> Here’s the integrated experimental comparison and summary based strictly on the provided papers:
> 
> **Scope** — Across the four methods described in the provided literature (
> • PBADet (Part-Body Association Detector)
> • Dale’s Law Spectral RNNs
> • JEPA vs MAE analysis
> • DoReMi (Domain Reweighting with Minimax Optimization)
> ), there are shared quantitative evaluation settings on identical datasets in some cases (e.g., COCO, BodyHands), and analogous setups for efficiency/generalization in others.
> 
> ---
> ## **1. PBADet vs baselines (BPJDet, Hier R-CNN, etc.) — identical datasets**
> 
> ### **On BodyHands dataset:**
> - **Metrics:** Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP.
> - **Identical setup** using YOLOv5l6 backbone for PBADet vs BPJDet.
> - **Results:**
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Cond. Acc. 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.
> - **Conclusion:** On identical backbone/dataset, PBADet edges BPJDet in all metrics (+2.2 AP points, +5.8 Cond. Acc, +1.34 Joint AP), thus better body-part association precision.
> 
> ### **On COCOHumanParts:**
> - **Metrics:** COCO-style APs for all categories & subordinate APs.
> - **Identical setup** with YOLOv5l6 backbone.
> - **Results:**
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 original/subordinate 43.0 / 41.8; APM 66.2 / 65.0.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 original/subordinate 43.6 / 43.3; APM 63.8 / 63.2.
> - **Conclusion:** PBADet slightly trails in the highest AP.5:.95 metric but leads in mid-size object AP (APM) and selected category AP (e.g., left/right foot), indicating stronger mid-scale generalization.
> 
> ---
> ## **2. Dale’s Law Spectral RNNs — Same tasks/datasets (Adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic Object Recognition)**
> 
> ### **All models tested on identical synthetic and real sequence datasets across baselines**:
> - **ColEI vs standard RNN vs DANN** under same hidden sizes, epochs, optimizers.
> - **Results pattern:**
>   - On every dataset, ColEI underperforms both Standard and DANN.
>   - DANN matches or beats Standard while obeying Dale’s Law.
>   - Quantitatively: For sequential MNIST with 3×100 hidden units, DANN and Standard achieve >~92% accuracy significantly earlier; ColEI converges slower and to lower accuracy.
> 
> **Conclusion:** In identical sequential learning setups, spectral properties (unimodal clustered singular values in DANN/Standard) lead to faster and higher final accuracy than ColEI’s dispersed multimodal spectra.
> 
> ---
> ## **3. JEPA vs MAE — Similar datasets and conditions**
> 
> ### **Synthetic Gaussian features with matched λ (variance proxy) and ρ (regression coeff.) patterns:**
> - **Findings:**
>   - MAE learns features in order of λ regardless of ρ.
>   - JEPA prioritizes high-ρ features especially with depth >1.
>   - On distributions where λ and ρ have opposing trends, JEPA inverts learning order compared to MAE.
> - **Implication:** Even when reconstruction/perception tasks see similar covariances, JEPA’s latent prediction bias yields faster prioritization of predictive (high-ρ) features.
> 
> ---
> ## **4. DoReMi — Same main model, different proxy scales & baseline weights**
> 
> ### **On The Pile (8B model main):**
> - **Identical downstream tasks and validation splits for baseline vs DoReMi-optimized weights.**
> - **Results:**
>   - DoReMi (280M→8B) vs baseline: +6.5% avg one-shot EM accuracy; achieves baseline accuracy 2.6× faster.
>   - Perplexity: Lowered *across all* 22 domains despite some being downweighted.
> 
> ### **On GLaM (iterated DoReMi):**
> - **Baseline:** Uniform weights; Oracle tuned on downstream.
> - **Iterated DoReMi:** Achieves oracle-matching downstream accuracy after round 2 without any downstream task data.
> 
> **Conclusion:** In identical final-model training conditions, DoReMi’s weight reallocation improves both speed and final EM accuracy, showing transfer from small proxy optimization to large model efficiency.
> 
> ---
> ## **Cross-method comparison where datasets/tasks align partially**
> 
> 1. **COCO/BodyHands vision tasks:** PBADet’s anchor-free single-offset design yields superior association accuracy over BPJDet. These gains are in absolute metrics per category.
> 2. **Sequence modeling (MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, synthetic):** DANN & Standard RNNs outperform ColEI consistently — analogous to PBADet’s improvement by removing representational inefficiency.
> 3. **Pretraining efficiency (The Pile, GLaM):** DoReMi achieves broad-domain perplexity reduction and faster downstream accuracy gains akin to spectral-RNN or PBADet’s early-stage efficiency boost.
> 4. **Feature-preference bias:** JEPA’s tendency to learn high-ρ features complements DoReMi’s reweighting toward medium-entropy domains — both focus capacity on data yielding maximal predictive generalization.
> 
> ---
> **Overall Summary:**
> - **Identical-dataset wins:** PBADet > BPJDet; DANN ≥ Standard >> ColEI; DoReMi weights > default weights.
> - **Similar-task trends:** JEPA prioritizes high-influence features, which parallels DoReMi’s shift to domains offering greatest marginal utility, while ColEI’s spectral inefficiency resembles default-weight underperformance.
> - **Efficiency gain commonality:** All advanced methods here (PBADet, DANN, JEPA, DoReMi) show faster rise to target accuracy or perplexity thresholds than their direct baselines under matched training budgets.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers that collectively cover your stack, with a comparative analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The papers (one per required piece)
> 
> 1. **Hands/face→person association in crowded scenes**: *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024). Detects body+parts (face, left/right hand, feet) and links each part to its parent body via a single part-to-body center offset; trained with SGD on YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones.
> 
> 2. **Biologically inspired E/I RNN stability**: *Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023). Shows why sign-constrained (excitatory/inhibitory) RNNs train poorly and how to keep them stable/learnable.
> 
> 3. **Faster language-backbone pretraining via reweighting**: *DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining*. Reweights domains with a small GroupDRO proxy model to cut perplexity.
> 
> 4. **Self-supervised prediction that avoids noisy pixel details**: *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024). Analyzes why JEPA-style latent prediction beats MAE-style pixel reconstruction.
> 
> 5. **Anytime-valid, online safety layer under label budget**: *Active, Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets* (Xu, Karampatziakis, Mineiro). E-process/betting-based risk control valid at all times, with active labeling under a fixed budget.
> 
> ## Experimental comparison and analysis
> 
> **Detection/association (PBADet vs. prior art).** On **BodyHands**, PBADet (YOLOv7) reaches hand AP 89.1 / joint AP 92.62 / conditional accuracy 85.98, versus BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 86.91 / 84.39 / 85.9, and far above BodyHands (2022), MaskRCNN variants, and OpenPose. On **COCOHumanParts**, it matches BPJDet on AP but achieves the lowest average mMR-2 (fewest part-body mismatches) across head, face, both hands, right foot, and beats the pose estimator ED-Pose by large margins in precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet (e.g., left hand F1 46.50 vs. 22.87). On **CrowdHuman** face-body association, its edge over BPJDet shrinks (body MR-2 36.5 vs. 40.7; face AP 81.6 vs. 81.6)—the authors attribute this to the single-part nature of the task; the part-to-body offset design pays off most with many parts. Notably, it achieves this with a smaller model (36.9M params) than BPJDet(YOLOv5m6) (41.2M).
> 
> **E/I RNN (spectral view).** Across adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition, ColEI (naive E/I partitioning) learns worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs; no spectral-radius value lets ColEI match the others. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum contributes more than sign constraints (sign constraints ≈0.7–1% error cost vs. spectrum ≈1.5–2% of the total 2.3±0.6% gap). Reducing inhibitory-neuron count or network size worsens both the spectrum and learning (anti-correlation between normalised SVD entropy and final error). Practical takeaways for your controller: prefer DANN-style reparameterization (robust even with one inhibitory neuron) and/or use gradient clipping, which benefits ColEI "substantially more" than other networks.
> 
> **Data reweighting (DoReMi).** With a 280M proxy tuning weights for an 8B model on The Pile, perplexity improves on *all* 22 domains (worst-case log-ppl 1.71→1.46), even where a domain is downweighted; average one-shot downstream accuracy rises 6.5 points, and baseline accuracy is reached 2.6× faster (75k vs. 200k steps). At matched scales (280M→1B) it is ~4× faster on average. On GLaM, iterated DoReMi (3 rounds) matches oracle weights tuned on downstream tasks. Cost: only ~8% of main-model FLOPs. Caveat: the 1B proxy underperforms its main model but still yields useful weights—suggesting robustness to proxy quality.
> 
> **JEPA vs. MAE (noise avoidance).** In deep linear networks, JEPA's learning order follows regression coefficients ρ (influential, semantically rich features), while MAE follows eigenvalue λ (high-variance features, including noisy ones); with ρ anti-correlated to λ, the two objectives learn almost disjoint feature sets, and the bias only appears with deep encoders. Critical-time analysis shows depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA aligns faster (CCA) with the low-variance perceptual subspace than MAE. So for your visual backbone, latent-space (JEPA) prediction is the theoretically and empirically supported choice over pixel reconstruction.
> 
> **Safety layer (active anytime-valid RCPS).** With θ=0.1, α=0.05, budget B=0.3, both the "pretrain" (predictor from a pretrained model) and "learned" (online-updated predictor/policy) methods reach the optimal β* faster than labeling-all or random ("oblivious") policies in simulations and on ImageNet, while all methods keep the safety-violation rate below α=0.05. Theory gives the optimal policy (label probability ∝ conditional risk std. dev.), the optimal predictor (conditional risk), and regret bounds tying estimation error to how fast β̂t converges to β*—and bad predictions slow convergence but never break the anytime-valid guarantee.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting design notes
> 
> - **Coherence of the stack**: PBADet (CNN/YOLO + SGD) and DoReMi (Transformer + Adam/Adafactor) both assume standard deep-learning training loops, so they integrate with your CNN/Transformer + SGD/Adam stack; PBADet even trains on the same COCO-family data your multimodal system targets.
> - **Complementarity of the two "regularization" pieces**: the JEPA analysis motivates predicting in latent space (skip pixel noise), while LDReg (local dimensionality regularization) in the same collection is an orthogonal fix for the dimensional-collapse risk JEPA-style objectives carry—useful if your self-supervised features collapse locally.
> - **Safety layer is model-agnostic**: the RCPS method explicitly supports any black-box model and uses the deployed model itself as a control variate, and can be updated online as new labeled pairs arrive—fitting your "anytime-valid under limited budget" requirement without retraining the full assistant.
> - **What the context does not cover**: no single paper in this collection combines all five components into one multimodal system, and end-to-end integration (e.g., how PBADet's detections feed the JEPA encoder or the RCPS risk function) is left to you; the RCPS guarantee is proven only under i.i.d. streaming data, a stated limitation.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are five papers covering your five requirements, with a comparison of their experimental results:
> 
> ## 1. Hands/face → person association in crowded scenes
> **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset; trained with YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones (CNN-based, SGD/Adam-compatible).
> - **BodyHands:** PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params, 1024px) beats all baselines — hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 vs BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (86.91/86.91/84.39), BodyHands (83.44/63.48), Mask R-CNN+IoU (74.52/51.74). It surpasses BPJDet even with a smaller model, and beats BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 on the same backbone.
> - **COCO-HumanParts (6 parts incl. face/hands/feet):** AP on par with BPJDet but leads AP_M/AP_L and feet, and achieves the lowest average mMR-2 for head, face, both hands, and right foot.
> - **CrowdHuman (face-body):** best body MR-2, AP comparable to DETR-based PED-DETR and Iter-E2EDET; advantage over BPJDet shrinks for this single-part task.
> - **vs ED-Pose (pose estimation, COCO val):** far higher precision/recall/F1 for hands/feet (e.g., left-hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87; all parts 48.52 vs 31.51), showing its association formulation outperforms keypoint-grouping approaches.
> 
> ## 2. Biologically inspired E/I RNN controller
> **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** — compares standard RNNs, column-constrained E/I RNNs (ColEI), and recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN).
> - ColEI networks train worse on all four benchmarks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition) and with higher variance; gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> - **Key comparison:** spectrum-transplant experiments show the initial singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints — spectrum accounts for ~1.5–2% of the performance gap vs ~0.7–1% for sign constraints.
> - ColEI has a multimodal, dispersed spectrum with a large singular-value mode; standard RNNs and DANNs have unimodal spectra (random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur forms).
> - Smaller networks and fewer inhibitory units degrade ColEI spectra/performance; DANNs stay robust even with a single inhibitory neuron (NSE ≈ 0.95). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) is predictive of EI-RNN learning, so use DANN-style or spectrally healthy E/I RNNs for stability.
> 
> ## 3. Faster LM pretraining via data reweighting
> **DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining (Google DeepMind)** — a 280M proxy trained with GroupDRO reweights domains; the weights are used to train the full model (Transformers with Adam).
> - **The Pile (280M→8B):** reduces perplexity on *all* domains (even down-weighted ones), raises average one-shot downstream accuracy by **+6.5 points**, and reaches baseline accuracy **2.6× faster** (75k vs 200k steps). DRO overhead is only ~8% of main-model compute.
> - **GLaM:** iterated DoReMi matches oracle domain weights tuned on downstream tasks; round-2/3 weights nearly identical. Effect is smaller (8 vs 22 domains).
> - **Scaling:** consistent gains across 280M/510M/760M/1B; weights stabilize after ~50k steps. This is the strongest fit for "pretrain faster by lowering perplexity."
> 
> ## 4. SSL feature prediction avoiding noisy pixels
> **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)** — theory/experiments comparing JEPA (latent-space prediction) vs MAE (pixel reconstruction).
> - JEPA is biased toward *influential* features (high regression coefficient ρ), while MAE prioritizes high-covariance features (λ), even noisy ones. On Distribution 2 (λ increasing, ρ decreasing), JEPA reverses learning order to ρ while MAE keeps the λ order — they can learn entirely different features.
> - Depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression: fixed-point encoder weight ∝ ρ^L (JEPA) vs ρ^(L/(L+1)) (MAE); a 1-layer JEPA matches infinite-depth MAE dynamics.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace of perceptual features than MAE (CCA), confirming the theoretical bias in practice. This validates JEPA-style latent prediction for avoiding noisy pixel details.
> 
> ## 5. Anytime-valid safety layer under a labeling budget
> **Active, Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets (NeurIPS 2024)** — extends RCPS to sequential, adaptively collected data via betting/e-processes, with an active labeling policy respecting a label budget.
> - **Simulations:** "pretrain" and "learned" policies reach lower β̂_t (closer to β* = 0.5578) uniformly across labels queried than "all"/"oblivious" baselines; all methods keep safety-violation rate below α = 0.05.
> - **ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05, B=0.3, 3,000 labels):** same ordering — pretrain/learned policies achieve β* ≈ 0.8349 with ~overlapping performance, beating both baselines while controlling violation rate.
> - The optimal labeling policy is proportional to the conditional risk standard deviation; regret bounds link policy/predictor estimation error to how quickly β̂_t can be safely shrunk. This directly supports an online, budget-aware safety layer.
> 
> ## End-to-end design summary
> - **Perception/association:** PBADet for part-body (hands/face) association on COCO-like data.
> - **Temporal/controller:** use DANN-style (or spectrally healthy) Dale's-law RNNs; monitor NSE to predict stability/learning quality.
> - **Language backbone:** DoReMi domain reweighting to cut pretraining steps ~2.6× while improving perplexity/accuracy.
> - **Vision SSL pretraining:** JEPA-style latent feature prediction instead of pixel reconstruction to avoid noisy features.
> - **Safety:** active anytime-valid RCPS as the online safety layer with a bounded labeling budget.
> 
> All methods are compatible with CNN/Transformer backbones and SGD/Adam training.

### paperscope:results_comparison:20 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m looking for a small set of papers that collectively explain how to train deep networks more efficiently and robustly across different modalities and tasks: (1) analyses of training dynamics and spectral diagnostics/regularization in recurrent models that respect excitatory–inhibitory constraints, (2) self-supervised representation learning via self-distillation that predicts in latent space (rather than pixel space) to down‑weight noisy features, (3) memory-lean training using optimizers that store first/second moments at very low precision while keeping Adam/AdamW/SGD‑style behavior and accuracy, (4) graph foundation models that map heterogeneous node attributes into a unified text feature space for cross-graph transfer, fine-tuning, and evaluation (e.g., AUROC/F1), and (5) one‑stage, anchor‑free part–whole detection trained end‑to‑end with classification/regression losses. Ideally these works discuss implicit bias, interpretability, regularization, use feature embeddings (often Transformer/CNN backbones), and report standard downstream metrics (e.g., cross-entropy losses, F1, AUROC) and fine‑tuning protocols.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## The Five Papers
> 
> 1. **Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly** (NeurIPS 2023) – training dynamics & spectral diagnostics for excitatory–inhibitory (E/I) recurrent models
> 2. **Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features** (NeurIPS 2024) – SSL via latent-space self-distillation
> 3. **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023) – low-precision first/second moments for Adam/AdamW/SGD
> 4. **Text-space Graph Foundation Models: Benchmarks & New Insights** (NeurIPS 2024) – mapping heterogeneous node attributes into a unified text space
> 5. **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024) – end-to-end part–whole detection
> 
> ## Experimental Results & Comparison
> 
> **1. EI RNN (spectral robustness):** On adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition, ColEI (sign-constrained columns) learns worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs; spectral properties (normalized SVD entropy, NSE) matter more than sign constraints (sign constraints cost ~0.7–1% error, but don't explain the full ~2.3%±0.6% gap). NSE anti-correlates with final test error; fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks degrade both NSE and learning, while DANN (reparameterized) stays robust. Gradient clipping mitigates the deficit. Key insight: the spectral *initialization* is a diagnostic/predictor of trainability.
> 
> **2. JEPA (latent-space self-distillation):** Theoretical + ImageNet-1K experiments show JEPA has a distinct implicit bias: it prioritizes high-ρ (highly influential, low-noise) features in a step-wise/greedy fashion, with depth strengthening noise suppression, whereas MAE orders features mainly by covariance λ. I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA), and JEPA converges to lower-amplitude weights on noisy features—down-weighting noise.
> 
> **3. 4-bit optimizers (memory-lean training):** Across RoBERTa-L, Swin-T, GPT-2M, Transformer, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B, 4-bit AdamW/AdamW+factorization match or slightly *exceed* 32-bit AdamW (NLU 88.9→89.1; QA 94.6→94.5; NLG 67.7→67.8; CLS 81.2→80.8; MT 26.61→26.28) while cutting memory up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB). Sublinear baselines (Adafactor, SM3) save more memory but lose accuracy, especially on classification—4-bit is the sweet spot.
> 
> **4. Text-space GFM (unified feature space):** Text-space projection preserves/improves performance on text attributes (Arxiv NC 71.53→73.10) and, with good prompts, matches on non-text data (HIV AUC-ROC 75.52→74.20), but hurts categorical features (Tolokers 83.25→78.16). Co-training benefits depend on inductive bias: node↔link co-training helps OneForAll (74.05→79.30) but not LLaGA; link-prediction-specific BUDDY benefits strongly from domain co-training (75.48→86.18 average) while GCN shows no gain; graph-level co-training eliminates the text-space gap. Cross-graph/cross-task in-context learning remains unsolved (existing GFMs often underperform simple LLM-embedding baselines).
> 
> **5. PBADet (part–whole detection):** One-stage, anchor-free, end-to-end trained with IoU/DFL/classification + dedicated association losses. On BodyHands it beats SOTA across all metrics (Hand AP 89.1 vs BPJDet 85.9; conditional accuracy 92.62 vs 86.91; JointAP 85.98 vs 84.39) with a smaller model (36.9M vs 86.1M). On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet on joint AP (AP.5:.95 ≈43.6) but leads on AP_M/AP_L and person/feet detection, with the lowest mismatching rate (mMR-2). Versus the pose estimator ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands/feet, and the single part-to-body offset extends to quadruped (AnimalPose/AP-10K).
> 
> ## Cross-cutting Analysis
> 
> - **Common principle — implicit bias / spectral structure drives trainability:** Papers 1 and 2 both show that what a model learns and how well depends on spectral/eigen structure (NSE; λ vs ρ ordering) rather than just capacity; diagnostics at initialization predict downstream performance.
> - **Robustness without sacrificing accuracy:** Papers 3 and 2 achieve "lossless" efficiency—4-bit states keep accuracy while cutting memory; JEPA keeps/down-weights only noisy features, retaining useful signal.
> - **Regularization as a unifying thread:** spectral diagnostics (1), implicit-bias-based noise suppression (2), quantization as state compression (3), text-space unification as feature regularization (4), and task-alignment loss regularization (5).
> - **Transfer/fine-tuning results are mixed and modality-dependent:** 4-bit optimizers give consistent near-lossless fine-tuning across language/vision; text-space GFM transfer works for homophilous/co-training settings but fails for heterophilous graphs and cross-task in-context learning; JEPA's advantage shows specifically in perceptual/robust features.
> - **Metrics used are standard and complementary:** test error/NSE (1), CCA/PCA alignment + linear probing (2), GLUE/accuracy/BLEU/F1/AUC (3), Accuracy/AUC-ROC/Hits@100 (4), AP/JointAP/conditional accuracy/mMR-2 (5), so the set reports cross-entropy-style losses, F1, AUROC, and fine-tuning protocols consistently as requested.

**community 最终答案**

> Here is the set of five papers and a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The five papers
> 
> 1. **Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly (spectral analysis of E/I networks)** — Shows poor learning in excitatory–inhibitory RNNs is caused mainly by the *initial recurrent-weight spectrum* (multimodal, dispersed singular values from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), not by sign constraints. Proposes **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** as a pre-training diagnostic: higher NSE anti-correlates with final error. Gradient clipping mitigates the deficit; recurrent DANN (Dale's ANN) matches standard RNNs in spectrum and performance.
> 
> 2. **Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features (deep linear analysis)** — Analyzes JEPA (predict in latent space) vs MAE (reconstruct in pixel space). Derives critical-time dynamics: JEPA prioritizes high-influence (high regression coefficient ρ) features and suppresses noisy/low-ρ directions, with suppression *strengthened by depth*; MAE's ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA features align faster to the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA).
> 
> 3. **4-bit Optimizers (Adam/AdamW states at 4-bit)** — Compresses optimizer first/second moments to 4-bit via smaller blocks (B128), rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluding linear quantization of the second moment. On GLUE (RoBERTa-L), SQuAD (F1 94.5), ImageNet (Swin-T), E2E-NLG, WMT14 and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning, 4-bit AdamW **matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW** (e.g., MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7 at 7B) while saving up to 57.7% memory and fitting LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU.
> 
> 4. **Text-space Graph Foundation Models (benchmark)** — Maps heterogeneous node attributes into a unified LLM-embedding text space across 23 datasets. Text-space preserves/improves text-attribute performance (Arxiv 71.53→73.10 acc) but can hurt categorical Tolokers (83.25→78.16). Co-training benefits graph-level tasks (e.g., OFA Node→Link 74.05→79.30; PCBA 0.233→0.282) but not node/link tasks; fine-tuning transfer on Cora/History/Ratings shows pre-train gains are marginal because LLM embeddings alone are strong; simple SBERT (no pre-training) often beats in-context-learning GFMs.
> 
> 5. **PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part-body detection)** — Treats parts as objects linked to a parent body by a single part-to-body center offset, trained end-to-end with IoU + DFL + classification + association losses and TOOD-style task alignment. On BodyHands it beats SOTA across the board (e.g., YOLOv7: HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98, surpassing larger BPJDet). On COCOHumanParts it matches BPJDet on AP (43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3) while leading on AP_M/AP_L and person/feet metrics and lowest average mMR−2, and gives much higher precision/recall/F1 than ED-Pose for hands/feet.
> 
> ## Cross-paper analysis
> 
> - **Common theme — implicit bias/regularization from the objective or architecture:** (1) and (2) are both training-dynamics analyses that attribute robustness (EI spectral health; noise suppression) to *implicit* properties rather than explicit constraints; (2) and (5) rely on CNN/Transformer feature backbones; (3) and (4) target efficiency/scalability.
> 
> - **Trade-off structure:** (1) and (2) diagnose *why* training is hard or robust (spectral pathology; latent-space prediction bias) and validate with controlled, small-scale theory-plus-experiments (adding, sMNIST, PTB; deep linear + ImageNet CCA). (3) and (4) are large-scale empirical/system papers reporting standard downstream metrics (accuracy, F1, AUC, MMLU, perplexity) and fine-tuning protocols, with a consistent finding that their efficiency interventions are **nearly lossless** (4-bit ≈ 32-bit; text-space ≈ original features after co-training).
> 
> - **Performance, not a single winner:** (3) shows accuracy is essentially invariant to the memory-saving trick (lossless), (4) shows gains depend on task level (co-training helps graph classification, not node/link), (5) shows the one-stage anchor-free design is more efficient *and* more accurate than multi-stage/heavier baselines, while (1) and (2) provide diagnostics/predictions (NSE, critical time) rather than headline accuracy improvements.
> 
> - **Robustness/limitations noted:** ColEI needs gradient clipping; JEPA analysis is limited to deep linear networks/special initialization; 4-bit optimizers tested only on language/vision; text-space projection can lose performance on categorical/non-text features; PBADet's advantage narrows to a single-part task on CrowdHuman.
> 
> All five report standard metrics (error/accuracy, cross-entropy-type losses, F1, AUROC, AP/mMR−2, MMLU) and fine-tuning or transfer protocols, making them a coherent, small set covering training-dynamics diagnostics, representation learning, memory-lean optimization, graph foundation modeling, and part–whole detection.

**问题：** I’m building a resource‑constrained multi‑modal system for on‑device analytics: it must (a) detect which person is gesturing to a camera in real time (part–body association), (b) analyze heterogeneous graphs from text‑heavy sources using a single backbone, (c) forecast time‑series with recurrent models that follow biological E/I constraints without tanking learnability, and (d) train/finetune with limited VRAM but near full‑precision accuracy using AdamW/SGD. Please point me to research that covers: ultra‑low‑memory optimizers for moment states; self‑distillation in latent space that avoids latching onto noisy details; spectral measures and initialization tricks that stabilize E/I recurrent nets; text‑aligned graph foundation models for cross‑dataset transfer; and compact one‑stage, anchor‑free part–whole detectors. Compatibility with standard fine‑tuning and metrics (e.g., cross‑entropy, AUROC/F1) is important.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

> 4) Spectrally‑stable E/I recurrent nets (Dale’s Law) for time‑series with preserved learnability
> Identical datasets within paper: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, naturalistic object recognition.
> 
> - Across identical tasks (Fig. 2): ColEI (column‑constrained E/I RNNs) learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs on all four benchmarks.
> - Sign constraints vs performance gap (Fig. 4A): free/frozen signs explain only a fraction of the gap (≈0.7% ± 0.3% for RNNs; 1% ± 1% for ColEI), leaving ~2.3% ± 0.6% unaccounted.
> - Spectrum “transplants” (Fig. 4B–C): swapping singular value spectra has larger impact than sign constraints (final test error changes ≈1.5% ± 0.3% for RNNs; 2% ± 1% for ColEI), isolating spectrum pathology as the main cause.
> - Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance: higher NSE (more clustered, unimodal singular values) correlates with lower test error across EI ratio and network width experiments (Figs. 5–7). Small ColEI with few inhibitory units are worst; DANNs remain robust.
> 
> Takeaway for (c) in your system: To keep E/I (Dale) constraints without losing learnability, ensure unimodal, clustered singular spectra at initialization (high NSE) and/or use DANN‑style parameterization. This stabilizes long‑sequence tasks like sequential MNIST and language modeling.
> 
> 5) Self‑distillation in latent space that avoids latching onto noisy details (JEPA vs MAE)
> - Deep‑linear dynamics and ODE simulations (Figs. 2, 4): JEPAs learn features in a greedy order by regression influence (ρ) when encoders are deep, prioritizing predictive, low‑variance (“non‑noisy”) features; MAEs prioritize high covariance (λ) irrespective of ρ.
> - Temporal generative model (Fig. 3): closed‑form λ and ρ show how JEPA down‑weights noisy modes; simulations match predictions as sequence length varies.
> - ImageNet (Appendix D): with I‑JEPA vs MAE on 64×64 inputs, feature similarity (CCA) shows I‑JEPA aligns more with the bottom variance subspace (believed semantic) and less with top variance subspace than MAE throughout training.
> 
> Takeaway for (b) and (e): For representation learning that resists spurious/high‑variance noise, JEPA‑style latent prediction (with deep encoders) implicitly biases toward influential, predictive features and away from pixel‑level variance—consistent with better transfer for perception tasks.
> 
> What’s comparable across papers?
> - No single dataset is shared across all five works. Identical datasets exist within each paper’s experiments (e.g., BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman; GLUE/ImageNet/E2E/SQuAD/WMT14; Cora/CiteSeer/PubMed/Arxiv/E‑commerce; adding/sequential‑MNIST/PTB; ImageNet‑64×64 CCA). We highlighted head‑to‑head results on those identical datasets.
> - By task type: vision (PBADet vs 4‑bit Swin‑T) both maintain or improve standard metrics at fixed or lower compute; graphs (TS‑GFM) benefit strongly on graph/LP tasks when structural priors are encoded; sequences/time‑series (Dale’s Law) show spectral‑initialization is key for learnability; SSL in latent space (JEPA) improves focus on predictive (less noisy) features.

> Practical mapping to your system
> - (a) Real‑time part–body association: PBADet improves BodyHands Conditional Accuracy by ~+6 points and reduces CrowdHuman MR−2 body to 36.5 while maintaining simplicity (one‑stage, offset‑to‑center decoding).

> - (c) E/I RNNs with stability: prefer DANN‑style recurrent architectures or initialize ColEI with high NSE spectra; spectrum dominates sign constraints in determining performance.
> - (d) Low‑VRAM training: 4‑bit states (rank‑1 normalization + zero‑free mapping) reach near‑FP32 accuracy, cut total training memory up to ~58%, and expand maximum trainable model size 4× within fixed VRAM.
> - (e) Self‑distillation/latent prediction: JEPA’s deep‑encoder bias toward high‑ρ features helps avoid noisy details compared to MAE; validated via ODE sims and ImageNet CCA trends.

**naive 最终答案**

> I found research covering all five requested areas. Here is the mapping and comparison of experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Ultra-low-memory optimizers for moment states
> **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Compresses Adam/AdamW moment states to 4-bit using smaller blocks (B128) for the 1st moment, and zero-point-excluding linear quantization + rank-1 normalization (optionally factorized second moment) for the 2nd. The compression framework also supports SGD(M).
> - Results: matches or slightly beats 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (RoBERTa-L GLUE 88.9→89.1; GPT-2M BLEU 67.7→67.8; QA F1 94.6→94.5) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 81.2→80.8; WMT14 MT 26.61→26.28). LLaMA-7B instruction tuning is essentially lossless (MMLU 38.7→38.9). Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU; 4-bitFactor gives ~2× memory saving over 8-bit. Sublinear methods (Adafactor/SM3) save more memory but degrade accuracy, especially on image classification. Limitation: best setting is task-dependent; only tested on language/vision tasks.
> 
> ## 2. Self-distillation in latent space avoiding noisy details
> **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Analyzes JEPA self-distillation (online encoder predicts a target encoder in latent space) vs MAE (input-space reconstruction). Theory (deep linear networks, exact ODEs) shows JEPA has an implicit bias toward high-influence features and learns noisy features more slowly, converging to lower-amplitude weights for noise — so noise is not latched onto downstream. Depth strengthens this suppression.
> - Experimental result: on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (measured by CCA). This is largely a mechanism/qualitative result; no standard accuracy/AUROC numbers are reported in the retrieved content.
> 
> ## 3. Spectral measures & initialization for E/I recurrent nets
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Shows that E/I (Dale's Law) recurrent nets can learn well **without tanking learnability** if the spectrum is right. The simple column-constrained ColEI partitioning produces multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), causing poor/high-variance learning; recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) retain standard-RNN-like unimodal spectra and learn just as well — even with only 1 inhibitory neuron.
> - Key tool: **Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE)** — a spectral "pathology" measure that anti-correlates with final test error (can predict performance before training); higher NSE ⇒ better training. Spectrum transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints for learning; gradient clipping substantially mitigates ColEI's deficit.
> - Benchmarks are sequential RNN tasks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition), not dedicated time-series forecasting — that specific gap is not covered in the collection.
> 
> ## 4. Text-aligned graph foundation models for cross-dataset transfer
> **"Graph Foundation Models: A Text-Space Benchmark and Co-Training Study"**
> - Unifies heterogeneous graphs by projecting node attributes into a shared **text space** via LLM encoders, enabling one backbone across datasets/tasks (node/link/graph classification).
> - Results: text-space projection preserves/improves text attributes (Arxiv accuracy 71.53→73.10; Pubmed Hits@100 53.05→66.13) but can hurt categorical features (Tolokers 83.25→78.16). Cross-task co-training helps OneForAll (Node→Link Hits@100 74.05→79.30) but not LLaGA; cross-graph/cross-task in-context learning is still far from solved. Simple SBERT + feature propagation beats most graph in-context-learning methods on homophilous graphs. Metrics used: Accuracy, AUC-ROC, Hits@100.
> 
> ## 5. Compact one-stage, anchor-free part–whole detectors
> **"PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association"** (ICLR 2024)
> - Extends YOLOv5/v7 anchor-free heads with a single **part-to-body center offset** plus task-alignment learning; one-to-one part↔body correspondence, scales to any number of parts, and stays valid when parts are occluded (fixing BPJDet's body-to-part offsets).
> - Results (BodyHands): HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 vs BPJDet (85.3 / 86.80 / 78.13); the anchor-free variant beats its own anchor-based version (88.4/92.31/85.28), validating both the anchor-free design and the part-to-body definition. On COCO-HumanParts AP .5:.95 reaches 42.7 (YOLOv7) / 43.0 (YOLOv5l6). Versus the pose estimator ED-Pose, PBADet has far higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet (all-parts F1 31.51→48.52). Advantage over BPJDet is smaller for the single-part face-body task on CrowdHuman (leading MR-2, competitive AP).
> 
> ## Cross-cutting analysis
> - **Compatibility:** 4-bit optimizers plug into standard AdamW/SGD(M) fine-tuning and keep accuracy metrics (F1/BLEU/accuracy); the GFM benchmark reports AUROC/Hits@100; PBADet reports AP/precision/recall/F1 — all standard. JEPA (latent-space) and the E/I RNN paper are more about representation/learning dynamics than end-task metrics, so direct metric compatibility is weaker there.
> - **Trade-offs across your pipeline:** the 4-bit optimizer and PBADet are the most directly deployable on-device (memory savings + compact single-stage detection). The E/I RNN work gives you a concrete initialization rule (maximize NSE, prefer DANN-style reparameterization) to keep biologically constrained recurrent models learnable. Text-space GFM is a strong fit for heterogeneous, text-heavy graphs but warns that positive cross-dataset/cross-task transfer is not guaranteed and depends on LLM embedding quality and inductive bias.
> 
> **Gaps not covered by the collection:** no paper addresses E/I recurrent nets specifically for time-series forecasting (only sequential classification/language modeling), and no paper combines latent-space self-distillation with the on-device/optimizer constraints directly.

**community 最终答案**

> ## 1. Ultra-low-memory optimizers for moment states
> **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> 
> - **Method**: Quantizes Adam/AdamW/SGD(M) first moment with small block size (B128/Dynamic-Exponent), second moment with Rank-1 normalization + linear quantizer excluding the zero-point (fixes the zero-point problem), optionally factorized ("4-bit Factor").
> - **Results**: On GLUE (RoBERTa-L) 89.1 vs 88.9 for 32-bit AdamW; Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2 E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; WMT14 MT 26.28 vs 26.61 — i.e., matches/exceeds 32-bit AdamW on all fine-tuning tasks, comparable on pretraining. LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning is comparable or slightly better (e.g., 13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5); convergence curves closely align.
> - **Memory**: up to 57.7% total-memory savings; trains LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; 4× larger OPT models under a fixed budget. Sublinear-memory baselines Adafactor/SM3 degrade (SM3: CLS 79.0, MT 22.72), unlike 4-bit AdamW.
> - **Compatibility**: drop-in for standard AdamW/SGD(M) with the same hyperparameters; evaluated with standard metrics (accuracy, F1, BLEU, SacreBleu), including LLaMA instruction fine-tuning; a convergence proof covers quantized SGD(M).
> 
> ## 2. Self-distillation in latent space avoiding noisy details
> **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> 
> - **Mechanism**: Deep-linear analysis shows JEPA self-distillation is implicitly biased toward high-influence (high regression coefficient ρ) features, whereas MAE orders by variance λ. JEPA suppresses noisy/low-ρ directions, and suppression strengthens with depth (fixed points: JEPA ρ^L vs MAE ρ^(L/(L+1))); a 1-layer JEPA equals infinite-depth MAE. Critical-time analysis shows JEPA learns high-ρ features first and can invert learning order when λ and ρ conflict.
> - **Experiments**: ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA), i.e., it avoids latching onto noisy, low-influence details.
> - **Caveat**: theory assumes deep linear networks, balanced orthogonal init, simultaneous diagonalizability; generalization to nonlinear models is qualitative. A related alternative is **LDReg** (local-dimensionality regularization), which improved linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE on ImageNet.
> 
> ## 3. Spectral measures and initialization for E/I recurrent nets
> **"Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> 
> - **Findings**: Column-constrained E/I RNNs (ColEI) train worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN-style reparameterized E/I nets on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn TreeBank, and object recognition. Gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially.
> - **Cause**: Not sign constraints per se — spectrum-transplant experiments show the *initial singular-value spectrum* matters more. ColEI's column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values, whereas standard/DANN match the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle. Fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks worsen spectra and performance; DANNs stay robust even with one inhibitory neuron.
> - **Diagnostic/trick**: Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error across sizes and E/I ratios, so it predicts trainability pre-training; the paper explicitly motivates an alternative spectral-aware initialization for ColEI. This gives you both a spectral measure (NSE) and guidance (match quarter-circle/random-matrix spectra; use DANN-style reparameterization) for E/I-constrained forecasting RNNs.
> 
> ## 4. Text-aligned graph foundation models for cross-dataset transfer
> **"Text-space Graph Foundation Models: Comprehensive Benchmarks and New Insights"**
> 
> - **Setup**: 23 text-attributed graph datasets (academic, e-commerce, molecular, wiki); four GFM paradigms (co-training vs pretraining × task-specific vs cross-task) with LLM encoders providing a unified feature space, plus graph SSL, graph prompts, and LLM+graph projectors.
> - **Results**: Text-space projection preserves/improves text attributes (Arxiv accuracy 71.53→73.10) and non-text with good prompts (HIV AUC-ROC 75.52→74.20), but categorical Tolokers drops (83.25→78.16). Cross-task node+link co-training benefits OneForAll (Node→Link Hits@100 74.05→79.30) but not LLaGA (85.03→84.10); node→graph fine-tuning transfers positively. Negative transfer depends on dataset traits (heterophily, feature heterogeneity), not data ratios; strong LLM encoders mitigate feature heterogeneity; SGC fails on heterophilous graphs. Pre-trained LLM embeddings + feature propagation beat most graph in-context learning on homophilous graphs, but **cross-graph, cross-task in-context learning is still far off** — direct transfer/fine-tuning of co-trained GFMs to new data is an open challenge. Metrics used: accuracy, AUC-ROC, Hits@100, F1-compatible settings.
> 
> ## 5. Compact one-stage, anchor-free part–whole detectors
> **"PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection"** (ICLR 2024)
> 
> - **Method**: Extends anchor-free detection with a single 2-D part-to-body center offset (one-to-one, always valid), multi-scale features, TOOD task-alignment anchor assignment, and a dedicated association loss; YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones.
> - **Results (BodyHands)**: PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params, 1024 input) → Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98, beating BPJDet-YOLOv5m6 (85.3/86.80/78.13 with 41.2M at 1536) and Mask R-CNN/BodyHands baselines (Joint AP ~50–64). YOLOv5l6 variant (86.1M) gives 88.1/92.71/85.73.
> - **Results (COCOHumanParts, 6 parts)**: AP on par with BPJDet while leading person/feet and AP_M/AP_L, and the lowest average mMR-2 for head, face, both hands, right foot. On CrowdHuman face-body association it leads body MR-2 with competitive AP; vs ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet. Extends to quadruped part-body association (AnimalPose, AP-10K).
> - **Ablations**: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment each improve association; part-to-body beats body-to-part definition (Joint AP 85.98 vs 78.13); anchor-free beats anchor-based (89.1 vs 88.4 Hand AP). Trained with SGD, AMP, 100 epochs on 4 V100s — standard detection fine-tuning with AP/mMR-2/F1 metrics.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting analysis and compatibility
> - **Memory vs accuracy trade-off**: 4-bit AdamW is the only method that gets near-full-precision accuracy at ~4× smaller optimizer states and works as a drop-in for AdamW/SGD fine-tuning (accuracy/F1/BLEU), directly addressing your limited-VRAM requirement; sublinear (Adafactor/SM3) saves more but loses accuracy.
> - **For E/I-constrained forecasting**: use DANN-style reparameterization (learns like standard RNNs) or spectral-aware init monitored by NSE; gradient clipping is the pragmatic stabilizer — this is about *trainability*, not memory.
> - **For text-heavy heterogeneous graphs**: text-space GFMs give one backbone across datasets/tasks, but cross-dataset transfer is still unreliable (negative transfer is dataset-dependent); co-training node+link tasks (OneForAll-style) is the currently working pattern, with AUC-ROC/F1/Hits@100 as standard metrics.
> - **For real-time person detection/association**: PBADet is the smallest, single-stage, anchor-free option with a strong accuracy/params trade-off (36.9M for SOTA on BodyHands) and standard AP/F1 evaluation.
> - **For latent-space self-distillation**: JEPA-style objectives are the principled way to avoid noisy features (verified on ImageNet-1K), though the theory is linear; LDReg is an alternative regularization with solid downstream gains.
> 
> One gap: no paper in the collection specifically combines these components or reports cross-entropy/AUROC/F1 on a single integrated multimodal benchmark, so end-to-end compatibility across all five modules must be inferred from each method's individual standard-training compatibility.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:26 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that unify reliable training, inference, and calibration across vision, language, and control systems, including: (1) self-supervised learning that avoids noisy features (e.g., JEPA-style) using MSE/CE losses, cosine similarity, and SGD/Adam; (2) diffusion models with amortized posterior sampling and End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning; (3) anchor-free, part–body association on COCO with Transformers/ResNet-50 backbones; (4) active, online implementation of anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets with evaluations on MNIST/CIFAR-100; and (5) deep networks with biologically inspired constraints analyzed via spectral properties. I’m looking for works reporting F1/Precision/AUROC and using datasets like COCO, MNIST, SVHN, CIFAR-100, with fine-tuning and feature embeddings.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：4→3（Δ-1）；rounds：6→4（Δ-2）。**

**naive 最终答案**

> I found papers matching each of your five themes, but they are **separate papers, not one unified framework**. No single work in the collection unifies reliable training, inference, and calibration across vision/language/control. Here is what each covers and how their experiments compare.
> 
> ## 1. JEPA/self-supervised that avoids noisy features (MSE, cosine similarity, SGD/Adam)
> **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024). Using deep linear networks and gradient-flow ODEs, it proves JEPA's implicit bias is to learn high-ρ (high-regression-coefficient) features and suppress noisy ones, increasingly with depth; MAE ordering depends only on λ (variance). It confirms via SGD simulations and ImageNet-1K CCA (I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace than MAE). **Results are theoretical/qualitative** — no accuracy/F1/AUROC tables. Related SSL papers in the collection: LDReg (local-dimensionality regularization; ImageNet linear eval, COCO detection/segmentation gains for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE) and "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (cosine-similarity analysis; SimCLR/DCL/DHEL + variance-reduction loss improves top-1 on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, full ImageNet, e.g., 51.79→52.48 top-1 on ImageNet; more gains at small batch sizes).
> 
> ## 2. Diffusion with amortized posterior sampling + end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning
> **RTB: "Amortizing intractable inference in diffusion models for vision, language, and control"** (NeurIPS 2024) — the only paper that genuinely spans vision, language, and control. The posterior is parameterized with **LoRA weights (~3% of prior params)**. Results (Table 2): on classifier-guided posterior sampling over **MNIST, MNIST even/odd, CIFAR-10**, RTB achieves FID 1.182 (MNIST), 1.179 (even/odd), 0.472 (CIFAR-10) with high diversity — better balancing reward vs. diversity than DPS/LGD-MC (high FID, low log-reward), DPOK (biased), and DDPO (mode collapse, near-zero reward). In offline RL (D4RL medium-replay), RTB beats pure online training on 2 of 3 tasks; for Stable Diffusion fine-tuning it matches/outperforms DPOK in reward and CLIP-cosine diversity. Metrics are FID/reward/diversity, not F1/AUROC.
> 
> ## 3. Anchor-free part–body association on COCO
> **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset, with YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 backbones (not ResNet-50 or Transformers). **This is the only paper reporting Precision/Recall/F1**: vs. ED-Pose on COCO (Table 7), all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, **F1 48.52 vs 31.51**. On BodyHands: HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (beats BPJDet's 85.9/86.91/84.39 with fewer params). On COCO-HumanParts: all-category AP 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate), leading AP_M/AP_L; lowest mMR⁻² on CrowdHuman face-body. Note: the Transformer/Swin-L and ResNet baselines (ED-Pose, Hier-R50) appear only as comparisons.
> 
> ## 4. Active, online, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets
> **"Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"** (NeurIPS 2024) matches the method: anytime-valid RCPS via e-processes/betting, active labeling with a budget, and ML control variates. **But its experiments are on numerical simulations and ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05), not MNIST/CIFAR-100.** "pretrain"/"learned" policies reach lower β̂_t faster than "all"/"oblivious" baselines while keeping safety-violation rates below α=0.05 (β*=0.8349 on ImageNet). No F1/Precision/AUROC reported — the metric is miscoverage risk control.
> 
> ## 5. Biologically inspired constraints analyzed via spectral properties
> Two relevant papers:
> - **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023): EI (Dale's Law) networks analyzed spectrally. ColEI networks have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error. Results on sequential MNIST, adding, PTB, object recognition (e.g., test errors ~0.7–2.3% ranges; NSE predicts performance across network size/EI ratio).
> - **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (ICML 2025): Hessian spectra of well-trained nets follow a power law across **MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100** (LeNet/ResNet-18, SGD and Adam); power-law emerges with SGD (d_ks 0.009 on MNIST vs 0.0796 random), is lost with small width/noisy labels/large batches, and correlates with generalization (Pearson 0.72 on CIFAR-10; d_ks predicts LLM generalization up to 0.98). Notably, LoRA-only fine-tuning does **not** induce the power law (relevant to your fine-tuning/LoRA thread).
> 
> ## Comparison and gaps
> - **Cross-cutting consistency**: The RTB diffusion paper is the only one unifying vision/language/control (with LoRA fine-tuning); the JEPA, PBADet, RCPS, and spectral papers are single-domain. No paper unifies all five sub-areas.
> - **Metrics requested vs. available**: F1/Precision appear **only in PBADet** (Table 7). **No AUROC values appear anywhere** in the retrieved content. The RCPS work does not use MNIST/CIFAR-100 (it uses ImageNet), and the part-body work does not use ResNet-50/Transformer backbones as its own architecture. **SVHN does not appear** in any retrieved paper.
> - **Datasets**: COCO (PBADet; LDReg transfer), MNIST (JEPA analysis, RTB, Dale's Law, Hessian paper), CIFAR-10/100 (RTB, contrastive similarity, Hessian paper), ImageNet (JEPA CCA, contrastive, RCPS, LDReg). Fine-tuning appears in RTB (LoRA) and the Hessian paper (LoRA adapters); feature embeddings appear in the contrastive-similarity paper (projection heads, cosine) and RTB (Inception/CLIP feature diversity).
> 
> If you specifically need a single source reporting F1/Precision/AUROC on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 with Transformer/ResNet-50 part-body detection and risk control on those datasets, the collection does not contain such a unified work — those exact combinations are not established in the available documents.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, no single paper unifies all five areas, but each of your five criteria maps to a distinct paper. Here are the matches and an analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Papers found
> 
> 1. **JEPA / noise-avoiding SSL** — *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features* (deep-linear analysis; ImageNet-1K I-JEPA vs MAE, CCA) and *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (InfoNCE/cosine similarity, SGD 200 epochs, ResNet-18/50, CIFAR-10/100 & ImageNet-100, top-1 accuracy).
> 2. **Diffusion + amortized posterior + LoRA** — *Amortizing Intractable Inference in Diffusion Models for Vision, Language, and Control* (RTB objective; posterior parameterized by LoRA ≈3% of params; MNIST, CIFAR-10, text-to-image, offline RL/D4RL).
> 3. **Anchor-free part–body association on COCO** — *PBADet* (part-to-body center offset on YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7 backbones; COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman; compared against ED-Pose with Swin-L Transformer).
> 4. **Active, anytime-valid RCPS** — *Active, Anytime-Valid Risk Controlling Prediction Sets* (e-process/betting; active labeling with IPW; optimal policy ∝ conditional-risk std).
> 5. **Biologically constrained networks via spectral analysis** — *Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (E/I sign constraints; singular-value spectra, NSE; sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition). Related: *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (power-law Hessian spectra; LeNet/ResNet18; MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100; SGD/Adam/AMSGrad…).
> 
> ## Comparison / analysis of experimental results
> 
> **SSL (1):** The JEPA paper is primarily theoretical (deep linear MLP, gradient-flow ODEs, critical-time analysis). It shows JEPA prioritizes high-influence, low-variance (noise-free) features and that this bias grows with depth; ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns with the perceptual low-variance PCA subspace faster than MAE (measured by CCA). No F1/AUROC — the contrastive-embeddings paper instead reports top-1 accuracy and shows a variance-reduction auxiliary loss generally improves SimCLR/DCL/DHEL accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet, plus temperature robustness and small-batch stability. LDReg (related) improves linear eval, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE on ImageNet (ResNet-50, ViT-B).
> 
> **Diffusion (2):** RTB on MNIST/CIFAR-10 classifier-guided posterior sampling: RTB achieves best FID (MNIST 1.18, CIFAR-10 0.47) and balanced reward/diversity; DPS and LGD-MC fail to model the posterior (high avg log r(x)) and DDPO mode-collapses. Mixed off-policy/on-policy RTB beats pure online on 2 of 3 D4RL medium-replay control tasks; Stable Diffusion LoRA fine-tuning uses timestep subsampling/batched gradients for memory efficiency with a reward-vs-diversity tradeoff. No F1/AUROC reported.
> 
> **Part–body (3):** PBADet (anchor-free) outperforms anchor-based BPJDet on BodyHands: HandAP 89.1 vs 85.3, Conditional Accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, JointAP 85.98 vs 78.13. On COCO-HumanParts it is on par with BPJDet (AP 43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3) and leads on AP_M/AP_L. Against ED-Pose (Swin-L Transformer) on COCO, PBADet is substantially higher in Precision/Recall/F1 (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51). Note: PBADet uses YOLO backbones rather than ResNet-50/Transformer; the Transformer (ED-Pose) appears only as a baseline.
> 
> **RCPS (4):** Evaluated on simulations and **ImageNet** (not MNIST/CIFAR-100 as requested — that criterion is not met in this collection). Learned/pretrained labeling policies cut risk faster (lower average β̂_t) than "all"/"oblivious" baselines while keeping safety-violation rate below α=0.05 (β* = 0.5578 simulation, 0.8349 ImageNet).
> 
> **Spectral/bio (5):** Dale's-law (ColEI) RNNs learn worse with higher variance than standard RNNs; the cause is the initial recurrent-weight spectrum (multimodal, dispersed singular values; rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure) rather than sign constraints — DANN E/I RNNs match standard spectra and performance. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error. The Hessian paper shows power-law spectra hold for well-trained nets across MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 (KS tests), hold across SGD/Adam/AMSGrad/AdaBound/etc., with slope magnitude correlating with sharpness/generalization (Pearson 0.72 on CIFAR-10 LeNet; d_ks predicts LLM generalization up to 0.98), and LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power law as full fine-tuning does.
> 
> ## Caveats
> 
> - **No F1/AUROC** is reported by these papers (F1 appears only in PBADet's comparison vs ED-Pose; AUROC nowhere).
> - **MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100**: MNIST and CIFAR-10/100 appear (RTB, Hessian paper, contrastive SSL), but SVHN is absent.
> - **RCPS** evaluates on ImageNet + simulations, not MNIST/CIFAR-100.
> - **PBADet** uses YOLO backbones; ResNet-50/Transformer part-body detection is not directly present in the collection (HASSOD, however, uses DINO ViT-B/8 features + Cascade Mask R-CNN for self-supervised COCO detection with AR metrics).
> - The "unified training-inference-calibration across vision/language/control" framing best matches the RTB diffusion paper (vision, language, control) and, to a lesser degree, the RCPS calibration paper; the other three papers are task-specific.

### paperscope:results_comparison:32 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find a concise reading list that spans: (1) a modern, anchor‑free method for associating human parts with people on large benchmarks like COCO; (2) theoretical and empirical analyses explaining the implicit bias of self‑supervised objectives (e.g., MSE vs cross‑entropy) and their interpretability in deep networks; (3) memory‑lean optimizers that replace 32‑bit Adam/AdamW/SGD states with 4‑bit variants suitable for fine‑tuning (including LoRA) on Transformers; (4) a modular library for decision‑making based on diffusion models with transformer‑based conditional guidance; and (5) a study of biologically constrained recurrent nets (excitatory/inhibitory, a.k.a. Dale’s Law) from a spectral perspective. Prefer works that evaluate on datasets like CIFAR‑100/MNIST/COCO, report metrics such as F1/AUROC/Precision, and discuss attention, feature embeddings, and multi‑task learning.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Concise Reading List (with experimental results)
> 
> **1. Human parts ↔ person association — PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — *One-stage anchor-free part-body association*
> - Method: single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale anchor-free heads (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones); a part-to-body (vs. body-to-part) definition; task-alignment + association loss.
> - Results: On **BodyHands**, PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M) beats BPJDet(YOLOv5m6, 41.2M): HandAP 89.1 vs 85.3, Cond. Accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, JointAP 85.98 vs 78.13. On **COCOHumanParts** AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate) vs BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3 — on par but leads AP_M/AP_L and person/feet; lowest mMR⁻² for head/face/hands/right-foot. On **CrowdHuman** it has best body MR⁻² but smaller advantage for the single-part case; vs ED-Pose it gives higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands & feet.
> 
> **2. Implicit bias of self-supervised objectives — "Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Method: exact gradient-flow ODEs for deep *linear* JEPA vs MAE (MSE-type) self-distillation.
> - Results: JEPA prioritizes **high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ)**, MAE only high-covariance (noisy) features; the bias grows with depth (fixed points: MAE ρ^{L/(L+1)} vs JEPA ρ^L); JEPA suppresses noisy directions as depth increases. On **ImageNet-1K** (CCA analysis), I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace than MAE. No CIFAR/MNIST metric table; largely theoretical + ImageNet correlation experiments.
> 
> **3. Memory-lean optimizers — "4-bit Optimizers"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Method: 4-bit first/second moments (small block B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, optional factorization) replacing 32-bit Adam/AdamW/SGD states; compatible with LoRA-style fine-tuning.
> - Results: matches 32-bit AdamW on **GLUE** (RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 89.1), ImageNet-1k Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2, E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, WMT 26.28 vs 26.61. LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning matches 32-bit across MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA (e.g., LLaMA-13B 47.4 vs 47.4 MMLU, ARC-e 64.1 vs 63.6); memory saved up to 57.7%, enables LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU (vs 4× larger OPT under same budget). 4-bitFactor has ~2× less memory than 4-bitAdamW.
> 
> **4. Diffusion decision-making library — CleanDiffuser** (NeurIPS 2024 D&B)
> - Method: modular library with decoupled diffusion models/solvers, network architectures, and guided sampling (CG/CFG); includes transformer-based **DiT1d** and Chi_Transformer (cross-attention conditioning) alongside UNet1d/MLP architectures.
> - Results: on **D4RL** (offline RL), DQL/EDP/IDQL average 89.0/82.4/84.1 vs Diffuser 78.2, Decision Diffuser 83.2, BC 51.9 (e.g., Hopper Medium-Expert DQL 111.1, HalfCheetah Medium 52.3). Diffusion policies excel in **imitation learning**; **DiT1d (transformer) gives better training stability and sample quality than Janner_UNet1d**; ablations: ~5 sampling steps usually enough, more steps can degrade, algorithm choice dominates model size.
> 
> **5. Biologically constrained RNNs (Dale's Law) — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Method: compares standard RNNs vs column-constrained EI (ColEI) vs recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) via singular-value/eigenvalue spectra and normalized SVD entropy (NSE).
> - Results: ColEI learns worse and with higher variance on adding, **sequential MNIST**, Penn TreeBank, and object recognition; the cause is **not sign constraints but the initial spectrum** — ColEI has multimodal, dispersed singular values (rank-one column-mean nilpotent structure), while standard/DANN match the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle. Spectrum transplants confirm this. Fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks worsen spectra/performance; **NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error** and predicts performance; DANN learns as well as standard RNNs even with 1 inhibitory unit.
> 
> ### Cross-method comparison
> - **Metrics/benchmarks**: PBADet uses COCO-derived AP/F1/Precision/Recall (COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands); the 4-bit paper uses F1 (SQuAD QA), accuracy, BLEU, SacreBLEU; CleanDiffuser uses D4RL/robomimic return scores; Dale's Law uses MNIST/PTB error; the JEPA paper reports no standard classification table (CCA on ImageNet).
> - **Where each is strongest**: PBADet (1) is the strongest at multi-part association accuracy; (2) the 4-bit optimizer matches 32-bit baselines while cutting memory ~2–4×, ideal for LoRA fine-tuning; (3) CleanDiffuser shows transformer-conditioned diffusion (DiT1d/Chi_Transformer) is most stable in IL/RL; (4) Dale's Law work shows that spectral (not sign) constraints govern EI RNN learnability — with NSE as a pre-training diagnostic.
> - **Common threads**: all five emphasize feature/embedding design, attention (DiT1d, Chi_Transformer cross-attention, PBADet multi-scale features), and multi-task/task-alignment loss (PBADet) or multi-benchmark evaluation — aligning with the requested attention/feature-embedding/multi-task criteria. Caveat: the JEPA paper lacks CIFAR-100/MNIST/F1/AUROC numbers, and CleanDiffuser/4-bit papers do not report AUROC/Precision.

**community 最终答案**

> Here is a concise reading list mapped to the five requested topics, followed by a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Reading List
> 
> 1. **Anchor-free human part association** — *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024). Detects hands/face/feet and links each part to a person via a single part-to-body center offset on COCO-based benchmarks.
> 2. **Implicit bias of self-supervised objectives & interpretability** — *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis* (NeurIPS 2024; JEPA-style MSE latent prediction vs. MAE reconstruction); supporting analyses: *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (cross-entropy/InfoNCE structure) and *LDReg: Local Dimensionality Regularized Self-Supervised Learning* (dimensional-collapse/feature interpretability).
> 3. **Memory-lean 4-bit optimizers** — *4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States* (NeurIPS 2023). Quantizes Adam/AdamW (and factorized second moments) states to 4-bit; validated on Transformer fine-tuning incl. LoRA (GPT-2) and LLaMA.
> 4. **Modular diffusion decision-making library** — *CleanDiffuser* (NeurIPS 2024 D&B). A modular library for diffusion-based decision-making with decoupled diffusion models, network architectures, and guided sampling (incl. transformer-based conditional guidance, e.g., Chi_Transformer with cross-attention masks).
> 5. **Dale's-Law constrained recurrent nets from a spectral view** — *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023). E/I (excitatory–inhibitory) RNNs analyzed via singular-value spectra and normalised SVD entropy.
> 
> ## Comparison / Analysis of Experimental Results
> 
> - **PBADet vs. anchor-based/pose baselines:** On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) reaches HandAP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 — clearly beating anchor-based BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13) at larger size, and far surpassing ED-Pose (pose estimation) on Precision/Recall/F1 (e.g., all parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; ~2× precision on hands/feet). On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet in AP (43.0/41.8 for YOLOv5l6) but leads in person/feet AP_M/AP_L and achieves the lowest average mMR-2. Ablations confirm the part-to-body offset, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each add accuracy. Its single-part (CrowdHuman face) advantage over BPJDet is smaller.
> - **Implicit-bias analyses:** The JEPA analysis shows MSE-style latent prediction is biased toward *influential* (high regression coefficient ρ) features while MAE reconstruction biases toward high-variance (λ) features; the order can fully reverse and depth amplifies noise suppression — empirically confirmed on ImageNet-1K where I-JEPA features align faster with the perceptual PCA subspace (CCA). The contrastive-embedding analysis proves a positive/negative-pair alignment trade-off and that mini-batch training inflates negative-pair variance; its proposed auxiliary loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100/ImageNet and small-batch robustness. LDReg adds local-dimensionality regularization that improves linear evaluation and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE.
> - **4-bit optimizers:** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (GLUE 89.1, SQuAD F1 94.5, E2E BLEU 67.8) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 SacreBleu 26.28 vs 26.61), while cutting total memory up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU) and making optimizer states ~2× smaller than 8-bit AdamW (4× for 4-bitFactor). Unlike Adafactor/SM3, it avoids the CLS accuracy drop; convergence curves align closely with full precision.
> - **CleanDiffuser:** Benchmarking 9 algorithms on 37 RL/IL environments shows reproduced (sometimes exceeded) official baselines, with DQL best among policies (D4RL avg 89.0 vs IDQL 84.1, Decision Diffuser 83.2, Diffuser 78.2; Antmaze 81.3 vs planners' 3–13). Key finding: diffusion *planners* underperform diffusion *policies* and are sensitive to guided sampling; in IL, transformer/DiT variants (Chi_TFM) hit ~1.00 success on pushT/kitchen/lift/can, while Pearce_MLP/Chi_UNet drop off on harder Robomimic tasks — showing conditional transformer guidance matters.
> - **Dale's-Law RNNs:** Column-constrained E/I (ColEI) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and Dale's-ANN (DANN) RNNs across sequential MNIST, adding, PTB, and object recognition. Spectral transplant/ablation experiments show the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed, rank-one nilpotent contribution) matters *more* than the sign constraints themselves; normalised SVD entropy at initialization anti-correlates with final test error, and smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units worsen both spectrum and performance (DANN stays robust). Gradient clipping mitigates but does not eliminate the deficit.
> 
> Overall, the strongest empirical payoffs are PBADet's large margins over anchor-based and pose baselines, the lossless accuracy of 4-bit optimizers with major memory savings, and the finding in CleanDiffuser and the Dale's-Law work that *architecture/spectral design choices dominate hyperparameters or sign constraints*. The self-supervised analyses are more theory-driven, using datasets (CIFAR-100/ImageNet/COCO) and metrics (top-1, F1, transfer AP) to validate the derived biases.

### paperscope:results_comparison:35 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource‑constrained perception‑to‑control stack for robots: the vision front‑end must robustly link hands/face to the right person in crowded, COCO‑style scenes; the control side will use diffusion‑driven planners/policies with transformer‑conditioned guidance; and model updates must rely on low‑memory optimizers while I LoRA‑fine‑tune large SFT backbones. I also want self‑supervised pretraining that avoids latching onto noisy pixels for better interpretability, and my time‑series modules should respect excitatory/inhibitory neuron separation yet still train stably. What set of papers covers these components end‑to‑end?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
