> Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results reported in the five provided papers, restricted to the tabulated/figure results and their accompanying descriptions.
> 
> 1) Part–body association in crowded, COCO‑style scenes (PBADet vs prior art)
> Identical datasets: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman.
> - BodyHands (hand–body association; Table 1)
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39
>   - Outcome: PBADet outperforms BPJDet on all three metrics (higher AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP) using the same or smaller backbones.
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (6 parts; Tables 2–3)
>   - Overall detection AP (AP.5:.95; All categories): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3. Detection AP is very close; BPJDet is slightly higher on overall AP, while PBADet leads or ties in some size splits (e.g., APM/APL) and several per‑category APs (e.g., feet; Table 2).
>   - Association robustness (average mMR−2 across parts; lower is better; Table 3): PBADet (YOLOv7) averages lower mMR−2 than BPJDet across head, face, left/right hand, and close on feet. Example: head mMR−2 PBADet 29.2 vs BPJDet (l6) 30.8; left hand 41.1 vs 41.6; right hand 42.7 vs 42.2 (near tie); indicates improved part–body association.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (face–body association; Tables 5–6)
>   - Body MR−2 (lower better): PBADet (YOLOv7) 36.5 (best vs BPJDet l6 40.7).
>   - Face MR−2: PBADet (YOLOv7) 44.7 vs BPJDet (l6) 46.3 (better).
>   - Body AP: PBADet (YOLOv7) 91.6 vs BPJDet (l6) 89.5 (better).
>   - mMR−2 body‑face pairing: PBADet (YOLOv7) 50.8 vs BPJDet (l6) 50.1 (slightly worse; lower is better). Overall: PBADet improves detection quality and MR−2; association mMR−2 is comparable/slightly worse on this single‑part (face) case.
> 
> Conclusion for this component: On identical datasets, PBADet achieves stronger part–body association accuracy and detection robustness than prior methods on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts; on CrowdHuman, PBADet improves MR−2 and AP while body–face pair mMR−2 is roughly on par.
> 
> 2) Time‑series modeling under Dale’s Law (Standard RNN vs ColEI vs DANN)
> Identical tasks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task (Fig. 2 A–D).
> - Across all four benchmarks, ColEI (column‑constrained E/I) learns worse than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs. DANNs match or approach standard RNN performance.
> - Gradient clipping benefits ColEI “substantially more,” stabilizing training, but does not close the gap (Fig. 2; text).
> - Spectral findings: ColEI shows multimodal, dispersed singular‑value spectra linked to degraded learning; DANN and standard RNNs have unimodal, clustered spectra. These spectral properties—not merely sign constraints—best explain performance differences (Figs. 3–4, 5–7). These are relative findings from figures; no competing numerical tables were provided.
> 
> Conclusion: On identical tasks, DANN recurrent models and standard RNNs learn faster/more reliably than ColEI; stability/accuracy differences are attributed primarily to spectral (singular‑value) distribution.
> 
> 3) Self‑supervised learning front‑end (JEPA vs MAE)
> Datasets/tasks: synthetic linear settings; temporal linear model; ImageNet‑64 (CCA analysis only).
> - In deep linear settings, JEPA exhibits a distinct implicit bias for “influential features” (high regression coefficients), whereas MAE prioritizes highly covarying (possibly noisy) features. JEPA’s prioritization strengthens with depth (Theorems 3.2–3.6; Fig. 1–2).
> - Temporal linear model (Eqs. 15–16; Fig. 3): JEPA learns “slow/noise‑robust” features (higher ρ) sooner; MAE remains tied to covariance ordering.
> - ImageNet‑64 validation (Appendix D, Fig. 7): JEPA features from “full vs bottom PCA” subspace show higher similarity than MAE (curves), while MAE aligns more with the “top PCA” variance. No explicit numeric tables were provided; curves indicate JEPA better aligns with low‑variance, semantic subspace quickly.
> 
> Conclusion: While not evaluated on the vision/robotics datasets used elsewhere here, the experimental figures support that JEPA front‑ends emphasize noise‑robust, predictive features (beneficial for interpretability), compared to MAE’s reconstruction bias.
> 
> 4) Memory‑efficient optimizers for LoRA/SFT fine‑tuning (4‑bit optimizers vs full precision)
> Identical datasets: GLUE (RoBERTa‑L), ImageNet‑1K (Swin‑T), E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2‑M), SQuAD & SQuAD2.0 (RoBERTa‑L), WMT14 En‑De (Transformer), LLaMA‑Alpaca tuning (7B/13B/33B) (Tables 2–6).
> - GLUE (mean): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9 vs 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 vs 8‑bit AdamW 89.1; SM3 87.5 (lower); Adafactor ~89.1–89.3 (comparable). 4‑bit matches or slightly exceeds 32‑bit.
> - ImageNet‑1K (Swin‑T): 32‑bit 81.2 vs 4‑bit 80.8 vs 8‑bit 81.0; the 4‑bit drop (≤0.4%) is small; within noise of 8‑bit.
> - E2E‑NLG (BLEU): 4‑bit 67.8 vs 32‑bit 67.7 (parity); Adafactor/SM3 similar (±0.8 BLEU).
> - SQuAD (F1) and SQuAD2.0 (F1): 4‑bit 94.5 (SQuAD) vs 94.6 (32‑bit); 4‑bit 88.4 (SQuAD2.0) vs 88.8 (32‑bit). Close parity.
> - WMT14 En‑De (SacreBLEU): 4‑bit 26.28 vs 32‑bit 26.61 vs 8‑bit 26.66; Adafactor ~26.45; all within ~0.3 BLEU.
> - LLaMA instruction‑tuning (MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA; Table 3): 4‑bit matches 32‑bit over sizes:
>   - 7B: MMLU 38.9 (4‑bit) vs 38.7 (32‑bit); other tasks within ±1.
>   - 13B: 4‑bit often slightly better (e.g., MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5).
>   - 33B: mixed but close (e.g., MMLU 54.9 vs 56.4; OBQA 45.4 vs 43.8), showing robust parity.
> - Efficiency (Table 4):
>   - LLaMA‑7B (FSDP, 2×A100 80GB): total memory 75.40GB (32‑bit) → 31.87GB (4‑bit), saving 57.7%, with similar wall‑time (3.35h → ~3.1h).
>   - RoBERTa‑L (RTE): total memory 5.31GB → 3.00GB (4‑bit fused), 43.5% saved; fused time 3.17min vs 3.93min (faster than 32‑bit and 8‑bit); 4‑bit Factor saves up to 46.7%.
>   - GPT‑2‑M (E2E‑NLG): total memory 6.89GB → 4.62GB (4‑bit), ~34% saved; fused time similar to 32‑bit.
> 
> Conclusion: On identical datasets across NLP/CV/MT/LLM tuning, 4‑bit optimizers match 32‑bit accuracy while reducing peak memory by ~35–58% and often preserving or improving throughput when fused kernels are used.
> 
> 5) Diffusion‑driven planners/policies (CleanDiffuser benchmarks)
> Identical datasets: D4RL offline RL (MuJoCo, Kitchen, AntMaze) and IL (PushT, Relay‑Kitchen, Robomimic). CleanDiffuser integrates and re‑benchmarks 9 DM‑based algorithms under a single modular stack (Tables 1–2).
> - Offline RL (Table 1; normalized scores; higher better unless stated):
>   - Locomotion averages (HalfCheetah/Hopper/Walker2d, 9 datasets): DQL (policy) leads overall (average 89.0 on locomotion block), e.g., Hopper‑medium‑replay 101.6 (best), Walker2d‑medium‑expert 111.6 (best). IDQL is also strong, typically second.
>   - Kitchen (Mixed/Partial): IDQL highest averages (66.6), exceeding Diffuser/DD/AdaptDiffuser and DQL/EDP; on Mixed Kitchen, IDQL 66.5 vs AdaptDiffuser 62.5 vs DD 75.0 on Mixed (DD tops that single split), but averaged over Mixed+Partial: IDQL ranks best (66.6).
>   - AntMaze (Play/Diverse; Medium/Large): DQL dominates with large margins (average 81.3) vs Diffuser/DD (<~13.3) and IDQL (59.8). Example: AntMaze‑Medium‑Diverse DQL 94.7; AntMaze‑Large (Play) DQL 83.3.
>   - Diffusion planners (Diffuser, DD, AdaptDiffuser) perform variably: strong on some locomotion splits, but generally behind diffusion policies (DQL/IDQL) on AntMaze and average scores.
>   - SynthER (data synthesizer) improves over BC, but policies (DQL/IDQL) still lead on most splits.
> 
> - Offline IL (Table 2; success rate or coverage; LAST/MAX):
>   - DiffusionPolicy generally outperforms DiffusionBC on both low‑dim and image splits across PushT, Relay‑Kitchen, and Robomimic.
>   - Best architecture for DiffusionPolicy is Chi_UNet1d: e.g., Robomimic (low‑dim) average LAST/MAX 0.90/0.96 vs DiffusionBC DiT1d 0.73/0.81; on image tasks, DiffusionPolicy Chi_UNet1d 0.88/0.91 vs DiffusionBC DiT1d 0.42/0.48.
>   - Task examples: Transport‑MH (image) DiffusionPolicy (DiT1d) 0.61/0.62; Chi_UNet1d 0.59/0.66; DiffusionBC methods ≤0.16; Square‑PH (image) DiffusionPolicy (DiT1d) 0.95/0.98, Chi_UNet1d 0.81/0.86; DiffusionBC ≤0.22.
> 
> - Cross‑paper consistency on identical IL datasets: The 4‑bit optimizer paper’s DiffusionPolicy/DiffusionBC results on PushT/Robomimic/Relay‑Kitchen match the CleanDiffuser ranges (e.g., PushT and Robomimic “lift/can/square/transport/toolhang” rows show the same best‑in‑class trends for DiffusionPolicy Chi_UNet1d), supporting reproducibility.
> 
> - Diffusion backbone & sampling analyses (Figs. 6–7; Appendix D):
>   - On several D4RL tasks, more sampling steps did not help and sometimes degraded performance (“sampling degradation”), especially on medium‑expert MuJoCo and Kitchen. First‑order solvers (DDPM, SDE‑DPM‑Solver++(1)) generally suffice; 5 steps often adequate.
>   - EMA rate: higher EMA (e.g., 0.999–0.9999) improves/stabilizes learning curves across IDQL, DD, DiffusionBC, DiffusionPolicy; near‑convergence around 5×10^5 gradient steps.
> 
> Overall conclusions across components (integrated view)
> - Vision front‑end for crowded COCO‑style scenes: PBADet sets stronger association/detection on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts, with robust MR−2/AP on CrowdHuman; it is the most suitable among compared detectors for reliable part‑to‑person linking.
> - Time‑series modules honoring E/I separation: recurrent DANNs retain Dale’s Law while matching standard RNN accuracy and outperforming simple E/I column‑partitioned (ColEI) models; spectral clustering (unimodal singular‑value spectra) predicts trainability.
> - Self‑supervised pretraining (JEPA) for interpretability and robustness: JEPA prioritizes high‑influence, low‑variance (semantic) features and avoids fixation on noisy pixels more than MAE (supported by linear dynamics, temporal model, and ImageNet CCA curves).
> - Low‑memory optimizers for LoRA/SFT updates: 4‑bit optimizers achieve parity with 32‑bit across GLUE, SQuAD/SQuAD2.0, E2E‑NLG, WMT14, and LLaMA instruction‑tuning, while saving 35–58% memory and maintaining throughput (often faster with fused ops).
> - Diffusion‑driven planners/policies: CleanDiffuser’s unified benchmarks show diffusion policies (DQL/IDQL) consistently lead on identical D4RL datasets (especially AntMaze) and DiffusionPolicy (Chi_UNet1d) leads on identical IL datasets (PushT/Robomimic/Relay‑Kitchen). Sampling steps/EMA/solver choices materially affect outcomes; 5 steps and higher EMA are strong defaults.
> 
> Note: All numbers and comparisons are taken strictly from the provided tables/figures and their captions; where only curves were given (e.g., Dale’s Law paper, JEPA vs MAE ImageNet), we report relative trends rather than specific numeric values.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Paper set (end-to-end coverage)
> 
> | Component | Paper(s) |
> |---|---|
> | Vision: hand/face→person association in COCO-style crowds | **PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free part-body association) |
> | Control: diffusion planners/policies + transformer-conditioned guidance | **CleanDiffuser** (planners: Diffuser/DD/AdaptDiffuser; policies: Diffusion Policy/DiffusionBC/DQL/EDP/IDQL; DiT1d & Chi_Transformer backbones, CG/CFG guided sampling); support: **Universal Guidance**, **RTB** |
> | Low-memory optimizer + LoRA/SFT fine-tuning | **4-bit Optimizers** (4-bit AdamW/Adam) |
> | SSL pretraining avoiding noisy pixels / interpretability | **JEPA** (noisy-feature avoidance); support: **HASSOD** (hierarchical part-whole interpretability) |
> | Time-series respecting E/I separation, stable training | **"Why Dale's Law RNNs Learn Poorly"** (ColEI vs DANN); support: **BSO/T-BSO** (stable online spiking training) |
> 
> ## Experimental comparison and analysis
> 
> **PBADet (vision):** On BodyHands it beats all SOTA: hand AP 92.62 (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) vs BPJDet 86.91 (YOLOv5l6, 86.1M) — smaller model, better accuracy, and higher conditional/joint AP. On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet in all-category AP but leads in AP_M/AP_L and has the lowest average mMR-2 for head/face/hands/right-foot. On CrowdHuman it achieves the best body MR-2 (36.5, YOLOv7) and competitive AP (91.6), though its edge over BPJDet narrows on this single-part task. Against pose estimator ED-Pose it is dramatically better on hand/foot association (left-hand F1 46.5 vs 22.9). Analysis: the single part-to-body center offset balances detection and association and scales to many parts without BPJDet's representation bloat.
> 
> **CleanDiffuser (control):** On D4RL, diffusion policies beat planners — DQL averages 89.0 (best), EDP 82.4, IDQL 84.1, while planners score 78.2–83.2 and collapse on Antmaze (planner avg 3.0–13.3 vs DQL 81.3), being sensitive to guided sampling and OOD trajectories. On IL benchmarks, Diffusion Policy with DiT1d/Chi_UNet1d reaches ~1.00 on PushT and near-1.00 on Robomimic tasks, outperforming ACT/LSTM-GMM, whereas DiffusionBC is weaker (transport-mh 0.00). DiT1d gives better training stability and sample quality than Janner_UNet1d; Chi_Transformer ≈ Chi_UNet1d; 5 sampling steps often suffice and more steps can degrade. Universal Guidance achieves quality comparable to specialized text-conditional diffusion (CLIP 0.2632 vs 0.2818) with no retraining but slower sampling. RTB attains the true posterior with the highest diversity/FID (vs biased classifier guidance and mode-collapsing KL-penalized RL), matches/outperforms DPOK on Stable Diffusion fine-tuning, and mixed off/on-policy RTB beats pure online training on 2/3 D4RL medium-replay tasks.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers (updates):** Match or slightly exceed 32-bit AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, ImageNet, WMT, and Alpaca fine-tuning of LLaMA-7B/13B/33B (e.g., LLaMA-7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7), while sublinear-memory Adafactor/SM3 degrade (especially CLS). Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB) and LLaMA-7B fits one 80 GB GPU — directly complementing LoRA (which freezes weights and tunes low-rank adapters). Ablations: smaller block size (B128) recovers first-moment accuracy; factorized second moment adds memory savings without loss.
> 
> **JEPA (SSL):** Theory and dynamics show JEPA's implicit bias toward high-ρ "influential" features while MAE greedily learns high-λ features even when noisy; depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression (fixed points ρ^L vs ρ^{L/(L+1)}), and critical-time analysis shows JEPA's learning order is ρ-driven while MAE's is λ-driven. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features than MAE (CCA), explaining its robustness/interpretability. HASSOD additionally provides interpretability by discovering whole/part/subpart object hierarchies (SA-1B Mask AR 17.0→26.0, LVIS 20.2→22.5) with 1/5 the data and 1/12 the iterations of CutLER.
> 
> **Dale's Law RNNs (time-series):** Sign-constrained ColEI networks learn consistently worse and with higher variance than DANN and standard RNNs on all four tasks (adding, sMNIST, PTB, object recognition); gradient clipping helps ColEI most. The failure is traced not to sign constraints or singular vectors but to the initial recurrent-weight spectrum (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure → multimodal dispersed singular values), quantified by normalised SVD entropy, which anti-correlates with final error. DANN remains robust even with a single inhibitory neuron, whereas ColEI degrades with fewer I units — so E/I separation can train stably via DANN-style structure/spectral initialization. BSO/T-BSO support stable training under memory constraints: memory drops to O(n²L/32) vs BPTT's O(n²L), with sublinear regret O(√T)/O(T^{3/4}) and state-of-the-art online-BSNN accuracy (CIFAR-10 94.86%, CIFAR-100 74.27%, DVS-CIFAR10 81.00%, GSC 96.12%), largely closing the gap to full-precision spiking networks.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, the following set of papers covers your perception‑to‑control stack end‑to‑end:
> 
> **Vision front‑end (hands/face → person in crowded COCO‑style scenes)**
> - **PBADet** (One‑Stage Anchor‑Free Part‑Body Association Detection) — the part‑to‑body center‑offset design directly addresses left/right hand, face, and foot‑to‑body association in crowded multi‑person scenes, evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman.
> 
> **Control side (diffusion planners/policies + transformer‑conditioned guidance)**
> - **RTB** (Reward Trajectory Balance) — reward‑guided diffusion/fine‑tuning for posterior sampling in vision/language and continuous control.
> - **Universal Guidance** — training‑free guidance of frozen diffusion models (incl. face/segmentation/object‑detection guidance).
> - **CleanDiffuser** — modular library benchmarking diffusion planners, policies (Diffusion Policy with transformer/DiT variants), and data synthesizers.
> 
> **Model updates (low‑memory optimizers + LoRA fine‑tuning of large SFT backbones)**
> - **4‑bit Optimizers** — 4‑bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states; evaluated alongside LoRA/instruction‑tuning (Alpaca) of LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B.
> 
> **Self‑supervised pretraining avoiding noisy‑pixel latching / interpretability**
> - **JEPA self‑distillation analysis** ("How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features") — explains why latent‑space prediction suppresses noisy pixels.
> - **HASSOD** — self‑supervised detection with hierarchical part/whole pseudo‑labels for interpretability.
> - (Optional: **LDReg** for local dimensionality collapse in SSL.)
> 
> **Time‑series modules respecting E/I separation with stable training**
> - **Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly** — why E/I (Dale's)‑constrained recurrent nets underperform and how to stabilize them.
> - **BSO/T‑BSO** — binary spiking online optimization (spiking/E‑I style dynamics, online, low‑memory, stable training).
> 
> ---
> 
> **Comparison & analysis of experimental results**
> 
> **Vision front‑end.** On **BodyHands**, PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9 GFLOPs) reaches hand AP 89.1 and joint AP 85.98, beating BPJDet (YOLOv5m6, 41.2 GFLOPs: 85.3/78.13) and BodyHands (83.44/63.48) with a smaller model. On **COCOHumanParts** it is on par with BPJDet overall but leads in AP_M/AP_L and person/feet AP, and has the lowest average mMR⁻² across head, face, both hands, and right foot. On **CrowdHuman** face‑body association, the advantage narrows (best body MR⁻² and body AP with YOLOv7, comparable AP to BPJDet), since a single part gives the part‑to‑body formulation less benefit. Against multi‑person pose estimator ED‑Pose on COCO val, PBADet's hand/feet precision‑recall‑F1 are far higher (e.g., left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87), showing the part‑object formulation is better suited to part‑body association than keypoint‑only pose methods.
> 
> **Diffusion control.** **RTB** matches state‑of‑the‑art on D4RL (halfcheetah/hopper/walker2d; vs Diffuser, Decision Diffuser, D‑QL, IDQL, QGPO), and outperforms pure on‑policy training on two of three medium‑replay tasks using mixed off/on‑policy data; in image/language it improves reward coverage over classifier guidance and KL‑constrained RL (which are biased/mode‑collapse prone), with a reward‑vs‑diversity tradeoff in Stable Diffusion fine‑tuning. **Universal Guidance** generates quality images guided by face recognition, segmentation, object location, and style without retraining, comparable to specialized conditional models (Stable Diffusion and ImageNet), at the cost of slower generation and per‑network tuning. **CleanDiffuser** shows diffusion policies excel in imitation learning (PushT, Relay‑Kitchen, Robomimic; 22 tasks) matching/beating official baselines but are slower than ACT; ablations find ~5 sampling steps often enough (more can degrade), solver choice matters, and the algorithm choice dominates model size.
> 
> **Low‑memory optimization.** 4‑bit Adam/AdamW match or slightly exceed 32‑bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa‑L), SQuAD, ImageNet (Swin‑T), E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2), WMT14 en‑de, and Alpaca instruction tuning of LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B (e.g., LLaMA‑7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7 for 32‑bit; LLaMA‑13B 47.4 vs 46.5), while cutting total training memory up to 57.7% and fitting LLaMA‑7B on one 80 GB GPU — i.e., LoRA‑style large‑backbone fine‑tuning without accuracy loss. Sub‑linear‑memory alternatives (Adafactor, SM3) degrade, especially on classification.
> 
> **Self‑supervised pretraining.** The JEPA analysis (ImageNet‑1K with I‑JEPA) shows JEPA features align faster with the low‑variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features than MAE, whose feature ordering depends mainly on eigenvalues — i.e., JEPA's implicit bias to high‑influence features is why it avoids latching onto unpredictable pixel noise, favoring interpretable representations. **HASSOD** improves zero‑shot Mask AR from 17.0→26.0 on SA‑1B and 20.2→22.5 on LVIS (Box AR +3.2/+3.3 on Objects365/LVIS) using 1/5 the images and 1/12 the iterations of CutLER, and adds hierarchical part/whole labels for interpretability and controllable detection granularity.
> 
> **E/I time‑series stability.** Dale's‑law ColEI RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN across all four tasks (Adding, sMNIST, Penn TreeBank, naturalistic object recognition); the paper shows via singular‑value transplantation that the culprit is the initial recurrent weight spectrum (multimodal/dispersed singular values), not the sign constraint — gradient clipping substantially mitigates it, and normalized SVD entropy anti‑correlates with error. **BSO/T‑BSO** gives an orthogonal route: online spiking training with per‑layer moments and adaptive flipping thresholds achieves 94.86%/74.27% on CIFAR‑10/100, 57.76% on DVS‑CIFAR10, 96.12% on Google Speech Commands with ~20–31× smaller models and near‑constant memory across timesteps, with sublinear regret guarantees (O(√T)/O(T^(3/4))) — i.e., E/I‑respecting spiking dynamics that train stably under low memory.
> 
> **End‑to‑end takeaway.** PBADet supplies the perception output (part‑to‑body association) that feeds diffusion planners/policies; RTB/Universal Guidance/CleanDiffuser cover reward‑guided and transformer‑conditioned diffusion control; 4‑bit optimizers make LoRA fine‑tuning of large SFT backbones memory‑feasible on‑device; the JEPA analysis/HASSOD provide noise‑robust, interpretable self‑supervised pretraining; and Dale's‑law/BSO work guides stable E/I‑separated time‑series modules. Together these cover every requested component; the main cross‑cutting caveat is that the vision and control components are validated on disjoint benchmarks (COCO‑family vs D4RL/robotic IL), so end‑to‑end integration gains are not directly quantified by any single paper.

</details>

<a id="case-paperscope-results_comparison-41"></a>

### paperscope:results_comparison:41 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a production system with three needs: (1) a medical vision module that reliably links hands/faces to the right person in crowded rooms (COCO-style benchmarks, anchor-free detection, evaluate with F1/Precision); (2) an LLM service that decides cache contents and ranked lists using only offline logs (bandit-style offline learning, no online exploration); and (3) a training stack for Transformers/ResNet-50 that must fine-tune with self-supervised objectives while keeping optimizer state tiny (prefer 4-bit AdamW/SGD) and steering representations away from noisy features. We also have an RNN component that should obey excitatory/inhibitory constraints but remain trainable via spectral guidance. Are there papers that bring together anchor-free part–body detection, offline combinatorial bandits, JEPA-style self-supervised learning, memory-efficient optimizers, and spectral perspectives on biologically constrained RNNs—using CE/MSE, cosine similarity, and LoRA fine-tuning?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：3→4（Δ+1）；rounds：3→3（Δ+0）。**

工具安排：naive 为第1轮4次、第2轮2次；community 为第1轮5次、第2轮4次。最终回答另占一轮。

两边均为 3 轮，但工具总数 6→9，同轮并发安排及工具工作量仍可能不同。

Gold 1：

> Below is a method-by-method comparison and summary of experimental results strictly extracted from the figures, tables, and text you provided. I group results by problem area and dataset, call out identical datasets when they exist, and state who performs better/worse under the reported metrics.
> 
> 1) Anchor‑free part–body detection (PBADet) vs prior detectors and pose methods
> Datasets with identical evaluation across methods: BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman.
> 
> - BodyHands (Narasimhaswamy et al., 2022)
>   Metrics: Hand AP (↑), Conditional Accuracy (↑), Joint AP (↑). Table 1.
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Acc 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1, 92.71, 85.73
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9, 86.91, 84.39
>   Result: On the identical BodyHands test split, both PBADet variants outperform BPJDet on all three metrics. The best absolute numbers are from PBADet (YOLOv7), with +3.2 AP and +5.71 cond. acc. vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6), and +1.59 joint AP.
> 
> - COCO-HumanParts (Yang et al., 2020)
>   Metrics: All-categories APs (original/subordinate), APM/APL, and per-category APs (person, head, face, hands, feet). Table 2; association quality via mMR−2 (↓). Table 3.
>   Detection AP (Table 2):
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.6/43.3; APM 63.8/63.2; APL 61.8/58.9
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 43.0/41.8; APM 66.2/65.0; APL 67.2/64.4
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): 42.7/41.5; APM 65.8/64.4; APL 66.7/63.3
>   Per-category APs (person/head/face/r-hand/l-hand/r-foot/l-foot):
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 61.3/56.6/46.3/40.4/39.6/30.2/30.9
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 62.4/54.6/44.6/39.0/37.7/30.9/31.5
>   Findings:
>   – Overall AP.5:.95 is slightly higher for BPJDet (43.6 vs 43.0); however, PBADet has substantially higher APM/APL (e.g., APL 67.2 vs 61.8), indicating stronger performance on medium/large objects.
>   – Per-category, PBADet (YOLOv5l6) outperforms for person and feet (r-foot 30.9 vs 30.2; l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9); BPJDet has higher APs for head, face, and hands.
>   Association mMR−2 (↓) (Table 3):
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): head 27.9, face 30.5, l-hand 36.2, r-hand 40.8, r-foot 50.4, l-foot 47.9
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, l-hand 41.6, r-hand 42.2, r-foot 49.1, l-foot 50.4
>   Findings: Lower is better. PBADet (YOLOv5l6) achieves lower (better) mMR−2 for head, face, and both hands; BPJDet is lower on r-foot (49.1 vs 50.4). PBADet is lower on l-foot (47.9 vs 50.4).
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Shao et al., 2018) face–body association (Appendix Tables 5, 6)
>   Metrics: MR−2 body/face (↓), AP body/face (↑), mMR−2 body–face (↓).
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): MR−2 body 36.5 (best), face 44.7; AP body 91.6; face 81.6; mMR−2 50.8
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 body 40.7; face 46.3; AP body 89.5; face 81.6; mMR−2 50.1 (better)
>   Findings: PBADet achieves better body detection (lower MR−2 and higher AP); BPJDet has slightly better association (lower mMR−2).
> 
> - Comparison to multi‑person pose estimation (ED‑Pose) on COCO (Appendix Table 7)
>   Metric: Precision/Recall/F1 for left/right hands and feet (PBADet uses IoU>0.5; ED‑Pose keypoint-in-box match). PBADet (YOLOv5l6) vs ED‑Pose (Swin‑L):
>   • All parts F1: 48.52 vs 31.51; also higher precision/recall for each part (e.g., l‑hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87).
>   Finding: On identical COCO validation images (2,693), PBADet substantially outperforms ED‑Pose for part localization/association under the reported matching protocols.
> 
> - Ablations (BodyHands, Table 4; Appendix Table 8)
>   • Adding the association head+loss (Lassoc) dramatically boosts Conditional Accuracy (80.78→92.62) and Joint AP (78.07→85.98) without harming Hand AP (89.1→89.1).
>   • Anchor‑free and part‑to‑body design both contribute: anchor‑free part‑to‑body yields higher Cond. Acc/Joint AP vs anchor‑based versions using the same backbone.
> 
> 2) Offline learning for combinatorial multi‑armed bandits (CLCB/Off‑CMAB)
> Datasets with identical evaluation across methods: synthetic cascading bandits (learning‑to‑rank), Yelp learning‑to‑rank, synthetic LLM cache, SciQ LLM cache.
> 
> - Cascading bandits (learning to rank)
>   Synthetic (Fig. 1a): Compared with CUCB‑Offline and EMP, CLCB reduces suboptimality gap by 47.75% and 20.02%, respectively, across the same synthetic setup (m=100, K=5, n varied).
>   Yelp dataset (Fig. 1b): For K=4 and K=8 (n=100), CLCB consistently has the lowest suboptimality gap vs CUCB‑Offline and EMP; gaps shrink as K increases (consistent with the reward form 1−∏(1−µ)).
>   Offline data generation study (Fig. 2): Across random, UCB‑based, LCB‑based, and empirical‑based logging, CLCB maintains the smallest suboptimality gap; the win is largest when logging used UCB‑based selection.
> 
> - LLM cache
>   Synthetic (Fig. 3a): CLCB‑LLM‑C achieves ≥1.32× improvement over LFU and LEC on identical synthetic cache tasks (100 queries, cache size 40, power‑law query frequency).
>   SciQ real‑world (Fig. 3b): Using GPT‑4‑o (“o200k base”) tokenization and API pricing, CLCB‑LLM‑C reduces cost by up to 36.01% vs LFU and 20.70% vs LEC (cache sizes K=10, 20). Results are robust to another LLM (GPT‑4‑turbo, “cl100k base”).
> 
> 3) Memory‑efficient optimizers with 4‑bit states
> Datasets with identical evaluation across optimizers: GLUE (RoBERTa‑L), ImageNet‑1k (Swin‑T), E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2‑M), SQuAD and SQuAD 2.0 (RoBERTa‑L), WMT14 en‑de (Transformer‑Base), LLaMA instruction‑tuning.
> 
> - Accuracy vs full precision and 8‑bit (Table 2; Tables 7–9)
>   • NLU (RoBERTa‑L mean over GLUE): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit Factor 88.9; SM3 87.5. 4‑bit matches 8‑bit and full precision; SM3 underperforms.
>   • ImageNet‑1k (Swin‑T top‑1): 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit 81.0; 4‑bit 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9; SM3 79.0. 4‑bit is within ~0.3–0.4 of 32‑bit and on par with 8‑bit; SM3 lags.
>   • E2E‑NLG BLEU (GPT‑2‑M): 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5; 4‑bit 67.8; 4‑bit Factor 67.6; SM3 66.9. 4‑bit slightly exceeds 32‑bit and 8‑bit.
>   • QA F1 (RoBERTa‑L on SQuAD): 32‑bit 94.6; 8‑bit 94.5; 4‑bit 94.5; 4‑bit Factor 94.6; SM3 91.7. 4‑bit matches full precision; SM3 is notably lower.
>   • WMT14 en‑de SacreBLEU: 32‑bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; 4‑bit 26.28; 4‑bit Factor 26.45; SM3 22.72. All AdamW/Adafactor variants are close; SM3 trails substantially.
>   • LLaMA instruction‑tuning (Table 3, identical eval sets): 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit AdamW across MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC‑e/ARC‑c, OBQA for 7B/13B/33B; e.g., LLaMA‑13B MMLU 47.4 (4‑bit) vs 46.5 (32‑bit); HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8.
> 
> - Memory and time (Table 4)
>   • LLaMA‑7B finetune (2×A100‑80GB): 32‑bit 75.40 GB, 3.35h; 4‑bit 31.87 GB (−57.7%), 3.07h; fused 3.11h. Identical setup shows 4‑bit both reduces memory and shortens wall‑time.
>   • RoBERTa‑L (single RTX 4090): 32‑bit 5.31 GB, 3.93 min; 8‑bit 3.34 GB, 3.38 min; 4‑bit fused 3.00 GB (−43.5%), 3.17 min.
>   • GPT‑2‑M (4×4090): 32‑bit 6.89 GB, 2.13h; 8‑bit 4.92 GB, 2.04h; 4‑bit fused 4.62 GB (−34.4%), 2.11h. 4‑bit reduces memory vs 8‑bit and is time‑comparable when fused.
> 
> - Largest trainable model under fixed GPU memory (Table 5)
>   • 24 GB GPU: 32‑bit up to OPT‑350M vs 4‑bit up to OPT‑1.3B.
>   • 80 GB GPU: 32‑bit up to OPT‑1.3B vs 4‑bit up to OPT‑6.7B and LLaMA‑7B.
> 
> - Stability and second‑moment quantization (Table 1)
>   • Naïve 4‑bit (B2048/DE like 8‑bit) is unstable (up to 66% runs) and degrades BLEU; removing the zero‑point (DE‑0) restores stability and BLEU (e.g., B2048/DE‑0: BLEU 67.5). Best BLEU (67.8) with Rank‑1 normalization + Linear mapping; factoring second moment is also stable (BLEU 67.6).
> 
> 4) JEPA‑style self‑supervised learning vs MAE (linear analyses + controlled experiments)
> Datasets/Settings: synthetic linear ODE simulations; temporal generative model; ImageNet‑1K (64×64) encoders compared via CCA similarity (Appendix D Fig. 7). No absolute accuracies are reported; comparisons are about learning order and feature subspace.
> 
> - Feature learning order (Figs. 1–2)
>   • On distributions where feature covariance (λ) and regression coefficient (ρ) diverge, JEPA prioritizes features with higher ρ (influential/predictive) even when λ is small, whereas MAE prioritizes features with larger λ. This produces an inverted learning order between JEPA and MAE when λ increases but ρ decreases across features.
> 
> - Depth dependence (Fig. 4; simulations Fig. 4 in Appendix A)
>   • The JEPA bias toward high‑ρ features strengthens with encoder depth (L>1). For shallow encoders, the difference vs MAE diminishes; for deeper encoders, JEPA shows wider temporal separation favoring high‑ρ features.
> 
> - ImageNet‑64 empirical proxy (Appendix D Fig. 7)
>   • I‑JEPA vs MAE: over training, I‑JEPA features show higher mean CCA similarity between full vs “bottom‑variance” data (and lower similarity between full vs “top‑variance”), indicating JEPA emphasizes lower‑variance, more semantic subspaces; MAE aligns more with top‑variance subspace. (Trends only; no numeric CCA values reported.)
> 
> 5) Spectral perspectives on Dale’s‑law RNNs (standard RNN vs ColEI vs DANN)
> Datasets with identical evaluation across architectures: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, naturalistic object recognition task.
> 
> - Overall learning performance (Fig. 2 A–D)
>   • Across all four tasks, ColEI (column‑sign‑constrained EI) learns worse and with higher variance vs standard RNNs and DANN RNNs; gradient clipping helps ColEI more but does not close the gap.
> 
> - Spectral radius sweep (Appendix Fig. 9)
>   • ColEI behaves differently with spectral radius ρ: it performs better than standard/DANN at larger ρ but worse at smaller ρ; standard and DANN have similar, smoother dependence on ρ.
> 
> - Spectrum transplant experiments (Fig. 4B–C)
>   • Freezing spectrum vs sign constraints: Changing the singular value spectrum accounts for a larger fraction of the performance gap than adding/removing sign constraints (e.g., sign constraints degrade RNN by ~0.7%±0.3% error, ColEI by ~1%±1%, whereas spectrum swaps shift errors by ~1.5%±0.3% for RNNs and ~2%±1% for ColEI on sequential MNIST; similar on naturalistic task, Appendix Table 2). Conclusion: spectrum dominates sign constraints in driving learning differences.
> 
> - EI ratio and network size (Figs. 5–7)
>   • ColEI degrades as fraction of inhibitory units decreases and as network gets smaller; normalized SVD entropy predicts performance across EI ratios and sizes. DANN maintains unimodal spectra and trains well even with a single inhibitory neuron.
> 
> How these results map to your stated needs
> - Medical vision module (anchor‑free part–body detection on COCO‑style data): PBADet achieves state‑of‑the‑art BodyHands results and competitive COCO‑HumanParts performance. It improves medium/large AP and offers strong association (mMR−2) for head/face/hands vs BPJDet, and its one‑stage, anchor‑free design is validated via ablations. Evaluation includes AP and mMR−2; F1/Precision/Recall were also contrasted against ED‑Pose (PBADet higher F1 across hands/feet on COCO val).
> - LLM cache and ranked lists with offline logs only: Off‑CMAB’s CLCB reduces suboptimality gaps substantially on synthetic and real learning‑to‑rank data (Yelp) and cuts LLM inference cost vs LFU/LEC by up to 36.01% on SciQ, consistent across two GPT‑4 variants. The comparisons are on identical datasets/logging distributions.
> - Memory‑efficient fine‑tuning for Transformers/ResNet‑50 with tiny optimizer state: 4‑bit AdamW/Factor match or nearly match 32‑bit/8‑bit accuracy across NLU, QA, NLG, and MT; enable much larger model sizes on fixed GPU memory (e.g., LLaMA‑7B on a single 80GB GPU) and reduce memory up to 57.7% in LLaMA‑7B finetuning. Stability requires excluding the zero‑point for second moment (DE‑0) or Rank‑1 Linear quantization.
> - Spectral guidance for EI‑constrained RNNs: DANN RNNs match standard RNNs across tasks, whereas naïve ColEI RNNs underperform due to pathological singular value spectra; spectrum transplant experiments quantify that spectra matter more than sign constraints.
> 
> Notes on metrics and identical datasets across methods
> - BodyHands, COCO‑HumanParts, CrowdHuman are identical datasets across PBADet vs baselines; evaluations include AP, AP.5:.95, APM/APL, per‑category APs, and mMR−2.
> - GLUE, ImageNet‑1k, E2E‑NLG, SQuAD/SQuAD2.0, WMT14 en‑de are identical across optimizers; the 4‑bit methods are compared to 32‑bit and 8‑bit under the same training setups.
> - Cascading bandits synthetic/Yelp and LLM cache synthetic/SciQ are identical tasks across CLCB and baselines (CUCB‑Offline, EMP; LFU, LEC).
> 
> All numbers and findings above are taken directly from the provided tables, figures, and captions without adding external assumptions.

**naive 最终答案**

> **No single paper in this collection combines all five components.** They are covered by five separate works; here is how each matches your needs and what their experiments show.
> 
> **1. Anchor-free part–body detection — PBADet (ICLR 2024)**
> Matches: one-stage, anchor-free, part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-style benchmarks with Precision/Recall/F1. Results: on COCO HumanParts all-categories AP 42.7–43.0; vs. ED-Pose (pose estimator) on COCO it wins clearly (e.g., left-hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87; all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51); on CrowdHuman face-body it beats BPJDet (body MR-2 36.5 vs 40.7, body AP 91.6 vs 89.5, mMR-2 50.8 vs 50.1). Ablations: anchor-free part-to-body (89.1 HandAP) > anchor-based part-to-body (88.4) > BPJDet body-to-part (85.3).
> 
> **2. Offline combinatorial bandits — Off-CMAB/CLCB (ICML 2025)**
> Matches: no online exploration, decisions from pre-collected logs (ranked lists, LLM cache). Results: CLCB cuts suboptimality gaps by 47.75% vs CUCB-Offline and 20.02% vs EMP on synthetic cascading bandits; on real LLM caching reduces inference cost by 36.01% vs LFU and 20.70% vs LEC; achieves near-optimal gap matching the lower bound up to a log factor.
> 
> **3. JEPA-style SSL / steering away from noisy features**
> - *Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features* (NeurIPS 2024): deep linear analysis shows JEPA self-distillation biases toward high-influence features and suppresses noise (depth strengthens this); on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (measured by CCA).
> - *LDReg* (ICLR 2024): local-dimensionality regularization improves linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE, MoCo, VICReg, Barlow Twins.
> - *Embedding Similarities in Contrastive Learning*: cosine-similarity analysis; optimal embeddings give positive-pair similarity 1 and negative-pair −1/(n−1); a variance-reduction auxiliary loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and full ImageNet, especially at small batch sizes.
> 
> **4. Memory-efficient optimizers — 4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)**
> Matches: 4-bit AdamW states (also SGD(M) convergence proof). Results: matches/exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (89.1), Swin-T ImageNet (80.8), E2E-NLG (67.8), SQuAD (94.5), WMT14 (26.28); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning comparable or better (e.g., MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7 at 7B; 47.4 vs 46.5 at 13B); up to 57.7% memory savings and LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU.
> 
> **5. Spectral perspective on biologically constrained RNNs — "Learning better with Dale's Law" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> Matches: E/I constraints with spectral guidance. Results: sign constraints alone explain only part of the deficit (0.7%±0.3% for RNNs, 1%±1% for ColEI of the total 2.3%±0.6% gap on sequential MNIST); singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints. ColEI's multimodal dispersed spectrum hurts learning (worse in small networks/fewer inhibitory units), while DANN RNNs keep standard-like spectra and learn just as well; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error and can predict performance before training; gradient clipping mitigates the ColEI deficit.
> 
> **On CE/MSE, cosine similarity, and LoRA:** cosine similarity is central to the contrastive-learning paper (and used in JEPA-style feature analysis); cross-entropy appears only as an assumption (e.g., additive-loss analyses) and MSE is not a reported objective in these papers. LoRA is referenced in the 4-bit optimizer paper for LLaMA fine-tuning; the Hessian-spectrum paper finds LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does. None of the papers jointly use CE/MSE + cosine similarity + LoRA across all five components, so that specific combination cannot be confirmed from the context.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Answer
> 
> **No paper in this collection brings all of these together.** There is no unified work combining anchor-free part–body detection + offline combinatorial bandits + JEPA-style SSL + 4-bit optimizers + spectral E/I RNN analysis. Instead, each need maps to a separate paper:
> 
> | Need | Closest paper |
> |---|---|
> | (1) Anchor-free part–body detection, COCO, F1/Precision | **PBADet** (doc `08b70bc3…`) |
> | (2) Offline combinatorial bandits, no exploration | **Off-CMAB / CLCB** (doc `d8faaa7f…`) |
> | (3a) JEPA-style SSL avoiding noisy features | **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc `40fde037…`) |
> | (3b) Memory-efficient 4-bit AdamW | **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (doc `8d5e1455…`) |
> | (4) Spectral perspective on E/I (Dale's law) RNNs | **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (doc `e63a94c4…`) |
> 
> Note: none of these five papers uses CE/MSE + cosine similarity + LoRA jointly. LoRA appears only tangentially (referenced in the 4-bit optimizer paper; analyzed in a separate Hessian-spectrum paper), and CE/MSE/cosine similarity are not the training recipe of any single paper.
> 
> ## Experimental results compared
> 
> **PBADet (detection):** One-stage anchor-free with a single part-to-body center offset. On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) reaches HandAP 89.1 / Cond. Accuracy 92.62 / JointAP 85.98, beating BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 86.1M) at 85.9/86.91/84.39 and BodyHands (700.3M) at 84.12/84.12/63.87. On COCOHumanParts, it is on par with BPJDet overall (AP 43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3) but leads in AP_M/AP_L, person, and feet metrics, and gives the lowest mean MR-2 for head/face/hands. Versus ED-Pose on COCO val, PBADet roughly doubles Precision/Recall/F1 for left/right hands (e.g., F1 46.50/47.34 vs 22.87/24.17) and feet (~51 vs ~40). On CrowdHuman face–body association it achieves leading body MR-2 but only competitive AP. Trained with SGD, IoU/DFL/classification losses — not CE/MSE/cosine or LoRA.
> 
> **Off-CMAB/CLCB (bandits):** First offline CMAB framework; CLCB combines pessimistic base-arm lower confidence bounds with a combinatorial solver. Theoretical suboptimality gap Õ(K*√(C*/n)) matches the lower bound up to a log factor, under two new data-coverage conditions. Empirically, for LLM caching it cuts inference cost by **36.01% vs LFU and 20.70% vs LEC**, robust across GPT-4-o/GPT-4-turbo, and substantially reduces cascading-bandit suboptimality on synthetic and Yelp data. This matches need (2) — decisions from offline logs only, no online exploration.
> 
> **JEPA analysis (SSL):** Theoretical (deep linear networks) result that JEPA self-distillation implicitly prioritizes high-influence features and suppresses noise, with depth strengthening noise suppression, whereas MAE ordering depends mainly on eigenvalues. ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features (CCA) than MAE features. No experimental accuracy numbers vs optimizers/LoRA — it is an analysis, not a training-stack method.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers (training stack):** 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor match or slightly exceed 32-bit AdamW: NLU (RoBERTa-L GLUE) 89.1 vs 88.9; CLS (Swin-T ImageNet) 80.8–80.9 vs 81.2; NLG 67.8 vs 67.7; QA 94.5 vs 94.6; MT 26.28–26.45 vs 26.61. Memory: LLaMA-7B fine-tuning drops from 75.4 GB to 31.9 GB (**57.7% saved**; optimizer states ~4× smaller for 4-bit Factor); LLaMA-7B fits on one 80 GB GPU. Sub-linear-memory baselines (Adafactor β₁=0, SM3) degrade more, especially on CLS. No self-supervised (JEPA) training or LoRA used.
> 
> **Dale's-law RNNs (spectral):** Constraining columns of the recurrent weight matrix (ColEI) learns worse and with higher variance across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum at initialization matters **more than the sign constraints themselves**: ColEI's rank-one-nilpotent column-mean structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values, while DANN (separate E/I units) keeps standard-RNN-like quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra and learns as well as standard RNNs. Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially. So it provides spectral guidance (NSE as a diagnostic), not a training objective like CE/MSE or spectral regularization.
> 
> **Bottom line:** The collection supports each of your four components individually with strong, complementary results — PBADet (detection accuracy/F1), CLCB (offline bandit regret + cache-cost savings), the JEPA paper (noise-avoidance mechanism), 4-bit AdamW (lossless accuracy at 57.7% memory savings), and the Dale's-law spectral paper (why E/I RNNs fail and how to diagnose them). But there is **no paper that unifies them** into one production stack, and none jointly uses CE/MSE + cosine similarity + LoRA fine-tuning as you specified.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:44 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that leverage internal signals to make deep networks more efficient and reliable across tasks: (1) spectral analyses of weight matrices in EI-constrained recurrent nets (Dale’s law) for time-series modeling; (2) implicit biases of joint-embedding self-distillation versus pixel-space reconstruction that avoid noisy features; (3) token-level decoding probability signatures to decide when chain-of-thought helps; (4) memory-lean optimizers that quantize first/second moments to ~4-bit for fine-tuning Transformers or ResNet-50–scale backbones; and (5) anchor-free, one-stage part–whole association detectors that replace heavy attention heads. I’m interested in works that report Precision/accuracy with cross-entropy or MSE losses, compare against cosine-similarity–style representation checks, optionally use feedforward classifier heads with Transformer-based conditional guidance, and include clear method diagrams, with references to standard vision sets (e.g., MNIST/SVHN) or COCO-style detection.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：4→3（Δ-1）；rounds：3→3（Δ+0）。**

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

> {'answer': 'Below is a comparison and summary of the experimental results reported across the five papers, using only the figures/tables and metrics provided in the literature.\n\n1) PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association)\nDatasets and metrics: BodyHands (AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP), COCOHumanParts (COCO AP metrics with per-category APs; subordinate association APs; mMR−2 for association), CrowdHuman (MR−2, AP, mMR−2).\nKey tables/figures: Table 1 (BodyHands), Tables 2–3 (COCOHumanParts), Tables 5–6 (CrowdHuman).\nComparative results:\n- BodyHands (Table 1):\n  • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.\n  • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.\n  • Best BPJDet baseline: YOLOv5l6 Joint AP 84.39, Conditional Accuracy 86.91.\n  → PBADet (both backbones) improves Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP over BPJDet on identical BodyHands test set.\n- COCOHumanParts (Table 2, all-category and per-category APs):\n  • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate), AP.5 70.0/68.4; strong APM/APL and per-category APs (e.g., person 62.4, r-foot 37.7, l-foot 31.5).\n  • PBADet (YOLOv7) comparable: AP.5:.95 42.7/41.5, AP.5 69.5/67.9.\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.6/43.3, AP.5 70.6/69.8; per-category APs slightly higher for some parts.\n  → On COCOHumanParts, PBADet matches BPJDet overall AP, and leads on some scales (APM/APL) and specific categories (feet/person), while BPJDet slightly edges on aggregate AP in some rows. **naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers identified
> 
> 1. **Spectral analysis of EI-constrained RNNs (Dale's Law)** — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023)
> 2. **Implicit bias of JEPA self-distillation vs. pixel reconstruction** — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks" (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024)
> 3. **Token-level decoding probabilities to decide when CoT helps** — "Token Signature: Predicting Chain-of-Thought Gains with Token Decoding Feature in LLMs" (Liu et al., ICML 2025)
> 4. **~4-bit optimizer states** — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023)
> 5. **Anchor-free one-stage part–body association detector** — "PBADet" (Gao et al., ICLR 2024)
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **1. Dale's Law RNNs (spectral perspective).** ColEI (column-partitioned E/I) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs on all four tasks: adding problem (MSE/identity output), row-wise sequential MNIST (softmax), Penn Tree Bank language modeling, and naturalistic object recognition. Gradient clipping helps ColEI disproportionately. SVD "spectrum transplant" experiments prove the singular-value distribution (not sign constraints or singular vectors) drives the deficit: ColEI's spectrum is multimodal/dispersed due to a rank-one nilpotent column-mean term, while DANN matches the unimodal random-matrix spectrum of standard RNNs. **Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with test error** across network size and E:I ratio — a diagnostic usable *before* training. Sequential MNIST is the standard vision set used.
> 
> **2. JEPA vs. MAE implicit bias.** This is largely a theory paper (deep linear networks, exact ODE dynamics). The empirical part compares I-JEPA and MAE on ImageNet-1K at 64×64: representations are checked by **canonical-correlation analysis (CCA)** between encoders trained on full vs. PCA-filtered images ("bottom" 25% / "top" 75% variance). I-JEPA's features align faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace (higher CCA for full-vs-bottom, lower for full-vs-top), i.e., it avoids noisy features, whereas MAE prioritizes high-variance/noisy directions. No accuracy numbers are reported — evidence is representational-similarity (CCA), not classification accuracy.
> 
> **3. Token Signature (CoT gating).** Prediction accuracy for when CoT helps: **Instance SC = 69.6%**, **Aggregated SC = 89.2%** across four open-source models; per-model Aggregated SC reaches 92.9% (Llama-3.2-3B, Llama-3.1-8B). **Dynamic CoT** (logistic regression on instance-level SC) selects CoT vs. direct answer per question: top-2 in **92.8% of 56 setups**, cuts token consumption by **39.1%** (open-source) and **35.8%** when transferred to GPT-4o/GPT-4o-mini. It roughly matches CoT accuracy on CoT-beneficial benchmarks (e.g., GSM8K ~71 vs. 72; FOLIO 54.05 vs. 53.93) and avoids CoT's negative gains on soft-reasoning/commonsense tasks (e.g., StrategyQA −11.3 gap avoided). Accuracy (correct-answer rate) is the metric; no cross-entropy/MSE reported.
> 
> **4. 4-bit optimizers.** On Table 2 metrics: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs. 89.1 (32-bit AdamW 88.9); **Swin-T ImageNet-1K 80.8 vs. 81.2** (cross-entropy classification); GPT-2 E2E BLEU 67.8 vs. 67.7; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs. 94.6; WMT14 Transformer SacreBLEU 26.28 vs. 26.61. LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning is comparable or better on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA (e.g., LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 vs. 46.5). Memory savings up to **57.7%** (LLaMA-7B: 31.87 GB vs. 75.40 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU. Ablations: quantizing both moments gives only marginal drop; smaller block size (B128) for the first moment and rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the second moment recover lossless accuracy; factorizing the second moment improves both accuracy and memory. Convergence curves closely track 32-bit AdamW. Note the vision backbone is Swin-T (Transformer), not ResNet-50 — the ImageNet scale matches but the architecture differs.
> 
> **5. PBADet (part–body association).** BodyHands (VOC AP, IoU=0.5): **Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98** (YOLOv7, 36.9 M params), beating BPJDet (85.9/86.91/84.39) and two-stage BodyHands baselines (84.8/84.12/63.87) by large margins; YOLOv5l6 variant: 88.1/92.71/85.73. COCOHumanParts: all-category AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6), leading on person/feet AP and lowest mMR-2 on most parts. CrowdHuman face–body: best body MR-2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6), competitive mMR-2 vs. BPJDet (advantage shrinks for the single-part case). vs. ED-Pose (Swin-L pose estimator): substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet (all-parts F1 48.52 vs. 31.51). Loss = weighted IoU + DFL + classification + association losses (λ_iou=7.5, λ_dfl=1.5, λ_cls=0.5, λ_assoc=0.2) with task-alignment learning. Ablations show the association head, multi-scale center offsets, and task alignment each improve conditional accuracy and joint AP. Method diagram (Figure 2) and COCO-style evaluation are present.
> 
> ## Cross-paper analysis
> 
> - **Metric diversity:** Papers 1 and 4 report error/accuracy with standard classification losses (cross-entropy; MSE for the adding problem in #1); paper 3 reports answer accuracy; paper 2 reports only CCA representational similarity (a cosine-similarity-style check) rather than task accuracy; paper 5 reports detection AP/conditional accuracy with IoU/DFL/classification/association losses. Only paper 2 directly matches your "cosine-similarity–style representation checks" criterion (via CCA).
> - **Efficiency vs. reliability trade-off:** Paper 4 shows the cleanest "efficiency with no accuracy loss" result (≤0.4 pt drops, up to 57.7% memory saved); paper 3 shows efficiency (token savings) *and* reliability (avoiding CoT's negative effects); paper 1 shows a spectral diagnostic (NSE) that predicts reliability before training; paper 5 shows a leaner one-stage head replacing heavier attention/DETR pipelines while improving AP; paper 2 explains *why* latent-space objectives are more reliable (noise avoidance) without reporting accuracy.
> - **Gaps vs. your criteria:** None of the five papers reports a feedforward classifier head with Transformer-based conditional guidance; none uses SVHN or MNIST/SVHN-style comparisons except paper 1 (sequential MNIST). ResNet-50-scale backbones specifically are not in paper 4 (Swin-T instead). Paper 2 has no method diagram with standard vision accuracy; its evidence is CCA-based, which is complementary to the accuracy-oriented papers.
> 
> **Caveats:** Exact final-error numbers for paper 1 are given in figures rather than text (only qualitative ordering and NSE correlations are stated); paper 2's claims rest on linear-model theory plus CCA experiments, so accuracy-level comparisons against the other works cannot be made from the provided context.

> I found all five papers in the collection. Here they are with their experimental results and a comparative analysis.
> 
> ## 1. Spectral analysis of EI-constrained RNNs (Dale's law)
> **"Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly"** (Li, Cornford, Ghosh, Richards — NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Setup:** Standard RNNs vs. ColEI (column sign-constrained) vs. DANN recurrent nets on adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition.
> - **Results:** ColEI nets learn worse and with higher variance across all four tasks; gradient clipping helps them most. Sign constraints alone only explain part of the gap (impairment ≈0.7±0.3% for RNNs, 1±1% for ColEI vs. a total gap of 2.3±0.6%). SVD "spectrum transplant" experiments show the singular-value spectrum at initialization matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors (~1.5±0.3% RNN / 2±1% ColEI). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error across sizes and E/I ratios; smaller nets with balanced E/I outperform larger nets with skewed ratios.
> - **Meets criteria:** uses cross-entropy (classification/PTB) and MSE (adding problem); sequential MNIST; clear method diagrams (Fig. 1); **no** cosine-similarity-style checks.
> 
> ## 2. Implicit bias of joint-embedding self-distillation vs. pixel reconstruction
> **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (Littwin et al., Apple — NeurIPS 2024)
> - **Setup:** Exact gradient-flow ODE analysis of deep linear JEPA vs. MAE; linear generative (static masking + temporal flickering) models; ImageNet-1K I-JEPA vs. MAE.
> - **Results:** JEPA greedily prioritizes high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ), while MAE orders learning by feature covariance λ only; JEPA's noise suppression strengthens with encoder depth (deep JEPA behaves like infinite-depth MAE, and vice versa). ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE.
> - **Meets criteria:** compares representations via **CCA/PCA-subspace alignment (cosine-similarity–style representation checks)** — this is the paper that matches that requirement; **no** cross-entropy accuracy reported; **no** vision sets like MNIST (ImageNet only).
> 
> ## 3. Token-decoding signatures for when CoT helps
> **"TokenSignature: Predicting Chain-of-Thought Gains with Token Decoding Feature in LLMs"** (Liu, Xu, Li — ICML 2025)
> - **Setup:** 12 benchmarks (GSM8K, MultiArith, FOLIO, ContextHub, ARC, CommonsenseQA, LSAT, PIQA, SIQA, etc.), open- and closed-source LLMs; Spearman correlation of token-probability monotonicity over the first 50 tokens.
> - **Results:** Instance SC predicts CoT usefulness at 69.6% accuracy; Aggregated SC at 89.2%. Dynamic CoT (logistic regressor = feedforward classifier head) selects CoT vs. direct answer per question, landing near the better option (top-2 in 92.8% of 56 setups) and cutting token consumption 39.1% (35.8% when transferred to closed-source models via voting). Robust to decoding variations and few-shot CoT; sequential tasks benefit, non-sequential tasks hurt (error snowballing).
> - **Meets criteria:** accuracy-based, logistic-regression head; **no** vision sets, **no** cosine-similarity checks, **no** MSE.
> 
> ## 4. Memory-lean 4-bit optimizers
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (Li, Chen, Zhu — NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Setup:** Quantized first/second moments (B128/DE for first; rank-1/linear zero-point-excluding for second; optional factored second moment); AdamW baselines.
> - **Results (Table 2):** RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 (vs. 88.9 32-bit); Swin-T ImageNet 80.8–80.9 (vs. 81.2); GPT-2 Medium E2E BLEU 67.8 (vs. 67.7); RoBERTa-L SQuAD F1 94.5 (vs. 94.6); Transformer WMT14 en-de SacreBleu 26.28–26.45 (vs. 26.61). LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca instruction tuning matches 32-bit AdamW on MMLU and commonsense benchmarks. Memory: up to 57.7% savings (LLaMA-7B: 31.87 GB vs. 75.40 GB), enables LLaMA-7B on a single 80 GB GPU; outperforms 8-bit Adam and beats Adafactor/SM3 (which degrade, especially on ImageNet classification).
> - **Meets criteria:** image classification (ImageNet/Swin-T) and Transformer fine-tuning; **no** cosine-similarity checks; **no** MNIST/SVHN; loss metrics are accuracy/BLEU/F1/bleu (not explicitly cross-entropy/MSE).
> 
> ## 5. Anchor-free, one-stage part–body association detector
> **"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** (Gao et al. — ICLR 2024)
> - **Setup:** YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones, conv detection heads (classification + localization + a single part-to-body center offset), TOOD task-alignment, IoU/DFL/classification (cross-entropy-style) + L1 association losses; no heavy attention heads.
> - **Results:** BodyHands — HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (YOLOv7, 36.9 M params) vs. BPJDet 85.3/86.80/78.13 (41.2 M) and BodyHands 84.8/83.44/63.48. COCOHumanParts — all-category AP 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6) and 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) vs. BPJDet 43.6/43.3, but PBADet leads AP_M (65.8–66.2) and AP_L (66.7–67.2) and has the lowest mMR⁻² for head, face, both hands, right foot. CrowdHuman: leading body MR⁻², competitive AP. Anchor-free beats anchor-based with the same offset definition (89.1 vs. 88.4 HandAP). Ablations: association loss lifts conditional accuracy 80.78→92.62 and joint AP 78.07→85.98; multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each add gains. Extends to quadruped part-body association (AnimalPose, AP-10K); clear pipeline diagram (Fig. 2).
> - **Meets criteria:** COCO-style detection, classification loss, method diagram, efficient conv heads replacing attention; **no** cosine-similarity checks.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis across the five
> - **Efficiency theme:** Paper 4 quantizes optimizer states (~4× memory cut) and Paper 3 cuts tokens (≈36–39%) while matching accuracy; Paper 5 replaces heavy two-stage/anchor/attention machinery with one-stage anchor-free conv heads at smaller model size (36.9 M vs. 41.2 M) and beats SOTA. Papers 1 and 2 are efficiency/reliability *diagnostics* rather than memory-saving methods: Paper 1's NSE predicts trainability before training (a reliability diagnostic), Paper 2 explains why latent-space prediction learns faster and with less noise.
> - **Reliability theme:** Paper 1 links spectrum pathology to poor learning; Paper 2 links objective choice to noisy-feature suppression; Paper 3 avoids CoT overthinking/error snowballing; Papers 4 and 5 show no accuracy loss despite heavy compression/simplification.
> - **Losses:** cross-entropy/MSE appear explicitly only in Paper 1 (softmax/identity outputs) and implicitly in Paper 5's classification loss; Papers 3–4 use accuracy/BLEU/F1; Paper 2 is analysis-based.
> - **Cosine-similarity–style representation checks:** only Paper 2 qualifies (CCA/PCA subspace alignment); Paper 3's logistic head is a feedforward classifier but with no representation-cosine comparison.
> - **Vision benchmarks:** Paper 1 (sequential MNIST, object recognition), Paper 4 (ImageNet/Swin-T), Paper 5 (COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands); Papers 2–3 use ImageNet/LLM benchmarks.
> - **Gaps vs. your criteria:** no paper in the collection combines a Transformer-based conditional guidance head with a feedforward classifier, none use SVHN, and Papers 1, 3, 4, 5 do not perform cosine-similarity-style representation checks. The best matches per criterion are Paper 1 (spectral EI + MNIST + CE/MSE), Paper 2 (representation-cosine comparison), Paper 3 (decoding-probability signatures + logistic head), Paper 4 (4-bit moments), and Paper 5 (anchor-free COCO-style association).

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:47 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** We’re building an edge AI system that must: (a) detect and associate body parts (e.g., hands→person) from video streams with high precision, (b) dynamically choose between chain-of-thought and a direct answer to save tokens, and (c) fine-tune large attention-based Transformers under very tight VRAM; we also have a small EI-constrained RNN handling time-series signals. Are there works showing how to use token-probability trends to trigger or skip CoT, quantize optimizer states to ~4-bit for memory-efficient fine-tuning, design anchor-free part–body association models, and analyze spectral properties to stabilize EI RNNs while guiding self-distillation to ignore noisy features? Ideally they report CE/MSE objectives, discuss feedforward heads and Transformer-based conditional guidance (ResNet-50–class backbones are fine), and provide implementation diagrams we can follow.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：3→4（Δ+1）；rounds：4→3（Δ-1）。**
