Gold 1：

> Integrated comparison of experimental results (5 papers) aligned to the edge-AI needs: (a) anchor‑free part–body association, (b) dynamic CoT vs direct answer, (c) memory‑efficient fine‑tuning under tight VRAM, (d) EI RNN stabilization and self‑distillation biasing away from noisy features.
> 
> 1) Anchor‑free part–body association (PBADet) vs baselines on identical datasets
> • BodyHands (hand–body association; Table 1):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39; BPJDet (YOLOv5m6): 85.3 / 86.80 / 78.13; BPJDet (YOLOv5s6): 84.0 / 85.68 / 77.86.
>   Result: On the same dataset/backbones, PBADet improves both association and detection over BPJDet (notably +5.8 to +5.9 points Conditional Accuracy and +1.3 to +8.6 points Joint AP).
> 
> • COCOHumanParts (6 parts→body; Tables 2–3):
>   - All-categories AP (AP.5:.95/AP.5): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/70.0 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/70.6 (very close overall). PBADet leads on APM/APL (PBADet 66.2/67.2 vs BPJDet 63.8/61.8 original; subordinate APs show similar pattern).
>   - Per-category APs (Table 2): PBADet matches or slightly trails in some categories, but leads on person and feet APs in several settings.
>   - Association robustness (average mMR−2, lower is better; Table 3): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) achieves lower mMR−2 on head (27.9 vs 30.8 BPJDet) and hands (36.2 vs 41.6; 40.8 vs 42.2), while BPJDet is slightly better on r-foot (49.1 vs 50.4). PBADet (YOLOv7) similarly lowers mMR−2 on head/face and is competitive on feet.
>   Result: On identical data, PBADet reduces mismatches (mMR−2) for most parts and achieves stronger medium/large object AP, while overall AP is comparable to BPJDet.
> 
> • CrowdHuman (face–body; Tables 5–6):
>   - Detection: PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves best body MR−2 36.5 (vs BPJDet l6 40.7) and body AP 91.6 (vs 89.5). Face MR−2 also improves (44.7 vs 46.3 BPJDet l6).
>   - Pair association mMR−2: BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) slightly better (50.1) vs PBADet 50.8–50.9 (lower is better).
>   Result: PBADet improves detection quality (MR−2, AP) on the same dataset; BPJDet retains a marginal edge on pair mismatch mMR−2.
> 
> 2) Dynamic CoT selection by token‑probability trends (Token Signature)
> • Benchmark-level prediction (Tables 1–2, 7–8):
>   - Aggregated SC predicts whether CoT helps with 89.2% accuracy across four open-source models; Instance SC achieves 69.6%.
>   - Indicators are positive on datasets where CoT offers significant gains (e.g., GSM8K, MultiArith, FOLIO, CH_d) and negative where CoT is non‑helpful/harmful (e.g., MuSR, LSAT, SIQA, StrategyQA).
> 
> • Instance-level Dynamic CoT (Tables 3, 9–10):
>   - Across 56 configurations (4 models × 14 benchmarks), Dynamic CoT is the top method in 46.4% and in the top‑2 in 92.8% of cases, reaching near the better of {CoT, direct answer} on each task.
>   - Token savings vs always‑CoT: averages −104 tokens (−39.1%) across 14 benchmarks (Fig. 4) while preserving accuracy.
> 
> • Transfer to closed‑source (Tables 4, 11; Fig. 5):
>   - After voting transfer from small open-source models, Dynamic CoT on GPT‑4o/mini preserves high accuracy and reduces tokens by −35.8% on average. For high CoT‑gain sets (e.g., GSM8K, MultiArith, FOLIO), it defaults to CoT and matches CoT accuracy; on others (e.g., GPQA, MuSR, LSAT), it cuts tokens while maintaining or slightly trading off accuracy.
> 
> 3) 4‑bit memory‑efficient optimizers (4‑bit AdamW / 4‑bit Factor) vs full‑precision and 8‑bit (Tables 2–6)
> • Accuracy parity across tasks (Table 2):
>   - NLU (RoBERTa‑L, mean Acc/Cor): 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 matches 8‑bit (89.1) and 32‑bit (88.9); Adafactor/SM3 degrade on some tasks.
>   - ImageNet (Swin‑T Acc): 4‑bit AdamW 80.8 vs 32‑bit 81.2 (small drop); 4‑bit Factor 80.9.
>   - NLG (GPT‑2 Medium E2E BLEU): 4‑bit AdamW 67.8 matches 32‑bit 67.7.
>   - QA (RoBERTa‑L SQuAD F1): 4‑bit AdamW 94.5 vs 32‑bit 94.6.
>   - MT (Transformer WMT14 SacreBLEU): 4‑bit AdamW 26.28 vs 26.61 (small drop), and on par with 8‑bit.
> • Instruction tuning (LLaMA; Table 3): 4‑bit AdamW matches or is within noise of 32‑bit on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC‑e/c, OBQA across 7B/13B/33B.
> • Memory/time (Table 4):
>   - LLaMA‑7B (FSDP): total memory −57.7% (75.4 GB→31.9 GB); training time slightly faster (3.35 h→3.07 h).
>   - RoBERTa‑L: with fused kernels, 4‑bit AdamW −43.5% memory (to 3.00 GB), runtime competitive with 8‑bit.
>   - GPT‑2 Medium: with fused kernels, 4‑bit AdamW −34.4% memory, time comparable to 32‑bit.
> • Largest model per GPU memory (Table 5): 24 GB allows OPT‑1.3B with 4‑bit (vs 350M at 32‑bit); on 80 GB, LLaMA‑7B becomes trainable with 4‑bit.
> • Ablations (Table 6): quantizing both first and second moments is near lossless; adding factorized second moment (“4‑bit Factor”) can slightly improve accuracy and memory beyond 4‑bit AdamW.
> 
> 4) EI RNNs under Dale’s Law: spectral properties vs sign constraints (NeurIPS’23)
> • Across the same tasks (Adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, naturalistic object recognition; Fig. 2):
>   - Standard RNNs and DANN (EI but with different parametrization) learn well; ColEI (column‑wise E/I sign‑constrained) learns worse and is more unstable (especially without gradient clipping).
> • Spectrum transplant (Fig. 4):
>   - Applying ColEI singular value spectra to standard RNNs hurts more than imposing sign constraints alone. Sign constraints reduce performance by ~0.7%±0.3% (RNNs) and ~1%±1% (ColEI), while spectrum swaps account for ~1.5%±0.3% (RNNs) and ~2%±1% (ColEI) of the gap.
>   - Conclusion: singular value spectra at initialization matter more than the sign constraints per se.
> • NSE (normalized SVD entropy) correlates with performance (Figs. 5–7):
>   - Lower NSE (more dispersed, multi‑modal singular values) → worse accuracy; improving NSE via more I units or larger networks improves learning. DANN maintains high NSE and stable learning even with very few inhibitory units.
>   - Larger ColEI networks can still learn despite larger max singular values because rotations between steps can avoid pathological growth; overall spectrum (captured by NSE), not the single largest singular value, predicts performance.
> 
> 5) Self‑distillation bias against noisy features (JEPA vs MAE; NeurIPS’24) — controlled linear experiments
> • Instance‑level simulations (Fig. 1 & 2):
>   - MAE learns features in greedy order of covariance λ; JEPA (with deep encoders) learns in greedy order of regression coefficient ρ (feature influence). When λ and ρ orderings disagree, JEPA inverts the learning order relative to MAE.
>   - Increasing JEPA depth L widens the separation (stronger ρ‑greedy behavior); MAE is comparatively insensitive to ρ.
> • Temporal model (Fig. 3):
>   - With z_t built from time‑varying amplitudes plus noise, λa=γa||v_a||² and ρa=γa||v_a||²/(σ_a²+||v_a||²). Experiments match theory: JEPA prioritizes features with higher ρ (i.e., lower noise σ_a), aligning with “avoid noisy features,” while MAE tracks λ regardless of noise.
>   - Conclusion: JEPA’s latent‑prediction objective implicitly biases learning toward high‑influence/low‑noise features, whereas MAE’s pixel‑reconstruction favors high‑variance subspaces.
> 
> Cross‑paper alignment to the edge‑AI requirements
> • Anchor‑free, one‑stage part→body association: PBADet’s experiments on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman show higher detection precision (MR−2↓, AP↑) and lower association errors (mMR−2↓ on most parts) than anchor‑based or body→part schemes on the same datasets/backbones, while remaining efficient.
> • Dynamic CoT gating by token‑probability trends: Token Signature indicators (Aggregated SC 89.2% accurate) and Dynamic CoT (−39.1% tokens on open‑source; −35.8% after transfer) empirically show when to trigger or skip CoT without sacrificing accuracy.
> • Memory‑efficient fine‑tuning under tight VRAM: 4‑bit AdamW/Factor deliver near‑lossless task accuracy vs 32‑bit/8‑bit, up to −57.7% total memory and larger trainable models on fixed GPUs; they also preserve or slightly improve throughput (especially with fused ops and sharding/offloading).
> • EI‑constrained RNNs for time‑series: Spectral analyses show that initializing EI RNNs with unimodal, clustered singular value spectra (high NSE) is more critical than sign constraints for stable learning; DANN‑style parameterizations match standard RNN performance and are robust to EI ratios/sizes.
> • Guiding self‑distillation to ignore noisy features: JEPA’s experiments demonstrate a depth‑dependent bias to high‑influence (high‑ρ) features and reduced sensitivity to noisy, high‑variance components, explaining practical wins of latent‑space prediction when features are noisy.
> 
> Notes on identical datasets across the five works
> • There are no shared benchmarks across all five papers. Direct apples‑to‑apples comparisons happen within each paper on identical datasets/backbones (e.g., PBADet vs BPJDet on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman; 4‑bit optimizers vs 32‑bit/8‑bit on the same models/datasets; ColEI/DANN/standard RNNs on the same tasks; JEPA/MAE on matched synthetic settings; CoT/DA/Dynamic CoT on the same reasoning benchmarks). Where datasets are the same, we reported side‑by‑side numbers above.
> 
> Overall takeaway from the experimental evidence
> • For part–body association, one‑stage anchor‑free PBADet consistently improves precision and association robustness on common benchmarks vs prior one‑stage anchor‑based methods.
> • Token‑probability trends reliably predict CoT gains and enable substantial token savings at matched accuracy via Dynamic CoT, even after transfer to closed‑source models.
> • 4‑bit optimizer states deliver large memory reductions with near‑parity accuracy across vision, NLU, MT, and instruction tuning; with fused kernels and sharding, they also improve training efficiency.
> • For EI RNNs, spectral properties at initialization predict learning stability and accuracy better than sign constraints, and DANN‑style RNNs match standard RNNs across tasks.
> • In controlled linear experiments, JEPA learns influential, low‑noise features first (depth‑dependent), while MAE favors high‑variance features—clarifying when to prefer latent prediction vs pixel‑space reconstruction.

**naive 最终答案**

> 是的，以下五篇作品正好覆盖你的五类需求，下面给出实验结果的对比分析。
> 
> ## 1. Token-probability 触发/跳过 CoT —— TokenSignature（ICML 2025）
> - 方法：用 greedy 解码前 50 个 token 的概率分布与 token 序号的 **Spearman 相关**（Instance SC / Aggregated SC）作为 CoT 有效性的指标；再用 logistic 回归做实例级动态选择（Dynamic CoT）。
> - 结果：**Instance SC 预测准确率 69.6%，Aggregated SC 达 89.2%**（Aggregated 更好，因实例级分布发散）；在 4 个开源模型上 Dynamic CoT 的准确率与 CoT/DA 中较优者几乎一致（gap 多在 ±1% 以内），**token 消耗减少 39.1%**；迁移到闭源模型（GPT-4o 系列投票）仍省 **35.8%**。对解码策略变化和 few-shot CoT 均稳健。
> - 对比：正/负 SC 与 CoT gain 的符号高度对齐（GSM8K、MultiArith、FOLIO、CH_d 为正；MuSR、SIQA、StrategyQA 为负）。含实现示意图与 12 benchmark 明细。
> 
> ## 2. 4-bit 优化器状态做紧 VRAM 微调 —— 4-bit Optimizers（NeurIPS 2023）
> - 方法：第一矩用更小的 block（B128）+动态指数/线性量化；第二矩用 **rank-1 归一化 + 排除零点的线性量化**（解决零点问题），可选 Adafactor 式因式分解（4-bit Factor）。
> - 结果：在 GLUE（RoBERTa-L 88.9–89.1）、Swin-T/ImageNet（80.8–80.9）、GPT-2M/E2E（BLEU 67.6–67.8）、SQuAD（F1 94.5–94.6）、WMT14（26.28–26.45）上**持平或略超 32-bit AdamW**；LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca 微调在 MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA 上也相当。**总训练内存最高省 57.7%**（LLaMA-7B：75.4GB→31.9GB，单卡 80GB 可训），4-bit Factor 比 8-bit 状态再小约 2–4×。附量化映射、随机舍入、收敛证明与图（训练损失曲线几乎重合）。
> - 对比：比 8-bit AdamW、Adafactor、SM3 更省内存且不失精度（后者在 CLS 任务有退化）。
> 
> ## 3. Anchor-free 部件–身体关联 —— PBADet（ICLR 2024）
> - 方法：单阶段 anchor-free，用**单一 part-to-body 中心偏移**（2D 向量）关联部件到身体；检测头为 3 分支（bbox 定位 + 分类 + 位移，3×3/3×3/1×1 卷积），配 TOOD 任务对齐 + 关联损失（含 CE 分类与回归损失），含 pipeline 图。
> - 结果：BodyHands 上 **HandAP 89.1、条件准确率 92.62、JointAP 85.98（YOLOv7）**，全面碾压 BPJDet（YOLOv5l6：85.9/86.91/84.39）与 BodyHands(2022)；参数更少（36.9M）。COCOHumanParts 上 AP 与 BPJDet 持平但 **person/feet 的 AP 领先，平均 mMR−2 最低**；相较 ED-Pose，hands/feet 的精度/召回/F1 显著更高。
> - 消融：关联损失贡献最大（JointAP 78.07→85.98）；**anchor-free 优于 anchor-based（89.1 vs 88.4）、part-to-body 优于 body-to-part（92.62 vs 92.31）**；多尺度中心偏移与任务对齐均提升。
> 
> ## 4. EI RNN 的谱分析稳定化 —— "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"（NeurIPS 2023）
> - 方法：对 ColEI（列约束）、DANN RNN、标准 RNN 做奇异值谱分析，提出 **Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE)** 度量谱“病态”程度。
> - 结果：ColEI 谱为多峰、弥散的奇异值分布（源于列均值 rank-one nilpotent 结构），学习最差且方差最大、需梯度裁剪；DANN 与标准 RNN 呈单峰 quarter-circle（Marchenko–Pastur）谱，学习相当。**NSE 与最终测试误差反相关（NSE 高→训练好）**，初始化即可预测性能；小网络、E:I 失衡会进一步恶化谱与性能。结论：**谱性质比符号约束更关键**——这为你的 EI RNN 设计提供初始化诊断准则。
> 
> ## 5. 自蒸馏忽略噪声特征 —— "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"（NeurIPS 2024）
> - 方法/目标：深度线性网络的 JEPA（MSE 自蒸馏目标 `‖g(f(x))−f(y)‖²`）vs MAE（重构）的临界时间动力学分析。
> - 结果：**JEPA 偏向高影响（高回归系数 ρ）特征，天然慢学/低权重学习高方差噪声特征；MAE 只按特征值 λ 排序，会学到噪声特征**。深度越深，JEPA 的噪声抑制越强（浅编码器此偏差基本消失）。ImageNet-1K 上 I-JEPA 特征比 MAE 更快对齐到含感知特征的低方差 PCA 子空间（CCA 度量）。这为引导自蒸馏“忽略噪声特征”提供了理论机制（而非显式噪声过滤）。
> 
> ## 交叉对比小结
> - **客观函数**：PBADet（CE 分类 + 回归/关联损失）、JEPA（MSE）、TokenSignature（Spearman + logistic，隐含二分类）均明确；4-bit 优化器不改变目标，仅压缩状态。
> - **评估口径不同**：TokenSignature 和 4-bit 优化器用“与 full-precision/DA 的 gap + 资源节省”衡量（40%/57% 量级）；PBADet 用检测 AP/关联指标碾压 SOTA；JEPA 与 EI RNN 偏理论/可解释性（动力学 + 谱）而非大表刷分。
> - **适用性**：前两者（TokenSignature、4-bit）直接适配你的 Transformer 大模型（文中即 LLaMA/RoBERTa）；PBADet 用 YOLOv7/v5 骨干（非 ResNet-50，但同为卷积 backbone，可直接替换）；EI RNN 谱方法直接服务你的时间序列 RNN；JEPA 给出无需显式去噪的自蒸馏设计原则。所谓“Transformer 条件引导 + ResNet-50 骨干”在你的四个核心需求中并非必需——Universal Guidance 一文的 ResNet-50-FPN 引导可作为可选参考，但与其核心需求相关性弱。
> 
> **注意事项**：JEPA 结论基于深度线性网络与特定初始化（文中有局限声明）；4-bit 优化器的最优量化可能任务相关、且目前为未融合算子时较慢；PBADet 未报告置信区间。这些点不影响上述主要结论。

**community 最终答案**

> All four needs are covered by works in this collection, with concrete experimental results to compare.
> 
> ## (a) Token-probability trends to trigger/skip CoT — **Token Signature / Dynamic CoT** (ICML 2025)
> - Uses the **monotonicity of token-probability distributions** (Spearman correlation over the first ~50 greedy-decoded tokens) as the "Token Signature." Two indicators: Instance SC and Aggregated SC, combined with a **logistic-regression (feedforward classifier) head** into Dynamic CoT, which picks **CoT vs. direct answer per question** (Figure 2 gives the instance-level schematic).
> - **Results:** Instance SC 69.6% and Aggregated SC 89.2% prediction accuracy for CoT gain; Dynamic CoT matches the better of CoT/DA while cutting token consumption **39.1%** (open-source) and **35.8%** (transferred to closed-source models); robust to decoding variations and few-shot CoT (Aggregated SC 78.6–92.9% across 4 models); 50 tokens is the optimal window.
> 
> ## (b) ~4-bit optimizer states — **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Quantizes Adam/AdamW **optimizer states to 4-bit**: first moment with small block size B128 + dynamic exponent; second moment with zero-point-excluding linear quantizer or **rank-1 normalization**, optionally factorized ("4-bit Factor"). Algorithm 1 provides the compress/decompress framework (implementation diagram).
> - **Results (vs. 32-bit AdamW):** RoBERTa-L GLUE 88.9→89.1, Swin-T ImageNet 81.2→80.8, GPT-2M E2E-NLG 67.7→67.8 BLEU, SQuAD 94.6→94.5, WMT14 26.61→26.28 — essentially lossless; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit (e.g., 13B MMLU 46.5→47.4; 33B ARC-c 43.8→45.4). Memory savings up to **57.7%** (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB, trainable on one 80 GB GPU); 4-bit Factor states ~4× smaller than 8-bit AdamW and beats Adafactor/SM3, which degrade (esp. on CLS).
> 
> ## (c) Anchor-free part–body association — **PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> - One-stage anchor-free detector with a **single part-to-body center offset** (2D displacement branch) plus classification/localization branches, three-layer **convolutional feedforward heads**, task-alignment learning; Figure 2 is the pipeline diagram. Generalizes to any part set (hands→body, face→body, multi-part, even quadruped parts). R50-class baselines (Faster/RetinaNet/FCOS-R50) are included in comparisons, though the method itself uses YOLOv5/v7 backbones.
> - **Results (BodyHands):** hand AP **89.1**, conditional accuracy **92.62**, joint AP **85.98** (YOLOv7, 36.9 M) vs. BPJDet(YOLOv5m6) 85.3/86.80/78.13 and BodyHands 84.8/83.44/63.48 — large margins. COCOHumanParts AP.5:.95 42.7–43.0 (leads AP_M/AP_L: 65.8–67.2 vs BPJDet 63.8/61.8); CrowdHuman body/face MR-2 36.5/44.7, AP 91.6/81.6. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each boost association; anchor-free + part-to-body (89.1/92.62/85.98) beats anchor-based + part-to-body (88.4/92.31/85.28) and BPJDet's anchor-based body-to-part (85.3/86.80/78.13); also beats ED-Pose (Swin-L) on hand/foot precision, recall, F1.
> 
> ## (d) Spectral stabilization of EI RNNs + self-distillation ignoring noise — **Dale's-Law RNNs (NeurIPS 2023)** + **JEPA self-distillation (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - **Dale's Law paper:** spectral analysis shows ColEI RNNs fail because of **multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra** (rank-one column-mean structure), not sign constraints. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization **anti-correlates with final test error** (predicts performance pre-training); DANN recurrent nets keep unimodal spectra and learn as well as standard RNNs, robust to E/I ratio (even 1 inhibitory unit); gradient clipping stabilizes ColEI substantially.
> - **JEPA paper:** self-distillation (online encoder predicting a target encoder) has an implicit bias toward **high-influence, low-variance features**, thereby **suppressing noisy features** (unlike MAE, whose ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ); on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA-based).
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Complements, not competitors:** each paper targets a different subsystem of your pipeline, and the results align well — (b) gives the VRAM headroom to fine-tune the large attention Transformers used in (a)/(c); (a) saves tokens at inference on the LLM side; (c) gives high-precision, scalable part–body association with a simple single-offset head; (d) explains *why* EI RNNs destabilize (NSE as a pre-training diagnostic) and why latent self-distillation inherently drops noisy features.
> - **Strength of evidence:** (b) and (c) report full benchmark tables with ablations and lossless/state-of-the-art margins (4-bit ≈ 32-bit across 6 task types; PBADet +3–5 hand AP and +6–9 conditional accuracy vs. BPJDet). (a) has the strongest token-efficiency story (≈36–39% token reduction at ~equal accuracy) but depends on the Spearman-trend assumption. (d) is more analytical/diagnostic than a drop-in method — the RNN results are on small-scale tasks (adding, sMNIST, PTB, object recognition) and the JEPA analysis is on deep *linear* networks with qualitative ImageNet support.
> - **Caveats:** (a) uses first 50 tokens only and needs small labeled samples for the logistic head; (b) notes slower 4-bit runs pre-operator-fusion and that optimal quantization may be task-dependent; (c) shows a slightly higher mMR-2 than BPJDet on the single-part CrowdHuman face task (50.8 vs 50.1); (d) hasn't validated spectral/diagnostic results on EI RNNs processing time-series signals specifically, and JEPA's noise-suppression mechanism is proven only in the linear setting.
> - **Implementation diagrams available:** (a) Figure 2/3 schematics, (b) Algorithm 1 framework + pseudocode, (c) Figure 2 pipeline + architecture/loss details, (d) spectrum-transplant and NSE methodology (figures/equations). CE/MSE-style objectives appear in (c) (classification + box/displacement regression with task alignment) and implicitly in (a) (logistic CE head) and (d) (predictive/classification losses); (b) reports training-loss curves rather than a task loss.

</details>

<a id="case-paperscope-results_comparison-50"></a>

### paperscope:results_comparison:50 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Find research that collectively examines how design choices in modern deep learning improve training efficiency and robustness across tasks: (a) one-stage, anchor-free detectors that associate human parts to the correct person on COCO-style benchmarks; (b) spectral analyses of deep networks with excitatory/inhibitory constraints showing how SGD/Adam or AdamW and loss choices (e.g., CE vs MSE) impact learning; (c) self-supervised learning theory contrasting latent prediction vs reconstruction (e.g., JEPA vs MAE) in deep linear settings; (d) open benchmarking of synthetic tabular and time-series data generators (GANs, VAEs, Diffusion models, Transformers) with utility, privacy, and fairness metrics; and (e) methods that reweight data mixtures via distributionally robust optimization to speed up Transformer pretraining. Please include works discussing optimizers (SGD/Adam), cross-entropy (CE)/MSE objectives, attention-based models, and evaluations on datasets like COCO and MNIST.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：4→3（Δ-1）；rounds：9→5（Δ-4）。**

> {'answer': 'Integrated comparison of experimental results across five works, organized by task and dataset, with explicit metrics from figures/tables.\n\nAnchor-free, one-stage part–body association (PBADet) vs baselines (COCO-style benchmarks)\n- BodyHands (Table 1):\n  - PBADet (YOLOv7, 1024 input): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.\n  - PBADet (YOLOv5l6, 1024): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.\n  - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 1536): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.\n  - Summary: On the identical BodyHands dataset, PBADet exceeds BPJDet in all three metrics; PBADet achieves higher AP and notably higher conditional and joint accuracy despite lower input resolution.\n- COCOHumanParts (Table 2 & Table 3):\n  - All-categories AP (original/subordinate): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3 (similar overall AP).\n  - Size-specific APs (APM/APL): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 66.2/67.2 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 63.8/61.8 — PBADet leads on medium and large objects.\n  - Category APs (person/head/face/r/l-foot): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 62.4/54.6/44.6/39.0/37.7/30.9/31.5 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 61.3/56.6/46.3/40.4/39.6/30.2/30.9 — mixed; PBADet stronger on feet categories.\n  - Association mMR−2 (average; Table 3): PBADet achieves lowest mMR−2 across head, face, hands, and right foot in both YOLOv7 and YOLOv5l6 backbones (e.g., PBADet YOLOv7 head 29.2 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 head 30.8).\n  - Summary: On the identical COCOHumanParts dataset, PBADet matches or exceeds BPJDet on size-based AP (especially medium/large) and improves association robustness (lower mMR−2), with slightly mixed per-part AP.\n- CrowdHuman (Tables 5 & 6):\n  - PBADet (YOLOv7): body MR−2 36.5 (best), body AP 91.6, body-face mMR−2 50.8.\n  - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR−2 40.7, body AP 89.5, body-face mMR−2 50.1.\n  - Summary: PBADet improves body detection (lower MR−2, higher AP) and keeps association competitive; all evaluated on the same CrowdHuman val set.\n- Optimizer/loss: PBADet trained with SGD; task-aligned learning (TOOD) with IoU loss, DFL loss, and classification loss Lcls, plus an association loss Lassoc; anchor-free head improves over anchor-based in ablations (Table 8).\n\nSpectral analyses of EI-constrained deep networks (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNN)\n- Datasets: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition. Identical dataset overlap across papers: MNIST appears only here.\n- Results (Figure 2): Across all four tasks, ColEI networks learn worse (higher error, lower accuracy) and are more variable than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs; gradient clipping benefits ColEI substantially more.\n- Spectral radius ablation (Appendix Figure 9): ColEI performance remains inferior across ρ settings; ColEI does relatively better at larger ρ but still below standard/DANN.\n- Spectrum transplant (Figure 4): Changing singular value spectra impacts performance more than sign constraints — spectrum-induced test error shifts are larger (e.g., RNNs: ~1.5%±0.3%; ColEI: ~2%±1%) than sign-freezing effects (~0.7–1%); sign constraints alone do not explain the performance gap.\n- EI ratio and size (Figures 5–6): Lower fraction of inhibitory units degrades ColEI spectra (multimodal, large singular values), lowers Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE), and harms test error; DANN spectra remain unimodal with high NSE and stable performance even with one inhibitory neuron. NSE anti-correlates with test error across EI ratios and sizes.\n- Optimizers/losses: Projected gradient descent maintains EI signs; gradient clipping is explicitly studied. Specific CE vs MSE choices are not varied in reported experiments.\n\nJEPA vs MAE (deep linear SSL; theory with supporting experiments)\n- Controlled synthetic data (Gaussian, temporal models):\n  - Feature learning order (Figure 1): With monotonically decreasing regression coefficients (ρ) but increasing covariance (λ), MAE learns high-λ features first; JEPA reverses order and learns high-ρ (influential) features first.\n  - Depth dependence (Figures 2 & 4): JEPA’s bias toward high-ρ strengthens with encoder depth; MAE’s critical time depends mainly on λ.\n  - Temporal model (Figure 3): With higher autocorrelation γ and lower noise σ, JEPA prioritizes “slow” (predictive, low-variance) features; MAE is less sensitive to ρ.\n- ImageNet feature similarity (Appendix D, Figure 7): JEPA’s learned features show higher mean CCA similarity between full and “bottom” PCA-subspace images and lower similarity for “top” variance subspace compared to MAE, indicating JEPA emphasizes discriminative, low-variance components.\n- Summary: On identical synthetic setups, JEPA and MAE learn different feature orders; JEPA’s implicit bias yields faster learning of predictive/low-noise features in deep encoders.\n\nOpen benchmarking of synthetic tabular/time-series generators (Synthcity)\n- Static tabular generation across 18 OpenML datasets (Table 4):\n  - Quality score (higher better): TVAE 0.5487 ≈ ARF 0.5475 ≥ CTGAN 0.5475 ≈ TabDDPM 0.5436 ≥ GOGGLE 0.4054.\n  - Detection score (lower better): ARF 0.6721 (best) < TabDDPM 0.7074 < TVAE 0.7389 < CTGAN 0.7758 < GOGGLE 0.9261.\n  - Summary: On identical OpenML datasets, ARF and TVAE deliver the highest fidelity; ARF makes synthetic data hardest to distinguish from real (best detection score).\n- Cross-domain augmentation for minority groups (SIVEP-Gripe; Table 5):\n  - Neural net AUROC: TabDDPM 0.7241 (best) > RadialGAN 0.7137 > CTGAN 0.6477 > TVAE 0.3623 > baseline 0.3244.\n  - XGBoost AUROC: TabDDPM 0.7786 ≈ TVAE 0.7794 > RadialGAN 0.7627 > CTGAN 0.7507 > baseline 0.7327.\n  - Summary: On the identical SIVEP-Gripe task, augmentation consistently improves minority-group AUROC; Diffusion-based TabDDPM (and TVAE with XGBoost) top performance.\n- Use-case coverage: Synthcity supports privacy (e.g., k-anonymity, l-diversity, simulated attacks), fairness (distribution balancing, algorithmic metrics), and time-series/survival generation; comparisons above derive only from reported case studies.\n\nDistributionally robust reweighting for LM pretraining (DoReMi)\n- The Pile (8B main model trained with 280M proxy weights; Figures 2–4, Tables 4–6):\n  - Downstream one-shot accuracy (avg of LAMBADA, NQ, WQ, SQuADv2, TriviaQA; Table 5): Baseline 20.03%; DoReMi (280M→8B) 26.56% (+6.53 points).\n  - Training efficiency: DoReMi reaches baseline accuracy in 75k steps vs 200k steps (2.6× fewer steps).\n  - Per-domain log-perplexity (Table 4): DoReMi reduces log-ppl on all 22 domains; worst-case from 1.71 (baseline) to 1.46; average from 1.64 to 1.40.\n  - Task specifics (Table 5): LAMBADA 29.19 vs 20.10; SQuADv2 51.89 vs 44.43; TriviaQA 34.86 vs 24.55 — consistent gains.\n- GLaM dataset (Figure 3 & Table 2):\n  - Iterated DoReMi converges in three rounds; downstream accuracy matches domain weights tuned using downstream tasks, without using those tasks during optimization.\n- Ablations across scales (Figures 5–6, Table 6):\n  - When proxy and main model sizes match (280M–1B), DoReMi improves downstream accuracy and reduces worst-case/average log-ppl (e.g., at 1B: worst-case 1.92 vs 1.94; average 1.83 vs 1.87; 19/22 domains beating baseline).\n  - Ablations show excess-loss DRO (reference-normalized) is critical; selecting only “hardest” or “easiest” domains fails to reduce perplexity (Table 7).\n- Optimizers: Adafactor for proxy training; standard optimizer used for main LM training.\n\nCross-work comparisons by dataset type and overlaps\n- Identical datasets:\n  - COCO appears only in the PBADet study (COCOHumanParts and COCO images for ED-Pose comparison within the same work); MNIST appears only in the spectral EI networks study. There are no identical datasets shared across the five works.\n- Similar dataset families:\n  - Vision benchmarks: PBADet’s detector AP/mMR−2 improvements on COCO-like data complement JEPA’s representation bias toward low-variance features (higher CCA on bottom PCA space); both point to design choices (anchor-free detection heads, latent prediction) improving robustness or semantic learning, but are evaluated on different datasets/metrics.\n  - Language modeling: DoReMi’s data-mixture reweighting lowers perplexity and accelerates training on The Pile and GLaM; spectral EI analysis shows RNN architectural/spectral choices strongly affect training stability/accuracy on Penn Tree Bank and sequential MNIST — both highlight training efficiency/robustness drivers but on different corpora.\n  - Tabular/time-series: Synthcity’s benchmarks show VAEs, diffusion models, and ARF can be strongest depending on utility metric (quality vs detection; augmentation AUROC) across identical OpenML and SIVEP datasets, covering privacy/fairness evaluations as a framework.\n\nDesign/optimizer/loss choices tied to outcomes (from reported experiments)\n- PBADet: One-stage, anchor-free heads + task-aligned learning (IoU+DFL+classification) and a simple 2D association offset deliver higher AP/association quality across BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman; trained with SGD.\n- EI spectral work: Projected gradient descent with sign constraints (ColEI) degrades spectra (multimodal singular values), harming learning; recurrent DANNs/standard RNNs with unimodal spectra learn well; gradient clipping notably stabilizes ColEI; NSE predicts performance.\n- JEPA vs MAE: In deep linear encoders, JEPA’s stop-grad self-distillation objective prioritizes high-regression-coefficient (predictive, low-noise) features (stronger with depth), while MAE prioritizes high-covariance features; on ImageNet, JEPA aligns representations more with low-variance, perceptual components.\n- Synthcity: Across identical static tabular tasks, ARF/TVAE top fidelity; diffusion (TabDDPM) and RadialGAN improve minority-group AUROC in augmentation; shows generator choice and downstream model (e.g., XGBoost vs NN) change utility outcomes.\n- DoReMi: Group DRO with online domain weight updates (excess loss vs reference) finds domain mixtures that reduce per-domain perplexity and boost downstream accuracy; iterated DoReMi removes need for downstream-tuned weights.\n\nOverall: Across diverse tasks, reported experiments consistently show that careful design choices — anchor-free detection heads with alignment losses, spectral properties (unimodal singular value spectra), latent prediction objectives (JEPA), principled generator selection/metrics (Synthcity), and distributionally robust data reweighting (DoReMi) — improve training efficiency and robustness. These improvements are evidenced on identical datasets within each task (BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman; OpenML; SIVEP-Gripe; The Pile/GLaM; sequential MNIST/Penn Tree Bank), with no cross-paper identical datasets.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, the five research threads map to the following works, whose experimental results can be compared and analyzed:
> 
> **1. PBADet — one-stage anchor-free part-body association (COCO-style)**
> - Design: single part-to-body center offset on YOLOv5/YOLOv7 anchor-free heads with classification/localization/displacement branches, TOOD task-alignment loss, SGD optimizer (100 epochs, AMP).
> - Results: On BodyHands, YOLOv7 variant (36.9M) reaches HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98, beating BPJDet (85.9/86.91/84.39) and far exceeding OpenPose (39.7/74.03/27.81) and BodyHands (84.8/84.12/63.87). On COCOHumanParts, AP.5:.95 ≈ 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6), leading on AP_M/AP_L and achieving lowest mMR−2 for several parts vs. BPJDet (43.6/43.3) and Hier-RCNN (42.0/38.8). Ablations show the association loss is the largest contributor (Cond. Acc 80.78→92.62; JointAP 78.07→85.98), with multi-scale offsets and task alignment adding smaller gains. vs. pose estimator ED-Pose on COCO, it gives much higher precision/recall/F1 for hands/feet.
> 
> **2. Spectral analyses with E/I constraints and optimizer/loss effects**
> - *"Learning better with Dale's Law"*: ColEI (column-constrained E/I) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs on sequential MNIST, adding, PTB, object recognition. Spectral analysis (normalised SVD entropy) shows multimodal dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization, not sign constraints, explain the gap: sign constraints account for only ~0.7–1% error vs. the full ~2.3% difference; gradient clipping mitigates; NSE anti-correlates with final test error, and small networks with balanced E/I outperform larger skewed ones.
> - *"Overlooked Hessian Structure"* (CNNs to LLMs): power-law Hessian spectra exist in well-trained networks (LeNet on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR, ResNet18, GPT-2, TinyLlama) but not random/untrained ones (KS tests). The power-law slope ŝ predicts sharpness and test error (MNIST Pearson 0.853; CIFAR-10 0.72; LLM generalization up to ~0.98), and holds across SGD, Vanilla SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, Yogi, RAdam, Adai, PNM, Lookahead, DiffGrad whenever training succeeds; AdamW is used for all LLM runs. Notably, SGD is worse than Adam for Transformers when Hessian spectra show blockwise heterogeneity, and the spectrum breaks with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large batch (sharp phase transition at 640<B<768). Eigengaps explain the robust, low-dimensional learning subspace.
> 
> **3. JEPA vs MAE in deep linear SSL theory**
> - Analytical solution of deep linear self-distillation shows JEPA is biased toward high-influence features (large regression coefficients), while MAE prioritizes high-covariance (possibly noisy) features; the bias exists only for deep encoders and vanishes for shallow ones. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features, confirming the theory.
> 
> **4. Synthcity — open benchmarking of synthetic tabular/time-series generators**
> - Benchmarks GANs (CTGAN, GOGGLE, TimeGAN…), VAEs (TVAE, TimeVAE…), Diffusion (TabDDPM), normalizing flows, plus Transformer/LSTM/GRU/TCN/InceptionTime architectures, with fidelity, utility, privacy (k-anonymity, l-diversity, DP, threat models, re-identification) and fairness metrics.
> - Static tabular (18 OpenML sets): quality/detection — ARF 0.5475/0.6721, GOGGLE 0.4054/0.9261, TabDDPM 0.5436/0.7074, CTGAN 0.5475/0.7758, TVAE 0.5487/0.7389; tree-based ARF is a strong competitor to deep models. Augmentation for minority-group COVID-19 mortality: TabDDPM best (AUROC 0.7241 NN / 0.7786 XGB), then RadialGAN (0.7137/0.7627), CTGAN (0.6477/0.7507), TVAE (0.3623/0.7794), all above baseline (0.3244/0.7327).
> 
> **5. DoReMi — DRO data-mixture reweighting for Transformer pretraining**
> - Trains a 280M reference + GroupDRO proxy (worst-case excess loss) to set domain weights for an 8B Transformer (30× larger), at ~8% of main-model compute. On The Pile: perplexity improves on every domain (even downweighted ones), +6.5 points average one-shot downstream accuracy, and baseline accuracy reached 2.6× faster. On GLaM it matches downstream-tuned oracle weights; weights stabilize after ~50k steps and iterate converges in 3 rounds.
> 
> **Cross-cutting comparison/analysis**
> - **Architecture/representation design**: PBADet shows a single explicit offset plus task alignment yields SOTA accuracy with fewer parameters (36.9M vs 86.1M) and smaller input (1024 vs 1536) than anchor-based BPJDet; the JEPA analysis similarly shows representation *objective* (latent prediction vs reconstruction) is what drives robustness (noise suppression), mirroring PBADet's finding that the association *loss* (not just detection capacity) is decisive.
> - **Optimizer choice**: the Hessian study shows the power-law spectral structure is optimizer-agnostic once training succeeds, yet optimizer-*interaction* matters — Adam/AdamW is needed for Transformers under blockwise-heterogeneous Hessians, and PBADet's detection training succeeds with plain SGD, whereas DoReMi's LM pretraining uses Adam/Adafactor; Dale's-Law RNNs additionally show spectral initialization, not the optimizer, dominates.
> - **Loss choices (CE vs MSE)**: DoReMi and PBADet rely on cross-entropy-type objectives (next-token/classification), whose landscapes exhibit the clean power-law spectra; reconstruction/MSE-style losses (MAE, square loss) are shown to be less selective about informative features, while the E/I study treats CE classification tasks where spectral pathology still predicts performance — tying objective choice to spectral geometry.
> - **Efficiency vs robustness trade-offs**: DoReMi converts data design into a 2.6× speedup at 8% overhead; Synthcity shows diffusion models (TabDDPM) maximize downstream utility/fairness, though ARF is best on raw fidelity/detection — i.e., no single generator dominates across utility, privacy, and fairness; the Hessian work shows the power-law measure predicts generalization where sharpness fails (LLMs), offering a diagnostic for when training choices degrade robustness.
> 
> All quantitative claims above come directly from the retrieved papers (PBADet, Dale's Law spectral study, Hessian power-law study, JEPA/MAE deep linear analysis, Synthcity, DoReMi).

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, I can identify four of the five requested research areas, with clear experimental results. I could not find a document that specifically studies CE vs MSE loss choices in the requested context.
> 
> ## (a) PBADet — One-stage, anchor-free part-body association (COCO)
> 
> **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) extends one-stage anchor-free detectors (YOLOv5/v7/FCOS/TOOD-style) with a single **part-to-body center offset**, guaranteeing one-to-one part→body correspondence that stays valid even when parts are invisible (unlike BPJDet's per-part body-to-part offsets).
> 
> **Experimental results:**
> - **COCO-HumanParts (vs ED-Pose, Swin-L):** PBADet (YOLOv5l6) is substantially better at associating small parts — e.g., left hand Precision/Recall/F1: **37.63/60.82/46.50 vs ED-Pose 18.36/30.34/22.87**; all parts F1 **48.52 vs 31.51**.
> - **BodyHands ablations (YOLOv7):** full model HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy **92.62**, JointAP **85.98**; removing the association loss drops Cond. Accuracy to 80.78 and JointAP to 78.07; removing multi-scale offsets or task alignment also degrades metrics.
> - **CrowdHuman face-body:** comparable body AP to DETR-based detectors (PED-DETR, Iter-E2EDET) and beats BPJDet, with a better detection/association balance.
> 
> ## (b) Spectral analyses of EI networks (SGD/Adam; MNIST)
> 
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023) studies RNNs with **excitatory (E)/inhibitory (I)** sign constraints (Dale's Law). It finds **spectral properties matter more than sign constraints**: ColEI networks have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (large singular-value mode), whereas standard RNNs and Dale's ANNs (DANNs) match random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur forms.
> 
> **Experimental results (sequential MNIST, adding problem, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition):**
> - ColEI networks learn **worse and with higher variance** across all four tasks; **gradient clipping** helps ColEI substantially more.
> - Sign constraints impair learning only ~1% (±1%) but don't explain the full ~2.3% (±0.6%) ColEI gap; spectrum-transplant experiments show the **singular-value spectrum contributes more than sign constraints and singular vectors** (~1.5% vs ~2% error).
> - Reducing inhibitory neurons (higher E:I ratio) **lowers NSE and impairs learning**; DANNs stay robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron. **Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error** — small networks with balanced E&I outperform larger networks with skewed ratios.
> 
> **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (ICML 2025) is a spectral analysis across optimizers: well-trained CNNs/LLMs (LeNet on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100; GPT-2, TinyLlama) show **power-law Hessian spectra** across **SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, RAdam, Yogi, Adai, PNM, Lookahead, DiffGrad, Vanilla SGD** — the power-law slope correlates with test error (LeNet CIFAR-10 Pearson 0.72–0.853), and power-law goodness predicts LLM generalization (up to 0.98). The structure is lost with random initialization, small width/depth, noisy labels, and large-batch training; it emerges during pretraining but not LoRA-only fine-tuning.
> 
> ## (c) JEPA vs MAE in deep linear SSL theory
> 
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024) exactly solves deep linear training dynamics for **latent prediction (JEPA, self-distillation)** vs **reconstruction (MAE, input-space MSE)**.
> 
> **Experimental results:**
> - JEPA is biased toward **"influential" features** (high regression coefficient ρ), while MAE prioritizes high-variance features even if noisy; JEPA converges to lower-amplitude weights on noisy modes.
> - Critical-time analysis: JEPA prioritizes high-ρ features (depth strengthens noise suppression); MAE's ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ.
> - **ImageNet-1K (ViT, I-JEPA vs MAE):** CCA shows I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (bottom 25% explained variance, which contains perceptual features) than MAE features; the trend reverses for the top 75% subspace — confirming JEPA learns perception-relevant low-variance features faster.
> - Bias takes hold only when the encoder is **deep** and diminishes when shallow.
> 
> ## (d) Synthcity — synthetic data benchmarking (GAN/VAE/Diffusion/Transformer)
> 
> **Synthcity** (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks) is an open-source library benchmarking synthetic tabular/time-series generators across **GANs (CTGAN, GOGGLE, TimeGAN, etc.), VAEs (TVAE, TimeVAE), Normalizing Flows, and Diffusion (TabDDPM)**, with utility, privacy, and fairness metrics, plus Transformer/LSTM/GRU/TCN/InceptionTime backbones.
> 
> **Experimental results (18 OpenML datasets, static tabular):**
> | Model | Quality ↑ | Detection ↓ |
> |---|---|---|
> | ARF (forest-based) | **0.5475** | **0.6721** |
> | GOGGLE | 0.4054 | 0.9261 |
> | TabDDPM | 0.5436 | 0.7074 |
> | CTGAN | 0.5475 | 0.7758 |
> | TVAE | **0.5487** | 0.7389 |
> 
> - **TVAE and ARF have the highest quality; ARF is hardest to detect.** Tree-based/VAE generators are strong competitors to deep generative models on tabular data.
> - Privacy evaluated via k-anonymity, l-diversity, DP, and attack simulations; fairness via Demographic Parity, Conditional Fairness, minority-group augmentation. **TabDDPM was best for COVID-19 mortality prediction after augmentation** (SIVEP-Gripe case study).
> 
> ## (e) DoReMi — DRO-based data-mixture reweighting for pretraining
> 
> **DoReMi** (NeurIPS 2023) reweights pretraining domains using **GroupDRO (distributionally robust optimization)** over worst-case excess loss — a 280M proxy model sets weights for an **8B (30× larger)** model, at ~8% of main-model compute.
> 
> **Experimental results (The Pile, GLaM):**
> - Improves perplexity on **all domains** (even down-weighted ones); **+6.5%** average few-shot downstream accuracy vs The Pile default weights; reaches baseline accuracy **2.6× faster**.
> - On GLaM, **matches domain weights tuned on downstream tasks** despite having no downstream-task knowledge; weights stabilize after ~50k steps; DRO also improves minority-subgroup fairness.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting comparison
> 
> - **Loss/objective choice:** PBADet uses classification + localization + task-aligned association losses (a CE-like classification head plus regression); Synthcity's benchmark and the JEPA/MAE analysis show MSE-style reconstruction vs latent prediction trade-offs (MAE learns high-variance/noisy features, JEPA learns influential features); no document directly compares CE vs MSE classification objectives.
> - **Optimizers:** The Hessian paper shows power-law spectral structure is optimizer-agnostic (SGD, Adam, and 8+ variants all exhibit it), while the Dale's Law paper shows gradient clipping (not optimizer choice per se) is what mitigates poor EI spectra.
> - **Datasets:** COCO (PBADet) and MNIST (Dale's Law RNNs, Hessian paper LeNet) appear as evaluation grounds; ImageNet-1K for JEPA/MAE; OpenML/SIVEP for Synthcity; The Pile/GLaM for DoReMi.
> - **Common theme:** training efficiency and robustness are consistently improved by structural/spectral/objective-aware design choices — better-conditioned spectra (EI networks), robust low-variance feature learning (JEPA), task-aligned association offsets (PBADet), and worst-case data reweighting (DoReMi) — rather than by any single optimizer or architecture.
> 
> **Gap:** No retrieved document explicitly analyzes **SGD/Adam vs AdamW** or **CE vs MSE** loss choices (e.g., for E/I networks), so that specific comparison cannot be established from the context.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the matching papers for each need, with their experimental results and a comparative analysis.
> 
> ## 1. Real-time gesture interface (anchor-free part-body detection)
> **PBADet** (doc `08b70bc3…`) — one-stage anchor-free detector linking hands/face to the right body via a single part-to-body center offset (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones, COCO-WholeBody/HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman).
> - Ablation (BodyHands, YOLOv7): BPJDet anchor-based body-to-part 41.2M params, Hand AP 85.3, Cond. Accuracy 86.80, Joint AP 78.13 → PBADet anchor-free part-to-body 36.9M, **89.1 / 92.62 / 85.98** (part-to-body definition and anchor-free head each add gains).
> - COCO-HumanParts (all categories): AP 42.7–43.0 (AP.5 69.5–70.0).
> - vs ED-Pose on COCO val: left-hand Precision 37.6 vs 18.4, Recall 60.8 vs 30.3, F1 46.5 vs 22.9; all-parts F1 48.5 vs 31.5.
> - Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offset, and task-alignment all boost association; on CrowdHuman face-body the edge over BPJDet is smaller (single-part task).
> 
> ## 2. Faster Transformer LM pretraining via data-mix reweighting (online DRO)
> **DoReMi** (doc `2c47f596…`) — GroupDRO over domains on excess loss vs a reference model, using the online GroupDRO optimizer and averaged domain weights; 280M proxy sets weights for an 8B model (30× larger), no downstream-task knowledge.
> - The Pile: perplexity improves on **every** domain (even downweighted ones); +6.5 points average one-shot downstream accuracy; reaches baseline accuracy **2.6× faster**; DRO costs ~8% of main-model compute; weights stabilize ~50k steps.
> - GLaM: matches downstream-task-tuned oracle weights. A unigram toy shows reweighting (weights [0.39, 0.61, 0.0]) reduces parameter error on all domains by downweighting very noisy/easy data.
> - Note: the DRO optimizer is the online GroupDRO update; AdamW is not the optimizer highlighted in this paper (AdamW appears only in other docs' fine-tuning details), so that specific detail is not established here.
> 
> ## 3. Self-supervised objectives: latent prediction vs pixel reconstruction
> **JEPA/MAE analysis** (doc `40fde037…`) — deep-linear theory of self-distillation (latent prediction, JEPA) vs masked autoencoding (pixel reconstruction, MAE).
> - JEPA is implicitly biased toward high-influence features (large regression coefficients) and is **slower to learn noisy features** than MAE; depth strengthens noise suppression, whereas MAE feature ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features than MAE (CCA). Limits: deep-linear MLPs, special initialization, simultaneous diagonalizability.
> 
> **Related, LDReg** (doc `51526068…`) — addresses the noisy-feature/collapse failure mode: adding local-intrinsic-dimensionality regularization improves SimCLR, BYOL, MAE, MoCo, VICReg, Barlow Twins on ImageNet linear eval, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation; longer pretraining helps more; forcing very low LID causes full collapse.
> - Caveat: no paper in this collection directly benchmarks the MSE-vs-CE objective choice on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100; the JEPA result is theory + ImageNet.
> 
> ## 4. Privacy-preserving synthetic tabular & time-series data
> **Synthcity** (doc `558c32ef…`) — unified benchmark for static tabular, regular/irregular time-series, censored, and composite data.
> - Generators: GANs (CTGAN, DPGAN, PATEGAN, ADSGAN, DECAF, TimeGAN, SurvivalGAN), VAEs (TVAE, RTVAE, TimeVAE, SurvivalVAE), flows (FourierFlow), TabDDPM, ARF, PrivBayes, AIM, GREAT.
> - Evaluation: fidelity (JS/Wasserstein/MMD, detection scores), downstream utility (Linear/MLP/XGBoost, time-series, survival), fairness (Demographic Parity, Fairness-Through-Unawareness, Conditional Fairness, minority-group utility), privacy (DP, k-anonymity/k-map, delta-presence, L-diversity, DOMIAS, identifiability).
> - Case studies: ARF strongest on static-tabular OpenML (18 datasets); **TabDDPM best for COVID-19 mortality prediction** after augmentation (AUROC on minority groups). Covers broader modalities/usecases than YData, Gretel, SDV, DataSynthesizer, SmartNoise, nbsynthetic.
> 
> ## 5. Why E/I-constrained recurrent controllers train poorly
> **Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (doc `e63a94c4…`) — ColEI (column sign-constrained E/I) vs standard RNNs vs DANN RNNs, on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank LM, and naturalistic object recognition.
> - ColEI learns worse with more variance and a **multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum** (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), while standard/DANN RNNs are unimodal (quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur).
> - Sign constraints hurt learning (0.7%±0.3% RNNs, 1%±1% ColEI) but don't explain the full gap (2.3%±0.6%); **spectrum transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors** (1.5%±0.3% vs 2%±1%).
> - Fewer inhibitory units → lower normalised SVD entropy (NSE) and worse learning; DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron (NSE ≈ 0.95). NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final error across sizes/ratios; small high-NSE networks beat larger low-NSE ones; gradient clipping mitigates ColEI instability.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Methodology**: All five works validate with controlled ablations (PBADet's association/task-alignment ablations; DoReMi's proxy-size and weight-stability studies; JEPA's critical-time theory matched to simulations; Synthcity's cross-library metric coverage; Dale's Law's spectrum transplants). The two theory papers (JEPA, Dale's Law) isolate *mechanisms* (implicit bias; initialization spectrum) rather than just reporting accuracy.
> - **Datasets**: Benchmarks span detection (COCO/BodyHands/CrowdHuman), LM pretraining (The Pile/GLaM), SSL (ImageNet-1K), synthetic data (OpenML + COVID-19), and RNN dynamics (MNIST/PTB/NOR) — so results are not directly comparable across the five needs; each is SOTA within its own benchmark.
> - **Key quantitative wins**: PBADet +5–10 points Joint AP over BPJDet and ~2× precision/recall over ED-Pose; DoReMi +6.5 points downstream / 2.6× speedup; JEPA suppresses noisy features by construction; Synthcity's TabDDPM best for mortality utility while ARF best for static fidelity; Dale's Law shows spectra (not sign constraints) dominate ColEI's 2.3% error gap.
> - **Gaps not established in context**: no direct MSE-vs-CE SSL comparison on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100; no explicit AdamW-based online DRO data-mix implementation; Synthcity is a benchmarking framework (reports which generators win per case study) rather than a single generator with end-to-end privacy+fairness+utility numbers on time-series.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers in the collection that map onto your stack, with their key experimental results and a brief analysis.
> 
> ## 1. Real-time gesture interface (hands/face → person)
> **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage, anchor-free part-body association with a single part-to-body center offset (COCO-WholeBody/COCO-HumanParts-style data).
> - BodyHands: HandAP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (YOLOv7); beats OpenPose, BodyHands, BPJDet.
> - COCOHumanParts: AP .5:.95 = 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6), on par with BPJDet but leading AP_M/AP_L and lowest mMR−2 on head/face/hands.
> - vs. ED-Pose (Swin-L pose estimator): far higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51).
> - Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task alignment each improve association accuracy (JointAP 78.07 → 85.98).
> - Analysis: the anchor-free, part-to-body formulation (vs. anchor-based body-to-part like BPJDet) scales to many parts without degrading detection and guarantees one-to-one correspondence, which is why it wins on association metrics.
> 
> ## 2. Faster LM pretraining via data-mix adjustment (online DRO + standard optimizer)
> **DoReMi (NeurIPS 2023)** — trains a 280M reference + GroupDRO proxy model to output domain weights; the online GroupDRO optimizer updates weights each step (proxy trained with Adam/Adafactor; main model trained standardly).
> - The Pile: perplexity reduced on **all 22 domains** even when domains are downweighted; average one-shot downstream accuracy +6.5 points; baseline accuracy reached **2.6× faster** (75k vs 200k steps); DRO compute ≈8% of the 8B main model.
> - GLaM: iterated DoReMi (3 rounds) matches domain weights tuned on downstream tasks (oracle).
> - Scale ablations: gains hold from 70M→8B through 1B→1B; matched-scale DoReMi (X→X) is ~4× faster on average; even a poorly trained 1B proxy yields weights that improve the 1B main model 2× faster.
> - Analysis: downweighting very-low- and very-high-entropy domains (e.g., ArXiv/PubMedCentral down, Pile-CC web up) drives positive transfer; the method needs no downstream-task knowledge.
> 
> ## 3. SSL objective choice (latent prediction vs pixel reconstruction; noisy features)
> **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024, Apple)** — deep linear network analysis of JEPA (latent-space prediction, MSE) vs MAE (input-space reconstruction).
> - JEPA is biased to learn **high-influence features** (large regression coefficient ρ); MAE only prioritizes high-covariance features (λ), including noisy, uninformative ones. Their learning orders invert when ρ and λ disagree.
> - Depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression (JEPA fixed point ∝ ρ^L vs MAE ∝ ρ^{L/(L+1)}); JEPA at depth L matches infinite-depth MAE.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA).
> - Analysis: reconstruction (MAE) targets the bulk of input variance (perception-irrelevant detail), so it learns noisy features; predicting in latent space with MSE (as in JEPA-style self-distillation) avoids this. (Related: LDReg regularizes local dimensionality to prevent dimensional collapse; contrastive CE-based losses like SimCLR get top-1 gains from variance-reduction on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet.)
> 
> ## 4. Privacy-preserving synthetic tabular + time-series data
> **Synthcity (NeurIPS 2023 Datasets & Benchmarks)** — benchmark library covering static tabular, regular/irregular time series, censored survival, and composite data; GAN/VAE/NF/diffusion (TabDDPM)/Bayesian/ARF generators; fidelity, downstream utility, fairness (Demographic Parity, Conditional Fairness), and privacy (DP via DPGAN/PATEGAN; threat-model metrics like k-anonymity, membership inference).
> - Static tabular (18 OpenML datasets): ARF best (quality 0.5475, detection 0.6721), TabDDPM 0.5436/0.7074, CTGAN 0.5475/0.7758, TVAE 0.5487/0.7389; GOGGLE worst quality (0.4054) and most detectable (0.9261).
> - Fairness/augmentation (SIVEP-Gripe COVID-19 mortality, minority ethnic groups): augmentation consistently beats baseline (AUROC 0.3244); TabDDPM best (0.7241 NN / 0.7786 XGBoost), then RadialGAN (0.7137/0.7627), CTGAN (0.6477/0.7507), TVAE (0.3623/0.7794).
> - Analysis: tree-based/forest (ARF) and diffusion (TabDDPM) generators are the strongest for fidelity and for downstream minority-group utility; deep generators (TVAE) can be poor for utility despite good fidelity, justifying Synthcity's use-case-specific evaluation.
> 
> ## 5. E/I-constrained recurrent controllers and spectra
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** — explains why column-wise excitatory/inhibitory (ColEI) RNNs train poorly.
> - ColEI is worse and higher-variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI far more.
> - Spectrum-transplant experiments: singular-value spectra at initialization matter **more than sign constraints** (spectrum accounts for ~1.5–2% test-error gap vs ~0.7–1% for sign constraints); singular vectors are not the cause.
> - ColEI's initial spectrum is multimodal/dispersed (eigenvalues clustered at origin, large unconstrained singular values), vs standard RNN/DANN quarter-circle (Marchenko–Pastur) spectra; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with test error. Smaller networks and fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance; DANNs stay robust even with one inhibitory neuron.
> - Analysis: the failure is not the E/I constraint per se but the resulting ill-behaved spectrum (gradient stretching along large singular-value directions); choosing/initializing for well-clustered spectra (or DANN-style reparameterization) fixes learning.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting comparison
> - All five papers are empirical/ablation-driven and show that **formulation/design choices beat added capacity**: part-to-body vs body-to-part association, DRO-reweighted data mix, latent vs pixel prediction, tree/diffusion vs naive GAN generators, and spectral initialization vs sign constraints.
> - Datasets: gesture/perception work is grounded in COCO-family data; SSL in CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet (and LDReg/BSO extend to CIFAR-100/MNIST-scale settings); RNN analysis uses sequential MNIST/PTB.
> - Caveat: DoReMi's experiments use Adafactor (the framework is optimizer-agnostic, i.e., "Adam, Adafactor, etc."); the collection does not contain a paper that specifically pairs an online DRO data-mix with AdamW — 4-bit-optimizer work (Adam/AdamW) is separate. Similarly, the "MSE vs CE" contrast appears mainly as JEPA (latent MSE) vs MAE (input MSE) vs contrastive (CE) objectives, not as a direct head-to-head on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 in this collection.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:56 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that modify training-time behavior to improve generalization and efficiency across deep networks: (1) adding stochastic perturbations to feature embeddings during instruction fine-tuning of Transformers; (2) studying joint-embedding predictive objectives that learn in latent space and their implicit bias under mean‑squared vs. cross‑entropy losses and angular (cosine) similarity; (3) compressing Adam/AdamW optimizer states to ultra‑low precision (≈4‑bit) for memory‑limited fine‑tuning; (4) analyzing spectral properties and interpretability of recurrent models that obey an excitatory/inhibitory constraint (Dale’s principle); and (5) one‑stage, anchor‑free part‑to‑whole association for human parts on COCO. Prefer works that discuss regularization during fine‑tuning, self‑supervised learning, attention‑based Transformers, and empirical results on benchmarks like COCO/MNIST/CIFAR‑100.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
