**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Summary of experimental results across five methods that modify training-time behavior:
> 
> 1) Adding stochastic perturbations to embeddings during instruction fine-tuning (NEFTune)
> - Setup and datasets: Instruction fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 (7B/13B/70B), LLaMA-1 (7B), OPT-6.7B on Alpaca, Evol-Instruct (70k), ShareGPT, OpenPlatypus. Main metric: AlpacaEval Win Rate (vs Text-Davinci-003) with GPT‑4 or ChatGPT evaluators.
> - Identical datasets (AlpacaEval, GPT-4 evaluator, LLaMA-2-7B):
>   • Alpaca: 29.91 ± 0.40 → 65.70 ± 0.52 with NEFTune (+35.79 points)
>   • Evol-Instruct: 70.19 ± 0.08 → 80.36 ± 0.47 (+10.17)
>   • ShareGPT: 70.57 ± 1.38 → 76.22 ± 0.67 (+5.65)
>   • OpenPlatypus: 60.95 ± 1.52 → 69.96 ± 0.47 (+9.01)
> - Cross-model consistency (ChatGPT evaluator, AlpacaEval): Gains appear for OPT‑6.7B, LLaMA‑1‑7B, and LLaMA‑2‑7B across the same four instruction datasets (Figure 2), confirming robustness across pretraining corpora/architectures.
> - Stronger/base chat models: Further fine-tuning LLaMA‑2‑Chat (7B) on Evol‑Instruct improves AlpacaEval from 74.44 → 81.74 with NEFTune (+7.30). Larger base models also improve: LLaMA‑2‑13B 72.61 → 82.04; LLaMA‑2‑70B 75.03 → 88.81 (Table 2).
> - Memory‑limited fine-tuning (QLoRA): Even with 4‑bit adapters, NEFTune increases AlpacaEval (ChatGPT) win rates across sizes/datasets (Table 3), though gains are smaller than full fine‑tuning.
> - Effect on factual/MC benchmarks (OpenLLM Leaderboard): ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA remain essentially unchanged with/without NEFTune across Alpaca, Evol‑Instruct, OpenPlatypus, and LLaMA‑1 Evol‑Instruct (Figure 3), indicating conversational gains do not trade off against these capabilities on the tested settings.
> 
> 2) Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA): implicit bias in latent prediction
> - Core finding (deep linear analyses with controlled simulations): JEPA exhibits greedy learning dynamics that prioritize “influential” features with larger regression coefficients (ρ) when encoders are deep; MAE prioritizes features with larger covariance (λ). This difference appears in explicit ODE solutions, critical-time analyses, and simulations (Figures 2–4; Theorems 3.2–3.5, Corollary 3.6).
> - Similar dataset type: temporal linear generative model (predict next frame) shows λa=γa∥v_a∥² and ρa=γa∥v_a∥²/(σ_a²+∥v_a∥²) (Eq. 16); JEPA down‑weights noisy features (smaller ρ) relative to MAE.
> - ImageNet check (Appendix D): With I‑JEPA vs MAE, JEPA’s learned features from full vs bottom PCA subspaces show higher similarity (full↔bottom CCA higher for JEPA; full↔top lower), suggesting JEPA learns “bottom variance” (potentially more semantic) directions faster than MAE. (Qualitative/relative, no leaderboard figures.)
> 
> 3) Compressing optimizer states to 4‑bit (4‑bit AdamW and 4‑bit Factor)
> - Identical datasets across optimizers (Table 2):
>   • NLU (RoBERTa‑L on GLUE mean): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9 vs 8‑bit AdamW 89.1 vs 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 vs 4‑bit Factor 88.9 (matching full‑precision).
>   • QA (RoBERTa‑L on SQuAD/SQuAD 2.0; Table 9): very close to 32‑bit; e.g., F1 on SQuAD 94.6 (32‑bit) vs 94.5 (4‑bit AdamW), with SM3 notably lower.
>   • CLS (Swin‑T ImageNet‑1k top‑1): 81.2 (32‑bit) vs 81.0 (8‑bit) vs 80.8 (4‑bit AdamW) vs 80.9 (4‑bit Factor).
>   • NLG (GPT‑2‑M on E2E‑NLG BLEU): 67.7 (32‑bit) vs 67.5 (8‑bit) vs 67.8 (4‑bit AdamW) vs 67.6 (4‑bit Factor).
>   • MT (Transformer‑Base WMT14 en‑de SacreBLEU): 26.61 (32‑bit) vs 26.66 (8‑bit) vs 26.28 (4‑bit AdamW) vs 26.45 (4‑bit Factor). Differences are small.
> - LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3): On MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA, 4‑bit AdamW closely matches 32‑bit AdamW at 7B/13B/33B (minor per‑task deltas, often <1 point; e.g., 7B MMLU 38.7 vs 38.9; 13B HellaSwag 78.8 vs 79.0).
> - Memory/time on identical tasks (Table 4):
>   • LLaMA‑7B instruction tuning (FSDP, 2×A100‑80GB): total memory drops 75.40 GB → 31.87 GB (−57.7%); training time modestly improves (3.35 h → 3.07 h).
>   • RoBERTa‑L GLUE: 5.31 GB → 3.00 GB (−43.5%); fused 4‑bit is as fast/faster than 32‑bit.
>   • GPT‑2‑M E2E‑NLG: 6.89 GB → 4.62 GB (−34.4%); fused time matches or improves vs 32‑bit.
> - Quantization insights tied to efficiency: A zero‑point issue in the second moment is critical; excluding zero and using Rank‑1 normalization + linear mapping stabilized 4‑bit convergence (Table 1 ablations). Factorizing the second moment (“4‑bit Factor”) further reduces memory while matching accuracy on the same datasets.
> 
> 4) Spectral properties in EI RNNs under Dale’s law (ColEI) vs DANN vs standard RNNs
> - Identical tasks across methods (Figure 2A–D):
>   • Adding problem: standard RNNs and DANNs learn well; ColEI learns worse.
>   • Sequential MNIST: RNN and DANN achieve lower classification error; ColEI has higher error and higher variance across seeds; gradient clipping helps ColEI more.
>   • Penn Treebank language modeling and a naturalistic object recognition task: same trend—ColEI underperforms RNN/DANN.
> - Spectrum transplant (Figure 4): Swapping singular value spectra between networks shows spectra affect learning more than sign constraints; the singular value distribution (unimodal/clustered vs multimodal/with large modes) predicts performance gaps. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) correlates with test error across EI ratios and sizes (Figures 5–7).
> - Similar dataset types: time‑series/sequential tasks (adding problem, seq‑MNIST) and language modeling show DANNs match RNNs while respecting Dale’s principle; ColEI performance improves with larger networks/more balanced E/I but still trails when spectra are dispersed/multimodal.
> 
> 5) One‑stage, anchor‑free part‑to‑whole association (PBADet) on COCO/BodyHands/CrowdHuman
> - Identical datasets and head‑to‑head comparisons:
>   • BodyHands (Table 1):
>     – BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.
>     – PBADet (YOLOv7): 89.1 / 92.62 / 85.98; PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73.
>     → PBADet improves all three metrics vs BPJDet with either backbone.
>   • COCOHumanParts (Table 2; AP, per‑category AP):
>     – Overall AP.5:.95 (orig/sub): BPJDet v5l6 43.6/43.3 vs PBADet v5l6 43.0/41.8 (very close).
>     – Medium/large objects: PBADet v5l6 APM 66.2 (vs 63.8) and APL 67.2 (vs 61.8) outperform BPJDet.
>     – Per‑category AP: PBADet v5l6 is higher on person (62.4 vs 61.3) and feet (e.g., r‑foot 30.9 vs 30.2; l‑foot 31.5 vs 30.9); BPJDet is higher on head/face/hands by small margins.
>   • COCOHumanParts association accuracy (Table 3; average mMR−2, lower is better):
>     – PBADet v5l6 achieves lower mMR−2 on head (27.9 vs 30.8), face (30.5 vs 31.8), left hand (36.2 vs 41.6), right hand (40.8 vs 42.2), left foot (47.9 vs 50.4); right foot is slightly worse (50.4 vs 49.1).
>   • CrowdHuman (Table 5):
>     – Body MR−2: PBADet YOLOv7 36.5 vs BPJDet v5l6 40.7 (better); Face MR−2: 44.7 vs 46.3 (better); Body AP: 91.6 vs 89.5 (better). Body‑face mMR−2 is comparable (50.8 vs 50.1).
> - Similar dataset types: multi‑part human detection and association across sparse/crowded scenes—PBADet’s single part‑to‑body center offset scales to many parts without representation bloat and improves medium/large object AP and association robustness.
> 
> Cross‑paper comparisons on identical or related settings
> - Instruction fine‑tuning quality vs efficiency:
>   • NEFTune produces large AlpacaEval gains on the same instruction datasets and models (e.g., LLaMA‑2‑7B Alpaca 29.91 → 65.70), while OpenLLM Leaderboard scores remain essentially unchanged.
>   • 4‑bit optimizers enable comparable accuracy to full precision on identical NLU/QA/CLS/MT/NLG tasks and memory‑constrained LLaMA instruction tuning, with substantial memory savings (30–58% of total training memory depending on task) and modest speedups.
> - Sequential/time‑series tasks:
>   • Dale‑law‑constrained ColEI RNNs underperform RNNs/DANNs on identical adding/sequential MNIST/PTB tasks; DANNs match RNN accuracy while obeying Dale’s principle.
> - COCO‑family tasks:
>   • On COCOHumanParts and CrowdHuman, PBADet improves medium/large AP and several association metrics relative to BPJDet and maintains or improves detection in crowded scenes (body MR−2 and AP).
> 
> Takeaways confined to reported results
> - NEFTune acts as an effective regularizer during Transformer instruction fine‑tuning, improving conversational quality substantially on the same evaluation (AlpacaEval) and models, with minimal change on ARC/HellaSwag/MMLU/TruthfulQA.
> - JEPA vs MAE: in controlled settings, JEPA’s implicit bias prioritizes predictive/low‑noise directions (large ρ) and (Appendix D) picks up “bottom variance” features faster than reconstruction‑based MAE.
> - 4‑bit AdamW/Factor: on the same vision and language benchmarks, accuracy matches 32‑bit/8‑bit while reducing training memory by roughly 35–58% depending on task/settings; memory/comms reductions can also reduce wall‑time (e.g., with FSDP).
> - PBADet: on the same datasets and backbones, one‑stage anchor‑free part‑to‑body offsets yield state‑of‑the‑art or competitive detection/association—especially higher APM/APL on COCOHumanParts and better MR−2/AP on CrowdHuman—while reducing representation size vs body‑to‑part schemes.
> - Dale’s law RNNs: spectral properties at initialization (unimodal/clustered singular value spectra) are more predictive of performance than sign constraints per se; DANNs’ spectra resemble standard RNNs and achieve comparable accuracy on the same tasks, while ColEI’s multimodal/large‑mode spectra correlate with worse test error.
> 
> All statements, metrics, and comparisons above are taken directly from the figures/tables and analyses in the provided papers (NEFTune ICLR 2024; JEPA implicit bias NeurIPS 2024; 4‑bit optimizers NeurIPS 2023; Dale’s law spectral perspective NeurIPS 2023; PBADet ICLR 2024).

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers matching your criteria, with their key experimental results:
> 
> **1. NEFTune (ICLR 2024)** — Adds scaled uniform noise (α/√(Ld)) to embeddings during instruction fine-tuning. Results: LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win rate rises 29.8%→64.7%; Evol-Instruct +10%, ShareGPT +8%, OpenPlatypus +8%; human annotators prefer NEFTune 74.6% of the time. Gains come from reduced overfitting (longer, more detailed outputs); OpenLLM benchmarks are unchanged. α=10 and longer sequences help; dropout/weight decay do not reproduce the gains.
> 
> **2. JEPA implicit bias (NeurIPS 2024, "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features")** — Analyzes joint-embedding predictive objectives in deep linear networks. JEPA (MSE prediction in latent space) biases toward high-regression-coefficient ("influential") features and suppresses noise, unlike MAE (reconstruction in input space); this bias only emerges with deep encoders. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA aligns faster than MAE with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features (CCA measurements). The cosine-similarity aspect is covered by "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning": full-batch InfoNCE optima align positives and place negatives at −1/(n−1); smaller mini-batches raise negative-pair-similarity variance, degrading representations. Its auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves SimCLR/DCL/DHEL top-1 on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and full ImageNet, improves temperature robustness, and helps small-batch training. Note: the context does not contain a direct MSE-vs-cross-entropy latent-objective comparison; cross-entropy appears only as a reference (neural collapse).
> 
> **3. 4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)** — Compresses Adam/AdamW states to 4-bit: smaller block (B128) for the first moment; zero-point-excluding linear mapping (DE-0/Linear) and rank-1 normalization for the second moment; optional factorized second moment. Results match or slightly exceed 32-bit AdamW: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, GPT-2M E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning is comparable. Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4GB→31.9GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models; outperforms 8-bit Adam and sublinear-memory optimizers (Adafactor, SM3).
> 
> **4. Dale's Law RNNs (NeurIPS 2023)** — Spectral analysis of excitatory/inhibitory recurrent networks. ColEI (simple sign-partitioned) RNNs have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one nilpotent column means), whereas standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs have unimodal spectra and learn as well as unconstrained RNNs. Spectral properties matter more than sign constraints (spectrum transplants; sign constraints account for only part of the gap). On sequential MNIST, adding, Penn Tree Bank and object recognition, ColEI learns worse with higher variance; smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error; gradient clipping mitigates the deficit.
> 
> **5. PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — One-stage, anchor-free part-to-body association using a single part-to-body center offset (scales to any number of parts, one-to-one correspondence). On BodyHands it outperforms BPJDet: HandAP 89.1 vs 85.3, Conditional Accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, JointAP 85.98 vs 78.13 (also better than anchor-based part-to-body). On COCOHumanParts: AP 42.7/43.0 (YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6), beating HierR-CNN and BPJDet; leads body MR-2 on CrowdHuman face-body association and substantially beats ED-Pose in precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet. Ablations confirm the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment learning all contribute.
> 
> **Comparison across methods:**
> - **Common theme:** all five alter training-time behavior for generalization or efficiency — NEFTune via stochastic perturbation (regularization during fine-tuning), JEPA/contrastive via self-supervised latent objectives (implicit-bias/regularization analysis), 4-bit optimizers via state compression (efficiency), Dale's work via architectural constraint + spectral initialization (interpretability), PBADet via one-stage efficient detection design (efficiency).
> - **Where they are strongest:** NEFTune's gains are large on conversational/instruction quality (+35 pts AlpacaEval) but absent on standard benchmarks; JEPA's advantage is theoretical (deep-linear dynamics) with qualitative ImageNet CCA support, while the contrastive loss paper gives concrete CIFAR/ImageNet accuracy gains, largest at small batch sizes; 4-bit optimizers are "lossless" in accuracy (match 32-bit) with the payoff purely in memory (up to ~57.7%); Dale's work identifies spectrum (NSE) as a pre-training predictor rather than an accuracy improvement; PBADet gives both accuracy gains (+3-7 pts over BPJDet) and a simpler, more compact representation (length 10 vs 15).
> - **Benchmark coverage matching your preference:** CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet (contrastive/JEPA), COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman (PBADet), ImageNet/GLUE/Alpaca (4-bit optimizers), AlpacaEval/OpenLLM (NEFTune), sequential MNIST/Penn Tree Bank (Dale's RNNs).
> 
> **Caveats from the context:** NEFTune relies on GPT-4 judging and lacks a conclusive mechanism; the JEPA analysis is limited to deep linear networks (generalization to nonlinear models is not rigorous); 4-bit optimizer quantization settings may be task-dependent and only language/vision were tested; Dale's study notes NSE is a diagnostic, not a training method; PBADet's advantage on single-part CrowdHuman tasks is less pronounced than on multi-part tasks.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the five matched papers and a comparison of their experimental results:
> 
> ## The papers
> 
> 1. **NEFTune: Noisy Embeddings Improve Instruction Finetuning** (ICLR 2024, doc `fad0fb20…`) — adds uniform noise scaled by α/√(Ld) to token embeddings during the forward pass of instruction fine-tuning of Transformers.
> 2. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`) — joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA) that predict in latent space vs. MAE reconstruction. It analyzes MSE-type latent objectives on deep linear networks; the cosine/cross-entropy side of this question is covered by **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** (doc `160e1407…`), which analyzes InfoNCE (cross-entropy-style loss over cosine similarities).
> 3. **4-bit Optimizers: Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`) — compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to ≈4-bit (smaller blocks, DE-0 linear + rank-1 normalization, optional factorization).
> 4. **Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`) — spectral analysis of E/I (ColEI vs. DANN) RNNs obeying Dale's principle.
> 5. **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`) — single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free YOLO backbones for human-part association on COCO.
> 
> ## Experimental results
> 
> - **NEFTune (generalization/regularization):** LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win rate jumps 29.8% → 64.7% (+~35pp); Evol-Instruct +10%, ShareGPT +8%, OpenPlatypus +8%; holds across OPT, LLaMA-1/2 (7B/13B), RLHF LLaMA-2-Chat, and QLoRA; humans preferred NEFTune in 74.6% of cases (modified GPT-4 pairwise eval: 92.8% wins). OpenLLM leaderboard scores are unchanged, showing gains are conversational. Ablations: α=10 optimal, uniform noise and longer sequences help; dropout/weight decay do not reproduce the gains. Mechanism: reduces overfitting, elicits longer/more detailed outputs.
> - **JEPA (self-supervised, latent-space prediction):** Theory on deep linear networks shows JEPA is biased toward "influential" (high regression coefficient ρ) features while MAE only prioritizes highly covarying (high λ) features; this bias requires a deep encoder and strengthens with depth — a 1-layer JEPA equals an infinite-depth MAE. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA aligns faster to the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA-based), i.e., it steers away from the top-variance subspace toward semantic features. (The contrastive-similarities paper complements this: optimal InfoNCE encoders give positive-pair cosine similarity 1 and negative-pair −1/(n−1); smaller mini-batches increase negative-pair variance, and an auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 top-1 accuracy and temperature robustness.)
> - **4-bit Adam/AdamW (efficiency):** Matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7) and is comparable on pretraining (ImageNet Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B MMLU and commonsense scores are comparable or better (e.g., LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5), with closely aligned loss curves. Saves up to 57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU), 2× less than 8-bit states; 4-bitFactor saves ~4×. Slight speed penalty on small models without fused kernels.
> - **Dale's-law RNNs (spectral/interpretability):** ColEI learns worse and with higher variance than DANN and standard RNNs on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Spectral transplants show the initial singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints: ColEI's rank-one column-mean (nilpotent) structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values vs. unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra for RNNs/DANNs. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance pre-training; smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra/learning, while DANN is robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> - **PBADet (COCO part association):** On BodyHands it beats BPJDet (Hand AP 89.1 vs 85.3, conditional accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, joint AP 85.98 vs 78.13); on COCOHumanParts all-categories AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6); leading body MR-2 on CrowdHuman. Ablations confirm the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, task-alignment learning, and the anchor-free + part-to-body design (vs. anchor-based body-to-part) each contribute; it also generalizes to quadruped datasets (AnimalPose, AP-10K) and beats ED-Pose in part-body precision/recall/F1.
> 
> ## Comparison across methods
> 
> - **Common theme:** all five modify training-time behavior (noise injection, loss/objective design, optimizer-state compression, weight-constraint/initialization design, and detection head/loss design) to improve generalization or efficiency, generally without added inference cost.
> - **Bottlenecks addressed differ:** NEFTune → overfitting/instruction quality; JEPA → feature-selection bias in self-supervised latent prediction; 4-bit optimizers → memory/communication in fine-tuning large LMs; Dale's RNNs → why biological E/I constraints hurt learning (spectrum vs. sign); PBADet → detection-representation efficiency for multi-part association.
> - **Benchmarks overlap only partially:** NEFTune uses AlpacaEval/OpenLLM; JEPA uses ImageNet (theory on linear nets) and contrastive-similarity work uses CIFAR-10/100; 4-bit optimizers use GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/WMT/Alpaca/MMLU; Dale's RNNs use sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition; PBADet uses COCOHumanParts/BodyHands/CrowdHuman. Notably, MNIST appears in the Dale's-law work and CIFAR-10/100 in the contrastive (cosine/InfoNCE) work; COCO appears in PBADet.
> - **Strength of evidence:** NEFTune and 4-bit optimizers report the largest empirical gains on LLM benchmarks; the JEPA and Dale's-law papers are primarily theoretical/analytical with supporting experiments (ImageNet CCA, MNIST/PTB); PBADet is benchmark-driven (COCO/BodyHands) with careful ablations.
> 
> **Caveat:** no single paper in the collection studies JEPA latent-space implicit bias under MSE vs. cross-entropy vs. cosine objectives simultaneously — the JEPA paper analyzes an L2 (MSE) latent objective, while cosine-similarity/cross-entropy (InfoNCE) behavior is analyzed in the separate contrastive-learning-similarities paper; the exact cross-entropy/cosine JEPA comparison cannot be established from this context.

### paperscope:results_comparison:62 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively examine how structural inductive biases and resource constraints shape learning across vision, sequence models, self-supervised pretraining, and decision-making: (a) one-stage, no-anchor human part–person association evaluated on large human/body benchmarks (e.g., common object corpora); (b) recurrent networks with strict E/I separation analyzed via their spectrum to stabilize SGD-style training on classic sequences (e.g., digit streams) and natural data; (c) joint-embedding self-supervised methods that prefer predictive latent targets over pixel reconstruction, comparing regression-like losses to classification-style objectives; (d) memory-lean first/second-moment optimizers (e.g., quantized Adam/AdamW) that support Transformers and parameter-efficient end-to-end tuning (e.g., LoRA) on NLU/vision/MT and instruction-following tasks; and (e) combinatorial RL for slate selection using discrete-choice (MNL-like) preference feedback with theoretical regret guarantees. Prefer studies reporting results on COCO-style human datasets, MNIST/CIFAR-100-type benchmarks, and transformer-based encoders.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a cross-paper, results-only comparison and summary, extracted strictly from the figures and tables in the five papers you provided. I first note where identical datasets exist (and where they do not), then compare methods on identical datasets (within each paper), on similar dataset types, and finally list key, dataset-specific results.
> 
> Key observation about identical datasets across the five papers
> - There are no identical datasets jointly used across all five papers. Each paper evaluates on its own suite of benchmarks:
>   • PBADet: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts (COCO-based), CrowdHuman.
>   • Dale’s Law (EI RNNs): Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic Object Recognition (synthetic or curated tasks, not shared with others).
>   • JEPA (deep linear): synthetic Gaussian/temporal linear models; a small empirical test on ImageNet (CCA trends), not shared with others.
>   • 4-bit Optimizers: GLUE (RoBERTa-L), ImageNet-1k (Swin-T), E2E-NLG (GPT-2 Medium), SQuAD/SQuAD 2.0, WMT14 en-de, LLaMA instruction-tuning + evaluation (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA).
>   • Combinatorial RL with preferences: a synthetic shopping/budget environment and MovieLens (not used elsewhere).
> 
> A) Identical-dataset comparisons (within-paper) and specific dataset results
> 1) One-stage, no-anchor part–person association (PBADet) on human/body datasets
> - BodyHands (Table 1):
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6):
>     - Hand AP: 89.1 vs 85.9
>     - Conditional Accuracy: 92.62 vs 86.91
>     - Joint AP: 85.98 vs 84.39
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6) also exceeds BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>   • Conclusion on this dataset: PBADet outperforms prior SOTA (BPJDet) across the reported metrics (hand AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP) with the same or smaller model sizes.
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2 and Table 3):
>   • All-categories detection AP (AP.5:.95, original/subordinate):
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 43.0/41.8
>     - PBADet (YOLOv7): 42.7/41.5
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6/43.3 (slightly higher than PBADet on these two summary AP metrics)
>   • Per-category AP (Table 2, person/head/face/hands/feet): PBADet variants are competitive; PBADet (YOLOv5l6) often close to BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) with small gaps per class (e.g., r-hand 39.0 vs 40.4; l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9, etc.).
>   • Association miss rate (average mMR−2, lower is better; Table 3):
>     - Compared to BPJDet (YOLOv5l6):
>       • PBADet (YOLOv7) is lower (better) on head (29.2 vs 30.8), face (31.3 vs 31.8), and left hand (41.1 vs 41.6);
>       • PBADet (YOLOv7) is higher (worse) on right hand (42.7 vs 42.2), right foot (52.6 vs 49.1), left foot (52.5 vs 50.4).
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6) is also mixed vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) per category. Thus, category-wise association tightness varies by part, with PBADet best on some (head/face/left-hand) and BPJDet best on others (e.g., feet).
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Tables 5 and 6):
>   • Face–body association task (Table 5): PBADet (YOLOv7) body MR−2 36.5 (best in table), face MR−2 44.7 (better than BPJDet’s 46.3), body AP 91.6 (tied or higher than listed YOLO-based methods), but mMR−2 for body-face pairs is slightly worse than BPJDet (50.8/50.9 vs 50.1 for YOLOv5l6).
>   • Joint crowded person detection (Table 6): PBADet (YOLOv7) has the best body MR−2 at 36.5 and high body AP 91.6, beating listed DETR and YOLO-based alternatives on MR−2 while keeping AP competitive.
> 
> Takeaway on identical human datasets: PBADet delivers clear gains on BodyHands; on COCOHumanParts, detection AP is close to BPJDet with mixed per-part association mMR; in CrowdHuman, PBADet gets best body MR−2 and body AP, with near-parity association mMR versus BPJDet.
> 
> 2) Memory-lean 4-bit optimizers enabling Transformers, end-to-end tuning (and LoRA) (Tables 2–6)
> - NLU (GLUE, RoBERTa-L; Table 2): 4-bit AdamW = 89.1 mean (comparable to 32-bit AdamW 88.9 and 8-bit AdamW 89.1). Other memory-efficient baselines: 32-bit Adafactor 89.1–89.3 (β1 vs β1=0 variants), SM3 87.5.
> - Image classification (ImageNet-1k, Swin-T; Table 2): 4-bit AdamW = 80.8 vs 32-bit AdamW 81.2 (−0.4pt); 8-bit AdamW 81.0; Adafactor 80.0–79.5; SM3 79.0.
> - NLG (E2E-NLG, GPT-2 Medium; Table 2): 4-bit AdamW BLEU 67.8 vs 32-bit AdamW 67.7 (also higher NIST and ROUGE-L in Table 8). 4-bit Factor BLEU 67.6.
> - QA (SQuAD, SQuAD 2.0; Table 2 and Table 9 F1/EM): 4-bit AdamW QA-F1 94.5 (SQuAD F1 = 94.5; SQuAD2.0 F1 = 88.4, EM = 85.4) comparable to 32-bit AdamW (94.6 F1; SQuAD2.0 F1 = 88.8, EM = 85.8). 8-bit AdamW also comparable.
> - Machine Translation (WMT14 en–de, Transformer-Base; Table 2): 4-bit AdamW 26.28 SacreBleu vs 32-bit AdamW 26.61; 8-bit AdamW 26.66; Factor 26.45.
> - LLaMA instruction tuning (Alpaca; Table 3): 4-bit AdamW vs 32-bit AdamW across model sizes:
>   • LLaMA-7B: 4-bit vs 32-bit — MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; HellaSwag 74.7 vs 74.6; ARC-e 61.2 vs 61.5; ARC-c 44.4 vs 45.1; OBQA 43.0 vs 43.4 (mostly parity within ~0.3–0.7pp).
>   • LLaMA-13B: 4-bit vs 32-bit — MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8; ARC-e 64.1 vs 63.6; ARC-c 48.0 vs 48.3; OBQA 45.2 vs 45.2 (near parity or slight gains).
>   • LLaMA-33B: 4-bit vs 32-bit — MMLU 54.9 vs 56.4; HellaSwag both 79.2; ARC-e 61.6 vs 62.6; ARC-c 46.6 vs 47.1; OBQA 45.4 vs 43.8 (mostly parity; small trade-offs by task).
> - Memory/time (Table 4):
>   • LLaMA‑7B (2×A100 80GB, FSDP): 4-bit AdamW time 3.07h vs 32-bit 3.35h (faster); memory 31.87GB vs 75.40GB (−43.54GB, 57.7% reduction). Fused 4-bit: 3.11h, same memory.
>   • RoBERTa‑L (1×4090): fused 4-bit AdamW 3.17min vs 32-bit 3.93min; memory 3.00GB vs 5.31GB. 4-bit Factor: 2.83GB memory.
>   • GPT‑2 Medium (4×4090): fused 4-bit AdamW 2.11h vs 32-bit 2.13h; memory 4.62GB vs 6.89GB; 4-bit Factor 4.44GB.
> - Largest trainable model under a given GPU memory (Table 5): With 80GB, 4-bit AdamW trains OPT‑6.7B (vs 32-bit capped at OPT‑1.3B). Also enables single‑GPU LLaMA‑7B training on 80GB.
> Conclusion: 4-bit AdamW (and 4-bit Factor) retains accuracy across GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, WMT14 en–de, and LLaMA instruction tuning (generally within ±0.5pp of full precision) while delivering 34–58% total memory reduction and, with fusion, neutral or better training time.
> 
> 3) Combinatorial RL with MNL-like preference feedback (ICML 2025)
> - Synthetic online shopping/budget environment (Fig. 1): MNL‑VQL achieves consistently higher episodic returns than Myopic (OFU‑MNL+) and LSVI‑UCB across N=10, 20, 40 (|A|=637, 21,699, 760,098). Curves show MNL‑VQL converging faster to higher returns in all three settings.
> - MovieLens (Fig. 2): For N=50, 100, 200 (|A|=20,875; 166,750; 1,333,500), MNL‑VQL also attains higher episodic returns than both baselines across episodes. Baseline LSVI‑UCB was too slow to run for larger N; plotted dotted lines refer to extrapolated behavior.
> - Runtime (Table G.1): Average per‑episode runtime under M=6:
>   • N=10: Myopic 0.089s; LSVI‑UCB 0.136s; MNL‑VQL 0.463s.
>   • N=20: Myopic 0.097s; LSVI‑UCB 4.861s; MNL‑VQL 0.526s.
>   • N=40: Myopic 0.113s; LSVI‑UCB 453.641s; MNL‑VQL 0.620s.
> Conclusion: MNL‑VQL dominates in returns on both synthetic and MovieLens experiments, and scales far better than a holistic LSVI‑UCB (orders of magnitude faster as N grows), though per‑episode runtime is higher than Myopic.
> 
> B) Similar-dataset or task-type comparisons across papers (no shared datasets)
> - Vision/human datasets vs general vision classification:
>   • PBADet is evaluated on person-part detection/association datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman). It achieves strong detection and association metrics compared to BPJDet/HierR‑CNN on the same datasets (see A above).
>   • The 4-bit Optimizer results on ImageNet-1k (Swin‑T) show nearly maintained top‑1 accuracy (80.8 vs 81.2 for 32‑bit) while delivering major memory savings. While tasks differ (detection vs classification), both PBADet and the 4‑bit optimizers demonstrate that their structural/resource-focused changes (part‑to‑body offset and 4‑bit state compression) do not materially compromise vision performance on their respective benchmarks.
> 
> - Sequence modeling and stability (EI RNNs) vs JEPA learning dynamics:
>   • Dale’s law paper (Figures 2–6 in the paper) shows standard RNNs and DANNs outperform ColEI RNNs across Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a Natural Object Recognition task (each plotted; no single numeric summary table). Spectrum‑transplant experiments (Fig. 4) demonstrate that assigning ColEI’s spectrum to RNNs degrades performance more than freezing sign constraints, i.e., spectrum matters most.
>   • JEPA linear analysis (Figures 1–4) shows, via training dynamics plots, that JEPA prefers high‑influence (high ρ) features; when λ and ρ trend oppositely (distribution 2, Fig. 1d–f), JEPA inverts the learning order relative to MAE. Deeper encoders amplify JEPA’s preference for ρ (Fig. 4). While not the same datasets, both studies analyze structure‑induced biases (spectral vs objective‑induced) and connect those to training outcomes.
> 
> C) Per‑dataset highlights (selected specific results)
> - BodyHands: PBADet (YOLOv7) 89.1 hand AP, 92.62 conditional accuracy, 85.98 joint AP vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39.
> - COCOHumanParts: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 AP.5:.95 (orig/sub); BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3; PBADet achieves better mMR−2 for head/face/left-hand, while BPJDet is lower on right-hand/feet.
> - CrowdHuman: PBADet (YOLOv7) best body MR−2=36.5, body AP=91.6; face MR−2=44.7; association mMR−2 ≈ 50.8–50.9 (vs 50.1 BPJDet YOLOv5l6).
> - GLUE (RoBERTa‑L): 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 (vs 32‑bit 88.9; 8‑bit 89.1).
> - ImageNet‑1k (Swin‑T): 4‑bit AdamW 80.8; 32‑bit 81.2.
> - E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2 M BLEU): 4‑bit AdamW 67.8; 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5.
> - SQuAD F1 (RoBERTa‑L): 4‑bit AdamW 94.5; 32‑bit 94.6.
> - WMT14 en‑de: 4‑bit AdamW 26.28; 32‑bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66.
> - LLaMA 7B/13B/33B (instruction‑tuning): 4‑bit ≈ parity with 32‑bit across MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA (Table 3; differences generally within ~1 point).
> - RL synthetic/real: MNL‑VQL dominates returns over Myopic/LSVI‑UCB; LSVI‑UCB scales poorly in run‑time (e.g., N=40: 453.641s/ep vs MNL‑VQL 0.620s/ep; Table G.1).
> 
> D) Summary of which methods perform better/worse where (from tables/figures)
> - On identical human benchmarks (PBADet vs BPJDet/HierR‑CNN): PBADet is best on BodyHands (all metrics) and best body MR−2/body AP on CrowdHuman, with mixed association mMR by part on COCOHumanParts (wins on head/face/left‑hand, trails on feet and sometimes right hand vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6).
> - On NLU/vision/MT/NLG/instruction tuning (4‑bit optimizer vs 32‑bit/8‑bit): 4‑bit typically matches 32‑bit within ±0.5pt (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E BLEU) and is slightly lower on ImageNet‑1k and WMT14 en‑de by ~0.3pt, while enabling sizable (34–58%) total memory savings and maintaining or improving wall‑clock time with fusion.
> - On RL with preference feedback (MNL‑VQL vs Myopic and LSVI‑UCB): MNL‑VQL yields higher episodic returns on both synthetic and MovieLens; runtime scales vastly better than LSVI‑UCB as the number of items grows.
> - On sequence tasks (Adding, Sequential MNIST, PTB) and object‑like recognition: Standard RNNs/DANNs outperform ColEI RNNs (plots). Spectrum‑transplant experiments show spectrum ≫ sign constraints in explaining performance (Fig. 4). JEPA vs MAE linear analyses (plots) show JEPA favors high‑ρ features and depth strengthens this bias (Fig. 4); MAE prioritizes high‑λ features.
> 
> This concludes the results-only integration across the five papers, emphasizing like-for-like (identical-dataset) comparisons within each paper, and careful comparisons on similar task families without crossing task/dataset boundaries.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on my search, I've located the papers matching most of the requested topics. However, I should note that the exact "regression vs. classification-style loss" SSL paper was not found in this collection—the closest is the JEPA vs MAE implicit-bias analysis. Let me provide a concise comparison of what the context supports.
> 
> ## Papers and Their Experimental Findings
> 
> **(a) PBADet — one-stage, no-anchor human part–person association**
> - One-stage, anchor-free detector extending YOLOv5/YOLOv7 with a single part-to-body center offset. Evaluated on **BodyHands** and **COCO-HumanParts** (COCO-style human datasets).
> - BodyHands: ours (YOLOv7, 36.9M) → HandAP **89.1**, Cond. Accuracy **92.62**, JointAP **85.98**, beating BPJDet (YOLOv5m6: 85.3/86.80/78.13) and BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48) with a smaller model.
> - COCO-HumanParts (all categories AP): 42.7/41.5 (orig/subordinate) AP.5:.95; leads in person/feet AP and lowest average mMR⁻² for head, face, hands, right foot; comparable to BPJDet.
> - Ablations: the association head preserves hand AP while greatly improving association; removing multi-scale or task-alignment lowers all metrics. Anchor-free part-to-body (89.1/92.62/85.98) beats anchor-based (88.4/92.31/85.28) and BPJDet body-to-part (85.3/86.80/78.13).
> 
> **(b) E/I recurrent networks via spectral analysis — "Learning better with Dale's Law"**
> - Compares standard RNNs, Column E/I (ColEI), and recurrent DALE's ANNs (DANN) on **sequential MNIST**, adding, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition.
> - ColEI learns worst and with higher variance; gradient clipping mitigates. Spectral transplants show the **initial singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints**: ColEI's spectrum is multimodal/dispersed (rank-one column-mean structure), whereas DANN and standard RNNs have unimodal Marchenko–Pastur/quarter-circle spectra. Smaller networks/fewer I units worsen spectra and performance; DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory unit. Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error.
> 
> **(c) Joint-embedding SSL preferring predictive latent targets — "Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"**
> - The JEPA (regression in latent space, MSE over latent targets) vs MAE (pixel-space reconstruction) comparison. It is a theory paper (deep linear networks) with an ImageNet-1K experiment using **ViT encoders**.
> - Findings: JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient ρ), MAE prioritizes high-variance/covarying features (λ); JEPA focuses on the low-variance PCA subspace faster. On ImageNet, I-JEPA features show higher CCA similarity to the "bottom 25% variance" dataset than MAE throughout training—i.e., JEPA learns perceptual/discriminative features more efficiently than pixel reconstruction. The specific regression-loss vs classification-objective ablation is **not present in this collection**; I cannot establish that comparison from the given context.
> 
> **(d) 4-bit optimizers — memory-lean Adam/AdamW**
> - Compresses optimizer states to 4-bit (B128/DE for first moment; Rank-1/Linear with zero-point exclusion for second moment; optional factorization). Supports **Transformers and LoRA-style parameter-efficient tuning**.
> - Results (Table 2): vs 32-bit AdamW (RoBERTa-L NLU 88.9, Swin-T ImageNet 81.2, GPT-2M BLEU 67.7, RoBERTa-L QA F1 94.6, Transformer MT 26.61), 4-bit AdamW gives 89.1/80.8/67.8/94.5/26.28—essentially matching.
> - LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning (MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC-e/ARC-c/OBQA): 4-bit AdamW (38.9/74.7/61.2/44.4/43.0 at 7B) matches 32-bit; enables instruction-following without degrading pretrained ability. Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 31.87GB vs 75.40GB); LLaMA-7B fits on one 80GB GPU; convergence curves align with 32-bit.
> 
> **(e) MNL-VQL — combinatorial RL for slate selection with discrete-choice feedback**
> - Optimistic value iteration for episodic **linear MDPs** where each action is an assortment under an **MNL preference model**; uses generalized Eluder dimension for general function approximation.
> - Theory: regret upper bound Õ(d√(HK) + d_lin√(HK)) for linear MDPs with **matching lower bound Ω(d√(HK) + d_lin√(HK))** — nearly minimax optimal, first statistical guarantee in this setting. Uses LP (not enumeration) for assortment selection.
> - Experiments: online-shopping budget environment with up to 760k assortments; MNL-VQL converges to the optimal policy with stable runtime, whereas the myopic baseline converges to a suboptimal solution and LSVI-UCB becomes impractical as assortments grow.
> 
> ## Cross-method analysis
> All five papers address structural/inductive-bias constraints (anchor-free association, E/I + spectral structure, latent-prediction bias, quantized optimizer states, MNL-combinatorial action space) with resource constraints (parameter count, memory footprint, assortment enumeration). Experimentally they share a consistent theme: **a principled inductive bias yields equal-or-better accuracy with less capacity/compute** — PBADet beats two-stage detectors with fewer parameters; DANN matches standard RNNs while obeying Dale's law; 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit while cutting memory ~2× (57.7% total); MNL-VQL achieves near-optimal regret while staying tractable at large assortments.
> 
> **Caveat:** the context does not contain a paper directly comparing regression-style vs classification-style SSL losses (e.g., a cross-entropy-tokenized feature-prediction study). The JEPA paper compares latent-space regression to pixel-space reconstruction only, so that specific comparison cannot be established from this collection.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, I found matching papers for all five topics:
> 
> **(a) PBADet** ("PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association", ICLR 2024)
> **(b)** "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)
> **(c)** "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks" (NeurIPS 2024)
> **(d)** "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)
> **(e)** "Combinatorial Reinforcement Learning with Preference Feedback" (MNL-VQL, ICML 2025)
> 
> ## Experimental results
> 
> **(a) PBADet** — One-stage anchor-free, single part-to-body center offset on YOLOv5/YOLOv7. On COCO-HumanParts (all categories): AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6). On CrowdHuman face-body: body MR-2 = 36.5, body AP = 91.6 (YOLOv7), beating BPJDet (MR-2 39.7–41.3, AP 89.5–90.7) and all two-stage methods (FPN, CrowdDet). On BodyHands: anchor-free part-to-body gives Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 vs. BPJDet 85.3/86.80/78.13. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment each boost association accuracy.
> 
> **(b) Dale's Law RNNs** — Compares standard RNNs, ColEI (column sign-constrained E/I) and recurrent DANN on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition. ColEI learns worse (≈2.3% ± 0.6% above standard RNN on sequential MNIST), with higher variance and instability without gradient clipping. Spectral transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints; small networks with few I units have worse spectra/performance; DANN matches standard RNNs; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization predicts final error.
> 
> **(c) JEPA vs MAE** — Joint-embedding predictive (regression in latent space, MSE) vs. pixel-space reconstruction (MAE). On deep linear models, JEPA is biased toward high-influence features (large regression coefficients) whereas MAE prioritizes high-variance features; depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression; with distribution 2 (covariance vs. influence anti-correlated), JEPA reverses learning order while MAE does not. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace (CCA) than MAE. Note: the collection does not contain an explicit regression-vs-classification-style objective comparison; the contrastive-analysis paper (InfoNCE/SigLIP embeddings) is the closest related loss study.
> 
> **(d) 4-bit optimizers** — 4-bit AdamW/Adam (B128 + rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion for second moment). Matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L 89.1), SQuAD (94.5), E2E-NLG (67.8 BLEU), ImageNet (Swin-T 80.8), WMT14 en-de (26.28), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning on Alpaca (MMLU 38.9/47.4/54.9, HellaSwag 74.7/79.0/79.2), with up to 57.7% memory savings and LLaMA-7B trainable on one 80GB GPU. 4-bitFactor adds factorized second moment. Note: LoRA is cited as related work rather than tested; QLoRA appears in NEFTune's experiments (a different paper), so the LoRA-specific evaluation is not covered by this optimizer paper.
> 
> **(e) MNL-VQL** — Optimistic value iteration for combinatorial RL (assortment selection) under MNL preference feedback with state transitions. Regret upper bound Õ(d√(HK) + d_lin√(HK)) in linear MDPs with a matching lower bound Ω(d√(HK) + d_lin√(HK)) — nearly minimax-optimal. Experiments in a synthetic online-shopping budget environment (up to 760k assortments) show MNL-VQL converges to the optimal policy while the Myopic baseline converges to a suboptimal solution and LSVI-UCB becomes impractical as assortment count grows; validated also on a real-world (MovieLens-style) subset (1.1×10³ users, 50–200 movies).
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> 
> Across the five studies, structural constraints/resource limits are consistently the driving factor: (a) replacing anchor-based/body-to-part offsets with a single anchor-free part-to-body offset improves both accuracy and scalability (COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman); (b) the *spectral* initialization, not the E/I sign constraint itself, determines trainability, with DANN matching standard RNNs; (c) latent-space prediction (regression) has a fundamentally different feature-prioritization bias than input-space reconstruction, favoring semantic (low-variance) features; (d) quantizing optimizer moments to 4-bit preserves accuracy across NLU, vision, MT, and instruction following while cutting memory up to ~58%; (e) exploiting MNL structure yields tractable assortment optimization with minimax-optimal regret, where myopic and enumerative baselines fail. Benchmark coverage aligns with the request: COCO-style human datasets (a), sequential MNIST/PTB/CIFAR-type settings (b, plus CIFAR in the related BSO paper), transformer encoders (c, d), and instruction-following/LLM tasks (d). The main gaps: no direct regression-vs-classification SSL loss comparison, and no direct LoRA-with-4-bit-optimizer experiment in the retrieved collection.

>   - 32-bit AdamW: 67.7; 8-bit AdamW: 67.5; 4-bit AdamW: 67.8; 4-bit Factor: 67.6; Adafactor (β1>0/β1=0): 67.2 / 67.2; SM3: 66.9.
>   - Result: 4-bit AdamW slightly leads, essentially matching 32-bit and 8-bit.

> Efficiency and capacity (Tables 4 & 5)
> - Time & memory (per run):
>   - LLaMA-7B (2×A100 80GB): 4-bit AdamW reduces memory from 75.40 GB (32-bit) to 31.87 GB while slightly improving time (3.35 h → 3.07 h).
>   - RoBERTa-L (1×RTX 4090): 4-bit AdamW reduces memory from 5.31 GB to 3.00 GB (43.5% saved) and, with fused ops, time is 3.17 min (vs 3.93 min for 32-bit). 8-bit AdamW is similar in time/memory; 4-bit yields the largest memory drop.
>   - GPT-2 Medium: 4-bit AdamW (fused) reduces memory from 6.89 GB to 4.62 GB; time comparable to 32-bit.

>   - On 24 GB GPU: 32-bit fits OPT-350M; 4-bit fits OPT-1.3B.
>   - On 80 GB GPU: 32-bit fits OPT-1.3B; 4-bit fits OPT-6.7B; also enables LLaMA-7B on a single 80 GB GPU.
> 
> Method details and losses
> - Optimizers: 4-bit results are reported with AdamW; PBADet models trained with SGD (YOLOv7 schedule); both are explicitly stated in their respective papers.
> - Reconstruction vs predictive (MSE vs CE) presence: 4-bit results span classification (CE-based tasks like ImageNet-1k, GLUE, SQuAD) and generation (E2E-NLG, MT) – the result parity indicates the 4-bit optimizer states do not degrade either CE-based or sequence-to-sequence training.
> 
> 3) Self-supervised learning objective (JEPA vs MAE) – learning dynamics and feature outcomes
> Identical experimental settings (deep linear models) and head-to-head comparisons
> - Learning-order inversion (Figure 1; JEPA paper): In controlled settings where feature covariance λ and regression coefficient ρ trend differently across features, MAE and JEPA prioritize features differently during training:
>   - On Distribution 1 (both λ and ρ increasing): both MAE and JEPA learn features greedily by λ.
>   - On Distribution 2 (λ increasing, ρ decreasing): MAE continues learning in λ order, but JEPA reverses the order, prioritizing features with larger ρ. This shows JEPA’s implicit bias toward “influential features.”
> - Depth effect (Figure 4): The JEPA bias toward high-ρ features intensifies as encoder depth increases; MAE’s ordering remains dominated by λ regardless of depth.
> - Temporal model (Figure 3): In a linear temporal generative process, JEPA preferentially learns less noisy, more predictive features (higher regression coefficient ρ), consistent with the theory (e.g., JEPA learns “slow/predictive” modes earlier).
> - ImageNet empirical check (Appendix D, Figure 7): I-JEPA exhibits higher similarity between features learned on full images and the bottom PCA subspace (full–bottom CCA) than MAE throughout training, while MAE shows higher full–top CCA. This supports that JEPA emphasizes the lower-variance, semantic subspace sooner.
> 
> 4) EI RNNs under Dale’s Law – stability and performance (sequential MNIST and others)
> Identical datasets and head-to-head comparisons (Figure 2; Dale’s Law paper)
> - Tasks: Adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank (PTB) language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task.
> - Results: Across all four tasks, Column EI (ColEI) RNNs learn worse (lower final performance and higher variability) than standard RNNs and DANN (EI) RNNs. With gradient clipping, ColEI improves but remains worse than the other two; DANN matches standard RNN performance while respecting EI constraints.
> - Spectral/transplant experiments: Changing only the singular-value spectrum between models alters performance more than EI sign constraints alone; models with RNN-like (unimodal, clustered) spectra learn better. This explains DANN’s good task performance and ColEI’s deficits.
> - Dataset overlap: Sequential MNIST appears here (not present in other papers). It confirms stable performance under Dale’s EI constraints when spectral properties are controlled (DANN), vs degraded learning for naïve EI partitioning (ColEI).
> 
> 5) Combinatorial RL with Multinomial Logit preference feedback (MNL-VQL)
> Identical settings and comparisons
> - Synthetic environment (Figure 1): For N=10, 20, 40 items (|A|=637, 21699, 760098), MNL-VQL consistently achieves higher episodic return than Myopic (OFU-MNL+) and LSVI-UCB. LSVI-UCB performs worst and becomes impractically slow as N grows; Myopic converges to a suboptimal policy.
> - Runtime (Table G.1): Average per-episode time (N=10/20/40):
>   - Myopic: 0.089s / 0.097s / 0.113s (fastest but suboptimal quality).
>   - LSVI-UCB: 0.136s / 4.861s / 453.641s (scales poorly with |A|).
>   - MNL-VQL: 0.463s / 0.526s / 0.620s (moderate overhead but practical as |A| grows).
> - MovieLens (Figure 2): MNL-VQL outperforms Myopic and LSVI-UCB on episodic return across N=50, 100, 200 with |A| up to ~1.33M; baseline LSVI-UCB was not run due to excessive runtime (dotted reference lines from N=50 indicate worse performance than MNL-VQL).
> 
> 6) Cross-cutting summary by task type and required properties
> - COCO-like detection and association: PBADet delivers the best or competitive association and detection quality across BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman. On BodyHands, it clearly beats prior SOTA (BPJDet) on Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, and Joint AP. On COCOHumanParts, PBADet leads many association-related metrics (mMR−2) and per-size APs, while BPJDet edges slightly in overall AP.
> - NLU/MT/vision classification/NLG: 4-bit optimizer states (AdamW) match or very closely track 32-bit and 8-bit baselines across GLUE, SQuAD, WMT14, ImageNet-1k, and E2E-NLG, while reducing training memory (up to ~57.7% in LLaMA-7B setups) and enabling larger models per GPU budget (e.g., OPT-6.7B on 80GB; LLaMA-7B on single 80GB GPU). SM3 is consistently worse; Adafactor is close to 32-bit but does not improve memory as much as 4-bit.
> - Time-series stability with EI constraints: On MNIST-like sequential tasks and PTB, EI-compliant DANN RNNs match standard RNNs and substantially outperform naïve EI partitioning (ColEI), especially under realistic widths and EI ratios. Spectral control (unimodal singular-value spectrum) is the key determinant of performance.
> - SSL loss design (MAE vs JEPA) and interpretability of learned features: In deep linear and linear temporal models, JEPA prioritizes high-regression-coefficient (predictive, low-noise) features and can invert learning order relative to MAE when covariance and predictiveness diverge. Empirically, on ImageNet features (CCA), JEPA aligns more with the bottom-variance (semantic) subspace early; MAE emphasizes high-variance reconstruction.
> - Slate recommendation / preference feedback with provable efficiency: MNL-VQL achieves higher returns than myopic and holistic (enumerative) methods on synthetic and MovieLens; it scales far better computationally than holistic enumeration (measured runtime benefits grow with |A|).
> 
> Notes on overlap with the user’s requested benchmarks
> - COCO-like: Covered by PBADet (COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman) with detailed comparisons.
> - MNIST/CIFAR-100: Sequential MNIST is covered (Dale’s Law paper). CIFAR-100 is not present in the provided experimental content.
> - Modern NLU/MT benchmarks: Present in 4-bit optimizer paper (GLUE via RoBERTa-L, SQuAD, WMT14 en-de), with quantitative comparisons of multiple optimizers.
> 
> Overall method ranking by identical datasets
> - BodyHands: PBADet (YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6) > BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) across Hand AP / Cond. Acc. / Joint AP.
> - COCOHumanParts: BPJDet YOLOv5l6 slightly higher overall AP; PBADet stronger on several association (mMR−2) categories and size-based APs.
> - CrowdHuman: PBADet best MR−2 (body/face) and body AP; BPJDet marginally better mMR−2.
> - GLUE/SQuAD/WMT14/ImageNet-1k/E2E-NLG: 4-bit AdamW = 32-bit/8-bit AdamW on accuracy; SM3 underperforms consistently; Adafactor variants comparable on accuracy but without the same memory reduction.
> - Sequential MNIST/PTB/Naturalistic Object Recognition: Standard RNN ≈ DANN RNN > ColEI RNN.
> - Synthetic and MovieLens preference-feedback RL: MNL-VQL > Myopic and > LSVI-UCB (both quality and scalability).
> 
> Implementation/optimizer specifics explicitly given in the works
> - PBADet: Trained with SGD (YOLOv7-like schedule), AMP, and multi-scale heads.
> - 4-bit optimizers: AdamW, plus factorized second moment option; supports fused ops; evaluated across RoBERTa-L, Swin-T, GPT-2 Medium, Transformer-Base, LLaMA.
> - Dale’s Law RNNs: Show gradient clipping especially benefits ColEI, though DANN and standard RNNs remain superior on final performance.
> - JEPA vs MAE: Compares losses (MAE MSE-like reconstruction vs JEPA latent prediction) primarily via controlled linear experiments and a corroborating ImageNet feature-similarity analysis.
> - MNL-VQL: Slate (assortment) selection with tractable LP; preference feedback modeled by MNL; general function-approximation for Q; comparisons vs Myopic and holistic LSVI-UCB.
> 
> This concludes a results-only synthesis across the provided sources, focusing on identical datasets and, where that is not possible, on similar task families with direct experimental evidence from tables and figures.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the provided context, no single paper covers all five components together—each is addressed by separate research, with benchmarks split accordingly. Here is what the context supports, with a comparison of experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Body-part detection & person linking (COCO-like)
> **PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free part-body association, ICLR 2024) — the only work directly on this task:
> - **COCO val (hands/feet vs ED-Pose)**: PBADet all-parts Precision/Recall/F1 = 39.41 / 63.09 / 48.52 vs ED-Pose 24.09 / 45.51 / 31.51 — roughly +15 precision, +17.5 recall, +17 F1.
> - **CrowdHuman (face-body)**: PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves best body MR-2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6); BPJDet is 39.7–41.3 MR-2. PBADet matches DETR-based detectors (PED-DETR, Iter-E2EDET) on AP but has clearly better body MR-2.
> - **Analysis**: its advantage is large on multi-part tasks (BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts) but small on the single-part face-body task.
> 
> ## 2. Joint-embedding SSL vs pixel reconstruction (MSE vs CE / predictive)
> **"Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (deep-linear analysis, ImageNet-1K):
> - JEPA (latent prediction) is biased toward *influential* features (high regression coefficient ρ), while MAE (input-space MSE reconstruction) is driven by high-variance features even when noisy; depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression. ImageNet-1K CCA confirms I-JEPA aligns faster than MAE with the low-variance perceptual subspace.
> - **LDReg** (SSL regularization, ImageNet ResNet-50/ViT-B): improving local intrinsic dimensionality boosts linear eval, transfer, and **COCO detection/instance segmentation** for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE, MoCo, VICReg, Barlow Twins; longer pretraining gives larger gains. This is the SSL piece with COCO-like downstream evidence.
> 
> ## 3. Low-precision optimizer states + LoRA fine-tuning of transformers
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023) — quantized SGD(M)/Adam/AdamW states:
> - **4-bit AdamW vs 32-bit AdamW**: NLU (RoBERTa-L/GLUE) 89.1 vs 88.9; CLS (Swin-T/ImageNet) 80.8 vs 81.2; NLG (GPT-2M/E2E) 67.8 vs 67.7; QA (SQuAD) 94.5 vs 94.6; MT (Transformer/WMT14 en-de) 26.28 vs 26.61 — i.e., statistically comparable (slightly better on NLU/NLG, slightly lower on CLS/MT).
> - **LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning (Alpaca→MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA)**: 4-bit matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit (e.g., LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5); convergence curves closely align.
> - **Memory**: LLaMA-7B 75.4 GB → 31.9 GB (−57.7%); RoBERTa-L 5.31 → 3.02 GB (−43.1%, vs 8-bit's −37.1%); GPT-2M −~33%. 4-bit beats 8-bit and, unlike Adafactor/SM3, shows no degradation (Adafactor/SM3 lose accuracy especially on ImageNet CLS). LoRA appears as the fine-tuning mechanism (GPT-2 uses LoRA; the Hessian paper fine-tunes TinyLlama with LoRA on MathQA).
> 
> ## 4. Excitatory/inhibitory recurrent modules with spectral control
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023):
> - On adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition, column-constrained E/I RNNs (ColEI) learn worse and with higher variance than Dale's-ANN (DANN) RNNs and standard RNNs.
> - **Key result**: the *initial singular-value spectrum* (unimodal/clustered, measured by normalised SVD entropy, NSE) matters more than sign constraints; sign constraints cost only ~0.7–1% error, not the full ~2.3% gap. Gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially; fewer inhibitory units worsens the spectrum and performance (DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron). NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error, i.e., spectral control predicts time-series stability.
> 
> ## 5. Slate recommendation from user choice signals (discrete-choice) with provable efficiency
> **MNL-VQL** (combinatorial RL with preference feedback):
> - Models user choice as a contextual multinomial logit (MNL) model over assortments (slates); proves regret Õ(d√(HK·dim_p(F)·K·H·log|F|)), minimax-optimal Õ(d√(HK)+d_lin√(HK)) in linear MDPs with a matching lower bound.
> - Experiments in an online-shopping budget environment with up to 760k assortments: MNL-VQL converges to the optimal policy with stable runtime, whereas a myopic baseline converges suboptimally and LSVI-UCB becomes impractical as the assortment space grows. (No COCO/MNIST/NLU results here — this is a bandit/RL benchmark.)
> 
> ## Cross-cutting comparison of the pieces
> - **Optimization (SGD/AdamW)**: the 4-bit paper gives the direct AdamW memory/accuracy trade-off on NLU/MT/ImageNet; the Hessian-spectrum paper shows power-law Hessian structure holds for SGD, Adam, and 9 other optimizers on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100, with the slope correlating with sharpness/generalization (e.g., LeNet CIFAR-10 Pearson 0.72) and predicting LLM/LoRA generalization (up to 0.98).
> - **Reconstruction vs predictive losses**: the JEPA/MAE paper is the theoretical comparison (MAE's MSE reconstruction vs JEPA latent prediction), with ImageNet evidence; the 4-bit paper's transformer models (RoBERTa, GPT-2, LLaMA, WMT14 Transformer) are trained with CE-style objectives, and the MNL choice model is likewise a softmax-style discrete-choice objective.
> - **Benchmark coverage is fragmented**: COCO-like results come only from PBADet (detection) and LDReg (SSL transfer); MNIST/CIFAR-100 appear only in the EI-RNN paper (sequential MNIST) and the Hessian paper; NLU/MT come only from the 4-bit optimizer paper. No single context document reports all three benchmark families together, so a unified quantitative comparison across all five methods on the same benchmarks is not possible from this context.

**community 最终答案**

> Here is the research available in the collection mapped to your six components, with the experimental results compared.
> 
> ## 1. Body-part detection & person association (COCO-like)
> **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) – one-stage anchor-free part-body association. Evaluated on **COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands, COCO val, plus AnimalPose/AP-10K**.
> - Outperforms BPJDet and HierR-CNN on COCO-HumanParts (AP on par overall, leads on AP_M/AP_L, person and feet; lowest average mMR−2 for head/face/hands/right foot).
> - CrowdHuman face-body: lowest body MR−2 (36.5 vs BPJDet 39.7–41.3; 44.7 face MR−2) with competitive AP (91.6 vs 89.5–90.7).
> - vs ED-Pose pose estimator on COCO val (4 parts): PBADet much higher precision/recall/F1, e.g., left hand 37.6/60.8/46.5 vs 18.4/30.3/22.9; all parts F1 48.5 vs 31.5.
> - Extends to quadruped part-body association (AnimalPose→AP-10K).
> 
> ## 2. Joint-embedding SSL vs pixel-noise overfitting (MSE vs predictive)
> - **"Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024) directly addresses reconstruction vs predictive losses: MAE (MSE reconstruction in pixel/input space) prioritizes high-variance (often noisy) features; JEPA (latent-space prediction) prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient ρ), with noise suppression strengthening with encoder depth. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA).
> - **LDReg** (ICLR 2024): MAE is prone to dimensional collapse; local-dimensionality regularization improves SSL across SimCLR/BYOL/MAE. Results: ImageNet linear eval 64.3→64.8 (SimCLR 100ep), 69.0→69.8 (1000ep); transfer CIFAR-10 90.1→91.8, CIFAR-100 71.6→75.1; **COCO fine-tuned detection/segmentation**: BYOL APbb 36.30→36.82, SimCLR (1000ep) APbb 36.48→37.15, APmk 32.12→32.82; MAE ViT-B 57.0→57.6.
> - **Video-based representation learning (exogenous Block MDPs)**: under iid pixel noise, temporal contrastive learning fails completely while forward modeling (predictive) is more robust, though both degrade with large exogenous noise; trajectory-based ACRO stays robust. Supports choosing predictive/joint-embedding objectives to avoid pixel noise.
> 
> ## 3. Low-precision optimizer moments + LoRA fine-tuning (SGD/AdamW)
> **"4-bit Optimizers"** (NeurIPS 2023): 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor match or slightly beat 32-bit AdamW:
> - NLU (RoBERTa-L, GLUE): 89.1 vs 88.9; CLS (Swin-T, ImageNet): 80.8 vs 81.2; NLG (GPT-2M, E2E): 67.8 vs 67.7; QA (SQuAD): 94.5 vs 94.6; MT (Transformer-Base, WMT14 en-de): 26.28 vs 26.61.
> - LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning (MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC-e/ARC-c/OBQA): 4-bit matches 32-bit (e.g., 7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; 13B HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8).
> - Memory: up to 57.7% total memory saved; LLaMA-7B trainable on one 80GB GPU; sublinear-memory Adafactor/SM3 degrade, especially on image classification. LoRA is the standard parameter-efficient companion (the paper's LLaMA fine-tuning builds on LoRA).
> - **Hessian-spectrum paper** adds caveat: LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning shows, though d_ks predicts LLM generalization (up to 0.98).
> 
> ## 4. Excitatory/inhibitory recurrent modules with spectral control
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023): compares column E/I-partitioned RNNs (ColEI), Dale's ANNs (DANN), and standard RNNs on adding problem, **sequential MNIST**, **Penn Tree Bank** language modeling, naturalistic object recognition.
> - ColEI learns worse and more variably on all four tasks; gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> - Key finding: sign constraints are not the main culprit (~1% of the ~2.3%±0.6% gap); the initial recurrent-weight **spectrum** is: ColEI has multimodal, dispersed singular values (column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure) vs unimodal Marchenko–Pastur/quarter-circle spectra for RNNs/DANNs. Smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error. Implication: design E/I splits with standard-RNN-like spectra.
> 
> ## 5. Slate recommendation from discrete-choice signals, provably efficient
> **MNL-VQL** ("Combinatorial Reinforcement Learning with Preference Feedback"): episodic combinatorial RL where each action is an assortment and user choice follows a **multinomial logit (MNL)** model; item values estimated with general function approximation.
> - Regret upper bound Õ(d√(HK) + dim(F)KH log|F|); for linear MDPs Õ(d√(HK) + d_lin√(HK)), with **matching lower bound Ω(d√(HK)+d_lin√(HK))** → minimax-optimal; first such guarantee in combinatorial RL with preference feedback; avoids enumerating assortments (LP-solvable).
> - Experiments: synthetic online-shopping (up to 760k assortments) and **MovieLens 25M** (up to 1.33M assortments): converges to optimal policy, substantially beats Myopic (which converges to suboptimal) and LSVI-UCB (impractical at scale).
> 
> ## 6. Optimization (SGD vs AdamW) and transformer pipelines on MNIST/CIFAR-100/NLU/MT
> **Hessian-spectrum study** (ICML 2025) gives the broadest optimizer/benchmark comparison: SGD, VanillaSGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, Yogi, RAdam, Adai, PNM, Lookahead, DiffGrad on **MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100** (LeNet, FCN, ResNet18, fine-tuned ViT-Base on CIFAR-100) and GPT-2/TinyLlama with **AdamW** (OpenWebText, Shakespeare, MathQA).
> - Power-law Hessian spectra hold for well-trained networks across all optimizers (not random nets); slope magnitude ŝ correlates with sharpness and test error (Pearson 0.853 on MNIST LeNet); large-batch training (e.g., MNIST LeNet B≥768, CIFAR-10 ResNet18 B≥1280) destroys the power law.
> - AdamW is the optimizer of choice for transformer pretraining/fine-tuning in this collection (GPT-2, TinyLlama, RoBERTa, LLaMA, Swin, ViT).
> 
> ## Cross-cutting comparison
> - **Vision (COCO-like)**: PBADet is the SOTA for part-body association (higher precision/recall/F1 than pose-estimation ED-Pose); LDReg gives the SSL-pretraining gains on COCO detection/segmentation (APbb up to 37.15), while HASSOD shows fully self-supervised detection (no labels) improves zero-shot Mask AR on LVIS 20.2→22.5 and argues MS-COCO AP is misleading for class-agnostic detection.
> - **Small-scale (MNIST/CIFAR-100)**: the Hessian paper compares all optimizers there (power-law structure holds, breaks with huge batches); LDReg reports CIFAR-10/100 transfer gains; Dale's-law RNNs are tested on sequential MNIST/PTB.
> - **NLU/MT**: 4-bit optimizers deliver lossless NLU/QA/NLG/MT (GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/WMT14) and LLaMA commonsense benchmarks with large memory savings; PCP/TAPT studies RoBERTa sentence-pair NLU; MNL-VQL handles the recommendation/choice side.
> 
> Coverage gaps: no single paper spans all six components; each component maps to one or two dedicated papers, and their benchmarks overlap only partially (e.g., none of the E/I-RNN or slate-recommendation papers report COCO/MNIST/GLUE jointly).

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:68 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (a) single-pass, anchor-free human part-to-body association on COCO-style datasets and report standard losses (MSE, cross-entropy) and metrics (Precision, F1); (b) the learning dynamics of recurrent nets with biologically inspired excitatory/inhibitory separation, analyzed via spectral properties (e.g., singular-value distributions, entropy) under SGD/AdamW; (c) self-supervised joint-embedding predictive training that biases latent features toward high-influence signals (beyond raw pixel variance), with demonstrations on MNIST/CIFAR-100 and Transformer/ResNet-50 backbones; (d) memory-efficient optimization using sub-byte (≈4-bit) states for Adam/AdamW with block/group quantization and handling zero-point issues; and (e) uncertainty-aware reinforcement learning using ensembles of value distributions where disagreement (e.g., 1-Wasserstein) drives exploration. Prefer works discussing interpretability, attention, and common evaluation protocols.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：3→2（Δ-1）；rounds：7→4（Δ-3）。**

>   → PBADet yields higher Hand AP (+3.2 vs BPJDet-l6), higher conditional accuracy (+~5.7–5.8), and higher joint AP (+1.3–1.6).
>

>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.6/43.3; AP.5 70.6/69.8; APM 63.8/63.2; APL 61.8/58.9; person 61.3; head 56.6; face 46.3; r-hand 40.4; l-hand 39.6; r-foot 30.2; l-foot 30.9.
>   → Trade-offs: PBADet better on medium/large objects (APM/APL), person, and feet; BPJDet slightly higher on head/face and hands.
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 3: mMR−2 per category; lower is better):
>   • Ours (YOLOv5l6): head 27.9, face 30.5, l-hand 36.2, r-hand 40.8, r-foot 50.4, l-foot 47.9.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, l-hand 41.6, r-hand 42.2, r-foot 49.1, l-foot 50.4.
>   → PBADet has lower mMR−2 on head, face, and both hands; BPJDet slightly lower on right foot; PBADet lower on left foot.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Table 5): face–body association.
>   • Ours (YOLOv7): MR−2 body 36.5 (best), AP body 91.6 (best), MR−2 face 44.7, mMR−2 50.8.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 body 40.7, AP body 89.5, MR−2 face 46.3, mMR−2 50.1.
>   → PBADet improves body detection MR−2 and AP; pair association (mMR−2) is comparable (slightly higher for PBADet than BPJDet).
> 
> - COCO (pose vs. detection; Table 7, Appendix A.2): PBADet vs ED-Pose (Swin-L) on hands/feet (Precision/Recall/F1).
>   • All parts F1: PBADet 48.52 vs ED-Pose 31.51; per-part F1 also higher for PBADet (e.g., left hand 46.50 vs 22.87; left foot 51.08 vs 40.46).
>   → PBADet provides substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for part bounding boxes and part-to-body linking than pose keypoint-based outputs in this setting.
