> 2) Vision classification/generative features and optimizer memory: 4-bit optimizers
> Identical datasets and metrics across methods in the paper
> - RoBERTa-L on GLUE (NLU; Table 2): mean score.
>   • 32-bit AdamW: 88.9; 8-bit AdamW: 89.1; 4-bit AdamW: 89.1; Adafactor 89.1; Adafactor (β1=0) 89.3; SM3 87.5.
>   → 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit and 8-bit; SM3 underperforms.
> 
> - Swin-T on ImageNet-1k (CLS; Table 2): accuracy.
>   • 32-bit AdamW: 81.2; 8-bit AdamW: 81.0; 4-bit AdamW: 80.8; 4-bit Factor: 80.9.
>   → 4-bit within ~0.3–0.4 points of FP32; comparable to 8-bit.
> 
> - GPT-2 Medium on E2E-NLG (BLEU; Table 2):
>   • 32-bit AdamW: 67.7; 8-bit: 67.5; 4-bit: 67.8; 4-bit Factor: 67.6.
>   → 4-bit equals or slightly exceeds FP32/8-bit under BLEU.
> 
> - RoBERTa-L on SQuAD (F1; Table 2, Table 9):
>   • 32-bit AdamW: 94.6; 8-bit: 94.5; 4-bit: 94.5.
>   → 4-bit matches FP32/8-bit.
> 
> - WMT14 En–De (Transformer; SacreBLEU; Table 2):
>   • 32-bit AdamW: 26.61; 8-bit: 26.66; 4-bit: 26.28; 4-bit Factor: 26.45.
>   → 4-bit and 4-bit Factor slightly below FP32/8-bit on this MT setting.
> 
> - LLaMA instruction tuning (Alpaca; Table 3): evaluation on MMLU and commonsense QA.
>   • 7B: 4-bit matches/edges FP32 on MMLU (38.9 vs 38.7) and HellaSwag (74.7 vs 74.6), similar on ARC/OBQA.
>   • 13B and 33B: 4-bit comparable to FP32 across tasks; no systematic regressions reported.
> 
> Memory and speed (Table 4, Table 5)
> - LLaMA-7B (two A100-80GB, FSDP): total mem 31.87 GB (4-bit) vs 75.40 GB (FP32) → 57.7% reduction; training time improved (3.07 h vs 3.35 h).
> - RoBERTa-L: total mem 3.00 GB (4-bit, fused) vs 5.31 GB (FP32) → 43.5% saved; wall time similar or faster with fused kernels.
> - GPT-2 Medium: total mem 4.62 GB (4-bit) vs 6.89 GB (FP32) → 34.4% saved; fused implementation recovers FP32 time.
> - Largest trainable model (Table 5): under 80 GB, FP32 trains OPT-1.3B; 4-bit trains OPT-6.7B and LLaMA-7B.
> 
> Key ablations tied to experimental results (Table 1, Table 6)
> - Second-moment quantization must exclude zero-point (DE-0 or Linear) to avoid catastrophic updates; with B2048/DE-0 or Rank-1/Linear, BLEU (E2E-NLG) remains at 67.4–67.8 and instability drops to 0%.
> - Rank-1 normalization + Linear mapping on v achieves stable convergence under 4-bit; factorizing v further saves memory with negligible accuracy change.
> 
> 3) RL: uncertainty-aware exploration with distributional ensembles
> Identical benchmark within paper, compared to baselines
> - Behavior Suite (468 envs; Fig. 4a): PE-DQN improves the exploration radar category and also lifts overall capability scores vs BDQN+P, IDS-C51, and DLTV-QR. The figure summarizes higher normalized scores across seven capability groups; exploration is the most improved.
> 
> - Deep Sea (hard exploration; Fig. 4b): episodic regret vs grid size up to 100.
>   • PE-DQN shows lower median regret than baselines (roughly half at larger sizes, per the plotted curves), scaling more gracefully as N increases.
>   • Ablations: using homogeneous projection ensembles (QR/QR or C51/C51) or removing bonus propagation (PE-DQN [Ind.]) degrades performance—both diverse projections and learned bonus propagation contribute to the gains.
> 
> - VizDoom MyWayHome (dense, sparse, very sparse; Fig. 5b): episodic return.
>   • Only PE-DQN reliably reaches high return across all three sparsity settings (the paper states it is the only method to find the object across all 10 seeds in all variants); BDQN+P, IDS-C51, DLTV-QR lag under sparse/very sparse.
> 
> 4) Learning dynamics and interpretability: EI RNNs under SGD/AdamW
> Datasets within paper and trends
> - Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic object recognition (Fig. 2):
>   • ColEI networks (simple EI sign-constrained columns) learn worse and with higher variance than DANNs and standard RNNs on all four tasks; gradient clipping helps ColEI disproportionately but does not close the gap.
> 
> - Sensitivity to E/I ratio and network size (Figs. 5, 6, 7):
>   • In ColEI, decreasing inhibitory proportion or using small networks increases spectral pathology (lower normalized SVD entropy), correlating with higher test error; larger networks and balanced E/I yield higher NSE and lower error.
>   • DANNs and standard RNNs show unimodal, clustered spectra and maintain high NSE (~0.95) and good learning even with few inhibitory units, matching standard RNN performance.
> 
> - Spectrum transplant experiments (Fig. 4):
>   • Swapping spectra vs. swapping sign constraints shows spectra account for a larger share of the performance gap than sign constraints alone; both matter, but spectral properties dominate in explaining ColEI underperformance.
> 
> 5) Self-supervised JEPA vs MAE: experimental indicators
> - Linear/controlled settings: synthetic Gaussian and linear generative models show JEPA learns influential features (higher regression coefficients ρ) earlier, while MAE prioritizes high-covariance (λ) features; in settings where λ and ρ trend oppositely, JEPA reverses feature learning order vs MAE (Fig. 1 & 2).
> - ImageNet feature dynamics (Appendix D, Fig. 7): JEPA’s features from full vs bottom-variance subspace have higher similarity (mean CCA) than MAE throughout training, whereas MAE aligns more with the top-variance subspace—supporting that JEPA learns perceptual/low-variance features more quickly. No direct accuracy head-to-head is reported here, but the CCA trend is experimentally measured.
> 
> Cross-paper comparisons by dataset overlap
> - There are no identical datasets shared across the five papers. Each paper’s experiments use domain-specific benchmarks:
>   • PBADet: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman, ED-Pose COCO comparison.
>   • 4-bit optimizers: GLUE (RoBERTa-L), SQuAD, ImageNet-1k (Swin-T), WMT14 En–De, LLaMA Alpaca evaluation (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA).
>   • PE-DQN: Behavior Suite and VizDoom.
>   • Dale’s Law: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, small naturalistic object recognition.
>   • JEPA: controlled synthetic/linear settings and ImageNet CCA analysis.
> 
> Comparisons across similar task types
> - Vision (detection vs classification): PBADet (detection/association) beats prior detectors/associators on the same COCO-style and BodyHands benchmarks, especially for medium/large objects and person/feet categories; the 4-bit optimizer study shows near-parity on ImageNet classification with large memory savings; JEPA shows faster alignment with low-variance perceptual subspaces on ImageNet (CCA), consistent with learning semantically relevant features quickly.
> - NLP: 4-bit optimizers match FP32/8-bit on GLUE and SQuAD, and are close on WMT14 En–De, while enabling larger models under fixed memory.
> - RL: PE-DQN outperforms strong exploration baselines on deep exploration (deep sea) and in sparse visual tasks (VizDoom); gains are attributable to diversity from mixing projections and propagating an epistemic bonus.
> - Recurrent learning dynamics: DANNs/standard RNNs outperform simple column EI networks across classic sequence/language tasks; spectral clustering (unimodal singular values, high NSE) correlates with better generalization.
> 
> Takeaways grounded in reported experiments
> - Detection/association (COCO-style, BodyHands): PBADet achieves state-of-the-art or best-in-class numbers on BodyHands and improves COCOHumanParts APM/APL and certain categories vs BPJDet, with nuanced trade-offs on head/face vs feet.
> - Efficiency (optimizers): 4-bit optimizers retain FP32/8-bit accuracy on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet-1k (close), E2E-NLG, and LLaMA instruction tuning, while halving or better the optimizer memory; zero-point handling for the second moment and rank-1 normalization are critical to stability and accuracy.
> - Exploration (RL): diverse projection ensembles (PE-DQN) deliver lower regret on deep sea and uniquely reliable success on sparse VizDoom tasks vs BDQN+P, IDS-C51, DLTV-QR, with ablations confirming both projection diversity and bonus propagation matter.
> - Learning dynamics (EI RNNs): ColEI’s multi-modal, dispersed singular-value spectra correlate with worse performance; spectrum transplant shows spectra outweigh sign constraints in explaining the gap; DANNs match standard RNNs across tasks.
> - JEPA vs MAE (feature learning bias): experiments confirm JEPA prioritizes high-influence (high ρ) features and aligns faster with low-variance perceptual subspaces on ImageNet (higher mean CCA full↔bottom), supporting reported practical advantages for perception.
> 
> Notes on losses, optimizers and interpretability where reported
> - Losses/optimizers used as standard within each domain: PBADet employs TOOD-style supervision (IoU, DFL, CE) and SGD; 4-bit experiments use Adam/AdamW with 4-bit states; PE-DQN uses distributional C51/QR losses and learns an epistemic bonus; Dale’s Law uses SGD/AdamW with gradient clipping where noted; JEPA/MAE linear analyses center on quantile (QR) loss vs reconstruction loss, with ODE-solved learning dynamics.
> 
> All numbers and conclusions above are drawn directly from the figures and tables of the provided papers and remain within their reported scopes; we found no datasets identically shared across papers.

**naive 最终答案**

> I have gathered sufficient evidence from the five target papers. Here is the answer.
> 
> ## Matching papers for each criterion
> 
> **(a) Part-to-body association (COCO-style, MSE/cross-entropy, Precision/F1)** — **PBADet** (ICLR 2024). One-stage, anchor-free (extending YOLOv5/YOLOv7/YOLOv8 with an anchor-free head). A single 2D part-to-body center offset gives one-to-one association. The total loss is a weighted sum of classification (cross-entropy-type), IoU, DFL, and an association loss (L1, not MSE); trained with SGD over 100 epochs on BodyHands and COCO-HumanParts/CrowdHuman. It reports AP/IoU=0.5, MR−2, conditional accuracy, joint AP, and Precision/Recall/F1: e.g., vs. ED-Pose on COCO val, all-parts P/R/F1 = 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs. 24.09/45.51/31.51. Note: **MSE is not used** in PBADet's association loss, so that specific claim is not fully matched.
> 
> **(b) E/I separation + spectral learning dynamics** — **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023). Compares sign-constrained (E/I) ColEI RNNs, DANN RNNs, and standard RNNs on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, natural-object recognition. Training uses SGD with gradient clipping (not AdamW); the spectral analysis is at initialisation, not throughout training. Results: ColEI learns worse and more variably; NSE (normalized SVD entropy) anti-correlates with final test error; singular-value spectra matter more than sign constraints (spectrum transplant: ColEI gap explained 2.0%±1% vs 0.7%±0.3% for sign constraints).
> 
> **(c) JEPA biased to high-influence signals** — **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024). Analyzes deep-linear JEPA vs MAE dynamics, showing JEPA's critical time depends on the regression coefficient ρ (high-influence features) increasingly with depth, while MAE depends mainly on covariance λ. Demonstrations are on **synthetic Gaussian data and ImageNet-1K (ViT, CCA vs PCA subspace)**, not MNIST/CIFAR-100 or ResNet-50; the Transformer/ResNet-50 and MNIST/CIFAR-100 claims do **not** match.
> 
> **(d) Sub-byte optimizer states** — **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023). Adam/AdamW with 4-bit first moment (B128 block + DE), second moment with rank-1 normalization and a linear quantizer that **excludes the zero point** (the zero-point problem) + optional factorization. Results: matches/exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet (Swin-T), E2E-NLG, WMT14, Alpaca; e.g., RoBERTa-L NLU 89.1 (vs 88.9), up to 57.7% memory saved, LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU. This criterion matches well.
> 
> **(e) Ensemble value distributions + 1-Wasserstein disagreement** — **PE-DQN "Diverse Projection Ensembles for Distributional RL"** (ICLR 2024). Ensembles of quantile and categorical projections; exploration bonus is ensemble disagreement measured by **average 1-Wasserstein distance**, propagated via distributional TD errors. On bsuite, 4 models roughly halve median episodic regret on deep sea (N up to 100) vs BDQN+P/IDS/DLTV; on VizDoom MyWayHome only PE-DQN solves all 10 seeds. This matches well.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis of experimental results
> 
> Across the five, the strongest quantitative stories are in (a), (d), and (e). PBADet gives clear SOTA gains over its anchor-based/body-to-part baseline BPJDet (JointAP 85.98 vs 78.13, HandAP 89.1 vs 85.3, all on the anchor-free variant) and over pose-estimator ED-Pose in P/R/F1 (~+15 F1). PE-DQN's core claim is efficiency: comparable or better exploration than larger baselines at only 4 ensemble members, with ablations confirming diverse projections and TD-error propagation are both required. The 4-bit optimizer achieves "lossless" fine-tuning and comparable pretraining to 32-bit across five task families, with the zero-point-excluding linear mapping (not block size or stochastic rounding) being the key factor for second-moment accuracy.
> 
> In contrast, (b) and (c) are diagnostic/theoretical. The Dale's Law paper's key quantitative contribution is correlational—NSE at initialisation predicts performance (and specifically small balanced networks beat large skewed ones)—rather than reporting SOTA accuracy; its spectral finding (multimodal/dispersed singular values for ColEI) explains the learning deficit more than sign constraints. The JEPA paper's result is a dynamic-ordering bias (JEPA greedily learns high-ρ features, MAE learns high-λ features), verified on linear models, with the ImageNet-1K ViT experiment confirming JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace than MAE.
> 
> ## Gaps to note (claims not supported by the evidence)
> 
> - (a) MSE is not the association loss (L1 is used); cross-entropy is implied via classification but not stated as such.
> - (b) The analysis is at initialisation and uses SGD/gradient clipping, not SGD/AdamW dynamics over training.
> - (c) MNIST/CIFAR-100 and ResNet-50/Transformer demonstrations are absent; the paper uses deep-linear models and an ImageNet-1K ViT (I-JEPA vs MAE) CCA experiment.
> 
> The five papers are not directly comparable to one another (different tasks, metrics, and experimental protocols), so a unified ranking is not meaningful; the overlaps are thematic (e.g., spectral analysis in (b) and (c); uncertainty via distribution disagreement in (e)).

**community 最终答案**

> Based on my searches, I found documents covering four of the five requested topics. Here is the summary with experimental comparison:
> 
> ## (a) Part-to-body association — **PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> One-stage, anchor-free part-body association using a single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale YOLO features. Losses: bounding-box IoU loss (L_iou), DFL loss (L_dfl), classification loss (L_cls, i.e., cross-entropy-type), and a dedicated ℓ1-style association loss (L_assoc), weighted λ_iou=7.5, λ_dfl=1.5, λ_cls=0.5, λ_assoc=0.2; trained with SGD, AMP, 1024×1024 input, batch 24, YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 backbones.
> 
> **Results comparison:**
> - BodyHands (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98, vs BPJDet (anchor-based, body-to-part): 85.3 / 86.80 / 78.13. Anchor-free part-to-body beats anchor-based body-to-part on every metric.
> - Ablations: removing association loss, multi-scale offset, or task-alignment each degrades all metrics.
> - COCO-HumanParts: AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7), 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6).
> - vs ED-Pose (COCO val, hands/feet): PBADet all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51 — large gains. Note: this paper reports Precision/Recall/F1 (vs ED-Pose), but its primary protocol is AP/conditional accuracy/joint AP, not standard MSE losses.
> 
> ## (b) EI-recurrent nets with spectral analysis — **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Compares standard RNN, column-constrained EI (ColEI), and Dale's ANN (DANN) recurrent nets on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition.
> 
> **Results:** ColEI learns worst and with highest seed variance across all four tasks; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Spectral analysis (eigenvalue complex-plane plots, singular-value distributions, normalised SVD entropy NSE) shows ColEI has multimodal, dispersed singular values (non-uniform, clustered near origin) vs quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur for standard/DANN. Spectrum-transplant experiments show singular-value spectra contribute more to the gap (≈1.5–2%) than sign constraints (≈0.7–1%) or singular vectors. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra/performance; DANN stays robust (NSE≈0.95) even with 1 inhibitory unit. Caveat: the paper does not explicitly mention SGD/AdamW by name, and it is an RNN-dynamics analysis, not a standard-metrics (Precision/F1) benchmark.
> 
> ## (d) 4-bit optimizer states — **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Adam/AdamW states compressed to 4 bits via smaller block size (B128/DE) for the first moment and, for the second moment, rank-1 normalization plus a linear quantizer that excludes the zero-point (fixing the identified zero-point problem); optional factorization of the second moment (4-bit Factor).
> 
> **Results:** On NLU (RoBERTa-L/GLUE), QA (SQuAD), NLG (E2E), CLS (Swin-T/ImageNet), MT (WMT14), 4-bit matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW (e.g., 89.1 vs 88.9 NLU; 80.8 vs 81.2 CLS; 94.5 vs 94.6 QA; 26.28 vs 26.61 MT), while 8-bit AdamW, Adafactor, SM3 degrade more on some tasks (SM3 22.72 MT). Memory: 4-bit AdamW saves 57.7% on LLaMA-7B (31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; 4-bit Factor is ~4× smaller states than 8-bit. Ablations show zero exclusion (DE-0/linear) is the key for second-moment quantization, and smaller block size improves first-moment accuracy.
> 
> ## (e) Uncertainty-driven RL — **PE-DQN: "Diverse Projection Ensembles for Distributional RL"** (ICLR 2024)
> Ensembles of diverse distributional projections (quantile and categorical) with an exploration bonus = average 1-Wasserstein disagreement, propagated via distributional TD errors; optimistic action selection a=argmax[Q̂+b].
> 
> **Results:** On bsuite, PE-DQN achieves the best exploration with only 4 distributional models, roughly halving median episodic regret on deep sea (up to N=100) vs larger baselines (BDQN+P, IDS, DLTV); ablations show diverse projections and TD-based uncertainty propagation are both necessary. In VizDoom MyWayHome (dense to very sparse), only PE-DQN succeeds on all 10 seeds. Projection choice significantly changes generalization of 2nd–4th moments in reward-free deep-sea probing.
> 
> ## (c) JEPA/self-supervised — **partial match only**
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024) exactly matches the mechanism: JEPA self-distillation is biased toward high-influence features (high regression coefficient ρ) rather than raw variance, increasingly so with depth, whereas MAE prioritizes by covariance λ; confirmed with I-JEPA vs MAE ViT encoders on ImageNet-1K (64×64) via CCA, showing JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace. **However, no MNIST/CIFAR-100 or ResNet-50 experiments are reported** — the empirical validation is ImageNet ViT only, and the rest is deep-linear theory.
> 
> ## Overall comparison
> - **Best supported matches:** PBADet (a), 4-bit optimizers (d), PE-DQN (e), and Dale's-law RNNs (b, with the caveat that optimizer names SGD/AdamW aren't explicitly stated).
> - **Partial matches:** (c) matches the mechanism and Transformer backbone but lacks the requested MNIST/CIFAR-100 and ResNet-50 demonstrations; (a) uses AP/conditional-accuracy/joint-AP and an ℓ1 association loss rather than MSE/cross-entropy, though it does report Precision/F1 against ED-Pose.
> - No single document in this collection covers all five topics; I could not find a paper demonstrating JEPA on MNIST/CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50 backbones, nor explicit SGD/AdamW spectral-dynamics results for EI RNNs.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:71 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an interactive vision and robotics system with tight GPU memory: we need robust per-person hand/face detection in crowded scenes (one-stage, anchor-free on COCO-like data) and an exploration-heavy control module where an RL agent uses distributional value ensembles to guide behavior via disagreement; our representation learning stack favors latent-space prediction to avoid noisy pixels for a feedforward classifier; training must fit in memory by using low-bit optimizer states for AdamW; and our time-series module should keep biologically plausible E/I separation in RNNs while remaining trainable. Are there papers that address these needs and discuss standard losses (MSE, CE), optimizers (SGD/Adam/AdamW), attention/Transformers, interpretability, and benchmarks like MNIST/CIFAR-100?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：3→4（Δ+1）；rounds：4→4（Δ+0）。**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results drawn strictly from the figures and tables of the five provided papers, organized to match your system needs. I highlight identical datasets where applicable, compare on similar benchmarks, and note per-dataset outcomes. 1) Per-person hand/face detection in crowded scenes (one-stage, anchor-free) Paper and methods compared on identical datasets: PBADet (ours, anchor-free) vs BPJDet (anchor-based) vs Hier R-CNN and others. Datasets: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts (COCO-based), CrowdHuman. • BodyHands (Table 1) – metrics: Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP (identical dataset across methods) – PBADet vs prior SOTA (BPJDet):   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Cond. Acc. 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Acc. 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.   Result: PBADet outperforms BPJDet on all three metrics (largest gains in conditional accuracy: +5.7 to +5.8 pts, and modest gains in joint AP). • COCOHumanParts (Tables 2 & 3) (identical dataset across methods) – detection AP and association quality (mMR−2) per category:   - Overall detection (Table 2): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) achieves AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate), APM 66.2/65.0, APL 67.2/64.4 versus BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3, APM 63.8/63.2, APL 61.8/58.9.   Result: PBADet shows notably higher APM (+2.4 pts) and APL (+5.4 pts) while overall AP.5:.95 is slightly lower.   - Per-category APs (Table 2): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) is higher for person (62.4 vs 61.3), right foot (30.9 vs 30.2), and left foot (31.5 vs 30.9); BPJDet is higher for head (56.6 vs 54.6), face (46.3 vs 44.6), hands (40.4/39.6 vs 39.0/37.7).   - Association mMR−2 (lower is better; Table 3): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) improves head (27.9 vs 30.8), face (30.5 vs 31.8), left hand (36.2 vs 41.6), right hand (40.8 vs 42.2), and left foot (47.9 vs 50.4); right foot is slightly worse (50.4 vs 49.1).   Result: PBADet yields lower (better) mismatch rates for most parts, especially hands. • CrowdHuman body–face association (Tables 5 & 6) (identical dataset across methods) – PBADet (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet and others:   - Body MR−2: PBADet (YOLOv7) 36.5 (best among listed), BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 40.7.   - Body AP: PBADet (YOLOv7) 91.6 (best among listed).   - Body–face mMR−2: PBADet (YOLOv7) 50.8 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 50.1 (similar order).   Result: PBADet achieves the lowest body miss rate and highest body AP; association mMR−2 comparable to BPJDet. Takeaway for your system: On COCO-like part-body association, PBADet’s one-stage anchor-free design delivers stronger association robustness (lower mMR−2 for key parts) and better detection at medium/large scales, with top body detection on CrowdHuman. PBADet uses SGD and standard detection/CE/IoU/DFL losses, aligning with your training stack. 2) Exploration-heavy control: distributional value ensembles with disagreement Paper and methods compared on identical benchmarks: PE-DQN vs BDQN+P, IDS-C51, DLTV-QR on the behavior suite and VizDoom. • Behavior Suite (Figure 4a): Radar of seven capability areas. Result: PE-DQN has the strongest exploration capability and wider coverage overall than baselines (BDQN+P, IDS-C51, DLTV-QR). • Deep Sea scaling (hard exploration; Figure 4b) (identical dataset across methods) – median episodic regret (lower is better) for sizes up to 100:   Result: PE-DQN scales more gracefully; the paper reports roughly half the median regret versus baselines at larger sizes. Ablations: diversity (quantile+categorical) and uncertainty propagation both matter; removing either degrades performance. • VizDoom MyWayHome (visual exploration) (Figure 5b) (identical dataset across methods):   - Dense/Sparse/Very Sparse variants: Only PE-DQN finds the target across all 10 seeds in all three settings; baselines fail on some runs (especially Sparse). Takeaway for your system: An ensemble with diverse distributional projections (categorical + quantile) and exploration bonus from average 1‑Wasserstein disagreement (plus uncertainty propagation) offers reliable deep exploration and is particularly strong in sparse/visual domains—exactly your “exploration-heavy” requirement. 3) Latent-space prediction (JEPA) vs pixel reconstruction (MAE) for representation learning Paper and methods compared on the same dataset: I‑JEPA vs MAE on ImageNet‑1K (64×64), evaluated via CCA between full data and PCA partitions (Appendix D, Figure 7). • Full-bottom (lower-variance PCA subspace) mean CCA vs epochs: I‑JEPA consistently higher than MAE across training, indicating faster alignment with low-variance (often semantic) features. • Full-top (high-variance components) mean CCA vs epochs: I‑JEPA lower than MAE, consistent with I‑JEPA de-emphasizing dominant pixel variance. Takeaway: On ImageNet‑1K (same dataset for both), JEPA learns predictive, low-variance features faster than MAE—directly supporting your choice to avoid noisy pixels with a feedforward classifier trained on latent predictions. 4) Memory-constrained training with low-bit optimizer states (AdamW) Paper and methods compared on identical datasets across multiple tasks (Table 2; Table 3); memory/time in Table 4; trainable model size in Table 5. • Natural Language Understanding (GLUE, RoBERTa‑L) – mean metric (Table 2):   - 32-bit AdamW 88.9; 8-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit Factor 88.9; Adafactor 89.1/89.3 (β1=0); SM3 87.5.   Result: 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit and 8‑bit at the same performance level. • Image classification (ImageNet‑1K, Swin‑T Top‑1, Table 2):   - 32-bit 81.2; 8-bit 81.0; 4-bit 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9; Adafactor 80.0; SM3 79.0.   Result: 4‑bit within ~0.4 pts of 32‑bit/8‑bit; better than SM3 and Adafactor. • NLG (E2E‑NLG, GPT‑2 Medium BLEU, Table 2):   - 32-bit 67.7; 8-bit 67.5; 4-bit 67.8 (best); 4-bit Factor 67.6; Adafactor 67.2; SM3 66.9. • QA (SQuAD F1, Table 2; also Table 9 EM/F1 per dataset):   - 32-bit 94.6; 8-bit 94.5; 4-bit 94.5; 4-bit Factor 94.6; SM3 91.7. • MT (WMT14 en‑de, SacreBLEU, Table 2):   - 32-bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; 4-bit 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45 (all close; SM3 22.72). • LLaMA fine‑tuning on identical eval suites (Table 3):   - 7B: 32‑bit vs 4‑bit → MMLU 38.7 vs 38.9; HellaSwag 74.6 vs 74.7; ARC‑e 61.5 vs 61.2; ARC‑c 45.1 vs 44.4; OBQA 43.4 vs 43.0 (comparable).   - 13B: 32‑bit vs 4‑bit → MMLU 46.5 vs 47.4; HellaSwag 78.8 vs 79.0; ARC‑e 63.6 vs 64.1; ARC‑c 48.3 vs 48.0; OBQA 45.2 vs 45.2.   - 33B: 32‑bit vs 4‑bit → MMLU 56.4 vs 54.9 (small drop); others similar. • Memory/time (Table 4):   - LLaMA‑7B finetuning: total GPU memory 75.40 GB (32‑bit) vs 31.87 GB (4‑bit) → 57.7% reduction; training time 3.35 h vs 3.07 h (faster).   - RoBERTa‑L: 5.31 GB (32‑bit) vs 3.00 GB (4‑bit fused) → 43.5% reduction; time 3.93 min vs 3.17 min (fused faster).   - GPT‑2 Medium: 6.89 GB → 4.62 GB (34.4% reduction), time parity with fused kernels. • Largest trainable model under budget (Table 5):   - On 24 GB: 32‑bit supports OPT‑350M; 4‑bit supports OPT‑1.3B.   - On 80 GB: 32‑bit supports OPT‑1.3B; 4‑bit supports OPT‑6.7B; and LLaMA‑7B on a single 80 GB GPU. • Second-moment quantization ablations (Table 1, E2E‑NLG):   - Zero-point removal is critical: B2048/DE (with zero) unstable runs 33% and BLEU 66.6; B2048/DE‑0 (without zero) 0% unstable, BLEU 67.5.   - Rank‑1 + Linear (no zero point) yields the best BLEU 67.8.   - Stable Embedding layers alone don’t fully recover accuracy without solving the zero‑point problem, but once zero is removed, Stable Embedding is no longer necessary. Takeaway for your system: 4‑bit AdamW (with rank‑1 normalization and a zero‑free linear mapping for second moments) matches or slightly exceeds 32‑bit/8‑bit results on GLUE, E2E‑NLG, SQuAD, and LLaMA finetuning, while saving 34–58% training memory and enabling larger models under the same GPU budget. 5) Time-series module with E/I separation (Dale’s Law) and trainability Paper and methods compared on identical datasets: ColEI (column E/I) vs DANN (Dale’s ANN) vs standard RNN on adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition task (Fig. 2 A–D). • Across all four tasks (same datasets for all three methods): ColEI performs worse than DANN and standard RNN; larger variance; gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially more (text; see Appendix Fig. 10 referenced). • Spectrum transplant experiments on identical tasks (Fig. 4 A–C):   - Sign constraints alone explain only part of the gap (impairs learning by ~0.7%±0.3% for standard RNNs, ~1%±1% for ColEI, vs total gap ~2.3%±0.6%).   - Singular value spectra differences contribute more to the gap (~1.5%±0.3% for RNNs, ~2%±1% for ColEI). • Effect of E/I ratio and network size on the same tasks (Figs. 5–7):   - Fewer inhibitory units and smaller networks → lower normalized SVD entropy and worse performance.   - Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts test error; increasing size or balancing E/I improves spectra and performance. • Conclusion from experiments: Recurrent DANNs (EI but with spectral properties like standard RNNs) learn as well as standard RNNs; ColEI’s poor learning is largely due to spectral pathologies, not just sign constraints. Takeaway for your system: To keep biologically plausible E/I separation with stable trainability in time-series models, adopt the DANN-style EI architecture (or otherwise control the recurrent weight spectra). Evidence on identical datasets shows DANN matches standard RNNs, while ColEI degrades performance unless spectra are corrected. 6) Cross-cutting comparisons on similar dataset types and training stacks • Optimizers and losses: PBADet trains with SGD and standard detection losses (IoU, DFL, CE) including an L1 association loss; the 4‑bit study uses AdamW across NLP/CV/MT tasks; both match your stated preferences. • Vision backbones and attention/Transformers: Swin‑T (Transformer) is used in the 4‑bit optimizer study (ImageNet‑1K), JEPA compares I‑JEPA vs MAE for ViT on ImageNet‑1K; PBADet uses YOLO-family (adapted anchor-free head). • Benchmarks: MNIST (sequential) appears in the Dale’s Law study; ImageNet‑1K in JEPA and the 4‑bit study; COCO-derived COCOHumanParts in PBADet; VizDoom and the behavior suite for RL exploration. Summary mapping to your requirements • Robust per-person hand/face detection in crowds (COCO-like): PBADet delivers superior association robustness and medium/large scale detection on COCOHumanParts, plus best body AP and MR−2 on CrowdHuman; it’s one-stage, anchor-free, and validated against strong baselines on the same datasets. • Exploration-heavy RL with distributional ensembles and disagreement: PE-DQN’s diverse projection ensemble (categorical + quantile), trained on shared TD targets, produces reliable disagreement and outperforms BDQN+P/IDS-C51/DLTV-QR on identical behavior suite/VizDoom tasks; ablations show both diversity and uncertainty propagation are essential. • Latent-space prediction to avoid noisy pixels: I‑JEPA vs MAE on ImageNet‑1K shows JEPA aligns faster with low-variance, semantically useful features (higher full‑bottom mean CCA), while de-emphasizing high-variance pixels (lower full‑top CCA). • Training with low-bit optimizer states (AdamW): 4‑bit AdamW retains accuracy across GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG, WMT14, and LLaMA finetuning while saving 34–58% memory; it also scales model size under fixed memory. Zero-point removal for the second moment is crucial to stability; rank-1 normalization + linear mapping (no zero) gives the best E2E numbers. • Biologically plausible E/I separation in RNNs with trainability: DANN-style EI recurrent networks match standard RNN performance on identical tasks (adding problem, seq. MNIST, PTB, object recognition), whereas ColEI degrades due to spectral issues; experiments show spectra (not just signs) govern performance and that normalized SVD entropy predicts learning quality. All comparisons above are taken directly from the papers’ figures/tables and concern identical datasets within each domain, comparisons on similar problem types, and specific per-dataset outcomes as required.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, here are papers matching each of your five needs, with experimental results compared.
> 
> **1. Hand/face detection in crowded scenes (PBADet, ICLR 2024)**
> One-stage anchor-free part-body association detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones; SGD optimizer; IoU+DFL+classification+association losses). On BodyHands: Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Acc 92.62, JointAP 85.98 with only 36.9M params (YOLOv7), beating BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39 (86.1M) and far ahead of OpenPose (39.7/74.03/27.81) and BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48). On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet while leading person/feet AP and AP_M/AP_L; on CrowdHuman face-body it achieves body MR-2=36.5, face AP=81.6. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each improve accuracy.
> 
> **2. Exploration via distributional value ensembles (PE-DQN, ICLR 2024)**
> Ensemble of categorical (C51) and quantile (QR-DQN) projections; exploration bonus = ensemble disagreement (avg 1-Wasserstein distance) propagated via distributional TD errors. On bsuite it gives the best exploration with only 4 models, roughly halving median episodic regret on deep sea (N up to 100) versus BDQN+P, IDS, DLTV. In VizDoom MyWayHome (dense to very sparse), only PE-DQN succeeds on all 10 seeds. Both diverse projections and TD-based uncertainty propagation are necessary.
> 
> **3. Latent-space prediction vs noisy pixels (JEPA, NeurIPS 2024)**
> Analyzes why predicting in latent space (JEPA, MSE in feature space) avoids noisy/pixel-level features that MAE (pixel reconstruction) must fit. Theory + ImageNet-1K: JEPA is biased toward high-influence (high regression coefficient) features and suppresses noise increasingly with depth, while MAE ordering follows eigenvalue magnitude; I-JEPA aligns faster with the perceptual (low-variance) PCA subspace than MAE (CCA metric). This supports your feedforward-classifier preference for latent prediction.
> 
> **4. Low-bit AdamW optimizer states (NeurIPS 2023)**
> 4-bit quantized first/second moments (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, optional factorization) apply to SGD/Adam/AdamW. Results: matches or slightly beats 32-bit AdamW — RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, GPT-2M E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7, QA 94.5 vs 94.6, MT 26.28 vs 26.61 — while cutting memory up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 31.87GB vs 75.40GB). 4-bit Factor beats Adafactor/SM3 in accuracy at similar memory efficiency.
> 
> **5. Biologically plausible E/I-separated, trainable RNNs (NeurIPS 2023)**
> Compares standard RNN, ColEI (sign-constrained E/I columns) and DANN (separate E/I projection matrices). On adding, sequential MNIST, Penn TreeBank, and object recognition, ColEI learns worse and with more variance; DANN stays robust and learns well even with a single inhibitory neuron, and is robust to EI-ratio/network-size changes. Gradient clipping mitigates ColEI's deficit. The cause is the initial singular-value spectrum (normalized SVD entropy anti-correlates with error), not the sign constraints — so DANN gives trainable E/I separation for your time-series module.
> 
> **On your other mentioned topics (from the collection):** MSE is used in the JEPA/MAE and G-Sim time-series losses; cross-entropy appears in classification heads (e.g., PBADet's classification loss, RZ-NAS). Optimizers SGD/Adam/AdamW appear in PBADet, the 4-bit paper, and a Transformer/GRU/SINDy time-series baseline (DyNODE uses Adam, the Transformer uses AdamW at lr 5e-5). Attention/Transformers appear in the time-series baselines, Swin-T (in the 4-bit paper), ViT (GRAFT), and interpretability works (mechanistic in-context meta-learning circuits, Neural Comprehension/CoNN, TuCo, G-Sim). MNIST/CIFAR-100 appear as benchmarks in the E/I-RNN paper (sequential MNIST) and Hessian/BSO/NFTS papers (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100). No single paper covers all your constraints; PBADet, PE-DQN, the JEPA analysis, the 4-bit optimizer paper, and the Dale's-Law RNN paper together cover each need, and all report quantitative comparisons of the type requested.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection contains papers for each module, and they report concrete experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Detection: PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free, hand/face + body association)
> - On **BodyHands**: PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves hand AP 89.1, cond. accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 vs. BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39 — better despite a smaller model (36.9M vs 86.1M params).
> - On **COCOHumanParts** (face/hands/feet with COCO-like data) it outperforms BPJDet and HierR-CNN; on **CrowdHuman** face-body it leads body MR-2 (36.5 vs 39.7–41.3) with competitive AP.
> - Losses: IoU + DFL + classification + association loss (L1); trained with SGD, AMP, 1024² input — a tight-memory-friendly one-stage anchor-free design.
> 
> ## 2. Exploration via distributional value ensembles + disagreement: PE-DQN
> - Uses an ensemble of categorical (C51) + quantile (QR-DQN) projections; exploration bonus = average **1-Wasserstein ensemble disagreement**, propagated through distributional TD errors.
> - **bsuite**: with only 4 models it roughly halves median episodic regret on deep-sea (up to N=100) vs. larger BDQN+P, IDS, DLTV ensembles; on **VizDoom MyWayHome** only PE-DQN succeeds across all 10 seeds in all sparsity variants. Ablations show diverse projections *and* TD-based uncertainty propagation are both necessary.
> 
> ## 3. Latent-space prediction for representation learning: JEPA vs MAE
> - "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" shows latent-space prediction (JEPA/self-distillation) is biased toward high-influence, low-variance (perceptual) features, while MAE pixel reconstruction chases variance/ noise.
> - **ImageNet-1K**: I-JEPA features align faster (higher CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace than MAE, and JEPA gives better downstream classification with fewer optimization steps — supports a feedforward classifier over latent features.
> - Related: LDReg (local dimensionality regularization) improves SSL linear-evaluation accuracy on ImageNet and COCO detection; the contrastive-embedding analysis improves top-1 on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100.
> 
> ## 4. Low-bit optimizer states for AdamW: 4-bit optimizers
> - 4-bit AdamW **matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW** on GLUE (RoBERTa-L 89.1), SQuAD (94.5), E2E-NLG (67.8), WMT14 (26.28), ImageNet Swin-T (80.8 vs 81.2), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning, with up to **57.7% memory savings** and LLaMA-7B trainable on one 80GB GPU. Ablations: smaller block (B128) for first moment, rank-1/zero-excluded quantization or factorization for second moment are what make 4-bit lossless.
> 
> ## 5. Biologically plausible E/I RNNs that stay trainable
> - "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" compares standard RNNs, column-constrained E/I (ColEI), and DANN (separate E/I populations) on adding, **sequential MNIST**, PTB, and object recognition.
> - ColEI trains poorly (worse final error, higher variance); **DANN keeps E/I separation but matches standard RNNs** and is robust — it learns well even with 1 inhibitory neuron. The gap is caused by the initial singular-value spectrum (normalized SVD entropy anti-correlates with error), not the sign constraint.
> 
> ## 6. Standard losses, optimizers, attention/interpretability, MNIST/CIFAR-100
> - The Hessian-spectrum study covers exactly these: LeNet/FCN/ResNet18/ViT on **MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100**, trained with SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, Yogi, RAdam, etc.; power-law Hessian spectra emerge only in well-trained nets and predict generalization (e.g., d_ks correlates with LLM generalization up to 0.98). It also uses Transformers (ViT, GPT-2, TinyLlama) and discusses interpretability of loss landscapes.
> - The attention-only transformer study (in-context meta-learning) is a mechanistic-interpretability paper identifying circuits/heads (induction-head-like Full-Context Circuit at 100% accuracy).
> - The 4-bit optimizer paper trains Transformer-base (WMT) and Swin-T (ImageNet) with AdamW.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Best matches to your stack**: PBADet (detection), PE-DQN (disagreement-driven exploration), JEPA (latent prediction for classifiers), 4-bit AdamW (memory), DANN (trainable E/I RNNs) — each is the direct counterpart of one of your requirements.
> - **Trade-offs**: PBADet is one-stage/anchor-free but its SOTA numbers come from large YOLO backbones (86.1M); the 4-bit optimizer offsets that by cutting ~43–58% of optimizer memory, so the combination fits a tight GPU budget. PE-DQN needs only 4 ensemble members (cheaper than 5–20-member baselines) yet gives the best exploration. JEPA is theoretically analyzed on deep *linear* networks with ImageNet confirmation (limits: nonlinear/general cases not proven). DANN gives biological plausibility without the learning penalty of naive ColEI, but the paper does not propose new E/I-specific training beyond projected gradient descent.
> - **No single paper covers all six needs**; they form a matched set: MSE/CE losses, SGD/Adam/AdamW optimizers, Transformers, interpretability, and MNIST/CIFAR-100 benchmarks appear in the Hessian/optimizer/contrastive papers, while each specialized module (detection, RL, JEPA, 4-bit, E/I) is validated on its own benchmark.

### paperscope:results_comparison:74 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively address: (1) avoiding local and global dimensional collapse in self-supervised learning via local intrinsic dimensionality regularization and analysis of feature embeddings; (2) the implicit bias of joint-embedding predictive approaches compared to reconstruction (e.g., how cosine-similarity vs. MSE objectives shape learned features); (3) memory-efficient fine-tuning with 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW and SGD on Transformers and ResNet-50; (4) spectral perspectives on recurrent networks under excitatory/inhibitory constraints for interpretability; and (5) a one-stage anchor-free method for associating detected human parts to the correct body, evaluated on COCO. I’m looking for works reporting results on datasets like ImageNet, COCO, CIFAR-100, and MNIST, using losses such as cosine similarity and cross-entropy (CE), and discussing regularization strategies, fine-tuning, and practical metrics.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of the experimental results reported across five works that collectively address (i) local/global dimensional collapse in self-supervised learning (SSL), (ii) JEPA’s implicit bias vis-à-vis reconstruction objectives (MAE), (iii) memory-efficient fine-tuning with 4-bit optimizer states, (iv) spectral perspectives on recurrent networks under Dale’s Law, and (v) a one-stage anchor-free method for part–body association on COCO.
> 
> 1) On identical datasets (or dataset families)
> - ImageNet (representation learning; linear probing and related analyses)
>   • LDReg (ICLR 2024): Improves linear evaluation Top-1 on ImageNet for multiple SSL baselines (ResNet-50 unless noted), while increasing effective rank and geometric mean of LID:
>     - SimCLR: 64.3 → 64.8 (+0.5); Effective rank: 470.2 → 529.6; LID geom. mean: 18.8 → 20.0 (Table 1).
>     - SimCLR-Tuned: 67.2 → 67.5; Effective rank: 525.8 → 561.7; LID geom. mean: 24.9 → 26.1 (Table 1).
>     - BYOL: 67.6 → 68.5 (+0.9); Effective rank: 583.8 → 594.0; LID geom. mean: 15.9 → 22.3 (Table 1).
>     - ViT-B encoder, SimCLR: 72.9 → 73.0; Effective rank: 283.7 → 326.1 (Table 1).
>     - ViT-B encoder, MAE: 57.0 → 57.6; Effective rank: 86.4 → 154.1; LID geom. mean: 25.8 → 29.8 (Table 1).
>   • JEPA vs MAE (NeurIPS 2024): On ImageNet (64×64), empirical CCA analyses show I-JEPA’s representations align more strongly with the bottom PCA subspace than MAE during training (Appendix D, Fig. 7): JEPA exhibits higher full–bottom mean CCA than MAE throughout training and lower full–top mean CCA, consistent with JEPA prioritizing predictive low-variance (semantic) features versus MAE prioritizing variance-heavy reconstruction.
>   • 4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023): ImageNet classification with Swin-T shows 4-bit AdamW maintains accuracy close to full precision: 80.8% vs 81.2% Top-1 (Table 2), while reducing memory (see below). 
> 
> - COCO family datasets
>   • PBADet (ICLR 2024): On COCOHumanParts, PBADet delivers competitive or superior multi-part detection/association versus state-of-the-art:
>     - All-category AP (original/subordinate, YOLOv5l6): 43.6/43.3 (BPJDet) vs 43.0/41.8 (PBADet); however PBADet achieves higher APM (66.2 vs 63.8) and APL (67.2 vs 61.8), and is comparable across per-category APs (Table 2). For part–body association robustness (average mMR−2; lower is better), PBADet achieves lower values across most categories (e.g., head: 27.9 vs 30.8; face: 30.5 vs 31.8; left hand: 36.2 vs 41.6; right hand: 40.8 vs 42.2; Table 3).
>   • LDReg: Fine-tuning RCNN-C4 on COCO detection shows consistent AP improvements when starting from LDReg-pretrained representations:
>     - SimCLR (100 epochs): APbb 35.24 → 35.26; APmk 31.30 → 31.38.
>     - BYOL (100 epochs): APbb 36.30 → 36.82; APmk 32.17 → 32.47.
>     - SimCLR (1000 epochs): APbb 36.48 → 37.15; APmk 32.12 → 32.82 (Table 3).
>   • PBADet vs crowd detectors (CrowdHuman): PBADet achieves best MR−2 on body (36.5) and highest body AP (91.6), with competitive mMR−2 for body–face associations (Table 5 & 6). 
> 
> 2) On similar dataset types and tasks
> - Vision classification and detection
>   • LDReg consistently boosts linear probing across transfer datasets (ResNet-50; 30 epochs probing): at longer pretraining and larger batch (4096; 1000 epochs), gains are larger, e.g., ImageNet 69.0 → 69.8; CIFAR-10 90.1 → 91.8; CIFAR-100 71.6 → 75.1; Birdsnap 37.5 → 38.7; Cars 35.3 → 41.6; DTD 70.7 → 70.8 (Table 2). 
>   • PBADet yields state-of-the-art on BodyHands: Hand AP 89.1 (YOLOv7), conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98; and improved metrics versus BPJDet at matched backbone (YOLOv5l6: joint AP 85.73 vs 84.39; Table 1). 
> - RNN sequence and language tasks under Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023)
>   • Across adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task, recurrent Dale’s ANNs (DANNs) and standard RNNs learn well, while simple column EI partitioning (ColEI) learns worse (Fig. 2 A–D). Spectrum transplant experiments show most of the performance gap stems from the singular value spectrum rather than sign constraints (Fig. 4 B–C): spectrum changes accounted for ~1.5–2.0% error differences versus ~0.7–1.0% for sign constraints. NSE (normalized SVD entropy) anti-correlates with test error across EI ratios and network sizes: fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks → lower NSE → higher errors (Figs. 5–7).
> 
> 3) On specific datasets
> - BodyHands (PBADet, Table 1)
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1; conditional accuracy 92.62; joint AP 85.98.
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1; conditional accuracy 92.71; joint AP 85.73.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9; conditional accuracy 86.91; joint AP 84.39.
>   → PBADet outperforms BPJDet on all three metrics at matched backbone size.
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (PBADet, Table 2–3)
>   • Overall AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate): PBADet 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6); BPJDet 43.6/43.3 (YOLOv5l6).
>   • Size-specific AP: PBADet higher APM/APL (66.2/67.2) than BPJDet (63.8/61.8). 
>   • Average mMR−2 per category (lower better): PBADet best or tied across head, face, hands, feet (e.g., head 27.9 vs 30.8; right hand 40.8 vs 42.2).
> 
> - CrowdHuman (PBADet, Tables 5–6)
>   • Face–body: PBADet (YOLOv7) yields best body MR−2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6); mMR−2 ~50.8 (competitive). 
> 
> - ImageNet + transfers (LDReg, Tables 1–2)
>   • Linear probing gains across SimCLR, BYOL, MAE; larger gains appear with stronger augmentations or longer pretraining; LDReg raises effective rank and geometric mean LID, addressing both local and global collapse.
> 
> - LLaMA instruction tuning and commonsense benchmarks (4-bit optimizers, Table 3)
>   • 4-bit AdamW matches or exceeds full-precision across sizes:
>     - LLaMA-13B: MMLU 47.4 (4-bit) vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8; ARC-e 64.1 vs 63.6; ARC-c 48.0 vs 48.3; OBQA 45.2 vs 45.2.
>     - LLaMA-7B and LLaMA-33B show similarly competitive results across tasks (Table 3).
> 
> - NLU, MT, CLS, NLG (4-bit optimizers, Table 2)
>   • 4-bit AdamW vs 32-bit AdamW:
>     - RoBERTa-L NLU mean: 89.1 vs 88.9.
>     - Swin-T ImageNet CLS: 80.8 vs 81.2.
>     - GPT-2 Medium E2E-NLG BLEU: 67.8 vs 67.7.
>     - RoBERTa-L QA F1: 94.5 vs 94.6.
>     - Transformer WMT14 en–de SacreBLEU: 26.28 vs 26.61.
>   • 4-bit Factor is also comparable, often within measurement noise (Table 2).
>   • Memory/time: large savings and competitive throughput (Table 4): e.g., LLaMA-7B total memory 75.40 GB → 31.87 GB (−57.7%); training time 3.35 h → 3.07 h; enables larger models (Table 5).
> 
> 4) Losses, regularization strategies, and optimizers used
> - Losses
>   • BYOL uses scaled cosine similarity; SimCLR uses InfoNCE (cross-entropy style); MAE and JEPA optimize squared error (MSE) variants in latent vs input spaces (Section 1 of JEPA paper: LJEPA vs LMAE). PBADet trains detection heads with IoU, DFL, classification loss and a quadratic part–body association loss (Eq. 3–4). 
> - Regularization and collapse
>   • LDReg explicitly regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality (LID) via asymptotic Fisher–Rao geometry, increasing geometric mean LID and effective rank (Tables 1–3; Fig. 2). 
>   • Dale’s Law study shows spectral pathologies (multimodal singular value spectra, low NSE) explain poor learning in ColEI; spectrum transplant and NSE–error anti-correlation confirm spectral properties are more predictive than sign constraints alone (Figs. 3–7). 
>   • JEPA vs MAE: deep linear analyses and simulations (Figs. 1–5) show JEPA prioritizes high-influence features (high regression coefficients ρ) while MAE favors high covariance λ, leading to different learning orders; experiments on ImageNet confirm JEPA’s stronger alignment to perceptual (low-variance) subspaces (Appendix D, Fig. 7).
> - Optimizers and fine-tuning
>   • 4-bit optimizers: Adam/AdamW/SGD variants with novel quantizers (rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion) reliably match 32-bit accuracy on Transformers and ResNet-50 while cutting memory by ~35–58% (Tables 2, 4, 5). 
>   • LDReg SSL pretraining used LARS for large-batch training; downstream COCO finetuning used SGD in RCNN-C4. PBADet training used SGD with NMS-decoding.
> 
> 5) Overall comparative trends
> - Avoiding collapse in SSL (local/global)
>   • LDReg consistently increases local LID and global effective rank, yielding accuracy gains in SimCLR, SimCLR-Tuned, BYOL, and MAE (Tables 1–3). Gains are larger with longer pretraining and stronger augmentations (Fig. 2b; Table 2). 
>   • JEPA’s implicit bias toward influential features complements LDReg’s dimensional regularization: JEPA focuses on low-variance semantic signals (ImageNet CCA) while LDReg enforces high local dimensionality to prevent underfilling.
> - Memory-efficient optimization
>   • 4-bit optimizer states enable training and finetuning of larger Transformers and CNNs under fixed memory, with near-parity accuracy to 32-bit baselines and better throughput in multi-GPU/FSDP settings (Tables 2, 4, 5). 
> - Spectral perspectives under Dale’s Law
>   • DANN and standard RNNs outperform ColEI across tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and naturalistic recognition). Most of the gap is explained by singular value spectra (and NSE), not merely sign constraints. Gradient clipping helps ColEI but does not close the gap (Fig. 2, Fig. 4).
> - One-stage anchor-free part–body association
>   • PBADet sets or matches SOTA on BodyHands and is competitive/on par with BPJDet/Hier R-CNN on COCOHumanParts, with stronger performance for medium/large objects (APM/APL) and lower mismatch rates mMR−2 across parts (Tables 1–3). On CrowdHuman, PBADet achieves best MR−2 and body AP (Tables 5–6).
> 
> In summary: (i) LDReg measurably improves SSL representations on ImageNet and transfers, addressing both local and global dimensional collapse. (ii) JEPA’s learning dynamics favor influential features (high ρ) compared to MAE’s covariance-driven order (high λ), with practical differences verified by CCA on ImageNet. (iii) 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW/SGD preserve accuracy across NLU, MT, CLS, NLG, and LLaMA instruction tuning, while substantially reducing memory and enabling larger models/training regimes. (iv) Under Dale’s Law, recurrent DANNs and standard RNNs outperform ColEI, with spectral properties (NSE, singular value distributions) predicting performance across sizes/EI ratios. (v) PBADet—an anchor-free, one-stage method—achieves strong part–body association on COCOHumanParts and state-of-the-art results on BodyHands and CrowdHuman, particularly excelling in medium/large object AP and lower mismatch rates.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers that match your five topics, followed by a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Matching papers
> 
> 1. **LDReg: Local Dimensionality Regularized Self-Supervised Learning** (Huang et al., ICLR 2024) — Addresses local and global dimensional collapse in SSL via local intrinsic dimensionality (LID) regularization based on an asymptotic Fisher-Rao metric; shows representations can span high-dimensional space globally but collapse locally.
> 
> 2. **Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features** (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024) — Analyzes the implicit bias of joint-embedding predictive (JEPA/self-distillation) vs. reconstruction (MAE) objectives; proves JEPA prioritizes high-influence features while MAE prioritizes high-covariance (even noisy) features, via cosine-similarity-style latent prediction vs. pixel-space MSE reconstruction.
> 
> 3. **4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States** (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023) — Memory-efficient optimization with 4-bit first/second moment states for Adam/AdamW (smaller block size B128, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, rank-1 normalization, optional second-moment factorization), evaluated on Transformers (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B) and vision (Swin-T on ImageNet). Note: the framework is general (SGD included in theory/convergence proof), but experiments focus on Adam/AdamW; no ResNet-50 result is reported in context.
> 
> 4. **Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly** (Li, Cornford et al., NeurIPS 2023) — Spectral perspective on recurrent networks under excitatory/inhibitory (Dale's law) constraints; shows initial singular-value spectrum (measured by normalized SVD entropy) matters more than sign constraints for interpretability of learning performance.
> 
> 5. **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association** (Gao et al., ICLR 2024) — One-stage anchor-free detector associating detected human parts (hands, face, feet) to the correct body via a single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on COCO (COCOHumanParts, COCO val), CrowdHuman, and BodyHands.
> 
> A closely related additional paper, **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (Lee et al.), analyzes cosine-similarity-based contrastive objectives, reporting top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-100.
> 
> ## Comparison and analysis of experimental results
> 
> **1. SSL representation quality (LDReg vs. JEPA/MAE).** LDReg (ImageNet, ResNet-50/ViT-B) improves linear evaluation and transfer across methods: SimCLR 64.3→64.8 (100 epochs), 69.0→69.8 (1000 epochs); BYOL and MAE also improve; CIFAR-100 71.2→70.6 (100 ep) but 71.6→75.1 (1000 ep), showing longer pretraining gives larger gains; COCO object detection APbb 35.24→36.30. Global covariance/variance regularizers barely helped, and forcing very low LID caused complete collapse. The JEPA paper (ImageNet-1K, CCA) shows I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace than MAE features — i.e., JEPA's implicit bias yields more semantic features, complementing LDReg's finding that locally low-dimensional features are undesirable. Both converge on "feature quality/locally informative embeddings matter."
> 
> **2. Cosine-similarity vs. MSE-style objectives.** The JEPA paper (deep linear networks + ImageNet) proves JEPA (latent-space prediction) prioritizes influential features, while MAE (MSE reconstruction) prioritizes noisy high-variance features; the bias strengthens with depth. The contrastive-similarity paper adds an auxiliary loss reducing variance of negative-pair cosine similarities: on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-100 it improves top-1 accuracy across temperatures (0.07–2.0) and small batch sizes — indicating cosine-similarity-based SSL benefits from controlling similarity variance.
> 
> **3. Memory-efficient fine-tuning (4-bit optimizers).** Results: 4-bit AdamW matches/exceeds 32-bit AdamW on all fine-tuning tasks (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; GPT-2 E2E BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning on Alpaca is on par (e.g., 13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5, HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8). Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9GB). Sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor β1=0, SM3) degrade, especially on classification, whereas 4-bit variants stay near-lossless — showing quantization with proper outlier handling beats factorization-only approaches. The convergence proof covers quantized SGD(M), though SGD was not empirically benchmarked.
> 
> **4. Spectral analysis of EI recurrent networks.** On sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, adding problem, and object recognition: standard RNNs and Dale's-ANN RNNs (DANN) learn well; column-constrained EI RNNs (ColEI) learn worse with higher variance across seeds. Sign constraints explain only ~1% of the gap (2.3±0.6%); the singular-value spectrum is the dominant factor — ColEI has multimodal dispersed singular values vs. unimodal quarter-circle (Marchenko-Pastur) spectra for standard/DANN RNNs. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance across sizes/EI ratios; smaller networks with fewer inhibitory units have worse spectra. Gradient clipping mitigates the deficit.
> 
> **5. Part-body association (PBADet).** On COCOHumanParts, PBADet (YOLOv7) reaches AP 42.7 and (YOLOv5l6) 43.0, outperforming prior state-of-the-art (HierR-CNN, BPJDet). On BodyHands, it achieves Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 vs. BPJDet 85.3/86.80/78.13; ablations show association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each help. On CrowdHuman face-body association, body MR-2 36.5–37.5 beats BPJDet (39.7–41.3) with competitive AP (~91.4–91.6). Against ED-Pose on COCO val, PBADet roughly doubles hand precision/recall/F1 (e.g., left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87), showing the anchor-free single-offset design is more efficient and accurate than two-stage/heuristic association.
> 
> ## Cross-paper synthesis
> 
> - All papers report that their **regularization/constraint design** (LID, spectral shape, low-bit states, single association offset) delivers near-lossless or improved performance relative to strong baselines, with the largest gains on hard settings (small batches, low-ratio inhibitory populations, crowded scenes, longer pretraining).
> - Datasets overlap as requested: ImageNet (LDReg, JEPA, 4-bit Swin-T), CIFAR-10/100 (LDReg, similarity paper), COCO (LDReg detection, PBADet), sequential MNIST (Dale's law paper). Cross-entropy fine-tuning (e.g., GLUE classification) appears in the 4-bit paper; cosine-similarity losses in the SSL papers.
> - **Caveats from the context:** no empirical ResNet-50 result for 4-bit optimizers (only Swin-T on ImageNet; SGD only in theory); the JEPA result is proven for deep linear networks with qualitative ImageNet support; LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch neighbors; PBADet's CrowdHuman advantage narrows for single-part tasks.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers addressing the five requirements
> 
> 1. **LDReg: Local Dimensionality Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning** (ICLR 2024) — regularizes *local intrinsic dimensionality* (LID) via a Fisher-Rao metric to avoid both local and global dimensional collapse of SSL embeddings (SimCLR, BYOL, MAE, etc.). ✔ requirement (1)
> 2. **Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024) — analyzes the implicit bias of joint-embedding predictive (JEPA) vs. reconstruction (MAE) objectives with deep linear networks; complements **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (cosine-similarity InfoNCE analysis, variance-reduction loss). ✔ requirement (2)
> 3. **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023) — 4-bit quantized first/second moments for Adam/AdamW (framework also covers SGD(M) with a convergence proof), for Transformers (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, Swin-T, Transformer, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B) and image classification on ImageNet (Swin-T). ✔ requirement (3)
> 4. **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023) — spectral analysis of recurrent networks under excitatory/inhibitory (Dale's law) constraints; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) as an interpretability/performance diagnostic. ✔ requirement (4)
> 5. **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024) — single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free YOLO-style detectors, evaluated on COCO (COCOHumanParts, COCO val), BodyHands, CrowdHuman. ✔ requirement (5)
> 
> ## Comparison and analysis of experimental results
> 
> **LDReg (dimensional-collapse regularization).** On ImageNet (ResNet-50, linear eval) LDReg improves SimCLR from 64.3→64.8 (100 epochs, bs 2048) and 69.0→69.8 (1000 epochs, bs 4096); on CIFAR-100 71.6→75.1 and CIFAR-10 90.1→91.8 at 1000 epochs (smaller gains at 100 epochs). On COCO detection, gains are modest but consistent: SimCLR APbb 35.24→35.26 (100ep) and 36.48→37.15 (1000ep); BYOL 36.30→36.82. Longer pretraining yields larger gains; effective rank correlates with quality within a method but not across methods. Global covariance/variance regularizers barely help, while forcing very low LID causes collapse — confirming low LID is undesirable.
> 
> **JEPA vs. MAE (implicit bias).** Exact ODE analysis shows JEPA learns features with high regression coefficient ρ first (greedy in ρ), whereas MAE orders by eigenvalue λ; with opposing trends JEPA can completely invert MAE's learning order. Depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression (fixed point w̄=ρ^L vs MAE ρ^(L/(L+1))), and a 1-layer JEPA matches an infinite-depth MAE. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features (CCA) than MAE, which spends capacity on high-variance but uninformative/noisy features. **Contrastive cosine-similarity analysis:** for full-batch InfoNCE, optimal embeddings give positive similarity 1 and negative −1/(n−1); mini-batch training preserves the expected negative similarity but raises its variance (worse for small batches), degrading representations; an auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves top-1 on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet plus temperature robustness.
> 
> **4-bit optimizer states.** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning tasks (RoBERTa-L GLUE 88.9→89.1; GPT-2 E2E-NLG 67.7→67.8; SQuAD 94.6→94.5) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 81.2→80.8; WMT14 26.61→26.28). LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning is comparable (e.g., 7B MMLU 38.7 vs 38.9). Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB; enables single-80GB-GPU fine-tuning); 4-bitFactor saves more (46.7% on RoBERTa-L). Sublinear-memory baselines Adafactor/SM3 degrade more, notably on ImageNet classification. So 4-bit states are effectively "lossless" with a clear memory-efficiency trade-off.
> 
> **Spectral E/I RNN analysis.** ColEI networks (column sign constraints) learn worse and with higher variance; spectrum-transplant experiments show the initial singular-value spectrum contributes more to the gap than sign constraints or singular vectors (sequential MNIST: spectrum ~1.5% error change vs ~0.7% from sign constraints). ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed (rank-one column-mean structure) while standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs match the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle; DANN stays robust even with a single inhibitory neuron. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error (sequential MNIST, naturalistic object recognition, Penn Tree Bank) — a practical pre-training diagnostic; smaller networks/fewer I units worsen both spectra and performance, and gradient clipping mitigates the ColEI deficit.
> 
> **PBADet (part-body association).** On COCOHumanParts, all-category AP is 42.7 (YOLOv7) and 43.0 (YOLOv5l6). On BodyHands it outperforms BPJDet (anchor-free part-to-body: HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 vs BPJDet 85.3/86.80/78.13), with ablations showing the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each contribute. On COCO val vs. the pose estimator ED-Pose, PBADet gives substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet (e.g., left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87). On CrowdHuman face-body association it leads in body MR-2 (36.5 vs BPJDet 40.7) with competitive face AP. The single part-to-body offset is scalable to many parts and always well-defined (one-to-one), unlike body-to-part offsets that fail when parts are invisible.
> 
> **Cross-paper observations:** (i) LDReg and the JEPA/contrastive analyses both tie representation quality to geometric/spectral structure of embeddings (LID, effective rank, negative-pair similarity variance, PCA subspace alignment) — regularizing these (local dimensionality, variance of similarities, noise suppression) improves downstream ImageNet/COCO/CIFAR results; (ii) the 4-bit optimizer work and the Dale's-law spectral work both show that careful low-precision/constrained training can be made "lossless" (4-bit AdamW) or explainable (NSE) without accuracy loss; (iii) PBADet demonstrates that a minimal anchor-free offset representation can beat multi-stage/anchor-based and even DETR/pose-estimation baselines on COCO-family benchmarks while being more efficient — analogous to how LDReg and 4-bit states achieve better efficiency/simplicity with equal or better accuracy. Datasets used span exactly the requested set: ImageNet (LDReg, 4-bit), COCO (LDReg detection, PBADet), CIFAR-10/100 (LDReg, contrastive similarity), and sequential MNIST (Dale's law).

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:77 — 数字已进入上下文，但方法标签被配错

**问题：** I am building a vision pipeline for a hospital HMI: cameras must detect hands/faces and reliably link them to the right person in crowded scenes, with a single-stage anchor-free detector evaluated on COCO. The backbone will be pretrained via self-supervised learning (we use cosine-similarity and MSE objectives) and then fine-tuned under tight GPU memory, so we need 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW/SGD. We also want to prevent local/global representation collapse, use Transformers plus some recurrent modules that respect biologically inspired excitatory/inhibitory constraints for interpretability, and validate on CIFAR-100/MNIST. Please point me to research on joint-embedding predictive learning, dimensionality regularization of feature embeddings, memory-efficient optimizers for fine-tuning, and anchor-free part-to-body association.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：4→2（Δ-2）；rounds：5→5（Δ+0）。**

两边都找到 LDReg 与 PBADet，轮次均为 5。community 将 ImageNet 的 69.0→69.8 写成 BYOL+LDReg，naive 则写作 SimCLR 长训练；这正是 judge 的主要扣分点之一。community 的 LDReg chunk 20 中可见 Markdown 表格的 4096/1000、69.0/69.8 数值，但局部表格行的模型标签不完整，容易脱离方法名解释。另有 BPJDet baseline 数值/骨干混用。更稳妥的诊断是表格结构保留和最终数字—方法—数据集绑定不足，而不是未召回数值。是否由 PDF 表格解析导致全部错误仍需对原 PDF 表格逐项比对，本报告不作这一跳跃推断。
