**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here is the research and a comparison of experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Joint-embedding predictive learning (JEPA)
> - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024): theoretically and empirically shows JEPA/self-distillation has an implicit bias toward *high-influence (predictive) features*, whereas MAE prioritizes high-covariance (often noisy) features; the bias strengthens with encoder depth. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (measured by CCA). Unlike MAE, the plain JEPA objective is susceptible to collapse (trivial constant solution), which is why stop-gradient/self-distillation is needed — relevant to your collapse-prevention requirement.
> 
> ## 2. Dimensionality regularization of embeddings
> - **LDReg (ICLR 2024)**: regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality (LID) via an asymptotic Fisher-Rao metric; increasing local dimensionality avoids *local* dimensional collapse (representations can fill space globally yet collapse locally, e.g., BYOL). Results: consistently improves linear evaluation and transfer for SimCLR, SimCLR-Tuned, BYOL, MAE, and also MoCo/VICReg/Barlow Twins. Selected numbers (ResNet-50, ImageNet): BYOL 67.6→68.5; SimCLR (1000 ep) 69.0→69.8 ImageNet, CIFAR-100 71.6→75.1; COCO detection APbb 36.48→37.15. Global covariance/variance regularizers (VICReg-style) barely helped (67.6→67.8), while LDReg gives ~1% gain — i.e., local regularization outperforms global decorrelation. Limitation: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch neighbors.
> 
> ## 3. Memory-efficient optimizers (4-bit states)
> - **"4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023)**: compresses first/second moments of Adam/AdamW to 4-bit (smaller block B128 for first moment; zero-point-excluding linear + rank-1 normalization, optionally factored "4-bit Factor" for second moment). Results: matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning) and is comparable on pretraining (ImageNet Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14). Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B fits one 80GB GPU; 4× larger OPT models trainable under a budget). Comparison: 8-bit AdamW is worse on memory (37.1% vs 43.1% saving on RoBERTa-L); sublinear-memory Adafactor/SM3 save more memory but degrade accuracy, particularly on image classification. Caveat: without fused kernels 4-bit is slower than 8-bit; the paper covers SGD(M) convergence theoretically as well (quantized SGD), so SGD is supported too.
> 
> ## 4. Anchor-free part-to-body association
> - **PBADet (ICLR 2024)**: one-stage, anchor-free detector with a *single part-to-body center offset* (part→body), built on YOLOv5/YOLOv7 with three heads (box, class, displacement) and task-alignment supervision. Experimental comparison (BodyHands, VOC AP): PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M) achieves HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 86.1M) 85.9/86.91/84.39 — better association with a smaller model. Ablations: adding the association loss boosts Cond. Accuracy from 80.78→92.62 (hand detection AP unchanged); multi-scale offsets and task alignment each add gains. On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet in AP but leads AP_M/AP_L and person/feet detection, with lowest miss-matching rate (mMR-2) for head/face/hands/right foot. Anchor-free part-to-body (89.1/92.62/85.98) beats anchor-based part-to-body (88.4/92.31/85.28) and anchor-based body-to-part BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13). This directly matches your hands/face-to-person linking in crowded scenes (CrowdHuman face-body results also reported, with leading body MR-2).
> 
> ## Cross-method comparison / gaps
> - Complementary roles: JEPA gives your pretraining objective (latent prediction, semantic features) and LDReg prevents local/global collapse of those embeddings; 4-bit AdamW/Adam/SGD gives tight-memory fine-tuning; PBADet provides the single-stage anchor-free COCO-style detector that natively links parts (hands/face) to bodies via one center offset.
> - Note: no single paper in this collection combines all four; no results exist here for 4-bit optimizers or JEPA on CIFAR-100/MNIST (4-bit is tested on ImageNet/LLaMA; LDReg transfer includes CIFAR-10/100; Dale's Law RNN paper evaluates on sequential MNIST/PTB). The Dale's Law RNN study ("Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective") is the relevant work for your excitatory/inhibitory recurrent modules: naive column-partitioned E/I (ColEI) networks learn worse due to multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra, whereas Dale's ANNs (DANN) respect the constraint and match standard RNN performance — spectral initialization matters more than the sign constraints. This suggests using DANN-style E/I recurrent modules for interpretability without sacrificing accuracy, though no results tie it to detection or CIFAR-100 in this collection.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the relevant works and how their results compare.
> 
> ## 1. Joint-embedding predictive learning (JEPA) + collapse prevention
> - **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024): theoretically shows JEPA's latent-prediction objective (e.g., MSE in latent space with StopGrad) prioritizes "influential" features while MAE prioritizes high-variance ones, even noisy ones. JEPA alone is susceptible to trivial collapse (all inputs → same vector), so non-contrastive JEPA (BYOL, SimSiam, I-JEPA) relies on StopGrad/asymmetry to prevent it. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual-feature PCA subspace than MAE (measured by CCA).
> - **LDReg** paper confirms collapse is the core risk: representations can span a high-dimensional space globally yet collapse **locally**; it regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality (LID) using a Fisher-Rao metric.
> 
> ## 2. Dimensionality regularization of feature embeddings
> - **LDReg** (ICLR 2024): adds L1/L2 penalties on negative log-LID to any SSL loss (SimCLR, SimCLR-Tuned, BYOL, MAE; also MoCo, VICReg, Barlow Twins). Results: on ImageNet linear eval, BYOL+LDReg improved 69.0→69.8 (1000-epoch/4096 batch) and CIFAR-100 71.6→75.1; on COCO detection/segmentation (ResNet-50), SimCLR 1000-epoch APbb rose 36.48→37.15 and BYOL 36.30→36.82. Longer pretraining gives larger gains. Covariance/variance global regularizers barely helped (BYOL 67.6→67.8), whereas LDReg gave ~1% gain on linear eval, and forcing very low LID caused complete collapse. Limitation: LID estimation degrades in high dimensions and uses minibatch neighbors.
> 
> ## 3. Memory-efficient optimizers (4-bit states for Adam/AdamW/SGD)
> - **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023): pushes state bitwidth to 4-bit (previously 8-bit), applicable to SGDM/Adam/AdamW. Uses small block size (B128) for first moment; second moment uses linear quantizer excluding zero-point + rank-1 normalization, optionally factorized ("4-bitFactor"). Results: matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD, E2E-NLG, ImageNet (Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2), MT, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning; up to 57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B 75.4→31.9GB). Convergence curves closely align. Sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor, SM3) save more but degrade, especially on classification. Limitation: optimal quantization may be task-dependent; tested only language/vision.
> 
> ## 4. Anchor-free part-to-body association
> - **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage anchor-free detector linking parts (hands, face, feet) to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset (vs. BPJDet's body-to-part offsets). Results on BodyHands: Hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62%, joint AP 85.98 (YOLOv7), beating BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13) and BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48) with a smaller model. On COCOHumanParts it matches/leads BPJDet (e.g., AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 with YOLOv5l6, higher part/feet APs) and beats HierR-CNN; on CrowdHuman face-body association it leads body MR-2 and is competitive in AP. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment each improve association. It also beats ED-Pose in precision/recall/F1 for hands/feet.
> 
> ## 5. Transformers + biologically-inspired E/I recurrent modules
> - **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023): recurrent networks respecting excitatory/inhibitory constraints (ColEI: column-wise E/I partition; DANN: separate E-to-E, E-to-I, I-to-E projections) for interpretability/biology. Results: ColEI RNNs learn worse and with higher variance on adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition; gradient clipping mitigates the deficit. The cause is not sign constraints but the initial recurrent weight spectrum (multimodal/dispersed singular values); DANN and standard RNNs have unimodal spectra and learn well. Normalised SVD entropy anti-correlates with final error.
> 
> ## Validation datasets
> - **CIFAR-100/MNIST**: LDReg reports CIFAR-10/100 linear eval (CIFAR-100 up to 75.1 with LDReg); the embedding-similarity/contrastive paper validates variance-reduction loss on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-100 (improves SimCLR accuracy and temperature robustness, helps small-batch training); the Dale's-law RNN paper uses sequential MNIST; BSO validates memory-efficient binary spiking training on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet.
> 
> **Caveat:** No single paper in the collection covers the full pipeline (SSL pretraining → dimensionality regularization → 4-bit fine-tuning → anchor-free part-body detection with E/I recurrent modules). Each addresses one component, and no document validates that exact combination on COCO/CIFAR-100/MNIST, so end-to-end conclusions across all four methods cannot be drawn from this collection.

</details>

<a id="case-paperscope-results_comparison-80"></a>

### paperscope:results_comparison:80 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that tie together implicit priors and inductive biases in modern deep learning: joint-embedding self-supervised training that favors predictive features over noisy ones; restoration networks used as plug-and-play priors for inverse problems; spectral perspectives on biologically constrained E/I recurrent networks for time-series; memory-lean optimizers with low-bit (sub-byte) state that work with Adam/AdamW; and one-stage, anchor-free vision systems that associate detected parts to the right body. I’m interested in connections to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (low-rank adapters), similarity-based feature embeddings (cosine-like comparisons), standard losses (MSE and cross-entropy), Transformers and diffusion-style approaches, and evaluations on common vision benchmarks (handwritten digits, 100-class small images) with Precision/F1.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：4→3（Δ-1）；rounds：7→6（Δ-1）。**

Gold 1：

> Below is a dataset- and task-centric comparison of the experimental results reported in the five papers you provided. I only use results explicitly reported in their figures/tables and accompanying captions/text.
> 
> 1) Human part–body association (PBADet) vs prior detectors on identical datasets
> - Dataset: BodyHands (hand–body association)
>   • Metrics: Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP (Table 1)
>   • Identical methods compared: OpenPose; Keypoint Com.; MaskRCNN variants (FD/FS/LD/IoU); BodyHands; BPJDet (YOLOv5s6/m6/l6); PBADet (Ours YOLOv7, Ours YOLOv5l6)
>   • Best overall: PBADet
>     - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.62; Joint AP 85.98
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.71; Joint AP 85.73
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9; Conditional Accuracy 86.91; Joint AP 84.39
>   • Takeaway: On the identical BodyHands test set, PBADet improves over the strongest published one-stage baseline (BPJDet) across all three metrics.
> 
> - Dataset: COCOHumanParts (multi-part–body association)
>   • All-categories detection AP (Table 2)
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.6/43.3 (original/subordinate), AP.5 70.6/69.8
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8, AP.5 70.0/68.4
>     - PBADet (YOLOv7): AP.5:.95 42.7/41.5, AP.5 69.5/67.9
>     - Interpretation: BPJDet is marginally higher on overall detection AP; however…
>   • Association accuracy (average mMR−2, lower is better; Table 3)
>     - PBADet (YOLOv7): head 29.2; face 31.3; l-hand 41.1; r-hand 42.7; r-foot 52.6; l-foot 52.5
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8; face 31.8; l-hand 41.6; r-hand 42.2; r-foot 49.1; l-foot 50.4
>     - Interpretation: PBADet achieves lower or comparable mMR−2 (better association) for most parts, particularly head/face/hands, while BPJDet retains a small edge on overall AP.
> 
> - Dataset: CrowdHuman (face–body association; Appendix Tables 5 and 6)
>   • mMR−2 (body–face), MR−2, and AP
>     - PBADet (YOLOv7): best MR−2 body (36.5), face MR−2 44.7, body AP 91.6, mMR−2 ~50.8–50.9
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 body 40.7, face MR−2 46.3, body AP 89.5, mMR−2 50.1
>     - Interpretation: On the identical CrowdHuman val set, PBADet yields lower miss rates and higher body AP, with similar face–body mMR−2.
> 
> - Dataset: COCO val (qualitative F1/Precision/Recall vs ED-Pose; Appendix A.2 Table 7)
>   • Parts chosen (lefthand, righthand, leftfoot, rightfoot) and “all parts” aggregate
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): all parts Precision 39.41, Recall 63.09, F1 48.52
>     - ED-Pose (Swin-L): all parts Precision 24.09, Recall 45.51, F1 31.51
>     - Interpretation: On identical data, PBADet’s box + association approach substantially improves F1 over a SOTA pose estimator in the four chosen body parts.
> 
> 2) Image restoration with a pre-trained restoration prior (DRP) vs denoiser-based PnP methods on identical datasets
> - Task: Image Deblurring (Gaussian kernels, σ=1.6 and 2.0) with AWGN 2.55/255 (Table 1)
>   • Datasets: Set3c, Set5, CBSD68, McMaster; Metrics: PSNR↑/LPIPS↓
>   • σ=1.6
>     - Set3c: DRP 30.69/0.056; DPIR 29.53/0.110; PnP-ADMM 29.11/0.099
>     - Set5: DRP 32.79/0.109; DPIR 32.38/0.152; PnP-ADMM 32.31/0.137
>     - CBSD68: DRP 29.10/0.246; DPIR 28.86/0.307
>     - McMaster: DRP 32.79/0.107; DPIR 32.42/0.151
>     - DRP best across all four sets (higher PSNR, lower LPIPS).
>   • σ=2.0
>     - Set3c: DRP 27.89/0.088 vs DPIR 27.52/0.159
>     - Set5: DRP 31.04/0.143 vs DPIR 30.94/0.188
>     - CBSD68: DRP 27.46/0.296 vs DPIR 27.52/0.376 (DRP lower LPIPS, similar PSNR)
>     - McMaster: DRP 30.79/0.141 vs DPIR 30.78/0.193
>     - DRP ties or improves over DPIR on identical datasets and kernels.
> 
> - Task: Single-Image Super-Resolution (SISR) under known blur (Table 2)
>   • Datasets: Set3c, Set5, CBSD68, McMaster; Factors: ×2 and ×3; Gaussian kernels std 1.6 and 2.0; Metrics: PSNR↑/LPIPS↓
>   • Across all combinations (×2/×3 and both kernels), DRP typically gives the best PSNR and lowest LPIPS. Example subsets:
>     - ×2, kernel std=2.0: Set3c DRP 27.41/0.107 vs DPIR 26.80/0.171; Set5 DRP 30.42/0.163 vs DPIR 30.36/0.241
>     - ×3, kernel std=2.0: Set3c DRP 26.84/0.108 vs DPIR 25.84/0.195; Set5 DRP 29.88/0.162 vs DPIR 29.70/0.225
>   • Conclusion: On identical SR test beds (same kernels, same datasets), DRP outperforms denoiser-based PnP baselines (DPIR, PnP-ADMM, SD-RED, IRCNN+), both quantitatively (PSNR/LPIPS) and visually (figures indicate sharper details with fewer artifacts).
> 
> - Additional internal comparisons on identical datasets (supplement)
>   • Against GS-PnP (HQS-free convergent PnP): DRP is best or tied for best PSNR on Set3c/CBSD68 for both deblurring and SR (Tables 3–4, supplement)
>   • Against diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) with face priors (FFHQ validation, deblurring): DRP yields higher PSNR, while DPS is more perceptually realistic (Table 5)
>   • SSIM corroborates LPIPS/PSNR trends (Tables 6–7): DRP generally improves SSIM and LPIPS over PnP-ADMM/DPIR on the same datasets/kernels
>   • Ablation: when the SwinIR SR prior is directly applied to mismatched SISR (bicubic-trained prior vs Gaussian-kernel SR), its performance is poor—but within DRP, it adapts and becomes SOTA on the same SISR setups (Fig. 9, supplement)
> 
> 3) Memory-efficient training (4-bit optimizers) on identical tasks/datasets
> - Natural Language Understanding (GLUE with RoBERTa-L)
>   • Mean score (Table 2): 4-bit AdamW 89.1 ≈ 8-bit AdamW 89.1 and 32-bit AdamW 88.9; SM3 lower (87.5)
>   • Per-task (Table 7, appendix): 4-bit AdamW matches or is within rounding error of 32-bit AdamW on MNLI, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST-2, MRPC, CoLA, STS-B
> 
> - Question Answering (SQuAD/SQuAD 2.0)
>   • F1 (Table 2 + Table 9): 4-bit AdamW 94.5 vs 32-bit AdamW 94.6 (SQuAD); similar EM/F1 on SQuAD 2.0
> 
> - Natural Language Generation (E2E-NLG with GPT-2 Medium)
>   • BLEU (Table 2): 4-bit AdamW 67.8 vs 32-bit AdamW 67.7; 4-bit Factor 67.6; 8-bit AdamW 67.5
> 
> - Machine Translation (WMT14 En–De, Transformer-Base)
>   • SacreBLEU (Table 2): 4-bit AdamW 26.28 vs 32-bit AdamW 26.61; 4-bit Factor 26.45 (minor gap)
> 
> - Image Classification (ImageNet-1K with Swin-T)
>   • Top-1 Acc (Table 2): 4-bit AdamW 80.8 vs 32-bit AdamW 81.2; 8-bit AdamW 81.0
> 
> - Instruction tuning (LLaMA on Alpaca → MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA; Table 3)
>   • 4-bit AdamW ≈ 32-bit AdamW at 7B/13B/33B on all benchmarks (e.g., LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5)
> 
> - Throughput and memory (Table 4)
>   • LLaMA-7B (FSDP, 2×A100 80GB): 4-bit AdamW reduces peak memory from 75.4 GB to 31.9 GB (−57.7%) and offers similar or slightly better wall-clock (3.07h vs 3.35h)
>   • RoBERTa-L/GPT-2 Medium: 4-bit methods reduce total memory by ~34–47%; fused kernels recover training speed comparable to 8-bit
>   • Largest trainable model under a given budget (Table 5): on 24 GB GPU memory, 32-bit AdamW fits OPT-350M vs 4-bit AdamW fits OPT-1.3B; on 80 GB, 4-bit supports LLaMA-7B
>   • Takeaway: On identical datasets and tasks, 4-bit optimizers match 32-bit accuracy while substantially reducing memory and often preserving or improving speed (with fused ops/offloading).
> 
> 4) Spectral analysis of EI-constrained RNNs (sequential tasks and classification/language benchmarks)
> - Tasks: Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, Naturalistic object recognition (Figure 2)
>   • Identical setup across methods: Standard RNN vs Column EI (ColEI) vs DANN RNN
>   • Reported outcome (curves, not single fixed numbers): ColEI learns worse and is more variable than both Standard RNN and DANN on all four tasks; DANN learns as well as Standard RNN
>   • Spectral correlates: ColEI exhibits dispersed, multimodal singular values with larger modes; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) correlates with error: higher NSE → lower error
>   • Architectural sensitivity: ColEI degrades as inhibitory ratio shrinks and in smaller networks; DANN robust across sizes/E:I ratios and attains high NSE
>   • Practical implication on the identical benchmarks: If Dale’s Law is enforced via ColEI, expect lower final accuracy and higher variance; DANN recovers standard-RNN-like accuracy while respecting excitatory/inhibitory structure
> 
> 5) Joint-embedding SSL (JEPA) vs MAE (training-dynamics and Imagenet features)
> - Deep linear and ODE simulations (Figures 1–2)
>   • With controlled synthetic feature distributions, JEPA exhibits greedy learning with respect to regression coefficients (ρ), whereas MAE is greedy w.r.t. covariance (λ). In “Distribution 2” (λ increases, ρ decreases), MAE learns high-λ features first, JEPA reverses order and learns high-ρ features first
>   • ODE experiments corroborate: only JEPA shows “greedy in ρ,” which intensifies with depth
> 
> - Temporal linear generative model (Figure 3)
>   • Theoretical predictions of λ and ρ match simulations as log10(T) varies; JEPA prioritizes less noisy (higher ρ) modes
> 
> - Imagenet-1K (64×64) empirical probe (Appendix D, Figure 7)
>   • CCA between representations: I-JEPA’s features show higher similarity between “full” and “bottom (low-variance) subspace,” and lower similarity between “full” and “top (high-variance) subspace,” compared to MAE, across epochs
>   • Interpretation: JEPA focuses learning sooner on the semantically-informative low-variance subspace; MAE emphasizes reconstruction-heavy high-variance subspace
>   • Note: No accuracy numbers are reported for this setup; comparison is via representation similarity (CCA) on the same Imagenet data
> 
> Cross-paper observations on similar data families
> - Imagenet family
>   • 4-bit Optimizers: Swin-T on ImageNet-1K classification—4-bit matches 32-bit within ~0.4% top-1 (80.8 vs 81.2)
>   • JEPA paper: On the same dataset family (ImageNet-1K resized to 64×64), I-JEPA learns features aligned with low-variance subspace more strongly than MAE (CCA-based), suggesting better “semantic” focus but without reporting accuracy
>   • Not directly comparable (different protocols/metrics), but both indicate that resource/architecture decisions (4-bit states; choice of JEPA vs MAE) can preserve or shift feature quality/efficiency on Imagenet
> 
> - MNIST family
>   • Spectral EI RNN paper uses sequential MNIST (sequence modeling). DANN and Standard RNNs attain higher final performance than ColEI on identical sequential MNIST; PBADet/DRP/4-bit papers do not report MNIST results, so no cross-paper numerical comparison is possible
> 
> - COCO family
>   • PBADet evaluates association F1/Precision/Recall on COCO val for small parts—PBADet substantially outperforms ED-Pose in F1 on identical images; other papers don’t report COCO-based detection/association, so no cross-paper comparison here
> 
> Summary of specific-dataset winners (from the provided tables)
> - BodyHands: PBADet best (Hand AP 89.1; Joint AP 85.98; CondAcc >92%)
> - COCOHumanParts: BPJDet slightly higher overall detection AP; PBADet lower (better) part–body association mMR−2 for most parts
> - CrowdHuman: PBADet yields lower MR−2 (body/face) and higher body AP than BPJDet
> - Set3c/Set5/CBSD68/McMaster (deblurring/SISR): DRP (with SwinIR prior) consistently best or tied for best PSNR and LPIPS vs DPIR/PnP-ADMM/SD-RED/IRCNN+ (and GS-PnP in supplement)
> - GLUE/SQuAD/E2E-NLG/WMT14/ImageNet-1K (training optimizers): 4-bit AdamW/Factor match 32-bit AdamW accuracy on identical benchmarks while cutting memory 34–58%; with fused ops, speed matches or improves
> - Sequential MNIST/Adding/PTB/Naturalistic object recognition: On identical setups, DANN ≈ Standard RNN > ColEI in final performance; NSE of the recurrent spectrum predicts performance
> - ImageNet (representation probe): On identical images, I-JEPA’s features are more aligned with low-variance (bottom) subspace than MAE (higher full–bottom CCA; lower full–top CCA)
> 
> Overall conclusions (strictly from reported results)
> - When the task is part–body detection/association on crowded human datasets, the one-stage anchor-free PBADet is the strongest reported method on BodyHands and CrowdHuman and provides superior association accuracy (mMR−2) on COCOHumanParts.
> - For ill-posed inverse problems (deblurring/SISR) with arbitrary blur, using a restoration network as an implicit prior (DRP with SwinIR) consistently yields higher PSNR and better perceptual quality (LPIPS/SSIM) than PnP-ADMM/DPIR/SD-RED/IRCNN+ on the same Set3c/Set5/CBSD68/McMaster benchmarks.
> - Memory-efficient training via 4-bit optimizers achieves near-identical accuracy to 32-bit Adam/AdamW on the same NLU/QA/NLG/MT/ImageNet-1K benchmarks, while drastically reducing optimizer-state memory (and enabling larger models on the same hardware).
> - Spectral constraints matter in time-series modeling: on identical sequential benchmarks, Dale-constrained EI RNNs (ColEI) underperform; the DANN architecture matches standard RNN performance, with NSE explaining the differences; results generalize across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB LM, and a naturalistic vision task.
> - In self-supervised representation learning, JEPA vs MAE comparisons (on identical inputs) show JEPA prioritizes high-influence, low-variance (bottom) features, as validated by CCA on ImageNet-1K; this is a qualitative difference in learned representations rather than an accuracy metric.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the relevant papers in the collection, mapped to your topics, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Papers found
> 
> **1. Joint-embedding SSL favoring predictive over noisy features**
> - *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features* (doc `40fde...`): proves JEPA's implicit bias toward high-influence (high-ρ regression coefficient) features vs. MAE's bias to high-variance (λ) features; depth amplifies noise suppression. ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (measured by CCA). Theory restricted to deep linear MLPs with balanced orthogonal init.
> - *LDReg* (doc `51526068...`): fixes local dimensional collapse in SSL. ImageNet linear eval (ResNet-50, 100 ep): SimCLR 64.3→64.8, BYOL 67.6→68.5; ViT-B (200 ep): SimCLR 72.9→73.0, MAE 57.0→57.6. Transfer (SimCLR, 1000 ep, bs4096): CIFAR-10 90.1→91.8, CIFAR-100 71.6→75.1, Food-101 71.1→73.3, Cars 35.3→41.6.
> 
> **2. Cosine-like similarity embeddings**
> - *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (doc `160e14...`): InfoNCE optimal state = positive pairs aligned, negatives at similarity −1/(n−1); mini-batching inflates negative-pair similarity variance. Variance-reduction loss improves top-1: ImageNet-100 72.30→74.04 (t=0.3), 73.80→73.94 (t=0.2); full ImageNet 51.79→52.48; consistent gains on CIFAR-10/100 across temperatures and small batch sizes. Limitation: may suppress meaningful semantic variance.
> 
> **3. Restoration networks as plug-and-play priors**
> - *A Restoration Network as an Implicit Prior (DRP)* (doc `79c498...`): any MMSE restoration operator (e.g., SwinIR SR) serves as an implicit prior via prior refinement + scaled proximal data fidelity. Deblurring (Set3c, σ=1.6): DRP PSNR 30.69 vs DPIR 29.53, PnP-ADMM 29.11; 2×SISR Set3c 29.26 vs DPIR 28.18, and leads on Set5/CBSD68/McMaster in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS, also beating DPS/diffusion-prior baselines in supplementary. Theory assumes MSE-trained (MMSE) priors.
> - *Universal Guidance* (doc `9134ed...`): training-free diffusion guidance (forward/backward), comparable to specialized conditional models, but slower and needs tuning — a diffusion-style counterpart rather than PnP-restoration.
> 
> **4. Spectral perspective on biologically constrained E/I recurrent networks**
> - *Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly* (doc `e63a94...`): ColEI (column-constrained E/I) RNNs learn worse and with more variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition. The initial singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints (spectrum transplant: 1.5%±0.3% vs 2%±1% error changes); normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error; small networks and skewed E:I ratios worsen both spectrum and performance.
> 
> **5. Memory-lean optimizers with sub-byte state**
> - *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (doc `8d5e14...`): 4-bit Adam/AdamW (B128 + rank-1/linear quantizers, zero-point-excluded 2nd moment; optional factorized 2nd moment). Matches or beats 32-bit AdamW: GLUE 88.9→89.1 (4-bit), Swin-T ImageNet 81.2→80.8 (comparable), SQuAD F1 94.6→94.5, E2E-NLG 67.7→67.8, WMT14 26.61→26.28; up to 57.7% memory savings; LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU. Works with LoRA-style fine-tuning pipelines.
> - *BSO/T-BSO* (doc `4741ca...`): 1-bit (binary) states for spiking networks, using first/second-order moments with adaptive flip thresholds (Adam-like). CIFAR-10 94.86%, CIFAR-100 74.27%, ImageNet 57.76%, DVS-CIFAR10 81.00%, GSC 96.12%; constant memory (2.9–3.1GB) vs BPTT's linear growth (2.86→58.18GB). Not Adam/AdamW-compatible but shares the low-bit state idea.
> 
> **6. One-stage anchor-free part-body association**
> - *PBADet* (doc `08b70b...`): single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free YOLOv5/YOLOv7. BodyHands: HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (vs BPJDet-m6 85.3/86.80/78.13, with fewer params 36.9M vs 41.2M). COCOHumanParts: on par with BPJDet overall, leads AP_M/AP_L and feet, lowest avg mMR−2 for most parts. CrowdHuman: best body MR−2 36.5 and body AP 91.6. Vs. ED-Pose (Swin-L): Precision/Recall/F1 all-parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs 24.09/45.51/31.51 — the only Precision/F1 numbers in the collection. Ablations: association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment each add gains (JointAP 78.07→85.98).
> 
> ## Connections across the set
> - **Implicit priors/inductive biases**: JEPA's bias toward predictive low-noise features, LDReg's dimensionality prior, and DRP's MMSE-restoration prior are all instances of *priors implemented through training objectives/architectures rather than explicit densities* — DRP makes this explicit by linking the restoration operator to a density via Tweedie/MMSE theory.
> - **Low-rank adaptation**: LoRA appears as the fine-tuning mechanism in the 4-bit optimizer (fine-tuning benchmarks), Themis (Vicuna-7B reward model), NFTS (adapter search for few-shot, 80.7 vs 76.6 with 16M vs 82M params), and the Hessian power-law paper (LoRA-only fine-tuning does *not* induce the power-law Hessian structure of full fine-tuning, and Hessian trace is a better generalization indicator for LoRA).
> - **Losses**: MSE (JEPA/MAE objectives, DRP's data fidelity), cross-entropy (classification/PTB tasks), IoU/DFL/classification + L1 association loss (PBADet), InfoNCE (embedding similarity paper).
> - **Benchmarks**: MNIST (sequential, EI-RNN paper), CIFAR-100 (LDReg transfer, embedding-similarity, BSO/T-BSO), ImageNet (LDReg, 4-bit, embedding-similarity, BSO), COCO-based part datasets (PBADet).
> - **Not established**: no single paper ties all these topics together; the "common vision benchmarks with Precision/F1" criterion is only met by PBADet (vs ED-Pose); the sub-byte-state optimizer criterion is met by 4-bit AdamW (4-bit, works with Adam/AdamW) and BSO/T-BSO (1-bit, but spiking-specific, not Adam/AdamW); diffusion-style approaches appear only as guidance/prior references in DRP and Universal Guidance, with no direct quantitative overlap with the other methods.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, I found five papers that match your topics. Here is a comparison and analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The Five Papers
> 
> 1. **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024) — implicit prior / inductive bias in joint-embedding SSL. Proves via deep linear networks that JEPA prioritizes high-regression-coefficient ("influential") features, increasingly with depth, while MAE only prioritizes high-variance features even if noisy.
> 2. **"Deep Restoration Priors (DRP) for Solving Inverse Problems"** (ICLR 2024) — a SwinIR super-resolution network used as a plug-and-play implicit prior for deblurring/SISR, with convergence to a stationary point of a global functional under MMSE assumptions.
> 3. **"Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023) — spectral perspective on biologically constrained E/I RNNs (ColEI vs DANN) for time-series tasks.
> 4. **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023) — 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states (sub-byte), with rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, factorization.
> 5. **"PBADet"** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage anchor-free part-body association detection (single part-to-body center offset).
> 
> Two additional works are strongly relevant to your requested connections: **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (cosine-similarity embeddings, CIFAR/ImageNet-100) and **"LDReg"** (SSL representation regularization, CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet transfer).
> 
> ## Experimental Results Compared
> 
> **Representation quality (accuracy):** LDReg improves linear evaluation on ImageNet across SimCLR (64.3→64.8), BYOL (67.6→68.5), and MAE (57.0→57.6), with larger gains at 1000 epochs; on CIFAR-10 transfer it reaches 91.8 vs 90.1, CIFAR-100 75.1 vs 71.6. The embedding-similarity paper's variance-reduction loss improves SimCLR top-1 on CIFAR-10 (~85→88), CIFAR-100 (~56→62), ImageNet-100 (74.04 at t=0.3), and full ImageNet (51.79→52.48), and stabilizes accuracy across temperatures 0.07–2.0.
> 
> **Inverse problems (PSNR/LPIPS):** DRP using a SwinIR SR prior consistently outperforms PnP-ADMM, DPIR, GS-PnP, and diffusion-posterior-sampling (DPS) on Set3c, Set5, CBSD68, McMaster for deblurring and SISR. Theory: fixed points satisfy first-order optimality; iterates converge at O(1/t) under MMSE priors; works even with mismatched (L1-trained, bicubic) priors, but performance is bounded by the pre-trained model and theory assumes MSE-trained (MMSE) priors.
> 
> **E/I RNNs (error):** ColEI learns worse and more variably than DANN and standard RNNs across all four tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, Penn TreeBank, naturalistic object recognition). Spectrum transplant shows the singular-value spectrum, not sign constraints, drives the gap: ColEI has multimodal, dispersed spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure); DANN/standard RNNs match the quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur law. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Small networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen both spectra and performance; DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> 
> **Memory-efficient optimizers (accuracy vs memory):** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (89.1), SQuAD (94.5), E2E-NLG (67.8), ImageNet Swin-T (80.8), and WMT14 (26.28 BLEU); 4-bitFactor slightly better memory. Saves up to 57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9GB), enables LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models. The key insight: excluding zero from the second-moment quantizer (DE-0/Linear, rank-1 normalization) is essential—B2048/DE (with zero) causes 33% unstable runs, while Rank-1/Linear achieves 0% instability. Note: the paper cites LoRA only as related work (delta tuning); the "LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce power-law Hessian structure" result comes from the Hessian-spectrum paper in the collection, not this optimizer paper.
> 
> **Part-body detection (AP/F1):** On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98—surpassing BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13) and BodyHands baselines (84.8/84.12/63.87), with fewer parameters (36.9M vs 41.2–86.1M). On COCOHumanParts it matches BPJDet's AP (42.7/41.5 vs 43.6/43.3) but leads on medium/large objects and per-category mMR-2 (e.g., head 27.9 vs 30.8; l-foot 47.9 vs 50.4 with YOLOv5l6). Against the Swin-L ED-Pose pose estimator, PBADet gives substantially higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands and feet. Ablations: the association loss L_assoc boosts conditional accuracy from 80.78→92.62 and JointAP from 78.07→85.98; multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each add gains.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting Analysis
> 
> - **Implicit priors/bias is the unifying theme:** JEPA's implicit bias (feature influence ρ) is what makes restoration networks (DRP) effective as implicit priors, and spectral properties (singular-value distribution) explain E/I RNN learning. In each case, the *initialization/objective structure*, not the explicit loss, determines what is learned.
> - **Depth and low-rank structure matter in both theory and practice:** JEPA's noise suppression strengthens with depth; DRP relies on a pre-trained (low-rank-like) restoration operator; LoRA-style low-rank adapters appear as related work in the optimizer paper, and a separate Hessian-spectrum paper in the collection shows LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does (TinyLlama, MathQA).
> - **Losses and metrics:** All papers use standard losses—MSE (DRP's MMSE/Tweedie interpretation, JEPA's regression), cross-entropy (RNN classification, detection classification head), IoU/DFL (PBADet), InfoNCE/cosine (contrastive SSL). Evaluations use PSNR/LPIPS (DRP), AP/mMR-2/F1 (PBADet), top-1 accuracy (SSL, optimizers), BLEU/F1 (optimizers), and test error/NSE (RNNs). Sequential MNIST (handwritten digits) and CIFAR-100 (100-class small images) appear in the RNN paper (sequential MNIST) and LDReg/embedding-similarity papers (CIFAR-10/100), respectively.
> - **Transformer and diffusion connections:** DRP explicitly compares against diffusion posterior sampling (DPS) and uses SwinIR (a Swin-Transformer); the 4-bit optimizer is evaluated on Transformer/Llama models; PBADet contrasts with transformer-based ED-Pose; contrastive embeddings use cosine similarity (which the InfoNCE loss is built on).
> 
> **Caveats:** The papers do not share a common benchmark, so direct cross-paper comparison is not possible. JEPA's ImageNet-1K experiments are qualitative (CCA alignment of I-JEPA features with the low-variance PCA subspace), not accuracy numbers. The 4-bit optimizer's limitations note optimal quantization may be task-dependent. DRP's theory assumes MMSE (MSE-trained) priors.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> This set of five papers collectively covers the requested toolkit. Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results, strictly derived from the figures and tables in the papers, organized by (a)–(e), and highlighting performance on identical datasets, similar dataset types, and specific datasets.
> 
> (a) Anchor‑free, one‑stage part–whole human detection (PBADet)
> - Identical datasets and direct comparisons:
>   • BodyHands (Table 1): PBADet (YOLOv7, YOLOv5l6) outperforms BPJDet across all metrics. Hand AP: 89.1 (YOLOv7), 88.1 (YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet up to 85.9; Conditional Accuracy: 92.62 (YOLOv7), 92.71 (YOLOv5l6) vs 86.91; Joint AP: 85.98 (YOLOv7), 85.73 (YOLOv5l6) vs 84.39. These methods use YOLO backbones and SGD training (Implementation Specifics).
>   • COCOHumanParts (Table 2): PBADet achieves comparable overall AP to BPJDet. AP.5:.95: 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6 PBADet) vs 43.6/43.3 (YOLOv5l6 BPJDet); AP.5: 70.0/68.4 (PBADet) vs 70.6/69.8 (BPJDet). PBADet leads on several category APs with the same backbone: person AP: 62.4 (PBADet YOLOv5l6) vs 61.3 (BPJDet YOLOv5l6); r-foot/l-foot: 37.7/31.5 (PBADet YOLOv5l6) vs 39.6/30.9 (BPJDet YOLOv5l6) — feet are mixed; PBADet YOLOv7 is similar.
>   • COCOHumanParts association quality (Table 3): PBADet achieves lower mMR−2 (better association) than BPJDet for head, face, hands, and is competitive on feet. Example averages: PBADet YOLOv7 head/face mMR−2 = 29.2/31.3 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 30.8/31.8; right/left hand PBADet YOLOv7 42.7/41.1 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 42.2/41.6.
>   • CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6): PBADet improves body MR−2 and body AP vs BPJDet. PBADet YOLOv7: body MR−2 36.5 (best), face MR−2 44.7, body AP 91.6, body-face mMR−2 50.8; BPJDet YOLOv5l6: body MR−2 40.7, face MR−2 46.3, body AP 89.5, body-face mMR−2 50.1. Against broader crowded detectors (Table 6), PBADet achieves the best body MR−2 while matching or closely trailing DETR-based APs.
> - Similar dataset types: On multi-part association (COCOHumanParts) PBADet’s subordinate APs (association-aware APs) are competitive with state-of-the-art anchor-based methods and improve person AP and large-object APs (APL 67.2/64.4 for YOLOv5l6 PBADet).
> - Specific datasets: The animal experiments (Appendix A.3) qualitatively show scaling to quadruped parts; ablations (Appendix A.4) show anchor-free part-to-body outperforms anchor-based designs.
> 
> (b) Spectral/implicit‑bias analyses of EI-constrained recurrent nets (Dale’s Law, NeurIPS 2023)
> - Identical datasets (within this paper across methods):
>   • Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition (Fig. 2): ColEI networks learn worse than DANNs and standard RNNs across all four tasks (curves show lower final accuracy/performance).
> - Similar dataset types: sequential classification (Sequential MNIST) and language modeling (PTB) reveal consistent trends: ColEI performance is degraded and highly variable; DANN and standard RNNs are robust.
> - Specific experimental findings (from figures/tables):
>   • Gradient clipping benefits ColEI substantially more (Appendix Figure 10), indicating instability tied to spectrum pathologies.
>   • Spectrum transplant (Fig. 4B–C): singular value spectra matter more than sign constraints. Quantified changes: spectrum contributes 1.5% ± 0.3% (RNNs) and 2% ± 1% (ColEI) to final test error gaps; sign constraints contribute ~0.7% ± 0.3% (RNNs) and ~1% ± 1% (ColEI).
>   • EI ratio and network size (Figs. 5–7): normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts test error; lower inhibitory fraction decreases NSE and worsens performance; DANN remains robust even with a single inhibitory neuron; larger networks improve NSE and performance even if maximum singular value increases.
> - Interpretation support: unimodal, clustered singular value spectra (high NSE) correlate with better learning; multimodal dispersed spectra (ColEI) correlate with poor learning; empirical curves substantiate interpretability via spectral diagnostics.
> 
> (c) JEPA vs reconstruction; filtering noisy features (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Identical datasets (within this paper’s scope): synthetic Gaussian-feature settings; linear deep networks; plus ImageNet-1K (64×64) for feature similarity diagnostics (Appendix D, Fig. 7).
> - Similar dataset types: vision representations; comparisons of JEPA vs MAE in latent vs pixel space.
> - Specific results:
>   • ODE simulations and deep linear training (Figs. 2, 4, 5) show JEPA exhibits greedy learning by regression coefficients (ρ), prioritizing “influential features,” whereas MAE prioritizes covariance (λ); JEPA’s depth amplifies bias toward predictive (low-variance) features; MAE favors high-variance subspaces.
>   • Temporal linear generative model (Fig. 3) aligns with theory: JEPA ignores noisy features (ρ increases when noise standard deviation decreases) and learns predictive “slow” features earlier.
>   • ImageNet representation similarity (Appendix D, Fig. 7): mean CCA between full and “bottom-PC” subsets is higher for I-JEPA than MAE, and lower for “top-PC” subsets, consistent with JEPA more rapidly learning low-variance perceptual features (as per Balestriero & LeCun 2024).
> 
> (d) Memory‑lean 4‑bit optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Identical datasets across optimizers (Tables 2, 7–9):
>   • NLU (GLUE, RoBERTa-L): 4-bit AdamW = 89.1 mean; matches 8-bit AdamW (89.1) and exceeds 32-bit AdamW (88.9); Adafactor variants are ≥ 89.1 (up to 89.3 with β1=0) and SM3 lower (87.5). Task-level (Table 7) shows similar parity per dataset (e.g., MNLI/SST-2/STS-B).
>   • CLS (ImageNet-1k, Swin-T): 32-bit AdamW 81.2; 8-bit 81.0; 4-bit AdamW 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9 — 4-bit methods are comparable to full/8-bit on this modern vision backbone.
>   • NLG (E2E-NLG, GPT-2 Medium): BLEU (Table 2): 4-bit AdamW 67.8 (best), 32-bit AdamW 67.7, 8-bit 67.5; full metrics (Table 8) show parity (NIST/METEOR/ROUGE-L/CIDEr).
>   • QA (SQuAD/SQuAD2.0, RoBERTa-L): 4-bit AdamW F1 94.5 vs 32-bit 94.6; EM/F1 per dataset (Table 9) are nearly identical among 4-bit and full; SM3 notably lower.
>   • MT (WMT14 en-de, Transformer-Base): SacreBleu: 32-bit AdamW 26.61; 8-bit 26.66; 4-bit AdamW 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45 — 4-bit close to full/8-bit.
> - LLaMA fine-tuning (Table 3, identical tasks across sizes):
>   • 7B: 4-bit AdamW vs 32-bit AdamW — MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; HellaSwag 74.7 vs 74.6; ARC-e/c and OBQA are within ~1 point.
>   • 13B: 4-bit equals or slightly better than full (e.g., MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8).
>   • 33B: parity across tasks (e.g., MMLU 54.9 both; HellaSwag 79.2 both; small differences in ARC).
> - Memory/time efficiency (Table 4):
>   • LLaMA‑7B (FSDP): total memory 31.87 GB (4-bit) vs 75.40 GB (32-bit) → 57.7% savings; training time improves (3.07 h vs 3.35 h).
>   • RoBERTa-L: memory 3.00 GB (4-bit fused) vs 3.34 GB (8-bit) and 5.31 GB (32-bit); 4-bit fused is fastest (3.17 min) including fused kernels.
>   • GPT-2 Medium: 4-bit fused memory 4.62 GB vs 4.92 GB (8-bit) and 6.89 GB (32-bit); time near parity (2.11 h fused 4-bit vs 2.04 h 8-bit).
> - Trainable model size under fixed budgets (Table 5):
>   • 24 GB GPU: 4-bit enables OPT‑1.3B vs 32-bit OPT‑350M.
>   • 80 GB GPU: 4-bit enables OPT‑6.7B and LLaMA‑7B vs 32-bit OPT‑1.3B.
> - Second-moment quantization ablations (Table 1, E2E-NLG):
>   • Zero-point removal is critical: DE-0 and Rank‑1/Linear yield stable training (0% unstable) with BLEU up to 67.8; naïve DE often unstable (up to 66% unstable).
>   • Rank‑1 normalization + Linear mapping attains the best stability/accuracy (BLEU 67.8 ± 0.51, 0% unstable) without relying on stable embeddings.
> - First/second moment ablations (Table 6, Swin‑T): quantizing both moments plus factorizing second moment maintains accuracy (~81%) — factorization improves memory while preserving pretraining performance.
> 
> (e) Video‑only representation learning for RL with iid vs exogenous noise (ICLR 2024)
> - Identical domains across methods: GridWorld and ViZDoom (Basic and Defend the Center). Methods compared: forward modeling, temporal contrastive, autoencoder (video‑only), and ACRO (trajectory‑based).
> - No exogenous noise (Figures 2(a), 4(a), 7(a)): forward modeling and temporal contrastive succeed (learning curves reach high returns); autoencoder is task‑dependent (better in ViZDoom than gridworld); ACRO also strong.
> - With observation/reward/exogenous noise (Figures 2(b)–(d), 4(b)–(d), 7(b)): temporal contrastive often fails (curves near zero/impaired returns); forward modeling degrades but can retain partial robustness; ACRO remains high across noise settings.
> - Noise scale and count ablations (Figures 6, 9): as exogenous noise (size or number of distractors) increases, video‑only methods (especially temporal contrastive) drop sharply; ACRO remains comparatively stable.
> - Iid noise robustness (Figure 10(a) vs 10(b); Figure 11(a)): forward modeling and ACRO handle iid noise; temporal contrastive performs well under iid Gaussian noise but fails with temporally correlated exogenous noise (Fig. 11(b)), matching theory.
> 
> Cross‑paper overlaps and benchmarks
> - COCO‑style detection: PBADet vs BPJDet on COCOHumanParts (Tables 2–3) — identical dataset comparison shows PBADet is competitive or better in several APs and has better association mMR−2.
> - MNIST/Sequential MNIST: spectral EI RNN paper uses Sequential MNIST (Fig. 2); JEPA work focuses on linear settings and ImageNet feature similarity rather than MNIST; hence, direct identical dataset comparison is within the RNN paper.
> - Modern backbones: Swin‑T in 4‑bit optimizer CLS experiments (Table 2); YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7 in PBADet (Implementation Specifics and tables).
> 
> Summary of “which method performs better/worse” by dataset/type
> - Part–whole detection (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman): PBADet (anchor‑free, one‑stage) outperforms or matches BPJDet (anchor‑based) on identical datasets; stronger conditional/joint AP on BodyHands and better body MR−2 on CrowdHuman.
> - EI‑RNNs: DANN and standard RNNs outperform ColEI on identical tasks (Adding, Sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition); spectrum (singular values) is the decisive factor; NSE anti‑correlates with error.
> - JEPA vs MAE: JEPA prioritizes predictive, low‑variance features (ρ‑driven) and learns them earlier than MAE; on ImageNet, JEPA’s bottom‑spectrum feature similarity exceeds MAE, consistent with stronger perceptual representations.
> - 4‑bit optimizers vs 8‑bit/full precision on identical tasks: 4‑bit AdamW/Factor match or surpass 32‑bit/8‑bit on NLU/NLG/QA and are near‑parity on CLS/MT; LLaMA fine‑tuning shows parity across sizes; memory/time reduced substantially; robust second‑moment quantization requires zero‑point‑free mappings and rank‑1 normalization.
> - Video‑only RL: forward modeling and temporal contrastive succeed without exogenous noise; temporal contrastive degrades most under exogenous noise; ACRO (with trajectory labels) consistently outperforms video‑only methods as noise increases.
> 
> All results above are drawn directly from the figures and tables in the papers, using the reported metrics (AP, AP.5:.95, mMR−2, MR−2, BLEU, NIST, METEOR, ROUGE‑L, CIDEr, F1/EM, SacreBleu, mean CCA, training time/memory) and the provided experimental comparisons on identical datasets and similar task types.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers matching your toolkit, with a cross-paper comparison of their experimental setups and results.
> 
> ## (a) PBADet — One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)
> - **Method:** Extends anchor-free dense detection (FCOS/TOOD-style, YOLOv5/v7 heads) with a single part-to-body center offset, so one offset serves any number of parts; task-alignment (TOOD) supervision; losses = IoU + DFL + classification + association.
> - **Setup:** SGD optimizer, YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 backbones, 1024×1024, 4×V100, 100 epochs.
> - **Results (BodyHands):** HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 — beating BPJDet (85.9/86.91/84.39) and Mask-RCNN baselines. **COCOHumanParts:** AP.5:.95 42.7/41.5, APL 66.7/63.3; leads person/feet AP and mMR−2 for head/face/hands/right-foot. Anchor-free head beats its own anchor-based version (89.1 vs 88.4 HandAP; 85.98 vs 85.28 JointAP).
> 
> ## (b) Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Method:** Theory of why E/I sign-constrained RNNs (ColEI) train poorly; gradient-descent/projected-gradient training with spectral-radius control.
> - **Setup:** Sequential MNIST, adding problem, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition (standard SGD-like training, 5–30 seeds).
> - **Results:** ColEI learns worst and with high variance; gradient clipping helps it most. SVD "spectrum transplant" shows the **singular-value spectrum at initialization, not the sign constraints**, is the main cause (ColEI = multimodal/dispersed spectrum vs Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle for standard RNNs/DANNs). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with test error — a pre-training diagnostic.
> 
> ## (c) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)
> - **Method:** Deep-linear self-distillation; both objectives are **squared-error** (JEPA predicts latent `VWx` vs target `SG(W)y`; MAE reconstructs `y`). Trained by gradient flow/SGD.
> - **Results:** Exact ODE analysis gives critical times: **MAE orders features by covariance λ; JEPA orders by regression coefficient ρ**, an effect that grows with depth (JEPA fixed point `w̄=ρ^L` vs MAE `w̄=ρ^(L/(L+1))`). Noise-suppression is thus an emergent implicit bias. **ImageNet-1K (ViT)**: I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance (bottom-PCA) perceptual subspace than MAE by CCA, confirming JEPA suppresses noisy features — a purely theoretical result, with empirical confirmation.
> 
> ## (d) 4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Method:** Adam/AdamW with first/second moments stored at ~4-bit: smaller blocks (B128) for first moment, zero-exclusion (DE-0/Linear) + rank-1 normalization (or factorization) for second moment.
> - **Results:** Matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 (vs 88.9), Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 (vs 81.2), GPT-2 E2E BLEU 67.8 (vs 67.7), Transformer MT SacreBLEU 26.28 (vs 26.61), LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tune with no drop; convergence curves align. Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU); no Stable-Embedding requirement once zero-point is fixed.
> 
> ## (e) Towards Principled Representation Learning from Videos for RL (ICLR 2024)
> - **Method:** Theory + practice of autoencoding, temporal contrastive, and forward modeling pretraining from video only, for downstream RL (Block MDPs, iid vs exogenous noise). Pretraining with Adam (lr 1e-3, batch 128, 400 epochs), downstream PPO on frozen features.
> - **Results:** PAC upper bounds for forward modeling and temporal contrastive (polynomial sample complexity) under iid noise; an **exponential lower bound** under exogenous noise. Empirically (GridWorld, ViZDoom Defend the Center): both work without noise; temporal contrastive **completely fails** under exogenous noise (it latches onto predictive noise), forward modeling degrades gracefully, and trajectory-based ACRO stays best — matching theory.
> 
> ---
> 
> ### Cross-paper analysis
> - **Shared toolchain:** All five use standard optimizers — SGD (PBADet), projected/plain SGD or gradient flow (Dale's Law, JEPA), Adam/AdamW (4-bit optimizer; video pretraining + PPO). All revolve around **squared-error/ℓ₂ objectives**: JEPA/MAE literally; Adam's second moment (d); PBADet's association and box losses; and the video paper's forward-model/reconstruction losses. This makes them a coherent "principled representation learning and training" stack.
> - **Benchmark commonality:** COCO-style detection (a) on COCOHumanParts; MNIST/Sequential MNIST (b, and c's Gaussian data); ImageNet-1K (c, d's Swin-T); modern backbones — YOLOv5/v7, ViT, Swin-T, RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, LLaMA.
> - **Relative strengths:**
>   - (a) is the strongest on detection **accuracy + association** (large margins on Joint AP), but is task-specific and uses L1/IoU losses rather than pure squared error.
>   - (b) and (c) are the most **diagnostic/theoretical**: (b) predicts learning success *before* training via NSE; (c) gives exact critical-time ordering showing why latent prediction beats pixel reconstruction for noise robustness. Both are limited to simplified settings (sequential MNIST/deep linear), with (c) only qualitatively confirmed on ImageNet.
>   - (d) is the strongest on **training efficiency**: lossless (even slight gains over) 32-bit AdamW while cutting memory up to ~58%, unlike factorization baselines (Adafactor/SM3) that lose accuracy, especially on image classification.
>   - (e) is the most cautionary: video-only pretraining has provable limits under exogenous noise — temporal contrastive fails entirely, forward modeling degrades, and only trajectory-based ACRO stays robust. So for the RL leg of the toolkit, expect degradation in real noisy video.
> - **Main caveat across the set:** each is validated in its own regime (detection AP, sequential-MNIST error, CCA/feature dynamics, GLUE/MMLU, GridWorld/ViZDoom returns), so no single benchmark unifies them; the links are the shared optimizers, squared-error objectives, and the implicit-bias theme (b and c) that explains why latent-prediction methods suppress noise, complemented by (d)'s memory-lean training and (a)/(e)'s empirical scaling.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the provided context, I found five papers matching the requested toolkit:
> 
> **1. Part–whole human detection — PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> One-stage anchor-free part-body association built on YOLOv5/YOLOv7. Results: outperforms SOTA (BPJDet, HierR-CNN, ED-Pose) on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman (face-body); ablations show the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning each improve association accuracy; extends to quadruped AnimalPose/AP-10K.
> 
> **2. Spectral/implicit-bias analysis of EI recurrent nets — "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> On sequential MNIST (plus adding, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition): ColEI networks learn worse (2.3% higher error) with more variance; sign constraints explain only part of the gap (≈1%), while the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal/dispersed vs unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur) matters more. Normalized SVD entropy at initialization anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance across sizes and EI ratios; DANN RNNs match standard RNNs.
> 
> **3. JEPA vs pixel reconstruction — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> Deep linear analysis with exact gradient-flow ODEs: latent-space squared-error prediction biases JEPA toward high-influence, low-variance features and filters noisy ones (with depth strengthening suppression), whereas MAE's feature ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA embeddings align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA perceptual subspace than MAE features.
> 
> **4. Memory-lean optimizers — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor (AdamW with quantized first moment B128, rank-1/linear zero-exclusion quantization and optional factorization of the second moment). On GLUE (RoBERTa-L), ImageNet (Swin-T), E2E-NLG (GPT-2), SQuAD, WMT14 (Transformer), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca instruction tuning, it matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW (e.g., LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5) while cutting memory up to 57.7% and enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; Adafactor/SM3 save more memory but degrade accuracy, especially on ImageNet.
> 
> **5. Video-only pretraining for RL — "Towards Principled Representation Learning from Videos for RL"** (ICLR 2024)
> PAC upper bounds for forward modeling and temporal contrastive learning under iid noise (polynomial sample complexity), and a lower bound showing exogenous noise makes video-only learning exponentially harder than trajectory-based. GridWorld/ViZDoom experiments: without exogenous noise both methods enable successful PPO downstream RL; with exogenous noise temporal contrastive collapses (it can exploit noise), forward modeling degrades more gracefully, and trajectory-based ACRO remains best; temporal contrastive is better than forward modeling for iid Gaussian pixel noise.
> 
> **Cross-paper comparison:**
> - **Optimizers:** (4) explicitly uses Adam/AdamW (32-bit baseline and its quantized variants); (1) uses YOLO-family training (SGD/Adam-style); (3) uses gradient-flow/MSE; (5) uses PPO downstream with frozen encoders — consistent with standard stochastic optimizers.
> - **Objectives:** (3) centers on squared-error latent prediction; (5) compares autoencoding, forward modeling (prediction), and contrastive objectives; (4) preserves the AdamW squared-gradient moment structure; (1) uses detection losses (box/class/association) with task alignment.
> - **Benchmarks:** COCO-style detection (BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman), Sequential MNIST (2), ImageNet/Swin-T, GLUE/SQuAD/WMT/E2E, LLaMA (4), GridWorld/ViZDoom (5).
> - **Key takeaways:** the theory papers (2, 3, 5) each identify an implicit bias or spectral/statistical mechanism — spectrum over sign constraints, high-influence feature prioritization over variance, and exogenous noise as an exponential barrier — while the engineering papers (1, 4) show that principled designs (single part-to-body offset; zero-exclusion/rank-1 4-bit quantization) achieve SOTA/lossless results with better efficiency (accuracy and association robustness; ~43–58% memory savings).

**问题：** I’m building an embodied‑AI pipeline where: (1) we need real‑time hand/face and body‑part association in crowded scenes; (2) pretraining has to use only unlabeled gameplay videos before reinforcement learning; (3) training must fit into tight GPU memory, so optimizer states should be quantized to about 4‑bit; and (4) one module is an interpretable RNN with separate excitatory/inhibitory units. We fine‑tune Transformers and some RNNs with SGD/AdamW and mostly squared‑error losses. Which research should I read to choose between latent prediction vs reconstruction and contrastive vs forward strategies, to understand spectral issues in EI‑constrained RNNs, to deploy low‑precision optimizers, and to implement anchor‑free part–whole detection, ideally with evidence on COCO‑like human‑parts data and classic benchmarks such as MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

> Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results reported by the five papers you provided. I organize findings by identical datasets (direct head‑to‑head), then by similar dataset type, and finally by specific datasets, citing concrete numbers where tables/figures report them.

> 1) Part–whole detection on COCO‑like human‑parts data (PBADet)
> Identical datasets and metrics:
> - BodyHands (hand–body association; AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP; Table 1):
>   • Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Acc. 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
>   • Ours (PBADet, YOLOv5l6): 88.1, 92.71, 85.73
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9, 86.91, 84.39
>   • Other two‑stage or non‑joint baselines are far lower (e.g., BodyHands (2022) Cond. Acc. 83.44, Joint AP 63.48; OpenPose Joint AP 27.81).
>   Result: PBADet improves all three metrics vs. BPJDet (same backbone) and prior systems.
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (multi‑part association; Table 2 and Table 3):
>   • Overall AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate):
>     – BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6/43.3 (best overall AP among the listed methods)
>     – Ours (PBADet, YOLOv5l6): 43.0/41.8; Ours (YOLOv7): 42.7/41.5

>     – Head/face/hands AP: BPJDet higher (e.g., head 56.6 vs. ours 54.6; face 46.3 vs. ours 44.6; r‑hand 40.4 vs. ours 39.0; l‑hand 39.6 vs. ours 37.7).

>     Result: PBADet reduces mismatches across head/face/hands/left‑foot, slightly worse on right‑foot.

> Summary for COCO‑like human‑parts: PBADet achieves SOTA on BodyHands, improves medium/large‑scale and person/feet metrics on COCOHumanParts, and improves MR−2/AP on CrowdHuman, while BPJDet slightly leads in overall COCO AP and head/face/hands AP.

> 2) Video pretraining for RL (representation learning from videos; forward vs. contrastive vs. autoencoder vs. ACRO)
> Identical environments and settings (figures referenced):
> - GridWorld (Fig. 2, Fig. 3, Fig. 6, Fig. 9, Fig. 10):
>   • No exogenous noise: forward modeling and temporal contrastive both support successful downstream RL; autoencoder performance is inconsistent; ACRO also succeeds.
>   • With exogenous observation noise (moving diamonds): temporal contrastive degrades markedly (learns to rely on exogenous pixels; reconstructions in Fig. 3(d) show noise), forward modeling is more robust but degrades as noise increases (Fig. 6, Fig. 9), autoencoder is unpredictable, ACRO remains strong.
>   • With IID noise (diamonds re‑randomized each step): forward modeling and ACRO retain strong learning (Fig. 10).
> - ViZDoom Defend the Center (Fig. 4, Fig. 5, Fig. 13):
>   • No exogenous noise: forward modeling and temporal contrastive both enable successful control; autoencoder also works here.
>   • With exogenous noise (in obs/reward/both): temporal contrastive fails; forward modeling degrades but is more robust than contrastive; ACRO remains reliable.
> - ViZDoom Basic (Fig. 7–8, Fig. 11):
>   • IID Gaussian noise: temporal contrastive handles IID noise best (expected), forward modeling also learns; ACRO remains strong.
> 
> Summary across RL tasks: In the absence of exogenous noise, forward modeling and temporal contrastive both work; with temporally correlated exogenous noise, temporal contrastive tends to fail (representation latches onto noise), forward modeling is somewhat robust but degrades as noise strength or count increases; ACRO (trajectory‑based) is consistently strongest and most robust. These empirical trends match the theory in the paper: forward/contrastive are provably sound without exogenous noise, while exogenous noise creates a statistical gap vs. trajectory‑based pretraining.
> 
> 3) Low‑precision (4‑bit) optimizers vs. 8‑bit/32‑bit and sublinear‑memory baselines
> Identical datasets and metrics (Table 2, A‑Tables; Table 3; Table 4–5):
> - Natural Language Understanding (GLUE, RoBERTa‑L; Table 2): mean score
>   • 32‑bit AdamW: 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW: 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW: 89.1; 4‑bit Factor: 88.9; SM3: 87.5; Adafactor: 89.1; Adafactor β1=0: 89.3
>   Result: 4‑bit AdamW matches 8‑bit and full precision; SM3 underperforms.
> - Question Answering (SQuAD/SQuAD2; Table 2 and App. Table 9): SQuAD F1 (RoBERTa‑L)
>   • 32‑bit AdamW: 94.6; 8‑bit AdamW: 94.5; 4‑bit AdamW: 94.5; 4‑bit Factor: 94.6; SM3: 91.7; Adafactor: 94.6–94.7
>   Result: 4‑bit matches 32‑bit and 8‑bit; SM3 is notably worse.
> - Natural Language Generation (GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG, BLEU; Table 2, Table 8):
>   • 32‑bit AdamW: 67.7; 8‑bit: 67.5; 4‑bit AdamW: 67.8; 4‑bit Factor: 67.6; SM3: 66.9
>   Result: 4‑bit equals or slightly exceeds full precision; SM3 lower.
> - Image classification (Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k Top‑1; Table 2):
>   • 32‑bit: 81.2; 8‑bit: 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW: 80.8; 4‑bit Factor: 80.9; SM3: 79.0; Adafactor: 79.5–80.0
>   Result: 4‑bit is within ~0.3–0.4 points of 32‑bit and 8‑bit; sublinear‑memory optimizers are lower.
> - Machine Translation (Transformer‑Base WMT14 En‑De SacreBLEU; Table 2):
>   • 32‑bit: 26.61; 8‑bit: 26.66; 4‑bit AdamW: 26.28; 4‑bit Factor: 26.45; SM3: 22.72
>   Result: 4‑bit is close to full/8‑bit; SM3 far lower.
> - LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3): 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit across MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC‑e/ARC‑c/OBQA for 7B and 13B (minor deltas); at 33B, 4‑bit MMLU is slightly lower (54.9 vs. 56.4) while other tasks are comparable.
> - Memory/time (Table 4):
>   • LLaMA‑7B, FSDP (2×A100 80GB): 4‑bit reduces total memory from 75.4 GB to 31.9 GB (~57.7% saved) and slightly reduces wall‑time vs. 32‑bit (3.35h → 3.07h).
>   • RoBERTa‑L (single GPU): total memory 5.31 GB → ~3.00 GB (~43–44% saved); with fused kernels, 4‑bit speed equals or surpasses 8‑bit.
>   • GPT‑2 Medium: total memory ~6.89 GB → 4.62 GB (34%), with fused kernels 4‑bit time ~2.11h, near 8‑bit (2.04h) and faster than 32‑bit (2.13h).
> - Trainable model size under a budget (Table 5):
>   • 24 GB: 32‑bit up to OPT‑350M; 4‑bit up to OPT‑1.3B.
>   • 80 GB: 4‑bit trains OPT‑6.7B and LLaMA‑7B (vs. 32‑bit OPT‑1.3B).
> Summary: 4‑bit AdamW achieves near‑lossless accuracy across NLU/QA/NLG/MT and LLaMA tuning while cutting optimizer memory ~2× vs. 8‑bit and much more vs. 32‑bit, with practical speed on par when fused. Sublinear‑memory optimizers (SM3) are more memory‑efficient but substantially worse in accuracy on these benchmarks.
> 
> 4) JEPA (self‑distillation) vs. MAE (reconstruction) — empirical trends
> - Deep linear simulations (Figures 1–4): both learn features greedily by covariance (λ), but only JEPA shows added prioritization by high regression coefficient (ρ) with deeper encoders; when λ and ρ conflict, JEPA and MAE learn different features (order inversion in Fig. 1 and ODE sims Fig. 2–4).
> - ImageNet features (Appendix D, Fig. 7): trained on ImageNet‑1k (64×64), JEPA features have higher mean CCA alignment between full and bottom‑variance data subspace than MAE over training; conversely, MAE aligns more with the top‑variance subspace. Empirically, this supports the claim that JEPA focuses earlier on semantic/low‑variance features while MAE emphasizes high‑variance pixels.
> Summary: Experiments corroborate the theory that JEPA (latent prediction) prioritizes predictive/low‑variance (influential) features as depth increases; MAE (reconstruction) prioritizes variance coverage. This shows up in CCA trends on ImageNet.
> 
> 5) EI‑constrained RNNs (Dale’s Law) — spectral effects and task performance
> Identical tasks across standard/ColEI/DANN (Fig. 2):
> - Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic Object Recognition
>   • ColEI (column‑constrained EI) learns poorly vs. standard RNN and DANN across all four tasks; more variance across seeds; notably stabilized but still worse even with gradient clipping.
>   • DANN (EI reparametrization) matches standard RNN performance across benchmarks.
> - Sensitivity to network size and E/I ratio (Figs. 5–7):
>   • ColEI performance degrades in small networks and with fewer inhibitory units; improves with larger networks and balanced E/I; Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) increases with size/balanced E/I and anti‑correlates with test error (higher NSE → lower error).
>   • DANN spectra and performance are robust across sizes and E/I ratios (good NSE ≈ 0.95 even with 1 inhibitory neuron).
> Summary: Across identical sequence/vision/language benchmarks, standard RNN ≈ DANN ≫ ColEI in learning quality; spectral clustering (high NSE, unimodal singular values) predicts performance; ColEI’s multimodal dispersed spectra (with large singular values) correlate with poor/unstable learning.
> 
> Cross‑cutting comparisons by dataset type
> - Vision detection (COCO/BodyHands/CrowdHuman): PBADet achieves state‑of‑the‑art association on BodyHands and stronger medium/large‑scale and person/feet results on COCOHumanParts; BPJDet slightly higher COCO overall AP; on CrowdHuman, PBADet lowers MR−2 and raises body AP.
> - Vision classification (ImageNet): 4‑bit optimizers keep Swin‑T top‑1 near full/8‑bit; JEPA’s CCA analyses indicate faster alignment to bottom‑variance subspace vs. MAE (no top‑1 numbers reported in that paper, only feature analyses).
> - RL from pixels: With no exogenous noise, latent‑prediction (forward) and contrastive both achieve good control; with exogenous noise, contrastive fails and forward degrades; trajectory‑based ACRO remains best.
> - Language tasks (GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/WMT/LLaMA): 4‑bit AdamW matches 8‑bit/32‑bit baselines across all tasks (minor deltas in ImageNet/MT), while sublinear SM3 lags.
> - Classic benchmarks: Sequential MNIST is shared only within the Dale’s RNN paper; there, ColEI underperforms vs. standard/DANN; MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR are not used in the other papers you provided.
> 
> Key takeaways tied to your pipeline components (from experimental evidence only):
> - Anchor‑free part–whole detection: PBADet yields strong state‑of‑the‑art association on BodyHands and robust improvements (medium/large/person/feet) on COCOHumanParts; BPJDet slightly higher overall AP on COCO.
> - Video self‑supervision: For RL, forward modeling (latent prediction) is empirically and theoretically superior to temporal contrastive under exogenous noise; autoencoding is unpredictable across domains.
> - Low‑precision training: 4‑bit AdamW (with rank‑1 normalization/zero‑free second‑moment quantization) preserves accuracy across NLU/QA/NLG/MT/ImageNet/LLaMA while cutting optimizer memory and enabling larger models under fixed GPU budgets.
> - EI RNNs: DANN‑style EI networks match standard RNN results on adding/Sequential‑MNIST/PTB/NOR and are robust; straightforward ColEI partitions degrade learning, with spectral pathologies (low NSE, multimodal singular values) correlating with poor results.
