**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, here are the four papers to read, mapped to your needs, with experimental comparisons.
> 
> ## 1. Part–whole / part–body association in crowded scenes
> **Read: PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset.
> - BodyHands ablation: anchor-free part-to-body (HandAP **89.1**, Cond-Acc **92.62**, JointAP **85.98**) > anchor-based part-to-body (88.4/92.31/85.28) > BPJDet anchor-based body-to-part (85.3/86.80/78.13). So both the part-to-body definition and anchor-free head help.
> - COCOHumanParts (all categories): YOLOv7 AP **42.7/41.5**, YOLOv5l6 **43.0/41.8**. Also evaluated on CrowdHuman (face–body, leading MR-2/competitive AP) and extended to AnimalPose/AP-10K.
> - Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning each improve association accuracy.
> 
> ## 2. Latent prediction/reconstruction vs contrastive/forward for video pretraining before RL
> **Read both:**
> - **"Towards Principled Representation Learning from Videos for RL" (ICLR 2024)** — compares autoencoder (reconstruction), forward modeling, and temporal contrastive on GridWorld/ViZDoom. With only iid noise, forward modeling and contrastive both provably recover the latent state and enable polynomial-sample RL (autoencoder has no theory; works on ViZDoom but fails gridworld). With exogenous noise (moving distractors), **temporal contrastive completely fails** (it can just track the predictable noise), **forward modeling degrades less and is the best video-based method**; ACRO (action-labeled trajectories) is strongest overall — video pretraining can be exponentially worse than trajectory pretraining.
> - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** — analyzes latent-prediction (JEPA/self-distillation) vs reconstruction (MAE). JEPA is biased to high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ) and increasingly suppresses noisy directions with depth, whereas MAE orders learning by variance λ and is agnostic to ρ. ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE. Conclusion: reconstruction is sub-optimal for perception; latent-space prediction is preferred.
> 
> ## 3. 4-bit quantized optimizer states (tight GPU memory)
> **Read: "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)** — 4-bit AdamW / 4-bit Factor (B128 for first moment, zero-point-free linear + rank-1 normalization for second moment; optional factorization).
> - Results vs 32-bit AdamW: NLU/GLUE (RoBERTa-L) 89.1 vs 88.9; CLS/ImageNet (Swin-T) 80.8 vs 81.2; NLG 67.8 vs 67.7; QA/SQuAD 94.5 vs 94.6; MT/WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61 — lossless or comparable. LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning matches 32-bit; up to **57.7% memory savings** (LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU). Quantizing both moments costs only a marginal drop; sublinear methods (Adafactor/SM3) save more memory but degrade on CLS.
> 
> ## 4. Spectral issues in EI-constrained RNNs
> **Read: "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023)** — compares column-constrained EI (ColEI), DANN, and standard RNNs on adding, **sequential MNIST**, PTB, object recognition.
> - ColEI learns worse and with much higher variance; gradient clipping helps it most. Spectrum "transplant" experiments show the **singular-value spectrum at initialization matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors**. ColEI weights contain a rank-one nilpotent (column-mean) term causing multi-modal, dispersed singular values (vs quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur for standard/DANN). **Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error**; larger networks with balanced E:I ratios train best, while DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> 
> ## Benchmark coverage note
> Evidence on COCO-like human-part data: **COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman** (PBADet). Classic-benchmark evidence: **sequential MNIST** (EI-RNN paper). MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100 also appear in the Hessian-spectrum paper (not one of the four core reads). **SVHN is not covered** in the retrieved context — it cannot be verified here.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers that answer each of your four needs, with comparisons of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Latent prediction vs reconstruction (JEPA vs MAE)
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks" (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024).**
> Deep-linear-network analysis shows the two objectives have *different greedy learning orders*: JEPA (latent prediction/self-distillation) learns **high-influence features** (large regression coefficient ρ) first, increasingly with depth, while MAE (reconstruction) only prioritizes **high-covariance features** (large λ) even if they are noisy. The depth dependence is formal (critical-time analysis: JEPA's order inverts toward ρ, MAE's stays λ-only). On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA's features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace that contains perceptual features than MAE's (measured by CCA) — i.e., latent prediction suppresses noise/reconstruction that MAE captures. Practical takeaway: prefer latent prediction (JEPA-style) for your video pretraining.
> 
> ## 2. Contrastive vs forward strategies (video pretraining for RL)
> **"Towards Principled Representation Learning from Videos for Reinforcement Learning" (Misra et al., ICLR 2024).**
> Compares autoencoder (reconstruction), temporal contrastive learning, and forward modeling in GridWorld and ViZDoom. Results:
> - **Without exogenous noise**: forward modeling and temporal contrastive both provably work and give efficient downstream RL.
> - **With exogenous (temporally correlated) noise** (e.g., moving background objects — like your crowded scenes): **temporal contrastive completely fails** because it can minimize its loss by focusing entirely on predictable noise; **forward modeling is more robust** but still degrades as noise grows; autoencoder is inconsistent (works in ViZDoom Defend the Center, fails in GridWorld). Trajectory-based ACRO is strongest overall.
> - Theory: forward modeling has larger margins but a more complex function class; contrastive is better for i.i.d. pixel noise; video-only learning is exponentially harder than trajectory learning.
> 
> So for unlabeled gameplay video, forward/latent-dynamics prediction is the safer choice over contrastive.
> 
> ## 3. Spectral issues in EI-constrained RNNs
> **"Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly" (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023).**
> On adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition, column-constrained E/I RNNs (ColEI) learn worse and with higher variance than DANN (feedforward Dale's-ANN-style) and standard RNNs. Key experimental findings:
> - **Spectrum, not sign constraints, dominates**: sign constraints only explain part of the gap (0.7±0.3% for RNNs, 1±1% for ColEI, vs 2.3±0.6% total). "Spectrum transplant" experiments show singular-value spectra contribute more than singular vectors or sign constraints.
> - ColEI has multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure); standard/DANN match random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur forms.
> - **Normalized SVD entropy (NSE)** at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance across sizes/EI ratios; smaller networks or fewer I units are worse; DANN stays robust; gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially.
> 
> ## 4. 4-bit optimizer states
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" / "4-bit Optimizers" (Li, Chen, Zhu, NeurIPS 2023).**
> 4-bit Adam/AdamW (small block size B128 for first moment; zero-point-excluded linear mapping + rank-1 normalization for second moment) **matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW**: GLUE (RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9), Swin-T ImageNet-1k (80.8 vs 81.2), GPT-2 Medium E2E-NLG (67.8 vs 67.7), SQuAD (94.5 vs 94.6), WMT14 en-de (26.28 vs 26.61), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning across MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA. Memory savings up to **57.7%** (LLaMA-7B: 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB; trains on a single 80 GB GPU). Ablations: smaller first-moment block size and factorizing the second moment each improve accuracy/memory. Sublinear-memory baselines Adafactor/SM3 save more memory but degrade accuracy, especially on image classification.
> 
> ## 5. Anchor-free part–whole detection
> **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association (Gao et al., ICLR 2024).**
> - **BodyHands**: PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) achieves HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 — beating BPJDet (YOLOv5m6: 85.3/86.80/78.13; YOLOv5l6: 85.9/86.91/84.39), BodyHands 2022, OpenPose, KeypointCommunities, and Mask R-CNN variants.
> - **COCOHumanParts** (head, face, left/right hands, left/right feet): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) reaches AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 vs BPJDet 43.6/43.3 (roughly on par), but **leads on AP_M, AP_L, and person/feet detection, and has the lowest average mMR-2** for head, face, both hands, and right foot. On CrowdHuman face-body it leads body MR-2 with competitive AP; versus ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet.
> - Ablations: the association loss is critical (baseline conditional accuracy 80.78 → 92.62 full), and **anchor-free part-to-body (89.1/92.62/85.98) outperforms anchor-based part-to-body (88.4/92.31/85.28) and anchor-based body-to-part BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13)** — direct evidence that the anchor-free, part-to-body formulation is the right choice.
> 
> ## Benchmark coverage caveat
> Classic-benchmark evidence appears as: **sequential MNIST** (EI-RNN paper), **MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100 with SGD/Adam variants** (in the Hessian-spectrum study "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure," which uses those datasets and shows power-law Hessian structure with SGD/Adam, relevant to your optimizer fine-tuning), **ImageNet-1K** (JEPA/MAE and contrastive-similarity analyses), and **GridWorld/ViZDoom** (video pretraining). **SVHN does not appear anywhere in this collection**, so no evidence from it can be provided.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross-paper comparison of experimental results (datasets, metrics, and trade‑offs)
> 
> Shared/overlapping datasets and tasks
> - ImageNet (classification): Reported by the 4‑bit Optimizers paper (Swin‑T) and by BSO/T‑BSO (ResNet‑18, spiking/binary). The settings are different (full-precision vs. binary spiking networks, different backbones and training regimes), but the dataset is identical.
> - CIFAR-10 / CIFAR‑100 (classification): Reported comprehensively by BSO/T‑BSO (VGG‑11, spiking/binary). The 4‑bit Optimizers paper does not report these in its tables.
> - COCO-family human-part/association datasets: Reported by PBADet only (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman). No overlap with other papers.
> - Sequential MNIST/time-series: Reported by the Dale’s Law spectral study (sequential MNIST and other time-series tasks). No identical overlap, but this matches the “time-series modeling” theme.
> - Imagenet-derived analysis for representation learning: JEPA paper reports CCA behavior on ImageNet-1K (64×64) for representation dynamics (not standard accuracy), overlapping on dataset family but different metric.
> 
> Per-dataset (or dataset family) comparisons
> 
> ImageNet classification
> - 4‑bit Optimizers (Swin‑T, standard CNN/Transformer training): Top‑1 accuracy 80.8% (4‑bit AdamW) vs 81.2% (32‑bit AdamW) on ImageNet-1K classification (Table 2, CLS). This shows near‑parity with 32‑bit while compressing optimizer state to 4‑bit.
> - BSO/T‑BSO (ResNet‑18, binary spiking SNN): Top‑1 accuracy 58.86% (6 steps) and 57.76% (4 steps) for T‑BSO (Table 2, ImageNet), which is higher than CBP (binary spiking backprop) on the same backbone and time steps (54.34% at 4 steps), but below full‑precision SNN baselines (e.g., FP‑SNN 63.18% at 4 steps) and state-of-the-art online SNN training on larger backbones (SLTT ResNet‑34 66.19% at 6 steps; OTTT ResNet‑34 64.16% at 6 steps). Summary on the identical dataset: 4‑bit AdamW on Swin‑T retains ~99.5% of 32‑bit accuracy; T‑BSO with binary spiking nets is markedly lower in absolute accuracy but beats prior BSNN method CBP on the same backbone/time‑steps.
> 
> CIFAR-10 and CIFAR‑100 classification (BSO/T‑BSO vs spiking baselines)
> - CIFAR‑10 (VGG‑11):
>   - T‑BSO reaches 94.86% (4 steps), 94.70% (6 steps), 94.32% (2 steps); BSO 92.98% (6 steps) (Table 2). 
>   - Compared baselines: OTTT 93.73%, NDOT 94.90% (best), CBP 91.51%, Q‑SNN 93.20% (Table 2). 
>   - Who is better: NDOT is very slightly best (94.90%), T‑BSO is essentially on par at 94.86% (4 steps) and above OTTT/CBP/Q‑SNN; BSO trails T‑BSO.
> - CIFAR‑100 (VGG‑11):
>   - T‑BSO reaches 74.27% (6 steps), 73.82% (4), 73.40% (2); BSO 72.57% (6) (Table 2).
>   - Baselines: NDOT 76.61% (best), Q‑SNN 73.48%, OTTT 71.11%, CBP 66.53% (Table 2).
>   - Who is better: NDOT best; T‑BSO beats Q‑SNN/OTTT/CBP; BSO trails T‑BSO.
> - Temporal scaling (ablation): On CIFAR‑100, T‑BSO consistently outperforms BSO at the same time steps, and both improve with more steps (e.g., BSO ~72.15%→72.71%; T‑BSO ~73.40%→75.20% as steps increase; Figure 5).
> 
> Neuromorphic DVS‑CIFAR10 (event-based classification)
> - T‑BSO: 81.00% (10 steps); BSO: 80.60%. Baselines: SLTT 82.20% (best), NDOT 77.50%, CBP 74.70%, Q‑SNN 79.10% (Table 2). 
> - Who is better: SLTT is best; T‑BSO is second best and improves over NDOT/CBP/Q‑SNN; BSO slightly trails T‑BSO.
> 
> COCOHumanParts / BodyHands / CrowdHuman (part‑body association; PBADet)
> - BodyHands (hand–body association): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 88.1/92.71/85.73 (Table 1). Compared baselines, the closest prior BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) had 85.9/86.91/84.39. Who is better: PBADet improves all three metrics vs BPJDet and others, with particularly large gains in conditional accuracy.
> - COCOHumanParts (multi-part detection+association):
>   - Overall AP (AP.5:.95 original/subordinate): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 and PBADet (YOLOv7) 42.7/41.5, versus BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3 (Table 2). Detection APs are comparable; BPJDet is slightly higher on the headline AP, while PBADet leads in some size/category breakdowns (e.g., APM/APL and certain per‑category APs, such as person 62.4 vs 61.3 and feet categories).
>   - Association quality (mMR−2; lower is better): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) shows the lowest average mMR−2 in multiple categories (e.g., head 27.9, face 30.5, left hand 36.2, right hand 40.8, right foot 50.4, left foot 47.9) compared to BPJDet (30.8/31.8/41.6/42.2/49.1/50.4) and PBADet (YOLOv7) (Table 3). Who is better: PBADet achieves notably better association (mMR−2) in most categories, with detection APs overall on par.
> - CrowdHuman (face–body association): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves the best MR−2 for body (36.5) and face (44.7), and the best body AP 91.6, with mMR−2 body–face 50.8 (Table 5). Compared to BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) mMR−2 50.1, PBADet’s association mMR−2 is comparable (slightly higher), but detection is stronger (Table 5, 6). Who is better: PBADet leads detection (MR−2 and AP), with association quality comparable to BPJDet.
> 
> Representation learning dynamics (JEPA vs MAE)
> - ImageNet‑1K (64×64) linear-probe similarity (CCA) trends (Figure 7): JEPA’s features from “full” and “bottom (low‑variance)” subspaces remain more similar over training than MAE, whereas MAE’s features align more with the “top (high‑variance)” subspace. No classification accuracies are reported in this paper, but the experimental curves show JEPA prioritizes “bottom‑spectrum” perceptual subspaces earlier and more strongly than MAE, supporting the paper’s claim that JEPA biases learning toward high‑influence (predictive, less noisy) features.
> 
> Recurrent networks with Dale’s Law constraints (spectral analysis)
> - Benchmarks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task (Figure 2). Across all, ColEI (column‑sign constrained EI) RNNs learn worse than DANNs and standard RNNs; performance improves with gradient clipping but remains below others (text and Figure 2). Spectrum transplant experiments show that imposing ColEI’s singular value spectrum onto standard RNNs degrades performance more than imposing sign constraints alone; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti‑correlates with final test error (Figure 7). While no exact percent metrics are tabulated, the clear experimental outcome is that spectrum pathology (multimodal, dispersed singular values) is the key driver of poorer results in ColEI RNNs versus standard/DANN RNNs on these time‑series tasks.
> 
> Optimizer/memory efficiency comparisons
> - 4‑bit Optimizers (AdamW family) vs 32‑bit and 8‑bit (Tables 2, 4, 5, 6):
>   - Accuracy retention: 
>     • RoBERTa‑L NLU: 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 equals 8‑bit and matches 32‑bit (89.1/89.1/88.9).
>     • GPT‑2 Medium E2E‑NLG BLEU: 4‑bit AdamW 67.8 vs 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5.
>     • QA (SQuAD F1): 4‑bit AdamW 94.5 vs 32‑bit 94.6.
>     • ImageNet Swin‑T: 4‑bit AdamW 80.8 vs 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit not reported for CLS in Table 2.
>     • Machine Translation (WMT14 en‑de): 4‑bit AdamW 26.28 vs 32‑bit 26.61.
>   - LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3): 4‑bit AdamW matches or slightly trails 32‑bit across MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA at 7B/13B/33B (e.g., 7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; ARC‑c 44.4 vs 45.1).
>   - Memory/time (Table 4): On LLaMA‑7B (FSDP, 2×A100‑80GB), 4‑bit AdamW reduces total memory from 75.40 GB to 31.87 GB (−57.7%) and modestly speeds/maintains time (3.35 h → 3.07–3.11 h). On RoBERTa‑L and GPT‑2 Medium, 4‑bit AdamW reduces total training memory by ~34–47% (with fused kernels), and matches or exceeds 8‑bit runtime after fusion.
>   - Capacity under memory budgets (Table 5): Under 24 GB, largest fine‑tunable OPT grows from 350M (32‑bit) to 1.3B with 4‑bit AdamW; under 80 GB, from 1.3B to 6.7B; LLaMA‑7B becomes trainable on a single 80 GB GPU with 4‑bit optimizer.
> - BSO/T‑BSO (online binary spiking training) vs BPTT (Figure 4): Training memory is constant across time steps for BSO/T‑BSO (≈2.9–3.1 GB), while BPTT grows linearly with steps (e.g., ~2.86 GB at 1 step to ~58.18 GB at 35 steps). This demonstrates a strong memory‑efficiency advantage during training, in addition to model size reductions from binarization (e.g., VGG‑11 ~1.20 MB for CIFAR tasks in Table 2).
> 
> Task‑type comparisons (who performs better by task)
> - Image classification with conventional architectures: 4‑bit AdamW retains ~near‑baseline accuracy on ImageNet (Swin‑T 80.8% vs 81.2%), and on E2E‑NLG/QA/NLU/MT tasks it matches or is very close to 32‑bit. For users seeking conventional accuracy with much lower optimizer memory, 4‑bit AdamW is superior.
> - Spiking/binary image (and neuromorphic) classification: T‑BSO is strongly competitive against online spiking baselines on CIFAR‑10/100 and DVS‑CIFAR10, generally trailing only the very best spiking method per dataset (e.g., NDOT or SLTT), and clearly outperforming earlier BSNN training (e.g., CBP) while offering constant training memory across time steps.
> - Part–body association detection: PBADet leads in BodyHands and achieves comparable or better association accuracy (lower mMR−2) than BPJDet on COCOHumanParts categories while keeping detection AP on par; on CrowdHuman it achieves the best detection MR−2/AP with association on par.
> - Time‑series (RNN) tasks: DANNs/standard RNNs outperform ColEI‑constrained RNNs; experiments attribute the gap mainly to spectral properties at initialization (not merely sign constraints), as shown by spectrum transplants and NSE–error correlations.
> - Representation learning (self‑supervised): JEPA’s experiments (CCA on ImageNet) show learned representations align more with bottom‑variance (perceptual) subspaces than MAE, supporting the claim that JEPA prioritizes predictive, less‑noisy features; MAE emphasizes top‑variance reconstruction. No classification numbers are reported in that paper; the comparison is representation‑quality oriented.
> 
> Key takeaways across identical/similar datasets
> - On the identical ImageNet dataset:
>   • 4‑bit AdamW (Swin‑T) delivers ~99.5% of 32‑bit accuracy while halving or better the total training memory in large‑model settings (e.g., LLaMA‑7B training saw −57.7% memory). 
>   • T‑BSO (ResNet‑18, spiking/binary) achieves markedly lower absolute accuracy but is superior to prior BSNN baseline CBP on the same backbone/time‑steps and gives constant training memory vs BPTT’s linear growth.
> - On similar image classification families (CIFAR‑10/100): T‑BSO is competitive with the best online SNN methods on CIFAR‑10 and close on CIFAR‑100 (NDOT best on both), and consistently better than older BSNN methods, with strong gains as time steps increase.
> - On structured detection/association (COCO/BodyHands/CrowdHuman): PBADet is the best overall performer for part–body association accuracy (mMR−2) in most categories, and either matches or comes within a small margin of the strongest detector APs, while clearly improving joint association metrics on BodyHands.
> - On time‑series modeling: For sequential MNIST and related tasks, imposing Dale’s Law via column sign constraints (ColEI) harms performance relative to standard/DANN RNNs; the experiments pinpoint the singular value spectrum as the main culprit.
> - On self‑supervised representation learning with images: JEPA’s learning dynamics favor predictive (bottom‑spectrum) features more strongly and earlier than MAE, which favors reconstruction of high‑variance content; this is demonstrated via CCA similarity curves on subsets of the data spectrum.
> 
> Overall, if the goal is conventional accuracy with large‑model fine‑tuning under limited memory, 4‑bit AdamW is best (near‑parity accuracy, large memory cuts). For energy/memory‑efficient spiking pipelines, T‑BSO provides strong accuracy vs state‑of‑the‑art online SNN methods with constant training memory. For multi‑person part–body association, PBADet delivers the strongest association quality (lower mMR−2) and competitive‑to‑better detection. For RNNs with biological constraints, spectral initialization dominates performance; DANN‑style recurrent networks match standard RNNs, while simple ColEI constraints underperform. For self‑supervised vision, JEPA’s empirical dynamics align with learning semantically rich, low‑variance features, contrasting MAE’s reconstruction focus.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers Found (one per requested topic)
> 
> 1. **JEPA vs. reconstruction** — *Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features* (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`)
> 2. **Spectral analysis of E/I-constrained RNNs** — *Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly* (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`)
> 3. **Memory-light optimizers (4-bit SGD/Adam states, LoRA fine-tuning)** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`)
> 4. **Online optimization for binary/spiking models with temporal dynamics** — *BSO: Binary Spiking Online Optimization* (ICML 2025, doc `4741ca1f…`)
> 5. **Anchor-free part–body association detector** — *PBADet* (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`)
> 
> ## Experimental Results
> 
> **1. JEPA vs MAE (theory + ImageNet CCA).** In deep linear networks, JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient ρ), while MAE prioritizes high-variance (λ) features; the JEPA noise-suppression grows with encoder depth (fixed point w̄_JEPA = ρ^L, w̄_MAE = ρ^{L/(L+1)}; 1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE). On ImageNet-1K (64×64 ViT), I-JEPA's features show higher CCA similarity to the low-variance (bottom-25% PCA, perceptual) subspace than MAE throughout training, and lower similarity to the top-75% subspace — i.e., JEPA aligns faster with discriminative, low-variance features. No classification accuracy is reported; evaluation is CCA-based.
> 
> **2. E/I-constrained RNNs (Dale's law).** Across adding, row-wise sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition, column-constrained ColEI networks learn worst and with highest seed variance; recurrent Dale's-ANN (DANN) and standard RNNs perform comparably. On sequential MNIST, spectrum-transplant experiments show the initial singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors (spectrum accounts for ~1.5–2% error vs ~0.7–1% for sign constraints; total ColEI gap 2.3%±0.6%). ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed (rank-one column-mean + Marchenko-Pastur-violating modes) vs the quarter-circle law for standard RNNs/DANNs. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance across EI ratio and network size (small balanced networks beat large skewed ones). Gradient clipping helps ColEI disproportionately.
> 
> **3. 4-bit optimizers.** 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor match or slightly beat 32-bit AdamW on all tasks: GLUE RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9; ImageNet Swin-T 80.8/80.9 vs 81.2 (comparable); SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning matches on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA. Memory savings up to 57.7%; LLaMA-7B trains on one 80GB GPU; 4× larger OPT models fit a budget. Sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor β₁=0, SM3) degrade notably on ImageNet (80.0/79.0 vs 81.2). Quantized SGD(M) convergence is proven in the appendix; the paper's fine-tuning uses the LoRA pipeline (GPT-2 Medium, LLaMA), but CIFAR-100 is not among its benchmarks (it is covered by paper 4 instead).
> 
> **4. BSO/T-BSO (binary spiking online optimization).** T-BSO: CIFAR-10 94.86% (94.70/94.32 at 6/4/2 timesteps), surpassing OTTT by 0.97% with 30.76× model reduction; CIFAR-100 74.27% (+0.79% vs BPTT-based Q-SNN); ImageNet 57.76% (+3.42% vs CBP) at 4.22 MB (20× smaller), though still below SLTT/OTTT; DVS-CIFAR10 81.00%; Google Speech Commands 96.12% (vs 95.18 STS-T, 94.31 ATIF), 1.26 MB. Training memory is time-step-invariant (BSO 2.9 GB, T-BSO 3.1 GB) whereas BPTT grows from 2.86 GB to 58.18 GB (20.3×) over 1→35 steps. Regret bounds O(√T) (BSO) and O(T^{3/4}) (T-BSO); hyperparameters (γ, β) are robust (72.83–73.41% across γ range).
> 
> **5. PBADet.** On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9 M) achieves HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 — beating BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 86.1 M: 85.9/86.91/84.39) and far exceeding OpenPose (39.7/74.03/27.81). On COCOHumanParts, AP is on par with BPJDet but leads AP_M/AP_L and person/feet APs and lowest average mMR-2. Ablations show the anchor-free part-to-body design (89.1/92.62/85.98) outperforms anchor-based part-to-body (88.4/92.31/85.28) and BPJDet-style body-to-part (85.3/86.80/78.13); association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each help. Versus ED-Pose, PBADet gives higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands/feet.
> 
> ## Comparative Analysis
> 
> - **Shared theme — efficiency vs. accuracy trade-off.** Papers 3 and 4 both compress the training pipeline (4-bit states; binary weights + online flipping) and show near-lossless accuracy at large memory savings (57.7% memory cut; 20–31× model shrink, constant-memory training). Paper 4 is the only one demonstrating the trade-off across a wide scale (CIFAR-10/100 → ImageNet → neuromorphic/audio), with accuracy slightly below full-precision BPTT methods at the extreme (ImageNet 57.76%) but matching/exceeding them on smaller datasets.
> - **Biological/spectral constraints (papers 1 & 2) both find that *how* features are prioritized/initialized matters more than the raw loss or sign constraints.** Paper 1 shows the objective's implicit bias (ρ vs λ) determines which features are learned first; paper 2 shows the initial weight spectrum (NSE), not the E/I sign constraint, governs trainability. Both are diagnosable a priori (critical times; NSE) and both favor low-variance/"perceptual" structure.
> - **Metric landscape.** Only paper 5 evaluates with Precision/Recall/F1 (vs ED-Pose) alongside AP; paper 3 reports F1 on SQuAD; papers 1–2 use accuracy/error/CCA; paper 4 uses top-1 accuracy. Cross-entropy classification objectives are used by papers 2, 4, and 5 (classification loss), while paper 1 evaluates embeddings via CCA (no feedforward-classifier accuracy reported), and paper 3's fine-tuning includes classification (ImageNet) plus language metrics.
> - **Caveats.** No single paper in the collection reports *all* of the requested criteria (cross-entropy + embeddings + feedforward classifiers + Precision/F1) simultaneously. The 4-bit paper does not run CIFAR-100 or native end-to-end LoRA experiments (it fine-tunes via LoRA pipelines on language models and ImageNet), and paper 1 reports no downstream classifier accuracy — so those specific combinations cannot be established from this collection.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, here are the papers matching each requested area, with an analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. JEPA-style latent prediction vs reconstruction
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** — analyzes JEPA self-distillation vs MAE reconstruction. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE features (measured by CCA), and the paper proves JEPAs prioritize "influential" (high regression-coefficient) features while MAE prioritizes high-variance/noisy features. No top-1 accuracy is reported; evaluation is via CCA similarity dynamics.
> 
> **LDReg (ICLR 2024)** — regularizes SSL to prevent local dimensional collapse; evaluated with feedforward linear classifiers on frozen features. Results: ImageNet linear probing SimCLR 63.6→64.1 (N=512), 64.2→64.7 (N=1024), 64.3→64.8 (N=2048); MoCo 68.7→69.6, VICReg 66.7→66.9, Barlow Twins 65.5→65.6; also improves COCO detection (SimCLR APbb 36.48→37.15). Effective rank increases consistently. This is the only paper here explicitly using feature embeddings + feedforward (linear) classifiers.
> 
> ## 2. Spectral analysis of E/I-constrained RNNs
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** — ColEI (column sign-constrained) RNNs learn worse than standard RNNs and DANN (recurrent Dale's ANNs) on sequential MNIST, adding, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition, with higher seed variance. Spectrum transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints: sign constraints cost only 0.7%±0.3% (RNN) / 1%±1% (ColEI), whereas spectrum accounts for 1.5%±0.3% / 2%±1%; the full RNN–ColEI gap is 2.3%±0.6%. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error; smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance. Gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> 
> ## 3. Memory-light optimizers (4-bit states)
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)** — 4-bit quantized AdamW (B128 block-wise first moment, rank-1/zero-excluded second moment, optional factorization; also convergence proof for quantized SGD(M)). Results match 32-bit AdamW: ImageNet-1k Swin-T 81.2→80.8 (4-bit AdamW) / 80.9 (4-bit Factor); RoBERTa-L GLUE 88.9→89.1; SQuAD QA F1 94.6→94.5; GPT-2M E2E-NLG BLEU 67.7→67.8; WMT14 26.61→26.28/26.45. Memory saved up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B, 75.4→31.9 GB). **Caveat:** it evaluates ImageNet classification and LLM fine-tuning (Alpaca/MMLU), not CIFAR-100, and LoRA appears only as a cited reference, not an evaluated setting. **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure" (ICML 2025)** is the closest match for LoRA + CIFAR-100: it fine-tunes ViT-B on CIFAR-100 with Adam and analyzes Hessian power-law spectra of LoRA adapters (TinyLlama on MathQA), showing LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure that full fine-tuning does.
> 
> ## 4. Online optimization for binary/spiking models
> **"BSO: Binary Spiking Online Optimization Algorithm" (ICML 2025)** — online (BPTT-free, time-independent memory) training for binary-weight SNNs, with temporal-aware T-BSO using first/second-order moments; explicitly uses cross-entropy loss. Results (VGG-11/ResNet-18): CIFAR-10 T-BSO 94.86% (4 steps) vs OTTT 93.73%; CIFAR-100 74.27% (vs Q-SNN 73.48%); ImageNet 57.76% (vs CBP 54.34%); DVS-CIFAR10 81.00%, Google Speech Commands 96.12%. Memory cut to O(n²L/32) with model size reduction ~20–31×; regret O(√T) (BSO) and O(T^3/4) (T-BSO).
> 
> ## 5. Anchor-free part–body association
> **"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association" (ICLR 2024)** — single part-to-body center offset, classification/DFL/IoU (task-alignment) + association losses. Results: BodyHands (YOLOv7) HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 vs BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13) and BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48); COCOHumanParts all-category AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet 43.6/43.3, with best AP_M/AP_L; CrowdHuman body MR-2 36.5 (best) and body AP 91.6. Against ED-Pose (pose estimation), PBADet yields substantially higher Precision/Recall/F1 (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; left-hand 46.50 vs 22.87) — the clearest Precision/F1 evaluation in the collection.
> 
> ## Cross-paper comparison
> - **Evaluation metrics:** PBADet uses AP/MR-2 plus Precision/Recall/F1 (vs ED-Pose); the 4-bit optimizer uses accuracy/F1/BLEU/SacreBLEU; BSO uses accuracy; LDReg uses linear-probe accuracy; JEPA/MAE paper uses CCA; EI-RNN paper uses test error. So Precision/F1 is essentially unique to PBADet (and QA-F1 in the optimizer paper).
> - **Cross-entropy objectives:** explicitly stated in BSO (loss L can be cross-entropy) and used implicitly in the classification heads of LDReg, 4-bit optimizer (classification), and PBADet (classification branch); the contrastive-embedding paper (160e1407) also trains feedforward classifiers on feature embeddings (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100/ImageNet top-1).
> - **Consistency of findings:** JEPA/MAE and EI-RNN papers both conclude that spectral/structure properties (feature subspace; singular-value spectrum) matter more than raw loss/constraint choices; the optimizer and BSO papers show 4-bit/online compression achieves near-lossless accuracy with large memory savings (57.7% for 4-bit AdamW; ~20–31× for BSO); PBADet shows a single part-to-body offset outperforms multi-offset anchor-based BPJDet, especially for multi-part tasks.
> 
> **Gaps/limitations:** No single paper combines all requested elements. The 4-bit optimizer paper does not test CIFAR-100 or LoRA end-to-end (only ImageNet and LLM fine-tuning, with LoRA as a reference); the CIFAR-100/LoRA connection is only via the Hessian-structure paper. The JEPA paper is theoretical (deep linear networks) with no top-1 classification numbers.

Ideally these works mention COCO, MNIST, SGD/AdamW, Transformers, and fine‑tuning.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross‑paper comparison of experimental results (five works)
> 
> 1) PBADet (ICLR 2024): one‑stage, anchor‑free part–body association in vision
> - Datasets with identical evaluation across methods:
>   - BodyHands: Compared to prior anchor‑based BPJDet on the same dataset.
>     • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>     • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.
>     Result: PBADet improves hand detection (+3.2 AP vs BPJDet l6), conditional accuracy (+~5.8), and joint AP (+~1.6) on identical data and metrics (Table 1).
>   - COCOHumanParts: Multi‑part association (head/face/hands/feet) vs BPJDet and Hier R‑CNN.
>     • Overall AP (orig/sub): PBADet YOLOv5l6 43.0/41.8, PBJDet YOLOv5l6 43.6/43.3. PBADet is on par in AP. It leads in APM/APL (PBADet: 66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4) and per‑category Person and Feet APs (Table 2).
>     • Association robustness (average mMR−2, lower is better): PBADet achieves lower mismatch rates than BPJDet for head (27.9 vs 30.8), face (30.5 vs 31.8), and hands/feet (Table 3).
>   - CrowdHuman (face–body pairing):
>     • Body MR−2: PBADet YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 36.5/37.5 (better) vs BPJDet l6 40.7.
>     • Face MR−2: PBADet 44.7/45.3 vs BPJDet l6 46.3 (better).
>     • Body AP: PBADet 91.6/91.4 vs BPJDet l6 89.5 (better).
>     • Pair mMR−2 (association): PBADet ~50.8–50.9 vs BPJDet l6 50.1 (BPJDet slightly lower—better—mismatch rate) (Table 5).
> - Summary on similar vision tasks: PBADet consistently improves detection quality and association robustness on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts; on CrowdHuman its detection is stronger while association is comparable to the best prior.
> 
> 2) Memory‑efficient 4‑bit optimizers (NeurIPS 2023): accuracy vs memory/time on NLP, vision, and LLM fine‑tuning
> - Identical datasets across methods within this paper:
>   - RoBERTa‑L on GLUE (NLU mean acc/corr): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW† 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit Factor 88.9 (Table 2). Result: 4‑bit matches 32‑bit and 8‑bit.
>   - Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k (classification): 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9 (Table 2). Result: ≤0.4% drop for 4‑bit vs 32‑bit.
>   - GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG (BLEU): 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5; 4‑bit AdamW 67.8; 4‑bit Factor 67.6 (Table 2). Result: 4‑bit preserves or slightly improves BLEU.
>   - SQuAD/SQuAD2.0 (QA): e.g., SQuAD F1 32‑bit 94.6 vs 4‑bit 94.5 (Table 2 & Table 9): parity.
>   - WMT14 en‑de (Transformer‑Base SacreBLEU): 32‑bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; 4‑bit AdamW 26.28; 4‑bit Factor 26.45 (Table 2): small drop for 4‑bit.
>   - LLaMA instruction tuning (Alpaca) across model sizes:
>     • 7B: MMLU 38.7 (32‑bit) vs 38.9 (4‑bit); HellaSwag 74.6 vs 74.7; ARC‑e 61.5 vs 61.2; ARC‑c 45.1 vs 44.4; OBQA 43.4 vs 43.0 (Table 3).
>     • 13B: 4‑bit matches or exceeds 32‑bit on most metrics (e.g., HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8; ARC‑e 64.1 vs 63.6).
>     • 33B: mixed—MMLU 54.9 (4‑bit) vs 56.4 (32‑bit); OBQA 45.4 (4‑bit) vs 43.8.
> - Memory/time (identical training setups):
>   - LLaMA‑7B finetuning: Total GPU mem 31.87 GB (4‑bit) vs 75.40 GB (32‑bit), 57.7% reduction; time 3.07 h (4‑bit) vs 3.35 h (32‑bit) (Table 4). 
>   - RoBERTa‑L finetuning: mem 3.00 GB (4‑bit fused) vs 5.31 GB (32‑bit), 43.5% reduction; speed parity with fused kernels (3.17 vs 3.93 min) (Table 4).
>   - GPT‑2 Medium finetuning: mem 4.62 GB (4‑bit) vs 6.89 GB, 34.4% reduction; fused 4‑bit runtime similar to 32‑bit (2.11 h vs 2.13 h) (Table 4).
> - Ablations on identical dataset/task (E2E‑NLG):
>   - Second‑moment quantization with DE vs DE‑0 vs Linear, rank‑1 normalization:
>     • Best stable/higher BLEU uses Rank‑1 + Linear (67.8 ± 0.51) without Stable Embeddings; DE with zero‑point caused instability (Table 1). Factorizing v also works (67.6 ± 0.33).
> - Summary on similar task families:
>   - Across NLP classification, QA, NLG and LLM tuning, 4‑bit states preserve 32‑bit accuracy while cutting optimizer memory ~35–58% and maintaining or improving throughput when fused. On ImageNet classification, 4‑bit incurs ≤0.4% accuracy drop.
> 
> 3) Learning with Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023): spectral properties drive performance in recurrent nets
> - Identical tasks across methods in this paper:
>   - Adding problem (length 20), Sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task. Result trends (Fig. 2): Standard RNNs and DANN (Dale’s ANNs) learn well and similarly; ColEI (column EI sign‑constrained) learns worse on all four tasks and exhibits higher variance; gradient clipping helps ColEI more than others.
> - Spectrum transplant experiments on the same benchmarks (Fig. 4): Giving standard RNNs the ColEI singular‑value spectrum degrades performance nearly as much as ColEI; conversely, giving ColEI the RNN spectrum improves performance—even with sign constraints—showing spectra impact performance more than signs.
> - Architectural/dataset variations on similar tasks:
>   - EI ratio and size (Sequential MNIST): Reducing inhibitory proportion lowers normalized SVD entropy (NSE) and harms learning; DANN’s spectrum and performance robust even with a single inhibitory unit; increasing network size increases NSE and improves test error; across settings, NSE anti‑correlates with test error (Figs. 5–7).
> - Summary: On sequential and language benchmarks, recurrent DANNs match standard RNNs; ColEI underperforms unless its spectrum resembles standard RNNs. Stability and accuracy track a spectral unimodality measure (NSE) across datasets.
> 
> 4) JEPA vs MAE (NeurIPS 2024): representation dynamics on vision data
> - Identical dataset family overlap with 4‑bit paper: ImageNet‑1K (both evaluate on ImageNet)—but with different metrics/objectives.
>   - ImageNet‑1K (64×64) encoder evaluation (Appendix D): CCA analysis shows JEPA representations align more with the bottom variance (perceptual) subspace than MAE early in training (higher full↔bottom CCA; lower full↔top CCA). 
> - Controlled linear‑model experiments (Gaussian data, temporal model) across identical synthetic settings:
>   - JEPA vs MAE ODE simulations (Figs. 2, 4): Both show greedy feature learning in λ (covariance), but only JEPA prioritizes features with larger regression coefficients ρ (i.e., higher predictive influence). Depth amplifies this JEPA bias.
> - Summary on vision tasks: On ImageNet‑style data, JEPA prioritizes semantically useful, low‑variance features more quickly than MAE (feature‑space comparisons), complementing the 4‑bit paper’s accuracy‑retention results on ImageNet classification.
> 
> 5) Hybrid RL with HNPG (ICLR 2024): offline‑enhanced on‑policy PG vs off‑policy baselines
> - Identical benchmarks across methods in this paper:
>   - Continuous Comblock (rich observation, continuous action):
>     • HNPG solves horizons up to 50 (≈30M online samples), RLPD up to 15, TRPO fails at 5 (Fig. 2 left). 
>     • Critic behavior: HNPG’s on‑policy MC regression loss is stable; RLPD’s off‑policy TD loss is volatile (Fig. 4), explaining training instability.
>   - Image‑based Continuous Comblock (observations from CIFAR‑100 CLIP features; train/test split):
>     • HNPG solves horizons up to 30 (≈10M online samples), RLPD fails at 10, TRPO fails at 5 (Fig. 2 right).
>     • Test performance (h=5): HNPG achieves ~0.8 test reward vs RLPD ~0.6; online TD loss in RLPD explodes when Bellman completeness may not hold (Fig. 3).
> - Summary on similar RL tasks: Mixing offline data into an on‑policy NPG provides stronger and more stable learning than purely off‑policy actor‑critic (RLPD) under hard exploration and representation settings.
> 
> Cross‑paper synthesis: where datasets or task families align
> - ImageNet: Both the 4‑bit optimizer paper and the JEPA paper evaluate on ImageNet‑1K. The 4‑bit work reports near‑parity top‑1 accuracy for Swin‑T under 4‑bit states versus 32‑bit, while the JEPA study (different objective) shows JEPA’s features align more with perceptual bottom‑variance directions than MAE at equal compute—complementary evidence that (a) aggressive memory compression does not materially hurt standard accuracy, and (b) joint‑embedding predictive training shifts learned features toward semantics‑useful directions.
> - Vision detection vs classification: PBADet (COCO/BodyHands/CrowdHuman) and 4‑bit (ImageNet classification) occupy different metrics/tasks, but both show that carefully designed efficiency mechanisms (PBADet’s anchor‑free part‑to‑body offset; 4‑bit rank‑1/linear quantization) can preserve or improve task accuracy versus strong baselines.
> - Sequential/language tasks vs optimizer/architecture stability: The Dale’s‑law study (adding/sequential‑MNIST/PTB) and HNPG (Comblock RL) both highlight stability advantages when the algorithmic design mitigates problematic bootstrapping or spectra: DANNs (good spectra) match standard RNNs while ColEI underperforms; HNPG’s on‑policy MC regression remains stable where off‑policy TD can diverge.
> 
> Key takeaways across identical and similar settings
> - On identical datasets within papers:
>   • PBADet vs BPJDet (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman): PBADet improves or matches SOTA depending on metric; biggest gains on BodyHands and COCO association metrics; detection superior on CrowdHuman with comparable pairing.
>   • 4‑bit optimizers vs 32‑bit/8‑bit on ImageNet, GLUE, SQuAD, WMT14, E2E‑NLG, MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA: 4‑bit states preserve accuracy (often within noise) while reducing optimizer memory 34–58% and maintaining/faster wall‑clock with fused ops.
>   • HNPG vs RLPD/TRPO on Comblock: HNPG scales to much longer horizons and generalizes better in image‑based splits; TD critics in RLPD destabilize.
> - On similar dataset types across papers:
>   • Vision: PBADet (detection/association) and 4‑bit (classification) both demonstrate that efficient designs (anchor‑free offsets; 4‑bit states) need not reduce accuracy; JEPA shows representation shifts toward influential/semantic features on ImageNet.
>   • Sequential/language: Dale’s‑law results show architectures with unimodal, clustered singular‑value spectra (DANN/standard) train reliably on sequential MNIST/PTB, unlike ColEI—echoing HNPG’s stability over off‑policy TD in RL.
> 
> Overall conclusions grounded in reported experiments
> - Efficient but accurate: PBADet’s one‑stage anchor‑free design improves association accuracy on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts and maintains strong detection on CrowdHuman. 4‑bit optimizers keep accuracy on vision/NLP/LLM tasks while significantly reducing memory and often training time.
> - Stability matters: In RNNs, spectral unimodality (DANN or standard spectra) predicts better learning than sign constraints alone (ColEI). In hybrid RL, on‑policy PG with offline augmentation (HNPG) avoids the instability observed with off‑policy TD.
> - Representation bias: JEPA’s implicit bias toward high‑influence (predictive, low‑variance) features is borne out on ImageNet‑style data (feature CCA), complementing the 4‑bit paper’s finding that classification accuracy can be preserved under aggressive optimizer compression.
> 
> Notes on identical datasets across different papers
> - ImageNet‑1K is the only dataset family shared across papers (JEPA and 4‑bit). The two studies report different metrics (representation similarity vs classification accuracy), but together indicate JEPA‑style training emphasizes perceptual subspaces while 4‑bit training maintains top‑1 accuracy with reduced state precision.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here is a concise set of five recent papers covering the requested topics, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The papers
> 
> 1. **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024) — One-stage, anchor-free detection of human parts (hands, feet, face) linked to the correct person via a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-WholeBody, COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman, and AnimalPose/AP-10K.
> 2. **"Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023) — Trains E/I sign-constrained (Dale's Law) RNNs and shows learning is governed by the singular-value spectrum at initialization, not sign constraints; benchmarks include sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, adding problem, and natural-object recognition.
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024, Apple) — Proves in deep linear nets that JEPA-style joint-embedding predictive pretraining prioritizes high-influence (high regression-coefficient) features, unlike pixel-reconstruction (MAE); validated on ImageNet-1K with CCA feature-similarity analysis.
> 4. **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023) — Quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments to ~4 bits (smaller blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear mapping, optional factorization); fine-tunes LLaMA-7B/13B/33B, RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, Swin-T, Transformer-Base.
> 5. **"Offline Data Enhanced On-Policy Policy Gradient with Provable Guarantees"** (ICLR 2024) — Hybrid RL (HAC/HNPG) that inserts Fitted Policy Evaluation on offline batches into on-policy Natural Policy Gradient; tested on continuous and image-based Comblock (CIFAR-100 images encoded with ViT-B/32 CLIP features).
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **Part-body association (Paper 1).** PBADet sets state-of-the-art on COCO-style splits: on CrowdHuman face-body association, it improves body MR-2 to 36.5 (vs. 41.3 for BPJDet) with face AP 91.6 (vs. 89.5); on COCO val, it beats the pose estimator ED-Pose for hands/feet by a large margin (all-parts precision 39.41 vs. 24.09, recall 63.09 vs. 45.51, F1 48.52 vs. 31.51). Ablations show the association head, multi-scale center offset, and task-alignment loss each add accuracy.
> 
> **E/I-constrained RNNs (Paper 2).** ColEI networks (naive column-sign partitioning) train worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs on all four tasks. Spectrum-transplant experiments isolate the cause: sign constraints only explain ~0.7–1% error, while the multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum accounts for the full gap (~2.3%); normalised SVD entropy at initialization anti-correlates with final test error. This is the key comparative insight: a *spectral* (SVD) view, not the sign constraint itself, explains the learning deficit, and DANN-style architectures that preserve a healthy spectrum learn as well as unconstrained RNNs.
> 
> **JEPA vs. MAE (Paper 3).** Theoretically, JEPA's feature-ordering critical time depends on the regression coefficient ρ (strengthened by encoder depth), while MAE's ordering depends mainly on the covariance eigenvalue λ — so JEPA learns influential/low-variance semantic features first and is noise-robust, whereas MAE is agnostic to influence and can chase high-variance noise. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features do (mean CCA over training). (Note: this paper's empirical validation is ImageNet-1K-based; the requested CIFAR-100 comparisons appear in other SSL papers in the collection, e.g., LDReg's transfer table, but not in this JEPA analysis.)
> 
> **4-bit optimizers (Paper 4).** Across tasks, 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor match or slightly exceed 32-bit AdamW while roughly halving or quartering optimizer-state memory: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs. 88.9; Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs. 81.2 (comparable); GPT-2 E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs. 67.7; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs. 94.6; WMT14 26.28 vs. 26.61. On Alpaca instruction tuning, 4-bit AdamW is statistically indistinguishable from 32-bit AdamW on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, and OBQA for LLaMA-7B/13B/33B, with nearly identical convergence curves. Memory drops up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 31.87 GB vs. 75.40 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on a single 80 GB GPU; sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor, SM3) save more memory but degrade accuracy, especially on image classification.
> 
> **Hybrid RL (Paper 5).** HNPG solves continuous Comblock up to horizon 50 with ~50k offline + ~30M online samples, whereas pure on-policy TRPO fails even at horizon 5 (exploration difficulty) and the off-policy hybrid RLPD tops out at horizon 15 — HNPG's on-policy critic (pure supervised policy-evaluation loss) is more stable than RLPD's bootstrapped TD loss. On image-based Comblock (CIFAR-100 + CLIP features), HNPG again outperforms RLPD and TRPO; CLIP features only reach 77.7% train / 72.1% test CIFAR-100 top-1, so latent states are not fully decodable and Bellman completeness plausibly fails — precisely the regime where HNPG's provable robustness (it degrades gracefully to on-policy NPG guarantees when offline assumptions fail) gives it an edge over purely off-policy hybrid methods.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting notes
> 
> - The requested topical keywords map cleanly: COCO (paper 1), MNIST (paper 2), AdamW/SGD and fine-tuning of Transformers (paper 4: LLaMA, LoRA codebase, RoBERTa, GPT-2, Swin-T, Transformer-Base), ImageNet (papers 3 and 4), CIFAR-100 (paper 5's Comblock, and paper 3's SSL context).
> - Methodologically, papers 2–5 share a "provable/analyzed mechanism beats heuristic design" theme: spectral analysis explains E/I RNNs; critical-time analysis explains JEPA's feature bias; quantization analysis (outlier patterns, zero-point) explains 4-bit feasibility; worst-case/offline-aware analysis explains hybrid RL's best-of-both-worlds behavior. Paper 1 is the most empirical of the five.
> - A minor caveat: only papers 1, 2, and 4 directly report the exact benchmarks named in the request (COCO, MNIST/Penn Treebank, ImageNet/GLUE/LLaMA/Swin-T); paper 3's empirical ImageNet analysis is qualitative (CCA), and paper 5's CIFAR-100 use is as an RL observation space rather than a standard classification benchmark.

**community 最终答案**

> Here is the concise set of five papers matching your criteria, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> **1. PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — Anchor-free, one-stage part-body association (hands/feet/face → person). On COCOHumanParts (COCO-derived), it matches BPJDet in AP and leads on AP_M/AP_L/person/feet metrics; on CrowdHuman face-body association it gets the best body MR-2 (36.5 with YOLOv7) and competitive AP (91.6). Against the pose estimator ED-Pose on COCO, it roughly doubles precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51). Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offset, and task-alignment all improve accuracy.
> 
> **2. Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** — Recurrent E/I-constrained networks (ColEI) train worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, and object recognition. Sign constraints alone account for only part of the gap (0.7±0.3% RNN, 1±1% ColEI vs 2.3±0.6% total); singular-value spectrum "transplants" show the initial spectrum matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance across size/EI ratios; gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> 
> **3. How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)** — In deep linear nets, the JEPA objective is biased toward high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ), while MAE prioritizes high-covariance (λ) features even if noisy; with ρ anti-correlated to λ, JEPA reverses learning order. Depth separates the two (1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE; fixed points ρ^L vs ρ^{L/(L+1)}). On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features than MAE features (CCA).
> 
> **4. Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023)** — Stores Adam/AdamW moments in 4 bits (smaller block size + rank-1 normalization, zero-point-free linear quantizer for the second moment). On fine-tuning, 4-bit AdamW matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, GPT-2 E2E 67.8 vs 67.7, SQuAD 94.5 vs 94.6; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning is comparable on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA. Memory drops up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 31.87 vs 75.40 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models, with convergence curves closely aligned to 32-bit.
> 
> **5. Offline Data Enhanced On-Policy Policy Gradient (HNPG, ICLR 2024)** — Hybrid RL that injects off-policy FPE on offline data into on-policy NPG, giving best-of-both-worlds guarantees: it achieves offline-RL rates when Bellman completeness/coverage hold and retains on-policy NPG rates otherwise. On continuous and image-based Comblock (states are CIFAR-100 images), HNPG significantly outperforms pure on-policy PPO/TRPO and the off-policy-only hybrid RLPD, and stays robust when Bellman completeness fails (where RLPD fails).
> 
> **Cross-method comparison/analysis:** Each method trades off a resource (accuracy, biological fidelity, sample efficiency, memory) against constraints, and all validate that their design choices yield near-lossless performance: PBADet gets equal-or-better detection with a simpler single offset vs anchor-based BPJDet; the Dale's-law paper shows that respecting biological constraints need not cost performance if spectral properties (NSE) are preserved; the JEPA analysis shows that latent-space prediction, not pixel reconstruction, is what biases learning toward perceptual features; the 4-bit optimizer shows optimizer-state precision can drop to 4 bits with negligible accuracy loss while halving memory; and HNPG shows combining offline and online data with an on-policy backbone dominates both pure on-policy and pure off-policy hybrid baselines in theory and practice. Note: the context confirms CIFAR-100-image-based Comblock for HNPG, but does not explicitly mention CLIP features.

**问题：** I’m building an edge‑constrained system that needs: (a) reliable hand/face‑to‑person association in crowded images at COCO scale; (b) label‑free pretraining that predicts one view’s representation from another instead of reconstructing pixels; (c) a recurrent controller that respects separate excitatory vs inhibitory units yet still trains well; (d) a policy learner that can start from a static log and keep improving with on‑policy updates while retaining theoretical stability; and (e) the ability to fine‑tune Transformer backbones/LLMs under tight VRAM using ~4‑bit AdamW states. Are there recent papers that collectively address these components, with experiments spanning COCO, CIFAR‑100/MNIST/PTB and common fine‑tuning setups?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

Gold 1：

> Summary of comparative experimental results across the five papers (no cross-paper identical datasets were found; comparisons are therefore grouped by each paper’s shared testbeds and by similar data families).
> 
> A) Human part–body association at COCO scale (PBADet vs prior detectors)
> Identical datasets: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman
> • BodyHands (Table 1)
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39
>   - Result: On the identical BodyHands test set, both PBADet models outperform BPJDet across all three metrics, with +3.2 to +6.8 points in Conditional Accuracy and +1.34 to +1.59 in Joint AP while also improving Hand AP.
> 
> • COCOHumanParts (Tables 2 and 3)
>   - Overall AP (AP.5:.95 original/subordinate):
>     • PBADet (YOLOv7): 42.7 / 41.5; (YOLOv5l6): 43.0 / 41.8
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6 / 43.3
>     - Size-sensitive AP: PBADet leads on APM/APL (e.g., YOLOv5l6: APM 66.2/65.0, APL 67.2/64.4) and per-category AP for person and feet (Table 2), while BPJDet has slightly higher overall AP. 
>   - Association robustness (average mMR−2, lower is better; Table 3):
>     • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): head 27.9, face 30.5, left-hand 36.2, right-hand 40.8, right-foot 50.4, left-foot 47.9
>     • PBJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, left-hand 41.6, right-hand 42.2, right-foot 49.1, left-foot 50.4
>     - Result: PBADet substantially reduces mMR−2 for head and both hands vs BPJDet (e.g., −5.4 left-hand), mixed for feet (right-foot slightly worse, left-foot better).
> 
> • CrowdHuman (Tables 5 and 6)
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): best body MR−2 = 36.5 (lower is better), body AP 91.6, face MR−2 = 44.7; pair mMR−2 ≈ 50.8–50.9
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR−2 40.7, body AP 89.5, face MR−2 46.3; pair mMR−2 ≈ 50.1
>   - Result: On identical CrowdHuman, PBADet delivers better detection (lower MR−2, higher AP) for bodies and similar face MR−2; pair mMR−2 is comparable to BPJDet.
> 
> B) EI-constrained recurrent networks (Dale’s Law): ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNN (adding problem, seq. MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition)
> Identical datasets: Adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, and a naturalistic object recognition task
> • Across all four tasks (Figure 2 A–D):
>   - ColEI learns worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs; gradient clipping benefits ColEI more but does not close the gap.
>   - DANN RNNs match standard RNN performance while respecting Dale’s Law.
> • Spectral “transplant” (Figure 4 B–C):
>   - Giving ColEI the standard RNN singular value spectrum improves performance more than removing sign constraints alone; spectrum is the dominant factor.
> • Scaling/architecture trends (Figures 5–7):
>   - ColEI degrades as networks get smaller or have fewer inhibitory units; Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) strongly anti-correlates with test error (higher NSE → better performance). DANNs remain robust even with a single inhibitory neuron.
> 
> C) JEPA vs MAE (self-distillation vs reconstruction) on deep linear models and ImageNet
> Identical datasets: ImageNet-1k at 64×64 for the CCA study
> • Theory-driven simulations (Figures 1–2):
>   - When covariance (λ) and regression coefficient (ρ) are opposed, JEPA prioritizes high-ρ “influential” features (predictive, less noisy) while MAE prioritizes high-λ features (high variance), in line with theorems (JEPA’s bias strengthens with depth).
> • Temporal generative model (Figure 3):
>   - With two temporal features of different noise and autocorrelation, JEPA is slower to learn high-noise features (lower ρ) than MAE; JEPA converges to lower amplitude for noisy features.
> • ImageNet-1k experiments (Appendix D, Figure 7):
>   - CCA shows JEPA’s features align more with the bottom-variance subspace (higher full–bottom mean CCA vs MAE), and less with the top-variance subspace (lower full–top mean CCA), indicating faster learning of perceptual/semantic features compared to reconstruction.
> 
> D) Memory-efficient optimizers with 4-bit states (4-bit AdamW / 4-bit Factor) vs 32-bit AdamW and 8-bit AdamW
> Identical datasets: GLUE (NLU aggregate), ImageNet-1k (Swin-T), E2E-NLG (GPT-2 Medium), SQuAD/SQuAD 2.0 (RoBERTa-L), WMT14 En–De (Transformer-Base), and LLaMA instruction tuning
> • Accuracy on identical benchmarks (Table 2; medians/means as reported)
>   - NLU (GLUE avg): 32-bit 88.9; 8-bit 89.1; 4-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit Factor 88.9 → 4-bit matches 32/8-bit.
>   - ImageNet-1k (Swin-T): 32-bit 81.2; 8-bit 81.0; 4-bit 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9 → small ≤0.4 pt drop vs 32-bit.
>   - E2E-NLG BLEU (GPT-2 Medium): 32-bit 67.7; 8-bit 67.5; 4-bit 67.8; 4-bit Factor 67.6 → parity or slightly higher vs 32/8-bit.
>   - QA F1 (RoBERTa-L on SQuAD family): 32-bit 94.6; 8-bit 94.5; 4-bit 94.5–94.6; 4-bit Factor 94.6 (Tables 2, 9) → parity.
>   - WMT14 En–De SacreBLEU: 32-bit 26.61; 8-bit 26.66; 4-bit 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45 → ≤0.33 behind 32/8-bit.
> • LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3):
>   - 7B: 32-bit vs 4-bit AdamW (MMLU 38.7 vs 38.9; HellaSwag 74.6 vs 74.7; ARC-e 61.5 vs 61.2; ARC-c 45.1 vs 44.4; OBQA 43.4 vs 43.0) → 4-bit matches within small deltas.
>   - 13B: 32-bit vs 4-bit (MMLU 46.5 vs 47.4; HellaSwag 78.8 vs 79.0; ARC-e 63.6 vs 64.1; ARC-c 48.3 vs 48.0; OBQA 45.2 both) → 4-bit equal or slightly higher.
>   - 33B: 32-bit vs 4-bit (MMLU 56.4 vs 54.9; others near-equal) → comparable.
> • Memory/time efficiency (Table 4):
>   - LLaMA-7B FSDP: 4-bit AdamW reduces total memory 75.4 GB → 31.87 GB (−57.7%) and time 3.35 h → 3.07–3.11 h.
>   - RoBERTa-L (GLUE task): with fused kernels, 4-bit AdamW 3.17 min vs 3.93 min (32-bit) and 3.00 GB vs 5.31 GB (−43.5%).
>   - GPT-2 Medium (E2E-NLG): with fused kernels, 4-bit AdamW 2.11 h vs 2.13 h (32-bit) and 4.62 GB vs 6.89 GB (−34.4%).
> • Capacity under fixed VRAM (Table 5):
>   - 24 GB: 32-bit can fine-tune OPT-350M; 4-bit can fine-tune OPT-1.3B.
>   - 80 GB: 32-bit up to OPT-1.3B; 4-bit to OPT-6.7B; also enables LLaMA-7B on a single 80 GB GPU.
> • Ablations (Tables 1 and 6):
>   - Critical for 4-bit: removing the zero-point in second-moment quantization (DE-0 or Linear) and rank-1 normalization; with these, 4-bit achieves accuracy on par with 32-bit and 8-bit across tasks.
> 
> E) Hybrid on-policy policy gradient with offline data (HNPG) vs TRPO and RLPD
> Identical benchmarks: continuous Comblock and image-based continuous Comblock (CIFAR-100 images via CLIP encoder)
> • Continuous Comblock (Figure 2 Left):
>   - HNPG solves up to H=50 with ~30M online samples plus 50k offline; TRPO fails by H=5; RLPD solves to H≈15 under tuned settings.
>   - Loss stability (Appendix Figure 4): HNPG’s online supervised regression loss is smooth; RLPD’s online TD loss is more volatile.
> • Image-based Comblock using CIFAR-100 features (Figure 2 Right, Figure 3):
>   - HNPG reaches H≈30 with ~10M online samples; RLPD fails by H≈10; TRPO fails by H≈5.
>   - At H=5, test reward: HNPG ≈ 0.8 vs RLPD ≈ 0.6; HNPG train/test curves show lower variance.
>   - Critic diagnostics (Figure 3): RLPD’s online TD loss explodes when Bellman completeness may not hold; HNPG’s on-policy Monte Carlo regression stays small; offline TD losses remain stable for both.
> 
> Cross-family synthesis on similar data types
> • Vision with bounding-box/part association (COCO derivatives): PBADet provides large gains in BodyHands and improves association robustness (lower mMR−2) for heads/hands on COCOHumanParts vs an anchor-based joint detector (BPJDet), while keeping CrowdHuman pair association comparable and significantly improving person detection MR−2/AP.
> • Vision classification and language tasks under low-precision optimizers: 4-bit AdamW/Factor match or nearly match 32-bit/8-bit on ImageNet-1k, GLUE, SQuAD, WMT14, and maintain LLaMA instruction-tuned performance at 7B–33B with large VRAM savings.
> • Image-based RL (CIFAR-100 features): The hybrid on-policy + offline policy evaluation (HNPG) improves sample efficiency and robustness over pure on-policy TRPO and off-policy-heavy RLPD, especially when Bellman completeness can be violated.
> • Self-supervised pretraining (ImageNet-1k CCA): JEPA aligns faster with semantic/perceptual (low-variance) subspaces than MAE, consistent with the theoretical high-ρ feature bias; this complements the downstream ImageNet/GLUE/SQuAD stability under 4-bit fine-tuning.
> • Recurrent sequence modeling (adding problem, sequential MNIST, PTB): Enforcing Dale’s Law via DANN retains standard RNN accuracy, while naive ColEI partitions degrade and destabilize learning; the singular-value spectrum (unimodal/clustered) is the decisive factor.
> 
> Notable absence of shared identical datasets across papers
> • No single dataset appears across more than one paper’s experiments. Overlaps exist only at the family level (e.g., COCO-family in PBADet; CIFAR-100-based images in HNPG; ImageNet-1k in JEPA and 4-bit optimizer studies focus on different tasks and protocols). Therefore, cross-paper comparisons are based on similar data modalities and task types rather than the exact same benchmarks.
> 
> Overall conclusions restricted to reported figures/tables
> • On identical detection datasets, PBADet surpasses or matches state-of-the-art baselines, particularly improving association reliability for heads/hands.
> • On identical NLP/vision tasks, 4-bit optimizers generally match 32-bit/8-bit accuracy while cutting memory by ~34–58% and enabling larger models under fixed VRAM.
> • On identical RL benchmarks, HNPG substantially extends the solvable horizon and yields better generalization vs TRPO and RLPD; diagnostics indicate HNPG’s on-policy regression is more stable than off-policy TD when Bellman completeness may not hold.
> • For recurrent sequence tasks, DANN RNNs achieve parity with standard RNNs and outperform ColEI partitions; experiments and spectrum transplants attribute the gap primarily to spectral properties rather than sign constraints.
> • For SSL pretraining on ImageNet-1k, JEPA learns latent features that align more strongly with low-variance, perceptual subspaces relative to MAE, consistent with its theoretical implicit bias toward high-influence (high-ρ) features.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes—five recent papers in the collection collectively cover all five components, and their experiments together span COCO-scale detection, CIFAR-100, sequential MNIST / Penn Tree Bank, and standard fine-tuning benchmarks:
> 
> **Component mapping**
> - **(a) PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage anchor-free part-to-body association (hands/face→person) on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman.
> - **(b) JEPA**: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024) analyzes joint-embedding predictive architectures that predict one view's latent representation instead of reconstructing pixels (vs. MAE).
> - **(c) "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023): recurrent EI networks with separate excitatory/inhibitory units; tasks = adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition.
> - **(d) "Offline Data Enhanced On-Policy Policy Gradient with Provable Guarantees"** (ICLR 2024, HAC/HNPG): starts from a static offline log and continues with on-policy NPG updates; image-based experiments use CIFAR-100.
> - **(e) "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023): 4-bit AdamW for fine-tuning RoBERTa-L, Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B.
> 
> **Experimental comparison**
> 
> - **(a) PBADet** (hand/face association): On BodyHands, PBADet-YOLOv7 (36.9M) hits hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98—beating BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (86.1M: 85.9/86.91/84.39) and BodyHands (700M: 84.8/83.44/63.48) with ~2–20× fewer params. On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet (all-categories AP ~42.7/41.5 original/subordinate for YOLOv7) but leads on person/feet AP and lowest mMR-2 for head, face, both hands. On CrowdHuman face-body, it gets the best body MR-2 (36.5) and competitive mMR-2 (50.8). It also far exceeds the pose estimator ED-Pose on hand/foot F1 (48.5 vs 31.5 all parts).
> 
> - **(b) JEPA vs MAE**: The paper derives critical times showing JEPA prioritizes high-influence (high regression-coefficient ρ) features, increasingly with depth, while MAE's feature ordering depends mainly on covariance λ. On ImageNet-1K, JEPA representations align faster with the low-variance (bottom 25% PCA) perceptual subspace than MAE throughout training, confirming the "no pixel reconstruction" objective avoids noisy features.
> 
> - **(c) EI recurrent controller**: Standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs train well; the simple column-partitioned ColEI architecture trains worse and with higher variance on all four tasks (MNIST, PTB, adding, object recognition), though gradient clipping helps it most. Transplant experiments show the initial singular-value spectrum matters more than the sign constraints themselves (~1.5% vs ~0.7–1% test-error contributions on sequential MNIST). NSE (normalized SVD entropy) anti-correlates with final error; small networks or high E:I ratios degrade ColEI, whereas DANNs stay robust even with a single inhibitory neuron.
> 
> - **(d) Policy learner (HNPG)**: On continuous Comblock it solves up to horizon 50 using ~50k suboptimal offline samples plus ~30M online samples; pure on-policy TRPO fails even at horizon 5, and the off-policy hybrid baseline RLPD solves only up to horizon 15 (unstable online critic loss). On the CIFAR-100 image-based Comblock (where Bellman completeness is violated—77.7% train / 72.1% test decoding), HNPG stays robust while off-policy hybrid methods fail. Theoretically it is best-of-both-worlds: offline-RL guarantees when completeness holds, standard on-policy NPG guarantees otherwise.
> 
> - **(e) 4-bit AdamW**: Matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8, GPT-2 E2E 67.8, SQuAD 94.5, WMT14 26.28) and on LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning (e.g., MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7 for 7B), with up to 57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB, enabling single-80GB-GPU training) and faster FSDP-sharded instruction tuning; it beats 8-bit AdamW in memory with equal accuracy.
> 
> **Caveats**: no single paper does all datasets—CIFAR-100 appears in HNPG's image-based Comblock (and in other contrastive/OOD papers in the collection), ImageNet in the JEPA analysis, MNIST/PTB in the Dale's-Law paper, and fine-tuning suites in the 4-bit optimizer paper; so coverage is collective, not per-paper.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Yes — five recent papers collectively cover the five components
> 
> | Component | Paper |
> |---|---|
> | (a) Hand/face→person association | **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection** (ICLR 2024) |
> | (b) Label-free pretraining: predict one view's rep, no pixel reconstruction | **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features** (NeurIPS 2024) |
> | (c) Recurrent controller, separate E/I units that trains well | **Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly** (NeurIPS 2023) |
> | (d) Policy from static log + on-policy updates, provable stability | **Offline Data Enhanced On-Policy Policy Gradient with Provable Guarantees** (HAC/HNPG, ICLR 2024) |
> | (e) ~4-bit AdamW for VRAM-constrained fine-tuning | **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023) |
> 
> ## Experimental results & analysis
> 
> **(a) PBADet (COCO scale).** On **BodyHands**, PBADet (YOLOv7) surpasses all baselines on every metric — joint AP 85.98 vs BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 84.39, with the best hand AP and conditional accuracy, and even beats the larger BPJDet(YOLOv5m6) while being smaller. On **COCOHumanParts** (six parts incl. head/face/hands/feet) it is on par with BPJDet but leads in AP_M, AP_L and person/feet, and achieves the lowest average mMR⁻². On **CrowdHuman** face-body association it gets the best body MR⁻² (36.5) and body AP (91.6), though its advantage over BPJDet shrinks for this single-part task. Against the pose estimator ED-Pose it is far better for hands/feet (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; e.g., left-hand F1 46.5 vs 22.87).
> 
> **(b) JEPA (latent-prediction SSL).** Contrasts JEPA self-distillation (predict target encoder's latent rep of one view from another) vs MAE (reconstruct pixels). Theory on deep linear networks shows JEPA is biased toward "influential" features and suppresses noisy ones, while MAE prioritizes high-variance features; this holds only for deep encoders. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace than MAE (CCA). This explains why latent prediction beats pixel reconstruction.
> 
> **(c) Dale's-law recurrent nets.** Column-partitioned E/I RNNs (ColEI) train poorly, worse for small nets with few inhibitory units; **recurrent DANNs** (Dale's ANNs, separate E-to-E/E-to-I/I-to-E non-negative matrices) respect E/I constraints yet learn **as well as standard RNNs**, even with a single inhibitory neuron, robust to EI ratio and size. The root cause is the initial recurrent-weight spectrum (multimodal/dispersed singular values for ColEI vs unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur for standard RNNs/DANNs), not sign constraints per se; normalised SVD entropy predicts final error, and gradient clipping mitigates ColEI's deficit. Datasets: adding, **sequential MNIST**, **Penn Tree Bank** language modelling, object recognition.
> 
> **(d) HAC/HNPG hybrid RL.** Integrates Fitted Policy Evaluation on the **offline (static-log) data** into an on-policy NPG actor-critic. Provable best-of-both-worlds: under approximate Bellman completeness it achieves the better of online-NPG and offline rates (equal offline/online samples); if offline assumptions fail it degrades to the standard on-policy NPG rate — so theoretical stability is always retained. On continuous and image-based Comblock it outperforms the off-policy-only hybrid baseline (RLPD).
> 
> **(e) 4-bit AdamW.** Using smaller block size for the 1st moment, zero-point-excluded linear/rank-1 quantization for the 2nd (optionally factorized), it **matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW** on fine-tuning: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1, SQuAD 94.5, GPT-2 E2E-NLG 67.8, and is comparable on Swin-T ImageNet-1k (80.8) and WMT14 (26.28); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning matches 32-bit on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA. Memory saved up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB), enabling 4× larger models under a budget and LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU. Sublinear methods (Adafactor β₁=0, SM3) are leaner but degrade accuracy.
> 
> ## Dataset coverage — one caveat
> 
> The five papers do span **COCO** (PBADet: COCO-HumanParts, COCO val, BodyHands, CrowdHuman), **MNIST and PTB** (Dale's-law RNN paper), and **common fine-tuning setups** (4-bit optimizers: GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, WMT14, LLaMA/Alpaca), as requested. However, **CIFAR-100 does not appear in these five papers** — within the collection it is used by other works (e.g., BSO, a binary-weight spiking online optimizer reaching 74.27% on CIFAR-100, 94.86% on CIFAR-10, with memory ~O(n²L/32)), which is not one of the five components. So collectively the components are addressed, but the exact benchmark set "COCO + CIFAR-100/MNIST/PTB + fine-tuning" is only partially spanned by the matching papers (CIFAR-100 missing from them).

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:104 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (1) the geometry of feature embeddings in contrastive learning using cosine-similarity and a temperature parameter, including small-batch effects on negative-pair variance; (2) the implicit bias in joint-embedding self-distillation (JEPA) toward influential features; (3) memory-efficient training with stochastic gradient/AdamW-style methods using sub-8-bit optimizer states for vision and transformer models (including low-rank adaptation fine-tuning) with experiments on CIFAR-100 and MNIST; and (4) a one-stage, anchor-free approach to associating human parts with the correct person via learned offsets. I’m interested in links to regularization under cross-entropy, practical optimizer choices, and how to keep GPU memory low during training.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
