**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is an integrated, results-only comparison drawn strictly from the figures and tables you provided. I group the findings along your four requested themes and call out identical or comparable datasets where they exist.
> 
> 1) Geometry of feature embeddings in contrastive learning (cosine similarity, temperature; small-batch variance)
> - Full-batch vs mini-batch theory and practice (On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning, ICML 2025)
>   • Full-batch optimum: positive pairs align to 1 and negative-pair cosine similarities concentrate at −1/(n−1) (Theorem 5.1). 
>   • Mini-batch effect: negative-pair similarities exhibit strictly positive variance that increases as batch size decreases (Theorem 5.5). 
>   • Measured variance on CIFAR-100 with SimCLR (Table 1):
>     - Batch 32: variance 0.1649 (SimCLR) → 0.1008 (SimCLR + proposed variance-reduction)
>     - Batch 64: 0.1505 → 0.0952
>     - Batch 128: 0.1444 → 0.0929
>     - Batch 256: 0.1404 → 0.0921
>     - Batch 512: 0.1396 → 0.0917
>     This confirms the small-batch increase in negative-pair variance and shows the proposed auxiliary loss consistently reduces it.
>   • Accuracy under temperature sweeps (Figure 3; CIFAR-10/100): adding the variance-reduction term to SimCLR yields consistently higher and more stable top-1 accuracy across a wide range of temperatures (curves show systematic gains; no numerical table provided).
>   • Across methods and batch sizes (Figure 4; CIFAR-10/100): adding the variance-reduction term improves top-1 accuracy for SimCLR, DCL, and DHEL, with visibly larger gains at smaller batch sizes (bar charts; relative improvements shown without explicit numbers).
>   • ImageNet family:
>     - ImageNet-100 (Table 4, SimCLR vs SimCLR+Ours; Top-1 / Top-5):
>       t=0.2: 73.80/93.14 → 73.94/93.08
>       t=0.3: 72.30/92.94 → 74.04/93.24
>       t=0.4: 69.92/92.10 → 73.12/92.98
>       (Other temperatures similarly favor the proposed loss in Top-1, with a few small trade-offs in Top-5.)
>     - Full ImageNet (Table 5, 100 epochs): Top-1 51.79 (SimCLR) → 52.48 (SimCLR + variance-reduction).
>   • Gradient sensitivity to batch size (Theorem 5.6): smaller batches increase the loss gradient magnitude w.r.t. negative-pair similarities, further encouraging separation (qualitative effect; no numeric table).
> 
> Identical datasets in this theme:
> - CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet variants are evaluated repeatedly within this paper (and across multiple methods: SimCLR/DCL/DHEL; baseline vs proposed auxiliary loss). This enables direct method-to-method comparisons reported above.
> 
> 2) Implicit bias in JEPA toward influential features (deep linear self-distillation)
> - Learning order and bias (How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features, NeurIPS 2024):
>   • In deep linear settings, JEPA prioritizes “influential” features (those with larger regression coefficients ρ), while MAE prioritizes high covariance λ (Figures 1–2; Theorem 3.2 and Corollary 3.6). This difference is depth-dependent: the JEPA bias toward high-ρ features strengthens as encoder depth increases (Figure 4; ODE simulations). 
>   • Temporal model experiment (Figure 3): the derived formulas λa=γa||va||^2 and ρa=γa||va||^2/(σ_a^2+||va||^2) match simulations; features with higher γ and smaller noise σ are learned earlier by JEPA. 
>   • ImageNet-style evidence (Appendix D, Figure 7): JEPA-trained features from “full vs bottom-PCA variance” subsets exhibit higher representational similarity than MAE across training (CCA curves), consistent with JEPA focusing on semantically useful, low-variance “slow” features (qualitative; no numeric table).
> 
> Notes on comparability:
> - The JEPA vs MAE evidence here is largely theoretical and curve-based (figures), not tabular accuracy. No identical dataset overlap exists with the optimizer or detection papers suitable for numeric cross-paper benchmarking.
> 
> 3) Memory-efficient training with sub‑8‑bit optimizer states (4‑bit) and LoRA-style fine-tuning
> - Core result across tasks (Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States, NeurIPS 2023)
>   • Summary table (Table 2) — 4-bit AdamW and 4-bit Factor vs 32-bit AdamW, 8-bit AdamW, Adafactor, SM3:
>     - Natural Language Understanding (RoBERTa-L, GLUE mean):
>       32-bit AdamW 88.9; 8-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit Factor 88.9; Adafactor 89.1; SM3 87.5.
>       (4-bit matches 8-bit and full precision on mean GLUE.)
>     - Image classification (Swin-T, ImageNet-1k top-1):
>       32-bit 81.2; 8-bit 81.0; 4-bit AdamW 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9; Adafactor 80.0; SM3 79.0.
>       (4-bit stays close to 32-bit; Adafactor/SM3 lower.)
>     - Natural language generation (GPT-2 Medium E2E-NLG BLEU):
>       32-bit 67.7; 8-bit 67.5; 4-bit AdamW 67.8; 4-bit Factor 67.6; Adafactor 67.2; SM3 66.9.
>       (4-bit ties/exceeds 32-bit; best BLEU is 67.8.)
>     - Question answering (RoBERTa-L, SQuAD F1):
>       32-bit 94.6; 8-bit 94.5; 4-bit AdamW 94.5; 4-bit Factor 94.6; Adafactor 94.6; SM3 91.7.
>       (4-bit matches 32-bit.)
>     - Machine translation (Transformer-base, WMT14 en-de SacreBLEU):
>       32-bit 26.61; 8-bit 26.66; 4-bit AdamW 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45; Adafactor 26.52; SM3 22.72.
>       (4-bit close to 32-bit/8-bit; SM3 lagging.)
>   • LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3) — 4-bit AdamW vs 32-bit AdamW:
>     - LLaMA‑7B: MMLU 38.7→38.9; HellaSwag 74.6→74.7; ARC‑e 61.5→61.2; ARC‑c 45.1→44.4; OBQA 43.4→43.0.
>     - LLaMA‑13B: MMLU 46.5→47.4; HellaSwag 78.8→79.0; ARC‑e 63.6→64.1; ARC‑c 48.3→48.0; OBQA 45.2→45.2.
>     - LLaMA‑33B: MMLU 56.4→54.9; HellaSwag 79.2→79.2; ARC‑e 62.6→61.6; ARC‑c 47.1→46.6; OBQA 43.8→45.4.
>     Net: 4-bit closely tracks 32-bit across sizes; some ups and downs per benchmark.
>   • Memory/time (Table 4):
>     - LLaMA‑7B (2× A100 80G, FSDP): total mem 75.40 GB (32-bit) → 31.87 GB (4-bit), saving 43.54 GB (57.7%); time 3.35 h → 3.07 h (and 3.11 h fused).
>     - RoBERTa‑L (single GPU): 5.31 GB → 3.00 GB (4-bit fused), saving 2.31 GB (43.5%); time 3.93 min → 3.17 min (4-bit fused). 4-bit Factor uses 2.83 GB (46.7% saved) with slightly longer time.
>     - GPT‑2 Medium: 6.89 GB → 4.62 GB (4-bit), saving 2.37 GB (34.4%); fused runtime 2.11 h vs 2.13 h (32-bit). 4-bit Factor: 4.44 GB (35.6% saved).
>   • Largest trainable model on a single 80 GB GPU (Table 5): OPT‑1.3B (32-bit AdamW) vs OPT‑6.7B (4-bit AdamW). LLaMA‑7B becomes trainable with one 80 GB GPU under 4-bit.
>   • Stability and ablations (Table 1): solving the “zero‑point” quantization problem for second moments is critical. Using DE‑0 or Linear mapping for v, plus rank‑1 normalization, eliminates instabilities (Unstable% → 0) and achieves BLEU on GPT‑2 E2E comparable to 32‑bit. Stable Embeddings are unnecessary once zero‑point is handled (e.g., Rank‑1/Linear: 0% unstable; BLEU 67.8±0.51).
>   • Swin‑T (ablation Table 6): quantizing 1st+2nd moments with (B128/DE for m; Rank‑1/Linear for v) yields top‑1 ≈80.8; factorizing 2nd moment yields ≈80.9. Both are near 32‑bit 81.2.
> 
> Identical datasets in this theme:
> - ImageNet‑1k is used consistently within the optimizer paper (Swin‑T). That dataset is different in scope from ImageNet‑100 used in the contrastive paper, so no cross‑paper numeric comparison is made.
> - GPT‑2 E2E, GLUE, SQuAD, WMT14, and LLaMA benchmarks are only in the optimizer paper.
> 
> Practical optimizer/memory tips from these results:
> - Preference for AdamW with 4‑bit moments works across vision (ImageNet‑1k) and NLP/NLG/MT, with near‑parity accuracy and large memory cuts.
> - Rank‑1 normalization for 2nd moment + linear mapping (excluding zero) is key for stability and accuracy at 4 bits; block size 128 suffices for 1st moment.
> - Factorizing the 2nd moment yields further memory savings with minimal accuracy loss where applicable.
> 
> 4) One-stage, anchor-free part–body association via learned offsets
> - BodyHands (Table 1): PBADet vs prior methods
>   • Ours (YOLOv7, 1024): Hand AP 89.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.62; Joint AP 85.98.
>   • Ours (YOLOv5l6, 1024): 88.1; 92.71; 85.73.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 1536): 85.9; 86.91; 84.39.
>   PBADet improves both conditional accuracy (+5.7–5.8 points) and joint AP (~+1.3–1.6) over BPJDet on the same backbone scale (v5l6 vs v5l6) despite lower input resolution.
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2; All categories AP):
>   • Ours (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.0 / subordinate 41.8; APM 66.2/65.0; APL 67.2/64.4; person AP 62.4.
>   • Ours (YOLOv7): 42.7/41.5; APM 65.8/64.4; APL 66.7/63.3; person 62.1.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6/43.3; APM 63.8/63.2; APL 61.8/58.9; person 61.3.
>   Interpretation: PBADet (v5l6) brings higher APM/APL and foot-category APs (e.g., r‑foot 30.9, l‑foot 31.5) vs BPJDet, while overall AP.5:.95 is close (43.0 vs 43.6). 
> - COCOHumanParts, association accuracy (Table 3; mMR−2, lower is better):
>   • Ours (YOLOv7): head 29.2, face 31.3, l‑hand 41.1, r‑hand 42.7, r‑foot 52.6, l‑foot 52.5.
>   • Ours (YOLOv5l6): 27.9, 30.5, 36.2, 40.8, 50.4, 47.9.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 30.8, 31.8, 41.6, 42.2, 49.1, 50.4.
>   PBADet reduces mMR−2 on head/face/hands vs BPJDet; feet trade-offs depend on backbone.
> - CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6; face–body association):
>   • Ours (YOLOv7): body MR−2 36.5 (best among joint methods), face MR−2 44.7, body AP 91.6, body–face mMR−2 50.8.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR−2 40.7, face MR−2 46.3, body AP 89.5, mMR−2 50.1.
>   PBADet improves body MR−2 and body AP; mMR−2 remains comparable (50.8 vs 50.1).
> - Ablations (Table 4 & Table 8):
>   • Removing association loss Lassoc severely hurts joint metrics (BodyHands): baseline joint AP 78.07 vs full 85.98 (YOLOv7); conditional accuracy +11.84 with Lassoc.
>   • Anchor-free part‑to‑body vs anchor-based body‑to‑part: on BodyHands, anchor-free gives Hand AP 89.1 and Joint AP 85.98 vs anchor-based 85.3 and 78.13 (Table 8), indicating both the association direction and anchor-free head contribute to gains.
> 
> Identical datasets in this theme:
> - BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman are used across multiple methods (PBADet vs BPJDet vs Hier R‑CNN and other detectors). The tables above give direct, like-for-like numeric comparisons on the same benchmarks.
> 
> 5) Connections to optimizer choice, regularization under cross-entropy, and keeping GPU memory low
> - Practical optimizer choices:
>   • 4-bit AdamW with (B128/DE for m) + (rank‑1 normalization + Linear mapping for v) consistently preserves accuracy vs 8/32‑bit while cutting optimizer memory (Table 2 & Table 4). 
>   • For association detection, PBADet uses SGD like YOLOv7’s schedule and benefits from task-alignment learning (no extra memory overhead beyond the added 2D offset head).
> - Batch-size regularization in contrastive learning:
>   • Smaller batches inherently increase negative‑pair similarity variance (Table 1 and Theorem 5.5), which can degrade representation quality. Adding the variance-penalty term (LVRNS) acts as a regularizer that stabilizes performance (Figure 3, Table 4–5).
> - Spectral regularization in EI RNNs (Learning better with Dale’s Law, NeurIPS 2023):
>   • Networks trained under Dale’s constraint learn worse unless their singular value spectra resemble standard RNNs; Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) at initialization predicts performance across tasks such as sequential MNIST and Penn Tree Bank (Figures 5–7). Gradient clipping benefits EI networks more (Appendix Figure 10), suggesting a practical training regularizer for such constrained models.
> - Keeping GPU memory low:
>   • Use 4‑bit optimizers (memory cut up to ~58% end-to-end for LLaMA‑7B; Table 4) and factorize the 2nd moment where possible (Table 2 & 4). 4‑bit enabled training of larger models (OPT‑6.7B vs OPT‑1.3B on a single 80GB GPU; Table 5).
> 
> Final note on cross-paper identical datasets:
> - There are no exact identical datasets jointly used by the optimizer paper (ImageNet‑1k, GLUE/SQuAD/WMT14, E2E-NLG, LLaMA) and the detection paper (BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman) suitable for direct numeric cross-comparison.
> - Within contrastive learning, identical datasets (CIFAR‑10/100 and ImageNet‑100/Full ImageNet) are used across baseline and improved methods in the same paper (SimCLR/DCL/DHEL with and without variance reduction), and all comparisons above reflect those matched settings only.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers found (matching all 4 topics)
> 
> **1. Contrastive-learning embedding geometry** — *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (doc 160e1407…): analyzes embeddings under cosine similarity with InfoNCE/SimCLR-style losses and temperature τ. Proves that in mini-batch settings, **smaller batch sizes increase the variance of negative-pair similarities** (optimal value −1/(n−1)), causing "excessive separation." Proposes an auxiliary variance-reduction loss (VRNS).
> 
> **2. JEPA implicit bias** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (doc 40fde037…): shows JEPA self-distillation is biased toward **high-influence features (large regression coefficients)**, while MAE prioritizes high-variance/noisy features; depth strengthens the effect.
> 
> **3. Memory-efficient sub-8-bit optimizers** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (doc 8d5e1455…): 4-bit AdamW/Adam optimizer states (B128 block + rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer), evaluated on vision (Swin-T) and transformers (RoBERTa, GPT-2, Transformer, LLaMA fine-tuning), referencing LoRA. A second relevant paper, *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (doc 582d138d…), experiments on CIFAR-100 (ViT-Base) and MNIST (LeNet/FCN) with SGD/AdamW and LoRA fine-tuning.
> 
> **4. One-stage anchor-free part-body association** — *PBADet* (doc 08b70bc3…): extends anchor-free detection with a single learned **part-to-body center offset** to associate human parts (hands, face, feet) to the correct body.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Experimental comparison & analysis
> 
> **Contrastive geometry (paper 1).** Negative-pair variance grows monotonically as batch shrinks: batch 32→512 gives variance 0.1649→0.1396; the VRNS loss cuts this to ~0.09–0.10 at all batch sizes. It improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet (SimCLR 51.79→52.48 on full ImageNet; largest gain at τ=0.3), stabilizes performance across temperatures, and helps DCL/DHEL, especially at small batches. Caveats: it can suppress meaningful semantic variance and adds a λ hyperparameter.
> 
> **JEPA (paper 2).** Theoretical critical-time analysis: JEPA learns high-ρ (influential) features first and converges to lower weights on noisy features; MAE orders by eigenvalue λ and learns noise. On ImageNet, I-JEPA's features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE's — matching the "semantic vs. pixel" advantage, with the bias only appearing for deep encoders.
> 
> **Optimizers/memory (paper 3).** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW: Swin-T/ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2 (4-bitFactor 80.9); GLUE 89.1 vs 89.1; GPT-2 67.8 vs 67.7; QA 94.5 vs 94.6; MT 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B Alpaca→MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7, HellaSwag 74.7 vs 74.6. Memory savings: LLaMA-7B 75.4→31.9 GB (−57.7%), enabling single-80GB-GPU training; RoBERTa-L −43.1%. Sublinear-memory Adafactor(β₁=0)/SM3 save more but degrade accuracy, notably on classification — so 4-bit quantization is the better accuracy/memory trade-off.
> 
> **Hessian/regularization (paper 4, cross-entropy link).** Power-law Hessian spectra hold for cross-entropy-trained models on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 (LeNet d_ks ≈ 0.009–0.032; random nets fail) and across SGD, VanillaSGD, Adam, AMSGrad, RAdam, Yogi, etc. Slope magnitude correlates with sharpness/generalization (Pearson 0.72 on CIFAR-10), linking optimizer choice (SGD vs AdamW) to the loss landscape; the power-law breaks with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large batches (MNIST B≥768), and emerges during ViT-Base/CIFAR-100 training and LLM (GPT-2) fine-tuning. Notably, **LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law as full fine-tuning does** (TinyLlama/MathQA: random d_ks 0.0552 → fine-tuned 0.0249), and during LoRA adaptation the Hessian trace decreases while d_ks initially rises — so LoRA changes generalization behavior and is also a parameter-efficient, low-memory alternative to full fine-tuning.
> 
> **PBADet (paper 5).** Ablations quantify each design choice: anchor-free part-to-body (89.1 HandAP / 92.62 conditional / 85.98 joint AP) beats its anchor-based counterpart (88.4/92.31/85.28) and BPJDet's body-to-part scheme (85.3/86.80/78.13) with fewer parameters (36.9M vs 41.2M); removing the association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task-alignment learning each degrades metrics. On COCOHumanParts all-category AP is 42.7–43.0, and it surpasses SOTA (BPJDet, HierR-CNN) on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts and ED-Pose on hand/foot precision-recall.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Cross-cutting takeaways for your stated interests
> - **Regularization under cross-entropy:** the Hessian paper treats weight decay (AdamW) and the power-law/sharpness slope as generalization proxies for cross-entropy-trained CNNs/transformers; the VRNS loss is an analogous "geometry regularizer" pulling negative-pair similarities toward the optimal value.
> - **Practical optimizer choices:** SGD and Adam/AdamW all converge to the same power-law structure when well trained; among memory-efficient options, 4-bit AdamW preserves accuracy while Adafactor/SM3 do not.
> - **GPU memory:** 4-bit optimizer states give up to ~58% total-memory savings, and LoRA (used in the Hessian paper and referenced by the 4-bit optimizer paper) keeps trainable parameters low — but note LoRA fine-tuning produces a different Hessian/generalization signature than full fine-tuning.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers matching your four topics
> 
> **1. Contrastive embedding geometry — "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (doc `160e1407…`)
> - Theory: under InfoNCE-style losses, full-batch optimum is positive-pair similarity = 1 and negative-pair similarity = −1/(n−1); mini-batches preserve the expected negative similarity but **smaller batches increase the variance of negative-pair similarities** ("excessive separation"). Gradient magnitude pushing negatives apart grows as batch size shrinks.
> - Experiments (SimCLR/DCL/DHEL, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, ImageNet): negative-similarity variance rises from 0.1396 (batch 512) to 0.1649 (batch 32); the proposed VRNS auxiliary loss cuts it to 0.0917/0.1008 and improves top-1 accuracy, most at small batches; it also stabilizes accuracy across temperatures 0.07–2.0. On full ImageNet: SimCLR 51.79 → 52.48 top-1. Caveat: it may suppress meaningful semantic variance and adds a λ hyperparameter.
> 
> **2. JEPA implicit bias — "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc `40fde037…`)
> - Deep-linear analysis: JEPA is implicitly biased toward **high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ)**; MAE prioritizes high-variance (eigenvalue λ) features even if noisy. The bias appears only for deep encoders; depth strengthens noise suppression; JEPA learns noisy features more slowly and at lower amplitude.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster (higher CCA) with the low-variance (bottom-25%-explained-variance) perceptual subspace than MAE, which favors the top subspace — explaining why JEPA learns semantic features more quickly.
> 
> **3. Memory-efficient optimizers — "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (doc `8d5e1455…`), plus **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (doc `582d138d…`) for the CIFAR-100/MNIST and regularization/optimizer-choice link.
> - 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor (smaller B128 blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for the second moment, optional factorization) match or slightly beat 32-bit AdamW: GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, SQuAD 94.5 vs 94.6, E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7; comparable on Swin-T ImageNet (80.8 vs 81.2) and WMT14 (26.28 vs 26.61); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA is on par. Memory: LLaMA-7B 75.4→31.9 GB (57.7% saved), RoBERTa-L 43.5% saved, 4-bit Factor ≈4× smaller states than 8-bit; enables LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU. Adafactor(β₁=0) and SM3 save more but degrade accuracy, especially on image classification. LoRA (freezing pretrained weights, tuning low-rank adapters) is discussed as a complementary memory saver for language-model fine-tuning.
> - The Hessian paper supplies the CIFAR-100/MNIST experiments: power-law Hessian spectra hold across many optimizers (SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, Yogi, RAdam, Adai, PNM, Lookahead, DiffGrad) on LeNet/ResNet18/ViT on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 (weight decay λ=0.0005 default; AdamW for ViT-Base fine-tuning on CIFAR-100 with weight decay 0.1, lr 1e-4, batch 4096). Slope magnitude ŝ tracks sharpness/generalization (Pearson 0.72 on CIFAR-10); power-law is lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training; LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure that full fine-tuning does.
> 
> **4. Part-body association — "PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection"** (doc `08b70bc3…`)
> - One-stage, anchor-free detector with a **single part-to-body center offset** (guaranteed one-to-one part↔body), multi-scale feature maps, task-alignment learning, YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 backbones.
> - BodyHands: beats all prior SOTA — Ours(YOLOv7, 36.9M params) HandAP 89.1, Cond. Acc 92.62, JointAP 85.98 vs BPJDet(YOLOv5l6, 86.1M) 85.9/86.91/84.39. COCOHumanParts: on par with BPJDet and leading in AP_M/AP_L and per-category APs (person/head/face/hands/feet) with the lowest average mMR−2 on most parts; higher precision/recall/F1 for hands/feet vs ED-Pose. Ablations: association loss lifts Cond. Acc 80.78→92.62 and JointAP 78.07→85.98; multi-scale offsets and task alignment each help.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis of experimental results
> 
> - **Batch size is a recurring lever.** The contrastive paper shows smaller batches degrade representations by inflating negative-pair similarity variance, and its auxiliary loss acts as a variance regularizer; the Hessian paper independently finds large-batch training destroys the power-law Hessian structure (a generalization correlate). Both point to batch size as a first-order practical choice.
> - **Regularization ties.** The contrastive VRNS term regularizes embedding geometry toward the −1/(n−1) optimum (also improving temperature robustness — temperature behaves like an implicit regularizer); in supervised cross-entropy settings, weight decay (λ=0.0005–0.1) is the standard regularizer, and the Hessian slope ŝ provides a generalization/sharpness diagnostic across optimizers.
> - **Optimizer choice.** The 4-bit paper's key practical finding: Adam/AdamW can be quantized to 4-bit states losslessly (out-of-the-box hyperparameter transfer), whereas sublinear-state baselines (Adafactor β₁=0, SM3) trade away accuracy — so 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor is the recommended memory/accuracy sweet spot; the Hessian paper confirms that all major optimizers behave alike spectrally when they train well, and that LoRA changes the loss-landscape structure versus full fine-tuning.
> - **GPU memory budget.** Complementary: 4-bit optimizer states (up to ~57.7% total-memory savings, 2× vs 8-bit, ~4× for 4-bit Factor), LoRA (fewer trainable parameters, smaller computation graph), plus offloading/sharding/activation compression/checkpointing (also used for memory-efficient Hessian computation via SLQ). PBADet's memory angle is different — smaller models (36.9M vs 86.1M params) achieving SOTA with AMP on 4×V100s.
> - **Caveat on matching.** Within this collection, no single paper combines sub-8-bit optimizer states *and* CIFAR-100/MNIST experiments: the 4-bit optimizer paper's vision benchmark is Swin-T on ImageNet-1k (plus transformer/LLM tasks), while the CIFAR-100/MNIST experiments with Adam/AdamW/SGD and regularization come from the Hessian-structure paper. Together they cover your (3) fully; neither individually does.

Gold 1：

> Here is a cross-paper comparison of the experimental results, organized by shared/identical datasets, similar dataset types, and per-dataset specifics. All numbers and claims are taken from the figures and tables in the provided papers.
> 
> A) Results on identical datasets
> 
> 1) CIFAR-10/100 (contrastive learning)
> - Baseline vs. variance-reduced contrastive loss (ICML 2025 “Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning”):
>   • Variance of negative-pair cosine similarities (CIFAR-100): with SimCLR, variance decreases as batch size grows (Table 1):
>     - Batch 32→512: 0.1649→0.1396 (SimCLR)
>     - With the proposed variance-reduction auxiliary loss (LVRNS), variance is consistently lower at every batch size (e.g., 0.1008 at 32; 0.0917 at 512).
>   • Classification accuracy across temperatures (Fig. 3): the auxiliary loss improves top-1 accuracy consistently on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 across temperatures (0.07–2.0), reducing sensitivity to temperature. The figure shows the +LVRNS curves are uniformly above the baselines.
>   • Accuracy vs. batch size and across methods (Fig. 4): incorporating the auxiliary loss improves top-1 accuracy for SimCLR, DCL, and DHEL on CIFAR-10/100, with larger gains at smaller batch sizes.
> 
> 2) ImageNet (contrastive learning and JEPA)
> - SimCLR vs. SimCLR + variance reduction (ICML 2025): On ImageNet-100, top-1 improves for multiple temperatures (Appendix E, Table 4):
>   • t=0.3: 72.30% → 74.04%
>   • t=0.4: 69.92% → 73.12%
>   • t=0.5: 68.60% → 72.88%
>   • t=0.2: 73.80% → 73.94%
>   On full ImageNet (Table 5): 51.79% → 52.48% top-1.
> - JEPA vs. MAE (NeurIPS 2024): On ImageNet (Appendix D), IJEPA’s learned features show higher mean CCA with the “bottom” (low-variance) PCA subspace and lower CCA with the “top” (high-variance) subspace than MAE over training epochs, indicating IJEPA emphasizes more perceptual/semantic directions than reconstruction (trend from Fig. 7; qualitative result, no single-number tables reported).
> 
> B) Results on similar dataset types
> 
> 1) Real-time hand/face/body part association in crowded scenes (ICLR 2024, PBADet)
> - Across large-scale human datasets, PBADet’s anchor-free, one-stage detector consistently improves hand/face/body detection and maintains competitive or superior association accuracy compared with anchor-based joint detectors (BPJDet) and two-stage approaches.
>   • On BodyHands (Table 1): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; PBADet (YOLOv5l6) Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73. These surpass BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) Joint AP 84.39 and older two-stage or pose-based baselines by large margins.
>   • On COCOHumanParts (Table 2, 3): Overall AP.5:.95 for BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) is slightly higher (43.6/43.3) than PBADet (YOLOv5l6) (43.0/41.8), but PBADet leads on size-specific metrics (APM 66.2/65.0 vs. 63.8/63.2; APL 67.2/64.4 vs. 61.8/58.9) and in several per-category APs (e.g., person 62.4 vs. 61.3; r-foot 30.9 vs. 30.2; l-foot 31.5 vs. 30.9). For association robustness (average mMR−2, Table 3), PBADet lowers mismatch rates on some parts (e.g., head 29.2 vs. BPJDet l6 30.8; face 31.3 vs. 31.8; left hand 41.1 vs. 41.6) while slightly higher on others (e.g., feet).
>   • On CrowdHuman (Appendix Table 5/6): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves best body MR−2 (36.5) and strong body AP (91.6), while mMR−2 for face-body association (50.8) is close to BPJDet (50.1). PBADet remains competitive versus specialized crowded-person detectors (Table 6), often with better body MR−2 and comparable AP.
> 
> 2) Memory- and compute-constrained fine-tuning (NeurIPS 2023, 4-bit optimizers)
> - Accuracy vs. full-precision/8-bit optimizers (Table 2): 4-bit AdamW matches or closely tracks 32-bit AdamW across varied tasks:
>   • NLU (RoBERTa-L/GLUE mean): 32-bit 88.9 vs. 4-bit 89.1
>   • QA (RoBERTa-L/SQuAD F1): 94.6 vs. 94.5; SQuAD v2 EM/F1 are also comparable (Appendix Table 9)
>   • NLG (GPT-2 M/E2E BLEU): 67.7 vs. 67.8 (Table 2; Appendix Table 8 shows other metrics unchanged)
>   • Image classification (Swin-T/ImageNet-1k): slight drop 81.2 → 80.8
>   • Machine translation (Transformer-Base, WMT14 en-de): 26.61 → 26.28 SacreBleu (small drop)
>   • Compared to 8-bit AdamW, 4-bit AdamW is similar or better on NLU and NLG and within noise on the rest.
> - Instruction-tuned LLaMA (Table 3): 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit AdamW across MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-e/c, OBQA for 7B, 13B, 33B (e.g., LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 vs. 46.5 for 32-bit; identical or within 0.1–0.5 points elsewhere).
> - Memory and throughput (Table 4):
>   • LLaMA-7B (FSDP, 2×A100-80GB): total memory 75.40 GB → 31.87 GB (–57.7%); time 3.35 h → 3.07 h (due to lower communication). 
>   • RoBERTa-L (single GPU): 5.31 GB → 3.00 GB (–43.5% with fused ops); GPT-2 M: 6.89 GB → 4.62 GB (–34.4% with fused ops).
> - Largest model trainable (Table 5): with 24 GB, fine-tunable model grows from OPT-350M to OPT-1.3B; with 80 GB, from OPT-1.3B to OPT-6.7B; LLaMA-7B becomes trainable on a single 80 GB GPU.
> - Ablations (Tables 1 & 6): Stable convergence at 4-bit requires addressing second-moment zero-point quantization; Rank-1 normalization + linear mapping for v (and small blocks for m) remove instabilities and recover full-precision accuracy; factorizing the second moment further improves memory with negligible accuracy loss.
> 
> 3) Mini-batch vs. full-batch representation quality (NeurIPS 2023, Dale’s Law RNNs; ICML 2025, CL Similarities; NeurIPS 2024, JEPA)
> - CL mini-batch effect (ICML 2025): The paper proves and empirically shows that smaller batches increase the variance of negative-pair cosine similarities (Table 1) and that this hurts downstream accuracy. Their auxiliary loss directly reduces this variance and improves accuracy (Figs. 3–4; Tables 4–5 on ImageNet too).
> - Spectral properties and small networks (NeurIPS 2023, Dale’s Law): For recurrent networks subject to Dale’s Law, the classic column-wise E/I partition (ColEI) trains worse than standard RNNs and the EI architecture DANN across tasks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, PTB language modeling, naturalistic object recognition). Spectrum “transplant” experiments show that the singular value spectrum of the recurrent weight matrix explains more of the performance gap than the mere sign constraint. Performance degrades with fewer inhibitory units and smaller network sizes in ColEI, matching a drop in normalized SVD entropy (NSE); DANN’s spectrum and performance remain robust even with a single inhibitory neuron.
> - JEPA vs. MAE (NeurIPS 2024): In linear deep encoders, JEPA focuses on high-regression-coefficient (more predictive, less noisy) features; MAE prioritizes high covariance, even if noisy. On ImageNet (Appendix D), IJEPA aligns more with the low-variance (perceptual) subspace than MAE throughout training (mean CCA trend).
> 
> C) Per-dataset specifics (detailed numbers)
> 
> 1) BodyHands (ICLR 2024, PBADet, Table 1)
> - PBADet vs. BPJDet (same YOLOv5l6 backbone): Joint AP 85.73–85.98 (PBADet YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7) vs. 84.39 (BPJDet YOLOv5l6). Conditional accuracy 92.71–92.62 vs. 86.91. Hand AP 88.1–89.1 vs. 85.9.
> 
> 2) COCOHumanParts (ICLR 2024, PBADet, Tables 2–3)
> - All-category AP.5:.95: BPJDet l6 43.6/43.3 vs. PBADet v5l6 43.0/41.8 (PBADet comparable). PBADet leads on APM/APL (66.2/65.0 & 67.2/64.4 vs. 63.8/63.2 & 61.8/58.9) and on several categories (e.g., person AP 62.4 vs. 61.3). 
> - Association mismatch rate (average mMR−2, lower is better): PBADet reduces head/face/hand mismatch compared with some BPJDet variants (e.g., YOLOv7: head 29.2 vs. l6 30.8; face 31.3 vs. 31.8) but is higher on feet in that table (e.g., right foot 52.6 vs. 49.1 for BPJDet l6).
> 
> 3) CrowdHuman (Appendix Tables 5–6)
> - PBADet YOLOv7: Body MR−2 36.5 (best in table), Face MR−2 44.7 (better than BPJDet l6 46.3), Body AP 91.6; Pair mMR−2: 50.8 vs. BPJDet l6 50.1.
> 
> 4) GLUE (RoBERTa-L, Table 2; Appendix Table 7)
> - Mean accuracy/correlation: 4-bit AdamW 89.1 vs. 32-bit 88.9; across individual tasks, 4-bit either matches or is within the variance of 32-bit and 8-bit baselines.
> 
> 5) SQuAD / SQuAD 2.0 (Appendix Table 9)
> - SQuAD F1: 94.5 (4-bit) vs. 94.6 (32-bit); SQuAD 2.0 EM/F1 also comparable with 32-bit.
> 
> 6) E2E-NLG (GPT-2 Medium; Tables 1–2; Appendix Table 8)
> - With correct second-moment quantization (Rank-1/Linear): BLEU recovers to or surpasses 32-bit (67.8 vs. 67.7). Table 1 shows unstable training with standard DE zero-point mapping; excluding zero or using linear mapping stabilizes and restores accuracy (e.g., Rank-1/Linear BLEU 67.8±0.51; no instability).
> 
> 7) ImageNet-1k (Swin-T, Table 2)
> - 80.8% (4-bit) vs. 81.2% (32-bit) top-1; small drop from full precision, typical for pretraining.
> 
> 8) WMT14 en-de (Transformer-Base, Table 2)
> - SacreBleu 26.28 (4-bit) vs. 26.61 (32-bit), close match.
> 
> 9) LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3)
> - 7B/13B/33B: 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-e/c, OBQA (e.g., 13B MMLU 47.4 vs. 46.5; other tasks within ~0–0.5 points).
> 
> 10) ImageNet (contrastive, Appendix E Tables 4–5)
> - SimCLR + variance reduction improves top-1 on ImageNet-100 for several temperatures (e.g., t=0.3: 72.30→74.04), and on full ImageNet (51.79→52.48).
> 
> D) Practical takeaways (grounded in the reported results)
> - For anchor-free, one-stage part–body association under tight compute: PBADet consistently lifts association-ready detection in crowded and multi-part scenarios, with best or competitive results vs. BPJDet and Hier R-CNN on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman, especially with smaller or moderate backbones (Tables 1–3, 5–6).
> - For small-batch pretraining with contrastive learning: Mini-batches increase the variance of negative-pair cosine similarities (proven and measured), especially at small batch sizes, which hurts accuracy; adding the variance-reduction term reduces that variance at every batch size (Table 1) and improves accuracy across methods and datasets (Figs. 3–4; Tables 4–5).
> - For understanding JEPA vs. reconstruction: Deep-linear analysis and ImageNet CCA trends show JEPA gravitates to high-influence (predictive, low-variance) features, complementing the CL results on bottom-subspace alignment, while MAE emphasizes high-variance (often less semantic) components.
> - For memory-limited fine-tuning (including LoRA backbones): 4-bit AdamW (with correct second-moment quantization) matches 32-bit accuracy on NLU/QA/NLG and instruction tuning, slightly trailing on ImageNet/MT, while cutting total memory 34–58% and enabling 2–4× larger models under the same budget (Tables 2–5). This integrates cleanly with standard PyTorch optimizers and is compatible with transformer fine-tuning.
> 
> These comparisons are strictly derived from the reported tables and figures in the provided papers.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Recommended works
> 
> **1. Mini-batch contrastive behavior — "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (Lee et al., ICML 2025)**
> - In full-batch settings, optimal InfoNCE embeddings align positives (cosine sim = 1) and separate negatives at −1/(n−1). In mini-batch settings, expected negative similarity stays the same, but **smaller batches increase the variance of negative-pair similarities** ("excessive separation"), degrading representation quality; the gradient magnitude pushing negatives apart grows as batch size shrinks. Temperature controls the similarity distribution and needs careful tuning.
> - **Results:** With SimCLR (t=0.2, CIFAR-100), negative-pair similarity variance rises as batch size drops (0.1396 at 512 → 0.1649 at 32). Their proposed auxiliary variance-reduction loss cuts variance (e.g., 0.1649→0.1008 at batch 32) and consistently improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100/ImageNet across SimCLR/DCL/DHEL, with gains **most pronounced at small batch sizes**, and makes accuracy higher and more stable across temperatures 0.07–2.0. Caveat: it may suppress meaningful semantic variance.
> 
> **2. JEPA's feature bias — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks" (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024)**
> - JEPA objectives are biased toward **high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ)**, while MAE prioritizes high-variance (high-λ) features; this bias only appears with **deep encoders** and strengthens with depth. JEPA learns low-variance (semantically rich, discriminative) subspaces faster and is slower to learn noisy features.
> - **Results (ImageNet-1K, ViT at 64×64):** CCA shows I-JEPA's features from full vs. bottom-25%-variance datasets are more similar than MAE's throughout training, while the trend reverses for top-75% images — JEPA focuses on the bottom (perceptual) PCA subspace faster than MAE.
> 
> **3. 4-bit optimizer states — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023)**
> - Compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit via small block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, optional second-moment factorization ("4-bit Factor"); suitable for fine-tuning transformers including with LoRA (referenced).
> - **Results:** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L: 89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD (94.5 vs 94.6), Swin-T ImageNet (80.8 vs 81.2), E2E-NLG (67.8 vs 67.7), WMT14 (26.28 vs 26.61), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning (e.g., 7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; 13B HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8). Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB, enabling single-80GB-GPU training); 4-bit Factor ~4× smaller optimizer states than 8-bit. Convergence curves closely track 32-bit AdamW. Note: fused operators needed for speed parity on small models.
> 
> **4. Anchor-free one-stage part–body association — "PBADet" (Gao et al., ICLR 2024)**
> - One-stage anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones, 1024×1024 input) using a **single part-to-body center offset** (representation length 10 vs BPJDet's 15 for 3 parts), guaranteeing one-to-one part–body correspondence; valid even when parts are occluded, and scalable to any number of parts.
> - **Results (BodyHands):** Ours(YOLOv7, 36.9M params) → Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98, beating BPJDet(YOLOv5l6, 86.1M): 85.9/86.91/84.39, and far exceeding BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48) and two-stage Mask R-CNN variants — superior with fewer parameters. **CrowdHuman (face–body):** body MR-2 36.5 (YOLOv7) / 37.5 (YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet 39.7–41.3 — best miss rate, though AP advantage over BPJDet is smaller for this single-part task (e.g., body AP 91.6 vs 90.7; face AP 81.6 vs 82.2 for BPJDet m6). Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale center offset, and task-alignment learning each improve association quality.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Representation learning (works 1–2):** Contrastive and JEPA objectives complement each other. Contrastive learning in **small batches** suffers from inflated negative-pair similarity variance (harmful for identity discrimination in crowded scenes); the variance-reduction loss is a cheap fix, and temperature tuning matters. JEPA's bias toward influential, low-variance features aligns well with identity/perceptual cues and is more sample-efficient, but its bias requires depth and can latch onto slow/spurious features. For your HMI, contrastive (with variance reduction) gives instance discrimination; JEPA gives noise-robust semantic features — the papers are complementary rather than competing.
> - **Efficiency (work 3):** 4-bit optimizer states give near-lossless fine-tuning (≤~0.5 pt drops or slight gains) with ~43–58% total memory reduction — ideal for your limited-GPU transformer/LoRA fine-tuning; the "4-bit Factor" variant adds memory savings with no accuracy loss.
> - **Detection (work 4):** PBADet is the strongest fit for hands/face-to-individual matching: one-stage anchor-free keeps compute low, and on BodyHands it beats all two-stage/anchor-based/pose-based methods on every metric with fewer parameters; on crowded face–body (CrowdHuman) it leads in miss rate (fewer missed people) with roughly on-par AP, so in dense scenes pair it with a strong classifier/embedding from works 1–2 for reliable identity matching.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the available documents, I can point you to the following works and analyze their experimental results:
> 
> ## 1. Mini-batch contrastive behavior (cosine similarity & temperature)
> **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (PMLR/ICML 2025) directly addresses your question:
> - In full-batch settings, optimal encoders align positive pairs (similarity 1) and separate negative pairs uniformly to **−1/(n−1)**; negative-pair alignment is unattainable below that threshold (mitigated by within-view negatives).
> - In **mini-batch settings, smaller batch sizes induce higher variance in negative-pair similarities** ("excessive separation"), which degrades representation quality. Gradient magnitude of InfoNCE on negative pairs grows as batch size shrinks.
> - The loss **temperature** shapes the distribution of embedding similarities and affects accuracy; they propose a variance-reduction auxiliary loss that lowers variance (e.g., batch size 32: variance 0.1649→0.1008) and improves/stabilizes top-1 accuracy across temperatures (0.07–2.0) and small batches, on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and full ImageNet (SimCLR 51.79→52.48). Limitations: suppresses meaningful semantic variance; gains shrink at large batches; adds hyperparameter λ.
> 
> ## 2. JEPA's feature bias
> **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis"** (NeurIPS 2024):
> - JEPA is **biased toward "influential" features** (high regression coefficient ρ), whereas MAE prioritizes features by covariance λ — even noisy ones. In a case where λ and ρ conflict, JEPA **reverses the feature-learning order** (learns high-ρ features first) while MAE keeps its λ-based order; this bias only holds for deep encoders and is a mechanism for avoiding noisy features.
> - ImageNet-1K experiments: I-JEPA's features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (containing perceptual features) than MAE's (higher CCA for full vs bottom-filtered data; reversed for top).
> 
> ## 3. 4-bit optimizer states + LoRA for fine-tuning
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023):
> - Covers **4-bit optimizer states** (Adam/AdamW) via smaller block size (B128) for the first moment, and for the second moment zero-point-excluding linear quantization and **rank-1 normalization**, optionally factorized — matching 32-bit AdamW accuracy on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet, E2E-NLG, and LLaMA fine-tuning (e.g., RoBERTa-L NLU 88.9→89.1; Swin-T 81.2→80.8) while saving up to 57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B fits one 80GB GPU). This is the memory-reduction tool to pair with low-rank adapters (LoRA, cited therein) during transformer fine-tuning.
> 
> ## 4. Anchor-free, one-stage part–body association
> **"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** (ICLR 2024) fits your hand/face-to-person matching task under tight compute:
> - Uses a single **part-to-body center offset** on anchor-free detectors (YOLOv5/YOLOv7), guaranteeing one-to-one part–body correspondence; it's compute-lean (e.g., 36.9M params @1024 for YOLOv7) vs. multi-stage/BPJDet representations.
> - Experimental results: on **COCOHumanParts**, PBADet (YOLOv5l6) achieves 43.0/41.8 all-category AP vs BPJDet 43.6/43.3, with much higher subordinate-part APs (e.g., 67.2 vs 61.8), and beats HierR-CNN (40.6/37.3); on **BodyHands** it outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN; on **CrowdHuman** face–body association it gives the leading body MR-2 (36.5) and competitive AP (91.6 body/81.6 face). Ablations show the association loss (JointAP 78.07→85.98), multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment learning each help. It also beats ED-Pose on hand/feet precision, recall, and F1, and extends to quadruped (AnimalPose/AP-10K).
> 
> **Comparison of the methods' results:** the contrastive paper shows small batches hurt representations via increased negative-pair variance and that a variance-reduction term restores accuracy robustly across temperatures; the JEPA analysis shows self-distillation (no negatives) avoids noisy features by biasing to influential/low-variance features — complementary to contrastive approaches. For efficiency, 4-bit optimizer states give near-lossless accuracy with large memory savings, suitable for small-GPU LoRA fine-tuning. PBADet demonstrates that one-stage anchor-free association is both accurate and budget-friendly, though its CrowdHuman advantage over BPJDet is smaller for the single part (face) task.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> The experimental comparison in the provided papers shows that AMP (Adaptive Message Passing) and the 4-bit Optimizers each improve over their respective baselines, but on different problem domains.
> 
> **Adaptive Message Passing (AMP)**
> - **Synthetic long-range tasks** (Diameter, SSSP, Eccentricity): Wrapping AMP around GCN, GIN, and ADGN consistently reduced log10(MSE) versus the unmodified architecture. Average relative error improvements are −63% for Diameter, −72% for SSSP, and −32% for Eccentricity.
> - **Chemical graph benchmarks** (peptides-func [AP↑], peptides-struct [MAE↓]): AMP improves all base MP architectures. Gains on peptides-func range +2.0 to +3.4 AP points over the base, and MAE reductions on peptides-struct put AMP variants at or near the top of the leaderboard.
> - Improvements come from jointly learning the effective depth and filtering messages, which mitigates oversmoothing/oversquashing and adapts depth per task. Figures show higher Dirichlet energy across layers and task-dependent learned depth distributions.
> 
> **4-bit Optimizers**
> - **Language & vision fine-tuning tasks** (NLU/GLUE, QA/SQuAD, NLG/E2E, CLS/ImageNet, MT/WMT14): 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW and 8-bit AdamW across all tasks. For example:
>   - RoBERTa-Large on GLUE: mean NLU score 89.1, matching 8-bit and 32-bit.
>   - GPT-2 Medium on E2E-NLG: BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7 (32-bit) and 67.5 (8-bit).
>   - Swin-T on ImageNet: 80.8% vs 81.0% (8-bit) and 81.2% (32-bit).
>   - Transformer on WMT14: 26.28 BLEU vs 26.66 (8-bit) and 26.61 (32-bit).
> - **Instruction tuning** (LLaMA-7B/13B/33B on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA): 4-bit maintains comparable performance to 32-bit.
> - Memory savings up to ~57% vs 32-bit with minimal or no loss in convergence, plus potential throughput gains when optimizer state comms dominate.
> 
> **Summary of performance comparison on identical tasks:**
> - For graph-structured long-range dependency problems (synthetic and molecular graphs), AMP-equipped message passing nets outperform their non-adaptive base versions substantially, addressing oversmoothing, oversquashing, and underreaching.
> - For transformer and CNN training/fine-tuning in NLP and vision, 4-bit optimizers preserve full-precision accuracy while significantly reducing optimizer state memory.
> - The two methods target different bottlenecks (graph depth/message quality vs optimizer state memory), but in their respective domains, both deliver consistent gains over standard baselines without sacrificing accuracy.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## The Five Papers (matching the requested topics)
> 
> **(a) PBADet — One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage, anchor-free part↔person association; a single part-to-body center offset replaces BPJDet's per-part body-to-part offsets. **Experiments (COCO-style benchmarks):**
> - **BodyHands:** Ours(YOLOv7) HandAP **89.1**, Cond. Acc. **92.62**, JointAP **85.98** vs BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39 and BodyHands 84.8/83.44/63.48 — beats all baselines on every metric with a smaller model.
> - **COCOHumanParts:** Ours(YOLOv5l6) AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 (orig/subordinate), AP.5 70.0/68.4; on par with BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3, and **leads in AP_M (66.2) and AP_L (67.2)** and per-part AP for person/feet; lowest average mMR⁻² for head/face/hands/right-foot.
> - **CrowdHuman (face-body):** Ours(YOLOv7) body MR⁻² 36.5, face AP 81.6, mMR⁻² 50.8, best body MR⁻² overall.
> - **Ablations:** association loss adds +11.8 Cond. Acc. (80.78→92.62) and +7.9 JointAP; multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each add ~0.5–1; anchor-free part-to-body (89.1/92.62/85.98) beats anchor-based (88.4/92.31/85.28) and BPJDet's body-to-part (85.3/86.80/78.13).
> 
> **(b) Adaptive Message Passing (AMP, ICML 2025)** — variational learning of message-passing depth + per-layer message filtering to counter oversmoothing/oversquashing/underreaching. **Experiments:**
> - **Synthetic long-range (Diameter/SSSP/Eccentricity):** AMP improves mean log₁₀(MSE) for every base model — AMPGCN −81%/−57%/−26%, AMPGIN −81%/−99%/−69%, AMPADGN −27%/−61%/−1%; avg relative improvement −63%/−72%/−32%.
> - **peptides-func:** Test AP AMPGCN **0.7161** vs GCN 0.5930, AMPGINE 0.7065 vs 0.5498, AMPGATEDGCN 0.6943 vs 0.6069 — competitive with SOTA NBAGCN (0.7207)/IPR-MPNN (0.7210). **peptides-struct:** MAE AMPGCN 0.2446 vs GCN 0.3496.
> - **Mechanism analyses:** Dirichlet energy stays higher (no exponential decay) → oversmoothing mitigated; learned depth ~10–22 layers (peptides diameter ~57) → underreaching solved; message-filtering ablation (input- and embedding-based) consistently improves over no filtering.
> 
> **(c) Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)** — deep-linear analysis showing JEPA (latent-space prediction) vs MAE (pixel-space MSE). **Results:**
> - **Critical-time theory:** MAE orders feature learning by input covariance λ; JEPA additionally orders by regression coefficient ρ, with the ρ-priority growing with depth (t\* ratio ∝ Δ_ρ ε^(L−1)). Fixed points: JEPA w̄(∞)=ρ^L vs MAE ρ^(L/(L+1)).
> - **Simulations:** both objectives show greedy dynamics in λ, but **only JEPA is greedy in ρ**; when λ and ρ trends oppose, JEPA inverts the learning order vs MAE; deeper encoders widen the temporal spread, suppressing noisy features (verified with randomly initialized SGD deep linear nets and a temporal flickering-image model).
> - **ImageNet-1K:** I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features than MAE — confirming the bias toward high-influence latent features over pixel-space MSE.
> 
> **(d) Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** — spectral analysis of RNNs obeying E/I sign rules (ColEI vs DANN). **Results:**
> - **Benchmarks (adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition):** ColEI learns worse and with more seed variance than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs on all four tasks; gradient clipping helps ColEI far more.
> - **Spectral findings:** ColEI's recurrent matrix (rank-one nilpotent column-means + zero-mean random matrix) gives a **multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum with a large-value mode**, unlike the unimodal Marchenko–Pastur/quarter-circle spectra of RNNs/DANNs. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the **singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints** (sign constraints account for only ~0.7–1% vs a 2.3±0.6% total gap).
> - **Predictive diagnostic:** normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error across sizes and E:I ratios; fewer inhibitory units degrade both spectrum and learning, while DANNs stay robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> 
> **(e) Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023)** — 4-bit quantized Adam/AdamW (framework also covers SGD(M)) via smaller blocks (B128), zero-point-excluding linear/DE-0 mapping, and rank-1 normalization/factorization of the second moment. **Results:**
> - **Accuracy (Table 2):** 32-bit AdamW vs 4-bit AdamW vs 4-bit Factor — NLU (RoBERTa-L/GLUE) 88.9 / **89.1** / 88.9; CLS (Swin-T/ImageNet-1k) 81.2 / 80.8 / 80.9; NLG (GPT-2M, BLEU) 67.7 / **67.8** / 67.6; QA (RoBERTa-L/SQuAD, F1) 94.6 / 94.5 / 94.6; MT (Transformer-Base/WMT14) 26.61 / 26.28 / 26.45. **Matches or exceeds 32-bit on all fine-tuning tasks and is comparable on pretraining**, while Adafactor/SM3 degrade (esp. CLS).
> - **LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning:** 4-bit AdamW ≈ 32-bit on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-e/c, OBQA; convergence curves closely align.
> - **Memory:** up to **57.7%** total-memory saving (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB; RoBERTa-L 43.1%; GPT-2M 34.4%; 4-bit Factor 46.7%); enables LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU and ~4× larger OPT models under fixed budgets. Ablations confirm the zero-point exclusion is the key enabler for second-moment quantization.
> - *Note:* this paper's benchmarks are ImageNet-1k/GLUE/SQuAD/E2E-NLG/WMT14/Alpaca (Swin-T, RoBERTa, GPT-2, Transformer-Base, LLaMA) — the CIFAR-100/COCO/ResNet-50 fine-tuning scenario you described is **not** what this paper evaluated in the retrieved context.
> 
> ## Comparative Analysis of the Experimental Results
> 
> - **Headline pattern:** every method either *matches a strong full-precision/SOTA baseline at lower cost* (4-bit optimizer ≈ 32-bit AdamW with ~57% memory cut; AMPGCN ≈ graph SOTA with no rewiring) or *beats SOTA on its benchmark* (PBADet exceeds BPJDet/BodyHands on all association metrics; JEPA theory explains I-JEPA's faster perceptual-feature alignment than MAE).
> - **Metric diversity:** (a) uses detection/association metrics (AP, Cond. Acc., JointAP, mMR⁻²); (b) uses task-error/energy metrics (log₁₀MSE, Test AP/MAE, Dirichlet energy); (c) uses dynamical metrics (critical times, CCA subspace alignment); (d) uses test error plus a spectral diagnostic (NSE); (e) uses task accuracy/F1/BLEU plus memory savings. They are not directly comparable quantitatively — the "comparison" is at the level of methodology (each ablates its core component: association loss/offset definition; depth learning + filtering; latent-vs-pixel objective; spectrum-vs-sign constraints; zero-point exclusion/factorization).
> - **Common insight — component ablations matter:** PBADet's association loss (+11.8 Cond. Acc.), AMP's message filtering (consistent gains over no-filter), the 4-bit optimizer's zero-point exclusion (turns unstable 33–66% runs into 0% unstable), and the Dale's-law paper's spectrum transplant (spectrum > sign constraints) all show that a single design choice drives most of the gain.
> - **Consistency with theory:** (c) derives exact ODEs and confirms predictions numerically and on ImageNet; (b) proves a sensitivity bound and confirms with Dirichlet-energy/sensitivity analyses; (d) uses random-matrix theory and confirms with SVD transplants; (e) provides a convergence proof for quantized SGD(M) and empirically matches it. PBADet is the purely empirical entry, validated across three datasets and an animal-pose transfer setting.
> - **Caveats from the papers:** JEPA analysis is limited to deep linear nets/special initializations; AMP's very deep learned architectures cost more readout parameters; ColEI RNNs remain unstable without gradient clipping; 4-bit quantization's optimal settings are task-dependent and unverified for RL/audio/graph tasks; PBADet's advantage over BPJDet narrows on the single-part CrowdHuman task.
> 
> If you need, I can pull the exact per-category tables (e.g., PBADet per-part APs, 4-bit optimizer per-task numbers) for a finer-grained comparison.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the matching papers and their experimental results:
> 
> ## Papers found
> 
> **(a)** **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage, anchor-free part↔body association via a single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on COCO-style benchmarks (BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman).
> 
> **(b)** **Adaptive Message Passing (AMP)** (ICML 2025) — variational framework that learns message-passing depth and per-layer message filtering to mitigate oversmoothing, oversquashing, and underreaching.
> 
> **(c)** **Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024) — proves JEPA prioritizes high-influence (high-ρ) features over pixel-space MSE reconstruction.
> 
> **(d)** **Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly** (NeurIPS 2023) — spectral analysis of E/I sign-constrained RNNs (ColEI vs DANN vs standard).
> 
> **(e)** **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023) — 4-bit quantized optimizer states (Adam/AdamW/SGD framework).
> 
> ## Experimental results comparison
> 
> **(a) PBADet.** On BodyHands, it beats all SOTA: YOLOv7 gives Hand AP 89.1 / Cond. Accuracy 92.62 / Joint AP 85.98 vs BPJDet(YOLOv5m6) 85.3/86.80/78.13 — with fewer parameters (36.9M vs 41.2M). On COCO-HumanParts it is on par with BPJDet on total AP (42.7–43.0) but leads on person/feet AP and has the lowest mMR-2; vs the pose-estimator ED-Pose it gives far higher Precision/Recall/F1 (all parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51). Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each matter.
> 
> **(b) AMP.** On synthetic long-range tasks (Diameter/SSSP/Eccentricity) AMP reduces test error by 63%/72%/32% on average vs base GCN/GIN/ADGN. On peptides-func it improves AP by 2–3.4% (AMP-GCN 0.7161, AMP-GINE 0.7065) and lowers peptides-struct MAE to 0.2446, placing at SOTA level. Qualitatively, AMP keeps higher Dirichlet energy (less oversmoothing) and reduces message squashing; it learns deep architectures only when needed.
> 
> **(c) JEPA vs MAE.** Theory (deep linear networks): JEPA's critical time depends on ρ (regression coefficient) increasingly with depth, so it learns high-influence, low-variance features first; MAE's ordering depends only on eigenvalue λ. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (bottom portion) than MAE, measured by CCA — i.e., JEPA favors discriminative latent features over pixel-space MSE.
> 
> **(d) Dale's Law RNNs.** ColEI networks learn worse and more variably than standard RNNs and DANN-RNNs on all four benchmarks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition). Singular-value "transplant" experiments show the spectrum matters more than sign constraints: sign constraints cost ~0.7–1% error but the full gap is ~2.3%; the initial singular-value spectrum contributes ~1.5–2%. ColEI has a multimodal, dispersed spectrum (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure) vs the unimodal quarter-circle spectrum of standard/DANN RNNs; normalised SVD entropy anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance before training.
> 
> **(e) 4-bit optimizers.** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on all reported tasks: GLUE NLU 89.1 vs 88.9, ImageNet (Swin-T) 80.8 vs 81.2, GPT-2 E2E BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, WMT Transformer SacreBleu 26.28 vs 26.61; on LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning it matches 32-bit AdamW on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA. Memory saving up to 57.7%; LLaMA-7B fits on one 80GB GPU. Adafactor/SM3 save more memory but degrade (especially image classification).
> 
> ## Important caveat on (e)
> 
> The question's specific claims for (e) — fine-tuning on **CIFAR-100 and COCO** with **ResNet-50 or feedforward classifiers**, **cosine-similarity-based embeddings**, and **Precision/F1** metrics — are **not supported by any document in the collection**. The 4-bit optimizer paper's closest matches are "Transformer" (Transformer-Base on WMT14) and "Adam/SGD" (its compression framework explicitly covers SGD(M)/Adam/AdamW), and it does report **F1** (SQuAD QA). But it uses Swin-T on ImageNet, RoBERTa/GPT-2/LLaMA, and Transformer — not CIFAR-100, COCO, ResNet-50, feedforward classifiers, or cosine-similarity embeddings. Those specific experimental claims therefore cannot be established from the provided context.
> 
> ## Cross-paper analysis
> 
> - The papers cover unrelated subfields (detection, graph learning, SSL theory, RNN spectral analysis, optimization), so there is **no shared benchmark** allowing direct comparison; only qualitative cross-cutting themes apply.
> - **Common theme — signal vs. noise/robustness:** JEPA (c) prefers predictive, low-noise latent features; AMP (b) reduces unnecessary message propagation while retaining task-relevant signal; PBADet (a) keeps a single clean one-to-one association offset instead of many body-to-part offsets; the Dale's-law paper (d) shows performance is governed by spectral "pathology" (dispersed, multimodal spectra) rather than sign constraints.
> - **Memory/parameter efficiency with no accuracy loss:** PBADet achieves SOTA with fewer parameters than BPJDet; 4-bit optimizers match 32-bit with up to 57.7% memory savings; AMP avoids costly depth grid-search by learning depth.
> - **Failure modes are dataset-dependent:** e.g., the 4-bit optimizer has a marginal drop on vision classification (80.8 vs 81.2) while matching on NLU/QA; PBADet's edge over BPJDet is large on BodyHands (multi-part) but smaller on CrowdHuman single-part face-body association; the JEPA advantage holds only for deep encoders (shallow encoders diminish the bias); the Dale's-law deficit shrinks for large/balanced networks (high NSE).

Which works address these needs end-to-end?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Here’s a precise comparison and summary of the experimental results from the AMP paper:
> 
> **1. Synthetic Long-Range Tasks (Diameter, SSSP, Eccentricity — Table 1)**
> - AMP consistently **improves over the base GCN, GIN, and ADGN** architectures across all three synthetic datasets.
> - **Relative error reductions**: ~63% on Diameter, ~72% on SSSP, ~32% on Eccentricity (averaged across bases).
> - Gains are largest for base models that relied on shallow optimal depths (e.g., GIN), showing that the learned depth and filtering are more effective than fixed-depth tuning.
> 
> **2. Chemical Long-Range Graph Benchmark (peptides-func, peptides-struct — Table 2)**
> - AMP improves **AP by +2–3.4%** over base GCN/GINE/GatedGCN on peptides-func.
> - On peptides-struct regression (lower MAE better), AMP variants achieve **state-of-the-art** or near SoTA performance within error margins, improving over all three base models.
> - Improvements hold without changing base architecture except for adaptive depth and learned filtering.
> 
> **3. Oversmoothing / Oversquashing Analysis (Figures 3, 4, 5)**
> - AMP keeps **Dirichlet energy** higher and more stable vs. baselines → mitigates oversmoothing.
> - Sensitivity patterns vary but AMP improves task scores, suggesting filtering can reduce oversquashing despite lower sensitivity.
> - Learned depth adapts to task: more layers for Eccentricity, fewer for SSSP, ~10 for peptides-struct.
> - Message filtering changes drastically by task; ablation shows both input-based and embedding-based filtering improve performance over no filtering.
> 
> **4. Node Classification Benchmarks (Table 3)**
> - Across 8 graphs (heterophilic + homophilic), AMPGCN outperforms vanilla GCN on **all datasets** (sometimes by large margins, e.g., +28% accuracy on Texas, +36% on Wisconsin).
> 
> **5. Fixed Depth Ablation (Table 6)**
> - Freezing AMP to the ‘best’ fixed depth found via its learned distribution yields **slightly worse performance** — validating the benefit of dynamic depth.
> 
> **Summary**
> - **AMP > base models** in all tested settings and metrics when long-range dependencies matter.
> - Works across architectures (GCN, GIN, ADGN, GINE, GatedGCN) and tasks (synthetic, chemical, node classification).
> - Gains come from two adaptive mechanisms: **layer-wise learned depth** (mitigates underreaching) and **soft message filtering** (mitigates over-smoothing & over-squashing).
> - Analysis shows AMP can operate deeper when needed, prune irrelevant messages, and adjust differently for each dataset/task.
> 
> If you’d like, I can prepare a **side-by-side table of base vs AMP scores** for all datasets to make the improvements more visually clear.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Which works address these needs
> 
> No single work covers the entire pipeline end-to-end; each requirement maps to a separate paper:
> 
> 1. **Hands/face→person association in crowded COCO-like scenes**: **PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free part-body association)
> 2. **Graph long-range dependencies without oversmoothing/oversquashing**: **Adaptive Message Passing (AMP)**
> 3. **Latent-space SSL that avoids noisy pixels**: **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (theoretical analysis of JEPA vs MAE), plus **LDReg** (anti-collapse regularization) and **HASSOD** (self-supervised object detection)
> 4. **Memory-efficient fine-tuning via 4-bit optimizer states**: **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"**
> 
> ## Experimental comparison and analysis
> 
> **PBADet (vision/association).** On BodyHands (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; ablations show the association loss matters most (Joint AP drops to 78.07 without it; multi-scale and task-alignment add ~0.5 each). On COCOHumanParts it matches BPJDet in AP (43.0/41.8 original/subordinate with YOLOv5l6) but with higher AP_M (66.2) and AP_L (67.2) and the lowest average mMR-2 on head, face, both hands and right foot. On CrowdHuman (face-body) it is best in body MR-2 (36.5, YOLOv7) and comparable in AP to DETR-based crowded detectors, though its edge over BPJDet is smaller for this single-part task. Against the pose estimator ED-Pose (Swin-L) on COCO, it roughly doubles Precision/Recall/F1 for hands and feet (e.g., all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51).
> 
> **AMP (graph).** On chemical benchmarks AMP consistently improves its base GNNs: AMPGCN 0.7161, AMPGINE 0.7065, AMPGATEDGCN 0.6943 on peptides-func/struct († = improvement over base architecture), competing with state-of-the-art graph transformers. Analysis shows AMP's Dirichlet energy stays higher across layers (less oversmoothing) and sensitivity is reduced (less oversquashing); it learns depth from data (Poisson distributions), often needing deeper nets than the standard 10 layers (peptide average diameter is 57).
> 
> **JEPA/MAE analysis (SSL).** Theoretically, JEPA's feature order depends on the regression coefficient ρ (JEPA fixed point w̄=ρ^L), while MAE orders by eigenvalue λ (w̄=ρ^{L/(L+1)}); JEPA suppresses noisy directions and this suppression grows with depth. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA measure), empirically supporting latent-space prediction over pixel reconstruction. **LDReg** complements this by preventing (local) dimensional collapse: on ImageNet it improves linear eval, transfer (incl. CIFAR) and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE, MoCo, VICReg and Barlow Twins with ResNet-50/ViT-B.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers (fine-tuning).** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on all tasks: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, GPT-2M NLG 67.8 vs 67.7, WMT 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning is comparable on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA. Memory savings reach 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB) and 43.5% for RoBERTa-L (5.31→3.00 GB); "4-bit Factor" saves more. Key techniques: smaller block (B128) for the first moment, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer and rank-1 normalization for the second moment.
> 
> **Takeaway.** Assemble the pipeline from these four works: PBADet handles part-body association on COCO-like crowded data; AMP provides the long-range graph component; JEPA-style latent-space SSL (with LDReg to avoid collapse) supplies noise-robust pretraining; and the 4-bit optimizer paper enables Adam/AdamW fine-tuning within tight GPU memory. Caveats from the papers: PBADet's advantage shrinks on single-part tasks; AMP results are on molecule/node-classification graphs, not vision graphs; the JEPA analysis is limited to deep linear models; and 4-bit results were tested on language/vision tasks with optimal quantization possibly task-dependent.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, four works map cleanly onto your four needs, plus one supporting SSL paper that matches your exact benchmark/backbone combo.
> 
> ## 1. Vision: hands/face → correct person in crowded COCO-like scenes → **PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> One-stage, anchor-free part-body association using a single part-to-body center offset, so it reliably links parts (face, left/right hands, feet) to the parent person. Experiments compare directly with BPJDet and HierR-CNN on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts (a COCO-family dataset), and CrowdHuman:
> - **BodyHands**: HandAP 89.1 (YOLOv7) / 88.1 (YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet 85.9 and BodyHands 84.8; Conditional accuracy 92.62/92.71 vs 86.91; JointAP 85.98/85.73 vs 84.39. The smaller 36.9M-param YOLOv7 beats larger rivals.
> - **COCOHumanParts** (head, face, both hands, both feet): AP 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6), on par with BPJDet (43.6/43.3), with the best AP_M/AP_L and feet APs; also best average mMR⁻² on face and hands.
> - **CrowdHuman** (crowded face-body): best body MR⁻² (36.5) and body AP (91.6); on this single-part task the advantage over BPJDet is smaller.
> - vs **ED-Pose** (Swin-L, Transformer): all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51 — directly supplying the F1/Precision numbers you want on COCO. Trained with SGD.
> 
> ## 2. Graph: long-range dependencies without oversmoothing/oversquashing → **Adaptive Message Passing (AMP)**
> A variational framework that learns *how many* message-passing layers to use and *which messages to filter*, directly targeting oversmoothing, oversquashing, and underreaching. Results: it consistently improves base GCN/GINE/GatedGCN/ADGN on synthetic long-range tasks and chemical benchmarks — e.g., peptides-func AMPGCN 0.7161 vs REWGCN 0.7150 (AMP is marked † = improvement over its base); AMPGCN 0.7207±0.0028 vs NBAGCN 0.7207. Empirically the Dirichlet energy no longer decays exponentially (oversmoothing mitigated) and a proved sensitivity bound limits oversquashing; AMP learns deeper (~10–20+ layer) architectures on long-range tasks.
> 
> ## 3. SSL: avoid noisy pixels by predicting in latent space → **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> This is exactly your requirement: it analyzes why JEPA-style self-distillation (predicting in latent space) suppresses noisy/uninformative features that MAE-style pixel reconstruction would learn. Result: JEPA's implicit bias favors "influential" features (high regression coefficient) and converges to lower weights on noisy features, while MAE only prioritizes high-variance features regardless of noise. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace than MAE (CCA), confirming latent-space prediction avoids noisy pixels.
> 
> ## 4. Fine-tuning with Adam/SGD under tight GPU memory via 4-bit states → **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Compresses Adam/AdamW (and the framework covers SGDM/Adam too) optimizer states to 4-bit using smaller block size (B128), zero-point-excluded linear mapping, and rank-1 normalization/factorization. Results vs 32-bit AdamW: NLU (RoBERTa-L/GLUE) 89.1 vs 88.9; CLS (Swin-T/ImageNet) 80.8 vs 81.2; NLG (GPT-2, BLEU) 67.8 vs 67.7; QA (RoBERTa-L, F1) 94.5 vs 94.6; MT (Transformer-Base) 26.28 vs 26.61. Memory savings up to 57.7%; 4-bit AdamW lets LLaMA-7B fit on a single 80GB GPU, and is lossless across LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning.
> 
> ## Bonus: LDReg (ICLR 2024) — matches your CIFAR-100/COCO + ResNet-50/ViT tracking requirement
> If you also need an SSL regularizer validated on your exact backbones/benchmarks, LDReg improves SimCLR/BYOL/MAE representations (ResNet-50 and ViT-B) with linear evaluation gains (e.g., BYOL ImageNet 67.6→68.5, SimCLR-tuned 67.2→67.5, MAE 57.0→57.6), transfer gains on CIFAR-100 (e.g., 71.6→75.1), and COCO detection/segmentation AP gains (e.g., BYOL APbb 36.30→36.82, SimCLR 36.48→37.15 at 1000 epochs).
> 
> ## Summary comparison
> - **PBADet** is the only work covering hand/face-to-person association, and it reports the exact F1/Precision/AP/MR⁻² you need on COCO-derived data (COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman) plus BodyHands.
> - **AMP** is the sole graph method targeting oversmoothing/oversquashing/underreaching with consistent gains over strong baselines.
> - **The JEPA analysis** is theoretical/analytical (deep linear nets + ImageNet CCA) rather than a new SOTA model, so it explains *why* latent-space SSL avoids noisy pixels but doesn't itself give CIFAR-100/COCO detection numbers.
> - **4-bit Optimizers** directly delivers lossless Adam/SGD fine-tuning under tight GPU memory, with image-classification (Swin-T) and Transformer MT results.
> - **LDReg** is complementary: it gives the ResNet-50/ViT + CIFAR-100/COCO evaluation you mention, but addresses dimensional collapse, not latent-space prediction per se.
> 
> One caveat: no single paper in the collection jointly covers all four sub-problems end-to-end; you would combine PBADet (vision), AMP (graph), JEPA-style latent pretraining (with LDReg as a drop-in regularizer), and 4-bit optimizers (memory-efficient fine-tuning).

I’m especially interested in works that discuss regularization choices, approximations, and how these methods integrate with AdamW/SGD and end-to-end fine-tuning (including low-rank adapters).Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
