Gold 1：

> The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed cubic regularization-based hyper-parameter optimization method consistently outperforms other approaches across synthetic and real-world tasks.
> 
> **Synthetic Data (Fig. 1a & 1b):** The cubic regularization method achieves higher validation AUC than gradient descent, natural gradient, and Newton methods using stochastic relaxation. It also yields Hessian eigenvalue spectra with less significant negative eigenvalues, suggesting better avoidance of saddle points.
> 
> **Knowledge Graph Completion (Fig. 2a & 2b):** On FB15k237 and WN18RR datasets, the method attains higher maximum MRR more quickly than Random Search, Bayesian Optimization, Hyperband, and RL-based methods, indicating faster convergence and better final performance.
> 
> **Schedule Search with Noisy Labels (Fig. 3a & 3b):** On CIFAR-10 with 50% symmetric noise and 45% pair-flipping noise, it reaches higher validation accuracy faster than all baselines, showing both efficiency and quality of the schedules found.
> 
> **Ablation Study (Fig. 4):** Larger sample size K improves gradient/Hessian estimation and model performance, but overly large K reduces upper-level iterations when total budget is fixed. More training epochs in the lower-level problem improve performance by producing more accurate approximate solutions.
> 
> **Time Cost (Table 2):** Across all datasets, most computation time is spent on lower-level model training; the cubic regularization update of the hyper-parameter distribution parameters is negligible in comparison.
> 
> Overall, experiments show that the proposed method converges faster, escapes saddle points more effectively, and finds hyper-parameters yielding better-performing models than competing methods.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, here are the papers covering each area and a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Papers found (one per area)
> 
> **(a) Sub-byte optimizer states → "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> AdamW/SGDM states compressed to 4-bit (vs. prior 8-bit minimum). Uses smaller block-wise normalization (B128/DE) for the first moment, and for the second moment a zero-point-excluding linear quantizer (DE-0/Linear) plus rank-1 normalization, optionally factorized. Results: on fine-tuning (RoBERTa-L on GLUE/SQuAD, GPT-2 Medium on E2E-NLG, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B on Alpaca) 4-bit AdamW **matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW** (e.g., NLU 89.1 vs 88.9; QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6; E2E BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT BLEU 26.28 vs 26.61). Memory savings up to 57.7%; convergence curves closely align. Ablations show zero-point exclusion, not block size or stochastic rounding, is the key for second moment; quantization of both moments gives only marginal loss. Sublinear optimizers (Adafactor, SM3) degrade on CLS. Integrates with fine-tuning/LoRA (LoRA used for GPT-2; delta-tuning cited as an alternative).
> 
> **(b) Curvature-aware HPO without gradients → "Efficient Hyper-parameter Optimization with Cubic Regularization" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> Stochastic relaxation + **cubic regularization** (a curvature-aware, beyond-quadratic surrogate) over the relaxed distribution, needing only objective values (no hyper-gradients), so it handles discrete hyperparameters and non-differentiable metrics. Experiments: synthetic feature-mask (AUC), knowledge-graph completion with **MRR** (FB15k237, WN18RR), noisy-label schedule search on **CIFAR-10** (validation accuracy). It outperforms Random, BO, Hyperband, RL and first-order stochastic-relaxation (GD/NG/Newton) methods, converging faster (theory: ε-second-order stationary point in O(1/ε^1.5) iterations, O(1/ε^3.5) samples vs O(1/ε^4) for first-order) and escaping saddle points (negative Hessian eigenvalues suppressed). Ablations: larger sample K and more exact lower-level solves help. **Caveat**: the exact benchmarks you cite (maximizing F1/Precision on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100) are not tested; the paper uses MRR/AUC/accuracy instead, so that specific claim isn't established in these documents.
> 
> **(c) JEPA/teacher–student inductive bias → "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> Analyzes MSE latent-space self-distillation (BYOL/SimSiam/I-JEPA) vs pixel-space MAE. Derives exact ODE dynamics: JEPA prioritizes features with **high regression coefficient ρ** (influence), MAE prioritizes high-variance features λ; the ρ-bias strengthens with encoder depth (critical time depends on ρ·ε^(L−1) for JEPA, not MAE). Fixed points: JEPA w̄=ρ^L vs MAE w̄=ρ^(L/(L+1)). ImageNet-1K experiments (ViT, 64×64): I-JEPA features align faster (higher mean CCA) with the low-variance "bottom 25%" PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE, which aligns with the top-variance subspace — explaining why JEPA avoids pixel noise. Depth separation: 1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE. Limitations: deep linear MLPs, balanced/diagonalizable initializations.
> 
> **(d) E/I sign constraints → "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> Compares sign-constrained ColEI RNNs, DANN (Dale's ANN) RNNs, and standard RNNs on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition. Key finding: **the initial singular-value spectrum matters more than the sign constraints themselves**. Spectrum-transplant experiments (8 configurations) show spectra contribute ~1.5–2% error vs ~0.7–1% for sign constraints; sign constraints alone don't explain the full 2.3% ColEI deficit. ColEI weight matrices (column means) yield multimodal, dispersed spectra vs. the quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra of standard/DANN RNNs; small networks or few inhibitory units worsen both spectrum and learning; gradient clipping mitigates ColEI instability; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization predicts final error. DANN stays robust even with one inhibitory neuron.
> 
> **(e) Anchor-free part-body detector → "PBADet" (ICLR 2024)**
> One-stage anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center offset (vs. BPJDet's body-to-part offsets). BodyHands: hand AP 89.1 vs BPJDet 85.9, conditional accuracy 92.62 vs 86.91, joint AP 85.98 vs 84.39 (with a smaller model, 36.9M vs 41.2M). COCOHumanParts: AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 vs BPJDet 43.6/43.3 (on par, but leads on AP_M/AP_L, person and feet; lowest mMR-2 for head/face/hands/right foot). CrowdHuman: best body MR-2 (36.5) with competitive AP. vs ED-Pose (Swin-L) on COCO val: substantially higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet (all parts: P 39.4 vs 24.1, R 63.1 vs 45.5, F1 48.5 vs 31.5). Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning each improve accuracy. Trained with SGD (YOLOv7 recipe), 100 epochs, AMP; generalizes to quadruped part-body association.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting comparison relevant to your interests
> 
> - **Regularization choices**: (b) is explicitly a *curvature-aware (cubic)* regularizer beyond quadratic, the strongest theoretical convergence guarantee of the set; (d) treats sign constraints and (via NSE) spectral initialization as the effective regularizers; (c) is an implicit-bias (no explicit regularizer) analysis, though companion work (LDReg) shows explicit local-dimensionality regularization further improves SSL representations (ImageNet linear eval, transfer, COCO detection) for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE.
> - **Approximations**: (a) is purely about approximation of optimizer states (quantization + factorization), with ablation evidence that approximation error is lossless only when the zero-point is handled; (b) uses approximate (inexact lower-level) solutions and Monte-Carlo gradient/Hessian estimates; (c) and (d) are exact-dynamics/spectral analyses.
> - **Integration with AdamW/SGD and fine-tuning/LoRA**: (a) is built on AdamW and validated on LoRA-based GPT-2 and LLaMA instruction fine-tuning, preserving full-precision accuracy out-of-the-box (no re-tuning); (e) uses SGD end-to-end; (b) uses SGD for lower-level training. The related Hessian-spectrum study shows LoRA-only fine-tuning does *not* induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does, and that power-law slope predicts generalization (up to 0.98 correlation on LLMs) — a useful caveat that low-rank adapters change the loss landscape in ways relevant to (a), (b), and (d).
> 
> **Gaps not covered by the context**: no document tests F1/Precision HPO on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 specifically for (b), and (c) does not treat CE losses directly (MSE only). Those claims cannot be established from this collection.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers from the collection matching your topics, with their key experimental results and a comparison.
> 
> ## (a) Sub-byte optimizer state storage — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Compresses first/second moments of stateful optimizers (framework covers SGDM, Adam, AdamW; Appendix gives a convergence proof for quantized SGD(M)) from 32-bit to **4-bit**, going below the prior 8-bit minimum (Dettmers et al.).
> - **Approximations/regularization choices:** smaller block size (B128) for the first moment; **zero-point-excluded linear mapping (DE-0/Linear)** and **rank-1 normalization** for the second moment (fixing the "zero-point problem"); optional **factorization** of the second moment ("4-bit Factor"); decoupled weight decay (AdamW) is preserved.
> - **Results:** matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW on all fine-tuning tasks — GLUE RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9; GPT-2 E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6 — and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61). LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning matches 32-bit AdamW; up to **57.7% memory savings** (LLaMA-7B in 31.87GB vs 75.40GB), LLaMA-7B trainable on one 80GB GPU, 4× larger OPT models under a memory budget. Ablations: excluding zero from the second-moment mapping is the key factor (training instability drops from 33–66% to 0%); factorizing the second moment improves both accuracy and memory. **LoRA** is discussed as a complementary memory technique (only tuning low-rank parameters), which the 4-bit optimizer can be combined with.
> 
> ## (b) Curvature-aware (beyond-quadratic) HPO without gradients — "Hyper-Parameter Optimization via Stochastic Relaxation and Cubic Regularization" (NeurIPS 2023)
> - For **non-differentiable metrics and discrete hyper-parameters** where hyper-gradients are unavailable, uses stochastic relaxation + **cubic regularization** (the ρ/6·‖δ‖³ term — curvature beyond quadratic) to escape saddle points, with gradients/Hessians estimated from K sampled hyper-parameters and **inexact lower-level solves**.
> - **Results:** on knowledge-graph completion (FB15k237, WN18RR; discrete hyper-parameters, MRR metric) it converges faster than random search, BO, Hyperband, and RL and is closer to the global optimum; on noisy-label **schedule search (CIFAR-10)** it outperforms stochastic-relaxation baselines and standard HPO; ablation: larger K and accurate lower-level solutions help, runtime dominated by lower-level training. Theory: O(1/ε^1.5) iterations and O(1/ε^3.5) samples vs O(1/ε^4) for gradient-based stochastic relaxation.
> - **Note:** retrieved content shows MRR/accuracy (KG, CIFAR-10 noisy labels) rather than the exact F1/Precision on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 you mentioned; the mechanism (non-differentiable/discrete objectives) is the same, but those exact datasets/metrics are not in the context.
> 
> ## (c) Inductive bias of non-contrastive JSSL — "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis" (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Analyzes JEPA (teacher–student with stop-gradient, latent-space MSE) vs MAE (pixel MSE) in deep linear networks; JEPA prioritizes **"influential" features (large regression coefficient ρ)** and suppresses noisy/high-variance features, an implicit bias that emerges only when the encoder is **deep** (depth strengthens noise suppression). The stop-gradient (SG) is the architectural regularization preventing collapse; JEPA learns "slow," low-variance features.
> - **Results:** ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA), matching the theory; toy-model dynamics show JEPA reverses learning order when ρ decreases while λ increases, whereas MAE does not.
> - Related (adjacent) works: LDReg (local dimensionality regularization to counter dimensional collapse) and the contrastive-embedding similarities paper (variance-reduction loss) — but the JEPA paper is the direct match for (c).
> 
> ## (d) E/I sign constraints, spectrum, learning dynamics — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Shows that **sign constraints themselves are not the main cause** of poor learning in Dale's-law (excitatory/inhibitory) RNNs; the **initial recurrent weight spectrum** is. Column-constrained E/I networks (ColEI) have a multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), whereas standard RNNs and Dale's ANNs (DANN) match random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur forms.
> - **Results (sequential MNIST):** removing sign constraints improves both networks only modestly (RNNs 0.7%±0.3%, ColEI 1%±1%), not enough to close the full gap (2.3%±0.6%); spectrum-transplant experiments show singular-value spectra matter more than sign constraints or singular vectors. Fewer inhibitory units and smaller networks worsen both spectrum and performance; **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** at initialization anti-correlates with final test error across EI ratios/sizes (also on natural object recognition and Penn Tree Bank). **Gradient clipping** mitigates ColEI instability; DANN RNNs are robust to EI ratio (learn well even with 1 inhibitory neuron).
> - **Regularization/integration notes:** sign maintenance uses projected gradient descent (clipping weights that change sign to 0); training uses standard optimization (no AdamW/LoRA specifics in the retrieved content).
> 
> ## (e) Anchor-free one-stage part-to-body association — "PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection" (ICLR 2024)
> - One-stage anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones) using a **single part-to-body center offset** (vs BPJDet's body-to-part offsets); decodes via NMS + Euclidean distance to enclosing unassigned bodies.
> - **Results (BodyHands):** Ours (YOLOv7, 36.9M) — HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98, beating BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 86.1M) at 85.9/86.91/84.39 and all prior methods (BodyHands 2022: 84.8/83.44/63.48). **COCOHumanParts:** 43.0/41.8 AP (original/subordinate), on par with BPJDet and leading on person/feet AP; lowest mMR−2 on most categories. **CrowdHuman face-body:** body MR-2 36.5 vs BPJDet 40.7 with competitive AP. Against ED-Pose it reports **substantially higher precision, recall, and F1** for hands/feet. Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and **task-alignment learning** each improve association accuracy; anchor-free part-to-body (89.1) beats anchor-based part-to-body (88.4) and anchor-based body-to-part BPJDet (85.3).
> - **Integration:** uses **SGD** (consistent with YOLOv7), AMP, 100 epochs, fine-tunes pretrained YOLO weights; loss weights λ_iou=7.5, λ_dfl=1.5, λ_cls=0.5, λ_assoc=0.2, NMS thresholds tuned per dataset.
> 
> ## Cross-paper comparison and analysis
> - **Approximation/regularization theme:** (a) uses quantization/factorization approximations that preserve AdamW's decoupled weight decay and full-precision accuracy; (b) adds cubic (third-order) curvature beyond quadratic to escape saddle points in discrete/non-differentiable search; (c) relies on stop-gradient/depth as the implicit regularizer for latent-space MSE; (d) shows sign-constraint regularization is secondary to spectral initialization (NSE as pre-training diagnostic); (e) uses task-alignment + association loss weighting on top of a standard anchor-free detector.
> - **Optimizer integration:** (a) is explicitly compatible with AdamW/SGD(M) (the only paper directly about AdamW/SGD), including end-to-end fine-tuning of LLMs and discussion of LoRA as a complementary memory saver; (e) trains with SGD end-to-end (fine-tuning pretrained YOLO); (b) is optimizer-agnostic (searches hyper-parameters like learning rate/schedule for any lower-level trainer, e.g., CIFAR-10 noisy-label training); (c) and (d) are about dynamics/spectra rather than optimizer memory (d) uses projected-gradient sign enforcement with gradient clipping for stability).
> - **Gaps vs your request:** no retrieved paper tests (b)'s method on F1/Precision with MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 specifically (it uses MRR and validation accuracy on KG/CIFAR-10); (a)'s SGD results are mostly covered by the framework/convergence proof rather than headline SGD experiments (the headline results are AdamW-based); (c) is a deep-linear theoretical analysis (its ImageNet validation uses CCA alignment, not downstream accuracy), and the CE-variant is not covered (JEPA uses latent MSE); (d) doesn't discuss AdamW/LoRA; (e) reports AP/MR−2/JointAP/Precision-Recall-F1 (F1 reported vs ED-Pose) rather than Precision/F1 as primary metrics.

### paperscope:results_comparison:197 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a real-time vision system for a hospital robot that must tell a technician’s hand from a patient’s and link each hand to the correct person in crowded scenes. The device runs on a tight GPU budget, so I need memory-lean optimizers (sub‑8‑bit states) that still work with AdamW/SGD during end-to-end fine-tuning (sometimes with low‑rank adapters). Our evaluation metric is F1/Precision on non-differentiable validation criteria, so I also need a hyper-parameter search method that doesn’t rely on hyper‑gradients and can leverage curvature (beyond simple quadratic penalties). We pretrain with a joint-embedding self-teaching setup and want to understand why this avoids focusing on noisy pixels and yields robust feature embeddings. Finally, our control stack uses recurrent modules with excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints inspired by biology, so I need guidance on spectral conditions for stable training. Are there works that address these needs together and report results on standard image datasets before deployment?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

> - **Methods compared**: Cubic (proposed), Gradient Descent (GD), Natural Gradient (NG), Newton's Method.
> - **Performance (Validation AUC)**: Cubic clearly achieves higher AUC than GD, NG, and Newton throughout training.
> - **Saddle Point Escape Capability**: Eigenvalue spectrum analysis shows Cubic yields fewer significant negative eigenvalues compared to positive ones, indicating better escape from saddle points; other methods retain strong negative eigenvalues.
> 
> **2. Knowledge Graph Completion (FB15k237, WN18RR) – Hyperparameter Optimization (Fig. 2)**
> - **Methods compared**: Cubic (proposed), Random Search, Bayesian Optimization (BO), Hyperband, RL.
> - **Metric**: Validation MRR.
> - **Results**:
>   - FB15k237: Cubic converges faster and reaches near-optimal MRR value earlier than baselines.
>   - WN18RR: Cubic outperforms baselines, achieving higher MRR and converging rapidly. This aligns with the theoretical advantage of avoiding poor saddle points.
> 
> **3. Noisy Label Learning – Schedule Search (CIFAR-10, Fig. 3)**
> - **Noise settings**: 50% symmetric noise, 45% pair-flip noise.
> - **Methods compared**: Cubic (proposed), Random, BO, Hyperband, RL.
> - **Metric**: Validation Accuracy.
> - **Results**:
>   - In both noise scenarios, Cubic converges faster to higher accuracy than baselines.
>   - Superior final accuracy reflects better schedule discovery via the curvature exploitation of cubic regularization.
> 
> **4. Ablation Studies (Synthetic Data, Fig. 4)**
> - **Factor K (samples per iteration)**:
>   - Larger K improves performance when update steps are fixed; excessive K under fixed overall runtime can lower performance due to fewer parameter updates.
> - **Factor Epochs (lower-level training)**:
>   - More epochs improve upper-level optimization by yielding more precise lower-level solutions.
> 
> **5. Time Cost (Table 2)**
> - Across all experiments, the time spent updating upper-level parameter θ is negligible compared to lower-level model training.
> 
> **Overall Comparison & Trends**:
> - Cubic Regularization (proposed) consistently outperforms GD, NG, Newton, and derivative-free baselines (Random, BO, Hyperband, RL) in synthetic and real-world hyperparameter optimization tasks.
> - Stronger curvature exploitation leads to faster convergence and better optima.
> - Demonstrated robustness to saddle points.
> - In ablations, performance scales with quality of gradient/Hessian estimation (K) and accuracy of lower-level solutions (epochs).

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Answer
> 
> No single work addresses all four needs together. Each component is covered by a separate paper, and none reports a combined hospital-robot vision pipeline. Here is the comparison of their experimental results on standard image datasets:
> 
> ### 1. Memory-lean optimizers (sub-8-bit states) — *4-bit Optimizers* (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Method: quantizes Adam/AdamW/SGDM first/second moments to 4-bit (smaller block size B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, optional factorized second moment). It is drop-in for AdamW/SGD fine-tuning; LoRA is only discussed as a related (language-only) approach, not combined.
> - Image result: Swin-T on ImageNet-1k — 32-bit AdamW 81.2 vs 4-bit AdamW 80.8 vs 4-bit Factor 80.9 (vs 8-bit AdamW 81.0). It matches/exceeds 32-bit on fine-tuning (NLU 89.1 vs 88.9; QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6; NLG 67.8 vs 67.7) and is comparable on pretraining; sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor β1=0, SM3) degrade, especially on ImageNet.
> - Memory: 57.7% saved (LLaMA-7B, 75.4→31.9 GB); 43.1% (RoBERTa-L); 4-bit Factor is ~4× smaller states than 8-bit.
> - Caveat: optimal quantization may be task-dependent; only Swin-T on ImageNet among image tasks.
> 
> ### 2. Hyper-parameter search without hyper-gradients, with curvature — *Stochastic Relaxation + Cubic Regularization* (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Method: no hyper-gradients; works on non-differentiable metrics (F1/MRR-type) and discrete hyper-parameters; uses stochastic relaxation to obtain gradient **and Hessian**, then cubic regularization (goes beyond quadratic penalties, escapes saddle points).
> - Theory: converges to an ε-second-order stationary point in O(1/ε^1.5) iterations / O(1/ε^3.5) samples — strictly faster than gradient-based stochastic-relaxation baselines (O(1/ε^4)).
> - Image result: schedule search on noisy-label CIFAR-10 (plus knowledge-graph MRR on FB15k237/WN18RR); beats Random, Bayesian optimization, Hyperband, RL, converging closer to the global optimum.
> - Caveat: not evaluated on large-scale vision datasets; Hessian computation limits it to low-dimensional hyper-parameter spaces.
> 
> ### 3. Joint-embedding self-teaching (JEPA) robustness — *Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features* (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Method/analysis: deep-linear analysis of self-distillation shows JEPA is implicitly biased toward **high-influence (high regression coefficient ρ) features**, while MAE prioritizes by eigenvalue λ; depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression. This explains why JEPA avoids noisy/unpredictable pixels and yields robust embeddings.
> - Image result: ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA measurement), i.e., semantic/low-noise features.
> - Caveat: rigorous results are for deep linear networks and special initialization; extension to nonlinear models is qualitative.
> 
> ### 4. Excitatory/inhibitory RNN spectral conditions — *Dale's Law RNNs: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Result: sign constraints (Dale's law) impair learning only slightly (RNN +0.7%, ColEI +1%), but account for only part of the gap; **the singular-value spectrum at initialization matters more** (transplant experiments: spectrum contributes ~1.5–2% vs ~0.7–1% for sign constraints).
> - Spectral guidance: column-constrained EI networks (ColEI) have multimodal/dispersed singular values (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure); standard RNNs and Dale's-ANN RNNs match the quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur unimodal form. Balanced E/I ratios, larger networks, and higher normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predict better training; without gradient clipping, ColEI is highly unstable.
> - Image result: sequential MNIST, plus adding problem, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object-recognition task.
> 
> ### Comparison / analysis
> - **Optimizer vs HPO**: the 4-bit optimizer gives near-lossless accuracy with 43–58% memory savings but tests only Swin-T on ImageNet and doesn't natively target LoRA; the cubic-regularization HPO is the only method designed for exactly your non-differentiable F1/Precision criterion and curvature use, but its image evidence is limited to CIFAR-10 noisy-label scheduling.
> - **JEPA vs HPO complementarity**: the JEPA analysis (robust embeddings) is theoretical with ImageNet-1K validation, while the HPO method is practical but on smaller datasets — no paper combines them.
> - **RNN spectral results**: give actionable initialization/architecture rules (unimodal clustered spectrum, balanced E/I, gradient clipping, NSE as a pre-training diagnostic) but are not coupled to the optimizer or HPO work.
> 
> **Bottom line:** you would need to assemble these four components yourself; the works are complementary, each validated on standard image benchmarks (ImageNet-1k, CIFAR-10, sequential MNIST), and no existing study reports the full stack together or results on a hand/patient crowded-scene deployment dataset.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Direct answer
> 
> No single paper in this collection addresses all four needs together in one system. They are covered piecewise by separate papers, and each is validated on standard image benchmarks. Here is the per-need comparison of experimental results.
> 
> **1. Memory-lean optimizers (sub-8-bit states, AdamW/SGD-compatible)**
> "4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023) compresses first/second moments to 4-bit via B128 block-wise + rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, optionally factorizing the second moment (4-bit Factor). It is optimizer-agnostic (AdamW, Adam, SGDM). Results: Swin-T on ImageNet-1k CLS = 80.8 (4-bit AdamW) and 80.9 (4-bit Factor) vs 81.2 (32-bit AdamW); QA F1 (RoBERTa-L/SQuAD) = 94.5 vs 94.6; LLaMA-7B fine-tuning memory 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB (57.7% saved); states 2× smaller than 8-bit AdamW and ~4× smaller than 32-bit; convergence curves align with full precision. LoRA is cited as a compatible PEFT method, but its LoRA experiments are language-only. The BSO paper offers an even leaner alternative (memory O(n²L/32), ~20–31× model shrink) for binary spiking online training: T-BSO reaches CIFAR-10 94.86%, CIFAR-100 74.27%, ImageNet 57.76%, DVS-CIFAR10 81.00%, GSC 96.12%.
> 
> **2. Hyper-parameter search without hyper-gradients, using curvature**
> "HPO via Stochastic Relaxation and Cubic Regularization" (NeurIPS 2023) needs only objective values (so F1/Precision are fine) and exploits Hessian curvature via cubic regularization (stronger than quadratic penalties; escapes saddle points). Convergence to ε-second-order stationary point in O(1/ε^1.5) iterations. Results: on FB15k237/WN18RR it beats Random search, Bayesian optimization, Hyperband, and RL in MRR per trained model; on CIFAR-10 noisy-label schedule search (50% symmetric / 45% pair-flip noise) it reaches higher validation accuracy faster. Ablations: larger K (gradient/Hessian samples) helps; update cost is negligible vs lower-level training.
> 
> **3. Why joint-embedding self-teaching (JEPA) avoids noisy pixels**
> "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024) proves an implicit bias: JEPA self-distillation prioritizes high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ), while MAE prioritizes high-variance features (λ) even if noisy/uninformative; depth strengthens noise suppression. ImageNet-1K experiments: I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features than MAE features. Caveat: the analysis is deep-linear/ODE theory with special initialization, generalized qualitatively.
> 
> **4. Spectral conditions for E/I-constrained recurrent training**
> "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023) shows the singular-value spectrum at initialization matters more than sign constraints: naive ColEI (column-constrained) RNNs have multimodal, dispersed singular values (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), whereas DANN-style reparameterization matches standard RNN quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur spectra and learns as well. Results: ColEI worse across adding, sequential MNIST, Penn TreeBank, naturalistic object recognition, with high seed variance; spectrum-transplant experiments attribute ~1.5% vs 0.7–1% error differences to spectra vs sign constraints; gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance pre-training; fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks worsen spectra and performance. Guidance: design E/I networks with standard-RNN-like spectra (DANN-style) or better initialization.
> 
> **5. The deployment-relevant piece (hand↔person linking, crowded scenes)**
> PBADet (ICLR 2024) directly matches your task: one-stage anchor-free part-to-body association (each hand linked to its person) on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts, trained end-to-end with SGD (no adapters). Results on BodyHands: hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet 86.91/86.80/84.39 and Mask R-CNN+IoU 74.52/51.74. On COCOHumanParts: all-category AP 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate) vs BPJDet 43.6/43.3, with better subordinate (association) APs; vs the pose estimator ED-Pose, hand precision/recall/F1 ≈ 37.6/60.8/46.5 and 38.6/61.3/47.3 vs 18.4/30.3/22.9 and 19.6/31.6/24.2. On CrowdHuman it achieves the best body MR−2. NFTS (ICLR 2024) is the complementary piece for low-rank-adapter fine-tuning search (evolutionary, no hyper-gradients) on image datasets: 79.2 avg on Meta-Dataset single-domain (vs ~77 for TSA/ETT) and >5% margin at 5-way/5-shot on Meta-Album.
> 
> **Bottom line:** no work in the collection integrates 1–4 into the hospital-robot system; the closest end-to-end deployment evidence is PBADet (hand-person association, F1/precision vs pose estimators) plus the 4-bit optimizer for GPU budget, cubic-regularization HPO for non-differentiable F1, the JEPA analysis for robust pretraining, and the Dale's-Law spectral analysis for the recurrent control stack — each validated separately on standard image datasets (ImageNet-1K, CIFAR-10, BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, Meta-Dataset/Meta-Album, sequential MNIST).

Prefer works that touch standard datasets (MNIST/CIFAR-100/COCO), use Transformers/RNNs, and discuss common losses (cross-entropy, MSE) and feature embeddings.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross-paper experimental comparison and summary along five requested themes
> 
> Scope and dataset overlap
> - There are no identical benchmark datasets shared across all five works. Each paper evaluates its own method on task-appropriate datasets: (1) PBADet on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts (built on COCO), and CrowdHuman; (2) 4-bit Optimizers on GLUE (NLU), ImageNet-1k (CLS), E2E-NLG (NLG), SQuAD (QA), WMT14 En–De (MT), and LLaMA instruction tuning; (3) JEPA vs. MAE largely in controlled deep-linear settings, plus an ImageNet (64×64) feature-similarity study; (4) TuCo on HH-RLHF vs. OpenWebText, plus GCG/Conjugate Prompting/Many-Shot jailbreaks; (5) Dale-like EI-RNNs on adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank (PTB), and a naturalistic object recognition task. Where identical datasets exist within a paper, we compare variants; across papers we compare task types and trends.
> 
> (1) Anchor-free, one-stage human part–to–body association (PBADet)
> Shared datasets and metrics vs. prior methods:
> - BodyHands (Table 1). PBADet improves both detection and association over BPJDet and other baselines:
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7, 1024): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6, 1024): Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 1536): Hand AP 85.9, Cond. Acc. 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.
>   PBADet thus outperforms anchor-based BPJDet on all BodyHands metrics despite using lower input resolution (1024 vs 1536) and matches or exceeds other two-stage or anchor-based detectors listed in Table 1.
> 
> - COCO-HumanParts (Tables 2–3). Detection APs (original/subordinate):
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6/43.3.
>   • PBADet is slightly lower on overall AP but leads in certain sub-categories: person AP (62.4 vs 61.3) and feet APs (r-foot 30.9 vs 30.2; l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9). It is lower on head/face/hands APs.
>   Association robustness (mMR−2, lower is better; Table 3): PBADet improves average mMR−2 for head (27.9 vs 30.8), face (30.5 vs 31.8), left hand (36.2 vs 41.6), right hand (40.8 vs 42.2), and left foot (47.9 vs 50.4), but is slightly worse on right foot (50.4 vs 49.1).
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6). For the face–body association task, PBADet achieves the best detection errors while pairing accuracy is comparable to BPJDet:
>   • Body MR−2: PBADet (YOLOv7) 36.5 (best) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 40.7.
>   • Face MR−2: PBADet (YOLOv7) 44.7 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 46.3.
>   • Body AP: PBADet (YOLOv7) 91.6 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 81.6–90.7.
>   • Pair mMR−2: PBADet (YOLOv7) 50.8 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 50.1—nearly tied.
> 
> Takeaway for (1): On identical BodyHands and CrowdHuman tasks PBADet consistently improves detection and association (especially conditional/joint metrics) over prior one-stage/two-stage baselines; on COCO-HumanParts it trades slight overall AP for better association reliability (lower mMR−2) on most parts and higher AP for person/feet.
> 
> (2) Memory-lean training via 4-bit optimizer states (Adam/AdamW/SGD behavior preserved)
> Across identical downstreams (Table 2): 4-bit AdamW vs 32-bit AdamW, 8-bit AdamW, Adafactor, SM3
> - NLU (RoBERTa-L, mean): 32-bit 88.9; 8-bit 89.1; 4-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit Factor 88.9. 4-bit matches 8-bit and full precision.
> - CLS (Swin-T/ImageNet-1k top-1): 32-bit 81.2; 4-bit AdamW 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9; 8-bit 81.0. Minor (≤0.4 pt) drop vs 32-bit, on par with 8-bit.
> - NLG (GPT-2 M, E2E BLEU): 32-bit 67.7; 8-bit 67.5; 4-bit AdamW 67.8; 4-bit Factor 67.6 (no loss; slight gain).
> - QA (RoBERTa-L, SQuAD F1): 32-bit 94.6; 8-bit 94.5; 4-bit AdamW 94.5; 4-bit Factor 94.6 (parity).
> - MT (Transformer-Base WMT14 En–De SacreBLEU): 32-bit 26.61; 8-bit 26.66; 4-bit AdamW 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45 (tiny drop ≤0.33).
> 
> Instruction tuning (Table 3, LLaMA): 4-bit AdamW preserves instruction-following gains vs pretrained across sizes.
> - Example (LLaMA-13B, MMLU 5-shot): Original 47.4 → 32-bit FT 46.5 → 4-bit FT 47.4 (4-bit equals original and tops 32-bit FT); similar pattern on HellaSwag and ARC.
> 
> Memory/time (Table 4):
> - LLaMA-7B (FSDP, 2×A100 80GB): total memory 75.40 GB → 31.87 GB (−57.7%); time 3.35 h → 3.07 h (speedup).
> - RoBERTa-L (RTE): 5.31 GB → 3.00 GB (−43.5%), with fused kernels 3.17 min vs 3.93 min (speedup).
> - GPT-2 M (E2E): 6.89 GB → 4.44–4.62 GB (−34–36%), fused time 2.11 h vs 2.13 h.
> 
> Ablations on second moment quantization stability (Table 1):
> - Using DE (dynamic exponent) with zero point causes instability (up to 66% runs unstable); removing zero (DE-0) or using linear mapping with Rank-1 normalization yields 0% instability and best BLEU (Rank-1/Linear: 67.8±0.51, matching 32-bit 67.7±0.67) without special embeddings. Factorizing v (second moment) is also stable and matches BLEU (67.6±0.33).
> 
> Takeaway for (2): On identical tasks (GLUE, ImageNet, SQuAD, E2E, WMT14), 4-bit AdamW achieves parity with 8-bit and 32-bit in accuracy while cutting total training memory up to 58% and maintaining or improving throughput; stability hinges on excluding zero for v and using Rank-1/Linear or factorization.
> 
> (3) Self-supervised JEPA vs. MAE: predictive, high-influence features over pixel MSE (deep linear + cosine space)
> Controlled deep-linear dynamics (Figures 1–2, 4):
> - Feature-learning order differs: MAE greedily prioritizes high covariance (λ) features; JEPA (for deep encoders, L>1) prioritizes high regression-coefficient (ρ) features—even reversing learning order when λ and ρ oppose (Fig. 1d–f, Fig. 2c,f). Spectrum/ODE analysis shows JEPA’s critical time depends more strongly on ρ than MAE.
> - Depth effect (Fig. 4): Increasing encoder depth amplifies JEPA’s greedy tendency w.r.t. ρ (no such amplification for MAE).
> 
> Temporal model and simultaneous diagonalization (Fig. 3):
> - With per-mode autocorrelation γ and noise σ, λa=γa∥va∥2, ρa=γa∥va∥2/(σa^2+∥va∥2); JEPA learns less noisy (higher ρ) modes earlier and with smaller final amplitude for noisy features—consistent with favoring predictive, high-influence features.
> 
> ImageNet (64×64) feature similarity (Appendix D, Fig. 7):
> - Mean CCA shows I-JEPA representations on “full” vs “bottom-variance” (perceptual) subspace are more similar than MAE (higher CCA); conversely, on “full” vs “top-variance” subspace, JEPA is lower than MAE. This supports JEPA emphasizing predictive/semantic (low-variance) subspace over high-variance pixel detail.
> 
> Takeaway for (3): Experiments confirm the theoretical bias—JEPA learns and retains high-influence (predictive, low-noise/low-variance) features earlier and more strongly than MAE, especially with depth; in representation space (CCA), JEPA aligns more with bottom-variance (semantic) directions than MAE.
> 
> (4) Per-prompt interpretability for alignment: TuCo (fine-tuning contribution) and jailbreaks (AUROC/F1/Precision)
> Discriminating prompt types (Table 1): TuCo (FTC/PTC magnitude ratio over layers) is lower for pretraining-like inputs, higher for chat-like/aligned inputs.
> - HH-RLHF vs OpenWebText (y=1 for HH-RLHF): AUC = 1.0 (Llama 2 7B, 13B), 0.98–0.99 (Vicuna 7B/13B), 0.93 (Gemma 7B), 0.98 (Mistral v0.1), 0.89 (Mistral v0.2), 0.63 (Zephyr Gemma).
> 
> Jailbreaks reduce TuCo (Table 1, Fig. 4):
> - GCG adversarial prefixes (attacked vs vanilla harmful prompts): AUC ≥ 0.78 for 4/5 models, up to 1.0 (Vicuna 7B/13B; Llama 2 7B), showing TuCo reliably drops under attack.
> - Conjugate Prompting (AdvBench in low-resource languages): On Llama 2 13B, languages sort by web prevalence and TuCo: English (highest) > Japanese > Hungarian > Swahili/Malayalam (lowest), with AUC 1.0/1.0/0.98 for several models.
> - Many-Shot Jailbreaking: TuCo decreases monotonically with number of harmful shots (Llama 2 7B/13B, Gemma 7B), paralleling rising harmful response rates (Fig. 4 bottom; Fig. F.3).
> 
> Predicting attack success (Table 2):
> - For prompts labeled by success (≥2/8 non-refusal completions), TuCo is consistently lower on successful jailbreaks. Example AUCs: 0.87 (Llama 2 13B), 0.83 (Llama 2 7B), 0.94 (Gemma 7B), 0.87 (Vicuna 7B). (Llama 3 8B AUC ~0.51; attacks rarely succeed.)
> 
> Takeaway for (4): TuCo quantifies how much SFT contributes per prompt; it (i) separates pretraining-like vs chat-like inputs, (ii) reliably drops under multiple jailbreak families (GCG/CP/MSJ), and (iii) is lower for successful than unsuccessful attacks (AUC up to 0.94). This provides a per-prompt, inference-time interpretability signal tied to alignment robustness.
> 
> (5) Dale-like EI RNNs: constraints, spectra, and singular-value entropy vs performance
> Across identical tasks (Fig. 2): ColEI (column-wise E/I) vs standard RNNs vs DANNs (EI architecture that learns well):
> - Adding problem, sequential MNIST, PTB language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task: ColEI learns worse than both DANN and standard RNNs on final performance curves across all four tasks (Fig. 2A–D); ColEI is also more unstable without gradient clipping.
> 
> Spectral analysis and spectrum transplant (Fig. 3–4):
> - ColEI recurrent matrices have dispersed, multimodal singular spectra with large modes; standard/DANN exhibit unimodal quarter-circle-like spectra. Transplant experiments show spectra matter more than sign constraints: swapping spectra changes final errors more than freezing/unfreezing signs (e.g., RNN gains/losses ~1.5%±0.3%, ColEI ~2%±1% in Fig. 4C), indicating spectral properties dominate learning outcomes.
> 
> E/I ratio and size effects (Figs. 5–7):
> - Reducing inhibitory fraction reduces Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) and degrades performance; NSE anti-correlates with test error across EI ratios and sizes. Small, imbalanced ColEI nets have low NSE and high error; larger nets and more balanced E/I increase NSE and reduce error, despite occasional large max singular values—highlighting the full-spectrum effect captured by NSE.
> 
> Takeaway for (5): Experiments isolate spectral pathology (dispersed, multimodal singular spectra) as the main cause of poor learning in naive Dale-constrained RNNs; the proposed NSE (singular-value entropy) predicts performance across EI ratio/size better than just max singular value or sign constraints, and DANNs match standard RNNs by maintaining unimodal spectra.
> 
> Cross-theme synthesis (similar task types and trends)
> - Classification-type vision tasks: both PBADet and 4-bit optimizer studies quantify improvements without sacrificing accuracy—PBADet boosts part–body association on COCO-family datasets; 4-bit training maintains ImageNet top-1 with minimal drop while halving optimizer memory.
> - Sequence modeling: Dale’s EI-RNNs vs standard/DANN on sequential MNIST and PTB show that spectral properties (quantified by NSE) tightly track performance; in contrast, TuCo focuses on per-prompt contribution of SFT in LLMs, producing AUC-based alignment diagnostics.
> - Self-supervision vs reconstruction: JEPA–MAE results (linear + ImageNet CCA) empirically support JEPA’s preferential learning of predictive (high-ρ, low-variance) features; this aligns with TuCo’s finding that “pretraining-like” inputs (OpenWebText) have lower SFT contribution.
> 
> What to use when (evidence-backed):
> - For multi-part association on COCO-family datasets, PBADet is preferred to BPJDet: BodyHands Hand AP 89.1/Joint AP 85.98 and lower mMR−2 on multiple parts; on COCO-HumanParts it trades small overall AP for improved association reliability and person/feet APs.
> - For memory-lean training, 4-bit AdamW with Rank-1/Linear (v) or factorized v achieves parity on GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/WMT14 and ~58% memory reduction—prefer these quantizers over DE with zero point (unstable).
> - For self-supervised pretraining favoring predictive semantics, JEPA over MAE: it learns high-ρ features earlier (deep encoders) and aligns better with low-variance perceptual subspace (CCA trends).
> - For alignment diagnostics per prompt, TuCo provides strong AUCs for distinguishing aligned vs pretraining-like prompts and detects jailbreak attenuation of SFT; it also correlates with jailbreak success odds.
> - For Dale-like recurrent models, prefer architectures (e.g., DANNs) or initializations that maintain unimodal singular spectra; use NSE to predict performance when varying EI ratio/size.
> 
> Notes on identical datasets across papers
> - No benchmark is shared across all five works. Identical datasets are used within papers to compare their methods to baselines (e.g., PBADet vs BPJDet on BodyHands/COCO-HumanParts/CrowdHuman; 4-bit vs 32-bit/8-bit on GLUE/ImageNet/SQuAD/E2E/WMT14; Dale variants on adding/sequential MNIST/PTB). Where present, we highlighted those head-to-head results explicitly above.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here is a compact set of five papers covering the requested areas, followed by a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The set
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage, anchor-free part-body association via a single part-to-body center offset. Evaluated on **COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman** (COCO-style detection benchmarks) against BPJDet, HierR-CNN, ED-Pose.
> 2. **4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)** — quantizes Adam/AdamW (and SGDM) first/second moments to **4-bit** with B128 block, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear mapping, optional factorized second moment.
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** — joint-embedding predictive objective vs. MAE pixel reconstruction, analyzed in **deep linear networks** and via **cosine-similarity/CCA** space; supplementary cosine-space analysis: **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100).
> 4. **TuCo (ICML 2025)** — per-prompt **fine-tuning contribution** at inference via exact PTC/FTC decomposition of Transformers; linked to **jailbreak success** (AUC reporting).
> 5. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** — RNNs with excitatory/inhibitory (ColEI/DANN) partitions, analyzed via **singular-value spectra and normalized SVD entropy (NSE)** on sequential MNIST, adding problem, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition.
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> | Paper | Key result | Standard benchmarks | Losses |
> |---|---|---|---|
> | PBADet | COCOHumanParts all-category AP 43.0/41.8 (AP.5 70.0/68.4, AP.75 66.2/65.0) with YOLOv5l6, beating BPJDet (43.6/43.3 at same backbone) on subordinate APs and HierR-CNN; CrowdHuman face-body MR-2 36.5 (YOLOv7) vs 39.7–41.3 for BPJDet; BodyHands JointAP 85.98; higher precision/recall/F1 than ED-Pose | COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands, AnimalPose/AP-10K | classification + box localization + association loss (task-aligned) |
> | 4-bit optimizers | Matches 32-bit: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2M 67.8 vs 67.7; LLaMA-7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; **memory −57.7%** (LLaMA-7B, 31.9GB vs 75.4GB); 4-bit Factor slightly better memory, comparable accuracy | ImageNet-1k (Swin-T), GLUE, SQuAD, E2E, WMT14, Alpaca/MMLU | CE (classification/LM) — preserves Adam/AdamW/SGD behavior |
> | JEPA deep-linear | JEPA bias to **high-influence (high-ρ) features** with critical-time ordering; depth strengthens noise suppression; ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA aligns faster to low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA) | ImageNet-1K (theory: deep linear nets) | MSE in latent (predictive) vs pixel (MAE) |
> | Similarities of embeddings | Mini-batch negative-pair variance degrades representations; auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, full ImageNet; better temperature robustness | CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, ImageNet | InfoNCE/DCL/DHEL (cosine similarities) |
> | TuCo | Jailbreaks (GCG, conjugate, many-shot) **lower TuCo**; successful attacks lower than failed; attack success predicted with **AUC 0.87** (Llama 13B); GCG discriminative AUC >0.78; OpenWebText vs HH-RLHF AUC >0.80; FTC scaling modulates MWE accuracy (±) and MMLU | Llama 2/3, Gemma, Vicuna, Mistral, Zephyr (≤13B); MMLU, MWE | (analysis metric; CE-trained LLMs) |
> | Dale's Law RNNs | ColEI (simple E/I partition) learns worse and with higher variance on all 4 tasks; spectrum transplants show **singular-value spectrum, not sign constraints, dominates** the gap; NSE anti-correlates with final test error; DANN stays robust (NSE ≈0.95) even with 1 inhibitory unit | Adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition | CE (classification/LM), MSE (adding) |
> 
> ## Analysis / caveats
> 
> - **Coverage fit**: items (2)–(5) match well. Item (1) is partially matched: PBADet is one-stage and anchor-free on COCO-family benchmarks, but its backbones are **YOLO (CNN), not Transformer-style**; Transformers appear only in baselines (ED-Pose with Swin-L) that PBADet outperforms. No Transformer-backbone variant of PBADet is reported in the collection.
> - **Metrics alignment**: TuCo reports **AUC (AUROC)** for jailbreak detection but not F1/Precision; PBADet reports AP/MR-2/F1 (F1 vs ED-Pose). So the requested AUROC/F1/Precision are present across papers, not all in one.
> - **Cross-paper themes**: all show a "lossless compression / implicit-bias" pattern — 4-bit AdamW is accuracy-neutral vs 32-bit; JEPA and the Dale's Law paper both attribute performance to spectral/implicit-bias structure (feature influence; singular-value spectrum) rather than superficial factors (bitwidth, sign constraints); TuCo links fine-tuning magnitude directly to safety behavior. Standard datasets covered: COCO (PBADet), ImageNet/CIFAR (optimizers, JEPA, contrastive), MNIST/PTB (Dale RNNs).
> - **Unverifiable**: no single work in the collection combines these five criteria; the Transformer-backbone part-to-body requirement and explicit F1/Precision jailbreak metrics cannot be fully established from the available context.

**community 最终答案**

> Here is a compact set of five papers covering your five topics, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Recommended set
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (doc `08b70bc…190`) — one-stage, anchor-free part-to-body association (ICLR 2024).
> 2. **4-bit Optimizers / "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (doc `8d5e14…0e1`) — 4-bit optimizer-state quantization (NeurIPS 2023).
> 3. **"Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc `40fde0…103`) — joint-embedding predictive objective vs. MAE pixel reconstruction, deep-linear analysis; optionally paired with **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (doc `160e14…21a`) for the cosine-similarity-space analysis.
> 4. **TuCo** (doc `e20e76…d2c`) — per-prompt fine-tuning contribution, jailbreak prediction.
> 5. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (doc `e63a94…0c8`) — E/I-constrained RNNs, SVD-spectrum/entropy analysis (NeurIPS 2023).
> 
> ## Experimental results and analysis
> 
> **1) PBADet (part–body association).** On BodyHands, the anchor-free part-to-body design beats the anchor-based body-to-part baseline (BPJDet): HandAP 89.1 vs 85.3, Conditional Accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, JointAP 85.98 vs 78.13; even the same part-to-body definition in an anchor-based YOLOv7 is worse (88.4/92.31/85.28), showing the anchor-free formulation itself helps. On COCO Human Parts it reaches AP 42.7–43.0 (AP50 ≈ 69.5–70.0); on CrowdHuman face–body it improves body MR-2 (36.5 vs BPJDet's 39.7–41.3) with competitive AP. Caveat vs. your request: the backbone is YOLOv5/YOLOv7 (CNN), **not a Transformer**; Transformer-based part/body detectors (HOTR, ED-Pose) appear only as related work/comparison baselines in the collection.
> 
> **2) 4-bit optimizer states.** Across tasks, 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor match or slightly exceed 32-bit AdamW: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9 (4-bit wins), Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2 (within noise), GPT-2 E2E 67.8 vs 67.7, SQuAD 94.5 vs 94.6, WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61. On LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning, 4-bit AdamW matches or beats 32-bit (e.g., LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8) with convergence curves closely aligned. Memory savings reach 57.7% (LLaMA-7B fits on one 80 GB GPU). Compared with the other methods, this is the only one whose "loss" is memory rather than accuracy—it preserves the baseline optimizer's behavior by design.
> 
> **3) JEPA vs. MAE (joint-embedding vs. pixel MSE).** In deep linear networks, JEPA's implicit bias is to prioritize **high-influence features** (large regression coefficients), while MAE prioritizes high-covariance features even when noisy; the bias strengthens with encoder depth (a critical time separates the two, and noise suppression improves with depth). ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE features (CCA). Complementing this, the contrastive-learning cosine-similarity paper proves optimal embeddings give positive-pair similarity 1 and negative-pair −1/(n−1), shows mini-batches inflate negative-pair similarity variance (smaller batches worse), and its variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and full ImageNet while improving temperature robustness. Together they give the requested deep-linear + cosine-similarity analyses favoring predictive features over pixel-level MSE.
> 
> **4) TuCo (alignment/jailbreak interpretability).** TuCo decomposes a fine-tuned LLM into pre-training (PTC) and fine-tuning (FTC) components and measures FTC magnitude per prompt (≈ two forward passes). Results: (a) scaling FTC up/down (α∈[0.75,1.25]) steers behavior—maximizing agreement raises MWE accuracy up to ~6.9 and MMLU by 1.03–2.69%, minimizing it drops accuracy by up to −25%; (b) jailbreaks (GCG, conjugate prompting in low-resource languages, many-shot) all significantly lower TuCo; (c) TuCo is lower on **successful** jailbreaks, predicting attack success with AUC 0.87 (Llama-13B) and AUC >0.78 for GCG on four of five models; it separates OpenWebText vs. HH-RLHF with AUC >0.80. Note the reported metric is AUC (AUROC); F1/Precision tables are not in the retrieved content.
> 
> **5) Dale's-law RNNs (E/I-partitioned).** On adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and naturalistic object recognition, simple column-partitioned E/I RNNs (ColEI) learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANN E/I architectures. The cause is spectral, not just sign constraints: spectrum-transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum contributes ~1.5%±0.3% test-error degradation vs ~0.7%±0.3% from sign constraints; ColEI's column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values, unlike the quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra of standard RNNs/DANNs. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization **anti-correlates with final test error** across network sizes and E:I ratios, and gradient clipping substantially mitigates ColEI's instability—an actionable diagnostic.
> 
> ## Cross-method observations
> - The two "analysis" papers (JEPA, Dale's RNN) both attribute performance to *initialization/objective biases* rather than architecture expressivity, and both use standard benchmarks (ImageNet-1K; sequential MNIST/PTB) with spectral/similarity diagnostics (CCA/PCA, SVD entropy, cosine similarity).
> - The two "efficiency/safety" papers (4-bit optimizers, TuCo) are the only ones reporting exact match-to-baseline behavior: 4-bit AdamW preserves full-precision accuracy while TuCo preserves/quantifies the fine-tuned model's behavior at inference.
> - PBADet is the only one targeting COCO-family detection; it also shows the largest relative gains come from the representation choice (part-to-body vs body-to-part offset) rather than the loss function—consistent with the other papers' emphasis on implicit bias over loss magnitude.

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of the experimental results reported in the five provided papers, organized by (A) identical datasets, (B) similar dataset families, and (C) each paper’s specific datasets and outcomes. All numbers and statements come directly from the cited figures and tables in the papers.
> 
> A) Identical datasets across papers
> 
> 1) MMLU (5-shot) appears in two papers
> - 4-bit Optimizers (Table 3):
>   • LLaMA‑7B: 4-bit AdamW 38.9 vs 32-bit AdamW 38.7
>   • LLaMA‑13B: 4-bit AdamW 47.4 vs 32-bit AdamW 46.5
>   • LLaMA‑33B: 4-bit AdamW 54.9 vs 32-bit AdamW 56.4
>   Interpretation: 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly improves MMLU at smaller sizes (7B, 13B), and is close at 33B.
> - TuCo (Appendix F.1/Table 3 and Figure 7): scaling the fine-tuning component (FTCα-scaling) yields statistically significant mean increases in MMLU category-level accuracy across models, typically ~1–3%:
>   • Example per-model deltas (Table 3): LLaMA‑2 13B: Humanities +1.03%, STEM +0.90%, Social Sciences +0.83%; Mistral V0.2 7B: Humanities +3.26%, Social +4.14%.
>   Comparison: Both papers report small but consistent MMLU gains from their interventions. 4-bit AdamW preserves/recovers baseline MMLU while saving memory; TuCo’s FTC scaling (α>1) provides ~1–3% boosts in many categories.
> 
> 2) COCO validation set (parts) within PBADet vs ED‑Pose (quantitative from PBADet Appendix A.2, Table 7)
> - On COCO val (4 small parts: left/right hand, left/right foot):
>   • ED‑Pose: Precision/Recall/F1 (all parts): 24.09/45.51/31.51
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Precision/Recall/F1 (all parts): 39.41/63.09/48.52
>   Per-part F1 examples: left hand 22.87 (ED‑Pose) vs 46.50 (PBADet); right hand 24.17 vs 47.34; left foot 40.46 vs 51.08; right foot 40.34 vs 50.34.
>   Comparison: On the same COCO validation set (for small parts), PBADet substantially outperforms ED‑Pose in F1/Precision/Recall for all parts in the table.
> 
> B) Similar dataset families (vision; language; safety)
> 
> Vision
> - Object detection (PBADet) vs image classification (4-bit Optimizers): metrics differ (AP/MR vs top-1 accuracy), so we compare trends:
>   • PBADet achieves SOTA or competitive detection/association on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman. On COCOHumanParts (Table 2), Ours (YOLOv5l6) has AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 (orig/subordinate) vs BPJDet l6 43.6/43.3 (very close overall), but PBADet improves APM/APL (66.2/67.2 vs 63.8/61.8) and boosts per-category “feet” AP (30.9/31.5 vs 30.2/30.9). Association miss rates (Table 3) favor PBADet (YOLOv5l6) on 5/6 categories (head, face, left/right hands, left foot) with lower mMR−2 than BPJDet l6; right foot is slightly worse.
>   • 4-bit Optimizers (ImageNet‑1k, Table 2) show top‑1 ACC: Swin‑T 32‑bit 81.2 vs 4‑bit AdamW 80.8 vs 8‑bit 81.0 (nearly identical), indicating 4‑bit optimizer states preserve classification accuracy while saving memory.
> 
> Language
> - 4-bit Optimizers (GLUE/SQuAD/WMT/E2E) vs TuCo (MWE behaviors/MMLU deltas):
>   • 4-bit Optimizers match 32‑bit baselines across standard language tasks (Table 2):
>     – GLUE mean: 32‑bit 88.9 vs 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 (NLU)
>     – SQuAD F1: 32‑bit 94.6 vs 4‑bit AdamW 94.5; EM 89.0 vs 88.8 (Table 9)
>     – WMT14 en‑de SacreBleu: 26.61 vs 26.28 (close)
>     – E2E‑NLG BLEU: 67.7 vs 67.8
>   • TuCo shows that up‑scaling the fine‑tuning component (FTC) can steer behaviors and improve performance:
>     – Behaviors (MWE, Figure 6; Table 3): increases in agreement when maximizing α; e.g., LLaMA‑2 13B: +5.90% (Political), +5.18% (Religious); vice‑versa decreases when minimizing α.
>     – MMLU deltas (Appendix F.1/Table 3 & Fig. 7): average improvements ~1–3% in many categories across models.
> 
> Safety/jailbreaks
> - TuCo provides consistent evidence (Table 1, Table 2; Figure 4) that successful jailbreaks reduce the tuning contribution:
>   • OpenWebText vs HH‑RLHF AUC (Table 1): near‑perfect separability by TuCo for most models (e.g., Llama‑2 7B, 1.0), indicating HH‑RLHF prompts have much higher TuCo than web‑text.
>   • Conjugate prompting (low‑resource languages) and GCG adversarial suffixes: TuCo AUCs often 0.96–1.0 in some cases (e.g., Llama‑2 7B for Japanese/Hungarian in Table 1), reflecting strong TuCo decrease under attacks.
>   • Many‑shot jailbreaks (Figure 4 bottom): TuCo decreases as the number of shots increases for several models.
>   • Predicting attack success (Table 2): AUC 0.94 (Gemma‑7B), 0.87 (Llama‑2 13B), 0.83 (Llama‑2 7B), meaning lower TuCo correlates with successful jailbreaks.
> 
> C) Per-paper: specific datasets and results
> 
> 1) PBADet (ICLR 2024)
> - BodyHands (Table 1): Ours (YOLOv7) outperforms prior SOTA in all metrics:
>   • Hand AP: 89.1 (Ours YOLOv7) vs 85.9 (BPJDet YOLOv5l6)
>   • Conditional Accuracy: 92.62 vs 86.91; Joint AP: 85.98 vs 84.39
>   • Ours (YOLOv5l6) similarly strong: 88.1/92.71/85.73
> - COCOHumanParts (Tables 2 and 3):
>   • Overall AP close to BPJDet l6; PBADet improves mid/large object AP (APM/APL) and maintains competitive per-category AP.
>   • Association quality (mMR−2, lower is better): Ours (YOLOv5l6) is lower than BPJDet l6 on head (27.9 vs 30.8), face (30.5 vs 31.8), left hand (36.2 vs 41.6), right hand (40.8 vs 42.2), left foot (47.9 vs 50.4), and slightly higher on right foot (50.4 vs 49.1).
> - CrowdHuman (Appendix Tables 5 & 6):
>   • Face‑body association: Ours (YOLOv7) achieves best MR−2 for body (36.5) and face (44.7), and highest body AP (91.6). Pair mMR−2 is close (50.8 vs BPJDet l6 50.1).
> - COCO val parts vs ED‑Pose (Appendix A.2/Table 7): PBADet’s F1/Precision/Recall notably exceed ED‑Pose (all parts F1: 48.52 vs 31.51).
> 
> 2) Learning with Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Identical datasets within the paper: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task (Fig. 2).
>   • Across all four tasks, ColEI (column-sign‑constrained E/I) learns worse and is more variable than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs (Fig. 2 A–D). Gradient clipping disproportionately helps ColEI.
> - Spectrum transplant (Fig. 4B–C): changing singular value spectra has larger impact on performance than sign constraints alone; sign constraints explain only part of the gap.
> - NSE (Normalized SVD Entropy) correlates with performance (Figs. 5G, 6G, 7): lower NSE (more dispersed spectra) degrades ColEI training; DANN and standard RNNs maintain higher NSE and better learning across E/I ratios and sizes.
> 
> 3) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)
> - In deep linear settings, JEPA prioritizes high‑influence (high regression coefficient ρ) features before high-variance (λ) features; MAE prioritizes high‑λ features. ODE simulations (Fig. 2, Fig. 4) confirm JEPA’s ρ‑greedy learning appears with deeper encoders.
> - Temporal generative model (Fig. 3): JEPA learns less‑noisy features (higher ρ) earlier; aligns with prediction.
> - ImageNet experiment (Appendix D/Fig. 7): mean CCA shows I‑JEPA features align more with the bottom PCA subspace (associated with perceptual/semantic features) than MAE, while MAE aligns more with the top variance subspace; curves show I‑JEPA full↔bottom CCA higher and full↔top CCA lower than MAE across training.
> 
> 4) Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Accuracy across tasks (Table 2; Tables 7–9): 4‑bit AdamW matches/very slightly improves over 32‑bit baselines on GLUE (NLU mean 89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD (F1 94.5 vs 94.6; EM 88.8 vs 89.0), E2E‑NLG (BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7), WMT14 en‑de (26.28 vs 26.61). 8‑bit also strong; SM3 and Adafactor can underperform in some settings.
> - ImageNet‑1k (Swin‑T): 4‑bit AdamW 80.8 vs 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit 81.0 (close).
> - Instruction tuning (Table 3): 4‑bit AdamW maintains capabilities while adding instruction following; e.g., LLaMA‑13B: MMLU 47.4 (4‑bit) vs 46.5 (32‑bit); HellaSwag 79.0 (4‑bit) vs 78.8; ARC‑c 48.0 vs 48.3; OBQA 45.2 vs 45.2.
> - Memory/time (Table 4): up to 57.7% total memory saved (LLaMA‑7B finetuning: 75.4GB → 31.9GB) and training time gains with FSDP due to reduced optimizer communication; RoBERTa‑L/GPT‑2 Medium see 34–47% memory savings, with speed parity after fused kernels.
> 
> 5) TuCo (ICML 2025)
> - FTC scaling controls model behavior/performance (Fig. 2–3; Table 3):
>   • Behaviors (MWE): choosing α to maximize agreement yields +1.55% to +5.18% mean gains depending on model; minimizing α reduces agreement by −2.80% to −25.24%.
>   • MMLU: statistically significant improvements for 71% of tasks; average gains ~1–3% across models/categories (e.g., LLaMA‑2 13B humanities +1.03%, political views +5.90%, religious +5.18%).
> - Safety signals via TuCo:
>   • Web vs chat: AUC near 1.0 separating OpenWebText vs HH‑RLHF using TuCo (Table 1 left column), indicating higher TuCo on chat-like prompts.
>   • Attacks (GCG; Conjugate Prompting; Many‑Shot): TuCo decreases under attacks; AUCs typically high (0.78–1.0 depending on model/language). Many‑shot TuCo monotonically drops with more shots (Fig. 4 bottom).
>   • Success prediction: TuCo lower on successful jailbreaks; AUC 0.94 (Gemma‑7B), 0.87 (Llama‑2 13B), 0.83 (Llama‑2 7B) (Table 2).
> 
> Summary of who is better where (from the reported tables/figures)
> - On identical COCO validation (parts), PBADet surpasses ED‑Pose on F1/Precision/Recall across all parts in Table 7.
> - On identical MMLU, 4‑bit AdamW preserves or slightly improves over 32‑bit for LLaMA‑7B/13B and is comparable at 33B; TuCo’s FTC scaling yields additional ~1–3% category-level gains across many models/tasks.
> - On multi-part detection/association, PBADet is SOTA or competitive vs BPJDet/Hier‑R‑CNN, with improved APM/APL and lower association miss rates on most categories.
> - For RNN training tasks, standard RNNs and DANN RNNs outperform ColEI; spectral properties (NSE, singular value dispersion) predict learning dynamics and stability.
> - For SSL pretraining objectives, JEPA (vs MAE) preferentially learns high‑influence (low‑variance) features (temporal model and ODE simulations) and aligns with bottom ImageNet subspace faster (higher bottom CCA).
> - For optimizer memory, 4‑bit states cut total memory markedly (up to 57.7% in LLaMA finetuning) with near‑identical accuracy to 32‑bit baselines.
> - For safety/jailbreak analyses, TuCo provides a per‑prompt quantitative marker: lower TuCo under attacks and especially for successful jailbreaks (AUC up to ~0.94), and high AUC in discriminating web vs chat prompts.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the papers to read for each piece, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Recommended papers per requirement
> 
> **(a) Hand/face detection + person association → PBADet** ("PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association")
> One-stage anchor-free detector that links parts (hands, face, feet) to their parent body via a single part-to-body center offset.
> 
> **(b) Joint-embedding SSL pretraining (no pixel reconstruction) → "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (Apple) + LDReg**
> The JEPA paper analyzes JEPA/self-distillation vs MAE (pixel reconstruction) and shows JEPA learns high-influence, noise-robust features. LDReg is a regularization layer that improves SSL encoders (SimCLR, BYOL, MAE, etc.).
> 
> **(c) Per-prompt instruction/SFT contribution + jailbreak detection via AUROC → TuCo** ("Measuring the Contribution of Fine-Tuning to Individual Responses of LLMs")
> Exactly matches your requirement: an exact decomposition of a fine-tuned LLM into pre-training (PTC) and fine-tuning (FTC) components, giving a per-prompt TuCo metric, and showing jailbreaks attenuate it (evaluated with AUC).
> 
> **(d) Small recurrent control loop with E/I separation, still trainable → "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"**
> Compares ColEI (naive E/I sign-constrained RNNs) vs recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) and shows DANN respects Dale's Law (E/I separation) yet trains as well as standard RNNs; identifies spectral initialization as the key factor.
> 
> **(e) Tight-VRAM training with low-bit optimizer states on Adam/SGD → "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"**
> Quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, optional factorization). **BSO** is a complementary spiking/online option with binary weights and O(n²L/32) memory.
> 
> **Adapter-style PEFT → NFTS** (NAS for adapter placement/fine-tune subsets; tables include CIFAR-100, MNIST, MSCOCO) and **NEFTune** (noisy-embedding instruction tuning; works with QLoRA).
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **(a) PBADet results:** On BodyHands it beats BPJDet and HierR-CNN across all metrics (body/hand AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP); its YOLOv7 model outperforms larger BPJDet(YOLOv5m6). On COCOHumanParts it matches BPJDet in AP and leads in AP_M/AP_L and feet detection. On CrowdHuman face-body association it gets the best body MR-2 (36.5 vs BPJDet's 40.7) and competitive face AP. Vs. ED-Pose (multi-person pose), PBADet gives much higher precision/recall/F1 for hands (F1 ≈ 46–47 vs ≈ 23–24) and all parts (48.52 vs 31.51) — directly supplying your F1/Precision metrics on COCO.
> 
> **(b) JEPA vs MAE:** On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (measured by CCA), supporting the claim that JEPA suppresses noise relative to reconstruction. LDReg adds local-intrinsic-dimensionality regularization: on ImageNet (ResNet-50/ViT-B) it improves linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO object detection/instance segmentation for SimCLR, SimCLR-Tuned, BYOL, and MAE (also MoCo, VICReg, Barlow Twins); longer pretraining gives larger gains; L1/L2 variants perform similarly.
> 
> **(c) TuCo results:** TuCo is lower on pre-training-like (OpenWebText) than chat (HH-RLHF) inputs, AUC>0.80. Jailbreaks (GCG, conjugate, many-shot) significantly decrease TuCo; GCG gives AUC>0.78 for 4 of 5 models, and attack success is predicted with AUC 0.87 for Llama-13B; many-shot intensity scales TuCo down as harmful responses rise. Scaling the FTC by α∈[0.75,1.25] steers behavior: maximizing TuCo agreement improves MWE accuracy (up to ~6.9), minimizing lowers it (≈ −2.3 to −13.3); MMLU gains are mostly positive but variable. Caveat: AUC dips to 0.66 (Vicuna v1.5 13B) and is uninformative when jailbreak success is negligible (Llama 3 8B, 0.24%).
> 
> **(d) E/I RNN results:** On adding, sequential MNIST, Penn TreeBank, and object recognition, ColEI learns worse and with higher variance; gradient clipping mitigates the deficit. Recurrent DANN matches standard RNNs (unimodal, random-matrix-like spectra) and stays robust even with a single inhibitory neuron, whereas small ColEI networks with few I units degrade. Normalized SVD entropy at initialization anti-correlates with final error — spectral properties, not sign constraints, determine trainability.
> 
> **(e) 4-bit optimizer results:** 4-bit AdamW matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), E2E-NLG (67.8 vs 67.7), and is comparable on ImageNet-1K Swin-T (80.8 vs 81.2) and WMT14 (26.28 vs 26.61); LLaMA-7B Alpaca tuning saves 57.7% memory (75.4→31.9 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU; 4-bit Factor saves more. Adafactor/SM3 are more memory-efficient but degrade, especially on classification. (Note: this paper benchmarks ImageNet/GLUE, not CIFAR-100/MNIST/COCO; the MNIST/CIFAR-100/COCO results appear in the NFTS Meta-Dataset table and in the Hessian-structure paper, which tests LeNet/FCN on MNIST/CIFAR-10/100 with SGD/Adam.) BSO additionally shows memory that is nearly constant across timesteps with ~20–31× model-size reduction and 74.27% on CIFAR-100, but for spiking networks.
> 
> **PEFT comparison:** NFTS shows per-layer adapter placement matters (adapters favored in early/late layers, not middle), combining fine-tuning with adapters helps, and NFTS-N (80.7 avg) beats fixed top-1 (76.6) with far fewer parameters (16M vs 82M). NEFTune gives the largest single gain: AlpacaEval win rate 29.8%→64.7% (LLaMA-2-7B), +10% Evol-Instruct, +8% ShareGPT/OpenPlatypus, human preference 74.6%, works under QLoRA, with no change on OpenLLM benchmarks.
> 
> **Coverage note:** All six pieces are covered by the above set (PBADet; JEPA+LDReg; TuCo; Dale's-Law/DANN RNN; 4-bit optimizers; NFTS/NEFTune). The context does not contain a single paper combining hand-face association with JEPA pretraining, nor one that jointly reports CIFAR-100/MNIST/COCO with Adam/SGD and F1/Precision — you would combine PBADet (F1/COCO), NFTS (CIFAR-100/MNIST/MSCOCO accuracy), and the 4-bit optimizer (Adam memory) to assemble those results.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers that cover each piece of your system, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Paper mapping
> 
> | Requirement | Paper |
> |---|---|
> | (a) Hand/face detection + person linking | **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection** (ICLR 2024) — detects hands/face/feet and links each part to its parent body via a single part-to-body center offset; one-stage anchor-free (YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7), trained with SGD |
> | (b) Joint-embedding SSL instead of pixel reconstruction | **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024) — JEPA/self-distillation vs MAE; (optional: **LDReg**, ICLR 2024, for SSL regularization against dimensional collapse) |
> | (c) Per-prompt SFT contribution + jailbreak AUROC | **TuCo: Measuring the Contribution of Fine-Tuning to Individual Responses of LLMs** (ICML 2025) — exact per-prompt decomposition into pre-training/fine-tuning components |
> | (d) Recurrent E/I loop that stays trainable | **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023) — ColEI vs recurrent DANN under E/I constraints |
> | (e) Low-bit optimizer states in tight VRAM | **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023) — 4-bit Adam/AdamW with quantization + factorization |
> | (f) Adapter-style, end-to-end parameter-efficient fine-tuning | **NFTS: Neural Fine-Tuning Search for Few-Shot Learning** (ICLR 2024) — NAS over per-layer freeze/fine-tune + adapter insertion for CNNs and ViTs |
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **PBADet (a).** On COCO validation (vs multi-person pose estimator ED-Pose), PBADet roughly doubles Precision/Recall/F1 for hands and feet: all-parts F1 **48.52 vs 31.51**, left-hand F1 **46.50 vs 22.87**, right-hand **47.34 vs 24.17** (Precision 37.63 vs 18.36, Recall 60.82 vs 30.34 for left hand). On COCOHumanParts it matches BPJDet in AP but achieves the lowest mismatch rate (mMR⁻²) on head/face/both hands/right foot; on CrowdHuman face-body association it beats BPJDet in body MR⁻² (36.5–37.5 vs 39.7–41.3) and AP (91.4–91.6 vs 89.5–90.7). It's the strongest fit for both detection and correct person-linkage with F1/Precision metrics on COCO.
> 
> **JEPA paper (b).** Theory (deep linear nets) plus ImageNet-1K experiments show I-JEPA features align **faster** with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA measure) — i.e., predicting in latent space suppresses noisy/high-variance pixel information that reconstruction objectives prioritize. The bias toward "influential" features strengthens with encoder depth. This is the direct justification for choosing joint-embedding over pixel reconstruction.
> 
> **TuCo (c).** All three jailbreak families (GCG adversarial prefixes, conjugate prompting, many-shot) **significantly reduce TuCo**, and successful attacks reduce it more than failed ones. GCG jailbreak-vs-harmless discrimination reaches **AUC > 0.78 for 4 of 5 models**; attack-success prediction hits **AUC 0.87** (Llama 13B); TuCo drops monotonically with many-shot attack intensity and separates OpenWebText vs HH-RLHF at AUC > 0.80. Scaling the fine-tuning component by 25% shifts behaviors (e.g., +24% Christian-belief alignment on Llama 2 13B) and improves MWE accuracy up to ~6.9 points, with mostly-positive but variable MMLU gains. This is exactly the per-prompt attribution + jailbreak-AUROC monitor you need.
> 
> **Dale's Law RNN (d).** The naive E/I implementation (ColEI, sign-partitioned columns) **learns worse and more variably** on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn TreeBank, and object recognition, while recurrent **DANN** (E/I separated via W_EE/W_EI/W_IE reparameterization with clipping) **matches standard RNNs**. The cause is not the sign constraint but the initial recurrent-weight spectrum: ColEI has multimodal, dispersed singular values vs the quarter-circle (Marchenko–Pastur) form of DANN/standard RNNs; gradient clipping helps ColEI most; normalized SVD entropy anti-correlates with final error. Takeaway: use DANN-style E/I, not ColEI partitioning, for a small trainable control loop.
> 
> **4-bit Optimizers (e).** 4-bit AdamW **matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW** on GLUE (RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD **F1 94.5 vs 94.6**, E2E-NLG, Swin-T ImageNet (80.8 vs 81.2), and WMT14, while saving up to **57.7% memory** (LLaMA-7B: 75.4 → 31.9 GB, trainable on one 80 GB GPU); 4-bit Factor adds further savings (46.7% on RoBERTa-L). Key fixes: smaller block size (B128) for the first moment and zero-point-excluding linear / rank-1 quantization for the second moment. This beats 8-bit Adam (28.6–37.1% savings).
> 
> **NFTS (f).** Searching per-layer fine-tune/freeze + adapter placement achieves SOTA on Meta-Dataset/Meta-Album; deferring architecture selection per episode (NFTS-N, N=3 best) beats a fixed top-1 architecture, especially single-source domains (**80.7 vs 76.6 with 16M vs 82M params**). Notably, **combining full fine-tuning with adapters works best** — a result prior adapter work missed.
> 
> **Coverage caveat:** no single paper in the collection runs low-bit Adam/SGD across COCO + CIFAR-100 + MNIST with F1/Precision simultaneously. Closest partial matches: PBADet covers COCO with SGD and reports Precision/Recall/F1; the Hessian-spectra paper (582d138d…) trains LeNet/ResNet18 with SGD/Adam on MNIST/CIFAR-10/100, but it addresses loss-landscape analysis, not optimizer-state memory. So the 4-bit optimizer paper (GLUE/SQuAD F1, ImageNet) plus PBADet's COCO F1 numbers together cover your benchmark/metric needs.

### paperscope:results_comparison:206 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find a small set of papers that, taken together, cover: (1) anchor‑free part‑to‑object association in vision (e.g., hand/face to person) with detection heads trained using common losses like cross‑entropy and MSE and evaluated by F1/Precision/AUROC on datasets such as MNIST/CIFAR‑100/SVHN; (2) analysis of deep networks under neurobiological excitatory/inhibitory constraints using spectral tools (e.g., singular value distributions, normalized entropy) and their impact on SGD/AdamW training; (3) joint‑embedding self‑distillation methods that bias toward high‑influence features (often measured via cosine similarity) rather than pixel‑level reconstruction; (4) sub‑8‑bit (e.g., 4‑bit) optimizer‑state quantization for Transformers/ResNet‑50 with end‑to‑end fine‑tuning (including LoRA-style setups) using AdamW; and (5) rigorous sample‑complexity guarantees for differentially private optimization on nonsmooth, nonconvex objectives, including single‑pass and multi‑pass algorithms. I’m looking for works that collectively address these themes across optimization, representation learning, spectral analysis, privacy, and efficient detection.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
