> {'answer': 'Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results reported in the five works, grouped by shared or comparable datasets and task types. All quantities and conclusions are taken directly from the papers’ figures and tables (or from textual statements where plots do not give exact numbers). Identical datasets are called out explicitly.\n\n1) Part–body association in vision (PBADet vs. baselines) — identical datasets\n- BodyHands (identical dataset across methods; Table 1)\n  • Metrics: Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP.\n  • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.\n  • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.\n  • Conclusion: PBADet outperforms BPJDet on BodyHands across all reported metrics (Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP). Even on identical backbone (YOLOv5l6), PBADet yields higher Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP.\n\n- COCOHumanParts (identical dataset across methods; Tables 2 and 3)\n  • All-categories APs (AP.5:.95 / AP.5) and scale APs (APM, APL):\n    – BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.6 / 43.3; AP.5 70.6 / 69.8; APM 63.8 / 63.2; APL 61.8 / 58.9.\n    – PBADet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.0 / 41.8; AP.5 70.0 / 68.4; APM 66.2 / 65.0; APL 67.2 / 64.4.\n    – Conclusion: Overall AP.5:.95 is slightly higher for BPJDet, but PBADet has higher APM/APL (medium/large scales), indicating better performance on larger instances.\n  • Per-category APs (Table 2):\n    – BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): person 61.3, head 56.6, face 46.3, right-hand 40.4, left-hand 39.6, right-foot 30.2, left-foot 30.9.\n    – PBADet (YOLOv5l6): person 62.4, head 54.6, face 44.6, right-hand 39.0, left-hand 37.7, right-foot 30.9, left-foot 31.5.\n    – Conclusion: PBADet is better on person and both feet (right-foot, left-foot), BPJDet is better on head/face/hands.\n  • Average miss-matching rate (mMR−2; lower is better) (Table 3):\n    – BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, left-hand 41.6, right-hand 42.2, right-foot 49.1, left-foot 50.4.\n    – PBADet (YOLOv5l6): head 27.9, face 30.5, left-hand 36.2, right-hand 40.8, right-foot 50.4, left-foot 47.9.\n    – Conclusion: PBADet achieves lower mMR−2 for head/face/hands and left-foot; BPJDet slightly better on right-foot.\n\n- CrowdHuman (identical dataset across methods; Tables 5 and 6)\n  • PBADet (YOLOv7): body MR−2 36.5, face MR−2 44.7, body AP 91.6, body-face mMR−2 50.8.\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR−2 40.7, face MR−2 46.3, body AP 89.5, body-face mMR−2 50.1.\n  • Conclusion: PBADet has better detection (lower MR−2, higher AP) but similar/slightly worse association (mMR−2) relative to BPJDet on CrowdHuman.\n\n- Multi-person pose estimation comparison on COCO validation (ED-Pose vs. PBADet; Appendix Table 7)\n  • Selected parts (PBADet vs. ED-Pose; Precision/Recall/F1):\n    – Left hand: PBADet P/R/F = 37.63 / 60.82 / 46.50 vs. ED-Pose 18.36 / 30.34 / 22.87.\n    – Right hand: 38.58 / 61.26 / 47.34 vs. 19.57 / 31.59 / 24.17.\n    – Left foot: 41.56 / 66.24 / 51.08 vs. 29.32 / 65.28 / 40.46.\n    – Right foot: 40.86 / 65.55 / 50.34 vs. 29.13 / 65.58 / 40.34.\n  • Conclusion: PBADet substantially outperforms ED-Pose on part detection and association for the evaluated parts.\n\n2) Deep networks under Dale’s Law — identical tasks\n- Tasks used across methods: Adding problem (sequence length 20), Sequential MNIST (row-wise), Penn Tree Bank language modeling, naturalistic object recognition (Figure 2).\n- Methods compared: Standard RNNs, Column EI (ColEI), DANN RNNs.\n- Reported outcomes (from plots and text):\n  • Across all four tasks, ColEI networks “did not learn as well” as DANNs and standard RNNs (Figure 2 A–D). DANNs match standard RNN performance.\n  • Gradient clipping benefits ColEI substantially more than the other networks (Appendix Figure 10); ColEI shows higher variance across random seeds.\n  • Spectral analyses: ColEI exhibits multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra (including large singular values), which correlates with poorer learning; DANNs and standard RNNs show unimodal clustering.\n  • Sensitivity to EI ratio and network size (Figures 5–6): Lower proportion of inhibitory units and smaller networks reduce Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) and degrade performance; DANN performance is robust even with very few inhibitory units. NSE anti-correlates with test error (Figure 7); higher NSE predicts better performance.\n  • Conclusion: On identical benchmarks (Adding, Sequential MNIST, PTB, naturalistic classification), DANNs ≈ standard RNNs > ColEI; spectral clustering (higher NSE) is predictive of better results.\n\n3) Joint-embedding self-distillation (JEPA) vs. Masked Autoencoders (MAE) — identical dataset family (ImageNet)\n- ImageNet-1K (64×64) experiments (Appendix D, Figure 7): ViT encoders trained with I-JEPA vs. MAE; metric is mean CCA similarity between representations from full vs. “bottom” or “top” PCA subspaces.\n  • Full vs. bottom PCA similarity: I-JEPA consistently higher mean CCA than MAE throughout training.\n  • Full vs. top PCA similarity: MAE shows relatively higher mean CCA (JEPA lower), indicating JEPA prioritizes lower-variance (perceptual) subspace.\n  • Conclusion: On ImageNet representations, JEPA aligns more strongly with bottom-spectrum (perceptual) features than MAE, consistent with the paper’s analytical findings.\n\n4) Sub-8-bit optimizer-state quantization (4-bit) — identical datasets across optimizers (Table 2, Table 3, Tables 7–9, Table 4)\n- GLUE (RoBERTa-L; NLU mean score; Table 2)\n  • 32-bit AdamW: 88.9.\n  • 8-bit AdamW: 89.1.\n  • 4-bit AdamW: 89.1.\n  • 4-bit Factor: 88.9.\n  • 32-bit Adafactor: 89.1; 32-bit Adafactor (β1=0): 89.3; 32-bit SM3: 87.5.\n  • Conclusion: 4-bit AdamW matches 8-bit and 32-bit AdamW; Adafactor with β1=0 is slightly higher; SM3 is lower.\n- ImageNet-1k classification (Swin-T; CLS; Table 2)\n  • 32-bit AdamW: 81.2.\n  • 8-bit AdamW: 81.0.\n  • 4-bit AdamW: 80.8.\n  • 4-bit Factor: 80.9.\n  • 32-bit Adafactor: 80.0; Adafactor (β1=0): 79.5; SM3: 79.0.\n  • Conclusion: 4-bit methods are comparable (≤0.4 pt from 32-bit); Adafactor/SM3 lower.\n- E2E-NLG (GPT-2 Medium; BLEU; Table 2)\n  • 32-bit AdamW: 67.7 ± 0.67.\n  • 8-bit AdamW: 67.5 ± 0.87.\n  • 4-bit AdamW: 67.8 ± 0.51.\n  • 4-bit Factor: 67.6 ± 0.33.\n  • 32-bit Adafactor: 67.2; ARC-e 63.6 vs 64.1; ARC-c 48.3 vs 48.0; OBQA 45.2 vs 45.2.\n  • LLaMA-33B: 56.4 vs 54.9 (MMLU); HellaSwag 79.2 vs 79.2; ARC-e 62.6 vs 61.6; ARC-c 47.1 vs 46.6; OBQA 43.8 vs 45.4.\n  • Conclusion: 4-bit AdamW is comparable to 32-bit AdamW across sizes, with small task-dependent deltas.\n- Memory/time (identical tasks; Table 4)\n  • LLaMA‑7B (FSDP, 2×A100 80GB): 32‑bit AdamW total mem 75.40 GB vs 4‑bit AdamW 31.87 GB (57.7% saved); time 3.35 h vs 3.07 h.\n  • RoBERTa‑L (RTE): 32‑bit 5.31 GB vs 4‑bit AdamW 3.00–3.02 GB (≈43–44% saved); LLaMA‑7B trainable with 4‑bit on single 80 GB GPU.\n- Ablations on second moment quantization (Table 1): excluding zero-point (DE‑0 or Linear mapping) stabilizes 4‑bit convergence; rank‑1 normalization (Linear) yields BLEU 67.8 ± 0.51 on E2E‑NLG (matching 32‑bit). Factorization further reduces memory without accuracy loss.\n\n5) Differentially private nonsmooth nonconvex optimization — algorithmic performance (Table 1)\n- Reported sample-complexity (not empirical datasets):\n  • Single‑pass (SP): n = Õ(√d/(αβ³) + d/(εαβ²)), improving over prior Õ(d/(αβ³) + d^{3/2}/(εαβ²)).\n  • Multi‑pass (MP) ERM: n = Õ(d^{3/4}/(εα^{1/2}β^{3/2})). For stochastic losses, generalization adds Õ(d/β²).\n  • First‑order variant reduces oracle complexity by Õ(d²) relative to zero‑order, with same sample‑complexity.\n  • Note: This paper does not report experimental datasets; the outcomes are theoretical bounds.\n\nSummary across similar task families and identical datasets\n- Vision, part–to–body association (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman): PBADet generally improves association accuracy (lower mMR−2) for several parts and raises detection accuracy (AP) vs. BPJDet, with nuances (e.g., better person/feet APs; BPJDet slightly better on head/face/hands APs; CrowdHuman association mMR−2 very close).\n- Pose vs detection: On COCO validation parts, PBADet yields markedly higher Precision/Recall/F1 than ED‑Pose for hands and feet.\n- Deep networks under EI constraints: DANN RNNs perform comparably to standard RNNs and better than ColEI on identical tasks (Adding, Sequential MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition). Spectral clustering (higher NSE) correlates with better performance and training stability.\n- Representation learning (ImageNet family): JEPA encoders show higher CCA alignment to bottom‑variance features than MAE; the 4‑bit optimizer maintains classification accuracy close to 32‑bit/8‑bit AdamW on ImageNet.\n- Optimizer‑state quantization: Across identical NLP and vision fine‑tuning/pretraining datasets, 4‑bit AdamW and 4‑bit Factor match 32‑bit and 8‑bit AdamW on accuracy (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG), remain close on ImageNet/MT, and yield large memory savings with comparable throughput (especially with fused ops and FSDP).\n- Private optimization: New bounds improve sample complexity vs. prior DP methods; no empirical datasets are reported.\n\nNotes\n- All numeric results above are directly from the cited tables/figures. Where plots are qualitative (e.g., Dale’s Law spectral/entropy trends; JEPA CCA curves), conclusions follow the paper’s text accompanying the figures.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Here is a small set of papers from the collection that best covers your five themes, with a brief comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The five papers (one per theme)
> 
> 1. **Detection / part–object association** — *PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024; doc `08b70bc3…`). One-stage anchor-free detector linking hands/face/feet to a parent body via a single part-to-body center offset; detection heads for classification, localization (IoU/DFL), and association (L1 offset regression), trained with task-alignment supervision.
> 2. **Spectral analysis under neurobiological E/I constraints** — *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023; doc `e63a94c4…`). RNNs with excitatory/inhibitory (Dale's law) sign constraints; analyzes singular-value distributions and normalized SVD entropy (NSE), showing the initial weight spectrum matters more than sign constraints for learning.
> 3. **Joint-embedding self-distillation** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features* (NeurIPS 2024; doc `40fde037…`). Shows JEPA self-distillation is biased to high-influence (high-regression-coefficient, ρ) features in latent space rather than pixel-level reconstruction (MAE), with depth strengthening this bias.
> 4. **4-bit optimizer-state quantization** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023; doc `8d5e1455…`). 4-bit AdamW states (B128/dynamic-exponent first moment; rank-1/linear second moment with zero-point exclusion), covering end-to-end fine-tuning of Transformers (RoBERTa-L, GPT-2 via LoRA codebase, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B) and Swin-T, using AdamW.
> 5. **DP sample complexity for nonsmooth nonconvex** — *Improved Private Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization* (ICML 2025; doc `b6c41b18…`). (ε,δ)-DP algorithms returning Goldstein-stationary points with both single-pass and multi-pass guarantees.
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **PBADet (theme 1):** On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7) reaches Hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 — beating BPJDet (YOLOv5l6: 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39) with a smaller model. On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet on AP.5:.95 (42.7/41.5 vs 43.6/43.3 for YOLOv5l6) but leads on AP_L (66.7 vs 61.8) and has the lowest average mMR⁻² on head/face/hands. Against the pose estimator ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands/feet. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment each improve association metrics (joint AP 78.07 → 85.98).
> 
> **Dale's Law spectral paper (theme 2):** ColEI networks (simple E/I column sign constraints) learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DALE's-ANN (DANN) architectures across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the initial singular-value distribution contributes more (≈1.5–2% error) than sign constraints or singular vectors; NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error, and small/imbalanced (few inhibitory) networks have worse spectra and performance.
> 
> **JEPA vs MAE (theme 3):** In deep linear networks, critical-time analysis shows MAE orders feature learning only by covariance λ, whereas JEPA additionally prioritizes features with high regression coefficient ρ, increasingly with depth (depth makes encoders low-rank toward the highest-ρ feature). On ImageNet-1K (ViT, 64×64), I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (bottom 25% explained variance) than MAE — measured by CCA similarity — confirming JEPA learns perceptual/discriminative features without pixel reconstruction.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers (theme 4):** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning is near-identical to 32-bit AdamW. Memory savings reach 57.7% for LLaMA-7B (31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU; sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor, SM3) degrade accuracy, especially on image classification.
> 
> **DP nonsmooth nonconvex (theme 5):** The single-pass algorithm achieves sample complexity Õ(√d/(αβ³) + d/(εαβ²)) — a √d improvement over Zhang et al. (2024) — plus a sublinear dimension-dependent non-private term. The multi-pass polynomial-time ERM algorithm improves this to Õ(d/β² + d^{3/4}/(εα^{1/2}β^{3/2})), with generalization from empirical to population loss when n = Õ(d/β²).
> 
> ## Cross-cutting analysis and caveats
> 
> - **Methodology diversity:** The five papers span detection (empirical, AP/F1-based), neuroscience-inspired optimization (spectral diagnosis of training failure), representation learning (theory + ImageNet CCA), systems/efficiency (memory-accuracy trade-off), and privacy theory (sample-complexity bounds) — collectively covering optimization, representation learning, spectral analysis, privacy, and efficient detection.
> - **Common theme:** all five attribute performance to a mechanism beyond raw loss value — spectral properties (theme 2, 3), association geometry (theme 1), quantization error patterns (theme 4), and stationarity definitions (theme 5).
> - **Limitations relative to your request:** (a) PBADet is evaluated on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman/AnimalPose with AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP, mMR⁻², and precision/recall/F1 — **not** MNIST/CIFAR-100/SVHN with AUROC; no paper in the collection matches that exact detection protocol. (b) The 4-bit optimizer paper uses Swin-T (not ResNet-50) for image classification; ResNet-50 with 4-bit AdamW is not covered in the collection. (c) The Dale's Law paper trains with gradient descent/gradient clipping, not explicitly SGD vs AdamW comparisons, and its spectral analysis is on RNNs, not general deep nets. (d) The JEPA paper measures feature similarity via CCA, not cosine similarity per se.
> 
> These are the closest available matches; the specific MNIST/CIFAR-100/SVHN + AUROC detection setting and ResNet-50 4-bit fine-tuning results cannot be established from this collection.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on my searches, the collection provides a good match for four of the five themes, with one partial match. Here is the small set of papers:
> 
> ## Recommended papers (one per theme)
> 
> **Theme 1 – Anchor-free part-to-object association (partial match):**
> **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc...`)
> - One-stage anchor-free approach associating hands/face to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset; detection head with classification, localization, and displacement branches.
> - **Losses:** classification loss L_cls, IoU loss, DFL loss, and an ℓ1-style association loss (not explicitly cross-entropy/MSE). **Evaluation:** AP, MR⁻², mMR⁻², and F1/Precision/Recall (vs. ED-Pose) on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman — not MNIST/CIFAR-100/SVHN, and no AUROC. Trained with SGD, not cross-entropy/MSE exactly.
> - Results: on BodyHands YOLOv7 achieves hand AP 89.1, cond. accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 (vs. BPJDet ~85.9/86.9/84.4); on CrowdHuman lowest body MR⁻² 36.5; vs. ED-Pose, all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51.
> 
> **Theme 2 – EI constraints + spectral analysis:**
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c...`)
> - Analyzes excitatory/inhibitory (Dale's Law) RNNs using singular value distributions and normalized SVD entropy (NSE); finds singular-value spectra matter more than sign constraints; NSE anti-correlates with test error; gradient clipping helps ColEI networks.
> - Trained on sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition. Note: it uses RNNs/gradient clipping rather than SGD/AdamW comparisons.
> 
> **Theme 3 – Joint-embedding self-distillation bias:**
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde03...`)
> - Shows JEPA self-distillation is biased toward high-influence features (high regression coefficients, often low-variance/slow features) vs. MAE pixel-level reconstruction; analyzed via deep linear networks, with ImageNet-1K CCA experiments confirming faster alignment of I-JEPA with low-variance PCA subspace.
> 
> **Theme 4 – Sub-8-bit optimizer-state quantization:**
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e145...`)
> - Pushes Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit (B128 blocks, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for second moment). Results: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 (vs 88.9 32-bit), Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 (vs 81.2), GPT-2 E2E 67.8 (vs 67.7), LLaMA-7B MMLU 38.9 (vs 38.7), LLaMA-33B 47.4 (vs 47.4); memory savings up to 57.7%. Note: covers LoRA-style GPT-2 fine-tuning via LoRA codebase, and Swin-T (not ResNet-50).
> 
> **Theme 5 – DP nonsmooth nonconvex sample complexity:**
> **"Improved Sample Complexity for Private Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization"** (ICML 2025, doc `b6c41b1...`)
> - Single-pass (ε,δ)-DP algorithm with sample complexity Õ(√d/αβ³ + d/εαβ²) — √d better than Zhang et al. (2024); multi-pass algorithm Õ(d/β² + d^(3/4)/εα^(1/2)β^(3/2)) with Goldstein-stationary point guarantees and generalization from ERM to population.
> 
> ## Coverage summary
> - ✅ Theme 1: PBADet (anchor-free part-to-body, F1/precision reported) — but the exact "cross-entropy + MSE losses" and "MNIST/CIFAR-100/SVHN + AUROC" details are **not** present in the collection; PBADet uses IoU/DFL/classification losses and AP/mMR⁻²/F1 on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman.
> - ✅ Theme 2: spectral (SVD, NSE) EI analysis; SGD/AdamW impact specifically not detailed.
> - ✅ Theme 3: high-influence features, cosine/CCA-based measurement, no pixel reconstruction.
> - ✅ Theme 4: 4-bit AdamW quantization, fine-tuning incl. LoRA-style setups; ResNet-50 not covered (Swin-T instead).
> - ✅ Theme 5: single-pass + multi-pass DP guarantees on nonsmooth nonconvex objectives.
> 
> A truly exact match for theme 1's loss/dataset specifications (cross-entropy, MSE, AUROC, MNIST/CIFAR-100/SVHN) was not found in the collection.

### paperscope:results_comparison:215 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an edge ML pipeline that: detects hands/face and links them to the correct person in crowded scenes with high Precision/F1; fine-tunes models under tight VRAM using Adam-like optimizers with low-bit states; guides diffusion-model image generation by optimizing a differentiable objective using adjoint methods; learns robust representations with a joint-embedding approach (using similarity in the embedding space rather than pixel-wise MSE); and explores EI-constrained RNNs for control/time-series tasks without sacrificing training stability. Are there works that address these needs across training efficiency, gradient computation for diffusion models, representation learning biases, spectral analysis in deep networks, and anchor-free part–body association?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：2→3（Δ+1）；rounds：6→6（Δ+0）。**

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a consolidated, results-only comparison drawn directly from the figures and tables of the five papers you provided. I organize the summary by task family, then detail per-dataset results (pointing out identical datasets within each comparison) and then comment on similar-task trends across works. Note: there are no identical datasets shared across these five papers; all identical-dataset comparisons occur within each paper’s own evaluation suite.
> 
> 1) Anchor‑free part–body association in crowded scenes (PBADet)
> Identical datasets (within-paper): BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman.
> 
> - BodyHands (Table 1; Hand AP↑, Conditional Accuracy↑, Joint AP↑)
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7, input 1024): 89.1 Hand AP, 92.62 Cond. Acc., 85.98 Joint AP
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6, 1024): 88.1, 92.71, 85.73
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 1536): 85.9, 86.91, 84.39
>   • Best overall: PBADet (YOLOv7) and PBADet (YOLOv5l6) both outperform BPJDet across all three metrics; the YOLOv7 variant attains the highest Cond. Acc. (92.62) and Joint AP (85.98).
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (Tables 2–3; COCO APs↑/subordinate APs↑, per-category APs↑, mMR−2↓)
>   • Overall AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate):
>     – PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 43.0 / 41.8
>     – PBJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6 / 43.3 (slightly higher overall APs) 
>   • Scale APs (original/subordinate): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) is higher on APM (66.2/65.0 vs 63.8/63.2) and APL (67.2/64.4 vs 61.8/58.9), indicating better medium/large-scale performance.
>   • Per-category APs (Table 2): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) shows higher Person AP (62.4 vs 61.3) and competitive-to-better feet APs (right foot 30.9 vs 30.2; left foot 31.5 vs 30.9) relative to BPJDet (YOLOv5l6).
>   • mMR−2 (Table 3; lower is better): PBADet yields lower average mMR−2 than BPJDet for head and face, and substantially lower for both hands. For example, vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) Head 27.9 vs 30.8; Face 30.5 vs 31.8; Left hand 36.2 vs 41.6; Right hand 40.8 vs 42.2; Left foot 47.9 vs 50.4; Right foot 50.4 vs 49.1 (here BPJDet is better). Net: PBADet improves mismatching (lower mMR−2) for head/face/hands and left foot, and is slightly worse on right foot.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6; MR−2↓, AP↑, mMR−2↓)
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7) attains the best MR−2 for body and face and the highest body AP: MR−2 (body/face) 36.5/44.7; AP (body/face) 91.6/81.6; mMR−2 (body–face) 50.8.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 (body/face) 40.7/46.3; AP (body/face) 89.5/81.6; mMR−2 50.1. PBADet improves MR−2 and body AP; mMR−2 is comparable (slightly higher/worse than BPJDet by 0.7).
> 
> Summary for this family: On identical datasets, PBADet consistently improves hand/face/body association quality in dense scenes vs prior one-stage baselines, with especially strong gains on BodyHands and in medium/large scales on COCOHumanParts; on CrowdHuman, PBADet achieves the best detection quality (MR−2/AP), with mMR−2 roughly on par.
> 
> 2) Memory-efficient 4‑bit optimizers for efficient training/finetuning (4‑bit states)
> Identical datasets (within-paper): GLUE (NLU, RoBERTa‑L), ImageNet‑1k (Swin‑T CLS), E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2 M), SQuAD/SQuAD 2.0 (QA, RoBERTa‑L), WMT14 en‑de (Transformer MT), LLaMA instruction tuning (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-e/c, OBQA).
> 
> - Main accuracy vs precision (Table 2)
>   • NLU (GLUE, mean): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9; 8‑bit 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit Factor 88.9. 4‑bit matches 32‑bit and 8‑bit.
>   • Image classification (Swin‑T, ImageNet‑1k): 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9. 4‑bit within ~0.3–0.4 points of 32‑bit.
>   • NLG (GPT‑2 M, E2E‑NLG, BLEU): 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5; 4‑bit AdamW 67.8; 4‑bit Factor 67.6. 4‑bit AdamW attains the best BLEU.
>   • QA (SQuAD, F1): 32‑bit 94.6; 8‑bit 94.5; 4‑bit AdamW 94.5; 4‑bit Factor 94.6. Parity.
>   • MT (WMT14 en‑de, SacreBleu): 32‑bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; 4‑bit AdamW 26.28; 4‑bit Factor 26.45. 4‑bit close (≤0.33 absolute from 32‑bit).
> 
> - LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3; different model sizes)
>   • 7B MMLU (5‑shot): 4‑bit 38.9 vs 32‑bit 38.7 (parity or small win). Similar parity on HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA.
>   • 13B MMLU: 4‑bit 47.4 vs 32‑bit 46.5 (small win).
>   • 33B MMLU: 4‑bit 54.9 vs 32‑bit 56.4 (small deficit). Other tasks are close.
> 
> - Memory/time efficiency (Table 4)
>   • LLaMA‑7B with FSDP (2× A100 80GB): 4‑bit AdamW reduces total memory from 75.40 GB to 31.87 GB (−57.7%) and is slightly faster (3.07 h vs 3.35 h).
>   • RoBERTa‑L (RTE): 4‑bit AdamW achieves −43.1% total memory vs 32‑bit; with fused ops, training time improves over 8‑bit (3.17 min vs 3.38 min).
>   • GPT‑2 M (E2E‑NLG): 4‑bit AdamW fused matches or slightly beats 32‑bit time (2.11 h vs 2.13 h) and cuts memory by −34.4%; 4‑bit Factor saves slightly more memory (−35.6%).
> 
> - Capacity expansion (Table 5)
>   • Under 24 GB GPU RAM: 32‑bit AdamW can fine‑tune up to OPT‑350M; 4‑bit AdamW up to OPT‑1.3B.
>   • Under 80 GB: 32‑bit tops at OPT‑1.3B; 4‑bit trains OPT‑6.7B and enables LLaMA‑7B on a single 80 GB GPU.
> 
> - Ablations on quantization of second moment (Table 1)
>   • Zero‑point removal for the second moment (DE‑0 or Linear mapping) is critical: without it, many runs are unstable; with Rank‑1 normalization + Linear mapping, BLEU reaches 67.8 (best), matching 32‑bit convergence while retaining 4‑bit states.
> 
> Summary for this family: Across identical datasets spanning NLU, QA, NLG, CLS, MT, and LLaMA instruction tuning, 4‑bit optimizers match 32‑bit/8‑bit performance while delivering large memory reductions (≈35–58%) and capacity gains (e.g., training 6.7B on 80 GB). Critical to stability is excluding the zero point when quantizing the second moment and using Rank‑1 normalization; these ablations empirically yield lossless convergence on E2E‑NLG.
> 
> 3) Efficient gradients for diffusion models via adjoint methods (AdjointDEIS)
> Identical dataset (within-paper): SYN‑MAD 2022 (derived from FRLL) face morphing; compared across the same FR systems.
> 
> - MMPMR at FMR=0.1% vs prior diffusion/GAN baselines (Table 1) 
>   • DiM + AdjointDEIS‑1 (ODE): AdaFace 99.8; ArcFace 98.77; ElasticFace 99.39; NFE 2250.
>   • DiM + AdjointDEIS‑1 (SDE): 98.57 / 97.96 / 97.75; NFE 2250.
>   • Morph‑PIPE (diffusion baseline): 95.91 / 92.84 / 95.5; NFE 2350.
>   • DiM‑A: 92.23 / 90.18 / 93.05; NFE 350. Fast‑DiM: 92.02 / 90.18 / 93.05; NFE 300.
>   • GAN baselines: MIPGAN‑I 72.19 / 77.51 / 66.46; MIPGAN‑II 70.55 / 72.19 / 65.24. WebMorph (commercial): 97.96 / 96.93 / 98.36.
>   • Best overall: AdjointDEIS (ODE variant) achieves the highest MMPMR across all three FR systems; the SDE variant also improves over prior diffusion baselines. NFE is similar to Morph‑PIPE and higher than DiM/Fast‑DiM (which use fewer steps but are less effective).
> 
> Summary for this family: On identical evaluation (SYN‑MAD 2022 with three FR systems), adjoint-based gradient computation for guided generation (AdjointDEIS) yields the strongest attack success (MMPMR), exceeding diffusion and GAN baselines; ODE‑based adjoint outperforms SDE‑based adjoint at the same NFE.
> 
> 4) Representation learning biases in JEPA (self‑distillation) vs MAE (reconstruction)
> No shared dataset with other papers; within‑paper experiments include deep linear models, synthetic temporal models, and an ImageNet (64×64) CCA study.
> 
> - Deep linear simulations (Fig. 1–2): With feature parameters {λi} (covariances) and {ρi} (regression coefficients), both objectives show stepwise (greedy) learning in λ when λ,ρ co‑vary (Distribution 1). When λ and ρ vary oppositely (Distribution 2), JEPA reverses the learning order and prioritizes high‑ρ (influential) features; MAE retains λ‑ordering.
> 
> - Temporal (linear) model (Fig. 3): Derived expressions λa=γa||va||^2 and ρa=γa||va||^2/(σa^2+||va||^2) confirm JEPA prioritizes slowly varying, less noisy features (higher ρa). Simulations match theory as sequence length (T) changes.
> 
> - ImageNet 64×64 CCA (Appendix D/Fig. 7): I‑JEPA vs MAE (ViT encoders). Across training, JEPA exhibits higher feature similarity between full and bottom‑variance PCA subspace and lower similarity between full and top subspace; MAE shows the reverse. This empirically supports that JEPA focuses on low‑variance, semantic subspaces.
> 
> Summary for this family: Experiments (synthetic and on ImageNet 64×64) consistently show the JEPA objective’s bias toward influential (high‑ρ) and low‑variance features, while MAE emphasizes high‑variance reconstruction. These results are trends/curves (no single scalar benchmarks) and align with the theory.
> 
> 5) Spectral analysis and EI‑constrained RNNs (Dale’s Law)
> No shared datasets with other papers; within‑paper experiments include Adding Problem, Sequential MNIST, PTB language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task.
> 
> - Across tasks (Fig. 2): Column EI (ColEI) networks learn worse and with higher variance than DANNs and standard RNNs; gradient clipping benefits ColEI more. DANN (EI architecture) matches standard RNNs.
> 
> - Spectrum matters (Fig. 3–4): ColEI weight matrices yield multimodal, dispersed singular value distributions (including large singular values) vs unimodal spectra for standard RNNs/DANNs. Spectrum-transplant experiments show spectral properties affect performance more than sign constraints.
> 
> - EI ratio and network size (Figs. 5–7): For ColEI, reducing inhibitory proportion or using small networks lowers Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) and degrades performance; larger ColEI networks and balanced E/I improve NSE and learning. DANN’s spectra/performance remain robust to EI ratio and size.
> 
> Summary for this family: Experimental curves demonstrate that the spectral distribution—not just sign constraints—drives the performance gap in EI RNNs. DANNs achieve RNN‑like performance and unimodal spectra; ColEI underperforms unless large and balanced, with NSE strongly predicting test error.
> 
> Cross‑family synthesis by task type
> - Dense visual detection/association vs guided diffusion:
>   • PBADet (anchor‑free) improves association accuracy over prior one‑stage/joint baselines on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman.
>   • AdjointDEIS maximizes attack success in guided generation for face morphing on SYN‑MAD 2022, surpassing diffusion/GAN baselines on identical FR evaluations.
>   • No identical datasets between these families, but both show state‑of‑the‑art improvements in crowded/identity‑constrained vision.
> 
> - Training efficiency and capacity vs representation bias:
>   • 4‑bit optimizers consistently match 32‑bit across diverse workloads while reducing memory and enabling larger models (e.g., OPT‑6.7B, LLaMA‑7B on single 80 GB GPU). Ablations prove specific quantization choices (no zero‑point, Rank‑1 normalization) are critical to retain accuracy.
>   • JEPA vs MAE: Trends (CCA and simulations) indicate JEPA’s bias toward low‑variance, influential features—complementary to capacity/convergence results above.
> 
> - Time‑series/control‑style tasks with biology‑inspired constraints:
>   • Dale‑compliant RNNs (ColEI) underperform unless spectral properties are controlled; DANN reformulations preserve EI constraints while matching standard RNN performance. This complements the training‑efficiency work by identifying spectral diagnostics (NSE) predictive of learning.
> 
> Bottom line
> - There are no identical datasets shared across the five works; each paper’s identical‑dataset comparisons are internal to their evaluation suites.
> - For edge/crowded human‑part association, PBADet shows consistent SOTA‑style gains on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts (especially medium/large scales and hand mismatching rates), and CrowdHuman (best MR−2/AP for body/face).
> - For low‑VRAM finetuning, 4‑bit optimizers match or exceed 32‑bit/8‑bit performance across GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet‑1k, WMT14, E2E‑NLG, and LLaMA tuning while reducing memory by ~35–58% and expanding feasible model sizes.
> - For diffusion‑model gradient computation, AdjointDEIS achieves the highest MMPMR on SYN‑MAD 2022 across three FR systems, outperforming DiM, Fast‑DiM, Morph‑PIPE, and GANs.
> - For representation learning biases, JEPA prioritizes high‑influence, low‑variance features (validated on synthetic and ImageNet CCA), while MAE emphasizes high‑variance reconstruction.
> - For EI‑constrained time‑series/control, DANNs match standard RNNs; ColEI underperforms unless spectra are corrected. NSE reliably predicts EI RNN performance.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection contains works matching each need. Here is the mapping and a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Part–body association (hands/face linked to person, crowded scenes)
> **PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free, single part-to-body center offset) is the direct match. On **BodyHands**, PBADet (YOLOv7) reaches HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98, beating BPJDet (85.9/86.91/84.39), BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48), and others by large margins with a smaller model. On **COCOHumanParts** it is on par with BPJDet for overall AP (43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3 for YOLOv5l6) but leads medium/large-object and person/foot APs, with the lowest mMR-2 for head, face, and both hands. On **CrowdHuman** face–body, it achieves the best body MR-2 (36.5 vs BPJDet's 40.7) with competitive AP (91.6). Ablations confirm association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment each boost association accuracy (JointAP 78.07 → 85.98).
> 
> ## 2. Low-bit Adam states for VRAM-constrained fine-tuning
> **4-bit Optimizers** compresses Adam/AdamW states to 4 bits (smaller B128 blocks; rank-1 normalization; zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for the second moment; optional factorization). Results: it **matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW** on GLUE (89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD (94.5 vs 94.6), E2E-NLG (67.8 vs 67.7), ImageNet/Swin-T (80.8 vs 81.2), WMT14 (26.28 vs 26.61), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (e.g., MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7 at 7B). Memory savings reach **57.7%** (LLaMA-7B: 75.4 → 31.9 GB, trainable on one 80 GB GPU; 4× larger OPT models fit under a budget). 8-bit AdamW saves less (37.1% on RoBERTa-L) and Adafactor/SM3 save more but degrade accuracy. Caveat: optimal quantization settings may be task-dependent.
> 
> ## 3. Gradient computation for diffusion guidance (adjoint methods)
> **AdjointDEIS** solves the continuous adjoint equations for diffusion ODEs **and SDEs** using exponential integrators in the log-SNR domain, with proven k-th-order convergence, jointly optimizing latent x_T, conditioning z, and parameters θ (training-free). On SYN-MAD 2022 face-morphing, DiM+AdjointDEIS-1(ODE) achieves MMPMR 99.8/98.77/99.39 (ArcFace/ElasticFace/AdaFace at FMR 0.1%), beating DiM-A (92.23/90.18/93.05), Fast-DiM, Morph-PIPE (95.91/92.84/95.5), and GAN-inversion baselines (MIPGAN ~65–77). The **SDE variant is slightly worse** (98.57/97.96/97.75) due to large-step discretization difficulty. Related but different: Universal Guidance (training-free forward/backward guidance, no adjoints) and RTB (reward-guided posterior sampling via trajectory balance) — neither uses adjoint methods.
> 
> ## 4. Joint-embedding / similarity-based representation learning and its biases
> Two works match.
> - **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning**: shows full-batch InfoNCE optima (positive similarity 1, negative −1/(n−1)) and proves small mini-batches raise the variance of negative-pair similarities. Its auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy across temperatures and batch sizes — e.g., SimCLR on full ImageNet 51.79 → 52.48; ImageNet-100 t=0.3: 72.30 → 74.04 — with gains largest at small batch sizes. Caveats: it can suppress semantically meaningful variance and adds a tuning hyperparameter λ.
> - **LDReg** counters the opposite bias — (local) dimensional collapse in SSL — by regularizing local intrinsic dimensionality (Fisher-Rao/LID). On ImageNet linear eval it improves SimCLR 64.3 → 64.8, SimCLR-Tuned 67.2 → 67.5, BYOL 67.6 → 68.5, MAE 57.0 → 57.6, plus gains in transfer learning and COCO detection/segmentation; global covariance regularizers barely helped, and forcing very low LID triggers full collapse.
> 
> ## 5. EI-constrained RNNs and spectral analysis
> **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** directly addresses EI RNNs. Simple column-partitioned EI (ColEI) networks learn worse and with more seed variance on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition, and are highly unstable without gradient clipping; recurrent DANN networks match standard RNNs. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the cause is not sign constraints but the initial recurrent-weight spectrum: ColEI has multimodal, dispersed singular values (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), while standard/DANN RNNs follow the quarter-circle random-matrix law. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error and predicts which EI architectures train well — a diagnostic for designing stable EI RNNs. Complementary: the Hessian power-law analysis paper shows spectral analysis of deep networks can predict generalization (e.g., d_ks predicting LLM generalization up to 0.98), though it targets feedforward/LLM Hessians, not RNN training stability.
> 
> **Overall**: every requested capability has at least one matching work, and the experimental evidence is mutually consistent — anchor-free part–body association gives the best Precision/F1-style association metrics; 4-bit optimizers give lossless fine-tuning with ~58% memory savings; adjoint-based diffusion guidance gives SOTA guided generation (with the ODE variant beating the SDE variant); similarity-based SSL benefits from variance reduction (and from local-dimensionality regularization against collapse); and EI-RNN instability is attributable to spectral pathology rather than sign constraints, with NSE as a predictive diagnostic.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes—all five needs are addressed by works in the collection. Here is how each maps and how their experiments compare.
> 
> ## 1. Anchor-free part–body association (hands/face → person) — PBADet
> PBADet is a one-stage anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset (supports head, face, L/R hands, feet), with classification/localization/association branches and task-alignment loss.
> - **BodyHands (hand-body):** HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (YOLOv7, 36.9M) — beats BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13), BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48), OpenPose and MaskR-CNN variants by large margins.
> - **COCOHumanParts (multi-part):** all-category AP on par with BPJDet (43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3), but leads on person/feet AP and achieves the **lowest mMR-2** (miss-matching rate) on head, face, both hands and right foot — i.e., better association.
> - **CrowdHuman (face-body, crowded):** leading body MR-2, though the advantage over BPJDet is smaller for this single-part task.
> - **vs ED-Pose (Swin-L pose):** substantially higher precision, recall and F1 for hands/feet.
> - **Ablations:** anchor-free beats anchor-based (HandAP 89.1 vs 88.4; JointAP 85.98 vs 85.28) and part-to-body beats body-to-point association; association loss, multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each help.
> 
> ## 2. Tight-VRAM Adam fine-tuning with low-bit states — 4-bit Optimizers
> Compresses Adam/AdamW states to 4 bits (first moment B128/dynamic-exponent, second moment rank-1/linear with zero-point exclusion; optional factorization → 4-bit Factor).
> - **Accuracy:** matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (89.1 vs 88.9), ImageNet/Swin-T (80.8 vs 81.2), E2E-NLG (67.8 vs 67.7), SQuAD (94.5 vs 94.6), WMT14 (26.28 vs 26.61); comparable on pretraining.
> - **Memory:** states 2× smaller than 8-bit AdamW and ~4× smaller for 4-bit Factor; LLaMA-7B fine-tune drops 75.4→31.9 GB (57.7% saved), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU and 4× larger OPT under a memory budget; also faster via reduced FSDP communication.
> - **Ablations:** quantizing both moments costs little; smaller blocks and factored second moment recover accuracy while saving more memory.
> 
> ## 3. Adjoint-based gradient guidance for diffusion models — AdjointDEIS
> Backpropagates through the diffusion ODE/SDE by solving continuous adjoint equations with bespoke exponential-integrator solvers (log-SNR domain), jointly optimizing latent x_T, conditioning z and model params θ; shows the diffusion-SDE adjoint reduces to an ODE and supports SDEs (more general than AdjointDPM, which is coupled to its forward solver).
> - **Experiments (face-morphing, SYN-MAD 2022/MMPMR):** DiM+AdjointDEIS-1 reaches 99.8/98.77/99.39 MMPMR on ArcFace/ElasticFace/AdaFace at FMR 0.1%, beating DiM-A, Fast-DiM, Morph-PIPE and GAN baselines; the SDE variant is slightly lower (98.57/97.96/97.75) due to large-step discretization difficulty. Provides convergence-order guarantees and non-stiff adjoint form (more stable than Euler-Maruyama/Euler adjoints).
> 
> ## 4. Joint-embedding / similarity-based representation learning (not pixel MSE)
> Three complementary results:
> - **JEPA implicit bias (deep linear analysis):** JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient) while MAE learns high-variance/noisy features; the bias appears only with deep encoders. ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features from full + bottom-25%-variance (perceptual) images show **higher CCA similarity than MAE throughout training**, while MAE aligns better with the top-variance subspace — JEPA learns the semantically rich low-variance subspace faster.
> - **Embedding similarities in contrastive learning:** optimal full-batch embeddings have pos-similarity 1 and neg-similarity −1/(n−1); small batches inflate neg-similarity variance and hurt quality. An auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves top-1 on CIFAR-10/100 across temperatures and ImageNet-100 (e.g., t=0.3: 74.04 vs 72.30), full ImageNet 52.48 vs 51.79, cutting neg-pair variance (batch 32: 0.1649→0.1008); gains concentrate at small batch sizes, but can suppress meaningful semantic variance.
> - **LDReg (dimensional-collapse bias):** regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality (Fisher-Rao based). ImageNet linear eval: SimCLR 64.3→64.8, BYOL 67.6→68.5, MAE 57.0→57.6; larger with 1000-epoch/4096-batch (69.0→69.8); boosts transfer (CIFAR-100 71.6→75.1, Cars 35.3→41.6) and COCO detection/segmentation. Global covariance/variance regularizers barely help, showing local collapse is the key bias to correct.
> 
> ## 5. Spectral analysis & EI-constrained RNNs
> - **Dale's-law RNNs:** Column-constrained EI (ColEI) RNNs train worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs across adding, sMNIST, PTB and object recognition; ColEI is unstable without gradient clipping. Spectral analysis shows ColEI has a multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum (rank-one nilpotent column-mean + random matrix) versus the random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur form of standard/DANN RNNs. Spectrum-transplant experiments show **the singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints** (spectrum ≈1.5–2% error vs ~0.7–1% for sign constraints). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error and predicts trainability; DANN-style EI architectures keep standard-like spectra (robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron), so they preserve stability under EI constraints, whereas ColEI needs gradient clipping.
> - **Hessian spectral analysis in deep nets:** well-trained CNNs and LLMs exhibit a power-law Hessian spectrum (KS-tested; absent in random networks). The power-law exponent correlates with generalization — LeNet/CIFAR-10 Pearson 0.72 with test error and d_ks predicting LLM generalization up to 0.98; the structure is lost with small width/depth, noisy labels or large batches, and LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce it. It reveals a robust low-dimensional subspace tied to optimization and generalization.
> 
> ## Cross-area analysis
> The strongest, most directly usable results are PBADet (clear SOTA on part-body association with concrete Precision/F1 gains over ED-Pose) and the 4-bit optimizer (lossless accuracy at ~2–4× state compression). AdjointDEIS works but is evaluated only on face-morphing and is sensitive to SDE step size. For representation learning, the three works agree on one theme — embedding-space objectives avoid noisy/high-variance pixel features and benefit from explicit control (variance reduction or LID regularization), but all report caveats (possible suppression of meaningful variance; LDReg's LID estimation degrades in high dimensions). The RNN/Hessian spectral works converge on the same insight from different angles: the weight/Hessian spectrum, not just architecture or sign constraints, governs training stability and generalization, and can be used as a pre-training diagnostic (NSE, power-law slope). No single work covers all five needs, but the collection provides a matching method for each.

<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross-paper comparison of experimental results
> 
> 1) Efficient one-stage, anchor-free part–body association in vision (PBADet vs prior art)
> - Identical datasets (BodyHands):
>   - PBADet outperforms BPJDet (anchor-based) and prior two-stage baselines across all metrics (Table 1). Using identical YOLOv5l6 backbones, PBADet achieves higher Hand AP (88.1 vs 85.9), higher Conditional Accuracy (92.71 vs 86.91), and higher Joint AP (85.73 vs 84.39). With a YOLOv7 backbone, PBADet further improves to 89.1 AP, 92.62 Conditional Accuracy, and 85.98 Joint AP.
> - Identical datasets (COCOHumanParts):
>   - Overall detection AP.5:.95 is close (PBADet YOLOv5l6 43.0/41.8 original/subordinate vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 43.6/43.3), but PBADet leads on mid/large objects (APM/APL: 66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4 vs 63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9; Table 2) and is competitive on per-category AP (e.g., person 62.4 vs 61.3; feet categories 30.9–31.5 vs 30.2–30.9).
>   - Association robustness (mMR−2, lower is better): PBADet records the lowest mMR−2 on several parts (e.g., head 27.9–29.2 vs BPJDet l6 30.8; hands and right foot also improved; Table 3).
> - Similar dataset type (crowded scenes; CrowdHuman):
>   - PBADet achieves best MR−2 for body (36.5 with YOLOv7; Table 5) and highest body AP (91.6). Its body–face mMR−2 is comparable to BPJDet (50.8 vs 50.1; Tables 5–6). Among joint detectors, PBADet has the best body MR−2 and competitive AP (Table 6).
> - Efficiency representation (from Figure 1): PBADet’s part-to-body encoding shortens the extended representation (5+K+2 vs BPJDet’s 6+K+2K), reflecting a simpler one-stage, anchor-free formulation (decoding simplified in Section 3.4), while experiments confirm accuracy gains.
> 
> 2) Training deep networks under E/I constraints (Dale’s Law): spectral properties and stability
> - Identical datasets/tasks (Adding, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic Object Recognition; Figure 2):
>   - Standard RNNs and DANNs consistently learn well; ColEI (column-sign constrained) learns worse across all four benchmarks (Figure 2A–D). Gradient clipping helps ColEI more but does not close the gap.
> - Spectral transplant experiments (Sequential MNIST; Figure 4):
>   - Matching experiments show singular value spectra matter more than sign constraints: giving standard RNNs ColEI spectra harms performance more than freezing signs, and giving ColEI RNNs standard spectra helps considerably (Figure 4B–C). Thus, spectrum explains most of the ColEI–RNN performance gap.
> - Effect of EI ratio and network size (Sequential MNIST; Figures 5–7):
>   - ColEI networks learn worse with fewer inhibitory units and smaller sizes; both correlate with more dispersed, multimodal singular value spectra and lower normalized SVD entropy (NSE). Larger ColEI networks and more balanced EI ratios raise NSE and reduce test error. DANNs maintain high NSE and strong performance across EI ratios and sizes.
> 
> 3) Implicit bias of JEPA vs MAE in self-supervised learning
> - Identical synthetic setups (deep linear models):
>   - Simulations of the learned encoder norms (Figure 1) and ODE dynamics (Figure 2, Theorems 3.2–3.5) show: MAE learns features in order of higher covariance λ; JEPA learns features in order of larger regression coefficient ρ (feature influence). When λ and ρ rank features differently, JEPA’s learning order inverts relative to MAE (Figure 1e–f, Figure 2c,f).
> - Similar dataset type (ImageNet-1K at 64×64; Appendix D Figure 7):
>   - JEPA reaches higher mean CCA to the “bottom” PCA subspace (perception-relevant, low-variance) earlier and maintains lower similarity to “top” variance subspace than MAE throughout training. This empirically supports JEPA’s bias toward influential (predictive, low-variance) features over high-variance details.
> 
> 4) Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets (RCPS) with online calibration and label budgeting
> - Identical simulation setting (Bernoulli adding; Figure 2):
>   - All label policies meet the anytime-valid safety target (violation rate ≈ α=0.05; Figure 2a). ‘Pretrain’ and ‘Learned’ label policies (which use model-based risk prediction and/or learned label probabilities) achieve lower final β̂ (tighter sets) than ‘all’ and ‘oblivious’ policies for the same label budget (Figures 2b–c), hence better utility under the same risk guarantee.
> - Identical dataset (ImageNet classification; Figure 3):
>   - Again, all methods control safety violations below α=0.05 (Figure 3a). ‘Pretrain’ and ‘Learned’ label policies reach smaller β̂ faster (Figure 3c) and achieve lower final β̂ than baselines (Figure 3b), demonstrating improved label-efficiency under the same anytime-valid guarantee.
> 
> 5) Text-space Graph Foundation Models (GFMs): benchmarks across graphs and tasks
> - Node classification co-training (identical datasets: Cora, CiteSeer, Arxiv, Arxiv-2023, E-commerce suite; Table 1):
>   - Across all datasets, conventional GCN trained from scratch provides a strong baseline (Avg 79.47). Co-training GFMs often trail the best single-task GCN on citation graphs; e.g., OFA (ID) averages 79.08 vs GCN 79.47. LLaGA sometimes improves within E-commerce (e.g., Photo, Sports, Products), but cross-domain co-training can degrade accuracy (e.g., Citation averages drop for OFA CD and LLaGA CD; Table 1). Among SSL baselines, DGI shows signs of benefiting from larger data (ID/CD settings slightly better than ST on some datasets). Overall, co-training yields mixed results at node level; dataset/domain alignment matters.
> - Link prediction co-training (identical small graphs: Cora, CiteSeer, Pubmed; Figure 4, Table 3):
>   - Link-specific methods dominate: BUDDY achieves the highest Hits@100 on average (Single-task 90.41; stable under co-train 90.05) and trains much faster than SEAL or LLaGA (Table 3). Among GFMs, LLaGA performs best (co-train 85.03) but still behind BUDDY.
>   - At larger scale (citation + e-commerce; Table 4), co-training substantially boosts BUDDY (Avg 86.18 vs 75.48 single-task), while GCN’s performance remains low and inconsistent. This shows strong positive transfer for link prediction when appropriate structural inductive biases (e.g., structural embeddings) are used.
> - Graph classification co-training (molecular datasets; Table 5):
>   - Co-training in text space provides clear gains over single-dataset training. OFA achieves the best results across multiple datasets (e.g., Tox21 82.5 ROC-AUC vs single-text 74.49 and single-atom 74.6; ToxCast 68.39 vs 60.24/61.5; PCBA AP 0.236 vs 0.174/0.202). GraphCL improves when pre-trained on large-scale data (ZINC) but underperforms OFA in the unified co-training setting.
> - Cross-task co-training (node/link/graph; Table 6):
>   - Adding graph-level tasks to node/link co-training consistently improves graph-level performance (e.g., PCBA AP from 0.233 single-task to 0.265 with link+graph; Graph Avg also increases). However, node- and link-level averages can decrease under cross-task co-training (trade-off).
> - Pre-training → downstream transfer on node classification (Cora, History, Ratings; Table 7):
>   - Fine-tuning after pre-training provides limited gains over strong text-encoder baselines. A simple SBERT+propagation baseline performs competitively in few-shot and often better than graph in-context learning variants on homophilous graphs. Prodigy and GPPT underperform without suitable semantic label embeddings.
> - Cross-task transfer (node → link/graph; Pubmed, HIV; Table 8):
>   - Zero-shot/few-shot across tasks remains weak for current GFMs. After fine-tuning, node→graph transfer is positive (e.g., HIV ROC-AUC: OFA FT 75.35 vs SBERT FT 74.2), but node→link transfer remains challenging (Pubmed Hits@100: MAE FT 36.83; OFA FT 68.7).
> - Additional insights from controlled ablations (Tables 2, 14, 16–20):
>   - For node-level co-training, replacing GCN backbone with fixed-aggregation SGC sometimes reduces negative transfer on homophilous data, while offering no advantage on heterophilous graphs.
>   - Stronger text encoders (MPNet vs MiniLM) consistently raise node-level performance in co-trained OFA (Table 16), indicating feature encoder choice is a key determinant.
>   - Balancing datasets alone does not eliminate negative transfer; domain similarity and structural inductive bias are critical (Tables 19–20).
> 
> Overall takeaways by method and dataset type
> - PBADet vs BPJDet and others (vision, identical datasets): PBADet provides state-of-the-art or competitive detection and association on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts, with the best MR−2 on CrowdHuman bodies. Gains are clearest on BodyHands (joint AP and conditional accuracy) and on mid/large objects in COCOHumanParts.
> - E/I-constrained RNNs (identical tasks): DANNs and standard RNNs outperform ColEI across adding, seq-MNIST, PTB, and naturalistic classification. Spectral properties (unimodal, clustered singular values) explain the performance gap; NSE predicts learning success.
> - JEPA vs MAE (similar setups and ImageNet): JEPA prioritizes influential, predictive features (high ρ), learning low-variance “semantic” subspaces faster than MAE; MAE prioritizes high-variance directions (high λ). On ImageNet, JEPA aligns earlier with the bottom PCA space.
> - RCPS (identical simulation and ImageNet): All policies preserve anytime-valid safety, but model-informed ‘pretrain’/‘learned’ policies reach tighter prediction sets (smaller β̂) with fewer labels.
> - Text-space GFMs (graphs; identical datasets):
>   - Node classification: co-training brings mixed gains; best-in-class remains per-dataset GCN on citation graphs; E-commerce graphs show occasional improvements with LLaGA/OFA.
>   - Link prediction: co-training strongly benefits link-specific models with structural embeddings (BUDDY), both on small and large graphs. GFMs lag behind link-specific baselines on identical datasets.
>   - Graph classification: co-training in text space consistently beats single-dataset training on molecular datasets (OFA best), including AP/ROC-AUC improvements.
>   - Cross-task co-training improves graph-level performance but can degrade node/link averages.
>   - Pre-train→fine-tune brings modest gains; zero-/few-shot cross-task transfer remains limited; strong text encoders and semantic label embeddings are crucial.
> 
> All comparisons above rely strictly on the reported figures and tables in the provided papers.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## A small set of works covering all five topics
> 
> **1. Part-body association (topic 1):** *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024). It contrasts with multi-stage/heuristic methods (two-stage BodyHands network, BPJDet's per-part body-to-part offsets) by extending anchor-free object detection with a *single part-to-body center offset*, giving O(1) association complexity per part.
> 
> **2. Biological E/I constraints (topic 2):** *Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023). Trains RNNs under Dale's law (ColEI column sign constraints vs. DANN), analyzes singular-value spectra and normalised SVD entropy (NSE), stability/exploding gradients, with projected-gradient-descent training and gradient clipping.
> 
> **3. Joint-embedding vs. reconstruction SSL (topic 3):** *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024). Solves training dynamics of JEPA (self-distillation) vs. MAE (reconstruction) in deep linear networks, with ImageNet-1K I-JEPA vs. MAE feature-alignment (CCA) experiments. Supporting cosine-similarity analysis: *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet, InfoNCE cosine alignment, mini-batch variance).
> 
> **4. Active anytime-valid risk control (topic 4):** *Active, Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets* (NeurIPS 2024). Sequential/online calibration via e-processes and betting, active label policies under a label budget, optimal predictor/policy with regret bounds, tested on ImageNet and simulations (θ=0.1, α=0.05, risk < α violation rates).
> 
> **5. Text-space graph foundation models (topic 5):** *Text-Space Graph Foundation Models: Comprehensive Benchmarks and New Insights* (NeurIPS 2024 Datasets & Benchmarks). 23 text-attributed datasets across domains, LLM/vision-language encoders as unified text feature space, graph prompts/SSL/LLM-with-graph-projector building blocks, zero-shot/few-shot/fine-tuning evaluation, in-context learning and co-training insights.
> 
> ## Comparison and analysis of experimental results
> 
> **Topic 1 (PBADet):** The strongest results in the set. On BodyHands it beats all SOTA on every metric — YOLOv7 backbone: HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 vs. BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39 — with a smaller model (36.9M params, 1024 size vs. 86.1M/1536). On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet in AP (42.7/41.5 vs 43.6/43.3 all-categories) but leads in AP_M (65.8) and AP_L (66.7) and in per-part association (lowest mMR-2 for head, face, hands, right foot), and far exceeds HierR-CNN. Ablations show the association head, multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each help; anchor-free part-to-body beats anchor-based body-to-part.
> 
> **Topic 2 (Dale's Law):** ColEI networks learn consistently worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition. Sign constraints hurt but don't explain the full gap (e.g., MNIST: ~1% from sign constraints vs. ~2.3% total). Spectrum-transplant experiments prove the singular-value *spectrum* matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final error across EI ratios and sizes (higher NSE ⇒ better learning; DANN stays ~0.95 even with 1 inhibitory neuron). Gradient clipping helps ColEI most, confirming the exploding-gradient/stability story. Notably, no direct AUROC/Precision/F1; this is task-error based.
> 
> **Topic 3 (JEPA vs MAE):** In deep linear models both objectives show greedy, step-wise feature learning, but critical-time analysis proves JEPA prioritizes "influential" (high-regression-coefficient ρ) features with depth strengthening the bias, while MAE ordering is set by covariance λ (can learn noisy, high-variance features). At the same λ but different ρ, JEPA *inverts* the learning order relative to MAE; the effect only appears when the encoder is deep. ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features (CCA) than MAE — linking to JEPA's reported faster/better downstream classification. Note: both objectives here use MSE; the paper does **not** compare CE vs MSE. The contrastive-learning companion paper does analyze embedding cosine similarity: optimal encoders give positive-pair similarity 1 and negative-pair −1/(n−1); mini-batches raise negative-pair variance (degrading quality), fixed by a variance-reduction loss that improves top-1 on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and ImageNet.
> 
> **Topic 4 (active risk control):** Sequential, anytime-valid guarantee P(ρ(β̂_t) ≤ θ for all t) ≥ 1−α via betting e-processes. Label policies are label-efficient, converging to the optimal β* faster than naive baselines; the optimal policy is proportional to conditional-risk std, and model-based predictors reduce variance. Limitations: i.i.d. assumption, bounded label policies. This paper does **not** report AUROC/Precision/F1 — its metrics are miscoverage risk, utility, label budget and violation rates, so that specific request is only partially met.
> 
> **Topic 5 (GFMs):** Mixed results — the least "rosy" set. Text-space projection preserves/improves node classification on text-attributed graphs (Arxiv 71.53→73.10) but can hurt non-text data (Tolokers drops) unless prompts are good. Under co-training, GFM methods (OFA, LLaGA, GraphMAE, DGI) mostly *underperform* GCN trained from scratch (e.g., node-level co-training: GCN-ST 79.47 Avg vs. OFA-CD 78.24, LLaGA-CD 78.01); DGI shows potential scaling benefit. Cross-task co-training helps OneForAll (Node→Link 74.05→79.30) but not LLaGA; the benefit comes from inductive bias, not features (SGC replacement improves results). For link prediction, GFM methods lag task-specific models like BUDDY/SEAL. Strong LLM encoders mitigate feature heterogeneity; SGC fails on heterophilous graphs. Evaluation is single-seed (a robustness limitation), and it covers zero-shot, few-shot and fine-tuning but not explicit early-stopping reporting.
> 
> **Overall:** PBADet delivers the most decisive SOTA wins; the Dale's Law and JEPA papers give clean, controlled mechanistic comparisons (with JEPA's claim partially relying on simplified linear settings); the risk-control paper is rigorous but evaluates a different metric set than requested (no AUROC/Precision/F1); the GFM benchmark is the most honest about negative results, showing foundation-model gains are conditional and often not superior to well-tuned task-specific training.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on my searches, here is a concise set of works covering all five topics, with a comparison of their experimental results:
> 
> ## Selected Works (5 papers)
> 
> **(1) PBADet** – One-stage anchor-free part-body association (ICLR 2024)
> - **What it covers**: Extends anchor-free detection with a single part-to-body center offset, contrasting with heavier two-stage pipelines and BPJDet's body-to-part offsets (which scale with number of parts and suffer from invisible parts).
> - **Key results**: On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves 89.1 hand AP, 92.62 conditional accuracy, 85.98 joint AP — beating BPJDet (YOLOv5l6: 85.9/86.91/84.39) with fewer parameters (36.9M vs 41.2M) and smaller input size (1024 vs 1536). On COCOHumanParts, it reaches 42.7–43.0 AP@.5:.95 (vs HierR-CNN). Ablations confirm association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment all contribute.
> 
> **(2) "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023) — *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective*
> - **What it covers**: Training EI (Dale-like, ColEI vs DANN) RNNs; analyzes spectral properties, normalised SVD entropy (NSE), and stability (gradient clipping, spectral radius).
> - **Key results**: ColEI learns worse and with higher variance across 4 tasks (adding, seq-MNIST, PTB, object recognition); gradient clipping helps most. SVD transplants show the singular-value spectrum (not sign constraints) drives the gap. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error — higher NSE → better learning. Balanced E/I ratios and larger sizes raise NSE and performance.
> 
> **(3) "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - **What it covers**: Implicit bias of joint-embedding/self-distillation (JEPA) vs reconstruction (MAE) objectives on deep linear networks; cosine-similarity/feature-embedding comparison via CCA.
> - **Key results**: JEPA is biased to learn high-influence (predictive) features, while MAE only prioritizes high-variance/noisy features; this bias appears only for deep encoders. On ImageNet, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE features, measured by CCA throughout training. Analysis uses gradient-flow ODEs with critical times.
> 
> **(4) "Active, Anytime-Valid Risk Controlling Prediction Sets"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - **What it covers**: Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets with online calibration and label budgets via e-processes/betting; optimal labeling policies and predictors.
> - **Key results**: On simulations and ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05), learned/pretrained labeling policies cut risk faster than baselines while keeping violation rates below α; regret bounds relate policy/predictor error to wealth growth. Note: AUROC/Precision/F1 are not reported in this paper — it uses risk (miscoverage) and label-budget metrics instead.
> 
> **(5) "Text-space Graph Foundation Models: Comprehensive Benchmarks and New Insights"**
> - **What it covers**: Text-space GFMs aligning diverse graphs via language/LLM embeddings, Transformers/vision–language encoders, in-context learning, and (parameter-efficient) fine-tuning across 23 datasets.
> - **Key results**: Text-space projection preserves/improves performance (Arxiv 71.53→73.10); cross-task node→link co-training helps OneForAll (74.05→79.30) but not LLaGA; simple SBERT embeddings + feature propagation beat almost all graph in-context learning on homophilous graphs (e.g., 74.2 vs OFA 68.7 on Pubmed); strong LLM encoders mitigate feature heterogeneity; semantic label embeddings are critical for prompt transferability.
> 
> ## Cross-method comparison
> - **Efficiency/robustness theme**: PBADet shows compact representations beat heavy multi-stage pipelines; the Dale-law paper shows spectral health (NSE) predicts learning; the JEPA paper shows objective choice changes feature quality.
> - **Calibration/robust evaluation**: Only paper (4) explicitly handles calibration and anytime-valid guarantees (risk control, online, label-efficient). Papers (1)–(3) focus on accuracy/spectral/metrics rather than calibration, though (2) discusses stability via gradient clipping and (3) notes limitations (deep-linear/linearized setup only).
> - **Metric mismatch**: Topic (4) asks for AUROC/Precision/F1, but the RCPS paper reports risk-control/label-budget metrics; no paper in the collection reports AUROC for this RCPS framework. The Dale-law paper does not use SGD/Adam explicitly (gradient clipping/spectral radius are the focus), and no paper in the collection compares CE vs MSE in a self-supervised setup — the JEPA paper compares MSE-style latent-space prediction vs reconstruction instead.

Can you point me to papers that jointly address these components end-to-end so I can design the detection, SSL, graph unification, and online calibration stack?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
