**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross-paper comparison of experimental results (only from the provided figures/tables)
> 
> 1) Part–body association detection (PBADet vs prior art) on identical datasets
> - BodyHands (Table 1):
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1, 92.71, 85.73.
>   • Best prior one-stage baseline (BPJDet YOLOv5l6): 85.9, 86.91, 84.39.
>   • Result: PBADet tops all metrics on BodyHands; with same backbone YOLOv5l6 it improves Joint AP from 84.39 to 85.73.
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2; identical protocol with “original/subordinate” APs, and per-category):
>   • Overall AP.5:.95: PBADet YOLOv5l6 43.0/41.8; BPJDet YOLOv5l6 43.6/43.3.
>   • Size breakdown: PBADet YOLOv5l6 APM 66.2/65.0 and APL 67.2/64.4 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 APM 63.8/63.2 and APL 61.8/58.9 (PBADet higher for M/L).
>   • Per-category APs: PBADet YOLOv5l6 (person 62.4, feet 30.9 & 31.5) marginally better on person/feet; heads/faces comparable (54–55). 
>   • Association robustness (mMR−2, Table 3, lower is better): PBADet YOLOv5l6 (head 27.9, face 30.5, l-hand 36.2, r-hand 40.8, r-foot 50.4, l-foot 47.9) improves over BPJDet YOLOv5l6 (30.8, 31.8, 41.6, 42.2, 49.1, 50.4), notably on hands.
>   • Result: PBADet improves association reliability (lower mMR−2) and medium/large-scale APs; BPJDet slightly higher overall AP.5:.95, but PBADet leads on key size/per-category and association metrics.
> - CrowdHuman (Tables 5 & 6; identical dataset):
>   • Body MR−2 (↓): PBADet YOLOv7 36.5 vs BPJDet variants 39.7–41.3.
>   • Body AP (↑): PBADet YOLOv7 91.6 (best).
>   • Face–body mMR−2 (↓): PBADet 50.8–50.9 vs BPJDet 50.1–51.4 (comparable; best single is BPJDet l6=50.1).
>   • Result: PBADet reduces miss rates and raises body AP; association miss-matching rates are roughly tied.
> 
> 2) Text-space Graph Foundation Models (TS-GFMs): across identical/similar datasets and tasks
> 2.1 Node classification co-training (Table 1)
> - Identical datasets: Cora, CiteSeer, Arxiv, Arxiv-2023 (citation); History, Child, Photo, Computers, Sports, Products (E-commerce); Pubmed, WikiCS (other).
> - Single-task GCN (trained per-graph) averages: Cit-Avg 76.39, Ecom-Avg 81.52, Avg 79.47.
> - Co-training outcomes:
>   • OFA (ID or CD) and GraphMAE/DGI (ID or CD) generally do not surpass single-task GCN; e.g., OFA-CD Avg 78.24, GraphMAE-ID Avg 76.99, DGI-CD Avg 76.96.
>   • LLaGA co-training similarly trails single-task GCN; e.g., LLaGA-CD Avg 78.01.
> - Backbone/probing (Table 2): replacing task backbone shows that SGC (fixed aggregation) can outperform learnable GCN in co-training averages on citation graphs (SGC-CT 72.51 vs GCN-CT 69.97), while in E-commerce, co-training maintains performance (SGC-CT 82.90; GCN-CT 81.93).
> - Result: With current approaches, co-training does not beat well-tuned single-task GCN on node classification; fixed aggregation (SGC) can help stabilize co-training.
> 
> 2.2 Link prediction on small identical graphs (Cora, CiteSeer, Pubmed)
> - Per-graph single-task backbones (Table 17, Hits@100):
>   • BUDDY: 91.37 (Cora), 96.57 (CiteSeer), 83.29 (Pubmed) – best on all three.
>   • GCN: 83.12, 88.91, 66.14; MLP and SIGN vary lower.
> - Co-training averages and efficiency (Table 3, Cora/CiteSeer/Pubmed):
>   • LLaGA co-train avg 85.03; BUDDY co-train avg 90.05 (best) with lower training time than LLaGA/SEAL.
>   • OFA/GraphMAE co-training do not match BUDDY.
> - Scaling to larger graphs via co-training (Table 4):
>   • BUDDY: Avg increases from 75.48 (single) to 86.18 (domain co-train), with across-graph gains (e.g., History 75.57→91.17, Sports 77.00→93.60).
>   • GCN: Avg remains low (43.27→42.29), showing no co-training benefit.
> - Result: Link-specific models with strong structural features (BUDDY) benefit substantially from co-training and scale better than TS-GFMs and plain GCNs.
> 
> 2.3 Graph classification (molecule property prediction; Table 5)
> - Identical datasets: PCBA (AP), HIV/TOX21/BACE/BBBP/MUV/TOXCAST (ROC-AUC).
> - Co-training vs single-graph:
>   • OFA (co-train) achieves best or near-best across datasets (e.g., TOX21 82.5 vs 74.6 single-atom and 74.49 single-text; BACE 77.32 vs 72.4/72.25; TOXCAST 68.39 vs 61.5/60.24). PCBA AP improves to 0.236 from 0.202 (single-atom) and 0.174 (single-text).
>   • GraphCL co-train lags OFA but shows that pre-training on large ZINC (GraphCL pre-train) can help HIV/BACE/BBBP.
> - Result: Co-training in text space consistently improves molecule graph classification over single-graph training.
> 
> 2.4 Cross-task co-training (Table 6, Table 13)
> - Across graphs and tasks (node/link/graph):
>   • Graph-level benefits: multi-task co-training increases graph classification (e.g., Graph Avg from 72.24 single-task to 75.48–76.43 when adding link/node tasks; PCBA AP from 0.233 to 0.265–0.282).
>   • Node/Link tasks: do not consistently improve and may decline under cross-task training; small complementary gains appear in specific node↔link joint setups (Table 13 shows OFA gains in Node->Link Hits@100 and Link->Node Acc vs task-specific co-train).
> - Result: Cross-task co-training reliably boosts graph-level tasks; node/link tasks see mixed results.
> 
> 2.5 Encoder strength matters (Table 16)
> - Upgrading Sentence-BERT encoder from minilm to mpnet within OFA (co-train across node/link/graph) raises Node Avg from 76.06→78.37 while keeping Graph Avg similar (~75.4–75.5), indicating stronger text encoders improve node performance.
> 
> 3) Dale’s Law in recurrent networks: performance comparisons
> - On identical tasks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, naturalistic object recognition), ColEI (column-sign-constrained EI) consistently learns worse than both standard RNNs and DANNs (EI architecture) across all four tasks (Fig. 2A–D), with higher variance and greater sensitivity to gradient clipping.
> - Quantified ablations (Section 3.3):
>   • Sign constraints alone reduce accuracy modestly (~0.7%±0.3% for RNNs; ~1%±1% for ColEI), insufficient to explain the full gap to standard RNNs (~2.3%±0.6%).
>   • Transplant experiments show singular value spectrum accounts for larger performance changes (≈1.5%±0.3% for RNNs; ≈2%±1% for ColEI) than sign constraints or singular vectors, across sequential MNIST and naturalistic object recognition.
> - Spectrum/size/ratio effects (Figs. 5–7):
>   • ColEI performs worse when inhibitory fraction is small and networks are small; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) strongly anti-correlates with test error across sizes and E/I ratios.
>   • DANNs match standard RNNs and are robust to E/I ratio and size (e.g., even with 1 inhibitory neuron), exhibiting unimodal clustered spectra and stable training.
> - Result: DANNs ≈ standard RNNs > ColEI across tasks; spectral properties (unimodal, clustered singular values; high NSE) predict better learning more than sign constraints per se.
> 
> 4) JEPA vs MAE (self-distillation vs masked reconstruction) on identical/similar settings
> - In linear deep models, ODE-solutions (Theorem 3.2) and simulations (Fig. 2, Fig. 4) show:
>   • Both exhibit greedy learning by covariance λ, but only JEPA is also greedy in regression coefficient ρ, prioritizing influential (high-ρ) features.
>   • When λ and ρ trends conflict, JEPA reverses feature learning order relative to MAE (Fig. 1e–f; Fig. 2c vs 2f), emphasizing predictive, less noisy features.
>   • Depth effect: JEPA’s ρ-prioritization strengthens with deeper encoders; shallow MAE behaves like 1-layer JEPA.
> - Temporal linear generative model (Eq. 16; Fig. 3e): Higher λ modes can be noisier (lower ρ); JEPA prefers modes with larger ρ, learning “slow/noise-robust” features that MAE does not.
> - Imagenet (Appendix D, Fig. 7): Feature similarity (mean CCA) indicates JEPA aligns better with the bottom (low-variance, perceptual) subspace than MAE (higher full–bottom CCA; lower full–top CCA) during ViT training.
> - Result: JEPA avoids noisy features and more quickly captures influential/low-variance semantics than MAE, especially with deeper encoders; supported by linear theory, simulations, and small-scale ImageNet analyses.
> 
> 5) Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets (sequential/active RCPS) on identical datasets
> - Safety validity: On both synthetic simulations and ImageNet (Figs. 2a, 3a), all methods keep safety-violation (ever unsafe β̂) below α=0.05 over time.
> - Label efficiency on identical datasets:
>   • Synthetic (β* = 0.5578): “pretrain” and “learned” labeling policies reach lower β̂ (closer to β*) with fewer queried labels than “all” (label everything) and “oblivious” (uniform sampling) (Fig. 2b–c).
>   • ImageNet (β* = 0.8349): same ordering—“pretrain” ≈ “learned” achieve smaller final β̂ and faster convergence than baselines with far fewer labels (Fig. 3b–c), while preserving anytime-valid risk control.
> - Result: Predictor-informed active labeling policies dominate naive strategies in label budget vs utility tradeoff, without compromising anytime-valid guarantees.
> 
> Cross-cutting takeaways on similar dataset types
> - Object/person-part detection in crowded or multi-part settings: anchor-free PBADet improves association reliability (lower mMR−2) and body detection miss rates versus anchor-based multi-part encodings (BPJDet), and scales better to multiple parts and occlusions (BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman).
> - Graph tasks:
>   • Node classification: co-training across graphs in text space generally does not surpass strong single-task GCN baselines; encoder upgrades (mpnet) help.
>   • Link prediction: structure-aware link models (BUDDY) benefit markedly from co-training and scale well; general TS-GFMs lag here.
>   • Graph/molecule classification: co-training in text space (OFA) consistently improves over single-graph training across HIV/TOX21/BACE/BBBP/PCBA/etc.
> - Sequence modeling with E/I constraints: recurrent DANNs match standard RNNs and outperform simple ColEI on adding, sMNIST, PTB, and a naturalistic recognition task; spectral properties (high NSE, unimodal spectra) are a reliable proxy for trainability and final accuracy.
> - SSL pretraining choice: JEPA emphasizes influential/low-variance features and shows faster alignment to perceptual subspaces than MAE, explaining empirical speed/semantic advantages observed in small-scale ImageNet probes.
> - Online safety calibration: active, anytime-valid RCPS with predictor-informed sampling achieves smaller prediction sets (lower β̂) with fewer labels while preserving guarantees, both in synthetic and ImageNet settings.
> 
> Datasets where multiple papers overlap
> - ImageNet: used in JEPA vs MAE (feature subspace CCA dynamics) and in RCPS (label-efficiency of active policies). Both show clear improvements of the proposed method over baselines in their respective metrics (JEPA: higher bottom-subspace CCA; RCPS: faster approach to β* with fewer labels).
> - Cora/CiteSeer/PubMed: used in TS-GFM studies. For link prediction, BUDDY > GCN/SEAL/TS-GFMs on Hits@100; for node classification, single-task GCN remains competitive to co-trained TS-GFMs.
> 
> Overall ranking per task/dataset family (from reported tables/figures)
> - Part–body association (BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman): PBADet > BPJDet/Hier R-CNN on most detection/association metrics (with minor exceptions in overall AP).
> - Graph link prediction (Cora/CiteSeer/PubMed and larger e-commerce/citation graphs): BUDDY (with co-training) > LLaGA/OFA/GraphMAE/GCN.
> - Graph/molecule classification (PCBA/HIV/Tox21/BACE/BBBP/MUV/ToxCast): OFA co-train > GraphCL co-train ≈ single-graph baselines.
> - Node classification across many graphs: single-task GCN ≥ co-trained OFA/LLaGA/GraphMAE/DGI; upgrading text encoders helps TS-GFMs.
> - RNNs with EI constraints: DANN ≈ Standard RNN > ColEI on all four tested tasks; spectrum > sign constraints in explaining performance gaps.
> - SSL objective: JEPA > MAE for prioritizing influential/low-variance features and for early semantic alignment (theory + small-scale ImageNet measurements).
> - RCPS active calibration on ImageNet: predictor-informed “pretrain/learned” labeling > “all/oblivious” for reaching tighter sets faster under the same label budget while maintaining α-control.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on my search of the collection, here is what I found.
> 
> ## Key finding: No single paper addresses all five components
> 
> The collection contains **no paper that jointly addresses detection + SSL + graph unification + online risk control + EI-constrained recurrent controllers** end-to-end. These are separate, domain-specific papers. However, each component has a directly relevant paper, and two papers bridge two components each. I'll list them and compare their experimental results.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Per-component papers
> 
> ### (a) Hand/face detection + tracking relative to person
> **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage anchor-free part-body association detection (face, left/right hands, feet). It is the strongest match for your detection+tracking-person-relative requirement.
> - BodyHands & COCOHumanParts: outperforms SOTA (BPJDet, HierR-CNN); best AP on person and feet, lowest mMR⁻² on head/face/hands.
> - CrowdHuman face-body: leading body MR⁻² (36.5–37.5) with competitive AP (~91.6) — but its advantage over BPJDet shrinks for this single-part task.
> - Against pose estimator ED-Pose: substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands/feet.
> 
> ### (b) Heterogeneous graph fusion via text + unified backbone
> **Text-space GFM benchmark** (TSGFM, NeurIPS 2024 D&B) — maps node attributes to text via LLM encoder, unified backbone across 20+ datasets.
> - Text-space projection preserves/improves: Arxiv 71.53→73.10 Acc; Pubmed Hits@100 53.05→66.13; but categorical Tolokers drops 83.25→78.16, and HIV AUC-ROC 75.52→74.20.
> - Cross-task co-training helps OneForAll (Node→Link 74.05→79.30) but not LLaGA. Negative transfer depends on dataset traits, not ratios.
> 
> **Graph World Model (GWM)** — a second candidate that unifies graph + multi-modal data (image/table/text) via text (GWM-T) or embeddings (GWM-E). Single GWM matches/beats domain-specific baselines across 6 tasks; GWM-E often beats GWM-T at 5–10× lower token cost; multi-hop graphs give ≥20% relative gain but excess hops over-smooth.
> 
> ### (c) SSL avoiding noisy features (joint-embedding over masked reconstruction)
> **"Why JEPA avoids noisy features"** (NeurIPS 2024) — directly supports your (c) design choice.
> - Deep-linear analysis: JEPA self-distillation is implicitly biased toward high-influence (low-variance) features and suppresses noise with depth, whereas MAE (masked reconstruction) orders features mainly by eigenvalue.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA representations align faster to the low-variance PCA (perceptual) subspace than MAE, measured by CCA.
> 
> **LDReg** (ICLR 2024) — complements this: counters (local) dimensional collapse in SSL. On ImageNet, improves linear eval, transfer, COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE (and MoCo, VICReg, Barlow Twins); longer pretraining gives larger gains.
> 
> ### (d) Anytime-valid risk control + active label budget
> **"Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Active Labeling"** (NeurIPS 2024) — exact match for (d).
> - Extends RCPS to sequential, adaptively-collected data with simultaneous risk control at all times (anytime-valid), using e-processes/betting.
> - Guarantees expected queried-labels below a fixed label budget; optimal labeling policy ∝ conditional-risk std; regret bounds.
> - Simulations + ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05): learned/pretrained policies cut risk faster than baselines while keeping safety-violation rates below α; reports 95% error bars.
> 
> ### (e) Recurrent controllers with E/I sign constraints, trainable & stable
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023) — exact match for (e).
> - Sign-constrained (Dale's-law) RNNs. Finding: poor learning of simple column-partitioned EI networks (ColEI) is caused by initial recurrent-weight **spectrum** (multimodal/dispersed singular values), not the sign constraint itself.
> - Recurrent DANN architectures have standard-RNN-like spectra and **learn just as well while respecting E/I signs**; robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> - ColEI is unstable without gradient clipping; NSE (normalised SVD entropy) at init anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance pre-training.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Cross-component bridges (closest to "joint" coverage)
> 
> 1. **JEPA + (b)-style unification?** — none found.
> 2. **HASSOD** — bridges detection and SSL: self-supervised object detection (no labels) via hierarchical clustering on frozen DINO features + Mean-Teacher; improves Mask AR on LVIS 20.2→22.5 and SA-1B 17.0→26.0, at 1/5 images and 1/12 iterations of CutLER. This is the closest existing bridge between your (a) and (c) components, but it's class-agnostic (no explicit person/face/hand association like PBADet).
> 3. **DiffusionFake / deepfake & forgery works** — SSL-style representations + AUROC monitoring on face data; not a joint stack.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Bottom line on experimental comparison
> 
> - **Detection:** PBADet is the SOTA anchor-free person-part detector, beating BPJDet/HierR-CNN and the two-stage BodyHands approach, with the caveat of a smaller margin on single-part (face-only) tasks.
> - **SSL:** JEPA-family objectives are validated to suppress noisy/low-influence features relative to MAE (I-JEPA aligns faster to perceptual subspace); LDReg adds a regularizer that consistently lifts downstream metrics across contrastive and MAE baselines.
> - **Graph unification:** TSGFM quantifies that text-mapping works for text/semantic attributes but can lose on non-text/categorical attributes; co-training gains are method-dependent. GWM extends this to genuinely multi-modal graph data at lower token cost.
> - **Risk control:** the anytime-valid active-labeling method provably enforces the safety guarantee at all times under a label budget, with label-efficient policies beating naive baselines on ImageNet.
> - **EI recurrent:** the evidence says use DANN-style (recurrent) architectures for sign-constrained controllers — they match standard RNN performance because their spectra are healthy — rather than naive ColEI, whose pathology (and instability without gradient clipping) is what historically "harmed" training.
> 
> No paper in the collection integrates all of these into one end-to-end system, so you would need to assemble the stack from the individual works above.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Direct answer
> 
> **No single paper in this collection jointly addresses all five components end-to-end.** The stack must be assembled from separate papers, one per component. The relevant papers and their experimental results:
> 
> ### (a) Hand/face detection & person association — **PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> - **BodyHands:** PBADet-YOLOv7 (36.9M params, 1024px) gets HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 — beating BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (85.9/86.91/84.39) and BodyHands-2022 (84.8/83.44/63.48) with a smaller model at lower resolution. Association (JointAP) gains are the largest.
> - **COCOHumanParts:** PBADet is on par with BPJDet on AP.5:.95 (43.0 vs 43.6) but leads on subordinate/association APs (AP.5 66.2 vs 63.8; APL 67.2 vs 61.8) and achieves the lowest mMR−2 for head/face/hands/feet.
> - **vs ED-Pose (pose SOTA):** PBADet roughly doubles hands/feet F1 (all-parts 48.52 vs 31.51).
> - **Analysis:** the one-stage anchor-free part-to-body formulation improves association efficiency without sacrificing detection; advantage shrinks for single-part tasks (CrowdHuman face-body) where it's only comparable.
> 
> ### (b) Heterogeneous graph unification via text — **Text-space GFM benchmark** and **Graph World Model (GWM)**
> - TSGFM benchmark: text-space projection preserves/improves text-attribute tasks (Arxiv 71.53→73.10) and matches non-text attributes with good prompts (HIV 75.52→74.20; Pubmed Hits@100 53.05→66.13), but categorical Tolokers drops (83.25→78.16). Cross-task co-training benefits OneForAll (Node→Link 74.05→79.30) but not LLaGA; negative transfer depends on dataset traits, not mixing ratios.
> - GWM (the closest thing to an end-to-end multi-modal graph stack): one unified model matches/beats domain-specific baselines across 6 tasks (recommendation, graph prediction, multi-agent, RAG, planning, multi-modal generation). GWM-E outperforms GWM-T in 5/7 tasks at 5–10× lower token cost; on LongBench v2 RAG, GWM-E with 2k context (33.32 overall) beats GPT-4o-mini with 128k context (29.01). Multi-hop graphs give ≥20% relative gain on graph tasks but too many hops cause over-smoothing.
> 
> ### (c) SSL favoring joint-embedding over masked reconstruction — **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Theory (deep linear networks): JEPA's critical learning time depends on the regression coefficient ρ (not just eigenvalue λ), so it learns high-ρ, low-noise, predictive features first — increasingly so with depth — while MAE orders learning mainly by λ. Fixed points: JEPA suppresses noisy directions more with depth (w̄→ρ^L vs MAE's ρ^(L/(L+1))).
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA), confirming noise avoidance empirically. This validates your design choice of joint-embedding over masked reconstruction.
> 
> ### (d) Anytime-valid risk control with active label budgeting — **"Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Guarantees P(ρ(β̂_t) ≤ θ for all t) ≥ 1−α on adaptively collected data (e-processes/betting); optimal labeling policy ∝ conditional risk std-dev, optimal predictor = conditional risk.
> - Simulations (β*=0.5578) and ImageNet (β*=0.8349): "pretrain" and "learned" active policies reach lower β̂ (tighter, safer sets) uniformly across queried labels than "all"/"oblivious" baselines, while all methods keep safety violation rates below α=0.05. Learned/pretrained policies cut risk faster with far fewer labels — exactly your online-safety + budget design.
> 
> ### (e) Recurrent E/I sign-constrained controllers — **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - ColEI RNNs (column-wise E/I sign constraints) learn worse and with more variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs. Key finding: sign constraints cause only ~1% of the gap; the initial **singular-value spectrum** is the dominant factor — ColEI's column-mean rank-one structure gives multimodal, dispersed spectra, while DANN/standard RNNs match the quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur form.
> - Gradient clipping restores stability; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance before training. **Design implication for you:** a trainable, stable sign-constrained recurrent controller is achievable by using a DANN-style architecture or engineering the recurrent weight spectrum (unimodal, clustered), not merely clipping signs.
> 
> ### Cross-component analysis
> The papers are orthogonal and don't share benchmarks, so no apples-to-apples joint comparison exists. Notable tensions/alignments if you combine them: PBADet's SGD/CE + YOLO detection training is compatible with your fine-tuning stack; GWM already uses an LLM-as-unified-text-space backbone (with frozen LLM + projector fine-tuning, like LoRA); the JEPA result theoretically justifies using joint-embedding pretraining for the detector/encoder backbone; the anytime-valid RCPS paper explicitly demonstrates its method on ImageNet classifiers, which matches your detection monitoring; the Dale's-law paper's spectral findings directly answer how to keep E/I-constrained recurrent time-series controllers trainable (spectrum design + gradient clipping). No paper covers tracking specifically, and none integrates (a)–(e) jointly — that integration would be a novel contribution.

Gold 1：

> Integrated comparison of experimental results across five papers that jointly cover: (1) self-supervised learning (JEPA vs MAE-style objectives), (2) memory-efficient optimizers with 4-bit states, (3) one-stage anchor-free part–body detection on COCO-style benchmarks, (4) hierarchical Transformer+Diffusion+GNN pipelines for structure generation, and (5) interpretability of recurrent EI models via spectral analysis. Below we summarize results strictly from the papers’ figures/tables.
> 
> A) Identical datasets across papers and direct comparisons
> - Sequential MNIST, Adding problem, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic Object Recognition
>   • Both “Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective” (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs) and “How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features” (JEPA vs MAE) evaluate on these tasks.
>   • Dale’s Law paper (Fig. 2A–D) shows ColEI RNNs learn worse than standard RNNs and DANNs on Adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task; sign constraints alone explain only part of the gap. Quantified on sequential MNIST: sign constraints impaired learning by 0.7% ± 0.3% (RNNs) and 1% ± 1% (ColEI), while spectrum transplant affected performance more (1.5% ± 0.3% for RNNs; 2% ± 1% for ColEI) (Fig. 4B–C).
>   • JEPA vs MAE paper analyzes dynamics rather than final accuracy; on sequential MNIST and the Adding problem it demonstrates (Fig. 2) objective-dependent greedy learning: both prioritize high covariance λ features, but JEPA increasingly prioritizes high regression-coefficient (ρ) features with depth, sometimes reversing the learning order relative to MAE when λ and ρ are antagonistic (Fig. 1e–f, Fig. 2c,f). Thus, while both papers use the same tasks, Dale’s provides performance gaps attributable to spectral properties; JEPA paper provides mechanistic dynamics (no tabulated final accuracies on these tasks).
> 
> B) Per-paper results on specific datasets (with cross-paper links when datasets are similar types)
> 1) One-stage anchor-free part–body detection (PBADet, ICLR 2024)
> - BodyHands (Table 1; identical dataset across compared methods in the paper):
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, anchor-based): 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39.
>   • PBADet improves Conditional Accuracy by ~5.7–5.8 pts over BPJDet at similar backbone scale and raises Joint AP by ~1.3–1.6 pts (Table 1, Fig. 3).
> - COCO-HumanParts (COCO-style, Tables 2–3; identical dataset across compared methods in the paper):
>   • All-categories AP (original/subordinate): PBADet YOLOv5l6: 43.0/41.8; PBADet YOLOv7: 42.7/41.5; BPJDet YOLOv5l6: 43.6/43.3.
>   • Category APs (PBADet YOLOv5l6 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6): person 62.4 vs 61.3; head 54.6 vs 56.6; face 44.6 vs 46.3; r-hand 39.0 vs 40.4; r-foot 37.7 vs 39.6; l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9 (Table 2). PBADet’s APM/APL are notably strong (66.2/67.2 vs 63.8/61.8 for BPJDet’s original/subordinate-based values).
>   • Association robustness (lower is better): average mMR−2 across parts—PBADet YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6: (head 29.2/27.9, face 31.3/30.5, l-hand 41.1/36.2, r-hand 42.7/40.8, r-foot 52.6/50.4, l-foot 52.5/47.9) vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 (30.8, 31.8, 41.6, 42.2, 49.1, 50.4) (Table 3). PBADet yields lower mMR−2 in several categories (notably hands) and comparable in others.
> - CrowdHuman (Appendix Tables 5–6; identical dataset across compared methods in the paper):
>   • PBADet YOLOv7 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6: MR−2 body 36.5 vs 40.7 (better), body AP 91.6 vs 89.5, mMR−2 body–face 50.8 vs 50.1 (comparable). PBADet also competitive with DETR-based models in AP (Table 6) while achieving best body MR−2.
>   • Net: PBADet’s single part-to-body offset yields consistent SOTA or comparable results on COCO-style datasets with simpler decoding vs anchor-based counterparts.
> 
> 2) Memory-efficient optimizers with 4-bit states (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Cross-task evaluation on NLU (GLUE with RoBERTa-L), image classification (Swin-T on ImageNet-1k), NLG (GPT-2 Medium on E2E-NLG), QA (RoBERTa-L on SQuAD), MT (Transformer-Base on WMT14 en–de) (Table 2; identical datasets across compared optimizers within the paper):
>   • Mean NLU accuracy/correlation: 4-bit AdamW = 89.1 equals or exceeds 32-bit AdamW (88.9) and 8-bit AdamW (89.1†), and > SM3 (87.5). “4-bit Factor” is 88.9.
>   • ImageNet-1k (Swin-T): Top-1 Acc: 4-bit AdamW 80.8 is close to 32-bit (81.2) and 8-bit (81.0†); Adafactor variants and SM3 trail.
>   • E2E-NLG BLEU: 4-bit AdamW 67.8 slightly > 32-bit (67.7) and 8-bit (67.5†); consistent across other NLG metrics (Table 8 in appendix).
>   • QA SQuAD F1: 4-bit AdamW 94.5 ~ 32-bit (94.6) and 8-bit (94.5†); SQuAD 2.0 shows similar parity (Table 9).
>   • MT SacreBLEU: 4-bit 26.28 is close to 32-bit 26.61; “4-bit Factor” 26.45.
> - Instruction tuning (LLaMA-7B/13B/33B on Alpaca; evaluated on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA) (Table 3; identical datasets across compared optimizers within the paper):
>   • 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly improves 32-bit AdamW across model sizes (e.g., 13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8; ARC-ch 48.0 vs 48.3; OBQA 45.2 vs 45.2).
> - Memory/time (Table 4):
>   • LLaMA‑7B: memory reduced from 75.4 GB (32-bit) to 31.9 GB (4-bit AdamW), saving 57.7%, and with fused kernels 3.11h time vs 3.35h.
>   • RoBERTa‑L and GPT‑2 M: 43–36% total memory reduction; fused versions recover speed relative to 8-bit implementations.
> - Capacity (Table 5): with 80 GB GPU, largest fine-tunable increases from OPT‑1.3B (32-bit) to OPT‑6.7B (4-bit); LLaMA‑7B becomes trainable on a single 80 GB GPU.
> - Second-moment zero-point ablation (Table 1):
>   • Naïve 4-bit (B2048/DE) is unstable on GPT‑2 M E2E-NLG (33% unstable, BLEU 66.6). Excluding zero-point (DE‑0) stabilizes training and recovers BLEU (67.5). Rank‑1 normalization with Linear mapping achieves best BLEU (67.8) without stable embeddings. Factorization of the second moment retains BLEU (67.6) while further reducing memory.
> 
> 3) Hierarchical generative pipeline (GenMS: LLM + Diffusion + GNN for crystals) (NeurIPS 2024)
> - End-to-end generation from language on three crystal families (Table 1; identical family tasks across methods in the paper):
>   • Perovskites: GenMS achieves CIF validity 1.00 (vs 0.88–1.00 for prompting), Structural validity 1.00 (vs max 0.66), Composition validity 0.85 (vs ≤0.45), Uniqueness 0.90 (vs ≤0.68), Match rate 0.93 (vs ≤0.36). Predicted/DFT Ef: −0.47/−1.32 eV/atom, lower (better) than prompting baselines (several N/A or higher Ef).
>   • Pyrochlore: GenMS CIF/struct/comp validity 1.00/0.95/0.89 (vs ≤0.64/0.36/0.22), Uniqueness 0.49 (competitive), Match rate 0.86 (vs ≤0.04). Ef: −1.37/−2.56 vs prompting degenerate values (e.g., +1.28, +1.19 eV/atom).
>   • Spinel: GenMS achieves 1.00/1.00/1.00 validity trio; Uniqueness 0.44; Match rate 0.89; Ef −1.38/−1.77 vs prompting alternatives (e.g., Ef −0.85 to −1.37 predicted).
> - Branching-factor study (Table 2; specific dataset setting within the paper): increasing language (H) and structure (L) branches consistently lowers DFT Ef (e.g., perovskite Ef from −0.55 at H=1,L=1 to −2.91 at H=25,L=100).
> - Component ablations:
>   • Retrieval augmentation (Table 4): valid formula rate improves to 1.00 (from 0.97), match rate to 0.89 (from 0.72).
>   • Compact representation vs UniMat (Table 5): DFT convergence 0.93 vs 0.62; mean Ef −0.49±0.03 vs −0.40±0.06 (lower is better).
>   • Compared to CrystalLM finetuned LLMs (Table 6): success (valid crystal) 0.93 vs 0.86–0.87; match to unseen 0.48 vs 0.26 (small LLM) / 0.37 (large LLM).
>   • Best‑of‑N guided by GNN: for 1,000 compositions, best‑of‑10 improves Ef over single sample ~80% of the time; GNN-predicted energy differences mirror DFT-calculated differences (Fig. 4).
> 
> 4) Self-supervised learning (JEPA vs MAE) (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Dynamics on toy and benchmark tasks (Figs. 1–2):
>   • On distributions where λ (covariance) and ρ (regression coefficient) align, JEPA and MAE learn features in similar order; when λ increases but ρ decreases across features, JEPA reverses order (prioritizes high‑ρ), MAE retains λ‑priority (Fig. 1e–f). This holds across ODE simulations and deep linear nets trained on Gaussian data (Fig. 2).
>   • Theoretically and empirically, deeper encoders amplify JEPA’s bias for high‑ρ features (Fig. 4), consistent with its fixed-point scaling (ρ^L) vs MAE’s (ρ^{L/(L+1)}).
> - Imagenet 64×64 representation probe (Appendix D, Fig. 7): during pretraining, I‑JEPA shows higher mean CCA similarity between full and bottom‑variance images (and lower for full vs top) than MAE, indicating faster focus on the low‑variance, perceptual subspace; this complements Balestriero & LeCun [20].
> 
> 5) Interpretability of recurrent EI models via spectral analysis (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Spectral diagnostics predict learning: Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE) anti‑correlates with test error across EI ratios and sizes (Figs. 5–7). ColEI’s multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra (Fig. 3D) yield worse performance and higher variance than DANN/standard RNNs (Fig. 2), especially for small networks with few inhibitory units; performance improves with size and balanced EI ratios.
> - Causal tests (Fig. 4): on sequential MNIST, spectrum transplant changes performance more than sign constraints; sign‑constraints alone account for ~1% error change, whereas transplanting singular values explains 1.5–2% change.
> 
> C) Performance on similar types of datasets (beyond strictly identical ones)
> - Vision classification vs recognition:
>   • Swin‑T ImageNet‑1k (4-bit optimizer): 80.8% Top‑1 shows near-parity to full precision, indicating 4-bit state quantization does not materially harm large‑scale vision training (Table 2).
>   • COCO‑style detection (PBADet): strong AP/AP.5 and association accuracy on COCO‑HumanParts and CrowdHuman (Tables 2, 5–6), showing that anchor‑free part‑to‑body offsets scale to crowded, multi-part scenes.
> - Language modeling/perception:
>   • PTB/sequential MNIST/Adding (Dale’s Law): spectral properties, particularly singular value dispersion, are the primary factor behind degraded learning in EI‑constrained nets (Figs. 2–4), a result generalizing across synthetic and naturalistic tasks.
>   • JEPA vs MAE: on structured synthetic distributions and deep linear settings, JEPA targets influential, low‑variance features earlier (Figs. 1–2), in line with the Imagenet CCA probe (Appendix D).
> - Generative pipelines with property predictors:
>   • GenMS: language→(LLM) formula→(diffusion) structure→(GNN) energy/lattice checking, with DFT verification. Numerically, it clearly surpasses direct LLM CIF prompting and prior diffusion/LLM baselines on validity/matching/energy across three families (Table 1) and converges better (Table 5).
> 
> D) Notable dataset-level takeaways
> - Identical datasets explicitly compared:
>   • COCO‑HumanParts and CrowdHuman: PBADet vs Hier‑R‑CNN and BPJDet (Tables 2, 5–6) show PBADet’s advantage in AP, MR−2, and association mMR−2.
>   • GLUE, ImageNet‑1k, E2E‑NLG, SQuAD, WMT14 en–de: across all, 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit (Table 2) with substantial memory savings (Table 4), and “4‑bit Factor” remains competitive.
>   • LLaMA instruction tuning: 4‑bit AdamW maintains 32‑bit performance across MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA (Table 3).
>   • Sequential MNIST/Add/PTB/Naturalistic recognition: Dale’s Law vs DANN vs RNN (Fig. 2A–D) on identical tasks; JEPA/MAE also use these benchmarks but primarily to show dynamics/greedy learning differences (Fig. 2), not final scores.
> - Similar dataset classes:
>   • Natural image recognition (Swin‑T) and naturalistic object recognition (RNN papers) both show that proposed methods maintain or elucidate performance trends in realistic vision-like tasks (near-parity for 4‑bit, spectral pathologies predict failures for ColEI).
>   • COCO‑style dense scenes vs structure generation with property constraints: both PBADet and GenMS show that adding the right inductive bias (part‑to‑body offsets; compact crystal representation + best‑of‑N with GNN) yields consistent, quantifiable gains over baselines.
> 
> E) Practical notes linked to the query’s desiderata
> - Self-supervised learning (JEPA/MAE): empirical dynamics and Imagenet probing support that JEPA (latent-space prediction) prioritizes high‑influence (high‑ρ) features earlier than MAE; this matches the intent of studying MSE‑style (JEPA’s squared error in latent space) vs reconstruction (MAE) objectives.
> - Memory efficiency with Adam/AdamW and quantized states: 4‑bit states with rank‑1 normalization and linear mapping for v_t remove the zero‑point failure mode and achieve parity across NLU/Vision/QA/MT while saving 43–58% total memory and enabling larger models (Tables 1–5).
> - One-stage, anchor-free detection on COCO‑style benchmarks: PBADet’s single part‑to‑body center offset attains strong APs and notably lower MR−2 and mMR−2 (Tables 2, 5–6), outperforming anchor‑based/2‑stage baselines.
> - Hierarchical pipeline (Transformers + Diffusion + GNN): GenMS’s LLM→Diffusion→GNN loop, with tree search and best‑of‑N selection, achieves higher validity, uniqueness, match rate, and lower DFT energies than CIF‑prompting and earlier structure generators (Tables 1, 4–6; Fig. 4).
> - Interpretability via spectral analysis under EI constraints: spectrum pathology (multimodal, dispersed singular values) explains ColEI’s poorer learning vs DANN/standard RNNs; improving NSE correlates with error reductions (Figs. 3–7), and spectrum transplant causally improves outcomes (Fig. 4).
>

> **1. SSL: MSE vs CE objectives / implicit bias (JEPA/self-distillation)**
> - **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`). Compares JEPA (latent-space MSE-style prediction, self-distillation with stop-grad) vs MAE (pixel reconstruction). Proves JEPA is implicitly biased toward high-influence (high-regression-coefficient) features, while MAE prioritizes high-variance/covarying features; the bias only appears with *deep* encoders. ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features.
> - Supporting: **LDReg** (`51526068…`, ICLR 2024) – regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality of SSL embeddings (SimCLR/BYOL/MAE) on ImageNet, transfer and COCO detection; **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (`160e1407…`) – analyzes InfoNCE vs optimal embedding similarity, proposes variance-reduction loss, evaluated on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and full ImageNet.
> 
> **2. Memory-efficient training with quantized Adam/AdamW moments (fine-tuning)**
> - **"4-bit Optimizers"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`). Quantizes first/second moments of Adam/AdamW to 4-bit (B128 block for 1st moment; rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for 2nd moment; optional factorization). Results: 4-bit AdamW **matches or slightly exceeds** 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), E2E-NLG BLEU (67.8 vs 67.7), Swin-T ImageNet (80.8 vs 81.2), WMT14 (26.28 vs 26.61); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning preserves MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OpenBookQA. Memory: up to **57.7% savings** (LLaMA-7B 75.4→31.9 GB, trainable on one 80 GB GPU); 4-bit Factor further reduces memory while keeping accuracy. Adafactor(β₁=0)/SM3 save more memory but degrade accuracy, especially on image classification. LoRA is discussed in related work (frozen weights + low-rank tuning), and the paper is complementary to it.
> 
> **3. One-stage anchor-free detection, part-body association (COCO-style, Precision/F1)**
> - **PBADet** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`). One-stage anchor-free YOLOv5/v7 detector with a single part-to-body center offset. Results: on BodyHands, anchor-free PBADet beats BPJDet (Hand AP 89.1 vs 85.3, Cond. Accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, Joint AP 85.98 vs 78.13); on CrowdHuman face-body, leading body MR-2 (36.5 vs BPJDet 39.7–41.3) with competitive AP (91.6 body/81.6 face); on COCOHumanParts, AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6); against the pose estimator ED-Pose it yields substantially higher **precision, recall, and F1** for hands/feet; also extends to AnimalPose/AP-10K quadruped part-body association. Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, task-alignment each improve accuracy; anchor-free > anchor-based.
> 
> **4. Hierarchical generative pipelines: Transformer + Diffusion + GNN for property-guided generation**
> - **GenMS** (ICLR 2024, doc `277849d4…`). LLM generates intermediate textual info (formulae) → diffusion model generates crystal structures → GNN predicts properties (formation energy), with forward tree search. Outperforms LLM-only baselines in validity, uniqueness, instruction following, match rate, and low formation energy (verified by VASP DFT); GNN-selected best-of-N improves energies for >80% of compositions; generates double perovskites, pyrochlores, spinels.
> - **GeoBFN** (ICLR 2024, doc `ad5cfba8…`). Bayesian Flow Networks + equivariant GNNs for 3D molecules; QM9 molecule/atom stability 90.87%/99.08%, GEOM-DRUG 85.60% atom stability; conditional (property-guided) generation beats baselines; 50-step sampling ≈20× speedup.
> - **FMG** (`4888a3c3…`) – multi-modal foundation models inducing molecular graph grammars for property prediction/generation.
> 
> **5. Spectral interpretability of recurrent models under E/I constraints**
> - **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`). Spectral analysis of E/I (excitatory/inhibitory) RNNs: ColEI networks have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one column-mean nilpotent structure), while standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs have unimodal Marchenko–Pastur/quarter-circle spectra. Sign constraints explain only ~0.7–1% of the error gap vs the ~2.3±0.6% total on sequential MNIST; **spectral properties matter more than sign constraints**. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; small networks with fewer I units and skewed E:I ratio train worst; DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> 
> ## Comparative Analysis of Experimental Results
> - **Loss/objective choice matters most in deep models**: The JEPA analysis shows the latent-prediction (MSE-style) objective's feature-ordering bias appears only for deep encoders and explains faster semantic-feature learning on ImageNet; the 4-bit optimizer results independently show the second moment (variance-like statistics) is the critical state to quantize carefully (zero-point problem), mirroring the theme that second-order statistics determine learning quality.
> - **Memory efficiency without accuracy loss**: 4-bit AdamW is the only method matching 32-bit accuracy across all tasks (vs 8-bit AdamW which skips embedding quantization and sublinear optimizers Adafactor/SM3 that degrade on classification). This pairs naturally with LoRA-style PEFT used in related collection works (NEFTune's QLoRA; Themis's LoRA fine-tuning of Vicuna-7B), but no single paper in the collection studies "end-to-end LoRA" merging explicitly—only LoRA as frozen-backbone low-rank tuning is described.
> - **Detection results favor the simpler association design**: PBADet's single part-to-body offset beats body-to-part offsets (BPJDet) by ~4–8 points across Hand AP/Cond. Accuracy/Joint AP and improves MR-2 on CrowdHuman, while keeping one-stage efficiency; ablations show each component (association loss, multi-scale offsets, task alignment) contributes, and anchor-free beats anchor-based at equal capacity.
> - **Hierarchical generation beats single-stage**: GenMS's LLM→diffusion→GNN pipeline with search outperforms direct LLM structure generation in both instruction satisfaction and low formation energy (DFT-validated); GeoBFN shows GNN-based equivariant diffusion/flow modeling reaches high stability at far fewer sampling steps. Both validate property-guided structure generation on scientific benchmarks (crystals, QM9/GEOM-DRUG).
> - **Spectral structure predicts RNN trainability**: NSE at initialization is a pre-training diagnostic of E/I RNN performance; architectural fixes (DANN parameterization) that restore unimodal spectra learn as well as unconstrained RNNs, whereas sign constraints alone cannot explain the deficit.
> 
> ## Coverage gaps (cannot be fully established from this collection)
> - No paper here directly compares **MSE vs cross-entropy** as training objectives head-to-head in one study (JEPA paper compares latent-prediction vs reconstruction, not CE); neural-collapse-under-CE is only cited in a reference list.
> - **"End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning"** is not a studied subject in any retrieved paper; LoRA appears only as related work (4-bit optimizer paper) or as a used method (NEFTune/QLoRA, Themis, LoRA-Hessian analysis).
> - Evaluation is well beyond MNIST/CIFAR-100 (ImageNet, COCO, GLUE/SQuAD, WMT, Alpaca, QM9, crystal datasets), though the Dale's-Law paper does use sequential MNIST among its benchmarks; feature embeddings are discussed in the SSL papers, NEFTune (embedding noise) and PBADet (feature maps), but not as a unifying theme.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:227 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource-constrained AI stack for materials discovery and human–robot interfaces: we need (a) self-supervised pretraining that avoids noisy features (MSE vs CE) before fine-tuning, (b) a one-stage anchor-free detector that associates hands/faces to bodies on COCO-like data with strong Precision/F1, (c) a language-to-structure generator that uses Transformers, Diffusion models, and a GNN to propose low-energy crystals, (d) Adam/AdamW variants with tiny optimizer states for efficient updates, and (e) guidance on designing EI-constrained RNNs with spectral diagnostics for interpretability. Which papers collectively address these needs, including tips for End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Who addresses which need in your stack
> • (a) Self-supervised pretraining that avoids noisy features (JEPA vs MAE/MSE): “How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features” (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024) shows, in deep linear settings and controlled generative models, that JEPA (latent-space prediction with MSE and stop-grad) prioritizes high-influence (predictive) features over high-variance (potentially noisy) features that MAE tends to emphasize. Appendix D further shows, on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align earlier with the low-variance (bottom-PCA) subspace than MAE.
> • (b) One-stage anchor-free hand/face-to-body association with strong Precision/F1 on COCO-like data: PBADet (ICLR 2024) is a one-stage, anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center-offset head that outperforms or matches anchor-based joints (e.g., BPJDet) across BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, and CrowdHuman, and yields higher F1 than a top multi-person pose estimator on COCO imagery.
> • (c) Language→structure generation using Transformers, Diffusion models, and a GNN for low-energy crystals: Generative Hierarchical Materials Search (GenMS, NeurIPS 2024) composes a retrieval-augmented LLM (Transformer), a compact-representation diffusion generator, and a property GNN into a tree search that optimizes satisfaction of language constraints and low formation energy (DFT-validated).
> • (d) Adam/AdamW with tiny optimizer states for efficient updates: Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023) provides 4-bit AdamW that matches 32-bit accuracy on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet (Swin-T), WMT14 en-de, and instruction-tuned LLaMA, while saving up to 57.7% total training memory and maintaining or improving wall-clock.
> • (e) EI-constrained RNNs with spectral diagnostics for interpretability: “Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective” (NeurIPS 2023) shows that spectral properties (singular-value distribution) dominate learning quality under Dale constraints; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance, offering a concrete diagnostic. Recurrent DANNs match standard RNNs, while column EI (ColEI) lags—especially in small networks and unbalanced E/I ratios.
> 
> Head-to-head experimental comparisons (from the papers)
> (b) One-stage anchor-free part–body association (PBADet) vs baselines
> Identical/similar datasets
> • BodyHands (hand–body association; Table 1). Metrics: Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP.
>   – PBADet (YOLOv7): 89.1 AP, 92.62 cond. acc., 85.98 joint AP.
>   – PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 AP, 92.71 cond. acc., 85.73 joint AP.
>   – BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9 AP, 86.91 cond. acc., 84.39 joint AP.
>   Outcome: PBADet improves over BPJDet with the same backbone (YOLOv5l6) on all three metrics (e.g., +2.2 AP, +5.8 pp cond. acc., +1.34 pp joint AP), and a smaller PBADet model (YOLOv7) still surpasses BPJDet (YOLOv5m6).
> • COCO-HumanParts (multi-part association; Tables 2–3). All-categories AP (original/subordinate) and per-category AP, plus association mMR−2 (lower is better).
>   – All AP (original/subordinate): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3. While BPJDet has slightly higher AP, PBADet leads on important sub-slices and association robustness:
>     ◦ APM/APL: PBADet (v5l6) 66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4 vs BPJDet (v5l6) 63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9 (PBADet higher mid/large APs).
>     ◦ Per-category AP: PBADet (v5l6) beats BPJDet (v5l6) for “person” (62.4 vs 61.3) and both feet (30.9–31.5 vs 30.2–30.9). 
>   – Association mMR−2 (Table 3): PBADet (YOLOv7) yields lower (better) mMR−2 than BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) across most parts, e.g., head 29.2 vs 30.8, face 31.3 vs 31.8, r-hand 42.7 vs 42.2 (close), l-foot 52.5 vs 50.4 (close). Overall average trends favor PBADet in association robustness.
> • CrowdHuman (face–body association; Tables 5–6). PBADet (YOLOv7) attains the best body MR−2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6) while mMR−2 is comparable (≈50.8–50.9) to BPJDet. Among crowded-person detectors, PBADet matches DETR-class AP while improving MR−2 versus prior CNN/DETR methods.
> • COCO (pose baseline; Table 7 and Fig. 5). Against ED-Pose (Swin-L), PBADet achieves much higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet (e.g., all-parts F1: 48.52 vs 31.51). This indicates stronger part detection plus reliable part–body association compared with state-of-the-art multiperson pose estimation when bounding boxes for parts matter.
> Ablations on PBADet (Table 4, Table 8)
> • Adding association loss (Lassoc) lifts association quality substantially at the same Hand AP: cond. acc. 92.62 vs 80.78 baseline and joint AP 85.98 vs 78.07.
> • Anchor-free and part-to-body offset together outperform anchor-based body-to-part and anchor-based part-to-body setups on BodyHands (Table 8).
> 
> (c) Language→structure (GenMS) vs prompting LLMs and other structure generators
> Identical/similar generation targets
> • End-to-end from language on classic families (Table 1): perovskites, pyrochlores, spinels. Metrics: CIF validity, structural validity, composition validity, uniqueness vs MP/ICSD, match-rate to family, and formation energy (Ef, lower is better). GenMS vs prompting with 1/5/25-shot and max-long-context CIF examples.
>   – Perovskites: GenMS (CIF/struct/comp validity) 1.00/1.00/0.85; match-rate 0.93; Ef (GNN/DFT) −0.47/−1.32. Prompting max context lags (e.g., match-rate 0.19; comp-validity 0.00; Ef DFT not reported).
>   – Pyrochlores: GenMS 1.00/0.95/0.89; match-rate 0.86; Ef −1.37/−2.56. Prompting max has lower comp-validity (0.00) and match-rate (0.00).
>   – Spinels: GenMS 1.00/1.00/1.00; match-rate 0.89; Ef −1.38/−1.77. Prompting max: match-rate 0.08 and lower validity in several columns.
>   Conclusion: Across all three families, GenMS simultaneously satisfies language constraints and produces low-energy and valid structures far more reliably than LLM prompting.
> • Sampling/search depth study (Table 2): Increasing language (H) and structure (L) branching lowers DFT Ef consistently (e.g., Perovskite: H=1,L=1 → −0.55; H=25,L=100 → −2.91), at higher inference cost. This quantifies the value of hierarchical tree search.
> • Compact diffusion vs uni- and LLM-based structure generators:
>   – UniMat (periodic-table tensor; Table 5): DFT convergence rate 0.62 vs GenMS 0.93, with better mean Ef (−0.49 vs −0.40 eV/atom). 
>   – CrystalLM (LLM directly generating CIF; Table 6): GenMS diffusion achieves higher success (0.93 vs 0.86–0.87) and higher match on unseen compositions (0.48 vs 0.26–0.37).
> • Best-of-N selection with GNN (Fig. 4): Best-of-10 (vs single sample) improves Ef in >80% of cases per both the GNN and DFT, validating the GNN’s utility as a selection heuristic during search.
> • Retrieval augmentation (Table 4): RAG improves valid-formula rate (1.00 vs 0.97) and downstream match-rate (0.89 vs 0.72) for family-constrained generation.
> 
> (d) 4‑bit Adam/AdamW vs 32‑bit and 8‑bit (identical datasets; Tables 2, 4–6)
> Accuracy (no significant loss vs 32‑bit) across tasks
> • GLUE (RoBERTa‑L; mean acc/corr): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9; 8‑bit 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit Factor 88.9. Per-task details (Table 7) show parity within noise across MNLI, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST‑2, MRPC, CoLA, STS‑B.
> • SQuAD/SQuAD2.0 (RoBERTa‑L, Table 9): 4‑bit AdamW EM/F1 (SQuAD) 88.8/94.5 vs 32‑bit 89.0/94.6; for SQuAD2.0 85.4/88.4 vs 85.8/88.8 (within variance).
> • ImageNet‑1K (Swin‑T CLS acc): 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9 (comparable pretraining accuracy).
> • E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2‑M; BLEU): 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5; 4‑bit AdamW 67.8; 4‑bit Factor 67.6 (Table 8 for full metrics: NIST/METEOR/ROUGE‑L/CIDEr near‑identical).
> • WMT14 en‑de (Transformer SacreBleu): 32‑bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; 4‑bit AdamW 26.28; 4‑bit Factor 26.45 (minor differences).
> • Instruction tuning (LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B; Table 3): 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit across MMLU and commonsense benchmarks (e.g., LLaMA‑13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8; ARC‑e 64.1 vs 63.6; ARC‑c 48.0 vs 48.3; OBQA 45.2 vs 45.2).
> Memory, speed, and scale (Tables 4–5)
> • Memory: up to 57.7% total memory reduction with 4‑bit vs 32‑bit (LLaMA‑7B: 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB). RoBERTa‑L: 3.00 GB (4‑bit fused) vs 5.31 GB; GPT‑2‑M: 4.62 GB vs 6.89 GB.
> • Throughput: with fused kernels, 4‑bit meets or beats 32‑bit and 8‑bit (e.g., RoBERTa‑L: 3.17 min/epoch vs 3.93 for 32‑bit; GPT‑2‑M 2.11 h vs 2.13 h).
> • Scale: with 24 GB GPU, 4‑bit fine‑tunes OPT‑1.3B vs 350M (32‑bit); with 80 GB, trains LLaMA‑7B (4‑bit; not feasible in 32‑bit).
> Ablations that matter (Table 1)
> • Second moment zero‑point: Quantizing v with a mapping that includes zero collapses 1/sqrt(v) (Figure 3). Excluding zero with a linear mapping and Rank‑1 normalization stabilizes and preserves accuracy (e.g., GPT‑2‑M BLEU 67.8 ± 0.51 with Rank‑1/Linear), removing need for “stable embeddings”.
> • First moment block size: smaller B=128 with DE mapping captures varied outlier patterns better than B=2048, improving approximation.
> • Factorized v: combining factorization (Adafactor‑style) for v with 4‑bit m retains accuracy and improves memory (Table 2 & ablations).
> 
> (a) Self-supervised pretraining (JEPA vs MAE): empirical dynamics and ImageNet evidence
> • Controlled dynamics (Figs. 1–2, 4): JEPA exhibits greedy learning by regression coefficient (ρ, influence) while MAE is greedy by covariance (λ, variance). When λ and ρ are opposed (Distribution 2), JEPA inverts the MAE learning order—prioritizing predictive, low-noise features. The depth dependence (“JEPA effect” grows with L) is quantified by the critical-time expansions; simulations show deeper JEPA separates time‑scales by ρ, MAE does not.
> • Temporal linear model (Fig. 3): Analytic λa=γa||v||^2 and ρa=γa||v||^2/(σa^2+||v||^2) confirm JEPA learns “slow but clean” modes earlier; experiments match predictions.
> • ImageNet‑1K (Appendix D): I‑JEPA features measured by CCA align faster with the low‑variance subspace (“bottom” PCA) than MAE, consistent with JEPA’s implicit bias toward informative, lower‑variance features.
> 
> (e) EI‑constrained RNNs with spectral diagnostics (Dale’s ANNs vs ColEI vs standard)
> Identical/similar tasks (Fig. 2)
> • Adding problem (length 20), sequential MNIST (28 steps), Penn Tree Bank LM, naturalistic object recognition: across tasks, ColEI networks learn worse and are more variable; DANNs match standard RNNs.
> Key controlled comparisons
> • Sign constraints vs spectrum (Fig. 4A–C): Freezing signs hurts both RNNs and ColEIs slightly (≈0.7% ± 0.3% and 1% ± 1% final error increases), but spectrum “transplants” explain most of the performance gap: singular‑value spectra account for ~1.5% ± 0.3% (RNNs) and ~2% ± 1% (ColEIs) changes—larger than sign effects.
> • EI ratio and size (Figs. 5–7): With fewer inhibitory units, ColEI spectra become multimodal with large singular modes, NSE drops, and test error rises; larger ColEI networks improve NSE and accuracy even when max singular value grows. DANNs and standard RNNs keep unimodal spectra and high NSE across sizes/EI ratios.
> • Diagnostic: Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) strongly anti‑correlates with ColEI test error over EI ratios and sizes, offering an actionable spectral criterion to design EI RNNs that learn well while respecting Dale’s law.
> 
> Actionable integration tips (grounded in the papers)
> • End‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning under tight memory:
>   – Use 4‑bit AdamW with B128/DE for the first moment and Rank‑1/Linear for the second (Table 1): this removes the zero‑point failure mode, so “stable embeddings” are not necessary.
>   – Combine with FSDP and fused 4‑bit kernels to recover/beat 32‑bit speed (Table 4). In practice, the 4‑bit paper trains GPT‑2‑M with the LoRA codebase and instruction‑tunes LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B to 32‑bit‑comparable scores while saving up to 57.7% memory.
>   – Follow the implementation heuristics used in experiments: avoid quantizing tiny tensors (≤4096 elements) and embedding layers; offload/ZeRO or FSDP shard if available.
> • One‑stage anchor‑free human‑part association:
>   – Prefer PBADet’s part‑to‑body center offset over body‑to‑part (BPJDet) and anchor‑based heads; it scales to more parts without representation blow‑up and yields higher cond. accuracy and joint AP on BodyHands, lower mMR−2 on COCO‑HumanParts (Tables 1–3). Task‑aligned learning and multi‑scale features further improve joint scores (Table 4).
> • Language→structure generation:
>   – Use GenMS’s RAG→LLM→Diffusion→GNN tree search instead of direct LLM CIF generation. It yields ≥0.89 match rates and low DFT energies on perovskite/pyrochlore/spinel from language only (Table 1), outperforms UniMat and CrystalLM on DFT‑convergence, success, and unseen‑match (Tables 5–6), and benefits monotonically from higher branching factors (Table 2) and best‑of‑N GNN selection (>80% Ef gains).
> • Self‑supervised pretraining resistant to noisy features:
>   – Prefer JEPA‑style latent prediction over MAE reconstruction when the goal is to emphasize predictive signal over high‑variance pixels. The paper’s controlled analyses and ImageNet evidence show JEPA prioritizes high‑ρ features and aligns faster with the discriminative, low‑variance subspace; MAE tends to chase high‑variance components.
> • EI RNNs with interpretability and stability:
>   – If you must respect Dale’s law, use recurrent DANNs (EI “fast-feedforward inhibition” architecture) rather than ColEI; monitor and optimize NSE (higher is better). Maintain balanced E/I ratios and sufficient width; spectra that are unimodal and clustered (quarter‑circle‑like) train better; spectrum quality matters more than sign constraints alone.
> 
> Bottom line for your stack
> • (a) JEPA (Littwin et al.) supports your “avoid noisy features” goal before fine‑tuning; (d) 4‑bit AdamW enables end‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning within tight memory and even accelerates with fused kernels; (b) PBADet gives you a one‑stage anchor‑free part–body association detector with higher F1/precision‑linked metrics on COCO‑style datasets; (c) GenMS provides a practical LLM+Diffusion+GNN pipeline to propose low‑energy crystals from language that DFT‑validates well; (e) DANN‑style EI RNNs with NSE monitoring deliver interpretable, stable Dale‑law‑constrained recurrent models. All performance claims above are taken directly from the reported tables/figures in the cited papers.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers that collectively address your stack
> 
> **(a) Noise-robust self-supervised pretraining (MSE vs CE):**
> - **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** — analyzes JEPA (predicting in latent space, MSE-style regression) vs MAE (data-space reconstruction/CE) and shows JEPA is biased toward high-influence, informative features while suppressing noise.
> - **NEFTune** (noisy embeddings during fine-tuning) and **LDReg** (local-dimensionality regularization against collapse) are complementary for fine-tuning/SSL quality.
> 
> **(b) One-stage anchor-free hand/face→body association:** **PBADet** — introduces a single part-to-body center offset on top of anchor-free heads (YOLOv5/v7/v8); evaluated on COCO, COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman.
> 
> **(c) Language→structure generator:** **GenMS** — LLM (Transformer) proposes formulae, a diffusion model generates crystal structures, and a GNN predicts properties, with forward tree search for low-energy crystals (DFT-verified).
> 
> **(d) Tiny-state Adam/AdamW:** **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** — quantizes first/second moments to 4-bit (block-size B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, factorized 2nd moment).
> 
> **(e) EI-constrained RNN design with spectral diagnostics:** **"Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** — shows spectral properties (singular-value spectrum at initialization), not sign constraints, determine EI-RNN learning; proposes Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) as a diagnostic.
> 
> **(LoRA tips):** **NEFTune** (noise works with QLoRA) and the **Hessian-structure paper** (diagnostics for LoRA fine-tuning).
> 
> ## Comparison and analysis of experimental results
> 
> - **(a) JEPA vs MAE:** On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (measured by CCA). Theoretically, JEPA's ordering depends on high-influence feature coefficients ρ (noise suppression strengthened by depth), whereas MAE's ordering depends mainly on eigenvalues λ. NEFTune adds: LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win-rate **29.79%→64.69%** (+10% Evol-Instruct, +8% ShareGPT/OpenPlatypus), with no change on OpenLLM; LDReg improves linear eval/transfer/COCO detection for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE.
> 
> - **(b) PBADet:** Strongest quantitative edge is vs ED-Pose on COCO — left hand: Precision **37.63 vs 18.36**, Recall **60.82 vs 30.34**, F1 **46.50 vs 22.87**; all parts F1 **48.52 vs 31.51**. It also beats BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands/COCO-HumanParts; on CrowdHuman face-body, body MR-2 **36.5** (best) but AP advantage over BPJDet is smaller for this single-part task. Ablations show association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each matter.
> 
> - **(c) GenMS:** Satisfies user instructions **>80%** of the time for perovskites/pyrochlores/spinels, vs ~0% for zero-shot LLM CIF generation; **100% CIF validity** (vs LLM baselines); match rate up to **0.89**; compact representation improves DFT convergence **~50%**; GNN best-of-10 selection lowers formation energy (GNN and DFT) for **>80%** of compositions; DFT-verified low Ef (e.g., ~-1.38/-1.77 eV/atom).
> 
> - **(d) 4-bit optimizers:** Match or slightly exceed 32-bit AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet (Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2), E2E-NLG, WMT14, and LLaMA Alpaca/MMLU — while saving **up to 57.7%** memory (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; enables ~4× larger OPT). Beats 8-bit AdamW and clearly outperforms Adafactor/SM3 on classification.
> 
> - **(e) EI-RNNs:** ColEI networks learn worse and with higher variance across 4 tasks; gradient clipping helps a lot. Spectrum-transplant experiments show **singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints**. ColEI has a multimodal, dispersed spectrum (from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean matrix), unlike unimodal standard-RNN/DANN spectra; smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units worsen both spectrum and learning. **NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error** — usable as a pre-training diagnostic.
> 
> - **(LoRA fine-tuning tips):** NEFTune's noisy-embedding trick transfers to QLoRA-based instruction tuning. The Hessian paper adds: **LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does**; for well-pretrained models the power-law pattern can diverge and **Hessian trace is a more reliable generalization indicator** (structure forms after ~500 steps; merged LoRA changes the Hessian minimally).
> 
> **Bottom line:** the set {JEPA-noisy-features, PBADet, GenMS, 4-bit Optimizers, Dale's-Law spectral RNN} plus {NEFTune, Hessian/LoRA} covers all five needs and the LoRA guidance; where the papers overlap (COCO association, low-energy generation, memory savings, spectral diagnostics), the reported metrics consistently favor these methods over their baselines.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers that collectively address your stack, with a comparison of their key experimental results.
> 
> ## (a) Self-supervised pretraining avoiding noisy features (MSE vs CE)
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (JEPA vs MAE). In deep linear networks, JEPA's latent-space (MSE-style) objective orders feature learning by the regression coefficient ρ, prioritizing high-influence features and learning noisy features slower and with lower amplitude; MAE (pixel reconstruction) orders features mainly by eigenvalue λ and cannot defer noise. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA), supporting the claim that JEPA avoids noisy features before fine-tuning. **Complement:** **LDReg** improves SSL representation quality by regularizing local intrinsic dimensionality (countering dimensional collapse), boosting ImageNet linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR, BYOL, and MAE.
> 
> ## (b) One-stage anchor-free part–body association detector
> **PBADet** (one-stage, anchor-free; single part-to-body center offset; YOLOv5/v7 backbones). On BodyHands and COCOHumanParts it outperforms BPJDet and HierR-CNN; on CrowdHuman face–body it achieves the leading body MR-2 (36.5 with YOLOv7) and competitive AP (91.6 body / 81.6 face). Against ED-Pose on COCO parts, it gives substantially higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands and feet (all parts: P 39.41 / R 63.09 / F1 48.52 vs ED-Pose 24.09 / 45.51 / 31.51). Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning each improve association accuracy.
> 
> ## (c) Language-to-structure generator (LLM + Diffusion + GNN)
> **GenMS** (Generative Hierarchical Materials Search): an LLM proposes formulae → a diffusion model generates structures from a compact A×4 representation → a GNN ranks/selects via forward tree search. Results: >80% instruction-following success on perovskites/pyrochlores/spinels vs ~0% for zero-shot LLM prompting; 100% CIF validity; the compact representation improves DFT convergence by 50%; GNN-based best-of-N selection yields lower-energy structures >80% of the time; DFT-verified low formation energies (e.g., spinel E_f ≈ −1.77 eV/atom). Limitations: weaker on MXenes/Kagome lattices, no synthesizability check.
> 
> ## (d) Adam/AdamW with tiny optimizer states
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (4-bit Adam/AdamW with B128/DE first-moment, rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluded linear quantization of second moment, optional factorization). Results: matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1, SQuAD 94.5, GPT-2 E2E 67.8) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T 80.8, WMT14 26.28); up to 57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B 75.4→31.9 GB, trainable on one 80GB GPU); convergence curves closely align with 32-bit. 4-bit Factor further reduces memory (46.7% saved on RoBERTa-L). Sublinear optimizers (Adafactor, SM3) save more but degrade accuracy, especially on classification.
> 
> ## (e) EI-constrained RNNs with spectral diagnostics
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly). Comparing standard RNNs, ColEI (column-constrained) and recurrent DANN (Dale's ANNs): ColEI learns worse and with higher variance across all four tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition) and is highly unstable without gradient clipping. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the initial singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors. **Normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** measures unimodal singular-value clustering and anti-correlates with final test error, serving as a pre-training diagnostic: higher NSE at initialization ⇒ better learning; small balanced-EI networks outperform large skewed ones; recurrent DANNs match standard RNNs because their spectra match.
> 
> ## End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning tips (from this collection)
> - **NEFTune**: add uniform noise to embeddings during fine-tuning (scale α/√(Ld), α≈10); works with QLoRA. LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win rate rises from 29.8% to 64.7% with no extra compute/data; consistent gains on Evol-Instruct (+10%), ShareGPT (+8%), OpenPlatypus (+8%). Dropout/weight decay do not reproduce the gains.
> - **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (LoRA diagnostic): power-law Hessian structure emerges in full fine-tuning but **not** with LoRA-only fine-tuning (suggesting LoRA and full fine-tuning differ in generalization); during LoRA tuning the KS distance d_ks first rises then falls alongside test loss, and the Hessian trace Tr(H) consistently decreases — Tr(H) may be a more reliable LoRA generalization indicator than the power-law slope.
> - **4-bit optimizers**: pair LoRA with 4-bit AdamW states for further memory savings during adapter fine-tuning.
> - **RTB (diffusion fine-tuning)**: for memory-efficient LoRA fine-tuning of diffusion models, use stochastic timestep subsampling, batched gradient computation, loss clipping, and relative VarGrad to fit long diffusion trajectories in memory.

### paperscope:results_comparison:230 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that, taken together, cover: (1) one-stage, anchor‑free part–body association evaluated on COCO/COCO‑WholeBody style benchmarks; (2) the implicit bias of label‑free representation learning (JEPA/self‑distillation) versus masked reconstruction, contrasting MSE vs cross‑entropy losses and using cosine similarity on feature embeddings; (3) spectral analyses of excitatory–inhibitory recurrent deep networks for time‑series modeling, explaining stability via singular‑value properties; (4) memory‑efficient training via 4‑bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW and stochastic gradient methods, including end‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning; and (5) diffusion models with Transformer‑based conditional guidance that improve cross‑domain deepfake detection, using attention and reporting Precision/F1. Prefer works that reference COCO, use SGD/Adam variants, and discuss practical architectures (e.g., ResNet‑50/ViT).Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
