Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results reported by the five papers you provided. All numbers and claims come directly from the papers’ tables and figures.
> 
> 1) One-stage, anchor‑free part–body association on COCO/COCO‑WholeBody style datasets (PBADet vs. prior methods)
> Identical datasets and metrics
> - BodyHands (Table 1, PBADet):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39
>   - Observation: On the same dataset, both PBADet variants outperform BPJDet on joint AP and conditional accuracy, with YOLOv7 PBADet strongest overall.
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (Tables 2, 3): All methods evaluated on the same dataset with COCO-style metrics (AP.5:.95/AP.5/APM/APL) and association mMR−2 per part.
>   - Overall detection AP (All categories, original/subordinate):
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6/43.3 (AP.5:.95), 70.6/69.8 (AP.5), APM 63.8/63.2, APL 61.8/58.9
>     - PBADet (YOLOv7): 42.7/41.5, 69.5/67.9, APM 65.8/64.4 (better than BPJDet in APM), APL 66.7/63.3 (better than BPJDet in APL)
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 43.0/41.8, 70.0/68.4, APM 66.2/65.0 (best APM), APL 67.2/64.4 (best APL)
>   - Per-category AP (sub-set): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) and PBADet (YOLOv7) are competitive with BPJDet; PBADet tends to be better on person and feet categories and holds parity elsewhere (Table 2).
>   - Association mMR−2 (lower is better) (Table 3): PBADet achieves the lowest mMR−2 on head/face and several parts:
>     - PBADet (YOLOv7): head 29.2, face 31.3, left hand 41.1, right hand 42.7, right foot 52.6, left foot 52.5
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): head 27.9, face 30.5, left hand 36.2, right hand 40.8, right foot 50.4, left foot 47.9
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, left hand 41.6, right hand 42.2, right foot 49.1, left foot 50.4
>     - Observation: PBADet yields the strongest (lowest) average mMR−2 across many categories, indicating better part–body association.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Appendix Table 5, 6): face–body association in crowded scenes.
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): best body MR−2 (36.5) and high AP (body 91.6); mMR−2 for body‑face ~50.8—comparable to BPJDet; improves overall detection while keeping association competitive.
>   - Observation: On identical CrowdHuman settings, PBADet offers the best body MR−2 and competitive association mMR−2.
> 
> Additional notes
> - Architectures/datasets: PBADet is anchor‑free and leverages multi‑scale features; training uses SGD with YOLO-style backbones. Evaluations include COCOHumanParts (built on COCO), BodyHands, and CrowdHuman, covering whole-body/parts and crowded cases.
> 
> 2) Memory‑efficient training via 4‑bit optimizer states (Adam/AdamW/SGD variants) including end‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning
> Identical tasks and metrics (Table 2 unless noted)
> - Natural Language Understanding (RoBERTa‑Large, GLUE mean):
>   - 32‑bit AdamW: 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW: 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW: 89.1; 4‑bit Factor: 88.9
>   - Observation: 4‑bit matches 32‑bit/8‑bit accuracy on GLUE mean.
> 
> - Image classification (Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k, accuracy):
>   - 32‑bit AdamW: 81.2; 8‑bit AdamW: 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW: 80.8; 4‑bit Factor: 80.9
>   - Observation: 4‑bit within ~0.4% of 32‑bit; comparable to 8‑bit.
> 
> - Natural language generation (GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG, BLEU):
>   - 32‑bit AdamW: 67.7; 8‑bit AdamW: 67.5; 4‑bit AdamW: 67.8; 4‑bit Factor: 67.6
>   - Observation: 4‑bit AdamW slightly best BLEU (67.8) among all.
> 
> - Question answering (RoBERTa‑Large on SQuAD, F1):
>   - 32‑bit AdamW: 94.6; 8‑bit AdamW: 94.5; 4‑bit AdamW: 94.5; 4‑bit Factor: 94.6
>   - Observation: 4‑bit matches 32‑bit/8‑bit F1.
> 
> - Machine translation (Transformer‑Base, WMT14 en‑de, SacreBLEU):
>   - 32‑bit AdamW: 26.61; 8‑bit AdamW: 26.66; 4‑bit AdamW: 26.28; 4‑bit Factor: 26.45
>   - Observation: Small drop for 4‑bit; still comparable magnitude to 32‑bit/8‑bit.
> 
> Instruction tuning on LLaMA (Table 3)
> - LLaMA‑7B (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC‑e, ARC‑c, OBQA): 4‑bit AdamW ≈ 32‑bit AdamW (e.g., MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; ARC‑e 61.2 vs 61.5; similar on others).
> - LLaMA‑13B: 4‑bit AdamW matches/exceeds 32‑bit on several metrics (e.g., MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; ARC‑e 64.1 vs 63.6).
> - LLaMA‑33B: 4‑bit AdamW stays comparable (e.g., MMLU 54.9 vs 56.4; OBQA 45.4 vs 43.8).
> 
> Memory/time and model size (Table 4, Table 5)
> - Memory savings: Up to 57.7% total‑memory reduction vs 32‑bit during instruction tuning (LLaMA‑7B: 75.40 GB→31.87 GB), with similar or slightly better runtime in fused implementations.
> - Trainable model size: With 4‑bit AdamW, can fine‑tune larger models under fixed memory (e.g., 24 GB GPU: OPT‑1.3B vs OPT‑350M with 32‑bit; 80 GB: LLaMA‑7B becomes feasible).
> 
> Ablations (Table 6)
> - Compressing both moments in 4‑bit (B128/DE for first moment; Rank‑1/Linear or DE‑0 for second) preserves accuracy near full‑precision. Factorizing the second moment often improves accuracy and memory even further.
> 
> Takeaway: Across identical tasks/datasets, 4‑bit AdamW/Factor generally matches 32‑bit/8‑bit performance while substantially cutting memory; on some tasks (NLG) it slightly improves metrics.
> 
> 3) Diffusion models with Transformer‑based conditional guidance for cross‑domain deepfake detection
> Cross‑dataset generalization (trained on FF++(HQ), tested cross‑domain; Table 1)
> - EfficientNet‑B4 backbone (baseline vs +DiffusionFake), AUC/EER on identical test sets:
>   - Celeb‑DF: 73.51/34.17 → 83.17/24.59
>   - Wild Deepfake: 70.04/37.03 → 75.17/33.25
>   - DFDC‑P: 70.51/33.98 → 77.35/30.17
>   - DFD: 87.57/21.31 → 91.71/16.27
>   - DiffSwap: 77.38/29.44 → 82.02/25.55
>   - Average across five: 75.80/31.19 → 81.88/25.97
>   - Observation: Plug‑and‑play DiffusionFake consistently improves cross‑dataset AUC and lowers EER without adding inference parameters.
> 
> - ViT‑B backbone, identical tests:
>   - Celeb‑DF: 74.64/33.07 → 80.46/27.51
>   - Wild Deepfake: 75.46/31.53 → 80.14/29.62
>   - DFDC‑P: 74.24/34.29 → 80.95/27.66
>   - DFD: 84.38/24.15 → 90.36/19.73
>   - DiffSwap: 78.50/28.14 → 86.98/21.32
>   - Average: 77.44/30.24 → 83.78/25.17
>   - Observation: Similar gains for ViT‑B; on average, DiffusionFake surpasses strong SOTA baselines (e.g., DCL avg AUC 80.40).
> 
> Ablations (Tables 2–3)
> - Removing Stable Diffusion (SD) or the Feature Filter or Weight module reduces gains. The full system (SD + Filter + Weight) yields best cross‑domain AUC/EER.
> - Backbone coverage: DiffusionFake improves ResNet‑34, EfficientNet‑B0, ViT‑Small as well—indicating generality.
> 
> Takeaway: On the same training/testing splits used by prior work, the guided Stable Diffusion framework (with attention modules for feature filtering/weighting and ControlNet‑style injection) improves cross‑domain deepfake detection across multiple backbones and datasets.
> 
> 4) Spectral analyses of EI recurrent deep networks (time‑series modeling) and stability via singular‑value properties
> Identical tasks and comparisons (Figure 2; §3.1–3.3)
> - Tasks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task. Across all, Column EI (ColEI; columns constrained to excitatory/inhibitory) learns worse than Standard RNNs and DANN EI architectures; performance is also more variable.
> - Role of sign constraints vs. spectra (Figure 4A–C):
>   - Sign constraints alone explain only part of the gap (impair learning by ~0.7% ± 0.3% for RNNs, ~1% ± 1% for ColEI), while the difference in singular‑value spectra explains more of the gap (changes of ~1.5% ± 0.3% for RNNs and ~2% ± 1% for ColEI when spectra are transplanted).
>   - Conclusion: Singular‑value spectra (multimodal, dispersed, with large modes in ColEI) are more detrimental than sign constraints per se.
> - Network size and E/I ratio (Figures 5–7):
>   - Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) is predictive: higher NSE (more clustered singular values) correlates with lower test error across EI ratios and network sizes. Small networks with few inhibitory units learn poorly and have more pathological spectra; larger or more balanced networks improve spectra and performance.
> 
> Takeaway: Across identical tasks, Standard/DANN RNNs learn best; ColEI performs worse unless spectrum pathologies are mitigated. The spectral profile (singular‑value distribution) is a stronger predictor of performance than the presence/absence of sign constraints.
> 
> 5) Implicit bias of label‑free representation learning (JEPA/self‑distillation) vs. masked reconstruction (MAE)
> Consistent experimental contrasts (Figures 1–2; §3–4; Appendix D)
> - Deep linear training dynamics (simulations): With features characterized by covariance (λ) and regression coefficient (ρ), JEPA prioritizes high‑influence features (high ρ) as depth increases, while MAE prioritizes highly covarying features (high λ). In distributions where λ increases but ρ decreases, JEPA reverses the learning order relative to MAE.
> - Spectrum/time‑series generative models: In a temporal linear model, JEPA learns predictive, less noisy features (higher ρ) sooner than MAE, aligning with its implicit bias against noisy reconstruction targets. MAE remains agnostic to ρ.
> - ImageNet (Appendix D): Using I‑JEPA vs. MAE on ImageNet‑1k (64×64), the linear probing alignment (mean CCA) indicates I‑JEPA features align faster/better with the low‑variance (bottom) subspace, while MAE emphasizes the top‑variance subspace; this matches the theory that perceptual/semantic features often live in low‑variance subspaces.
> 
> Takeaway: On matched synthetic and ImageNet settings, JEPA and MAE learn different features: JEPA focuses earlier on influential (predictive, low‑variance) features, while MAE emphasizes high‑variance reconstruction. This difference becomes stronger with deeper encoders.
> 
> Summary by dataset/type
> - Identical COCO‑style settings (COCOHumanParts and derivatives): PBADet achieves best per‑size AP (APM/APL) and lowest mMR−2 for many parts, outperforming BPJDet on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman.
> - Identical language/vision/QA/MT tasks: 4‑bit AdamW/Factor matches 32‑bit/8‑bit across GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG BLEU, and is within ~0.5% on ImageNet; instruction tuning on LLaMA remains comparable across sizes with major memory reductions.
> - Identical deepfake cross‑dataset splits: With EfficientNet‑B4 and ViT‑B backbones, DiffusionFake improves average AUC by ~6 points and reduces EER consistently across Celeb‑DF, WildDeepfake, DFDC‑P, DFD, DiffSwap; it surpasses or matches prior SOTA averages and requires no extra inference-time parameters.
> - Time‑series modeling and sequence tasks: DANN/Standard RNNs > ColEI on adding/sMNIST/PTB/naturalistic recognition; spectral transplantation proves spectra dominate sign constraints in driving performance gaps; NSE tracks error across EI ratios/sizes.
> - JEPA vs. MAE: On controlled linear settings and ImageNet, JEPA shows a depth‑dependent bias toward influential features (high ρ) and faster alignment to low‑variance, semantic subspaces; MAE prioritizes high‑variance reconstruction.
> 
> Overall, taken together, the five works provide consistent experimental evidence across identical datasets, similar dataset types, and specific benchmarks that: (i) one‑stage anchor‑free part–body association (PBADet) outperforms anchor‑based/extended representations on COCO‑style benchmarks; (ii) JEPA and MAE have distinct, empirically observed implicit biases; (iii) EI RNN performance differences stem primarily from spectral properties rather than sign constraints; (iv) 4‑bit optimizer states preserve task performance while enabling substantial memory savings and larger models; and (v) diffusion‑guided conditional feature learning (DiffusionFake) generalizes better across deepfake domains on the same evaluation suites.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers matching the five topics
> 
> **1. Part–body association — PBADet** (`08b70bc3…`): One-stage, anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/v7 backbones + TOOD task-alignment) using a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman (COCO-WholeBody-style).
> 
> **2. JEPA vs MAE implicit bias** (`40fde037…`, "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"): Deep-linear analysis showing JEPA (self-distillation, latent-space **MSE** prediction) prioritizes high-ρ "influential" features while MAE (data-space **MSE** reconstruction) only prioritizes high-variance features; depth strengthens the bias. Cosine similarity appears via CCA feature-similarity analysis (I-JEPA vs MAE on ImageNet). The complementary paper "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (`160e1407…`) covers **cross-entropy-style InfoNCE loss with cosine similarity on embeddings** (SGD, ResNet-18/50).
> 
> **3. EI recurrent networks — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (`e63a94c4…`): Explains stability/learning via singular-value spectra (NSE, multimodal dispersed spectra, max singular value) on time-series tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition).
> 
> **4. 4-bit optimizer states** (`8d5e1455…`, "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"): Adam/AdamW/SGDM first+second moments quantized to 4-bit (B128/DE, Rank-1/Linear, zero-point exclusion, factorization). Note: LoRA is only cited as related work — the paper does **not** run end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning experiments itself.
> 
> **5. Deepfake detection — DiffusionFake** (`fc4f3d19…`): Frozen Stable Diffusion + ControlNet-inspired Guide Module (cross-attention/self-attention) guides detector encoders to disentangle source/target features for cross-domain generalization. Note: it reports **AUC/EER**, not Precision/F1.
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **Part–body association (PBADet):** On BodyHands, anchor-free part-to-body (Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98) beats anchor-based BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13). On CrowdHuman face-body, it improves body MR-2 (36.5 vs 41.3) with competitive face AP (91.6 vs 89.5). Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each add accuracy; COCOHumanParts AP ≈ 42.7. It also reports higher precision/recall/F1 than ED-Pose for hands/feet.
> 
> **JEPA vs MAE:** Theoretically, with deep encoders the two objectives learn the same features in *different order* — JEPA inverts learning order toward influential (low-variance, predictive) features; on ImageNet, I-JEPA features align faster with the perceptual low-variance PCA subspace than MAE (CCA). Implication: reconstruction (MAE) wastes capacity on noisy, high-variance features; JEPA is more sample-efficient for downstream tasks. LDReg (SSL regularization) complements this by showing MAE/SimCLR-style methods suffer local dimensional collapse, which its Fisher-Rao-based LID regularization fixes (better ImageNet linear eval, COCO transfer).
> 
> **EI RNNs:** ColEI (simple Dale's-law partitioning) learns worse and with higher variance on all four tasks; gradient clipping helps a lot. Singular-value analysis shows sign constraints matter less than the initial spectrum: ColEI has multimodal, dispersed spectra (NSE low), whereas standard RNNs and DANN follow the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle law; NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance across EI ratio/size.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers:** 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor match or slightly exceed 32-bit AdamW across NLU (88.9–89.1), ImageNet Swin-T (80.8–80.9), NLG, QA (F1 94.5), MT, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning, while cutting memory up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU) and reducing communication cost; sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor, SM3) degrade, especially on image classification.
> 
> **DiffusionFake:** Training FF++ → unseen datasets, En-B4 average AUC rises 75.80 → 81.88 (Celeb-DF +11%) and ViT-B 77.44 → 83.78 (DFDC +6%), with lower EER than all SOTA baselines (Xception, F3-Net, MAT, DCL, RECCE, etc.); it also wins cross-manipulation and multi-source protocols (+8% vs backbone, +7% under low-quality). Inference adds no parameters.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting observations
> - **Optimizers/backbones:** PBADet uses YOLO (anchor-free) with TOOD task alignment; DiffusionFake uses Adam (lr 1e-5, 20 epochs) with EfficientNet-B4/ViT-B; the contrastive-embedding paper uses SGD + ResNet-18/50; the 4-bit paper covers Adam/AdamW/SGDM; the JEPA and EI-RNN papers rely on (stochastic) gradient descent.
> - **Architecture trend:** CNN/YOLO for detection, ViT and Transformer-based guidance for deepfakes and SSL — consistent with the "ResNet-50/ViT" preference.
> - **Metrics gaps vs. your request:** no paper here reports Precision/F1 for deepfake detection (DiffusionFake uses AUC/EER); the 4-bit paper does not actually test end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning with 4-bit states; and the JEPA paper contrasts MSE (latent vs data space) but not MSE vs cross-entropy directly — the cross-entropy/cosine-similarity angle is covered by the contrastive-learning embedding paper.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers identified (one per topic)
> 
> **1. PBADet (ICLR 2024, doc 08b70b…)** — One-stage, anchor-free part–body association. Evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman (COCO/COCO-WholeBody-style benchmarks; explicitly cites COCO and COCO-WholeBody). Built on YOLOv5/v7 (anchor-free heads), trained with the **SGD** optimizer + AMP over 100 epochs. Results: BodyHands HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (YOLOv7); COCOHumanParts all-category AP 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6); vs ED-Pose (Swin-L) on COCO parts it beats it in Precision/Recall/F1 (all parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs 24.09/45.51/31.51).
> 
> **2. "Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024, doc 40fde0…)** — Implicit bias of JEPA/self-distillation vs MAE (masked reconstruction) in label-free representation learning, analyzed via deep linear networks. Shows JEPA prioritizes high-influence features while MAE prioritizes high-variance (noisy) ones; verified with I-JEPA vs MAE on ImageNet-1K using CCA (JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace). The companion **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (doc 160e14…) supplies the **cosine-similarity on feature embeddings** analysis and the **cross-entropy-style InfoNCE vs sigmoid/SigLIP** contrast (positive-pair similarity = 1, negative = −1/(n−1); smaller batches raise negative-pair variance).
> 
> **3. "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023, doc e63a94…)** — Spectral analysis of excitatory–inhibitory recurrent networks (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNN) on sequence tasks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, PTB language modeling, object recognition). Explains poor learning via **singular-value spectrum** rather than sign constraints: ColEI's column-mean nilpotent structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values (vs Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle), causing exploding gradients; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance across EI ratio/size.
> 
> **4. "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023, doc 8d5e14…)** — 4-bit optimizer states for **Adam/AdamW and SGD(M)** (B128 block, DE-linear mapping, rank-1 normalization, zero-point exclusion, second-moment factorization), including a convergence proof for quantized SGDM; used in **LoRA-based fine-tuning** of GPT-2 and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning. Results: 4-bit AdamW matches/exceeds 32-bit on GLUE/SQuAD/E2E-NLG and is comparable on ImageNet (Swin-T) and WMT; LLaMA-7B runs on one 80 GB GPU with up to **57.7% memory savings** (75.4→31.9 GB) with near-identical loss curves.
> 
> **5. DiffusionFake (doc fc4f3d…)** — **Diffusion-model-guided cross-domain deepfake detection**: a frozen Stable Diffusion reconstructs source/target images via a ControlNet-inspired GuideModule, with Feature-Filter/Weight modules (attention-based, ViT-B/EfficientNet-B4/ResNet backbones). Cross-dataset FF++→{Celeb-DF, WildDeepfake, DFDC-P, DFD, DiffSwap}: En-B4 average AUC 75.80→81.88, ViT-B 77.44→83.78 (+~6%); En-B4+Ours on Celeb-DF 83.17, DiffSwap 82.02. Ablations: removing SD weights drops ~5 AUC, Filter −5, Weight −3. **Note:** it reports AUC/EER/ACC, not Precision/F1 (Precision/F1 appear in PBADet's ED-Pose comparison instead).
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> 
> - **Benchmarks are heterogeneous**, so the five papers cannot be ranked on a single scale; each claims SOTA within its own task/regime.
> - **Optimizer/architecture preferences:** PBADet uses SGD + CNN backbones (YOLO); DiffusionFake uses Adam + ViT/EfficientNet/ResNet; the 4-bit optimizer paper focuses on AdamW (with SGD(M) theory). This matches your preference for SGD/Adam-variant and ResNet/ViT-style backbones, but none of the papers share a common network or dataset.
> - **Common methodological theme:** all five gain accuracy/efficiency by adding a *guiding signal* to the main objective — a part-to-body center offset (PBADet), a latent-space prediction loss (JEPA), spectral shaping/initialization of recurrent weights (Dale's-law paper), quantization of optimizer states (4-bit optimizers), and diffusion-based source/target reconstruction (DiffusionFake). In each case, ablations show the added component is the main driver of the gain (e.g., PBADet +1.2 JointAP from anchor-free part-to-body; DiffusionFake +8 AUC from SD+Filter+Weight; 4-bit optimizer matched full precision only with the zero-point-exclusion fix).
> - **Representation quality vs. memory:** the JEPA paper shows theoretical (implicit-bias) gains transfer to ImageNet CCA alignment; the 4-bit optimizer shows the practical cost of that: near-lossless training at 4-bit with big memory savings. These are complementary rather than competing.
> - **Caveats:** DiffusionFake's gains are reported as AUC/EER without error bars (per the overview); PBADet's COCOHumanParts AP is only on par with BPJDet for some categories (leads on person/feet); the Dale's-law RNN paper uses small (≤1000-unit) RNNs, and the JEPA theory is limited to deep linear networks/special initialization. These limitations prevent any claim of a single "best" method across the five topics.

Gold 1：

> Below is a consolidated, results‑only comparison across the five papers you provided. We report exactly what is in their tables/figures and note when datasets are identical or only similar in type.
> 
> 1) Identical datasets across methods (none) and within‑paper head‑to‑head comparisons
> - Across the five papers, there are no shared benchmark datasets used by more than one of the five methods. Therefore, direct cross‑paper head‑to‑head on the same dataset is not available. We instead report (a) each paper’s within‑paper comparisons (their method vs. baselines on identical datasets) and (b) cross‑paper comparisons on similar task types.
> 
> 2) Per‑paper experimental results on identical datasets (within each paper)
> A. PBADet (ICLR 2024): anchor‑free part–body association
> - BodyHands (Table 1; identical train/test splits for all methods)
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Acc. 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>   Summary: PBADet improves all three metrics over the strongest BPJDet baseline on the same dataset (e.g., +3.2 AP, +5.71% conditional accuracy, +1.59 joint AP for PBADet‑YOLOv7 vs. BPJDet‑YOLOv5l6).
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2; identical protocol)
>   • Overall AP (AP.5:.95, original/subordinate):

>   • Scale APs: PBADet leads on mid/large objects: APM/APL = 66.2/67.2 (PBADet‑YOLOv5l6) vs. 63.8/61.8 (BPJDet‑YOLOv5l6); subordinate APM/APL 65.0/64.4 vs. 63.2/58.9.
>   • Per‑category APs (examples): Person AP: 62.4 (PBADet‑YOLOv5l6) vs. 61.3 (BPJDet‑YOLOv5l6). Left foot AP: 31.5 (PBADet‑YOLOv5l6) vs. 30.9. Right foot AP: 37.7 (PBADet‑YOLOv5l6) vs. 39.6 (BPJDet‑YOLOv5l6).
>   • Association quality (Table 3, mMR−2 lower is better):
>     – BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, l‑hand 41.6, r‑hand 42.2, r‑foot 49.1, l‑foot 50.4.
>     – PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 27.9, 30.5, 36.2, 40.8, 50.4, 47.9.
>   Summary: PBADet substantially reduces average mismatch rates for head/face/hands (e.g., head mMR−2 30.8 → 27.9; l‑hand 41.6 → 36.2) and improves mid/large‑object AP, with similar or slightly lower small‑part APs vs. BPJDet.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Appendix Tables 5–6)
>   • Face‑body association (Table 5): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves best body MR−2 (36.5 vs. 40.7 for BPJDet‑l6) and equal/better face/body AP (body AP 91.6 vs. 89.5). Part‑pair mMR−2 is comparable (≈50–51).
>   • Versus crowded‑person detectors (Table 6): PBADet attains the best body MR−2 (36.5) and competitive AP vs. DETR‑based baselines while preserving joint detection.
> 
> - Pose baseline comparison (Appendix A.2, Table 7; COCO val)
>   • Against ED‑Pose (Swin‑L), PBADet reports higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet (e.g., “all parts” F1: 48.52 vs. 31.51) using its own model and IoU>0.5 criteria.
> 
> B. DiffusionFake (NeurIPS 2024): guided Stable Diffusion for generalizable deepfake detection
> - Cross‑dataset generalization (Table 1; trained on FF++ HQ, identical test sets for all listed methods)
>   • Celeb‑DF (AUC/EER): En‑B4 baseline 73.51/34.17 → En‑B4+Ours 83.17/24.59; ViT‑B baseline 74.64/33.07 → ViT‑B+Ours 80.46/27.51. DiffusionFake exceeds or matches SOTA reported baselines (e.g., DCL 82.30 AUC, UIA‑ViT 82.41 AUC).
>   • WildDeepfake: En‑B4 70.04/37.03 → 75.17/33.25; ViT‑B 75.46/31.53 → 80.14/29.62.
>   • DFDC‑Preview: En‑B4 70.51/33.98 → 77.35/30.17; ViT‑B 74.24/34.29 → 80.95/27.66.
>   • DFD: En‑B4 87.57/21.31 → 91.71/16.27; ViT‑B 84.38/24.15 → 90.36/19.73.
>   • DiffSwap (diffusion‑based swap): En‑B4 77.38/29.44 → 82.02/25.55; ViT‑B 78.50/28.14 → 86.98/21.32.
>   • Average (over 5 test sets): En‑B4 75.80/31.19 → 81.88/25.97; ViT‑B 77.44/30.24 → 83.78/25.17.
>   Summary: On identical test sets across many baselines, DiffusionFake delivers consistent AUC gains and lower EER, especially strong on difficult cross‑domain sets and the new diffusion‑swap data.
> 
> - Ablations (Table 2): Adding the pre‑trained Stable Diffusion (SD), feature filter, and weight modules cumulatively improves Celeb‑DF AUC from 71.87 (no SD/filter/weight) to 83.17 and DFDC‑P AUC from 71.78 to 77.35. Removing SD degrades both detection and reconstruction metrics (Appendix Table 6, SSIM/PSNR correlate with AUC/EER changes).
> 
> C. Memory‑efficient optimizers with 4‑bit states (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Accuracy vs. baselines on identical tasks (Table 2)
>   • NLU (GLUE, RoBERTa‑L, mean score): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9 → 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 8‑bit ≈ 89.1; Adafactor/SM3: 89.1/87.5.
>   • ImageNet‑1k (Swin‑T, top‑1 Acc): 32‑bit 81.2 → 4‑bit 80.8 (−0.4); 8‑bit 81.0; Adafactor/SM3: 80.0/79.0.
>   • E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2 M, BLEU): 32‑bit 67.7 → 4‑bit 67.8; 8‑bit 67.5; Adafactor/SM3: 67.2/66.9.
>   • SQuAD (RoBERTa‑L, F1): 32‑bit 94.6 → 4‑bit 94.5; 8‑bit 94.5; SM3 91.7.
>   • WMT14 En‑De (Transformer‑Base, SacreBLEU): 32‑bit 26.61 → 4‑bit 26.28; 8‑bit 26.66; Adafactor 26.52; SM3 22.72.
>   Summary: Across diverse vision/NLP tasks, 4‑bit states match or nearly match 32‑bit and 8‑bit optimizers; they substantially outperform SM3 in most settings and are competitive with Adafactor.
> 
> - LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3; identical evaluation protocols)
>   • 7B model (MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC‑e/ARC‑c/OBQA): 32‑bit 38.7/74.6/61.5/45.1/43.4 vs. 4‑bit 38.9/74.7/61.2/44.4/43.0 (very close).
>   • 13B, 33B: 4‑bit closely tracks 32‑bit across all benchmarks.
> 
> - Memory/time (Table 4):
>   • LLaMA‑7B FSDP: total training memory 75.40 GB (32‑bit) → 31.87 GB (4‑bit), −57.7%; training time modestly improves (3.35 h → 3.07 h).
>   • RoBERTa‑L and GPT‑2 M: total memory reduced by ≈34–47% with 4‑bit, throughput parity once fused ops are used.
> 
> D. Learning with Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023): RNN spectral properties dominate performance
> - Across four standard RNN tasks—Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank LM, and a naturalistic object recognition task (Figure 2)—ColEI (column‑signed EI) networks learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs.
> - Sign‑constraint vs. spectrum (Figure 4): Freezing signs degrades performance only partially (e.g., +0.7% ± 0.3% test error for RNNs; +1% ± 1% for ColEI), whereas transplanting singular value spectra accounts for most of the gap (summary in Fig. 4C: spectrum explains ≈1.5% ± 0.3% of RNN error change and ≈2% ± 1% for ColEI), indicating spectrum is the dominant factor.
> - Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) predicts performance (Figures 5–7): Lower NSE (more dispersed/multimodal singular values) correlates with higher test error; increasing inhibitory ratio and/or width increases NSE and lowers error. These are reported as consistent trends with plotted correlations; exact numeric errors vary by task/size in the figures.
> 
> E. JEPA implicit bias (NeurIPS 2024): JEPA vs. MAE dynamics
> - Controlled linear‑network simulations and ODE analysis show JEPA learns features with higher regression coefficients ρ earlier than MAE (Figures 1–2), reversing the learning order when λ (covariance) and ρ differ (no hard numbers in the figures; the result is qualitative but consistent across runs).
> - On ImageNet (Appendix D, Figure 7), JEPA encoders show higher CCA similarity between features learned on full vs. bottom‑variance PCA data than MAE, and lower CCA for full vs. top‑variance PCA—consistent with JEPA prioritizing predictive, lower‑variance/perceptual subspaces compared to pixel reconstruction.
> 
> 3) Cross‑paper comparisons on similar task types
> - Detection with structured guidance vs. baselines: PBADet (anchor‑free, task‑aligned) and DiffusionFake (guided SD) both demonstrate improvements over strong in‑domain baselines by enforcing structure at training time: PBADet via a 2D part‑to‑body offset and task‑alignment (e.g., BodyHands joint AP 85.98 vs. 84.39 for BPJDet), DiffusionFake via reconstructing source/target with frozen Stable Diffusion (e.g., Celeb‑DF AUC 83.17 vs. 73.51 for En‑B4 baseline).
> - Generalization strength: DiffusionFake’s cross‑dataset AUC gains (up to +11 AUC on Celeb‑DF with En‑B4) parallel PBADet’s improved association mMR−2 across occlusion‑prone categories on COCOHumanParts. Both methods emphasize conditioning/guidance (Transformer attention in DiffusionFake’s filters and ControlNet‑style zero‑conv; task‑aligned learning and anchor‑free offsets in PBADet).
> - Resource‑constrained training: The 4‑bit optimizer states paper shows accuracy parity with 32‑bit across vision/NLP tasks while cutting optimizer memory >50% in large‑model FSDP training; this complements DiffusionFake/PBADet by enabling their backbones/head fine‑tuning on small GPUs. Reported optimizers: Adam/AdamW (4‑bit, 8‑bit), SGD/SGDM (PBADet uses SGD); these satisfy the standard stochastic optimizer requirement.
> - Objective choice (latent vs. pixel) and cosine similarity: JEPA (latent prediction) vs. MAE (pixel reconstruction) shows JEPA’s bias toward predictive/low‑variance features; in DiffusionFake, the weight module is trained with cosine similarity between VAE latents of fake vs. source/target, explicitly using cosine similarity as supervision. In PBADet, classification losses are cross‑entropy; in DiffusionFake, the reconstruction objectives are MSE‑style denoising losses (Eqs. 10–11) combined with CE for detection (Eq. 12).
> 
> 4) Performance by dataset category (specific highlights)
> - Part–body joint detection (PBADet)
>   • BodyHands: Hand AP 89.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.62; Joint AP 85.98 (beats prior BPJDet at 85.9/86.91/84.39).
>   • COCOHumanParts: Higher mid/large‑scale APs and lower mMR−2 for key parts than BPJDet; comparable to better on per‑category association quality.
>   • CrowdHuman: Best body MR−2 (36.5) and strong body AP (91.6), with comparable face‑body pairing mMR−2.
> 
> - Deepfake detection generalization (DiffusionFake)
>   • Celeb‑DF: En‑B4 AUC/EER 73.51/34.17 → 83.17/24.59; ViT‑B 74.64/33.07 → 80.46/27.51.
>   • DFDC‑P: En‑B4 70.51/33.98 → 77.35/30.17; ViT‑B 74.24/34.29 → 80.95/27.66.
>   • DFD: En‑B4 87.57/21.31 → 91.71/16.27; ViT‑B 84.38/24.15 → 90.36/19.73.
>   • DiffSwap: En‑B4 77.38/29.44 → 82.02/25.55; ViT‑B 78.50/28.14 → 86.98/21.32.
> 
> - Memory‑efficient fine‑tuning (4‑bit states)
>   • RoBERTa‑L GLUE: 88.9 (32‑bit) vs. 89.1 (4‑bit).
>   • SQuAD F1: 94.6 vs. 94.5; GPT‑2 M E2E BLEU: 67.7 vs. 67.8; ImageNet‑1k top‑1: 81.2 vs. 80.8.
>   • LLaMA‑7B: MMLU 38.7 vs. 38.9 and similar across other tasks; total memory −57.7% with FSDP.
> 
> - RNNs under Dale’s Law (spectral stabilization)
>   • Spectrum (not just sign constraints) explains most performance gaps (≈1.5–2% test error impact depending on setting) across adding/seq.‑MNIST/LM/object recognition; increasing NSE improves learning stability.
> 
> - JEPA vs. MAE (latent vs. pixel)
>   • In controlled linear tasks, JEPA prioritizes high‑influence (high ρ) features; when λ and ρ disagree, JEPA reverses learning order vs. MAE; on ImageNet, JEPA shows higher CCA on bottom‑variance subspace and lower on top‑variance than MAE.
> 
> 5) Optimizers, cosine similarity, and loss types (from the papers)
> - Optimizers used: PBADet (SGD); DiffusionFake (Adam, LR=1e−5); 4‑bit optimizers (Adam/AdamW, with 4‑bit states); Dale’s/JEPA analyses use gradient descent/flow.
> - Cosine similarity: DiffusionFake’s weight modules are trained against cosine similarity of VAE latents between fake and source/target images (Eqs. 6–7).
> - Loss types: PBADet uses IoU/DFL/CE plus association L1; DiffusionFake uses denoising MSE‑type losses for source/target guidance (Eqs. 10–11) plus cross‑entropy detection (Eq. 12); 4‑bit studies retain task‑standard losses (e.g., CE for ImageNet, BLEU/SacreBLEU, EM/F1 for QA); JEPA vs. MAE are analyzed under squared losses; Dale’s RNNs train under standard task losses.
> 
> Overall takeaways from the experiments
> - For anchor‑free association, PBADet consistently improves association metrics and mid/large‑scale AP over prior joint detectors on identical datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman).
> - For deepfake generalization, DiffusionFake yields robust, cross‑dataset AUC/EER gains on the same test sets as strong baselines, including on diffusion‑swap data, without inference‑time overhead.
> - For resource‑limited fine‑tuning, 4‑bit optimizer states maintain accuracy within noise of 32‑bit across vision/NLP (and instruction‑tuned LLMs) while cutting optimizer memory ≥50%.
> - For EI‑constrained RNNs, experiments show spectral initialization (unimodal/clustered singular values) matters more than sign constraints for learning stability and accuracy.
> - For learning objective choice, controlled experiments and ImageNet probes indicate JEPA’s latent‑space prediction biases towards predictive, low‑variance (perceptual) features, in contrast to reconstruction objectives that emphasize variance‑heavy components.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the papers to read for each requirement, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## (a) Anchor-free hand/face→person linking on common-objects datasets
> **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage, anchor-free part-body association via a single part-to-body center offset (YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7 backbones).
> - **Results**: On COCO-HumanParts, AP is on par with BPJDet while leading on person/feet AP and achieving the lowest average mMR-2 across head, face, and both hands; on CrowdHuman face-body it attains leading body MR-2 and competitive AP (advantage over BPJDet is smaller for this single-part task). Against ED-Pose, PBADet is much stronger: all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51.
> - **Ablations**: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning each improve association accuracy.
> 
> ## (b) Face-swap detection that generalizes to unseen forgeries via diffusion guidance
> **DiffusionFake (NeurIPS 2024)** — injects detector features (Filter/Weight modules) into a frozen pre-trained Stable Diffusion via a ControlNet-style GuideModule (trainable copy + zero convolutions) to reconstruct source/target faces; trains with CE classification + MSE diffusion losses; no extra inference parameters.
> - **Results (FF++→unseen datasets)**: EfficientNet-B4 average AUC 75.80→81.88 (e.g., Celeb-DF 73.51→83.17, DiffSwap 77.38→82.02); ViT-B 77.44→83.78 (Celeb-DF 74.64→80.46, DiffSwap 78.50→86.98). This beats baselines in the same table (Xception 72.67, F3-Net 74.96, GFF 75.46, LTW 77.07, DCL 80.40). Ablations confirm Filter/Weight modules and the pre-trained SD are critical.
> - **Related diffusion-guidance works**: Universal Guidance (ICLR 2024) — training-free guidance of frozen diffusion models (face recognition, object detection, segmentation signals); AdjointDEIS — training-free guidance via continuous adjoints for face-morphing attacks (DiM+AdjointDEIS-1 reaches 99.8/98.77/99.39 MMPMR on SYN-MAD 2022 with ArcFace/ElasticFace/AdaFace at FMR=0.1%).
> 
> ## (c) Stabilizing an EI-constrained RNN with exploding gradients
> **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023)** — the closest match. ColEI (excitatory/inhibitory sign-constrained) RNNs have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra with a large-singular-value mode → exploding activations/gradients; they train worse and with more variance across adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object-recognition tasks. Key findings:
> - **Gradient clipping benefits ColEI networks substantially more** than standard/DANN RNNs (without it they are "highly unstable").
> - Sign constraints matter less than the spectrum: spectral transplants and ablation show the singular-value distribution drives the deficit; DANN RNNs keep standard-RNN-like spectra and learn equally well.
> - Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance.
> - Note: the paper uses benchmark tasks, not sensor streams; if you need an RNN-on-time-series reference, G-Sim trains GRUs/DyNODE with Adam (lr 1e-2) and a Transformer with AdamW + gradient clipping at 0.7 for sequence prediction.
> 
> ## (d) Low-rank (LoRA) fine-tuning on small GPUs with 4-bit optimizer states
> **"4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023)** — compresses Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit (B128 blocks for first moment; rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for second moment; optional factorization), and uses LoRA in its LLaMA experiments (github.com/microsoft/LoRA).
> - **Results vs 32-bit AdamW**: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2 Medium E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7; QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B Alpaca MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7, LLaMA-13B 47.4 vs 46.5, LLaMA-33B comparable. So 4-bit matches/beats 32-bit while cutting memory up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B on a single 80 GB GPU); Adafactor/SM3 save more memory but degrade (esp. on classification).
> - **LoRA/Hessian reference** ("Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure", ICML 2025): analyzes LoRA adapters (TinyLlama on MathQA) and shows power-law Hessian spectra hold across SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, RAdam, Yogi, Adai, PNM, Lookahead, DiffGrad; slope magnitude predicts test error (Pearson 0.72–0.85) — useful for your optimizer comparison.
> 
> ## Latent-space prediction vs pixel reconstruction (MSE vs CE) and cosine-similarity probes
> - **DiffusionFake** itself contrasts a latent-space (LDM) MSE noise-prediction objective with a CE classification head; latent-space modeling "reduces computational cost and memory while preserving high quality."
> - **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)**: direct MAE (MSE on pixels/reconstructed input space) vs JEPA (MSE on latent representation) comparison. JEPA suppresses noise earlier/stronger (depth strengthens it); on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance PCA perceptual subspace faster than MAE (measured by CCA).
> - **Video-based representation learning (ICLR 2024)**: forward modeling (pixel prediction) beats temporal contrastive under exogenous noise; both degrade as noise grows; trajectory-based ACRO is strongest.
> - **Cosine-similarity probes**: "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" proves optimal encoders give positive-pair cosine sim = 1 and negative = −1/(n−1); smaller mini-batches raise variance of negative similarities, and an auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet. AdvI2I uses latent-space cosine similarity against NSFW concept vectors (SafetyChecker) with ASR ~82.5%; Visual Data-Type Identification uses a 0.85 cosine threshold for semantic search (correlation r≈0.80 with performance).
> 
> **Summary recommendation**: PBADet (a), DiffusionFake + Universal Guidance/AdjointDEIS (b), the Dale's Law EI-RNN paper + G-Sim's Adam/gradient-clipping setup (c), 4-bit Optimizers + LoRA/Hessian paper (d), and JEPA-vs-MAE plus the contrastive-similarity paper for your MSE-vs-CE and cosine-probe questions. Caveat: no collection paper covers an EI-constrained RNN on actual sensor streams, and none directly compares latent-prediction vs pixel-reconstruction as a controlled head-to-head with both MSE and CE objectives beyond the JEPA/MAE and DiffusionFake setups.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the papers that map to your four needs, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## (a) Anchor-free part–body association for HMI
> **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024).**
> - Fast, one-stage, anchor-free; uses YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones with a single part-to-body center offset for hands/face→person. Evaluated on COCO-WholeBody, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands, and it extends to animal parts.
> - Results: on BodyHands (YOLOv7), anchor-free part-to-body achieves Hand AP 89.1 / Conditional Accuracy 92.62 / Joint AP 85.98 vs. the anchor-based BPJDet's 85.3 / 86.80 / 78.13. On COCO-HumanParts it reaches 42.7 AP. On CrowdHuman face–body association it gives leading body MR-2; against the pose estimator ED-Pose it yields substantially higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands/feet. Ablations show association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment learning all help.
> 
> ## (b) Face-swap detection generalizing to unseen forgeries via guided diffusion
> **DiffusionFake: Enhancing Generalization in Deepfake Detection via Guided Stable Diffusion.**
> - Injects detector features into a **frozen pre-trained Stable Diffusion** through a ControlNet-style (zero-convolution) Guide Module to reconstruct source/target images—this is the Transformer-style/conditioning-guided diffusion approach. A Weight Module is trained with **cosine-similarity** supervision; training uses **Adam** (lr 1e-5), classification + diffusion **MSE** losses; no inference overhead.
> - Results (trained on FF++, cross-dataset): EfficientNet-B4 average AUC 75.80→**81.88** (+11% on Celeb-DF, +6% avg); ViT-B 77.44→**83.78** (+6% on DFDC, +6% avg). Ablations confirm the Filter/Weight modules and the pre-trained SD are critical.
> - *Alternative:* **Universal Guidance for Diffusion Models (ICLR 2024)**—training-free guidance of frozen diffusion using face-recognition/segmentation/CLIP cosine losses; comparable to specialized conditional models but slower and needs differentiable guidance functions.
> 
> ## (c) Stabilizing EI-constrained RNNs with exploding gradients
> **Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023).**
> - Shows EI (excitatory/inhibitory, Dale's-law) RNNs (ColEI) train poorly and unstably; **gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially more** than standard RNNs—directly addressing exploding gradients. Diagnosis: the problem is initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal/dispersed), not sign constraints; Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE) predicts trainability before training. DANN-RNNs retain good spectra and learn as well as standard RNNs across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition.
> - Practical takeaway: prefer DANN-style EI RNNs or spectral-aware initialization + gradient clipping for sensor streams.
> 
> ## (d) 4-bit optimizer states for small-GPU fine-tuning
> **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (4-bit optimizers, NeurIPS 2023).**
> - Quantizes **Adam/AdamW** first/second moments to 4-bit (small block B128 + rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer), with a factorized 4-bitFactor variant.
> - Results: matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW—RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, GPT-2 E2E 67.8 vs 67.7, LLaMA fine-tuning comparable—while cutting memory up to **57.7%** (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; RoBERTa-L 43.1% savings, GPT-2 34.4%). Full-precision accuracy/F1 is retained.
> - For the low-rank-adapter side, **NFTS (Neural Fine-Tuning Search)** searches per-layer freeze/adapter choices for few-shot adaptation (uses AdamW; +1.9%/+2.3% over TSA on Meta-Dataset ResNet-18, 16M vs 82M params).
> 
> ## On latent-space vs pixel reconstruction (MSE vs CE) + cosine probes
> **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024).**
> - Directly compares **latent-space prediction (JEPA)** vs **pixel reconstruction (MAE)**. Both are MSE-type, but the paper isolates the core bias: JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient, increasingly with depth) and learns the low-variance, perceptually rich subspace faster; MAE prioritizes high-covariance features regardless of informativeness. Verified on ImageNet-1K via CCA (I-JEPA aligns with the perceptual subspace faster than MAE). Uses SGD with stochastic gradients in experiments.
> - **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** supplies the **cosine-similarity probe** angle: analyzes embedding cosine similarities (optimal negative-pair similarity −1/(n−1)), proposes variance-reduction loss, and evaluates via linear probes with SGD, improving SimCLR/DCL/DHEL top-1 on CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet-100. Relatedly, **LDReg** and the JEPA/contrastive works use AdamW/LARS linear-evaluation probes.
> - MSE vs CE in this collection: DiffusionFake contrasts MSE reconstruction with CE classification; the 4-bit optimizer and Contrastive papers benchmark CE-based objectives. No single paper in the collection makes a direct "latent MSE vs pixel CE" head-to-head, so that specific contrast can only be inferred piecewise.
> 
> **Bottom line:** PBADet → (a); DiffusionFake (+ Universal Guidance as fallback) → (b); the Dale's-Law spectral RNN paper → (c); 4-bit optimizers (+ NFTS for adapters) → (d); the JEPA-vs-MAE paper + contrastive embedding-similarity paper for the latent-vs-pixel and cosine-probe comparison.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results drawn directly from the five papers, grouped by the five topics in your query. I highlight identical datasets where methods are compared head‑to‑head and summarize trends across similar dataset types. 1) Anchor‑free part–body association (PBADet) vs prior art on identical datasets • BodyHands (identical dataset; Table 1): – BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39. – PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98. – PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73. Result: PBADet improves Hand AP by +3.2–3.7 pts and Conditional Accuracy by +5.7–5.8 pts over BPJDet (v5l6), and slightly improves Joint AP. • COCOHumanParts (identical dataset; Table 2 & 3): – All‑categories AP (AP.5:.95 original/subordinate): BPJDet (v5l6) 43.6/43.3 vs PBADet 43.0/41.8 (v5l6) and 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7). – Scale APs: PBADet yields higher APM/APL (e.g., PBADet v5l6: APM 66.2/65.0, APL 67.2/64.4) than BPJDet v5l6 (APM 63.8/63.2, APL 61.8/58.9). – Per‑category APs: BPJDet slightly higher for head/face; PBADet slightly higher for person and feet (PBADet v5l6 person 62.4 vs 61.3 for BPJDet; l‑foot 31.5 vs 30.9). – Association metric (average mMR−2; Table 3): PBADet reduces miss‑matching vs BPJDet in most categories; PBADet v5l6: head 27.9 vs 30.8, face 30.5 vs 31.8, l‑hand 36.2 vs 41.6, r‑hand 40.8 vs 42.2; feet mixed (r‑foot 50.4 vs 49.1; l‑foot 47.9 vs 50.4). Result: PBADet achieves better mid/large‑scale and association accuracy (lower mMR−2), while BPJDet holds slight AP edge on some small parts (head/face). • CrowdHuman (identical dataset; Tables 5–6): – PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves best body MR−2 (36.5 vs BPJDet v5l6 40.7) and best body AP (91.6 vs 89.5). Part (face) AP is tied (81.6); mMR−2 for body‑face pairs is comparable (50.8 vs 50.1). Result: PBADet improves detection (body MR−2/AP) with similar association mMR−2. • Precision/Recall/F1 vs multi‑person pose (COCO val; Appendix A.2, Table 7): – ED‑Pose vs PBADet (YOLOv5l6): lefthand F1 22.87→46.50; righthand 24.17→47.34; leftfoot 40.46→51.08; rightfoot 40.34→50.34; all parts F1 31.51→48.52. Result: PBADet substantially improves Precision, Recall, and F1 over a strong pose baseline in bounding‑box part‑association. Notes on design: PBADet uses multi‑scale anchor‑free heads with task‑align learning and an explicit part‑to‑body center offset; ablations (Table 4, Table 8) show the association head, multi‑scale definition, and anchor‑free design all contribute to higher Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP. 2) Spectral and interpretability analyses with EI constraints (Dale’s ANNs vs ColEI vs standard RNNs) • Across identical tasks (Figures 2A–D): – Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic Object Recognition: ColEI (column‑sign‑constrained EI) consistently learns worse (slower convergence, higher final error) than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs. DANNs match standard RNNs despite enforcing Dale’s Law. Gradient clipping helps ColEI more (noted in text, Appendix Fig. 10). • Spectral diagnostics (Figures 3D–F; text): – ColEI initial singular value spectra are multimodal and dispersed with a notable large‑singular‑value mode, unlike the unimodal Marchenko–Pastur‑like spectra of standard RNNs and DANNs. – Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance: higher NSE (more clustered singular values) correlates with lower test error across EI ratios and widths (Figures 5G, 6G, 7C–D). • Spectrum vs sign‑constraints (Figure 4B–C; text): – Spectrum transplant experiments show spectra matter more than sign constraints for the performance gap. Quantitatively, the spectrum accounts for ~1.5% ± 0.3% (RNNs) and ~2% ± 1% (ColEI) absolute error changes, larger than the ~0.7–1.0% hit from freezing/relaxing sign constraints. • Scaling trends (Figures 5–6): – ColEI degrades as inhibitory ratio decreases (biologically realistic E:I) and improves with larger widths (higher NSE), even though max singular values grow; DANN remains robust across EI ratios and sizes. Takeaway: For EI‑constrained RNNs, spectral properties (singular value clustering) are the principal driver of optimization and generalization, surpassing the impact of the sign constraint itself. 3) Implicit bias of JEPA (self‑distillation) vs MAE (masked reconstruction) in deep linear models • Identical synthetic settings (Figures 1–2, 4–5; theory Theorems 3.2–3.5): – Greedy learning order: MAE prioritizes features with larger covariance λ (co‑variance with inputs), whereas JEPA prioritizes features with larger regression coefficient ρ (predictive influence). – Depth separation: The JEPA bias towards high‑ρ features strengthens with deeper encoders; shallow MAE (L→∞) approaches 1‑layer JEPA dynamics (Corollary 3.3 / Eq. 10). • Temporal model (Figure 3, Eq. 16): – In a simple video generative process, λa=γa||va||^2 and ρa=γa||va||^2/(σa^2+||va||^2); JEPA focuses on high‑ρ “slow, less‑noisy” features, while MAE tracks high‑λ correlated components even if noisy. • ImageNet study (Appendix D, Figure 7): – CCA trends indicate JEPA learned features align earlier with the “bottom” PCA variance subspace (where perceptual features reside), while MAE aligns more with the “top” variance subspace; JEPA thus reaches discriminative representations faster. Takeaway: With MSE‑style objectives in linear networks, JEPA’s implicit bias is to favor high‑influence (high‑ρ) features—especially at depth—whereas MAE favors high‑variance (high‑λ) features. 4) Memory‑efficient 4‑bit optimizer states (supports AdamW and end‑to‑end LLaMA fine‑tuning) Accuracy on identical datasets (Table 2, Table 9): • NLU (RoBERTa‑L/GLUE mean): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9 vs 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 8‑bit AdamW 89.1. Per‑task medians show close parity (e.g., MNLI/QNLI/QQP/SST‑2, etc.). • QA (RoBERTa‑L/SQuAD F1): 32‑bit 94.6 vs 4‑bit 94.5 (SQuAD v1.1); similar EM/F1 on SQuAD 2.0 (Table 9). • Vision classification (Swin‑T/ImageNet‑1K Top‑1): 32‑bit 81.2 vs 4‑bit 80.8 (−0.4 pt). • NLG (GPT‑2 Med/E2E‑NLG BLEU): 32‑bit 67.7 vs 4‑bit 67.8 (Table 2; other metrics NIST/METEOR/ROUGE‑L/CIDEr closely match, Table 8). • MT (Transformer‑Base/WMT14 en‑de SacreBleu): 32‑bit 26.61 vs 4‑bit 26.28; 8‑bit 26.66. LLaMA instruction‑tuning (Table 3): • LLaMA‑7B: 4‑bit AdamW ≈ 32‑bit across MMLU (38.9 vs 38.7), HellaSwag (74.7 vs 74.6), ARC‑e (61.2 vs 61.5), ARC‑c (44.4 vs 45.1), OBQA (43.0 vs 43.4). • LLaMA‑13B: 4‑bit slightly better on most (e.g., MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8). • LLaMA‑33B: 4‑bit comparable with small shifts (e.g., MMLU 54.9 vs 56.4) but OBQA improves (45.4 vs 43.8). Memory/throughput and capacity (Table 4–5): • Memory savings: – LLaMA‑7B FSDP: 32‑bit 75.4 GB → 4‑bit 31.9 GB (−57.7%); similar or faster wall‑clock (3.35 h → 3.11 h fused). – RoBERTa‑L: 5.31 GB → 3.00 GB with 4‑bit fused (−43.5%); training time also improves (3.93 → 3.17 min). – GPT‑2 Med: 6.89 GB → 4.62 GB (−34.4%), matched time when fused. • Max trainable model under fixed budget: – 24 GB GPU: 32‑bit up to OPT‑350M vs 4‑bit up to OPT‑1.3B. – 80 GB GPU: 32‑bit up to OPT‑1.3B vs 4‑bit up to OPT‑6.7B, and LLaMA‑7B becomes trainable on a single 80 GB. Key techniques validated by figures/tables: smaller blocks (B=128) for first moment; zero‑point‑free linear mapping and rank‑1 normalization for second moment (Table 1 ablations), achieving stable 4‑bit convergence without stable embeddings. 5) Cross‑domain policy adaptation via Value‑Guided Data Filtering (VGDF) Online dynamics adaptation (identical environments; Figure 4): • Across 8 Mujoco transfer settings (HalfCheetah/Ant/Walker/Hopper; kinematic and morphology shifts), VGDF consistently outperforms DARC, GARAT, and IW‑Clip in sample‑efficiency and asymptotic return; Finetune is strong in some cases, but the paper notes VGDF is the only method that matches/surpasses the target‑trained Oracle in 4/8 settings. Offline‑source + online‑target (identical tasks; Table 1): • HalfCheetah‑broken back thigh: H2O 5761±148 > VGDF+BC 4834±250 > Symmetric 2439±390 > Offline‑only 1128±156. • HalfCheetah‑no thighs: VGDF+BC 3910±160 > H2O 3023±77 > Symmetric 2211±77 > Offline‑only 361±39. • Hopper‑broken hips: VGDF+BC 2785±75 > H2O 2435±325 > Symmetric 2607±181 > Offline‑only 155±19. • Hopper‑short feet: VGDF+BC 3060±60 > Symmetric 2144±509 > H2O 868±73 > Offline‑only 399±5. • Walker‑broken right thigh: H2O 3743±50 > VGDF+BC 3000±388 > Offline‑only 1453±412 > Symmetric 709±128. • Walker‑no right thigh: VGDF+BC 3293±306 > H2O 2600±355 > Offline‑only 975±131 > Symmetric 872±301. PyBullet generalization (identical tasks; Table 3): • HalfCheetah: with (200k,20k) src/target samples: DARC 304±211, Finetune 653±51, VGDF 770±203; with (1M,100k): DARC 679±131, Finetune 678±38, VGDF 808±89. • Hopper: with (200k,20k): 73±20, 240±189, 957±39; with (1M,100k): 99±20, 869±32, 1006±2 (DARC, Finetune, VGDF). Ablations/training dynamics: • Data ratio Γ: Higher Γ (more source data) improves returns with fixed target data (Figure 5). • Selection ratio ξ%: VGDF robust in 10–50% range; naive mixing (no filtering) works on kinematic shifts but fails on morphology shifts (Figure 6). • Optimistic exploration policy π_E: boosts sample efficiency in most settings (Figure 7). • Fictitious Value Proximity (FVP): lower in kinematic than morphology shifts, quantifying domain closeness via value difference (Figure 8, Appendix Fig. 11). Cross‑topic synthesis on identical/similar dataset types • Detection (PBADet): On identical datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman), the anchor‑free, multi‑scale, attention‑aligned PBADet improves Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP, and reduces association errors (mMR−2) vs BPJDet; it also yields much higher Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED‑Pose on COCO. • Sequence modeling (Dale’s): On identical tasks (adding, sMNIST, PTB, natural objects), DANN (EI with better spectra) matches RNN performance, while ColEI underperforms; spectrum statistics (singular values, NSE) track generalization. • Representation learning (JEPA vs MAE): In identical linear settings, JEPA learns high‑ρ features first (especially with depth); MAE learns high‑λ features; ImageNet CCA curves show JEPA aligns faster to “bottom” variance subspace important for perception. • Fine‑tuning at scale with 4‑bit states: On identical datasets across NLP/vision/MT, 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit accuracy (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG) with small drops on ImageNet/WMT; for LLaMA (identical evaluation suites), 4‑bit closely matches 32‑bit; memory is cut by ~35–58% and allows 4× larger models on fixed GPUs. • RL adaptation (VGDF): On identical Mujoco/PyBullet tasks, VGDF reliably beats DARC/GARAT/IW‑Clip; in offline‑online, VGDF+BC often wins or is runner‑up depending on the task; training dynamics over t (learning curves) show consistent gains from value‑guided filtering and exploration. Notes aligning with your requested entities • Optimizers/SGD/AdamW: 4‑bit results use AdamW; RNN/DANN/ColEI trained with SGD (per paper) in controlled settings; • Losses: JEPA and MAE analyses center on MSE objectives in linear settings; classification tasks report cross‑entropy outcomes (e.g., ImageNet, GLUE); • Spectral diagnostics: singular value histograms, NSE correlations; • Training dynamics over t: Figures in Dale’s (test error over updates), JEPA (ODE learning curves; CCA over epochs), VGDF (returns vs steps) explicitly track dynamics; • Fine‑tuning setups: LLaMA 7B/13B/33B instruction tuning (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA) and ImageNet (Swin‑T) are directly reported; LoRA codebase is used for GPT‑2 finetuning, while LLaMA experiments demonstrate end‑to‑end 4‑bit AdamW fine‑tuning feasibility. Overall conclusions from the reported experiments • PBADet achieves state‑of‑the‑art part–body association on identical detection datasets, with strong Precision/F1 vs pose baselines, especially on hands/feet. • For EI‑constrained RNNs, getting the singular value spectrum “right” (DANN) is more important than the sign constraint alone; NSE is a practical predictor of performance. • JEPA’s implicit bias (high‑ρ features, amplified by depth) explains its rapid emergence of semantic features compared to MAE (high‑λ bias). • 4‑bit optimizer states deliver near‑parity accuracy across GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/WMT/ImageNet and LLaMA instruction tuning, with 35–58% lower memory and higher capacity, enabling practical end‑to‑end fine‑tuning. • VGDF (value‑guided filtering) consistently improves cross‑domain RL adaptation under limited target interactions, outperforming dynamics‑discrepancy baselines on identical environments and extending to offline‑online regimes.

> Here are the papers found in the collection, mapped to your five topics, followed by a brief comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1) Anchor-free part–body association — PBADet
> **"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** (ICLR 2024). One-stage anchor-free detector extending YOLOv5/YOLOv7 with a single part-to-body center offset over multi-scale feature maps, with task-alignment learning.
> - **BodyHands (YOLOv7):** HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (vs. BPJDet-YOLOv5m6: 85.3 / 86.80 / 78.13; BPJDet-YOLOv5l6: 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39).
> - **COCOHumanParts (YOLOv5l6):** AP.5:.95 = 43.0/41.8, AP.5 = 70.0/68.4 (original/subordinate), leading AP_M, AP_L and lowest mMR−2 for head/face/hands/right-foot.
> - **vs. ED-Pose (Precision/Recall/F1, all parts):** PBADet 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs. ED-Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51 — substantially higher precision, recall and F1.
> - Ablations: removing association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task-alignment each degrades metrics.
> 
> ## 2) Spectral/interpretability of excitatory–inhibitory sign-constrained networks
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023). Analyzes RNNs with E/I sign constraints (ColEI vs. DANN vs. standard RNNs) on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition.
> - ColEI learns worse and with higher variance; gradient clipping helps most.
> - Sign constraints alone explain only part of the gap (≈1% of 2.3%); **singular-value spectra matter more** (spectrum "transplant" experiments). ColEI has multimodal/dispersed spectra; standard RNNs/DANNs match the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle form.
> - Diagnostic: **Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE)** at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance.
> - Note: the retrieved content does not explicitly document cosine-similarity diagnostics or MSE vs. cross-entropy comparisons; the training is projected gradient descent (sign-projection), so that specific detail of your request is not covered here. (The Hessian power-law paper, **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (ICML 2025), is related: SGD-trained LeNet/ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/100 show power-law Hessian spectra that predict generalization.)
> 
> ## 3) Implicit bias of joint-embedding self-distillation vs. masked reconstruction
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024). Solves deep linear encoder dynamics for JEPA (self-distillation, StopGrad) vs. MAE (MSE reconstruction).
> - ODEs differ by one exponent: JEPA prioritizes high-regression-coefficient (ρ) "influential" features; MAE orders by covariance λ. With deep encoders JEPA reverses feature-learning order toward high-ρ, low-variance features, suppressing noise increasingly with depth; fixed points: w̄_JEPA(∞)=ρ^L vs. w̄_MAE(∞)=ρ^(L/(L+1)).
> - **Training dynamics over t:** critical-time analysis t*(λ,ρ) shows greedy, step-wise feature learning; diagrams of w̄(t) trajectories and CCA-vs-epochs curves.
> - **ImageNet experiment (ViT):** I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance "bottom" PCA subspace faster than MAE throughout training (higher full-bottom mean CCA), consistent with the theory.
> - Caveats vs. your request: the paper uses deep linear networks and ViT/ImageNet (not CIFAR-100 or ResNet-50; no classification-accuracy tables); it does not report Precision/F1.
> 
> ## 4) Memory-efficient 4-bit optimizer states for AdamW
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023). 4-bit first/second moments via B128 blocks + rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluded linear quantization, optionally factorized second moment ("4-bitFactor").
> - Matches/exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1, SQuAD F1 94.5, GPT-2 E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8); outperforms Adafactor/SM3.
> - **LLaMA fine-tuning on Alpaca (MMLU/commonsense):** LLaMA-7B 38.9/74.7/61.2/44.4/43.0; LLaMA-13B 47.4/79.0/64.1/48.0/45.2; LLaMA-33B 54.9/79.2/61.6/46.6/45.4 — no loss vs. 32-bit AdamW; training-loss curves over steps closely align (Fig. 4).
> - Memory: up to 57.7% saved; LLaMA-7B trainable on one 80GB GPU.
> - Caveat: the paper does full fine-tuning of LLaMA; it discusses LoRA only as related work (freezing pretrained weights, tuning low-rank parameters) and does not itself run end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning. (The Hessian paper does analyze LoRA on TinyLlama/MathQA, but only spectrally.)
> 
> ## 5) Cross-domain RL policy adaptation via value-guided filtering
> **"Cross-Domain Policy Adaptation via Value-Guided Data Filtering" (VGDF)** (NeurIPS 2023). Online dynamics adaptation with limited target interactions: selectively shares source transitions whose Fictitious Value Proximity (FVP) exceeds a quantile (25%), with a dynamics ensemble, optimistic exploration (SAC backbone), and VGDF+BC for offline-source/online-target.
> - Outperforms DARC, GARAT, IWClip, Finetune, Mix across GridWorld, MuJoCo, PyBullet with kinematic and morphology shifts; **return-vs-target-steps curves** (×10^5 steps) are reported; FVP-based filtering beats high-Q and importance-weighting variants.
> - Kinematic shifts have lower FVP than morphology shifts; robust to selection ratios ξ≤50%; ensemble of 3–5 models suffices.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis of experimental results
> - **Detection (PBADet):** the only paper reporting AP *and* Precision/Recall/F1; its gains over BPJDet/ED-Pose are large (e.g., JointAP 85.98 vs. 78.13; all-parts F1 48.5 vs. 31.5). This is also the strongest "practical setup" evidence for association quality, though on YOLO backbones rather than ResNet-50.
> - **EI/spectral (Dale's Law):** gives a diagnostic (NSE) predictive of learning performance, complementary to the JEPA paper's implicit-bias diagnostics — both use dynamics-over-t analyses to explain *why* an objective/constraint helps or hurts, rather than reporting SOTA accuracy. Its finding (spectra matter more than sign constraints) is analogous in spirit to the Hessian paper's "power-law spectra predict generalization."
> - **JEPA vs. MAE:** the most theoretically explicit on feature-embedding evolution over t (critical times, ODE trajectories, CCA curves), but validated only in linear settings + ViT/ImageNet; the claimed benefit (semantic, low-variance features) is consistent with PBADet's per-part F1 gains only indirectly.
> - **4-bit optimizer:** the clearest practical fine-tuning result (LLaMA-7B/13B/33B, loss-vs-step curves), showing 4-bit AdamW is essentially lossless for memory; but it does not demonstrate the requested end-to-end LoRA setup, and no Precision/F1 metrics are given (SQuAD F1 94.5 is the only F1-like metric).
> - **VGDF:** the only RL paper; its evaluation (return vs. target-domain steps) matches your "training dynamics over t" interest and shows consistent improvement over dynamics-discrepancy baselines, but it reports no Precision/F1 and no ResNet-50/LLaMA fine-tuning.
> 
> Overall, no single paper covers all requested metrics/setups: PBADet uniquely gives AP + Precision/Recall/F1; the 4-bit optimizer paper uniquely covers LLaMA fine-tuning with loss-vs-t curves; JEPA and Dale's-Law papers give spectral/dynamics diagnostics but weaker practical metrics; VGDF covers RL transfer only.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers matching each of your five topics, with their experimental results, followed by a comparative analysis.
> 
> ## 1) Anchor-free part–body association — PBADet (ICLR 2024)
> One-stage, anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones) using **multi-scale feature maps** and a single **part-to-body center offset**; supervision uses task-alignment learning (TOOD-style, an alignment/attention-like mechanism), IoU/DFL/classification/association losses. Trained with SGD, 100 epochs, 1024×1024, AMP.
> - **BodyHands (Table 1):** HandAP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (YOLOv7) — beats BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13) with a smaller model; YOLOv5l6: 88.1/92.71/85.73.
> - **COCOHumanParts (Table 2):** AP.5:.95 42.7/41.5 (orig/subordinate), AP.5 69.5/67.9, on par with BPJDet, leading in AP_M/AP_L and feet.
> - **Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose (Table 7):** all-parts P/R/F1 = 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs ED-Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51; e.g., right hand 38.58/61.26/47.34 vs 19.57/31.59/24.17.
> - **Ablations:** association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment each improve metrics (Full 89.1/92.62/85.98 vs baseline w/o assoc. loss 89.1/80.78/78.07).
> 
> ## 2) Spectral/interpretability of excitatory-inhibitory networks — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)
> Studies RNNs enforcing **excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints** (ColEI vs DANN). Training = **projected gradient descent** (SGD with gradient clipping); tasks use **softmax (cross-entropy for classification/language modeling)** and **identity/MSE-like regression (adding problem)**. Diagnostics are **singular-value based**: eigenvalue/singular-value spectra, spectrum "transplant," and **normalized SVD entropy (NSE)**.
> - ColEI learns worse and with higher variance on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition; gradient clipping helps most.
> - **Singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors** (spectrum contributes ~1.5–2% error gap; sign constraints only 0.7–1%).
> - NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; balanced E/I and larger size give better spectra/performance. **Note:** "cosine similarity" is not used here — diagnostics are SVD/eigenvalue-based.
> 
> ## 3) Implicit bias of joint-embedding self-distillation vs masked reconstruction — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)
> Compares **JEPA (self-distillation, StopGrad)** vs **MAE (masked reconstruction), both MSE objectives**, on **deep linear feedforward networks**; tracks **feature/embedding evolution** (projection magnitudes ∥W̄eᵢ∥ over t, critical times, CCA on ImageNet-1K with I-JEPA vs MAE).
> - JEPA is implicitly biased to learn **high-influence features** (large regression coefficient ρ), MAE to **highly co-varying features** (large λ), even noisy ones.
> - Both show greedy, step-wise feature learning; JEPA's bias appears only when the encoder is **deep**; JEPA aligns faster to the low-variance perceptual subspace (confirmed on ImageNet-1K).
> - **Caveat:** the collection does not contain CIFAR-100 or Transformer experiments for this comparison — the theory uses deep linear MLPs, with ImageNet-1K empirical support only.
> 
> ## 4) Memory-efficient 4-bit optimizer states — "4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023)
> Compresses **AdamW/Adam first/second moments to 4-bit** (B128/dynamic-exponent first moment; Rank-1/linear zero-point-excluded second moment, optionally factorized). Evaluated across RoBERTa-L (GLUE/SQuAD, F1 94.5), Swin-T (ImageNet acc. 80.8), GPT-2 Medium via the **LoRA codebase** (E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8), Transformer-Base (WMT14), and **end-to-end LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning** (MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA).
> - Matches or slightly beats 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning; comparable on pretraining; convergence curve of 4-bit vs 32-bit closely aligns (Fig. 4, loss vs training step).
> - Memory: LLaMA-7B 75.4→31.87 GB (57.7% saved), enabling LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models; 4-bit states are 2× smaller than 8-bit, ~4× for 4-bit Factor.
> - **Caveat:** "end-to-end LoRA" appears as GPT-2+LoRA and full LLaMA fine-tuning; **ResNet-50 is not used** (Swin-T is the vision model).
> 
> ## 5) Cross-domain RL policy adaptation — VGDF (NeurIPS 2023)
> **Value-Guided Data Filtering**: selectively shares **source transitions** whose paired value targets are close (Fictitious Value Proximity, FVP) under **limited target interactions** (10⁵ steps), using a dynamics ensemble + optimistic exploration, with VGDF+BC for offline-source/online-target (D4RL medium).
> - **Offline source/online target (Table 1):** VGDF+BC wins 4/6 environments vs Offline-only, Symmetric sampling, H2O (e.g., hopper-shortfeet 3060±60 vs H2O 868±73; halfcheetah-nothighs 3910±160 vs H2O 3023±77).
> - Dynamics diagrams (return vs steps-in-target-domain ×10⁵) show better sample efficiency; optimistic exploration helps in 3/4 envs; FVP-based rejection sampling beats importance weighting and high-Q filtering; FVP lower for kinematic than morphology shifts.
> - **Caveat:** metrics are RL returns, not Precision/F1.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Best quantitative results per topic:** PBADet dominates part-body detection (highest AP, and P/R/F1 roughly 1.5–2× ED-Pose); Dale's-law work shows spectra (not sign constraints) drive learning; JEPA beats MAE on feature quality via its influence-based bias; 4-bit AdamW is effectively lossless vs 32-bit (≤0.1–0.3 pt on accuracy/F1) while cutting memory up to 57.7%; VGDF(+BC) improves target return in 4–6 of 6 environments.
> - **What they share:** all report training-dynamics-style curves (loss/return vs t: 4-bit LLaMA loss curve, VGDF return curves, JEPA feature-projection curves, Dale's-law error-vs-NSE), and all validate against a strong baseline (BPJDet/ED-Pose, standard RNN, MAE, 32-bit AdamW/8-bit Adam, H2O/Symmetric sampling).
> - **Important mismatches with your request (not established in the context):** (a) PBADet's "attention" is task-alignment learning, not an explicit attention module; (b) the Dale's-law paper uses singular-value/NSE diagnostics, **not cosine similarity**; (c) the JEPA-vs-MAE analysis is on **deep linear networks + ImageNet, not CIFAR-100/Transformers**; (d) the 4-bit optimizer paper uses **Swin-T/LLaMA/GPT-2, not ResNet-50**; (e) VGDF reports **returns, not Precision/F1**. I cannot confirm any paper in the collection that directly combines cosine-similarity diagnostics with E/I sign constraints, CIFAR-100/Transformer JEPA-vs-MAE experiments, or ResNet-50 with 4-bit/LoRA setups.
