Gold 1：

> Here is a comparison and summary of experimental results across the five works, organized to match your deployment needs and grounded only in their reported figures/tables and text.
> 
> 1) Reliable hand/face detection for a gesture UI (PBADet vs prior detectors/pose estimators)
> - Identical datasets and direct comparisons:
>   • BodyHands (Table 1): PBADet using YOLOv7 achieves Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; PBADet using YOLOv5l6 achieves Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73. The best BPJDet baseline (YOLOv5l6) reports Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39. Thus, on BodyHands, PBADet outperforms BPJDet on all metrics.
>   • COCOHumanParts (Table 2): On AP.5:.95, PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6 (slightly lower), but PBADet leads or matches in several per-category APs: person 62.4 vs 61.3; r-foot 37.7 vs 39.6 (slightly lower); l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9 (higher). Association quality (Table 3, mMR−2 averages): PBADet YOLOv7 achieves lower average mismatch rates (e.g., r-hand 42.7 vs BPJDet 42.2 comparable; l-hand 41.1 vs 41.6 slightly better; feet categories often comparable to better), indicating robust part-body association.
>   • CrowdHuman (Table 5/6): For face-body association, PBADet (YOLOv7) has best MR−2 body 36.5 and body AP 91.6, with comparable mMR−2 to BPJDet, showing strong performance in crowded scenes.
> - Similar dataset type (pose vs detection) using Precision/Recall/F1: PBADet vs ED-Pose (Appendix A.2, Table 7) on COCO validation for hands/feet shows PBADet has much higher F1:
>   • left hand F1: PBADet 46.50 vs ED-Pose 22.87; right hand F1: 47.34 vs 24.17; left foot F1: 51.08 vs 40.46; right foot F1: 50.34 vs 40.34. Precision and Recall are both higher for PBADet across parts, confirming superior detection quality for a gesture UI.
> - Practical training settings and heads: PBADet trained 100 epochs on 4×V100 with AMP, SGD optimizer, YOLOv7 scheduler; image size 1024×1024, batch size 24; loss weights λiou=7.5, λdfl=1.5, λcls=0.5, λassoc=0.2; anchor-alignment K=13, α=1.0, β=6.0; NMS thresholds (BodyHands): τ_conf^b=0.05, τ_iou^b=0.6; τ_conf^p=0.05, τ_iou^p=0.6. Detection heads: per-scale branches for classification, localization, and a new 2D displacement (part-to-body center offset). This end-to-end, anchor-free design improves association robustness without extra anchors.
> 
> 2) End-to-end Transformer fine-tuning under tight GPU memory (4-bit optimizers)
> - Identical datasets across optimizers (Table 2): 4-bit AdamW achieves parity with 32-bit AdamW across tasks:
>   • NLU (RoBERTa-L, GLUE mean): 4-bit 89.1 vs 32-bit 88.9.
>   • Image classification (Swin-T on ImageNet-1K): 4-bit 80.8 vs 81.2 (slightly lower).
>   • NLG (GPT-2 Medium on E2E-NLG): BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7.
>   • QA (RoBERTa-L on SQuAD): F1 94.5 vs 94.6 (almost identical); SQuAD 2.0 EM/F1 comparable (Table 9).
>   • Machine translation (Transformer WMT14 en-de, SacreBLEU): 4-bit 26.28 vs 26.61 (slightly lower but close).
> - LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3; Figure 4): 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit AdamW on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA across 7B, 13B, 33B models (e.g., 7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; 13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5), while saving 57.7% memory on 2×A100 80GB (Table 4). Training loss curves overlap (Figure 4).
> - Practical AdamW and data settings: The paper uses AdamW for all tasks; examples include LR 1e-5–2e-5 for GLUE (Table 10), SQuAD LR 1.5e-5 (Table 11), GPT-2 LR 4e-5 (Table 12). The 4-bit scheme uses B128/DE for first moment and Rank-1 normalization + Linear mapping for second moment to avoid zero-point quantization issues; these settings retain stability without “stable embeddings.” Memory/time gains (Table 4) show 4-bit faster or comparable wall-clock with fused kernels and largest trainable model increases 4× under fixed budget (Table 5).
> 
> 3) Pretraining choice: joint-embedding self-distillation (JEPA) vs reconstruction (MAE)
> - Deep linear analyses show JEPA’s implicit bias toward “influential features” (high regression coefficients ρ) vs MAE favoring high covariance λ (Sections 2–3; Figure 1, Figure 2). In distribution 2 (λ increases while ρ decreases), JEPA reverses learning order to prioritize more predictive, less noisy features; MAE maintains λ-first order. This difference becomes stronger as encoder depth L increases (Corollary 3.6; Figure 4 with varying L), indicating deeper JEPA encoders learn semantically predictive features earlier.
> - On ImageNet-1K (64×64) ViT encoders, JEPA features show higher CCA similarity between full-and-bottom PCA subspace than MAE (Appendix D, Figure 7), consistent with JEPA prioritizing the low-variance, perceptually relevant subspace highlighted in [20]. This supports using JEPA-style self-distillation (with an MSE loss to the stop-grad target) when semantic robustness is the goal.
> 
> 4) Spectral tools to keep EI RNN controllers stable (Dale’s ANNs vs simple EI partition)
> - Across identical tasks (Figure 2): ColEI (column-constrained EI RNN) learns worse than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs on the adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition; variance across seeds is higher. Gradient clipping benefits ColEI substantially more.
> - Spectrum transplant experiments (Figure 4B–C) show that giving an RNN the ColEI singular value spectrum degrades performance more than imposing sign constraints; spectra contributed ∼1.5–2% test error changes vs ∼0.7–1% for sign constraints on sequential MNIST (RNN 5 seeds, ColEI 30 seeds). Thus, singular value distribution is the dominant determinant of learning quality.
> - NSE (normalized SVD entropy) predicts performance across EI ratios and sizes (Figures 5–7): small networks or few inhibitory units lower NSE, increasing large singular values and hurting learning. Larger ColEI networks learn well despite large max singular values because rotations (U,V) steer activity away from unstable directions. Practically, initialize recurrent weights to unimodal, clustered singular-value spectra and prefer DANN-style EI architectures to keep controllers stable without sacrificing performance.
> 
> 5) Sim-to-real policy transfer with small online budget via value-guided filtering (VGDF)
> - Identical Mujoco target domains (Figure 4): With Γ=10 (source:target data), VGDF outperforms GARAT (action transformation) and IW Clip (importance weighting), and is competitive with or better than DARC (domain-classifier reward correction). VGDF matches or exceeds Oracle (1M target-only training) in 4/8 environments despite the limited online budget.
> - Offline-source/online-target setting (Table 1): VGDF+BC (behavior cloning regularization) achieves the highest mean returns in 4/6 tasks (e.g., HalfCheetah “broken back thigh” 4834±250 vs H2O 5761±148 best, but VGDF+BC close; “no thighs” 3910±160 vs H2O 3023±77; Hopper “short feet” 3060±60 vs H2O 868±73), showing robust gains over “Offline only” and symmetric sampling.
> - Additional PyBullet results (Table 3): VGDF consistently outperforms DARC and finetune across different target data amounts in HalfCheetah and Hopper.
> - Practical recipe: Use an ensemble Gaussian dynamics model on the target domain to generate fictitious next-states, score source transitions by Fictitious Value Proximity (likelihood of source value under the ensemble’s fictitious value distribution), and perform rejection sampling (e.g., top 25%) to share only value-consistent source data. The paper shows importance weighting via FVP underperforms rejection sampling (Figure 13), and filtering by raw value (Figure 14) or by dynamics gap (Figure 15) is inferior to the proposed value-based filtering.
> 
> Cross-cutting notes on evaluation metrics and designs
> - Precision/F1: PBADet achieves higher Precision/Recall/F1 than ED-Pose on hands/feet (Appendix Table 7), and 4-bit AdamW matches SQuAD F1 compared to 32-bit (Table 9), satisfying your evaluation preference.
> - Attention/feature embeddings: PBADet uses multi-scale dense detection heads with a part-to-body offset branch rather than attention; JEPA/MAE experiments use ViT encoders and show JEPA’s bottom-subspace alignment; Swin-T is used for image classification in the 4-bit study.
> - Optimizers: SGDM is used in PBADet (YOLO-style training); AdamW is used throughout the 4-bit optimizer study (practical LRs and batch sizes provided in Tables 10–12). For EI RNNs, gradient clipping is recommended especially for ColEI.
> 
> Summary by need
> - Gesture UI detection: PBADet provides state-of-the-art hand/face detection and association on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman; it surpasses BPJDet and substantially exceeds ED-Pose on F1 for hands/feet.
> - Memory-constrained Transformer fine-tuning: 4-bit AdamW yields near-parity accuracy with large memory savings (up to 57.7%) and supports end-to-end instruction tuning (LLaMA) and typical NLU/QA/NLG/MT tasks.
> - JEPA vs reconstruction: Deep-linear and ImageNet experiments indicate JEPA-style self-distillation (MSE to stop-grad targets) learns semantically predictive, low-noise features earlier than MAE, especially at larger encoder depths.
> - EI RNN stability: Prefer recurrent DANNs or standard RNN spectra; use NSE to diagnose spectra and gradient clipping for ColEI; spectral properties matter more than sign constraints for performance.
> - Sim-to-real with small online budget: VGDF’s value-guided selective sharing consistently outperforms or matches baselines across kinematics/morphology shifts, and extends well to offline-source/online-target settings.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection covers all five needs, with concrete experimental results:
> 
> **1. Hand/face detection for gesture UI (resource-constrained):** **PBADet** (one-stage, anchor-free part-body association on YOLOv5/YOLOv7; practical settings: SGD per YOLOv7 protocol, 1024×1024 input, batch 24, AMP). On BodyHands it beats BPJDet: HandAP 89.1 vs 85.9, JointAP 85.98 vs 84.39, using a smaller YOLOv7 (36.9M vs 86.1M). On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet and leads in AP_M/AP_L/feet; on CrowdHuman face-body it gets lower body MR-2 (36.5 vs 39.7–41.3). vs ED-Pose (pose estimation) it is much better in **Precision/Recall/F1** (all-parts P 39.41 vs 24.09, R 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51; left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87). For on-device compute, **BSO/T-BSO** (binary spiking online training) cuts memory to O(n²L/32) and model size ~20–31× (T-BSO: 94.86% CIFAR-10, 74.27% CIFAR-100, 96.12% GSC).
> 
> **2. Memory-tight LoRA fine-tuning:** **4-bit AdamW** quantizes optimizer states; it matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/E2E-NLG/Alpaca, with up to 57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; 4× larger OPT models under a fixed budget). Practical hyperparameter advice: keep the original optimizer's settings unchanged ("out-of-box" transfer; ablation shows B128 first-moment blocks and rank-1/factorized second moment are near-lossless). The Hessian-structure paper adds LoRA fine-tuning analysis (Tr(H) decreases, KS-distance predicts generalization up to 0.98).
> 
> **3. JEPA (MSE self-distillation) vs reconstruction:** The deep-linear analysis shows JEPA is biased toward high-regression-coefficient (influential) features with depth strengthening noise suppression, while MAE orders features by covariance λ and keeps noisy features. ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster (higher CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE, which matches the top-variance subspace. So for perception pretraining, joint-embedding self-distillation beats reconstruction.
> 
> **4. Spectral tools for E/I RNN stability:** The Dale's-Law paper provides **Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE)** as a spectrum-pathology diagnostic; ColEI singular-value spectra are multimodal/dispersed (vs unimodal for standard RNNs/DANNs), spectra matter more than sign constraints, gradient clipping helps ColEI most, and NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error (balanced E/I ratios and larger networks → better spectra/performance; DANNs are robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron).
> 
> **5. Sim-to-real with small online budget via value-target filtering:** **VGDF** filters source transitions by Fictitious Value Proximity (FVP) with 25% rejection sampling. It outperforms DARC, GARAT, IWClip, Finetune, and dynamics-discrepancy filtering: PyBullet-HC 770±203 vs DARC 304±211; PyBullet-Hopper 957±39 vs DARC 73±20; VGDF+BC (offline-source/online-target) beats Symmetric sampling and H2O on most D4RL tasks (e.g., hopper-shortfeet 3060±60 vs 2144±509/868±73). FVP-based filtering beats high-Q filtering in 4 of 8 environments. **ASID** is an alternative: one real rollout with Fisher-information exploration + system identification → zero-shot transfer (rod balancing 6/9 vs DR 0/9; shuffleboard 7/10 vs 3/10).
> 
> **Attention/feature-embedding design:** the 4-bit paper covers attention (Swin-T ImageNet), PBADet covers multi-scale anchor-free heads with task-alignment, and GOT-D shows embedding choice for data selection is not critical (sentence-transformer ≈ distilled-BERT). Overall, the closest match per need is PBADet + BSO (detection/compute), 4-bit AdamW (LoRA memory), the JEPA analysis (pretraining choice), NSE spectral diagnostics (E/I RNN), and VGDF/ASID (sim-to-real transfer).

**community 最终答案**

> Yes — works in the collection cover each need, with quantitative results to compare.
> 
> **1. Hand/face detection for a gesture UI (resource-constrained).**
> PBADet (ICLR 2024) is a one-stage anchor-free part–body detector (body, face, left/right hand) on YOLOv5/YOLOv7, using a compact part-to-body offset (representation length 10 vs BPJDet's 15) — a leaner design suited to constrained robots. On COCOHumanParts its AP is on par with BPJDet while leading on person/feet AP; on CrowdHuman face–body association it attains the best body MR-2 (36.5 vs BPJDet-YOLOv5l6's 40.7). Evaluation includes Precision/F1: vs ED-Pose (Table 7), PBADet gets left-hand P/R/F1 = 37.63/60.82/46.50 vs 18.36/30.34/22.87, right-hand 38.58/61.26/47.34 vs 19.57/31.59/24.17, all-parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs 24.09/45.51/31.51 — a clear win for small parts.
> 
> **2. LoRA fine-tuning of a Transformer under tight GPU memory + practical SGD/AdamW settings.**
> The 4-bit-optimizer paper (NeurIPS 2023) is directly applicable: quantizing AdamW's moments (B128 first moment, rank-1/linear second moment) gives up to 57.7% memory savings, trains LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models under a fixed budget, with lossless results: NLU 89.1 vs 88.9, CLS 80.8 vs 81.2, NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6 (32-bit AdamW). Reported settings: β₁=0.9, β₂=0.999, ε=1e-6, weight decay 0.01, linear schedule. The Hessian paper also gives a concrete LoRA recipe (TinyLlama-1B on MathQA: rank=16, α=32, dropout=0.1, AdamW lr=1e-4 → 1e-5, batch 32, weight decay 0.1, 1000 steps), and notes LoRA improves task performance but, unlike full fine-tuning, does not induce the power-law Hessian structure — implying different generalization behavior worth checking on your task.
> 
> **3. Joint-embedding self-distillation (MSE) vs reconstruction pretraining.**
> The JEPA analysis (NeurIPS 2024) answers this: with the same MSE-style latent-prediction objective, JEPA beats MAE-style reconstruction. Theory (deep linear networks) shows JEPA is implicitly biased to learn high-influence, low-variance "slow" features and suppresses noise (depth strengthens this), whereas MAE orders features by eigenvalue and can fit uninformative pixel-level structure. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace of perceptual features than MAE. Caveat from the text: the bare JEPA objective is collapse-prone, so stop-gradient/predictor tricks are needed.
> 
> **4. Spectral tools for excitatory/inhibitory RNN stability.**
> The Dale's-Law RNN study (NeurIPS 2023) is exactly this. Tools: eigenvalue/singular-value spectra, spectrum "transplants," and normalised SVD entropy (NSE). Results: column-constrained E/I (ColEI) networks have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra (mode of large singular values) and learn worse/higher variance, while DANN E/I networks have unimodal Marchenko–Pastur spectra like standard RNNs and learn well even with 1 inhibitory unit. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance across EI ratio/size (balanced E/I and larger networks → higher NSE → better learning); gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially. Conclusion: check the singular-value spectrum (NSE), not just eigenvalues, to keep the controller stable.
> 
> **5. Sim-to-real transfer with a small online budget via value-target filtering.**
> VGDF matches your description almost exactly: it filters source transitions by Fictitious Value Proximity — proximity of paired value targets V(s′_tar) vs V(s′_src) — and rejection-samples the top 25% for a small target budget (1e5 target vs 1e6 source steps). Results: outperforms DARC, GARAT, IWClip, and Finetune; PyBullet-HalfCheetah 770±203 vs DARC 304±211 and Finetune 653±51, PyBullet-Hopper 957±39 vs 73±20/240±189; it matches or exceeds the Oracle in 4/8 environments. Value-based (FVP) filtering beats both high-Q filtering and dynamics-discrepancy (DGDF) filtering. In the offline-source/online-target setting, VGDF+BC beats Symmetric sampling and H2O on 4 of 6 D4RL tasks (e.g., hopper-shortfeet 3060±60 vs 2144±509/868±73). ASID is a complementary option (active Fisher-information exploration + system ID; real rod-balancing 6/9 vs DR 0/9, shuffleboard 7/10 vs 3/10) but uses exploration rather than value-target data filtering.
> 
> **Bottom line.** All five needs are covered: PBADet (detection, Precision/F1), 4-bit AdamW + LoRA (memory, SGD/AdamW settings), the JEPA analysis (latent MSE > reconstruction), the Dale's-Law spectral study (NSE/stability), and VGDF (value-target filtering for small-budget sim-to-real). Attention/feature-embedding design is addressed indirectly (PBADet's center-offset head, JEPA's encoder/predictor, and a contrastive-learning paper showing a variance-reduction loss improves small-batch embedding quality).

> Here is a comparison-driven guide to the works most relevant to your on-device, self-supervised perception-and-control stack. It integrates only the reported experimental results and figures/tables from the cited papers, and highlights identical datasets where methods can be compared directly.
> 
> 1) Self-supervised multi-object and part-aware detection (COCO-like scenes, cosine-similarity clustering)
> - HASSOD (Cao et al., NeurIPS 2023)
>   - How it discovers many objects and parts: Uses a frozen self-supervised ViT (DINO) and merges adjacent regions by cosine similarity of feature embeddings via hierarchical adaptive clustering; ensembles multiple merge thresholds to adaptively determine many objects per image, and infers whole/part/subpart hierarchies by mask coverage relations.
>   - Identical datasets versus prior SOTA:
>     • Objects365 (val): HASSOD vs CutLER vs FreeSOLO vs SAM (Table 1)
>       - Box AR: HASSOD 39.0 vs CutLER 35.8 vs FreeSOLO 10.2 vs SAM 54.9
>       - (No mask GT on Objects365.)
>     • LVIS v1.0 (val): HASSOD vs CutLER vs FreeSOLO vs SAM (Table 1)
>       - Box AR: 26.9 vs 23.6 vs 6.4 vs 42.7; Mask AR: 22.5 vs 20.2 vs 5.9 vs 46.1
>       - Improvement over CutLER on Mask AR = +2.3; stronger recall on small and medium scales too.
>     • SA-1B subset (50k images): HASSOD vs CutLER vs FreeSOLO vs SAM (Table 1)
>       - Box AR: 29.0 vs 18.8 vs 2.4 vs 60.5; Mask AR: 26.0 vs 17.0 vs 2.2 vs 60.8
>       - Large improvements over CutLER (+10.2 Box AR, +9.0 Mask AR; relative gains ≈ +54% Mask AR).
>     • Efficiency (Section 4.1): HASSOD trains on ~0.24M MS-COCO images (≈ 1/5 of ImageNet used by CutLER) and 40k iterations (≈ 1/12 of CutLER), ~20h on 4×A100.
>   - Qualitative: Recovers many more objects per image than CutLER and predicts hierarchical whole/part/subpart (Figure 5), enabling part-aware detection without supervision.
> 
> - When you also need supervised, robust part-body association (for evaluation or downstream benchmarks): PBADet (Gao et al., ICLR 2024)
>   - Datasets identical across methods:
>     • BodyHands (Table 1): Ours (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6)
>       - Hand AP: 89.1 vs 85.9; Conditional Accuracy: 92.62 vs 86.91; Joint AP: 85.98 vs 84.39. PBADet is better on all three metrics.
>     • COCOHumanParts (Table 2): Ours (YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6)
>       - All-categories AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate): 43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3 (ours slightly lower overall), but ours is stronger on APM/APL and on specific categories (person, both feet). Per-category AP: person 62.4 vs 61.3; right foot 30.9 vs 30.2; left foot 31.5 vs 30.9 (ours better). BPJDet is higher on head/face/hands AP.
>       - Association robustness (mMR−2, lower is better; Table 3): Ours (YOLOv5l6) achieves best (lowest) for head (27.9), face (30.5), left hand (36.2), right hand (40.8), and left foot (47.9); BPJDet (l6) is best on right foot (49.1) while ours is close (50.4).
>     • CrowdHuman (Tables 5 and 6): For face–body association, PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves best MR−2 body (36.5) and face (44.7), and best body AP (91.6); mMR−2 is comparable (50.8 vs BPJDet l6 50.1). Against crowded-person detectors, PBADet gets the best body MR−2 and competitive AP.
>   - Takeaway: For annotated part–body association, PBADet’s one-stage, anchor-free part-to-body offset design improves robustness and association accuracy on BodyHands and is competitive/comparable on COCOHumanParts and CrowdHuman.

> 2) Memory-lean end-to-end training (4-bit optimizers on Transformers/ResNet-50 backbones)
> - Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023)
>   - Identical model/dataset setups across optimizers (Table 2):
>     • NLU (RoBERTa-L/GLUE, mean): 32-bit AdamW 88.9; 8-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit Factor 88.9 (4-bit is on par with 32/8-bit).
>     • Image classification (Swin-T/ImageNet-1k): 32-bit 81.2; 8-bit 81.0; 4-bit 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9 (negligible drops).
>     • NLG (GPT-2 M/E2E-NLG BLEU): 32-bit 67.7; 8-bit 67.5; 4-bit 67.8; 4-bit Factor 67.6.
>     • QA (RoBERTa-L/SQuAD F1): 32-bit 94.6; 4-bit 94.5; 4-bit Factor 94.6.
>     • Machine translation (Transformer-Base/WMT14 en-de SacreBleu): 32-bit 26.61; 4-bit 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45 (very close).
>   - Instruction tuning (LLaMA-7B/13B/33B; Table 3): 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit across MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-e/c, OBQA.
>   - Memory/time (Table 4):
>     • LLaMA-7B, 2×A100 80GB: total mem 75.4GB (32-bit) → 31.87GB (4-bit), −57.7%; time 3.35h → 3.07h (4-bit) with offload/fusion.
>     • RoBERTa-L (GLUE): total mem 5.31GB → 3.00GB (4-bit fused), −43.5%; time 3.93 min → 3.17 min.
>     • GPT-2 M (E2E): total mem 6.89GB → 4.62GB (4-bit fused), −34.4%; time similar or faster with fusion.
>   - Implication for your stack: You can train Cascade Mask R-CNN (ResNet-50) or ViT-based heads end-to-end with 4-bit AdamW and retain accuracy, while fitting tight GPU memory and even improving throughput with offloading.
> 
> 3) Interpretable recurrent module with excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) constraints
> - Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023)
>   - Identical tasks across recurrent architectures (Figures 2–6): standard RNN vs ColEI (columns constrained E/I) vs DANN (Dale’s ANN-inspired EI with good spectra)
>     • Adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task: ColEI learns worse (higher error, slower/unstable) than standard RNN and DANN; DANN matches standard RNN performance with stable training.
>     • Spectrum transplant (Figure 4): Matching a ColEI singular value spectrum onto an RNN causes degraded performance; matching an RNN spectrum onto ColEI improves performance—showing spectrum matters more than sign constraints per se.
>     • Size/E–I ratio (Figures 5–7): Small networks and few inhibitory units harm ColEI learning and produce dispersed, multimodal singular value spectra; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) of the singular values correlates with performance (higher NSE → better). DANN remains robust even with very few inhibitory neurons.
>   - Implication: For an interpretable E/I-constrained recurrent controller, favor a DANN-style EI reparameterization (which respects Dale’s Law but keeps unimodal, clustered singular spectra) over naïve column-sign ColEI. The paper quantifies that spectral properties (via NSE) predict performance across tasks.
> 
> 4) Vision backbone pretraining with a JEPA-style latent objective (cosine/MSE in latent space)
> - How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024)
>   - Deep linear theory and controlled experiments show JEPA (self-distillation with latent MSE) preferentially learns “influential” features (high regression coefficients), while MAE prioritizes highly covarying (potentially noisy) features; the effect strengthens with encoder depth (Theorems 3.2–3.6, Figures 1–2, 4).
>   - Empirical check on ImageNet-64 (Appendix D, Figure 7): I-JEPA features align (higher mean CCA) with the bottom PCA subspace sooner than MAE, consistent with learning more semantic, less noisy features.
>   - Implication: A JEPA-style pretrain for your detector backbone (ViT/ResNet-50) complements HASSOD’s cosine-similarity-based region grouping by emphasizing predictive, low-variance features.
> 
> Putting it together for your system
> - Self-supervised detector that discovers many objects and their parts with cosine-similarity grouping: Study HASSOD for its hierarchical adaptive clustering (cosine similarity on DINO features), hierarchical level prediction, and Mean Teacher with adaptive targets. On the same datasets, HASSOD substantially outperforms prior self-supervised detectors in recall (Objects365, LVIS, SA-1B).
> - Supervised part–body association when annotations exist: Study PBADet. On identical datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman), PBADet improves association accuracy and robustness (e.g., BodyHands Joint AP 85.98 vs BPJDet 84.39; best MR−2/AP on CrowdHuman body/face) and achieves strong mMR−2 across parts on COCOHumanParts.
> - Memory-tight end-to-end training on Transformers/ResNet-50: Adopt 4-bit AdamW from Li et al. 2023. Across identical tasks, 4-bit matches 32/8-bit accuracy while cutting optimizer memory and often the end-to-end training memory/time (e.g., −34–58% total memory).
> - Interpretable recurrent controller under E/I constraints: Use a DANN-style EI recurrent module to satisfy Dale’s Law without the performance pitfalls of simple column sign constraints (ColEI). The paper’s experiments demonstrate DANN ≈ standard RNN across four benchmarks, while ColEI underperforms.
> - Pretrain visual backbone with JEPA: The deep linear analysis and the empirical ImageNet-64 comparison indicate JEPA focuses on predictive (low-noise) features, aligning with your goal to avoid pixel-level noise and to support robust cosine-similarity clustering.
> 
> Notes on datasets where methods are directly comparable
> - Self-supervised detection (HASSOD vs CutLER vs FreeSOLO vs SAM): Identical datasets—Objects365, LVIS, SA-1B (Table 1 in HASSOD). HASSOD yields higher Box/Mask AR in all cases, with especially large gains on SA-1B.
> - Part–body association (PBADet vs BPJDet): Identical datasets—BodyHands (Table 1), COCOHumanParts (Tables 2–3), CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6). PBADet leads on BodyHands across metrics; on COCOHumanParts, PBADet is stronger on several categories and sizes (APM/APL) and best (lowest) mMR−2 on most parts; on CrowdHuman, PBADet shows best MR−2/AP for body/face and comparable mMR−2.
> - 4-bit optimizers: Identical model/dataset comparisons (Table 2) demonstrate 4-bit parity with 32/8-bit on GLUE, ImageNet-1k, E2E-NLG, SQuAD, WMT14; instruction-tuning parity on LLaMA benchmarks (Table 3) and significant memory savings (Table 4).
> - EI recurrent networks: Identical benchmarks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, natural-object recognition) show DANN and standard RNN outperform ColEI; spectrum transplants and NSE-performance correlations are demonstrated in figures.
> 
> These works, in combination, give you: (i) a self-supervised detector that scales to many objects and their parts via cosine-similarity grouping and hierarchical prediction (HASSOD), (ii) an optional supervised association head with strong empirical association accuracy (PBADet), (iii) a training recipe that fits tight memory (4-bit AdamW) without accuracy loss, (iv) an EI-constrained, interpretable recurrent controller (DANN RNN) validated across tasks, and (v) a JEPA pretrain whose implicit bias aligns with learning stable, predictive visual features rather than noisy pixels.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Recommended works
> 
> 1. **HASSOD** (Hierarchical Adaptive Self-Supervised Object Detection) — discovers many objects and whole/part/subpart composition in COCO-like scenes via agglomerative clustering of **cosine-similarity** of DINO ViT patch features, then trains a Cascade Mask R-CNN (ResNet-50, DINO-initialized) end-to-end on COCO with a Mean-Teacher self-training stage. Covers your detector + parts requirement.
> 2. **LDReg** (Local Dimensionality Regularization) — regularizes SSL embeddings (incl. JEPA-style self-distillation like BYOL, and MAE) to avoid local dimensional collapse; improves representation quality for downstream COCO detection/segmentation. Useful for the cosine-similarity embedding quality and ResNet-50/ViT-B backbones.
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** — theory + experiments for your **JEPA-style latent-space MSE pretraining** (I-JEPA vs MAE dynamics).
> 4. **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** — 4-bit AdamW/Adam optimizer states (B128 block + rank-1 normalization + zero-exclusion linear quantizer) for **tight-GPU end-to-end training** of Transformers/ResNet (tested on Swin-T, Transformer, LLaMA, RoBERTa).
> 5. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** — recurrent **E/I (excitatory/inhibitory) constrained RNNs** (ColEI vs DANN), including why sign-constrained RNNs fail and how to make them trainable; the closest match for an interpretable recurrent control module.
> 
> ## Experimental results comparison
> 
> **HASSOD:** Zero-shot class-agnostic detection (AR, not AP, since AP penalizes valid unlabeled objects): Mask AR on **LVIS 20.2→22.5**, on **SA-1B 17.0→26.0**, and Box AR gains of +3.2/+3.3 on Objects365/LVIS. Achieved with only **1/5 the images and 1/12 the iterations** of CutLER (~40k iters, ~20h on 4×A100). Ensembling 3 merge thresholds captures objects of varied sizes/levels; the hierarchy (whole/part/subpart) head improves both detection and interpretability. Limitations: hierarchy can misalign with human perception; struggles with overlapping similar objects and text.
> 
> **LDReg:** ImageNet linear eval gains: SimCLR 64.3→64.8, SimCLR-Tuned 67.2→67.5, BYOL 67.6→68.5 (ResNet-50, 100ep); ViT-B SimCLR 72.9→73.0, MAE 57.0→57.6 (200ep). COCO fine-tuning (ResNet-50): SimCLR APbb 35.24→35.26, BYOL 36.30→36.82, SimCLR (1000ep) 36.48→37.15. Longer pretraining gives larger gains; global covariance/variance regularizers barely help (BYOL +0.0–0.2), confirming local LID is the key factor; results stable across β/k/batch size.
> 
> **JEPA analysis:** In deep linear nets, JEPA's latent MSE objective prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient), while MAE tracks high-variance features even if noisy; JEPA's noise suppression strengthens with depth, MAE's doesn't. On ImageNet, I-JEPA features match the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) faster than MAE (higher full-bottom CCA, lower full-top CCA), and JEPA generally reaches better downstream classification with fewer steps. Caveat: analysis is for deep linear MLPs with specific initialization.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers:** Match or slightly beat 32-bit AdamW across tasks: GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2 (comparable), SQuAD 94.5 vs 94.6, E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7, WMT14 en-de 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B fine-tuning accuracy is preserved with **57.7% memory savings** (e.g., 75.4→31.9GB for LLaMA-7B) and enables training LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; 4-bitFactor saves more. Sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor β₁=0, SM3) degrade, especially on vision.
> 
> **E/I RNN (Dale's Law):** Standard sign-partitioned ColEI RNNs learn **worse across all four tasks** (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition) with higher seed variance; gradient clipping helps ColEI disproportionately. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the **initial recurrent-weight spectrum, not the sign constraints**, is the main cause (ColEI: multimodal dispersed singular values; RNN/DANN: unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur). DANN (E→E, E→I, I→E non-negative projections) learns **as well as standard RNNs** while respecting Dale's Law and stays robust to small networks/few inhibitory units; normalized SVD entropy predicts final error. Note: results are on sequence modeling/classification tasks, not explicitly time-series control — you'd need to validate on your control task.
> 
> ## Gaps
> No single work in the collection covers all your requirements jointly; the collection provides no direct evidence for combining a 4-bit optimizer with a JEPA-pretrained detector, nor an E/I RNN evaluated specifically on control. Design your stack by composing these five works and validate on your own benchmarks.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the context, the works to study for your stack are:
> 
> **1. Detector (self-supervised, cosine-similarity, objects + parts, COCO-like): HASSOD** ("Hierarchical Adaptive Self-Supervised Object Detection")
> **2. Part/body association (plug-in for part control): PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free part-body association)
> **3. 4-bit optimizer for end-to-end training: "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (4-bit AdamW / 4-bit Factor)
> **4. JEPA-style latent-MSE pretraining: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (deep-linear analysis of the L = ½E‖g(f(x))−f(y)‖² objective); optionally **LDReg** (local-dimensionality regularization that improves ResNet-50/ViT-B SSL backbones)
> **5. Interpretable E/I recurrent module: "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (ColEI vs DANN recurrent networks)
> 
> **Comparison and analysis of experimental results**
> 
> - **HASSOD** is the core match for your detector: it runs hierarchical agglomerative clustering on frozen DINO ViT-B/8 features using **pairwise cosine similarity** of patch embeddings, adaptively deciding the number of objects per image and classifying them into **whole/part/subpart** via coverage-relation trees; it then trains a Cascade Mask R-CNN (ResNet-50) end-to-end on MS-COCO with Mean-Teacher self-training. Results (class-agnostic AR, zero-shot): Objects365 Box AR 39.0 (vs CutLER 35.8, FreeSOLO 10.2, supervised SAM 54.9), LVIS Box AR 26.9 / Mask AR 22.5 (vs CutLER 23.6/20.2), SA-1B Box AR 29.0 (+54% over CutLER's 18.8) and Mask AR 26.0 (+53% over 17.0). Small/medium objects benefit most (SA-1B small AR is 2.6× CutLER). Critically for tight compute, it needs only **1/5 the images and 1/12 the iterations** of CutLER (~40k iterations, ~20h on 4 A100s). It evaluates with AR rather than AP because AP penalizes valid out-of-category detections. Limitations: hierarchy can misalign with human part perception; fails on overlapping similar objects, heterogeneous wholes, and text.
> 
> - **PBADet** complements HASSOD on the "parts" side: it extends anchor-free detection (YOLOv5/YOLOv7) with a single 2D part-to-body center offset, giving one-to-one part-body association without anchor complexity. On BodyHands, Ours(YOLOv7, 36.9M params) achieves HandAP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 — beating BPJDet(YOLOv5l6, 86.1M) at 85.9/86.91/84.39 and BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48). On COCOHumanParts it matches BPJDet overall but leads in AP_M/AP_L and feet detection, and has the lowest mMR-2 for head, face, hands, and right foot; it also extends to quadruped (AnimalPose, AP-10K). Caveat: it is a **supervised** formulation (needs part/body labels), so use it for the association head design rather than self-supervision.
> 
> - **4-bit optimizer states** deliver the GPU-memory savings for training the Transformer/ResNet backbone: 4-bit AdamW quantizes the first moment with smaller blocks (B128) and the second moment with rank-1 normalization plus a zero-point-excluding linear quantizer (optionally factorized as 4-bit Factor). Results are near-lossless across tasks: Swin-T on ImageNet 81.2 (32-bit AdamW) → 80.8 (4-bit AdamW) / 80.9 (4-bit Factor); RoBERTa-L GLUE 88.9→89.1; GPT-2 E2E 67.7→67.8; QA 94.6→94.5; WMT 26.61→26.28; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning matches 32-bit. Memory: up to 57.7% total training-memory reduction (LLaMA-7B 75.4→31.9GB, enabling it on one 80GB GPU), optimizer states 2× smaller than 8-bit and ~4× smaller for 4-bit Factor; it also speeds up sharded training via reduced communication. Caveats: smaller unfused models are slower than 8-bit, and optimal quantization may be task-dependent.
> 
> - **JEPA analysis** supports your latent-space-MSE pretraining choice: it shows JEPA (BYOL/data2vec/SimSiam/I-JEPA/V-JEPA, using stop-gradient) learns **high-influence features** and suppresses noisy ones, unlike MAE which prioritizes high-variance (often noisy) features; depth strengthens this. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster than MAE with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features (higher CCA similarity on full-vs-bottom variance data). So JEPA-style pretraining is preferable to reconstruction for your downstream perception. Caveat: the JEPA objective is collapse-prone and needs stop-gradients/architectural tricks; the analysis uses deep linear networks with special initialization. **LDReg** is a practical add-on: it raises local intrinsic dimensionality and consistently improves ResNet-50/ViT-B SSL backbones — e.g., ImageNet linear eval BYOL 67.6→68.5, MAE 57.0→57.6, SimCLR(1000ep) 69.0→69.8; COCO detection with ResNet-50 RCNN-C4: BYOL APbb 36.30→36.82 (APbb75 38.82→39.62), APmk 32.17→32.47, with negligible compute overhead (27.8h→27.1h). This matters because low LID (local collapse) hurts downstream detection.
> 
> - **Dale's Law recurrent module** gives you the interpretable E/I constraint for time-series control, but with an important experimental caveat: naively partitioning a standard RNN into excitatory/inhibitory columns (ColEI) trains **worse and with higher variance** on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and naturalistic object recognition — the cause is not the sign constraint but the **initial recurrent-weight spectrum** (multimodal, dispersed singular values vs the unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur form of standard RNNs). The fix is the **DANN** reparameterization (E-to-E, E-to-I, I-to-E non-negative matrices), which respects Dale's Law yet matches standard RNN performance and stays robust even with one inhibitory neuron. Gradient clipping helps ColEI disproportionately; normalized SVD entropy predicts E/I RNN performance. So: use DANN-style (or spectrally well-behaved) E/I RNNs, not ColEI, and consider spectral initialization.
> 
> In sum: **HASSOD** (discovery + part hierarchy via cosine similarity, efficient Mean-Teacher training) + **PBADet** (part-body association head) + **4-bit optimizers** (memory) + **JEPA/LDReg** (backbone pretraining) + **Dale's Law/DANN spectral analysis** (E/I recurrent control) cover all your requirements; the experimental evidence shows HASSOD's efficiency and recall gains, PBADet's association accuracy, 4-bit's near-lossless memory savings, JEPA's feature-quality advantage, and DANN's spectral remedy for E/I RNN training failures.

### paperscope:results_comparison:254 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Find research that improves deep networks’ efficiency, stability, and interpretability across architectures: (1) transformer-based modules that execute symbolic rules via attention for exact arithmetic with clear reasoning traces; (2) analyses of recurrent models under biologically inspired E/I sign constraints (Dale’s law) using spectral tools to explain training stability; (3) theory of non-contrastive joint-embedding self-distillation versus reconstruction objectives (e.g., JEPA vs MAE) showing biases under MSE/CE losses; (4) memory‑saving optimizers that quantize first/second moments to 4‑bit yet match Adam/SGD fine‑tuning accuracy; and (5) one‑stage, anchor‑free detectors that learn part‑to‑whole associations with attention‑like offsets. Prefer works using Transformers/attention, feature embeddings, cross‑entropy and MSE metrics, fine‑tuning (incl. parameter‑efficient methods), and reporting precision on benchmarks like MNIST/CIFAR for interpretability.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：3→3（Δ+0）；rounds：4→6（Δ+2）。**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison-only synthesis of experimental results reported in the five papers. We use only the figures/tables and explicit statements in the papers, grouped by: (A) identical datasets across compared methods; (B) similar dataset/task types; and (C) per‑paper, per‑dataset specifics. Where the same dataset is shared, we highlight which method performs better or worse.
> 
> A) Identical datasets (direct, same-benchmark comparisons)
> 1) Human part–body association detection (one-stage detectors)
> - Datasets shared: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman (PBADet vs prior art, mainly BPJDet; tables and figures: PBADet Tables 1–3, 5–6, 9; Figs. 3–4)
> - BodyHands (Table 1):
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 (best across all listed methods).
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73 (beats prior BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9/86.91/84.39).
>   → Winner: PBADet on all three metrics (AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP) while using an anchor‑free, one‑stage design.
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2, APs across sizes/categories):
>   • Overall AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate): BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3 vs PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 and PBADet (YOLOv7) 42.7/41.5 (BPJDet slightly higher on overall AP.5:.95).
>   • APM/APL (mid/large objects): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4; PBADet (YOLOv7) 65.8/64.4 and 66.7/63.3 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9 (PBADet higher on APM/APL).
>   • Per‑category APs (Table 2): BPJDet better on head/face/hands by small margins; PBADet better on feet (e.g., r-foot 30.9 vs 30.2; l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9) and “person” (62.4 vs 61.3 for YOLOv5l6 backbones).
>   • Association quality (mMR−2, Table 3; lower is better): PBADet (YOLOv7) lower (better) for head (29.2 vs 30.8) and face (31.3 vs 31.8) than BPJDet (YOLOv5l6), similar on hands (41.1/42.7 vs 41.6/42.2), worse on feet (e.g., r-foot 52.6 vs 49.1; l-foot 52.5 vs 50.4).
>   → Mixed: BPJDet slightly higher overall AP.5:.95; PBADet decisively better for APM/APL and some categories (person, feet), and better mMR−2 (head/face), but worse mMR−2 on feet.
> - CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6):
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7) yields best body MR−2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6), better face MR−2 (44.7) than BPJDet (YOLOv5l6: 40.7 MR−2 body, 89.5 body AP, 46.3 face MR−2). mMR−2 (body–face) is slightly worse for PBADet (50.8–50.9) than BPJDet (50.1).
>   → Winner on detection MR−2/AP: PBADet; association mMR−2: BPJDet slightly lower (better).
> 
> B) Similar task types (cross‑paper comparisons, different datasets)
> 1) Symbolic/arithmetic reasoning
> - Neural Comprehension (ICLR 2024) vs LLM few‑shot/CoT/Algorithmic baselines on symbolic operations (Fig. 4):
>   • Length generalization: Neural Comprehension achieves near‑perfect solve rates in‑ and out‑of‑distribution (digit lengths up to 40) for Parity, Reverse, Addition, Subtraction; fine‑tuning and few‑shot baselines degrade markedly outside the training length range; CoT/Algorithmic improve generalization but are compute‑heavy.
>   • On arithmetic reasoning (AddSub+ digit‑controlled; Fig. 6) with GPT‑class LLMs: NC improves solve rates vs vanilla CoT and competes with/exceeds tool‑calling PAL in several digit settings (figures show consistent gains especially at higher digit counts), while being end‑to‑end neural (no external interpreter).
>   • GSM8K‑Hard subsets (Table 2): In Mixed (add+sub), NC boosts solve rate for llama‑2‑7b from 11.1 (CoT) and 11.1 (PAL) to 27.8; for llama‑2‑70b, from 16.7 (CoT) and 27.8 (PAL) to 33.3. In single‑op subsets, NC matches or slightly exceeds CoT/PAL on average.
>   → Conclusion: For symbolic/arithmetic, NC offers near‑perfect symbolic execution and better length generalization than LLM learning‑based baselines; on real arithmetic reasoning, NC often improves over CoT and is competitive with tool methods while keeping high efficiency.
> - JEPA vs MAE (NeurIPS 2024) on self‑supervised dynamics (Figures 1–5, 7):
>   • On synthetic linear tasks: both exhibit greedy learning w.r.t. feature covariance (λ), but only JEPA is greedy w.r.t. regression coefficient (ρ)—JEPA prioritizes high‑influence (predictive, low‑noise) features; in “Distribution 2” experiments, JEPA reverses learning order vs MAE when λ and ρ trends conflict.
>   • Depth sensitivity: JEPA’s preference for high‑ρ strengthens with encoder depth; MAE’s ordering remains λ‑driven.
>   • ImageNet (Fig. 7): JEPA’s representations align more with the low‑variance (bottom‑PCA) subspace, while MAE aligns more with the top‑variance subspace; JEPA shows higher similarity between features learned on full vs bottom components and lower similarity for full vs top—consistent with emphasizing semantically predictive features.
>   → Conclusion: For representation learning, JEPA is empirically biased to influential (predictive) directions, learning them earlier and more with depth; MAE emphasizes high‑variance reconstructions. This difference is experimentally demonstrated on synthetic setups and with CCA trends on ImageNet.
> 2) Training stability and interpretability across architectures
> - Dale’s Law RNNs (NeurIPS 2023) on Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Natural Object Recognition (Fig. 2):
>   • Ordering: Standard RNN ≈ recurrent DANNs > ColEI (column sign‑constrained E/I) across all tasks (ColEI learns worse, with higher variance; gradient clipping helps ColEI more).
>   • Spectrum transplant (Fig. 4): Performance is impacted more by the singular‑value spectrum at initialization than sign constraints per se; transplanting spectra changes performance more than freezing signs.
>   • Size and E/I ratio (Figs. 5–7): Smaller networks and fewer inhibitory units (higher E:I) hurt ColEI performance and increase spectral pathologies (lower normalized SVD entropy, NSE). Larger ColEI nets have spectra closer to standard/DANN and learn better despite some large singular values. NSE anti‑correlates with test error.
>   → Conclusion: Training stability and performance in EI RNNs are best explained by spectral properties (unimodal/clustered singular values) rather than sign constraints alone; DANNs and standard RNNs exhibit unimodal clustered spectra and train well; ColEI’s multimodal dispersed spectra predict worse learning unless network size/E:I is favorable.
> 3) Memory/efficiency for deep networks
> - 4‑bit optimizers (NeurIPS 2023) vs 32‑bit AdamW, 8‑bit AdamW, Adafactor, SM3 across NLP/CV (Table 2, 4, 5):
>   • Accuracy (identical datasets):
>     – NLU (RoBERTa‑L, GLUE mean): 32‑bit 88.9; 8‑bit 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit Factor 88.9; Adafactor 89.1; Adafactor β1=0 89.3; SM3 87.5.
>     – CLS (Swin‑T ImageNet): 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9; Adafactor 80.0; SM3 79.0.
>     – NLG (GPT‑2 M on E2E‑NLG BLEU): 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5; 4‑bit 67.8; 4‑bit Factor 67.6; Adafactor 67.2; SM3 66.9.
>     – QA (RoBERTa‑L SQuAD F1): 32‑bit 94.6; 8‑bit 94.5; 4‑bit 94.5; 4‑bit Factor 94.6; SM3 91.7.
>     – MT (Transformer WMT14 en‑de SacreBLEU): 32‑bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; 4‑bit 26.28; 4‑bit Factor 26.45; Adafactor 26.52; SM3 22.72.
>     → 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit/8‑bit on NLU/NLG/QA and is close on CLS/MT; Adafactor is close; SM3 is consistently worse. 
>   • LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3): 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit AdamW across MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA for 7B/13B; small regressions at 33B MMLU (54.9 vs 56.4) but similar elsewhere.
>   • Memory/time (Table 4): 4‑bit saves 43–58% total training memory (e.g., LLaMA‑7B: 75.40→31.87 GB; RoBERTa‑L: 5.31→3.00 GB) with neutral or improved time (e.g., LLaMA‑7B: 3.35 h → 3.07 h; RoBERTa‑L 3.93 min → 3.17 min with fused ops). Largest trainable model (Table 5): single‑GPU budget jumps (e.g., OPT‑1.3B→6.7B on 80GB; LLaMA‑7B becomes feasible on 80GB).
>   • Ablations (Table 1): removing zero from second‑moment quantization and using Linear mapping (Rank‑1/Linear) stabilizes 4‑bit training and matches BLEU of 32‑bit on GPT‑2/E2E‑NLG; stochastic rounding or smaller block sizes without zero‑exclusion are insufficient alone.
>   → Conclusion: 4‑bit optimizers (with rank‑1 normalizer + zero‑free linear mapping for v) preserve accuracy across NLP/CV, enable large memory savings and speedups in sharded/offloaded setups, and scale to instruction tuning on multi‑B models.
> 
> C) Per‑paper, per‑dataset specifics
> 1) PBADet (ICLR 2024, anchor‑free one‑stage part‑to‑body offsets)
> - BodyHands (Table 1): PBADet outperforms prior SOTA across all three metrics (Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP), even when matching the YOLOv5l6 backbone used by BPJDet.
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2–3): PBADet leads in APM/APL (mid/large), “person” and feet AP, and reduces mMR−2 for head/face; BPJDet slightly higher overall AP.5:.95 and better feet mMR−2.
> - CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6): PBADet achieves best detection MR−2 and AP for body (and better face MR−2), with a small disadvantage on combined body–face mMR−2.
> 
> 2) Dale’s Law RNNs (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Across Adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, Natural Object Recognition (Fig. 2): ColEI < DANN ≈ standard RNN; gradient clipping produces a larger improvement for ColEI.
> - Spectrum transplant (Fig. 4): Changing singular value spectra alters performance more than sign constraints; NSE (singular value clustering) anti‑correlates with test error across EI ratio and size sweeps (Figs. 5–7).
> 
> 3) JEPA vs MAE (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Synthetic distributions (Figs. 1–2): Both greedy in λ; only JEPA greedy in ρ; in distributions where λ↑, ρ↓ (Distribution 2), JEPA flips feature learning order vs MAE.
> - Depth (Fig. 4): Increasing depth widens JEPA’s ρ‑driven separation; MAE’s ordering remains λ‑driven.
> - ImageNet (Fig. 7): JEPA yields higher mean CCA between full/bottom PCA representations and lower between full/top, consistent with JEPA emphasizing low‑variance (semantically predictive) subspaces.
> 
> 4) 4‑bit optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Accuracy: On GLUE/SQuAD/E2E‑NLG/WMT14/ImageNet, 4‑bit AdamW matches or is within noise of 32‑bit/8‑bit; Adafactor close; SM3 worse.
> - Efficiency: 43–58% total memory savings; similar/faster training with fused kernels; unlocks larger models under fixed memory.
> - Stability ablations: Zero‑free linear mapping for second moment and rank‑1 normalization are key to stable 4‑bit convergence (Table 1).
> 
> 5) Neural Comprehension with CoNNs (ICLR 2024)
> - Symbolic operations (Fig. 4): Near‑100% solve rates in‑ and out‑of‑distribution lengths (up to 40 digits) vs notable degradation for fine‑tuned/few‑shot LMs; CoT/Algorithmic more compute‑intensive.
> - Symbolic reasoning training dynamics (Fig. 5): Faster/better convergence than vanilla fine‑tuning on Last‑Letter and Coin‑Flip intermediate targets across T5 sizes.
> - Arithmetic reasoning (Fig. 6; Table 2): Gains over CoT; competitive with PAL under many settings (while remaining end‑to‑end neural). Combining multiple CoNNs improves performance; irrelevant CoNNs rarely degrade it.
> - Inference overhead (Appendix Table 8): ~1–3% latency increase vs vanilla on T5; scales well with model size.
> 
> Summary of winners by setting
> - Human part–body association (identical datasets): PBADet leads on BodyHands; on COCOHumanParts it wins on APM/APL/person/feet and some mMR−2, while BPJDet slightly edges overall AP.5:.95 and feet mMR−2; on CrowdHuman PBADet leads on detection MR−2/AP.
> - Symbolic/arithmetic: Neural Comprehension attains near‑perfect symbolic execution and best length generalization; improves arithmetic reasoning vs CoT and is competitive with tool‑based PAL while being more efficient end‑to‑end.
> - Self‑supervised representation (JEPA vs MAE): Experiments show JEPA prioritizes high‑influence (predictive) features (high ρ), learns them earlier and more with depth, and aligns with bottom‑variance subspaces on ImageNet; MAE remains variance (λ) driven.
> - EI RNN stability: DANN/standard RNNs outperform ColEI; spectrum (singular values) matters more than sign constraints; NSE predicts performance. 
> - Memory‑efficient training: 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit/8‑bit accuracy across NLP/CV while cutting total memory up to ~58% and enabling larger models; zero‑free v‑quantization and rank‑1 normalization are critical for stable 4‑bit convergence.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Five research works found and comparison
> 
> **1. Symbolic-rule Transformers — "Neural Comprehension" (ICLR 2024).** Compiled Neural Networks (CoNNs) are transformer modules whose attention/MLP weights are *compiled* (RASP/Tracr) to encode rules as Select/Aggregate/Zipmap operations, giving exact arithmetic with interpretable execution traces. Results: **flawless (100%) execution** of symbolic tasks (parity, reverse, last-letter, coin-flip, concatenation) across T5 Small/Base/Large; robust length generalization to OOD inputs (3–30 digits); on GSM8K-Hard AddSub it beats CoT (avg 9.3) and tool-calling PAL (14.8) with a mixed-task average of **22.2**, generalizing to Llama-2-7B/70B, GLM-130B, GPT-3.5 with only ~1–3% latency overhead. It trains faster than vanilla fine-tuning and is end-to-end differentiable. Limits: AutoCoNN fails on addition/subtraction; gating tested with ≤5 CoNNs.
> 
> **2. Dale's-law RNNs — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023).** RNNs with E/I sign constraints (ColEI) train worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition. Spectrum-transplant experiments show sign constraints explain only part of the gap (≈0.7–1%) while the **initial singular-value spectrum matters more** (≈1.5–2%); ColEI's rank-one column-mean nilpotent structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values vs. the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle of standard/DANN RNNs. **Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error**, predicting performance before training (small balanced-E/I networks beat large skewed ones); DANN stays robust (NSE≈0.95 even with 1 inhibitory neuron); gradient clipping stabilizes ColEI most.
> 
> **3. JEPA vs. MAE theory — "Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024).** Exact gradient-flow analysis of deep linear self-distillation shows JEPA (non-contrastive, StopGrad, MSE in latent space) is biased toward **high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ)**, while MAE (reconstruction MSE) prioritizes high-variance (λ) features regardless of informativeness; depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression and can make the encoder low-rank. ImageNet-1K CCA confirms I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance perceptual subspace faster than MAE. Key difference: JEPA can be slower to learn noisy features, MAE is not.
> 
> **4. 4-bit optimizers — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023).** Quantizes first moment with B128/dynamic-exponent and second moment with rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluding linear quantizer (optionally factorized). **Matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on all fine-tuning tasks**: GLUE RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9, SQuAD 94.5 vs 94.6, E2E GPT-2 67.8 vs 67.7, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, WMT 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning matches 32-bit AdamW on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA with closely aligned convergence. Memory savings up to **57.7%** (LLaMA-7B: 31.9GB vs 75.4GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; 4-bitFactor saves more. Sublinear optimizers (Adafactor β1=0, SM3) degrade, especially on classification.
> 
> **5. Anchor-free part-body detection — PBADet (ICLR 2024).** One-stage, anchor-free detector extending FCOS/TOOD-style dense prediction with a **single 2D part-to-body center offset** (multi-scale, task-aligned supervision) linking parts to bodies. Results (BodyHands): HandAP **89.1**, Cond. Accuracy **92.62**, JointAP **85.98** with YOLOv7 (36.9M params, 1024 input) vs. BPJDet(YOLOv5m6) 85.3/86.80/78.13; same-backbone comparison (YOLOv5l6) 88.1/92.71/85.73 vs. 85.9/86.91/84.39. On COCOHumanParts AP 42.7–43.0 (all categories). Ablations show anchor-free > anchor-based, part-to-body > body-to-part, and that the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment each matter.
> 
> ## Cross-method comparison
> 
> - **Efficiency**: NC removes step-by-step tracking/external tools (fewer compute steps than CoT/PAL); 4-bit optimizers cut memory 35–58% and speed FSDP fine-tuning via reduced communication; PBADet uses fewer parameters (36.9M vs 41.2M) and smaller input (1024 vs 1536) than BPJDet while beating it.
> - **Stability**: Dale's-law work explains poor training stability of sign-constrained RNNs via spectra (NSE as pre-training diagnostic) and shows gradient clipping recovers it; 4-bit optimizers preserve Adam's convergence (loss curves align) and even improve throughput; NC gives OOD length stability not achievable by gradient-based LMs.
> - **Interpretability**: NC provides explicit, human-controllable rule modules with clear reasoning traces (Select/Aggregate/Zipmap); the JEPA analysis gives a mechanistic, theoretical explanation of feature-selection bias (ρ vs λ) verified by CCA on ImageNet; NSE is an interpretable spectral diagnostic; PBADet's single offset gives a well-defined, one-to-one part–body correspondence simplifying post-processing.
> - **Precision metrics**: interpretability/accuracy quantified on sequential MNIST (Dale's), solve rates on arithmetic (NC), CCA similarity on ImageNet (JEPA), accuracy/BLEU/F1 on fine-tuning benchmarks (4-bit), and AP/conditional accuracy/JointAP on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts (PBADet).
> 
> Overall, the works share a theme: encoding structure (compiled rules, E/I constraints, latent-space objectives, low-bit states, part-to-body offsets) improves efficiency/stability/interpretability with **little or no accuracy loss** — NC and PBADet exceed baselines, 4-bit optimizers match full-precision, JEPA explains why latent prediction beats reconstruction, and Dale's-law analysis shows *how* to design stable constrained RNNs rather than avoiding them.

**community 最终答案**

> Below are the five matched works from the collection, with their experimental results compared/analyzed.
> 
> **1. Neural Comprehension (CoNNs for symbolic rules) — ICLR 2024**
> Compiled Neural Networks (CoNNs) are transformer modules whose attention/MLP weights are compiled (via RASP/Tracr) to encode rules as Select/Aggregate/Zipmap operations; a sparse MoE-style gate routes rule-intensive tokens to CoNNs, leaving an interpretable, human-controllable reasoning trace. Results: near-perfect/flawless symbolic execution (parity, reverse, copy, last letter) with strong length generalization (3–30 digits; OOD beyond 10-digit training range), whereas Vanilla fine-tuning and few-shot degrade OOD. On arithmetic (AddSub), Neural Comprehension beats PAL baselines (mixed-task avg 22.2 vs 14.8/9.3), adds only ~1–3% latency, and works from T5-Small (60M) to GLM-130B/GPT-3.5 (175B). It outperforms CoT/Scratchpad in efficiency and interpretability, and auto-generates new CoNNs (AutoCoNN), though it fails to auto-generate addition/subtraction.
> 
> **2. "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" — NeurIPS 2023**
> ColEI RNNs (column-wise E/I sign constraints per Dale's law) train worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANN on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn TreeBank, and object recognition; gradient clipping mitigates the deficit. Spectrum-transplant experiments (SVD decomposition swapping singular values/vectors) show the initial singular-value spectrum — not sign constraints — is the dominant cause: ColEI's column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values, whereas RNNs/DANNs match random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance pre-training; larger networks or balanced E/I ratios (higher NSE) train better. DANNs remain robust even with one inhibitory neuron.
> 
> **3. "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (JEPA vs MAE) — NeurIPS 2024**
> Solves deep-linear self-distillation (JEPA) vs reconstruction (MAE) dynamics under MSE. Fixed points: w̄_MAE(∞,L)=ρ^{L/(L+1)} vs w̄_JEPA(∞,L)=ρ^L, with a 1-layer JEPA equivalent to infinite-depth MAE. Critical-time analysis shows MAE orders feature learning by covariance λ only, while JEPA also prioritizes regression coefficient ρ ("influential features"), with that bias strengthening with depth and able to reverse learning order when λ and ρ anti-correlate; JEPA suppresses noisy directions. ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster than MAE with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features (CCA similarity), consistent with JEPA's advantage in interpretable/perceptual representation. (CE-loss comparisons were not reported in the retrieved material.)
> 
> **4. "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" — NeurIPS 2023**
> Quantizes Adam/AdamW first moment (B128 dynamic-exponent) and second moment (rank-1 normalization + linear mapping excluding zero-point, optionally factorized). Results: 4-bit matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (GLUE RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7; LLaMA-7B/13B Alpaca→MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7, 47.4 vs 46.5) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61 SacreBLEU). Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B fits one 80GB GPU; 4× larger OPT models trainable), with near-identical convergence curves; Adafactor/SM3 degrade, especially on image classification. Note: the paper reports Adam/AdamW (not SGD) fine-tuning parity; the zero-point problem in the second moment was the key bottleneck, solved by zero-excluding linear mapping.
> 
> **5. PBADet: one-stage anchor-free part-body association — ICLR 2024**
> Extends anchor-free dense prediction with a single part-to-body center offset (a learned 2D displacement vector with one-to-one part↔body correspondence, decoded by Euclidean distance to enclosing body centers), multi-scale feature maps, and TOOD task-alignment learning (IoU/DFL/classification + association losses). Results: on BodyHands, YOLOv7 variant reaches 89.1 HandAP, 92.62 conditional accuracy, 85.98 JointAP — beating BPJDet (85.9/86.91/84.39) with fewer parameters (36.9M vs 86.1M); on COCOHumanParts, AP 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate) with YOLOv5l6, leading on medium/large objects and feet, with lower mMR-2 (fewer part-body mismatches) than BPJDet; ablations confirm association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment each help. It generalizes to quadruped part-body association (AnimalPose/AP-10K).
> 
> **Cross-cutting comparison/analysis**
> - **Interpretability/efficiency trade-offs:** CoNNs give exact, traceable symbolic execution but require hand/auto-compiled modules; PBADet trades a single extra 2D offset for strong association accuracy with fewer parameters than anchor-based competitors; 4-bit optimizers are "lossless" in accuracy while cutting memory by ~35–58%, directly improving fine-tuning scalability (LLaMA-7B on one GPU).
> - **Stability:** the Dale's-law analysis shows training instability stems from spectral properties (multimodal singular values, low NSE) rather than constraints — NSE is a pre-training diagnostic; likewise the 4-bit optimizer paper identifies quantization-induced instability (zero-point problem) and fixes it by design rather than by more bits.
> - **Bias in representation learning:** JEPA vs MAE theory shows objective choice biases *which* features are learned first (influential/low-variance vs high-variance), explaining JEPA's perceptual advantage — an interpretability-relevant finding echoed by the ImageNet CCA experiments; MAE-type reconstruction is biased toward variance, JEPA toward regression coefficients.
> - **Precision reporting:** symbolic (CoNNs) results are reported as accuracy/length-generalization on synthetic tasks; RNN and JEPA/MAE analyses report MNIST/ImageNet metrics; 4-bit optimizers report GLUE/ImageNet/MMLU; PBADet reports AP/conditional accuracy/JointAP/mMR-2 on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman. The methods' gains are consistent: each outperforms its direct baseline while adding explicit structure (compiled rules, spectral diagnostics, quantizer design, or a single association offset) rather than capacity.

</details>

**问题：** I’m building an end‑to‑end system under tight GPU memory: an HCI module must robustly associate hands/faces to the correct person in crowded scenes; our LLM must perform exact multi‑digit arithmetic without tool calls; our SSL pretraining seems to chase noisy pixels; and our small RNN control loop must remain stable under E/I constraints. I’m looking for papers on: anchor‑free part–whole association detectors; compiled attention programs that plug into Transformers for rule‑based symbolic operations; 4‑bit state optimizers that keep Adam‑level accuracy for fine‑tuning (compatible with LoRA); analyses of joint‑embedding self‑distillation (vs reconstruction) explaining biases via MSE/CE; and spectral perspectives on Dale’s law for training stability. We rely on attention/Transformers, SGD/Adam, regularization and interpretability, and care about precision under edge‑device constraints.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the documents found in the collection, here's a comparison of the experimental results for the five requested methods.
> 
> ## 1. Anchor-free part–whole association — PBADet (ICLR 2024)
> - **BodyHands**: PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) beats BPJDet(YOLOv5m6, 41.2M) with a *smaller* model: HandAP 89.1 vs 85.3, conditional accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, JointAP 85.98 vs 78.13. The anchor-free part-to-body formulation beats both anchor-based body-to-part (BPJDet) and its own anchor-based variant (89.1/92.62/85.98 vs 85.3/86.80/78.13).
> - **COCOHumanParts** (6 parts): AP .5:.95 on par with BPJDet (42.7 vs 43.6), but leads in AP_M/AP_L, person and feet, and achieves the lowest average mMR-2 across head/face/hands. Per-category mMR-2: head 29.2, face 31.3, r-hand 42.7.
> - **CrowdHuman** (single-part face-body): advantage over BPJDet is *less pronounced* (body MR-2 36.5 vs 39.7, face MR-2 44.7 vs 45.0, body AP 91.6 vs 90.7) — the benefit shows mainly in multi-part settings.
> - **vs ED-Pose** (pose estimator): much higher precision/recall/F1, e.g. F1 all parts 48.52 vs 31.51.
> - Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task alignment each boost association accuracy.
> 
> ## 2. Compiled attention for symbolic ops — Neural Comprehension (ICLR 2024)
> - **Symbolic tasks**: achieves ~flawless (100%) execution on parity/reverse/last-letter/coin-flip, robust to **length generalization** (3–30 digits; >10 digits is OOD), unlike vanilla LMs whose accuracy collapses with length.
> - **Arithmetic (GSM8K-Hard AddSub+)**: NC mixed average 22.2 vs CoT 9.3 vs PAL 14.8; addition 21.2 vs PAL 20.8; subtraction 15.6 vs PAL 14.1 — matching/exceeding **tool-calling (PAL)** without external tools.
> - **Efficiency**: end-to-end differentiable, adds only ~1–3% latency, works across T5/Llama-2/GLM-130B scales. Caveats: AutoCoNN generator fails on addition/subtraction; sparse gating tested only up to 5 CoNNs.
> 
> ## 3. 4-bit state optimizer — 4-bit AdamW (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Fine-tuning** (NLU/QA/NLG): matches/exceeds 32-bit AdamW — RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, GPT-2M BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6. **Pretraining** (CLS/MT): comparable — Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2, WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61.
> - **LLaMA instruction tuning**: MMLU 7B 38.9 vs 38.7; 13B 47.4 vs 46.5; 33B 54.9 vs 56.4 (small dip at largest scale).
> - **Memory**: up to 57.7% savings (LLaMA-7B: 31.9GB vs 75.4GB, fits one 80GB GPU; ~4× larger OPT models under budget). Beats Adafactor/SM3 on CLS (80.8 vs 79.5–80.0).
> - **LoRA compatibility**: LoRA is described as combinable ("can be utilized by these methods" to cut communication); the paper notes LoRA itself freezes pretrained weights and only tunes low-rank params. Compatibility is asserted, but no dedicated LoRA+4-bit benchmark table is reported in the collection.
> - Key designs: smaller block (B128) + rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the second moment; factorization for extra savings.
> 
> ## 4. Joint-embedding self-distillation vs reconstruction — JEPA (NeurIPS 2024)
> - This is a deep-linear analysis of **MSE** objectives (predicting in latent space vs reconstructing in input space); the collection does not contain an explicit MSE-vs-CE comparison paper.
> - **Mechanism**: JEPA is implicitly biased to learn **high-influence features** (high regression coefficient ρ), and this bias *grows with encoder depth*; MAE orders feature learning by covariance λ, so it "chases noisy pixels" (high-variance, uninformative directions).
> - **Fixed points**: JEPA w̄(∞)=ρ^L vs MAE ρ^(L/(L+1)) — JEPA suppresses noisy directions with depth, converging to lower weights on noisy features.
> - **ImageNet-1K** (ViT, 64×64): I-JEPA features align *faster* with the low-variance "bottom" PCA subspace (where perceptual features live) than MAE by CCA; MAE aligns more with the top-variance subspace.
> - Limitations: deep linear MLPs, special initialization, simultaneous diagonalizability.
> 
> ## 5. Spectral perspective on Dale's law — EI RNNs (NeurIPS 2023)
> - ColEI (column-constrained E/I) RNNs learn poorly with **multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra**; standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs have unimodal clustered (quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur) spectra and learn as well as standard RNNs.
> - **Spectrum matters more than sign constraints**: sign constraints hurt (RNN +0.7%, ColEI +1%) but don't explain the full gap (2.3%±0.6%).
> - **E/I ratio & size**: fewer inhibitory units degrades spectra and learning (NSE drops); DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron. Small balanced networks beat large skewed ones.
> - **Stability**: without gradient clipping ColEI is highly unstable; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance before training.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting takeaways for your system
> - For the HCI module, PBADet is the strongest fit: one-stage anchor-free, handles many parts without representation bloat, best on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts; note the CrowdHuman (single face) gain is modest, and it's CNN/YOLO-based rather than attention-based.
> - For exact arithmetic, compiled attention (CoNN/Neural Comprehension) delivers flawless, length-generalizing symbolic ops and beats tool-calling on GSM8K-Hard, at ~1–3% latency — ideal under edge/GPU constraints, but limited to ~5 stacked CoNNs and imperfect AutoCoNN.
> - For fine-tuning memory, 4-bit AdamW gives Adam-level accuracy with up to 57.7% memory savings; LoRA compatibility is discussed but not empirically benchmarked in these docs (and LoRA-only fine-tuning has its own noted spectral caveat in the Hessian-structure paper).
> - For SSL, the JEPA result explains why reconstruction-based pretraining chases noisy pixels (ordering by variance λ) vs latent prediction (ordering by influence ρ) — directly relevant to your noisy-pixel concern, with the caveat of linear-model analysis.
> - For the RNN control loop, the spectral analysis says the reason EI constraints impair learning is the initialization spectrum, not the sign constraints — so use DANN-style architectures or monitor NSE at initialization for stable training under E/I constraints.

> Here is a comparison and analysis of the experimental results for the five methods you identified.
> 
> ## 1. Anchor-free part–whole association — PBADet
> - **BodyHands**: PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) achieves HandAP 89.1 / Cond. Accuracy 92.62 / JointAP 85.98, beating BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 86.1M: 85.9/86.91/84.39) and far surpassing BodyHands (700M: 84.8/83.44/63.48) — with a much smaller model. The **anchor-free part-to-body** variant outperforms the anchor-based part-to-body variant (89.1 vs 88.4 HandAP; 85.98 vs 85.28 JointAP), and both beat BPJDet's anchor-based body-to-part (78.13 JointAP).
> - **COCOHumanParts** (6 parts): on par with BPJDet in overall AP (43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3 for YOLOv5l6), but **leads in AP_M/AP_L, feet/person APs, and lowest average mMR-2** (better association robustness), and beats Hier-R-CNN. On **CrowdHuman** (single-part face-body), the advantage over BPJDet is less pronounced.
> - **Ablations**: association loss is the key — removing it collapses Cond. Accuracy from 92.62 to 80.78; multi-scale offsets (+1 to JointAP) and task-alignment each help.
> - **Analysis**: the single part-to-body offset is memory/param-efficient (shorter representation: 10 vs 15 dims) and degrades gracefully as part count grows — a good fit for your crowded-scene HCI module under GPU memory limits.
> 
> ## 2. Compiled attention programs — Neural Comprehension (CoNNs)
> - **Symbolic tasks**: reaches ~100% on parity/reverse/last-letter/coin-flip across T5 Small/Base/Large, converging faster than vanilla fine-tuning, and **generalizes to OOD digit lengths** (robust 3–30 digit arithmetic where vanilla LMs collapse past ~10 digits).
> - **Arithmetic (GSM8K-Hard)**: NC mixed add/sub solver rate 22.2% avg vs PAL 14.8% and CoT 9.3%; on addition NC (21.2) roughly matches PAL (20.8); on subtraction it leads (15.6 vs 14.1). Works across Llama-2, GLM-130B, GPT-3, T5.
> - **Efficiency**: adds only ~1–3% latency; end-to-end differentiable (unlike tool-calling/PAL), so it fits "exact arithmetic without tool calls."
> - **Caveats**: AutoCoNN generator fails on addition/subtraction; sparse gating tested only up to 5 CoNNs; gains over CoT on simpler in-distribution tasks are modest.
> 
> ## 3. 4-bit state optimizers — Memory-Efficient Optimizers
> - **Accuracy (fine-tuning)**: matches or slightly beats 32-bit AdamW — RoBERTa-L GLUE 88.9 (both 89.1 for 4-bit), GPT-2M NLG 67.7→67.8, QA 94.6→94.5; comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 81.2→80.8; WMT14 26.61→26.28). LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tune: MMLU 38.7→38.9, 46.5→47.4, 56.4→54.9 — **does not degrade with model scale**.
> - **Memory**: LLaMA-7B training memory 75.4→31.9 GB (**57.7% saved**); RoBERTa-L 5.31→3.00 GB; enables LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models. Beats 8-bit memory (2× smaller states).
> - **Speed**: faster than 8-bit on large sharded models (reduced communication), slower on small models until fused kernels.
> - **Key tricks**: smaller block size (B128) + rank-1 normalization + zero-point exclusion for second moment; factorizing second moment improves both accuracy and memory. LoRA is used for the GPT-2 NLG task, confirming compatibility in that setting. Ablations show quantizing both moments costs only marginal accuracy.
> 
> ## 4. Joint-embedding self-distillation vs reconstruction — JEPA deep linear analysis
> - This paper **explains your "noisy pixel chasing"** theoretically: JEPA prioritizes **influential features (high regression coefficient ρ)**, while MAE/reconstruction prioritizes **high-variance (λ) features even if noisy**. Critical-time: MAE order depends only on λ⁻¹; JEPA order depends on both λ and ρ, so it *reverses* feature-learning order when ρ and λ conflict.
> - Depth amplifies the bias: JEPA fixed-point w̄=ρᴸ vs MAE ρ^(L/(L+1)); **1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE**; deeper JEPA increasingly suppresses noisy/low-ρ directions. Note this analysis is for **MSE (L2)**; the CE/InfoNCE angle is covered by related contrastive theory in the same collection but not this paper.
> - **Empirical validation**: on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE (CCA). Implication: for your SSL, JEPA-style latent prediction (not pixel reconstruction) is the principled fix for noisy-pixel bias.
> 
> ## 5. Spectral perspective on Dale's law — Why Dale's Law RNNs Learn Poorly
> - **Results**: ColEI (E/I column-constrained) RNNs train worse with higher variance on all 4 tasks (adding, sMNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition) vs standard RNNs and DANN (recurrent) networks. **Gradient clipping** helps ColEI substantially — directly relevant to your small control-loop stability.
> - **Key finding — spectrum, not sign constraints**: sign constraints alone account for only ~0.7–1% error; the full gap is 2.3±0.6%. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the **singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints and singular vectors** (1.5±0.3% vs 2±1% error).
> - **Mechanism**: ColEI weights = rank-one nilpotent (column means) + zero-mean random matrix → **multimodal, dispersed singular values with a large-singular-value mode**; RNNs/DANNs match the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle law. Small networks / few inhibitory units worsen the spectrum and performance. **Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error** — a pre-training stability diagnostic.
> 
> ---
> 
> ## Cross-cutting analysis for your constraints
> - **Edge precision**: PBADet (smaller param count, 1024 input) and 4-bit optimizers (57.7% memory cut, Adam-level accuracy, LoRA-compatible) are the two directly deployable under tight GPU memory. Neural Comprehension gives exact arithmetic with only ~1–3% latency and no external tools — ideal for your "no tool calls" requirement.
> - **Stability**: the Dale's-law paper tells you that if your small RNN is E/I-constrained, its poor learning is a *spectral initialization* problem, fixable by spectral-aware init/gradient clipping and measured via NSE — not an inherent cost of the constraint.
> - **SSL**: prefer JEPA-style latent self-distillation over reconstruction to avoid noisy-pixel chasing; expect the benefit to grow with encoder depth (per the depth-separation result).
> - **Precision trade-offs to note**: 4-bit optimizer's only real regression is vision pretraining (Swin-T ~0.4 drop); NC's gains over CoT shrink on simple in-distribution arithmetic; PBADet's CrowdHuman (single-part) advantage over BPJDet is small — the multi-part COCOHumanParts and BodyHands results are where it decisively wins.
