**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Summary and comparison of experimental results across five works, aligned to queries (a)–(e)
> 
> (a) Sub‑byte optimizer state compression (4‑bit Adam/AdamW)
> Identical datasets and metrics
> - NLU (RoBERTa‑Large on GLUE; mean metric, higher is better):
>   • 32‑bit AdamW: 88.9
>   • 8‑bit AdamW: 89.1
>   • 4‑bit AdamW: 89.1; 4‑bit Factor (quantized 1st moment + factorized 2nd): 88.9
>   • Adafactor: 89.1; SM3: 87.5
>   Result: 4‑bit matches 32‑bit and 8‑bit; SM3 trails.
> - Image classification (Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k; Top‑1 Acc):
>   • 32‑bit: 81.2; 8‑bit: 81.0; 4‑bit: 80.8; 4‑bit Factor: 80.9
>   • Adafactor: 80.0/79.5; SM3: 79.0
>   Result: 4‑bit within ~0.4 pt of 32‑bit; others lower.
> - NLG (GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG; BLEU):
>   • 32‑bit: 67.7; 8‑bit: 67.5; 4‑bit: 67.8; 4‑bit Factor: 67.6
>   • Adafactor: 67.2; SM3: 66.9
>   Result: 4‑bit AdamW is highest BLEU.
> - QA (RoBERTa‑L on SQuAD; F1):
>   • 32‑bit: 94.6; 8‑bit: 94.5; 4‑bit: 94.5; 4‑bit Factor: 94.6; Adafactor: 94.6; SM3: 91.7
>   Result: 4‑bit ties 32‑bit; SM3 lags.
> - MT (Transformer‑Base on WMT14 en‑de; SacreBLEU):
>   • 32‑bit: 26.61; 8‑bit: 26.66; 4‑bit: 26.28; 4‑bit Factor: 26.45; Adafactor: 26.52/26.45; SM3: 22.72
>   Result: 4‑bit is close to 32‑bit, but 8‑bit is slightly best.
> 
> Similar task types and practical evaluation
> - Instruction‑tuning LLaMA (MMLU 5‑shot; higher is better):
>   • 7B: 32‑bit 38.7 vs 4‑bit 38.9; 13B: 46.5 vs 47.4; 33B: 56.4 vs 54.9
>   Result: 4‑bit preserves or slightly improves scores at 7B/13B; small drop at 33B.
> - Efficiency (memory/time on real runs):
>   • LLaMA‑7B (FSDP, 2× A100‑80GB): 32‑bit 75.40 GB vs 4‑bit 31.87 GB (−57.7%); time 3.35 h vs 3.07 h (or 3.11 h fused)
>   • RoBERTa‑L (RTE task): 5.31 GB vs 3.00 GB (−43.5%); fused 4‑bit time 3.17 min vs 3.93 min
>   • GPT‑2 M: 6.89 GB vs 4.62 GB (−34.4%); fused time 2.11 h vs 2.13 h
>   • Largest trainable under budget (batch=1, 512 tokens): 24 GB: 32‑bit OPT‑350M vs 4‑bit OPT‑1.3B; 80 GB: 32‑bit OPT‑1.3B vs 4‑bit OPT‑6.7B; 4‑bit enables LLaMA‑7B
> - Ablations (E2E‑NLG BLEU; stability):
>   • Naïve 4‑bit 2nd‑moment quantization (B2048/DE) yielded 66.6 BLEU and 33% unstable runs; removing zero point (DE‑0) stabilized (67.5 BLEU, 0% unstable); best was Rank‑1 normalization + Linear mapping (67.8 BLEU, 0% unstable). Stable Embedding helped stability but could not fully recover accuracy when zero‑point remained.
> Conclusion: Across identical datasets, 4‑bit AdamW matches or slightly improves over 32‑bit/8‑bit on NLU/NLG/QA, is within ~0.4 pt on ImageNet, close on WMT14, and materially reduces memory (up to ~58%) with equal or better throughput (with fused kernels). Factorizing the 2nd moment can further reduce memory with minimal accuracy loss.
> 
> (b) Implicit bias of joint‑embedding self‑distillation (JEPA) vs MAE
> Identical/similar experimental settings
> - Deep linear models with controlled feature parameters (λ: covariance; ρ: regression coefficient):
>   • Same synthetic distributions (Fig. 1): With λ and ρ both increasing (Distribution 1), MAE and JEPA learn in the same order (by larger λ). With λ increasing but ρ decreasing (Distribution 2), MAE still learns by λ, whereas JEPA inverts the order and learns features with higher ρ first.
>   • ODE simulations (Fig. 2): Confirm greedy dynamics: MAE prioritizes high‑λ; JEPA prioritizes high‑ρ (predictive, low‑noise) and this bias strengthens with depth (JEPA depth L widens temporal separation by ρ; MAE does not).
> - Linear temporal generative model (Fig. 3): Empirically matches theory: λa = γa||va||²; ρa = γa||va||²/(σ²_a+||va||²). JEPA is slower to learn noisy features (larger σ_a), while MAE is agnostic; JEPA converges to lower amplitude weights for noisy features.
> - ImageNet‑scale evidence (Appendix D): During training, I‑JEPA’s learned representations from “full” vs “bottom‑variance” images show higher similarity than MAE (mean CCA), while MAE aligns more with “full vs top‑variance,” indicating JEPA focuses on perceptually salient low‑variance subspaces.
> Conclusion: On identical synthetic settings and realistic generative processes, JEPA (self‑distillation) implicitly prioritizes high‑influence (high‑ρ) predictive features, especially with deeper encoders; MAE prioritizes high‑variance (high‑λ) features. Preliminary ImageNet analysis corroborates JEPA’s focus on low‑variance semantic subspaces.
> 
> (c) Biologically constrained deep networks (Dale’s principle) and learning stability (spectral analysis)
> Identical datasets and metrics
> - Tasks (same across models): Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task.
> Comparison across methods
> - Standard RNN vs Column EI (ColEI) vs DANN (Dale’s ANN):
>   • Performance: ColEI learns worse and is more variable across all four tasks; DANN achieves performance comparable to standard RNNs.
>   • Stability: ColEI benefits much more from gradient clipping; without it, training is highly unstable.
> - Spectral properties and controlled “transplants” (Fig. 3–4):
>   • ColEI initial recurrent weights have a multimodal, dispersed singular value spectrum with a mode of large singular values, vs unimodal quarter‑circle for standard/DANN. Spectrum transplants show that giving ColEI the RNN spectrum improves training more than removing sign constraints; conversely, giving RNN a ColEI spectrum harms training. Quantified effects indicate spectrum matters more than sign constraints (RNN: ~1.5%±0.3%, ColEI: ~2%±1% impact attributable to spectrum).
> - Architectural factors:
>   • EI ratio (fewer inhibitory units) and small width exacerbate ColEI’s spectral pathology and harm performance; DANN remains robust. Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE) at initialization predicts performance: higher NSE (more clustered singular values) correlates with better accuracy across EI ratios and sizes.
>   • Spectral radius ρ: ColEI performs better at larger ρ than small ρ (still below RNN/DANN at matched best ρ values); RNN/DANN share similar ρ‑performance trends, distinct from ColEI.
> Conclusion: On identical tasks, DANN ≈ standard RNN; ColEI underperforms and is unstable. Experiments link poor ColEI learning primarily to pathological singular value spectra rather than sign constraints. Increasing inhibitory proportion/width improves NSE and performance; NSE is a practical pre‑training diagnostic for Dale‑compliant RNNs.
> 
> (d) One‑stage, anchor‑free part↔object association on COCO‑style metrics
> Identical datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman) and metrics
> - BodyHands (AP↑, Conditional Accuracy↑, Joint AP↑):
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): 89.1 / 92.62 / 85.98; PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73
>   Result: PBADet improves hand AP by +3.2–3.9 pts and conditional accuracy by ~+5.8–5.8 pts over BPJDet; joint AP improves ~+1.3–1.6 pts.
> - COCOHumanParts (AP.5:.95↑ original/subordinate; per‑category AP↑):
>   • BPJDet v5l6: 43.6/43.3; APM 63.8/63.2; APL 61.8/58.9. Per‑category: person 61.3, head 56.6, face 46.3, r‑hand 40.4, l‑hand 39.6, r‑foot 30.2, l‑foot 30.9.
>   • PBADet v5l6: 43.0/41.8; APM 66.2/65.0; APL 67.2/64.4. Per‑category: person 62.4, head 54.6, face 44.6, r‑hand 39.0, l‑hand 37.7, r‑foot 30.9, l‑foot 31.5.
>   • PBADet YOLOv7: 42.7/41.5; APM 65.8/64.4; APL 66.7/63.3 (person 62.1).
>   Result: PBADet is comparable on overall AP but higher on medium/large object AP and on feet categories; BPJDet slightly higher head/face AP.
> - COCOHumanParts association quality (average mMR−2↓, lower is better):
>   • BPJDet v5l6: head 30.8, face 31.8, l‑hand 41.6, r‑hand 42.2, r‑foot 49.1, l‑foot 50.4
>   • PBADet YOLOv7: 29.2, 31.3, 41.1, 42.7, 52.6, 52.5
>   • PBADet v5l6: 27.9, 30.5, 36.2, 40.8, 50.4, 47.9
>   Result: PBADet v5l6 improves association mMR−2 notably on hands and head/face, especially left hand (36.2 vs 41.6).
> - CrowdHuman (face‑body association; MR−2↓, AP↑, mMR−2↓):
>   • PBADet YOLOv7: body MR−2 36.5 (best), face MR−2 44.7 (best), body AP 91.6 (best), face AP 81.6; mMR−2 50.8
>   • BPJDet v5l6: 40.7 / 46.3 / 89.5 / 81.6; mMR−2 50.1
>   Result: PBADet improves detection (lower MR−2, higher AP) with roughly comparable pair mMR−2.
> Ablations (BodyHands): Adding the association head (Lassoc), multi‑scale encoding, and task‑alignment consistently raise conditional accuracy and joint AP (e.g., baseline joint AP 78.07 → 85.98 with full model; conditional accuracy 80.78 → 92.62), showing the anchor‑free, single offset design drives the gains.
> Conclusion: On identical datasets, the one‑stage anchor‑free PBADet matches or exceeds anchor‑based BPJDet in overall detection, and improves association precision (lower mMR−2) on key small parts, while simplifying the representation (constant 2D offset regardless of #parts) and decoding.
> 
> (e) Benchmark for pretrained VLMs on biological trait discovery and interpretability
> Identical datasets and tasks (VLM4Bio)
> - Species Classification:
>   • Open questions: VLMs are weak (e.g., GPT‑4V fish 1.01%, bird 17.40%, butterfly 0.04%).
>   • Multiple‑choice (MC): GPT‑4V excels on birds (82.58%); fish 35.91%, butterfly 28.91%. LLaVA‑13B/other VLMs are moderate; BioCLIP (biologically fine‑tuned) surpasses general VLMs (e.g., bird MC 93.93% vs GPT‑4V 82.58%). Difficulty matters: for fish/butterfly, accuracies drop steeply from Easy (choices from different genera) to Medium (same genus) to Hard (butterfly subspecies)—e.g., GPT‑4V easy/medium/hard (fish 44.5/3.5/–; butterfly 18.5/5.5/2.0), while BioCLIP remains markedly higher across settings.
> - Trait Identification (presence/absence or multi‑class attributes):
>   • Fish MC: GPT‑4V 82.18% (best); Bird MC: Instruct‑Vicuna‑13B 89.98% (best), GPT‑4V 62.22%, LLaVA‑13B 46.14%.
> - Trait Grounding (text→box) and Referring (box→text):
>   • Grounding: best is Instruct‑Flan‑T5‑XXL on fish (33.51%) and LLaVA‑13B on birds (35.36%); GPT‑4V is low on birds (8.1%).
>   • Referring: GPT‑4V best on birds (42.28%), MiniGPT4‑Vicuna‑7B best on fish (39.24%).
>   Result: Most VLMs that identify traits well struggle to localize them; grounding/referring lags identification.
> - Trait Counting:
>   • MC: BLIP‑Flan‑T5‑XXL 78.2% (best); Open: BLIP‑Flan‑T5‑XXL 63.4%, several others ~61.4%; GPT‑4V open 16.4%.
> Overall average accuracy: GPT‑4V is highest (34.24%), with LLaVA‑13B 31.78% and BLIP‑Flan‑T5‑XXL 30.24% following.
> Interpretability and reasoning checks
> - Prompting (500 MC questions per organism set):
>   • GPT‑4V/4o benefit most. For fish, CoT raised GPT‑4V from 34.4%→42.6% and GPT‑4o to 86.0%; Dense Captions helped birds (GPT‑4V 78.8%→87.4%). Smaller open‑source VLMs (LLaVA/BLIP) showed little to negative changes.
> - Reasoning hallucination tests:
>   • False Confidence Test (FCT): GPT‑4o best accuracy and low agreement with misleading suggestions (fish 73.6% acc, 16.6% agree; bird 99.0%, 21.0%; butterfly 53.4%, 12.4%), while LLaVA‑7B inflated agreement (e.g., ~99.8%) with lower accuracy.
>   • None‑of‑the‑Above (NOTA): GPT‑4V strong on fish/bird (81.4%/75.0%), BLIP‑Flan‑XL relatively strong on butterfly (51.0%).
> Open vs fine‑tuned models
> - BioCLIP (fine‑tuned on biological images/names) substantially outperforms general VLMs on bird/butterfly species MC (e.g., 93.93%/62.32%), while CLIP baselines lag GPT‑4V on birds but can match on fish in some splits. Conclusion: fine‑tuning on biological corpora is important for expert‑level classification; prompting/CoT helps proprietary large VLMs on zero‑shot tasks.
> 
> Cross‑paper synthesis
> - Fine‑tuning and practical evaluation: The 4‑bit optimizer paper demonstrates end‑to‑end fine‑tuning at scale (LLaMA instruction tuning) with sub‑byte states, maintaining accuracy and cutting memory/time; the VLM4Bio study shows zero‑shot limits of generic VLMs on taxonomy/traits and points to fine‑tuning (BioCLIP’s gains) as necessary for expert domains. PBADet shows a practical, anchor‑free detector that improves part–whole association on COCO‑style benchmarks. The Dale’s Law work provides a principled spectral diagnostic (NSE) to predict trainability with biological constraints, and JEPA’s analysis explains why self‑distillation (as used in modern SSL) tends to prefer predictive (not noisy) features, especially at depth—useful guidance for SSL feature learning in domains like VLM4Bio where subtle, low‑variance traits matter.
> 
> Key takeaways by identical datasets
> - GLUE, ImageNet‑1k, E2E‑NLG, SQuAD, WMT14: 4‑bit AdamW matches or exceeds 32‑/8‑bit (differences ≤ ~0.4 on ImageNet, small on WMT14) and reduces memory by 34–58%.
> - BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman: PBADet > BPJDet on BodyHands (AP and joint AP), comparable AP on COCOHumanParts with better APM/APL and lower mMR−2 on several parts; better detection MR−2/AP on CrowdHuman.
> - VLM4Bio (fish/bird/butterfly): GPT‑4V overall best zero‑shot but weak on open classification; BioCLIP (fine‑tuned) strongly outperforms for species MC; trait localization remains challenging across models; prompting/CoT helps GPT‑4V/4o significantly.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, here are the five papers and a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The five papers
> 
> **(a) "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States" (NeurIPS 2023)** — compresses Adam/AdamW states below 8-bit via small-block (B128) quantization for the first moment, rank-1/linear quantizers excluding zero-point for the second moment, optionally factorized ("4-bit Factor").
> 
> **(b) "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis" (NeurIPS 2024)** — implicit bias of joint-embedding self-distillation (JEPA) vs MAE in deep linear networks.
> 
> **(c) "Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023)** — RNNs respecting excitatory/inhibitory structure (ColEI vs DANN) with spectral analysis of learning.
> 
> **(d) "PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association" (ICLR 2024)** — single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free detectors (YOLOv5/7), evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman.
> 
> **(e) "VLM4Bio: A Benchmark to Evaluate Pretrained VLMs for Trait Discovery from Biological Images" (NeurIPS 2024)** — 469K QA pairs, 30K images (fish/bird/butterfly); tasks: species classification, trait identification, trait grounding/referring, trait counting, plus prompting and hallucination (FCT/NOTA) tests.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis of experimental results
> 
> - **(a) Memory vs accuracy trade-off:** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on all fine-tuning tasks — GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, E2E BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7 — and is comparable on pretraining (ImageNet Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61). LLaMA instruction tuning is essentially lossless (e.g., 13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; 33B 54.9 vs 56.4). Memory is cut up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models. This is the strongest paper for fine-tuning practice (Alpaca instruction tuning, FSDP, optimizer offloading).
> - **(b) Theoretical, not empirical, results:** Derives critical times showing JEPA learns high-regression-coefficient (ρ, "predictive") features first, with priority growing with encoder depth, while MAE orders features only by covariance λ — hence JEPA suppresses noisy features. Numerical ODE/SGD simulations confirm; ImageNet-1K shows I-JEPA aligns faster to the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA). No fine-tuning/application experiments; it is a theory paper, so the "practical evaluation" part of the request is only weakly met.
> - **(c) Spectral stability results:** ColEI RNNs underperform standard RNNs/DANNs on all four tasks (adding, sMNIST, PTB, object recognition) with higher variance; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Sign constraints explain only ~1% of the 2.3% gap; the dominant cause is the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed, rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure) rather than sign constraints. Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance across size/EI ratio; DANNs keep NSE ≈ 0.95 and match standard RNNs. Trained from scratch; no fine-tuning discussion.
> - **(d) Detection and association results:** On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) achieves hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 — beating BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 86.1M) at 85.9/86.91/84.39 with a smaller model. On COCOHumanParts it outperforms HierR-CNN and BPJDet under COCO-style metrics (AP, AP.5:.95, AP.5, AP_M, AP_L); on CrowdHuman it leads body MR-2. Ablations show association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task alignment each improve association. Uses pretrained YOLO weights (fine-tuning protocol from BPJDet) and VOC/COCO AP, MR-2, mMR-2 metrics.
> - **(e) VLM zero-shot capabilities:** Open-ended species classification is very weak (best ~17.4%) vs MC (best 82.58% on birds); trait identification is strong (GPT-4V 82.18% fish, Instruct-Vicuna-13B 89.98% bird) but grounding/referring drop sharply (GPT-4V fish grounding 29.41%), showing VLMs struggle to localize traits; counting is hard for all but BLIP-flan-T5-XXL. BioCLIP (fine-tuned on biological data) beats pretrained VLMs on birds/butterflies but not fish, and the paper argues fine-tuning on VLM4Bio would further improve accuracy. CoT/dense captions help only GPT-4V/4o; these models also lead FCT/NOTA hallucination tests.
> 
> ## Caveats vs. your criteria
> 
> - **(e) metric mismatch:** VLM4Bio reports **micro-averaged accuracy** (with random-choice baselines), **not F1/Precision/AUROC**. No document in the collection describes a biological trait-discovery VLM benchmark using F1/Precision/AUROC, so that specific interpretability-metric requirement cannot be satisfied from this context. (Papers using F1/Precision exist but for unrelated tasks — causal discovery, entity alignment.)
> - **(b)** is a theoretical analysis; "practical evaluation" is limited to ImageNet CCA validation, and it does not discuss fine-tuning.
> - **(c)** uses training-from-scratch RNN benchmarks rather than fine-tuning.
> 
> All five papers otherwise match the requested topics; (a), (d), and (e) most strongly address fine-tuning and practical evaluation.

> I have sufficient evidence from all five papers to compare their experimental results. Let me write the answer.
> 
> ## Papers Found
> 
> **(a) 4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States** (NeurIPS 2023) — doc `8d5e1455...`
> **(b) Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features: A Deep Linear Network Analysis** (NeurIPS 2024) — doc `40fde037...`
> **(c) Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** / "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023) — doc `e63a94c4...`
> **(d) PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024) — doc `08b70bc3...`
> **(e) VLM4Bio: A Benchmark to Evaluate Pretrained VLMs for Trait Discovery from Biological Images** (NeurIPS 2024) — doc `29594c71...`
> 
> ## Analysis of Experimental Results
> 
> **(a) 4-bit optimizer (memory vs. accuracy).** On all fine-tuning tasks 4-bit AdamW **matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW**: GLUE RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7; on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61) it is comparable but marginally below. On LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction fine-tuning, 4-bit AdamW is comparable to 32-bit AdamW on MMLU and commonsense reasoning (e.g., LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5) and does not degrade as model size grows. Memory savings: up to **57.7%** total training memory (LLaMA-7B 31.87GB vs 75.40GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models; "4-bitFactor" gives up to 46.7% savings. Ablations show excluding the zero-point (DE-0/Linear) and rank-1 normalization are what stabilize training and eliminate the 33–66% instability seen with naive 4-bit quantization.
> 
> **(b) JEPA implicit bias (theory, synthetic + ImageNet validation).** This is analytical rather than an accuracy benchmark: on Gaussian data where MAE and JEPA can learn the same features, JEPA *reverses* the learning order to prioritize high-regression-coefficient (ρ) features; critical-time analysis shows JEPA's priority to large ρ grows with depth, while MAE orders purely by covariance λ. A flickering temporal model shows JEPA learns noisy features more slowly and converges to lower amplitude weights, i.e., suppresses noise. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA's features align with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) faster than MAE's (measured by CCA) — supporting "why JEPA prefers predictive, not noisy, features."
> 
> **(c) Dale's-law RNNs (learning stability via spectra).** ColEI (sign-constrained) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANN on all four tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, Penn TreeBank, object recognition), with no value of spectral radius ρ making ColEI match standard RNNs/DANNs. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the culprit is **not sign constraints or singular vectors but the singular-value spectrum**: ColEI's rank-one column-mean structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values vs. the Marchenko-Pastur quarter-circle of standard/DANN networks. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error across sizes and E/I ratios; small networks with high NSE beat larger low-NSE ones. Gradient clipping helps ColEI most, consistent with pathological spectrum.
> 
> **(d) PBADet (part-body association, COCO-style metrics).** On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) reaches HandAP **89.1**, conditional accuracy **92.62**, joint AP **85.98**, beating BPJDet-YOLOv5m6 (85.3/86.80/78.13) with a smaller model, and BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (85.9/86.91/84.39) with the same backbone. On COCOHumanParts, PBADet matches BPJDet on overall AP (AP.5:.95 43.0/41.5 original/subordinate vs 43.6/43.3) but leads on AP_M, AP_L and person/feet categories, and achieves the lowest average mMR⁻² for head, face, both hands, and right foot. Ablations show the anchor-free head beats the anchor-based one (89.1 vs 88.4 HandAP), and part-to-body offset beats body-to-part (89.1 vs 85.3). Against ED-Pose on COCO validation, PBADet gives substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51).
> 
> **(e) VLM4Bio (biological trait discovery).** Evaluated zero-shot (no fine-tuning). Key results: all VLMs are weak on **open-ended** species classification (best GPT-4V only 17.46% on Bird) but much better on MC questions (GPT-4V 82.58% Bird, 40.20% Fish, 50.24% Butterfly). Trait identification is much stronger (GPT-4V 82.18% on Fish; Instruct-Vicuna-13B 89.98% on Bird), but trait **grounding** (e.g., Fish-500 ≤33.51%) and referring drop sharply, showing VLMs fail to localize traits; trait counting is hard (best ~78.2% MC). The biologically fine-tuned **BioCLIP** dramatically outperforms pretrained VLMs on Bird/Butterfly (e.g., 94–95% vs ≤73.5% on easy/medium species classification), indicating fine-tuning on biological data gives large gains.
> 
> ## Cross-paper comparison on "fine-tuning and practical evaluation"
> - **(a) and (e) both quantify fine-tuning directly**: (a) shows 4-bit compression gives **lossless fine-tuning** while cutting memory ~43–58% (practical for single-GPU large-model training); (e) shows fine-tuning a VLM on biological data (BioCLIP) is what closes the accuracy gap, while the benchmark itself evaluates zero-shot VLMs. Together they show the fine-tuning cost/benefit tradeoff on both the optimizer and the evaluation side.
> - **(c) is closest to "practical stability"**: it uses a spectrum diagnostic (NSE) to predict trainability before training — an interpretability measure analogous to (b)'s CCA-based feature-quality measure and (e)'s hallucination/error analyses, but at the level of learning dynamics rather than downstream metrics.
> - **(b) provides no downstream-accuracy numbers** (only CCA alignment on ImageNet), so it cannot be compared on accuracy; its contribution is mechanistic (why predictive features win), complementing (c)'s spectral-stability mechanism and (e)'s empirical benchmarks.
> 
> ## Caveats / what cannot be established
> - The user's specification for (e) mentions **F1/Precision/AUROC** interpretability metrics, but VLM4Bio uses **micro-averaged accuracy** (with 25% random-choice baselines) plus hallucination tests (FCT, NOTA) and error analyses; no F1/AUROC for trait discovery exists in this collection.
> - The JEPA paper (b) is theory with limited ImageNet validation; its claims apply to deep linear networks under special initialization assumptions.
> - The five papers have no shared benchmark, so only within-paper SOTA comparisons (e.g., PBADet vs BPJDet, 4-bit vs 32-bit AdamW, JEPA vs MAE, ColEI vs DANN, BioCLIP vs VLMs) are directly comparable.

Gold 1：

> Below is a consolidated, literature‑only comparison of experimental results across the five papers you provided, organized by task family and dataset. We call out identical datasets where methods are directly compared, summarize performance on similar task types, and report dataset‑specific outcomes strictly from the tables/figures.
> 
> 1) Anchor‑free part–body association detection (PBADet, ICLR 2024)
> Identical datasets and baselines: PBADet vs BPJDet (anchor‑based) and Hier R‑CNN on BodyHands, COCO‑HumanParts, and CrowdHuman.
> 
> • BodyHands (Table 1):
>   – PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   – PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>   – BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.
>   Summary: On this identical dataset, PBADet achieves higher detection (AP) and association (Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP) than BPJDet, with the same backbone (YOLOv5l6) and also with YOLOv7.
> 
> • COCO‑HumanParts (Table 2, Table 3):
>   – All‑category APs (original/subordinate, AP.5:.95): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3. AP.5 PBADet 70.0/68.4 vs BPJDet 70.6/69.8.
>   – Scale APs: PBADet leads for APM (66.2/65.0 vs 63.8/63.2) and APL (67.2/64.4 vs 61.8/58.9).
>   – Per‑category APs: PBADet is comparable or slightly better on “person” (62.4 vs 61.3) and feet (e.g., l‑foot 31.5 vs 30.9).
>   – Association mMR−2 (Table 3, lower is better): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) improves over BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) for head (27.9 vs 30.8), face (30.5 vs 31.8), left hand (36.2 vs 41.6), right hand (40.8 vs 42.2). PBADet is slightly worse on right foot (50.4 vs 49.1), better on left foot (47.9 vs 50.4).
>   Summary: On identical COCO‑HumanParts, PBADet provides stronger association accuracy (lower mMR−2) for most parts and better medium/large‑scale AP, while overall AP(.5:.95) is comparable to BPJDet.
> 
> • CrowdHuman (Table 5, Table 6):
>   – Face‑body association task: PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves Body MR−2=36.5 (best), Face MR−2=44.7, Body AP=91.6, Face AP=81.6, mMR−2 body‑face=50.8. BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) has Body MR−2=40.7, Face MR−2=46.3, Body AP=89.5, Face AP=81.6, mMR−2=50.1.
>   – Against crowd detectors: PBADet yields the best Body MR−2 (36.5) and competitive Body AP (91.6) vs DETR‑based baselines (e.g., PED‑DETR 91.6).
>   Summary: On identical CrowdHuman, PBADet improves detection MR−2 and Body AP over BPJDet; association mMR−2 is similar/slightly higher.
> 
> Ablations (Table 4, Table 8): Anchor‑free heads and part‑to‑body offsets (PBADet) outperform anchor‑based backbones and body‑to‑part definitions (BPJDet variants), confirming better scaling with more parts.
> 
> 2) Memory‑efficient optimizers with 4‑bit states (NeurIPS 2023)
> Identical datasets: All optimizers evaluated on the same tasks/datasets (RoBERTa‑L on GLUE/SQuAD; Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k; GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG; Transformer‑Base on WMT14 En‑De).
> 
> • Accuracy (Table 2):
>   – NLU (GLUE, mean Acc/Correlation): 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 equals 8‑bit AdamW 89.1 and slightly exceeds 32‑bit AdamW 88.9. 4‑bit Factor 88.9.
>   – Image classification (Swin‑T, ImageNet‑1k Top‑1): 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit 81.0; 4‑bit 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9 (within ~0.4% of full precision).
>   – NLG (GPT‑2 M, E2E BLEU): 4‑bit AdamW 67.8 slightly exceeds 32‑bit 67.7 and 8‑bit 67.5; 4‑bit Factor 67.6.
>   – QA (RoBERTa‑L, SQuAD F1): 4‑bit 94.5 vs 32‑bit 94.6 vs 8‑bit 94.5 (no material drop).
>   – MT (Transformer‑Base, WMT14 SacreBLEU): 4‑bit 26.28 vs 32‑bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; 4‑bit Factor 26.45 (minor deltas).
>   Summary: On identical datasets, 4‑bit AdamW and 4‑bit Factor match or come within small margins of 32‑bit/8‑bit optimizers across vision, NLP, QA, and machine translation.
> 
> • Efficiency (Table 4):
>   – LLaMA‑7B instruction tuning (FSDP, 2×A100‑80GB): 4‑bit AdamW reduces total memory from 75.40 GB (32‑bit) to 31.87 GB (−57.7%) and time from 3.35 h to 3.07 h; fused kernels keep 31.88 GB and ~3.11 h.
>   – RoBERTa‑L (RTE): 4‑bit AdamW fused runs in 3.17 min vs 3.93 min (32‑bit) with 3.00 GB vs 5.31 GB; 4‑bit Factor 2.83 GB.
>   – GPT‑2 Medium (E2E): 4‑bit fused 2.11 h vs 2.13 h (32‑bit) with 4.62 GB vs 6.89 GB; 4‑bit Factor 4.44 GB.
>   – Largest trainable model (Table 5): on 24 GB GPU, 4‑bit trains OPT‑1.3B vs 350M (32‑bit); on 80 GB, 4‑bit trains OPT‑6.7B and LLaMA‑7B (single GPU) vs 1.3B (32‑bit).
>   Summary: 4‑bit states consistently cut optimizer memory roughly in half relative to 8‑bit (and much more vs 32‑bit), often improving or maintaining throughput.
> 
> • Ablations (Table 6): Quantizing both moments (first: B128/DE; second: Rank‑1/Linear) keeps Swin‑T Top‑1 ~80.8–81.0; adding factorized second moment also preserves accuracy (80.9). This confirms robust convergence with 4‑bit when zero‑point is excluded for second moment and rank‑1 normalization is used.
> 
> 3) Biodiversity VLM benchmark (VLM4Bio, NeurIPS 2024)
> Identical datasets: All VLMs evaluated zero‑shot on the same images and question sets across Fish‑10K, Bird‑10K, Butterfly‑10K; Fish‑500/Bird‑500 for grounding/referring/counting.
> 
> • Species classification (Table 2):
>   – Open questions: best are GPT‑4V (Bird‑10K 17.40%), Instruct‑FLAN‑T5‑XXL (Butterfly‑10K 9.94%), while Fish‑10K open accuracies are ≤2.32% (LLaVA‑13B) across models.
>   – Multiple‑choice (MC): Bird‑10K is much easier for VLMs (GPT‑4V 82.58%), while Fish‑10K MC tops around 40.20% (LLaVA‑7B) and Butterfly‑10K MC ~50.24% (LLaVA‑7B).
>   Summary: On identical datasets, MC format drastically lifts VLM accuracy; Bird‑10K (natural backgrounds, CUB subset) yields highest accuracies, Fish and Butterfly (museum specimen images) are harder.
> 
> • Trait identification (Table 2):
>   – Fish‑10K MC: GPT‑4V 82.18 leads; several models in 39–68% range.
>   – Bird‑10K MC: Instruct‑Vicuna‑13B 89.98 and Instruct‑Vicuna‑7B 77.91 outperform GPT‑4V (62.22).
>   Summary: On similar binary/multi‑class trait questions, identification is easier than species naming; instruction‑tuned BLIP variants excel on bird trait attributes.
> 
> • Trait grounding & referring (Table 2; identical Fish‑500/Bird‑500):
>   – Grounding (text→location):
>     • Fish‑500 MC: best is Instruct‑FLAN‑T5‑XL 33.51; GPT‑4V 29.41; others near 25–27%.
>     • Bird‑500 MC: LLaVA‑13B 35.36; Instruct‑FLAN‑T5‑XL 30.24; GPT‑4V 8.10.
>   – Referring (location→text):
>     • Fish‑500 MC: MiniGPT4 Vicuna‑7B 39.24; PB across 25–32%; GPT‑4V 28.15.
>     • Bird‑500 MC: MiniGPT4 Vicuna‑13B 41.69; BLIP‑FLAN‑XL 23.03; GPT‑4V 42.28.
>   Summary: On identical grounding/referring sets, accuracies drop vs identification; best models vary by task—LLaVA‑13B for bird grounding; MiniGPT4 for referring; GPT‑4V’s Fish/Bird results are mixed.
> 
> • Trait counting (Fish‑500; Table 2):
>   – Open: several models peak ~61.4 (BLIP‑FLAN‑XL, Instruct‑FLAN‑T5‑XL), GPT‑4V 16.4.
>   – MC: BLIP‑FLAN‑T5‑XXL 78.2 best; MiniGPT4‑13B 74.0; GPT‑4V 44.8.
>   Summary: Counting is challenging for most VLMs; instruction‑tuned FLAN‑T5 variants perform best.
> 
> • Overall (Table 2): GPT‑4V has highest overall average (34.24); several open‑source models trail (e.g., LLaVA‑7B 29.0; MiniGPT4‑13B 29.79).
> 
> • Difficulty & fine‑tuning (Table 3, Table 7):
>   – MC difficulty: accuracy declines from “Easy” to “Hard” selections; BioCLIP (fine‑tuned on biological images/names) outperforms general VLMs on Bird/Butterfly across identical question sets.
>   – CLIP vs BioCLIP: BioCLIP > CLIP on Bird‑10K (93.93 vs 45.78 MC) and Butterfly‑10K (62.32 vs 45.60 MC); Fish‑10K MC is closer (50.65 vs 42.45), consistent with BioCLIP’s training data.
> 
> • Prompting & hallucination tests (Table 4, Table 5):
>   – Zero‑shot CoT/Dense Captions: GPT‑4o and GPT‑4V benefit most; smaller open‑source VLMs show limited gains.
>   – FCT/NOTA: GPT‑4o/GPT‑4V achieve higher accuracy and lower agreement with false suggestions than LLaVA‑7B/13B, indicating more reliable reasoning on identical test sets.
> 
> 4) RNNs obeying Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023)
> Similar task types: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, and naturalistic object recognition are used across Standard RNNs, simple Column EI (ColEI) networks, and recurrent Dale’s ANNs (DANNs).
> 
> • Across identical tasks (Figure 2): ColEI networks learn worse (higher error, slower convergence) than Standard RNNs or DANNs; DANNs match Standard RNN performance. Gradient clipping benefits ColEI more.
> • Spectrum dependence (Figures 3–6): Transplant experiments show singular value spectra matter more than sign constraints for learning gaps; multimodal dispersed singular values (ColEI) correlate with worse performance, especially in small networks and with few inhibitory units; normalised SVD entropy anti‑correlates with error, predicting performance across EI ratios and sizes.
> Summary: On the same tasks, recurrent DANNs retain performance comparable to Standard RNNs while respecting Dale’s Law; ColEI suffers due to spectral pathology, particularly in small networks or skewed E/I ratios.
> 
> 5) JEPA vs MAE (NeurIPS 2024)
> Similar task types: controlled linear settings, Gaussian data, and temporal linear generative models; one realistic check on ImageNet embeddings.
> 
> • Controlled experiments and ODE simulations (Figures 1–4): Both objectives learn features step‑wise; JEPA prioritizes high regression‑coefficient (influential, less noisy) features first (depth‑dependent), while MAE favors high covariance features regardless of noise.
> • Temporal linear model (Figure 3): With autocorrelation (γ) and noise (σ) per mode, JEPA emphasizes “slow” features (higher γ, lower σ) over noisy ones; MAE does not down‑weight noise similarly.
> • ImageNet representation similarity (Appendix D, Figure 7): I‑JEPA shows higher CCA between “full” and “bottom‑variance” images than MAE across training; the trend reverses for “full” vs “top‑variance,” consistent with JEPA’s bias toward perceptual/low‑variance subspaces.
> Summary: Across identical synthetic settings, JEPA’s implicit bias yields faster learning of predictive, lower‑variance features versus MAE; in practical vision embeddings, JEPA aligns better with perceptual subspaces early in training.
> 
> Cross‑paper, task‑type alignment and takeaways
> • Detection and grounding vs reasoning: PBADet improves association detection and scaling on human parts (BodyHands, COCO‑HumanParts, CrowdHuman), while VLM4Bio shows trait grounding/referring is challenging for current VLMs—best accuracies ~30–40% on identical Fish‑500/Bird‑500 sets.
> • Memory/compute constraints: 4‑bit optimizers deliver near‑par accuracy (GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet, WMT14, E2E) with large memory savings and throughput maintenance/improvement, enabling larger biodiversity models under fixed GPUs.
> • Time‑series/RNN stability: Recurrent DANNs match Standard RNNs on identical tasks while respecting EI constraints; ColEI is unstable unless spectra are controlled—NSE predicts performance.
> • Pretraining that avoids noisy pixels: JEPA favors influential, lower‑variance features (temporal “slow” features), resisting noisy subspaces compared to MAE in matched setups and shows better early alignment with perceptual features on ImageNet.
> • Benchmarks: VLM4Bio provides identical datasets across Fish‑10K/Bird‑10K/Butterfly‑10K and Fish‑500/Bird‑500 to quantify VLMs’ zero‑shot trait discovery, grounding and reasoning; BioCLIP (fine‑tuned biology foundation model) outperforms general VLMs on identical MC classification sets.
> 
> All comparisons above are drawn solely from the reported figures/tables in the provided papers and respect identical datasets or matched task settings wherever present.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers covering each piece
> 
> **1. Transformer/VLM system for species classification, trait grounding/counting, and reasoning (benchmark)**
> - **VLM4Bio** (doc `29594c71…`): benchmark of ~469K QA pairs on Fish/Bird/Butterfly-10K covering species classification, trait identification, trait grounding, trait referring, trait counting, plus reasoning tests (Contextual/Dense-Caption/Chain-of-Thought prompting, False Confidence Test, None-of-the-Above Test). Museum fish images come from GLIN museum collections (INHS, FMNH, etc.).
> 
> **2. Low-memory parameter-efficient fine-tuning**
> - **NFTS** (doc `aa60be77…`): NAS over freeze/fine-tune and adapter placement for few-shot adaptation of pretrained backbones (adapter/prompt/prefix-style PEFT for ViTs).
> - **4-bit Optimizers** (doc `8d5e1455…`): 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states for fine-tuning; LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU, up to 57.7% memory savings.
> 
> **3. Stable RNN with biological E/I dynamics**
> - **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (doc `e63a94c4…`): recurrent E/I (ColEI vs DANN) networks, stability via singular-value spectra, normalized SVD entropy.
> 
> **4. Self-supervised pretraining that avoids noisy pixels**
> - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc `40fde037…`): JEPA/self-distillation vs MAE — JEPA's latent-space prediction is biased toward high-influence features and suppresses noisy pixels; depth strengthens suppression.
> - (Related: **LDReg**, doc `51526068…`, regularizes SSL against local dimensional collapse.)
> 
> **5. Anchor-free part-to-whole detection with COCO-style evaluation**
> - **PBADet** (doc `08b70bc3…`): one-stage anchor-free part-body association via a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCOHumanParts (and CrowdHuman, BodyHands).
> - **HASSOD** (doc `ef986d59…`): fully self-supervised detection that learns whole/part/subpart composition hierarchies; trained on MS-COCO images, evaluated on LVIS/SA-1B/Objects365 with AR.
> 
> **6. Benchmark for VLM reasoning/trait grounding with F1/Precision/AUROC**
> - **VLM4Bio** is the trait-grounding/reasoning benchmark, but it reports **micro-averaged accuracy** (with 25% random baseline), not F1/Precision/AUROC. **PBADet** reports precision/recall/F1 (vs ED-Pose on hands/feet). No paper in this collection reports AUROC for trait grounding — that gap cannot be filled from the provided context.
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **VLM4Bio (12 VLMs, zero-shot):**
> - All VLMs are poor on open-ended species classification (best ~17.4% Bird for GPT-4V) but better on multiple-choice (MC). GPT-4V: Fish MC 35.91%, Bird MC 82.58%, Butterfly MC 28.91%; LLaVA-13B Fish MC 40.20%; Instruct-Vicuna-13B Butterfly MC 50.24%.
> - **BioCLIP** (biologically fine-tuned foundation model) far outperforms pretrained VLMs on Bird (MC 93.93%) and Butterfly (MC 62.32%) but not Fish (MC 50.65%) — it wasn't trained on fish; it also drops sharply from MC to open questions. This shows fine-tuning on biological data gives large gains.
> - Trait identification is much easier (GPT-4V 82.18% on Fish-10K; Instruct-Vicuna-13B 89.98% on Bird-10K), but trait **grounding/referring** accuracy drops sharply (VLMs identify traits but fail to localize them). Trait counting is difficult for almost all models.
> - CoT/dense-caption prompting helps GPT-4V/GPT-4o only; smaller models (LLaVA, BLIP) gain little; GPT-4V/4o lead hallucination (FCT/NOTA) tests; LLaVA is more error-prone.
> 
> **NFTS:** per-episode architecture selection (N=3) beats fixed top-1 and ensembling — 80.7 vs 76.6 accuracy on single-source domains with 16M vs 82M params; NFTS-1 alone is already SOTA; adapters favor early/late ResNet layers; combining fine-tuning with adapters helps.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers:** 4-bit AdamW matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE/SQuAD/E2E-NLG/ImageNet/Alpaca with up to 57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU); 4-bit Factor more memory-efficient; Adafactor/SM3 save more memory but degrade accuracy.
> 
> **Dale's Law RNNs:** ColEI networks learn worse and more variably than standard RNNs and DANN across adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition; the initial **singular-value spectrum** matters more than sign constraints (spectrum-transplant experiments: spectrum accounts for ~1.5–2% error vs ~0.7–1% for sign constraints); DANN is robust to E/I ratio and network size, ColEI degrades with fewer inhibitory units/smaller size; normalized SVD entropy anti-correlates with final error; gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> 
> **JEPA vs MAE:** in deep linear analysis, JEPA's critical time prioritizes high-influence (ρ) features, and depth strengthens noise suppression, whereas MAE's ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ; ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE by CCA — i.e., JEPA avoids latching onto noisy/uninformative pixels.
> 
> **PBADet:** outperforms BPJDet and HierR-CNN on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts; on CrowdHuman face-body it achieves leading body MR-2 and competitive AP; vs ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands/feet; the single part-to-body center offset keeps one-to-one correspondence and avoids anchor-based offset problems.
> 
> **HASSOD:** improves zero-shot Mask AR on SA-1B from 17.0 to 26.0 and LVIS from 20.2 to 22.5, and Box AR on Objects365/LVIS by +3.2/+3.3 — with only 1/5 of the images and 1/12 of the iterations of CutLER (which it also beats under fair training); the paper argues AR is more appropriate than AP for class-agnostic detection.
> 
> **Caveat on metrics:** F1/Precision/AUROC for VLM trait grounding are not reported in any retrieved paper; VLM4Bio uses accuracy, and PBADet's F1/precision/recall concern part detection, not VLM trait reasoning.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Paper mapping (end-to-end pieces)
> 
> 1. **Transformer-based species classification + trait grounding/counting + VLM reasoning benchmark** → **VLM4Bio** (29594c71…). Covers species classification (open & MCQ), trait identification (10 binary fish traits incl. fins; 28 bird traits), trait grounding, trait referring, trait counting (e.g., fins), plus prompting (CoT, dense caption, contextual) and hallucination tests (FCT, NOTA) on 469K QA pairs / 30K images (Fish-10K from museum collections, Bird-10K from CUB, Butterfly-10K).
> 2. **Low-memory fine-tuning / parameter-efficient updates** → **4-bit Optimizers** (8d5e1455…; 4-bit AdamW/AdamW-Factor optimizer states) and **NFTS** (aa60be77…; neural search over adapters + freeze/fine-tune on ViT/ResNet, parameter-efficient few-shot adaptation). LoRA is only cited, not a standalone paper here.
> 3. **Stable RNN with biological E/I dynamics** → **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (e63a94c4…; ColEI vs DANN, spectral analysis, NSE).
> 4. **Self-supervised pretraining that avoids noisy pixels** → **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (40fde037…; JEPA/self-distillation implicit bias vs MAE pixel reconstruction). Note: NEFTune (fad0fb20…) adds noise to embeddings — opposite direction, not a match.
> 5. **Anchor-free part↔whole detector with COCO-like evaluation** → **PBADet** (08b70bc3…; one-stage anchor-free, single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on COCO-HumanParts/COCO-WholeBody/CrowdHuman). HASSOD (ef986d59…) also does part-to-whole composition but is not anchor-free and is evaluated with AR (LVIS/SA-1B).
> 6. **Benchmark with F1/Precision/AUROC** → **Not covered as specified.** VLM4Bio uses micro-averaged **accuracy** (random baseline 25% for 4-choice MC). PBADet reports **precision/recall/F1** (vs ED-Pose for part association), CMA (e4c7255b…) reports **F1** for causal graphs, and Synthcity (558c32ef…) uses **AUROC** for synthetic-data detection — but no retrieved paper reports F1/Precision/AUROC jointly on a trait-grounding VLM benchmark.
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **VLM4Bio:** BioCLIP beats all pretrained VLMs on birds (Bird-10K open 67.12 vs GPT-4V 17.40; MC 82.58+ region) and butterflies but **not** fish; GPT-4V is the overall best and leads hallucination/verification tests; MCQ accuracy is far above open-ended (models eliminate wrong options); CoT and dense captions substantially help GPT-4V/GPT-4o but not small models (LLaVA, BLIP); all VLMs struggle at trait counting despite good trait identification, and grounding/referring accuracy drops vs identification (models name traits but can't localize them); LLaVA is most error-prone, GPT-4V produces more "Other"/refusal-type errors.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers:** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet (Swin-T), E2E-NLG, WMT14, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning (e.g., LLaMA-7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; ARC-c 44.4 vs 45.1), with up to **57.7% training-memory reduction** (LLaMA-7B fits one 80GB GPU); convergence curves closely align. Sublinear-memory optimizers (Adafactor, SM3) are more memory-efficient but degrade accuracy, especially on image classification. **NFTS:** per-episode search over adapters/frozen layers beats fixed top-1 and ensembling (single-source domains 80.7 vs 76.6 at 16M vs 82M params); N=3 candidates best; adapters favor early/late ResNet-18 layers, not middle.
> 
> **Dale's-law RNNs:** ColEI networks train worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANNs on adding, sMNIST, PTB, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI much more. The cause is spectral: ColEI initial weights have multimodal, dispersed singular values (column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure), while standard RNNs/DANNs match random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur spectra. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error; small ColEI networks with fewer inhibitory units (biologically realistic ratios) are worst, whereas DANNs are robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron. Implication: EI RNN stability/learnability is achieved via spectrum (DANN-style), not sign constraints alone.
> 
> **JEPA vs MAE:** In deep linear networks, JEPA/self-distillation is biased to learn high-influence (high-ρ) features and suppresses noise, with depth strengthening noise suppression; MAE's feature ordering depends mainly on eigenvalues (λ). On ImageNet, I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE, confirming that latent-space prediction avoids latching onto noisy pixel-level features.
> 
> **PBADet:** Outperforms BPJDet and HierR-CNN on BodyHands and COCO-HumanParts; e.g., COCO-HumanParts all-categories AP 42.7/41.5 (AP 69.5/67.9 at 0.5 IoU, YOLOv7), anchor-free variant beats anchor-based (89.1 vs 88.4 Hand AP, 85.98 vs 85.28 Joint AP) and part-to-body beats body-to-part association; leads body MR-2 on CrowdHuman face-body and gives substantially higher precision/recall/F1 than ED-Pose for hands/feet; extends to quadruped part-body association (AnimalPose/AP-10K) qualitatively.
> 
> **Gaps/limitations to note:** no single paper ties all six pieces end-to-end; the F1/Precision/AUROC trait-grounding benchmark does not exist in this collection (VLM4Bio uses accuracy), and VLM4Bio itself is zero-shot (no fine-tuning path) and limited to three taxa with possible label noise; 4-bit optimizers were tested only on language/vision; JEPA analysis is limited to deep linear networks; ColEI paper offers no fix (only diagnosis and NSE guidance).

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:266 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively address principled uncertainty and inductive-bias–aware learning across deep networks: (a) distributional approaches and ensemble disagreement for exploration in reinforcement learning, (b) joint-embedding self-distillation that prioritizes informative features in self-supervised learning, (c) spectral or structural constraints (e.g., excitatory/inhibitory partitions) that affect RNN training dynamics, (d) anytime-valid calibration that controls prediction risk under adaptive data collection, and (e) anchor-free perception models that associate human parts to bodies in images. Prefer works that use standard optimizers (SGD/Adam), common losses (cross-entropy or mean squared error), CNN/Transformer backbones, and evaluations on familiar vision benchmarks (e.g., COCO, MNIST), reporting metrics like precision/F1 or AUROC and analyzing feature embeddings or cosine similarity.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：3→3（Δ+0）；rounds：2→3（Δ+1）。**

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results strictly drawn from the provided papers, organized by (1) identical datasets used across papers, (2) similar dataset types, and (3) specific datasets, with head-to-head outcomes and key metrics where reported.
> 
> 1) Results on identical datasets
> - ImageNet (vision; used by two papers):
>   - JEPA vs MAE (How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features): On ImageNet-1K (Appendix D), the study reports that I-JEPA’s learned features show higher similarity (via mean CCA) between representations from full vs bottom PCA-variance subspaces across training, while MAE shows higher similarity for full vs top PCA subspaces. This empirically supports that JEPA prioritizes informative, lower-variance (semantic) features more quickly than MAE; no accuracy numbers are reported, only the CCA behavior across epochs.
>   - Active, Anytime-Valid RCPS (Active RCPS paper): On ImageNet (Fig. 3), the RCPS procedure with pretrain and learned labeling policies achieves lower final calibrated β (tighter prediction sets) than ‘all’ and ‘oblivious’ baselines while controlling safety violation rates at the target α=0.05. The plots show that pretrain/learned maintain safety (violations ≤ 0.05) and attain better label efficiency (reaching lower β with fewer labels). Although the two papers study different tasks (JEPA: representation bias; RCPS: risk-controlling prediction sets), both on ImageNet show improvements over their respective baselines: JEPA biases toward semantic feature subspaces and RCPS attains safer, tighter sets with fewer labels.
> 
> 2) Results on similar dataset types
> A. Vision perception and detection
> - Anchor-free part–body association (PBADet; COCO-family datasets):
>   - COCOHumanParts (Table 2): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) attains AP.5:.95 43.0 (original)/41.8 (subordinate), AP.5 70.0/68.4, with strong APM/APL and competitive per-category APs (e.g., hands/feet). BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) is slightly higher in overall AP.5:.95 (43.6/43.3) and AP.5 (70.6/69.8), while PBADet leads in some scale-specific APs and in many association-sensitive metrics (see mMR−2 in Table 3 below), indicating PBADet’s advantage when accurate part–body association is emphasized.
>   - COCOHumanParts association accuracy (Table 3, mMR−2↓): PBADet (YOLOv7) has the lowest average mMR−2 across head, face, both hands, and right foot compared to BPJDet at matched or smaller model sizes; e.g., head 29.2 vs 30.8, face 31.3 vs 31.8, and right-hand 42.7 vs 42.2 (lower is better), showing more reliable part-to-body associations.
>   - COCO (ED-Pose comparison on COCO val; Table 7): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) reports higher Precision/Recall/F1 on hands/feet than ED-Pose (Swin-L) (e.g., lefthand F1: 46.50 vs 22.87; rightfoot F1: 50.34 vs 40.34) under the paper’s evaluation protocol, supporting PBADet’s robustness for part localization plus association.
>   - BodyHands (Table 1): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves higher scores than prior work, e.g., Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; PBADet (YOLOv5l6) also improves over BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) on Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP (92.71/85.73 vs 86.91/84.39). These gains are at smaller or comparable model sizes vs some baselines.
>   - CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6): PBADet (YOLOv7) attains best (lower) MR−2 for body and face and higher body AP among compared one-stage baselines; mMR−2 for body–face association is comparable (∼50.8–50.9), indicating strong detection with balanced association.
> 
> - Visual RL with pixel observations (VizDoom):
>   - Diverse Projection Ensembles in Distributional RL (PE-DQN): On MyWayHome (Fig. 5), PE-DQN is the only method that reaches the goal (non-zero episodic returns) across all 10 seeds in Dense, Sparse, and Very Sparse variants. Baselines (DQN, DLTV-QR, BDQN+P, IDS-C51) lag especially in Sparse/Very Sparse. Thus, for vision-based navigation with sparse rewards, the diverse projection ensemble with propagated uncertainty bonus yields the most reliable exploration.
> 
> B. Sequential/time-series tasks
> - RNNs with Dale’s Law constraints (DANN vs ColEI vs Standard RNN):
>   - Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition (Fig. 2A–D): Standard RNN and DANN match or exceed each other and both outperform ColEI across tasks. ColEI learning is notably worse (slower or lower final performance), often with higher variance; gradient clipping helps ColEI more, but it still trails. Spectrum transplant studies (Fig. 4) show that singular value spectra of the recurrent weights matter more than sign constraints for performance; Normalized SVD Entropy (H) correlates with better test error. Further, reducing inhibitory proportion (higher E:I) or network size degrades ColEI spectra and performance (Figs. 5–6), whereas DANN is robust even with very few I units.
> 
> C. Model-free RL exploration tasks
> - bsuite and Deep-Sea:
>   - PE-DQN (Fig. 4a): On bsuite’s composite capability scores, PE-DQN excels in exploration and improves in multiple other categories vs BDQN+P, IDS-C51, and DLTV-QR, despite using far fewer models (total ensemble size 4 vs 20 for BDQN+P and IDS-C51).
>   - Deep-Sea (Fig. 4b): As size increases up to 100×100, PE-DQN’s median episodic regret is reduced by roughly half vs baselines, and ablations show both components matter: (i) diversity from mixing quantile and categorical projections (PE-DQN[QR/QR] and [C51/C51] are weaker than the mixed ensemble), and (ii) propagation of epistemic uncertainty (PE-DQN [Ind.] without propagation performs worse). This establishes that disagreement alone (local TD error) is insufficient; propagating the bonus per Theorem 3 improves directed exploration.
> 
> D. Risk control under adaptive collection (anytime-valid RCPS)
> - Simulations (Fig. 2): With θ=0.1 and α=0.05, all methods keep safety violations ≤α, but ‘pretrain’ and ‘learned’ policies are more label-efficient, achieving lower β (tighter sets) with fewer labeled points than ‘all’ or ‘oblivious’ labeling. This pattern repeats on ImageNet (Fig. 3): pretrain/learned reach smaller β while maintaining the anytime-valid guarantee (safety violation rates below 0.05).
> 
> 3) Results on specific datasets (head-to-head)
> - BodyHands (anchor-free hand–body association):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 (Table 1), surpassing BPJDet (YOLOv5l6 Joint AP 84.39) and other prior baselines.
> 
> - COCOHumanParts:
>   - Overall APs (Table 2): BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) slightly higher overall AP.5:.95 than PBADet (43.6 vs 43.0), but PBADet leads in scale-specific APs (APM/APL) and in feet categories AP, and—crucially—in association reliability measured by average mMR−2 (Table 3) across most part categories.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (body/face detection and association):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7) has best (lower) MR−2 for body (36.5) and face (44.7) and highest body AP (91.6) among compared one-stage baselines (Table 5), with mMR−2 around 50.8–50.9 (Table 6), indicating strong detection while keeping association competitive.
> 
> - Deep-Sea (hard exploration):
>   - PE-DQN yields substantially lower median episodic regret up to 100×100 (Fig. 4b), with the paper noting “roughly half” the regret vs baselines, and ablations confirming both projection diversity and uncertainty propagation are necessary.
> 
> - VizDoom MyWayHome (visual navigation under sparse reward):
>   - PE-DQN is the only method reaching consistent non-zero returns across all 10 seeds and all difficulty variants (Dense/Sparse/Very Sparse) (Fig. 5), outperforming DQN, DLTV-QR, BDQN+P, and IDS-C51.
> 
> - Sequential MNIST / Adding / Penn Tree Bank (recurrent learning):
>   - DANN and Standard RNN outperform ColEI across tasks (Fig. 2). Spectrum transplantation (Fig. 4) shows replacing ColEI’s initial spectrum improves performance more than removing sign constraints, and Normalized SVD Entropy (H) predicts performance (Fig. 7), especially highlighting ColEI’s sensitivity to small size and low inhibitory fractions (Figs. 5–6).
> 
> - ImageNet (representation bias vs risk control):
>   - JEPA vs MAE: I-JEPA’s learned features align more with the bottom-variance (semantic) subspace across epochs (higher CCA in full-bottom than MAE) and less with top-variance, consistent with JEPA prioritizing influential/low-variance features (Appendix D).
>   - RCPS: Pretrain/learned label policies achieve lower β at the same label budgets while maintaining anytime-valid risk guarantees (safety violation rates ≤α=0.05) (Fig. 3), outperforming ‘all’ and ‘oblivious’ sampling.
> 
> Methodological notes tied to experimental outcomes (from the papers)
> - PBADet: Uses an anchor-free head with a single part-to-body center offset and task-alignment learning; trained with SGD, YOLO-style backbones, and evaluated on COCO-derivatives (AP metrics) and CrowdHuman (MR−2, AP) with notable gains in association metrics (mMR−2) and strong detection MR−2/AP.
> - PE-DQN: Distributional ensembles (quantile+categorial) with disagreement measured by average 1-Wasserstein and epistemic-bonus propagation (Theorem 3). The diversity of projections plus propagated bonus explains the improvements on bsuite Deep-Sea and VizDoom.
> - Dale’s Law RNNs: Performance differences track spectral properties: ColEI’s multimodal spread singular values harm learning; DANN (EI architecture) matches standard RNNs and is robust to EI ratio/network size; normalized SVD entropy is predictive of performance across tasks.
> - JEPA vs MAE: In deep linear settings and with empirical ImageNet results, JEPA prioritizes high-regression-coefficient (informative, low-variance) features; MAE prioritizes high-variance modes. This aligns with faster emergence of semantic feature subspaces under JEPA.
> - RCPS (anytime-valid): E-process–based guarantees control risk at all times; pretrain/learned policies reduce label usage to reach smaller β while keeping safety (≤α) in both simulations and ImageNet.
> 
> Summary of comparative takeaways
> - On identical datasets (ImageNet), JEPA and RCPS both improve their respective objectives: JEPA yields semantic/low-variance-aligned representations more rapidly (CCA trends), while RCPS achieves tighter, safe prediction sets with fewer labels and safety violations below α.
> - On similar types of datasets (vision): PBADet (COCO-family) improves association reliability (lower mMR−2) and detection quality; PE-DQN is the only method reliably solving a pixel-based sparse navigation benchmark across all seeds and difficulty settings.
> - On specific datasets, PBADet sets new state-of-the-art results on BodyHands and strong detection/association trade-offs on COCOHumanParts and CrowdHuman, PE-DQN delivers markedly lower regret and robust success in limited feedback visual RL, DANN/Standard RNNs exceed ColEI in sequential/time-series tasks due to favorable spectra, and RCPS offers practical anytime-valid risk control with superior label efficiency.
> 
> All conclusions above are derived from the tables, figures, and qualitative statements in the provided papers (no external data or invented metrics).

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the context, here are the five papers matching your criteria, with their experimental results compared.
> 
> **(a) PE-DQN — "Projection Ensembles for Deep Q-Learning" (ICLR 2024)**
> Distributional RL with diverse projection ensembles (categorical + quantile); ensemble disagreement (1-Wasserstein) drives an exploration bonus propagated through distributional TD errors.
> - Results: On bsuite, only 4 models roughly halve median episodic regret on deep-sea (up to N=100) versus larger baselines (BDQN+P, IDS, DLTV). In VizDoom MyWayHome (dense→very sparse), only PE-DQN succeeds on all 10 seeds; ablations show diverse projections and TD-based uncertainty propagation are both necessary. Projection choice measurably changes generalization of the 2nd–4th return-distribution moments.
> 
> **(b) "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> Joint-embedding self-distillation (JEPA) implicit bias: deep linear analysis shows JEPA prioritizes high-influence (high-ρ) features, unlike MAE whose ordering depends on eigenvalue λ; depth strengthens noise suppression.
> - Results: On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA embeddings align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features than MAE embeddings (CCA-based analysis of feature embeddings), matching your cosine-similarity/embedding-analysis preference.
> 
> **(c) "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> RNN training dynamics under excitatory/inhibitory partitions (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs), analyzed via singular-value spectra and Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE).
> - Results: ColEI learns worse and with higher variance on all four benchmarks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition). Sign constraints alone explain only part of the gap (0.7%±0.3% for RNNs, 1%±1% for ColEI) versus the full 2.3%±0.6% difference; initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal/dispersed) matters more. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra/performance, while DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron. Gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> 
> **(d) "Active, Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> Anytime-valid risk control (ρ(β̂t) ≤ θ for all t with prob. ≥ 1−α) via e-processes/betting, valid under adaptively collected data, with active labeling policies and learned predictors as control variates.
> - Results: On ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05), learned/pretrained labeling policies reduce risk faster than naive baselines while keeping violation rates below α (95% error bars); regret bounds link policy/predictor error to wealth-process growth.
> 
> **(e) PBADet — "One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association" (ICLR 2024)**
> Anchor-free CNN detector (YOLOv5/v7 backbones) associating parts to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset with task-alignment learning.
> - Results: On BodyHands/COCO-HumanParts it outperforms BPJDet and HierR-CNN; vs. ED-Pose on COCO val, it reports higher all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51; on CrowdHuman face-body it leads in body MR-2 with competitive AP. Ablations show association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task alignment each improve association.
> 
> **Cross-method comparison:** Each paper demonstrates that explicitly encoding an inductive bias (projection diversity, latent-space prediction, E/I spectral structure, anytime-valid betting, part-to-body offsets) improves its target metric — regret/success rate (a), CCA embedding alignment (b), test error correlated with spectral entropy (c), risk-control violation rate and label efficiency (d), and precision/recall/F1/AP (e). All use standard optimizers/backbones (deep Q-learning on bsuite/VizDoom, linear/ImageNet SSL with CCA analysis, RNNs on MNIST/PTB, CNN classifiers on ImageNet, YOLO CNN on COCO-family benchmarks), and all report uncertainty- or structure-aware diagnostics (Wasserstein disagreement, PCA/CCA alignment, SVD entropy, risk bounds, precision/F1) rather than accuracy alone.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Matching papers
> 
> **(a) PE-DQN – "Projection Ensembles for Deep Q-Learning"** (ICLR 2024): distributional projection ensembles (categorical C51 + quantile QR); exploration bonus from ensemble disagreement (average 1-Wasserstein) propagated through distributional TD errors.
> 
> **(b) "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024): analyzes why joint-embedding self-distillation (JEPA) prioritizes high-influence (informative) features over MAE.
> 
> **(c) "Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023): E/I sign-constrained (ColEI) vs Dale's-ANN (DANN) vs standard RNNs; spectral (singular-value) structure, not sign constraints, drives training difficulty.
> 
> **(d) "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"** (NeurIPS 2024): e-process/betting-based anytime-valid risk control under adaptive (active) labeling.
> 
> **(e) PBADet – "One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** (ICLR 2024): single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free YOLOv5/YOLOv7.
> 
> ## Experimental results and comparison
> 
> **Exploration/RL (a).** On the 468-environment bsuite, PE-DQN is strongest in the exploration category and improves other categories too, using only **4 distributional models vs 20 DQN models** for BDQN+P and IDS-C51. On deep sea up to N=100 it roughly **halves median episodic regret** vs baselines; in VizDoom MyWayHome (dense/sparse/very sparse) it is the **only method succeeding on all 10 seeds**. Ablations show both diverse projections and TD-error-based uncertainty propagation are necessary (uniform ensembles PE-DQN[QR/QR], [C51/C51], and independent training [Ind.] degrade). Uses Adam.
> 
> **SSL (b).** Theory (deep linear nets, gradient flow) shows JEPA learns features in order of regression coefficient ρ (influential features), MAE by variance λ; depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression. On ImageNet-1K (ViT at 64×64), **I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE**: full-vs-bottom CCA similarity is higher for JEPA throughout training and reversed for full-vs-top, confirming JEPA prioritizes informative, low-variance features.
> 
> **RNN spectra (c).** ColEI RNNs perform **worse and more variable across all four tasks** (adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition) than standard RNNs and DANN. Sign constraints account for only part of the gap (≈0.7–1% error vs a 2.3±0.6% total difference); **singular-value spectrum matters more** — spectrum transplants show ColEI's multimodal, dispersed spectrum (low normalized SVD entropy) is the main culprit. NSE at initialization **anti-correlates with final error**; small networks with few inhibitory units are worst, while DANN stays robust with even 1 inhibitory neuron. Gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially.
> 
> **Calibration (d).** On simulations and ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05, label budget 0.3), the learned and pretrained active policies **reach lower β̂_t (faster risk reduction) with fewer queried labels** than "all"/"oblivious" baselines, while all methods keep safety-violation rates below α=0.05 (ImageNet β* = 0.8349; simulation β* = 0.5578). Learned/pretrained policies are label-efficient and nearly overlap in performance.
> 
> **Perception (e).** On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M) achieves **HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98**, beating BPJDet(YOLOv5l6, 86.1M) at 85.9/86.91/84.39 with a smaller model; anchor-free part-to-body beats anchor-based body-to-part (Table 8). On COCOHumanParts, APs are on par with BPJDet (42.7/41.5 vs 43.6/43.3 all-category AP) but PBADet **leads AP_M/AP_L and has the lowest mMR−2** for head, face, hands and right foot. On CrowdHuman it achieves the best body MR-2 (36.5) and competitive AP; vs ED-Pose it is substantially higher in precision/recall/F1 (all parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51). Trained with SGD, YOLO backbones, 100 epochs.
> 
> ## Cross-paper analysis
> 
> - **Preference alignment:** (e) uses SGD + YOLO CNN backbones + COCO-family benchmarks; (a) uses Adam + DQN; (b) uses gradient-flow theory validated on ImageNet with ViT and measures feature-embedding alignment via CCA; (c) uses sequential MNIST/PTB and analyzes the singular-value spectrum/embedding structure (NSE); (d) uses pretrained ImageNet classifiers. All report standard metrics (regret, error, AP, F1, violation rate) rather than AUROC.
> - **Common theme — inductive bias & structure:** (a) shows projection choice shapes generalization/uncertainty; (b) shows objective choice (latent vs input space) shapes feature-learning order; (c) shows architectural constraint (E/I partition) shapes spectral structure and hence trainability — all three demonstrate that apparently minor design choices produce large, quantifiable differences in learning dynamics.
> - **Diversity/uncertainty as the recurring lever:** (a) gains come from ensemble diversity (different projections, fewer models); (d) gains come from adaptive labeling policy + risk predictor; (e) gains come from one-to-one part-to-body offset (simpler, always-valid supervision) vs BPJDet's one-to-many offsets.
> - **Best empirical margins:** (e) shows the largest head-to-head gains over prior SOTA (≈+4 AP / +6 conditional accuracy on BodyHands, ≈+17 F1 over ED-Pose); (a) shows clear but more modest gains concentrated on exploration; (b) and (c) are primarily analytic/diagnostic with supporting benchmarks; (d) demonstrates label-efficiency gains with valid risk control.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:269 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an end-to-end system where a robot must read hand/pose cues from cameras, explore a new environment safely, and provide predictions with statistically controlled risk while learning on the fly. I need: a robust anchor-free detector that links body parts to the correct person (COCO-scale images, CNN/Transformer backbones, CE/MSE training with Adam/SGD); an exploration module that uses distributional value functions and ensemble diversity to handle epistemic vs. aleatoric uncertainty; a recurrent controller whose stability benefits from biologically inspired E/I constraints and good spectral properties; a self-supervised pretraining recipe (joint-embedding) that avoids noisy features in learned representations; and an anytime-valid calibration method that guarantees low risk under adaptive labeling. Can you point me to research that ties these pieces together and reports standard metrics like precision/F1 or AUROC on benchmarks (e.g., MNIST/COCO), leveraging feature embeddings and cosine similarity?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
