**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison-and-summary of the experimental results reported across the five papers that match the system you described (anchor‑free part–body detection and association, distributional exploration with ensembles, recurrent control with E/I constraints and spectral guarantees, joint‑embedding self‑supervision, and anytime‑valid risk calibration). I only use quantitative results and qualitative findings explicitly reported in the papers you provided.
> 
> How the five works map to your system
> - Part/pose cues (COCO-scale, anchor-free, CE/MSE, Adam/SGD): PBADet (ICLR 2024) proposes an anchor‑free, one‑stage part‑to‑body association detector; trained with YOLO-style heads and SGD; evaluated on BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman; includes a COCO-based comparison to ED‑Pose with Precision/Recall/F1.
> - Exploration with distributional ensembles (epistemic vs. aleatoric): Diverse Projection Ensembles (ICLR 2024) (PE‑DQN) uses distributional value functions with mixed projections (quantile + categorical) and ensemble disagreement to separate epistemic vs. aleatoric uncertainty; evaluated on the behavior‑suite and VizDoom.
> - Recurrent controller with E/I constraints and spectral stability: Learning better with Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023) (DANN vs. ColEI vs. standard RNNs); tasks include adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task.
> - Self‑supervised joint-embedding pretraining avoiding noisy features: How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024) provides theory + experiments (Imagenet 64×64) showing JEPA prioritizes influential (predictive, low-variance) features vs. MAE.
> - Anytime‑valid calibration under adaptive labeling: Active, anytime-valid RCPS (NeurIPS 2024) produces risk‑controlling prediction sets with label‑efficiency; evaluated on simulations and Imagenet; reports safety violation control at α=0.05 and label‑efficiency vs. baselines.
> 
> Identical and similar datasets across methods
> - COCO/COCO‑HumanParts (identical within PBADet): PBADet reports detailed detection/association performance on COCO‑HumanParts; also compares to a pose estimator (ED‑Pose) on COCO validation with Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet.
> - Imagenet (similar across JEPA and RCPS): both use Imagenet but for different objectives—JEPA assesses representation dynamics via CCA similarity (not classification accuracy), while RCPS evaluates label‑efficiency and safety violation rates for miscoverage control.
> - Sequential MNIST (unique to RNN paper): used to compare recurrent architectures (ColEI vs. DANN vs. standard RNNs) by test error dynamics.
> - Behavior‑suite and VizDoom (unique to distributional RL): used to compare PE‑DQN vs. BDQN+P, IDS‑C51, DLTV‑QR; metrics include episodic regret and return.
> 
> 1) Part/pose: identical datasets (BodyHands, COCO‑HumanParts, CrowdHuman) and COCO‑scale comparisons
> BodyHands (hand–body association; higher is better)
> - PBADet vs. BPJDet (Table 1)
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9; Conditional Accuracy 86.91; Joint AP 84.39.
>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.62; Joint AP 85.98.
>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.71; Joint AP 85.73.
>   Summary: On the same dataset, PBADet improves hand AP (+2.2–3.2), conditional accuracy (+~5.8), and joint AP (+~1.3) over BPJDet (YOLOv5l6).
> 
> COCO‑HumanParts (multi‑part to body; AP higher is better; mMR−2 lower is better)
> - Detection AP, original/subordinate (Table 2):
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.6/43.3; AP.5 70.6/69.8; APM 63.8/63.2; APL 61.8/58.9.
>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7): 42.7/41.5; 69.5/67.9; APM 65.8/64.4; APL 66.7/63.3.
>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv5l6): 43.0/41.8; 70.0/68.4; APM 66.2/65.0; APL 67.2/64.4.
>   Summary: PBADet leads on medium/large (APM/APL) vs. BPJDet, while overall AP.5:.95 is comparable.
> - Per‑category AP (Table 2):
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): person 61.3; head 56.6; face 46.3; r‑hand 40.4; l‑hand 39.6; r‑foot 30.2; l‑foot 30.9.
>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7): person 62.1; head 54.5; face 44.7; r‑hand 38.7; l‑hand 37.5; r‑foot 30.4; l‑foot 30.9.
>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv5l6): person 62.4; head 54.6; face 44.6; r‑hand 39.0; l‑hand 37.7; r‑foot 30.9; l‑foot 31.5.
>   Summary: PBADet improves the person AP (62.1–62.4 vs. 61.3) and feet APs (esp. l‑foot 31.5 vs. 30.9; r‑foot mixed: 30.9 vs. 30.2–30.4), while BPJDet is slightly higher on head/face/hands.
> - Average mMR−2 by part (Table 3; lower is better):
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8; face 31.8; l‑hand 41.6; r‑hand 42.2; r‑foot 49.1; l‑foot 50.4.
>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7): head 29.2; face 31.3; l‑hand 41.1; r‑hand 42.7; r‑foot 52.6; l‑foot 52.5.
>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv5l6): head 27.9; face 30.5; l‑hand 36.2; r‑hand 40.8; r‑foot 50.4; l‑foot 47.9.
>   Summary: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) achieves lower (better) mMR−2 for head, face, both hands, and left foot vs. BPJDet; right foot mMR−2 is mixed (50.4 vs. 49.1).
> 
> CrowdHuman (face–body association; lower MR−2/mMR−2 is better; AP higher is better) (Tables 5 & 6)
> - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7): body MR−2 36.5 (best reported); face MR−2 44.7; body AP 91.6; body‑face mMR−2 50.8.
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR−2 40.7; face MR−2 46.3; body AP 89.5; body‑face mMR−2 50.1.
>   Summary: PBADet improves body MR−2 and face MR−2 and matches strong AP; body‑face mMR−2 is similar (≈50–51) across methods.
> 
> COCO (pose vs. detection F1 on small parts) — PBADet vs. ED‑Pose (Appendix A.2 table)
> - Precision/Recall/F1 (PBADet vs. ED‑Pose, COCO val; hands/feet):
>   - Left hand: P/R/F1 — ED‑Pose 18.36/30.34/22.87 vs. PBADet 37.63/60.82/46.50.
>   - Right hand: 19.57/31.59/24.17 vs. 38.58/61.26/47.34.
>   - Left foot: 29.32/65.28/40.46 vs. 41.56/66.24/51.08.
>   - Right foot: 29.13/65.58/40.34 vs. 40.86/65.55/50.34.
>   - All parts: 24.09/45.51/31.51 vs. 39.41/63.09/48.52.
>   Summary: On identical COCO‑val subsets (for parts defined), PBADet substantially increases F1 over ED‑Pose across hands/feet and overall.
> 
> 2) Exploration with distributional ensembles (similar type: RL benchmarks)
> Behavior‑suite (bsuite) (capabilities; higher is better)
> - Summary radar (Fig. 4a): PE‑DQN improves most in exploration and also raises multiple other capability scores compared to BDQN+P, IDS‑C51, and DLTV‑QR.
> Deep‑sea (hard exploration; episodic regret lower is better)
> - Scaling to N×N up to 100 (Fig. 4b): PE‑DQN reduces median regret roughly by half relative to baselines (BDQN+P, IDS‑C51, DLTV‑QR) with most pronounced gains on larger mazes.
> Ablations (Fig. 4b, right):
> - Diversity (quantile+categorical) and uncertainty propagation both matter: using homogeneous ensembles (QR/QR or C51/C51) or dropping propagation (independent training) degrades exploration (higher regret) relative to full PE‑DQN.
> VizDoom MyWayHome (pixel observations; episodic return higher is better)
> - Dense/Sparse/Very‑Sparse (Fig. 5b): Only PE‑DQN reliably reaches the goal across all seeds and tasks; baselines (DQN, DLTV‑QR, BDQN+P, IDS‑C51) underperform, especially in sparse settings.
> 
> 3) Recurrent controller with E/I constraints (identical/similar datasets within this family)
> Adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition (Fig. 2)
> - Across all four tasks, simple “Column EI” (ColEI) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs; gradient clipping benefits ColEI more, indicating instability.
> Effect of spectral radius ρ (Appendix Fig. 9)
> - Standard/DANN show similar performance vs. ρ; ColEI improves at large ρ but underperforms at small ρ, consistent with differing spectral properties.
> Spectrum vs. sign‑constraints (Fig. 4)
> - Freezing signs or removing sign‑constraints changes test error by ~0.7–1.0%, but transplanting the singular value spectrum shifts test error more (Fig. 4C: changes on the order of ~1.5%±0.3% for RNNs and ~2%±1% for ColEI), indicating spectrum dominates sign constraints in explaining performance gaps.
> EI ratio and network size (Figs. 5–6)
> - Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) increases with more balanced EI and larger networks and anti‑correlates with test error; small networks with balanced EI (high NSE) can outperform larger ones with skewed EI (low NSE).
> Takeaway: For stability/performance, the spectral properties (singular value distribution) are the key driver; DANN RNNs match standard RNNs, while ColEI needs careful spectral control.
> 
> 4) JEPA vs. MAE (Imagenet and synthetic; similar dataset family)
> Gaussian simulations + theory (Figs. 1–2, Theorems):
> - In deep linear encoders, JEPA prioritizes “influential features” (high regression coefficient ρ) as depth grows; MAE prioritizes high covariance λ. This leads to distinct learning orders when λ and ρ conflict.
> Imagenet 64×64 (Appendix D; Fig. 7)
> - Feature similarity (CCA) dynamics:
>   - Full vs. Bottom‑variance subspace: I‑JEPA shows higher CCA than MAE through training (better alignment with low‑variance, semantic features).
>   - Full vs. Top‑variance subspace: I‑JEPA shows lower CCA than MAE (avoids high‑variance, fine‑grained/pixel features), consistent with avoiding noisy features.
> 
> 5) Anytime‑valid RCPS (identical dataset within this paper; similar dataset to JEPA)
> Simulations (Fig. 2)
> - Label policies “pretrain” and “learned” reach lower β̂ (closer to optimal β*) with fewer labels compared to “all” and “oblivious” strategies, while maintaining safety violation rates ≤ α=0.05.
> Imagenet (Fig. 3)
> - Same ranking: “pretrain” and “learned” policies use fewer labels to reach a smaller β̂ than “all”/“oblivious”; safety violation rate remains controlled (below 0.05).
> Takeaway: Under adaptive labeling, the anytime‑valid e‑process RCPS maintains risk control and improves label‑efficiency by leveraging predictors/labeling policies.
> 
> Cross‑component takeaways for your integrated system
> - Anchor‑free detector for part–body association (COCO scale): PBADet improves Hand AP/Joint AP/Conditional Accuracy on BodyHands; on COCO‑HumanParts it lifts medium/large AP and person/feet APs and improves head/face/hand mMR−2 (with mixed feet), and it substantially outperforms a pose‑based approach (ED‑Pose) on COCO parts F1. Training uses YOLO‑style CNN heads with SGD (matching your requested setup).
> - Distributional exploration separating epistemic vs. aleatoric: PE‑DQN (quantile+categorical projections) uses ensemble disagreement (1‑Wasserstein) with a propagation scheme to guide optimism, yielding best exploration on bsuite (esp. deep‑sea) and reliable success on VizDoom under sparse rewards.
> - Recurrent controller stability with E/I constraints: DANN RNNs (EI‑respecting) match standard RNNs; simple EI column constraints (ColEI) underperform unless spectral properties are controlled. NSE predicts performance; spectrum dominates sign‑constraints in determining learning.
> - Self‑supervised pretraining to avoid noisy features: JEPA’s implicit bias favors predictive, low‑variance (semantic) features; on Imagenet, JEPA aligns more with bottom‑variance subspace than MAE throughout training, and less with top‑variance (pixel‑level) features.
> - Anytime‑valid calibration under adaptive labeling: Active RCPS controls miscoverage with α=0.05 at all times and uses predictors/label policies to reduce labels vs. naïve baselines, both in simulations and on Imagenet.
> 
> Notes on metrics and datasets
> - Identical datasets: COCO/COCO‑HumanParts (within PBADet) and the COCO‑val parts comparison vs. ED‑Pose; Imagenet (used by JEPA and RCPS but for different objectives/metrics).
> - Standard metrics reported: Precision/Recall/F1 on COCO parts (PBADet vs. ED‑Pose); AP/AP.5:.95/APM/APL and mMR−2 (COCO‑HumanParts); MR−2/AP/mMR−2 (CrowdHuman); error/test error (RNNs on adding/sequential MNIST/PTB/NOR); CCA (JEPA/MAE on Imagenet); safety violation rate and β̂ progression (RCPS); episodic regret/return (distributional RL on bsuite/VizDoom).
> 
> Overall: The five works provide complementary, benchmark‑validated pieces for your system. PBADet supplies robust anchor‑free part–body association on COCO‑scale images; PE‑DQN supplies distributional exploration with ensemble diversity distinguishing epistemic from aleatoric uncertainty; DANN‑style EI RNNs deliver stable recurrent control with favorable spectra; JEPA pretraining avoids noisy features and emphasizes semantically predictive components; and active, anytime‑valid RCPS offers statistically controlled risk under adaptive labeling with strong label‑efficiency.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## The five research pieces (one per module)
> 
> **1. Anchor-free detector — PBADet** (`08b70bc3…`): One-stage anchor-free part-body association via a single part-to-body center offset, with classification/localization/association branches on YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones. No single paper ties the whole stack together; these five each address one module.
> 
> **2. Exploration — Projection Ensembles for Deep Q-Learning (PE-DQN)** (`5ebc98c7…`): Ensemble of distributional projections (quantile + categorical); 1-Wasserstein ensemble disagreement propagated through distributional TD errors as an optimism/exploration bonus.
> 
> **3. Recurrent E/I controller — "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (`e63a94c4…`): Compares sign-constrained ColEI, DANN, and standard RNNs; shows the learning deficit is driven by the initial singular-value spectrum (measured by Normalised SVD Entropy, NSE), not sign constraints per se.
> 
> **4. Joint-embedding pretraining — JEPA self-distillation analysis** (`40fde037…`): Shows JEPA suppresses noisy features by biasing toward high-ρ "influential" features, with depth strengthening noise suppression (vs. MAE's eigenvalue-driven ordering). **LDReg** (`51526068…`) is the complementary regularization recipe against local dimensional collapse.
> 
> **5. Anytime-valid calibration — Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets** (`cda0aa75…`): Extends RCPS to sequential/adaptive data with a simultaneous anytime-valid risk guarantee via e-processes/betting and active labeling (IPW, conditional-risk control variates).
> 
> ## Comparison & analysis of experimental results
> 
> **Detector (COCO-scale).** On COCO-HumanParts, PBADet's AP is on par with BPJDet but leads in AP_M/AP_L and person/feet metrics, with the lowest average mMR⁻². Against the pose estimator ED-Pose (COCO val), PBADet roughly doubles hand precision (37.63 vs 18.36) and all-parts F1 (48.52 vs 31.51; precision 39.41 vs 24.09, recall 63.09 vs 45.51). On CrowdHuman face-body association it achieves leading body MR-2 but only competitive AP — its advantage over BPJDet shrinks for the single-part task. Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment all individually boost hand accuracy and joint AP. The formulation extends to AnimalPose/AP-10K quadruped parts.
> 
> **Exploration (bsuite/VizDoom).** PE-DQN attains the best exploration with only 4 distributional models, roughly halving median episodic regret on deep sea (up to N=100) relative to larger baselines (BDQN+P, IDS, DLTV). Ablations show both diverse projections *and* TD-based uncertainty propagation are necessary. On VizDoom MyWayHome, only PE-DQN solves all 10 seeds. Notably, the projection choice shapes generalization (the 2nd–4th moments behave differently for categorical vs quantile).
> 
> **Recurrent controller (MNIST + others).** ColEI RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard/DANN RNNs across all four tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition); gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially more. Sign constraints alone only account for ~0.7–1% error; the full ColEI deficit (~2.3±0.6% on sequential MNIST) is explained by the multimodal, dispersed initial singular spectrum (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure). Smaller networks and higher E:I ratios worsen the spectrum and learning; DANN remains robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron, and NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error (predicting performance before training).
> 
> **SSL pretraining (ImageNet/COCO + CIFAR).** The JEPA analysis (theory on deep linear nets + ImageNet-1K) shows I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features than MAE features (CCA), i.e., less noisy-feature contamination. LDReg empirically improves linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO object detection/instance segmentation for SimCLR, SimCLR-Tuned, BYOL, and MAE (also MoCo, VICReg, Barlow Twins) on ResNet-50 and ViT-B, with larger gains from longer pretraining; forcing very low local intrinsic dimensionality triggers full collapse.
> 
> **Calibration (ImageNet/simulations).** At θ=0.1, α=0.05, learned/pretrained label policies and risk predictors reduce risk faster and reach higher utility with fewer labels than naive baselines (all/oblivious), while keeping the average safety-violation rate below α. Regret bounds tie labeling-policy/predictor estimation error to the wealth-process growth rate; limitations are the i.i.d. assumption and bounded label-policy assumption.
> 
> ## Notes on metrics requested
> 
> - **Precision/Recall/F1**: only the detector reports these (PBADet vs ED-Pose); no other module uses them.
> - **MNIST**: only the E/I RNN paper reports MNIST (sequential-MNIST error rates); it does not report precision/F1/AUROC.
> - **AUROC**: none of the five methods report AUROC. AUROC appears in the corpus only in an unrelated tabular synthetic-data benchmark (Synthcity), so an AUROC comparison cannot be assembled from this collection.
> - **Cosine similarity / embeddings**: the contrastive-learning theory paper (`160e1407…`) analyzes embedding cosine similarity (positive-pair alignment, negative-pair separation, mini-batch variance) and reports top-1 accuracy gains on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and full ImageNet; the JEPA paper uses CCA on embeddings rather than cosine. So the cosine-similarity thread connects to SSL pretraining, not to the detector or calibration stack.
> 
> In sum, the collection supplies a paper per required component with benchmarks (COCO-HumanParts/COCO val, CrowdHuman, bsuite, VizDoom, sequential MNIST/PTB/object recognition, ImageNet-1K/COCO, CIFAR), but no single work integrates all five modules, and AUROC/precision-F1 are reported only within individual (mostly detector) evaluations rather than across the full system.

**community 最终答案**

> No single paper in this collection ties all five pieces into one end-to-end system, but each requested component maps to a specific paper whose experiments can be compared:
> 
> **1. Anchor-free part/body detector — PBADet (ICLR 2024)**
> - One-stage anchor-free detector (YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7 backbones, per-pixel dense prediction) adding a single part-to-body center offset; trained with IoU + DFL + classification (CE-type) + association (L1/MSE-type) losses under task alignment, SGD optimizer, COCO-scale images. It also compares against the Transformer-based (Swin-L) pose estimator ED-Pose.
> - BodyHands: PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) → HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98, beating BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 86.1M): 85.9/86.91/84.39 and BodyHands (700.3M): 84.8/84.12/63.87.
> - COCOHumanParts: PBADet ~on par with BPJDet on AP.5:.95 (42.7–43.0 vs 43.6) but leads on AP_M/AP_L and per-part association (lowest mMR−2 for hands/feet).
> - CrowdHuman (face-body): best body MR−2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6); advantage over BPJDet shrinks for the single-part task.
> - vs ED-Pose (all parts, Precision/Recall/F1): ED-Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51 vs PBADet 39.41/63.09/48.52 — roughly double precision/F1, driven by the four small parts (hands/feet).
> 
> **2. Exploration with distributional value functions + ensemble diversity — PE-DQN (ICLR 2024)**
> - Ensembles quantile (QR-DQN) and categorical (C51) projection value functions; ensemble disagreement (1-Wasserstein) propagated through distributional TD errors as an epistemic-uncertainty bonus (aleatoric noise handled by the distribution itself).
> - bsuite (468 envs): strongest in the exploration category with only 4 distributional models vs 20+ for BDQN+P/IDS. Deep-sea up to N=100: median episodic regret roughly halved vs baselines; ablations show diverse projections AND TD-based propagation are both necessary.
> - VizDoom MyWayHome (dense→very sparse): only PE-DQN solves all 10 seeds across all sparsity levels.
> 
> **3. Recurrent controller with E/I constraints + spectral stability — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - On adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition: simple column-partitioned E/I RNNs (ColEI) learn worse and with more variance than standard RNNs and DANN (recurrent Dale's ANNs); gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> - Spectrum-transplant experiments: singular-value distribution at initialization matters more than sign constraints (sign constraints account for only ~1% of the ~2.3% gap on sequential MNIST); normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance before training — i.e., the recipe for a stable EI recurrent controller is DANN-style reparameterization (unimodal, clustered spectrum) rather than naive column sign constraints.
> 
> **4. Self-supervised joint-embedding pretraining avoiding noisy features**
> - "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024): JEPA self-distillation implicitly prioritizes high-influence (high ρ) features and suppresses noisy directions, increasingly with depth (fixed-point w̄ = ρ^L); MAE orders features by variance λ. ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE.
> - LDReg (ICLR 2024): regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality (Fisher-Rao metric) to prevent local dimensional collapse; improves linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR, SimCLR-Tuned, BYOL, MAE (and MoCo/VICReg/Barlow Twins) on ImageNet with ResNet-50/ViT-B.
> - "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (ICML 2025): uses cosine similarity as the lens — full-batch InfoNCE optimum = positive similarity 1, negative −1/(n−1); mini-batches inflate negative-pair similarity variance, degrading representations; an auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, and full ImageNet (SGD, 200 epochs).
> 
> **5. Anytime-valid calibration under adaptive labeling — "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Extends risk-controlling prediction sets (RCPS) to sequential/adaptive data: e-process + betting gives P(ρ(β̂_t) ≤ θ for all t) ≥ 1−α; supports active label policies (IPW, lower-bounded query probability) and ML control variates. On ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05): learned/pretrained labeling policies cut risk faster than naive baselines while keeping violation rates below α.
> 
> **Analysis / cross-cutting observations**
> - The collection does not contain a paper that combines all modules or reports AUROC; standard metrics across these works are AP/F1 (COCO/BodyHands/CrowdHuman), episodic regret/exploration capability (bsuite/VizDoom), test error + NSE (MNIST/PTB), top-1 accuracy + CCA (ImageNet/CIFAR), and risk-violation rate (ImageNet). Embeddings and cosine similarity appear explicitly in the contrastive-learning paper (and CLIP-based works), not in the detector/RL papers.
> - The clearest "ties": PBADet's per-part F1 results are the only F1-style metrics on COCO-scale benchmarks; PE-DQN's learned uncertainty bonus is the natural interface to the anytime-valid risk-control layer (both operate online/adaptive); LDReg explicitly reports gains on COCO detection, connecting the SSL representation quality directly to the detector's downstream task; the Dale's-law work provides the diagnostic (NSE) to predict recurrent-controller stability before deployment.
> - If your goal is an end-to-end claim, it cannot be established from this collection: the pieces are individually validated on disjoint benchmarks, with no shared evaluation (no single precision/F1 or AUROC run across all components, and no evidence they compose).

### paperscope:results_comparison:272 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (1) one-stage, anchor-free perception methods that link body parts to their parent instance; (2) spectral perspectives on recurrent networks with excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints (Dale’s Law) and how such spectra influence learning dynamics under SGD/AdamW; (3) analyses of joint-embedding self-supervised objectives versus pixel reconstruction (e.g., explaining when representation learning avoids noisy features in deep networks); (4) memory-frugal training via ~4-bit optimizer states for AdamW/SGD to enable fine-tuning on image benchmarks like MNIST/CIFAR-100 and attention/Transformer backbones; and (5) discovering general reinforcement learning updates via adversarial/teacher-designed curricula. Please emphasize generalization, interpretability, attention mechanisms, and practical online implementation.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, here are the five papers and what their experiments show.
> 
> ## The five papers
> 
> **1. PBADet — One-stage anchor-free part-body association** (doc `08b70bc3…`)
> Introduces a single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free YOLO-style detectors (YOLOv5/v7), guaranteeing one-to-one part↔body correspondence. Results: on BodyHands, anchor-free part-to-body (Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98) beats anchor-based body-to-part BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13); ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and TOOD-style task-alignment each improve association. It generalizes to quadruped (AnimalPose, AP-10K) and CrowdHuman face-body. Practical upside: single-stage efficiency, no per-part anchors, simple post-processing.
> 
> **2. "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (doc `e63a94c4…`)
> ColEI RNNs (sign-constrained columns) learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps them most. Using SVD transplants, the authors show the *initial singular-value spectrum* (multimodal/dispersed, from a rank-one column-mean nilpotent structure), not the sign constraints or singular vectors, drives poor learning. Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; balanced E/I ratios and larger networks improve spectra and learning. Note: training is projected gradient descent (SGD-style); the retrieved text does **not** contain AdamW experiments for this setting — that link is not established in the context.
> 
> **3. "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc `40fde037…`)
> Deep-linear analysis of JEPA self-distillation vs MAE pixel reconstruction. Critical-time theorems show MAE orders feature learning mainly by covariance λ (so it can learn high-variance noisy features), while JEPA's next-to-leading order depends on the regression coefficient ρ, biasing it to "influential" (high-ρ) features — a bias that grows with encoder depth. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace (CCA) than MAE features. This explains when joint-embedding objectives generalize better than reconstruction for perception.
> 
> **4. "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (doc `8d5e1455…`)
> Compresses Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit (B128/DE for first moment; rank-1 normalization and zero-point-excluding linear mapping or factorization for second moment). Across GLUE (RoBERTa-L), SQuAD, E2E-NLG (GPT-2M), WMT14 (Transformer), ImageNet (Swin-T, an attention backbone), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning, 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor match or slightly exceed 32-bit AdamW while cutting memory up to 57.7% and enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU (4× larger OPT under budget). Caveats vs. the question: the vision benchmark is ImageNet with Swin-T, **not** MNIST/CIFAR-100; SGD appears via the quantized-SGD(M) convergence proof, while empirical results are AdamW-based. (MNIST/CIFAR-100 + SGD/Adam + ViT fine-tuning appear in a different retrieved doc, the power-law Hessian-spectrum paper `582d138d…`, which uses LeNet on MNIST/CIFAR-100 and ViT-B on CIFAR-100.)
> 
> **5. GROOVE — Discovering general RL updates via adversarial environment design** (doc `319440a3…`)
> Extends unsupervised environment design to policy meta-optimization (PMO): meta-learned RL update rules are trained on curricula maximizing a new "algorithmic regret" (AR) metric, with PLR-style level curation instead of a generative teacher. Meta-trained on Grid-Worlds, GROOVE gives superior out-of-distribution generalization vs. LPG, especially on Atari/Min-Atar/Procgen, and AR outperforms prior UED metrics and handcrafted curricula. Practical online implementation: a JAX implementation cuts meta-training from ~24h on TPU-v2 to ~3h on one V100 GPU.
> 
> ## Cross-paper comparison
> 
> - **Generalization**: GROOVE explicitly optimizes OOD generalization (AR-driven curricula beat LPG on unseen Atari); PBADet shows cross-dataset/cross-species transfer; the JEPA analysis gives a mechanistic explanation (high-ρ features, depth-dependent) for why joint-embedding generalizes better than reconstruction; NSE predicts EI-RNN test error before training; 4-bit optimizers retain full-precision accuracy across tasks, so generalization is not sacrificed.
> - **Interpretability**: PBADet's single explicit part-to-body offset is inherently interpretable; NSE is a pre-training diagnostic; JEPA's "influential feature" ordering makes the learned representation explainable; AR gives an interpretable curriculum signal; the 4-bit work interprets moment outlier patterns to design quantizers.
> - **Attention/transformers**: 4-bit optimizers are validated on Swin-T and Transformer/LLaMA backbones; JEPA analysis applies to I-JEPA (ViT-based) though the theory is linear; PBADet uses task-alignment (not attention); GROOVE and the Dale's paper do not involve attention.
> - **Practical online implementation**: PBADet is single-stage and fast; 4-bit states enable online fine-tuning with FSDP and reduced communication; GROOVE's JAX version enables affordable meta-training; NSE can be computed at initialization as a cheap go/no-go check; JEPA results are design guidance (depth amplifies noise rejection) rather than an implementation.
> 
> **Honest gaps**: no retrieved paper jointly covers Dale's-law spectra *and* AdamW dynamics; the 4-bit paper's image benchmarks are ImageNet/Swin-T rather than MNIST/CIFAR-100; and GROOVE's "teacher" is a regret-based curator rather than a learned adversarial generator, though it is motivated by adversarial environment design.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers covering each requested theme, with a comparative analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## (1) One-stage anchor-free part–body association
> **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — Adds a single part-to-body center offset onto one-stage anchor-free detectors (YOLOv5/YOLOv7), with three branches (box, class, association) and TOOD-style task-alignment loss. Results: on BodyHands, HandAP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98, beating BPJDet (85.3/86.8/78.13) and HierR-CNN; on COCOHumanParts, 43.0/41.8 AP (YOLOv5l6) and 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) vs ~30–32 for prior SOTA; on CrowdHuman face–body, lower body MR−2 (36.5 vs 39.7–41.3). Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment each improve metrics; anchor-free + part-to-body definition outperforms anchor-based + body-to-part. The design is attention-free but simple to deploy (single offset, one-to-one correspondence, simpler post-processing).
> 
> ## (2) Spectral perspective on Dale's-law RNNs
> **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023)** — Shows the poor learning of sign-constrained (E/I) RNNs is due to the **initial singular-value spectrum**, not the sign constraints. ColEI networks have multimodal, dispersed spectra (from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean term), whereas standard RNNs and recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) match the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle. Spectrum "transplant" experiments: spectra contribute more (1.5–2% error) than sign constraints (0.7–1%) or singular vectors; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error across EI ratio and size, and predicts performance pre-training. ColEI also shows higher variance, more instability without gradient clipping, and worse performance with fewer inhibitory units; DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron. Tasks: adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition. Note: this is gradient-descent based learning; the related **Hessian power-law paper (ICML 2025)** further shows spectra influence learning under **SGD vs Adam** (power-law slope correlates with generalization across both optimizers).
> 
> ## (3) Joint-embedding SSL vs pixel reconstruction
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** — Analytically solves deep linear JEPA vs MAE dynamics. JEPA prioritizes **high-influence features** (large regression coefficient ρ), while MAE prioritizes high-covariance features even if noisy; this bias holds only for deep encoders. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA-based). Practical implication: JEPA-style objectives avoid noisy features and learn semantic features more efficiently — supporting the user's generalization/interpretability emphasis. Related: **LDReg (ICLR 2024)** shows SSL representations can still collapse locally, and regularizing local intrinsic dimensionality improves ImageNet linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO detection for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE.
> 
> ## (4) Memory-frugal 4-bit optimizer states
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)** — Pushes optimizer-state bitwidth from 8 to 4 bits via small block size (B128) for the first moment and rank-1/linear zero-point-excluded quantization for the second moment, with optional factorization. Results: 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (89.1), SQuAD (94.5), E2E-NLG (67.8), ImageNet with **Swin-T transformer** (80.8 vs 81.2), WMT14, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning, saving up to 57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU) and speeding up FSDP-sharded training. Framework supports SGDM/Adam/AdamW (stateless SGD included). Caveats: the exact MNIST/CIFAR-100 and ViT fine-tuning settings with these 4-bit states are not in this paper — MNIST/CIFAR-100 and ViT fine-tuning with SGD/AdamW appear in the Hessian paper's experimental protocol (LeNet/FCN/ResNet18/ViT-Base on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, Fashion-MNIST), which is a spectral-analysis study rather than a memory-compression method.
> 
> ## (5) Discovering general RL updates via adversarial/teacher curricula
> **GROOVE (ICLR 2024)** — Applies Unsupervised Environment Design to policy meta-optimization, meta-learning update rules (building on LPG) with a PLR-style level curator and a new **algorithmic regret (AR)** metric co-trained against an antagonist. Results: on unseen Grid-Worlds, GROOVE has higher mean performance and robustness (LPG fails to exceed 75% A2C-normalized return on 187% more tasks); on Atari, GROOVE wins 39 vs 17 tasks over LPG with better IQM and optimality gap; high-AR static curricula beat random and handcrafted curricula at all sizes (5 handcrafted levels beat 2⁶=64 random levels; r=0.86 correlation with Min-Atar performance); AR is the only UED metric that consistently improves OOD generalization vs L1/positive value loss/uniform scoring. Fast JAX implementation cuts meta-training from ~24h (TPU-v2) to ~3h (single V100) — relevant to practical online implementation.
> 
> ## Cross-paper comparative takeaways
> - **Generalization**: GROOVE (RL OOD generalization via curriculum), JEPA (feature-prioritization for generalization), and the Hessian power-law work (spectral slope as generalization predictor) all show generalization benefits; PBADet shows robustness gains from task-aligned, multi-scale association.
> - **Interpretability/attention**: the Dale's-law paper offers an interpretable diagnostic (NSE spectrum pathology); the Hessian paper links power-law spectra to robust low-dimensional learning subspace; PBADet uses task-alignment rather than attention; the 4-bit optimizer targets Transformer/attention backbones (Swin-T, GPT-2, LLaMA) with no accuracy loss.
> - **Practical online implementation**: 4-bit optimizers give near-lossless training at large memory savings (with fused-operator speed caveat); GROOVE's fast JAX implementation enables practical meta-training; PBADet's single-offset design simplifies post-processing; Dale's-law NSE can predict performance before training.
> 
> Limitation: no single document covers 4-bit optimizer states on MNIST/CIFAR-100 with attention backbones explicitly — the two relevant papers cover complementary parts (4-bit states on ImageNet/Transformer/LLMs; MNIST/CIFAR-100/ViT only under full-precision SGD/AdamW in the Hessian study).

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:275 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource-constrained vision-and-control stack: we need an anchor-free approach to reliably associate hands, faces, and feet with the correct person; training must fit tight GPU memory budgets (preferably 4‑bit optimizer states with AdamW) for quick fine‑tuning on small datasets (e.g., MNIST/SVHN, CIFAR‑100) and Transformer/attention backbones; our SSL pipeline should favor joint-embedding objectives that avoid overfitting to pixel noise; our control module explores biologically motivated E/I constraints in recurrent nets for stability and interpretability; and our policy learning should benefit from adversarial environment design to discover RL algorithms that transfer. Are there works that address these combined needs across self-supervised learning, optimizer efficiency, spectral properties with Dale’s Law, anchor-free part–body detection, and adversarial curriculum design for RL?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Below is a consolidated, dataset-grounded comparison of experimental results from five works aligned with your stack: anchor-free part–body detection (PBADet), spectral EI RNN design (Dale’s ANNs vs ColEI vs standard RNNs), self-supervised joint-embedding objectives (JEPA vs MAE), memory-efficient training (4‑bit AdamW), and adversarial environment design for RL (GROOVE vs LPG). The comparisons use identical datasets where available, and otherwise group similar dataset types.\n\n1) Anchor-free part–body detection (PBADet) vs prior detectors on identical datasets\n- BodyHands (hand–body association; identical dataset across methods):\n  • Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7, 1024 px input): Hand AP 89.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.62; Joint AP 85.98.\n  • Ours (PBADet, YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.71; Joint AP 85.73.\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 1536 px): Hand AP 85.9; Conditional Accuracy 86.91; Joint AP 84.39.\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5m6/YOLOv5s6) perform lower than PBADet across these metrics. Thus, PBADet outperforms BPJDet and earlier baselines on BodyHands across all reported metrics.\n- COCOHumanParts (multi-part association; identical dataset across methods): All-categories AP (original/subordinate)\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.6/43.3; AP.5 70.6/69.8; APM 63.8/63.2; APL 61.8/58.9.\n  • Ours (PBADet, YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8; AP.5 70.0/68.4; APM 66.2/65.0; APL 67.2/64.4.\n  • Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7): AP.5:.95 42.7/41.5; AP.5 69.5/67.9; APM 65.8/64.4; APL 66.7/63.3.\n  Interpretation: While BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) has slightly higher aggregate AP.5:.95 and AP.5, PBADet (both backbones) leads on medium/large object AP (APM/APL) and category breakdown (person/feet). Association robustness (average mMR−2) across categories:\n  • PBADet (YOLOv7): head 29.2; face 31.3; l-hand 41.1; r-hand 42.7; r-foot 52.6; l-foot 52.5 (lowest or competitive vs BPJDet variants).\n  • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): head 27.9; face 30.5; l-hand 36.2; r-hand 40.8; r-foot 50.4; l-foot 47.9.\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8; face 31.8; l-hand 41.6; r-hand 42.2; r-foot 49.1; l-foot 50.4.\n  Thus, PBADet improves association mismatch rates notably for head/face and is competitive on hands/feet.\n- CrowdHuman (face–body association; identical dataset across methods):\n  • Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7): MR−2 body 36.5 (best); MR−2 face 44.7; body AP 91.6 (best); body–face mMR−2 50.8.\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 body 40.7; MR−2 face 46.3; body AP 89.5; mMR−2 50.1.\n  PBADet yields stronger detection metrics (MR−2 and body AP) with similar association mMR−2.\n\n2) Spectral EI recurrent networks: DANN vs ColEI vs standard RNN (identical task suites)\n- Tasks: Adding problem (length 20), Sequential MNIST (3 layers of 100 neurons), Penn Tree Bank language modeling (3 layers of 500 neurons), and a Naturalistic Object Recognition task.\n- Across all tasks, ColEI (column-wise sign-constrained EI) learns worse and shows higher variance than DANN and standard RNNs. Gradient clipping helps ColEI more substantially.\n- Spectrum transplant experiments (Sequential MNIST): Changing spectra contributes more to final test error gap than sign constraints (RNN: +1.5% ± 0.3%; ColEI: +2% ± 1%), i.e., spectral properties at initialization are the dominant factor.\n- Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE) predicts performance: lower NSE (more dispersed, multimodal singular values) correlates with worse test error. ColEI performance degrades with fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks; DANN and standard RNNs maintain high NSE (~0.95) and robust performance even with few I units.\n- Conclusion: For identical datasets, DANN and standard RNNs consistently outperform ColEI; spectrum (unimodal, clustered singular values) matters more than sign constraints.\n\n3) Self-supervised JEPA vs MAE (similar type, and identical image setting in one experiment)\n- Deep linear analyses (synthetic data):\n  • JEPA exhibits greedy learning by regression coefficient (ρ), prioritizing high-influence features; MAE prioritizes covariance (λ). When λ increases but ρ decreases (Distribution 2 in Fig. 1), JEPA reverses feature learning order relative to MAE.\n  • Derived critical times: JEPA’s feature learning times strongly depend on ρ and depth L; MAE depends primarily on λ (leading order). Thus, JEPA avoids overfitting to noisy/high-variance features by biasing toward predictive, lower-variance features.\n- Linear generative temporal model (synthetic videos): JEPA learns noisy features more slowly and converges with lower amplitude weights than MAE (consistent with preferring predictive over noisy features).\n- ImageNet-64×64 feature similarity (identical dataset and training protocol for I-JEPA vs MAE): I-JEPA’s representations show higher mean CCA between full and bottom-PCA-subspace images and lower CCA for full vs top-subspace than MAE over training, indicating JEPA learns perceptual/semantic (low-variance) features faster than MAE.\n\n4) Memory-efficient training: 4‑bit AdamW (identical downstream datasets across optimizers)\n- GLUE (RoBERTa-L, mean metric):\n  • 32-bit AdamW: 88.9.\n  • 8-bit AdamW†: 89.1.\n  • 4-bit AdamW (ours): 89.1.\n  • 4-bit Factor (ours): 88.9.\n  Comparable to full precision; 4-bit matches 8-bit and 32-bit.\n- SQuAD/SQuAD2.0 (RoBERTa-L; EM/F1): 32-bit vs 4-bit AdamW nearly identical (e.g., SQuAD F1: 94.6 vs 94.5; SQuAD2.0 F1: 88.8 vs 88.4).\n- Image classification (Swin-T on ImageNet-1k Top-1 Acc):\n  • 32-bit AdamW: 81.2.\n  • 8-bit AdamW†: 81.0.\n  • 4-bit AdamW: 80.8.\n  • 4-bit Factor: 80.9.\n  Slight drop (≤0.4 pp) vs 32-bit; close to 8-bit.\n- NLG (GPT-2 Medium, E2E-NLG BLEU): 32-bit 67.7 vs 4-bit AdamW 67.8; 4-bit Factor 67.6; matching or slightly better than full precision.\n- Machine Translation (Transformer-Base, WMT14 en-de SacreBLEU): 32-bit 26.61 vs 4-bit AdamW 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45; small degradation.\n- Instruction tuning (LLaMA-7B/13B/33B; identical evaluation tasks): 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit AdamW across MMLU and commonsense benchmarks; e.g., LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 (4-bit) vs 46.5 (32-bit), ARC-c 48.0 vs 48.3.\n- Memory and speed (identical training setups):\n  • LLaMA-7B: total GPU memory 75.4 GB (32-bit) vs 31.87 GB (4-bit) → 57.7% saved; training time 3.35 h (32-bit) vs 3.07 h (4-bit). Fused 4-bit stays ~3.11 h.\n  • RoBERTa-L: total memory 5.31 GB (32-bit) vs 3.00–3.02 GB (4-bit) → 43–44% saved; fused 4-bit time 3.17 min vs 3.38 min (8-bit) and 3.93 min (32-bit).\n  • GPT-2 Medium: total memory 6.89 GB (32-bit) vs 4.62 GB (4-bit) → 34% saved; fused 4-bit time 2.11 h ~ equal/slightly faster than 32-bit.\n- Ablations on identical E2E-NLG task: solving second-moment zero-point problem is critical—Rank‑1 + Linear mapping (4-bit) achieves BLEU 67.8 ± 0.51; removing zero in DE (DE‑0) stabilizes training; stochastic rounding alone insufficient.\n\n5) Adversarial environment design: GROOVE vs LPG (identical meta-training distribution and identical test suites)\n- In-distribution Grid-World (unseen levels): GROOVE’s score distribution dominates LPG on the lower-scoring half of tasks (more robust), with comparable performance on easy tasks.\n- Atari (aggregate metrics): GROOVE significantly improves IQM and reduces optimality gap vs LPG; per-task, GROOVE achieves higher mean score on 39 games vs 17 for LPG (1 tie), indicating broad transfer gains.\n- Min-Atar: AR-based level selection yields better generalization than random or handcrafted curricula across set sizes (e.g., positive performance gains at 2^2–2^6 levels), validating AR as a superior regret proxy for PMO.\n- Regret metrics (identical Min-Atar tasks): AR outperforms L1 value loss, positive value loss, and even optimal-policy regret (which can overemphasize artificially hard levels); antagonists: A2C/PPO antagonists outperform random/expert antagonists, with A2C best overall.\n\nSummary by identical datasets\n- BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman: PBADet consistently improves detection and association robustness over BPJDet on BodyHands and CrowdHuman; on COCOHumanParts, PBADet is competitive on overall AP and leads on APM/APL and several per-category metrics.\n- Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic Object Recognition: DANN and standard RNNs outperform ColEI on all; spectrum (NSE) more predictive than sign constraints.\n- ImageNet-64×64: JEPA yields higher CCA similarity to bottom-variance subspace and lower similarity to top-variance subspace vs MAE, consistent with learning semantic features and avoiding noisy pixel detail.\n- GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet-1k, E2E-NLG, WMT14, LLaMA instruction-tuning: 4‑bit AdamW matches or nearly matches 32‑bit/8‑bit baselines; delivers substantial memory saves and comparable/occasionally faster training.\n- Atari and Min-Atar: GROOVE (with AR) generalizes better than LPG across broad suites; on Atari, GROOVE wins most games; on Min-Atar, AR-based curation consistently outperforms random and handcrafted.\n\nBy dataset type\n- Detection/association (crowded, multi-part human): Anchor-free PBADet improves robustness and reduces mismatches without increasing representation size; best MR−2 and AP on CrowdHuman body/face.\n- Vision SSL: JEPA is empirically biased toward predictive, low-variance features (temporal/Imagenet analyses), supporting stable joint embeddings under noise.\n- Sequence/classification (MNIST/PTB): Spectral EI design (DANN) yields unimodal clustered spectra and strong learning; ColEI’s multimodal dispersed spectra hurt both stability and performance.\n- Language/vision fine-tuning: 4‑bit AdamW achieves near-parity with full precision across GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet, NLG, MT; largest memory/time gains on large models (LLaMA-7B).\n- RL algorithm discovery: GROOVE’s adversarial curricula (via AR) enhance OOD generalization from simple Grid-World meta-training to Atari/Min-Atar, outperforming LPG.\n\nOverall implications for the integrated stack\n- Anchor-free PBADet provides efficient, one-stage part–body association with improved robustness (BodyHands, CrowdHuman) and competitive multi-part performance (COCOHumanParts).\n- 4‑bit AdamW fine-tuning is validated across NLP/CV tasks with sizable memory savings and minimal accuracy loss, suitable for resource-constrained deployment.\n- JEPA’s implicit bias toward influential, low-variance features supports stable SSL under pixel noise, consistent with your joint-embedding objective requirements.\n- EI RNNs respecting Dale’s Law can learn well when spectral properties are controlled (DANN-like architectures); spectra are more consequential than sign constraints for stability and performance (MNIST/PTB/object recognition).\n- GROOVE’s AR-driven environment design discovers meta-optimizers that generalize better than LPG across Atari/Min-Atar, supporting adversarial curriculum design for RL transfer.\n'}}

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes—each of your five needs is addressed by a separate paper in the collection (no single work covers all of them):
> 
> 1. **Anchor-free part–body association** → **PBADet** (ICLR 2024): one-stage, anchor-free, with a single part-to-body center offset for hands/face/feet.
> 2. **Memory-efficient AdamW** → **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023): 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor optimizer states.
> 3. **SSL joint-embedding vs pixel noise** → **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024), plus **LDReg** (ICLR 2024) which regularizes joint-embedding methods.
> 4. **E/I (Dale's Law) recurrent nets, spectral view** → **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023).
> 5. **Adversarial curriculum design for RL** → **GROOVE** (ICLR 2024).
> 
> ## Experimental results compared
> 
> **Part–body detection (PBADet vs BPJDet/HierR-CNN):** On COCOHumanParts, PBADet(YOLOv5l6) is on par with BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) overall (AP 43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3; AP.5 70.0 vs 70.6) but leads on medium/large-person and feet AP (APM 66.2 vs 63.8; APL 67.2 vs 61.8) and achieves lower (better) average mMR-2 for head/face/hands (e.g., 27.9/30.5/36.2/40.8 vs 30.8/31.8/41.6/42.2). Ablations on BodyHands show anchor-free part-to-body beats anchor-based part-to-body (JointAP 85.98 vs 85.28) and far beats BPJDet's anchor-based body-to-part (78.13); association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each contribute (JointAP 78.07 → 85.98).
> 
> **4-bit optimizer:** On NLU (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9), CLS (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2), NLG (BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7), QA (F1 94.5 vs 94.6) and MT (26.28 vs 26.61), 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW, with ~2× smaller states than 8-bit (4-bit Factor ~4×). LLaMA-7B fine-tuning: 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB (57.7% saved), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU. Caveat: this paper's vision benchmark is ImageNet-1k with Swin-T; it does **not** test MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 (SVHN appears in no document here). The Hessian-spectra paper (ICML 2025) does use LeNet on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100 and ViT-B fine-tuning on CIFAR-100, but for loss-landscape analysis, not optimizer-state compression.
> 
> **SSL joint embedding (JEPA):** In deep linear networks, JEPA's fixed point is w̄=ρ^L vs MAE's ρ^(L/(L+1)): JEPA learns high-regression-coefficient ("influential") features first and suppresses noisy high-variance features, with suppression growing with depth (1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE). On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA). Complementarily, LDReg raises local intrinsic dimensionality and improves linear eval on ImageNet: SimCLR 64.3→64.8, SimCLR-Tuned 67.2→67.5, BYOL 67.6→68.5, MAE 57.0→57.6, with effective-rank and transfer gains (e.g., SimCLR CIFAR-100 71.6→75.1).
> 
> **Dale's Law/spectral properties:** ColEI RNNs trained worse and more variably than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs on all four benchmarks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition), and gradient clipping helped them most. ColEI's singular-value spectrum is multimodal/dispersed with a large-mode, vs the unimodal quarter-circle (Marchenko–Pastur) of RNNs/DANNs. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the spectrum matters more than sign constraints (sign constraints account for ~1% of a 2.3%±0.6% gap). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error; small networks with balanced E/I outperform larger, skewed-ratio ones. Recurrent DANNs learn as well as standard RNNs while respecting Dale's Law.
> 
> **Adversarial curriculum RL (GROOVE vs LPG):** Meta-trained on Grid-Worlds, GROOVE improves unseen Grid-World robustness (LPG fails to exceed 75% A2C-normalized return on 187% more tasks) and Atari generalization (higher mean score on 39 vs 17 tasks, one tie; better IQM and optimality gap). Its "algorithmic regret" (AR) metric beats L1/positive value loss, optimal-policy regret, and uniform sampling on all Min-Atar tasks (Asterix, Breakout, Freeway, SpaceInvaders), while prior UED value-loss metrics only beat random on one task. It also cuts meta-training cost (~3 h on one V100 vs ~24 h on TPU-v2).
> 
> **Bottom line:** Each method is validated within its own domain; none of the papers jointly addresses your full stack, so you would combine PBADet (vision), 4-bit AdamW + JEPA/LDReg (SSL), DANN-style E/I RNNs (control), and GROOVE (policy meta-learning) as complementary building blocks. Two gaps: the 4-bit optimizer work is not evaluated on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100, and SVHN appears nowhere in the collection.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection contains exactly five works mapping to your five requirements. Here is how they address each need and how their experimental results compare.
> 
> ## The five matching works
> 
> **1. Anchor-free part–body association — PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> One-stage, anchor-free detector that associates hands/face/feet with the correct person using a single part-to-body center offset (part-to-body rather than BPJDet's body-to-part offsets). Results: on BodyHands it achieves HandAP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 with a 36.9M-param YOLOv7, beating BPJDet's anchor-based body-to-part (85.3 / 86.80 / 78.13). Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each help. It also beats HierR-CNN and gives higher precision/recall/F1 than the pose estimator ED-Pose, and generalizes to animal part–body association.
> 
> **2. 4-bit AdamW optimizer states — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Uses smaller blocks (B128) for the first moment plus rank-1 normalization and zero-point-excluding linear quantization for the second moment. Results: matches or slightly beats 32-bit AdamW on all fine-tuning tasks (e.g., RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2) while cutting total training memory up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB), and 4× smaller optimizer states than 8-bit. Note: it is validated on Swin-T/ImageNet and LLaMA, not on MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 specifically.
> 
> **3. Joint-embedding SSL that avoids pixel noise — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> Theoretical/empirical analysis showing JEPA (latent-space prediction) is biased toward high-influence features and suppresses pixel noise, unlike MAE (input reconstruction), which orders learning by eigenvalue λ and can retain noise. JEPA's critical-time analysis shows it prioritizes features with high regression coefficient ρ (depth amplifies this), and ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance perceptual subspace faster than MAE. Complementing it, **LDReg** regularizes SSL (SimCLR, BYOL, MAE) against dimensional collapse, improving linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO detection for both CNN and ViT backbones.
> 
> **4. Dale's Law E/I spectral stability — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Shows sign constraints are not the main cause of poor EI-RNN learning; the initial singular-value spectrum is. ColEI (column sign-constrained) RNNs have multimodal, dispersed spectra and learn worse and with higher variance on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition; recurrent DANN variants keep unimodal spectra like standard RNNs and match their performance (even with 1 inhibitory neuron). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance.
> 
> **5. Adversarial curriculum for RL algorithm discovery — GROOVE** (ICLR 2024)
> Meta-learns RL update rules via Unsupervised Environment Design, using a new "algorithmic regret" (AR) metric that co-trains an antagonist. Results: meta-trained only on Grid-Worlds, GROOVE beats LPG on 39 vs 17 Atari tasks, improves IQM and optimality gap, and increases robustness on unseen Grid-Worlds (LPG fails to reach >75% A2C-normalized return on 187% more tasks). AR consistently outperforms L1 value loss, positive value loss, and optimal-policy regret; high-AR static curricula also beat handcrafted and random curricula, though the gap narrows as the level count grows. It is ~8× faster to meta-train than the reference LPG (3 h on one V100 vs 24 h on TPU-v2).
> 
> ## Cross-cutting comparison
> 
> - **Coverage gap:** No single paper combines these needs; they are five independent methods. The optimizer paper does not test the small datasets (MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100) or few-shot regimes you name, and GROOVE's meta-training uses only simple Grid-Worlds — the papers themselves note these limitations (task-dependent quantization settings, simple meta-training environments).
> - **Method type vs. empirics:** PBADet, the 4-bit optimizers, LDReg, and GROOVE are empirical methods with strong quantitative wins; the JEPA and Dale's-Law papers are primarily analytical (deep-linear/spectral theory) backed by smaller experiments. The former directly improve accuracy/memory/generalization; the latter provide explainability (NSE diagnostic, noise-suppression mechanism) rather than large accuracy gains.
> - **Stability/robustness theme:** Both the Dale's-Law paper (spectral initialization, NSE) and the JEPA paper (feature ordering, noise suppression) emphasize that *initialization/dynamics properties* — not just final accuracy — determine whether a method is usable, which is directly relevant to your resource-constrained, interpretability-oriented control and SSL modules.
> - **Recommended combination:** Use PBADet for detection, 4-bit AdamW for memory-constrained fine-tuning, JEPA-style objectives (+LDReg regularization) for SSL, DANN-style EI recurrency for the control module, and GROOVE/AR for adversarial RL curriculum design.
> 
> One caveat: nothing in the collection evaluates these methods together on the same stack, so any end-to-end comparison of the combined system cannot be established from the provided context.
