**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison-only summary of experimental results reported in the five papers, organized by shared or similar datasets and tasks, and highlighting where methods were evaluated on identical datasets. No claims outside the provided figures, tables, and descriptions are made.
> 
> 1) Object detection and part–body association (PBADet vs baselines) on identical datasets
> - BodyHands (identical dataset across methods):
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7, input 1024) achieved Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98. PBADet (YOLOv5l6, input 1024) achieved Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, input 1536) reported Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39 (Table 1). 
>   • Result: On BodyHands, PBADet outperforms BPJDet and prior baselines on conditional accuracy and joint AP, and improves hand AP relative to BPJDet.
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (identical dataset across methods):
>   • All-categories APs (AP.5:.95/AP.5): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3 (Table 2). 
>     – Medium/large scales: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) APM 66.2/65.0 and APL 67.2/64.4 outperform BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) APM 63.8/63.2 and APL 61.8/58.9. 
>     – Per-category APs: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) person 62.4 vs BPJDet 61.3; PBADet feet categories slightly improve (l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9), while BPJDet is higher for head/face/hands (e.g., head 56.6 vs PBADet 54.6).
>   • Average mismatched miss rate (mMR−2) per category (Table 3): PBADet achieves the lowest average mMR−2 in head, face, both hands, and right foot; example: head mMR−2 PBADet 27.9–29.2 vs BPJDet 30.8.
>   • Result: On COCOHumanParts, PBADet improves medium/large-object APs, person AP, and reduces association mMR−2 in several parts compared to BPJDet; BPJDet retains a slight edge in overall AP. 
> 
> - CrowdHuman (identical dataset across methods):
>   • Face–body association (Table 5): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves body MR−2 36.5 (best), face MR−2 44.7, body AP 91.6 (best), mMR−2 50.8; PBADet (YOLOv5l6) body MR−2 37.5, face MR−2 45.3, body AP 91.4, mMR−2 50.9. BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) body MR−2 40.7, face MR−2 46.3, body AP 89.5, mMR−2 50.1. 
>   • Wider comparison (Table 6): PBADet’s joint detector achieves best body MR−2 among joint methods and AP competitive with DETR-based detectors; BPJDet comparable but generally higher MR−2 than PBADet.
>   • Result: On CrowdHuman, PBADet improves body detection MR−2 and AP vs BPJDet, with similar mMR−2 for association.
> 
> - Additional datasets (qualitative and auxiliary results):
>   • COCO: PBADet qualitatively shows more robust part–body associations vs Hier R-CNN and BPJDet (Figures 4–5).
>   • AP-10K animals: PBADet extends part-body association (head/feet) effectively (qualitative Figure 6).
> 
> 2) Memory-efficient training (4-bit optimizer states) on identical or standard benchmarks
> - GLUE (RoBERTa-L; identical task across optimizers, Table 2 and Table 7):
>   • Mean score: 4-bit AdamW 89.1 ± 0.01, 8-bit AdamW 89.1 ± 0.00, 32-bit AdamW 88.9 ± 0.01; SM3 underperforms (87.5 ± 0.00). Per-task results show 4-bit AdamW closely matches 32-bit and 8-bit across MNLI, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST-2, MRPC, CoLA, STS-B.
>   • Result: 4-bit AdamW matches 8-bit and 32-bit baselines on GLUE; SM3 degrades.
> 
> - SQuAD and SQuAD 2.0 (RoBERTa-L; identical task across optimizers, Table 9):
>   • SQuAD F1/EM: 4-bit AdamW 94.5 ± 0.10 / 88.8 ± 0.08; 8-bit AdamW 94.5 ± 0.04 / 88.8 ± 0.15; 32-bit AdamW 94.6 ± 0.13 / 89.0 ± 0.10; SM3 lower (91.7/84.2). 
>   • Result: 4-bit AdamW retains accuracy comparable to 32-bit and 8-bit; SM3 inferior.
> 
> - ImageNet-1k (Swin-T; identical architecture across optimizers, Table 2):
>   • Top-1 accuracy: 4-bit AdamW 80.8 ± 0.02; 8-bit AdamW 81.0 ± 0.01; 32-bit AdamW 81.2 ± 0.05; SM3 79.0 ± 0.03. 
>   • Result: 4-bit within ~0.4% of 32-bit, better than SM3.
> 
> - E2E-NLG (GPT-2 Medium; identical task across optimizers, Tables 2 and 8):
>   • BLEU: 4-bit AdamW 67.8 ± 0.51; 8-bit AdamW 67.5 ± 0.87; 32-bit AdamW 67.7 ± 0.67; SM3 slightly lower (66.9 ± 0.58). Other metrics (NIST/METEOR/ROUGE-L/CIDEr) are comparable across 4-bit and 32-bit.
>   • Result: 4-bit matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit/8-bit on E2E-NLG.
> 
> - WMT14 En–De (Transformer-Base; identical task across optimizers, Table 2):
>   • SacreBLEU: 4-bit AdamW 26.28 ± 0.05; 8-bit AdamW 26.66 ± 0.10; 32-bit AdamW 26.61 ± 0.08; Adafactor ~26.45 ± 0.05 (4-bit Factor, Table 2). 
>   • Result: 4-bit essentially comparable; 8-bit slightly higher on this task.
> 
> - Instruction tuning of LLaMA (identical task metrics across optimizers, Table 3):
>   • MMLU (5-shot): 4-bit AdamW equals or closely matches 32-bit across sizes (e.g., 7B: 38.9 vs 38.7; 13B: 47.4 vs 46.5; 33B: 54.9 vs 56.4). 
>   • Commonsense tasks (HellaSwag, ARC-e, ARC-c, OBQA): 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit AdamW across sizes (minor diffs within reported values). 
>   • Result: 4-bit optimizer retains LLaMA performance during fine-tuning.
> 
> - Memory/time comparisons (Table 4 and Table 5):
>   • LLaMA-7B (FSDP): 4-bit AdamW saves 57.7% total memory (31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB) and trains in ~3.07 h (vs 3.35 h), with fused implementation similar speed. 
>   • RoBERTa-L: 4-bit (fused) saves 43.5% memory (3.00 GB vs 5.31 GB) and matches/exceeds 8-bit speed; 4-bit Factor saves 46.7%. 
>   • GPT-2 Medium: 4-bit (fused) saves 34.4% memory (4.62 GB vs 6.89 GB) and is comparable to 32-bit/8-bit time; 4-bit Factor saves 35.6%. 
>   • Largest model under budget (Table 5): 4-bit enables OPT-1.3B on 24GB (vs 350M with 32-bit), OPT-6.7B on 80GB, and LLaMA-7B on 80GB.
> 
> - Ablations (Table 6; quantization choices):
>   • Quantizing both first (B128/DE) and second moments (Rank-1/Linear) yields lossless fine-tuning vs 32-bit; factorizing the 2nd moment (4-bit Factor) maintains accuracy while improving memory.
> 
> 3) JEPA vs MAE (joint-embedding vs reconstruction; identical and similar settings)
> - Deep linear simulations (Figures 1–2, 4–5):
>   • On Gaussian synthetic data with controlled feature covariances (λ) and regression coefficients (ρ), both JEPA and MAE learn features greedily in λ; JEPA uniquely prioritizes high-ρ (influential) features, reversing learning order when λ increases but ρ decreases (Distribution 2). 
>   • ODE simulations confirm depth-dependent bias: JEPA’s critical times depend strongly on ρ (Corollary 3.6), while MAE’s depend mainly on λ.
> 
> - Temporal generative model (Figure 3):
>   • With time-correlated signals (γ) and mode-specific noise (σ), JEPA learns less noisy, more predictive modes earlier (higher ρa), while MAE is agnostic to noise in early learning; empirical λ and ρ predictions match simulations.
> 
> - ImageNet features (Figure 7):
>   • CCA between full and bottom-variance subspaces: I-JEPA exhibits higher similarity to bottom subspace than MAE throughout training; MAE aligns more with top-variance subspace. 
>   • Result: On vision data, JEPA more rapidly targets semantically useful (low-variance) features than MAE.
> 
> 4) Dale’s Law RNNs (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNN; identical tasks)
> - Adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, naturalistic object recognition (Figures 2A–D):
>   • ColEI (column-sign constrained) networks learn worse and more variably than DANNs and standard RNNs across all four tasks. Gradient clipping disproportionately benefits ColEI (Appendix Fig. 10). 
> 
> - Spectral-transplant and sign-constraint experiments (Figure 4A–C):
>   • Freezing parameter signs impairs learning modestly (RNN: 0.7% ± 0.3%; ColEI: 1% ± 1%), but does not explain total gap (2.3% ± 0.6%). 
>   • Transplanting ColEI singular values into RNNs produces a larger performance drop than transplanting singular vectors or imposing sign constraints (e.g., changes ≈1.5% ± 0.3% for RNNs; ≈2% ± 1% for ColEI). Result: spectrum (singular values) matters most.
> 
> - EI ratio and network size (Figures 5–7):
>   • For ColEI, fewer inhibitory units and smaller networks reduce Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) and worsen test error; NSE anti-correlates with error across EI ratios and sizes (Fig. 7D). 
>   • DANNs remain near-unimodal spectra (NSE ≈ 0.95) and learn well even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> 
> 5) Hessian spectra in CNNs and LLMs (power-law analyses; identical datasets across optimizers and models)
> - Power-law Hessian structure holds in trained LeNet on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 (Figure 1; Table 1/8): 
>   • KS tests accept power-law for trained networks (e.g., MNIST LeNet SGD dks 0.009 < 0.043, Fashion-MNIST 0.013 < 0.043, CIFAR-10 0.028 < 0.043; random networks fail, dks > 0.043).
>   • Across optimizers on CIFAR-10 (Table 3), trained spectra remain power-law; slope ŝ correlates with largest eigenvalue and trace (Figures 4, 23) and with test error (Pearson ~0.72–0.85).
> 
> - Batch-size phases (MNIST LeNet, Figure 7; Table 4):
>   • Phase I (B ≤ 640): spectra power-law and sharper minima as B grows (e.g., B=512 dks 0.0079 < 0.043); Phase II (768 ≤ B ≤ 50000): power-law breaks (e.g., B=1024 dks 0.129 > 0.043); Phase III (very large B): convergence issues, spectra resemble random.
> 
> - LLMs (GPT-2 family; identical datasets across training stages):
>   • Pretraining on OpenWebText: power-law emerges as training progresses; KS distance (dks) strongly correlates with test loss (Pearson up to 0.923), whereas sharpness measures (λ1, Tr(H)) correlate weakly or negatively (Figures 9–10, 12–13). 
>   • Fine-tuning on Shakespeare: dks correlates with test loss (Pearson up to 0.980) while sharpness fails (Figure 11). 
>   • Layer-wise in GPT-2 small: early/middle layers show clearer power-law than last (Figure 31). 
>   • ViT (CIFAR-100): random-init lacks power-law; trained ViT exhibits power-law (Figure 14).
> 
> - Power-law eigengaps (LeNet MNIST, Fashion-MNIST; GPT-2 small):
>   • Eigengaps decay as power-law (Figures 2, 21, 30), implying robust, low-dimensional learning subspaces (Davis–Kahan bound scales with gap; Appendix B).
> 
> 6) Cross-paper comparisons on identical or overlapping datasets
> - MNIST/seq-MNIST:
>   • Dale’s: DANN ≈ standard RNN > ColEI across tasks; spectrum quality (unimodal, clustered) predicts better learning. 
>   • Hessian: trained LeNet shows power-law spectra and eigengaps; random networks do not. Increasing batch beyond phase boundary breaks power-law and hurts generalization.
>   • Result: On MNIST, methods that produce unimodal/clustered spectra (DANN, standard RNN; power-law Hessians) show superior optimization/generalization, consistent across papers.
> 
> - CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100:
>   • Hessian: trained LeNet and ResNet-18 exhibit power-laws; ŝ tracks sharpness and test error; power-law breaks at large batch (ResNet phase boundary around B≈1280). 
>   • PBADet: evaluated on COCOHumanParts; ViT (CIFAR-100) power-law emerges with training (vision Transformer context). 
>   • Result: In vision classification, trained models tend towards power-law Hessians; large-batch can break this, aligning with observed generalization trends.
> 
> - COCO/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman/BodyHands (detection):
>   • PBADet vs BPJDet/Hier R-CNN on identical datasets: PBADet improves association accuracy (mMR−2) and medium/large APs; BPJDet slightly higher overall AP. 
>   • Result: On these datasets, one-stage anchor-free PBADet yields stronger association and robustness without large representation overhead.
> 
> - GLUE/SQuAD/E2E-NLG/WMT14 (NLP tasks):
>   • 4-bit AdamW retains accuracy vs 8-bit and 32-bit while reducing memory; SM3/Adafactor occasionally lower. 
>   • JEPA vs MAE (theoretical + empirical): JEPA prioritizes informative features (high ρ) and aligns with low-variance subspaces faster; relevant to downstream linear probing as shown via CCA.
> 
> 7) Key takeaways restricted to reported experiments
> - On identical detection datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman), PBADet achieves better or comparable detection/association metrics than prior one-stage/two-stage baselines, notably boosting Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP (BodyHands) and reducing mMR−2 (COCOHumanParts), while medium/large scale APs improve.
> - On identical NLP and vision benchmarks, 4-bit optimizer states (with rank-1 normalization and zero-excluding linear mapping for v) retain or match 32-bit/8-bit accuracy, reduce memory by up to ~58%, and enable larger models under fixed budgets.
> - Across RNN tasks (adding, seq-MNIST, Penn Treebank, naturalistic object recognition), DANNs and standard RNNs outperform ColEI. Spectrum-transplant studies and NSE analyses show singular-value spectra dominate learning differences.
> - Power-law Hessians consistently appear in trained CNNs/Transformers/LLMs and correlate with optimization/generalization. In LLMs, KS distance dks is a stronger generalization predictor than sharpness measures at training-time, whereas for CNNs sharpness correlates better near minima. Batch-size phase transitions can disrupt power-law and generalization.
> 
> This summary includes only experimental findings and numerical results present in the supplied papers/tables/figures, highlighting identical datasets and comparable metrics where available.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, here are the papers that collectively cover the requested topics:
> 
> **1. Spectral/curvature analysis (Hessian power laws, eigengaps, SGD/Adam generalization)**
> - *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs* (Tang et al., ICML 2025). Finds power-law Hessian spectra in well-trained CNNs and LLMs (GPT-2, TinyLlama, ViT) but not random networks. Power-law holds across SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, Yogi, RAdam, Adai, PNM, Lookahead, DiffGrad (LeNet on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100; ResNet18 on CIFAR-10). Slope magnitude ŝ correlates with sharpness and test error (Pearson 0.853 MNIST, 0.72 CIFAR-10); power-law eigengaps explain low-dimensional learning via Davis–Kahan. Notably, sharpness measures predict CNN generalization but fail for LLMs, where power-law goodness (d_ks, up to 0.98) predicts generalization better; LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power law as full fine-tuning does; SGD underperforms Adam for Transformers when Hessian spectra are blockwise heterogeneous.
> 
> **2. Biologically constrained E/I recurrent networks (Dale's principle)**
> - *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (Li, Cornford, Ghosh, Richards, NeurIPS 2023). ColEI RNNs (sign-constrained, Dale's law) have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure, whereas DANN RNNs and standard RNNs match random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur forms. Spectrum matters more than sign constraints (sign constraints cost ~0.7–1% error; spectrum accounts for the full 2.3%±0.6% gap on sequential MNIST). Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error; small networks with skewed E/I ratios learn worse (DANN robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron). Also tested on adding problem, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition.
> 
> **3. JEPA / joint-embedding self-distillation vs MSE reconstruction**
> - *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (Littwin et al., Apple, NeurIPS 2024). In exactly-solvable deep linear networks, JEPA prioritizes "influential" high-regression-coefficient (high-ρ) features, while MAE/MSE reconstruction prioritizes high-variance (λ) features even if noisy; the bias requires a deep encoder. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA metric). This explains why predicting in latent space (vs pixel MSE) prioritizes informative features.
> 
> **4. Memory-efficient 4-bit optimizer states**
> - *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (Li, Chen, Zhu, NeurIPS 2023). 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor use smaller block (B128) + rank-1 normalization and a zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the second moment. Results: RoBERTa-L on GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9 (32-bit), Swin-T (attention backbone) on ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, GPT-2M E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, WMT14 en-de 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning (LoRA-style/instruction tuning) matches 32-bit with up to 57.7% memory saving and LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU; enables 4× larger OPT models.
> 
> **5. One-stage anchor-free part-body detector**
> - *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (Gao et al., ICLR 2024). Extends anchor-free detection (YOLOv5/YOLOv7) with a single part-to-body center offset (vs BPJDet's body-to-part representation of length 15 vs 10). On BodyHands: Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 vs BPJDet 85.3/86.80/78.13; on COCO-HumanParts AP 42.7–43.0; on CrowdHuman face-body, best body MR-2 (36.5) with competitive AP; also outperforms ED-Pose on precision/recall/F1 and extends to AnimalPose/AP-10K quadrupeds. Ablations show association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment each help.
> 
> **Cross-cutting comparison of experimental results:**
> - **Loss function:** MSE/reconstruction (MAE) learns high-variance, often noisy features; JEPA's latent-space prediction learns informative low-variance features (better downstream), while cross-entropy classification is the standard for the Hessian/spectral and detection studies; MSE-based square loss also appears in the Dale's-law RNN analyses (adding problem/object recognition) with spectrum-determined performance.
> - **Optimizers:** Power-law Hessian structure holds for both SGD and Adam families; slope magnitude predicts generalization on CNN benchmarks (MNIST/CIFAR) but fails for LLMs, where 4-bit AdamW retains full-precision accuracy during fine-tuning; LoRA fine-tuning doesn't reproduce the full-fine-tuning Hessian power law.
> - **Benchmarks:** Digit/object benchmarks (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-1K) appear in items 1, 3, 4; detection benchmarks (COCO-WholeBody, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands) in item 5; sequential MNIST/PTB in item 2.
> - **Attention backbones:** ViT power-law emergence (CIFAR-100) and Swin-T ImageNet accuracy preserved under 4-bit optimization are reported; Adam's advantage over SGD for Transformers is linked to blockwise Hessian heterogeneity.
> 
> **Caveats:** No single retrieved document directly compares cross-entropy vs MSE head-to-head on the same benchmark, nor does any combine all five themes; the coverage above is assembled from independent papers, and some requested connections (e.g., eigengap-driven optimizer choice on detection benchmarks, or 4-bit optimizers on whole-body detection) are not established in the available context.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the matching papers, with their key experimental results, followed by a comparative analysis.
> 
> ## (a) Hessian spectra & generalization
> **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs"** (ICML 2025)
> - Power-law Hessian spectra (KS-tested) exist in well-trained CNNs (LeNet, ResNet18) and LLMs (GPT-2, TinyLlama) on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100; absent in random nets, underparameterized nets, limited data, and large-batch training (phase transition at batch 640→768 on LeNet/MNIST).
> - Holds across SGD, Vanilla SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, RAdam, Yogi, etc. Slope magnitude ŝ correlates with sharpness and test error (e.g., LeNet CIFAR-10 Pearson ≈ 0.72); d_ks predicts LLM generalization (up to 0.98) where sharpness measures fail.
> - Power-law eigengaps (Davis–Kahan analysis) explain a robust low-dimensional learning subspace.
> - **LoRA**: LoRA-only fine-tuning does *not* induce the power-law structure that full fine-tuning does. Covers CNNs and Transformers (ViT-base), SGD vs Adam, and digit/object benchmarks.
> 
> ## (b) Dale's-law E/I recurrent networks
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - ColEI RNNs (columns sign-constrained to E/I) learn worse and with higher variance; recurrent DANNs obeying Dale's principle learn as well as standard RNNs.
> - Singular-value spectrum of ColEI is multimodal/dispersed (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), vs. unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra for standard/DANN RNNs. Spectrum transplants show spectral properties matter more than sign constraints.
> - Smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error (sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition; gradient clipping mitigates deficits).
> 
> ## (c) JEPA vs reconstruction (MSE)
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Exact gradient-flow ODEs for deep linear networks show JEPA (latent-space prediction) prioritizes "influential" high-ρ features, whereas MAE (input-space MSE reconstruction) orders features mainly by eigenvalue λ and learns high-variance/noisy features.
> - Noise suppression strengthens with encoder depth; bias nearly vanishes for shallow encoders. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA measure).
> 
> ## (d) 4-bit optimizer states
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Adam/AdamW states compressed to 4-bit using smaller block size (B128) for first moment, rank-1 normalization and zero-point-excluding linear mapping for second moment, optionally factorized ("4-bit Factor").
> - Results: 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L, 89.1), ImageNet-1k (Swin-T, 80.8), E2E-NLG (GPT-2M, 67.8), SQuAD (94.5), WMT14 (26.28); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning on Alpaca retains accuracy (e.g., 4-bit AdamW 54.9 vs 32-bit 56.4 on MMLU-ish LLaMA-33B). Enables LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU and ~4× larger OPT models under a memory budget. Attention backbone (Swin-T) and fine-tuning covered.
> 
> ## (e) One-stage anchor-free part-body detector
> **"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** (ICLR 2024)
> - One-stage anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones) linking parts to a parent body via a single part-to-body center offset (vs BPJDet's body-to-part offsets).
> - Results: outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts (e.g., YOLOv7: HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98; COCOHumanParts AP 42.7). On CrowdHuman face-body: best body MR-2 (36.5) and competitive AP (91.6). Anchor-free beats anchor-based under the same part-to-body definition (85.98 vs 85.28 JointAP).
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Loss landscape vs architecture**: (a) shows optimizer choice (SGD vs Adam) barely changes the power-law spectrum, while (e) shows detection architecture choice (anchor-free vs anchor-based, YOLOv5 vs YOLOv7) and association direction (part-to-body vs body-to-part) materially change detection metrics — spectral structure is optimizer-agnostic but task-formulation-sensitive.
> - **Loss function matters**: (c) demonstrates that the *space* in which the loss operates (latent vs pixel/MSE) changes which features are learned and in what order, complementing (a)'s finding that Hessian shape (curvature) drives generalization; both point to loss geometry rather than the optimizer alone.
> - **Memory vs accuracy trade-offs**: (d) achieves near-lossless accuracy (≤~1.5 points on most tasks) with 4-bit states, whereas (b) shows biologically constrained (E/I) networks lose 2.3% accuracy on sMNIST unless spectra are fixed — constraints on states (quantization) are cheaper than constraints on weights (Dale's law).
> - **LoRA/fine-tuning**: (a) shows LoRA-only fine-tuning fails to induce power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning produces, while (d) shows full fine-tuning with 4-bit optimizer states retains accuracy — indicating the spectral signature of generalization may depend on full-parameter updates, not on parameter precision.
> - **Benchmarks**: (a) uses digit/small-image sets (MNIST, CIFAR), (b) sequential MNIST/PTB, (c) ImageNet, (d) ImageNet/GLUE/WMT/Alpaca, (e) COCO-WholeBody/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman — collectively covering digit, object, language, and whole-body detection benchmarks.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is an evidence-only comparison and summary of experimental results across the five papers you provided, organized around your needs (one‑pass part–body detection, low‑memory training, self‑supervised distillation that avoids noisy pixels, and curvature/spectral tracking under SGD/AdamW on CNN/Transformer backbones). I highlight identical datasets and direct, table/figure‑based comparisons first.
> 
> 1) One‑pass part–body detection (multi‑person hand/face association)
> - Identical dataset: BodyHands
>   - Methods compared: PBADet (ours, one‑stage anchor‑free) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5 variants) and prior systems.
>   - Results (Table 1):
>     - PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73.
>     - Best BPJDet on BodyHands (YOLOv5l6) achieves 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39.
>     - Therefore on BodyHands, PBADet > BPJDet across all three metrics; gains are largest in conditional accuracy (+~6 points) and joint AP (+~1.3–1.6 points).
>   - Additional per‑pair F1 vs a pose method (Appendix A.2, Table 7): on COCO validation parts, PBADet outperforms ED‑Pose strongly in F1 (all parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; left hand 46.50 vs 22.87; right hand 47.34 vs 24.17; left foot 51.08 vs 40.46; right foot 50.34 vs 40.34), showing more reliable part‑to‑body association quality.
> 
> - Identical dataset: COCOHumanParts
>   - Methods compared: PBADet (YOLOv5l6, YOLOv7) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5s6/m6/l6) and Hier R‑CNN variants (Table 2, Table 3).
>   - All‑category AP (AP.5:.95 / subordinate AP.5:.95): BPJDet‑l6 = 43.6 / 43.3; PBADet‑l6 = 43.0 / 41.8; PBADet‑v7 = 42.7 / 41.5. BPJDet slightly higher in these aggregate APs.
>   - Size‑wise AP: PBADet leads on APM/APL: 
>     - PBADet‑l6: APM 66.2/65.0, APL 67.2/64.4 vs BPJDet‑l6: APM 63.8/63.2, APL 61.8/58.9.
>   - Per‑category AP: PBADet‑l6 better on person (62.4 vs 61.3) and feet (r‑foot 30.9 vs 30.2; l‑foot 31.5 vs 30.9), but lower on head/face/hands compared to BPJDet‑l6 (e.g., head 54.6 vs 56.6, face 44.6 vs 46.3).
>   - Association robustness (average mMR−2; lower is better, Table 3): PBADet‑YOLOv7 attains the lowest mMR−2 for head (29.2) and face (31.3) and lower for left hand (41.1) than BPJDet‑l6 (30.8, 31.8, 41.6), but higher for feet (e.g., r‑foot 52.6 vs 49.1).
>   - Takeaway: On COCOHumanParts, BPJDet has a slight edge in overall AP, while PBADet favors medium/large scales, person/feet categories, and reduces mismatches on head/face (mMR−2) without post‑processing complexity.
> 
> - Identical dataset: CrowdHuman (Appendix Table 5–6)
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5 variants) and crowded‑person detectors.
>   - Face‑body association (Table 5): PBADet‑YOLOv7 achieves best body MR−2 (36.5 vs BPJDet‑m6 39.7) and best body AP (91.6 vs BPJDet‑m6 90.7); mMR−2 for body‑face pairs is comparable (~50–51).
>   - Against general person detectors (Table 6): PBADet attains the best body MR−2 (36.5) and competitive AP amid heavier DETR baselines; shows a balanced detection/association trade‑off.
> 
> 2) Low‑memory training with ≈4‑bit optimizer states
> - Identical datasets across methods:
>   - NLU (GLUE with RoBERTa‑Large), QA (SQuAD), NLG (E2E‑NLG with GPT‑2 Medium), MT (WMT14 with Transformer‑Base), and ImageNet CLS (Swin‑T) (Table 2, 7–9):
>     - 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit AdamW on NLU (89.1 vs 88.9 mean score) and NLG (BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7), and is comparable on QA F1 (94.5 vs 94.6). On MT, 4‑bit slightly trails (26.28 vs 26.61 SacreBleu). On ImageNet (Swin‑T), 4‑bit is slightly lower (80.8 vs 81.2 Acc), but within typical variance.
>     - 4‑bit Factor (quantized first moment + factorized v) yields similar accuracy to 4‑bit AdamW and 32‑bit on the same tasks, with added memory savings.
>   - Instruction tuning on LLaMA (Table 3): across 7B/13B/33B, 4‑bit AdamW preserves or matches 32‑bit performance (e.g., 7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; 13B 47.4 vs 46.5; 33B 54.9 vs 56.4), and similar trends on HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA.
> - Memory/time (Table 4–5):
>   - LLaMA‑7B (FSDP): total memory drops from 75.40 GB to 31.87 GB (−57.7%) with 4‑bit optimizer; fused kernels recover or surpass 32‑bit speed.
>   - RoBERTa‑L and GPT‑2 Medium: 4‑bit saves 34–47% total memory vs 32‑bit; fused ops restore runtime to near 32‑bit or 8‑bit levels.
> - Ablations that matter for 4‑bit stability (Table 1):
>   - Second‑moment zero‑point quantization is the main failure mode; removing zero (DE‑0) or using a linear mapping plus rank‑1 normalization stabilizes training and preserves accuracy. Smaller blocks (B128) help first moment; Stable Embedding alone cannot fix zero‑point issues.
> 
> 3) Self‑supervised distillation: avoiding noisy pixel cues (JEPA vs MAE)
> - Identical synthetic settings (deep linear encoders; Figures 1–2, Theorems 3.2–3.6):
>   - When feature covariance (λ) and regression coefficient (ρ) disagree (Distribution 2), JEPA inverts the learning order relative to MAE: JEPA prioritizes high‑ρ (predictive/low‑noise) directions, while MAE prioritizes high‑λ (high‑variance) directions. This inversion is visible in Figure 1(d–f) and ODE simulations in Figure 2(c,f).
>   - Depth amplifies JEPA’s bias toward influential features: increasing L widens temporal separation by ρ in JEPA (Figure 4), but MAE remains mostly λ‑driven even at depth.
> - Temporal model (Eq. 16; Figure 3):
>   - For sequences x=z_t, y=z_{t+1} with noise σ_a and auto‑correlation γ_a, JEPA’s effective ρ_a=γ_a||v_a||^2/(σ_a^2+||v_a||^2) climbs when noise is lower; experiments (Figure 3e) confirm that JEPA favors the higher‑ρ mode as T increases.
> - Realistic vision evidence (Appendix D, Figure 7):
>   - On ImageNet‑64, feature similarity (CCA) shows I‑JEPA’s representations align more with the low‑variance (“bottom”) PCA subspace than MAE across training (JEPA higher full↔bottom CCA; MAE higher full↔top CCA), supporting that JEPA avoids pixel‑level reconstruction bias and focuses early on semantic (predictive/low‑variance) content.
> 
> 4) Curvature/spectral tracking for generalization under SGD/AdamW
> - Identical datasets: MNIST and CIFAR‑10
>   - CNNs (LeNet/ResNet18) trained with SGD/Adam‑family optimizers exhibit a power‑law Hessian spectrum when trained (KS tests), but not at random initialization (Tables 1, 8, 10; Figure 1 & 24).
>   - On MNIST with LeNet (Figure 3–4): the Hessian’s rank–eigenvalue log–log slope magnitude ŝ correlates with generalization proxies and performance across optimizers:
>     - ŝ vs test error: Pearson 0.853 (smaller ŝ → better test error).
>     - ŝ vs λ_max and Tr(H): high positive correlation (e.g., Figure 4; smaller ŝ → smaller sharpness/trace), consistent with sharpness–generalization links.
>   - On CIFAR‑10 (LeNet; Figure 22–23): the same trend holds (e.g., ŝ vs test error Pearson 0.72; ŝ vs λ_max/Tr(H) ≈0.97), suggesting ŝ can be tracked as a curvature proxy during SGD training on typical digit/object datasets.
> - Batch size phases (MNIST; Figure 7; Table 4):
>   - With identical epochs, power‑law holds at B≤640 (e.g., B=640 d_ks=0.0125<0.043) but breaks sharply at B≥768 (e.g., B=768 d_ks=0.278>0.043), indicating a sudden loss of the learned spectral structure. With fixed iteration budget, extremely large B can recover power‑law (Table 5, B=16384 d_ks=0.0271<0.043) at much higher compute.
> - Overparameterization and data scaling (Figures 5–6):
>   - Deeper/wider networks and larger training sets yield clearer power‑laws; underparameterized 1‑layer FCN or very small data break the structure, mirroring generalization degradation.
> - LLMs (GPT‑2 family; Figures 8–13):
>   - Pretraining/fine‑tuning transitions the Hessian from non‑power‑law (random or pretrained checkpoints) to power‑law (trained), across GPT2‑small/medium/large and TinyLlama LoRA (Table 2).
>   - Generalization predictor during training: KS distance d_ks (power‑law goodness) tracks test loss strongly, while sharpness measures often fail in LLMs.
>     - GPT2‑nano (pretraining on Shakespeare): Pearson(Test loss, d_ks)=0.923 vs poor/negative correlations with λ_max and Tr(H) (Figure 10).
>     - GPT2‑small (fine‑tuning): Pearson(Test loss, d_ks)=0.980; λ_max and Tr(H) show weak/negative correlations (Figure 11). Thus, monitoring d_ks is more predictive for LLM generalization than sharpness in early/mid training.
> - Stable learning subspace from spectra (Dale’s Law and Hessian papers)
>   - Dale’s RNNs: The singular‑value spectrum’s clustering (NSE) predicts performance; lower NSE (more dispersed/multimodal spectra) leads to worse results, especially for ColEI at small sizes or high E:I ratios (Figures 5–7). DANNs and standard RNNs have unimodal clustered spectra and learn well; ColEI exhibits multi‑modal dispersed singular values and learns poorly. Spectrum‑transplant experiments show spectrum > sign constraints in impact on test performance (Figure 4B–C).
>   - Hessian eigengaps: top eigengaps follow a power‑law; with Davis–Kahan bounds, large top eigengaps imply robust, low‑dimensional eigenspaces; empirical eigengap power‑law verified on MNIST and GPT‑2 (Figures 2 & 30), supporting the practicality of subspace tracking.
> 
> What this means for your use case
> - One‑pass, real‑time part–body linking: PBADet is validated on multi‑person datasets with better conditional accuracy/joint AP than BPJDet on BodyHands, strong association robustness on head/face (mMR−2) and competitive category APs on COCOHumanParts; F1 analyses vs ED‑Pose on COCO val (Appendix) show large advantages on hands/feet.
> - Low‑VRAM training/finetuning: 4‑bit AdamW/Factor retain 32‑bit accuracy on GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG, and LLaMA instruction‑tuning while cutting optimizer memory ~2–4× (total memory −34% to −58%) and supporting fused kernels for speed.
> - Avoiding noisy pixel cues in distillation: JEPA (self‑distillation with stop‑grad) prioritizes high‑ρ (predictive/low‑noise) features, especially with deeper encoders, and empirically aligns with the bottom (semantic) PCA subspace on ImageNet, unlike MAE’s reconstruction bias.
> - Tracking generalization via curvature/spectra during SGD/AdamW:
>   - CNNs: monitor Hessian power‑law slope ŝ and sharpness (λ_max, Tr(H)); ŝ correlates with test error and sharpness on MNIST/CIFAR‑10.
>   - LLMs and ViTs: sharpness may not predict generalization in early/mid training; instead track the KS distance d_ks (goodness of power‑law fit) which correlates strongly with test loss during GPT‑2 pretrain/fine‑tune; ViT‑base also exhibits emergence of power‑law with training.
> 
> Dataset‑wise summary (who’s better on identical/similar datasets)
> - MNIST/Sequential MNIST (Dale’s RNNs; identical task/dataset across methods): Standard RNN ≈ DANN >> ColEI across Adding, seq‑MNIST, PTB, and a natural object‑recognition task; constraining columns to EI (ColEI) hurts learning; gradient clipping helps ColEI more but does not close the gap. Spectral clustering (high NSE) aligns with better accuracy.
> - MNIST/CIFAR‑10 (Hessian analysis; identical datasets across optimizers): On the same LeNet/ResNet backbones and datasets, optimizers with smaller ŝ (closer to power‑law with steeper decay) show better test error and lower sharpness (Figures 3–4, 22–23). Larger batches can break power‑law (worse generalization) unless training budget compensates (Tables 4–5).
> - COCO/BodyHands/CrowdHuman (PBADet vs BPJDet on identical datasets): PBADet best on BodyHands (hand AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP), achieves lower mismatch rates on head/face (mMR−2) and stronger medium/large object APs on COCOHumanParts, and best body MR−2/body AP on CrowdHuman; BPJDet holds a slight edge in overall COCO AP. Against ED‑Pose on COCO val parts, PBADet attains far higher Precision/Recall/F1.
> - GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/WMT/ImageNet/Instruction‑tuning (4‑bit vs 32‑bit/8‑bit/Adafactor/SM3, identical datasets): 4‑bit AdamW/Factor match 32‑bit accuracy on GLUE, SQuAD, E2E, and instruction‑tuning; are slightly lower on ImageNet/WMT but close; Adafactor/SM3 save more memory but degrade accuracy more notably on CLS/MT.
> 
> Metrics explicitly reported and useful for deployment validation
> - PBADet: AP (AP.5:.95, AP.5), APM/APL, per‑class APs; MR−2 (body/face), mMR−2 (pair mismatches), conditional accuracy, joint AP; part association F1/Precision/Recall vs ED‑Pose (Appendix Table 7).
> - 4‑bit optimizer: task metrics (GLUE mean, SQuAD EM/F1, E2E BLEU/NIST/METEOR/ROUGE‑L/CIDEr, WMT SacreBleu, ImageNet Acc), memory saved (%), wallclock.
> - JEPA vs MAE: ODE learning curves (feature‑wise projections), temporal model correlations; representation similarity (CCA) on ImageNet‑64 (JEPA higher full↔bottom CCA over training).
> - Spectral measures you can track online: Hessian λ_max, Tr(H), rank–eigenvalue slope ŝ; KS distance d_ks of power‑law fit; RNN singular‑value NSE (normalized SVD entropy). In LLM training, d_ks aligned with test loss (Pearson up to 0.979–0.990 across settings), while λ_max/Tr(H) often failed as predictors.
> 
> All statements above are taken directly from the reported tables/figures in the five papers; no additional claims were introduced.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the papers from the collection that match each requirement, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. One-pass detector linking hands/face to the correct person
> **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)** — exactly your clinical setting (the paper's motivating example is a technician's gestures in a medical scan room). It adds a single part-to-body center offset to an anchor-free detector (YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7), so parts (face, left/right hand, feet) are linked one-to-one to their parent body in one pass, unlike two-stage heuristic/BodyHands-style association networks or BPJDet's body-to-part offsets (which grow with part count and break when parts are occluded).
> 
> **Results comparison (BodyHands):**
> - PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params): Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
> - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, same backbone): 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39
> - BodyHands (700.3M): 84.8 / 83.44 / 63.48; OpenPose: 39.7 / 74.03 / 27.81
> 
> PBADet wins on every metric and, with a smaller model than BPJDet-YOLOv5m6, still outperforms it. On **COCOHumanParts** (head, face, both hands, both feet) it matches BPJDet in overall AP but leads in person/feet AP and achieves the lowest mMR−2 for head, face, hands and right foot. On **CrowdHuman** face-body association, it gives the best body MR−2 (36.5 vs BPJDet 39.7–41.3). Against the transformer pose estimator **ED-Pose**, PBADet's Precision/Recall/F1 are far higher (left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87; all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51). It also transfers to quadruped part-body association (AnimalPose/AP-10K). Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment sampling each materially improve association.
> 
> ## 2. 4-bit optimizer states for low-VRAM training
> **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023)** — compresses AdamW first/second moments to 4 bits (B128 dynamic-exponent block quantization for the first moment; Rank-1/linear zero-point-excluded quantization, optionally factorized, for the second moment). Works for end-to-end and adapter-style fine-tuning.
> 
> **Results vs 32-bit AdamW (same hyperparameters, no retuning):**
> - RoBERTa-L GLUE: 89.1 vs 88.9; SQuAD F1: 94.5 vs 94.6 (4-bit even slightly higher)
> - Swin-T ImageNet-1k: 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2M E2E-NLG BLEU: 67.8 vs 67.7; WMT14 en-de SacreBLEU: 26.28 vs 26.61
> - LLaMA-7B Alpaca fine-tune: MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7, HellaSwag 74.7 vs 74.6, ARC-c 44.4 vs 45.1, OBQA 43.0 vs 43.4 — no degradation as model size grows; convergence curves align.
> 
> Memory: up to 57.7% total-memory saving; trains 4× larger OPT models at a fixed budget and LLaMA-7B on a single 80 GB GPU. Compared with 8-bit AdamW, Adafactor and SM3: sublinear-memory baselines lose accuracy (especially on vision, e.g., Swin-T 79.0–80.0 vs 80.8), while 4-bit retains it. Ablations: quantizing both moments costs only marginally; smaller first-moment blocks help; factorizing the second moment improves both accuracy and memory.
> 
> ## 3. Avoiding noisy pixel cues in self-supervised distillation
> **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)** — directly supports preferring predictive latent features over raw MSE reconstruction. In a fully solvable deep-linear model, JEPA's critical learning time scales with the regression coefficient ρ (feature influence) as well as variance λ, while MAE's ordering depends mainly on λ — so JEPA is greedier for high-influence, low-variance (semantic) features and is strictly slower to learn noisy directions, converging to lower-amplitude weights on them; the suppression grows with encoder depth (a 1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE), and JEPA's solution is unreachable by MAE. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (measured via CCA). Caveat: the analysis assumes deep linear MLPs with special initialization; the authors argue qualitatively it generalizes. (Related, also in the collection: LDReg's local dimensionality regularization counters dimensional collapse in SimCLR/BYOL/MAE; and exogenous-noise RL studies show pixel-space reconstruction/temporal-contrastive objectives latch onto noise, whereas latent predictive objectives are more robust.)
> 
> ## 4. Tracking/forecasting generalization via curvature/spectral properties under CE with SGD/AdamW
> **Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs (ICML 2025)** — Hessian spectra of well-trained networks (CE-trained LeNet on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 under SGD and Adam/AMSGrad/AdaBound/Yogi/RAdam/Adai/PNM/Lookahead/DiffGrad; ViT-B fine-tuned on CIFAR-100; GPT-2 pretrained/fine-tuned with AdamW) follow a power law p(λ) ∝ λ^(−β), absent in random nets and in degenerate regimes (too-large batches, small width/depth, noisy labels, LoRA-only fine-tuning).
> 
> **Results/analysis:**
> - The KS-distance d_ks (power-law "goodness") predicts LLM generalization with Pearson correlation up to 0.923 during training, while sharpness (λ₁, Tr(H)) — reliable for CNNs (LeNet/CIFAR-10 power-law slope correlates ~0.72 with test error) — becomes nearly useless for transformers/LLMs (sharpness can rise while test loss drops).
> - Power-law structure emerges during training and tracks test loss synchronously, giving you a cheap in-training generalization forecast on both CNN and transformer backbones; power-law eigengaps link to robust top eigenvectors (Davis-Kahan analysis), explaining low-dimensional robust learning.
> - Complement: the Dale's-Law RNN study shows normalized SVD entropy (NSE) of the weight spectrum at initialization anti-correlates with final test error across RNNs on sequential MNIST, PTB, and object-recognition tasks — a spectral metric for predicting learnability before training.
> 
> **Bottom line for your system:** PBADet covers the one-pass hand/face-to-person association with strong Precision/Recall/F1 and AP wins over BPJDet/BodyHands/ED-Pose on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts and CrowdHuman; 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor gives near-lossless fine-tuning with up to ~58% memory savings on CNNs and transformers; the JEPA analysis justifies latent predictive distillation over pixel-reconstruction MSE for suppressing noise; and power-law Hessian/KS-distance analysis (plus NSE) provides spectral generalization tracking under SGD/AdamW on CNN and ViT backbones. One gap: the collection's 4-bit-optimizer results are on language + ImageNet/Swin classification rather than detection, and no paper here combines all four components on whole-body data, so that end-to-end integration would be your own contribution.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the relevant papers and a comparison of their experimental results, based only on the provided context.
> 
> ## 1. One-pass detector linking hands/face to correct person
> **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection** (doc `08b70bc...`) — a one-stage, anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset to associate hands/face to parent bodies in one pass.
> 
> - **BodyHands**: surpasses all baselines (BPJDet, BodyHands, Mask R-CNN variants) on hand AP, conditional accuracy, and joint AP. PBADet YOLOv7: hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 vs. BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39 — better despite a smaller backbone.
> - **COCOHumanParts** (6 parts): AP on par with BPJDet but leads AP_M/AP_L and feet detection, and achieves the lowest average mMR-2 across head, face, both hands, and right foot.
> - **CrowdHuman** (face–body): best body MR-2 (36.5, YOLOv7) with competitive AP; advantage over BPJDet is smaller since this is a single-part task.
> - **vs. ED-Pose (COCO val)**: far higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet — all-parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs. 24.09/45.51/31.51 — showing the one-stage part-body formulation beats a leading multi-person pose estimator at part association.
> 
> ## 2. 4-bit optimizer states for limited-VRAM fine-tuning
> **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (doc `8d5e1455...`) — 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor quantize first/second moments (B128 block, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, optional factorization).
> 
> - **Results**: matches 32-bit AdamW across GLUE (89.1 vs 88.9), Swin-T ImageNet-1k CLS (80.8 vs 81.2), GPT-2 E2E BLEU (67.8 vs 67.7), RoBERTa SQuAD F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), WMT14 en-de (26.28 vs 26.61); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning comparable on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA.
> - **Memory**: up to 57.7% total-memory savings; enables LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU and ~4× larger OPT models under a fixed budget; 4-bit Factor's states are ~4× smaller than 8-bit AdamW.
> - **Comparison**: Adafactor/SM3 are more memory-efficient but degrade, especially on image classification; ablation shows smaller first-moment blocks and factorized second moment improve accuracy.
> 
> ## 3. Self-supervised distillation avoiding noisy pixel cues
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation"** (doc `40fde037...`) — supports your preference for predictive latent features over raw reconstruction with MSE.
> 
> - JEPA self-distillation is implicitly biased toward high-influence (high regression coefficient) features and suppresses noise, whereas MAE-style reconstruction prioritizes high-variance pixel subspaces that explain most input variance.
> - ImageNet-1K experiments: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (measured by CCA), confirming the theoretical bias in practice.
> 
> **LDReg** (doc `51526068...`) is complementary: local dimensional collapse hurts SSL representations; LDReg increases local intrinsic dimensionality and improves linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE, MoCo, etc. (contrastive/non-contrastive alike).
> 
> ## 4. Tracking/forecasting generalization via curvature/spectral properties (CE under SGD/AdamW)
> **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs"** (doc `582d138d...`) — Hessian spectra of well-trained networks follow a power law; random/untrained networks do not.
> 
> - **Datasets/backbones**: LeNet on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 (trained with SGD and a range of optimizers including Adam/AdamW-family); GPT-2/TinyLlama pretrained with AdamW; ViT on CIFAR-100.
> - **Generalization forecasting**: power-law goodness (KS statistic d_ks) correlates with generalization — Pearson 0.72 with LeNet CIFAR-10 test error, and d_ks predicts LLM generalization up to 0.98, where conventional sharpness measures fail.
> - **Optimizer analysis**: power-law structure holds across SGD, Adam, RAdam, Yogi, etc.; it is lost with large batch sizes, small width/depth, limited data, and noisy labels; LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure that full fine-tuning does — relevant to your adapter-based fine-tuning.
> 
> ## Analysis / synthesis
> - For the detector, the evidence favors one-stage part-to-body association (PBADet) over two-stage matching and over DETR-style pose estimation: better AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP, lower mMR-2, and large Precision/Recall/F1 gains on hands/feet, with real-time backbones (YOLOv5/YOLOv7).
> - For memory-constrained fine-tuning, 4-bit AdamW is essentially lossless vs. 32-bit on all tested vision/language tasks, with the largest gains on LLM fine-tuning; prefer 4-bit Factor when further savings are needed.
> - For SSL pretraining, the JEPA analysis gives a principled reason to prefer latent-space prediction over MSE reconstruction (feature-prioritization by influence rather than variance), and LDReg guards against local collapse in the resulting representations.
> - For monitoring generalization, Hessian power-law goodness (d_ks) is a practical curvature/spectral proxy that works across CNNs and LLMs and across SGD/AdamW, but note the caveats: it fails for LoRA-only fine-tuning and very large batches, and it is computed on the CE loss landscape.
> 
> One caution: the Hessian power-law paper is an ICML 2025 work using CE-trained CNNs/LLMs; the context does not provide direct evidence of applying d_ks specifically to hand/body detectors or adapter fine-tuning on your datasets, so that part of your pipeline is supported by analogy rather than a directly matching experiment.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross-paper comparison of experimental results (only using reported figures/tables)
> 
> Scope and datasets overlap
> - There is no single dataset evaluated across all five papers. Each targets a different sub-domain: human-part detection and association (PBADet), recurrent nets with Dale’s Law (EI RNNs), self-distillation vs. masked reconstruction in SSL (JEPA vs MAE), sequential/active calibration (RCPS), and instruction fine-tuning of LLMs (NEFTune).
> - Partial overlap:
>   - Vision: PBADet uses BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman; RCPS uses ImageNet; JEPA includes an ImageNet study (feature similarity) but not the same metrics/tasks as RCPS, so results are not directly comparable.
>   - Language: NEFTune uses AlpacaEval and OpenLLM Leaderboard tasks; other papers do not evaluate these.
> 
> Within-domain, same-dataset comparisons
> 1) One-stage part–body association (PBADet)
> - BodyHands (Table 1):
>   - Baseline BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) vs PBADet with identical backbone (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9 → 88.1; Conditional Accuracy 86.91 → 92.71; Joint AP 84.39 → 85.73 (PBADet higher on all three).
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7) further improves: Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 (best overall in this table).
> - COCOHumanParts (Tables 2–3):
>   - All-categories AP (AP.5:.95, original/subordinate): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3 (BPJDet slightly higher overall AP), but PBADet excels on size-specific AP and association accuracy:
>     - Size AP: PBADet APM/APL = 66.2/67.2 (original) and 65.0/64.4 (subordinate) vs BPJDet 63.8/61.8 and 63.2/58.9 (PBADet higher for medium/large objects).
>     - Per-category AP: PBADet beats BPJDet for person (62.4 vs 61.3) and both feet (r-foot 30.9 vs 30.2; l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9), while BPJDet edges hands (r-hand 40.4 vs 39.0; l-hand 39.6 vs 37.7) and head/face slightly.
>     - Association error (average mMR−2, lower is better; Table 3): PBADet is lower on 5/6 categories (head 27.9 vs 30.8; face 30.5 vs 31.8; l-hand 36.2 vs 41.6; r-hand 40.8 vs 42.2; l-foot 47.9 vs 50.4), slightly higher on r-foot (50.4 vs 49.1).
> - CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6):
>   - Against BPJDet (YOLOv5l6/m6/s6): PBADet achieves better body MR−2 (37.5/36.5 vs 40.7–41.3), better face MR−2 (45.3/44.7 vs 45.0–46.3), and higher body AP (91.4/91.6 vs 89.5–90.7). Pair mismatch mMR−2 is comparable (PBADet 50.8–50.9 vs BPJDet 50.1–51.4).
>   - Versus wider crowded-person detectors (Table 6): PBADet (YOLOv7) gets best body MR−2 (36.5), with AP 91.6 comparable to stronger DETR variants.
> - Ablations (Table 8): Part-to-body and anchor-free choices matter. Anchor-free + part-to-body (PBADet) outperforms anchor-based variants and an anchor-based body-to-part design in joint AP/Cond. Acc.
> 
> 2) Instruction fine-tuning with noisy embeddings (NEFTune)
> - Identical datasets, same model family (LLaMA‑2‑7B, Table 1):
>   - Alpaca: 29.91 → 65.70 GPT‑4 win rate (+35.79 pp).
>   - Evol‑Instruct: 70.19 → 80.36 (+10.17 pp).
>   - ShareGPT: 70.57 → 76.22 (+5.65 pp).
>   - OpenPlatypus: 60.95 → 69.96 (+9.01 pp).
>   - Average: 57.91 → 73.06 (+15.15 pp).
> - Scaling and chat refinement (Table 2):
>   - LLaMA‑2‑Chat‑7B (already RLHF‑aligned), further finetuned on Evol‑Instruct: 74.44 → 81.74 (+7.30 pp).
>   - LLaMA‑2‑13B (Evol‑Instruct): 72.61 → 82.04 (+9.43 pp).
>   - LLaMA‑2‑70B (Evol‑Instruct): 75.03 → 88.81 (+13.78 pp).
> - Quantized finetuning (QLoRA, Table 3): still improves AlpacaEval (e.g., LLaMA‑2‑13B, Evol‑Instruct: 56.96 base → up to 61.30 with NEFTune), though gains are smaller than full finetuning.
> - Similar tasks, capability preservation (Figure 3): Across ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA, NEFTune maintains essentially unchanged accuracy vs. standard finetuning (differences ≤ ~1–1.5 pp across configurations shown), indicating conversational quality gains do not trade off factual QA metrics.
> 
> 3) Active, anytime-valid RCPS
> - Identical dataset: Synthetic simulation (Figure 2): “pretrain” and “learned” label policies reach lower (safer/smaller) β̂ faster vs. labeling all or oblivious random sampling; after fixed label budgets (e.g., 2500 labels) β̂ is closer to β* for the learned/pretrain policies. Safety violation rates for all methods remain controlled under α=0.05 (Figure 2a).
> - ImageNet (Figure 3): With class-probability predictors, “pretrain”/“learned” labeling policies again yield lower β̂ than “all”/“oblivious” for the same number of queried labels, and average safety violation rates remain below α=0.05.
> - Takeaway: Under identical streams, active policies using predictors are more label-efficient at achieving the same anytime-valid risk target than baselines, while preserving the advertised anytime validity.
> 
> 4) Dale’s Law in EI RNNs (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs)
> - Across identical tasks (Figures 2–7): Adding problem (regression), sequential MNIST (classification), Penn Tree Bank (language modeling), and a naturalistic object recognition sequence task:
>   - ColEI consistently learns worse than DANNs and standard RNNs (lower final performance, higher variance) across all four benchmarks.
>   - Gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially more than others (appendix result cited in text), indicating instability tied to spectrum.
>   - Spectrum transplant experiments (Figure 4): Giving ColEI the RNN singular value spectrum (or vice versa) shows that singular value spectra explain more of the performance gap than sign constraints alone; sign constraints still hurt but are secondary to spectral pathologies.
>   - E/I ratio and size (Figures 5–7): ColEI performance degrades with fewer inhibitory units and smaller networks; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) of the recurrent matrix at initialization correlates with final test error. DANN spectra and performance remain robust across sizes/ratios (including very few inhibitory units), matching standard RNNs.
> 
> 5) JEPA vs MAE (deep linear analysis + controlled generative processes)
> - Identical experimental setting (ODE simulations and Gaussian/temporal models, Figures 2–3):
>   - With matched encoders, JEPA shows greedy learning in both covariance (λ) and regression coefficient (ρ), prioritizing high‑ρ “influential” features; MAE exhibits greedy dynamics primarily in λ and is largely insensitive to ρ during training.
>   - Temporal model (Eq. 16, Figure 3): When one feature has lower covariance but higher ρ (less noisy, more predictive), JEPA learns it sooner; MAE continues to prioritize higher covariance, even if noisier.
> - ImageNet study (Appendix D, Figure 7 in appendix):
>   - For encoders trained on the full dataset, I‑JEPA’s features align more with the “bottom” (low-variance, perceptual) subspace (higher mean CCA between full and bottom representations) than MAE, and are less aligned with the “top” subspace; this matches the theory that JEPA prioritizes influential/low-variance features, while MAE tends toward variance-heavy subspaces.
> 
> Similar-type dataset comparisons (cross-paper)
> - Vision tasks: PBADet vs RCPS vs JEPA
>   - PBADet targets detection/association; on COCOHumanParts and CrowdHuman it improves association accuracy and medium/large-object detection (size AP), and reduces miss rates relative to YOLO-integrated BPJDet baselines. RCPS targets calibration: on ImageNet it reduces label usage to attain the same anytime-valid risk, not accuracy per se. JEPA’s ImageNet analysis addresses representational alignment: JEPA features emphasize perceptually useful, low-variance directions, unlike MAE.
> - Sequential learning: Dale’s Law vs JEPA theory
>   - EI RNN results emphasize that spectral properties (unimodal, clustered singular values) at initialization are decisive for learning quality; DANNs (EI‑compliant) match standard RNNs, while ColEI suffers unless spectra are corrected. JEPA theory similarly highlights representation‑level biases that influence what is learned first (ρ‑sensitivity), complementing the importance of spectral bias in recurrent settings.
> - Language / instruction following: NEFTune stands alone here
>   - On identical datasets (Alpaca/Evol‑Instruct/ShareGPT/OpenPlatypus), NEFTune consistently lifts model‑based preference win rates (often double‑digit percentage points) while preserving OpenLLM Leaderboard scores.
> 
> Per‑dataset summaries (specific highlights)
> - BodyHands (identical dataset within PBADet): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) beats BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) on Hand AP (88.1 vs 85.9), Conditional Accuracy (92.71 vs 86.91), Joint AP (85.73 vs 84.39). PBADet (YOLOv7) is stronger still (Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Acc. 92.62, Joint AP 85.98).
> - COCOHumanParts (PBADet Table 2–3): PBADet has better APM/APL and lower mean mismatch rates on most categories, while BPJDet slightly leads in overall AP and hand APs; PBADet leads on person/feet AP and on 5/6 categories of mMR−2.
> - CrowdHuman (PBADet Tables 5–6): PBADet yields lowest body MR−2 (36.5–37.5) and high body AP (~91.4–91.6), comparable or better than anchor-based YOLO variants and on par with heavier DETR-based methods; pair mismatch is roughly similar.
> - AlpacaEval (NEFTune, GPT‑4 evaluator): LLaMA‑2‑7B gains +35.79 pp (Alpaca), +10.17 pp (Evol‑Instruct), +5.65 pp (ShareGPT), +9.01 pp (OpenPlatypus); LLaMA‑2‑70B gains +13.78 pp (Evol‑Instruct). LLaMA‑2‑Chat‑7B improves +7.30 pp despite prior RLHF.
> - OpenLLM Leaderboard (NEFTune, Figure 3): Across ARC/HellaSwag/MMLU/TruthfulQA, scores remain essentially unchanged vs. standard finetuning.
> - Active RCPS (Figures 2–3): On synthetic data and ImageNet, “pretrain”/“learned” label policies achieve lower β̂ (closer to β*) with fewer labels than “all”/“oblivious,” all keeping safety violations ≤ α=0.05.
> - EI RNNs (Figures 2–7): On four benchmarks, ColEI underperforms DANNs and standard RNNs; spectrum transplant shows singular value distribution is the dominant factor; NSE at initialization predicts performance; small/few‑I ColEI nets suffer most.
> - JEPA vs MAE (Figures 2–3; Appendix D): In matched linear settings JEPA learns high‑ρ features earlier; in temporal generative models and ImageNet, JEPA prioritizes influential/low‑variance structure (higher full↔bottom CCA), while MAE emphasizes high‑variance structure.
> 
> Key takeaways across methods
> - Representation-level and training‑procedure choices shape what gets learned and how reliably: noisy token embeddings (NEFTune) markedly improve instruction‑following quality without hurting classical NLP benchmarks; JEPA’s latent prediction objective prioritizes influential/low-variance features, unlike reconstruction.
> - Architectural/initialization spectra strongly impact recurrent learning under Dale’s Law: EI‑compliant DANNs (with favorable spectra) match standard RNNs; ColEI’s multimodal, dispersed spectra correlate with poor learning; correcting spectra or using larger/more balanced EI networks mitigates this.
> - In detection, moving to a one‑stage, anchor‑free part‑to‑body offset improves association robustness, size‑specific AP, and miss rates relative to anchor‑based joint detectors, while keeping body detection competitive with state‑of‑the‑art.
> - For safety/reliability, active anytime‑valid RCPSes attain target risk with fewer labels by combining predictors and adaptive labeling, maintaining uniform‑in‑time guarantees (safety violation rates ≤ α) throughout.
> 
> Note on identical datasets
> - No dataset is shared across all five works. ImageNet appears in both RCPS (classification risk control) and JEPA (representation similarity), but tasks and metrics differ and are not directly comparable. All other named datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman, Alpaca/Evol‑Instruct/ShareGPT/OpenPlatypus, MNIST/seq‑MNIST/PTB) are unique to their respective studies.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the matching papers and a brief comparison of their experimental results:
> 
> **1. NEFTune — Noisy Embeddings Improve Instruction Finetuning (ICLR 2024)** — Adds uniform noise scaled by α/√(Ld) to token embeddings during instruction-tuning of attention-based LMs (LLaMA-1/2, OPT-6.7B, trained with Adam). Results: LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win rate jumps 29.8%→64.7%; +10% (Evol-Instruct), +8% (ShareGPT, OpenPlatypus); humans preferred NEFT in 74.6% of cases. It raises training loss but lowers test loss (less overfitting), longer outputs; OpenLLM benchmark unchanged. Dropout/weight decay don't reproduce gains; α=10, uniform noise, longer sequences best.
> 
> **2. How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)** — Analyzes joint-embedding predictive (JEPA) vs MAE objectives via solvable deep linear nets. Note: both objectives studied here use **mean-squared (L2) prediction losses**; I found no analysis in the collection comparing MSE against softmax cross-entropy for JEPA, so that specific loss comparison cannot be established. Results: JEPA prioritizes "influential" (high regression-coefficient ρ) features, with the bias strengthening with encoder depth; MAE orders features only by covariance λ and is agnostic to ρ. On ImageNet, I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE (measured by CCA), explaining JEPA's better perception performance and noise suppression.
> 
> **3. Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly (NeurIPS 2023)** — Biologically constrained recurrent nets with separate excitatory/inhibitory units (ColEI, DANN) examined via singular-value spectra. Results: ColEI learns worse and with higher variance on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, natural object recognition; gradient clipping helps most. SVD "transplant" experiments show the initial singular-value spectrum (not sign constraints or singular vectors) drives the gap — ColEI's spectrum is multimodal/dispersed, while standard RNNs/DANNs follow quarter-circle (Marchenko–Pastur) forms. Reducing inhibitory ratio worsens spectra and performance; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error.
> 
> **4. Active, Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Prediction Sets (NeurIPS 2024)** — Sequential calibration giving anytime-valid risk control with active labeling via e-processes/betting. Results: guarantees P(ρ(β̂_t)≤θ for all t)≥1−α on adaptively collected data; optimal labeling policy is proportional to conditional-risk std. Simulations and ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05) show "pretrain"/"learned" label policies cut risk faster than naive baselines while keeping safety-violation rates below α; it uses fewer labels to reach higher utility.
> 
> **5. PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)** — Anchor-free detector associating human parts (hands, face, feet) to parent bodies via a single part-to-body center offset, on YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 conv backbones with multi-scale feature maps, trained with SGD. Results (BodyHands): HandAP 89.1/88.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62/92.71, JointAP 85.98/85.73 — beating BPJDet, BodyHands, MaskRCNN baselines; on COCOHumanParts it matches/leads BPJDet on joint AP (43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3) and leads in AP_M/AP_L, feet, with lowest mMR−2 for most parts. Against ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands/feet. Note: it's evaluated with AP, joint AP, conditional accuracy, mMR−2 (and F1 vs ED-Pose) — **not** AUROC or perplexity; the question's mention of AUROC/perplexity does not match this paper.
> 
> **Cross-method comparison.** NEFTune shows that representation-level perturbation is a cheap, compute-free reliability/performance lever, echoing JEPA's finding that representation-level (latent) prediction beats input-space reconstruction for perception, and Dale's-Law work showing initialization spectra (representation geometry) dominate learning success. PBADet demonstrates that representation/association design choices (a single part-to-body offset + task alignment + multi-scale) yield large, consistent gains over two-stage or anchor-based alternatives, mirroring the theme that representation choices outweigh training-procedure tweaks. The anytime-valid method is different in kind: it provides formal statistical guarantees on risk (not accuracy) through sequential calibration, complementing the empirical gains of the others.
> 
> Caveats: the softmax cross-entropy vs MSE comparison within joint-embedding SSL, and AUROC/perplexity evaluations for PBADet, could not be established from the provided collection.

**community 最终答案**

> I found the five papers. Here is what each reports and a comparative analysis.
> 
> **1. NEFTune (noisy embeddings for instruction finetuning)** — Adding uniform noise (scaled α/√(Ld)) to token embeddings during post-training adaptation of LLaMA-2/OPT transformers: AlpacaEval win rate jumps from 29.79% to 64.69% on LLaMA-2-7B; +10% on Evol-Instruct, +8% on ShareGPT and OpenPlatypus; also helps LLaMA-2-Chat (RLHF) and QLoRA. It raises training loss but slightly lowers test loss (less overfitting) and yields longer, more coherent outputs; human annotators preferred it 74.6% of the time. OpenLLM benchmark scores are unchanged, and dropout/weight-decay do not reproduce the gains (α≈10, uniform noise, longer sequences are best). The noise rarely flips tokens (<0.4% flips) and does not change the embedding similarity spectrum.
> 
> **2. JEPA-style joint-embedding predictive SSL (deep linear analysis)** — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" analyzes self-distillation joint-embedding prediction against MAE reconstruction, both under **mean-squared (L2) objectives** (the user's "softmax cross-entropy" variant does not appear in this collection — no paper here compares MSE vs softmax-CE for joint-embedding predictive setups). The result: JEPA's MSE-in-latent objective is biased toward high-influence (high regression-coefficient ρ) features and suppresses noisy, high-variance directions, with suppression growing with encoder depth (fixed point w̄_JEPA(∞)=ρ^L vs w̄_MAE(∞)=ρ^{L/(L+1)}; 1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE). Feature learning order can invert relative to MAE when λ and ρ trend oppositely. ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster than MAE with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features (CCA).
> 
> **3. Dale's-law RNNs (E/I units) via singular-value spectra** — Constrained ColEI networks (separate excitatory/inhibitory columns) learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN variants across adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition. Spectrum "transplants" show the deficit is mostly due to the **initial recurrent-weight singular-value spectrum**, not the sign constraints or singular vectors (spectra contribute ~2% error vs ~1% for sign constraints). ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed (column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure) instead of the quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur form of standard RNNs/DANNs; normalised SVD entropy anti-correlates with final error, and fewer inhibitory units worsen both spectrum and performance. Gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> 
> **4. Anytime-valid risk control with active labeling** — Extends risk-controlling prediction sets to sequential, adaptively collected data: guarantees P(ρ(β̂_t) ≤ θ for all t) ≥ 1−α at every time step via e-processes/betting, with inverse-propensity-weighted active labeling, lower-bounded label policies, and ML control variates. Optimal labeling policy is proportional to conditional-risk standard deviation; regret bounds link policy/predictor error to wealth growth. On ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05), learned/pretrained label policies reach the target risk faster than "label all" or oblivious baselines while keeping violation rates below α, cutting label cost.
> 
> **5. PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part–body detection)** — Associates human parts to parent persons via a single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale features (YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7 backbones, trained with SGD). On BodyHands: HandAP 89.1 / Cond. Accuracy 92.62 / JointAP 85.98 (YOLOv7, 36.9M params), beating BPJDet (85.9/86.91/84.39) and BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48). On COCOHumanParts (six parts): AP_50:95 42.7 (original)/41.5 (subordinate) with YOLOv7, leading AP_M/AP_L and lowest average mMR−2 on most parts. On CrowdHuman face–body, it leads body MR−2 with competitive AP. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment learning all help; anchor-free beats anchor-based with the same representation. Against the pose estimator ED-Pose, it gives far higher precision/recall/F1 (e.g., all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; note the user's "AUROC/perplexity" metrics do not apply — the paper uses AP, MR−2, mMR−2, conditional accuracy, joint AP, and F1).
> 
> **Comparative analysis.** Across all five, a small representation- or procedure-level choice drives reliability/performance: (1) NEFTune shows noise at the embedding level during adaptation acts as a regularizer that improves conversational reliability with no compute overhead; (2) the JEPA analysis shows the latent-space MSE objective itself biases learning toward predictive, low-noise features — i.e., the objective choice, not just architecture, determines reliability; (3) the RNN study shows initialization-level spectral structure (not the biological constraint per se) explains training reliability, quantified by SVD entropy; (4) the calibration paper shows sequential betting-based calibration gives statistically guaranteed anytime-valid risk with fewer labels — reliability is formalized as a worst-case probability bound; (5) PBADet shows the representation of the association (a single part-to-body offset) plus anchor-free multi-scale detection gives consistent gains in detection and association accuracy across benchmarks. A caution for the request: the requested "MSE vs softmax cross-entropy" comparison for joint-embedding SSL and "AUROC/perplexity" evaluation for the detector are not present in the collection; the closest available evidence is the L2-based JEPA-vs-MAE analysis and AP/F1-based detector evaluation, respectively.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:287 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a real-world system that needs: (1) a lightweight single-pass model to detect hands/face and link them to the correct person in crowded scenes; (2) a practical way to boost a transformer assistant’s instruction-following via a simple fine-tuning tweak on feature embeddings; (3) online, label-efficient calibration that guarantees low risk at every time step; and (4) guidance on designing recurrent controllers that respect excitatory/inhibitory constraints. I’d also like theory explaining why predicting in a learned representation space can avoid noisy cues in self-supervised pipelines. Are there works that collectively cover these needs?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
