Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison-only synthesis of the experimental results reported in the five papers you provided. I only cite outcomes that appear in their figures/tables and refrain from adding external claims.
> 
> 1) Identical datasets: head–hand/face/body association (vision)
> - BodyHands (hand–body association)
>   - PBADet vs. prior methods (Table 1):
>     - LLaMA-2-7B not relevant here; the key comparison is PBADet vs. BPJDet and two-stage methods.
>     - Using the same backbone as BPJDet (YOLOv5l6), PBADet achieves higher Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, and Joint AP: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 88.1 Hand AP, 92.71 Conditional Accuracy, 85.73 Joint AP vs. BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 85.9, 86.91, 84.39. With a YOLOv7 backbone, PBADet further improves to 89.1, 92.62, 85.98 respectively.
>     - Conclusion on identical dataset: PBADet consistently outperforms BPJDet on BodyHands across all three metrics.
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (multi-part–to–body association)
>   - Overall and per-category APs (Table 2): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) achieves 43.0/41.8 AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate) vs. BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3 (slightly lower overall AP), but PBADet leads in APM, APL, and in person/feet APs (e.g., person 62.4 vs. 61.3, r-foot 30.9 vs. 30.2, l-foot 31.5 vs. 30.9). With a YOLOv7 backbone, PBADet records 42.7/41.5 with the strongest large-object APs.
>   - Association robustness (average mMR−2, Table 3): PBADet shows lower (better) mMR−2 than BPJDet in head, face, left/right hands, and right foot (e.g., head 27.9 vs. 30.8; face 30.5 vs. 31.8; r-hand 40.8 vs. 42.2).
>   - Conclusion on identical dataset: AP trade-offs exist, but PBADet improves association reliability (lower mMR−2) and performs best on medium/large scales and for person/feet categories.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (face–body association; Appendix Table 5 & Table 6)
>   - PBADet vs. BPJDet and crowded-pedestrian baselines: PBADet (YOLOv7) attains the best MR−2 for body (36.5) and face (44.7), and body AP 91.6, with comparable mMR−2 to BPJDet (≈50.8–50.9). PBADet also matches or exceeds several DETR-based detectors on body AP while staying efficient.
>   - Conclusion on identical dataset: PBADet achieves the best detection MR−2 and competitive AP; association mMR−2 is on par with BPJDet for this single-part task.
> 
> 2) Similar dataset types: instruction tuning and language understanding
> - Instruction tuning across four datasets (Alpaca, Evol-Instruct, ShareGPT, OpenPlatypus)
>   - LLaMA-2–7B (Table 1): AlpacaEval win-rate vs Text-Davinci-003 improves with NEFTune on all datasets:
>     - Alpaca: 29.91 → 65.70 (+35.79)
>     - Evol-Instruct: 70.19 → 80.36 (+10.17)
>     - ShareGPT: 70.57 → 76.22 (+5.65)
>     - OpenPlatypus: 60.95 → 69.96 (+9.01)
>     - Average: 57.91 → 73.06 (+15.15)
>   - Across models (Figure 2; Table 2):
>     - OPT-6.7B, LLaMA-1–7B, and LLaMA-2–7B all improve on AlpacaEval with NEFTune.
>     - Larger LLaMA-2 models also benefit: 13B improves (Evol-Instruct) 72.61 → 82.04; 70B improves 75.03 → 88.81.
>     - Even LLaMA-2-Chat–7B (already RLHF-tuned) gains: 74.44 → 81.74 on Evol-Instruct.
>   - OpenLLM Leaderboard (Figure 3): ARC, HellaSwag, MMLU, TruthfulQA scores remain essentially unchanged after NEFTune (e.g., for LLaMA-2–7B Alpaca: 56.4/80.0/47.9/41.6 vs 56.1/80.1/47.7/42.5), indicating no loss on these established tasks.
>   - Resource-constrained finetuning (Table 3): With QLoRA, NEFTune still yields win-rate gains on AlpacaEval across sizes/datasets (smaller boosts than full finetuning).
>   - Conclusion on similar dataset family: NEFTune consistently improves conversational quality (AlpacaEval) across multiple instruction datasets and model sizes, without degrading standard multiclass benchmarks.
> 
> 3) Similar dataset types: online calibration/label-efficiency and safety
> - Active, anytime-valid RCPS (Figures 2–3 in the paper)
>   - Simulation (θ = 0.1, α = 0.05, label budget B = 0.3): “pretrain” and “learned” labeling policies reduce β (the calibration parameter) faster and closer to the theoretical optimum β* (dotted line shown at 0.5578) using fewer labels than the baselines “all” (label everything) and “oblivious” (label uniformly at random).
>   - Safety: Average safety violation rate is controlled below the target α = 0.05 across methods (Figure 2a), with active policies maintaining the guarantee while being more label-efficient.
>   - ImageNet experiments: The same ranking holds—“pretrain”/“learned” policies reach smaller β with fewer labels than baselines, while obeying anytime-valid risk control.
>   - Conclusion: Under an identical evaluation protocol (anytime-valid e-process tests), using predictors and active policies improves label efficiency over baselines without sacrificing the safety guarantee.
> 
> 4) Similar dataset types: recurrent controllers with E/I constraints
> - Learning with Dale’s Law (Figures 2–7 in the paper)
>   - Across identical tasks (Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task), ColEI (column-constrained E/I) networks learn worse and exhibit higher variance than both standard RNNs and DANNs (recurrent Dale’s ANNs). DANNs match standard RNNs across these tasks.
>   - Spectral results explain performance: ColEI shows dispersed, multimodal singular-value spectra with a heavy tail; DANNs and standard RNNs exhibit clustered, unimodal spectra (quarter-circle behavior). Spectrum “transplant” experiments reveal spectrum dominates sign constraints in determining performance.
>   - Scaling studies: ColEI performance improves with larger network size and more balanced E/I ratios; Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) correlates with test error (higher NSE → better performance). DANNs remain robust even with very few inhibitory units, maintaining favorable spectra and performance.
>   - Conclusion: Under the same tasks, DANNs ≈ standard RNNs; ColEI underperforms. The experimental comparisons tightly link singular-value spectrum shape to learning outcomes.
> 
> 5) Similar dataset types: representation prediction vs input reconstruction
> - JEPA vs MAE (linear theory + controlled experiments)
>   - Controlled simulations (Figures 1–4): Deep JEPAs learn “influential” features (high regression coefficients ρ) earlier; MAEs prioritize high covariance (λ). When λ and ρ are in conflict, JEPA reverses learning order relative to MAE. This is most pronounced with deeper encoders.
>   - Temporal model (Figure 3): In a linear temporal generative setting, λa = γa||va||^2 and ρa = γa||va||^2/(σa^2+||va||^2). JEPA’s preference for high-ρ features slows learning of noisy modes relative to MAE.
>   - ImageNet-1K (Appendix D, Figure 7): With ViT encoders trained on identical data, I-JEPA features show higher similarity between full-data and bottom-PCA-subspace images (and lower similarity for full vs top-PCA-subspace) earlier in training than MAE. This empirically supports that predicting in representation space emphasizes informative (lower-variance, semantic) directions compared to pixel reconstruction.
>   - Conclusion: On identical training corpora (ImageNet-1K at 64×64) and controlled models, JEPA exhibits a bias toward predictive, low-noise features versus MAE. This mechanistic difference is experimentally visible in feature-similarity dynamics.
> 
> 6) Specific dataset highlights (numbers taken directly from the papers)
> - BodyHands: PBADet (YOLOv7) Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 88.1/92.71/85.73; vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39.
> - COCOHumanParts: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) APM/APL 66.2/67.2 (original) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 63.8/61.8 (original APs differ; PBADet leads on M/L and person/feet categories). Association mMR−2: PBADet lower across most parts (head 27.9 vs 30.8, face 30.5 vs 31.8, r-hand 40.8 vs 42.2, etc.).
> - CrowdHuman: PBADet (YOLOv7) body MR−2 36.5 (best), face MR−2 44.7 (best), body AP 91.6 (best), association mMR−2 ≈ 50.8–50.9 (comparable to BPJDet).
> - AlpacaEval (LLaMA-2–7B): Alpaca 29.91 → 65.70; Evol-Instruct 70.19 → 80.36; ShareGPT 70.57 → 76.22; OpenPlatypus 60.95 → 69.96; Average 57.91 → 73.06.
> - AlpacaEval (LLaMA-2–Chat 7B / 13B / 70B): Evol-Instruct 74.44 → 81.74 (Chat-7B); 72.61 → 82.04 (13B); 75.03 → 88.81 (70B).
> - OpenLLM Leaderboard (LLaMA-2–7B examples): Arc/HellaSwag/MMLU/TruthfulQA essentially unchanged pre/post NEFTune.
> - Active RCPS: In both simulation and ImageNet experiments, “pretrain” and “learned” policies reach smaller β (closer to the dotted β* = 0.5578 in sim) with fewer labels, while safety violation rate remains ≤ 0.05.
> - RNNs with Dale’s Law: On Adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and natural object recognition, ColEI underperforms; DANNs ≈ standard RNNs. Spectral pathology (multi-modal singular values with large modes) correlates with worse learning; larger networks and balanced E/I improve ColEI.
> - JEPA vs MAE: On synthetic/linear settings and ImageNet-1K (ViT) pretraining, JEPA prioritizes high-ρ (predictive/low-noise) features; MAE prioritizes high-λ (variance) features; I-JEPA aligns faster with bottom-PCA subspace than MAE.
> 
> 7) Overall comparative takeaways across methods
> - On identical vision association datasets, PBADet provides the strongest single-pass part/body detection-association trade-off: highest BodyHands metrics, better association robustness on COCOHumanParts (mMR−2), and best MR−2/AP on CrowdHuman body/face detection with competitive association.
> - On similar instruction-tuning datasets, NEFTune consistently increases conversational win-rate (AlpacaEval) across models/datasets without hurting standard multiple-choice benchmarks; gains persist even with QLoRA and on already RLHF-tuned LLaMA-2-Chat.
> - For online, label-efficient calibration, active anytime-valid RCPS policies using predictors are empirically more label-efficient than “all”/“oblivious,” converging faster toward optimal β* while controlling risk at every time.
> - For recurrent controllers under Dale’s Law, DANNs experimentally match standard RNNs, whereas ColEI underperforms; experiments attribute this primarily to spectral properties rather than sign constraints alone.
> - For self-supervised representation learning, I-JEPA vs MAE experiments on the same ImageNet-1K data corroborate theory: JEPAs focus on influential (predictive, low-variance) features, while MAEs stress high-variance reconstruction, explaining observed differences in learned feature subspaces over training.
> 
> These conclusions are strictly drawn from the reported tables/figures in the supplied papers.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — five works in this collection collectively cover all your needs:
> 
> **1. Hand/face detection + person association in crowds: PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> One-stage, anchor-free, single-pass detector linking parts (hands, face, head, feet) to parent bodies via a part-to-body center offset, built on YOLOv5/YOLOv7.
> - *BodyHands:* beats all baselines on hand AP, conditional accuracy, and joint AP; YOLOv7 is smaller than BPJDet(YOLOv5m6) yet performs better.
> - *COCOHumanParts:* AP on par with BPJDet but leads on AP_M/AP_L and has the lowest mMR−2 for head, face, both hands, right foot.
> - *CrowdHuman (face-body):* best MR−2 for body/face (YOLOv7), competitive AP — advantage over BPJDet shrinks because it's a single-part task.
> - *vs. ED-Pose:* much higher precision/recall/F1 on hands and feet (e.g., all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51).
> 
> **2. Instruction-following via embedding tweak: NEFTune** (ICLR 2024)
> Adds noise to embeddings during instruction fine-tuning only. LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win rate jumps 29.8→64.7 (+34.9); +10% Evol-Instruct, +8% ShareGPT, +8% OpenPlatypus; works on RLHF'd LLaMA-2-Chat and QLoRA. Humans prefer NEFT 74.6% of the time; OpenLLM benchmark scores unchanged (gain is conversational, not factual).
> 
> **3. Online, label-efficient, anytime-valid risk control: "Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> Extends RCPS to the sequential setting with guarantees holding simultaneously at *all* time steps (P(ρ(β̂ₜ)≤θ ∀t) ≥ 1−α), with active labeling under a budget. Experiments (θ=0.1, α=0.05; simulations + ImageNet) show learned/pretrained labeling policies reach the risk target with fewer labels and lower violation rates than naive baselines.
> 
> **4. Recurrent controllers respecting E/I constraints: "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Compares sign-constrained ColEI RNNs, DANN RNNs, and standard RNNs. Finding: poor learning of ColEI is due to multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization, not sign constraints; recurrent DANNs match standard RNN performance and are robust to E/I ratio (even 1 inhibitory neuron). Normalized SVD entropy at initialization predicts trainability — useful design guidance.
> 
> **5. Theory for latent-space prediction avoiding noise: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> Analyzes deep linear self-distillation: JEPA is implicitly biased toward high-influence (high regression-coefficient) features and is slower to learn noisy features than MAE; depth strengthens noise suppression. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE features (CCA).
> 
> **Comparative analysis across the set:**
> - All five are lightweight/simple in mechanism: one-stage detection, a noise-augmentation trick, betting-based calibration, reparameterized E/I weight structure, and gradient-flow analysis — no heavy pipelines.
> - Empirically strongest gains where each target: PBADet gives the largest margin over prior art on multi-part association (BodyHands/COCOHumanParts) and degrades to parity on the single-part CrowdHuman face task; NEFTune's gains are large but confined to conversational quality; the RCPS work's gains are label-efficiency (faster risk reduction at same violation rate); the Dale's Law work shows architecture choice (DANN vs ColEI) matters more than constraint type; JEPA analysis is validated qualitatively on ImageNet despite being derived for deep linear models.
> - Limitations noted: PBADet's advantage shrinks for single-part tasks; NEFTune's mechanism isn't fully explained; the calibration guarantees assume i.i.d. streams and bounded label policies; JEPA theory assumes linear networks/special initialization; ColEI performance is worst for small networks with few inhibitory units.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes — the collection contains works that collectively cover all five needs, one per area:
> 
> 1. **Hands/face detection + person linking in crowded scenes — PBADet** (one-stage, anchor-free part-to-body association detector on YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones; handles head/face/left/right hands/feet linked to the parent body via a single part-to-body center offset).
> 2. **Instruction-following boost via an embedding tweak — NEFTune** (adds uniform noise scaled by α/√(Ld) to embeddings during instruction fine-tuning).
> 3. **Online, label-efficient calibration with anytime-valid low risk — "Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Active Labeling"** (extends RCPS to the sequential/active setting via e-processes and betting, guaranteeing ρ(β̂ₜ) ≤ θ simultaneously for all t with probability ≥ 1−α).
> 4. **Recurrent controllers with excitatory/inhibitory constraints — "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (analyzes sign-constrained E/I RNNs and gives construction guidance via initial spectral properties).
> 5. **Theory for predicting in learned representation space avoiding noisy cues — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (deep linear self-distillation analysis; JEPA prioritizes high-influence features and learns noisy features more slowly than MAE, converging to lower amplitude weights on noise).
> 
> **Comparison and analysis of experimental results**
> 
> - **PBADet**: On BodyHands it surpasses all baselines on every metric — hand AP 89.1 (YOLOv7) and 88.1 (YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet's 84.0–85.9, with conditional accuracy 92.62/92.71 vs 85.68–86.91 and joint AP 85.98/85.73 vs 77.86–84.39 — and the YOLOv7 variant wins despite being smaller (36.9M params) than BPJDet-YOLOv5m6 (41.2M) and despite a lower input size (1024 vs 1536). On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet on overall AP but leads on person/feet APs and has the lowest average mMR−2 (e.g., 27.9/30.5 vs 29.7–30.8 head/face for YOLOv5l6). On CrowdHuman (face–body association) it achieves the best body MR−2 (36.5, YOLOv7) and competitive AP, though its advantage over BPJDet is smaller for this single-part task. Against pose estimator ED-Pose (Swin-L), PBADet is dramatically better on small parts (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51). Ablations show anchor-free part-to-body beats anchor-based body-to-part (JointAP 85.98 vs 78.13 at fewer params). Note the collection only covers detection/association of these parts and doesn't itself show "face" detection in PBADet's main two datasets — face appears in COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman — so the face+hand combination is partially covered.
> 
> - **NEFTune**: LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win rate rises from 29.8% to 64.7% (+34.9 points); Evol-Instruct +10%, ShareGPT +8%, OpenPlatypus +8% (average +15.1). Gains hold across model sizes, OPT, RLHF'd LLaMA-2-Chat, and QLoRA. Human annotators prefer NEFT in 74.6% of cases; a modified pairwise GPT-4 evaluation gives 92.8% wins. Crucially, OpenLLM benchmark performance stays the same — the improvement is conversational instruction-following, not factual tasks. Ablations: α=10 and uniform noise are best; longer sequences help; dropout/weight decay don't reproduce the gains.
> 
> - **Anytime-valid risk control**: Simulations and ImageNet experiments (θ=0.1, α=0.05) show learned/pretrained labeling policies (optimal policy ∝ conditional-risk standard deviation, with ML control variate) cut risk faster than naive baselines while keeping violation rates below α; the optimal policy/predictor choices are characterized with regret bounds relating estimation error to the wealth process. This gives the per-timestep risk guarantee (P(ρ(β̂ₜ)≤θ for all t) ≥ 1−α), with limitations of i.i.d. data and bounded label policies.
> 
> - **Dale's-law RNNs**: ColEI (column-constrained E/I) networks learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN networks; gradient clipping mitigates the deficit. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum at initialization (multimodal/dispersed for ColEI vs quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur for RNNs/DANNs) matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors (sign constraints explain ~0.7–1% error, spectrum ~1.5–2% of the ~2.3% gap). Reducing inhibitory neurons worsens spectra and performance; DANN stays robust even with one inhibitory neuron; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance across sizes/EI ratios — directly usable as design guidance for E/I recurrent controllers.
> 
> - **JEPA vs MAE theory**: In the linear setting, JEPA has an implicit bias toward high-influence (high regression coefficient) features, with derived critical times showing depth strengthens noise suppression, while MAE's ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ; JEPA converges to lower amplitude weights on noisy features, making them less likely to be used downstream. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features do. This is the theoretical explanation for why latent-space prediction avoids noisy cues, though it's formally proven only for deep linear networks under special initialization.
> 
> So collectively the four/five papers match your requirements, and their experimental results are each validated on appropriate benchmarks (crowded person/part datasets, AlpacaEval-style instruction evaluation, risk-control simulations + ImageNet, sequential MNIST/PTB/object recognition, and ImageNet CCA analysis respectively).

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:293 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m deploying a resource‑constrained system that must: (a) robustly detect which person’s hands/face belong to which body for gesture control, (b) ship a coding copilot fine‑tuned via supervised/instruction tuning, and (c) train efficiently on limited GPUs. I need references on: an anchor‑free part–body detector for multi‑person scenes; instruction‑tuning of code LLMs on permissive data; optimizer state compression to 4‑bit for Adam‑style training; why latent‑space prediction in self‑supervised setups outperforms pixel reconstruction for useful features; and how E/I (Dale‑style) constraints change RNN spectra and stability. We’ll evaluate with Precision/F1 and cosine‑similarity probes, train with CE/MSE losses using SGD/AdamW, and prefer lightweight, end‑to‑end LoRA updates. Which papers fit this end‑to‑end pipeline?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Papers that fit your end‑to‑end pipeline
> - Anchor‑free part–body detector for multi‑person scenes: PBADet (ICLR 2024)
> - Instruction‑tuning of code LLMs on permissive data: OCTOPACK (COMMITPACK/COMMITPACKFT, HUMANEVALPACK, models OCTOCODER/OCTOGEEX)
> - Optimizer state compression to 4‑bit for Adam‑style training: Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Why latent‑space prediction (JEPA) beats pixel reconstruction (MAE) in self‑supervised setups: How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)
> - How E/I (Dale‑style) constraints change RNN spectra and stability: Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)
> 
> Comparative summary of experimental results (derived from the papers’ figures and tables)
> 
> 1) Anchor‑free part–body association (PBADet) vs prior detectors on identical datasets
> - BodyHands (identical dataset across methods; Table 1):
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98, outperforming BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) at 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39. PBADet (YOLOv5l6) also improves to 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73.
> - COCOHumanParts (identical; Table 2 & 3):
>   • All‑categories detection AP: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) has AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 and AP.5 70.0/68.4 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3 and 70.6/69.8 (BPJDet slightly higher overall AP).
>   • Size stratification: PBADet leads on medium/large objects (APM 66.2/65.0; APL 67.2/64.4) vs BPJDet (63.8/63.2; 61.8/58.9).
>   • Per‑category APs: Mixed—PBADet improves person (62.4 vs 61.3) and feet (l‑foot 31.5 vs 30.9; r‑foot 37.7 vs 39.6 slightly lower) while BPJDet remains higher on head/face/hands in some cases.
>   • Association accuracy (lower mMR−2 is better; Table 3): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) reduces mismatch rates across categories (e.g., l‑hand 36.2 vs BPJDet 41.6; r‑hand 40.8 vs 42.2; head 27.9 vs 30.8; face 30.5 vs 31.8; r‑foot 50.4 vs 49.1; l‑foot 47.9 vs 50.4).
> - CrowdHuman (identical; Tables 5 & 6):
>   • Detection: PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves best body MR−2 36.5 and body AP 91.6 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 40.7 / 89.5. Face MR−2 also improves (44.7 vs 46.3). Pair mMR−2 is comparable (PBADet 50.8 vs BPJDet 50.1).
> - Ablations (Table 4, Table 8):
>   • Adding the association prediction head boosts conditional/joint metrics without hurting part AP; anchor‑free formulation and part‑to‑body offsets outperform anchor‑based definitions.
> 
> 2) Instruction‑tuned code LLMs on HUMANEVALPACK (3 tasks × 6 languages; identical benchmark across models)
> - Overall leaderboard (Table 2):
>   • Among permissive models, OCTOCODER (16B) attains the highest average pass@1 across HUMANEVALFIX, HUMANEVALEXPLAIN, HUMANEVALSYNTHESIZE (e.g., Python scores: 30.4 / 35.1 / 46.2).
>   • OCTOGEEX (6B) also surpasses prior permissive baselines and is the smallest model evaluated.
>   • GPT‑4 (closed) is highest overall (e.g., Python: 47.0 / 64.6 / 86.6), but OCTOCODER is best among commercially usable models.
> - Task difficulty and model behavior (Figures & Table 2):
>   • Code synthesis (HUMANEVALSYNTHESIZE) is easiest: GPT‑4 near saturation (Python pass@1 86.6); OCTOCODER leads permissive models (Python 46.2), improving over StarCoder (33.6).
>   • Code repair (HUMANEVALFIX) is most challenging: OCTOCODER improves targeted bug‑fix success across languages vs baselines; models often regenerate buggy code unchanged or introduce new bugs (qualitative failures noted in figures).
>   • Code explanation (HUMANEVALEXPLAIN): models must output natural language then reconstruct code; many pretrained code models (e.g., StarCoder, CodeGeeX2) fail by outputting code instead of text; OCTOCODER/OCTOGEEX, instruction‑tuned with NL outputs, achieve substantially higher pass@1 than pure code models.
> - Instruction data ablation (Figure 4):
>   • COMMITPACKFT+OASST yields the best average performance across the three tasks; COMMITPACKFT is particularly important for code repair (≈20% bug‑fix commits in its mix), while OASST contributes NL targets required for explanation.
> 
> 3) 4‑bit optimizer states for efficient training (identical tasks across optimizers)
> - Accuracy vs 32‑bit and 8‑bit baselines (Table 2):
>   • NLU (RoBERTa‑L, GLUE mean): 4‑bit AdamW 89.1, matching 8‑bit AdamW 89.1 and 32‑bit 88.9.
>   • Image classification (Swin‑T, ImageNet‑1k Acc): 4‑bit AdamW 80.8–80.9, comparable to 32‑bit 81.2 and 8‑bit 81.0.
>   • NLG (GPT‑2 Medium, E2E BLEU): 4‑bit AdamW 67.8, slightly above 32‑bit 67.7 and 8‑bit 67.5.
>   • QA (RoBERTa‑L, SQuAD F1): 4‑bit AdamW 94.5, matching 32‑bit 94.6 and 8‑bit 94.5.
>   • MT (Transformer‑Base, WMT14 en‑de SacreBleu): 4‑bit AdamW 26.28, on par with 32‑bit 26.61 and 8‑bit 26.66.
> - Instruction tuning of LLaMA (Table 3):
>   • Across MMLU and commonsense tasks, 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit performance at all scales (e.g., LLaMA‑7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; LLaMA‑13B 47.4 vs 46.5).
> - Memory/time and model size (Tables 4 & 5):
>   • Training memory drops up to 57.7% (LLaMA‑7B: 75.4 GB → 31.9 GB) with similar throughput (fused implementation); RoBERTa‑L and GPT‑2 Medium also reduce memory ~35–47%.
>   • Largest trainable models under fixed GPU memory increase (e.g., 24 GB: OPT‑350M → OPT‑1.3B; 80 GB: OPT‑1.3B → OPT‑6.7B; single 80 GB GPU can fine‑tune LLaMA‑7B).
> - Second‑moment quantization ablations (Table 1):
>   • Excluding the zero point in the second moment is critical for stability and accuracy (DE‑0 or Linear mapping). Rank‑1 normalization + Linear mapping yields BLEU 67.8 with 0% instability, matching/intentionally improving over 32‑bit baselines on E2E.
> 
> 4) JEPA vs MAE (latent‑space prediction vs pixel reconstruction) on identical simulation settings, plus an ImageNet probe
> - Feature learning order (Figure 2):
>   • With monotonically increasing covariances λ and regression coefficients ρ (Distribution 1), both JEPA and MAE show greedy dynamics w.r.t. λ.
>   • When λ increases but ρ decreases (Distribution 2), JEPA inverts the learning order—prioritizing high‑ρ features first—while MAE retains λ‑driven order. This difference appears in deeper encoders (Figure 4), where JEPA’s depth accentuates prioritization by ρ.
> - Temporal model (Figure 3):
>   • As temporal correlation γ and noise σ vary by mode, JEPA tracks higher‑ρ (more predictive, lower‑noise) features; the plots show JEPA’s learned λ and ρ matching simulations, indicating preference for informative features.
> - Vision experiment (Appendix D, Figure 7):
>   • Mean CCA over ImageNet representations: I‑JEPA aligns more with “bottom” PCA subspace (low‑variance, perceptual features) than MAE, and less with “top” variance subspace. Curves for I‑JEPA are consistently higher on full‑bottom and lower on full‑top than MAE, supporting JEPA’s useful feature bias.
> 
> 5) Dale‑style E/I constraints and RNN stability/spectra (identical tasks across architectures)
> - Benchmark tasks (Figure 2 A–D):
>   • ColEI (simple E/I column partition) underperforms DANN and standard RNN on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and naturalistic object recognition; training variance and instability are higher for ColEI, especially without gradient clipping.
> - Spectrum transplant experiments (Figure 4 B–C):
>   • Transplanting singular value spectra vs singular vectors vs sign constraints shows spectra matter most: changing spectrum accounts for larger test‑error shifts (e.g., ~1.5%±0.3% for RNN, ~2%±1% for ColEI) than freezing parameter signs (~0.7–1% changes). Conclusion: ColEI’s multimodal, dispersed singular values (with large modes) drive poor learning; DANN/standard RNNs have unimodal, clustered spectra.
> - EI ratio and network size (Figures 5–7):
>   • Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance: lower inhibitory proportion lowers NSE and hurts accuracy; larger networks increase NSE and improve accuracy even when max singular value grows. Plots show anti‑correlation between test error and NSE across EI ratios and network sizes.
> 
> Where identical datasets/benchmarks enable direct comparison
> - PBADet vs BPJDet/Hier R‑CNN: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman—all identical datasets with shared metrics (AP, MR−2, mMR−2).
> - OCTOPACK vs other code LLMs: HUMANEVALPACK (same tasks, languages, and pass@1 metric).
> - 4‑bit optimizers vs 8/32‑bit baselines: identical models/datasets across NLU (GLUE), CLS (ImageNet‑1k), NLG (E2E), QA (SQuAD), MT (WMT14); also identical instruction‑tuning evaluations for LLaMA.
> - JEPA vs MAE: identical deep‑linear settings and sampling distributions; a shared ImageNet probing setup.
> - E/I RNNs: identical tasks (adding, seq‑MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition) across ColEI, DANN, and standard RNNs, plus controlled spectrum‑transplant experiments.
> 
> Takeaways for your deployment
> - Robust multi‑person part–body association: PBADet’s anchor‑free, single part‑to‑body offset improves BodyHands and CrowdHuman detection and association metrics; on COCOHumanParts it trades slightly lower overall AP for notably better medium/large object AP and lower mismatches across hands/feet.
> - Coding copilot (SFT/instruction‑tuned): OCTOCODER (COMMITPACKFT+OASST) is the strongest permissive code LLM across HUMANEVALPACK; it handles synthesis, explanation, and targeted repairs better than prior permissive baselines.
> - Efficient training on limited GPUs: 4‑bit AdamW with Rank‑1 normalization + Linear second‑moment mapping achieves near‑parity accuracy with substantial memory savings and enables larger models under fixed budgets; ablations show excluding zero‑point for the second moment is key for stability.
> - Self‑supervised pretraining choice: JEPA’s latent prediction yields features more aligned with perceptual/low‑variance directions (higher mean CCA on bottom PCA space) and prioritizes informative (high‑ρ) features, unlike MAE’s reconstruction bias.
> - Stable recurrent dynamics under E/I constraints: Using DANN‑style architectures (which preserve Dale’s Law but exhibit unimodal, clustered spectra) recovers standard‑RNN‑like performance; ColEI’s multimodal singular value spectrum correlates with poor learning—NSE is a practical diagnostic for EI‑RNN initialization stability.
> 
> Metrics used in the papers match your evaluation choices
> - Precision/F1: Reported for pose/part association vs ED‑Pose (Appendix A.2 in PBADet) and for GLUE/SQuAD tasks (Tables 2, 7, 9 in 4‑bit optimizer).
> - Cosine similarity probes: Mean CCA curves in JEPA’s appendices (Figure 7) reflect representation similarity analyses.
> - CE/MSE losses, SGD/AdamW, LoRA: 4‑bit paper uses SGD/AdamW and reports AdamW variants; Octopack and LLaMA tuning follow supervised/instruction tuning regimes compatible with LoRA; PBADet uses IoU/DFL/CE losses; JEPA analysis is in deep linear settings with MSE.
> 
> All comparisons above are drawn directly from the cited tables and figures in the provided papers.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Papers that fit your pipeline
> 
> Your five requirements map to five papers (plus one alternative):
> 
> | Requirement | Paper |
> |---|---|
> | (a) Anchor-free part–body detection | **PBADet** (Gao et al., ICLR 2024) |
> | (b) Instruction-tuning code LLM on permissive data | **OctoPack** (Muennighoff et al.) |
> | (c) 4-bit Adam-style optimizer states | **4-bit Optimizers** (Li, Chen, Zhu, NeurIPS 2023) |
> | (d) Latent-space vs pixel-reconstruction SSL | **“Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features”** (Littwin et al.) |
> | (e) E/I (Dale) constraints on RNN spectra/stability | **“Why Dale’s Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly”** (Li, Cornford et al., NeurIPS 2023) |
> 
> A secondary fit for (b) is **NEFTune** (noisy embeddings during instruction fine-tuning), but for "permissive-data code instruction tuning," OctoPack is the direct match.
> 
> ## Experimental results — comparison and analysis
> 
> **(a) PBADet.** Uses a single part-to-body center offset, so association stays valid even when parts are occluded (unlike BPJDet's body-to-part offsets). Results (BodyHands): anchor-free part-to-body YOLOv7 gives Hand AP 89.1 / conditional accuracy 92.62 / joint AP 85.98 vs BPJDet anchor-based body-to-part 85.3 / 86.80 / 78.13 — better on all three, with fewer params (36.9M vs 41.2M). Ablations show the association head, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment all contribute; vs the pose estimator ED-Pose, PBADet yields substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet. Its advantage is largest for multi-part scenes; on single-part CrowdHuman face–body association the gap over BPJDet shrinks.
> 
> **(b) OctoPack.** COMMITPACKFT is ~2GB of permissively licensed commit-message instructions (filtered from 4TB). Instruction-tuning StarCoder → OctoCoder, the best *permissive* model on HumanEvalPack (Python synthesis pass@1 = 46.2% vs StarCoder 33.6; Table 2 beats CodeGeeX2, WizardCoder, etc.), but still below GPT-4 (86.6%). Ablations are the key insight: COMMITPACKFT drives the fix task, and natural-language targets (OASST) are required for explanation — pure code-target data alone fails explain. So the recipe is data mixing, not just data volume. (NEFTune shows an orthogonal lever: embedding noise lifts LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval 29.8→64.7 without extra compute, but it doesn't address permissive-data code tuning directly.)
> 
> **(c) 4-bit optimizer.** Matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE, SQuAD QA, ImageNet, E2E-NLG, MT, and LLaMA fine-tuning (e.g., LLaMA-33B 32-bit vs 4-bit scores are essentially tied), while cutting memory: LLaMA-7B 75.4→31.9GB (57.7% saved, trainable on one 80GB GPU), RoBERTa-L ~43%, GPT-2 ~33%, with 4-bitFactor going further. Technical findings: moments have heterogeneous outlier patterns; small block size (B128) helps the first moment, and a zero-point-excluding linear quantizer + rank-1 normalization solves the second moment's zero-point problem. It composes with LoRA-style delta tuning, and offloading/fusion recover speed (fused 4-bit AdamW ≈ 8-bit time).
> 
> **(d) JEPA vs MAE.** Latent-space prediction (JEPA/self-distillation) is biased toward *high-influence* features (high regression coefficients), learning high-variance but noise-correlated features slowly — i.e., it implicitly suppresses uninformative pixel noise. MAE reconstructs in input space and is ordered by eigenvalue, so it captures variance-explaining but often perceptually unhelpful content. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features (measured by CCA) than MAE. This is the mechanistic justification for your choice of latent prediction over reconstruction.
> 
> **(e) Dale's-law RNNs.** The naive "ColEI" (whole-column sign constraints) gives multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization (rank-one column-mean + random matrix structure), which impairs learning on all four benchmarks, raises variance, and makes networks unstable without gradient clipping. DANN-style E/I architecture (separate E/I units) restores a unimodal, random-matrix-like spectrum like standard RNNs and learns just as well, robust even to 1 inhibitory unit. Spectrum "transplants" show the spectrum matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors (2% vs ~1% error effect); normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at init predicts final error. So: E/I constraints *per se* aren't the problem — the induced spectrum is.
> 
> **Coherence check for your pipeline:** PBADet's detection precision feeds gesture control; OctoPack's permissive-data mixing (commit + natural language) fits your supervised/instruction fine-tuning with CE/MSE and SGD/AdamW; the 4-bit optimizer gives the limited-GPU training efficiency and composes with LoRA/AdamW; the JEPA result justifies latent-space SSL under your cosine-similarity probes; and the Dale's-law study tells you that if you add E/I constraints to any recurrent module, design it DANN-style (not ColEI) to keep a healthy spectrum and stability. Note one caveat: nothing in the collection evaluates these five methods jointly end-to-end — they are component-level matches, and any integration (e.g., 4-bit states + LoRA on the detector/LLM) is your own combination, not an experimentally validated pipeline here.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers fitting each pipeline stage
> 
> | Requirement | Paper | Doc |
> |---|---|---|
> | (a) Anchor-free part–body detector | **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024) | `08b70bc3…` |
> | (b) Instruction-tuning code LLMs on permissive data | **OctoPack: Instruction Tuning Code LLMs** (CommitPack/HumanEvalPack, OctoCoder) | `d7b75fa4…` |
> | (c) 4-bit Adam-style optimizer states | **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023) | `8d5e1455…` |
> | (d) Latent-space vs pixel prediction in SSL | **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation** | `40fde037…` |
> | (e) Dale-style E/I constraints on RNN spectra/stability | **Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023) | `e63a94c4…` |
> 
> Supporting fit: PBADet is one-stage/anchor-free (single part-to-body center offset, YOLOv5/v7/v8 backbones, multi-scale) — exactly (a). OctoPack is permissively licensed (CommitPack 4TB Git commits, 350 languages; CommitPackFT 2GB) with a human-written 3-task × 6-language benchmark — fits (b). The 4-bit optimizer paper enables LLaMA-7B fine-tuning on one 80GB GPU (57.7% memory savings) — fits (c) and limited GPUs; it also cites LoRA as a complementary memory saver. The JEPA paper explains why latent-space prediction wins — fits (d). The Dale's-law paper analyzes spectra/stability — fits (e).
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **PBADet (a).** On COCO vs. the multi-person pose estimator ED-Pose (Precision/Recall/F1): left hand 37.6/60.8/**46.5** vs 18.4/30.3/22.9; right hand 38.6/61.3/47.3 vs 19.6/31.6/24.2; all parts F1 **48.5** vs 31.5; feet F1 ~50–51 vs ~40. It also beats BPJDet (anchor-based, body-to-part offsets, degrades with more parts) and HierR-CNN on BodyHands/COCO-HumanParts, and leads CrowdHuman face–body association (MR-2) with competitive AP. Ablations: the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning each improve association; removing any one degrades hand accuracy, conditional accuracy, and joint AP.
> 
> **OctoPack (b).** OctoCoder (16B StarCoder) is the best permissively licensed model on HumanEvalPack: 46.2% pass@1 Python synthesis (≈38% relative gain over StarCoder), best across all 3 tasks/6 languages; OctoGeeX (6B) beats all prior permissive models while being smallest. GPT-4 leads overall (86.6% Python) but is closed/non-permissive. Ablations: CommitPackFT is essential for code repair (~20% bug-fix data); natural-language-target data (OASST) is required for explanation (code-only Self-Instruct always outputs code); all datasets give similar synthesis gains; CommitPackFT+OASST gives the best average (+23% absolute over StarCoder).
> 
> **4-bit optimizers (c).** 4-bit AdamW ≈ 32-bit AdamW on NLU (RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9), classification (Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2), NLG (GPT-2M 67.8 vs 67.7), QA F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), MT (26.28 vs 26.61), and lossless Alpaca instruction tuning; it beats 8-bit AdamW on memory (LLaMA-7B: 31.9GB vs 75.4GB = 57.7% saved; RoBERTa-L 43.1%). Key design: smaller block size (B128) + DE for the first moment; zero-point-excluded linear/rank-1 normalization for the second moment; factorized second moment (4-bitFactor) gives further savings. Convergence proof given for quantized SGD(M). Limitation: optimal quantization may be task-dependent.
> 
> **JEPA vs MAE (d).** In deep linear networks, JEPA has an implicit bias toward high-influence features (high regression coefficients) and prioritizes high-ρ features at critical times, with depth strengthening noise suppression; MAE's feature ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ, so it keeps noisy/unpredictable pixel information. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features — quantitatively explaining why latent-space prediction yields more useful, robust features.
> 
> **Dale's-law RNNs (e).** ColEI (column sign-constrained) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance on all four benchmarks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition); gradient clipping helps them most. Cause: the ColEI weight matrix = rank-one nilpotent (column-mean) matrix + zero-mean random matrix, giving a multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum, whereas standard RNNs/DANNs show unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the spectrum contributes more than sign constraints (sign constraints cost only ~0.7–1%, but the total gap is 2.3±0.6% on sMNIST). Smaller networks with fewer inhibitory units are worse; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance; recurrent DANNs stay robust even with a single inhibitory neuron.
> 
> **Pipeline-level takeaways.** PBADet is evaluated with exactly your Precision/F1 protocol; OctoPack covers your coding-copilot stage; the 4-bit optimizer is the GPU-memory lever (and pairs with LoRA); the JEPA analysis supports your cosine-similarity/latent-probe evaluation rationale; the Dale's-law paper explains how E/I constraints alter spectra and stability (NSE as a pre-training diagnostic). One caution from the context: none of these papers jointly trains all stages, and the Dale's-law/JEPA papers are analyses (deep-linear theory) rather than deployment recipes, so end-to-end integration would be your contribution.

> Below is a method-by-method, dataset-grounded comparison of the experimental results reported across the five papers. For each, we (1) extract only figures/tables from the papers you provided, (2) compare on identical datasets when available, (3) compare on similar task types, and (4) summarize dataset-specific outcomes.
> 
> 1) One-stage anchor-free part–body association (PBADet) vs prior detectors and pose estimators
> Identical datasets and head-to-head comparisons
> - BodyHands (Table 1):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Cond. Acc. 86.91, Joint AP 84.39
>   Outcome: PBADet outperforms BPJDet on all three metrics; gains are especially large in conditional accuracy (+5.71 to +5.80 points vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6) and joint AP (+1.34 to +1.59).

> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2 & Table 3):
>   - All categories AP (AP.5:.95, AP.5; original/subordinate): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 (AP.5:.95), 70.0/68.4 (AP.5); BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3 (AP.5:.95), 70.6/69.8 (AP.5). PBADet matches BPJDet on overall AP but trails slightly on AP.5:.95 (−0.6 to −1.5).
>   - Scale and category strengths: PBADet leads on APM/ APL (66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4 for YOLOv5l6) and on person and feet APs (person 62.4; r-foot 30.9; l-foot 31.5) vs BPJDet (person 61.3; r-foot 30.2; l-foot 30.9) (Table 2).
>   - Association robustness (average mMR−2; Table 3): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) achieves lower miss-matching rates on head (27.9 vs 30.8), face (30.5 vs 31.8), r-hand (40.8 vs 42.2) and competitive on feet vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6).
>   Outcome: PBADet improves association reliability (lower mMR−2) and medium/large-scale detection, while overall AP is on par or slightly below BPJDet depending on the slice.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Table 5 & 6):
>   - Face-body association (Table 5): PBADet (YOLOv7) yields best body MR−2 (36.5) and face MR−2 (44.7), and best body AP (91.6). Pair miss-match mMR−2 comparable (~50.8–50.9) to BPJDet (50.1–51.4).
>   - Against crowded-person detectors (Table 6): PBADet attains the best body MR−2 (36.5) and competitive AP (91.6), on par with strong DETR-based methods.
>   Outcome: In crowd scenarios, PBADet improves body/face detection robustness without sacrificing association accuracy relative to BPJDet and matches heavy detectors in AP.
> 
> Similar task-type comparison (part association vs pose)
> - Multi-person pose (ED-Pose; Table 7): PBADet substantially surpasses ED-Pose on selected part-level Precision/Recall/F1 on COCO val (e.g., all parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87; right hand F1 47.34 vs 24.17). Outcome: For localized parts and part–body linkage, PBADet delivers much higher F1 than a top-down pose estimator.
> 
> 2) Memory-efficient optimization with 4-bit states (4-bit AdamW/Factor) vs 32-bit/8-bit optimizers
> Identical datasets and head-to-head comparisons
> - GLUE (RoBERTa-L; NLU, Table 2): Mean 4-bit AdamW 89.1 vs 32-bit AdamW 88.9 and 8-bit AdamW 89.1; Adafactor/SM3 are lower/brittle across tasks. Outcome: 4-bit equals or slightly exceeds full-precision on average.
> - ImageNet-1k (Swin-T; classification, Table 2): 4-bit AdamW 80.8 vs 32-bit 81.2 vs 8-bit 81.0; Adafactor 80.0–79.5; SM3 79.0. Outcome: Small top-1 drop vs 32-bit (−0.4), outperforming Adafactor/SM3. 
> - E2E-NLG (GPT-2 Medium; Table 2 & 8): BLEU 4-bit 67.8 vs 32-bit 67.7 vs 8-bit 67.5. Outcome: 4-bit slightly higher BLEU.
> - SQuAD (RoBERTa-L; Table 9): F1 4-bit 94.5 vs 32-bit 94.6; SQuAD 2.0 F1 4-bit 88.4 vs 32-bit 88.8. Outcome: Near parity.
> - WMT14 en-de (Transformer-Base; MT, Table 2): SacreBLEU 4-bit 26.28 vs 32-bit 26.61 vs 8-bit 26.66. Outcome: Slightly lower than full precision.
> 
> Instruction tuning (LLaMA; Table 3)
> - Across sizes (7B/13B/33B), 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-e/c, OBQA (e.g., LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8; ARC-e 64.1 vs 63.6). Outcome: 4-bit maintains performance at scale.
> 
> Efficiency (Table 4 & 5)
> - Memory/time: LLaMA-7B finetuning: total memory 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB (−57.7%); training time drops from 3.35 h (32-bit) to 3.07 h (4-bit). RoBERTa-L: total memory 3.00 GB (4-bit fused) vs 5.31 GB (−43.5%). GPT-2 Medium: 4.62 GB vs 6.89 GB (−34.4%).
> - Capacity scaling (Table 5): On an 80 GB GPU, 4-bit enables OPT-6.7B finetuning (vs OPT-1.3B with 32-bit); LLaMA-7B becomes trainable on a single 80 GB GPU.
> Outcome: 4-bit states deliver near-32-bit accuracy while enabling substantially larger models and lowering memory/time.
> 
> 3) LLM-assisted causal discovery with deep structural causal models (CMA)
> Identical benchmarks and head-to-head comparisons (Table 2)
> - Arctic sea ice (12 nodes; 48 edges): CMA NHD/BHD ratio 0.46 vs TCDF 0.89; NOTEARS (best) 0.82; DAG-GNN 0.74–1.0; gpt-3.5 0.80; gpt-4 0.68. Outcome: CMA recovers graphs substantially better (lower is better). 
> - Alzheimer’s (11 nodes; 19 edges): CMA ratio 0.21 vs gpt-4 0.27; NOTEARS best 0.74; DAG-GNN ~0.83. Outcome: CMA best.
> - Sangiovese (15 nodes; 55 edges): CMA ratio 0.63 vs gpt-4 0.65; NOTEARS best 0.79–0.96; DAG-GNN 0.79–0.91. Outcome: CMA best or tied best.
> 
> Synthetic validation and real-world case study
> - Synthetic DAG/likelihood (Fig. 2; Table 1): Correct DAG (perfect map) yields highest data likelihood (4402.68 ± 26.70) vs misspecified DAGs (3857.53 ± 18.98; 3757.55 ± 60.80); all pairwise differences significant. Outcome: CMA’s model-fitting signal (log-likelihood) properly ranks correct DAGs higher.
> - ADNI multi-modal: CMA discovers novel plausible edges (e.g., Sex → tau) and validates with counterfactual tests (Welch’s t-tests |t|≈6, p<0.001) and proposes external variables (e.g., sTREM2 → tau with F=43.52, p<0.01 under counterfactual inference). Outcome: CMA not only outperforms on discovery benchmarks but also grounds hypotheses with counterfactual image/variable effects.
> 
> 4) Spectrum-aware RNNs obeying Dale’s Law (ColEI vs DANN vs Standard RNN)
> Identical tasks & direct comparisons (Fig. 2 A–D; Fig. 4)
> - Across adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, natural object recognition: ColEI consistently learns worse and with higher variance than standard RNN and DANN, while DANN matches standard RNN.
> - Quantified ablations (Fig. 4A–C):
>   - Sign constraints alone degrade performance modestly (absolute test-error changes ~0.7% ± 0.3% for RNNs; ~1% ± 1% for ColEI), but spectrum accounts for a larger gap (RNNs ~1.5% ± 0.3%; ColEI ~2% ± 1%).
>   - Spectrum-transplant experiments: giving RNNs the ColEI spectrum (or vice versa) shifts performance accordingly, highlighting spectral properties drive most of the performance delta.
> - Stability/regularization: Gradient clipping benefits ColEI substantially (Appendix Fig. 10); Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) correlates with generalization—higher NSE (more clustered singular values) predicts lower test error (Fig. 5G; Fig. 6G; Fig. 7D). Outcome: DANN (EI) is competitive with standard RNNs; ColEI’s poor learning is primarily spectral (not just sign constraints), with NSE a predictive interpretability tool.
> 
> 5) Self-distillation JEPA vs MAE (deep linear models + ImageNet)
> Empirical results (Figs. 1–2–4; Fig. 7)
> - Learning dynamics (ODE simulations; Figs. 2 & 4): Both MAE and JEPA show greedy feature learning in linear models, but only JEPA exhibits a depth-dependent bias toward high regression-coefficient (influential) features. When covariance (λ) and regression coefficient (ρ) are opposed (Fig. 1d–f), JEPA inverts learning order vs MAE.
> - ImageNet feature similarity (Appendix D, Fig. 7): With I-JEPA vs MAE trained on ImageNet-1K (64×64), JEPA’s learned representations show higher mean CCA between full and bottom-variance data than MAE across training, but lower mean CCA between full and top-variance data. Outcome: Empirically corroborates that JEPA prioritizes perceptual/low-variance, influential features (benefiting representation quality) over pixel-level reconstruction.
> 
> Cross-paper alignment on identical/similar datasets
> - ImageNet: 4-bit optimizers achieve Swin-T top-1 around 80.8–81.2% (Table 2), while the JEPA study (Fig. 7) evaluates mean CCA alignment—both operate on ImageNet-class images but with different objectives/metrics; thus not directly comparable numerically. Still, both show efficient/robust training of Transformer-family models on ImageNet-scale data.
> - MNIST family: Dale’s Law paper reports on sequential MNIST (Fig. 2B), not part of other studies—no direct overlap.
> - COCO family: PBADet evaluates on COCO-HumanParts/WholeBody variants; other papers do not.
> - GLUE/NLP and WMT: Exclusive to the 4-bit optimizer paper.
> - Causal discovery benchmarks: Exclusive to CMA.
> 
> What each method does best on its evaluated datasets
> - PBADet: Best conditional accuracy and joint AP on BodyHands; lowest mMR−2 (average) on COCOHumanParts; best MR−2 on CrowdHuman body/face, with strong AP.
> - 4-bit AdamW/Factor: Matches near-32-bit accuracy on GLUE/SQuAD/E2E while cutting memory ~34–58% and enabling larger models (OPT-6.7B/LLaMA-7B) on a single 80 GB GPU.
> - CMA: Best NHD/BHD on Arctic sea ice, Alzheimer’s, and Sangiovese benchmarks; additionally validates novel edges in ADNI with significant counterfactual tests and multi-modal outputs.
> - DANN vs ColEI RNNs: DANN (EI RNN) ≈ Standard RNN across adding problem, sequential MNIST, PTB, naturalistic recognition; ColEI degrades most due to pathological spectra (not just signs), with NSE an informative diagnostic.
> - JEPA vs MAE: On ImageNet representations, JEPA aligns more with bottom-variance (perceptual) subspaces than MAE (higher mean CCA for full-bottom; lower for full-top), consistent with JEPA preferring influential, less noisy features.
> 
> Overall synthesis
> - Efficient training: 4-bit optimizers deliver large practical gains with negligible accuracy loss; DANN architectures retain performance while respecting Dale’s Law; JEPA focuses representation learning on influential, low-variance directions, which can reduce training time to useful features. 
> - Interpretability/diagnostics: NSE (Dale’s) is predictive of learning quality; JEPA’s feature-prioritization emerges from measurable learning dynamics; CMA’s log-likelihood and NHD/BHD enable model selection and hypothesis vetting.
> - End-to-end impact: In detection (PBADet), NLP/Vision/MT (4-bit), graph discovery (CMA), and RNN training (DANN), the reported experiments demonstrate complementary advances in efficiency and interpretability, each evidenced on their respective benchmarks with head-to-head baselines and statistically grounded analyses (e.g., Tukey HSDs; Welch’s tests).

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, I found papers matching four of the five areas. No paper in the collection uses **AUROC** as an evaluation metric (the causal-discovery paper reports NHD/BHD ratio, Precision, Recall, and F1 instead), and no paper proposes a **spectrum-aware regularization** for RNNs (the Dale's Law paper is an *analysis* of spectra, not a regularizer). Here are the findings:
> 
> ## 1. Memory-efficient optimization (4-bit optimizer states)
> **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (NeurIPS 2023) — Adam/AdamW with 4-bit quantized states: B128 block + rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for the second moment; optional "4-bit Factor" variant factorizes the second moment (Adafactor-style).
> - **Results:** Matches/exceeds 32-bit AdamW: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8–80.9, GPT-2M E2E-NLG BLEU 67.6–67.8, RoBERTa-L SQuAD F1 94.5–94.6, Transformer WMT14 SacreBLEU 26.28–26.45; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (Alpaca→MMLU/common-sense) comparable. Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB, trainable on one 80GB GPU). Ablations: smaller block size and factorized second moment both improve accuracy.
> 
> ## 2. Self-distillation in JEPA vs CE/MSE/cosine objectives
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024) — theoretical analysis (deep linear networks) of JEPA self-distillation vs MAE reconstruction. JEPA uses an MSE-style latent prediction loss; it is biased toward high-influence (high regression coefficient ρ), low-variance features, whereas MAE's feature order depends on eigenvalue λ. Depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression; JEPA converges to lower amplitude on noisy features. ImageNet experiments: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE (CCA-based), explaining why JEPA "avoids noisy features." Note: cosine-similarity objectives appear only in a *different* document (contrastive-learning paper on embedding similarities, InfoNCE/cosine, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100); that paper is not a JEPA study.
> 
> ## 3. Spectrum-aware regularization for RNNs obeying Dale's Law — NOT FOUND
> The matching paper **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023) is an *analysis*, not a regularization method. It finds ColEI RNNs (sign-constrained) train poorly due to multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra at initialization, not sign constraints; recurrent DANNs keep RNN-like spectra and train well; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance. Gradient clipping helps ColEI stability — but no regularization term that shapes the spectrum to stabilize SGD is proposed.
> 
> ## 4. Anchor-free one-stage part–body association detector
> **"PBADet"** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage, anchor-free (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones) detector using a single part-to-body center offset, with association loss + task-alignment (TOOD).
> - **Results (BodyHands):** HandAP 89.1 (YOLOv7) / 88.1 (YOLOv5l6), Cond. Accuracy 92.62/92.71, JointAP 85.98/85.73 — surpassing BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13 for m6; 85.9/86.91/84.39 for l6) with fewer params (36.9M vs 41.2–86.1M).
> - **COCOHumanParts:** All-categories AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6), on par with BPJDet, with better person/feet AP and lowest mMR−2.
> - **F1/Precision vs ED-Pose (COCO val):** all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51 (e.g., left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87, right hand 47.34 vs 24.17, left foot 51.08 vs 40.46).
> - **CrowdHuman:** best body MR−2 (36.5 vs BPJDet 40.7) with competitive AP.
> - Ablations: association loss boosts Cond. Accuracy 80.78→92.62; multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each add gains; anchor-free beats anchor-based (JointAP 85.98 vs 85.28).
> 
> ## 5. LLM-assisted causal discovery with DSCMs
> **"Causal Modelling Agents (CMA)"** (ICLR 2024) — combines LLM metadata reasoning (as prior, critic, post-processor, hypothesis amender) with Deep Structural Causal Models, including chain-graph parameterization for unmeasured confounding; applied to multi-modal ADNI data (tabular + MRI) and time-series (Arctic sea ice, TCDF baseline).
> - **Results:** CMA achieves the best NHD/BHD ratio on all three benchmarks (Arctic sea ice 0.46, AD 0.21, Sangiovese 0.63), beating NOTEARS, DAG-GNN, TCDF, gpt-3.5-turbo, and gpt-4.
> - **F1:** Arctic sea ice F1 = 0.57 (best; gpt-4 up to 0.52, NOTEARS 0.092), AD consensus graph F1 = 0.81 with Precision = Recall = 0.81 (gpt-4 best 0.77; data-driven ≤0.52); robust under Gaussian noise perturbation.
> - **AUROC:** Not reported — evaluation uses NHD/BHD, Precision, Recall, F1, plus statistical significance tests.
> 
> ## Cross-paper comparison & analysis
> - **Efficiency vs accuracy trade-off:** The 4-bit optimizer achieves near-lossless accuracy (within ±0.1–0.3 points of 32-bit) while cutting memory ~43–58% and enabling 4× larger OPT models — the strongest efficiency–accuracy pairing among the papers.
> - **Interpretability mechanisms:** JEPA's implicit bias (predictive, low-variance features) and the Dale's Law spectral analysis (NSE as a pre-training diagnostic) both use spectral/statistical structure to explain learning dynamics; neither proposes an intervention (no regularization), while PBADet and CMA are applied systems where the interpretability is in the explicit structure (center offsets; causal graph + counterfactuals).
> - **Benchmark coverage:** The four found papers span the requested benchmarks — GLUE/ImageNet/MMLU (optimizer), CIFAR-100/ImageNet (contrastive/embedding paper), COCO/COCO-HumanParts/BodyHands/CrowdHuman (PBADet), and Arctic sea ice/ADNI time-series + multimodal (CMA). MNIST appears only in the Dale's Law/sequential-MNIST experiments and the Hessian-spectrum paper.
> - **Caveats:** (a) No AUROC-evaluated method exists in the collection; (b) no spectrum-regularization method exists — the Dale's Law paper only diagnoses the problem; (c) the cosine-similarity objective analysis belongs to a separate contrastive-learning paper, not the JEPA self-distillation study; (d) none of the papers report end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning results (LoRA appears only as a cited reference and in the Hessian paper, where LoRA-only fine-tuning is noted as not inducing power-law spectra).

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers identified (one per criterion)
> 
> **(a) "4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023)** — Memory-efficient fine-tuning via 4-bit Adam/AdamW states (smaller block size B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-free linear quantizer, factorized second moment).
> 
> **(b) "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** + companion **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** — analysis of JEPA self-distillation (latent-space MSE) vs MAE (input-space MSE), and of cosine-similarity/InfoNCE objectives.
> 
> **(c) "Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** — spectrum-aware analysis of E/I-constrained RNNs (ColEI vs DANN), normalised SVD entropy (NSE) as pathology measure.
> 
> **(d) "PBADet" (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage, anchor-free part–body association detector via a single part-to-body center offset (F1/Precision reported vs ED-Pose).
> 
> **(e) "Causal Modelling Agents (CMA)" (ICLR 2024)** (+ **G-Sim**) — LLM-assisted causal discovery with Deep Structural Causal Models on multi-modal/benchmark data, scored with F1.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis of experimental results
> 
> **Lossless compression vs full precision (a).** Across 32-bit AdamW → 4-bit AdamW: GLUE/RoBERTa-L 88.9→89.1 (NLU), ImageNet/Swin-T 81.2→80.8, E2E-NLG BLEU 67.7→67.8, SQuAD F1 94.6→94.5, WMT SacreBleu 26.61→26.28 — i.e., statistically matched or slightly better despite quantizing both moments. Memory drops up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB; LLaMA-7B fits one 80 GB GPU), and LLaMA 7/13/33B instruction-tuning stays on par with 32-bit on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA. So (a) trades no accuracy for large memory savings.
> 
> **Implicit-bias analysis, no accuracy tables (b).** This is a theoretical/dynamical study: JEPA prioritizes high-regression-coefficient (high-ρ) features and, as depth grows, suppresses noisy, low-ρ directions; a 1-layer JEPA is equivalent to infinite-depth MAE (fixed points ρ^L vs ρ^{L/(L+1)}). On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) faster than MAE (CCA dynamics). The cosine-similarity companion shows optimal InfoNCE encoders give positive-pair similarity 1 and negative-pair −1/(n−1); an auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, and ImageNet. These results are analytic/qualitative rather than competing benchmarks.
> 
> **Spectral properties dominate over sign constraints (c).** ColEI RNNs learn worse and with much higher variance than DANN/standard RNNs on all four tasks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition), and need gradient clipping most. Singular-value transplant experiments attribute more of the gap to the spectrum (RNN 1.5±0.3%, ColEI 2±1% error change) than to sign constraints (0.7±0.3% / 1±1%). NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error, predicting performance before training; smaller networks with fewer inhibitory units have worse spectra and learning, while DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> 
> **Strongest F1/precision gains (d).** On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7) reaches HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 — beating BPJDet (85.9/86.91/84.39) with a smaller model. On COCOHumanParts it is on par in AP (42.7/41.5) but leads in association-specific AP_M/AP_L and lower mMR−2. Against the pose estimator ED-Pose, PBADet's all-parts Precision/Recall/F1 are 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs 24.09/45.51/31.51 — roughly +1.5× F1, the largest relative metric gain among the five papers.
> 
> **LLM+DSCM beats data- or metadata-only causal discovery (e).** CMA achieves NHD/BHD ratios 0.25/0.46 (Arctic sea ice), 0.07/0.21 (Alzheimer's), 0.23/0.63 (Sangiovese), below NOTEARS, DAG-GNN, and gpt-3.5/gpt-4 alone; best F1 = 0.57 (Arctic sea ice, robust under added noise) and F1 = 0.81 on the AD consensus graph. G-Sim (LLM-proposed + calibrated simulators) reports even higher structural F1 (COVID 95.5%, supply chain 93.3%, hospital scheduling 100.0%) on time-series simulators. Note: in this collection the causal-discovery methods are evaluated with F1 (and SHD/NHD); AUROC appears only in unrelated domains (deepfake detection AUC 75.8→81.88; LLM tuning-contribution AUC >0.80; molecular ROC-AUC), not in the causal-discovery papers.
> 
> **Overall.** The common theme is matching or exceeding a strong baseline while adding efficiency/robustness: (a) matches full precision at 4-bit memory; (b) explains—rather than benchmarks—why latent-space objectives are noise-robust and cosine objectives benefit from variance reduction; (c) shows a spectral measure, not sign constraints, predicts RNN trainability; (d) gives the largest concrete accuracy/F1 improvements; (e) shows that fusing LLM priors with data-driven DSCM fitting beats either alone, with the best causal-structure F1 in the collection.

>   - Across rising noise levels (L1/L2/L3), CMA maintains lower NHD/BHD than NOTEARS and DAG-GNN (Tables 14–16; Figure 29).
