> 4) Similar dataset types (qualitative but on identical datasets within each study)
> - Recurrent stability under Dale’s Law (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNN)
>   - On adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task, ColEI RNNs learn worse than DANNs and standard RNNs; DANNs match standard RNNs while obeying Dale’s Law (Figure 2 A–D). Gradient clipping helps ColEI more, but spectral “spectrum transplant” shows singular value spectra matter more than sign constraints (Figure 4). 
>   - Size/EI-ratio sweeps: smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units degrade ColEI more; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with test error and predicts performance across EI ratios and sizes (Figures 5–7). 
>   - Takeaway: For time-series/classification/language tasks, DANN RNNs are the strongest way to impose spectral/biological stability under Dale’s Law, outperforming naive ColEI.
> 
> - JEPA vs MAE (self-distillation vs reconstruction) on controlled linear settings
>   - On synthetic Gaussian and temporal generative processes, JEPA exhibits greedy learning over “influential” features (large regression coefficients ρ), and can invert feature-learning order compared to MAE when λ and ρ rank orders differ (Figure 1; Figure 2; Theorem 3.4–3.6). 
>   - On ImageNet (64×64) splits, JEPA’s latent prediction yields features aligned with low-variance (“bottom”) subspace earlier than MAE (Appendix D Figure 7), consistent with more semantic feature emergence. 
>   - Takeaway: For noisy features, JEPA-style self-distillation resists learning high-variance but uninformative features, and prioritizes predictive/low-noise features compared to MAE in deep encoders.
> 
> 5) Specific datasets (called out by name in the papers)
> - BodyHands (PBADet): PBADet > BPJDet and others on Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP (Table 1). 
> - COCOHumanParts (PBADet): PBADet shows better association quality (mMR−2) and better APM/APL; BPJDet slightly higher overall AP (Tables 2–3). 
> - CrowdHuman (PBADet): PBADet achieves lowest body MR−2 and strong AP (Tables 5–6).
> - GLUE, ImageNet-1k, E2E-NLG, SQuAD, WMT14 (4-bit optimizers): 4-bit AdamW/Factor match or nearly match 32-bit/8-bit across these standard tasks (Tables 2, 8–9). 
> - Arctic Sea Ice, Sangiovese, Alzheimer’s (CMA): CMA achieves the lowest NHD/BHD ratios across all three benchmarks, with the largest gains on Alzheimer’s (Table 2). 
> - Sequential MNIST/PTB/adding/naturalistic object recognition (Dale’s Law RNNs): DANN/standard RNNs > ColEI (Figure 2), confirming spectral design improves training stability and performance.
> 
> Summary by requirement
> - Identical datasets: Clearly favored methods are PBADet (BodyHands, CrowdHuman; better association metrics and MR−2; on COCOHumanParts improves APM/APL and mMR−2), 4-bit AdamW (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E BLEU; parity with 32/8-bit), CMA (lowest NHD/BHD on Arctic/Sangiovese/AD), DANN RNNs (vs ColEI on adding/MNIST/PTB/naturalistic tasks).
> - Similar dataset types: For vision/language, 4-bit optimizers retain accuracy with major memory wins; for RNN sequence/temporal tasks, DANN respects Dale’s Law without training collapse, unlike naive ColEI; for representation learning under noise, JEPA prioritizes predictive, low-variance features versus MAE.
> - Specific datasets: 
>   - BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman: PBADet wins association robustness (and part F1 vs ED-Pose on COCO); 
>   - GLUE/ImageNet/SQuAD/WMT: 4-bit optimizers match 32/8-bit; 
>   - Arctic Sea Ice/Sangiovese/AD: CMA best NHD/BHD; 
>   - Sequential MNIST/PTB/adding: DANN/standard RNN > ColEI.
> 
> Practical implications for your stack (grounded in reported results)
> - Fine-tuning under tight VRAM with AdamW: 4-bit optimizer states deliver near-parity accuracy to 32/8-bit across GLUE, SQuAD, E2E, WMT and big gains in trainable model size/memory. 
> - Spectrum-aware RNNs (biological constraints): Use DANN RNNs; they match standard RNN performance while respecting Dale’s Law and remain stable versus ColEI baselines (sequential MNIST/PTB, etc.). NSE is a good spectral diagnostic. 
> - JEPA-style self-distillation vs CE/MSE: In linear deep encoders, JEPA is biased toward influential/predictive features and away from noisy/high-variance features; observed faster alignment to low-variance subspaces on ImageNet-64 splits. 
> - LLM+DSCM causal graphs for tabular/time-series/MRI: CMA’s NHD/BHD is best on three standard benchmarks and robust under noise; in real ADNI MRI use-case, it produced plausible image counterfactuals and surfaced missing edges. 
> - One-stage anchor-free detector (HCI hand/face to body): PBADet delivers higher association reliability (mMR−2, part F1 on COCO) and lower MR−2 in crowd datasets than prior detectors, with strong BodyHands gains.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here is the comparison of the five matched papers (each covers one of your stack pieces):
> 
> **1. 4-bit optimizer states for AdamW fine-tuning** — *"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"* (NeurIPS 2023)
> - 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly beats 32-bit AdamW across tasks: GLUE (RoBERTa-L) 89.1±0.01 vs 88.9±0.01; ImageNet (Swin-T) 80.8 vs 81.2; E2E-NLG (GPT-2M) 67.8 vs 67.7; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61.
> - LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning: 4-bit ≈ 32-bit (e.g., LLaMA-7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; HellaSwag 74.7 vs 74.6). Memory reduced up to 57.7%; enables LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU.
> - **Caveat vs your LoRA goal:** LoRA appears only as related work (freezes weights, tunes low-rank adapters, "only applicable to language model fine-tuning") — this paper validates the 4-bit-state path, not LoRA itself.
> 
> **2. Spectrum-aware recurrent stability under biological constraints** — *"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"* (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Tests standard RNN vs ColEI (Dale's-law sign-constrained) vs recurrent DANN on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition.
> - Key finding: the initial singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints. Sign constraints cost only ~0.7±0.3% (RNN) / 1±1% (ColEI) error, far short of the full 2.3±0.6% ColEI gap; spectrum transplant accounts for 1.5±0.3% vs 2±1%.
> - ColEI has a multimodal, dispersed spectrum (rank-one nilpotent column-mean term); DANN/standard RNNs follow random-matrix (Marchenko–Pastur) form. Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance pre-training; DANN stays stable even with 1 inhibitory unit (NSE ≈ 0.95). Without gradient clipping ColEI is highly unstable. Metrics are error/accuracy (softmax/CE objective), not F1/AUROC.
> 
> **3. Why JEPA self-distillation resists noisy features** — *"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"* (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Deep-linear analysis: JEPA's critical time prioritizes high-regression-coefficient (high-influence ρ) features, and this bias **strengthens with encoder depth** (Corollary 3.6), whereas MAE ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ. Noisy features (low ρ) are learned later and converge to lower-amplitude weights.
> - Empirical: on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA vs MAE feature similarity via CCA — JEPA matches the low-variance (bottom-25%-variance) perceptual subspace faster than MAE; trend reversed for top-variance images. This is a theoretical/CCA study (cosine/regression-style latent objectives), not F1/AUROC on MNIST/CIFAR-100.
> 
> **4. LLM + DSCM auto-constructed causal graphs (tabular, time-series, MRI)** — *"Causal Modelling Agents"* (ICLR 2024)
> - CMA (LLM prior/critic/post-processor + Deep Structural Causal Model) on tabular (Sangiovese, 15 nodes), time-series (Arctic sea ice, 12 nodes), and MRI (ADNI Alzheimer's, 11 nodes).
> - Best F1: 0.57 on Arctic sea ice and 0.81 on the AD consensus graph, beating NOTEARS (AD F1 ≈ 0.18), DAG-GNN (≈ 0.17), and LLM-only gpt-4 (0.46). NHD/BHD ratios: CMA 0.46/0.21/0.63 vs gpt-4 0.68/0.27/0.65 on the three benchmarks.
> - Robust to added noise: at L3 Gaussian noise CMA F1 = 0.64 vs NOTEARS 0.125 / DAG-GNN 0.222. Produces plausible brain-MRI counterfactuals (limitation: 2D MRI slices, Markov-equivalence classes).
> 
> **5. Anchor-free one-stage part-body (hand/face) association for HCI** — *"PBADet"* (ICLR 2024)
> - On BodyHands: hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 86.91/84.39 and BodyHands 84.12/63.87 — best on all metrics with fewer params.
> - On COCOHumanParts (COCO-derived): AP on par with BPJDet, leads AP_M/AP_L for person and feet, lowest average mMR−2 across head/face/hands/feet.
> - CrowdHuman face-body: body MR−2 36.5 (vs BPJDet 39.7–41.3), body AP 91.6, face AP 81.6, mMR−2 50.8.
> - vs ED-Pose on COCO: all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51.
> 
> **Cross-cutting analysis for your stack**
> - Coverage is complementary: #1 gives VRAM savings (memory/accuracy trade-off) with CE-trained vision/NLU; #2 gives stability guidance (use DANN-style spectrum or high-NSE init, avoid ColEI's dispersed spectrum) on MNIST-style tasks; #3 gives a theory that cosine-style latent objectives implicitly suppress noise, aligning with #2's biological-spectrum angle; #4 gives F1/Precision/Recall causal-graph metrics on your exact data types (tabular/time-series/MRI); #5 gives AP/F1 hand-face-body association metrics on COCO-family datasets.
> - Gaps to note: no single paper reports AUROC; the JEPA and Dale's-law papers use error/accuracy and CCA rather than F1/Precision; the 4-bit paper doesn't benchmark LoRA itself; the CMA's MRI is 2D-slice based; #2/#3 are theory-driven with limited dataset breadth (no CIFAR-100), so direct cross-method metric comparison is only possible within each paper's own benchmarks.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, here is a comparative analysis of the five pieces of your stack:
> 
> ## 1. Tight-VRAM fine-tuning with 4-bit optimizer states / AdamW / LoRA
> **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (NeurIPS 2023). Compression via smaller block size (B128) for the first moment, and rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the second moment, optionally factorized ("4-bit Factor").
> 
> - **Results:** 4-bit AdamW *matches or exceeds* 32-bit AdamW on all fine-tuning tasks: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; GPT-2 E2E BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7; LLaMA-7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61).
> - **Memory:** saves up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 31.9GB vs 75.4GB), enables LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; RoBERTa-L 43–47% saving. LoRA is discussed only as a complementary/reference technique (it freezes weights and tunes low-rank parameters); the Hessian paper notes LoRA-only fine-tuning does *not* induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does.
> - **Analysis:** the main trade-off is bitwidth vs. convergence — 4-bit is lossless for fine-tuning (unlike Adafactor/SM3, which degrade especially on image classification), so it's the safer choice for your VRAM-bound AdamW/LoRA setup.
> 
> ## 2. Spectrum-aware recurrent stability with biological constraints
> **"Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly"** (NeurIPS 2023). Naive biological E/I partitioning (ColEI, column sign constraints) produces **multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra**; this — not the sign constraints — is what impairs learning (sequential MNIST, adding problem, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition). Recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) respect Dale's Law yet keep a **unimodal, clustered spectrum** and learn as well as standard RNNs.
> 
> - **Quantitative:** sign constraints alone account for only ~1–2.3% error differences; spectrum "transplants" show the spectrum contributes more (≈1.5–2% of the gap). **Normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance across network size and E/I ratio; small networks with few I-units have worse spectra/performance and are unstable without gradient clipping.
> - **Analysis:** for your stable recurrent modules, the design rule is: enforce biological constraints *without* creating column-mean rank-one structure — replicate the DANN unimodal spectrum (NSE≈0.95) rather than ColEI's dispersed spectrum. This directly operationalizes spectrum-aware design.
> 
> ## 3. Why JEPA self-distillation resists noisy features vs. CE/MSE-style training
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024). In a solvable deep-linear setting, JEPA self-distillation exhibits **greedy dynamics w.r.t. the correlation coefficient ρ (regression coefficient / feature influence)** — it prioritizes high-influence features and learns noisy features slower, converging to **lower-amplitude weights** on them, so they are less used downstream. MAE-style (MSE/pixel-reconstruction) ordering instead depends mainly on the eigenvalue λ (variance), so it learns high-variance/noisy features early. Depth **strengthens** JEPA's noise suppression.
> 
> - **Experimental confirmation:** on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA's features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (where perceptual features reside) than MAE's, measured by CCA — higher mean CCA on bottom-25%-variance data, lower on top-75%.
> - **Analysis:** this is an *implicit bias of predicting in latent space*, not an explicit robustness loss; note it also implies JEPA can be **vulnerable to spurious/slow features**. The mechanism applies to self-distillation (BYOL/data2vec/I-JEPA), not contrastive or CE training, which explains the noise-resistance gap.
> 
> ## 4. LLM+DSCM auto-construction of interpretable causal graphs (tabular / time-series / MRI)
> **"Causal Modelling Agents (CMA): Causal Graph Discovery through Synergising Metadata- and Data-Driven Reasoning"** (ICLR 2024). CMA iterates: LLM hypothesis generation → DSCM model fitting (log-likelihood) → LLM post-processing → hypothesis amendment, with chain-graph parameterization for unmeasured confounding.
> 
> - **Results (NHD/BHD ratio, lower better):** CMA 0.46 / 0.21 / 0.63 vs NOTEARS 0.82/0.74/0.96, DAG-GNN 0.85/0.83/0.79, gpt-4-only 0.68/0.27/0.65 on Arctic sea ice / Alzheimer's / Sangiovese — CMA beats all purely data-driven and metadata-driven baselines. Per the overview, CMA reaches **F1 0.57 on Arctic sea ice** and **F1 0.81 on the AD consensus graph**, robust to added Gaussian noise.
> - **Multi-modal:** on ADNI, CMA jointly models tabular covariates + brain MRI, producing biologically plausible image-space counterfactuals (e.g., age → cortical degeneration/ventricular expansion; sex/P-tau/brain-volume relations statistically supported).
> - **Analysis:** the gain comes from combining the two signals (LLM priors prune graph space; data likelihood grounds and corrects LLM reasoning). Caveats: discrete relaxations, 2D MRI slices, and Markov-equivalence limitations.
> 
> ## 5. Anchor-free one-stage detector for hand/face–body association (HCI)
> **"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** (ICLR 2024). Extends anchor-free detection (YOLOv5/v7) with a single **part-to-body center offset** (one-to-one, always valid, scalable to any number of parts — unlike BPJDet's body-to-part offsets which grow and fail when parts are occluded).
> 
> - **BodyHands (hand-body):** Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) vs BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39 — PBADet leads on all metrics with a smaller model.
> - **COCOHumanParts (head/face/hands/feet):** AP 43.0 (YOLOv5l6), best on AP_L and feet/head categories, and **lowest average mMR-2** across categories (e.g., 29.2–31.3 for hands vs BPJDet 33.4–50.2).
> - **CrowdHuman (face-body):** best body MR-2 (36.5 YOLOv7) with competitive body/face AP (91.6/81.6). Against ED-Pose, PBADet gives substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands/feet.
> - **Ablations:** the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning each independently improve association accuracy (Cond. Acc. 92.62 vs 80.78 without association loss).
> - **Analysis:** the single part-to-body offset avoids the representation blow-up and occlusion-invalidity of BPJDet while being more precise than pose-estimation (ED-Pose) for part bounding boxes — a direct fit for HCI hand/face-to-body association.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting comparison
> - The five methods are complementary and use the exact objectives you target: 4-bit AdamW retains cross-entropy fine-tuning accuracy losslessly; JEPA's analysis specifically contrasts latent-space (cosine-like) prediction vs MSE reconstruction; CMA's model fitting uses data log-likelihood; PBADet uses classification (CE) + localization + association losses.
> - Dataset coverage matches your list: MNIST (spectrum paper: sequential MNIST; Hessian: LeNet/MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 label noise), CIFAR-10/100 (contrastive/SSL papers), COCO/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman (PBADet), ImageNet (4-bit optimizer, JEPA), plus domain-specific causal datasets.
> - **Main gaps:** no single paper combines 4-bit optimization *with* LoRA metrics (LoRA is referenced only); F1/AUROC/Precision are reported mainly for PBADet (AP/accuracy/F1) and CMA (F1) — the 4-bit optimizer and JEPA papers report accuracy/BLEU/F1/CCA rather than AUROC.
> 
> If you need, I can dig deeper into any specific metric table (e.g., PBADet's per-category AP breakdown or CMA's extended Arctic/AD appendix results).

### paperscope:results_comparison:302 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (1) a one-stage, anchor-free approach for linking detected human parts (e.g., hands, face) to the correct person and reporting AP/F1 and Precision; (2) spectral stability analysis for recurrent deep networks that respect excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints (Dale’s principle), going beyond simple sign clipping; (3) self-supervised joint-embedding prediction (non-contrastive self distillation) and its implicit bias toward high-influence features vs pixel reconstruction, with cosine-based similarity and log-loss used in downstream linear probes on a 100‑class image benchmark (e.g., CIFAR‑100); (4) training at scale with memory‑savvy optimizers that keep first/second moments in ~4‑bit while remaining compatible with Adam‑style decoupled weight decay and stochastic gradient descent fine‑tuning on attention/backbone models like a 50‑layer residual net or Transformers; and (5) learning‑augmented online algorithms that, with bandit access to multiple predictors, combine heuristics for metrical task systems and achieve sublinear regret. I’m specifically interested in work that mentions cross‑entropy, cosine similarity, F1/Precision, clean subset evaluation sets like D_k^c, and uses transformer‑based conditional guidance or similar, with near‑linear runtime in problem size.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of the experimental results reported in the five papers you provided, organized by topic and dataset. Only results explicitly reported in their figures/tables are used.
> 
> 1) One-stage, anchor-free part–body association (PBADet)
> Identical datasets and metrics
> - BodyHands (Table 1)
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39
>   - Summary: On BodyHands, PBADet improves all three metrics over the best BPJDet variant (higher Hand AP, higher Conditional Accuracy, higher Joint AP). 
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2: APs; Table 3: average mMR−2)
>   - All categories AP (.5:.95 / .5) and size breakdown:
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6/70.6 (AP.5:.95/AP.5); APM 63.8/63.2; APL 61.8/58.9
>     • Ours (YOLOv7): 42.7/69.5; APM 65.8/64.4; APL 66.7/63.3
>     • Ours (YOLOv5l6): 43.0/70.0; APM 66.2/65.0; APL 67.2/64.4
>   - Per category AP (APs↑; higher is better):
>     • Person: Ours v5l6 62.4 vs BPJDet l6 61.3; Ours v7 62.1
>     • Feet categories favor PBADet: r-foot Ours v5l6 30.9 vs BPJDet l6 30.2; l-foot Ours v5l6 31.5 vs BPJDet l6 30.9
>     • Hands/head/face: BPJDet l6 slightly higher AP in some; PBADet competitive.
>   - Average mMR−2 (lower is better; Table 3):
>     • BPJDet l6: head 30.8, face 31.8, l-hand 41.6, r-hand 42.2, r-foot 49.1, l-foot 50.4
>     • Ours (YOLOv7): 29.2, 31.3, 41.1, 42.7, 52.6, 52.5
>     • Ours (YOLOv5l6): 27.9, 30.5, 36.2, 40.8, 50.4, 47.9 (best in most categories)
>   - Summary: PBADet attains the lowest association miss-rate (mMR−2) across most categories, while AP is on par with BPJDet overall, and PBADet leads on medium/large-object AP (APM/APL) and feet AP.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Table 5)
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 body 40.7, face 46.3; AP body 89.5, face 81.6; mMR−2 body-face 50.1
>   - Ours (YOLOv7): MR−2 body 36.5, face 44.7; AP body 91.6, face 81.6; mMR−2 50.8
>   - Ours (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 body 37.5, face 45.3; AP body 91.4, face 81.2; mMR−2 50.9
>   - Summary: On CrowdHuman, PBADet improves body/face detection MR−2 and body AP over BPJDet; the pair mMR−2 is comparable (BPJDet slightly lower).
> 
> F1/Precision comparisons (ED-Pose vs PBADet; Table 7)
> - COCO (selected parts; Precision/Recall/F1):
>   - Left hand: PBADet P=37.63, R=60.82, F1=46.50 vs ED-Pose P=18.36, R=30.34, F1=22.87
>   - Right hand: 38.58/61.26/47.34 vs 19.57/31.59/24.17
>   - Left foot: 41.56/66.24/51.08 vs 29.32/65.28/40.46
>   - Right foot: 40.86/65.55/50.34 vs 29.13/65.58/40.34
>   - All parts aggregate: PBADet F1=48.52 vs ED-Pose 31.51
>   - Summary: PBADet substantially improves Precision, Recall, and F1 over a strong multi-person pose baseline for small parts.
> 
> Ablations (BodyHands, Table 4)
> - Adding the association loss (Lassoc), multi-scale offsets, and task-aligning anchor assignment boosts Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP vs baseline; the full model yields highest Joint AP (85.98) without reducing Hand AP.
> 
> 2) Spectral stability for EI RNNs under Dale’s Law
> Comparisons on identical tasks (Figures in paper)
> - Across four standard RNN tasks (Adding problem; Sequential MNIST; Penn Treebank; Naturalistic object recognition), ColEI (column-sign constrained) networks learn worse and exhibit higher variance than standard RNNs and DANNs, while DANN RNNs match standard RNNs.
> - Gradient clipping benefits ColEI substantially more than the other models (appendix figure), yet does not close the gap.
> Size/E–I ratio studies (Figures 5–7)
> - ColEI performance degrades as inhibitory fraction decreases; Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) decreases correspondingly, and the largest singular values grow—both correlating with higher error. DANN spectra and performance are robust even with very few inhibitory units (e.g., a single I unit).
> - Increasing network width improves ColEI (NSE increases and test error decreases), despite some singular values growing—global clustering (NSE) predicts performance better than max singular value. Overall: spectrum quality (high NSE) predicts learning performance; DANN maintains unimodal clustered spectra like standard RNNs and consequently learns well.
> 
> 3) JEPA (non-contrastive self-distillation) vs pixel reconstruction (MAE)
> Synthetic linear settings (Figures 1–2, 4–5)
> - In deep linear models, both JEPA and MAE show stepwise (greedy) feature learning, but with different implicit biases: JEPA prioritizes high-regression-coefficient (influential) features; MAE prioritizes high-variance (covarying) features. This distinction grows with encoder depth (JEPA’s bias intensifies as L increases).
> Temporal linear generative model (Figure 3)
> - For features with similar variance (λ) but differing informativeness (regression coefficients ρ), JEPA learns the more informative (higher ρ) modes earlier than MAE; in noisy settings, JEPA converges to lower-amplitude weights for noisy features, making them less likely to be used downstream.
> ImageNet study (Appendix D, Figure 7)
> - With ViT encoders, feature similarity (CCA) between Full and Bottom-variance images is higher for I-JEPA than for MAE across training, while Full to Top-variance CCA favors MAE. This supports that JEPA focuses more on the low-variance, semantically useful subspace than MAE. (No CIFAR-100 linear-probe experiments were reported.)
> 
> 4) Training at scale with ~4‑bit optimizer states (AdamW-compatible)
> Identical datasets across optimizers (Table 2)
> - NLU (GLUE; RoBERTa-L; Mean score):
>   • 32-bit AdamW 88.9; 8-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit Factor 88.9. (4-bit matches 32-bit/8-bit.)
> - CLS (ImageNet-1K; Swin-T; Top-1 Acc):
>   • 32-bit 81.2; 8-bit 81.0; 4-bit AdamW 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9. (4-bit within ~0.3–0.4 of 32-bit.)
> - NLG (E2E-NLG; GPT-2 M; BLEU):
>   • 32-bit 67.7; 8-bit 67.5; 4-bit AdamW 67.8; 4-bit Factor 67.6. (4-bit matches 32-/8-bit.)
> - QA (SQuAD; RoBERTa-L; F1):
>   • 32-bit 94.6; 8-bit 94.5; 4-bit AdamW 94.5; 4-bit Factor 94.6. (No loss.)
> - MT (WMT14 En–De; Transformer Base; SacreBLEU):
>   • 32-bit 26.61; 8-bit 26.66; 4-bit AdamW 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45. (4-bit roughly on par.)
> 
> Instruction tuning (Table 3; LLaMA 7B/13B/33B)
> - LLaMA‑7B: 32-bit vs 4-bit (MMLU 38.7→38.9; HellaSwag 74.6→74.7; ARC‑e 61.5→61.2; ARC‑c 45.1→44.4; OBQA 43.4→43.0) — comparable.
> - LLaMA‑13B: gains or parity (MMLU 46.5→47.4; HellaSwag 78.8→79.0; ARC‑e 63.6→64.1; ARC‑c 48.3→48.0; OBQA 45.2→45.2).
> - LLaMA‑33B: comparable (MMLU 56.4→54.9; others close).
> 
> Memory/time (Table 4) and capacity (Table 5)
> - LLaMA‑7B with FSDP on 2×A100‑80GB: memory cut from 75.40 GB to 31.87 GB (−57.7%); wall-clock 3.35 h→3.07 h.
> - RoBERTa‑L: total training memory 5.31 GB→3.00 GB (−43.5%) with fused 4-bit; time comparable or faster with fusion.
> - GPT‑2 M: 6.89 GB→4.62 GB (−34.4%) with fused 4-bit; time similar with fusion.
> - Largest trainable model (batch 1, seq 512): 24 GB GPU: 32-bit up to OPT‑350M vs 4-bit up to OPT‑1.3B; 80 GB: 32-bit up to OPT‑1.3B vs 4-bit up to OPT‑6.7B; 4-bit enables LLaMA‑7B on a single 80 GB GPU.
> 
> Ablations (Table 6)
> - Quantizing both moments to 4-bit with PBADet-style Rank‑1/Linear for v and B128/DE for m preserves ImageNet accuracy; factorizing v further improves memory while keeping accuracy (Swin‑T: 81.2 baseline → 80.9 with v factorized).
> 
> 5) Learning‑augmented online algorithms with bandit access (MTS)
> - This work is theoretical: it provides regret guarantees (e.g., O(OPT^{2/3}) with matching lower bound up to logs) for combining multiple predictors under m‑delayed bandit access. No empirical results are reported.
> 
> Cross‑paper observations on similar problem types
> - Detection/association (PBADet) consistently outperforms prior one-stage methods on identical human-part/body datasets in AP and association stability (mMR−2), and substantially improves F1/Precision over a strong pose estimator on small parts in COCO.
> - Optimizers: Across identical NLU, QA, MT, and ImageNet classification tasks, 4‑bit AdamW (and the factorized variant) matches or is within statistical noise of 32‑bit AdamW and 8‑bit AdamW, while delivering large memory savings and enabling larger models.
> - Representation learning (JEPA vs MAE): While largely analytical/synthetic, the ImageNet CCA evidence supports JEPA learning features aligned with the low‑variance, more semantic subspace faster than MAE, complementing the empirical improvements observed in one‑stage association when small, semantically crucial parts must be linked (note: this is a conceptual complement; no shared datasets between these two works).
> - Recurrent stability under biological constraints: DANN RNNs empirically match standard RNN baselines across tasks, while ColEI RNNs underperform unless spectrum pathologies are mitigated (no shared datasets with other papers).
> 
> Notes on requested items not present in the reported experiments
> - CIFAR‑100 linear‑probe evaluations with cosine similarity/log‑loss, ResNet‑50 backbones, Bayesian Flow Networks, conditional guidance, or clean‑subset sets like D_k^c were not reported in the provided papers, so no experimental comparisons can be made for those.
> 
> Overall conclusion
> - The experimental evidence shows: (i) a new one-stage, anchor‑free PBADet method that achieves state‑of‑the‑art part–body association on BodyHands and competitive/better results on COCOHumanParts and CrowdHuman, including strong Precision/Recall/F1 on small parts; (ii) 4‑bit memory‑efficient optimizers that preserve accuracy across a wide set of vision and NLP benchmarks while notably reducing memory and enabling larger models/training configurations; (iii) JEPA’s empirically observed focus on informative, low‑variance features (via CCA on ImageNet) versus MAE’s reconstruction bias; and (iv) for Dale’s‑law RNNs, spectra with high SVD entropy correlate with good learning, and architectures (DANN) that match standard RNN spectra perform best; (v) a learning‑augmented MTS framework with bandit access offering provable sublinear regret but no experiments to compare.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the papers matching each topic, with their key experimental results and a comparison.
> 
> ## Papers identified
> 
> **(1) Part-body association — PBADet** (ICLR 2024, `08b70bc3…`)
> One-stage anchor-free part-to-body association (hands/face/feet → person) via a single part-to-body center offset.
> - BodyHands: HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (anchor-free part-to-body), vs BPJDet 85.3/86.80/78.13; anchor-based version is worse, proving the anchor-free design helps.
> - vs ED-Pose (COCO val, Precision/Recall/F1): all-parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs ED-Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51; left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87. PBADet is markedly more robust in precision/F1.
> - COCOHumanParts: AP on par with BPJDet, leads AP_M, AP_L, person/feet; lowest mMR-2. CrowdHuman: body AP 91.6, MR-2 36.5 (YOLOv7), besting BPJDet (89.5–90.7 AP, 39.7–41.3 MR-2). Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offsets and task-alignment all improve joint AP.
> 
> **(2) Dale's Law / spectral stability — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023, `e63a94c4…`)
> - Sign constraints alone explain little of the gap: freezing signs costs only ~0.7–1%, but the full ColEI-vs-RNN gap is 2.3% (sequential MNIST).
> - Spectrum-transplant experiments: the singular-value spectrum at initialization matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors.
> - ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), unlike standard RNNs/DANNs; smaller networks and fewer I units worsen both spectra and performance. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error; DANNs stay robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron (NSE ≈ 0.95). ColEI is unstable without gradient clipping. This goes beyond sign clipping: the paper shows clipping isn't the culprit — the spectrum is.
> 
> **(3) JEPA implicit bias — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (`40fde037…`)
> Non-contrastive self-distillation (StopGrad) vs MAE pixel reconstruction in deep linear nets: JEPA is biased to high-influence (high regression-coefficient ρ) features, increasingly with depth; MAE ordering depends only on λ. Critical-time analysis (t* ∝ λ⁻¹ρ^(1−2L)…) shows JEPA learns low-noise, high-influence features first and suppresses noisy directions. ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA). **Note:** the paper's validation is theoretical + ImageNet CCA; the specific "cosine-similarity/log-loss linear probes on CIFAR-100" detail you mention is not in this paper — the closest CIFAR-100 linear-probe results (normalized/cosine features, SGD linear classifier, top-1) are in the contrastive-learning paper "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (`160e1407…`), which is contrastive (SimCLR + variance-reduction loss), not non-contrastive.
> 
> **(4) 4-bit optimizers — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023, `8d5e1455…`)
> 4-bit first/second moments (B128 + dynamic-exponent first moment; rank-1/zero-excluded linear second moment; optional factorization), built on 32-bit AdamW (decoupled weight decay).
> - Matches/beats 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; GPT-2M BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; Transformer-Base WMT 26.28 vs 26.61); better than Adafactor/SM3.
> - Memory: LLaMA-7B −57.7% (43.5 GB), RoBERTa-L −43–47%, ~2× smaller states than 8-bit, ~4× for 4-bitFactor; trains LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU and 4× larger OPT. **Note:** experiments use Transformers (Swin-T, Transformer-Base, RoBERTa, GPT-2, LLaMA); ResNet-50 and SGD fine-tuning are not among the evaluated setups (SGD-M appears only in the framework/convergence proof).
> 
> **(5) Learning-augmented MTS — "Learning-Augmented Algorithms for MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors"** (ICML 2025, `c97e745c…`)
> Bandit access (m-delayed) to ℓ heuristics for MTS; combines heuristics via HEDGE/SHARE with exploration/exploitation and MTS rounding.
> - Regret O((Dℓ ln ℓ)^{1/3} m^{2/3} OPT_{≤0}^{2/3}), sublinear in OPT, so competitive ratio → (1+o(1)) vs the best heuristic; tight lower bounds Ω̃(ℓ^{1/3}T^{2/3}) and Ω̃((kℓ)^{1/3}T^{2/3}) (Dekel et al. construction); policy-regret extension O((mℓ ln ℓ)^{1/3}T^{2/3}) for memory-bounded adversaries; guess-and-double estimates OPT online with R^{2/3} overhead. **Note:** this is a theory-only paper (no empirical results), and "near-linear runtime in problem size" is not explicitly claimed.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting terms you flagged
> - **Cross-entropy:** Universal Guidance (`9134ed60…`, ℓ_ce classifier-guidance extension) and RZ-NAS (implementation).
> - **Cosine similarity:** Universal Guidance (CLIP/style guidance uses negative cosine similarity; DrawBench CLIP score 0.2632 vs conditional Stable Diffusion 0.2818), the contrastive-embeddings paper (negative-pair cosine similarities), Visual Data-Type Identification (0.85 threshold), AdvI2I.
> - **F1/Precision:** PBADet (Table 7), GOT-D (GLUE F1), GEEA (dangling-entity Precision/Recall/F1).
> - **Transformer-based conditional guidance:** Universal Guidance (compares guidance vs text-conditional Stable Diffusion; "Adding conditional control…" cited); its time complexity scales linearly with the number of refinement steps k.
> - **Clean subset D_k^c:** This notation does **not** appear anywhere in the collection — I cannot confirm it. Closest are GOT-D's "clean" target subsets (TOXICITY ≤ 0.1) and the Hessian paper's "clean labels/clean test" terminology.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> Across the five methods, the common thread is "match or beat a strong full-information/full-precision baseline with a restricted mechanism": PBADet removes two-stage association and beats BPJDet/ED-Pose in precision-F1; the Dale's-law paper shows the restriction (sign constraint) is not the real cost — the initialization spectrum is; JEPA's restriction (latent prediction) buys noise suppression that MAE lacks; 4-bit optimizers retain 32-bit AdamW accuracy while cutting memory up to ~58%; and the MTS algorithm attains (1+o(1))-competitive behavior against the best heuristic despite bandit feedback. The strongest empirical evidence is in PBADet (large AP/F1 gains) and the 4-bit optimizer (lossless accuracy across 6 tasks); the Dale's-law and JEPA papers are primarily analytical/theory with supporting experiments; the MTS paper provides no empirical results. Several details you listed (D_k^c, CIFAR-100 cosine/log-loss probes in the JEPA paper, ResNet-50/SGD evaluation in the optimizer paper, near-linear runtime claims) could not be verified in this collection.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, here are the papers matching your five topics and a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Papers identified
> 
> 1. **Part-body association** — *PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association* (ICLR 2024)
> 2. **Spectral stability of Dale's-law RNNs** — *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023)
> 3. **JEPA/self-distillation implicit bias** — *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks* (NeurIPS 2024)
> 4. **4-bit optimizer states** — *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023)
> 5. **Learning-augmented MTS with bandit predictors** — *Learning-Augmented Algorithms for MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors* (ICML 2025)
> 
> ## Experimental results and comparison
> 
> **1. PBADet (AP / Precision / Recall / F1):** On BodyHands it beats all SOTA: hand AP 89.1 (YOLOv7) / 88.1 (YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet 85.9; conditional accuracy 92.62/92.71 vs 86.91; joint AP 85.98/85.73 vs 84.39 — with a smaller backbone (36.9M vs 86.1M params). On COCOHumanParts AP is on par with BPJDet while leading AP_M/AP_L and feet detection, and it achieves the lowest average mMR⁻² for head, face, both hands, right foot. On CrowdHuman it attains the best body MR⁻² (36.5) and body AP (91.6). vs ED-Pose (Swin-L): all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51 — roughly doubling precision and F1 on hands/feet.
> 
> **2. Dale's Law RNNs:** Sign constraints alone impair learning (≈0.7%±0.3% for RNNs, ≈1%±1% for ColEI) but do not explain the full gap (2.3%±0.6%). Singular-value spectrum "transplant" experiments show the spectrum matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors (1.5%±0.3% / 2%±1% contributions). ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure) while DANN RNNs match standard RNN spectra and learn just as well, robust even with a single inhibitory neuron. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error; gradient clipping mitigates the ColEI deficit. This is empirical (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition), not just theory.
> 
> **3. JEPA vs MAE:** Theory (deep linear nets, exact ODEs) shows JEPA learns high-influence (high-ρ) features greedily, with depth amplifying the bias, whereas MAE order depends mainly on covariance λ; at depth L, JEPA converges to ρ^L vs MAE ρ^(L/(L+1)). On ImageNet, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance (bottom PCA) subspace containing perceptual features than MAE, which tracks the top-variance subspace (CCA over training). Limitations: deep-linear MLPs and special initializations only. Note: the cosine-similarity + CIFAR-100 linear-probe (normalized features, top-1 accuracy) evaluation appears in the companion contrastive-learning paper *On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning* (ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10/100; e.g., CIFAR-100 ~55–62% top-1 across batch sizes), not in the JEPA paper itself, which uses CCA on ImageNet.
> 
> **4. 4-bit optimizers:** Match or exceed 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; GPT-2M E2E BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7; QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6) and are comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 Transformer 26.28 vs 26.61 SacreBleu). Sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor β₁=0, SM3) degrade more (e.g., CLS 79.0–80.0). Memory: 57.7% savings on LLaMA-7B (75.4→31.9 GB, enabling single-80GB-GPU training), 43–47% on RoBERTa-L, 34–36% on GPT-2M; 4-bitFactor ≈2× smaller than 8-bit, ≈4× smaller than 32-bit; convergence curves closely track 32-bit. Tested on Transformers (Swin-T, Transformer-Base, LLaMA, RoBERTa, GPT-2); the collection does not contain a ResNet-50 experiment for this optimizer.
> 
> **5. MTS with bandit predictors:** Theoretical only — no datasets. Algorithm 2 (HEDGE/SHARE with exploration/exploitation and surrogate costs) achieves regret O((Dℓk lnℓ)^{1/3}m^{2/3}OPT≤₀^{2/3}) against the best heuristic and Õ(k^{1/3}OPT≤ₖ^{2/3}) against k-switching benchmarks, i.e., competitive ratio →1 (sublinear in OPT). A matching lower bound Ω̃(OPT^{2/3}) via Dekel et al. (2013) shows tightness; also gives O(T^{2/3}) policy regret for m-memory-bounded bandits and an online doubling scheme for OPT estimation with R^{2/3} overhead.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting observations
> 
> - **Empirical vs theoretical:** PBADet and the 4-bit optimizer paper are fully empirical with strong numeric wins; the Dale's-law paper is empirical-theoretical (NSE as a predictive diagnostic); JEPA is largely theory with ImageNet validation; the MTS paper is purely theoretical (no experiments reported).
> - **Robustness theme:** PBADet keeps accuracy while simplifying representation; 4-bit optimizers keep accuracy while cutting memory; DANN keeps performance while respecting Dale's law; JEPA keeps useful features while suppressing noise; the MTS algorithm keeps near-optimal competitive ratio while restricting feedback.
> - **Requested specifics present in the collection:** cross-entropy (Universal Guidance uses per-pixel cross-entropy for segmentation/classifier guidance, and cosine similarity/negative cosine for CLIP guidance, with time complexity linear in refinement steps k — matching "near-linear runtime"); F1/Precision (PBADet vs ED-Pose); cosine similarity and log-loss linear probes on CIFAR-100 (contrastive-embeddings paper).
> - **Requested specifics NOT found:** the exact clean-subset notation **D_k^c** does not appear in any retrieved document (only GOT-D's "clean" 2.5K low-toxicity subsets and generic "data subsetting" appear); no paper in the collection reports a 4-bit-optimizer run on a 50-layer ResNet; the JEPA paper does not itself use CIFAR-100 cosine/log-loss linear probes.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results across the five works, organized around your four system needs. I only report results and claims that appear explicitly in the papers you provided.
> 
> A) Anchor‑free part–body association under multi‑person scenes (PBADet vs prior work)
> Identical datasets and metrics
> - BodyHands (Narasimhaswamy’22)
>   - Metrics: Hand AP (IoU=0.5), Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP.
>   - Results (Table 1):
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5s6/m6/l6): Hand AP = 84.0/85.3/85.9; Cond. Acc. = 85.68/86.80/86.91; Joint AP = 77.86/78.13/84.39.
>     • PBADet (Ours YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6, 1024×1024): Hand AP = 89.1/88.1; Cond. Acc. = 92.62/92.71; Joint AP = 85.98/85.73.
>   - Takeaway: On the same dataset, PBADet improves all three metrics over BPJDet, with +3.2–5.1 AP and +5.8–6.9 Cond. Acc.; Joint AP also higher (best 85.98 vs 84.39).
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (Yang’20)
>   - Metrics: COCO APs (original/subordinate) and per‑category APs; association quality via mMR−2 (lower is better).
>   - Detection AP (Table 2):
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 = 43.6/43.3; AP.5 = 70.6/69.8; APM = 63.8/63.2; APL = 61.8/58.9.
>     • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 = 43.0/41.8; AP.5 = 70.0/68.4; APM/APL higher (66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4).
>     • PBADet (YOLOv7): AP.5:.95 = 42.7/41.5; AP.5 = 69.5/67.9; APM/APL = 65.8/64.4 and 66.7/63.3.
>   - Per‑category AP (Table 2): PBADet matches or is close to BPJDet, and leads on person and feet categories (e.g., PBADet‑l6 r‑foot/l‑foot 30.9/31.5 vs BPJDet‑l6 30.2/30.9).
>   - Association mMR−2 (Table 3, lower is better):
>     • Hands: PBADet‑l6 36.2 (l‑hand), 40.8 (r‑hand) outperform BPJDet‑l6 41.6/42.2; heads/faces also slightly better (27.9/30.5 vs 30.8/31.8).
>   - Takeaway: On COCOHumanParts, PBADet improves association robustness (lower mMR−2), with comparable overall AP and noticeably better medium/large object APs.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Shao’18)
>   - Metrics: body MR−2, face MR−2, body/face AP, body‑face mMR−2.
>   - Results (Table 5): PBADet‑YOLOv7 yields best body MR−2=36.5 (vs BPJDet‑m6 39.7/l6 40.7) and highest body AP=91.6; face/body‑face mMR−2 comparable to BPJDet.
>   - Takeaway: On crowded scenes, PBADet reduces miss rates and increases body AP while maintaining similar association mMR−2.
> 
> Similar tasks / qualitative comparisons
> - Compared to multi‑person pose (ED‑Pose), on COCO (Appendix A.2, Table 7), PBADet attains substantially higher F1 on four small parts: LF/RF = 51.08/50.34 vs 40.46/40.34; LH/RH = 46.50/47.34 vs 22.87/24.17; precision and recall higher for all parts. Qualitative figures show fewer speculative limb predictions.
> 
> Ablations directly tied to your setting
> - Anchor‑free head and part‑to‑body center‑offset decoding are key: Anchor‑free + part‑to‑body outperforms anchor‑based and body‑to‑part (Table 8), and dedicated association loss (Lassoc) significantly boosts Conditional Accuracy/Joint AP (Table 4). Multi‑scale offsets and task‑alignment further improve metrics (Table 4).
> 
> B) Low‑memory, 4‑bit optimizers (first/second moments) vs full precision
> Identical datasets across optimizers
> - Natural language understanding (RoBERTa‑L on GLUE; Table 2 and Table 7): Mean NLU score
>   • 32‑bit AdamW: 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW: 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW: 89.1; 4‑bit Factor: 88.9; SM3 degrades to 87.5.
>   • Per task (e.g., MNLI/QNLI/QQP/RTE/SST‑2/MRPC/CoLA/STS‑B), 4‑bit matches 32‑bit/8‑bit within noise; SM3 consistently worse on several tasks.
> 
> - Question answering (RoBERTa‑L on SQuAD/SQuAD2.0; Table 9):
>   • 32‑bit AdamW: F1=94.6; 4‑bit AdamW: 94.5; 4‑bit Factor: 94.6; 8‑bit AdamW: 94.5; SM3: 91.7.
> 
> - Machine translation (Transformer‑Base on WMT14 en‑de; Table 2):
>   • 32‑bit AdamW: 26.61; 8‑bit AdamW: 26.66; 4‑bit AdamW: 26.28; 4‑bit Factor: 26.45; SM3: 22.72.
>   • Takeaway: 4‑bit maintains accuracy close to full precision and 8‑bit; SM3 shows large drops on MT.
> 
> - Image classification pretraining (Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k; Table 2):
>   • 32‑bit AdamW: 81.2; 8‑bit: 81.0; 4‑bit: 80.8; 4‑bit Factor: 80.9; Adafactor variants and SM3 underperform (80.0/79.5 and 79.0).
> 
> - Natural language generation (GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG; Table 2 & 8):
>   • BLEU: 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5; 4‑bit 67.8; 4‑bit Factor 67.6. Other metrics (NIST/METEOR/ROUGE‑L/CIDEr) remain aligned across 32/8/4‑bit.
> 
> - Instruction tuning (LLaMA 7B/13B/33B on Alpaca; Table 3):
>   • 7B MMLU: 32‑bit 38.7 vs 4‑bit 38.9 (comparable); other tasks (HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA) nearly identical.
>   • 13B MMLU: 46.5 vs 47.4 (4‑bit slightly higher); 33B MMLU: 56.4 vs 54.9 (small drop), while other benchmarks remain close.
> 
> Memory/time efficiency (identical training regimes)
> - LLaMA‑7B with FSDP (Table 4): total mem 75.4 GB (32‑bit) → 31.87 GB (4‑bit), 57.7% savings; time improves (3.35 h → 3.07 h). 
> - RoBERTa‑L fine‑tuning (Table 4): total mem 5.31 GB → 3.00–3.02 GB (4‑bit), 43% savings; with fused kernels, 4‑bit is faster than 8‑bit (3.17 vs 3.38 min).
> - GPT‑2 Medium (Table 4): total mem 6.89 GB → 4.62 GB (4‑bit), 34% savings; training time matches/exceeds 8‑bit when fused.
> 
> Key ablations tied to second‑moment quantization (directly relevant to ~4‑bit moments)
> - Zero‑point problem is decisive: Using DE‑0 or Linear mappings that exclude zero for the 2nd moment removes instability and preserves accuracy, unlike DE with zero (Table 1). Rank‑1 normalization plus Linear mapping yields the best BLEU (67.8) with 0% instability.
> - Factorization of 2nd moment (Adafactor‑style) with 4‑bit first moment attains comparable accuracy and further memory savings (Table 1 & 2).
> 
> C) Recurrent modules with EI constraints and spectral stability (Dale’s ANNs vs ColEI vs standard RNN)
> Identical tasks and networks
> - Adding problem (length 20), sequential MNIST (row‑wise), Penn Tree Bank language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task (Fig. 2 A–D):
>   • Across all four tasks, ColEI networks learn worse and exhibit higher variance than DANNs and standard RNNs. DANN RNNs match standard RNNs.
>   • Gradient clipping benefits ColEI significantly more (Appendix Fig. 10 in the paper’s text), indicating sensitivity to spectral pathologies.
> 
> Spectral findings tied to performance (measured across many random inits)
> - ColEI shows multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with a large‑value mode (Fig. 3D), unlike the unimodal spectra of DANN/standard RNNs (Fig. 3E–F); eigenvalues of ColEI concentrate near the origin (Fig. 3A–C). Spectrum transplants confirm that spectra matter more than sign constraints for performance gaps (Fig. 4B–C): transplanting ColEI’s spectrum into an RNN hurts more than freezing signs.
> 
> Scaling and EI‑ratio sensitivity (sequential MNIST focus)
> - Vary EI ratio (Fig. 5): Reducing inhibitory fraction degrades ColEI accuracy and reduces NSE (normalized SVD entropy); DANNs remain robust even with only 1 inhibitory neuron.
> - Vary width (Fig. 6): Larger ColEI nets improve NSE and test error despite growing max singular values; performance anti‑correlates with NSE across sizes and EI ratios (Fig. 7D). Small balanced ColEI networks can beat larger skewed ones if their initial NSE is higher (Fig. 7A–B).
> 
> Interpretation for your constraint: For EI‑constrained recurrent modules, DANN‑style parameterization (with sign‑constrained submatrices WEE, WEI, WIE but unconstrained effective W) achieves standard‑RNN‑like spectra and performance. ColEI’s poor spectra—not the sign constraints alone—align with instability/under‑performance; thus, controlling the singular value distribution (high NSE) is predictive of stability and learning quality.
> 
> D) Online bandit‑style selection among predictors/heuristics (bandit access with m‑step memory)
> Regret guarantees (identical model/settings)
> - New learning‑augmented MTS bandit setting (ICML’25): with m‑delayed bandit access to ℓ heuristics in a metric space of diameter D, the algorithm attains (Theorem 3.9):
>   • Expected cost E[ALG] ≤ OPT≤0 + O((D·ℓ·lnℓ)^{1/3}·m^{2/3}·OPT^{2/3}_{≤0}).
>   • Competitive ratio tends to 1 as OPT≤0 grows; tight up to log factors via a matching lower bound Ω(OPT^{2/3}_{≤0}) (Theorem 1.3).
> - Against a switching benchmark (≤k switches), the regret is O~(k^{1/3}·OPT^{2/3}_{≤k}) (Theorem 1.2), giving (1+ε) competitiveness for k up to Ω~(ε^3·OPT≤k).
> - In the related m‑memory‑bounded adversary model, adapting the same dynamics yields O(T^{2/3}) regret with slightly improved dependence on m (Appendix D).
> 
> Summary by dataset/task type
> - Human part–body association tasks (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman): PBADet consistently lowers miss rates and improves (or matches) detection AP and association quality relative to BPJDet and prior detector baselines; it also beats pose‑based ED‑Pose on part detection/association F1 on COCO.
> - Foundation‑model fine‑tuning (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG, WMT14 en‑de, ImageNet‑1k, Alpaca/MMLU/ARC/OBQA): 4‑bit optimizers (with 4‑bit moments and either rank‑1/Linear 2nd‑moment quantization or factorization) match full‑precision/8‑bit accuracy within noise on all benchmarks tested, while shrinking optimizer memory by ~34–58% and often holding or improving wall‑clock.
> - Recurrent time‑series modeling tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition): DANN‑style EI RNNs match standard RNNs, while simple EI partitioning (ColEI) lags; spectrum quality (high NSE, unimodal singular values) predicts performance and stability.
> - Online selection among multiple predictors/heuristics: The presented bandit framework achieves sublinear regret in OPT (Θ(OPT^{2/3})) with tight lower bounds, providing a principled way to pick among heuristics online when only one can be queried per step and costs depend on m previous queries.
> 
> Notes on entities present in the results
> - Optimizers: AdamW (used across 32‑bit/8‑bit/4‑bit experiments) and SGD (used to train PBADet per YOLOv7 schedule).
> - Self‑supervised learning: JEPA analysis (Non‑contrastive self‑distillation) provides empirical evidence that JEPA learns more semantic, low‑variance features faster than MAE (Appendix D, CCA trends on ImageNet‑64), and controlled linear experiments show JEPA prioritizes high‑influence features.
> - F1/Precision/Recall: Reported for PBADet vs ED‑Pose on COCO small parts (Appendix A.2), with PBADet higher on all metrics.
> - Backbone references: ResNet‑50 baselines (Faster‑FPN‑R50, FCOS‑R50) appear in COCOHumanParts Table 2 and are outperformed by joint detectors (Hier R‑CNN, BPJDet, PBADet) in that table.
> 
> What these results imply for your pipeline
> - (a) Use PBADet (anchor‑free, part‑to‑body center‑offset) as the detector/tracker: it yields higher part AP, higher joint AP, and lower mismatching/miss rates than BPJDet across BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman, and higher F1 than ED‑Pose for small parts on COCO.
> - (b) Use the 4‑bit optimizer with: small‑block (B128) for 1st moment, rank‑1 normalization + Linear (zero‑excluded) for 2nd moment, or factorize 2nd moment. This preserves accuracy across GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/WMT/ImageNet and compresses memory by up to ~58%; fused kernels restore/increase throughput.
> - (c) For EI‑constrained recurrent attention/recurrent modules, prefer DANN‑style EI parameterization to preserve unimodal spectra and stability. Monitor normalized SVD entropy as a pre‑training indicator of stability; adjust EI ratio and width to raise NSE. These choices empirically closed the gap to standard RNNs on adding, sMNIST, PTB, and object recognition.
> - (d) For online predictor/heuristic selection under bandit access and m‑step memory, the presented algorithm achieves E[ALG] ≤ OPT + O(OPT^{2/3}) with a tight Ω(OPT^{2/3}) lower bound; against k‑switch benchmarks, regret scales as O~(k^{1/3}·OPT^{2/3}).
>

> I have enough evidence from the document collection to answer. Let me compile the answer.
> 
> ## Summary
> 
> **Requested capability → matched work (and experimental results):**
> 
> **(a) Anchor-free detector linking parts to bodies — PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> One-stage anchor-free detector that links hands/face to the right body via a single **part-to-body center offset** (2D vector from each part location to its parent body's bounding-box center), guaranteeing one-to-one part↔body correspondence even when parts are occluded — exactly the "associate hands/face to the right body" need. Results: on **BodyHands** (hand-body association) it beats all SOTA — hand AP 89.1, **conditional accuracy 92.62**, joint AP 85.98 (vs. BPJDet's 85.3/86.80/78.13) with fewer parameters (36.9M, 1024 input vs 1536); on **COCOHumanParts** (6 parts: head, face, l/r hand, l/r foot) it matches/leads BPJDet on AP (e.g., AP_M 65.8 vs 63.8) with the **lowest mismatch rate mMR−2**; on **CrowdHuman** it gets the best body MR−2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6). Ablations: removing the association loss drops conditional accuracy from 92.62→80.78 (joint AP 85.98→78.07); multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each add ~1 point. It also outperforms the pose estimator **ED-Pose** in precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet. Evaluation uses clean-part metrics (conditional accuracy, joint AP) — the closest thing to "clean subset evaluation."
> 
> **(b) Low-memory 4-bit-moment optimizer — "4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023).**
> Compresses AdamW first/second moments to **4-bit** (smaller block B128 quantization for 1st moment; zero-point-excluding linear quantizer + rank-1 normalization for 2nd; optional factorized 2nd moment). Results: matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9), ImageNet (Swin-T 80.8–80.9 vs 81.2), QA F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), NLG BLEU (67.8 vs 67.7), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (e.g., 4-bit AdamW 38.9/47.4/54.9 MMLU vs 38.7/46.5/56.4 for 32-bit — comparable or better at 7B/13B); memory savings up to **57.7%** (LLaMA-7B 31.9GB vs 75.4GB) and 4-bit Factor adds more. Note: small-model non-fused versions can be slower (throughput improves with fusion/offloading).
> 
> **(c) Excitatory/inhibitory recurrent modules with spectral stability — "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023).**
> Directly answers the design guidance: E/I sign constraints (ColEI) alone don't explain poor learning — **the singular-value spectrum of the recurrent weights at initialization** matters more. ColEI has a multimodal, dispersed spectrum with a mode of large singular values (unstable/exploding gradients); standard RNNs and the reparameterized **DANN** (E-to-E, E-to-I, I-to-E non-negative projections) have the desirable unimodal quarter-circle (Marchenko-Pastur) spectrum. Results: ColEI is worse and higher-variance on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI most; smaller nets / fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and learning; **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** anti-correlates with final test error (predictive of performance). Guidance: use DANN-style parameterization (keeps E/I structure but recovers stable spectrum) or initialize/constrain the spectrum (unimodal singular values, monitor NSE); don't rely on spectral-radius-only constraints.
> 
> **(d) Online bandit-style predictor selection with sublinear regret — "Learning-Augmented Algorithms for MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors" (ICML 2025).**
> Combines ℓ heuristics/predictors online, querying only **one per step** (bandit feedback with m-delayed cost observation, needed because a heuristic's cost at t requires its state at t−1 — exactly your "predictors/heuristics" setting). Algorithm (HEDGE/SHARE with exploration/exploitation and MTS-style rounding) achieves **regret O(OPT²ᐟ³)** vs. the best heuristic (sublinear in OPT; competitive ratio →1+o(1)), Õ(k^⅓·OPT^⅔) vs. k-switching benchmarks, and tight lower bounds Ω̃(T^⅔); it also gives O(T^⅔) policy regret for m-memory-bounded adversarial bandits. This is the bandit-style sublinear-regret combination method.
> 
> **Other requested topics — what the collection does/doesn't support:**
> - **Joint-embedding self-supervised pretraining + cosine scoring on a 100-class benchmark + SGD/ResNet-50/Transformer fine-tuning + F1/log-loss**: the contrastive-learning paper ("On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning") matches the setup (SimCLR-style joint embedding, cosine-similarity analysis, ResNet-50 on **ImageNet-100**, SGD, linear eval): its variance-reduction loss improves top-1 on ImageNet-100 (e.g., 74.04 vs 73.80 at t=0.3; 52.48 vs 51.79 on full ImageNet), but it reports **top-1 accuracy, not F1/precision/log-loss**; "LDReg" also regularizes SSL embeddings (ResNet-50/ViT, ImageNet). No document in the collection reports F1/Precision/log-loss on a 100-class cosine-scored benchmark, so that specific evaluation chain cannot be fully confirmed.
> - **"D_k^c"**: no document in the collection contains the notation "D_k^c"; the clean-set evaluations found are conditional accuracy/joint AP (PBADet) and clean-vs-noisy-label analyses (Hessian paper), so I cannot point to a work with D_k^c.
> - **Transformer-style conditional guidance**: "Universal Guidance for Diffusion Models" (ICLR 2024) gives training-free guidance with arbitrary guidance functions (face, segmentation, object-location, CLIP-text guidance) using gradients on predicted clean images — matches "transformer-style conditional guidance" broadly (it's diffusion/transformer-agnostic guidance; results comparable to specialized conditional models on Stable Diffusion/ImageNet).
> - **Near-linear-time implementations**: the linear-time HSIC framework (O(n) estimators, tests 100k samples in <10s vs quadratic baselines) and the output-sensitive parametric-DP algorithms (e.g., ray search O(R·T_DP), near-linear in output size) are the near-linear-time results in the collection; neither is a part-body/gesture system, so "near-linear-time" for your specific pipeline is only partially covered by these algorithmic works.
> 
> **Bottom line:** PBADet (a), 4-bit optimizers (b), the Dale's-Law RNN spectral paper (c), and the MTS bandit-combination paper (d) together cover all four explicit needs with strong experimental evidence; the joint-embedding/cosine-100-class chain is partially matched (accuracy, not F1/log-loss), "D_k^c" does not appear anywhere in the collection, and near-linear-time results exist but outside the part-body domain.

> Here is a mapping of your four needs to works in the collection, with their experimental results compared.
> 
> ## (a) Anchor-free part→body association
> **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage, anchor-free detector that links parts (hands, face, feet) to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset, avoiding anchor-based body-to-part offsets (BPJDet). On COCO (vs. ED-Pose, Swin-L), PBADet (YOLOv5l6) is substantially better: all-parts F1 **48.52 vs 31.51**, left hand F1 **46.50 vs 22.87**, right hand **47.34 vs 24.17**, left/right foot **51.08/50.34 vs 40.46/40.34**. On BodyHands/COCO-HumanParts it beats BPJDet and HierR-CNN; on CrowdHuman it leads body MR-2 with competitive AP. Ablations: removing the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, or task-alignment each degrade hand accuracy, conditional accuracy, and joint AP — so all three components matter. It also extends to quadruped (AnimalPose/AP-10K) part-body association.
> 
> ## (b) 4-bit-moment optimizer
> **4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)** — compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (smaller block B128 + dynamic exponent for m; rank-1 normalization / zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for v; optional factorized second moment "4-bit Factor"). Results: matches 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (89.1 vs 88.9), ImageNet Swin-T (80.8 vs 81.2), E2E BLEU (67.8 vs 67.7), SQuAD F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), WMT14 (26.28 vs 26.61), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7 for 7B). Memory: LLaMA-7B total memory drops **75.40 GB → 31.87 GB (57.7% saved)**, enabling single-80GB-GPU training; with fused ops it is also faster than 8-bit AdamW. It beats 8-bit AdamW, Adafactor, and SM3 on accuracy retention.
> 
> ## (c) E/I-constrained recurrent modules with spectral stability
> **"Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** — the key guidance is that **spectral properties, not sign constraints, dominate learning**: column-constrained (ColEI) RNNs get a multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum (rank-one column-mean nilpotent term) and train poorly with high variance; recurrent Dale's-ANNs (DANN) keep a unimodal, clustered spectrum like standard RNNs and match them. Gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance across EI ratio and size (smaller networks / fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra). Recommendation: build E/I recurrent modules with unimodal clustered spectra (e.g., DANN-style, orthogonal-like initialization) rather than naive column sign-partitioning, and monitor NSE.
> 
> ## (d) Online bandit-style predictor selection with sublinear regret
> **"Learning-Augmented Algorithms for MTS with Bandit Access to Multiple Predictors"** — combines heuristics online querying only one at a time; regret is sublinear, **O((Dℓlnℓ)^{1/3} m^{2/3} OPT_{≤0}^{2/3})**, with a tight lower bound **Ω̃(ℓ^{1/3} T^{2/3})** (Dekel-style switching-cost reduction), so it is near-optimal; competitive ratio approaches 1 + o(1) w.r.t. the best heuristic. Related: **Off-CMAB (CLCB)** for offline combinatorial bandits gives O(√(m log(mn/δ)/n)) regret (e.g., 36% LLM-cache cost reduction), and **BSO** for online binary-weight training achieves O(√T) regret with memory O(n²L/32).
> 
> ## Supporting items you asked to discuss
> - **Transformer-style conditional guidance**: **Universal Guidance (ICLR 2024)** — training-free guidance of frozen diffusion models with any differentiable function (face, segmentation, object location, style, CLIP text). CLIP text guidance uses **cosine similarity** between image and text embeddings; CLIP score 0.2632 vs. 0.2818 for a dedicated text-conditional model (comparable). Its time complexity **scales linearly with the number of refinement steps k** (near-linear). A related linear-time method: **Learning Kernels for Fast HSIC-Based Independence Testing** runs in seconds on up to 100k samples with favorable power-runtime trade-off.
> - **Joint-embedding SSL pretraining**: **Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features** (JEPA/MAE feature-dynamics analysis on ImageNet-1K), **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** (InfoNCE/SigLIP, CIFAR-10/100 top-1 gains), and **LDReg** (LID regularization improving SimCLR/BYOL/MAE, including COCO detection).
> - **Clean-subset evaluation (D_k^c) and a 100-class cosine-scoring benchmark**: the exact **D_k^c notation does not appear anywhere in the provided collection**, and no 100-class benchmark evaluated purely by cosine scoring was found (closest are CIFAR-100-based evaluations in the contrastive-learning and AGL papers, and 27-class cosine-matching in the Visual Data-Type ID paper). Closest related work is **GOT-D**, which selects "clean" subsets (TOXICITY ≤ 0.1) for fine-tuning and evaluates on disjoint clean test samples — its 20k-subset cuts worst-case toxicity 0.33 vs. GPT-2's 0.62 while keeping downstream accuracy ~0.408 vs. 0.422. I cannot confirm the specific D_k^c evaluation scheme from this context; it would need a source outside the collection.
