**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Summary of experimental results and cross-paper comparisons (strictly from the provided figures/tables)  
> 
> Identical datasets across the five papers  
> - None of the five works evaluate on the same dataset. Each paper reports results on its own benchmarks (e.g., PBADet on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman; 4‑bit optimizers on GLUE/ImageNet/SQuAD/WMT/E2E‑NLG/Alpaca; GWM on Goodreads/Multi‑Modal‑Paper/Baby–Sports–Clothing/Cora–PubMed–HIV/AgentClinic/LongBench v2/ALFWorld; Dale’s Law on adding/sequential‑MNIST/Penn Tree Bank/naturalistic object recognition; JEPA vs MAE on controlled linear settings plus an ImageNet diagnostic without shared metrics).  
> 
> Comparisons on similar task types (within each paper’s datasets)  
> 1) Human part–body association (detection/association; PBADet)  
> - BodyHands (Table 1): PBADet outperforms BPJDet on all metrics with the same or smaller backbones.  
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39.  
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73 also surpasses BPJDet (YOLOv5l6).  
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2, Table 3):  
>   • Overall AP(.5:.95): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 (orig/subord) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3 (BPJDet slightly higher on overall AP).  
>   • Size‑specific AP: PBADet leads on APM/APL (e.g., PBADet YOLOv5l6 APM 66.2/65.0, APL 67.2/64.4) vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 (63.8/63.2; 61.8/58.9).  
>   • Per‑category AP: mixed; PBADet improves feet (e.g., r‑foot 30.9, l‑foot 31.5) over BPJDet (30.2/30.9), while BPJDet keeps higher head/face/hands AP.  
>   • Association quality (average mMR−2, lower is better): PBADet achieves lower (better) averages across key parts; notably PBADet (YOLOv5l6) improves head (27.9 vs 30.8), face (30.5 vs 31.8), hands (36.2/40.8 vs 41.6/42.2) compared to BPJDet (YOLOv5l6).  
> - CrowdHuman (Table 5, Table 6): PBADet achieves the best MR−2 for body detection (36.5 with YOLOv7) and best AP for body (91.6), while mMR−2 for body‑face association is comparable to BPJDet (≈50–51).  
> - Comparison to ED‑Pose (Appendix A.2, Table 7): On COCO validation for parts (hands/feet), PBADet has substantially higher Precision/Recall/F1 than ED‑Pose (e.g., all parts F1: 48.52 vs 31.51).  
> 
> 2) Sequence modeling and spectral/implicit dynamics (Dale’s Law)  
> - Across four tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition; Fig. 2): simple column EI (ColEI) networks learn worse (higher error/worse accuracy) than standard RNNs and Dale’s ANNs (DANNs); DANNs learn comparably to standard RNNs.  
> - Gradient clipping helps ColEI much more than others (Appendix Figure 10).  
> - Varying spectral radius ρ (Appendix Fig. 9): no ρ where ColEI matches the best standard RNN/DANN; ColEI can look better at large ρ but worse at small ρ.  
> - Spectrum transplant (Fig. 4): singular value spectra matter more than sign constraints. Quantitatively, sign constraints alone reduce performance modestly (≈0.7%±0.3% for RNNs; ≈1%±1% for ColEI), while imposing ColEI‑like spectra on RNNs yields larger degradations (reported in Fig. 4C; e.g., 1.5%±0.3% effect for RNNs, 2%±1% for ColEI).  
> - Network size/E:I ratio (Figs. 5–7): for ColEI, fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks lower normalised SVD entropy (NSE) and worsen performance; larger networks increase NSE and improve performance despite a larger max singular value. DANNs remain robust (high NSE, good learning) across EI ratios and sizes.  
> 
> 3) Latent prediction vs reconstruction in self‑supervision (JEPA vs MAE)  
> - In deep linear analyses, JEPA learns features in an order biased toward high regression coefficients (ρ), while MAE learns by covariance (λ); JEPA’s depth amplifies this bias (Theorem results and Fig. 2, 4).  
> - Spectrum of findings borne out by ODE simulations and SGD on synthetic Gaussian data (Fig. 2, 4, 5): JEPA reverses learning order when λ increases but ρ decreases, while MAE does not.  
> - Temporal generative setting (Fig. 3): JEPA deprioritizes noisy features (smaller ρ) more than MAE.  
> - ImageNet diagnostic (Appendix D, Fig. 7): I‑JEPA’s features maintain higher similarity (mean CCA) between full and bottom‑variance subspaces during training than MAE, consistent with JEPA focusing faster on low‑variance/perceptual subspaces; the trend reverses for full vs top‑variance subspace.  
> 
> 4) Memory‑efficient training with 4‑bit optimizer states (4‑bit AdamW and Factor)  
> - Accuracy vs full precision (Table 2):  
>   • NLU (RoBERTa‑L, GLUE mean): 4‑bit AdamW 89.1±0.01 vs 32‑bit AdamW 88.9±0.01; matches or slightly improves.  
>   • Image classification (Swin‑T/ImageNet‑1k): 4‑bit 80.8–80.9 vs 32‑bit 81.2 (≤0.4% drop).  
>   • NLG (GPT‑2‑M on E2E‑NLG): BLEU 67.8±0.51 vs 67.7±0.67 (parity).  
>   • QA (RoBERTa‑L SQuAD F1): 94.5±0.10 vs 94.6±0.13 (parity); SQuAD2.0 F1 88.4±0.26 (4‑bit) vs 88.8±0.15 (32‑bit).  
>   • MT (Transformer‑Base WMT14 en‑de): SacreBLEU 26.28±0.05 (4‑bit) vs 26.61±0.08 (small gap).  
> - Instruction tuning (Table 3): LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B: 4‑bit AdamW matches or slightly improves 32‑bit on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA (e.g., 7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; 13B HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8; 33B close on all).  
> - Memory/time (Table 4):  
>   • LLaMA‑7B FSDP: 57.7% total memory saved (75.40→31.87 GB); training time improved (3.35 h→3.07 h).  
>   • RoBERTa‑L: 43.5% memory saved (5.31→3.00 GB); fused 4‑bit faster than 32‑bit (3.17 min vs 3.93 min).  
>   • GPT‑2‑M: 34.4% memory saved; fused 4‑bit time 2.11 h vs 2.13 h for 32‑bit.  
>   • Largest trainable model (Table 5): with 24 GB GPU, 4‑bit trains OPT‑1.3B vs 32‑bit OPT‑350M; with 80 GB, 4‑bit can train LLaMA‑7B.  
> - Ablations (Table 1, Table 6): For second moment, excluding zero in quantization (DE‑0 or Linear mapping) is critical; Rank‑1 normalization + Linear for v achieves stable, lossless convergence at 4‑bit; factorizing v (when dim>1) yields best memory/accuracy trade‑off.  
> 
> 5) Graph World Model (GWM) across diverse domains  
> - Multi‑modal generation (Table 2):  
>   • Goodreads: INSTRUCTG2I achieves highest CLIP/DINOv2 (50.37/25.54). GWM‑T is competitive (47.46/20.91), better than SD‑1.5/ControlNet on DINOv2; GWM‑E similar.  
>   • Multi‑Modal‑Paper: GWM‑E yields the best DINOv2 (26.03) and high CLIP (59.84), outperforming SD‑1.5 FT (24.13 DINOv2) and INSTRUCTG2I (18.80 DINOv2).  
> - Multi‑modal matching (Table 3):  
>   • Goodreads (text–image): CLIP‑FT best (Acc/Rec/F1 ≈92.6); GWM‑E strong (88.82/89.73/89.06).  
>   • Multi‑Modal‑Paper (text–image/table): GWM‑E best (96.23/97.21/97.13), far above Contrastive MLP.  
> - Recommendation (Table 4): GWM‑E generally best or near best:  
>   • Baby: Recall/F1 76.72/84.74 (best).  
>   • Sports: Recall 88.78 (best); LightGCN has slightly higher F1 (91.32) vs GWM‑E 90.32.  
>   • Clothing: 75.27/84.06 (best).  
> - Traditional graph prediction (Table 5):  
>   • Cora node: LLAGA 89.22 (highest); GWM‑E 83.03; GAT 82.76.  
>   • Cora link: GWM‑E 94.31 (highest).  
>   • PubMed node: LLAGA 95.03 (highest); GWM‑E 84.22.  
>   • PubMed link: OFA 96.39 (highest); GWM‑E 94.01.  
>   • HIV graph: GWM‑E 93.86 (highest).  
> - Multi‑agent collaboration (AgentClinic; Table 6): GWM‑T achieves the highest Accuracy/Recall/F1 (50.00/46.42/48.20), outperforming CoT/ToT/Few‑shot/Longformer and a fine‑tuned baseline (FT).  
> - RAG (LongBench v2; Table 7): With only 2k context, GWM‑E achieves the best Accuracy overall/easy/hard (33.32/39.16/29.52), outperforming RAG baselines (BM25/Dragon) and long‑context LLMs at 128k (e.g., GPT‑4o mini 29.01 overall).  
> - Planning/Optimization (ALFWorld; Table 8): GWM‑E achieves the best BERTScore Precision/Recall/F1 (93.27/92.36/92.13), above T5‑FT (92.06/91.52/91.82) and CoT.  
> - Multi‑hop graph utility (Fig. 4): Adding multi‑hop aggregation improves GWM across all tasks vs “no graph”; too many hops can over‑smooth.  
> 
> Performance on specific datasets (highlights)  
> - BodyHands (PBADet): PBADet (YOLOv7) 89.1/92.62/85.98 (Hand AP/CondAcc/Joint AP) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39.  
> - COCOHumanParts (PBADet): PBADet improves APM/APL over BPJDet while mixed per‑category AP; association mMR−2 lower for PBADet on head/face/hands (Table 3).  
> - CrowdHuman (PBADet): Best MR−2 (body) 36.5; body AP 91.6; association mMR−2 ≈50.8 (comparable to BPJDet).  
> - GLUE (4‑bit): 4‑bit equals or slightly exceeds 32‑bit (89.1 vs 88.9).  
> - ImageNet‑1k (4‑bit): 80.8–80.9 vs 81.2 (≤0.4% gap).  
> - E2E‑NLG (4‑bit): BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7.  
> - SQuAD (4‑bit): F1 94.5 vs 94.6; SQuAD2.0 F1 88.4 vs 88.8.  
> - WMT14 en‑de (4‑bit): 26.28 vs 26.61.  
> - LLaMA instruction tuning (4‑bit): 7B/13B/33B—4‑bit matches 32‑bit across MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA.  
> - Multi‑Modal‑Paper (GWM): Best generation DINOv2 26.03 (GWM‑E); best matching (Acc/Rec/F1) 96.23/97.21/97.13 (GWM‑E).  
> - Goodreads (GWM): INSTRUCTG2I best for generation; CLIP‑FT best for matching; GWM competitive but not SOTA on this dataset for these subtasks.  
> - Recommendation (GWM): GWM‑E best on Baby and Clothing (both Recall/F1), and best Recall on Sports (F1 slightly below LightGCN).  
> - Graph learning (GWM): GWM‑E tops Cora link & HIV graph; LLAGA/OFA lead on Cora/PubMed node and PubMed link.  
> - AgentClinic (GWM): GWM‑T best Accuracy/Recall/F1.  
> - LongBench v2 (GWM): GWM‑E best Accuracy across overall/easy/hard with only 2k context.  
> - ALFWorld (GWM): GWM‑E best BERTScore F1.  
> 
> Training/optimization choices that relate to reported results  
> - PBADet trained with SGD (YOLO‑style) and CE/IoU/DFL losses plus a quadratic‑style association L1 loss (task‑aligned anchor selection, metric t=s^α u^β; K=13); these settings underpin the reported AP/F1/mMR−2 gains.  
> - Dale’s Law experiments isolate effects of singular value spectra vs sign constraints; spectrum transplants and NSE analyses quantify effects on test error (Fig. 4, 5–7).  
> - JEPA vs MAE results are from exactly solvable deep‑linear dynamics and simulations (feature‑learning order differences) and an ImageNet CCA diagnostic indicating faster alignment to low‑variance subspaces for JEPA.  
> - 4‑bit Optimizers: core results hinge on 4‑bit quantization of moments with Rank‑1 normalization + Linear mapping for v (zero‑point excluded) and B128/DE for m; across tasks, 4‑bit AdamW/Factor match 32‑bit while saving 34–58% total memory and sometimes time.  
> - GWM: Two instantiations—GWM‑T (tokens) and GWM‑E (embeddings)—use graph message passing; GWM‑E’s multi‑hop projector and small token budget explain its advantage on long contexts and several domains.
> 
> Bottom line across similar task categories  
> - Detection/association (vision): On BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman, PBADet consistently improves association accuracy (mMR−2) and size‑specific APs over anchor‑based BPJDet while achieving best MR−2/AP on CrowdHuman body detection.  
> - Long‑context question answering (RAG): GWM‑E outperforms strong RAG baselines and 128k‑context LLMs on LongBench v2 with only 2k context.  
> - Text/image generation/classification: 4‑bit AdamW maintains full‑precision performance on GLUE, SQuAD, WMT14, ImageNet and E2E‑NLG while cutting memory >30%; GWM attains SOTA on Multi‑Modal‑Paper generation/matching.  
> - Graph tasks: GWM is competitive or best on several graph benchmarks (Cora link, HIV graph) but specialized methods (LLAGA/OFA) lead on some node/link tasks.  
> - Sequential/implicit dynamics: DANNs and standard RNNs dominate ColEI; spectral properties (singular value clustering, NSE) are the key driver.  
> - Self‑supervised representation learning: In linear theory and simulations, JEPA prioritizes influential (high‑ρ) features and avoids noisy ones; MAE prioritizes highly covarying directions; ImageNet diagnostics show faster JEPA alignment to low‑variance perceptual subspaces.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## The five works
> 
> 1. **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage, anchor-free part-body association via a single part-to-body center offset (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones). Trained with **SGD** (YOLOv7 schedule, 100 epochs, AMP) using IoU/DFL/classification losses plus an L1 association loss under task-alignment. Benchmarks: COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman; reports Precision/Recall/**F1** vs ED-Pose (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51, Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51) and AP on COCO HumanParts (42.7–43.0). The requested CE/MSE details are not stated in the document.
> 2. **"Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** — RNNs under excitatory–inhibitory constraints (ColEI vs DANN vs standard). Using singular-value spectra and **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** for interpretability: the initial singular-value spectrum (not sign constraints) drives learning; NSE anti-correlates with final test error across tasks, EI ratio, and network size.
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** — latent-space prediction bias of self-distillation (JEPA) vs reconstruction (MAE) in deep linear networks. JEPA prioritizes high-regression-coefficient (high-ρ) features and suppresses noise increasingly with depth; MAE ordering follows covariance λ. ImageNet-1K I-JEPA vs MAE via CCA confirms JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace. **The paper does not address fine-tuning effects on feature embeddings** — that aspect is not covered in this collection.
> 4. **"4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023)** — sub-byte optimizer states (4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor: B128 block quantization, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer). Matches 32-bit AdamW: GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, GPT-2 E2E 67.8 vs 67.7, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning comparable; memory saved up to 57.7%.
> 5. **Graph World Model (ICML 2025)** — multi-modal states as graphs with action nodes; implicit edges via **cosine-similarity/embedding similarity retrieval** (RAG), **multi-hop message passing**, and transformer-guided decoders (LLM + Stable Diffusion with graph conditioning tokens; diffusion MSE + SFT cross-entropy objectives). Reports **F1/Recall/Accuracy** (beats LightGCN/MMGCN/GRCN on recommendation; multi-hop gives ≥20% relative gains, but over-smoothing with excess hops; GWM-E beats GWM-T at 5–10× lower token cost). **AUROC, BPR/ranking losses, and explicit regularization are not found in this document.**
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> - **Accuracy vs efficiency trade-off:** PBADet shows a one-stage anchor-free design matches cumbersome DETR-style detectors in AP while beating BPJDet (anchor-free vs anchor-based ablation: Hand AP 89.1 vs 85.3, Cond. Accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, Joint AP 85.98 vs 78.13). Similarly, 4-bit AdamW preserves accuracy while cutting memory by ~58%, and GWM-E matches GWM-T accuracy at 5–10× lower token cost — both demonstrate that aggressive compression/approximation need not sacrifice performance.
> - **What drives performance:** The EI-spectral paper finds the *initial weight spectrum* (measured by NSE) matters more than explicit sign constraints — an interpretability-driven predictor of learning outcomes. The JEPA paper likewise explains *why* JEPA generalizes better for perception: it learns high-influence, low-noise features, whereas MAE learns variance-dominated, less informative features. Both thus attribute performance differences to spectral/feature-prioritization dynamics rather than raw capacity.
> - **Match to full precision:** 4-bit optimizers are near-lossless (differences ≤0.5 points; sometimes slightly better, e.g., NLU 89.1 vs 88.9, GPT-2 NLG 67.8 vs 67.7), outperforming 8-bit AdamW on several tasks while using less memory; the largest gains appear at LLaMA scale (57.7% memory saving, LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU).
> - **Generality:** GWM demonstrates that one model transfers across six domains (generation, matching, recommendation, graph prediction, multi-agent, RAG, planning), with zero-shot RAG even exceeding task-specific training; PBADet likewise extends from humans to quadruped part-body association — both emphasize cross-task/domain transfer.
> - **Gaps to note:** (3) fine-tuning's effect on embeddings is not covered by the retrieved JEPA paper; (5) AUROC/BPR/regularization claims are not supported by the retrieved GWM text (only F1/Recall/Accuracy and diffusion/SFT objectives appear).

**community 最终答案**

> ## The five research threads and their experimental results
> 
> **1. PBADet — one-stage anchor-free part-body association** (ICLR 2024)
> - One-stage, anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones) with a single part-to-body center offset; losses = classification (CE-style) + IoU/DFL + association (L1/MSE-style) with task-alignment; trained with **SGD**, 100 epochs, 4×V100, AMP.
> - COCO results: vs ED-Pose on COCO-val, all parts **Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51**; COCO-HumanParts AP 42.7–43.0; CrowdHuman face-body MR-2 36.5, AP 91.6. Anchor-free part-to-body beats anchor-based BPJDet (Hand AP 89.1 vs 85.3; JointAP 85.98 vs 78.13); ablations show association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each help.
> 
> **2. Dale's-Law EI RNNs** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Recurrent nets obeying excitatory–inhibitory sign constraints (ColEI) learn worse and with higher variance than DANN/standard RNNs on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition. Spectrum "transplant" experiments show the **singular-value spectrum at initialization (not sign constraints/vectors) drives the gap**; **normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error**, predicting performance across EI ratio and size; smaller/fewer-I networks worsen the spectrum; gradient clipping mitigates the deficit. Diagnostic rather than task-metric oriented (error rates, no F1/AUROC).
> 
> **3. JEPA vs MAE latent-space prediction bias** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Deep-linear analysis proves JEPA self-distillation is implicitly biased to learn **high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ)** while MAE reconstruction learns high-variance features (large λ); with deep encoders JEPA even reverses learning order on data where ρ and λ conflict. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA). Related collection work on fine-tuning effects: Agreement-on-the-Line shows fine-tuned CLIP/LLM embeddings only exhibit AGL with **random head initialization** (data ordering/subsetting don't), and Visual Data-Type ID shows **freezing the vision encoder improves both ID and OOD** while freezing the text encoder hurts OOD.
> 
> **4. 4-bit AdamW optimizer states** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - 4-bit quantized first/second moments (small blocks B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear mapping, optional factorized 2nd moment) match full precision across Transformers: GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9 (RoBERTa-L), ImageNet CLS 80.8 vs 81.2 (Swin-T), E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7 (GPT-2), SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, WMT BLEU 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7. Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 31.87 vs 75.40 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU; convergence curves closely track 32-bit AdamW.
> 
> **5. Graph World Model (GWM)** (ICML 2025)
> - World model with multi-modal (image/table/text) states as graphs, action nodes, **cosine-similarity/Top-k retrieval (RAG)**, **multi-hop GCN message passing**, and LLM (Llama-3-8B) + Stable Diffusion generative decoders. A single GWM matches/beats domain baselines on 6 tasks; GWM-E often beats GWM-T at 5–10× lower token cost; multi-hop graphs give ≥20% relative gains but **excessive hops cause over-smoothing** (regularization concern); RAG: GWM-E with 2k context scores 33.32 vs GPT-4o-mini (128k) 29.01 on LongBench v2; recommendation F1 beats FREEDOM/LightGCN/MMGCN/GRCN; multi-agent and planning SOTA; strong zero/few-shot with only projector fine-tuning. **Note:** it reports accuracy/Recall/F1 and discusses over-smoothing + token-efficiency approximations, but the retrieved content shows **no AUROC or BPR/ranking-loss results** (HIV graph task uses accuracy).
> 
> ## Cross-cutting comparison
> - **Spectral/interpretability thread:** both (2) and (3) use spectral tools (SVD entropy; PCA/eigenvalue dynamics) to explain *why* models behave as they do, rather than reporting task metrics — (2) links spectrum to trainability, (3) links it to feature quality/SSL success.
> - **Efficiency thread:** (1), (4), (5) all trade off accuracy vs. cost: PBADet's single-offset design vs anchor-based multi-offset; 4-bit AdamW achieves near-lossless accuracy at ~half memory; GWM-E trades token cost for embeddings. (4) is the only one with controlled lossless claims (matching full precision within noise); GWM shows efficiency gains with some accuracy loss vs. its own token variant; PBADet improves both accuracy and simplicity vs. prior art.
> - **Representation/fine-tuning thread:** (3) explains latent-space bias at pretraining; the fine-tuning effect is best evidenced by the companion AGL/data-type papers (random head init; freezing vision encoder), which study *how* fine-tuning changes feature-embedding behavior (OOD linear agreement, ID/OOD shifts).
> - **Caveats:** PBADet's "CE/MSE" claim is only partially supported (CE-style classification + L1 association, not explicitly documented as MSE); GWM lacks the preferred AUROC/BPR reporting; the JEPA paper itself does not analyze fine-tuning of embeddings — that is covered by adjacent works in the collection.

### paperscope:results_comparison:317 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource‑constrained perception‑and‑control stack: a camera system must detect hands/face and reliably associate them to the correct person in crowded scenes (COCO‑style), while the onboard model is continually fine‑tuned with LoRA under tight GPU memory—so I need 4‑bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW. Our control module uses time‑series RNNs that must respect excitatory/inhibitory constraints, and I want spectral guidance to keep training stable with SGD/AdamW. For vision pretraining I’m considering JEPA‑style self‑distillation (cosine similarity/MSE) and want to understand why it learns robust feature embeddings. Finally, the robot should rapidly transfer to new manipulation rewards via self‑supervised RL using random features and MPC. Which papers cover these components end‑to‑end so I can architect this system?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

Gold 1：

> Mapping papers to the stack components you asked about
> - Part–body association for hands/face in crowded scenes: PBADet (ICLR 2024)
> - Memory‑efficient continual fine‑tuning (4‑bit Adam/AdamW, LoRA‑friendly): Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Time‑series RNNs with excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) constraints and spectral guidance: Learning better with Dale’s Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)
> - JEPA‑style self‑distillation (cosine/MSE) and robust feature embeddings: How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Fast transfer to new rewards via self‑supervised RL with random features + MPC: Self‑Supervised Reinforcement Learning that Transfers using Random Features (NeurIPS 2023)
> 
> Comparisons on identical datasets (must‑match datasets and reported metrics)
> 1) Human part–body association (PBADet vs baselines)
> - BodyHands (identical dataset)

> 4) JEPA vs MAE (controlled deep‑linear settings and ImageNet; same tasks per comparison)
> - Deep linear experiments (Figs. 1–2):
>   - On feature distributions where covariance (λ) and regression coefficients (ρ) trend differently, JEPA inverts the learning order, prioritizing high‑ρ “influential” features; MAE remains driven by λ (co‑variance) and can over‑prioritize noisy features.
>   - The effect strengthens with encoder depth; formalized via critical time analysis (Theorems 3.4–3.5): JEPA’s learning times depend on ρ at NLO, MAE’s do not.
> - Temporal model (Fig. 3):
>   - With two temporal modes (γ1=0.99, γ2=0.95) and different noise levels, learned λ decreases while ρ increases across modes; JEPA tracks influential (less noisy) modes as predicted.
> - ImageNet (Appendix D Fig. 7):
>   - I‑JEPA vs MAE: higher mean CCA similarity between features trained on “full” vs “bottom‑variance” subspace; lower similarity between “full” vs “top‑variance” subspace. Empirically, JEPA focuses on the low‑variance (perceptually relevant) subspace faster than MAE; MAE emphasizes top‑variance components.

>   - RaMP maintains best adaptation across long‑horizon tasks; MBPO slower; Successor Features reasonable (benefits from reduced compounding error) when goals are close to training distribution; CQL performs well when test goal lies near the training goal range (e.g., Sprint) and poorly when OOD.

>   - With 9‑DoF actions/16‑D state, RaMP outperforms baselines in adaptation speed and final return.

>   - Pendulum: Ours 65.1 ± 0.4 vs MBRL 395.4 ± 5.8
>   - Conclusion: RaMP’s implicit long‑horizon modeling via random‑feature Q‑bases reduces compounding error compared to one‑step dynamics models.

> - Vision detection/association vs vision representation:

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the papers covering each component, with their key experimental results compared.
> 
> ## 1. Perception: hand/face detection + person association in crowds
> **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association Detection (ICLR 2024)** — detects body, hands, face and links each part to its person via a single part-to-body center offset; the anchor-free property makes any point inside a part box automatically associate to the body.
> 
> Experimental results (vs. SOTA):
> - **BodyHands (hand–body)**: PBADet (YOLOv7) hand AP 89.1 / conditional acc 92.62 / joint AP 85.98 vs. BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39 and BodyHands 84.8/83.44/63.48 — wins on all metrics with a smaller backbone and lower input resolution (1024 vs 1536).
> - **COCO-HumanParts (6 parts: head, face, hands, feet)**: AP on par with BPJDet; leads in AP_M, AP_L and per-category person/feet; lowest average mMR-2 across head, face, both hands, right foot.
> - **CrowdHuman (face–body in crowds)**: best body MR-2 (36.5) and face MR-2 (44.7), body AP 91.6 — advantage over BPJDet is smaller for this single-part task.
> - **vs. pose estimator ED-Pose (COCO)**: all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51 — substantially better hand/foot detection.
> 
> ## 2. 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW (tight GPU memory, LoRA-style fine-tuning)
> **4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States (NeurIPS 2023)** — quantizes first moment (B128/DE) and second moment (rank-1/linear, zero-point excluded), optionally factorized ("4-bit Factor").
> 
> Results: matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; SQuAD 94.5 vs 94.6; E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61); convergence curves align. Memory: LLaMA-7B fine-tuning 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB (**−57.7%**), RoBERTa-L −43.1%, GPT-2 −34.4%; enables LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU. Compared with 8-bit AdamW it saves ~2× state memory; Adafactor/SM3 save more but degrade accuracy (especially image classification). Note: the paper's LLaMA fine-tuning uses the LoRA repo's setup, and it's designed for exactly this low-memory fine-tuning regime.
> 
> ## 3. E/I-constrained RNNs + spectral guidance for stable training
> **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** — the primary match. It shows why sign-constrained (excitatory/inhibitory) RNNs train poorly and what to do: spectral properties, not sign constraints, dominate.
> 
> Results: ColEI RNNs learn worse and with higher variance on all 4 benchmarks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition). Sign constraints alone explain only part of the gap (0.7±0.3% RNNs, 1±1% ColEI vs. 2.3±0.6% total); SVD "spectrum transplant" shows the singular-value spectrum contributes more (1.5±0.3% / 2±1%) than sign constraints or singular vectors. ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed with a large-singular-value mode, while standard RNNs and DANN (biologically inspired E/I architecture) have unimodal Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle spectra. **Guidance**: normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance pre-training; gradient clipping helps unstable ColEI networks substantially; DANN recurrent nets learn as well as standard RNNs even with one inhibitory neuron. Caveat: this paper studies spectral diagnostics/initialization and gradient clipping — no paper in the collection explicitly ties spectral guidance to SGD-vs-AdamW stability. A secondary, complementary match for spectral analysis of optimizers/LoRA is **Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure (ICML 2025)**: Hessian spectra follow a power law for SGD/Adam-trained nets (power-law slope correlates with sharpness/generalization; d_ks predicts LLM generalization up to 0.98), and for LoRA adapters the power law forms after ~500 steps with Hessian trace as the more reliable generalization indicator (LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the structure as full fine-tuning does).
> 
> ## 4. JEPA self-distillation (cosine/MSE) and why it learns robust embeddings
> **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)** — the mechanism: in a deep-linear model, JEPA (predicting latent targets, e.g., cosine/MSE self-distillation with stop-grad) is biased toward high-influence features (large regression coefficients) and learns noisy features slowly; depth strengthens this noise suppression. MAE's ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue (variance). ImageNet-1K experiment: I-JEPA representations from full and bottom-PCA (low-variance, perceptual) datasets have higher CCA similarity than MAE's throughout training, and the reverse for top-PCA — JEPA captures the discriminative low-variance subspace faster. Related cosine-similarity analysis: **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** (positive-pair alignment = 1, negative separation −1/(n−1); small batches raise negative-pair variance and degrade quality, mitigated by a variance-reduction auxiliary loss) — useful if your JEPA loss includes contrastive/cosine terms.
> 
> ## 5. Rapid transfer to new manipulation rewards: self-supervised RL + random features + MPC
> **Self-Supervised Reinforcement Learning that Transfers using Random Features — RaMP (ICLR 2024)**: pre-trains multi-step Q-basis functions on unlabeled offline data using random features as pseudo-rewards (fully self-supervised), then at test time regresses features to the new reward and plans via MPC (random shooting) — no explicit dynamics model, avoiding compounding error.
> 
> Results: on Meta-World (Reach, Wall, Door Open, Faucet Open, Button Press), Hopper (Stand, Jump, Backward) and D'Claw, RaMP adapts to novel rewards (including out-of-distribution goals) markedly faster than MBPO, PETS, Successor Features, and CQL. Neural-network random features beat polynomial/Gaussian features; multi-step Q-functions reduce compounding error. On pixel observations it matches Dreamer on Pixel Reach/Faucet Open but not Pixel Door Open (Monte-Carlo value-estimation variance is a stated limitation). Theory guarantees Q-approximation with polynomially many random features and multi-step policy improvement.
> 
> ## Summary / gaps
> - All five components have a dedicated paper, forming a coherent stack: PBADet (perception) → 4-bit optimizers (fine-tuning memory) + LoRA noted in Hessian/LoRA analyses → Dale's Law spectral RNN (control, with NSE diagnostics) → JEPA self-distillation (vision pretraining) → RaMP (RL transfer via random features + MPC).
> - Not covered in this collection: an explicit "spectral constraint applied during SGD/AdamW training for stability" method (the Dale's Law paper gives pre-training spectral diagnostics and gradient clipping, not an optimizer-level spectral regularizer), and a standalone LoRA method paper (LoRA appears only as the fine-tuning setting in the 4-bit-optimizer and Hessian papers).

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers in the collection covering each component, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Hand/face detection + person association (COCO-style, crowded) → **PBADet** (08b70bc3…)
> One-stage anchor-free part-body association (part-to-body center offset) on YOLOv5/YOLOv7.
> - **COCOHumanParts** (6 parts: head, face, L/R hand, L/R foot): AP on par with BPJDet but leads on AP_M/AP_L/AP_s for person and feet, and lowest average mMR-2 for head/face/hands/right foot.
> - **CrowdHuman** face-body task: PBADet (YOLOv7) has best MR-2 (body 36.5, face 44.7) and body AP 91.6; advantage over BPJDet is smaller here because it's a single-part task.
> - **vs. pose estimator ED-Pose**: much higher hand precision/recall/F1 (left hand F1 46.5 vs 22.9; all parts 48.5 vs 31.5), showing joint detection + association beats keypoint-only pose estimation.
> 
> ## 2. 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states for LoRA-style fine-tuning → **4-bit Optimizers** (8d5e1455…)
> Compresses optimizer states to 4-bit (small-block B128 quantization, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for the 2nd moment, optional factorization). LoRA is discussed as the complementary parameter-efficient approach.
> - **Results**: 4-bit AdamW matches/exceeds 32-bit on GLUE (RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD, E2E-NLG, Swin-T ImageNet (80.8 vs 81.2), WMT14; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning comparable to 32-bit with closely aligned loss curves.
> - **Memory**: up to 57.7% total memory saved (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB, enabling single-80GB-GPU training); ~2× saving vs 8-bit AdamW; 4-bitFactor is most memory-efficient. Trade-off: slightly slower on small models until fused operators; optimal quantization may be task-dependent.
> 
> ## 3. E/I-constrained time-series RNNs + spectral stability guidance → **Dale's Law RNNs** (e63a94c4…) and **Hessian power-law** (582d138d…)
> - **Dale's Law paper**: Column-constrained E/I RNNs (ColEI) learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN (E/I-separated) architectures across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Singular-value transplants prove **spectral properties matter more than sign constraints or singular vectors**: ColEI's multimodal, dispersed spectrum (rank-one nilpotent column-mean + random matrix) vs unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur for RNNs/DANNs. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance pre-training; small networks/fewer I units worsen both spectrum and learning, while DANN stays robust even with 1 I unit.
> - **Hessian paper** (closest "spectral guidance for SGD/AdamW"): well-trained nets (CNNs, GPT-2, TinyLlama) show power-law Hessian spectra; power-law slope correlates with sharpness/generalization (LeNet CIFAR-10 Pearson 0.72; d_ks predicts LLM generalization up to 0.98). Structure holds across SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, RAdam, etc. and emerges during LLM AdamW pretraining/fine-tuning; it is lost with very large batches, small width/depth, noisy labels, and LoRA-only fine-tuning — i.e., it provides a spectral diagnostic and batch-size guidance for stable training. (Caveat: it does not propose spectral normalization itself.)
> 
> ## 4. JEPA self-distillation robustness → **Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features** (40fde037…)
> Deep-linear-network analysis of self-distillation (online encoder predicts target encoder's latent output; BYOL/data2vec/SimSiam/I-JEPA/V-JEPA). Mechanism: JEPA implicitly prioritizes **high-influence features** (large regression coefficients) and the **low-variance subspace where perceptual features live**, with depth strengthening noise suppression; MAE's feature ordering instead depends mainly on eigenvalue, so it learns high-variance/noisy pixel structure.
> - **ImageNet-1K experiments**: I-JEPA representations match the low-variance (bottom-25% PCA) subspace faster than MAE throughout training (higher CCA similarity on full-bottom, reversed on full-top), empirically confirming the bias. This explains why JEPA gives robust, semantic embeddings. (The retrieved content analyzes latent-space prediction generally; it doesn't explicitly compare cosine vs MSE losses.)
> 
> ## 5. Self-supervised RL + random features + MPC for manipulation transfer → **RaMP** (528b3e89…)
> Pre-trains multi-step "Q-basis" functions on reward-free offline trajectories using random-feature pseudo-rewards (fully self-supervised); at test time a new reward is fit by simple linear regression over the basis and acted on via MPC — no autoregressive dynamics model, avoiding compounding error.
> - **Results**: on Meta-World, Hopper, and D'Claw, RaMP adapts to new rewards faster than MBPO, PETS, successor features, and CQL, especially out-of-distribution goals; NN random features beat polynomial/Gaussian features; multi-step Q-functions reduce compounding error. On pixel observations it matches Dreamer on Pixel Reach/Faucet Open but not Pixel Door Open. Limitation: variance in Monte-Carlo value estimation.
> 
> ## Summary / architectural mapping
> - Perception: **PBADet** (best part-body association; its single-part face task is the weakest margin vs BPJDet — prefer it for multi-part hand+face association).
> - Memory-constrained continual fine-tuning: **4-bit Optimizers** (lossless vs 32-bit, up to ~58% memory savings; combine with LoRA as related-work approach).
> - E/I RNN control: **Dale's Law paper** (use DANN-style architecture or monitor NSE; constrain spectra, not just signs; use gradient clipping).
> - Spectral stability: **Hessian power-law paper** (diagnostic: keep batch size moderate so power-law structure emerges; works across SGD/Adam/AdamW).
> - Vision pretraining: **JEPA paper** (justifies JEPA over MAE for robust low-variance perceptual features).
> - Fast reward transfer: **RaMP** (self-supervised random-feature Q-basis + MPC).
> 
> No single paper spans the whole stack; the collection covers each component with these papers.

### paperscope:results_comparison:320 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively tackle efficient and interpretable deep learning across perception and physical modeling, including: anchor-free part–body association in vision; training EI-constrained recurrent nets under Dale’s principle via spectral analysis; non-contrastive self-distillation (JEPA) that biases latent feature embeddings toward high-influence dimensions; memory-light optimizers that compress Adam/AdamW states to sub-byte levels for parameter-efficient Transformer fine-tuning (e.g., low-rank adapters end-to-end); and adaptive hierarchical graph simulators for time-series meshes. I’m looking for work that discusses squared-error metrics (MSE), cosine-similarity style objectives, cross-entropy loss, regularization trade-offs (quadratic penalties/Pareto), shallow predictors vs. feedforward classifiers, and reports Precision/F1/AUROC. Benchmarks can range from MNIST/ResNet-scale vision to large Transformers.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

Gold 1：

> Cross-paper comparison of experimental results (grouped by domain), with explicit datasets, metrics, and head-to-head rankings.

> 1) Mesh-based physical simulation (adaptive hierarchical GNNs)
> Methods compared on identical datasets: EvoMesh vs MGN, Lino et al., BSMS-GNN, Eagle, HCMT.
> 
> Datasets and metrics (lower is better; RMSE reported ×10^-2):
> - CylinderFlow
>   - One-step (RMSE-1): EvoMesh 0.1568; best prior: Eagle 0.1733. EvoMesh improves 9.53% over prior best.
>   - Long-rollout (RMSE-All): EvoMesh 6.571; best prior: BSMS-GNN 16.98. EvoMesh improves 61.3%.
> - Airfoil
>   - RMSE-1: EvoMesh 41.41; best prior: HCMT 48.62. Improvement 14.8%.
>   - RMSE-All: EvoMesh 2002; best prior: Lino et al. 2080. Improvement 3.75%.
> - FlyingFlag
>   - RMSE-1: EvoMesh 0.3049; best prior: MGN 0.3459. Improvement 11.9%.
>   - RMSE-All: EvoMesh 76.16; best prior: HCMT 90.32. Improvement 15.7%.
> - DeformingPlate
>   - RMSE-1: EvoMesh 0.0282; best prior: Lino et al. 0.0291 (also close to HCMT 0.0295). Improvement 3.10%.
>   - RMSE-All: EvoMesh 1.296; best prior: BSMS-GNN 1.811. Improvement 28.5%.
> 
> Time-varying mesh (FoldingPaper)
> - EvoMesh vs MGN on identical data:
>   - RMSE-1: 0.0544 vs 0.0618 (12.0% better).
>   - RMSE-All: 7.412 vs 24.08 (69.2% better).
> 
> Out-of-distribution mesh resolutions (train low-res, test higher-res)
> - CylinderFlow: RMSE-1 0.4855 (EvoMesh) best; RMSE-50 1.077 (EvoMesh) best.
> - Airfoil: RMSE-1 126.7 (EvoMesh) best; RMSE-50 812.5 (EvoMesh) best.
> - FlyingFlag: MGN outperforms EvoMesh (RMSE-1 0.4215 vs 0.5536; RMSE-50 55.96 vs 58.29).
> - DeformingPlate: MGN/HCMT edge out EvoMesh (e.g., RMSE-1 0.0354 HCMT vs 0.0368 EvoMesh; RMSE-50 0.2467 MGN vs 0.3780 EvoMesh).
> 
> Ablations (within EvoMesh, same datasets):
> - Static hierarchy + anisotropic intra-level aggregation already beats BSMS-GNN; adding learnable inter-level propagation further reduces error; making the hierarchy dynamic yields the largest gains (e.g., CylinderFlow RMSE-All drops from 9.621 → 8.317 → 7.793 → 6.571).
> 
> Interpretability/diagnostics (same datasets):
> - EvoMesh’s anisotropic weights vary most where physical quantities vary most over time (visual correlation shown). Learned hierarchies place more coarse nodes in high-dynamics regions and evolve over time to track flow features.
> 
> Conclusion in this domain: Across four standard benchmarks and a time-varying mesh setting, EvoMesh consistently lowers one-step and rollout error versus fixed-hierarchy baselines, sometimes by large margins (notably CylinderFlow RMSE-All). Generalization to higher resolutions is strongest on Eulerian flow (Cylinder/Airfoil), while MGN remains competitive on certain Lagrangian tasks under OOD resolution.
> 
> 2) Human part–body association detection (anchor-free, part-to-body offsets)
> Methods compared on identical datasets: PBADet vs BPJDet (and other baselines where reported).
> 
> BodyHands (single-part hand–body association)
> - Metrics: Hand AP (IoU=0.5), Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP.
> - PBADet (YOLOv7, 1024): Hand AP 89.1; Cond. Acc. 92.62; Joint AP 85.98.
> - PBADet (YOLOv5l6, 1024): 88.1; 92.71; 85.73.
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 1536): 85.9; 86.91; 84.39.
> Result: On identical backbone (YOLOv5l6) PBADet improves Conditional Accuracy (92.71 vs 86.91) and Joint AP (85.73 vs 84.39). With a smaller model (YOLOv7 vs YOLOv5m6), PBADet still surpasses BPJDet on all three metrics.
> 
> COCOHumanParts (multi-part association: head, face, hands, feet)
> - All-category AP (original/subordinate association-aware):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.0 / 41.8; AP.5 70.0 / 68.4; APM 66.2 / 65.0; APL 67.2 / 64.4.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.6 / 43.3; AP.5 70.6 / 69.8; APM 63.8 / 63.2; APL 61.8 / 58.9.
>   - By category (AP.5:.95): PBADet v5l6 vs BPJDet v5l6 — person 62.4 vs 61.3; head 54.6 vs 56.6; face 44.6 vs 46.3; r-hand 39.0 vs 40.4; l-hand 37.7 vs 39.6; r-foot 30.9 vs 30.2; l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9.
> - Association accuracy (average mMR−2, lower better):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): head 27.9; face 30.5; l-hand 36.2; r-hand 40.8; r-foot 50.4; l-foot 47.9.
>   - PBJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8; face 31.8; l-hand 41.6; r-hand 42.2; r-foot 49.1; l-foot 50.4.
> Result: PBADet achieves better mid/large-object APs and lower mismatching rates across most parts (notably hands) while per-part AP.5:.95 is close, with BPJDet slightly higher on some head/face/hand categories.
> 
> CrowdHuman (face–body association)
> - PBADet (YOLOv7): MR−2 body 36.5 (best); face 44.7; AP body 91.6 (best); AP face 81.6; mMR−2 body-face 50.8.
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 body 40.7; face 46.3; AP body 89.5; AP face 81.6; mMR−2 50.1.
> Result: PBADet improves detection MR−2 and body AP; mMR−2 is comparable (50.8 vs 50.1).
> 
> Conclusion in this domain: On datasets shared with prior art, PBADet consistently raises Conditional/Joint association metrics and reduces mismatches, with competitive per-category detection AP, validating its anchor-free part-to-body offset design.
> 
> 3) Memory-efficient optimizers with 4-bit states (training across NLP/Vision/MT)
> Methods compared on identical datasets: 4-bit AdamW vs 32-bit AdamW vs 8-bit AdamW (and Adafactor/SM3 where reported).
> 
> Language understanding (RoBERTa-L on GLUE, mean score)
> - 32-bit AdamW 88.9; 8-bit 89.1; 4-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit Factor 88.9. Result: 4-bit matches or equals full precision.
> 
> Question answering (SQuAD F1 with RoBERTa-L)
> - 32-bit 94.6; 8-bit 94.5; 4-bit AdamW 94.5; 4-bit Factor 94.6. Result: parity.
> 
> Natural language generation (E2E-NLG, BLEU with GPT-2 Medium)
> - 32-bit 67.7; 8-bit 67.5; 4-bit AdamW 67.8; 4-bit Factor 67.6. Result: 4-bit slightly best BLEU among listed.
> 
> Image classification (ImageNet-1k, Swin-T top-1 accuracy)
> - 32-bit 81.2; 8-bit 81.0; 4-bit AdamW 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9. Result: ≤0.4 pt drop vs 32-bit.
> 
> Machine translation (WMT14 en–de SacreBLEU)
> - 32-bit 26.61; 8-bit 26.66; 4-bit AdamW 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45. Result: small degradation vs 32-bit/8-bit.
> 
> Instruction tuning (LLaMA; identical evaluation sets)
> - 7B (after fine-tuning): 4-bit AdamW ≈ 32-bit on HellaSwag/ARC; MMLU 38.9 (4-bit) vs 38.7; mixed small differences across tasks.
> - 13B: 4-bit slightly improves most tasks (e.g., MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5).
> - 33B: mixed (e.g., MMLU 54.9 vs 56.4), with some gains on OBQA.
> 
> Efficiency (identical training setups)
> - RoBERTa-L: total memory ↓ ~43% vs 32-bit; throughput comparable with fused kernels (3.17 min/epoch 4-bit fused vs 3.93 min 32-bit).
> - GPT-2 Medium: memory ↓ ~34%; fused 4-bit runtime matches 32-bit (2.11 h vs 2.13 h).
> - LLaMA-7B with FSDP (2× A100 80GB): total memory ↓ 57.7% (75.4 GB → 31.9 GB) and total training time slightly reduced (3.35 h → 3.07 h).
> 
> Ablations relevant to stability and accuracy
> - Second-moment quantization must avoid a zero point: DE-0 or linear mapping (with rank-1 normalization) stabilizes training and matches 32-bit accuracy on GPT-2 Medium E2E and RoBERTa tasks, whereas including zero or using large blocks degrades or destabilizes training.
> 
> Conclusion in this domain: Across shared datasets, 4-bit AdamW (with rank-1 normalization and zero-excluding quantization for v) provides accuracy at or near 32-/8-bit levels while substantially reducing optimizer memory (up to ~58%) and maintaining or improving throughput with fused kernels.
> 
> 4) Dale’s Law–constrained recurrent nets (EI RNNs) vs standard/DANN
> Shared datasets within this paper: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, a naturalistic object classification task.
> 
> Head-to-head results (qualitative and percentage deltas reported)
> - Across all four benchmarks, ColEI (column sign-constrained EI) learns worse than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs; DANNs match standard RNNs.
> - Spectrum vs sign constraints (Sequential MNIST and a natural object task):
>   - Freezing parameter signs harms test accuracy by ~0.7% (RNNs) to ~1% (ColEI), but transplanting ColEI’s singular value spectrum into an RNN degrades performance by ~1.5% (RNNs) to ~2% (ColEI)—indicating spectrum explains more of the gap than sign constraints.
> - Stability: ColEI benefits much more from gradient clipping; small networks or low inhibitory ratios perform poorly and have dispersed, multimodal singular value spectra; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) strongly anticorrelates with test error.
> 
> Conclusion in this domain: When compared on identical tasks, DANN and standard RNNs attain better accuracy and training stability than simple ColEI, and controlled experiments attribute most of the performance gap to spectral properties at initialization rather than the EI sign constraints per se.
> 
> 5) JEPA vs MAE (non-contrastive self-distillation vs reconstruction) in deep linear settings
> Experimental comparisons (same synthetic settings; analytical + numeric ODEs)
> - On synthetic feature distributions where covariance (λ) and regression coefficient (ρ) orders differ, JEPA and MAE learn entirely different features first:
>   - When λ increases but ρ decreases across features, MAE learns by λ (covariance-dominant), while JEPA prioritizes high-ρ (influential) features; the gap grows with encoder depth.
> - Temporal linear generative model (predict next frame): closed-form shows that for two modes with similar covariance but different noise (σ), JEPA’s effective ρ=γ‖v‖^2/(σ^2+‖v‖^2) favors less noisy (higher ρ) modes; simulations match theory.
> - ImageNet probe (CCA, not accuracy): JEPA’s learned representations align earlier with low-variance (“bottom”) subspace than MAE, consistent with the theoretical bias toward influential/less-noisy features.
> 
> Conclusion in this domain: Although not reported with standard accuracy metrics here, the controlled experiments show a distinct learning bias: deep JEPAs prioritize predictive, influential features (high ρ), whereas MAE favors highly covarying (high-λ) features—even if they are noisier. This explains faster emergence of semantic features in JEPA-style training observed in practice.
> 
> Cross-domain notes and shared elements
> - Optimizers/backbones: Adam/AdamW appear across several works (4-bit optimizer, EvoMesh training schedules, PBADet’s detector training), but datasets are distinct; no direct cross-paper accuracy comparisons are applicable.
> - Sequential MNIST appears in Dale’s Law paper only among the provided works; no identical MNIST results elsewhere.
> - All comparisons above are restricted to the datasets and metrics reported in the respective papers; where identical datasets exist within a domain (e.g., physical simulation benchmarks; BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman; GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/ImageNet/WMT14/LLaMA evaluations), we reported head-to-head rankings and absolute numbers.
> 
> Overall summary
> - Physical simulation: EvoMesh (dynamic, learned hierarchies with anisotropic propagation) consistently reduces RMSE against fixed-hierarchy GNNs on shared benchmarks, with particularly large gains on long-range Eulerian flows and time-varying meshes.
> - Human part–body association: PBADet (one-stage, anchor-free, part→body center offsets) improves association accuracy (Conditional/Joint AP; lower mMR−2) on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman versus prior joint detectors while maintaining competitive per-part AP.
> - Memory efficiency: 4-bit AdamW matches 32-/8-bit accuracy on GLUE/SQuAD/E2E and is close on ImageNet/WMT14 while cutting optimizer memory by ~34–58% and preserving or improving throughput with fused ops; instruction tuning results show parity at 7B–13B and mixed but close results at 33B.
> - EI-constrained RNNs: DANN/standard RNNs outperform simple ColEI across identical tasks; spectrum at initialization accounts for most of the gap, with NSE predicting performance.
> - JEPA vs MAE: In deep linear tests, JEPA learns high-influence (high-ρ) features first, diverging from MAE’s high-variance focus—clarifying observed practical differences in representation quality.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, the five papers you're looking for are:
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) – one-stage anchor-free part-body association in vision.
> 2. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023) – EI-constrained recurrent nets under Dale's principle via spectral analysis.
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024) – non-contrastive self-distillation (JEPA) biased toward high-influence features.
> 4. **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023) – Adam/AdamW states compressed to 4-bit (sub-byte, vs. prior 8-bit minimum) for parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
> 5. **EvoMesh** (ICML 2025) – adaptive hierarchical graph simulator for time-series meshes.
> 
> **Comparison & analysis of experimental results:**
> 
> **PBADet (perception, detection):** Reports AP/Precision/Recall/F1 and miss-rate. On BodyHands it beats all SOTA: HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (vs. BPJDet 85.9/86.91/84.39), at smaller model size (36.9M). On COCOHumanParts it matches BPJDet on AP (42.7/41.5) while leading on AP_M/AP_L, and achieves the lowest mMR⁻² on most parts. On CrowdHuman, body MR⁻² 36.5 and body AP 91.6 are best. Against the pose estimator ED-Pose, PBADet gives far higher Precision (39.41 vs. 24.09), Recall (63.09 vs. 45.51), and F1 (48.52 vs. 31.51) for hands/feet. Ablations confirm the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each matter (without the association loss, conditional accuracy collapses to 80.78). Uses IoU/DFL/classification (cross-entropy-style) losses.
> 
> **Dale's Law EI RNNs (interpretable/neuroscience-inspired modeling):** Tested on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn TreeBank, natural object recognition. ColEI (column-sign-constrained) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs across all four tasks. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum at initialization matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors (sign constraints account for only ~0.7–1% of a 2.3% gap). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error; gradient clipping helps ColEI much more. Conclusion: spectral properties, not Dale's sign constraints per se, drive EI training difficulty.
> 
> **JEPA (self-distillation):** Theoretical + toy-MLP simulations show JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (large regression coefficient ρ), whereas MAE orders learning by covariance λ; the effect strengthens with encoder depth (fixed point w̄=ρ^L for JEPA), and only appears with deep encoders (diminishes for shallow predictors). On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the bottom (perceptual) PCA subspace than MAE features, measured by CCA. No classification-accuracy table is given — results are qualitative/theoretical (deep linear MLPs; acknowledged limitations).
> 
> **4-bit optimizers (efficiency):** 4-bit AdamW/AdamF match or exceed 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning tasks — NLU 89.1 vs. 88.9, QA F1 94.5 vs. 94.6, NLG BLEU 67.8 vs. 67.7 — and are comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs. 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs. 26.61). LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning is on par with full precision on MMLU and commonsense benchmarks. Memory savings reach 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.40→31.87 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU and ~4× larger OPT models. Rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluded linear mapping is the key for stable second-moment quantization (BLEU 67.8, 0% unstable runs). LoRA/delta-tuning are discussed as complementary parameter-efficient methods.
> 
> **EvoMesh (physical modeling):** Reports RMSE (squared-error family) on CylinderFlow, Airfoil, Flag, DeformingPlate. EvoMesh beats fixed-hierarchy baselines by large margins: RMSE-1 0.1568 vs. 0.2263 (BSMS-GNN) and 0.9190 (HCMT) on Cylinder; RMSE-All on Cylinder 6.571 vs. 16.98 (BSMS, 61.3% improvement), Airfoil 2002 vs. 2080–2816, Plate 1.296 vs. 1.811 — roughly 20% average improvement over fixed-hierarchy models. It also generalizes best to OOD mesh resolutions and time-varying mesh topologies (FoldingPaper). Ablations show anisotropic message passing, dynamic (learnable, Gumbel-Softmax) hierarchy construction, and learnable inter-level propagation each contribute; it does so at modest cost (~2.3–3.2M params).
> 
> **Cross-cutting analysis:** Across domains the papers target different objectives — PBADet uses detection losses (IoU/DFL/cross-entropy) with AP/F1/miss-rate metrics; EvoMesh uses MSE/RMSE rollout error; the 4-bit optimizer optimizes convergence accuracy under a memory budget (BLEU/F1/accuracy); the JEPA paper analyzes squared-error (L2) prediction with a shallow linear predictor vs. feedforward reconstruction and a cosine-like latent-space objective; the Dale's Law paper uses classification/regression error with spectral diagnostics. Common themes are efficiency (memory-4-bit vs. anchor-free one-stage vs. dynamic graph pooling) and interpretability/spectral-regularization trade-offs. PBADet and EvoMesh report the strongest absolute empirical wins over SOTA baselines; the JEPA and Dale's Law papers are more analytical (toy models/theory with supporting empirical evidence), and the optimizer paper shows lossless accuracy with large memory savings.

**community 最终答案**

> I have all the evidence. Here's the analysis:
> 
> ## Papers found and their experimental results
> 
> **1. PBADet (ICLR 2024) — anchor-free part–body association** (doc `08b70b…`)
> - **Method**: One-stage, anchor-free detector (YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 backbones) using a single part-to-body center offset; loss = weighted IoU + DFL + classification + association (task-aligned).
> - **BodyHands**: Ours (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) → Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 — beats BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 86.1M: 85.9/86.91/84.39) and all baselines with a smaller model. Anchor-free beats anchor-based (89.1 vs 88.4 HandAP; 85.98 vs 85.28 JointAP).
> - **COCOHumanParts**: On par with BPJDet on AP (43.0/41.8 AP.5:.95; YOLOv5l6), leads in AP_M/AP_L and feet; lowest average mMR−2 on most categories.
> - **vs. ED-Pose (Swin-L pose estimator)**: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) substantially higher Precision/Recall/F1, e.g., left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87, right foot 50.34 vs 40.34, all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51.
> - **Ablations**: association loss is decisive for association (JointAP 78.07 → 85.98); multi-scale offsets and task alignment each help.
> - **Extends to quadruped animal part–body association (AnimalPose/AP-10K).**
> - **Metrics**: AP, conditional accuracy, JointAP, mMR−2, Precision/Recall/F1.
> 
> **2. "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** (doc `e63a94…`)
> - **Method**: EI-constrained RNNs — sign-constrained ColEI vs. spectral-friendly recurrent DANN, analyzed via singular-value spectrum at initialization.
> - **Results (all tasks: adding, sequential MNIST, PTB language modeling, naturalistic object recognition)**: ColEI learns worse and with higher variance; DANN RNNs match standard RNNs. Sign constraints alone explain only part of the gap (sequential MNIST: ~1% of ~2.3%); singular-value spectrum is the dominant factor — spectrum "transplant" experiments show spectrum contributes more than sign constraints or singular vectors.
> - **EI ratio / size**: fewer inhibitory units and smaller networks degrade ColEI's spectrum (multimodal, dispersed) and performance; DANN is robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron. Larger networks with balanced E/I ratios learn better.
> - **Normalized SVD entropy (NSE)** at initialization anti-correlates with final test error — a predictive diagnostic; gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially.
> - **Metrics**: test error, SVD entropy; benchmarks at MNIST/PTB scale.
> 
> **3. "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks" (NeurIPS 2024)** (doc `40fde0…`)
> - **Method**: Non-contrastive JEPA self-distillation (deep linear encoders, MSE objective ‖VW̄x − SG(W̄)y‖²) vs. MAE reconstruction.
> - **Results**: JEPA and MAE both show greedy feature learning w.r.t. covariance λ, but JEPA (unlike MAE) also prioritizes features with high regression coefficient ρ — an implicit bias that strengthens with encoder depth; the ODE analysis shows JEPA fixed point w̄=ρ^L vs MAE ρ^(L/(L+1)); critical-time theorems (JEPA t* depends on ρ via the NLO term; MAE only on λ).
> - **Numerical experiments**: ODE simulations (L=5), stochastic-gradient deep linear nets with default initialization, and linear generative models (random masking; temporal/flickering model) reproduce the predicted ordering inversion; a 1-layer JEPA matches infinite-depth MAE (depth separation).
> - **ImageNet-1K (I-JEPA vs MAE)**: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE features, measured by CCA on full vs. bottom/top-variance-filtered images.
> - **Metrics**: MSE objectives, CCA similarity/accuracy; theory validated at linear scale plus ImageNet.
> 
> **4. "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)** (doc `8d5e14…`)
> - **Method**: Compress Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (B128/DE for 1st; Rank-1/Linear with zero-point exclusion for 2nd; optional factorization).
> - **Results (Table 2)**: matches/exceeds 32-bit AdamW across tasks — RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 (vs 88.9), Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 (vs 81.2), GPT-2M E2E BLEU 67.8 (vs 67.7), QA F1 94.5, Transformer MT SacreBleu 26.28 (vs 26.61); beats sublinear optimizers (Adafactor, SM3) on CLS.
> - **LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3)**: 4-bit AdamW ≈ 32-bit on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA at 7B/13B/33B (e.g., 13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5, HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8); convergence curves closely align.
> - **Memory**: up to 57.7% total memory savings (LLaMA-7B: 75.40→31.87GB); optimizer states 2× smaller than 8-bit, ~4× for 4-bitFactor; trains 4× larger OPT models and LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU.
> - **Ablations**: smaller block (B128) improves first-moment accuracy; zero-point exclusion (DE-0/Linear) is the key to stable second-moment quantization (unstable runs 33–66% → 0%); factorization improves accuracy + memory.
> - **Metrics**: accuracy, BLEU, F1, SacreBleu, memory; benchmarks MNIST-scale vision (Swin-T ImageNet) to large Transformers (LLaMA-33B, RoBERTa-L, GPT-2M, Transformer-Base).
> 
> **5. EvoMesh: Adaptive Physical Simulation with Hierarchical Graph Evolutions (ICML 2025)** (doc `8eb806…`)
> - **Method**: Fully differentiable adaptive hierarchical GNN; Gumbel-Softmax node selection (DiffSELECT) + anisotropic message passing (AMP) + learned REDUCE/EXPAND; trained end-to-end with one-step L2 (squared-error/MSE) supervision.
> - **Main results (Table 2, 3 seeds)**: On CylinderFlow/Airfoil/Flag/DeformingPlate, EvoMesh beats all fixed-hierarchy baselines (MGN, Lino, BSMS-GNN, Eagle, HCMT) — e.g., RMSE-1 (×10⁻²): Cylinder 0.1568 vs BSMS-GNN 0.2263; Flag 0.3049 vs 0.5080; RMSE-All: Cylinder 6.571 vs 16.98, Flag 76.16 vs 168.1; ~20% average improvement over the second-best.
> - **Time-varying meshes (FoldingPaper)**: RMSE-1 0.0544 vs MGN 0.0618; RMSE-All 7.412 vs 24.08 (69.2% improvement).
> - **OOD generalization**: strong zero-shot on unseen (2× node, 3× edge) resolutions for Cylinder/Airfoil; MGN better on regular-structure Flag/Plate.
> - **Ablations**: each component contributes — Static-hierarchy→Dynamic (M3→M4), unlearnable→learnable weights, isotropic→anisotropic; K=2 edge enhancement optimal; hierarchy depth ~7 best; stable across seeds (small std) and AMP beats GATConv/CrossAttention variants.
> - **Metrics**: RMSE-1, RMSE-All, RMSE-50 (squared-error based).
> 
> ## Cross-paper comparison
> 
> | Paper | Domain | Objective | Key metric | Best result |
> |---|---|---|---|---|
> | PBADet | Perception (vision detection) | IoU+DFL+cls+assoc (cross-entropy-like cls) | AP / JointAP / F1 | 89.1 HandAP, 92.62 Cond.Acc, 48.52 F1 vs ED-Pose 31.51 |
> | Dale's Law RNN | Physical modeling (recurrent dynamics) | MSE (adding) / cross-entropy (MNIST, PTB) | test error | DANN RNNs match standard RNNs; NSE predicts error |
> | JEPA analysis | Perception (representation learning) | MSE (self-distillation) | CCA / learning order | JEPA prioritizes high-ρ (influential) features, depth-strengthened |
> | 4-bit optimizers | Efficient training (large Transformers) | cross-entropy (LM), BLEU, F1 | accuracy/BLEU/F1/memory | matches 32-bit AdamW, saves up to 57.7% memory |
> | EvoMesh | Physical modeling (mesh time-series) | MSE (L2 one-step) | RMSE | ~20% better than fixed-hierarchy GNNs; 69.2% better long-term on folding |
> 
> **Cross-cutting observations**: (1) **Squared-error/MSE objectives** are central to three works: JEPA's latent-space regression (where its implicit bias emerges), EvoMesh's one-step L2 supervision (RMSE metrics), and the Dale's-law RNN adding task; (2) **Cosine-similarity-style/CCA alignment** appears in the JEPA work's ImageNet feature-similarity analysis (CCA similarity between full and filtered-image representations); (3) **Regularization trade-offs**: the Dale's-law paper shows sign constraints (a form of structured regularization) trade off against spectral health — spectra matter more than constraints, echoing a Pareto-type trade-off between biological plausibility and learnability, while EvoMesh's temperature annealing (5→0.1) trades exploration vs. stability in hierarchy selection; (4) **Shallow predictors vs feedforward classifiers**: the JEPA work explicitly contrasts deep encoders with shallow linear decoders/predictors (depth separation result: 1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE), and PBADet compares its dense anchor-free head against DETR-style/pose feedforward classifiers; (5) **Benchmark span**: from MNIST/ResNet-scale (sequential MNIST, Swin-T ImageNet) to large Transformers (LLaMA-33B, GPT-2, RoBERTa-L) and mesh simulation datasets (CylinderFlow, Airfoil, Flag, Plate, FoldingPaper); (6) **Precision/F1/AUROC**: Precision/Recall/F1 are explicitly reported only in PBADet (vs ED-Pose); AUROC is not reported in any of these five papers — no paper in this set reports AUROC, so that specific metric cannot be attributed to these works.
> 
> **Note on the question's framing**: the question mentions "cosine-similarity style objectives," "Pareto trade-offs," "AUROC," and "low-rank adapters end-to-end" — of these, cosine-similarity appears in the JEPA CCA analysis, and the 4-bit optimizer paper addresses parameter-efficient fine-tuning (its ablation/LLaMA tuning) and cites LoRA, but the collection does not contain a paper that trains low-rank adapters end-to-end with sub-byte states, nor one reporting AUROC or explicit Pareto/quadratic-penalty multi-objective optimization. Those specific elements cannot be established from this collection.

**问题：** We’re building a resource-constrained robotics pipeline that must: 1) reliably associate hands and faces to the correct person for HMI, 2) fine-tune large Transformers with LoRA under tight GPU memory budgets using compressed-state optimizers, 3) understand why self-distilled representations focus on useful signals rather than noisy pixels, 4) keep recurrent models biologically consistent (excitatory/inhibitory) without killing performance, and 5) run adaptive mesh-based physics simulators that evolve graph hierarchies over time. We plan to evaluate with MSE and cross-entropy, use cosine-style similarity in the embedding space, and track Precision/F1/AUROC. Are there works covering these design and training strategies end-to-end?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
