Gold 1：

> Here is a consolidated, literature‑only comparison of experimental results across the five methods, organized by task domain. Where identical datasets exist across competing methods, I state who performs better/worse and by how much. Where only similar datasets exist, I summarize trends and metrics that are directly reported.
> 
> A) Part–body association for hands/faces (PBADet vs. prior detectors)
> Identical datasets and metrics
> 1) BodyHands (hand–body association; metrics: Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP)
> - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Acc. 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
> - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1, 92.71, 85.73
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Cond. Acc. 86.91, Joint AP 84.39
> Result: On identical BodyHands, PBADet consistently outperforms BPJDet on all three metrics (e.g., +3.2 Hand AP and +5.7–5.8 points Conditional Accuracy, +1.3–1.6 Joint AP depending on backbone).
> 
> 2) COCOHumanParts (6 parts; metrics: COCO AP series and per‑class AP; association accuracy via mMR−2)
> Detection AP (higher is better):
> - Overall AP.5:.95 / AP.5: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) = 43.0/41.8 & 70.0/68.4 vs. BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) = 43.6/43.3 & 70.6/69.8 (BPJDet slightly ahead on these two overall lines)
> - PBADet leads on size‑conditioned APs: APM 66.2 vs. 63.8; APL 67.2 vs. 61.8
> - Per‑category AP: PBADet higher for person (62.4 vs. 61.3) and feet (r‑foot 30.9 vs. 30.2; l‑foot 31.5 vs. 30.9), while BPJDet is higher on head and face (head 56.6 vs. 54.6; face 46.3 vs. 44.6)
> Association accuracy (mMR−2, lower is better):
> - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): head 27.9, face 30.5, left‑hand 36.2, right‑hand 40.8, right‑foot 50.4, left‑foot 47.9
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 30.8, 31.8, 41.6, 42.2, 49.1, 50.4
> Result: PBADet achieves lower (better) average miss matching rates in most part categories (notably both hands), while BPJDet is better on one foot; PBADet also improves medium/large object AP and person/feet APs.
> 
> 3) CrowdHuman (face–body association; metrics: MR−2 body/face/AP and pair mMR−2)
> - PBADet (YOLOv7): body MR−2 36.5 (best), face MR−2 44.7, body AP 91.6, face AP 81.6, body–face mMR−2 50.8
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR−2 40.7, face MR−2 46.3, body AP 89.5, face AP 81.6, mMR−2 50.1
> Result: PBADet reduces body/face MR−2 and raises body AP, while pair mMR−2 is comparable (BPJDet 50.1 vs. PBADet 50.8).
> 
> 4) Multi‑person pose baseline (ED‑Pose) vs. PBADet (Precision/Recall/F1 on COCO parts)
> - All parts (hands/feet only): ED‑Pose F1 31.51 vs. PBADet 48.52; PBADet has higher Precision (39.41 vs. 24.09) and Recall (63.09 vs. 45.51). This directly shows higher Precision/F1 for PBADet on equivalent part‑association evaluation.
> 
> B) Memory‑efficient 4‑bit optimizers for fine‑tuning (vs. 32‑bit AdamW, 8‑bit AdamW/Adam)
> Identical datasets by task family
> 1) Natural language understanding (RoBERTa‑Large on GLUE; metric: mean Accuracy/Correlation)
> - 32‑bit AdamW: 88.9
> - 8‑bit AdamW: 89.1
> - 4‑bit AdamW (ours): 89.1; 4‑bit Factor: 88.9
> Result: 4‑bit matches 8‑bit and 32‑bit aggregate GLUE performance; per‑task tables (Appendix A) show parity across tasks.
> 
> 2) Question answering (SQuAD/SQuAD 2.0; metric: F1/EM)
> - 32‑bit AdamW: F1 94.6 (SQuAD); 4‑bit AdamW: 94.5; 4‑bit Factor: 94.6. SQuAD 2.0: small deltas within reported std.
> Result: 4‑bit maintains SQuAD F1 within run variability compared to full precision.
> 
> 3) Machine translation (Transformer‑Base on WMT14 En‑De; SacreBLEU)
> - 32‑bit AdamW: 26.61; 8‑bit AdamW: 26.66; 4‑bit AdamW: 26.28; 4‑bit Factor: 26.45
> Result: 4‑bit remains comparable to 32‑/8‑bit within ~0.3–0.4 BLEU.
> 
> 4) Image classification (Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k; Accuracy)
> - 32‑bit: 81.2; 8‑bit: 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW: 80.8; 4‑bit Factor: 80.9
> Result: 4‑bit within ~0.3–0.4% of 32‑bit.
> 
> 5) Natural language generation (GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG; BLEU)
> - 32‑bit AdamW: 67.7; 8‑bit: 67.5; 4‑bit AdamW: 67.8; 4‑bit Factor: 67.6
> Result: 4‑bit slightly tops or matches full precision.
> 
> 6) LLaMA instruction tuning (Alpaca; downstream eval on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA)
> - LLaMA‑7B: 32‑bit vs. 4‑bit AdamW: MMLU 38.7 vs. 38.9; other tasks within ~0.1–0.7 absolute
> - LLaMA‑13B: 32‑bit vs. 4‑bit: MMLU 46.5 vs. 47.4; others similar
> - LLaMA‑33B: 32‑bit vs. 4‑bit: MMLU 56.4 vs. 54.9; others similar or slightly higher for 4‑bit on OBQA
> Result: 4‑bit preserves instruction‑tuned accuracy across model sizes within small margins.
> 
> Efficiency comparisons (same training setups)
> - LLaMA‑7B fine‑tune: Total memory drops from 75.4 GB (32‑bit AdamW) to 31.87 GB (4‑bit AdamW), a 57.7% reduction; time modestly faster (3.35 h → 3.07 h)
> - RoBERTa‑L: memory 5.31 GB → 3.00 GB (4‑bit fused); GPT‑2 Medium: 6.89 GB → 4.62 GB (4‑bit fused)
> - Largest trainable model (single GPU): on 24 GB, 32‑bit trains OPT‑350M vs. 4‑bit trains OPT‑1.3B; on 80 GB, 32‑bit trains OPT‑1.3B vs. 4‑bit trains OPT‑6.7B; 4‑bit enables single‑GPU LLaMA‑7B.
> Ablations directly tied to stability/quality
> - 4‑bit second‑moment quantization requires excluding zero point (DE‑0 or Linear) and/or rank‑1 normalization; with these, 4‑bit achieves “lossless” convergence on finetuning benchmarks, while naive 4‑bit DE with zero point destabilizes training (Table 1, GPT‑2 Medium E2E‑NLG).
> 
> C) Why self‑distilled JEPA focuses on useful signals (JEPA vs. MAE)
> Identical/similar settings
> - Linear deep networks: analytic/simulation results show JEPA prioritizes features with high regression coefficients (ρ) when depth L>1, whereas MAE prioritizes high covariance (λ). In mixed settings (ρ decreases while λ increases), JEPA reverses the learning order relative to MAE and learns the more predictive, lower‑variance (less noisy) features earlier. This is demonstrated in the controlled synthetic experiments (Figure 1, Figure 2) and the temporal generative model where λa=γa||va||² and ρa=γa||va||²/(σa²+||va||²): JEPA slows learning of noisy features (larger σa) compared to MAE.
> - ImageNet‑1k (64×64) probing: JEPA learned features show higher similarity (mean CCA) between full and bottom‑variance PCA subspaces than MAE, and lower similarity between full and top subspaces (Appendix D Figure 7). No exact numbers are reported, but the plotted curves consistently show JEPA aligns faster/stronger with the “bottom” subspace commonly linked to perceptual/semantic content.
> Result: Across these comparable settings, JEPA’s implicit bias toward influential (high‑ρ), lower‑variance features is supported; MAE is biased to reconstruct high‑variance (often noisy) details.
> 
> D) Dale’s‑law RNNs without performance collapse (ColEI vs. DANN vs. standard RNN)
> Identical datasets and outcomes (qualitative/graphical)
> - Tasks: Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, and a naturalistic object‑recognition sequence
> Findings across all four tasks
> - ColEI (columns constrained E/I) learns worse: higher final errors and more variance across seeds, benefiting disproportionately from gradient clipping
> - DANN RNNs (EI architecture extended to recurrent) learn as well as standard RNNs
> Mechanistic comparisons
> - Spectrum transplant experiments show singular value spectra, not just sign constraints, account for most of the ColEI vs. RNN/DANN performance gap. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) of the recurrent weights at initialization predicts performance: lower NSE (dispersed, multi‑modal singular values) correlates with worse learning. Small networks or few inhibitory units worsen ColEI spectra and learning; DANN spectra remain unimodal and robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> Result: For identical tasks, DANNs match standard RNNs; ColEI underperforms unless spectral pathologies are fixed. These are consistent across all reported benchmarks; exact numerical scores weren’t tabulated, but the figures show consistent rank ordering.
> 
> E) Adaptive mesh simulators with evolving hierarchies (EvoMesh vs. MGN/Lino/BSMS/Eagle/HCMT)
> Identical datasets and metrics (RMSE; lower is better)
> 1) Standard benchmarks (Table 2)
> One‑step RMSE‑1 (×10⁻²):
> - CylinderFlow: EvoMesh 0.1568 (best) vs. Eagle 0.1733, BSMS 0.2263, MGN 0.3046, HCMT 0.9190, Lino 3.9352 (EvoMesh best by 9.53% vs. second best)
> - Airfoil: EvoMesh 41.41 vs. HCMT 48.62, Eagle 51.55, BSMS 71.69, MGN 77.38, Lino 85.66 (EvoMesh best by 14.8%)
> - FlyingFlag: EvoMesh 0.3049 vs. Eagle 0.3805, HCMT 0.4013, BSMS 0.5080, MGN 0.3459, Lino 0.9993 (EvoMesh best by 11.9%)
> - DeformingPlate: EvoMesh 0.0282 vs. HCMT 0.0295, Lino 0.0291, Eagle 0.0392, MGN 0.0579, BSMS 0.0632 (EvoMesh best by 3.10%)
> Long‑term RMSE‑All (×10⁻²):
> - CylinderFlow: EvoMesh 6.571 vs. BSMS 16.98, Eagle 20.05, HCMT 23.59, Lino 27.60, MGN 59.78 (61.3% lower than second best)
> - Airfoil: EvoMesh 2002 vs. Lino 2080, Eagle 2344, BSMS 2493, MGN 2816, HCMT 3238 (3.75% lower than second best)
> - FlyingFlag: EvoMesh 76.16 vs. HCMT 90.32, Eagle 127.7, MGN 115.3, Lino 118.2, BSMS 168.1 (15.7% lower than second best)
> - DeformingPlate: EvoMesh 1.296 vs. BSMS 1.811, Lino 2.090, HCMT 2.468, MGN 3.982, Eagle 7.797 (28.5% lower than second best)
> 
> 2) FoldingPaper with time‑varying meshes (Table 3; vs. MGN)
> - RMSE‑1: 0.0544 vs. 0.0618 (12.0% better)
> - RMSE‑All: 7.412 vs. 24.08 (69.2% better)
> Result: Across identical datasets (fluids, flag, plates; and a dynamic topology cloth task), EvoMesh sets the best or near‑best RMSEs, with especially strong long‑horizon gains on CylinderFlow and DeformingPlate.
> 
> 3) Out‑of‑distribution mesh resolution (Table 4, test meshes ≈2× nodes, 3× edges)
> - CylinderFlow RMSE‑1/RMSE‑50: EvoMesh 0.4855 / 1.077 vs. BSMS 0.9177 / 2.097 and others (best)
> - Airfoil RMSE‑1/RMSE‑50: 126.7 / 812.5 (best)
> - FlyingFlag, DeformingPlate: MGN is best; EvoMesh remains competitive but not top
> Result: EvoMesh generalizes best on fluid OOD resolutions; for smoother Lagrangian deformation tasks, MGN can edge it.
> 
> 4) Physical variation generalization (Table 5)
> - With higher variance/norm dynamics at test time on Cylinder and Airfoil, EvoMesh yields lowest RMSE‑1 and RMSE‑All among compared models (e.g., Cylinder RMSE‑All 0.665 vs. next best 1.035; Airfoil 22.57 vs. 30.32).
> 
> 5) Ablations (Table 8/Figure 4)
> - Replacing fixed hierarchies with learned time‑evolving ones and using anisotropic intra‑level plus learnable inter‑level propagation reduces errors over the same datasets (e.g., Cylinder RMSE‑All: BSMS 16.98 → EvoMesh 6.571; Flag 168.1 → 76.16). Learned inter‑level weights further improve over unlearnable degree‑based propagation; uniform sampling underperforms adaptive selection.
> 
> Cross‑paper alignment to the requested metrics
> - MSE family: EvoMesh reports RMSE; 4‑bit optimizer tasks report task‑standard metrics (BLEU, Accuracy, F1) rather than MSE
> - Cross‑entropy: implied in classification fine‑tuning (e.g., ImageNet, GLUE), but papers report accuracy/F1 not CE values
> - Cosine‑style similarity: JEPA reports representational similarity via CCA trends (higher mean CCA for full↔bottom subspace than MAE)
> - Precision/F1/AUROC: PBADet reports Precision/Recall/F1 vs. ED‑Pose, with significant F1 gains; AUROC is not reported in these works
> 
> What these results imply for the proposed robotics pipeline
> - Robust hand/face association (PBADet): On identical hand/face datasets, PBADet provides quantifiably higher association accuracy (BodyHands/COCO/ CrowdHuman) and markedly higher F1 than pose‑estimation baselines on COCO hands/feet.
> - Memory‑tight LoRA fine‑tuning (4‑bit optimizers): 4‑bit first/second moments (with zero‑point‑free second moment and rank‑1 normalization) match full‑precision accuracy across GLUE, SQuAD, WMT14, ImageNet, and LLaMA instruction tuning, while cutting optimizer memory up to ~58% and enabling much larger models per GPU.
> - Why self‑distilled features de‑noise (JEPA): Experiments/theory show JEPA’s depth‑dependent bias prioritizes high‑ρ (predictive) low‑variance features, explaining empirical focus on “useful signals” (bottom PCA subspace) over pixel noise (top variance) compared to MAE.
> - EI‑consistent recurrent controllers (Dale’s law): Recurrent DANNs match standard RNNs on adding/sMNIST/PTB/object‑recognition, whereas simple column EI (ColEI) underperforms; spectrum (NSE) diagnostics predict learnability and can guide stable EI designs.
> - Adaptive simulators with evolving graphs (EvoMesh): On identical CFD/elastic/cloth benchmarks, EvoMesh lowers short‑ and long‑horizon RMSEs—especially on fluids—while adapting hierarchies to evolving flow/strain regions; it also generalizes to OOD mesh resolutions and distributions.
> 
> Limitations of cross‑paper comparison
> - No single dataset is shared across all five works; comparisons are within domain (detectors, optimizers, JEPA/MAE dynamics, EI‑RNNs, mesh simulators)
> - Some results are qualitative or trend‑based (JEPA CCA, Dale’s‑law spectra) rather than tabulated metrics
> 
> Bottom line
> - For each part of your pipeline there are literature‑validated methods with strong experimental evidence on identical or closely related datasets: PBADet (association), 4‑bit optimizers (memory‑tight fine‑tuning), JEPA analyses (useful‑feature bias), DANN RNNs plus spectrum diagnostics (EI consistency without performance loss), and EvoMesh (adaptive multi‑scale simulation). Their reported metrics collectively support the design/training strategies you outlined under realistic evaluation protocols.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes—the collection contains one work per requirement, though no single paper covers all five end-to-end. Here is the comparison and analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> **1) Hand/face-to-person association (HMI): PBADet** — One-stage anchor-free part-body association (ICLR 2024).
> - On BodyHands: Ours(YOLOv7) hand AP 89.1 / conditional accuracy 92.62 / joint AP 85.98, and Ours(YOLOv5l6) 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73, vs. BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39 and BodyHands 84.8 / 83.44 / 63.48 — outperforming all baselines including a smaller model than BPJDet(YOLOv5m6).
> - On COCOHumanParts: AP on par with BPJDet, but leads on AP_M/AP_L/AP_s and achieves the lowest mMR-2 for head, face, both hands, and right foot.
> - On CrowdHuman face-body: best body MR-2 (36.5) and competitive AP (body 91.6, face 81.6), though mMR-2 (50.8) is slightly worse than BPJDet (50.1) for this single-part task.
> - vs. ED-Pose (pose estimation): much higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet (e.g., all parts F1 48.52 vs. 31.51; left-hand F1 46.50 vs. 22.87). This matches the requested Precision/F1 evaluation; AUROC is not reported.
> 
> **2) LoRA + compressed-state optimizers under GPU budget: "4-bit Optimizers"** (NeurIPS 2023).
> - On LLaMA-7B Alpaca fine-tuning (LoRA-style parameter-efficient setting, Alpaca codebase), 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit: MMLU 38.9 vs. 38.7, HellaSwag 74.7 vs. 74.6, ARC-e 61.2 vs. 61.5, ARC-c 44.4 vs. 45.1, OBQA 43.0 vs. 43.4; results stay comparable at 13B and 33B.
> - Memory: LLaMA-7B drops from 75.40 GB (32-bit) to 31.87 GB (4-bit), a 57.7% saving, enabling LLaMA-7B on a single 80 GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models; also matches/exceeds 32-bit on GLUE, SQuAD, E2E-NLG, ImageNet (Swin-T), and WMT14. GPT-2 Medium experiments explicitly use the LoRA codebase. Convergence curves closely align with 32-bit AdamW.
> 
> **3) Why self-distillation ignores noisy pixels: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024).
> - Theory (deep linear nets, gradient-flow ODEs): JEPA's critical time depends on the regression coefficient ρ (increasingly with encoder depth), i.e., an implicit bias to learn high-influence/low-variance features first, whereas MAE's ordering depends mainly on the eigenvalue λ — explaining noise/pixel suppression.
> - Experiment: on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (measured by CCA). This supports cosine-style embedding-similarity evaluation of representation quality.
> 
> **4) Biologically consistent (E/I) recurrent models: "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023).
> - Simply partitioning units into E/I (ColEI) impairs learning (worse final error, higher variance on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB); gradient clipping mitigates the deficit.
> - The Dale's-ANN (DANN) reparameterization learns well while respecting Dale's Law — robust even with only 1 inhibitory neuron, whereas ColEI degrades with fewer I units. The cause is spectral, not sign constraints: ColEI has multimodal/dispersed singular values vs. the unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur spectra of standard RNNs/DANNs; normalized SVD entropy anti-correlates with final error.
> 
> **5) Adaptive mesh physics with evolving graph hierarchies: EvoMesh** (ICML 2025).
> - On CylinderFlow/Airfoil/Flag/DeformingPlate/FoldingPaper it outperforms fixed-hierarchy baselines (MGN, BSMS-GNN, Eagle, HCMT), e.g., RMSE-1 2.14e-3 vs. BSMS-GNN 2.58e-3 / Eagle 2.49e-3 / HCMT 7.35e-3 (14.1% gain) and 63.7%/28.6%/25.6% gains on other metrics; on average ~20% better than fixed-hierarchy models.
> - On time-varying meshes (FoldingPaper with remeshing), RMSE-All 7.412e-2 vs. MGN 24.08e-2 (69.2% gain), showing adaptive hierarchies are needed when meshes change; generalizes to unseen resolutions/OOD dynamics. Uses RMSE (an MSE-family metric, matching your MSE choice).
> 
> **Analysis / gaps:** The five needs map onto PBADet, 4-bit Optimizers (+LoRA), JEPA analysis, Dale's-Law RNNs, and EvoMesh, respectively, and their metrics cover your plan: MSE/RMSE (EvoMesh), cross-entropy-based benchmarks (4-bit optimizers' NLU/instruction tasks, RNN classification/language modeling), cosine-style embedding similarity/CCA (JEPA), and Precision/F1/AP/mMR-2 (PBADet). However, the works are independent—none integrates all five strategies end-to-end—and AUROC is not explicitly evaluated in any of these papers, so that specific metric is not supported by the context.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Answer
> 
> No single work in the collection covers all five components end-to-end, but there is one paper per component, and their experimental results can be compared as follows:
> 
> **1) Hands/face→person association (HMI): PBADet (ICLR 2024)**
> - One-stage anchor-free part-body association using a single part-to-body center offset.
> - BodyHands: hand AP 92.71 / joint AP 85.73 (YOLOv5l6, 1024px) vs BPJDet 86.91/84.39 (1536px); the smaller YOLOv7 variant (36.9 GFLOPs) reaches 92.62 hand AP — beating larger BPJDet models.
> - COCOHumanParts: on par with BPJDet on AP but leads in AP_M, AP_L and person/feet; lowest mMR⁻² for head, face, both hands, right foot.
> - vs ED-Pose (COCO val, all parts): Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51 — large gains on hands/feet.
> - On CrowdHuman face-body association the margin over BPJDet shrinks (single-part task), though body MR-2 is leading. Uses AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP, Precision/Recall/F1.
> 
> **2) LoRA + compressed-state optimizers under tight GPU memory: "4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states (smaller B128 blocks; zero-point-excluded linear second-moment quantizer; optional rank-1 factorization).
> - LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning: 4-bit matches 32-bit AdamW (e.g., MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8 for 13B), lossless on fine-tuning, comparable on pretraining.
> - Up to 57.7% total memory saving; LLaMA-7B fits on one 80GB GPU; 4× larger OPT models trainable at fixed budget. LoRA is cited as the parameter-efficient complement (it freezes pretrained weights so only low-rank adapters are tuned). RTB (Stable Diffusion fine-tuning) also combines LoRA with memory-efficient batched gradient computation.
> 
> **3) Self-distillation focusing on useful signals, not noisy pixels: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Theory (deep linear networks): JEPA self-distillation is biased toward high-influence features (high regression coefficients ρ), with depth strengthening noise suppression; MAE orders features by eigenvalue λ and learns noisy features faster.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA-based). JEPA converges to lower-amplitude weights for noisy features.
> - Companion analysis on embedding-space similarity ("On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning", covering your cosine-style similarity metric): optimal encoders give positive-pair cosine similarity 1 and negative-pair −1/(n−1); an auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, full ImageNet, temperature robustness, and small-batch training.
> 
> **4) Biologically consistent (E/I) recurrent models without losing performance: "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - ColEI (column-partitioned E/I) learns worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs; gradient clipping mitigates the deficit.
> - The cause is the *initial recurrent-weight spectrum* (multimodal/dispersed singular values from column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure), not sign constraints: singular-value transplants show spectra matter most.
> - Recurrent DANN (Dale's ANNs) respects E/I sign structure while keeping RNN-like unimodal spectra — it learns well even with 1 inhibitory neuron (NSE ≈ 0.95) and is robust to E/I ratio changes; normalised SVD entropy anti-correlates with final error across adding, sMNIST, PTB, and object recognition.
> 
> **5) Adaptive mesh physics simulators with evolving graph hierarchies: EvoMesh (ICML 2025)**
> - Fully differentiable hierarchy evolution: Gumbel-Softmax node selection + anisotropic message passing within/across levels.
> - On CylinderFlow/Airfoil/Flag/DeformingPlate it beats fixed-hierarchy baselines by ~20% on average (e.g., RMSE 2.14×10⁻³ vs BSMS-GNN 2.58×10⁻³, Eagle 2.49×10⁻³, HCMT 7.35×10⁻³; and 0.091 vs 0.251/0.273/1.047 on a second metric).
> - FoldingPaper (time-varying meshes, where BSMS/HCMT are inapplicable): RMSE-1 0.0544 vs MGN 0.0618 (−12%), RMSE-All 7.412 vs 24.08 (−69.2%); generalizes to novel resolutions and OOD dynamics.
> 
> **Cross-cutting analysis of your evaluation plan:** MSE/RMSE is used by EvoMesh, DiffusionFake (classification + diffusion + MSE losses), and JEPA theory; cross-entropy underlies the classification/LoRA fine-tuning tasks in the 4-bit optimizer and PBADet papers; cosine embedding similarity is directly analyzed in the contrastive-embedding paper; Precision/F1 appear in PBADet (vs ED-Pose) and AUC in DiffusionFake (cross-dataset deepfake AUC rises 75.80→81.88 for EfficientNet-B4, 77.44→83.78 for ViT-B). So the collection covers each strategy and each evaluation metric, but as separate works rather than one unified end-to-end system — you would need to assemble them.

Gold 1：

> {'answer': 'Integrated comparison of experimental results across the five papers, organized by shared datasets, similar dataset types, and task-specific outcomes.\n\n1) Methods and scope covered by the five papers\n- Anchor‑free detectors for part–body association: PBADet (ICLR 2024)\n- Active exploration for system identification for sim‑to‑real manipulation: ASID (ICLR 2024)\n- Low‑bit (4‑bit) optimizer states compatible with SGD/Adam/AdamW: Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States (NeurIPS 2023)\n- Spectral analyses of EI recurrent nets under Dale’s Law: Learning better with Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023)\n- Non‑contrastive self‑distillation in joint‑embedding SSL (JEPA) and its implicit bias: How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)\n\n2) Comparisons on identical datasets\nA. COCO‑style, instance‑level human part association (PBADet vs BPJDet vs Hier‑R‑CNN) — COCOHumanParts (identical dataset)\n- Overall AP (all categories; original/subordinate):\n  • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 43.0 / 41.8; PBADet (YOLOv7): 42.7 / 41.5\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6 / 43.3\n  • Takeaway: BPJDet attains slightly higher overall AP, while PBADet narrows the gap.\n- Size-specific AP and per-category (Table 2):\n  • APM/APL: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 66.2/67.2 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 63.8/61.8 — PBADet leads on medium/large.\n  • Person AP: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 62.4 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 61.3 — PBADet higher.\n  • Feet AP: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) r‑foot 30.9, l‑foot 31.5 vs BPJDet 30.2/30.9 — PBADet slightly higher on feet; BPJDet higher on head/face/hands.\n- Qualitative and decoding: PBADet reports simpler part‑to‑body decoding and robustness benefits from its one‑stage anchor‑free design.\n\nB. BodyHands hand–body association (identical dataset)\n- Metrics (Table 1):\n  • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.62; Joint AP 85.98\n  • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.71; Joint AP 85.73\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9; Conditional Accuracy 86.91; Joint AP 84.39\n  • Takeaway: On BodyHands, PBADet outperforms BPJDet by large margins in Conditional Accuracy (+5.8–5.9 points) and Joint AP (+1.3–1.6), and higher Hand AP.\n\nC. CrowdHuman face–body association (identical dataset)\n- Metrics (Table 5):\n  • PBADet (YOLOv7): MR−2 body 36.5; MR−2 face 44.7; AP body 91.6; AP face 81.6; mMR−2 body‑face 50.8\n  • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 body 40.7; MR−2 face 46.3; AP body 89.5; AP face 81.6; mMR−2 50.1\n  • Takeaway: PBADet achieves lower miss rates (better MR−2) and higher body AP; mMR−2 very close.\n\nD. Pose/association comparison (COCO val subset; identical images) — PBADet vs ED‑Pose\n- Precision/Recall/F1 (Appendix Table 7):\n  • All parts F1: PBADet 48.52 vs ED‑Pose 31.51 (+17.01)\n  • Hands (F1): left 46.50 vs 22.87; right 47.34 vs 24.17\n  • Feet (F1): left 51.08 vs 40.46; right 50.34 vs 40.34\n  • Takeaway: PBADet notably outperforms ED‑Pose in precision/recall/F1 for part detection+association on COCO images.\n\nE. ImageNet‑1K (identical dataset used by two papers; different aims/metrics)\n- 4‑bit Optimizers (Swin‑T, CLS): Top‑1 accuracy (Table 2)\n  • 32‑bit AdamW 81.2; 8‑bit AdamW 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9 — Low‑bit optimizers nearly match 32‑bit on ImageNet.\n- JEPA vs MAE (Appendix D): representation similarity (CCA) trends\n  • On ImageNet‑1K (64×64), I‑JEPA features from full ↔ bottom‑variance subsets exhibit higher CCA earlier than MAE, while full ↔ top CCA is lower for JEPA — indicating JEPA focuses sooner on low‑variance, perceptual subspaces. (Qualitative curve comparison; no accuracy reported.)\n\n3) Comparisons on similar dataset types (not identical)\nA. Robotic manipulation with sim‑to‑real (ASID)\n- Simulation tasks (Table 1):\n  • Rod balancing (tilt angle, ↓ better). (2019), enabling identification of multiple parameters (heatmaps in Fig. 4).\n\nB. Low‑bit optimizer states across NLP/CV tasks (same benchmarks across methods in the 4‑bit paper)\n- NLU (RoBERTa‑L, GLUE; mean acc/corr, Table 2): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit Factor 88.9 — 4‑bit matches 32‑bit/8‑bit.\n  • Per‑task detail (Table 7, medians over 5 runs): MNLI 90.2 (4‑bit AdamW), QNLI 94.5, QQP 92.0, RTE 85.2, SST‑2 96.3, MRPC 92.8, CoLA 67.3, STS‑B 92.5 — close to 32‑bit and 8‑bit.\n- QA (RoBERTa‑L, SQuAD/SQuAD2.0, Table 9):\n  • SQuAD F1: 32‑bit 94.6; 8‑bit 94.5; 4‑bit 94.5. SQuAD2.0 F1: 32‑bit 88.8; 8‑bit 89.0; 4‑bit 88.4 — parity within noise.\n- NLG (GPT‑2 Medium, E2E‑NLG, Table 2 & 8):\n  • BLEU: 32‑bit 67.7±0.67; 8‑bit 67.5±0.87; 4‑bit 67.8±0.51; 4‑bit Factor 67.6±0.33 — 4‑bit slightly best BLEU.\n- CLS (Swin‑T, ImageNet‑1K, Table 2): 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit 81.0; 4‑bit 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9 — small drop (≤0.4 pt) vs 32‑bit.\n- MT (Transformer‑Base, WMT14 en‑de SacreBLEU, Table 2): 32‑bit 26.61±0.08; 8‑bit 26.66±0.10; 4‑bit 26.28±0.05; 4‑bit Factor 26.45±0.05 — small degradation for 4‑bit.\n- LLaMA instruction‑tuning (Table 3):\n  • 7B MMLU: 4‑bit 38.9 vs 32‑bit 38.7; HellaSwag 74.7 vs 74.6; ARC‑e 61.2 vs 61.5; ARC‑c 44.4 vs 45.1; OBQA 43.0 vs 43.4 — comparable.\n  • 13B and 33B: similar parity; e.g., 13B MMLU 47.4 (4‑bit) vs 46.5 (32‑bit).\n- Memory/time (Table 4):\n  • LLaMA‑7B (FSDP, 2×A100‑80GB): 32‑bit 75.40GB, 3.35h vs 4‑bit 31.87GB, 3.07h — 57.7% memory reduction and slight speedup.\n  • RoBERTa‑L (single GPU): 5.31GB → 3.00GB (−43.5%) with fused 4‑bit; GPT‑2 Medium: 6.89GB → 4.62GB (−34.4%).\n\nC. Recurrent nets under Dale’s Law (same synthetic/benchmark families across variants)\n- Across adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank LM, and a naturalistic object recognition task (Fig. 2):\n  • ColEI (column EI sign constraints) underperform standard RNNs and DANNs; DANNs match standard RNNs.\n- Quantified effects (Sec. 3.3):\n  • Sign‑constraints alone degrade performance by ~0.7%±0.3% (RNNs) and ~1%±1% (ColEI), but total gap ColEI vs RNNs ~2.3%±0.6% — not fully explained by signs.\n  • Spectrum “transplant” experiments (Fig. 4): changes induced by spectrum were ~1.5%±0.3% (RNNs) and ~2%±1% (ColEI), larger than sign effects — spectrum is more impactful.\n  • Gradient clipping disproportionately helps ColEI; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts test error across EI ratio and network size (Figs. 5–7): higher NSE → lower error.\n  • Takeaway: DANN spectral properties (unimodal, clustered singular values) drive learning comparable to standard RNNs; ColEI multimodal/dispersed spectra impair learning, especially in small nets or with few inhibitory units.\n\nD. JEPA vs MAE (linear and controlled settings)\n- Training dynamics in deep linear models (Figs. 1–2; Theorems 3.2–3.6):\n  • Both objectives learn features stepwise; MAE prioritizes high covariance (λ), JEPA prioritizes high influence (regression coefficient ρ), increasingly so with depth.\n  • On data where λ increases but ρ decreases across features, JEPA reverses the order vs MAE, focusing on predictive, less noisy features.\n- Temporal linear model (Fig. 3):\n  • Analytical expressions show λa = γa‖va‖² and ρa = γa‖va‖²/(σ²_a+‖va‖²); JEPA is slower to learn noisy features (smaller ρ), consistent with simulations.\n- ImageNet‑1K (Appendix D):\n  • CCA analysis indicates I‑JEPA features align more with bottom‑variance (perceptual) directions earlier than MAE; for top‑variance, MAE CCA is higher — matching the implicit‑bias theory.\n\n4) Task‑specific highlights and takeaways\n- Part–body association on COCO‑style benchmarks: PBADet is competitive on overall AP vs BPJDet, and leads on APM/APL and “person/feet” categories; it delivers clear gains on BodyHands and lower miss rates on CrowdHuman. Against ED‑Pose on COCO images, PBADet substantially improves Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet.\n- Active exploration & system ID for sim‑to‑real: ASID’s Fisher‑information‑maximizing exploration plus optimization‑based system ID beats random/MI‑based exploration and DR both in simulation (near‑zero tilt in rod balancing; highest strike success for spheres) and real (6/9 rod successes vs 0/9 DR; 7/10 shuffleboard vs 3/10 DR), using very little real data.\n- Low‑bit (4‑bit) optimizers: 4‑bit AdamW (and 4‑bit Factor for second moment) deliver near‑parity with 32‑bit/8‑bit across GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet, WMT14, and LLaMA instruction‑tuning, while cutting optimizer memory by ~35–58% and even improving throughput in multi‑GPU FSDP settings.\n- Spectral EI RNNs: Recurrent DANNs perform on par with standard RNNs, while ColEI generally underperform unless networks are large and EI ratios balanced; spectral properties (NSE, singular‑value clustering) are strongly predictive of performance.\n- JEPA implicit bias: In deep linear settings, JEPA prioritizes high‑influence (ρ) features, steering away from noisy/high‑variance directions; corroborated by ImageNet CCA trends where JEPA homes in earlier on bottom‑variance (perceptual) subspace than MAE.\n\n5) Notes on models/backbones, losses, and adapters (as reported)\n- Backbones: PBADet uses YOLOv5/YOLOv7 heads, with comparisons to Faster‑R50/FPN‑R50/RetinaNet‑R50 and Hier‑R‑CNN (R50/X101) on COCO‑style tasks. 4‑bit optimizers evaluate Swin‑T (ImageNet), RoBERTa‑L (GLUE/SQuAD), GPT‑2 Medium (E2E‑NLG), Transformer‑Base (WMT14), and LLaMA (7B/13B/33B) — transformer/residual families are represented.\n- Losses: PBADet uses task‑alignment with IoU/DFL/classification losses plus an association loss (L1 on center offsets). JEPA vs MAE analyze squared‑error objectives in latent vs input space; the empirical CCA analysis compares learned representations rather than cross‑entropy.\n- Lightweight adapters: The 4‑bit study trains GPT‑2 via the LoRA codebase and performs LLaMA instruction tuning; the optimizer results are reported over the standard fine‑tuning setups used therein. (No new adapter results are introduced beyond those configurations.)\n\nOverall conclusion based on reported results in figures and tables\n- For COCO‑style instance‑level part detection/association, PBADet is SOTA or competitive, especially on BodyHands and certain COCOHumanParts categories/sizes, and clearly improves F1 vs pose‑based baselines.\n- For sim‑to‑real robotic control, ASID’s targeted exploration (Fisher information) and optimization‑based system ID consistently outperform random/MI‑based exploration and DR, enabling zero‑shot or few‑shot transfer in both simulation and real.\n- 4‑bit optimizer states (with careful quantization and factorization of moments) preserve accuracy across diverse NLP/CV tasks while substantially reducing memory and often maintaining or improving throughput.\n- In recurrent nets with EI constraints, spectral properties, not just sign constraints, drive learning success: DANN‑style recurrent architectures achieve standard‑RNN‑level performance; ColEI needs favorable spectra (large nets, balanced EI) to close the gap.\n- JEPA’s implicit bias favors high‑influence latent features, which helps it learn more perceptual, low‑variance structure earlier than MAE — consistent with its empirical CCA trends on ImageNet.'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, here are the five papers matching the requested topics, followed by a comparative analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The papers
> 
> 1. **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — One-stage anchor-free part-body association detector (hands/face/feet ↔ body). Uses YOLOv5/YOLOv7 (anchor-free heads) with classification/localization/displacement branches, TOOD-style task-alignment loss and DFL.
> 2. **ASID (ICLR 2024)** — Active exploration for system identification (mass, friction, stiffness, articulation, center of mass) for sim-to-real robot manipulation; Fisher-information-maximizing exploration policy, optimization-based identification, then zero-shot transfer.
> 3. **4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)** — Pushes Adam/AdamW (and the framework covers SGD with momentum) optimizer states to 4-bit via small block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, optional factorized second moment.
> 4. **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)** — Spectral (SVD) analysis of excitatory/inhibitory RNNs respecting Dale's Law (ColEI vs DANN), using normalised SVD entropy (NSE).
> 5. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)** — Theoretical/empirical analysis of the implicit bias of non-contrastive JEPA self-distillation in deep linear networks (with ImageNet I-JEPA experiments).
> 
> ## Comparative analysis of experimental results
> 
> **PBADet (detection, COCO-style metrics):** Anchor-free part-to-body (Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 on BodyHands) beats anchor-based body-to-part BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13) and its own anchor-based variant (88.4/92.31/85.28), showing both the part-to-body offset definition and anchor-free design help. On COCO-HumanParts, all-category AP is 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6). Against the pose estimator ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision, recall and F1 for hands/feet. Ablations show association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment each matter.
> 
> **ASID (robotics, success-rate metrics):** Real-world rod balancing: ASID 6/9 vs domain randomization 0/9 (DR fails catastrophically); shuffleboard: ASID 7/10 vs DR 3/10 (yellow 4/5 vs 2/5, blue 3/5 vs 1/5). A single real episode typically suffices. ASID also beats random exploration and learned estimators (Kumar et al. 2019). Limitation: center-of-mass ambiguity near the rod's middle can hurt identification.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers (efficiency, accuracy retained):** 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit AdamW on NLU (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9), image classification (Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2), NLG (GPT-2 67.8 vs 67.7), QA (94.5 vs 94.6), MT (26.28 vs 26.61), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning, while saving up to 57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU). Sublinear optimizers (Adafactor, SM3) save more memory but degrade (e.g., CLS 79.0/79.5 vs 81.2). Smaller block size on the first moment and factorizing the second moment improve accuracy and memory.
> 
> **Dale's Law spectral analysis (spectral pathology predicts learning):** ColEI RNNs learn worse and with higher variance (sequential MNIST gap ~2.3%±0.6%); sign constraints alone don't explain it — the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed due to a rank-one column-mean nilpotent structure) does. Standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs have unimodal, clustered spectra (Marchenko–Pastur/quarter-circle) and learn equally well. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error across network size and E/I ratio; gradient clipping mitigates the ColEI deficit.
> 
> **JEPA implicit bias (feature quality):** JEPA self-distillation prioritizes "influential" (high-regression-coefficient) features and suppresses noisy ones, an effect that strengthens with encoder depth; MAE instead prioritizes high-variance features regardless of informativeness. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA), explaining JEPA's semantic-feature advantage.
> 
> ## Fit with your stated preferences
> 
> - **Residual/transformer backbones:** Only partially evidenced. PBADet uses YOLOv5/v7 backbones; the 4-bit paper uses Swin-T and Transformer-Base; JEPA uses linear networks plus ImageNet I-JEPA; no paper centers on a 50-layer ResNet backbone, though LDReg/HASSOD (retrieved as related SSL/detection works) use ResNet-50 with DINO init.
> - **Precision/recall/F1 on COCO-style tasks:** PBADet reports AP-style metrics (BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman) and precision/recall/F1 vs ED-Pose; HASSOD reports AR on COCO/LVIS/SA-1B. The 4-bit optimizer, Dale's-law and JEPA papers do not report COCO P/R/F1.
> - **MSE vs log-softmax loss comparisons:** Not directly compared in these papers. JEPA analyzes a squared (MSE-like) latent-prediction objective vs MAE reconstruction; PBADet uses task-alignment classification plus DFL localization; the Dale's-law and optimizer papers don't compare these losses.
> - **Low-rank adapter fine-tuning and regularization:** The 4-bit optimizer paper explicitly discusses LoRA/delta-tuning (low-rank, parameter-efficient) as alternatives and uses low-rank factorization of the second moment; LDReg provides L1/L2 regularization of local intrinsic dimensionality for SSL (improving COCO APbb for SimCLR 35.24→35.26, BYOL 36.30→36.82 at 100 epochs, and ImageNet linear eval 64.3→64.8, 67.6→68.5). PBADet's task-alignment learning acts as a form of sample-selection regularization.
> 
> **Caveats:** No single retrieved paper jointly satisfies all preferences (50-layer backbones + COCO P/R/F1 + MSE-vs-log-softmax loss comparison + LoRA + regularization). The connections across papers are thematic (efficient training/memory, transfer to downstream tasks, regularization for representation quality) rather than a unified benchmark; cross-paper quantitative comparison is therefore limited to each paper's own baselines.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers found (one per requested topic)
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — one-stage **anchor-free** detector for part→body association on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman (YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 backbones).
> 2. **ASID** (ICLR 2024) — **active exploration** for system identification (mass, friction, articulation) for **sim-to-real** robot manipulation.
> 3. **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023) — **~4-bit optimizer states** for both SGD(M) and Adam/AdamW (quantized first/second moments).
> 4. **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023) — **spectral analysis** of excitatory/inhibitory RNNs respecting Dale's law (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs).
> 5. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features** (NeurIPS 2024) — **non-contrastive self-distillation in JEPA** and its implicit bias (prioritizing influential/low-variance features over noise).
> 
> The closest match to "transformer/residual-50 backbones + COCO-style AP + regularization + SSL" is **LDReg** (ICLR 2024), which regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality in SSL on ResNet-50/ViT-B and reports COCO detection/segmentation AP — it complements topic 5.
> 
> ## Comparison and analysis of experimental results
> 
> **PBADet (detection/association).** On BodyHands: HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) vs BPJDet(YOLOv5m6) 85.3/86.80/78.13 — PBADet wins on all metrics with a smaller model; the anchor-free part-to-body offset also beats anchor-based body-to-part (Table 8: 89.1/92.62/85.98 vs 85.3/86.80/78.13). On COCOHumanParts it matches BPJDet's overall AP (42.7/41.5 vs 43.6/43.3) and leads AP_M/AP_L and lowest mMR−2 on most parts; it reports higher precision/recall/F1 than the pose estimator ED-Pose (Swin-L) for hands/feet. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each matter (JointAP 78.07 → 85.98). Loss is a weighted sum (IoU + DFL + classification + association), i.e., not an MSE-vs-log-softmax study.
> 
> **ASID (sim-to-real).** In simulation, ASID+SysID achieves tilt angle 0.00°/0.72°/0.00° (rod, left/middle/right inertia) and 28.0% sphere-striking success vs random exploration (10.6%), Kumar et al. (9.5%), domain randomization (8.75%), and learned estimators (11.0%) — optimization-based identification generalizes far better than learned modules. In the real world, ASID solves rod balancing 6/9 vs DR 0/9, and shuffleboard 7/10 vs DR 3/10, using typically a single episode of real data. Fisher-information-based exploration also interacts with the object far more (80% vs 20% for naïve baselines).
> 
> **4-bit Optimizers.** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), E2E-NLG (67.8 vs 67.7), ImageNet/Swin-T (80.8 vs 81.2), WMT14 (26.28 vs 26.61) and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning, while saving up to 57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU); 4-bitFactor further factorizes the second moment. It is explicitly compatible with both SGD(M) (convergence proof for quantized SGD(M)) and Adam. The framework (compress/decompress states) is optimizer-agnostic, covering "stochastic gradient and adaptive-moment methods."
> 
> **Dale's Law spectral study.** ColEI RNNs learn worse and with higher variance on all four tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition); gradient clipping helps them most. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum at initialization matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors (sign constraints explain only ~0.7–1% of the 2.3% gap). ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure) vs the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle of standard/DANN RNNs; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance across network size and E:I ratio — small networks with balanced E/I outperform larger skewed ones.
> 
> **JEPA implicit bias.** In deep linear networks, JEPA self-distillation learns "influential" (high-regression-coefficient, low-variance) features first and suppresses noisy ones, whereas MAE (input-space MSE reconstruction) is biased toward high-variance/noisy features; this bias appears only for deep encoders. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA-based). This is a theoretical/dynamics analysis rather than a detection benchmark; the "loss" contrast is MSE in latent space (JEPA) vs MSE in input space (MAE), not MSE vs log-softmax.
> 
> **LDReg (SSL + COCO + ResNet-50).** Adding LDReg to SimCLR/BYOL/MAE raises ImageNet linear eval (e.g., BYOL 67.6→68.5, MAE/ViT-B 57.0→57.6) and COCO fine-tuning: BYOL APbb 36.30→36.82, APbb_75 38.82→39.62; SimCLR (1000 epochs) 36.48→37.15 APbb, APmk 32.12→32.82. Gains grow with longer pretraining; it increases both local (LID) and global (effective rank) dimensionality, addressing local dimensional collapse.
> 
> ## Caveats (not covered by available evidence)
> - **MSE vs log-softmax loss comparison**: no retrieved paper directly benchmarks mean-squared vs log-softmax classification losses; the closest is the JEPA paper's MSE-in-latent vs MSE-in-input-space analysis. PBADet uses detection losses (IoU/DFL/BCE), not MSE vs log-softmax.
> - **Low-rank adapter fine-tuning (LoRA)**: none of the five matched papers is a dedicated low-rank adapter method; the 4-bit optimizer paper targets memory-efficient (full) fine-tuning and references LoRA/delta-tuning only as related work. So "support for lightweight adapter fine-tuning" is not experimentally established in these documents.
> - **Precision/recall/F1 on COCO-style tasks**: only PBADet reports such metrics (AP, mMR−2, and P/R/F1 vs ED-Pose); LDReg reports COCO APbb/APmk for transfer evaluation; ASID and the RNN/JEPA papers use control success, error, and CCA/linear-eval metrics instead.

Comparisons of mean-squared vs classification losses and regularization effects would be helpful.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

>     - Overall AP (AP.5:.95 / subordinate): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0 / 41.8 vs PBJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6 / 43.3 (Table 2). While PBJDet is slightly higher in aggregate AP, PBADet leads on several practical slices:
>       - Person AP: 62.4 (PBADet) vs 61.3 (PBJDet)

>     - Part‑body association robustness (mMR−2, lower is better): PBADet exhibits lower (better) average mMR−2 for head, face, both hands and right foot (Table 3). 
>   - CrowdHuman (face‑body; identical task to PBJDet and other detectors)
>     - Body MR−2: PBADet (YOLOv7) 36.5 vs PBJDet (YOLOv5l6) 40.7 (Table 5/6) – best body detection miss‑rate; body AP also highest (91.6 vs 89.5–90.7 among BPJDet variants).
>     - Pair mMR−2 is comparable (~50.8–50.9), indicating PBADet maintains association accuracy while improving body detection in crowds.
>   - Precision/Recall/F1 on COCO validation (part localization vs pose): Against ED‑Pose (Swin‑L), PBADet shows higher Precision/Recall/F1 across hands/feet (Appendix Table 7):
>     - All parts F1: 48.52 (PBADet) vs 31.51 (ED‑Pose), with both Precision and Recall gains (e.g., righthand F1: 47.34 vs 24.17). This directly provides the requested Precision/F1 on a COCO‑like dataset.
> - Similar datasets/tasks (qualitative)
>   - Animal pose/parts (AP‑10K): PBADet transfers to quadrupeds with qualitative success in part‑to‑body association (Fig. 6), supporting versatility beyond human COCO variants.
> - Loss/regularization effects (ablation)
>   - Removing association loss (Lassoc) drops joint association quality (BodyHands: Joint AP from 85.98→78.07) while hand AP remains ~unchanged, indicating the L1 association head is the key regularizer for correct pairing (Table 4).
>   - Task‑alignment learning (TOOD‑style metric t=s^α·u^β) improves all metrics; removing it reduces Cond. Acc. and Joint AP (Table 4). Multi‑scale offsets also matter (w/o multi‑scale degrades all metrics).
>   - Anchor‑free design yields higher Joint AP than anchor‑based (Table 8), and the part‑to‑body offset outperforms body‑to‑part aggregate offsets for association robustness.

> 2) Active exploration for system identification and sim‑to‑real (ASID, ICLR’24)

>   - Rod balancing (single‑shot pick‑place; unknown inertia): lower tilt is better. ASID + SysID achieves near‑perfect placement (0.00±0.0° tilt for left/right masses; 0.72±1.0° for middle) vs Domain Randomization (DR) 26.69±7.0° (left), random exploration 12.44±19.6°, and Kumar et al. (mutual‑information exploration) 13.70±9.3°. Learned estimators (ASID+estimator) generalize poorly vs optimization‑based system ID.
>   - Sphere striking (unknown friction/stiffness): Success rate (%) PBADet’s—sorry—ASID + SysID achieves 28.0±9.7 vs DR 8.75±1.5, random 10.62±4.3, Kumar et al. 9.50±2.4 (Table 1). 
>   - Multi‑friction exploration coverage: Fisher information maximization (ASID) distributes sphere visitation across all friction patches (uniform coverage) while Kumar et al. exploration rarely leaves the starting region (Fig. 4), yielding more informative data for multi‑parameter ID.
> - Real‑world tasks (Tables 2–3)
>   - Rod balancing (real): Success counts (of 3 per inertia) – ASID 2/3 (left) 1/3 (middle) 3/3 (right) vs DR 0/3 across all (Table 2). 
>   - Shuffleboard (real): Hitting target zones with varying board wax friction – ASID succeeds 4/5 (yellow/near) and 3/5 (blue/far) vs DR 2/5 and 1/5 respectively (Table 3).
> - Takeaways on objectives/regularization
>   - Fisher‑information‑maximizing exploration yields higher‑quality trajectories for parameter estimation than mutual‑information or random exploration. ONE episode sufficed for real‑world ID in reported tasks.
>   - System‑ID via optimization on trajectory MSE (simulated vs real action‑replayed trajectories) was more reliable than fully learned estimators in extrapolation; i.e., a practical advantage for MSE‑style trajectory fitting in the identification stage.
> 
> 3) 4‑bit optimizers for SGD/Adam‑style training (NeurIPS’23)
> - Identical tasks/datasets across optimizers (Tables 2, 7–9)
>   - Natural Language Understanding (GLUE, RoBERTa‑Large): 4‑bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32‑bit AdamW and 8‑bit Adam on mean accuracy/correlation; per‑task scores remain within noise (Table 7).
>   - Question Answering (SQuAD/SQuAD2.0): 4‑bit AdamW is essentially on par with 32‑bit AdamW (Table 9; EM/F1 deltas within std).
>   - Image classification (ImageNet‑1k, Swin‑T): 4‑bit methods are comparable to 32‑bit, slightly below best 8‑bit in Top‑1 but within reported variance (Table 2).
>   - Machine Translation (WMT14 en‑de, Transformer‑Base): 4‑bit AdamW BLEU 26.28 vs 26.61 (32‑bit) and 26.66 (8‑bit) – competitive (Table 2).
>   - Instruction‑tuning LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B: 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC‑e/c, OBQA across model sizes (Table 3). Training loss curves overlap; zero divergence with 4‑bit fused kernels (Fig. 4).
> - Memory/time on identical setups (Table 4/5)
>   - LLaMA‑7B finetuning (FSDP, 2×A100‑80GB): Memory reduced from 75.4 GB (32‑bit) to 31.9 GB (4‑bit), saving 57.7%; training time slightly faster due to reduced communication.
>   - RoBERTa‑L/GPT‑2M: 4‑bit with fused ops recovers or beats 8‑bit wall‑clock time; saves 34–44% total memory vs 32‑bit and ~2× less optimizer‑state memory vs 8‑bit. 
>   - Largest model under fixed memory: On 80 GB, 4‑bit can fine‑tune LLaMA‑7B (not feasible with 32‑bit); on 24 GB, scales from OPT‑350M (32‑bit) to OPT‑1.3B (4‑bit) (Table 5).
> - Ablations tied to numerical design (Tables 1, 6)
>   - Second‑moment zero‑point pitfall: Using dynamic‑exponent mapping with zero (DE) collapses small v to zero, exploding updates. Removing zero (DE‑0) or using linear mapping solves the issue.
>   - Rank‑1 normalization for second moment + linear mapping achieves the most stable 4‑bit convergence (E2E‑NLG BLEU 67.8±0.5, matching 32‑bit 67.7±0.7). Factorizing 2‑D second moments (Adafactor‑style) on top of 4‑bit further reduces memory with minimal accuracy change (Tables 1–2).
>   - First moment: smaller block size (B128/DE) improves approximation vs B2048/DE under column/row outlier patterns; verified via histograms and performance retention.
> 
> 4) Recurrent controllers with EI sign rules and spectral analysis (NeurIPS’23)
> - Identical benchmarks across RNN variants (Fig. 2)
>   - ColEI (column‑signed E/I) vs DANN (Dale’s ANN) vs standard RNN on Adding, seq‑MNIST, Penn Treebank, Naturalistic Object Recognition: ColEI learns worse and with higher variance; DANN ≈ standard RNN across tasks.
>   - Gradient clipping benefits ColEI substantially more; without clipping, ColEI often unstable, consistent with “pathological” singular‑value spectra.
> - Spectrum vs sign constraints (Fig. 4)
>   - Spectrum transplant shows singular‑value distribution matters more than sign constraints for learning gaps: supplying ColEI with the RNN spectrum (or vice‑versa) narrows most of the performance gap; freezing signs has smaller effect sizes.
> - Dataset/task scaling effects (Figs. 5–7)
>   - EI ratio and network size: small ColEI with few inhibitory units → large max singular values, low Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE), poor accuracy. Larger networks or more balanced EI ratios increase NSE and improve accuracy even if max singular value remains large; NSE predicts final test error across seq‑MNIST, object recognition, and language modeling.
> - Practical guidance
>   - For memory‑limited controllers using EI constraints, initialize to unimodal, clustered singular‑value spectra (high NSE) rather than focus solely on sign enforcement; spectral shaping behaves like an effective regularizer for trainability.
> 
> 5) JEPA‑style self‑distillation vs MAE reconstruction (NeurIPS’24)
> - Controlled deep‑linear experiments with identical data regimes (Figs. 1–2)
>   - Critical difference in implicit bias with squared‑error objectives:
>     - MAE (MSE in pixel/data space) prioritizes features with high covariance λ (explains variance) – greedy learning order is set by λ with weak depth‑dependence.
>     - JEPA (latent prediction with stop‑grad; L2 in representation space) prioritizes high‑influence features with large regression coefficient ρ=λ/σ²; the bias strengthens with encoder depth L. When λ and ρ disagree, JEPA inverts MAE’s learning order (Fig. 1 & Theorems 3.4–3.6).
>   - ODE and spectrum transplant simulations confirm: with deeper encoders, JEPA accelerates convergence (smaller critical time t*) on high‑ρ features, while MAE’s t* scales mainly with λ and weakly with ρ.
> - Linear generative temporal model (Fig. 3)
>   - For x=z_t, y=z_{t+1} with per‑mode autocorrelation γ_a and noise σ_a, λ_a=γ_a||v_a||² and ρ_a=γ_a||v_a||²/(σ²_a+||v_a||²). JEPA focuses on “slow,” predictive, low‑noise features (high γ, low σ), matching empirical observations that joint‑embedding methods favor semantically useful, low‑variance subspaces over pixel details.
> - ImageNet sanity check (Appendix D)
>   - CCA shows JEPA’s learned features align more with the “bottom” PCA subspace (low variance), while MAE aligns more with the “top” variance components; consistent with [20]’s “reconstruction learns uninformative features”.
> - Takeaways for SSL pretraining under limited labels/compute
>   - For Transformers/ResNets pre‑training with later LoRA/adapter tuning, JEPA‑style self‑distillation accelerates acquisition of predictive, low‑noise features, particularly with deeper encoders; MAE’s MSE reconstruction biases toward high‑variance components unless heavily regularized or masked.
> 
> Cross‑paper synthesis for the target robot (hands/face perception → object interaction on embedded compute)
> - Perception (hands/face association): PBADet’s anchor‑free part‑to‑body association yields better association robustness (lower mMR−2) and higher Cond. Accuracy/Joint AP on BodyHands and improved F1/Precision/Recall on COCO vs pose‑estimation baselines. For multi‑person scenes and crowded settings (CrowdHuman), PBADet improves body detection MR−2 while keeping association stable, aiding reliable “watch people’s hands/face” prerequisites.
> - Exploration & sim‑to‑real: ASID demonstrates that one short, Fisher‑maximizing exploration trajectory in real suffices to ID friction/inertia/articulation parameters, enabling zero‑/few‑shot transfer of policies trained in the tuned simulator; outperforms domain randomization and mutual‑information exploration in both sim and real tasks.
> - Training on embedded GPUs: 4‑bit AdamW (with rank‑1 + linear for v and B128/DE for m) achieves near‑parity accuracy across GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet‑1k, WMT14 and LLaMA fine‑tuning while reducing total memory by ~35–58% and optimizer‑state memory by >2× relative to 8‑bit; factorizing v further reduces memory with negligible loss.
> - Recurrent control under EI constraints: if the controller must obey Dale’s law, ensure spectral properties (high NSE, unimodal spectrum) at initialization; DANN‑style architectures match standard RNNs and surpass naive ColEI on adding/seqMNIST/PTB/object recognition. Gradient clipping is more critical for ColEI.
> - SSL pretraining and adaptation: for minimal labels, JEPA‑style self‑distillation (stop‑grad) biases training toward predictive, low‑noise features; with deeper encoders this bias strengthens, complementing LoRA/adapter‑based downstream adaptation. MAE’s MSE reconstruction is less aligned with perception unless carefully masked/regularized.
> 
> Notes on losses and regularization across works
> - MSE vs classification/objective choice: PBADet couples classification loss with IoU/DFL and a dedicated L1 association loss; removing the association loss harms joint AP/association while leaving part AP nearly unchanged, indicating the association head is the crucial regularizer for pairing. ASID’s system‑ID optimizes MSE between real and simulated action‑replayed trajectories—this out‑generalizes learned estimators. JEPA vs MAE directly contrasts two L2 objectives: latent predictive (JEPA) vs pixel reconstruction (MAE), where the former selects high‑ρ features and the latter high‑λ features.
> - Regularization/initialization: Task‑alignment in PBADet improves consistency (better Cond. Acc./Joint AP). In EI RNNs, spectral shaping (high NSE) and gradient clipping act as effective trainability regularizers; sign constraints alone are insufficient and less important than the singular‑value spectrum.
> 
> Bottom line
> - The five works collectively cover the requested pipeline with measured advantages on shared/related datasets: PBADet provides state‑of‑the‑art association on COCO‑like data with Precision/Recall/F1; ASID delivers data‑efficient sim‑to‑real via Fisher‑information exploration; the 4‑bit optimizer enables training/inference on embedded GPUs with minimal accuracy loss; EI‑compliant recurrent controllers should be spectrally regularized; and JEPA‑style SSL pretraining offers a principled bias toward predictive, low‑noise features that adapt well with low‑rank adapters.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the suggested works and a comparison of their experimental results, based only on the retrieved context.
> 
> **1. Perception — PBADet (ICLR 2024, Gao et al.)**
> One-stage anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on COCO-like datasets (BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman). On COCO val vs. ED-Pose (pose-estimation baseline), it achieves much higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands and feet (e.g., left hand 37.63/60.82/46.50 vs ED-Pose 18.36/30.34/22.87; all parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51). On COCO-HumanParts all categories, AP:95 = 43.0 (YOLOv5l6) / 42.7 (YOLOv7); on BodyHands it beats BPJDet (anchor-based body-to-part), and the anchor-free part-to-body formulation outperforms the anchor-based one (Hand AP 89.1 vs 88.4, Joint AP 85.98 vs 85.28). Ablations show association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning each improve conditional accuracy and joint AP.
> 
> **2. Sim-to-real — ASID (ICLR 2024, Memmel et al.)**
> Active exploration maximizing Fisher information in simulation, one episode of real data for system identification, then zero-shot transfer. It identifies mass, friction, stiffness, articulation, center of mass on sphere manipulation, rod balancing, laptop articulation, shuffleboard. Real-world rod balancing succeeds 6/9 vs domain randomization 0/9; shuffleboard 7/10 vs 3/10. Fisher-based exploration gives more uniform coverage than Kumar et al. (2019); center-of-mass ambiguity near the rod middle can hurt transfer. This directly covers push/balance/articulated-object tasks and minimal real data.
> 
> **3. Memory-efficient training — 4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023, Li et al.)**
> 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW (and, via appendix convergence proof, SGD(M)-style quantized states) using smaller blocks (B128), zero-point-excluding linear quantizer and rank-1 normalization for the second moment, plus factorization. Matches 32-bit baselines on RoBERTa-L (GLUE 89.1), Swin-T (80.8), GPT-2 (67.8), Transformer MT (26.28), LLaMA fine-tuning, with ~57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B: 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB) — suitable for memory-limited/embedded GPUs. Ablations: quantizing both moments costs little accuracy; smaller first-moment block and factorized second moment are the key gains.
> 
> **4. Recurrent control with sign constraints — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023, Li, Cornford et al.)**
> Analyzes RNNs obeying excitatory/inhibitory sign rules (Dale's Law). Finding: poor learning of simple column-partitioned E/I RNNs (ColEI) is due not to sign constraints but to the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal/dispersed from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean term), whereas standard RNNs and Dale's ANNs (DANN) have unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra and learn well. Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance; fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks worsen both spectrum and learning; gradient clipping mitigates instability. Sign constraints cost only ~0.7–1% error, while spectral differences explain the larger gap (~1.5–2.3%).
> 
> **5. SSL pretraining — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024, Littwin et al.)**
> Analyzes JEPA self-distillation implicit bias in deep linear networks: JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (large regression coefficients) and suppresses noisy directions increasingly with depth, while MAE prioritizes high-variance features regardless of informativeness. ImageNet I-JEPA vs MAE experiments confirm JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) via CCA. Fixed points: JEPA(∞,L)=ρ^L vs MAE(∞,L)=ρ^L√(L+1); JEPA solutions are not reachable by MAE. Limitations: deep linear MLPs, balanced orthogonal init, simultaneous diagonalizability. This supports pretraining transformer/residual backbones with minimal labels; the collection's Hessian study additionally shows LoRA adapters on pretrained backbones (TinyLlama) develop power-law Hessian structure during fine-tuning, with Hessian trace a reliable generalization indicator for adapters.
> 
> **MSE vs. classification losses and regularization:** No single work in the collection directly compares mean-squared vs. classification losses or regularization effects for this pipeline. Closest evidence: the shallow-ReLU gradient-flow analysis (square loss, small init) proves convergence to zero loss with implicit bias to minimal-rank interpolators under a dataset-dependent condition; PBADet relies on task-aligned classification plus localization/association regression losses (ablation: removing association loss hurts); ASID matches simulated to real trajectories with an L2 (MSE-style) objective; the 4-bit optimizer paper discusses weight-decay/regularization only in the context of AdamW. So a dedicated MSE-vs-CE/regularization comparison for the perception module is **not established** from the available context.
> 
> **Overall analysis:** The five works are complementary and coherent for your deployment: PBADet provides label-efficient-ish perception with strong Precision/F1 on COCO-like data; ASID gives the active-exploration physical-parameter estimation and zero-shot sim-to-real for push/balance/articulation with minimal real data; 4-bit optimizers cut training memory ~2–4× with no accuracy loss; the Dale's-law spectral study tells you how to initialize/architect recurrent controllers so E/I sign constraints don't hurt learning; and the JEPA implicit-bias study justifies SSL pretraining of backbones that then adapt cheaply (e.g., LoRA-style adapters, as studied in the Hessian work). The main evidence gap is the direct MSE-vs-classification-loss/regularization comparison you requested.

> - vs ED-Pose (precision/recall/F1): all parts **39.41/63.09/48.52** vs 24.09/45.51/31.51; left hand 37.63/60.82/46.50; right hand 38.58/61.26/47.34; left foot 41.56/66.24/51.08; right foot 40.86/65.55/50.34.
> - COCO-HumanParts all-category AP: 43.0 (YOLOv5l6), 42.7 (YOLOv7).
> - Ablations: anchor-free part-to-body beats anchor-based body-to-part (BPJDet): Hand AP 89.1 vs 85.3, Conditional Accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, Joint AP 85.98 vs 78.13. Association loss, multi-scale offsets, and TOOD task-alignment each improve accuracy.
> 
> ## 2. Active exploration for sim-to-real physical parameter estimation
> **ASID** (ICLR 2024): decouples exploration (Fisher-information-maximizing exploration policy trained in sim, deployed once in real) → system identification (REPS/CEM matching simulated rollouts) → task policy in corrected simulator → zero-shot transfer. Identifies mass, friction, stiffness, articulation, center of mass. Real-world results: rod balancing **6/9 vs DR 0/9**; shuffleboard **7/10 vs DR 3/10** (yellow 4/5 vs 2/5, blue 3/5 vs 1/5). Exploration visits ~uniform coverage vs Kumar et al. (2019); interacts with articulated laptop 80% vs 20% for naive baselines. Caveat: center-of-mass ambiguity can break zero-shot transfer.
> 
> ## 3. 4-bit optimizer for embedded GPUs
> **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023): compresses Adam/AdamW (framework also covers SGD(M)) states to 4-bit — smaller block size (B128) for first moment; rank-1 normalization and zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for second moment; optional factorized second moment; convergence proof for quantized SGD(M). Results: matches 32-bit AdamW (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2M E2E 67.8 vs 67.7; SQuAD 94.5 vs 94.6; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61); up to **57.7% memory saving**; LLaMA-7B trainable on one 80 GB GPU; 4-bitFactor ~4× smaller states than 8-bit.
> 
> ## 4. Recurrent controllers with excitatory/inhibitory sign rules via spectral analysis
> **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023): finds the poor training of sign-constrained E/I RNNs (ColEI) is due to initial recurrent-weight spectrum, not sign constraints per se. ColEI weight matrix = rank-one nilpotent (column means) + zero-mean random → multimodal, dispersed singular values; standard/DANN RNNs match random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra and learn as well. Sign constraints alone impair learning only ~0.7–1%, vs total gap 2.3±0.6%. Gradient clipping mitigates instability; smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error (predicts performance pre-training). Guidance: use DANN-style reparameterization or spectrum-aware initialization; balanced E/I and larger size raise NSE.
> 
> ## 5. JEPA self-distillation implicit bias + low-rank adaptation of transformer/residual backbones
> **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features** (NeurIPS 2024): deep linear analysis shows JEPA self-distillation has an implicit bias toward high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ), suppressing low-ρ noise; MAE prioritizes high-variance/covarying (often noisy) features. The bias only appears with *deep* encoders (JEPA fixed point w̄=ρ^L vs MAE ρ^L·L/(L+1)); depth strengthens noise suppression; JEPA prioritizes "slow," low-variance semantic features. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features (CCA) than MAE. This supports SSL pretraining of transformer/residual backbones with minimal labels.
> - Low-rank adaptation context: **NFTS** (ICLR 2024) adapts SSL-pretrained backbones (URL-pretrained ResNet-18, DINO-pretrained ViT-small) via searched per-layer residual/prefix adapters + freeze/fine-tune, SOTA on Meta-Dataset (+1.9–2.3% over TSA); **Hessian power-law study** (ICML 2025) shows LoRA adapters (TinyLlama, MathQA) develop power-law Hessian spectra during fine-tuning, with Hessian trace Tr(H) a more reliable generalization indicator for adapters.
> 
> ## Cross-method comparison / analysis
> - **Loss design (MSE vs classification):** PBADet shows the classification branch alone is insufficient — task-aligned classification+regression (TOOD) and the association (regression) loss are needed (removing task-align or association loss degrades all metrics). ASID's system identification uses MSE trajectory matching (‖τ_real−τ_sim‖²), which suffices for parameter identification. The JEPA analysis shows MSE-style latent prediction has *different* implicit bias than reconstruction losses — for perception, predicting in latent space (MSE on features) beats pixel-space reconstruction, aligning with using low-rank adaptation on top of such SSL features. No direct head-to-head MSE-vs-cross-entropy study exists in the collection for a single task.
> - **Regularization effects:** LDReg (SSL) shows L1/L2 penalties on negative log-LID (local intrinsic dimensionality) improve linear evaluation/transfer/detection for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE, with geometric-mean aggregation preferred; NEFTune shows embedding noise (regularization) boosts instruction-tuning win rates (29.8→64.7 on AlpacaEval) while dropout/weight decay do *not* reproduce gains; 4-bit optimizer ablations show smaller block size and second-moment factorization improve accuracy (regularization via better quantization).
> - **Coverage gap:** no single document in the collection jointly studies JEPA pretraining *with* LoRA on detection backbones, nor directly compares MSE vs classification losses on the same robot task; those two connections are assembled from separate papers (JEPA analysis + NFTS/Hessian LoRA studies; PBADet task-alignment + ASID MSE matching). Also, ASID's downstream policies use PPO/CEM, not E/I-constrained recurrent controllers, so item 4 stands alone as guidance for controller architecture rather than an evaluated component of the full stack.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:338 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (1) anchor-free, part-to-body association detectors evaluated with AP/Precision/F1 on COCO-style benchmarks; (2) self-supervised joint-embedding (non-contrastive) methods whose implicit bias is analyzed with cosine similarity and MSE-style objectives; (3) memory-efficient fine-tuning using low-bit AdamW/SGD optimizer states; (4) safety and robustness of Diffusion models, including adversarial image-to-image attacks that bypass cosine-similarity safety checkers; and (5) interpretability and regularization via spectral analysis of deep networks, especially recurrent EI architectures. Ideally include works that discuss practical fine-tuning (e.g., end-to-end LoRA), metrics like cross-entropy and F1, and guidance for stable training on limited hardware.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：4→3（Δ-1）；rounds：3→3（Δ+0）。**
