> {'answer': 'Below is a dataset- and metric-grounded comparison of the experimental results reported across the five papers you provided. It only uses the tables/figures and numerical trends they reported, and highlights identical or similar datasets where applicable.\n\n1) Anchor-free part–body association detectors (PBADet vs. baselines)\nIdentical datasets: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman\n• BodyHands (Table 1):\n  - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98\n  - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73\n  - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) baseline: Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39\n  ⇒ PBADet outperforms BPJDet on all three metrics, with the largest gains in Conditional Accuracy (+5.71 to +5.80) and notable gains in Joint AP.\n• COCOHumanParts (Table 2, per-category APs):\n  - Overall AP.5:.95: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0 (subordinate 41.8) vs. BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6 (43.3). BPJDet has slightly higher overall AP, but PBADet leads on some AP subsets (e.g., person AP 62.4 vs. 61.3; left foot AP 31.5 vs. 30.9). PBADet trails BPJDet on right hand (39.0 vs. 40.4) and right foot (37.7 vs. 39.6).\n  - Size-wise AP: PBADet shows strong APM/APL (e.g., YOLOv5l6 APM 66.2/65.0; APL 67.2/64.4), matching or exceeding several baselines.\n• COCOHumanParts (Table 3, average mMR−2; lower is better):\n  - PBADet (YOLOv7): head 29.2 vs. BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 30.8; face 31.3 vs. 31.8; left hand 41.1 vs. 41.6; right hand 42.7 vs. 42.2; right foot 52.6 vs. 49.1; left foot 52.5 vs. 50.4.\n  ⇒ PBADet improves mMR−2 for head/face/left hand, but is worse on right hand and feet in this specific table.\n• CrowdHuman (Table 5,6):\n  - PBADet (YOLOv7): best body MR−2 (36.5) vs. BPJDet (39.7–41.3); body AP 91.6 (top among compared methods); mMR−2 for body–face pairs ≈50.8 (comparable to BPJDet’s 50.1–51.4).\n• Multi-person pose comparison on COCO (Appendix A.2, Table 7):\n  - PBADet outperforms ED-Pose on F1 for hands/feet (e.g., all parts F1: 48.52 vs. 31.51), with higher precision/recall across the selected parts.\nConclusion on identical datasets: PBADet clearly beats anchor-based BPJDet on BodyHands and achieves best body detection MR−2 and AP on CrowdHuman; on COCOHumanParts it is competitive, leading in several size- and category-specific APs while slightly trailing BPJDet on overall AP and some part categories.\n\n2) Self-supervised joint-embedding (JEPA) vs. MAE (linear/latent-space analyses)\nSimilar dataset: ImageNet (JEPA CCA analysis; not numerically identical to the Swin-T ImageNet training in the optimizer paper)\n• Deep linear simulations (Figures 1–2):\n  - On synthetic Gaussian “Distribution 1,” both JEPA and MAE learn features greedily in order of covariance λ.\n  - On “Distribution 2” (λ increases, ρ decreases), JEPA flips learning order to prioritize high regression coefficients ρ, while MAE retains λ-based order.\n  ⇒ JEPA exhibits a distinct bias toward influential features (high ρ) when encoders are deep; MAE remains driven by covariance.\n• Temporal generative model (Figure 3):\n  - Empirical λ and ρ trends: JEPA prioritizes temporally “slow” and less noisy features (higher ρ), consistent with theory; MAE emphasizes high-variance features (λ).\n• ImageNet CCA (Appendix D, Figure 7):\n  - JEPA features from full and “bottom-spectrum” datasets show higher similarity than MAE early in training; JEPA focuses faster on low-variance, perceptually relevant directions.\nConclusion on similar datasets: While exact metrics differ, JEPA learns predictive, low-variance (“semantic”) features earlier than MAE on ImageNet-style data; MAE prioritizes variance-heavy directions. Numerical results presented are curves/trends (CCA), not discrete AP/accuracy.\n\n3) Memory-efficient fine-tuning with 4-bit optimizer states\nIdentical/similar datasets: ImageNet-1k (Swin-T), GLUE, SQuAD, WMT14 en-de, E2E-NLG, LLaMA finetuning benchmarks\n• Accuracy vs. FP32 baselines (Table 2):\n  - NLU (GLUE mean): 4-bit AdamW 89.1 vs. 32-bit 88.9 (on par/slightly better). 4-bit Factor 88.9.\n  - ImageNet-1k (Swin-T top-1): 4-bit AdamW 80.8 vs. 81.2 (small drop). 4-bit Factor 80.9.\n  - E2E-NLG BLEU: 4-bit AdamW 67.8 vs. 67.7 (on par/slightly better). 4-bit Factor 67.6.\n  - SQuAD F1: 4-bit AdamW 94.5 vs. 94.6 (on par). 4-bit Factor 88.9 F1 on SQuAD 2.0 EM/F1 also comparable (Table 9).\n  - WMT14 en–de SacreBleu: 4-bit AdamW 26.28 vs. 26.61 (small drop). 4-bit Factor 26.45.\n  ⇒ Across identical NLP/vision datasets, 4-bit optimizers match or slightly trail FP32; drops are small.\n• LLaMA instruction finetuning (Table 3; same evaluation sets):\n  - 7B: 4-bit AdamW ~equals FP32 on most tasks (e.g., MMLU 38.9 vs. 38.7; ARC-c 44.4 vs. 45.1).\n  - 13B: 4-bit matches FP32 (e.g., HellaSwag 79.0 vs. 78.8; ARC-e 64.1 vs. 63.6).\n  - 33B: 4-bit slightly lower MMLU (54.9 vs. 56.4), but comparable on commonsense tasks.\n• Memory/time (Table 4):\n  - LLaMA-7B with FSDP: memory 31.87GB (4-bit) vs. 75.40GB (FP32), training time ~3.07h vs. 3.35h (4-bit fused ~3.11h).\n  - RoBERTa-L on RTE: 3.00GB (4-bit fused) vs. 5.31GB (FP32), time ~3.17min vs. 3.93min.\n  - GPT-2 M: 4.62GB (4-bit fused) vs. 6.89GB (FP32), time ~2.11h vs. 2.13h.\n• Capacity under fixed memory (Table 5):\n  - 24GB: 4-bit trains OPT-1.3B (FP32 only OPT-350M).\n  - 80GB: 4-bit enables LLaMA-7B; FP32 does not (table’s budget comparison).\nConclusion on identical datasets: On GLUE, SQuAD, WMT14, ImageNet-1k, and E2E-NLG, 4-bit AdamW and 4-bit Factor match FP32 accuracy within small deltas, while saving 34–58% memory and enabling larger models.\n\n4) Safety/robustness of diffusion models under adversarial image-to-image attacks (AdvI2I)\nIdentical models/datasets within the paper: InstructPix2Pix; SDv1.5-Inpainting; same NSFW prompts/defenses\n• Baselines vs. AdvI2I (Tables 3–4, ASR; higher is worse for safety):\n  - InstructPix2Pix, nudity: AdvI2I 81.5% (no defense), SC reduces to 18.0%; AdvI2I-Adaptive restores ASR to 70.5% under SC.\n  - InstructPix2Pix, violence: AdvI2I 80.0% (no defense), SC 32.5%; AdvI2I-Adaptive ~70.5% under SC.\n  - SDv1.5-Inpainting, nudity: AdvI2I 82.5% (no defense), SC 10.5%; AdvI2I-Adaptive 72.0% under SC.\n  - SDv1.5-Inpainting, violence: AdvI2I 81.0% (no defense), SC 31.5%; AdvI2I-Adaptive 71.5% under SC.\n  ⇒ Safety Checker (SC) is strongest single defense; AdvI2I-Adaptive remains high-ASR even with SC, indicating defense bypass.\n• Generalization (Table 5): unseen images/prompts retain high ASR (e.g., nudity ~68.5–76.5; violence ~63.5–75.0).\n• Noise bound ε (Table 6): larger ε increases ASR; even with defenses, AdvI2I-Adaptive remains high (e.g., SC ~72.0 at ε=64/255).\n• Transferability (Tables 7–9):\n  - From SDv1.5-Inpainting → SDv2.0/2.1: high ASR (≈73–84%).\n  - SDv3.0: ASR drops (~33–34%), consistent with cleaner training data.\n• Ablations (Tables 10–11):\n  - Removing the generator reduces ASR substantially (e.g., SDv1.5-Inpainting nudity 55.0% vs. 82.5%).\n  - Higher concept strength α can raise ASR but defenses still mitigate; AdvI2I-Adaptive balances attack strength vs. robustness.\n• Additional robustness/quality:\n  - DiffPure reduces ASR modestly (82.5 → 72.5; Table 17), showing partial purification effectiveness.\n  - Image quality metrics (Table 14, 15): AdvI2I’s attacked images maintain LPIPS/SSIM/FSIM/VIF comparable to generator-based baselines and show favorable NIQE/PIQE/FID against a diffusion-based face swap baseline.\nConclusion: Across identical models and defense settings, AdvI2I has the highest ASR without defenses and remains effective under SC when adapted (AdvI2I-Adaptive). Transferability holds for SDv2.x but degrades on SDv3.0.\n\n5) Interpretability/regularization via spectral analysis in EI RNNs (Dale’s Law)\nIdentical tasks within the paper: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition\n• Performance trends (Figure 2):\n  - ColEI networks converge worse and with higher variance vs. DANN and standard RNNs across all tasks.\n  - Gradient clipping helps ColEI more than others.\n• Spectral radius sweep (Appendix; summarized):\n  - ColEI performs better at larger ρ but worse at smaller ρ relative to DANN/RNN.\n• Spectrum transplant (Figure 4B–C):\n  - Sign constraints cause ~0.7–1.0% performance drop; spectral differences cause larger test error changes (~1.5–2.0%). Spectrum contributes more than sign constraints to the RNN–ColEI performance gap.\n• EI ratio and size (Figures 5–6,7):\n  - ColEI test error anti-correlates with normalized SVD entropy (NSE); fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks lower NSE and degrade performance.\n  - DANN spectra and performance remain robust across EI ratios and sizes.\nConclusion: On identical RNN benchmarks, DANN ≈ standard RNN, ColEI worse; spectral properties (unimodal clustered singular values) predict better learning and stability compared to sign constraints alone.\n\nCross-paper notes on identical/similar datasets:\n• Identical datasets across papers are rare. The anchor-free detector paper and optimizer paper both include “COCO-style” benchmarks, but the former uses COCOHumanParts and CrowdHuman with detection/AP/mMR−2 metrics, while the latter focuses on GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/WMT14/E2E with accuracy/BLEU/F1—so their metrics and tasks are not directly comparable.\n• Both the JEPA paper (CCA analysis) and the 4-bit optimizer paper include ImageNet, but they assess different objectives (representation similarity vs. top-1 accuracy); comparisons are qualitative (JEPA learns low-variance features earlier) rather than numeric.\n• Sequential MNIST appears in the EI RNN paper; the JEPA paper does not report comparable supervised accuracy on that dataset; hence no direct numeric comparison.\n\nOverall synthesis (method classes vs. outcomes):\n• Detection (COCO-style): PBADet achieves the top results on BodyHands and best body MR−2/AP on CrowdHuman; competitive on COCOHumanParts with strengths on person/size-specific APs.\n• Self-supervised JEPA vs. MAE: JEPA prioritizes high-ρ (predictive, low-noise) features, learning bottom-spectrum (“semantic”) directions sooner; MAE favors high-variance features. Observations are from CCA/time-to-learn plots.\n• Fine-tuning efficiency: 4-bit AdamW/Factor match FP32 accuracy across GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/E2E/WMT with sizable memory savings and slight speed gains; they also enable larger models under fixed budgets.\n• Diffusion safety: AdvI2I has highest ASR without defenses and maintains high ASR under Safety Checker when adaptive; transfer succeeds to SDv2.x and weakens on SDv3.0.\n• EI interpretability/regularization: DANN ≈ standard RNN across tasks; ColEI worse; spectral properties (NSE, singular value clustering) predict performance more strongly than sign constraints.\n'}

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the provided documents, here is a set of papers that collectively cover all five requested areas, followed by a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Papers by Topic
> 
> **(1) Anchor-free part-to-body association detector (AP/Precision/F1, COCO-style)**
> - **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`). Extends anchor-free detection (FCOS/TOOD) with a single part-to-body center offset; evaluated on COCO-HumanParts and compared to ED-Pose on COCO val with Precision/Recall/F1.
> 
> **(2) Non-contrastive joint-embedding, implicit bias via cosine/MSE-style objectives**
> - **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`). Analyzes JEPA (BYOL/SimSiam/I-JEPA-type, non-contrastive, MSE-style latent prediction) vs MAE, showing JEPA's implicit bias toward "influential" (high-regression-coefficient) features, with cosine-similarity/PCA-CCA analysis on ImageNet-1K.
> 
> **(3) Memory-efficient fine-tuning with low-bit AdamW/SGD optimizer states**
> - **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`). 4-bit quantization of AdamW/Adam/SGD(M) first/second moments (B128, rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, factorization).
> 
> **(4) Diffusion safety/robustness; adversarial I2I attacks bypassing cosine-similarity safety checkers**
> - **AdvI2I: Adversarial Image Attack on Image-to-Image Diffusion Models** (ICML 2025, doc `a49d1b5f…`). Image-condition-side attacks; the "Adaptive" variant adds a loss minimizing cosine similarity between generated images and the SafetyChecker's NSFW concept embeddings, bypassing it.
> 
> **(5) Spectral interpretability/regularization of deep networks, recurrent EI architectures**
> - **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`). Spectral (SVD/random-matrix) analysis of excitatory–inhibitory RNNs (ColEI vs DANN vs standard), with Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE) as a performance predictor.
> - **Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure** (ICML 2025, doc `582d138d…`). Power-law Hessian spectral analysis, generalization prediction, and LoRA fine-tuning behavior.
> 
> **Additional supporting works for practical fine-tuning (LoRA, F1, limited hardware):**
> - **NEFTune** (doc `fad0fb20…`): noisy-embedding instruction fine-tuning, works with QLoRA on constrained hardware.
> - **GOT-D** (doc `bb21f950…`): data selection for pre-fine-tuning LLMs, evaluated with F1/macro-F1 on GLUE-style domain adaptation.
> - **LDReg** (doc `51526068…`): local-dimensionality regularization for SSL (improves COCO detection for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE).
> - **On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning** (doc `160e1407…`): cosine-similarity analysis of embeddings (contrastive, complementary to topic 2).
> 
> ## Comparison of Experimental Results
> 
> **Detection (PBADet vs baselines).** On COCO-HumanParts (all categories, original/subordinate), PBADet (YOLOv5l6) reaches AP.5:.95 = 43.0/41.8, AP.5 = 70.0/68.4, AP_S = 31.5/30.3, AP_M = 66.2/65.0, AP_L = 67.2/64.4; YOLOv7 version is slightly lower (42.7/41.5 AP.5:.95). Ablations show the anchor-free part-to-body variant beats both anchor-based part-to-body and BPJDet (anchor-based body-to-part): HandAP 89.1 vs 88.4 vs 85.3, Conditional Accuracy 92.62 vs 92.31 vs 86.80, JointAP 85.98 vs 85.28 vs 78.13, with fewer parameters (36.9M vs 41.2M). Against the pose estimator ED-Pose on COCO val, PBADet dominates on all parts: Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51 (e.g., left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87). Anchor-free design gives both better accuracy and simpler post-processing.
> 
> **Self-supervised implicit bias (JEPA vs MAE).** The JEPA analysis proves, via deep-linear ODEs, that JEPA learns high-influence features in step-wise fashion with depth strengthening noise suppression, whereas MAE prioritizes high-variance (often noisy) features. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA measurement). So JEPA's MSE-style latent objective yields semantically richer representations than pixel-reconstruction MAE, at the cost of being collapse-prone (needing stop-gradient/EMA).
> 
> **Memory-efficient optimizers.** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW across tasks: GLUE (RoBERTa-L) 89.1 vs 88.9, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61. Memory savings: LLaMA-7B instruction tuning drops from 75.40GB to 31.87GB (57.7% saved), enabling LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU and ~4× larger OPT models; 4-bit Factor adds ~10% more savings. 8-bit AdamW and Adafactor/SM3 are either less memory-efficient or lose accuracy (SM3: 79.0 CLS, 22.72 MT). The trade-off: 4-bit is slower than 8-bit without fused operators (RoBERTa-L 5.59 min vs 3.38 min), but fused kernels restore speed.
> 
> **Diffusion safety (AdvI2I).** Without defense, AdvI2I achieves ASR 81.5% (nudity) on InstructPix2Pix and 82.5% on SDv1.5-Inpainting, beating text-attack baselines; adversarial prompt attacks are easily blocked (perplexity filter cuts ASR ~58%; LLM filter reduces to ~2%). SafetyChecker is the strongest defense (ASR down to 18.0% nudity / 32.5% violence; Gaussian noising only to 64.5%), but the cosine-similarity-aware AdvI2I-Adaptive still holds ~70.5–72% ASR under SafetyChecker, and attacks transfer across SD inpainting models, FLUX.1-dev, and SDXL-Turbo. Implication: current cosine-similarity-based post-hoc safety checkers are not sufficient.
> 
> **Spectral analysis (EI RNNs and Hessian).** Dale's-Law study: ColEI RNNs learn worse and with higher variance across all four tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition); gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Spectrum transplant experiments show spectral properties matter more than sign constraints (sign constraints account for ~0.7–1% error; the full ColEI deficit is ~2.3%±0.6%). NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error (higher NSE → better learning; DANN and standard RNNs stay at NSE≈0.95 even with 1 inhibitory unit, while ColEI's NSE drops with fewer I units). Hessian paper: well-trained networks show power-law spectra (absent in random nets); power-law slope correlates with generalization (LeNet CIFAR-10 Pearson 0.72; d_ks predicts LLM generalization up to 0.98), the structure is lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large batches, and—importantly—LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce power-law structure as full fine-tuning does, while Hessian trace Tr(H) is a more reliable generalization indicator for fine-tuned LoRA adapters.
> 
> **Fine-tuning support (NEFTune, GOT-D, Hessian).** NEFTune lifts LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win rate from 29.8% to 64.7% (+34.9), with gains on Evol-Instruct (+9.3), ShareGPT (+7.5), OpenPlatypus (+8.6) and across sizes/QLoRA, while reducing overfitting (lower ROUGE-L/BLEU vs training data) and keeping OpenLLM benchmarks unchanged. GOT-D improves F1 over BERT domain-adaptation baselines (DAPT, DSIR) and GLUE averages under 5k–10k budgets, runs in ~1 GPU hour. These complement the 4-bit optimizer (which already references LoRA) for stable, hardware-limited training.
> 
> **Overall takeaways.** The five areas are covered by: PBADet (detection), JEPA implicit-bias analysis (SSL), 4-bit optimizers (memory-efficient fine-tuning), AdvI2I (diffusion safety), and Dale's-Law/Hessian spectral studies (interpretability/regularization). Cross-cutting themes: (i) anchor-free/spectral/quantization designs consistently beat their constrained counterparts (anchor-based, sign-constrained, full-precision states) with equal or better metrics; (ii) cosine-similarity-based mechanisms appear both as useful analysis tools (embedding similarity, safety checkers) and as vulnerabilities (AdvI2I-Adaptive defeats them); (iii) LoRA/QLoRA-style parameter-efficient fine-tuning is the practical bridge, and the Hessian work cautions that LoRA-only tuning changes spectral structure, so generalization should be tracked via Tr(H) or NSE-like diagnostics rather than spectral power-law fit alone.
> 
> Note: no document in this collection provides a single "end-to-end LoRA with cross-entropy + F1 on limited hardware" benchmark paper; the closest supports are the 4-bit optimizer paper (F1 on SQuAD, LoRA mention), NEFTune (QLoRA), and GOT-D (F1), so a fully unified experimental comparison across all five topics is not available from the provided context.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the papers from the collection that collectively cover your five themes, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Anchor-free part-to-body association (PBADet, ICLR 2024)
> A one-stage anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset on COCO-style benchmarks (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman).
> - **BodyHands (YOLOv7):** HandAP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 — beats BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13) and anchor-based part-to-body variants (88.4/92.31/85.28).
> - **Ablations:** removing association loss drops Cond. Accuracy to 80.78; removing multi-scale offsets → 91.64; removing task-alignment → 92.08.
> - **vs ED-Pose (COCO val, Precision/Recall/F1):** all parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs ED-Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51; best for left foot (41.56/66.24/51.08).
> - **COCOHumanParts AP (all categories):** 43.0/41.8 (AP/AP50) with YOLOv5l6.
> 
> ## 2. Non-contrastive joint-embedding implicit bias (JEPA/MAE, NeurIPS 2024)
> "JEPA self-distillation implicit bias" analyzes joint-embedding (non-contrastive) models via deep linear networks with MSE-style (squared-error) objectives. JEPA prioritizes high-regression-coefficient "influential" features in a depth-dependent way; MAE orders features only by covariance λ. Critical-time theory: JEPA ordering depends on ρ (grows with depth L), MAE depends mainly on λ — verified in simulations and ImageNet-1K (I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace). Cosine-similarity analysis appears in the companion contrastive paper (optimal positive/negative similarity −1/(n−1), variance reduction improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR/ImageNet-100).
> 
> ## 3. Low-bit optimizer states (4-bit Optimizers, NeurIPS 2023)
> 4-bit AdamW/Adam (also applicable to SGD-M) optimizer states for memory-efficient fine-tuning.
> - **Results:** 4-bit AdamW matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L 89.1), SQuAD F1 94.5, GPT-2 E2E-NLG 67.8, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8, WMT14 26.28; LLaMA-7B fine-tuning memory 75.4→31.87GB (**57.7% saved**), enabling LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU.
> - Ablations: smaller block size (B128) for first moment, rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for second moment are key.
> 
> ## 4. Diffusion safety & adversarial I2I attacks (AdvI2I, ICML 2025)
> Adversarial image-to-image attacks on I2I diffusion models that bypass the cosine-similarity-based SafetyChecker (and SLD, SD-NP, GN).
> - **ASR (attack success rate, NudeNet/Q16):** no defense 82.5% (SDv1.5-Inpainting, nudity); SC cuts to 10.5–32.5%; the adaptive variant (explicitly minimizing cosine similarity to NSFW concept embeddings) retains **70–72% ASR under SafetyChecker**. Larger noise bound ε raises ASR to 84.5%; transfers to unseen images/prompts (>63.5%/68.5%) and other SD models/FLUX/SDXL.
> 
> ## 5. Spectral interpretability of recurrent EI networks (NeurIPS 2023)
> Dale's-law EI RNNs (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs): spectral analysis shows the colEI singular-value spectrum (multimodal, dispersed, from rank-one column-mean structure) matters more than sign constraints for learning. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with test error; DANN/standard RNNs have unimodal spectra and learn well even with 1 inhibitory unit; ColEI is worse on all 4 tasks with higher seed variance. Related: the Hessian power-law paper ties spectral structure to generalization and notes LoRA-only fine-tuning doesn't induce it as full fine-tuning does.
> 
> ## Practical fine-tuning items (cross-entropy, F1, stable training)
> - **4-bit optimizer** paper: LLaMA fine-tuning (cross-entropy) with out-of-box hyperparameters, lossless, on limited GPU memory.
> - **NEFTune** (ICLR 2024): noisy-embedding instruction fine-tuning raises LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval from 29.8→64.7 (no added compute/memory; works with QLoRA), while OpenLLM (cross-entropy-trained) metrics stay unchanged; less overfitting.
> - **GOT-D**: data-selection pre-fine-tuning, reports macro/micro F1, one-GPU hour-scale, boosts GLUE/BERT F1 under low budgets.
> - **RTB** (LoRA fine-tuning, AdamW, batch/grad-accum details, loss clipping for stability on a single A100).
> 
> **Comparative takeaway:** PBADet shows anchor-free beats anchor-based association on AP/Precision/F1; JEPA analysis shows non-contrastive objectives yield a distinct, depth-growing implicit bias measurable via spectral/regression analysis; 4-bit AdamW gives near-lossless fine-tuning with ~58% memory savings (complimentary to LoRA/QLoRA, which NEFTune further improves); AdvI2I demonstrates that cosine-similarity safety checkers can be bypassed by directly optimizing against them (adaptive ≈70% ASR vs 10–18% for non-adaptive); and spectral analysis of EI RNNs shows initial singular-value structure — not sign constraints — predicts trainability, with NSE as a pre-training diagnostic. Note: no single paper in the collection covers all five themes together; the set above collectively satisfies the request.

Gold 1：

> Here’s a detailed comparison and summary of experimental performance results across the provided methods and datasets, focusing on the key shared evaluation metrics:
> 
> **1. Comparison Across Defense Strategies — InstructPix2Pix (Table 3)**
> - **Without Defense:** AdvI2I achieves the highest ASR for Nudity (81.5%) and Violence (80%), outperforming MMA (68.5% / 71.5%) and VAE baseline (~19–22%).
> - **Under Strongest Defense (SC):** SC drops AdvI2I to 18% (Nudity) and 32.5% (Violence), but AdvI2I-Adaptive maintains ~70.5% for both — a clear improvement in robustness over the non-adaptive method.
> - **Other Defenses (SLD, SD-NP, GN):** All reduce ASR but less drastically; AdvI2I consistently leads MMA and VAE.
> 
> **2. Comparison Across Defense Strategies — SDv1.5-Inpainting (Table 4)**
> - **Without Defense:** AdvI2I again reaches the highest ASR — 82.5% (Nudity) and 81% (Violence), versus ~42–47% for MMA.
> - **SC Defense:** Non-adaptive AdvI2I drops sharply (to ~10.5% and 31.5%), while adaptive holds ~72% for both.
> - **Conclusion:** SC is the most effective defense, but the adaptive variant substantially mitigates SC’s impact.
> 
> **3. Generalization to Unseen Images/Prompts (Table 5)**
> - Strong generalization: ASR remains ≥63.5% across all cases for both concepts.
> - AdvI2I shows slightly better generalization on prompts than images.
> 
> **4. Effect of Noise Bound ε (Table 6)**
> - Larger ε increases ASR in all cases.
> - Adaptive AdvI2I sustains high ASR even at the lowest ε (32/255) — showing attack strength even with small perturbations.
> 
> **5. Ablation – Without Generator (Table 10)**
> - Direct perturbation without generator performs far worse (e.g., InstructPix2Pix Nudity: 18.5% vs 81.5%).
> - Confirms value of trained adversarial generator for universal, transferable perturbations.
> 
> **6. Ablation – Concept Strength α (Table 11)**
> - For non-adaptive, ASR peaks at α = 2.8 without defense (82.5%) but may drop more under defenses.
> - Adaptive maintains stronger performance under defense across α values.
> 
> **7. Transferability to Other Models (Appendix Tables 7–9)**
> - High ASR when transferring from SDv1.5 to SDv2.0/2.1 (~73–84%), weaker to SDv3.0 (~33%).
> - Transfers reasonably to unrelated models (e.g., FLUX ControlNet: 74%, SDXL-Turbo: 62.5%).
> 
> **8. Image Quality Metrics (Tables 14–15)**
> - AdvI2I matches Attack VAE in SSIM/LPIPS while far surpassing MMA.
> - Maintains high perceptual quality (better NIQE, PIQE, FID than Face-Adapter baseline).
> - Good balance between high ASR and imperceptible perturbations.
> 
> **9. Extended Concepts & Robustness**
> - Works on other NSFW concepts like Extremism (ASR ~74–76% w/o defense).
> - Resistant to DiffPure purification: ASR drop ~10% only (82.5%→72.5%).
> 
> **10. Defensive Use Case (Table 18)**
> - Embedding a benign concept (‘wearing clothes’) into input reduces ASR of explicit text prompts from 96.5% to 24.5%.
> 
> ---
> **Summary of Findings:**
> - **AdvI2I vs Baselines:** Outperforms MMA and VAE-based attacks across all metrics in ASR, robustness (especially adaptive variant), and image quality.
> - **Defense Evasion:** Adaptive formulation notably resists SC and GN defenses.
> - **Generality:** Strong transfer to unseen images/prompts/models (except heavily NSFW-filtered SDv3.0).
> - **Stealth:** Maintains high visual similarity to original images while embedding effective triggers.
> 
> AdvI2I thus poses a substantial, demonstrated risk to I2I diffusion models, revealing vulnerabilities that survive common safety measures, and its adaptive variant is particularly effective against state-of-the-art defenses.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here is the relevant research for each component, followed by a comparative analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Research pointers (per component)
> 
> 1. **Detection architecture (hands/face→body association):** **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) — a one-stage, anchor-free detector with a part-to-body center offset, evaluated on COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, and CrowdHuman, including F1/AP comparisons against the pose estimator ED-Pose on COCO.
> 2. **Low-bit optimizer for fine-tuning:** **4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)** — 4-bit AdamW states via smaller blocks (B128), rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, optional factorized second moment.
> 3. **Spectral analysis for EI stability:** **"Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** — analyzes why sign-constrained (excitatory/inhibitory) RNNs train poorly, using singular-value spectra and normalized SVD entropy (NSE).
> 4. **JEPA-style SSL interpretability / cosine-similarity bias:** **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** — deep-linear analysis of JEPA self-distillation vs MAE; also **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (cosine-similarity theory) and **LDReg** (dimensional-collapse regularization).
> 5. **Adversarial I2I attacks vs safety checkers:** **AdvI2I (ICML 2025)** — adversarial images that make I2I diffusion models (InstructPix2Pix, SDv1.5-Inpainting) generate NSFW content, bypassing SafeLatentDiffusion and SafetyChecker.
> 
> ## Comparison and analysis of experimental results
> 
> **Detection (PBADet vs SOTA).** On COCOHumanParts, PBADet (YOLOv5l6) reaches AP .5:.95 of 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate), on par with BPJDet (43.6/43.3) while leading in per-category person/feet APs; on BodyHands, PBADet-YOLOv7 (36.9M params) beats the larger BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (86.1M): hand AP 89.1 vs 85.9, conditional accuracy 92.62 vs 86.91, joint AP 85.98 vs 84.39. Against the pose estimator ED-Pose (Swin-L) on COCO validation, PBADet's F1 is roughly doubled for hands (46.50 vs 22.87 left hand; 47.34 vs 24.17 right hand) and feet. On CrowdHuman face-body, PBADet gets best body MR-2 (36.5 vs BPJDet's 40.7), but the advantage over BPJDet narrows because it's a single-part task — consistent with its design for multi-part association.
> 
> **Low-bit optimizer.** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly beats 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning: GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, ImageNet (Swin-T) 80.8 vs 81.2 (comparable), WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61 (comparable). Memory savings: RoBERTa-L −43.1%, GPT-2 −34.4%, LLaMA-7B −57.7% (75.4→31.9 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU and ~4× larger OPT models. Ablations show the first-moment block size and second-moment zero-point exclusion/factorization are what preserve lossless accuracy; 4-bitFactor is the most memory-efficient variant.
> 
> **EI stability (spectral).** Sign constraints alone account for only part of the gap (e.g., 1%±1% for ColEI vs 2.3%±0.6% total deficit on sequential MNIST) — the initial **singular-value spectrum** matters more. ColEI networks show multimodal, dispersed singular values (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), which constrain spectral radius but leave large unconstrained singular values, causing instability/exploding gradients; DANN (Dale's ANN) RNNs match standard RNNs' quarter-circle (Marchenko–Pastur) spectrum and learn as well, robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error, making it a usable pre-training diagnostic; reducing the fraction of inhibitory neurons worsens both spectrum and performance, and gradient clipping mitigates ColEI instability.
> 
> **JEPA / SSL interpretability.** The deep-linear analysis shows JEPA's implicit bias is toward **high-influence features** (high regression coefficient ρ), while MAE orders features mainly by eigenvalue λ; depth amplifies JEPA's noise suppression, and JEPA prefers "slow features" (low-variance modes). On ImageNet, I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE does. Complementarily, the cosine-similarity theory shows optimal full-batch encoders align positives to similarity 1 and separate negatives to −1/(n−1), but mini-batch training inflates negative-pair similarity variance (worse for small batches); adding a variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and full ImageNet, temperature robustness, and small-batch training. LDReg adds local intrinsic-dimensionality regularization, improving linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE, MoCo, VICReg, and Barlow Twins — countering both local and global dimensional collapse.
> 
> **Adversarial I2I vs safety checkers.** AdvI2I achieves ASR 81.5% (InstructPix2Pix, nudity) and 82.5% (SDv1.5-Inpainting) with no defense. SafetyChecker is the strongest post-hoc defense (dropping ASR to 18.0% nudity / 32.5% violence), while Gaussian noising is weak (64.5% nudity). Crucially, AdvI2I-Adaptive — which also evades the safety checker's embedding space and trains under Gaussian noise — retains ~70.5% ASR even under SafetyChecker at small noise bounds, and attacks transfer to other SD inpainting models, FLUX.1-dev, and SDXL-Turbo. This shows text-filter-based defenses are insufficient; the image-condition side is a distinct, currently under-mitigated attack surface.
> 
> **Cross-cutting takeaway.** For your system: PBADet gives the best accuracy/efficiency trade-off for part-body association (more so with multiple parts than single-part face-body); 4-bit AdamW provides lossless fine-tuning with up to ~57% memory savings, directly addressing the tight-GPU constraint; the EI-RNN work implies you should check singular-value spectra (via NSE) rather than just spectral radius when enforcing E/I constraints, and prefer DANN-style constraints or gradient clipping; JEPA's cosine-similarity bias means you can expect robustness to noisy/perceptual features but must manage collapse (LDReg, variance-reduction losses) and be aware of mini-batch similarity variance; and AdvI2I-Adaptive demonstrates that no current SafetyChecker-style defense reliably stops adversarial I2I inputs, so adversarial-robustness measures are still an open problem.

**community 最终答案**

> Here is the research matching each requirement, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Detection architectures for hand/face–body association
> **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset (more compact than BPJDet's body-to-part representation: length 10 vs 15 for 3 parts).
> - **COCO-HumanParts vs ED-Pose (SOTA pose estimator):** PBADet all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 **48.52 vs 31.51**; left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87, right hand 47.34 vs 24.17.
> - **CrowdHuman (face-body):** best body MR-2 (36.5) and AP (91.6, YOLOv7); comparable to BPJDet (advantage smaller for this single-part task).
> - Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment all boost association accuracy; outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN on BodyHands.
> 
> ## 2. Low-bit optimizers for fine-tuning
> **4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)** — quantized AdamW states (B128 block for 1st moment; rank-1/linear zero-point-excluding quantizer for 2nd; optional factorization).
> - **Matches or exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning** (GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, E2E 67.8 vs 67.7); comparable on pretraining (ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, MT 26.28 vs 26.61).
> - Memory: LLaMA-7B fine-tune 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB (**57.7% saved**, fits one 80 GB GPU); RoBERTa-L 43.1% saved; 4-bitFactor ~4× smaller states than 8-bit.
> - vs alternatives: Adafactor/SM3 are more memory-efficient but degrade (SM3 CLS 79.0, MT 22.72 vs 81.2/26.61); 8-bit AdamW is a worse memory/accuracy trade-off.
> 
> ## 3. Spectral analysis for E/I-constrained RNN stability
> **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023)** — compares ColEI (column sign-constrained) vs DANN vs standard RNNs.
> - ColEI learns worse and with higher variance across adding, sMNIST, PTB, object recognition; unstable without gradient clipping.
> - Spectrum-transplant experiments show **singular-value spectra matter more than sign constraints**: sign constraints account for only 0.7–1% error, while spectral mismatch explains the full ~2.3% gap.
> - **Normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; higher EI ratios (fewer inhibitory units) and smaller nets worsen the spectrum/performance, while DANN stays robust (NSE≈0.95 even with 1 inhibitory neuron). Larger, balanced-EI nets learn best — guidance for stable EI controllers.
> 
> ## 4. JEPA-style SSL interpretability and cosine-similarity bias
> - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024):** in deep linear nets, JEPA self-distillation biases toward *influential* (high-regression-coefficient) features, whereas MAE prioritizes high-variance/noisy features; the bias only holds for deep encoders. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA).
> - **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning":** full-batch optimum is positive-pair similarity 1 and negative-pair −1/(n−1); mini-batching keeps expected similarity but raises variance for small batches. Their variance-reduction auxiliary loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, and full ImageNet, plus temperature robustness and small-batch training.
> - (Related: LDReg counters local dimensional collapse, improving SimCLR/BYOL/MAE linear eval and COCO detection.)
> 
> ## 5. Adversarial I2I attacks against safety checkers
> **AdvI2I (ICML 2025)** — trains a generator to perturb input images so I2I diffusion models emit NSFW content under benign prompts; AdvI2I-Adaptive adds a loss minimizing cosine similarity to SafetyChecker NSFW concept embeddings.
> - **No defense:** ASR 81.5% (InstructPix2Pix, nudity), 82.5% (SDv1.5-Inpainting).
> - **Defenses:** SafetyChecker (cosine-similarity NSFW filter) is the strongest, cutting ASR to 18.0% (nudity) / 32.5% (violence); Gaussian-noise preprocessing only reduces to 64.5%. **AdvI2I-Adaptive retains ~70–72% ASR even under SafetyChecker** at small noise bounds.
> - Attacks transfer across SD inpainting models, FLUX.1-dev, SDXL-Turbo, and generalize to nudity/violence/extremism; embedding a benign "wearing clothes" concept cuts explicit-prompt ASR from 96.5% to 24.5%. Implication: current post-hoc safety checkers are insufficient against image-side attacks.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting analysis
> - **Detection vs optimization:** PBADet's accuracy gains are large on multi-part association (F1 +17 points vs ED-Pose) but modest on single-part face association (≈BPJDet) — the method's edge is multi-part scalability. The 4-bit optimizer gives near-lossless fine-tuning at ~43–58% memory savings, directly addressing tight-GPU fine-tuning of large backbones.
> - **Stability vs SSL:** the RNN work shows stability is determined by the *initial weight spectrum*, not just sign constraints — an actionable diagnostic (NSE) before training. The JEPA analysis likewise attributes behavior to an implicit spectral/feature-prioritization bias (influential vs noisy features), which the cosine-similarity analysis complements by quantifying embedding-space statistics and their small-batch degradation.
> - **Security:** the adversarial results show defenses are asymmetric — the strongest defense (SafetyChecker) is still bypassed at ~70% ASR by a single added loss term, whereas prompt-side attacks are easily filtered. This cautions against relying on safety checkers in the editing pipeline you describe.
> 
> Note: exact per-method numbers for LDReg and further PBADet BodyHands tables were not fully in retrieved chunks; the comparisons above rely only on the retrieved content.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Here’s a comparison and summary of experimental results from the provided papers:
> 
> **On identical datasets:**
> - **CIFAR-100**: The *4-bit optimizer* from “Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States” achieves 80.8–80.9% accuracy with quantized/factorized states (Tab. 2 in that paper). The *PBADet* paper doesn't use CIFAR-100, but the other works here don't compare directly on CIFAR-100.
> - **MNIST**: Appears only in PBADet indirectly for method descriptions; no numeric results from others.
> 
> **On similar distribution shift setups:**
> - **SQuAD → SQuAD-Shifts (Amazon, Reddit, NYT, New Wiki)**:
>   - *4-bit optimizers*: Retain near-identical F1 to baseline full-precision AdamW (Amazon: 67.8 vs 67.7 BLEU equivalent; see Tab. 2 and Table 9 in that paper).
>   - *AGL prediction method*: Can very precisely predict OOD F1 scores when ensembles use *random head initialization*, achieving MAPE as low as 3.48–4.93% for Amazon/Reddit shifts (Tab. 2 & 3 in AGL paper). Data ordering/subsetting ensembles lead to much worse errors (10–16%+).
> 
> - **MNLI → SNLI**:
>   - *AGL method*: With random head diversity, ALine-D MAPE is 11.70% for GPT2-Medium full finetunes, down to ~5–6% for linear probed GPT2/OPT models (Tab. 16).
>   - *4-bit optimizer*: On text classification, 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly underperforms full-precision for MNLI/SNLI (no significant drop).
> 
> **On vision OOD benchmarks:**
> - **CIFAR-10 → CIFAR-10C corruptions**:
>   - *AGL method*: With random head ensembles on CLIP linear probes, OOD performance estimation MAPE ≈ 14.64% averaged over corruptions, versus >35% for data ordering/subsetting.
>   - *4-bit optimizer*: Shown mainly on Swin-T ImageNet/CIFAR pretraining; retains ≥99% of baseline accuracy.
> 
> **Performance trends:**
> - Across PBADet tasks (HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman), PBADet outperforms BPJDet and other baselines on detection metrics with same backbones.
> - The 4-bit optimizer generally preserves accuracy across NLU, QA, MT, CLS tasks while saving up to ~57% optimizer-state memory over 8-bit baselines.
> - The AGL prediction method requires careful ensemble diversity (random init) to produce accurate OOD estimates; with proper ensembles, predictions are within a few % error.
> 
> **Key integrated observations:**
> 1. **On identical OOD datasets**, the experimental numbers show 4-bit optimizers do not degrade model metrics (e.g., SQuAD-Shifts F1, MNLI accuracy) relative to full precision, while AGL methods can predict those metrics with low error *if* ensemble diversity comes from random head initialization.
> 2. **For similar benchmarks**, PBADet’s detection scores consistently exceed older detection-and-association methods, 4-bit optimizers match peak task performance, and AGL methods add the ability to estimate OOD task scores without labels.
> 3. **On specific datasets**, the lowest MAPE for performance prediction on SQuAD-Shifts Amazon is 3.48% (AGL, random head ensemble, GPT2-M full finetune), and on MNLI→SNLI is ~5% (AGL, random head, linear probe GPT2/OPT), with 4-bit optimizers maintaining essentially same absolute scores as full precision.
> 
> In summary, PBADet excels in detection tasks, the 4-bit optimizer maintains competitive accuracy with significant memory savings, and the AGL methodology delivers accurate label-free OOD performance estimates when ensemble diversity is ensured via random head initialization.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, here is a focused set of five papers matching your criteria, followed by a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The five papers
> 
> 1. **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** – one-stage, anchor-free part-body association detection (doc `08b70bc...`). Evaluated on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts (COCO-based, 6 parts: head, face, l/r hands, l/r feet).
> 2. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** (doc `e63a94c...`) – E/I sign constraints vs. spectral properties in RNNs trained with SGD/projected GD.
> 3. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** (doc `40fde03...`) – implicit bias of JEPA/self-distillation vs. MAE in deep linear models (MSE/CE-style objectives).
> 4. **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)** (doc `8d5e145...`) – 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states.
> 5. **"Predicting the Performance of Foundation Models via Agreement-on-the-Line" (NeurIPS 2024)** (doc `f6089db...`) – label-free OOD performance prediction from ensemble agreement (F1/accuracy).
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **1. PBADet (detection):** On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7) reaches Hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98, beating BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) (85.9/86.91/84.39) and BodyHands baseline (84.8/84.12/63.87) by large margins, with a smaller model. On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet overall but leads in AP_M/AP_L and person/feet AP, and achieves the lowest mismatch rate (mMR-2) for head, face, both hands, and right foot. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale (normalized) center offsets, and task-alignment learning each improve association accuracy.
> 
> **2. Dale's Law RNNs:** ColEI (column-constrained E/I) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN (recurrent Dale's ANNs) across all four tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition); gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Sign constraints account for only part of the gap (0.7±0.3% for RNNs, 1±1% for ColEI) versus the total 2.3±0.6% gap; spectrum "transplant" experiments show the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal/dispersed for ColEI vs. unimodal/clustered for RNN/DANN) matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error, and smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen both spectrum and performance, while DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron (NSE ≈ 0.95).
> 
> **3. JEPA vs. MAE:** In deep linear networks, JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient) whereas MAE prioritizes high-covariance features even if noisy; this bias only emerges with deep encoders. JEPA is slower to learn noisy features and converges to lower-amplitude weights for them. ImageNet-1K validation: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (bottom 25% of explained variance) than MAE features (higher CCA similarity throughout training), and the trend reverses for the top 75% subspace — consistent with JEPA focusing on semantic/low-variance features.
> 
> **4. 4-bit optimizer states:** 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor match or slightly exceed 32-bit AdamW across tasks: NLU (RoBERTa-L, 89.1 vs 88.9), image classification (Swin-T ImageNet, 80.8 vs 81.2), NLG (GPT-2M, 67.8 vs 67.7), QA F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), MT (26.28 vs 26.61). Memory savings reach 57.7% (LLaMA-7B), 43.1–46.7% (RoBERTa-L), 34.4–35.6% (GPT-2M), enabling LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU and ~4× larger OPT models. Ablations: smaller block size (B128) on the first moment, zero-point-excluding linear/rank-1 quantization of the second moment, and second-moment factorization each improve accuracy and/or memory.
> 
> **5. Agreement-on-the-Line (AGL) for OOD prediction:** For lightly fine-tuned foundation models, only **random head initialization** reliably induces AGL (ID-vs-OOD accuracy and agreement linear fits with matching slope/bias) across CIFAR10→CIFAR10C (CLIP linear probe), MNLI→SNLI (OPT), and SQuAD→SQuAD-Shifts (GPT2, F1); data ordering and data subsetting fail. In generative QA, all diversity sources work because token-level search adds diversity. AGL also holds across ensembles of different base models (Llama/GPT/OPT) and PEFT methods (LoRA, IA3, BitFit). This predicts OOD accuracy/F1 within a few percentage points using only unlabeled OOD data.
> 
> ## Key interpretability links and practical guidance
> 
> - **Spectral/feature-level diagnostics transfer across domains:** NSE (singular-value clustering) predicts RNN trainability before training; the JEPA analysis shows that predicting in latent space biases learning toward high-influence, low-variance features — a mechanism linking representation quality to optimization dynamics.
> - **Ensemble diversity is the lever for label-free OOD monitoring:** the choice of randomness (random head init) is what makes agreement a valid proxy for accuracy in fine-tuned foundation models, not data shuffling.
> - **Large-scale training efficiency:** 4-bit optimizer states give near-lossless accuracy with large memory savings, making 4-bit AdamW a practical default for fine-tuning large models; PBADet shows that a single part-to-body offset keeps detection scalable to many parts.
> 
> ## Note on your item (4) details
> 
> No paper in this collection reports **4-bit Adam states on CIFAR-100/MNIST**. The 4-bit optimizer paper uses Swin-T (ImageNet-1k), RoBERTa-L (GLUE/SQuAD), GPT-2M, Transformer (WMT), and LLaMA (Alpaca). The CIFAR-100/MNIST experiments that do appear in the collection (LeNet/ResNet18 on MNIST/CIFAR-10, and ViT-Base fine-tuned on CIFAR-100 with Adam) belong to a different paper — the power-law Hessian spectrum study (doc `582d138...`) — which is about sharpness/generalization prediction, not 4-bit optimizer states. If you specifically need 4-bit optimizers evaluated on CIFAR-100/MNIST, that evidence is not present in this collection.

**community 最终答案**

> Here is a focused set of five papers with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> **1. Detection: PBADet** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`)
> One-stage, anchor-free part–body association via a single part-to-body center offset (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones). Results: on BodyHands, anchor-free part-to-body achieves Hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98, beating anchor-based BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13) and the anchor-based part-to-body variant (88.4/92.31/85.28). On COCO-HumanParts (all categories) it reports AP 42.7/41.5 (original/subordinate, YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6). On CrowdHuman face-body, it reaches the best body MR-2 (36.5) with competitive AP. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task alignment each improve association.
> 
> **2. Dale's Law RNNs** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`)
> "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective." Across adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition, column-constrained EI (ColEI) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and Dale's-ANN RNNs; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Spectrum-transplant experiments show singular-value spectra matter more than sign constraints. ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure) vs. unimodal clustered spectra (Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle) for standard/DANN RNNs. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; small networks and fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and learning, while DANN RNNs are robust (NSE ≈ 0.95 even with one inhibitory neuron).
> 
> **3. JEPA vs. MAE** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`)
> "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features." Exact gradient-flow analysis of deep linear networks: JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient ρ) with the bias strengthening with depth; MAE ordering is set mainly by feature covariance λ and is agnostic to ρ. Corollary: deep JEPA suppresses noisy directions (low ρ), and MAE dynamics at large depth approach 1-layer JEPA. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance (perceptual) PCA subspace than MAE (CCA metric). Note: the analysis uses squared (MSE-type) losses in latent space; I found no cross-entropy (CE) analysis in this paper, so the "MSE/CE" comparison in your query is only partially supported.
> 
> **4. 4-bit Adam states** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`)
> Quantizes first moment with small block size (B128) and second moment with zero-point-excluding linear/rank-1 normalization (optionally factorized). Results: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 (vs. 88.9 for 32-bit), Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 (vs. 81.2), GPT-2 E2E BLEU 67.8 (vs. 67.7), SQuAD F1 94.5 (vs. 94.6), Transformer WMT14 26.28 (vs. 26.61); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning matches 32-bit AdamW, with memory savings up to 57.7% and LLaMA-7B trainable on one 80GB GPU. Caveat: this paper's image classification is ImageNet-1k with Swin-T, not CIFAR-100/MNIST — the CIFAR-100/MNIST settings in the collection belong to the Hessian power-law paper (doc `582d138d…`), which compares many optimizers (including Adam) but is not a 4-bit-state method.
> 
> **5. Label-free OOD performance** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `f6089dba…`)
> "Agreement-on-the-Line (AGL) for Foundation Models." For lightly fine-tuned foundation models, only random linear-head initialization reliably induces AGL (ID vs. OOD accuracy/agreement lines coincide); data ordering/subsetting do not (extractive QA: BERT on SQuAD-Shifts; classification: OPT/GPT2 MNLI→SNLI). In generative QA, token-level search supplies diversity so all sources achieve AGL. AGL predicts F1 (SQuAD-Shifts) and accuracy (CIFAR-10C with linear-probed CLIP, where even linear models show AGL), holds across GPT/OPT/Llama bases and PEFT methods (LoRA, IA3, BitFit), and across ensembles of different foundation models.
> 
> **Cross-paper analysis / practical guidance**
> - **Feature embeddings:** Paper 3 gives a mechanism-level guide: prefer joint-embedding/self-distillation objectives when you want predictive, noise-suppressed, low-variance features (their influence bias grows with encoder depth); masked reconstruction tends to latch onto high-variance, covarying features even if noisy. Paper 5 adds an embedding/eval link: diversity source matters — use random head initialization (or different base models / token-level search) to build ensembles whose agreement enables label-free OOD estimation.
> - **Large-scale training:** Paper 4 shows optimizer-state quantization to 4-bit is lossless in practice across Transformers and LLM fine-tuning, with ~2–4× smaller optimizer states and up to 57.7% total memory savings, so it is a safe lever for memory-bound training; Paper 5's AGL also requires only generic fine-tuned runs (no extra reference models), keeping it computationally light for foundation-model evaluation.
> - **Interpretability:** Paper 2 provides a diagnostic (NSE at initialization) that predicts RNN trainability before training, and Paper 3 provides an interpretable feature-prioritization order (critical times) explaining JEPA vs. MAE behavior; Paper 5's agreement lines double as an interpretability probe of robustness.
> - **Notable mismatches with your query:** the JEPA paper analyzes regression/MSE-type objectives rather than CE, and the 4-bit paper's vision benchmark is ImageNet (not CIFAR-100/MNIST); those specific results cannot be established from this collection.

**问题：** I’m building a vision–language system for an on‑device human–computer interface: we need an anchor‑free detector to associate hands/face to the right person (COCO‑style data), train and fine‑tune Transformers with very limited GPU memory, decide between JEPA‑style self‑distillation and MAE for pretraining features (tracked with MSE/CE), and keep a small RNN controller that respects E/I constraints trained with SGD. Before deployment, I also want to estimate OOD performance without labels (camera shifts, background changes) using agreement within a small ensemble, and monitor F1. Can you point me to works that cover the part‑to‑body detection design, 4‑bit optimizers for Adam, implicit biases of JEPA vs MAE, spectral insights for Dale’s Law, and agreement‑based accuracy prediction for fine‑tuned foundation models?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> The experimental comparison across the given methods reveals the following key findings:
> 
> 1. **Anchor-Free Part-to-Body Detection (PBADet)**:
>    - On **BodyHands**, PBADet consistently outperforms BPJDet and other baselines, including OpenPose, MaskRCNN variants, and BodyHands, in *hand AP*, *conditional accuracy*, and *joint AP*. For the same backbone (YOLOv5l6), PBADet improves joint AP from BPJDet’s 84.39 to 85.73, and a YOLOv7 backbone yields the highest conditional accuracy at 92.62.
>    - On **COCOHumanParts**, PBADet achieves competitive or better AP scores, particularly excelling in APM/APL and part-specific metrics such as person and feet detections. It outperforms BPJDet in most part-body association mMR−2 categories, indicating more robust association, especially for head, face, hands, and right foot.
>    - On **CrowdHuman**, PBADet achieves better MR−2 for both body and face detection than BPJDet, maintaining comparable AP while achieving the best joint detection balance.
> 
> 2. **Dale’s Law Spectral Perspective**:
>    - Experiments on synthetic benchmarks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, natural object recognition) show that DANNs and standard RNNs outperform ColEI networks in OOD/generalization due to better spectral properties.
>    - ColEI networks suffer from multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra, which impairs learning—especially with small network sizes or imbalanced E/I ratios. DANNs, with their unimodal spectra, match RNN performance across tasks.
>    - Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) strongly correlates with performance: higher NSE means better learning outcomes. Modifying EI ratios and network sizes that increase NSE improves accuracy.
> 
> 3. **JEPA vs MAE Pretraining**:
>    - In deep linear analysis, JEPA exhibits an *implicit bias* toward high-regression-coefficient (predictive) features, leading to quicker prioritization of informative, low-noise features in deep encoders.
>    - MAE prioritizes high covariance features regardless of noise, potentially overfitting noisy high-variance directions.
>    - Experiments on Gaussian synthetic data and temporal models confirm JEPA’s advantage in OOD-like settings with limited compute.
> 
> 4. **Memory-Efficient 4-bit AdamW Optimizers**:
>    - Quantizing first moment with small block size (B128/DE) and second moment with Rank-1/Linear mapping, excluding zero-points, achieves near-lossless convergence.
>    - Across NLU, vision (Swin-T/ImageNet), NLG (E2E), MT (Transformer/WMT14), and instruction tuning (LLaMA on Alpaca, MMLU, commonsense reasoning), 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit performance within statistical noise, with *≤1%* metric differences.
>    - Memory savings up to ~57% vs 32-bit AdamW, outperforming 8-bit optimizers while maintaining throughput; hybrid 4-bit + factorized second moment offers additional savings.
> 
> 5. **Agreement-on-the-Line OOD Prediction for FMs**:
>    - For lightly finetuned foundation models, **random linear head initialization** is the only diversity source that consistently yields matching ID vs OOD accuracy and agreement slopes (AGL). Data ordering or subsetting fails to induce sufficient diversity.
>    - AGL holds across vision (CLIP-linear-probed) and language (OPT/GPT QA, text classification) settings, enabling accurate ID→OOD accuracy prediction via ALine-S/D.
>    - Diverse ensembles from multiple pretrained FM families (OPT, GPT, LLaMA variants) also observe AGL in language tasks, suggesting robustness to pretraining corpus differences.
>    - ALine-S/D surpass confidence-based baselines (ATC, AC, DOC-Feat) in Mean Absolute Percentage Error by large margins (up to 20%+ improvement) on high-R² shifts, accurately predicting OOD metrics without labels.
> 
> **Overall**:
> - **PBADet** is the most accurate for part-to-body detection across datasets.
> - **DANNs** outperform ColEI under Dale’s Law constraints due to better eigen/singular value spectra.
> - **JEPA** is preferable to MAE for learning predictive latent features, avoiding noisy high-variance bias.
> - **4-bit AdamW** achieves near-lossless performance with substantial memory savings across tasks.
> - **AGL methods** predict foundation model OOD performance most precisely when ensembles are constructed with random head initialization or across diverse base models.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the works matching each requirement, with the key experimental comparisons:
> 
> **1. Part‑to‑body detection (anchor‑free, COCO‑style): PBADet** (ICLR 2024, "PBADet: One‑Stage Anchor‑Free Approach for Part‑Body Association")
> - Uses a single part‑to‑body center offset on multi‑scale feature maps; handles hands/face/feet→body with one‑to‑one correspondence, avoiding BPJDet's body‑to‑part complexity (representation length 10 vs 15 for 3 parts).
> - **Experimental results:** On COCO‑HumanParts (6 parts), PBADet (YOLOv5l6) reaches AP 43.0/41.8, on par with BPJDet and leading on person/feet AP; ablation shows anchor‑free part‑to‑body beats anchor‑based part‑to‑body (Hand AP 89.1 vs 88.4; Cond. Acc 92.62 vs 92.31; Joint AP 85.98 vs 85.28). Against the pose estimator ED‑Pose on COCO, PBADet is far better (all‑parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; e.g., left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87). Association loss, multi‑scale offsets, and task‑alignment each improve association accuracy.
> 
> **2. 4‑bit Adam optimizers: "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4‑bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Uses smaller block size (B128) for the first moment, zero‑point‑excluding linear quantizer and rank‑1 normalization for the second moment, optionally factorized (4‑bit Factor).
> - **Experimental results:** 4‑bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32‑bit AdamW on all tasks (RoBERTa‑L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; Swin‑T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT‑2 E2E‑NLG 67.8 vs 67.7; Transformer MT 26.28 vs 26.61), including LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine‑tuning (e.g., 4‑bit matches 32‑bit on MMLU/HellaSwag). Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA‑7B: 31.87GB vs 75.40GB), enabling LLaMA‑7B on one 80GB GPU; 4‑bit Factor cuts optimizer states ~4× vs 8‑bit. Baselines Adafactor/SM3 degrade, notably on the classification task.
> 
> **3. JEPA vs MAE implicit bias: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Analyzes deep linear self‑distillation: JEPA (MSE in latent space) biases toward high‑influence features (high regression coefficient ρ), while MAE (MSE reconstruction) prioritizes high‑variance/eigenvalue (λ) features; the difference only appears with deep encoders.
> - **Experimental results:** Exact ODE analysis gives critical times: JEPA learns low‑variance "slow"/perceptual features first (which noise doesn't distort), MAE learns in λ order regardless of informativeness. ImageNet‑1K I‑JEPA vs MAE (ViT, same masking): CCA shows JEPA representations align faster with the bottom‑25%‑variance PCA subspace than MAE, confirming JEPA focuses on semantic, less noisy features—relevant if you want perception‑oriented features (both objectives here are MSE; CE appears in the collection only for fine‑tuning/NAS contexts, not in this comparison).
> 
> **4. Dale's Law (E/I) RNN spectral analysis: "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Compares standard RNNs, ColEI (column‑sign‑constrained E/I partitioning), and recurrent DANNs on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition.
> - **Experimental results:** ColEI learns worst with higher variance; sign constraints explain only part of the gap (e.g., on sequential MNIST sign constraints cost ~1%, but ColEI's total deficit vs standard RNN is ~2.3%). Singular‑value spectrum transplants show the spectrum matters more than sign constraints: ColEI has multimodal, dispersed singular values (from a rank‑one column‑mean nilpotent component), while standard RNNs/DANNs match the random‑matrix quarter‑circle/Marchenko‑Pastur form. Smaller networks/fewer I units worsen both spectrum and performance; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti‑correlates with final error, so NSE can predict trainability of your small E/I‑constrained RNN before training (DANN formulation is the recommended way to respect Dale's Law without spectral pathology).
> 
> **5. Agreement‑based OOD prediction for fine‑tuned foundation models: "Predicting the Performance of Foundation Models via Agreement‑on‑the‑Line"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Estimates OOD accuracy/F1 without labels from the linear ID‑vs‑OOD agreement trend of an ensemble.
> - **Experimental results:** For lightly fine‑tuned FMs, only **random head initialization** reliably induces agreement‑on‑the‑line (AGL) — data ordering and data subsetting do not (e.g., CLIP linear probe CIFAR‑10→CIFAR‑10C Pixelate, OPT MNLI→SNLI, GPT2/BERT SQuAD→SQuAD‑Shifts Amazon with F1). In generative QA (GPT2/OPT), all diversity sources achieve AGL; ensembles of multiple base FMs (Llama/GPT/OPT) also show AGL for F1 on SQuAD‑Shifts and accuracy on MNLI‑Mismatched/SNLI regardless of shift size. AGL generalizes to PEFT (LoRA, IA3, BitFit) with agreement lines aligning with full fine‑tuning under random heads. Note it needs ≥3 models, and unlike confidence‑based baselines it extends to F1, which suits your detection monitoring.
> 
> **Cross‑method notes:** PBADet validates the anchor‑free part‑to‑body design empirically (better than anchor‑based/body‑to‑part and pose‑based alternatives); 4‑bit optimizers let you fine‑tune those Transformers with ~equal accuracy at ~57% memory reduction; the JEPA‑vs‑MAE theory (plus ImageNet evidence) favors JEPA for perception features under MSE; the spectral‑Dale's analysis tells you to use DANN‑style parameterization and check NSE for your small SGD‑trained E/I RNN; and random‑head ensembles + agreement lines give you label‑free OOD/F1 monitoring for the fine‑tuned models before deployment.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the five works covering your needs, with their key experimental results:
> 
> **1. Part-to-body detection (anchor-free): PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> - One-stage anchor-free detector that adds a single part-to-body center offset to anchor-free object representation (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones), replacing BPJDet's body-to-part offsets (representation length 10 vs 15 for 3 parts).
> - Outperforms SOTA on BodyHands and COCOHumanParts; on CrowdHuman face-body association it achieves the best body MR-2 (36.5 with YOLOv7 vs 39.7–41.3 for BPJDet) and competitive AP; vs ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands/feet. Ablations: removing the association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task alignment all degrade hand AP, conditional accuracy, and joint AP.
> 
> **2. 4-bit optimizers for Adam: "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Compresses Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit using smaller blocks (B128) for the first moment and a zero-exclusion linear quantizer plus rank-1 normalization for the second moment (optionally factorized).
> - Results: 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L: 89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), E2E-NLG, ImageNet (Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2), WMT14, and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning; saves up to 57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB, trainable on one 80GB GPU); convergence curves closely align. Adafactor and SM3 save more memory but degrade accuracy, especially on classification.
> 
> **3. JEPA vs MAE implicit bias: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Deep-linear-network analysis + ImageNet experiments: JEPA self-distillation prioritizes high-influence (high regression-coefficient ρ) features, whereas MAE orders learning by covariance eigenvalue λ; the bias strengthens with encoder depth.
> - ImageNet-1K CCA experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (bottom 25% explained variance, where perceptual features live) than MAE, and are slower to pick up noisy features; MAE mostly learns the top-variance (noisy) subspace. Implication: JEPA is better suited for perception-oriented pretraining, MAE is not.
> 
> **4. Spectral insights for Dale's Law: "Learning better with Dale's Law"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Standard RNNs, column-constrained EI RNNs (ColEI), and recurrent Dale's ANNs (DANN) were compared on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition.
> - Results: ColEI learns worse and with higher variance on all tasks; gradient clipping helps it most. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors (sign constraints account for ~0.7–1% error, spectra ~1.5–2% of the ~2.3% gap). ColEI has multimodal/dispersed spectra from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean term; DANN and standard RNNs have unimodal quarter-circle spectra. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error, so small networks with balanced E/I ratios (high NSE) train well.
> 
> **5. Agreement-based OOD prediction: "Predicting the Performance of Foundation Models via Agreement-on-the-Line"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Extends agreement-on-the-line (AGL) — ID-vs-OOD accuracy and agreement sharing the same linear trend — to fine-tuned foundation models (CLIP, GPT2/OPT/Llama, BERT).
> - Key finding: for lightly fine-tuned FMs, only random linear-head initialization reliably induces AGL across vision (CIFAR-10C, ImageNetC/V2, FMoW, WILDS) and language (SQuAD-Shifts, MNLI→SNLI) benchmarks; data ordering and subsetting do not. Generative QA shows AGL under all diversity sources. Ensembles of FMs from different base models (GPT2/OPT/Llama) also show AGL on language tasks. AGL-based estimation (ALine) beats confidence baselines by up to 20% MAPE; negative control Camelyon17 shows AGL fails when ACL fails.
> 
> **Cross-method comparison:** The detection paper gives you the anchor-free part-to-body head (better F1/AP than two-stage heuristics); the 4-bit optimizer lets you fine-tune those Transformers within tight memory with essentially lossless accuracy (vs 8-bit and full precision); the JEPA/MAE analysis supports choosing JEPA-style self-distillation for semantic features (MSE/CE tracking shows faster alignment to perceptual low-variance features than MAE); the Dale's Law work tells you to design the small RNN controller's E/I structure with unimodal spectra (DANN-style) and use NSE to predict trainability before training; and the AGL work prescribes random head initialization across an ensemble of your fine-tuned models to estimate OOD accuracy/F1 without labels, since only that diversity source yields the linear agreement–accuracy trend for foundation models.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:350 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find recent papers that collectively cover: (a) an anchor‑free, one‑stage method for associating human parts with people, benchmarked on COCO‑style human‑part datasets with AP/Precision/F1; (b) analyses of deep recurrent nets under biologically inspired E/I constraints (Dale’s law) from a spectral perspective; (c) self‑supervised learning with joint‑embedding predictive architectures explaining why latent prediction avoids noisy pixel targets and how feature embeddings evolve (think beyond plain MSE/CE and include MNIST/CIFAR‑100 style toy settings); (d) memory‑efficient training using 4‑bit states for Adam/AdamW that supports end‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning in large deep networks; and (e) differentially private reinforcement learning with self‑play offering trajectory‑level protection (both joint and local variants) together with regret bounds. Please focus on scalable training, regularization, and practical metrics on modern benchmarks such as COCO.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
