**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparative summary of experimental results drawn only from the figures and tables of the provided papers. It is organized by topic, highlights identical datasets across methods, and reports which methods perform better or worse on those datasets. Where a paper reports only theory or curves without tabulated metrics, we state the qualitative findings attributable to the provided figures.
> 
> 1) Anchor‑free, one‑stage part–body association (PBADet vs baselines)
> Identical datasets and metrics: BodyHands (Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP), COCOHumanParts (COCO AP suite plus per‑category APs and subordinate APs; mMR−2), CrowdHuman (MR−2, AP, mMR−2).
> 
> BodyHands (Table 1)
> - PBADet (YOLOv7, 1024): Hand AP 89.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.62; Joint AP 85.98.
> - PBADet (YOLOv5l6, 1024): 88.1; 92.71; 85.73.
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 1536): 85.9; 86.91; 84.39.
> - Earlier baselines (OpenPose, MaskRCNN variants, BodyHands): substantially lower Joint AP than PBADet; e.g., BodyHands 63.48 Joint AP.
> Conclusion on BodyHands: PBADet consistently outperforms BPJDet and older baselines across all three metrics, with the largest gains in Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP. Between PBADet variants, YOLOv7 has slightly higher Hand AP and Joint AP than YOLOv5l6.
> 
> COCOHumanParts (Table 2, Table 3)
> All‑categories APs (Table 2):
> - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate), AP.5 70.0/68.4, APM 66.2/65.0, APL 67.2/64.4.
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.6/43.3, AP.5 70.6/69.8, APM 63.8/63.2, APL 61.8/58.9.
> Observations: BPJDet has slightly higher AP.5:.95 and AP.5, but PBADet has notably higher APM and APL, indicating stronger performance on medium and large objects.
> Per‑category APs (Table 2):
> - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Person 62.4; Head 54.6; Face 44.6; Right hand 39.0; Left hand 37.7; Right foot 30.9; Left foot 31.5.
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Person 61.3; Head 56.6; Face 46.3; Right hand 40.4; Left hand 39.6; Right foot 30.2; Left foot 30.9.
> Observations: PBADet better on Person, APM/APL, and slightly on feet (left foot and right foot are mixed), while BPJDet is stronger on head, face, and hands AP by small margins.
> Association robustness (average mMR−2, Table 3; lower is better):
> - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Head 27.9; Face 30.5; Left hand 36.2; Right hand 40.8; Right foot 50.4; Left foot 47.9.
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Head 30.8; Face 31.8; Left hand 41.6; Right hand 42.2; Right foot 49.1; Left foot 50.4.
> Observations: PBADet achieves lower mMR−2 for head, face, and both hands (better association accuracy); BPJDet has slightly lower mMR−2 on right foot.
> 
> CrowdHuman (Table 5 and Table 6)
> - PBADet (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet family: PBADet YOLOv7 attains best body MR−2 (36.5 vs 39.7–41.3 for BPJDet variants) and best body AP (91.6 vs 89.5–90.7), and competitive face MR−2. For mMR−2 (body‑face pairs), PBADet is comparable to BPJDet (e.g., 50.8 vs 50.1 for YOLOv5l6 BPJDet), showing similar association reliability under crowding.
> 
> Ablations (Tables 4 and 8)
> - Removing the association head (Lassoc) hurts Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP, confirming the benefit of explicit association.
> - Anchor‑free + part‑to‑body definition outperforms anchor‑based and body‑to‑part definitions (Table 8), supporting PBADet’s design.
> 
> 2) Deep recurrent nets under Dale’s Law (ColEI vs DANN vs Standard RNN) (Fig. 2)
> Datasets: Adding Problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank (language modeling), Naturalistic Object Recognition.
> - Qualitative performance curves (Figure 2) show ColEI networks have worse and more variable performance across all four tasks; DANNs and standard RNNs learn well.
> - Gradient clipping benefits ColEI substantially more than the other two, but does not close the gap.
> - Additional analysis (Appendix Figure 9 referenced in text) indicates ColEI performs relatively better only at large spectral radii (ρ), but worse at small ρ; DANNs and standard RNNs are less sensitive and perform stably.
> Conclusion: Across identical tasks (adding, seq‑MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition), DANNs and standard RNNs outperform ColEI consistently; ColEI’s training stability and final performance are inferior.
> 
> 3) Self‑supervised JEPA vs MAE (linear/CCA analyses) (Fig. 1, Fig. 2, Fig. 4, Fig. 7)
> Datasets and metrics: Synthetic linear settings and ImageNet‑1K (64×64) CCA between representations trained on full vs PCA‑filtered images.
> - Feature learning order (Fig. 1 and Fig. 2): In distribution 2 (λ increasing but ρ decreasing), JEPA learns features with larger regression coefficients (ρ) first, reversing the MAE’s learning order. This is visible in the heatmaps of encoder component magnitudes over training.
> - Encoder depth sensitivity (Fig. 4): Only JEPA exhibits increasingly pronounced greedy dynamics w.r.t. ρ as depth L grows; MAE’s dynamics are largely governed by covariance λ.
> - ImageNet CCA (Appendix D, Figure 7): I‑JEPA’s representations show higher mean CCA between full and “bottom” PCA subspace throughout training than MAE; JEPA’s mean CCA is lower for full vs “top” PCA subspace compared to MAE.
> Conclusion: On identical synthetic settings and the shared ImageNet‑1K analysis protocol, JEPA aligns more strongly with the bottom‑variance PCA subspace and prioritizes influential features (high ρ) in deep settings, while MAE focuses on high‑variance directions (high λ). These are qualitative, curve‑based outcomes rather than task accuracies.
> 
> 4) Memory‑efficient training with 4‑bit Adam/AdamW (supports end‑to‑end LoRA) (Tables 2–6, 7–9)
> Identical datasets: GLUE (RoBERTa‑L), SQuAD/SQuAD 2.0, E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2 M), ImageNet‑1K (Swin‑T), WMT14 En‑De (Transformer‑Base), LLaMA finetuning (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC‑e/c, OBQA).
> 
> Accuracy on common benchmarks (Table 2; medians/means as reported):
> - GLUE (RoBERTa‑L, mean across tasks): 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 vs 32‑bit AdamW 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW 89.1; SM3 87.5. Per‑task details (Table 7) show 4‑bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32‑bit on most tasks and clearly outperforms SM3.
> - ImageNet‑1K (Swin‑T): 4‑bit AdamW 80.8% vs 32‑bit 81.2%; 8‑bit 81.0%; Adafactor 80.0%. Slightly lower than full precision but comparable to 8‑bit.
> - E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2 M, Table 2 & Table 8): BLEU 4‑bit 67.8 vs 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5; Adafactor 67.2. Other metrics (NIST, METEOR, ROUGE‑L, CIDEr) similarly show parity.
> - SQuAD (Table 9): 4‑bit F1 94.5 vs 32‑bit 94.6; EM 88.8 vs 89.0; nearly identical; SM3 markedly lower (F1 91.7).
> - SQuAD 2.0 (Table 9): 4‑bit F1 88.4 vs 88.8; EM 85.4 vs 85.8; comparable; 8‑bit slightly higher F1 (89.0).
> - WMT14 En‑De (Transformer‑Base, Table 2): SacreBLEU 4‑bit 26.28 vs 32‑bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; Adafactor 26.52. All differences are small.
> - LLaMA finetuning (Table 3): On MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC‑e/c, OBQA across 7B/13B/33B models, 4‑bit AdamW matches or nearly matches 32‑bit AdamW (e.g., for 13B, MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8), showing preserved capability with instruction tuning.
> 
> Memory/time efficiency (Table 4)
> - LLaMA‑7B (FSDP, 2×A100 80GB): 4‑bit AdamW total memory 31.87GB vs 75.40GB (32‑bit); 57.7% saving; training time 3.07h vs 3.35h.
> - RoBERTa‑L (single RTX 4090): 4‑bit AdamW (fused) 3.17 min vs 3.93 min (32‑bit), with total memory 3.00GB vs 5.31GB; 43.5% saving.
> - GPT‑2 M: 4‑bit AdamW (fused) 2.11h vs 2.13h (32‑bit), memory 4.62GB vs 6.89GB; 34.4% saving.
> Largest trainable model under fixed budget (Table 5)
> - With 24GB: 4‑bit enables OPT‑1.3B vs 350M with 32‑bit.
> - With 80GB: 4‑bit enables OPT‑6.7B and LLaMA‑7B; 32‑bit only OPT‑1.3B.
> Ablations on Swin‑T (Table 6)
> - Quantizing 1st moment (B128/DE) and 2nd moment (Rank‑1/Linear): 80.8% top‑1; factorizing 2nd moment further yields 80.9%, both close to full precision (81.2%).
> Conclusion: Across identical datasets (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG, ImageNet‑1K, WMT14, and LLaMA evals), 4‑bit AdamW achieves accuracy comparable to 32‑bit and 8‑bit optimizers, while offering substantial memory savings (≈35–58%) and enabling larger models within the same hardware budget. Methods without first moments or with sublinear memory (SM3) often underperform on accuracy.
> 
> 5) Differentially Private RL with self‑play (theoretical regret comparisons) (Table 1)
> Setting: Two‑player zero‑sum Markov Games; regret bounds (no empirical datasets).
> - Non‑private: DP‑Nash‑VI reduces to Õ(√(H^2 SAB T))—matching Nash VI’s leading term.
> - Under ϵ‑JDP: DP‑Nash‑VI achieves Õ(√(H^2 SAB T) + H^3 S^2 AB / ϵ). Lower bounds: Ω̃(√(H^2 S(A+B)T) + HS(A+B)/ϵ). The additional term has optimal dependence on ϵ and near‑optimal leading term.
> - Under ϵ‑LDP: DP‑Nash‑VI achieves Õ(√(H^2 SAB T) + S^2 AB √(H^5 T)/ϵ). Lower bounds: Ω̃(√(H^2 S(A+B)T) + √(HS(A+B)T)/ϵ). The dependence on K and ϵ matches lower bounds; H,S,A,B dependence remains an open optimization.
> Conclusion: On identical theoretical settings, DP‑Nash‑VI matches the best known non‑private leading term and adds privacy‑dependent terms consistent with lower bounds for both JDP and LDP.
> 
> Cross‑paper overlaps and comparability notes
> - ImageNet‑1K appears in both the 4‑bit optimizer paper (Swin‑T classification) and the JEPA paper (CCA analyses). However, the optimizer paper reports top‑1 accuracy while JEPA reports representational similarity (CCA). These are not directly comparable metrics.
> - MNIST is used only in the Dale’s Law paper (Sequential MNIST curves); no other paper reports MNIST metrics.
> - COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, and CrowdHuman are unique to PBADet’s evaluation.
> - GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG, WMT14 En‑De, and LLaMA eval suites are unique to the 4‑bit optimizer paper.
> 
> Overall takeaways on identical datasets
> - Human part‑body association: PBADet delivers state‑of‑the‑art association on BodyHands (highest Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP), competitive or superior APs on COCOHumanParts for medium/large objects, and lower mismatches (mMR−2) for head/face/hands compared to BPJDet; on CrowdHuman it achieves best body detection MR−2/AP with similar pair association mMR−2.
> - RNNs with Dale’s Law constraints: Across the same four tasks (Adding, Seq‑MNIST, PTB, Naturalistic recognition), DANNs and standard RNNs consistently outperform ColEI; ColEI is more sensitive to hyperparameters and benefits disproportionately from gradient clipping.
> - 4‑bit training across standard NLP/Vision datasets: 4‑bit AdamW preserves accuracy on GLUE, SQuAD/SQuAD2.0, E2E‑NLG, WMT14, ImageNet‑1K and LLaMA instruction tuning versus 32‑bit/8‑bit Adam/AdamW, while substantially reducing memory and enabling larger models.
> - DP RL regret guarantees on the same Markov‑game setting: DP‑Nash‑VI achieves regret upper bounds that generalize best known single‑agent DP results and match non‑private leading terms, with privacy terms consistent with lower bounds.
> 
> Limits of comparability
> - JEPA results are representation‑centric (feature learning order and CCA) rather than task accuracies; comparisons to MAE are qualitative and based on provided curves.
> - DP RL paper reports theoretical regret tables rather than empirical datasets; comparisons are formal (upper vs lower bounds).

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the papers matching each topic, with key experimental results and a comparative analysis.
> 
> ## (a) Part-body association — **PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> One-stage, anchor-free detector adding a single **part-to-body center offset** to YOLO-style heads (classification + localization + displacement, with task-alignment loss). On **BodyHands**, PBADet (YOLOv7) reaches Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 — beating BPJDet (85.9/86.91/84.39), BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48) and others. On **COCO-HumanParts** it gets AP₅₀:₉₅ 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6), leading AP_M/AP_L and per-category person/feet; lowest mMR⁻² for head/face/hands/right-foot. Against ED-Pose on COCO val, PBADet gives much higher Precision/Recall/F1 (all-parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs 24.09/45.51/31.51). On CrowdHuman it lowers body MR⁻² to 36.5 (vs BPJDet 40.7) at AP 91.6. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each boost Joint AP.
> 
> ## (b) Dale's Law RNNs from a spectral view — **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Compares standard RNNs with sign-constrained ColEI and DANN E/I recurrent nets (adding, sMNIST, PTB, object recognition). Sign constraints alone explain little; the **initial singular-value spectrum** matters most. ColEI's column-mean nilpotent structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values, so it learns worse (sMNIST error 2.3±0.6% vs 0.3% for standard RNN; DANN matches standard RNN). Smaller nets / fewer I-units worsen spectra and performance; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance pre-training. Gradient clipping mitigates the ColEI deficit.
> 
> ## (c) JEPA self-supervised learning — **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> Derives why predicting in **latent space** (JEPA, e.g. self-distillation) beats pixel reconstruction (MAE). In exactly solvable deep-linear toy models, JEPA is biased to learn **high-influence features** (large regression coefficients ρ), steering away from high-variance/noisy pixels; MAE prioritizes only high-covariance features. The bias strengthens with encoder depth. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE. *Caveat:* the context's toy analysis uses Gaussian data, not explicitly MNIST/CIFAR-100; MNIST/CIFAR-100 toy settings appear in a separate paper (Hessian-spectrum study) on a different question.
> 
> ## (d) Memory-efficient training — **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Compresses Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4 bits (B128/DE for first moment; rank-1/linear zero-excluded mapping or factorization for second moment, solving the zero-point problem). Across GLUE, ImageNet (Swin-T), E2E-NLG, SQuAD, WMT and Alpaca, 4-bit matches/beats 32-bit: e.g. RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, GPT-2 BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, LLaMA-33B MMLU 54.9 vs 56.4 (no degradation as size grows). Memory savings up to **57.7%** (LLaMA-7B 31.9GB vs 75.4GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models. It is explicitly validated for **end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning** (GPT-2 Medium via the LoRA codebase, and LLaMA on Alpaca with FSDP).
> 
> ## (e) DP reinforcement learning with self-play — **"Differentially Private Reinforcement Learning with Self-Play"**
> Extends Joint DP (JDP) and Local DP (LDP) to two-player zero-sum episodic Markov Games with **trajectory-level protection**. The DP-Nash-VI algorithm (optimistic Nash value iteration + privatized Bernstein bonuses, Laplace mechanism) provably satisfies either notion. Regret: central JDP ~O(H²SAB√T + H³S²AB + H²S²AB·E) with privacy cost E=Õ(H/ε); LDP variant with E=Õ(H√K/ε). Bounds generalize the best single-agent DP-RL results and reduce to the best non-private multi-agent bound; first results for trajectory-wise privacy in multi-agent RL.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Scalable training (d vs a):** 4-bit optimizer states attack the dominant memory bottleneck of large-model fine-tuning, pairing naturally with LoRA/FSDP (a "regularization-free" memory lever); PBADet instead achieves scalability at the architecture level — one offset handles any number of parts without degrading detection AP, outperforming anchor-based BPJDet with fewer params (36.9M vs 41.2M).
> - **Regularization & representation (c vs b):** Both are "why does X work/fail" analyses from first principles. (c) frames latent prediction as an implicit-bias/regularization mechanism (noisy-pixel avoidance), while (b) reframes the E/I constraint failure as a spectral-pathology problem — in both, the *initialization/objective-induced* structure, not the constraint per se, drives learning dynamics.
> - **Practical metrics on modern benchmarks (a/e):** Only PBADet directly uses COCO-family metrics (AP₅₀:₉₅, AP, mMR⁻², Precision/F1) and modern backbones (YOLOv5/v7); the DP-RL and RNN papers report regret bounds and sMNIST/PTB errors rather than COCO-style metrics, and the 4-bit/JEPA papers report GLUE/ImageNet/E2E/BLEU and CCA. Thus COCO-relevant, modern-benchmark experimental evidence is strongest in PBADet; the others contribute scalable-training and theoretical guarantees.
> 
> All findings above come strictly from the retrieved documents.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, I found one paper per topic. Here they are with their experimental results and a comparative analysis.
> 
> ## (a) PBADet — one-stage anchor-free part–body association (ICLR 2024)
> - **Method**: single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free YOLOv5/YOLOv7; benchmarks on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman (AP, precision, recall, F1, mMR⁻², conditional accuracy, joint AP).
> - **BodyHands**: Ours(YOLOv7) → Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98, vs BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39 and BodyHands 84.8/83.44/63.48.
> - **COCOHumanParts** (all categories, original/subordinate): Ours(YOLOv5l6) AP .5:.95 = 43.0/41.8, AP .5 = 70.0/68.4, AP_M = 66.2/65.0, AP_L = 67.2/64.4 — on par with BPJDet but leading AP_M/AP_L and person/feet APs, and lowest average mMR⁻² on head, face, both hands, right foot.
> - **vs ED-Pose** (COCO val, hands/feet): Precision/Recall/F1 for all parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs ED-Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51 (e.g., left hand 37.63/60.82/46.50 vs 18.36/30.34/22.87).
> - **CrowdHuman**: body MR⁻² 36.5, AP 91.6 (YOLOv7), beating BPJDet (40.7, 89.5).
> 
> ## (b) "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Method/analysis**: spectral analysis of E/I (Dale's-law) RNNs; compares ColEI (sign-constrained columns) vs recurrent DANN vs standard RNNs; uses normalised SVD entropy (NSE) as a spectrum-pathology metric.
> - **Results**: ColEI has multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra and learns worse with higher variance (mitigated by gradient clipping); DANN RNNs have standard-RNN-like (unimodal, quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur) spectra and learn just as well, robust even with 1 inhibitory unit. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error across adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition. This is an analysis paper, not a benchmark-beating method.
> 
> ## (c) "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: Deep Linear Self-Distillation" (NeurIPS 2024)
> - **Method/analysis**: JEPA vs MAE objectives in exactly solvable deep linear networks; proves JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient ρ) while MAE prioritizes high-variance features even if noisy; critical-time ordering and depth separation (1-layer JEPA ≈ infinite-depth MAE).
> - **Results**: toy Gaussian data (two feature distributions) show JEPA reverses learning order under high-λ/low-ρ; on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA embeddings align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA measure). Note: the toy settings are Gaussian deep-linear models, not literally MNIST/CIFAR-100; MNIST/CIFAR-10/100 appear only in the related Hessian-spectrum paper, which is not an SSL paper.
> 
> ## (d) "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Method**: 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states (B128 block + rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluding linear quantizer, optional second-moment factorization).
> - **Results**: matches or slightly beats 32-bit AdamW — RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 (vs 88.9), Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 (vs 81.2), GPT-2M E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 (vs 67.7), RoBERTa-L SQuAD 94.5, WMT14 26.28; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca instruction tuning MMLU 38.9/47.4/54.9 vs 38.7/46.5/56.4 for 32-bit; memory savings up to 57.7%, enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models under a fixed budget.
> - **Caveat**: the context reports full fine-tuning; LoRA is only discussed as a combinable parameter-efficient method (e.g., with offloading), and no dedicated end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning experiment is documented.
> 
> ## (e) "Differentially Private Reinforcement Learning with Self-Play"
> - **Method**: extends Joint DP (JDP) and Local DP (LDP) to two-player zero-sum episodic Markov games with trajectory-wise protection; algorithm DP-Nash-VI (optimistic Nash value iteration + privatized Bernstein bonuses).
> - **Results (theoretical)**: central JDP regret Õ(H²S√(ABT) + H³S²AB + H²S²AB·E_{ε,β}) with E=Õ(H/ε); local variant E=Õ(H√K/ε); lower bounds combine non-private Ω̃(H²S(A+B)T) with single-agent JDP Ω(HSA/ε) and LDP Ω(√(HSAT)/ε); plus a PAC sample-complexity bound. No empirical benchmarks are reported.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Benchmark maturity**: only (a) provides COCO-scale, practical metrics (COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman, COCO val with AP/Precision/F1) and clearly outperforms SOTA (BPJDet, HierR-CNN, ED-Pose) with a smaller/same-size model; (d) provides strong practical benchmarks (GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet, WMT, LLaMA/Alpaca) showing lossless accuracy with large memory savings — the most "scalable training" contribution; (b) and (c) are analytical (toy/deep-linear settings + sequential MNIST/PTB/ImageNet-1K confirmations) and contribute understanding/regularization (spectral diagnostics, implicit bias) rather than new benchmark records; (e) is purely theoretical (regret/PAC guarantees, no experiments).
> - **Regularization/robustness themes**: (b) shows spectrum pathology (NSE) predicts poor learning, advocating spectral-aware initialization; (c) explains why latent prediction avoids noisy pixel targets (implicit bias toward influential features) — both are diagnostic/mechanistic. (a) uses task-alignment learning and a single valid part-to-body offset as its design "regularization."
> - **Efficiency vs accuracy**: (d) is the efficiency paper (up to 57.7% memory saved with no accuracy loss), while (a) also emphasizes efficiency (one-stage, no multi-stage association, fewer parameters than DETR-based pose estimators).
> - **Gaps/limitations**: (e) has no empirical validation; (d) lacks an explicit LoRA fine-tuning experiment in the reported context (and notes optimal quantization may be task-dependent, untested on RL/audio/graphs); (c)'s theory relies on deep-linear/simultaneously-diagonalizable assumptions; (b) requires gradient clipping for stable ColEI training. Across the five, only (a) and (d) directly address "scalable training/practical metrics on modern benchmarks such as COCO"; (b), (c), (e) are theory/analysis-oriented and cannot be compared on common metrics.

### paperscope:results_comparison:353 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m deploying a privacy‑preserving assistant that needs to: detect and associate hands/faces with the right person in crowded scenes (COCO‑like), learn robust visual/audio representations via latent‑space prediction (not raw pixel reconstruction), fine‑tune large models under tight GPU memory using low‑bit optimizers with LoRA, and train interactive policies with self‑play while guaranteeing strong per‑trajectory privacy (local/joint protections). Are there works that together cover an anchor‑free part‑to‑body detector, a spectral view of E/I‑constrained recurrent nets, joint‑embedding SSL (JEPA‑style), 4‑bit Adam/AdamW optimizers for end‑to‑end fine‑tuning, and DP reinforcement learning with regret guarantees?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：4→3（Δ-1）；rounds：4→3（Δ-1）。**

工具安排：naive 为第1轮5次、第2轮3次、第3轮2次；community 为第1轮5次、第2轮4次。最终回答另占一轮。

> 2) E/I‑constrained recurrent nets: ColEI vs DANN vs Standard RNN (figures report test error gaps)
> Across tasks (Adding, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic Object Recognition) (Fig. 2)
> - Consistent pattern: ColEI learns worse (higher error curves) than both Standard RNN and DANN; DANN ≈ Standard RNN.
> Impact of sign constraints vs spectra (Fig. 4A–C)
> - Freezing signs (adding sign constraints) increases error by 0.7% ± 0.3% (RNNs) and 1% ± 1% (ColEI), not explaining full gap (2.3% ± 0.6%).
> - Transplanting spectra accounts for larger performance changes: 1.5% ± 0.3% (RNNs) and 2% ± 1% (ColEI), indicating spectra matter more than signs.
> Effect of EI ratio and network size (Figs. 5–7)
> - Lower inhibitory fraction → larger max singular values, lower normalized SVD entropy (NSE), worse performance; DANN robust even with 1 inhibitory unit.
> - Larger networks increase singular‑value clustering (higher NSE) and reduce error even if max singular value grows; test error anti‑correlates with NSE across sizes/ratios.
> - Takeaway: Spectral properties at initialization (unimodal, clustered singular values) predict learning; DANN matches Standard RNN; ColEI suffers unless size and EI balance restore benign spectra.
> 
> 3) JEPA vs MAE (deep linear theory + simulations + ImageNet)
> Learning dynamics (Figs. 1–2, Theorems 3.2–3.6)
> - With monotonically increasing feature covariance λ and decreasing regression coefficient ρ, MAE still learns high‑λ first, whereas JEPA prioritizes high‑ρ (influential) features; depth increases JEPA’s bias toward high‑ρ.
> Temporal model & simulations (Fig. 3)
> - In a simple time‑varying linear model, features with larger temporal autocorrelation (γ) and lower noise (smaller σ) get higher ρ and are learned earlier by JEPA; MAE follows λ.
> ImageNet‑64 (Appendix D, Figure 7)
> - Canonical correlation (CCA) between representations learned on full vs bottom‑PCA variance images: I‑JEPA shows higher mean CCA than MAE throughout training, indicating JEPA emphasizes the low‑variance (perceptual) subspace; on full vs top‑variance, MAE shows higher CCA than I‑JEPA.
> - Takeaway: Empirically and theoretically, JEPA predicts in latent space and focuses on predictive, low‑variance (high‑ρ) features; MAE focuses on high‑variance (high‑λ) content.

> Markov Games (two‑player, zero‑sum) regret bounds with privacy
> - DP‑Nash‑VI (ours):
>   • No privacy: Õ(√(H² S A B T)) — matches best non‑private (Nash‑VI).
>   • ϵ‑JDP: Õ(√(H² S A B T) + H³ S² A B / ϵ)

> Single‑agent MDP special cases (B=1) recover best‑known bounds (Table 1).

> Comparisons on identical datasets/tasks (explicit winners)
> - Hand/face/hands association (BodyHands): PBADet > BPJDet on Cond. Acc. (92.62 vs 86.91) and Joint AP (85.98 vs 84.39), with higher Hand AP (89.1 vs 85.9).
> - Multi‑part detection/association (COCOHumanParts): PBADet reduces mismatching (mMR−2) on head/hands; BPJDet slightly higher AP on head/face/hands; PBADet higher APM/APL and feet AP.
> - Crowded scenes (CrowdHuman): PBADet best MR−2 for body (36.5) and face (44.7) and competitive AP; association mMR−2 similar to BPJDet (~50–51).
> - GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/WMT14 (optimizers): 4‑bit AdamW ≈ 32‑bit AdamW (often ±0.0–0.3 points); 4‑bit occasionally best (E2E BLEU 67.8); 8‑bit often ties for top (WMT14 26.66).
> - LLaMA instruction‑tuning: 4‑bit AdamW ≈ 32‑bit across MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA; small task‑specific fluctuations.

> Comparisons on similar dataset types
> - Vision detection in crowds (PBADet vs crowd baselines): PBADet yields lowest body MR−2 (36.5) and competitive AP among CNN/DETR‑family baselines (Tables 5–6).
> - Representation learning (JEPA vs MAE): On ImageNet‑64, I‑JEPA’s features show higher CCA alignment in the low‑variance subspace than MAE through training (Fig. 7 in appendix), consistent with theoretical bias to high‑ρ features.
> - Sequence modeling with biological constraints (RNN EI): DANN ≈ Standard; ColEI under‑performs across tasks; spectrum properties (unimodal clustered singular values) correlate with better performance (lower error) as measured by NSE.
> - RL privacy: DP‑Nash‑VI’s regret terms (Table 1) scale near‑optimally; JDP and LDP add separable terms consistent with lower bounds.
> 
> Per‑dataset highlights
> - BodyHands: Ours (YOLOv7) Hand AP 89.1 / Cond. Acc. 92.62 / Joint AP 85.98 (SOTA among reported).
> - COCOHumanParts: Ours (YOLOv5l6) APM/APL (66.2/67.2 original) higher than BPJDet (63.8/61.8); mMR−2 lowest on head (27.9) and hands (36.2/40.8) vs BPJDet (30.8/41.6/42.2).
> - CrowdHuman: Ours (YOLOv7) body MR−2 36.5 (best), face MR−2 44.7 (best), body AP 91.6 (top‑tier).
> - GLUE (mean): 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 (ties 8‑bit 89.1; ≈ 32‑bit 88.9).
> - E2E‑NLG BLEU: 4‑bit AdamW 67.8 (best among compared);
> - WMT14: 8‑bit 26.66 slightly > 32‑bit 26.61 > 4‑bit 26.28 (all close).
> - LLaMA‑7B MMLU: 4‑bit 38.9 vs 32‑bit 38.7 (tie); 33B OBQA: 4‑bit 45.4 vs 32‑bit 43.8 (4‑bit >).
> 
> Synthesis for deployment
> - For crowded, multi‑person vision (COCO‑like), PBADet provides an anchor‑free, one‑stage part–to–body association with improved joint metrics and simple decoding; achieves best body/face MR−2 on CrowdHuman and top metrics on BodyHands.
> - For recurrent policy modules under E/I constraints, DANN achieves RNN‑level performance; avoid naïve ColEI unless network size/ratios restore benign spectra (high NSE).
> - For SSL pretraining, JEPA‑style self‑distillation prioritizes high‑influence (high‑ρ) features and aligns better with low‑variance perceptual subspaces than MAE (CCA results), especially with deeper encoders.
> - For fine‑tuning large models under tight memory, 4‑bit Adam/AdamW preserves accuracy across GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/WMT14 and LLaMA while cutting optimizer memory ~40–58% and often maintaining or improving training time; 8‑bit remains a strong baseline.
> - For interactive privacy with self‑play, DP‑Nash‑VI gives trajectory‑wise JDP/LDP with near‑optimal regret; recovers best non‑private rates when ε→∞ and matches best single‑agent DP‑RL in the MDP limit.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes — five works in the collection jointly cover your stack. Comparisons of their experimental results:
> 
> **1. Anchor-free part-to-body detector — PBADet (ICLR 2024).** One-stage anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center offset (vs. BPJDet's body-to-part offsets). On BodyHands: HandAP 89.1, Cond. Acc 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) vs. BPJDet-l6 85.9/86.91/84.39 (86.1M) — better with fewer parameters. On COCOHumanParts it's on par overall (AP 43.0 vs. 43.6) but leads AP_M (66.2 vs. 63.8), AP_L (67.2 vs. 61.8), person/feet AP, and lowest mMR-2 for head/face/hands. On CrowdHuman it achieves the best body MR-2 (36.5). Ablations: association head, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment all help; anchor-free beats anchor-based (JointAP 85.98 vs. 85.28), and part-to-body beats body-to-part (85.28 vs. 78.13).
> 
> **2. Spectral view of E/I-constrained RNNs — "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023).** ColEI nets (sign-constrained columns) learn worse and with higher variance than DANN and standard RNNs on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition. Spectrum transplants show the singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints: sign constraints explain only ~0.7–1% of a 2.3% error gap. ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed with a large-singular-value mode; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error. DANNs stay robust to E/I ratio and size (learn well even with 1 inhibitory neuron).
> 
> **3. JEPA-style joint-embedding SSL — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024).** Deep-linear analysis: JEPA prioritizes high-regression-coefficient ("influential") features with a depth-dependent bias, while MAE orders learning by covariance λ only; when ρ and λ anti-correlate, JEPA reverses feature-learning order. On ImageNet, I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA (perceptual) subspace than MAE (higher CCA on bottom-25%-variance images, lower on top-75%), and converges to lower-amplitude weights for noisy features. Note: the context covers vision (I-JEPA/ImageNet), not audio.
> 
> **4. 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizers — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023).** On fine-tuning, 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW (GLUE 89.1 vs. 88.9; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs. 94.6; E2E BLEU 67.8 vs. 67.7); comparable on pretraining (ImageNet 80.8 vs. 81.2; WMT 26.28 vs. 26.61). LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning is comparable (MMLU 38.9/47.4/54.9 vs. 38.7/46.5/56.4), with up to 57.7% memory savings (75.4GB→31.9GB) and LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; 4-bitFactor adds more savings. Caveat: results are for end-to-end fine-tuning — the context does not demonstrate a combined 4-bit-optimizer + LoRA experiment.
> 
> **5. DP RL with self-play — "Differentially Private RL with Self-Play" (NeurIPS 2024).** DP-Nash-VI (optimistic Nash value iteration + privatized Bernstein bonuses) satisfies trajectory-wise JDP or LDP with regret O~(√(H²SABT) + H²S²AB·E_ε,β), E=O~(H/ε) (JDP) or O~(H√K/ε) (LDP). It matches the non-private best regret (Liu et al. 2021) as ε→∞, matches the best single-agent DP RL bound (Qiao & Wang 2023), and comes with PAC and lower-bound guarantees.
> 
> **Coverage gaps:** no work in context combines 4-bit optimizers with LoRA specifically, and the JEPA analysis is vision-only (no audio results). All other requested components are covered, and each paper reports strong, often state-of-the-art, results against its baselines.

> **1. PBADet (anchor-free part-to-body detector, ICLR 2024)**

Results: on BodyHands it beats all SOTA — HandAP 89.1 / Cond. Accuracy 92.62 / JointAP 85.98 (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) vs BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (86.1M) 85.9/86.91/84.39, and vs BPJDet-YOLOv5m6 (41.2M) 85.3/86.80/78.13 — better with a smaller model. On COCOHumanParts it is on par with BPJDet on overall AP but leads on AP_M/AP_L, feet, and has the lowest mMR-2 for head/face/both hands/right foot. Ablations: anchor-free part-to-body (89.1/92.62/85.98) > anchor-based part-to-body (88.4/92.31/85.28) > anchor-based body-to-part BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13); association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each add gains. Strongest empirical gains of the five.
> 
> **2. "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (spectral view of E/I RNNs, NeurIPS 2023)**
> ColEI (column-constrained E/I) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs/DANNs on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Spectrum-transplant experiments show the singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints (spectrum contributes ~1.5–2% error vs ~0.7–1% for sign constraints; total gap 2.3±0.6%). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with test error; small balanced-E/I networks with high NSE beat large skewed networks. DANN is robust to EI ratio/size (learns even with 1 inhibitory neuron; NSE ≈0.95). Diagnostic/analysis paper — no SOTA-accuracy claims.
> 
> **3. "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (joint-embedding SSL, NeurIPS 2024)**
> Theoretical analysis (deep linear self-distillation): JEPA is greedily biased toward high-ρ (high-influence) features while MAE orders learning only by eigenvalue λ; noise suppression strengthens with depth (JEPA fixed point ρ^L vs MAE ρ^(L/(L+1)); 1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE). Numerical ODE/SGD simulations confirm; ImageNet-1K shows I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA perceptual subspace than MAE (CCA). Limited to deep linear networks/special initialization; it explains robustness rather than reporting new task accuracy.
> 
> **4. "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (4-bit Adam/AdamW, NeurIPS 2023)**
> 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; GPT-2M E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7; SQuAD 94.5 vs 94.6) and is comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61). LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning matches 32-bit with aligned convergence curves. Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 31.9GB vs 75.4GB), enabling 4× larger OPT models and LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; 4-bit Factor saves more. Beats 8-bit AdamW in memory; Adafactor/SM3 are leaner but degrade, especially on classification. Note: LoRA is discussed only as a complementary method (related work), not combined in experiments.
> 
> **5. "Differentially Private Reinforcement Learning with Self-Play" (DP RL with regret, NeurIPS 2023)**
> DP-Nash-VI for two-player zero-sum episodic Markov games under Joint DP and Local DP, both guaranteeing trajectory-wise privacy. Regret under JDP: Õ(H²S√(ABT) + H³S²AB·E_{ε,β}) with E=Õ(H/ε); under LDP: E=Õ(H√K/ε). With ε→∞ it matches the best non-private MARL regret Õ(H²S√(ABT)), nearly matching the Ω̃(H²S√((A+B)T)) lower bound; with B=1 it reduces to the best single-agent DP-RL bound. Lower bounds: Ω(HSA/ε) (single-agent JDP), Ω(√(HSAT)/ε) (LDP). Purely theoretical — no empirical experiments.
> 
> **Cross-method analysis:** Only PBADet and the 4-bit optimizer report large-scale empirical results; the JEPA and E/I-RNN papers are analytical (theory + small simulations/ablations), and the DP-RL paper is theory-only. PBADet shows the largest SOTA improvements (association accuracy especially); the 4-bit optimizer demonstrates lossless fine-tuning at ~half the memory (the most directly deployable result for your GPU-constrained fine-tuning); the E/I-RNN and JEPA papers offer mechanistic explanations (spectrum pathology; latent-space implicit bias) rather than accuracy wins; DP-RL provides the regret guarantees you asked for but no empirical validation. Together they cover your stack, but note that (a) the 4-bit optimizer paper doesn't itself test LoRA, and (b) the JEPA work is a theory study of JEPA rather than a new JEPA method, and (c) DP-RL results are tabular/theoretical without benchmarks.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:356 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (1) joint-embedding self-supervised learning that biases feature embeddings toward informative signals rather than pixel noise (analyzing why squared-error vs entropy-based classification losses behave differently), (2) memory-lean training using sub-byte (around 4‑bit) optimizer states compatible with Adam‑style and stochastic gradient methods for end-to-end fine‑tuning of Transformers and adapter-based (e.g., low‑rank) updates, (3) an anchor‑free one‑stage approach for associating human parts with people that reports metrics like F1/Precision and uses standard objectives such as squared error or cross‑entropy, and (4) a rank‑based causal discovery framework that allows causally related hidden variables for interpretability. Prefer works that also discuss fine‑tuning on benchmarks (e.g., MNIST, CIFAR‑100) and report practical considerations for evaluation and optimization.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a consolidated, results-only comparison across the five works you provided, organized by domain. I only use the figures and tables (and accompanying text) you supplied, and I explicitly identify identical datasets and the metrics used.
> 
> 1) One-stage anchor-free part–body association (PBADet) vs baselines on identical datasets
> Identical datasets: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman
> 
> - BodyHands (Table 1; metrics: Hand AP↑, Conditional Accuracy↑, Joint AP↑)
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5m6): Hand AP 85.3, Cond. Acc. 86.80, Joint AP 78.13
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5s6): Hand AP 84.0, Cond. Acc. 85.68, Joint AP 77.86
>   • Conclusion on BodyHands: PBADet tops all metrics among one-stage methods reported; using the same backbone (YOLOv5l6), PBADet outperforms BPJDet on all three metrics. 
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2; All categories APs and per-category APs; Table 3; mMR−2↓ per category)
>   • All categories AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate):
>     – Ours (YOLOv5l6): 43.0 / 41.8  vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6 / 43.3
>     – Ours (YOLOv7): 42.7 / 41.5  vs BPJDet (YOLOv5m6): 42.0 / 41.7
>   • AP.5 (original/subordinate):
>     – Ours (YOLOv5l6): 70.0 / 68.4  vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 70.6 / 69.8
>     – Ours (YOLOv7): 69.5 / 67.9  vs BPJDet (YOLOv5m6): 68.9 / 68.1
>   • Scale APs (Ours YOLOv5l6): APM 66.2 / 65.0, APL 67.2 / 64.4 (notably strong large/small-scale subordinate APs compared to BPJDet variants)
>   • Per-category APs (Table 2):
>     – Relative to BPJDet (YOLOv5l6), Ours (YOLOv5l6) is higher on Person (62.4 vs 61.3) and both Feet (r-foot 30.9 vs 30.2; l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9), but lower on Head (54.6 vs 56.6), Face (44.6 vs 46.3), Right Hand (39.0 vs 40.4), and Left Hand (37.7 vs 39.6).
>   • Average mMR−2 per category (Table 3; lower is better):
>     – Ours (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Head 29.2 vs 30.8 (better), Face 31.3 vs 31.8 (better), Left Hand 41.1 vs 41.6 (better), Right Hand 42.7 vs 42.2 (slightly worse), Right Foot 52.6 vs 49.1 (worse), Left Foot 52.5 vs 50.4 (worse).
>     – Ours (YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Head 27.9 vs 30.8 (better), Face 30.5 vs 31.8 (better), Left Hand 36.2 vs 41.6 (better), Right Hand 40.8 vs 42.2 (better), Right Foot 50.4 vs 49.1 (slightly worse), Left Foot 47.9 vs 50.4 (better).
>   • Conclusion on COCOHumanParts: Overall APs are comparable between PBADet and BPJDet. PBADet shows advantages on person and feet APs and shows better average mMR−2 for head/face/hands in several settings; BPJDet holds advantages on some head/face/hand APs.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Appendix Table 5; metrics: MR−2↓ body/face, AP↑ body, mMR−2↓ body-face)

>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 body 40.7, MR−2 face 46.3, AP body 89.5, mMR−2 50.1 (slightly lower than ours on mMR−2)
>   • Conclusion on CrowdHuman: PBADet attains best MR−2 (body) and AP (body); mMR−2 is comparable across methods (50.8–50.9 vs ~50.1).

> - Comparison to multi-person pose estimation (ED-Pose) on COCO (Appendix Table 7; metrics: Precision/Recall/F1 per part)
>   • By F1, PBADet beats ED-Pose on left hand (46.50 vs 22.87), right hand (47.34 vs 24.17), left foot (51.08 vs 40.46), right foot (50.34 vs 40.34), and overall (48.52 vs 31.51).

> 2) Rank-based causal discovery with causally related hidden variables (RLCD) vs baselines on identical synthetic settings
> Identical settings: Three families of latent graphs with multiple sample sizes (2k, 5k, 10k)

>   • RLCD again highest F1 across latent tree, measurement, and general latent graphs (e.g., 0.79→0.97 latent-tree; 0.84→0.95 latent-measurement; 0.68→0.78 latent-general as sample size increases). Hier. rank and GIN are not applicable in this metric (assume no observed-adjacency), while PC/FCI/RCD lag RLCD across all cases.

>   • RLCD consistently achieves lowest SHD across latent-tree, latent-measurement, and general latent settings at each sample size, indicating the closest recovered structure to ground truth.

> - Real data (Big Five personality)
>   • RLCD identifies coherent clusters and directions (Fig. 5) consistent with domain structure. No numeric accuracy baselines are provided on this real dataset; the result is qualitative.

> 3) Memory-lean training with 4‑bit optimizer states (4-bit AdamW / 4-bit Factor) vs 32‑bit/8‑bit AdamW and adaptive baselines on identical datasets
> Identical datasets: GLUE (RoBERTa-L), SQuAD/SQuAD2.0 (RoBERTa-L), E2E-NLG (GPT-2 Medium), ImageNet-1k (Swin-T), WMT14 en-de (Transformer-Base), Alpaca → eval on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA (LLaMA-7B/13B/33B)
> 
> - Language understanding (GLUE, RoBERTa-L; Table 2)
>   • Mean score: 4-bit AdamW 89.1 matches or slightly betters 32-bit AdamW (88.9) and 8-bit AdamW (89.1); Adafactor ~89.1; SM3 87.5.
>   • Per-task breakdown (Table 7) shows 4-bit methods generally on par with 32-bit; occasionally 4-bit Factor achieves the best among 4-bit variants on some tasks.
> 
> - Question answering (RoBERTa-L on SQuAD/SQuAD2.0; Table 2 and Table 9)
>   • SQuAD: 4-bit AdamW F1 94.5, EM 88.8 (≈32-bit AdamW F1 94.6, EM 89.0; and 8-bit AdamW F1 94.5, EM 88.8)
>   • SQuAD2.0: 4-bit AdamW F1 88.4, EM 85.4 (≈32-bit AdamW F1 88.8, EM 85.8; 8-bit AdamW F1 89.0, EM 86.1)
>   • Conclusion: 4-bit retains QA performance comparable to 32-bit/8-bit.
> 
> - Natural language generation (E2E-NLG, GPT-2 Medium; Table 2 and Table 8)
>   • BLEU: 4-bit AdamW 67.8 (vs 32-bit 67.7; 8-bit 67.5), other metrics (NIST, METEOR, ROUGE-L, CIDEr) show close parity among 32-bit, 8-bit, and 4-bit.
> 
> - Image classification (ImageNet-1k, Swin-T; Table 2)
>   • Top-1 Acc: 32-bit 81.2; 8-bit 81.0; 4-bit AdamW 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9. Small drop (~0.3–0.4 pt) from 32-bit to 4-bit/8-bit.
> 
> - Machine translation (WMT14 en-de, Transformer-Base; Table 2)
>   • SacreBLEU: 32-bit 26.61; 8-bit 26.66; 4-bit AdamW 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45. All are close; 4-bit is slightly below 32/8-bit.
> 
> - Instruction tuning, LLaMA (Alpaca train; eval MMLU 5-shot + HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA; Table 3)
>   • LLaMA-7B: 4-bit ≈ 32-bit across all metrics (e.g., MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; HellaSwag 74.7 vs 74.6; ARC-e 61.2 vs 61.5; ARC-c 44.4 vs 45.1; OBQA 43.0 vs 43.4)
>   • LLaMA-13B: 4-bit ≈ 32-bit (MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; similar trends on other tasks)
>   • LLaMA-33B: 4-bit ≈ 32-bit (MMLU 54.9 vs 56.4; other tasks close)
>   • Conclusion: 4-bit maintains instruction tuning quality comparable to 32-bit across model scales.
> 
> - Memory / throughput (Table 4, Table 5)
>   • LLaMA-7B finetuning (2×A100 80GB): Training memory drops from 75.40 GB (32-bit) to 31.87 GB (4-bit AdamW), a 57.7% reduction; training time improves from 3.35 h to ~3.07–3.11 h.
>   • RoBERTa-L finetuning: Total memory from 5.31 GB (32-bit) to ~3.00 GB (4-bit AdamW fused), 43.5% reduction; fused implementation time 3.17 min vs 3.93 min (32-bit).
>   • GPT-2 Medium finetuning: Total memory from 6.89 GB (32-bit) to 4.62 GB (4-bit AdamW), 34.4% reduction; fused time 2.11 h vs 2.13 h.
>   • Largest trainable model (Table 5): With the same GPU memory, 4-bit enables larger models: on 24 GB, OPT-350M→OPT-1.3B; on 80 GB, OPT-1.3B→OPT-6.7B; enables LLaMA-7B on a single 80 GB GPU.
> 
> Summary for 4-bit optimizers: On identical datasets across NLP/vision/MT, 4-bit AdamW (and 4-bit Factor) match full-precision/8-bit accuracy in finetuning and are close in pretraining, while substantially reducing memory and sometimes improving throughput.
> 
> 4) Dale’s Law in recurrent networks (DANN vs ColEI vs standard RNN) on similar datasets
> Identical/standardized tasks within the paper: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition
> 
> - Comparative performance (Fig. 2 A–D)
>   • Across the four benchmarks, ColEI (column EI partition with sign constraints) learns worse (higher error / lower accuracy) and with higher variance; DANN (the extended Dale’s ANN architecture in recurrent form) learns comparably to standard RNNs.
>   • Gradient clipping helps ColEI more but does not close the gap to RNN/DANN.
> 
> - Spectrum transplant on sequential MNIST (Fig. 4B–C)
>   • Experiments show the singular value spectrum at initialization explains most of the performance difference: imposing ColEI spectra onto RNNs degrades performance more than imposing ColEI sign constraints alone. Reported relative changes in final test error (in the figure caption narrative) are on the order of ~1.5–2.0% depending on configuration; spectrum effects dominate sign constraints.
> 
> - Sensitivity to EI ratio and model size (Figs. 5–7)
>   • ColEI: fewer inhibitory neurons and smaller networks reduce normalized SVD entropy and harm learning (higher error); larger networks with more balanced E/I have better spectra (more clustered singular values) and better performance.
>   • DANN: robust across EI ratios and sizes; normalized SVD entropy remains high and performance remains strong.
> 
> Conclusion for Dale’s Law RNNs: On identical tasks (adding, seq-MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition), DANN achieves standard-RNN-like performance, while ColEI lags notably; spectral properties (not sign constraints alone) chiefly drive the performance gap.
> 
> 5) Joint-embedding SSL (JEPA) vs reconstruction (MAE) on similar tasks
> Experiments are diagnostic/qualitative rather than standardized benchmarks; the focus is the learning order and feature bias.
> 
> - Feature-learning order in deep linear experiments (Fig. 1, Fig. 2)
>   • Under “Distribution 1” (both covariance λ and regression coefficient ρ increasing), JEPA and MAE exhibit greedy learning by λ (larger-variance features learned earlier).
>   • Under “Distribution 2” (λ increasing, ρ decreasing), MAE maintains learning order by λ, but JEPA inverts the order and learns high-ρ (influential) features first. This inversion occurs more strongly with deeper encoders.
> 
> - Temporal model (Fig. 3)
>   • In a simple linear dynamical setting with noisy modes, JEPA prioritizes features with higher regression coefficient (γ·||v||^2/(σ^2+||v||^2)), i.e., more predictive and less noisy components; MAE emphasizes highly covarying features regardless of noise.
> 
> - ImageNet experiment (Appendix D, Fig. 7; CCA similarity over epochs)
>   • I-JEPA vs MAE: JEPA’s representations from full vs bottom-PCA images have higher mean CCA (more aligned), and from full vs top-PCA images have lower mean CCA; this indicates that JEPA focuses earlier on low-variance (semantic) subspace relative to MAE. 
> 
> Conclusion for JEPA vs MAE: On similar types of diagnostics, JEPA (self-distillation in latent space) exhibits an implicit bias toward high-ρ (predictive, less noisy) features, especially with deeper encoders; MAE prioritizes high-variance features. On ImageNet representations, JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance subspace than MAE.
> 
> Overall cross-paper comparisons by dataset family
> - Identical datasets within each domain were compared directly above (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman for detection; synthetic latent-graph families for causal discovery; GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/ImageNet/WMT/LLaMA evals for 4-bit optimization; adding/seq-MNIST/PTB/NOR for Dale’s Law RNNs). 
> - Across similar problem types, each approach dominates in its respective domain: PBADet achieves state-of-the-art part–body association on BodyHands and very competitive results on COCOHumanParts and CrowdHuman; RLCD has the best structural recovery (F1/SHD) across a variety of latent graph types; 4-bit optimizers retain full-precision quality on standard NLP/vision tasks with large memory savings; DANN matches standard RNNs while ColEI underperforms; JEPA learns informative, less noisy features sooner than MAE in controlled studies.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Recommended papers
> 
> **1. Joint-embedding SSL vs. pixel reconstruction (loss analysis)**
> - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (Littwin et al., Apple, NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037...`). Analyzes why JEPA (squared-error prediction in latent space) biases embeddings toward *influential* features (high regression coefficient ρ) and away from noisy, high-variance pixel-level features, whereas MAE (squared-error reconstruction in input space) prioritizes features by covariance λ and is agnostic to informativeness. Proves JEPA critical time depends on ρ (increasingly with depth) while MAE's depends only on λ; fixed points differ (w̄_JEPA=ρ^L vs w̄_MAE=ρ^(L/(L+1))). ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA).
> - **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (Lee et al., ICLR 2025, doc `160e1407...`). Contrastive/information-theoretic (softmax/entropy-type InfoNCE) counterpart: analyzes why entropy-based contrastive objectives behave differently — in full batch the optimum aligns positives and uniformly separates negatives (−1/(n−1)); smaller batches increase negative-pair similarity variance and degrade quality; a variance-reduction auxiliary loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, and full ImageNet and improves temperature robustness.
> 
> **2. Memory-lean 4-bit optimizer states**
> - **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (Li, Chen, Zhu; NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455...`). 4-bit Adam/AdamW and 4-bit Factor (factorized second moment) via small block size (B128), rank-1 normalization, and zero-point-excluding linear quantization of the second moment; compatible with SGD(M), Adam(W), Adafactor-style factorization, LoRA-based fine-tuning, and optimizer offloading. Benchmarks: RoBERTa-L (GLUE), SQuAD, GPT-2 Medium E2E-NLG, Swin-T ImageNet, Transformer WMT14, LLaMA-7B/13B/33B instruction tuning (Alpaca, MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA). 4-bit variants match or slightly beat 32-bit AdamW (e.g., GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6; ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2) with up to 57.7% memory savings and LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU. Adafactor(β₁=0) and SM3 degrade, especially on image classification.
> 
> **3. Anchor-free one-stage part-body association**
> - **"PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"** (Gao et al., ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3...`). Extends anchor-free detection (FCOS/TOOD) with a single part-to-body center offset; uses standard objectives — IoU/DFL bounding-box losses, cross-entropy classification loss, and an L1 (squared-error-type regression) association loss with task-alignment anchor selection. Metrics: Hand AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP, F1/Precision/Recall, MR-2/mMR-2. On BodyHands and COCO-HumanParts it outperforms BPJDet/HierR-CNN (e.g., YOLOv7: Hand AP 89.1 vs BPJDet 85.3, Cond. Acc. 92.62 vs 86.80, Joint AP 85.98 vs 78.13); vs ED-Pose on COCO, all-parts Precision/Recall/F1 = 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs 24.09/45.51/31.51. Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment all help.
> 
> **4. Rank-based causal discovery with causally related hidden variables**
> - **"A Versatile Causal Discovery Framework to Allow Causally-Related Hidden Variables"** (Dong, Huang, et al., ICLR 2024, doc `f8eb4c37...`). RLCD uses rank deficiency of sub-covariance matrices over observed variables (rank tests instead of pure CI) to locate latent variables, determine cardinalities, and recover the full causal structure including edges among latent variables (as confounders, mediators, effects, or hierarchical). Asymptotically identifies the Markov equivalence class; without latents it matches PC. Synthetic results: SHD consistently lowest (e.g., Latent+tree 10k: 0.7 vs 9.0–25.1 for baselines) and higher F1 than PC, FCI, GIN, RCD, Hier. Rank; real-world Big Five analysis (network-style, interpretable) with no neuroticism latent. F1 computed by aligning/permuting latent variables; α tuned per method for fairness.
> 
> **5. Practical evaluation/optimization on MNIST/CIFAR benchmarks** — no single paper covers all four topics; the relevant experimental-consideration content lives in the papers above. A complementary methodological reference from the collection: **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure: From CNNs to LLMs"** (Tang et al., ICML 2025, doc `582d138d...`), which reports detailed fine-tuning practice on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 with LeNet/ResNet/ViT and many optimizers (SGD, Adam, etc.), including LR schedules, batch sizes, weight decay, and ViT fine-tuning on CIFAR-100 (batch 4096, 200 steps, Adam, weight decay 0.1), and shows LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does — a practical caveat relevant to item (2)'s adapter-based updates.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis of experimental results
> 
> - **Loss behavior (squared error vs entropy):** The JEPA analysis shows squared-error latent-space prediction *suppresses noise* via the ρ-implicit bias (depth-strengthened), while MAE's squared-error input-space reconstruction *chases variance*; the contrastive-learning paper shows entropy/softmax-based (InfoNCE) objectives *behave differently* — they enforce alignment + uniformity, whose quality degrades with small batches (higher negative-pair variance) and is temperature-sensitive. So squared-error and entropy losses differ in *what feature order they learn* (JEPA: informativeness-first; MAE: variance-first) and in *optimization sensitivity* (entropy: temperature/batch-size sensitive; the variance-reduction fix improves CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet top-1, e.g., ImageNet-100 at t=0.3: 74.04 vs 72.30).
> - **Memory vs accuracy:** The 4-bit optimizer matches full precision across all benchmarks (GLUE 89.1, QA F1 94.5, ImageNet 80.8, MT 26.28–26.45 vs 26.61) while cutting memory ~43–58% (LLaMA-7B: 31.9GB vs 75.4GB), and unlike Adafactor/SM3 it does not sacrifice the vision classification task (80.8 vs 79.0–80.0). Its speedups come mainly from reduced communication in FSDP/offloading, not fused kernels (unfused 4-bit is slower than 8-bit on small models).
> - **Detection accuracy vs architecture:** PBADet's anchor-free, part-to-body design beats anchor-based body-to-part (BPJDet) and two-stage/pose methods on both association quality (Joint AP 85.98 vs 78.13; F1 48.52 vs 31.51) and efficiency (fewer params: 36.9M vs 41.2M), while keeping body detection AP comparable to DETR-based detectors.
> - **Causal discovery accuracy vs baselines:** RLCD's rank-based approach gives substantially lower SHD (e.g., 0.7 vs ≥9.0 on latent-tree 10k) and higher F1 than CI-based PC/FCI and other latent-variable methods, at moderate compute (~3h vs RCD's ~2 days); when graphical conditions are violated it either returns a correct-but-uninformative rank-equivalent graph or signals the violation.
> - **Cross-cutting practical notes:** The 4-bit optimizer and PBADet both stress out-of-the-box hyperparameter reuse (same hyperparameters across quantizations; task-alignment weights), and the Hessian paper documents how evaluation/optimization choices (LR schedule, batch size, weight decay, LoRA vs full fine-tuning) measurably change optimization structure and generalization on MNIST/CIFAR-100 — cautioning that adapter-only fine-tuning (item 2) alters the loss landscape compared with full fine-tuning.

**community 最终答案**

> I found four papers in the collection matching the four topics. Here they are with their experimental results and a comparison.
> 
> ## The four papers
> 
> **1. Joint-embedding SSL — "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde…`)**
> Analyzes, via deep linear networks, why JEPA (joint-embedding predictive) features are biased toward high-influence, informative features instead of pixel noise. It derives critical times showing JEPA orders feature learning by regression coefficient ρ (squared-error regression in latent space), whereas MAE orders mainly by eigenvalue λ; depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression (a 1-layer JEPA equals an infinite-depth MAE). **Results:** on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features than MAE features. (Complementary SSL paper: **LDReg** `51526…` regularizes local intrinsic dimensionality and improves linear-eval/transfer/detection of SimCLR, BYOL, MoCo, VICReg, Barlow Twins, MAE on ImageNet/COCO.)
> 
> **2. 4-bit optimizer states — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e…`)**
> Compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (B128/dynamic-exponent for m; rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluding linear map, optionally factorized, for v), and includes a convergence proof for quantized SGD(M), so it works with Adam-style and stochastic-gradient methods. **Results:** RoBERTa-L GLUE 88.9→89.1, Swin-T ImageNet 81.2→80.8, GPT-2M E2E-NLG BLEU 67.7→67.8, RoBERTa-L SQuAD F1 94.6→94.5, Transformer WMT14 26.61→26.28—matching or exceeding 32-bit AdamW while saving up to 57.7% memory and enabling LLaMA-7B fine-tuning on a single 80GB GPU; also used for GPT-2 fine-tuning (LoRA-linked repo) and LLaMA/Alpaca instruction tuning.
> 
> **3. Part-body association — "PBADet" (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70…`)**
> One-stage, anchor-free part-to-body association via a single part-to-body center offset, trained with IoU/DFL/classification (cross-entropy-style) losses plus an association loss (ℓ1/squared-error-style). **Results:** BodyHands hand AP 89.1 vs BPJDet 85.9, conditional accuracy 92.62 vs 86.91, joint AP 85.98 vs 84.39; on COCOHumanParts AP 43.0/41.8 (all categories) vs BPJDet 43.6/43.3 but leading person/medium/large AP and lowest mMR⁻²; CrowdHuman face-body: leading body MR⁻² with competitive AP; vs ED-Pose (COCO): all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51.
> 
> **4. Rank-based causal discovery — "RLCD" (ICLR 2024, doc `f8eb4…`)**
> Rank-based latent causal discovery that allows causally-related hidden variables (confounders, mediators, effects, hierarchies), using rank deficiency of covariance. **Results:** on synthetic latent-tree/measurement/general graphs, lower SHD and higher F1 than PC, FCI, GIN, RCD, and Hier. Rank; Big Five personality analysis recovers a network-style latent model (e.g., no neuroticism latent), yielding interpretable causal structure.
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results & practices
> 
> - **Evaluation metrics reflect each task**: the SSL papers report linear-eval/transfer accuracy and feature alignment (CCA); the optimizer paper reports task scores (GLUE accuracy, SQuAD F1, BLEU, SacreBLEU) plus memory/throughput; PBADet reports AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP, MR⁻², and Precision/Recall/F1 (the only one reporting F1, matching your preference); RLCD reports SHD/F1. Only RLCD and PBADet quantify "association/structural" quality directly with F1.
> - **Gains are consistent but modest on accuracy and large on efficiency/interpretability**: 4-bit states give ~equal accuracy (−0.1–+0.4) but up to 57.7% memory savings and 4× larger trainable models; PBADet gives the largest head-to-head accuracy gains among the four (up to +17 points F1 over a pose estimator, +1.6–6 points over BPJDet); JEPA is a theoretical/implicit-bias result with an ImageNet confirmation; RLCD gives clear F1/SHD gains over baselines plus interpretability.
> - **Optimization considerations**: the optimizer paper reports convergence curves aligning with 32-bit and lossless convergence without stable-embedding tricks, at the cost of being slower than 8-bit without operator fusion (task-dependent optimal quantization is a stated limitation). PBADet details practical training (4 V100s, 100 epochs, SGD, AMP, NMS thresholds). RLCD notes practical trade-offs (needs high-recall CI skeleton, ~3 h vs PC/FCI ~10 min but far faster than RCD ~2 days). SSL/JEPA notes limitations of linear/linearized analysis (deep linear MLPs, special initialization).
> - **Benchmark overlap**: only partially matches the stated MNIST/CIFAR-100 preference—the contrastive-embedding paper (`160e…`, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet) covers those benchmarks but addresses embedding similarities rather than the squared-error vs entropy question; the four matched papers instead use ImageNet, GLUE/SQuAD, WMT, COCO/BodyHands, and personality data. Fine-tuning is explicitly discussed in the optimizer (Transformers/LLaMA), PEFT-adjacent (GPT-2/LoRA), and PBADet (pretrained YOLO backbones) papers.
> 
> **Bottom line**: these four papers collectively cover all four requested topics; the strongest quantitative accuracy gains come from PBADet, the strongest efficiency result from the 4-bit optimizer, and the SSL and causal papers contribute principled analyses with benchmark confirmations rather than large accuracy jumps.
