**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a component‑wise comparison and summary of experimental results across the five papers, using only the figures/tables provided. For each component, I highlight identical datasets (when present), relative performance, and key metrics (F1/Precision/Recall where available, or the paper’s task metrics).
> 
> 1) One‑stage, anchor‑free detector for hand/face–to‑person association (PBADet, ICLR’24)
> - Identical datasets: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman. Baselines include BPJDet variants (YOLOv5{s6,m6,l6}) and earlier multi‑stage methods.
> - BodyHands (Table 1):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73.
>   - BPJDet YOLOv5l6: 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39; YOLOv5m6: 85.3 / 86.80 / 78.13; YOLOv5s6: 84.0 / 85.68 / 77.86.
>   - Conclusion: On the identical BodyHands test set, PBADet outperforms all BPJDet variants across all three metrics, with the largest gains in Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP.
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2 & 3):
>   - Overall AP (all categories): PBADet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate); BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3. PBADet (YOLOv7) 42.7/41.5. So overall detection AP is comparable.
>   - Size‑stratified: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) has higher APM/APL (66.2/67.2 original vs BPJDet 63.8/61.8) when comparing original APs; subordinate APs also favor PBADet in APM/APL.
>   - Per‑category APs (persons/parts): Mixed: BPJDet YOLOv5l6 slightly higher for head/face/right/left hand in AP, while PBADet is similar or slightly higher on feet and person (e.g., person 62.4 vs 61.3).
>   - Association quality (average mMR−2, lower is better; Table 3): PBADet improves over BPJDet on most categories (e.g., head 27.9 vs 30.8, face 30.5 vs 31.8; hands and feet also lower for PBADet).
>   - Conclusion: On the identical COCOHumanParts benchmark, overall AP is comparable, PBADet is stronger on mid/large sizes and reduces mismatching rates (mMR−2) across most parts, while BPJDet retains slightly higher per‑category AP for some parts.
> - CrowdHuman (Table 5 & 6):
>   - Association (mMR−2 body‑face pair, lower is better): BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 50.1 slightly better than PBADet 50.8/50.9. However, PBADet achieves better detection MR−2 and AP for the body (e.g., MR−2 36.5 vs 40.7; AP body 91.6 vs 89.5).
>   - Conclusion: On the identical CrowdHuman face‑body association task (single part), association mMR−2 is very close with a small edge to BPJDet, while PBADet achieves better body detection quality.
> - Additional F1/Precision/Recall comparison vs pose method (Appendix A.2):
>   - On COCO val (using ED‑Pose keypoints as comparator): PBADet shows higher F1 across all parts (e.g., all‑parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; left‑hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87; right‑hand 47.34 vs 24.17), with higher Precision/Recall as well.
> 
> 2) Self‑supervised pretraining (JEPA vs MAE, NeurIPS’24)
> - Identical settings (deep linear and synthetic/temporal models):
>   - From ODE simulations (Fig. 2 & 4): JEPA shows greedy learning prioritized by regression coefficient ρ (influential features), whereas MAE prioritizes features by covariance λ; JEPA’s prioritization becomes stronger with depth. Spectrum transplant experiments (Eq. 14) quantify this (ratios in critical time reflect depth‑dependent bias), indicating JEPA focuses on informative/less noisy features under deep encoders.
> - ImageNet‑64 experiment (Appendix D, Fig. 7):
>   - Feature similarity (mean CCA): JEPA’s features trained on full vs bottom PCA subspace exhibit consistently higher mean CCA across epochs than MAE; for full vs top, MAE is higher and JEPA lower. The plotted curves show JEPA aligns better with the “bottom” (low‑variance, more semantic) subspace; MAE aligns more with “top” (high‑variance) subspace. (Exact numeric values are read from the curves; JEPA’s full–bottom mean CCA remains visibly higher through training.)
>   - Conclusion: Across identical synthetic settings and a matched ImageNet‑64 setup, JEPA’s training dynamics and representation similarity indicate better focus on predictive/low‑variance (less noisy) features than MAE.
> 
> 3) Memory‑efficient training with 4‑bit optimizer states (NeurIPS’23)
> - Identical datasets (same tasks across optimizers):
>   - GLUE finetuning (RoBERTa‑L; Table 2 & 7): 4‑bit AdamW achieves NLU mean 89.1, matching 8‑bit AdamW (89.1) and slightly exceeding 32‑bit AdamW (88.9); SM3 is lower (87.5). Per‑task (Table 7) shows parity with full precision across MNLI/QNLI/QQP/RTE/SST‑2/MRPC/CoLA/STS‑B.
>   - SQuAD/SQuAD 2.0 (Table 9): 4‑bit AdamW achieves SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6 (32‑bit), with similar EM; on SQuAD 2.0, 4‑bit F1 88.4 vs 88.8 (32‑bit). SM3 lags (e.g., SQuAD F1 91.7).
>   - E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2 Medium; Table 2 & 8): BLEU 67.8 (4‑bit) vs 67.7 (32‑bit) vs 67.5 (8‑bit) vs 67.2 (Adafactor). Other metrics (NIST/METEOR/ROUGE‑L/CIDEr) are on par.
>   - ImageNet‑1k pretraining (Swin‑T; Table 2): CLS Top‑1 accuracy 80.8 (4‑bit) close to 81.2 (32‑bit) and 81.0 (8‑bit); Adafactor/SM3 lower (80.0/79.0). Ablations (Table 6) show that rank‑1/linear quantization of second moment and B128/DE for first moment give best 4‑bit results.
>   - WMT14 En–De (Transformer‑Base; Table 2): SacreBLEU 26.28 (4‑bit) vs 26.61 (32‑bit) vs 26.66 (8‑bit); essentially comparable.
>   - LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3): 4‑bit AdamW matches or slightly improves over 32‑bit on MMLU and commonsense (e.g., 13B: MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8; ARC‑e 64.1 vs 63.6; ARC‑c 48.0 vs 48.3; OBQA 45.2 vs 45.2). Training loss curves (Fig. 4) overlap.
> - Memory/time efficiency (Table 4 & 5):
>   - LLaMA‑7B (FSDP, two A100 80GB): total memory 31.87 GB (4‑bit) vs 75.40 GB (32‑bit); time 3.07 h vs 3.35 h.
>   - RoBERTa‑L (single 4090): 3.00 GB (4‑bit fused) vs 5.31 GB (32‑bit); similar or faster step time with fused kernels.
>   - GPT‑2 Medium (4×4090): 4.62 GB (4‑bit) vs 6.89 GB (32‑bit); time ~2.11 h (4‑bit fused) vs 2.13 h (32‑bit).
>   - Largest trainable model on 80GB (Table 5): 4‑bit AdamW fine‑tunes up to OPT‑6.7B and LLaMA‑7B on a single 80GB GPU, while 32‑bit is limited to OPT‑1.3B.
> - Conclusion: On identical tasks (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG, ImageNet‑1k, WMT14, LLaMA fine‑tuning), 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit/8‑bit accuracy while reducing optimizer memory by up to ~58% and enabling much larger models under fixed memory.
> 
> 4) Causal discovery with unobserved factors via rank constraints (RLCD, ICLR’24)
> - Identical datasets (synthetic categories): Latent tree, latent measurement, general latent models; baselines: Hier. rank, PC, FCI, GIN, RCD.
> - F1 on full skeleton (VG = observed+latent; Table 2):
>   - Latent tree: RLCD 0.98 (10k) vs Hier.rank 0.60, PC ~0.37, FCI ~0.38, GIN ~0.41, RCD ~0.33.
>   - Latent measurement: RLCD 0.91 (10k) vs PC/FCI ~0.49–0.51, Hier.rank ~0.53; GIN ~0.47; RCD ~0.34.
>   - Latent general: RLCD 0.80 (10k) vs Hier.rank 0.45, PC 0.32, FCI 0.28, GIN 0.35, RCD 0.36.
> - F1 on observed skeleton (XG; Table 3):
>   - RLCD leads across all categories/samples: e.g., latent general 0.78 (10k) vs PC 0.45, FCI 0.41, RCD 0.44.
> - SHD (Appendix D.1, Table 4): RLCD has consistently smaller SHD than baselines for all categories and sample sizes (e.g., latent tree 10k: SHD 0.7 vs ≥9.0; latent general 10k: 21.4 vs ≥26.0).
> - Real‑world: Big Five dataset (Fig. 5) shows a plausible latent+indicator network; (qualitative result, no baselines on this set).
> - Conclusion: On identical synthetic benchmarks, RLCD substantially improves F1 and reduces SHD vs rank‑based (Hier.rank) and CI‑based (PC/FCI) baselines, and vs GIN/RCD, especially on general latent structures.
> 
> 5) Spectrally constrained EI RNNs (Dale’s law, NeurIPS’23)
> - Identical datasets across methods (standard RNN, DANN RNN, ColEI RNN): adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition (Fig. 2).
>   - Across all four tasks, ColEI networks converge slower and to worse final performance than both standard RNNs and DANN RNNs; DANN and standard RNNs are comparable.
>   - Gradient clipping disproportionately benefits ColEI (Appendix Fig. 10), indicating instability without spectral control.
>   - Spectrum transplant experiments (Fig. 4) show that imparting ColEI‑like spectra to RNNs degrades accuracy more than freezing signs, i.e., spectral properties matter more than sign constraints per se.
> - Conclusion: On the same tasks (adding, sMNIST, PTB, naturalistic recognition), DANN RNNs match standard RNN performance and clearly outperform simple column‑partitioned EI (ColEI) RNNs; performance gaps are corroborated by spectral analyses and controlled transplants.
> 
> Cross‑component observations on similar dataset types
> - Vision tasks: PBADet achieves SOTA association on BodyHands and superior mMR−2 on COCOHumanParts; 4‑bit AdamW maintains ImageNet‑1k Top‑1 within ~0.4% of 32‑bit while cutting memory significantly; JEPA aligns learned features with bottom PCA subspace on ImageNet‑64.
> - NLP tasks: 4‑bit AdamW retains GLUE, SQuAD, WMT14, and instruction‑tuning (LLaMA) performance vs 32‑bit/8‑bit; Dale’s EI results on PTB favor DANN/standard RNNs over ColEI.
> - F1/Precision/Recall: PBADet reports explicit precision/recall/F1 vs ED‑Pose (large gains in F1 and precision/recall for hands/feet). RLCD reports F1 for graph skeleton recovery; 4‑bit optimizer NLP/vision tasks mostly report accuracy/F1/EM; JEPA/Dale’s present learning curves without explicit F1.
> 
> Overall guidance (end‑to‑end implication from quantitative results)
> - Detector: PBADet is best supported for one‑stage, anchor‑free part–body association; on identical datasets it improves BodyHands AP/Joint AP and COCOHumanParts mMR−2, and matches or betters detection AP on larger objects; on CrowdHuman the association error is similar to BPJDet but detection quality metrics are better.
> - Self‑supervised pretraining: The JEPA results (synthetic, temporal, and ImageNet‑64) support choosing a joint‑embedding self‑distillation scheme (e.g., I‑JEPA/V‑JEPA family) when the goal is to avoid noisy pixels and emphasize influential/semantic features; curves show stronger alignment with the low‑variance subspace than MAE.
> - Memory‑efficient training: The 4‑bit optimizer paper demonstrates across identical tasks that 4‑bit AdamW matches 8/32‑bit accuracy while enabling far larger models on fixed memory; for Transformer fine‑tuning (including adapter‑style setups) it delivers consistent wins in memory with no accuracy loss.
> - Causal auditability: RLCD’s F1/SHD advantages on identical synthetic latent graphs show it recovers latent structures using rank constraints better than prior rank/CI/Gaussian‑noise methods; applicable when hidden confounders/mediators are expected.
> - RNN design under Dale’s law: For sequential modules, recurrent DANNs (spectrally well‑behaved EI) equal standard RNNs and outperform simple ColEI partitioning on identical benchmarks; spectrum (not just sign constraints) is the key determinant of performance.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, the end-to-end paper set is:
> 
> **1. PBADet** — one-stage, anchor-free part-body association detector. It extends anchor-free detection with a single part-to-body center offset, so one model detects hands/face and associates them with the correct person (universal for multi-part: head, face, left/right hands/feet).
> - Results: On BodyHands, PBADet (YOLOv7, 36.9M params) reaches HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 — beating BPJDet (85.9/86.91/84.39) and all two-stage baselines (BodyHands, MaskRCNN variants) with a smaller model. On COCOHumanParts, it matches BPJDet in AP and leads in AP_M/AP_L and lowest mMR−2 across head/face/hands. On CrowdHuman face-body association it gives best body MR−2 (36.5) and competitive AP. Ablations show association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment all boost association accuracy; uses IoU/DFL/classification losses.
> 
> **2. "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** — analyzes joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA) self-distillation pretraining. It shows JEPA has an implicit bias to prioritize high-regression-coefficient (high-ρ, low-variance/noise) features, increasingly with depth, while MAE orders learning by covariance λ only.
> - Results: theory + simulations show JEPA learns "slow"/predictive low-noise features first; ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (measured by CCA), i.e., it avoids noisy pixels. So this justifies JEPA-style self-distillation over MAE for your pretraining.
> 
> **3. "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** — 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW (B128 block size + rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluded linear quantizer; optional factorized 2nd moment "4-bit Factor"). Works with Adam-like optimizers and fine-tuning, incl. LoRA-style/language-model fine-tuning of Transformers.
> - Results: on GLUE (RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD (94.5 vs 94.6), E2E-NLG, ImageNet (Swin-T), WMT14 and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning, 4-bit variants match or slightly exceed 32-bit AdamW and 8-bit Adam, with up to 57.7% memory savings (LLaMA-7B trainable on one 80GB GPU). Sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor, SM3) lose accuracy, particularly on classification.
> 
> **4. RLCD** — flexible rank-based latent causal discovery. Uses rank (deficiency) constraints on sub-covariance matrices (canonical correlation tests) to uncover causal structure among operator/behavior variables even with unobserved confounders/mediators, identifying the Markov equivalence class.
> - Results: on synthetic latent-tree/measurement/general graphs, RLCD achieves highest F1 (e.g., latent-general 10k: 0.80 vs Hier.rank 0.45, PC 0.32, FCI 0.28, GIN 0.35, RCD 0.36) and lowest SHD across settings; on Big Five data it recovered a network-style model with latent dimensions. Without latents it asymptotically matches PC.
> 
> These four map exactly to your pipeline: PBADet (one-stage anchor-free hand/face-person detection, evaluated with AP/F1-style metrics), the JEPA analysis (pretraining that avoids noisy pixels), 4-bit optimizers (low-GPU-memory Adam fine-tuning of Transformers with adapters), and RLCD (rank-constraint causal analysis under unobserved factors). Note that PBADet itself uses SGD, so the 4-bit Adam paper serves as a drop-in memory-saving optimizer for the Transformer fine-tuning stage rather than for PBADet training.

**community 最终答案**

> The best end-to-end set of papers is:
> 
> 1. **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024) — detector.
> 2. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024) — pretraining.
> 3. **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023) — low-memory training.
> 4. **RLCD: A Flexible Rank-Based Method for Latent Causal Discovery** (ICLR 2024) — auditability.
> 
> **Comparison and analysis of experimental results:**
> 
> - **PBADet (detection):** It is the only one-stage, anchor-free detector in the set that directly handles hand/face-to-body association via a single part-to-body center offset. Experiments show it outperforms BPJDet and HierR-CNN on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts and achieves the best body MR−2 (36.5 vs BPJDet's 39.7–41.3) on CrowdHuman face-body association. Against ED-Pose it yields substantially higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands and feet. Ablations confirm the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment learning each improve association accuracy. This matches your F1/Precision evaluation criterion.
> 
> - **JEPA paper (pretraining):** This explains why a joint-embedding self-distillation (JEPA-style) objective suppresses noisy pixels: it is biased to learn high-influence, low-variance features, whereas MAE learns features by eigenvalue order and keeps noise. ImageNet-1K experiments (CCA analysis) confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features. So it directly justifies your choice to avoid pixel-reconstruction pretraining.
> 
> - **4-bit Optimizers (training efficiency):** Quantizes Adam/AdamW first moment with block size B128 and second moment with rank-1 normalization plus zero-point-excluded linear quantization (optionally factorized). Results: 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (89.1), SQuAD (94.5 F1), ImageNet (80.8), E2E-NLG (67.8 BLEU), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning, while cutting total memory up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU vs 75.4GB for 32-bit). Adafactor and SM3 save more memory but degrade accuracy, especially on classification. It is tested with LoRA-based fine-tuning of GPT-2 and LLaMA, so it pairs with adapter-style Transformer fine-tuning under limited GPU memory.
> 
> - **RLCD (causal analysis):** Uses rank-deficiency constraints on observed-variable covariances (canonical-correlation tests) to locate latent variables (confounders/mediators/effects) and recover the Markov equivalence class under weaker conditions than Hier. Rank; without latents it asymptotically matches PC. Experiments on synthetic latent-tree/measurement/general data show lower SHD and higher F1 than PC, FCI, GIN, RCD, and Hier. Rank, and a Big Five analysis yields a network-style model with no neuroticism latent. This covers your requirement to uncover operator-behavior relationships with unobserved factors via rank constraints.
> 
> Together, these four papers cover your pipeline end-to-end: PBADet for anchor-free part-body association, the JEPA analysis for noise-avoiding joint-embedding self-distillation pretraining, 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW with adapter/LoRA-style fine-tuning under tight GPU memory, and RLCD for auditable causal discovery under latent confounding.

</details>

Gold 1：

> Cross‑paper comparison of experimental results (restricted to the reported figures/tables)
> 
> Overview of identical vs. similar datasets across the five works
> - Identical datasets used within each sub‑area (thus directly comparable):
>   • Human part–body detection: BodyHands, COCO‑HumanParts, CrowdHuman (PBADet vs. BPJDet/Hier R‑CNN baselines). 
>   • EI recurrent networks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task (standard RNN/DANN vs. ColEI). 
>   • Self‑supervised learning: linear/synthetic settings (JEPA vs. MAE) and an ImageNet‑64 setup (I‑JEPA vs. MAE) for CCA trends. 
>   • Memory‑efficient training: GLUE (RoBERTa‑L), ImageNet (Swin‑T), E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2 M), SQuAD/SQuAD2.0, WMT14 En‑De (Transformer‑Base), and LLaMA instruction‑tuning (4‑bit vs. 8/32‑bit Adam/AdamW).
>   • Interpretable molecular generation: small chemistry sets (Isocyanates, Acrylates, Chain Extenders) and real‑world HOPV/PTC (FMG vs. MHG/DEG/JT‑VAE/Hier‑VAE/MoLeR/CLMs/ICL).
> - Across the five topics there are no shared datasets spanning all papers; comparisons are therefore made within each task family, and via “similar‑type” tasks (e.g., image recognition/representation; sequence modeling; structure generation).
> 
> 1) Anchor‑free human part–body detection on identical datasets (PBADet)
> BodyHands (Table 1)
> - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
> - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73.
> - Best prior (BPJDet YOLOv5l6): 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39.
> Conclusion: On BodyHands, PBADet outperforms BPJDet across all three metrics (hand detection and association), with large gains in conditional accuracy and joint AP.
> 
> COCO‑HumanParts (Table 2; identical dataset across methods)
> - Overall AP (AP.5:.95, orig./subord.):
>   • BPJDet YOLOv5l6: 43.6 / 43.3 (highest overall AP).
>   • PBADet YOLOv5l6: 43.0 / 41.8; PBADet YOLOv7: 42.7 / 41.5.
> - AP by scale (PBADet vs. BPJDet):
>   • APM/APL: PBADet (v5l6) 66.2/67.2 vs. BPJDet 63.8/61.8 → PBADet better on medium/large objects.
> - Per‑category AP:
>   • Person: PBADet (v5l6) 62.4 vs. BPJDet 61.3 (PBADet better).
>   • Head/Face: PBADet (v5l6) 54.6/44.6 vs. BPJDet 56.6/46.3 (BPJDet better).
>   • Hands/Feet: hands slightly mixed; feet BPJDet leads (e.g., r‑foot 39.6 vs. 37.7 for PBADet).
> - Association quality (lower is better; Table 3 mMR−2):
>   • Heads/Face/Hands: PBADet YOLOv7 achieves 29.2 (head), 31.3 (face), 41.1 (l‑hand), 42.7 (r‑hand), improving or matching BPJDet (head 30.8, face 31.8, l‑hand 41.6, r‑hand 42.2). 
>   • Feet: PBADet is worse (e.g., r‑foot 52.6 vs. BPJDet 49.1).
> Conclusion: On COCO‑HumanParts, BPJDet attains the top overall AP, but PBADet improves detection/association for medium/large scales and for person/head/face/hands in several metrics, while trailing on feet.
> 
> CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6; identical dataset across methods)
> - Body MR−2 (lower better): PBADet YOLOv7 36.5 (best among all listed), vs. BPJDet YOLOv5l6 40.7.
> - Face MR−2 and AP: PBADet YOLOv7 44.7 (face MR−2), 81.6 (face AP) comparable to/above BPJDet.
> - Pair mMR−2 (body‑face): PBADet 50.8 vs. BPJDet 50.1–51.4 (comparable).
> Conclusion: On CrowdHuman, PBADet attains the best body detection MR−2 and competitive association.
> 
> ED‑Pose comparison (Table 7; identical keypoint‑to‑box matching protocol)
> - All parts (F1): PBADet 48.52 vs. ED‑Pose 31.51; hands and feet also show higher Precision/Recall/F1 for PBADet.
> Conclusion: For part localization+association, PBADet substantially outperforms ED‑Pose under the reported evaluation.
> 
> 2) Spectral analysis of EI constraints in RNNs (identical datasets; Dale’s Law study)
> Tasks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank (language modeling), and a naturalistic object recognition task.
> - Across all four tasks (Fig. 2 A–D), Column EI (ColEI) networks learn worse than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs, with higher variance across seeds; gradient clipping helps ColEI far more.
> - Spectral‑radius sweep (Appendix/Fig. 9): standard/DANN behave similarly; ColEI does better only at larger ρ but worse overall.
> - Spectrum transplant (Fig. 4B–C): Swapping singular‑value spectra impacts performance more than sign constraints:
>   • Final test error changes attributable to spectrum vs. sign constraints: for RNNs ~1.5% ± 0.3% (spectrum) vs. ~0.7% ± 0.3% (sign); for ColEI ~2% ± 1% (spectrum) vs. ~1% ± 1% (sign).
> Conclusion: On identical datasets, DANN/standard RNNs outperform ColEI; spectral properties (unimodal, clustered singular values) explain more variance in performance than the mere presence of EI sign constraints. Normalized SVD entropy correlates (anti‑correlates) with test error across EI ratio and network size.
> 
> 3) Self‑supervised learning in deep networks (JEPA vs. MAE)
> - Linear/synthetic settings (Figs. 2–4 & Thms. 3.2–3.6):
>   • JEPA exhibits greedy learning in regression‑coefficient ρ (feature “influence”), especially with deeper encoders (L>1), while MAE greedily follows variance/covariance λ. Critical‑time analysis (Eqs. 12–14) quantifies this difference.
>   • In temporal generative models (Fig. 3), JEPA prioritizes slowly varying, informative features (higher ρ), and converges to lower‑amplitude weights for noisy modes, consistent with avoiding noisy pixel features.
> - ImageNet‑64 CCA (Appendix D; identical data across JEPA vs. MAE):
>   • I‑JEPA shows higher mean CCA between full and “bottom‑PCA” images; MAE shows higher CCA on “top‑variance” images. 
> Conclusion: While not reported as accuracy numbers, experiments consistently show JEPA learns latent features with high predictive influence (ρ) and focuses on low‑variance, semantic subspaces; MAE emphasizes high‑variance reconstruction. (JEPA uses MSE‑style latent prediction; MAE uses pixel‑space MSE.)
> 
> 4) Memory‑efficient training with 4‑bit optimizer states (identical datasets per task; Adam/AdamW vs. 8/32‑bit)
> Main results (Tables 2–5):
> - GLUE (RoBERTa‑L; NLU mean): 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 vs. 32‑bit 88.9 and 8‑bit 89.1 (parity; per‑task Table 7 shows close or better on multiple tasks). Losses are standard CE for classification.
> - ImageNet (Swin‑T; classification top‑1): 4‑bit AdamW 80.8% vs. 32‑bit 81.2% (−0.4 pp); 4‑bit Factor 80.9%.
> - E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2 M; BLEU): 4‑bit AdamW 67.8 vs. 32‑bit 67.7 (parity), with stable training when the second moment excludes zero‑point (DE‑0/Linear mapping) and rank‑1 normalization (Table 1).
> - SQuAD F1: 4‑bit AdamW 94.5 vs. 32‑bit 94.6 (parity). SQuAD 2.0 F1: 88.4 vs. 88.8 (Table 9).
> - WMT14 En‑De (Transformer‑Base; SacreBleu): 4‑bit 26.28 vs. 32‑bit 26.61 (close).
> - LLaMA instruction‑tuning (MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA): 4‑bit matches or slightly exceeds 32‑bit across 7B/13B/33B settings (e.g., 7B MMLU 38.9 vs. 38.7).
> - Memory/time: 4‑bit cuts optimizer memory by >50% vs. 8/32‑bit, and total training memory by up to 57.7% (LLaMA‑7B: 75.4 GB → 31.9 GB). Largest trainable model on 80GB improves from OPT‑1.3B (32‑bit) to OPT‑6.7B (4‑bit) and enables LLaMA‑7B on a single 80GB GPU (Table 5). Fused kernels recover or improve throughput.
> Ablations tied to reported issues:
> - Zero‑point problem in second moment (Fig. 3 & Table 1): Excluding zero (DE‑0/Linear mapping) and rank‑1 normalization stabilize training; “Rank‑1 + Linear” attains best BLEU (67.8) with 0% instability.
> - First moment quantization: Smaller block size (B128/DE) better tracks outliers than B2048/DE (Fig. 1), improving accuracy.
> Conclusion: On identical datasets, 4‑bit AdamW/Factor match 8/32‑bit accuracy with substantially lower memory. The gains stem from handling moment outliers and removing zero‑point for the second moment; optimizers include SGD variants (SGD/Adam/AdamW), with AdamW the primary.
> 
> 5) Interpretable and synthesizable molecular generation via multi‑modal grammar (FMG)
> Small datasets (Table 1; identical datasets across methods)
> - Valid/Unique/Novelty: FMG reaches 100% across Isocyanates/Acrylates/Chain Extenders.
> - Diversity (Div): FMG 0.73/0.46/0.85 (respectively), competitive though not always the highest.
> - Synthesizability & class membership: Retro* success (RS) and membership are among the best:
>   • Isocyanates: RS 61.7%, Memb. 99.6%.
>   • Acrylates: RS 93.0%, Memb. 100%.
>   • Chain Extenders: RS 99.1%, Memb. 99.8%.
> - Compared baselines: VAE variants often collapse (very low Unique/Div), CLMs/ICL have validity/uniqueness issues despite strong RS/Memb. on the few valid generations; DEG/STONED/MHG cover syntax but trail FMG in RS/Memb.
> Real‑world datasets (Table 2; identical datasets across methods)
> - HOPV/PTC: FMG attains 100% Valid/Unique and ~0.92–0.93 RS; Novelty 100% (PTC 92%+);
> - Diversity: Top‑tier among methods (e.g., highest on HOPV); membership high for PTC, mixed for HOPV (trade‑off curves Fig. 4/6).
> - FMG‑Text (text‑only) is competitive but generally trails image‑based FMG on Div/RS.
> Interpretability and validation: LLM‑judge tournament correlates with expert preference (71% agreement; p=1.1e‑5), and expert case studies report mostly correct/partially correct step‑by‑step reasoning.
> Conclusion: On identical chemistry datasets, FMG achieves perfect validity/uniqueness, high Retro* success, and near‑perfect membership on small sets, while staying competitive on larger HOPV/PTC. Its interpretable chain‑of‑thought is validated by experts and used to select better grammars.
> 
> Cross‑domain synthesis (similar‑type datasets and losses)
> - Image tasks: PBADet (COCO/CrowdHuman) and Optimizers (ImageNet Swin‑T) both operate in the vision domain; PBADet’s anchor‑free association improves medium/large object detection/association on COCO and overall MR−2 on CrowdHuman, while 4‑bit AdamW preserves top‑1 accuracy on Swin‑T within −0.4 pp of 32‑bit.
> - Sequence modeling / language: Dale’s study (seqMNIST/PTB) shows spectral clustering (high SVD entropy) yields better training; 4‑bit AdamW maintains RoBERTa‑L GLUE and PTB‑style QA scores; JEPA linear theory explains why latent‑space prediction avoids noisy features (predictive features with high ρ), complementing Dale’s generalization findings.
> - Losses and metrics: MAE/JEPA use MSE‑type objectives (pixel vs. latent); PBADet uses classification + IoU/DFL losses (task‑aligned CE‑style Lcls + IoU + DFL); Optimizers keep task‑appropriate CE for classification and MSE‑family losses for regression/translation. Reported metrics include Precision/Recall/F1 (PBADet vs. ED‑Pose), AP/AP50, MR−2/mMR−2 (detection), BLEU/SacreBleu (NLG/MT), F1/EM (QA), and mean accuracy/correlation (GLUE).
> 
> Key takeaways per topic
> - PBADet: On identical COCO/CrowdHuman/BodyHands datasets, the proposed anchor‑free part‑to‑body association improves BodyHands across all metrics, wins CrowdHuman body MR−2, and offers better medium/large‑scale APs on COCO while trading some small‑part AP (feet) vs. BPJDet.
> - EI RNNs: On identical sequence and language datasets, DANN/standard RNNs consistently outperform ColEI. Spectral properties (unimodal, clustered singular values; higher SVD entropy) explain larger performance differences than sign constraints alone.
> - JEPA vs. MAE: JEPA prioritizes influential, predictive features (high ρ) and learns “slow”, low‑variance semantics; MAE prioritizes high‑variance reconstruction. On ImageNet‑64, I‑JEPA aligns better with “bottom‑PCA” features (higher mean CCA), consistent with avoiding noisy pixel features.
> - 4‑bit optimizers: On identical GLUE/ImageNet/NLG/QA/MT/LLaMA tests, 4‑bit AdamW achieves accuracy on par with 8/32‑bit while reducing total training memory up to 57.7%. Rank‑1 normalization and zero‑point‑free quantization are crucial.
> - FMG: On identical chemistry datasets, FMG yields 100% validity/uniqueness, strong synthesizability (RS), and near‑perfect class membership on small datasets; competitive Div/RS on HOPV/PTC with interpretable, expert‑aligned reasoning.
> 
> Notes on identical datasets across all five works
> - There are no datasets shared across all five papers. Identical‑dataset comparisons are therefore made within each task family as summarized above; for cross‑family context, we used “similar‑type” dataset groupings without mixing metrics or fabricating results.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, here are the papers addressing each theme, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Interpretable/synthesizable molecular generation with multi-modal models
> - **FMG (Foundation Molecular Grammar)** — renders molecules as images, describes them as text via MMFMs, and induces an interpretable graph grammar (prompt learning + chain-of-thought + LLM debate). Trained on only 0.05% of refined ZINC, it produces valid/unique/novel/diverse molecules on MOSES, but **weak distributional fidelity (FCD 26.30; SNN 0.29)**. GPT-4o expert case studies: 18 correct, 2 partially correct, none wrong.
> - Related: **CoBO** (latent-space Bayesian optimization) improves Perindopril MPO from 0.6844 to 0.7921 at 20k calls and is SOTA on Guacamol/TDC DRD3, with latent–objective correlation >0.7.
> 
> ## 2. Self-supervised learning predicting in latent space (JEPA)
> - **"Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** — analyzes deep linear self-distillation: JEPA is implicitly biased to learn **high-influence (high regression-coefficient) features**, suppressing noisy pixel-level features, whereas MAE's ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE (measured by CCA); depth strengthens noise suppression.
> - **LDReg** complements this: regularizing local intrinsic dimensionality improves linear evaluation/transfer/COCO detection for SimCLR, BYOL, and MAE (ResNet-50, ViT-B).
> 
> ## 3. Spectral analysis of E/I-constrained recurrent nets
> - **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** — ColEI RNNs (column-wise E/I sign constraints) learn worse with higher variance on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition. **Spectral properties matter more than sign constraints** (sign constraints explain only ~1% of a 2.3%±0.6% gap). ColEI's singular-value spectrum is multimodal/dispersed vs. the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle of standard RNNs/DANNs; **normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error** — small networks with balanced E/I and high NSE beat larger networks with skewed E/I. Gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> 
> ## 4. Anchor-free human part-body detection
> - **PBADet** — one-stage anchor-free part-body association via a single part-to-body center offset; trained/evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, COCO-WholeBody, CrowdHuman. Results: anchor-free part-to-body (HandAP 89.1, Cond. Acc. 92.62, JointAP 85.98) > anchor-based part-to-body (88.4/92.31/85.28) > BPJDet anchor-based body-to-part (85.3/86.80/78.13). COCOHumanParts all-category AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6), beating BPJDet and HierR-CNN. Against ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands/feet; ablation shows association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each help.
> 
> ## 5. Memory-efficient low-bit (4-bit) optimizer states
> - **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** — compresses Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (B128/DE + rank-1/zero-exclusion for second moment, optional factorization). Results: 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit on GLUE (89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), E2E-NLG (67.8 vs 67.7), MT (26.28 vs 26.61), and Swin-T ImageNet (80.8 vs 81.2); up to **57.7% memory savings** (LLaMA-7B: 75.4GB→31.9GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; 4-bitFactor roughly halves 8-bit optimizer-state memory.
> - Related: **BSO/T-BSO** (binary spiking online optimization) removes stored latent weights (memory O(n²L/32), near-constant across timesteps vs BPTT), reaching 94.86% (CIFAR-10), 74.27% (CIFAR-100), 96.12% (GSC) with ~20–31× smaller models; **MLMC** reduces distributed SGD compression bias on CIFAR-10/ResNet18 and BERT/SST-2.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting analysis
> - **Losses/embeddings:** GEEA combines **BCE** (prior reconstruction of graph/attribute features) and **MSE** (post-reconstruction of joint and image embeddings, using pretrained embeddings instead of pixels) for entity alignment (SOTA Hits@1/MRR on DBP15K). The contrastive-embeddings paper shows the optimal negative-pair similarity is −1/(n−1) and that a variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and full ImageNet and helps small-batch training.
> - **Metrics/benchmarks:** MNIST and CIFAR-10/100 appear in the Hessian-spectrum study (power-law spectra correlate with generalization; e.g., LeNet on CIFAR-10 Pearson 0.72 with test error; lost with noise/large batches) and in Edge-GCN (MNIST 94.37%, CIFAR-10 57.44%). **No document in this collection reports SVHN experiments** — that benchmark is not covered by the retrieved context. F1 is reported by CMA for causal discovery (Arctic sea ice F1=0.57; AD consensus F1=0.81) and by PBADet vs ED-Pose, not on MNIST/SVHN.
> - **Time-series considerations:** The Dale's Law paper uses row-wise sequential MNIST and PTB (temporal tasks); RaMP shows multi-step Q-functions reduce compounding error (matching Dreamer on pixel-based tasks); ChaosBench finds weather models lose skill vs climatology beyond ~15–20 days, with ensembles and direct training mitigating autoregressive error accumulation; Synthcity benchmarks regular/irregular time-series generation (TimeGAN, TimeVAE, FourierFlow). These are the only temporal-modeling contexts present.
> 
> **Caveats:** SVHN results and any exact Precision numbers on MNIST/CIFAR-100 are absent from the collection; the closest Precision/F1 evidence is PBADet's hand/foot detection and CMA's causal-graph F1.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the available context, here are the papers addressing each theme and a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> **1. Interpretable & synthesizable molecular generation with multi-modal models**
> - **FMG (Foundation Molecular Grammar)** (doc 4888a3c3): uses multi-modal foundation models to induce interpretable molecular graph languages (molecules rendered as images, described as text, aligned via prompt learning). Trained on only 0.05% of refined ZINC, it yields valid/unique/novel/diverse molecules on MOSES but with weak distributional fidelity (FCD 26.30; SNN 0.29). In GPT-4o expert case studies (HOPV, isocyanates, acrylates, chain extenders), 18/20 responses were correct and 2 partially correct (none wrong). Related: **GeoBFN** (3D molecule generation; QM9 stability 90.87% molecules/99.08% atoms, 94.25% at 4k steps) and **CoBO** (latent-space Bayesian optimization; improves latent–objective correlation >0.7, Perindopril MPO 0.6844→0.7921).
> 
> **2. Self-supervised learning predicting in latent space to avoid noisy pixel features**
> - **JEPA self-distillation analysis** (doc 40fde037): proves via deep linear networks that JEPA's latent-space prediction biases toward high-influence features and suppresses noise, unlike MAE's pixel reconstruction. Critical times show depth strengthens noise suppression; on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA (perceptual) subspace than MAE (measured by CCA).
> - **LDReg** (doc 51526068): counters local dimensional collapse via local intrinsic dimensionality regularization; on ImageNet (ResNet-50/ViT-B) it improves linear evaluation (e.g., SimCLR 64.3→64.8, BYOL 67.6→68.5, MAE 57.0→57.6), transfer to CIFAR-10/100, and COCO detection/segmentation.
> - **Contrastive embedding similarities** (doc 160e1407): variance-reduction auxiliary loss improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and ImageNet, and temperature robustness.
> 
> **3. Spectral analysis of excitatory/inhibitory constraints in recurrent nets**
> - **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (doc e63a94c4): ColEI (column E/I sign constraints) RNNs learn worse with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition. Sign constraints account for only part of the gap (RNNs 0.7±0.3%, ColEI 1±1%); the dominant factor is the initial spectrum — ColEI weight matrices have multimodal, dispersed singular values (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure) versus the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle of standard/DANN RNNs. Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance across sizes/EI ratios (small balanced networks beat large skewed ones). Gradient clipping substantially helps ColEI.
> 
> **4. Anchor-free human part–body detection trained on COCO**
> - **PBADet** (doc 08b70bc3): one-stage anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center offset. On BodyHands and COCOHumanParts it outperforms BPJDet and HierR-CNN. On COCOHumanParts: AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6) for original/subordinate categories. Anchor-free beats anchor-based (Hand AP 89.1 vs 88.4; Cond. accuracy 92.62 vs 92.31; Joint AP 85.98 vs 85.28). vs pose estimator ED-Pose on COCO val: PBADet gives far higher Precision/Recall/F1 (e.g., left hand 37.63/60.82/46.50 vs 18.36/30.34/22.87; all parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs 24.09/45.51/31.51). On CrowdHuman it leads body MR-2 with competitive AP. Related self-supervised alternative: **HASSOD** (improves zero-shot Mask AR on SA-1B 17.0→26.0 and LVIS 20.2→22.5; argues COCO AP is misleading for class-agnostic detection).
> 
> **5. Memory-efficient training with low-bit (4-bit) optimizer states**
> - **4-bit Optimizers** (doc 8d5e1455): quantizes Adam/AdamW first/second moments (B128 block + dynamic exponent; rank-1 normalization/zero-point exclusion for second moment; optional factorization). Across RoBERTa-L (GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9), Swin-T/ImageNet (80.8 vs 81.2), GPT-2 Medium (E2E BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7), Transformer MT (26.28 vs 26.61) and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (MMLU etc.), 4-bit matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW while saving up to 57.7% memory (LLaMA-7B trains on one 80GB GPU; 4x larger OPT trainable). Adafactor/SM3 save more but degrade, especially on image classification.
> - **MLMC compression** (doc fe0a4443): 2-bit fixed-point/QSGD compression for distributed SGD with ResNet-18 on CIFAR-10, improving communication efficiency and final accuracy vs biased 2-bit quantization and uncompressed SGD.
> 
> **Cross-cutting comparison/analysis**
> - **Losses/embeddings**: MSE appears in latent-space SSL (JEPA), in time-series forecasting (G-Sim's per-dimension MSE, e.g., COVID-19 val MSE 2.85→1.89), and in vector-graphics generation (VectorGrimoire, where smaller patches improve MSE); CE loss appears in in-context meta-learning transformers (3e359365) and classification tasks; embeddings (SimCLR/CLIP features) are central to the contrastive and graph foundation-model papers.
> - **Precision/F1**: PBADet's Precision/Recall/F1 gains over ED-Pose; CMA causal discovery (F1 0.57 on Arctic sea ice, 0.81 on AD consensus graph); RLCD latent causal discovery (higher F1 than PC/FCI/GIN/RCD).
> - **MNIST/CIFAR-100**: covered by the Hessian-spectrum study (582d138d; power-law Hessian spectra on MNIST/CIFAR-10/100 with SGD/Adam/etc., power-law slope correlates with generalization, e.g., LeNet CIFAR-10 Pearson 0.72) and BSO (CIFAR-10 94.86%, CIFAR-100 74.27%, ImageNet 57.76%).
> - **SVHN**: I found **no paper in the provided context that reports SVHN experiments** — this benchmark cannot be covered from this collection.
> - **Time-series**: G-Sim (LLM-proposed mechanistic simulators; COVID-19 validation Wasserstein loss 0.793→0.404 with MSE per compartment), ChaosBench (S2S prediction; most models lose skill vs climatology beyond ~15–20 days), Synthcity (synthetic time-series benchmarking; TabDDPM best for COVID-19 mortality after augmentation), and decision-aware spatiotemporal forecasting (DAML: direct BPR optimization improves decisions but degrades likelihood; DAML keeps BPR gains with little likelihood loss).
> 
> In short, the collection covers all five requested topics well except SVHN, and the strongest quantitative evidence is: FMG's interpretability at extreme data efficiency (with weak distributional fidelity), JEPA's implicit noise-avoidance bias, spectral NSE as a predictor of EI-RNN learning, PBADet's clear AP/F1 advantages on COCO-based part–body benchmarks, and 4-bit optimizer states achieving lossless-or-better accuracy with ~40–58% memory savings.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:365 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource‑constrained, multi‑modal pipeline: (1) on‑device hand/face association for HCI evaluated on COCO, (2) a chemistry assistant that proposes synthesizable molecules with interpretable substructures, and (3) LoRA end‑to‑end fine‑tuning of Transformers under tight GPU memory. I need research that shows how to use anchor‑free detection, avoid spurious high‑variance pixels via self‑supervised latent‑space prediction, understand how E/I constraints impact RNNs on sequential data, and shrink optimizer memory with 4‑bit Adam/AdamW while maintaining accuracy on MNIST/CIFAR‑100/SVHN and business metrics like Precision/F1. Practical guidance on losses (MSE, cross‑entropy), feature embeddings, and online implementation/diagrams would be ideal.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

Gold 1：

> Cross-domain comparison of experimental results from the five papers, grouped by identical datasets, similar task types, and dataset-specific outcomes:
> 
> 1) Hand/face association (anchor-free detection) — PBADET vs baselines
> Identical datasets and metrics
> • BodyHands (Table 1; identical splits and metrics):
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.
>   - PBADet (Ours, YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   - PBADet (Ours, YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>   Outcome: PBADet (both backbones) surpasses BPJDet on all three metrics; largest gains are in Conditional Accuracy (+~6 points) with comparable or slightly better Joint AP.
> 
> • COCOHumanParts (Table 2, identical tasks and per-category AP; Table 3, mismatch mMR−2):
>   - All categories AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate):
>     • BPJDet YOLOv5l6: 43.6/43.3
>     • PBADet YOLOv7: 42.7/41.5
>     • PBADet YOLOv5l6: 43.0/41.8
>   - Per-category AP: PBADet is competitive: Person (62.1–62.4), Head (54.5–54.6), Hands (~38.7–39.0), Feet (~37.5–31.5/30.9). PBADet leads in some size-specific APs (APM/APL) and selected categories vs BPJDet.
>   - Average mMR−2 (lower is better; Table 3):
>     • BPJDet YOLOv5l6: head 30.8, face 31.8, l-hand 41.6, r-hand 42.2, r-foot 49.1, l-foot 50.4
>     • PBADet YOLOv7: head 29.2, face 31.3, l-hand 41.1, r-hand 42.7, r-foot 52.6, l-foot 52.5
>     • PBADet YOLOv5l6: head 27.9, face 30.5, l-hand 36.2, r-hand 40.8, r-foot 50.4, l-foot 47.9
>   Outcome: PBADet reduces mismatch rate noticeably for heads, face, and hands (best with YOLOv5l6), while feet are mixed (sometimes similar/worse).
> 
> • CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6, identical face–body association and joint detection):
>   - Body MR−2 (lower better): PBADet YOLOv7 36.5 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 40.7 — best among joint detectors.
>   - Face MR−2: PBADet YOLOv7 44.7 vs BPJDet 46.3 — better (lower).
>   - Body AP: PBADet YOLOv7 91.6 vs BPJDet 89.5 — PBADet higher.
>   - Pair mMR−2 (body–face): PBADet ~50.8–50.9 vs BPJDet best 50.1 — comparable association mismatch rate.
>

>   - All parts: ED-Pose Precision/Recall/F1 = 24.09/45.51/31.51 vs PBADet 39.41/63.09/48.52 — PBADet substantially higher Precision, Recall, and F1 for hands/feet when evaluated with IoU>0.5 boxes and association success.
> 
> Dataset-specific takeaways
> • PBADet consistently improves practical HCI-relevant association metrics: highest Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP on BodyHands; lower MR−2 on CrowdHuman; competitive to better mMR−2 on COCOHumanParts for head/face/hands.
> 
> 2) Chemistry assistant (interpretable, synthesizable molecules) — FMG vs grammar/LLM baselines
> Identical datasets and metrics (Tables 1–2)
> • Small monomer sets (Isocyanates, Acrylates, Chain Extenders):
>   - FMG: Valid 100% and Unique 100% on all three; Diversity (Div) ≈ 0.73/0.46/0.85; Retro* success (RS) 61.7%/93.0%/99.1%; Membership ≈ 99.6%/100%/99.8%.
>   - DEG (data-efficient grammar): Valid 100% across; Unique 100%/100%/100%; Div ≈ 0.86/0.86/0.93; RS 27.2%/43.9%/67.5%; Membership 96.3%/69.6%/93.5%.
>   - MHG / JT-VAE / Hier-VAE / MoLeR / STONED show various trade-offs; notably VAEs often suffer from very low uniqueness on these tiny datasets (e.g., JT-VAE Unique as low as 0.5–5.8%).
>   - GPT-4 ICL: Often high RS/Membership when valid, but low Valid/Unique (e.g., on Chain Extenders Valid 35.1%, Unique 63.5%), highlighting fragility without a formal grammar.
>   Outcome: On identical small datasets, FMG jointly maximizes validity, uniqueness, high RS, and near-perfect class membership — outperforming grammar/LLM baselines especially on RS and Membership while keeping 100% Valid/Unique.
> 
> • Real-world datasets (HOPV and PTC):
>   - FMG: Valid 100%, Unique 100%, Novelty 100%, Diversity ≈ 0.93 on both datasets; RS reported at competitive levels (text notes FMG ties for top-2 diversity and achieves high RS while sustaining full validity/uniqueness). Membership is not strictly defined in these domains; FMG remains competitive against strong baselines.
>   - Compared baselines: MoLeR (FT/I), DEG, RW (expert), GPT-4 ICL, CLMs. FMG is among the only methods achieving 100% uniqueness with top diversity, while also maintaining high RS (≈0.93 average reported) — outperforming many baselines on the joint criteria of Valid/Unique/Div/RS.
> 
> Similar-task comparison
> • Against grammar learners (MHG/DEG) and neural scaffold models (JT-VAE/Hier-VAE/MoLeR), FMG’s tournament-ranked, interpretable grammar consistently preserves 100% validity/uniqueness and raises RS/Membership without expert-labeled vocabularies—meeting synthesizability and coverage simultaneously.
> 
> Dataset-specific takeaways
> • Small data regime: FMG maintains robustness where VAEs collapse (uniqueness near zero) and CLMs/ICL struggle with validity.
> • Larger, more complex domains (HOPV/PTC): FMG keeps 100% Unique, achieves top-tier diversity (~0.93) and strong RS, comparing favorably with expert methods (RW) and finetuned neural baselines.
> 
> 3) Memory-efficient optimizers (4-bit Adam/AdamW) — accuracy, time, and memory
> Identical datasets and metrics (Tables 2–4)
> • RoBERTa-L (GLUE; NLU mean Acc/Cor):
>   - 32-bit AdamW 88.9; 8-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit AdamW 89.1; 4-bit Factor 88.9 — 4-bit matches 32-bit and 8-bit within noise while cutting optimizer state to 4-bit.
> • Swin-T (ImageNet-1k Top-1):
>   - 32-bit 81.2; 8-bit 81.0; 4-bit AdamW 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9 — small drops (≤0.4) vs full-precision.
> • GPT-2 Medium (E2E-NLG BLEU):
>   - 32-bit 67.7; 8-bit 67.5; 4-bit 67.8; 4-bit Factor 67.6 — 4-bit equals or slightly exceeds full-precision.
> • RoBERTa-L (SQuAD F1):
>   - 32-bit 94.6; 8-bit 94.5; 4-bit 94.5; 4-bit Factor 94.6 — parity.
> • Transformer-Base (WMT14 en–de SacreBleu):
>   - 32-bit 26.61; 8-bit 26.66; 4-bit 26.28; 4-bit Factor 26.45 — small drop (≤0.33) for 4-bit AdamW, Factor recovers part of it.
> • LLaMA instruction tuning (MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA; identical evaluations):
>   - LLaMA‑7B (MMLU): 32-bit 38.7 vs 4-bit 38.9 (slight gain); other tasks show parity-level differences (HellaSwag 74.6 vs 74.7; ARC‑e 61.5 vs 61.2; ARC‑c 45.1 vs 44.4; OBQA 43.4 vs 43.0).
>   - LLaMA‑13B: 4-bit equals or slightly exceeds 32-bit on several tasks (e.g., MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5).
>   - LLaMA‑33B: small regressions on some tasks (e.g., MMLU 56.4 vs 54.9) but overall competitive.
> 
> Time/memory (Table 4)
> • LLaMA‑7B, FSDP (2×A100 80GB): 32‑bit: 75.40 GB; 4‑bit: 31.87 GB (−57.7% total memory), training time 3.35 h → 3.07 h (fused ~3.11 h).
> • RoBERTa‑L: 5.31 GB → 3.00 GB (−43.5%); time 3.93 min → 3.17 min (fused).
> • GPT‑2 Medium: 6.89 GB → 4.62 GB (−34.4%); time 2.13 h → 2.11 h (fused).
> 
> Takeaways
> • On identical NLP/CV/MT datasets, 4‑bit Adam/AdamW maintains accuracy at or near full precision while reducing optimizer-state memory to 4 bits and improving or matching wall-clock time when fused kernels are used.
> 
> 4) Dale’s Law in RNNs — spectral properties drive performance differences (identical tasks)
> Identical tasks
> • Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank (language modeling), and Naturalistic Object Recognition (Fig. 2):
>   - Standard RNN and DANN (Dale’s ANN with EI parameterization) learn well across tasks.
>   - Column EI (ColEI; strict sign-constrained columns) learns worse (higher error/poorer accuracy) across all four tasks; gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially more than others.
> Spectrum transplant & EI-ratio/size studies
> • Swapping spectra vs sign constraints (Fig. 4): Giving ColEI the RNN singular value spectrum narrows most of the performance gap. Conclusion: singular value spectrum (multimodal/large outliers in ColEI) matters more than sign constraints per se.
> • Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) correlates strongly with test performance; low NSE (dispersed/multimodal spectra) degrades learning. Increasing inhibitory fraction or network size raises NSE and improves performance; small networks with few inhibitory units show worst spectra and worst results.
> 
> Takeaways
> • For identical sequential benchmarks, DANN (EI but with good spectra) matches standard RNNs, while naive ColEI underperforms; spectral pathology (large singular values, multimodal spectra) is the primary factor.
> 
> 5) JEPA vs MAE — avoiding spurious pixels via latent prediction (controlled sims + ImageNet)
> Controlled linear experiments
> • Deep linear encoders trained with JEPA vs MAE (Eqs. (7), (8)): both show greedy learning by feature covariance λ, but only JEPA prioritizes high-influence features (high regression coefficient ρ). When λ and ρ trends oppose, JEPA reverses the learning order (learns high‑ρ features first), while MAE stays λ‑first. JEPA’s ρ‑bias strengthens with depth.
> 
> ImageNet-64 experiment (Appendix D)
> • Using the “full vs bottom/top PCA subspace” protocol, JEPA’s learned representations match the low‑variance, perceptually relevant subspace earlier and more strongly (higher mean CCA on full↔bottom; lower on full↔top) than MAE throughout training — consistent with JEPA suppressing spurious, high-variance pixel detail and prioritizing semantic structure.
> 
> Overall cross-paper synthesis (aligned to the resource‑constrained, multi‑modal pipeline)
> • On-device HCI association (COCO/CrowdHuman): Anchor-free PBADet achieves higher Conditional Accuracy/Joint AP (BodyHands), lower MR−2 on CrowdHuman, and improved mMR−2 for heads/face/hands on COCOHumanParts versus anchor-based BPJDet — matching the need for accurate, lightweight association.
> • Chemistry assistant with interpretable substructures: FMG delivers 100% Valid/Unique with high RS and near‑perfect class membership on small monomer datasets, and strong diversity/RS on real‑world HOPV/PTC — outperforming or matching grammar learners and neural baselines, while producing step‑by‑step interpretable grammars.
> • JEPA-style self‑distillation: Experiments demonstrate JEPA’s depth‑dependent bias toward high‑influence features and better alignment to perceptual/low‑variance subspaces on ImageNet, supporting the goal of avoiding spurious high‑variance pixels.
> • Time‑series modeling under biological constraints: Across identical RNN benchmarks, DANN (EI with sound spectra) matches standard RNNs, while naive ColEI fails; spectrum control (NSE) is predictive — clarifying how E/I constraints can be used without sacrificing performance.
> • 4‑bit Adam/AdamW: On identical GLUE/ImageNet/E2E‑NLG/SQuAD/WMT14/LLaMA tasks, 4‑bit optimizers retain accuracy vs 32‑bit and 8‑bit while cutting total memory up to ~58% and improving throughput with fused kernels — aligning with tight-GPU-memory, end‑to‑end finetuning (including LoRA setups).
> 
> Where identical datasets were used, these must be highlighted:
> • COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman (PBADet vs BPJDet/others): PBADet shows superior Conditional Accuracy/Joint AP (BodyHands) and lower MR−2 (CrowdHuman), with competitive to better association on COCOHumanParts.
> • GLUE, ImageNet‑1k, E2E‑NLG, SQuAD, WMT14 en–de, LLaMA downstream tasks (4‑bit vs 32‑bit/8‑bit/Adafactor/SM3): 4‑bit maintains accuracy and improves memory/time.
> • Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, PTB, Naturalistic Object Recognition (RNNs): DANN≈Standard RNN > ColEI.
> • Isocyanates, Acrylates, Chain Extenders, HOPV, PTC (FMG vs grammar/neural/LLM baselines): FMG dominates validity/uniqueness, boosts RS and class‑specific membership on small sets, and attains top diversity and strong RS on real‑world sets.
> 
> Notes on losses/embeddings/diagrams (as reported in the papers’ experiments)
> • PBADet trains an anchor‑free multi‑head with IoU+DFL box loss and classification loss; association is learned with an ℓ1 center‑offset objective and task‑aligned top‑K assignment.
> • JEPA and MAE are analyzed with squared errors in latent vs input space respectively; JEPA’s latent prediction governs the observed feature‑learning order.
> • 4‑bit optimizer results are obtained with standard cross‑entropy objectives across GLUE/ImageNet/WMT and MSE-style/sequence losses where applicable (e.g., NLG BLEU evaluation); quantization methods include per‑block (B128) first moment, rank‑1/linear second moment, and factorization for second moments.
> • All four domains include clear implementation diagrams (e.g., PBADet pipeline, FMG learning/judge tournament, JEPA/MAE learning curves, optimizer memory/time tables) that match the reported experimental protocols.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here is the comparison and analysis of the experimental results found in the context, organized by your three pipeline components.
> 
> ## 1. Anchor-free hand/face association for HCI (PBADet, ICLR 2024)
> - **Method**: One-stage anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7) with a single **part-to-body center offset**; three heads (box via DFL, class, displacement) trained with **task-alignment loss (TOOD)** plus association loss. More compact than BPJDet's body-to-part representation (length 10 vs 15 for 3 parts).
> - **BodyHands (hand-body)**: PBADet YOLOv7 (36.9M params, 1024 input) gets **Hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98** vs BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (86.1M, 1536) **85.9/86.91/84.39** and the 700.3M BodyHands model 84.8/83.44/63.48 — better accuracy at much lower compute.
> - **COCO-HumanParts (multi-part)**: AP 42.7/41.5 on par with BPJDet, leading AP_M, AP_L, person and feet.
> - **CrowdHuman (face-body)**: best body MR-2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6); advantage over BPJDet is small for this single-part task.
> - **vs ED-Pose on COCO val (2693 imgs)**: PBADet all-parts **P/R/F1 = 39.41/63.09/48.52** vs 24.09/45.51/31.51 — much higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet.
> - **Ablations**: anchor-free beats anchor-based (89.1 vs 88.4 Hand AP; 85.98 vs 85.28 joint AP); removing association loss, multi-scale offsets, or task-alignment all degrade metrics.
> 
> ## 2. Avoiding spurious high-variance pixels via self-supervised latent-space prediction
> - **JEPA analysis (NeurIPS 2024)**: JEPA/self-distillation predicts in **latent space**, and is biased to learn **high-influence features** (high regression coefficients), suppressing noise; depth strengthens noise suppression. MAE (pixel-space reconstruction) orders features mainly by eigenvalue λ. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the **low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features** than MAE (CCA), directly supporting latent-space prediction over pixel prediction to avoid noisy/uninformative high-variance pixels.
> - **Related**: LDReg shows SSL representations can collapse *locally*; increasing local intrinsic dimensionality improves linear eval, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation, whereas global variance/covariance regularizers barely help.
> 
> ## 3. E/I constraints on RNNs over sequential data (Dale's Law, NeurIPS 2023)
> - ColEI (E/I sign-constrained columns) learns **worse and with higher variance** than standard RNNs and DANNs on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> - **Cause**: not the sign constraints but the **singular-value spectrum at initialization** — ColEI's spectrum is multimodal/dispersed (rank-one nilpotent column structure) vs unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur for RNNs/DANNs. Spectrum transplant experiments: spectra contribute more to the 2.3±0.6% gap (1.5±0.3% for RNN, 2±1% for ColEI) than sign constraints (0.7±0.3% / 1±1%).
> - Smaller networks and fewer inhibitory units worsen both spectrum and performance; **normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** anti-correlates with final test error. DANNs are robust even with a single inhibitory neuron.
> 
> ## 4. 4-bit Adam/AdamW memory reduction + LoRA fine-tuning
> - **Method** (NeurIPS 2023): smaller block size B128 + dynamic-exp for the first moment; **rank-1 normalization** and a **linear quantizer excluding the zero point** for the second moment; optional factorization ("4-bit Factor").
> - **Results vs 32-bit AdamW**: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2M BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7; **SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6**; WMT 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7, HellaSwag 74.7 vs 74.6; LLaMA-13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; LLaMA-33B 54.9 vs 56.4. Convergence curves closely align.
> - **Memory**: LLaMA-7B fine-tuning 75.4 GB → 31.87 GB (**57.7% saved**), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU; ~4× larger OPT models fit. Adafactor(β₁=0)/SM3 save more but degrade, especially on image classification.
> - **LoRA**: the 4-bit paper treats LoRA/delta-tuning as an alternative (tuning a subset avoids optimizer states). The Hessian paper notes LoRA-only fine-tuning (TinyLlama, MathQA) does not induce the power-law Hessian of full fine-tuning, and Hessian trace is a more reliable generalization indicator for LoRA. RTB uses LoRA for Stable Diffusion fine-tuning with stochastic timestep subsampling/batched gradients to cut memory.
> 
> ## 5. Chemistry assistant: synthesizable molecules with interpretable substructures
> - **Foundation Molecular Grammar (FMG)**: MMFM-guided grammar induction over expert-derived motifs with interpretable design narratives. On a 1k (0.05%) ZINC/MOSES subset it produces valid/unique/novel/diverse samples but **weak distributional fidelity (FCD 26.30, SNN 0.29)**; it is one of only two methods reaching 100% uniqueness (HOPV) and beats RW on synthesizability (RS) by 12–18%; expert GPT-4o case studies: 18 correct, 2 partially correct, none wrong. Image inputs beat text (FMG-Text) on diversity and synthesizability.
> - **CoBO**: latent-space Bayesian optimization aligning latent distances with objective values (Lipschitz + correlation regularization); state-of-the-art on 9 molecule-design tasks (Guacamol, TDC DRD3), lifting Perindopril MPO from 0.6844 to 0.7921 at 20k calls with latent-objective correlation >0.7.
> 
> ## Gaps / what the context cannot establish
> - The 4-bit optimizer paper **does not report MNIST/CIFAR-100/SVHN** or Precision/F1 "business metrics" for those datasets; the closest evidence is Swin-T ImageNet accuracy (80.8 vs 81.2) and SQuAD F1 (94.5 vs 94.6). Claims of accuracy retention on those specific datasets are unsupported by this collection.
> - No direct experiment ties JEPA/LDReg to a specific on-device HCI pipeline; the support is theoretical/ImageNet-based.
> - The E/I study is on small RNN benchmarks, not on LoRA or detection backbones.
> - No end-to-end LoRA-vs-full-fine-tuning accuracy comparison with Precision/F1 exists in the collection; the Hessian paper only analyzes LoRA adapter spectra.
> 
> Overall, the context supports: anchor-free one-stage detection with a single part-to-body offset (PBADet) beats anchor-based/two-stage baselines on association P/R/F1 at lower cost; latent-space self-supervised prediction is theoretically and empirically biased away from noisy high-variance features; E/I-RNN deficits are spectral, not sign-based; and 4-bit Adam/AdamW preserves accuracy while cutting memory up to ~58%, with FMG/CoBO providing interpretable, synthesizability-aware molecule generation.

**community 最终答案**

> Based only on the provided collection, here is the comparison/analysis of the experimental results for each component of your pipeline.
> 
> ## 1. Anchor‑free detection (PBADet, ICLR 2024) — hand/face association on COCO
> - **Method:** one‑stage anchor‑free part‑to‑body detection with a *single* part‑to‑body center offset (vs. BPJDet's body‑to‑part representation of length 6+K+2K vs. 5+K+2).
> - **BodyHands (hand‑body):** Ours (YOLOv7) HandAP **89.1**, Cond. Acc **92.62**, JointAP **85.98** — beats BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) (85.9/86.91/84.39) and Mask‑RCNN/BodyHands baselines by large margins, with a smaller model.
> - **COCOHumanParts:** AP.5:.95 = **43.0/41.8** (original/subordinate), on par with BPJDet (43.6/43.3); leads on AP_M/AP_L for person and feet; lowest avg mMR‑2 for head, face, both hands and right foot.
> - **COCO val vs ED‑Pose (pose estimator):** substantially higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet, e.g., all‑parts F1 **48.52 vs 31.51**; left‑hand F1 **46.50 vs 22.87**.
> - **CrowdHuman (face‑body, single part):** best body/face MR‑2 and body AP, but the advantage over BPJDet shrinks because a single‑part task doesn't exploit multi‑part scalability.
> - **Ablations:** anchor‑free head beats anchor‑based (89.1 vs 88.4 HandAP); part‑to‑body beats body‑to‑part; association loss, multi‑scale center offsets and TOOD task‑alignment each add accuracy.
> 
> ## 2. Avoiding spurious high‑variance pixels via latent‑space prediction (JEPA, NeurIPS 2024)
> - **Design:** MAE predicts in *input* space with MSE (L = ½E‖VW̄x−y‖²); JEPA predicts in *latent* space (L = ½E‖VW̄x−SG(W̄)y‖²).
> - **Result (deep‑linear analysis + ImageNet‑1K):** JEPA is implicitly biased to learn *influential* features (high regression coefficient ρ), whereas MAE prioritizes high‑covariance (often noisy) features even when uninformative. This bias requires a **deep encoder** and diminishes when shallow.
> - **Empirically:** I‑JEPA features align faster with the low‑variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA measure) — i.e., latent‑space prediction genuinely avoids noise‑dominated pixel subspaces.
> 
> ## 3. E/I (Dale's Law) constraints on RNNs (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Setup:** ColEI (column‑sign E/I constraint), recurrent DANN, and standard RNN on adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, natural‑object recognition.
> - **Results:** ColEI learns worse on **all four tasks** and is more variable across seeds; gradient clipping helps ColEI far more than others. Recurrent DANN respects Dale's Law but learns as well as standard RNNs.
> - **Root cause:** not the sign constraint per se (only 0.7±0.3% error effect) but the **initial singular‑value spectrum** — ColEI has a multimodal, dispersed spectrum (rank‑one nilpotent column‑mean term) vs. the quarter‑circle Marchenko–Pastur form of standard/DANN RNNs. Spectrum transplant: singular values contribute more (1.5±0.3% / 2±1%) than singular vectors or sign constraints.
> - **Diagnostic:** Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) at initialization **anti‑correlates with final test error**; smaller networks with balanced E/I (high NSE) outperform larger networks with skewed ratios.
> 
> ## 4. 4‑bit Adam/AdamW memory compression (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Design:** B128/DE quantization of the first moment, DE‑0 linear quantizer with zero‑point exclusion for the second moment, rank‑1 normalization, optional factorized second moment.
> - **Accuracy vs 32‑bit AdamW (same hyperparameters):** NLU (RoBERTa‑L/GLUE) **89.1 vs 88.9**; CLS (Swin‑T/ImageNet) **80.8 vs 81.2**; NLG (GPT‑2M/E2E BLEU) **67.8 vs 67.7**; QA (RoBERTa‑L/SQuAD F1) **94.5 vs 94.6**; MT (Transformer/WMT14) **26.28 vs 26.61**. LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine‑tuning: 4‑bit matches 32‑bit on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC‑e/c, OBQA.
> - **Memory:** up to **57.7%** training‑memory saving; enables LLaMA‑7B on a single 80GB GPU; trains ~4× larger OPT models. 4‑bitFactor adds further savings with equal/lossless accuracy.
> - **Caveat (important for your request):** the paper does **not** test MNIST/CIFAR‑100/SVHN, and no Precision/F1 business metrics are reported — those datasets/metrics do not appear for this optimizer in the collection, so such claims **cannot be established** from context.
> 
> ## Cross‑cutting practical notes (from context)
> - **Losses/embeddings:** latent‑space MSE (JEPA) vs input‑space MSE (MAE) is the key distinction for feature quality; PBADet uses IoU/DFL + classification + association branches with task‑alignment learning; FMG (chemistry) aligns molecular images/text with in‑context learning, giving interpretable substructure grammars.
> - **Chemistry assistant (FMG, ICML 2025):** on MOSES (0.05% ZINC subset) it achieves valid/unique/novelty **1.00**, diversity 0.90 but weak distributional fidelity (FCD 26.30, SNN 0.29); on small/real‑world datasets it leads on validity, uniqueness, diversity and Retro* synthesizability (e.g., RS 70%/78%, membership 100%/92%), with image inputs better than text for global substructure reasoning and synthesizability.
> - **Diagrams:** PBADet includes a full multi‑scale pipeline diagram (backbone → P1–P5 → detection heads with classification/localization/displacement branches); FMG provides workflow figures with image/text alignment.
