Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results across the five papers, organized by domain, datasets, and baselines. Where identical datasets are used, we make head‑to‑head comparisons and report the table/figure-derived metrics. We also note that there is no cross-paper dataset overlap; all identical-dataset comparisons are within each paper’s domain.
> 
> 1) Anchor‑free part–body association (PBADet, ICLR 2024)
> Identical datasets: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman
> Baselines: BPJDet (YOLOv5s6/m6/l6), Hier R‑CNN variants; for CrowdHuman, multiple pedestrian detection baselines
> 
> BodyHands (Table 1)
> - Metrics: Hand AP (↑), Conditional Accuracy (↑), Joint AP (↑)
> - Ours (YOLOv7): 89.1 AP, 92.62 Cond. Acc., 85.98 Joint AP
> - Ours (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 AP, 92.71, 85.73
> - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9 AP, 86.91, 84.39
> Summary: On the same dataset, PBADet surpasses BPJDet and all earlier two‑stage or anchor‑based methods across all three metrics. With the same YOLOv5l6 backbone, PBADet still improves Joint AP (85.73 vs 84.39).
> 
> COCOHumanParts (Tables 2, 3)
> - All‑category APs (AP.5:.95/AP.5/APM/APL, original and subordinate). Ours (YOLOv5l6): 43.0/41.8 (AP.5:.95), 70.0/68.4 (AP.5), 66.2/65.0 (APM), 67.2/64.4 (APL); BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6/43.3, 70.6/69.8, 63.8/63.2, 61.8/58.9. PBADet leads on APM/APL while BPJDet holds a marginal edge on the headline AP.5:.95.
> - Average mMR−2 (lower is better) per part (Table 3). Ours (YOLOv7): head 29.2, face 31.3, left hand 41.1, right hand 42.7, right foot 52.6, left foot 52.5. Ours (YOLOv5l6): 27.9, 30.5, 36.2, 40.8, 50.4, 47.9. BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 30.8, 31.8, 41.6, 42.2, 49.1, 50.4.
> Summary: PBADet reduces mismatched pair rates for heads/faces and (especially with YOLOv5l6) hands and left foot; BPJDet (l6) remains slightly better on right foot mMR−2 (49.1 vs 50.4). Overall, PBADet improves association quality, particularly for hands and some feet categories.
> 
> CrowdHuman (Appendix, Tables 5–6)
> - Face–body association (Table 5): Our YOLOv7 achieves best body MR−2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6); mMR−2 for body–face pairs is comparable (50.8–50.9) to BPJDet (best 50.1 with YOLOv5l6).
> - Broader crowded detection comparison (Table 6): Our YOLOv7 gives best body MR−2 among joint detectors (36.5) and competitive AP to heavier DETR-based models while keeping joint association.
> 
> Takeaway: On identical datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman), PBADet’s anchor‑free, task-aligned supervision improves pairwise association quality and scales better with multiple parts; it beats or matches BPJDet on most metrics, with some feet categories competitive.
> 
> 2) Spectral effects and Dale’s Law in RNNs (NeurIPS 2023)
> Identical tasks: Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task (all within paper)
> Methods: Standard RNN, Column E/I (ColEI) with sign constraints, and Dale’s ANN (DANN) recurrent architecture
> 
> Learning curves across tasks (Fig. 2):
> - On all four benchmarks, ColEI learns worse and has higher variance than Standard and DANN RNNs; DANNs match standard RNNs.
> - Gradient clipping particularly benefits ColEI (Appendix Fig. 10), indicating sensitivity to spectral pathologies.
> 
> Spectrum transplant study on Sequential MNIST (Fig. 4):
> - Impact of sign constraints alone: hurts test error modestly (~0.7% ± 0.3% for standard RNNs, ~1% ± 1% for ColEI) but does not explain full gap (2.3% ± 0.6%).
> - Swapping singular value spectra: spectrum contributes more to the performance gap (1.5% ± 0.3% for RNNs; 2% ± 1% for ColEI) than sign constraints or singular vectors, isolating spectral dispersion/multimodality as the dominant factor.
> 
> EI ratio and network size (Figs. 5–7):
> - ColEI: fewer inhibitory units or smaller networks lower the normalized SVD entropy (NSE) and worsen performance; NSE anti‑correlates with test error across EI ratios and sizes.
> - DANN: robust to EI ratio and size; spectra remain unimodal and performance stable.
> 
> Takeaway: On identical tasks, DANNs (and standard) outperform ColEI primarily due to better singular value spectra (unimodal/clustered). The quantitative deltas (above) support the conclusion that spectral properties matter more than sign constraints for learning and generalization.
> 
> 3) Implicit bias in self‑supervised JEPA vs MAE (NeurIPS 2024)
> Identical synthetic settings and linear generative models; ImageNet‑64×64 snapshots for CCA trends (Appendix D)
> 
> Deep linear experiments (Figs. 1–2, 4–5):
> - With monotonically increasing feature covariance λ but decreasing regression coefficient ρ, JEPA inverts the learning order relative to MAE: MAE learns by λ (co‑variance) while JEPA prioritizes high‑ρ (influential) features; the effect strengthens with encoder depth L.
> - ODE analysis shows JEPA’s critical time has a leading ρ‑dependent term (Theorem 3.4), while MAE’s leading term depends on λ (Theorem 3.5). Result: JEPA is greedier in ρ; MAE in λ.
> 
> Temporal linear model (Fig. 3):
> - For two modes with different autocorrelations (γ) and noise σ, λa = γa‖v‖² and ρa = γa‖v‖²/(σ²+‖v‖²). JEPA learns less/noisy features later and converges to lower amplitudes for noisy modes; MAE is less sensitive to noise in learning order.
> 
> ImageNet‑64×64 feature similarity (Fig. 7 in Appendix D):
> - Mean CCA(full,bottom) is higher for I‑JEPA than MAE throughout training, indicating JEPA aligns faster with low‑variance “bottom” perceptual subspace; CCA(full,top) favors MAE.
> 
> Takeaway: On identical synthetic distributions and a controlled ImageNet setup, JEPA and MAE learn the same features in a stepwise manner but in different orders: JEPA prioritizes predictive, low‑noise (high‑ρ) directions and aligns better with the bottom variance subspace; MAE prioritizes high‑variance (high‑λ) directions.
> 
> 4) Memory‑efficient fine‑tuning with 4‑bit optimizer states (NeurIPS 2023)
> Identical datasets: GLUE (NLU), SQuAD/SQuAD2.0 (QA), E2E‑NLG, ImageNet‑1k with Swin‑T, WMT14 en‑de, Alpaca fine‑tuning of LLaMA‑7B/13B/33B
> Baselines: 32‑bit AdamW; 8‑bit AdamW; Adafactor (with/without β1), SM3; also a 4‑bit Factor variant (factorized second moment)
> 
> Main accuracy (Table 2):
> - NLU (GLUE mean): 4‑bit AdamW = 89.1, on par with 32‑bit AdamW (88.9) and 8‑bit AdamW (89.1); SM3 drops to 87.5.
> - Image classification (Swin‑T): 4‑bit AdamW 80.8 vs 81.2 (32‑bit); 8‑bit 81.0; 4‑bit Factor 80.9.
> - NLG (E2E‑NLG BLEU): 4‑bit AdamW 67.8 vs 67.7 (32‑bit). 4‑bit Factor 67.6; 8‑bit 67.5.
> - QA (SQuAD F1): 4‑bit AdamW 94.5 vs 94.6 (32‑bit); 8‑bit 94.5.
> - MT (WMT14 en‑de SacreBLEU): 4‑bit AdamW 26.28 vs 26.61 (32‑bit); 8‑bit 26.66.
> 
> LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3):
> - 7B: MMLU 38.9 (4‑bit) vs 38.7 (32‑bit); HellaSwag 74.7 vs 74.6; ARC‑e 61.2 vs 61.5; ARC‑c 44.4 vs 45.1; OBQA 43.0 vs 43.4.
> - 13B: 4‑bit slightly edges 32‑bit on most metrics (e.g., MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8).
> - 33B: close performance (MMLU 54.9 vs 56.4; OBQA 45.4 vs 43.8).
> 
> Efficiency (Table 4):
> - LLaMA‑7B with FSDP: total memory 75.40 GB → 31.87 GB (−57.7%); time 3.35 h → 3.07 h.
> - RoBERTa‑L (fused): 5.31 GB → 3.00 GB (−43.5%); time 3.93 min → 3.17 min; 4‑bit Factor reduces memory further to 2.83 GB.
> - GPT‑2 M (fused): time roughly matches 32‑bit (2.11 h vs 2.13 h) with 34.4% memory saving.
> 
> Ablations on second moment quantization (Table 1):
> - Using DE mapping with zero‑point at 4‑bit leads to instability or BLEU drops (e.g., 33% instability; 66.6 BLEU avg).
> - Removing zero point (DE‑0) or using a Linear mapping with Rank‑1 normalization fixes instability and restores BLEU ≈ 67.4–67.8.
> - Stable embeddings help stability when zero-point remains, but once zero is excluded, they are unnecessary.
> 
> Takeaway: On identical NLP/vision tasks, 4‑bit AdamW with per‑row/column (rank‑1) normalization and zero‑free second moment quantization matches or closely tracks 32‑bit/8‑bit accuracy while delivering large (≈35–58%) memory savings and, with FSDP, lower wall‑clock on LLaMA.
> 
> 5) Transient NeRFs for lidar view synthesis & 3D reconstruction (NeurIPS 2023)
> Identical datasets: Five simulated scenes (chair, ficus, lego, hotdog, statue) and six captured scenes (e.g., cinema, food, baskets). Supervision and evaluation are on the same scenes across methods.
> Baselines: Instant‑NGP; DS‑NeRF; Urban NeRF; Urban NeRF‑M (Urban NeRF + oracle masks)
> 
> Simulated (Table 1; 2/3/5 views; higher is better for PSNR, lower for LPIPS/L1 depth)
> - Proposed vs best baseline (Urban NeRF‑M):
>   • 2 views: PSNR 21.38 vs 20.91; LPIPS 0.172 vs 0.410; L1 depth 0.015 vs 0.051.
>   • 3 views: PSNR 23.48 vs 20.81; LPIPS 0.151 vs 0.382; L1 0.011 vs 0.038.
>   • 5 views: PSNR 28.39 vs 22.34; LPIPS 0.115 vs 0.339; L1 0.013 vs 0.029.
> - Depth quality: Proposed consistently achieves lowest L1 error; visual comparisons (lego, Fig. 5) show fewer floating artifacts.
> 
> Captured (Table 2; 2/3/5 views)
> - Intensity PSNR/LPIPS: Proposed leads by wide margins (e.g., PSNR 22.11–22.72 vs best baselines ≈19.1; LPIPS 0.172 vs ≥0.191) across views.
> - Depth L1: Proposed 0.005–0.010 vs best baselines 0.004–0.014; values are close and sensitive to small extrinsic misalignments noted by authors.
> - Novel-view transient rendering: qualitative slices (Fig. 7) show rendered transient histograms and depth consistent with ground truth.
> 
> Takeaway: On identical simulated and captured scenes, optimizing a time‑resolved volume rendering loss on the raw lidar histograms (after convolution with the lidar impulse response) yields state‑of‑the‑art novel‑view intensity and depth, particularly in sparse‑view (2–5 view) settings, outperforming point‑cloud‑supervised NeRF variants.
> 
> Cross‑domain synthesis and comparisons on similar dataset types
> - Sparse‑input regimes: Both PBADet and Transient NeRFs show clear gains in settings where structure or association is ambiguous (PBADet improves association mMR−2; Transient NeRFs improve PSNR/LPIPS/L1 under 2–5 views).
> - Regularization and spectra: The Dale’s Law study quantifies that spectral clustering (high NSE) correlates with lower error on identical tasks (e.g., Sequential MNIST), aligning with the benefits of task-aligned learning (PBADet) and lidar‑consistent rendering (Transient NeRF).
> - Optimizer memory reductions preserve accuracy across disjoint NLP/vision tasks (GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet, WMT) similar to how JEPA preserves predictive features under different noise/variance structures; both show that carefully chosen inductive biases (zero‑point‑free rank‑1 quantization; JEPA’s predictor objective) change training dynamics without sacrificing end metrics.
> 
> Summary of identical‑dataset winners by task
> - BodyHands: PBADet YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 best across AP/Cond. Acc./Joint AP.
> - COCOHumanParts: PBADet best or tied on APM/APL and most mMR−2 categories; BPJDet marginally ahead on overall AP.5:.95 and right foot mMR−2.
> - CrowdHuman: PBADet best body MR−2 and body AP; mMR−2 comparable to BPJDet.
> - Sequential MNIST/Adding/PTB/Naturalistic recognition: DANN/Standard RNN > ColEI; spectral properties drive the gap (quantified by transplant study).
> - JEPA vs MAE (synthetic, ImageNet‑64×64 CCA trends): JEPA learns high‑ρ features sooner and aligns better with bottom‑variance subspaces; MAE emphasizes high‑λ directions.
> - GLUE/SQuAD/E2E‑NLG/ImageNet/WMT: 4‑bit AdamW matches or nearly matches 32‑bit/8‑bit; 4‑bit Factor closely tracks while saving more memory.
> - Simulated & captured lidar scenes (2–5 views): Transient NeRF achieves best PSNR/LPIPS and low depth L1 versus Instant‑NGP/DS‑NeRF/Urban NeRF baselines.
> 
> Notes
> - No identical datasets are shared across the five papers; all comparisons above are made on the exact same datasets within each paper as required.
> - All numbers and claims are taken directly from the provided tables/figures and text (e.g., PBADet Tables 1–3, 5–6; Transient NeRF Tables 1–2; 4‑bit optimizer Tables 1–6; Dale’s Law Figs. 2–7 and spectrum transplant deltas; JEPA Figs. 1–5 & App. D).

> **1. Spectral/regularization effects in SGD-trained networks**
> - *Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective* (NeurIPS 2023) – RNNs with excitatory/inhibitory constraints (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs), tested on sequential MNIST (+ PTB, object recognition).
> - *Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure* (ICML 2025) – power-law Hessian spectra of SGD-trained LeNet on MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100; slope magnitude predicts test error (Pearson 0.72 on CIFAR-10).
> 
> **2. Implicit bias of SSL (JEPA vs MAE)**
> - *How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features* (NeurIPS 2024) – deep linear analysis: JEPA (self-distillation with predictor) learns high-influence features first, whereas MAE (masked reconstruction) ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue; the bias difference only appears with deep encoders. ImageNet I-JEPA vs MAE confirm alignment with perceptual PCA subspace. (The specific cosine-similarity-head vs MSE-head contrast is not detailed in this corpus.)
> 
> **3. Memory-efficient fine-tuning with 4-bit Adam**
> - *Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States* (NeurIPS 2023) – 4-bit first/second moments, smaller block size (B128), rank-1 (row×column) normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer for the second moment. Evaluated on Swin-T (ImageNet), RoBERTa-L, GPT-2, Transformer-Base, LLaMA. **No CIFAR-100/ResNet-50/F1-Precision experiments exist in this collection** — the vision metric is accuracy (Swin-T: 80.8–80.9 vs 81.2 32-bit), and QA F1 = 94.5 (RoBERTa-L/SQuAD).
> 
> **4. Anchor-free part–body association**
> - *PBADet* (ICLR 2024) – one-stage anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center offset, using TOOD-style task-alignment (anchor alignment metric t = s^α·u^β) rather than plain cross-entropy. On BodyHands (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 — beating BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13); on COCOHumanParts AP 42.7/43.0.
> 
> **5. Time-resolved NeRFs for lidar**
> - *Transient Neural Radiance Fields for Lidar View Synthesis and 3D Reconstruction* (NeurIPS 2023) – renders time-resolved photon-count histograms (transients) over t via a time-resolved volume rendering equation. On simulated data (2/3/5 views): PSNR 21.38/23.48/28.39 vs Instant-NGP 16.62–19.66, DS-NeRF ≤21.07, Urban-NeRF ≤22.34; LPIPS 0.172/0.151/0.115 and depth L1 ≈0.015 vs ≥0.029 baselines. Same trend on captured data.
> 
> ## Cross-method comparison of experimental results
> - **Spectral analyses** (1) converge on the same message: the *spectrum* — not sign constraints or loss design per se — dominates learnability. Hessian power-law slope predicts generalization; SVD entropy (NSE) of recurrent weights at initialization anti-correlates with final error (small high-NSE networks beat large low-NSE ones). Both are diagnostic tools that work before/without full training.
> - **SSL implicit bias** (2) extends this spectral/step-wise view to representation learning: JEPA's latent-space prediction gives a different feature-ordering bias than MAE's input-space reconstruction, explaining why JEPA learns perceptually useful features with fewer steps.
> - **4-bit optimizer** (3) shows quantization itself can be near-lossless: 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit within ≤0.5 accuracy points (Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2), keeps QA F1 at 94.5, while saving up to 57.7% memory and enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; sublinear-memory baselines (SM3, Adafactor β₁=0) degrade more, notably on classification.
> - **PBADet** (4) demonstrates that a simple task-alignment regularized association head outperforms anchor-based part-detectors (BPJDet) by ~4 AP points and boosts association accuracy; ablation shows removing task alignment hurts all metrics.
> - **Transient NeRF** (5) shows the largest relative gains: direct supervision of raw lidar transients beats point-cloud-supervised NeRFs by large margins in PSNR (+6–9 dB with 5 views), LPIPS (≈3× lower), and depth L1 (≈3–10× lower), especially in the few-view regime, because raw-histogram supervision avoids noisy, view-inconsistent point clouds.
> 
> **Caveats:** the corpus contains no paper matching the exact topic-3 configuration (Adam 4-bit on CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50/Swin and F1/Precision) — the closest is the 4-bit optimizer paper using Swin-T on ImageNet (accuracy) and F1 only for QA; and no explicit "cosine-similarity head vs MSE head in Transformers" ablation for topic 2 was found, so those specific claims cannot be verified from this context.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved context, I found the papers that match each of the five topics:
> 
> 1. **Spectral/regularization effects (Dale's Law RNNs)** – "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023)
> 2. **Implicit bias of SSL (JEPA vs MAE)** – "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks" (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024)
> 3. **Memory-efficient 4-bit Adam optimizer** – "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023)
> 4. **Anchor-free part–body association (PBADet)** – "PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association" (Gao et al., ICLR 2024)
> 5. **Time-resolved NeRF (Transient NeRF)** – "Transient Neural Radiance Fields for Lidar View Synthesis and 3D Reconstruction" (Malik et al., NeurIPS 2023)
> 
> **Comparison and analysis of experimental results:**
> 
> **(1) Dale's Law RNN (spectral perspective).** The paper tests ColEI (simple column E/I partitioning) vs. DANN (bio-inspired EI architecture) vs. standard RNNs on sequential MNIST (also adding, PTB, object recognition). Sign constraints alone only account for part of the gap (RNN ±0.3%, ColEI ±1%, gap 2.3±0.6%); spectral "transplant" experiments (8 configurations) show the singular-value spectrum at initialization matters more than sign constraints or singular vectors (spectra contribute ~1.5% vs ~2% for ColEI). Small networks with few inhibitory units have worse (multimodal, dispersed) spectra and worse learning; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error, and gradient clipping mitigates ColEI instability. DANN performs as well as standard RNNs.
> 
> **(2) JEPA vs MAE implicit bias.** Using deep linear networks with exact gradient-flow ODEs, JEPA prioritizes "influential" (high-regression-coefficient, ρ) features, MAE orders learning by eigenvalue λ. The bias only emerges for deep encoders and diminishes for shallow ones; JEPA converges to lower-amplitude weights on noisy features (noise suppression strengthens with depth). ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace (CCA) than MAE. (Note: the retrieved context describes both objectives as L2/MSE regression forms, Eq. (2) for JEPA and Eq. (1) for MAE; it does not explicitly compare cosine-similarity heads vs. MSE losses in Transformers.)
> 
> **(3) 4-bit optimizers.** 4-bitAdamW (first moment B128/DE; second moment Rank-1/Linear) and 4-bitFactor match/exceed 32-bit AdamW on fine-tuning (NLU 89.1 vs 88.9, QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6, NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7) and are comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8–80.9 vs 81.2; Transformer MT 26.28–26.45 vs 26.61), while sublinear-memory Adafactor/SM3 degrade (especially on classification). Memory savings reach 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB). Notably, the paper's image-classification benchmark is Swin-T on ImageNet-1k — **not** CIFAR-100/ResNet-50 — and reports accuracy (not Precision), and F1 is reported for SQuAD QA, not on CIFAR. So the specific "CIFAR-100 + ResNet-50 + F1/Precision" claims cannot be confirmed from this context.
> 
> **(4) PBADet.** One-stage anchor-free detector with a single part-to-body center offset plus TOOD-style task-alignment learning (t = s^α·u^β). Ablations on BodyHands (YOLOv7) show the association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task alignment each improve association accuracy (hand AP, conditional accuracy, joint AP); removing task alignment ("w/o Task-align") decreases all metrics. Anchor-free part-to-body (Hand AP 89.1, cond. acc. 92.62, joint AP 85.98) beats anchor-based part-to-body (88.4/92.31/85.28) and BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13); on CrowdHuman it leads body MR-2 and beats ED-Pose on precision/recall/F1 for hands/feet; COCOHumanParts AP 42.7–43.0.
> 
> **(5) Transient NeRF.** Using a time-resolved volume-rendering equation (squared transmittance, inverse-square falloff, impulse-response convolution, Poisson noise), it renders raw single-photon lidar histograms from novel views and recovers geometry. On simulated data (2/3/5 views) it dominates baselines: PSNR 21.38/23.48/28.39 vs. Instant-NGP 16.62/17.67/19.66, UrbanNeRF-mask 20.91/20.81/22.34; LPIPS 0.172/0.151/0.115 vs ~0.34–0.52; depth L1 0.015/0.011/0.013 vs 0.029–0.238. Captured results show the same trend (PSNR ~22.1–22.7, LPIPS 0.17–0.27, depth L1 0.005–0.010), with cleaner geometry from histogram supervision than point-cloud supervision.
> 
> **Cross-paper analysis.** The two "spectral" papers are complementary: the Dale's-Law paper shows initial weight spectra (not sign constraints) drive EI-RNN learnability, while the JEPA paper shows objective choice (latent prediction vs. reconstruction) drives feature-learning order/spectral bias; both use MNIST-adjacent settings (sequential MNIST) and argue spectra/dynamics predict performance. The 4-bit optimizer and Transient NeRF papers both trade memory/representation fidelity for efficiency, but the optimizer keeps accuracy essentially lossless (within ~0.1–0.5 points), whereas Transient NeRF *gains* large accuracy (PSNR +4.8 to +8.7 over best baseline) by switching supervision from point clouds to raw histograms. PBADet's task-alignment loss mirrors the "alignment" theme in the SSL paper (alignment of objectives/features improves quality). Note the context does not substantiate the CIFAR-100/ResNet-50/F1-Precision claims for the optimizer paper, nor an explicit cosine-similarity-head-vs-MSE-Transformer comparison for the SSL paper; those specific experimental details are absent from the retrieved material.

<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Here is a consolidated comparison of experimental results across five works that, together, address: (1) hand/body association in crowded scenes, (2) time‑resolved single‑photon lidar rendering and reconstruction along time t, (3) memory‑lean fine‑tuning with 4‑bit optimizer states, and (4) analyses of EI (excitatory/inhibitory) constraints and JEPA‑style objectives.
> 
> 1) Part–body association in crowded scenes (PBADet vs prior art)
> Identical datasets and metrics
> - BodyHands (hand–body association, single part type):
>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6):
>     - Hand AP: 89.1 vs 85.9
>     - Conditional Accuracy: 92.62 vs 86.91
>     - Joint AP: 85.98 vs 84.39
>   - Using the same backbone (YOLOv5l6), PBADet also exceeds BPJDet: Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73 vs 85.9/86.91/84.39.
> - COCOHumanParts (multi‑part associations: head/face/hands/feet): PBADet vs BPJDet and Hier‑R‑CNN
>   - All‑category AP (original/subordinate), identical test set:
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 43.0/41.8; PBADet (YOLOv7): 42.7/41.5
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6/43.3
>     - PBADet leads on APM/APL (medium/large), e.g., PBADet (YOLOv5l6): APM 66.2/65.0; APL 67.2/64.4 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): APM 63.8/63.2; APL 61.8/58.9.
>   - Per‑category AP (PBADet vs BPJDet, YOLOv5l6): person 62.4 vs 61.3; feet (r/l) 30.9/31.5 vs 30.2/30.9; heads/faces are similar or slightly lower with PBADet.
>   - Association difficulty (lower is better): average mMR−2 across parts:
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): head 27.9, face 30.5, l‑hand 36.2, r‑hand 40.8, r‑foot 50.4, l‑foot 47.9
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, l‑hand 41.6, r‑hand 42.2, r‑foot 49.1, l‑foot 50.4
>     - PBADet yields consistently lower miss‑match rates on head/face/hands, comparable on feet.
> - CrowdHuman (face–body association in heavy crowding):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves best body MR−2 and body AP among joint detectors: body MR−2 36.5 (lower is better), body AP 91.6 (higher is better); face MR−2 44.7; mMR−2 body‑face 50.8 (BPJDet l6: 50.1).
> - Precision/Recall/F1 for association vs multi‑person pose (ED‑Pose) on COCO val:
>   - All parts (hands/feet): PBADet Precision/Recall/F1 = 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs ED‑Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51.
>   - E.g., L‑hand F1: 46.50 vs 22.87; R‑hand F1: 47.34 vs 24.17; PBADet markedly improves F1 and Precision.
> Takeaway: On identical datasets, PBADet consistently outperforms prior body‑part linking methods in both detection and association metrics, with especially strong gains in conditional accuracy/joint AP (BodyHands) and reduced miss‑match rates (COCOHumanParts). It also achieves higher F1/Precision than a strong multi‑person pose baseline when both are evaluated against part boxes.
> 
> 2) Transient NeRF (time‑resolved lidar view synthesis along t) vs NeRF baselines
> Identical datasets and metrics
> - Simulated multiview single‑photon lidar (five scenes: chair/ficus/lego/hotdog/statue), trained with few views (2/3/5):
>   - Image synthesis (PSNR ↑ / LPIPS ↓):
>     - Proposed (Transient NeRF): 2 views 21.38/0.172; 3 views 23.48/0.151; 5 views 28.39/0.115
>     - Urban NeRF (w/mask): 20.91/0.410; 20.81/0.382; 22.34/0.339
>     - DS‑NeRF: 19.28/0.431; 19.35/0.436; 21.07/0.376
>     - Instant‑NGP (no depth): 16.62/0.520; 17.67/0.476; 19.66/0.387
>   - Depth accuracy (L1 ↓): Proposed 0.015/0.011/0.013 vs Urban NeRF‑M 0.051/0.038/0.029; DS‑NeRF 0.109/0.115/0.119; Instant‑NGP 0.238/0.195/0.178.
>   - Proposed is best for image quality and greatly reduces depth error, especially with just 2–3 views.
> - Captured multiview single‑photon lidar (e.g., cinema/food/baskets), trained with 2/3/5 views:
>   - Image synthesis PSNR/LPIPS: Proposed 22.11/0.271; 21.83/0.212; 22.72/0.172 versus Urban NeRF‑M 15.45/0.458; 18.26/0.269; 19.11/0.191, and others lower.
>   - Depth L1: Proposed 0.005/0.006/0.010; Urban NeRF‑M 0.014/0.006/0.004 (Proposed is best at 2 views; similar or slightly higher at 3–5 views).
> - Unique capability: renders the raw transient (time‑resolved photon count histograms) and x–y, x–t slices; captures transient light transport along time t that baselines (which use point clouds) cannot render.
> Takeaway: On identical simulated and captured datasets, Transient NeRF substantially improves few‑view image quality and depth accuracy while uniquely enabling lidar view synthesis in the time domain (x–t), critical for raw single‑photon lidar simulation and planning.
> 
> 3) Memory‑lean fine‑tuning with 4‑bit optimizer states
> Identical datasets and metrics
> - Natural Language Understanding (RoBERTa‑Large on GLUE, mean metric ↑): 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 ≈ 32‑bit AdamW 88.9 and 8‑bit 89.1; Adafactor/SM3 are competitive but can underperform on some tasks.
> - Image classification (Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k top‑1 Acc ↑): 4‑bit AdamW 80.8 vs 32‑bit 81.2 vs 8‑bit 81.0 (4‑bit within 0.4 pt of full precision).
> - Natural language generation (GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG, BLEU ↑): 4‑bit AdamW 67.8 vs 32‑bit 67.7 vs 8‑bit 67.5.
> - Question answering (RoBERTa‑Large on SQuAD/SQuAD2.0, F1 ↑): SQuAD F1 94.5 (4‑bit) vs 94.6 (32‑bit); SQuAD2.0 F1 88.4 (4‑bit) vs 88.8 (32‑bit).
> - Machine translation (Transformer‑Base, WMT14 en‑de, SacreBLEU ↑): 4‑bit AdamW 26.28 vs 26.61 (32‑bit) vs 26.66 (8‑bit);
> - Instruction‑tuning LLaMA (MMLU and commonsense QA, 5‑shot): 4‑bit matches or is very close to 32‑bit across 7B/13B/33B (e.g., MMLU: 7B 38.9 vs 38.7; 13B 47.4 vs 46.5; 33B 54.9 vs 56.4).
> - Memory/time efficiency on identical training setups:
>   - LLaMA‑7B (FSDP, 2×A100‑80GB): Total memory 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB (−57.7%); training time 3.07 h vs 3.35 h (speed‑up; fused kernel ~3.11 h).
>   - RoBERTa‑L (RTE): 3.00 GB vs 5.31 GB (−43.5%); time 3.17 min (fused) vs 3.93 min.
>   - GPT‑2 Medium: 4.62 GB vs 6.89 GB (−34.4%); time 2.11 h (fused) vs 2.13 h.
> - Largest trainable model under fixed GPU memory:
>   - 24 GB: 4‑bit trains OPT‑1.3B vs 32‑bit limited to OPT‑350M.
>   - 80 GB: 4‑bit trains OPT‑6.7B (and LLaMA‑7B) vs 32‑bit limited to OPT‑1.3B.
> - Ablations (all on identical tasks/datasets): rank‑1 normalization + linear quantizer for 2nd moment avoids zero‑point failure and yields the best BLEU on E2E‑NLG (e.g., 67.8), while 8‑bit‑style DE mapping at 4‑bit destabilizes training; factorizing 2nd moment (“4‑bit Factor”) preserves accuracy while further reducing memory.
> Takeaway: Across identical benchmarks, 4‑bit AdamW/Factor match 32‑bit accuracy (GLUE, SQuAD F1, E2E BLEU, WMT14) while cutting optimizer memory roughly in half vs 8‑bit and far below 32‑bit, enabling larger models on the same GPUs. This directly supports memory‑lean fine‑tuning of large Transformers with Adam/SGD tracking F1/Precision as reported (e.g., SQuAD F1).
> 
> 4) EI constraints and JEPA‑style objective analyses
> Identical datasets and tasks
> - EI (Dale’s Law) constraints in RNNs (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNN): adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task (same splits per method):
>   - ColEI consistently underperforms DANN and standard RNN in final accuracy across all tasks; benefits disproportionately from gradient clipping.
>   - Spectral transplant experiments (same datasets): modifying spectra impacts performance more than enforcing/removing sign constraints; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization strongly anti‑correlates with test error across EI ratios and network sizes.
>   - Small networks or large E:I ratios reduce NSE and degrade learning; DANN/standard RNNs maintain unimodal clustered spectra and learn well even with few inhibitory units (e.g., 1 I unit).
> - JEPA vs MAE (deep linear analyses with synthetic data; plus ImageNet‑64 study):
>   - On matched synthetic distributions, both objectives learn high‑variance features first, but JEPA additionally prioritizes large regression‑coefficient (influence) features; under opposing trends (high variance but low influence), JEPA reverses the learning order vs MAE.
>   - On ImageNet‑64, I‑JEPA’s features align earlier with the lower‑variance (perceptual) PCA subspace than MAE (reported via CCA trends), consistent with JEPA learning predictive, less noisy features.
>   - Note: No MNIST or CIFAR‑100 cosine‑similarity vs squared‑error results are reported in these papers; sequential MNIST is used in the EI study, and ImageNet‑64 is used to compare JEPA vs MAE representation dynamics.
> Takeaway: For time‑series modeling (adding task, seq. MNIST, PTB), EI architectural constraints degrade performance unless spectral properties are controlled; DANN recovers standard‑RNN‑like spectra and performance. For SSL objectives, JEPA’s latent prediction (squared error in latent with stop‑grad) implicitly biases toward high‑influence, low‑variance features vs pixel reconstruction (MAE) — a favorable property for robotics perception when pretraining under limited compute.
> 
> How these results map to the requested capabilities
> - Hand/body association in crowds: On identical datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman), PBADet is superior to BPJDet/Hier‑R‑CNN and gives higher F1/Precision than a pose baseline (ED‑Pose), directly addressing crowded‑scene association.
> - Transient NeRF along time t: On identical simulated and captured lidar datasets, Transient NeRF exceeds NeRF baselines in PSNR/LPIPS and depth L1 with few views, and uniquely renders time‑resolved histograms (x–t slices) for planning/simulation.
> - Memory‑lean fine‑tuning: Across identical NLU/QA/MT/NLG/ImageNet benchmarks, 4‑bit AdamW/Factor match 32‑bit accuracy while saving up to ~58% total memory (LLaMA‑7B) and enabling much larger models under fixed GPU memory.
> - EI constraints and JEPA‑style pretraining: On identical tasks (adding, seq. MNIST, PTB, object recognition), DANN ≈ standard RNN >> ColEI; spectra matter more than sign constraints. JEPA vs MAE analyses (synthetic + ImageNet‑64) explain why JEPA‑style SSL learns more semantic/low‑variance features than pixel reconstruction — aligning with your stated pretraining preference.
> 
> Notes on datasets requested but not reported
> - No results are reported on CIFAR‑100 or cosine‑similarity objectives in these papers; sequential MNIST is covered in the EI study, and ImageNet‑64 is used for JEPA vs MAE representation dynamics. All numerical comparisons above are taken directly from the papers’ figures/tables.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Yes — four works collectively cover your stack, plus two supporting analyses.
> 
> ### 1. Detection with part–body linking → **PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> One-stage anchor-free detector that links parts (hands/face/feet) to a body via a single **part-to-body center offset** — designed for crowded scenes (avoids BPJDet's one-to-many body-to-part offsets that break under occlusion). Uses SGD on YOLOv5/YOLOv7, and reports the **F1/Precision/Recall** you need.
> - **BodyHands:** hand AP **89.1**, cond. accuracy **92.62**, joint AP **85.98** (YOLOv7) vs. best BPJDet 85.9/86.91/84.39; smaller model, higher accuracy.
> - **vs. ED-Pose** (COCO): all-parts Precision **39.41 vs 24.09**, Recall **63.09 vs 45.51**, F1 **48.52 vs 31.51** — clearly better part-body association, at the cost of some body AP parity.
> - **CrowdHuman** (face-body): best body MR-2 (**36.5**), AP 91.6; advantage over BPJDet shrinks on this single-part task.
> 
> ### 2. Raw single-photon lidar simulation/reconstruction → **Transient NeRF** (NeurIPS 2023)
> Renders **raw time-resolved photon-count histograms** (not point clouds) using a time-resolved volume-rendering equation with Poisson noise, from 2–5 views. Uses Adam-style training on hash-grid Instant-NGP/NerfAcc.
> - 5 views: PSNR **28.39** vs Instant-NGP 19.66 / DS-NeRF 21.07 / UrbanNeRF 19.80; LPIPS **0.115** vs 0.339–0.476; depth L1 **0.013** vs 0.029–0.178.
> - Gains hold at 2 views (21.38 vs 20.91 best baseline). Limits: single-bounce/coaxial only.
> 
> ### 3. Memory-lean fine-tuning of large Transformers → **4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023)
> 4-bit Adam/AdamW states via smaller block size (B128) + rank-1 normalization / zero-point-free linear quantizer, optionally factorized second moment.
> - Matches 32-bit AdamW: NLU 89.1 vs 88.9, ImageNet Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2, GPT-2 BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, WMT BLEU 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning comparable.
> - Memory: up to **57.7%** saved; LLaMA-7B fits one 80GB GPU; 4-bitFactor states ~4× smaller. Convergence curves align with full precision.
> 
> ### 4. JEPA-style SSL + objective comparison
> - **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"**: in deep linear networks, JEPA (L2 predictive in latent space) orders feature learning by the **regression coefficient ρ** (influential, low-variance features), increasingly with depth, whereas MAE/reconstruction orders by covariance λ and learns noisy features. ImageNet CCA confirms I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace than MAE — supports your JEPA-over-reconstruction preference.
> - **"Learning better with Dale's Law"** (your E/I constraint question): ColEI networks obeying Dale's Law train worse than standard/DANN RNNs on sequential MNIST, but transplant experiments show this is **mostly the initial singular-value spectrum, not the sign constraints**; normalized SVD entropy at init anti-correlates with final error, and DANN networks are robust even with one inhibitory unit.
> - **Cosine-similarity analysis** ("Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning", SGD, CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100): proves optimal negative-pair cosine similarity is −1/(n−1), and that **small batches inflate negative-similarity variance**, degrading representations. A variance-reduction auxiliary term lifts top-1 accuracy on **CIFAR-10/100** consistently across temperatures (0.07–2.0) and batch sizes (32–512), helping tight-GPU-budget small-batch training.
> 
> ### Caveat on your exact query
> A **direct head-to-head of cosine-similarity vs squared-error objectives on MNIST/CIFAR-100** is **not** present in this collection. The contrastive paper studies cosine similarity on CIFAR-10/100; the JEPA paper studies L2/squared-error objectives on deep linear models (Gaussian data) with ImageNet CCA; the E/I paper uses sequential MNIST with L2-style classification. So the "cosine-vs-squared-error on MNIST/CIFAR-100" comparison you asked about specifically cannot be established from these documents.
> 
> **Bottom line:** the collection covers all four pillars with strong, complementary evidence — PBADet for linked detection (F1/P/R), Transient NeRF for raw-lidar planning data, 4-bit optimizers for GPU-lean training, and the JEPA/E-I/contrastive analyses for pretraining-objective and architectural-constraint guidance under Adam/SGD.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes—the collection contains works covering all four areas, though one match is only partial. Here is the comparison of their experimental results:
> 
> **1. Part–body linking detection (crowded scenes) — PBADet (ICLR 2024).** One-stage, anchor-free; a single part-to-body center offset replaces BPJDet's body-to-part offsets (representation length 10 vs 15 for 3 parts), giving one-to-one part→body correspondence that stays valid when parts are occluded. On BodyHands (YOLOv7), the full model reaches Hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98; ablations show the association loss boosts conditional accuracy from 80.78→92.62 and joint AP from 78.07→85.98, multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each add further gains. On CrowdHuman face–body, Ours(YOLOv7) leads MR-2 (body 36.5, face 44.7) and AP (91.6/81.6) vs BPJDet, and vs the pose estimator ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet.
> 
> **2. Raw single-photon lidar simulation/reconstruction along time t — Transient NeRFs (NeurIPS 2023).** Renders time-resolved photon-count histograms via a time-resolved volume-rendering equation with squared transmittance, inverse-square falloff, and a Poisson noise model. On simulated multiview scans, it beats RGB-supervised baselines decisively: PSNR 21.38/23.48/28.39 (2/3/5 views) vs Instant-NGP 16.62/17.67/19.66, DS-NeRF 19.28/19.35/21.07, UrbanNeRF 18.86/18.73/19.80, UrbanNeRF-M 20.91/20.81/22.34; LPIPS 0.172/0.151/0.115 vs ≥0.339 for the best baseline; depth L1 0.015/0.011/0.013 vs ≥0.029. Explicit histogram supervision also removes floating-density artifacts; it trains on a single A40 GPU.
> 
> **3. 4-bit optimizer states for memory-lean Transformer training — 4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023).** Uses smaller blocks (B128) for the first moment and rank-1 normalization/zero-point-excluded linear quantizers for the second moment, optionally factorized. 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly beats 32-bit AdamW on all tasks: NLU RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9; Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2M BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61. LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning: 4-bit AdamW MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7 (7B), 47.4 vs 46.5 (13B), with near-identical loss curves. Memory drops up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B 75.4→31.9 GB, enabling a single 80 GB GPU) and 4× larger OPT models fit a given budget. 8-bit AdamW is close but uses 2× the optimizer-state memory; Adafactor/SM3 degrade, especially on image classification (80.0/79.0 vs 81.2).
> 
> **4a. JEPA-style pretraining (vs pixel reconstruction) — "Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024).** Deep-linear analysis shows JEPA self-distillation is biased to learn high-influence features (prioritizing high-ρ modes, with depth strengthening noise suppression), whereas MAE orders features mainly by eigenvalue λ and reconstructs variance-dominated subspaces. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features do (CCA), supporting your preference for JEPA-style latent prediction over pixel reconstruction.
> 
> **4b. Excitatory/inhibitory architectural constraints — "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023).** Comparing sign-constrained column E/I RNNs (ColEI), Dale's ANNs (DANN), and standard RNNs on sequential MNIST, PTB, etc., ColEI learns worse and with more variance; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Sign constraints alone explain little (0.7–1% error increase); spectrum-transplant experiments show the initial singular-value spectrum matters more (1.5–2% gap), with ColEI's multimodal spectrum vs the unimodal quarter-circle spectrum of standard RNNs/DANNs. Fewer inhibitory units (higher E/I ratio) worsen both spectrum and learning; DANNs stay robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron. Normalized SVD entropy at initialization anti-correlates with final test error.
> 
> **4c. Cosine-similarity vs squared-error on MNIST/CIFAR-100 — partial match.** No document directly compares cosine-similarity vs squared-error objectives on MNIST/CIFAR-100. The closest is "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning" (ICML 2025), which analyzes embeddings through cosine similarity: optimal full-batch states are positive similarity 1 and negative −1/(n−1); smaller batches inflate negative-pair similarity variance and hurt representations. Adding an auxiliary variance-reduction loss to SimCLR/DCL/DHEL improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100 (and ImageNet-100/full ImageNet), improves temperature robustness across τ∈[0.07, 2.0] and small-batch performance (batch 32–512). This is cosine-similarity analysis rather than a head-to-head cosine-vs-MSE comparison, so that specific question cannot be fully answered from this collection.

### paperscope:results_comparison:374 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively cover: (1) selecting a small subset of open, unlabeled text to warm‑start fine‑tuning large language models using feature embeddings and distributional matching (rather than full continued pretraining), compatible with SFT/LoRA workflows and reported with F1/Precision style metrics; (2) memory‑lean training via compressing optimizer states to very low bitwidth while keeping Adam/AdamW/SGD behavior for Transformer backbones; (3) analyses of non‑contrastive self‑supervised objectives that predict in latent space (vs reconstruction losses like MSE) and their implicit bias in deep networks; (4) a spectral perspective on recurrent models with separate excitatory/inhibitory units (Dale‑style constraints) for stability/interpretability; and (5) an anchor‑free, one‑stage detector that associates parts to their parent instances on whole‑body benchmarks (e.g., COCO‑like), with attention backbones and standard detection metrics. Prefer works that discuss fine‑tuning, self‑supervised learning, cosine‑style similarity/embeddings, and common optimizers (Adam/AdamW).Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Cross-paper comparison of experimental results (only from the provided papers)
> 
> 1) Datasets shared across papers and head-to-head comparisons
> - GLUE (identical benchmark appears in two papers):
>   • GOT-D (ICLR’24, data selection for pre-fine-tuning, BERT-base): With 50k selected unlabeled samples for pre-fine-tuning, then full GLUE training per task, GOT-D achieves the best average among selection methods (Table 4): AVG 83.43 vs DSIR 83.25 and TAPT/c 83.18; it also improves over the vanilla BERT baseline (82.39). In a low-resource regime (pre-fine-tuning with 50k and GLUE fine-tuning capped at 5k/task), GOT-D again ranks first: AVG 78.43 vs DSIR 78.15 and TAPT/c 78.32; improves over vanilla (75.30) (Table 4, lower half).
>   • 4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS’23, training memory reduction): With RoBERTa-L, the NLU aggregate metric on GLUE is 89.1±0.01 for 4-bit AdamW, essentially matching 8-bit AdamW (89.1±0.00) and 32-bit AdamW (88.9±0.01) (Table 2). These results demonstrate 4-bit optimizer parity to higher-precision baselines on GLUE, while GOT-D targets data efficiency/selection (different models; not directly comparable). Still, both show improvements within their respective baselines on the same benchmark.
> - HellaSwag (appears in both GOT-D and 4-bit papers, with different models):
>   • GOT-D (detox/utility evaluation, GPT-2 base, zero-shot): Accuracy around ~29% across methods (Table 7), with GOT-Dcontrast reaching 29.1. 
>   • 4-bit Optimizers (LLaMA instruction tuning, Table 3): Accuracy is much higher with LLaMA models; after fine-tuning 4-bit AdamW, HellaSwag reaches 74.7 (7B), 79.0 (13B), 79.2 (33B), comparable to 32-bit AdamW. These are different model/capability regimes, but both papers report results on HellaSwag.
> 
> 2) Within-paper direct comparisons on identical datasets
> A) PBADet (ICLR’24): One-stage anchor-free part–body association
> - BodyHands (hand–body association): PBADet consistently outperforms prior BPJDet and other baselines (Table 1). For example, with YOLOv7 backbone, PBADet achieves Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; with the same YOLOv5l6 backbone as BPJDet, PBADet reaches 88.1/92.71/85.73 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 85.9/86.91/84.39. Gains come both from higher AP and much higher conditional/joint association accuracy.
> - COCOHumanParts (multi-part association; Table 2 and Table 3): On “All categories APs”, PBADet with YOLOv5l6 obtains 43.0/41.8 (AP.5:.95/AP.5 subordinate) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3. Per-category APs: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) matches or slightly trails BPJDet in some parts but leads on several size-specific metrics (e.g., APM 66.2 vs 63.8 subordinate reported by BPJDet; APL 67.2 vs 61.8 subordinate for BPJDet). Importantly, association robustness (average mMR−2 for head/face/hands/feet) is competitive (Table 3), and PBADet attains the lowest average mMR−2 in multiple categories (e.g., left/right hands with YOLOv7 41.1/42.7 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 41.6/42.2).
> - CrowdHuman (face–body association; Appendix Table 5, Table 6): PBADet achieves the best body MR−2 (lower is better): 36.5 (YOLOv7) and 37.5 (YOLOv5l6), beating BPJDet (40.7 best with YOLOv5l6). Body AP also improves (91.6 vs 89.5–90.7). Association mMR−2 is comparable (~50.8–50.9).
> Summary on identical datasets: PBADet either exceeds or matches prior state-of-the-art on BodyHands and CrowdHuman, and is on par with BPJDet on COCOHumanParts AP while demonstrating stronger association metrics and inference simplicity.
> 
> B) GOT-D (ICLR’24): Data selection for pre-fine-tuning LLMs
> - Detoxification (GPT-2 base; Perspective API; Table 1): On toxic prompts, Expected Max Toxicity drops from 0.62 (base) to 0.41–0.47 (GOT-D with 20k); Toxicity Probability from 0.67 to as low as 0.28 (clean) or 0.39 (contrast). Non-toxic prompts similarly improve (max toxicity from 0.38 to 0.26–0.28; probability from 0.25 to 0.07–0.10). Baselines RTP/DSIR/random show smaller reductions; GOT-D achieves the largest toxicity reductions at 10k and 20k budgets while largely preserving utility (average accuracy changes within ±~1 point) and perplexity within ~±4 points vs base.
> - Detoxification (Moderation API; Appendix Table 6): Consistent reductions: toxic Exp. Max Toxicity down to 0.33–0.40 (from 0.60) and Toxicity Probability to 0.29–0.38 (from 0.62), outperforming baselines.
> - Domain adaptation (8 NLU tasks; Table 2): With a 150k pre-fine-tuning selection budget, GOT-D attains the best average F1 (83.83) over DAPT (83.11), DSIR (82.98), All domains (82.81), and vanilla BERT (82.70). Per-task wins include ChemProt (81.97 vs DAPT 81.03; DSIR 80.69) and ACL-ARC (72.34 vs DAPT 70.51; DSIR 70.32). 
> - Resource-constrained regime (50k selection, 5k labeled; Table 3): GOT-D again leads in average F1 (81.51) over DSIR (80.92), TAPT/c (81.03), and vanilla (80.75).
> - GLUE (Table 4): With 50k pre-fine-tuning and full GLUE training, GOT-D is best (AVG 83.43) over DSIR (83.25), TAPT/c (83.18), and vanilla (82.39). With 5k/task fine-tuning, GOT-D remains best (78.43) vs DSIR (78.15), TAPT/c (78.32), and vanilla (75.30).
> - Zero-shot with larger LMs (Appendix E): 
>   • AGNews (GPT-2 XL): GOT-D improves accuracy from 49.5 (no pre-fine-tuning) to 63.4 with 40k, outperforming DSIR (54.7) and TAPT/c (59.1) at the same budget (Table 16).
>   • BoolQ (GPT-Neo 2.7B): GOT-D improves to 57.7 with 40k vs DSIR 53.3 and TAPT/c 51.2 (Table 18).
> Summary across similar tasks: For pre-fine-tuning on unlabeled text, GOT-D consistently outperforms distribution-matching baselines (DSIR, TAPT/c) across toxicity reduction, domain-specific NLU, GLUE, and zero-shot tests at low selection budgets.
> 
> C) 4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS’23): Memory-lean training while retaining accuracy
> - GLUE (RoBERTa-L; Table 2): 4-bit AdamW achieves 89.1±0.01 (NLU mean) vs 32-bit AdamW 88.9±0.01 and 8-bit AdamW 89.1±0.00; Adafactor and SM3 lag on average.
> - ImageNet-1k classification (Swin-T; Table 2 “CLS” column): 4-bit AdamW 80.8±0.02% top-1 accuracy; 4-bit Factor 80.9±0.06%; both comparable to 32-bit AdamW (81.2±0.05) and 8-bit AdamW (81.0±0.01). 
> - E2E-NLG (GPT-2 Medium; Table 2): BLEU 67.8±0.51 (4-bit AdamW) and 67.6±0.33 (4-bit Factor) vs 32-bit AdamW 67.7±0.67; on full metrics (Table 8), 4-bit matches 32-bit across BLEU/NIST/METEOR/ROUGE-L/CIDEr.
> - SQuAD/SQuAD2.0 (RoBERTa-L; Table 9): 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit within ±0.2 on EM/F1; 4-bit Factor similarly competitive.
> - WMT14 En–De (Transformer-Base; Table 2 “MT”): 4-bit AdamW 26.28±0.05 SacreBLEU, 4-bit Factor 26.45±0.05, matching 32-bit AdamW 26.61±0.08 and 8-bit AdamW 26.66±0.10; Adafactor is slightly lower.
> - LLaMA instruction tuning (Table 3): 4-bit AdamW delivers results comparable to 32-bit AdamW across MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-e, ARC-c, OBQA at scales 7B/13B/33B (differences within ~±1 point depending on task/model size).
> - Efficiency (Table 4): Memory savings up to 57.7% total memory (LLaMA-7B) and 43–47% on RoBERTa-L and GPT-2 Medium; training throughput improves for large sharded models (LLaMA-7B with FSDP), and fused 4-bit kernels close the small-model speed gap vs 8-bit.
> Summary across similar tasks: 4-bit optimizers (quantized moments + rank-1 normalization and zero-point-safe second moment quantization) retain or match full-precision performance on vision (ImageNet), NLU (GLUE), QA (SQuAD), MT (WMT14), NLG (E2E), and LLaMA instruction tuning, while substantially reducing optimizer memory footprint and sometimes training time.
> 
> D) Spectral perspective on EI RNNs (NeurIPS’23): Dale’s Law with recurrent DANNs vs column EI
> - Benchmarks (Figure 2A–D): On adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task, ColEI networks underperform standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs; they exhibit higher variance between seeds. Gradient clipping benefits ColEI more than others.
> - Spectrum–performance link (Figures 3–7): ColEI recurrent weights show multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large modes, correlating with worse learning; DANNs/standard RNNs show unimodal clustered spectra and better performance. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts performance: higher NSE (more clustered singular values) anti-correlates with test error across EI ratio and width sweeps; DANNs are robust over EI ratios and sizes, whereas ColEI improves with more units and balanced EI but remains sensitive.
> Summary: Empirically (plots), DANN RNNs learn as well as standard RNNs and outperform ColEI across all reported tasks; performance tracks spectral clustering metrics (NSE), not just sign constraints.
> 
> E) JEPA vs MAE (NeurIPS’24): Non-contrastive self-distillation (JEPA) vs reconstruction (MAE)
> - Linear deep network dynamics (Figures 1–2, 4): In controlled linear settings, both objectives learn features greedily, but with different biases:
>   • MAE prioritizes features with larger covariance (λ), regardless of regression coefficient (ρ), showing a consistent ordering across settings.
>   • JEPA prioritizes “influential” features with large regression coefficients (ρ), even reversing the learning order when λ and ρ trend oppositely; this preference strengthens with depth (L>1).
> - Temporal model and simultaneous diagonalizability (Figure 3): Empirical simulations match theory: with modes having different auto-correlations/noise (γ, σ), λ and ρ decouple; JEPA favors high-ρ (predictive, low-noise) modes and is slower to learn noisy high-λ modes; MAE tends to learn high-variance modes regardless of informativeness.
> - ImageNet probe (Appendix D): CCA analyses (plots) suggest I-JEPA focuses earlier on low-variance perceptual subspaces than MAE, consistent with theory.
> Summary: While not reporting absolute task metrics like accuracy/bleu on standard datasets, the paper’s experiments/plots consistently support that JEPA’s latent prediction objective implicitly biases towards high-ρ, informative features; MAE emphasizes high-variance reconstruction. Depth accentuates JEPA’s advantage.
> 
> 3) Performance on specific datasets (aggregated)
> - BodyHands: PBADet YOLOv7 89.1 Hand AP / 92.62 conditional / 85.98 joint; YOLOv5l6 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39 (Table 1).
> - COCOHumanParts: PBADet YOLOv5l6 AP.5:.95=43.0 (subordinate 41.8), per-class APs show competitiveness and often better size-specific APs (Table 2); association mMR−2 shows best/lower averages on many parts with YOLOv7 (Table 3).
> - CrowdHuman: PBADet best body MR−2 36.5 (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet 40.7 (YOLOv5l6); body AP 91.6 vs 89.5–90.7; mMR−2 ~50.8–50.9 (Tables 5–6).
> - Detox (Perspective API): GOT-D drops toxic Exp. Max. Toxicity from 0.62→0.41 and probability 0.67→0.28–0.39 at 20k; non-toxic max 0.38→0.26–0.28, prob 0.25→0.07–0.10 (Table 1). Moderation API shows similar gains (Table 6).
> - Domain NLU (8 tasks): GOT-D avg 83.83 (150k) and 81.51 (50k/5k regime), best among baselines (Tables 2–3).
> - GLUE: GOT-D avg 83.43 (50k + full per-task training) and 78.43 (50k + 5k/task), best among selection baselines (Table 4). 4-bit AdamW (RoBERTa-L) NLU=89.1±0.01, matching 8-bit and 32-bit (Table 2).
> - AGNews (zero-shot, GPT-2 XL): Accuracy 49.5→63.4 with 40k GOT-D (vs DSIR 54.7; TAPT/c 59.1) (Table 16).
> - BoolQ (zero-shot, GPT-Neo 2.7B): 51.1→57.7 with 40k GOT-D (vs DSIR 53.3; TAPT/c 51.2) (Table 18).
> - ImageNet-1k: 4-bit AdamW (Swin-T) 80.8–80.9, close to 32-bit (81.2) and 8-bit (81.0) (Table 2).
> - WMT14 En–De: 4-bit AdamW 26.28–26.45 SacreBLEU, near 32-bit (26.61) and 8-bit (26.66) (Table 2).
> - E2E-NLG: 4-bit AdamW BLEU 67.8±0.51 (Table 2, Table 8), matching 32-bit.
> - LLaMA instruction tuning: 4-bit AdamW comparable to 32-bit across MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA (Table 3), with up to 57.7% memory savings (Table 4).
> 
> 4) Takeaways by task family
> - Detection/association on human parts (PBADet): Best-in-class association accuracy and competitive AP across BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman; improvement is most pronounced for crowded/association-heavy settings (MR−2 and mMR−2).
> - LLM pre-fine-tuning via unlabeled selection (GOT-D): Consistently superior in low-budget regimes over DSIR/TAPT/c; strong toxicity reduction while preserving utility; gains on GLUE and domain NLU; meaningful zero-shot improvements on AGNews/BoolQ with larger LMs.
> - Memory-lean optimization (4-bit): 4-bit AdamW/Factor retains 32-bit accuracy across vision/NLP/MT/NLG while reducing training memory and in some settings time.
> - Recurrent models with EI structure (Dale’s Law): Recurrent DANNs achieve standard-RNN-level performance, whereas simple ColEI partitions learn worse; spectral properties (unimodal, clustered singular values) predict good learning; NSE is a reliable proxy.
> - JEPA vs MAE (self-supervised objectives): In linear settings, JEPA learns predictive (high-ρ) features first, resisting noisy/high-variance modes; depth amplifies this advantage; empirical trends (e.g., ImageNet CCA) align with theory.
> 
> Notes
> - Identical datasets explicitly noted: GLUE (GOT-D and 4-bit); HellaSwag (GOT-D and 4-bit). Due to different models and protocols, direct cross-paper score ranking is not meaningful, but both show gains relative to their baselines on the shared datasets.
> - All numbers and claims above are taken from the provided tables/figures; qualitative trends for spectral (Dale’s Law) and JEPA are drawn from their plots and stated results.

**naive 最终答案**

> I found all five matching papers in the collection. Here they are with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The five papers
> 
> 1. **GOT-D: Principled Data Selection for Warming Up Fine-Tuning in LLMs** (bb21f950…) — selects a small subset from open unlabeled text via Optimal Transport "gradients" to pull the pretraining distribution toward the target distribution, using feature embeddings. Compatible with two-stage SFT-style fine-tuning (mentions LoRA workflows) and reports F1-style metrics.
> 2. **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (8d5e1455…) — compresses Adam/AdamW (and SGD-family) optimizer first/second moments to 4-bit (B128 block-wise + rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer), on Transformer backbones (RoBERTa, GPT-2, LLaMA, Swin-T).
> 3. **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (40fde037…) — analyzes non-contrastive SSL that predicts in latent space (JEPA/self-distillation) vs reconstruction (MAE/MSE), proving the implicit bias of latent-space prediction.
> 4. **Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (e63a94c4…) — spectral (SVD) analysis of recurrent E/I (Dale-constrained) networks, explaining why constrained recurrent nets train poorly and how to make them stable/learnable.
> 5. **PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association** (08b70bc3…) — anchor-free, one-stage detector associating parts to parent bodies via a single part-to-body center offset, on COCO-WholeBody-type benchmarks with YOLO/attention-style backbones and AP/recall/F1 metrics.
> 
> ## Comparison of experimental results
> 
> **Fine-tuning/selection (GOT-D):** Outperformed vanilla BERT, DAPT, and DSIR in **F1** on BERT domain adaptation and improved **GLUE** averages under constrained (50K) budgets; large gains on small tasks. In zero-shot, +13.9% on GPT-2 XL AG News and +6.6% on GPT-neo BoolQ at 40K samples, beating DSIR and TAPT/c. Notably, cheap **sentence-transformer embeddings ≈ distilled-BERT embeddings** (cosine-style similarity suffices). Full selection runs in ~1 hour on one GPU. For GPT-2 detoxification it reduced toxicity more than baselines.
> 
> **Memory-lean optimizers (4-bit):** On RoBERTa-L NLU, 4-bit AdamW matched/exceeded 32-bit (89.1 vs 88.9); Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2 Medium NLG 67.8 vs 67.7; RoBERTa-L QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6; MT SacreBLEU 26.28 vs 26.61. On LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (Alpaca instruction tuning), 4-bit matched 32-bit AdamW on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA (e.g., LLaMA-7B MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7; 33B 54.9 vs 56.4), with closely aligned convergence curves. It beats 8-bit AdamW, Adafactor(β₁=0), and SM3 on accuracy while saving **up to 57.7% memory** and enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; 4-bitFactor (factorized 2nd moment) is most memory-efficient.
> 
> **Self-supervised implicit bias (JEPA):** Proved JEPA (latent prediction) prioritizes high-influence/low-variance "slow" features, while MAE (reconstruction/MSE) tracks high-variance noisy features; the bias appears only when the encoder is deep. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align **faster** with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (measured by CCA). The two learn the same features step-wise but in different order.
> 
> **Recurrent E/I spectral view (Dale's Law):** ColEI networks (simple sign-constrained E/I columns) have multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectra and train worse (sequential MNIST error ≈2.3%±0.6% vs 0.7%±0.3% for standard RNNs); sign constraints explain only part of the gap (1%±1%), spectra matter more. DANN-style E/I networks keep spectra close to standard RNNs and learn just as well. **Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error** across sizes and E/I ratios, serving as a pre-training diagnostic; gradient clipping mitigates ColEI instability.
> 
> **Part-body detection (PBADet):** On BodyHands/COCOHumanParts it beats prior SOTA (BPJDet, HierR-CNN). Anchor-free + part-to-body offset is best: on BodyHands, Hand AP 89.1 vs BPJDet's 85.3, Conditional Accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, Joint AP 85.98 vs 78.13, with fewer params (36.9M vs 41.2M). On CrowdHuman face-body, it achieves leading body MR-2 (36.5 vs 41.3 for BPJDet-YOLOv5s6) and higher face AP (81.6); on COCOHumanParts it reaches ~42.7/41.5 AP (original/subordinate). Against pose estimators it gives substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet.
> 
> **Cross-cutting observations:** GOT-D relies on embedding-space distributional matching (cosine/OT over features); the 4-bit optimizer preserves Adam/AdamW behavior at extreme compression for the same Transformer backbones used in fine-tuning; the JEPA analysis explains why latent-space (vs MSE-reconstruction) objectives generalize better for perception; the Dale's Law paper's spectrum diagnostic parallels the "predict in latent space" intuition of learning robust features; and PBADet is the one task-specific (vision) paper, using attention-free YOLO backbones but a similar anchor-free dense-prediction paradigm with AP/F1 metrics. Note that GOT-D's pre-fine-tuning, NEFTune, and PCP papers in the collection share the fine-tuning theme, but only GOT-D matches the "select small unlabeled subset via embeddings + distributional matching + F1" requirement.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the document collection, I identified five papers matching your five criteria:
> 
> **1. Data selection for warm-starting LLM fine-tuning → GOT-D** (doc `bb21f950…`, "Get More for Less: Principled Data Selection for Warming Up Fine-tuning in LLMs"). Selects a small subset from open unlabeled data via gradients of Optimal Transport (distributional matching) for a pre-fine-tuning stage, then targeted fine-tuning (compatible with LoRA-style SFT). Uses sentence-transformer/feature embeddings. Results: BERT domain adaptation beats DAPT/DSIR in F1 and GLUE average under constrained budgets; GPT-2 toxicity −30% at 10K samples; +1.13% average over 8 tasks at 150K; zero-shot gains of 13.9% (GPT-2 XL AG News) and 6.6% (GPT-neo BoolQ) at 40K; runs on one GPU in ~1 hour.
> 
> **2. Low-bitwidth optimizer states → 4-bit Optimizers** (doc `8d5e1455…`, "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"). Compresses Adam/AdamW (and SGDM) first/second moments to 4-bit (B128/DE first moment, Rank-1/Linear + zero-point-exclusion and optional factorization for second moment). Results: matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on all fine-tuning tasks (RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, GPT-2M E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7, SQuAD F1 94.5), comparable on pretraining; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA nearly identical to 32-bit; up to 57.7% memory saving and LLaMA-7B on a single 80GB GPU; beats 8-bit AdamW and Adafactor/SM3 (which degrade on CLS).
> 
> **3. Non-contrastive latent-space SSL analysis → "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks"** (doc `40fde037…`, NeurIPS 2024). Analyzes JEPA (predict in latent space) vs MAE (reconstruct in data space). Deep-linear gradient-flow analysis shows JEPA's implicit bias toward high-influence features (large regression coefficients), strengthened by depth, while MAE tracks high-variance/noisy features — explaining why reconstruction (MSE) losses are suboptimal for perception. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (CCA) than MAE features.
> 
> **4. Spectral view of E/I recurrent models → "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (doc `e63a94c4…`, NeurIPS 2023). Shows sign constraints are *not* the main cause of poor training in Dale's-law (E/I) RNNs; the initial recurrent weight spectrum is. ColEI partitioning yields multimodal, dispersed singular values vs unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur forms for standard RNNs and Dale's ANNs (DANN). Spectrum transplants and normalized-SVD-entropy show spectrum predicts performance; gradient clipping mitigates; small nets with few I units are worst; DANN is robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> 
> **5. Anchor-free one-stage part-body association → PBADet** (doc `08b70bc3…`, "PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association"). One-stage anchor-free detector linking parts to a parent body via a single part-to-body center offset. Results: outperforms BPJDet and HierR-CNN on BodyHands and COCO-HumanParts; on CrowdHuman face-body achieves best body MR-2 (36.5 vs 41.3 for BPJDet) with competitive AP; vs ED-Pose (Swin-L transformer) it raises hand/foot Precision/Recall/F1 substantially (e.g., left-hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87, all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51); ablations confirm association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each help.
> 
> **Comparison/analysis across methods:**
> - **Common threads:** All five favor fine-tuning-oriented, practical settings — GOT-D and 4-bit optimizers are explicitly built around SFT/LoRA fine-tuning workflows and Adam/AdamW; GOT-D uses embedding-similarity-style feature matching (sentence-transformer embeddings nearly as good as distilled-BERT), aligning with the cosine/embedding preference. The 4-bit optimizer paper keeps Adam/AdamW semantics intact, which is why it transfers losslessly out-of-the-box.
> - **Experiments differ in modality and metrics:** GOT-D reports classification-style metrics (F1, accuracy, toxicity) for LLMs; 4-bit optimizers report accuracy/F1/BLEU/SacreBLEU across NLU, QA, NLG, MT, plus memory/training-time; PBADet uses detection metrics (AP, MR-2, F1/Precision/Recall); the JEPA and Dale's-Law papers are more analytical — JEPA reports CCA alignment to perceptual subspaces on ImageNet, Dale's-Law reports error on adding/sMNIST/PTB plus spectral entropy correlations.
> - **Relative strengths/limitations:** GOT-D is strong at low selection budgets (50K) but assumes overlap with pretraining distribution and drifts with Perspective API; 4-bit optimizers are the most broadly validated across backbones (BERT, GPT-2, Swin, LLaMA up to 33B) but note optimal quantization may be task-dependent and only language/vision were tested; JEPA's result is proven in deep linear nets under specific initialization (qualitative generalization only); Dale's-Law work shows spectral initialization — not constraints — governs learnability; PBADet uses CNN (YOLO) backbones rather than attention backbones (attention/transformer backbones appear only via the ED-Pose/Swin-L comparison), so it only partially matches that sub-criterion.
> 
> If you need attention backbones for the detector specifically, PBADet itself is built on YOLOv5/v7 (CNN) and matches DETR-style baselines in AP, so it's the best available match in this collection but not transformer-based.
