**naive 最终答案**

> I found research covering all five areas, with some specific sub-interests only partially present. Here's what the collection contains, area by area, followed by a comparative analysis.
> 
> ## (a) One-stage anchor-free part–body association — **PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> Single part-to-body center offset built on YOLOv5/YOLOv7 anchor-free heads; one-to-one part→body correspondence simplifies post-processing (no anchor boxes, no heuristic matching).
> - **BodyHands**: Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 (anchor-free part-to-body) vs. BPJDet 85.3/86.80/78.13; anchor-based part-to-body 88.4/92.31/85.28.
> - **COCOHumanParts**: AP 42.7 (YOLOv7) / 43.0 (YOLOv5l6); **CrowdHuman** face-body: body MR-2 36.5, face 44.7, AP 91.6/81.6.
> - Against ED-Pose, PBADet gives substantially higher precision, recall, and F1 for hands/feet. Ablations: association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each help; anchor-free beats anchor-based.
> 
> ## (b) Spectral analyses of biologically-constrained RNNs — **"Learning better with Dale's Law"** (NeurIPS 2023) + **Hessian power-law** (ICML 2025)
> - Dale's Law paper: ColEI (column-constrained E/I) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs across adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition. The cause is **spectral**, not sign constraints: ColEI initial weights have multimodal, dispersed singular values; standard RNNs/DANNs match random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur spectra. Singular-value transplants show spectra matter more than sign constraints (sign constraints only explain part of the 2.3%±0.6% gap). **Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error**; smaller networks / fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra; gradient clipping helps.
> - Hessian paper: power-law Hessian spectra hold for well-trained nets (LeNet on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, ResNet18) but not random nets; SGD/Adam/etc. shape the spectrum; power-law is lost with small width/depth, limited data, **noisy labels**, and large-batch training; batch-size phases identified; LoRA-only fine-tuning doesn't induce power-law like full fine-tuning; d_ks predicts LLM generalization (up to 0.98). Also relevant: gradient-flow analysis (square loss, small balanced init) proving implicit rank-minimization bias in shallow ReLU nets.
> - **Caveat**: the user asked for "squared-error or log-loss" RNN analysis; the Dale's Law paper evaluates performance empirically (MNIST classification/log-loss tasks) rather than contrasting losses explicitly; the Hessian paper is the SGD/loss-landscape piece.
> 
> ## (c) Joint-embedding self-supervision (latent-target prediction) — **"Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Theoretical analysis of deep linear self-distillation: JEPA (predicting latent targets) is biased toward **high-influence features** (high regression coefficients, ρ), with critical times and depth-strengthened noise suppression; MAE (masked reconstruction) ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ, so it learns noisy/high-variance features that JEPA delays or suppresses.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE, measured by CCA.
> - **Caveats**: experiments are on ImageNet-1K, not MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100; **no SVHN results exist anywhere in this collection**. Classic-dataset SSL work here is the contrastive-similarity paper (CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 with ResNet-18/50 backbones) and LDReg (ResNet-50, ViT-B on ImageNet), which are joint-embedding-adjacent but not the JEPA-vs-MAE comparison.
> 
> ## (d) Anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets — **"Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"**
> - Extends RCPS (Bates et al., JACM'24) to sequential, adaptively-collected data: guarantees P(ρ(β̂t) ≤ θ for all t) ≥ 1−α simultaneously at all times.
> - Built on **e-processes** and **testing-by-betting** (Waudby-Smith–Ramdas betting e-process, Ville's inequality), with **active labeling** via IPW and a label budget; a model-based predictor acts as a control variate (optimal predictor = conditional risk; optimal labeling policy ∝ conditional risk std dev); regret bounds relate policy/predictor error to wealth-process growth.
> - Experiments: simulations + ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05); learned/pretrained policies cut risk faster than naive baselines while keeping violation rates below α.
> 
> ## (e) Instruction tuning of permissively-licensed code LLMs — **OctoPack** + **NEFTune**
> - **OctoPack** (ICLR 2024): instruction-tunes StarCoder (permissively licensed) end-to-end on CommitPack (4TB Git commits, 350 languages) and CommitPackFT (2GB, 277 languages); evaluates on HumanEvalPack (synthesis/repair/explanation × Python/JS/Java/Go/C++/Rust). **OctoCoder: 46.2% pass@1 on Python HumanEval** (≈38% relative gain over StarCoder), best among non-OpenAI-trained models; GPT-4 reaches 86.6%. Ablations: CommitPackFT is critical for repair; natural-language targets (OASST) are critical for explanation; all datasets help synthesis equally.
> - **NEFTune** (ICLR 2024): noisy embeddings during instruction tuning; LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win rate 29.8→64.7; Evol-Instruct 70.3→79.6, ShareGPT 68.7→76.3, OpenPlatypus 62.0→70.6; works with QLoRA; OpenLLM scores unchanged; human preference 74.6%.
> - **Caveats**: low-rank adapter tuning of code LLMs appears only as a citation (Astraios); **feature embeddings/angular similarity** as evaluation tools for code models were not found (cosine/angular similarity appears in contrastive-learning and causal-discovery papers, not code LLM evaluation).
> 
> ## Cross-cutting analysis & remaining interests
> - **Near-linear runtime**: linear-time HSIC independence tests (O(n), 100k samples in <10 s vs. quadratic baselines); output-sensitive parametric-DP algorithms (improved from O(m³K³) to O(mK log(mK)+R) for ℓ=1); GNN edge-embedding protocols with input-linear evaluation; MNL-VQL avoids enumerating 760k assortments with stable runtime.
> - **SFT backbones**: StarCoder (OctoPack) and LLaMA-2 (NEFTune) are the SFT backbones; Hessian paper shows power-law spectra emerge during pretraining/fine-tuning (LoRA-only fine-tuning does not).
> - **ResNet-50 baselines**: appear in GRAFT (SeCo, CACo ResNet-50 baselines), the contrastive-similarity paper (standard ResNet-50 for ImageNet-100), and LDReg (ResNet-50 on ImageNet for SSL).
> - **Clean-label subsets for calibration**: the Hessian paper contrasts clean labels vs. 40%/80% label noise (power-law breaks under noise); the Agreement-on-the-Line paper uses data ordering/subsetting and random-head init as calibration/diversity sources for ID-vs-OOD prediction across GPT/OPT/BERT and CLIP embeddings.
> 
> **Not established in this collection**: (1) any SVHN experiments; (2) JEPA-style latent-prediction results on MNIST/CIFAR-100 (JEPA analysis uses ImageNet-1K); (3) angular-similarity/feature-embedding analyses specifically for instruction-tuned code LLMs (only pass@k, BLEU/METEOR, and win-rate metrics); (4) a single paper combining "near-linear runtime" with the detection/LLM methods (that discussion lives in the statistics/graph papers).

**community 最终答案**

> I now have enough evidence to answer. Let me summarize the findings across the five research areas.
> 
> ## 1. (a) One-stage anchor-free part–body association — **PBADet** (ICLR 2024)
> - **Method**: Extends one-stage anchor-free detectors (YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6) with a single part-to-body center offset; one-to-one part–body correspondence guarantees valid ground truth and **simplified post-processing** (plain NMS; no embedding matching or heuristic association networks).
> - **Metrics**: On BodyHands, Hand AP 89.1 (YOLOv7), conditional accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 — beating BPJDet and all prior methods with fewer parameters. On COCOHumanParts: AP.5:.95 42.7/43.0, AP.5 69.5/70.0, AP_M 65.8/66.2, AP_L 66.7/67.2.
> - **Precision/Recall/F1** (vs. ED-Pose, COCO val, Table 7): all parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, **F1 48.52 vs 31.51**; per-part F1 (e.g., left hand 46.50 vs 22.87).
> - **Ablations**: association loss (Joint AP 78.07→85.98), multi-scale center offsets (85.46), task-alignment learning (85.78) each help; anchor-free part-to-body (85.98) beats anchor-based body-to-part (78.13).
> 
> ## 2. (b) Spectral analysis of biologically constrained recurrent nets — **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - ColEI (E/I sign-constrained) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than DANN and standard RNNs on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> - **Spectral finding**: poor learning is caused by the **initialization spectrum** (multimodal, dispersed singular values; column-mean rank-one nilpotent structure), not sign constraints per se — spectrum transplants confirm singular values matter more than sign constraints or singular vectors; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error across EI ratio and network size.
> - **Optimization/stochastic-gradient connection**: this paper analyzes gradient-clipping effects; the Hessian power-law work ("Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure", ICML 2025) complements it by showing well-trained LeNets/CNNs (SGD vs random init on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100) exhibit power-law Hessian spectra (log-loss classification), while random-initialized networks do not — i.e., initialization + SGD shape training; large-batch SGD (B>768) breaks the power law; 40–80% label noise also breaks it, and clean labels preserve it.
> 
> ## 3. (c) Joint-embedding self-supervision predicting latent targets — **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024, Apple)
> - JEPA (self-distillation, predicting latent target representations with stop-gradient) is contrasted with MAE (masked reconstruction in input space). Theory on deep linear networks shows JEPA is implicitly biased to high-influence features (high regression coefficients) and **learns noisy features more slowly than MAE**, converging to lower amplitude weights for noisy modes.
> - Experiments are on **ImageNet-1K (64×64)** with I-JEPA vs MAE ViT encoders using CCA on PCA-filtered (bottom 25% / top 75% variance) data: JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual subspace. Note: this paper does **not** use MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 — its vision experiments are ImageNet-based; I could not find an SVHN experiment in this collection, so that specific dataset match is unverified.
> 
> ## 4. (d) Anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets — **"Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Extends RCPS (Bates et al.) to the sequential, adaptive setting with **(θ,α)-anytime-valid risk control**: P(ρ(β̂t)≤θ for all t) ≥ 1−α, via **e-processes and testing-by-betting** (Waudby-Smith–Ramdas betting e-process, Ville's inequality).
> - **Active labeling**: labeling policy q_t(X_t) decides whether to query the gold label, with IPW reweighting, bounded label probability (q_min), and a predefined **label budget**; a machine-learning predictor (conditional risk estimate) acts as a control variate to reduce variance.
> - **Optimal policy/predictor**: optimal predictor is the conditional risk; optimal labeling policy is proportional to the conditional risk standard deviation; log-optimal regret bounds relate policy/predictor estimation error to the wealth process growth rate.
> - **Experiments**: simulations and ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05) — learned/pretrained policies cut risk faster than baselines while keeping violation rates below α. Limitations: i.i.d. assumption, bounded label policies.
> 
> ## 5. (e) Instruction tuning of permissively licensed code LLMs — **OctoPack** (ICLR 2024)
> - Instruction-tunes StarCoder (16B) end-to-end on CommitPackFT (permissively licensed Git commits; ~2GB filtered, 5,000 samples per language) + filtered OASST; **explicitly avoids OpenAI-output-trained models (non-permissive)**.
> - **HumanEval-style evaluation**: introduces HumanEvalPack (synthesis, repair, explanation; Python/JS/Java/Go/C++/Rust) with execution-based pass@1 (temp 0.2, top-p 0.95, n=20).
> - **Results**: OctoCoder 46.2% pass@1 on Python HumanEval (≈38% relative gain over StarCoder); best permissively licensed model on HumanEvalPack; GPT-4 reaches 86.6% pass@1. Ablations: CommitPackFT critical for repair, natural-language data for explanation, OASST mixing helps.
> - Related: NEFTune (ICLR 2024) adds noise to **embedding vectors** during instruction tuning (LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval 29.8→64.7), including QLoRA/low-rank settings, with embedding-similarity and singular-value analyses. Note: the requested "angular similarity" and "practical diagrams" for code LLM evaluation are not explicitly reported in these papers' text; the code-LLM papers here report pass@k, not angular similarity.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting comparison and honest caveats
> - **Verified matches**: (a) PBADet ✓; (b) Dale's-Law spectral paper ✓ (+ Hessian power-law/SGD paper as the stochastic-gradient complement); (d) anytime-valid RCPS ✓; (e) OctoPack ✓ (permissive licensing, end-to-end finetuning; LoRA appears in NEFTune/Hessian-LoRA analyses).
> - **Partial/uncertain**: (c) JEPA paper matches "predict latent targets vs masked reconstruction to avoid noisy features," but its experiments are on ImageNet, **not** MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100 — no SVHN results exist in the collection for this topic.
> - **Not found in this collection**: near-linear runtime discussions (the only near-linear/linear-time items are HSIC independence testing and parametric DP — unrelated to these five topics), ResNet-50 baselines specifically tied to these papers (ResNet-50 appears only as a backbone in unrelated GRAFT/contrastive-learning papers and as a KITTI-360 feature extractor), clean-label subsets used for calibration (the Hessian paper analyzes clean vs noisy labels but not calibration subsets; the RCPS paper uses unlabeled calibration streams, not "clean-label subsets"), and feature-embedding/angular-similarity/diagram evaluations for code LLMs.
> 
> Consequently, a faithful synthesis is only possible for items (a), (b), (d), and (e) (plus (c) with the caveat about datasets); the "near-linear runtime," "ResNet-50 baseline," "clean-label calibration subset," "SFT backbone," and "angular similarity/diagrams" specifics you asked about **cannot be established from this context** — they do not appear in the retrieved documents for the matched papers.

### paperscope:results_comparison:383 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a robotics + coding assistant platform. It needs a vision module that can associate hands/faces with the correct person in crowded rooms; a forecasting block that respects EI constraints yet trains stably; a self‑supervised backbone that learns robust features without overfitting to pixel noise; a deployment layer that guarantees low‑risk outputs at all times while querying only a fraction of labels; and a code copilot tuned from open Git commits (not closed APIs), possibly via low‑rank adapters. Please point me to works that collectively cover these needs and discuss stochastic gradient training, squared‑error vs. log‑loss, angular similarity in feature embeddings, common image benchmarks (MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR‑100), F1/Precision evaluation, and practical finetuning on ResNet‑50/SFT backbones with near‑linear time complexity.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：3→2（Δ-1）；rounds：5→6（Δ+1）。**

Gold 1：

> Cross-paper comparison of experimental results (only from figures/tables provided)
> 
> 1) Vision: Part–Body Association and Crowded Person Detection (PBADet vs baselines)
> - BodyHands (hand–body association, Table 1)
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7, 1024) achieves Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6, 1024) achieves Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>   - Best anchor-based BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 1536) reports Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.
>   - Conclusion: On the identical BodyHands dataset, both PBADet variants outperform BPJDet across all three metrics, with +3.2 to +3.9 AP, +5.7 to +5.8 points conditional accuracy, and +1.3 to +1.6 points joint AP.
> 
> - COCOHumanParts (multi-part-to-body association, Tables 2–3)
>   - Overall AP (all categories): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate), similar to BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3.
>   - Scale-specific AP: PBADet improves APM/APL (66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4) vs BPJDet (63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9).
>   - Per-category APs: PBADet competitive with BPJDet across person/head/face/hands/feet (e.g., person 62.4 vs 61.3; feet categories slightly higher with PBADet).
>   - Association quality (average mMR−2, lower is better, Table 3): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) achieves lower mMR−2 for head (27.9 vs 30.8), face (30.5 vs 31.8), left hand (36.2 vs 41.6), right hand (40.8 vs 42.2), left foot (47.9 vs 50.4); right foot slightly worse (50.4 vs 49.1). PBADet (YOLOv7) also lowers mMR−2 in most categories.
>   - Conclusion: On the identical COCOHumanParts dataset, PBADet matches or exceeds detection APs at medium/large scales and improves association robustness (lower mMR−2) in most part categories vs BPJDet.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (face–body association, Tables 5–6)
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): MR−2 body 36.5 (best among compared methods in Table 6), MR−2 face 44.7, AP body 91.6, AP face 81.6, mMR−2 50.8.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): MR−2 body 40.7, MR−2 face 46.3, AP body 89.5, AP face 81.6, mMR−2 50.1.
>   - Against crowded-scene detectors (e.g., Sparse-RCNN, Deformable-DETR, Table 6): PBADet attains lower body MR−2 and competitive AP.
>   - Conclusion: On the identical CrowdHuman dataset, PBADet improves body MR−2 and body AP over BPJDet; face AP parity; mMR−2 is close (PBADet +0.7 higher).
> 
> - Additional ablations (Tables 4 and 8)
>   - Removing association loss (Lassoc) reduces Conditional Accuracy (92.62→80.78) and Joint AP (85.98→78.07), confirming the association head’s impact.
>   - Anchor-free part-to-body vs anchor-based: PBADet’s anchor-free design achieves Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98, outperforming both anchor-based part-to-body (88.4/92.31/85.28) and anchor-based body-to-part (BPJDet 85.3/86.80/78.13).
>   - ED-Pose comparison (Table 7, COCO val): PBADet yields higher Precision/Recall/F1 across parts, e.g., all parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87; right hand F1 47.34 vs 24.17; left foot F1 51.08 vs 40.46; right foot F1 50.34 vs 40.34.
> 
> 2) Recurrent Networks with Dale’s Law (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNN)
> - Benchmarks (Figure 2): Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic Object Recognition.
>   - Across all four tasks, ColEI networks learn worse (higher test errors, more variance) than DANNs and standard RNNs; gradient clipping benefits ColEI substantially.
> - Spectrum transplant and sign constraints (Figure 4)
>   - Impact on sequential MNIST: Changing spectrum contributes more than sign constraints to the performance gap. Reported changes in final test error: spectrum effects ~1.5% ± 0.3% (RNNs) and ~2% ± 1% (ColEI); sign constraints effects smaller (~0.7% ± 0.3% for RNNs; ~1% ± 1% for ColEI).
> - EI ratio and network size (Figures 5–7)
>   - ColEI degrades with fewer inhibitory units and in small networks (lower Normalized SVD Entropy, larger max singular values), leading to worse accuracy across tasks; DANNs remain robust (consistent NSE, stable performance) even with very few inhibitory neurons.
>   - Normalized SVD Entropy predicts performance: higher NSE correlates with lower test error across EI ratios and sizes.
>   - Conclusion: On identical tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition), DANNs and standard RNNs outperform ColEI; spectral properties (unimodal clustered singular values) are key to good performance.
> 
> 3) Self-supervised learning in vision: JEPA vs MAE
> - Training dynamics (Figures 2, 4, 5): In deep linear settings, both exhibit greedy learning w.r.t. feature covariance (λ), but JEPA additionally prioritizes high-influence features with larger regression coefficients (ρ), especially with deeper encoders; MAE remains primarily sensitive to λ.
> - Spectrum-depth effect (Figure 4): Deeper JEPA encoders widen temporal separation favoring larger ρ; MAE’s ordering is largely unchanged by depth.
> - Identical dataset overlap (ImageNet-1K, 64×64; Figure 7)
>   - JEPA (I-JEPA) vs MAE on ImageNet: Mean CCA (feature similarity) between full and “bottom-variance” datasets is higher for JEPA than MAE throughout training (curves in Fig. 7), indicating JEPA learns perceptual, low-variance features faster; JEPA shows lower similarity on “top-variance” subsets than MAE.
>   - Conclusion: On the identical ImageNet setting, JEPA emphasizes influential, low-variance features and achieves higher representation similarity in the perceptual subspace than MAE during training.
> 
> 4) Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets (RCPS)
> - Numerical simulation (Figure 2)
>   - Target safety: α=0.05; β* dotted line 0.5578. Label-efficient methods (“pretrain”, “learned”) reach lower β̂ closer to β* with fewer labels than baselines (“all”, “oblivious”), while maintaining average safety violation rates below α.
> - ImageNet (Figure 3)
>   - On the identical ImageNet dataset, “pretrain” and “learned” policies achieve lower final β̂ and faster convergence (β̂ vs labels) than “all” or “oblivious” and respect the anytime-valid constraint (safety violation rates below α=0.05).
>   - Conclusion: On identical datasets (ImageNet), active RCPS improves label efficiency (better β̂ with fewer labels) while controlling risk at all times.
> 
> 5) Code LLMs and instruction tuning (OCTOPACK)
> - HUMANEVALPACK (3 tasks × 6 languages, Table 2)
>   - OCTOCODER (16B) vs permissive baselines: Highest average pass@1 across Fix/Explain/Synthesize among permissive models. Examples:
>     • HUMANEVALSYNTHESIZE (Python): 46.2 pass@1 (vs StarCoder 33.6; CodeGeeX2 35.9; BLOOMZ 15.6; StarChat- 33.5). Across languages, OCTOCODER averages 35.5 (best permissive).
>     • HUMANEVALEXPLAIN (Python): 35.1 pass@1 (vs StarCoder 0.0; CodeGeeX2 0.0; BLOOMZ 14.7; StarChat- 25.4); average 24.5 (best permissive).
>     • HUMANEVALFIX (Python): 30.4 pass@1 (vs StarCoder 8.7; CodeGeeX2 15.9; BLOOMZ 16.6; StarChat- 18.1); average 27.0 (best permissive).
>   - Non-permissive SOTA: GPT-4 outperforms all models (e.g., HUMANEVALSYNTHESIZE Python 86.6; average 78.3), but underperforms OCTOCODER only in permissive class comparisons.
> - Ablations on instruction sources (Figure 4; Python subset)
>   - COMMITPACKFT+OASST yields best average across Fix/Explain/Synthesize vs OASST alone, xP3x+OASST, or Self-Instruct. COMMITPACKFT, containing ~20% bug fixes, is especially important for Code Repair; OASST contributes natural language targets crucial for Explain.
>   - Conclusion: On identical HUMANEVALPACK tasks/languages, COMMITPACKFT+OASST-tuned OCTOCODER generalizes best among permissive models; GPT-4 remains strongest overall.
> 
> Cross-domain notes on overlapping or similar evaluation types
> - Identical dataset: ImageNet appears in both JEPA (representation learning) and RCPS (risk control). JEPA shows higher full–bottom representation similarity; RCPS shows lower β̂ and controlled violations with active labeling. Metrics differ (CCA vs safety β̂), but both show improved performance of the proposed methods on ImageNet.
> - Similar tasks across code benchmarks: HUMANEVALSYNTHESIZE is nearly saturated by GPT-4 (86.6 pass@1, Python), while HUMANEVALFIX and HUMANEVALEXPLAIN remain more challenging; OCTOCODER improves substantially vs StarCoder across all three tasks.
> - Vision detection vs pose/heads: On COCOHumanParts and CrowdHuman, PBADet’s anchor-free part-to-body design improves association accuracy (lower mMR−2) and body MR−2 vs BPJDet; relative to Faster R-CNN/FCOS/RetinaNet baselines (Table 2), PBADet matches/exceeds APs at medium/large scales and per-category APs.
> 
> Specific datasets summary (best vs worse performers)
> - BodyHands: Best PBADet (YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6) across AP/Conditional Accuracy/Joint AP; BPJDet worse.
> - COCOHumanParts: PBADet best for APM/APL and association mMR−2 in most categories; BPJDet slightly higher overall AP in some entries.
> - CrowdHuman: PBADet best body MR−2; close mMR−2 to BPJDet.
> - Sequential MNIST/Adding/PTB/Natural Object Recognition: DANN/standard RNN > ColEI across tasks; spectrum more decisive than sign constraints.
> - ImageNet (JEPA vs MAE): JEPA higher mean CCA in perceptual (bottom-variance) subspace; MAE higher on top-variance; JEPA learns “influential” features faster.
> - ImageNet (RCPS): Active policies (“pretrain”, “learned”) reduce labels and achieve lower β̂ with safety violation rate ≤ α.
> - HUMANEVALPACK: OCTOCODER best permissive across Fix/Explain/Synthesize; GPT-4 strongest overall.
> 
> Evaluation metrics appearing (only as reported)
> - AP/MR−2/mMR−2 (PBADet on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman).
> - Precision/Recall/F1 (PBADet vs ED-Pose on COCO validation; Table 7).
> - Test error/accuracy curves (Dale’s Law figures across benchmarks) and quantified deltas (Figure 4 spectrum/sign contributions).
> - CCA (JEPA vs MAE on ImageNet), β̂ and safety violation rate α (RCPS on simulation and ImageNet).
> - pass@1 (OCTOPACK across tasks/languages; Table 2).
> 
> Overall conclusion
> - On identical datasets, PBADet outperforms BPJDet on BodyHands and CrowdHuman, and improves association robustness on COCOHumanParts; JEPA shows better perceptual feature alignment than MAE on ImageNet; RCPS achieves label-efficient, anytime-valid risk control on ImageNet.
> - On similar dataset types, OCTOPACK’s COMMITPACKFT+OASST-tuned OCTOCODER delivers the strongest permissive performance across multi-language, multi-task code benchmarks; DANN and standard RNNs consistently outperform ColEI on standard sequence tasks due to favorable spectral properties.
> - Across specific datasets, the proposed methods (PBADet, JEPA with deep encoders, RCPS with active policies, OCTOCODER) show measurable gains over baselines as reflected directly in the reported tables/figures.

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Works covering your five modules
> 
> **1. Vision (hand/face→person association in crowds): PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free part-body association). Treats parts (hands, face, feet) as objects linked to a parent body via a single part-to-body center offset (part-to-body principle, vs BPJDet's body-to-part). Results: on **BodyHands** it beats all competitors on hand AP, conditional accuracy and joint AP (e.g., YOLOv7 model: 89.1 mMR-2/92.62 vs BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 85.9/86.91); on **COCOHumanParts** it matches BPJDet AP while leading person/feet APs and achieving the lowest mMR-2; on **CrowdHuman** face-body association it gets the best body MR-2 with competitive AP. Against the pose-estimator ED-Pose it is far better on **Precision/Recall/F1** (all-parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs 24.09/45.51/31.51).
> 
> **2. Forecasting that respects constraints yet trains stably:** two complementary works.
> - **DAML (Decision-Aware ML)** trains spatiotemporal forecasters by maximizing likelihood subject to a top-K BPR constraint. Experiments: NLL-only training gives suboptimal top-K decisions; BPR-only optimization sharply degrades likelihood; DAML improves BPR (up to ~0.05 over ML) with little/no likelihood loss, and its Pareto-frontier sweeps (ε thresholds) let you trade BPR vs log-likelihood — better than surrogate baselines PG and SPO+.
> - **Dale's Law / EI networks (spectral perspective)**: EI (excitatory/inhibitory) constraints alone don't explain poor training — the initial **singular-value spectrum** does. ColEI RNNs have multimodal dispersed spectra and train badly (higher variance, unstable without gradient clipping), while DANN (Dale's ANN) recurrent variants have standard-RNN-like spectra and train just as well, even with one inhibitory unit. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error. Practical takeaway: use DANN-style EI architectures + gradient clipping + spectrum check for stable EI-constrained training.
> 
> **3. Self-supervised backbone robust to pixel noise: "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features."** Deep-linear analysis shows JEPA/self-distillation is implicitly biased to learn high-influence (high-ρ) features and suppresses noise, while MAE's feature ordering depends on eigenvalues; depth strengthens noise suppression. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA representations align faster with the low-variance PCA (perceptual) subspace than MAE (measured by CCA). Related: **LDReg** counters local dimensional collapse (Fisher-Rao/LID regularization), improving SimCLR/BYOL/MAE linear eval, transfer (Food-101, CIFAR, Birdsnap, Cars, DTD) and COCO detection on ResNet-50/ViT-B; and the exogenous-noise RL paper showing **temporal contrastive learning beats forward modeling under iid pixel noise**.
> 
> **4. Deployment with guaranteed low-risk outputs and limited label queries: "Anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets" (RCPS + active labeling).** It guarantees ρ(β̂t) ≤ θ simultaneously for all t with probability ≥ 1−α on adaptively collected data (e-processes/testing-by-betting), with a label policy whose expected query fraction stays under a budget. Experiments (θ=0.1, α=0.05, budget B=0.3, incl. ImageNet) show learned/pretrained policies reach lower risk faster than "all"/"oblivious" baselines while keeping violation rates below α. Supporting label-efficiency works: **DSL** (consistent estimates from ~100 gold labels over imperfect surrogates) and **GOT-D** (optimal-transport data selection under 50M-token budgets, improving GLUE F1 and reducing GPT-2 toxicity).
> 
> **5. Code copilot from open Git commits + low-rank adapters: OctoPack.** Compiles **CommitPack** (~4TB permissively-licensed Git commits, 350 languages) and CommitPackFT; instruction-tunes StarCoder-16B (SFT) into **OctoCoder**, best permissively-licensed model on HumanEvalPack (synthesis/repair/explanation, 6 languages), **46.2% pass@1 on HumanEval Python (~38% relative gain over StarCoder)**. CommitPackFT is critical for repair; natural-language data for explanation. Low-rank adaptation is validated elsewhere in the corpus: **NEFTune + QLoRA** improves AlpacaEval across model sizes (milder than full FT), **Themis** fine-tunes a Vicuna-7B-SFT with LoRA (SFT+PPO), and the Hessian paper analyzes LoRA adapters on TinyLlama (LoRA-only tuning does *not* induce the power-law Hessian that full FT does, implying different generalization behavior).
> 
> ## Cross-cutting training/evaluation topics
> 
> - **Stochastic gradient training**: the Hessian-structure paper trains LeNet/FCN/ResNet-18 on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 with SGD/VanillaSGD/Adam/AMSGrad/etc. (batch 128, lr schedules). Well-trained networks show power-law Hessian spectra (predicts generalization; e.g., LeNet CIFAR-10 correlation ~0.72); spectra are lost with random init, label noise, and very large batches (≥B=768–1280), and SGD's gradient-noise covariance is heavy-tailed. The 4-bit-optimizer paper also gives a convergence proof for quantized SGD(M).
> - **Squared-error vs log-loss**: no single head-to-head comparison exists in this corpus. Evidence is split: the minimax data-selection paper explicitly uses **logistic (log) loss** L(y;z)=−yz+log(e⁻ᶻ+eᶻ) and analyzes misclassification error under misspecification; the shallow-ReLU gradient-flow paper analyzes **square loss** (rank-minimization bias); INN-TD uses MSE for regression; the video-based RL theory optimizes log-loss (KL). So: log-loss for probabilistic classification, square loss for regression/least-squares — but a direct empirical comparison isn't in the collection.
> - **Angular (cosine) similarity in embeddings**: "On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning." Optimal full-batch encoders give positive-pair similarity 1 and negative-pair similarity −1/(n−1); mini-batches preserve the expectation but raise negative-pair-similarity variance (worse for small batches). Their auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy and temperature robustness on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and ImageNet (e.g., negative-pair variance drops from 0.1649→0.1008 at batch 32). This is the theoretical basis for the angular geometry of your face/hand embeddings.
> - **Image benchmarks (MNIST/SVHN/CIFAR-100)**: MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 appear in the Hessian paper (SGD, power-law spectra); CIFAR-10/100 and ImageNet in the contrastive-embeddings paper and LDReg; sequential MNIST in the Dale's Law paper. **SVHN does not appear anywhere in the retrieved corpus** — that benchmark is not covered.
> - **F1/Precision evaluation**: PBADet reports Precision/Recall/F1 vs ED-Pose; RLCD defines F1 = 2·Recall·Precision/(Recall+Precision) and uses it for causal discovery (F1 0.81 on Alzheimer's graph); Agreement-on-the-Line uses macro-F1 for QA OOD estimation; CEGA uses F1/fidelity for budget-constrained GNN acquisition.
> - **Practical finetuning on ResNet-50/SFT backbones, near-linear time**: no paper demonstrates "near-linear time" finetuning directly. Closest evidence: **LDReg**'s standard protocol (ResNet-50 with SimCLR/BYOL; 100-epoch pretraining batch 2048; linear eval batch 4096; COCO RCNN-C4 finetuning; transfer eval with SGD+Nesterov), and the minimax data-selection paper's use of SwAV **ResNet-50** features (2048-d penultimate, ridge logistic regression). Efficiency results in the corpus: **4-bit optimizers** cut memory up to ~57.7% (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU) with no accuracy loss, and the **linear-time HSIC** framework achieves O(nD²) complexity (seconds on 100k samples vs slow quadratic baselines) — the latter is near-linear complexity, but for independence testing, not backbone finetuning. **SFT backbones** are concretely used by OctoPack (StarCoder SFT), Themis (Vicuna-7B-SFT + LoRA) and CodeSteer (Llama-3.1-8B SFT/DPO).
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> 
> - **Vision**: PBADet shows a one-stage part-to-body formulation beats multi-stage (BPJDet, Hier-RCNN, DETR-based) methods on both association quality (mMR-2, conditional accuracy, joint AP) and small-part F1 — strongest on multi-part (BodyHands/COCOHumanParts), less differentiated on single-part face-body (CrowdHuman).
> - **Forecasting**: DAML dominates the NLL-vs-BPR trade-off curve (Pareto frontier) over ML, BPR-only, PG, SPO+; the Dale's-Law work explains *why* constrained networks fail (spectrum, not sign constraints) and gives a pre-training diagnostic (NSE) — directly actionable for stable EI-constrained training.
> - **SSL backbone**: JEPA (latent prediction) is the principled choice against pixel noise; LDReg is orthogonal (fixes dimensional collapse) and stacks on top of SimCLR/BYOL/MAE; the exogenous-noise paper says use temporal contrastive when noise is iid pixel-level.
> - **Deployment**: anytime-valid RCPS is the only method here with simultaneous all-time risk guarantees + bounded label queries; DSL/GOT-D reduce label/data budgets upstream (statistical guarantees vs data-selection efficiency).
> - **Code copilot**: OctoPack is the only open-commit training corpus; LoRA/QLoRA (via NEFTune/Themis/Hessian papers) is the efficient adaptation path, with the caveat from the Hessian paper that LoRA and full FT induce different Hessian/generalization structure.
> - **Gaps in the corpus**: SVHN benchmarks, a direct squared-error-vs-log-loss comparison, and an explicit near-linear-time ResNet-50/SFT finetuning scheme are not present — those specific claims cannot be established from this collection.

**community 最终答案**

> Here is a concise mapping of each need to works in this collection, plus a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Vision: hands/faces → correct person in crowds
> **PBADet** (one-stage, anchor-free part–body association) directly targets this. It links each detected part (hands, face, feet) to its parent body via a single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman.
> - **Comparison/results:** On BodyHands it beats BPJDet, HierR-CNN, and BodyHands in hand-AP, conditional accuracy, and joint-AP; the YOLOv7 variant reaches ~89.1% body/part detection with 92.62 AP. On COCOHumanParts it leads AP/AP_M/AP_L and the lowest mMR⁻² for head, face, both hands. Against the pose estimator ED-Pose it is substantially better on **Precision/Recall/F1** (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; left-hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87, precision 37.6 vs 18.4, recall 60.8 vs 30.3). On CrowdHuman face–body association it wins body/face MR⁻² and stays competitive in AP (advantage over BPJDet is smaller for this single-part task).
> 
> ## 2. Forecasting with equivariance/invariance (EI) constraints, stable training
> - **GeoBFN** enforces SE(3)-invariant density modeling through equivariant GNNs with continuous-time training losses; state-of-the-art molecule stability (90.87% on QM9, 85.60% atom stability on GEOM-DRUG) and stable conditional generation.
> - **ChaosBench** (S2S climate forecasting) provides physics-based constraints/metrics. **Results:** weather-scale models collapse to unskilled climatology beyond ~15–20 days; ensembling, robust error-propagation control, and physics-informed models are the strategies that stabilize and extend skill (ECMWF ensembles best).
> - **DAML** (decision-aware spatiotemporal forecasting) shows a constrained objective trades off likelihood vs top-K decision metric, tracing a Pareto frontier (ML maximizes likelihood but poor top-K; direct BPR maximizes decisions but sharply hurts likelihood; DAML improves BPR with little likelihood loss). This is the closest explicit "constraint vs stable training" trade-off analysis.
> 
> ## 3. Self-supervised backbone robust to pixel noise
> - **JEPA/self-distillation analysis**: proves (via deep-linear gradient-flow ODEs) that JEPA prioritizes high-influence features and suppresses noisy pixel features (depth strengthens noise suppression), unlike MAE whose ordering depends mainly on eigenvalues. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance perceptual subspace than MAE.
> - **Video Block-MDP study**: temporal contrastive learning is more robust than forward modeling to i.i.d. pixel noise.
> - **LDReg**: local-dimensionality regularization counters dimensional collapse; improves linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE (ResNet-50 and ViT-B) without forcing collapse.
> 
> ## 4. Deployment: low-risk outputs at all times, querying a fraction of labels
> **Anytime-valid risk-controlling active labeling** is an exact match: it builds risk-controlling prediction sets with simultaneous risk guarantees ρ(β̂_t) ≤ θ for all t with probability 1−α on adaptively collected data, and an active labeling policy that keeps the expected label-query proportion under a budget. **Results:** learned/pretrained label policies cut risk faster than naive baselines on simulations and ImageNet while keeping violation rates below α (θ=0.1, α=0.05).
> 
> ## 5. Code copilot from open Git commits, low-rank adapters
> **OctoPack** is the canonical work: CommitPack (≈4TB of permissively licensed Git commits, 350 languages) + CommitPackFT for instruction tuning, benchmarked by HumanEvalPack (synthesis/repair/explanation, 6 languages). **Results:** OctoCoder is the best permissively-licensed model on HumanEvalPack with 46.2% pass@1 on Python synthesis (≈38% relative gain over StarCoder); CommitPackFT is critical for repair and OASST mixing for explanation. Companion works cover the low-rank adapter side: **4-bit optimizers** fine-tune LLaMA-7B/13B/33B on Alpaca matching 32-bit AdamW with large memory savings; **NEFTune** improves QLoRA instruction tuning (LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win 29.8→64.7, less overfitting); **Agreement-on-the-Line** shows PEFT (LoRA/IA3/BitFit) with random-head initialization reliably predicts OOD performance.
> 
> ## Cross-cutting methodological topics
> - **Stochastic gradient training:** the Hessian power-law study trains LeNet/ResNet18 with SGD/Adam etc. on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 — power-law Hessian spectra appear only for well-trained (SGD-type) nets and are lost with random labels, label noise, or very large batches. PPO-Clip is analyzed as a two-timescale SGD-type method with convergence/stationarity guarantees. Contrastive-learning experiments use SGD (200 epochs, cosine decay).
> - **Squared-error vs log-loss:** the shallow-ReLU gradient-flow paper analyzes **square loss** (rank-minimization bias, PL inequality, exponential convergence); the minimax data-selection and forecasting papers use **logistic/NLL (log-loss)**. Note: the collection has no direct head-to-head square-vs-log comparison.
> - **Angular similarity in embeddings:** the contrastive-learning paper shows InfoNCE-type losses yield positive-pair cosine 1 and negative-pair cosine −1/(n−1); smaller mini-batches inflate the variance of negative-pair similarities and degrade representations, mitigated by a variance-reduction loss that improves top-1 on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100/full ImageNet and temperature robustness. Angular-margin face losses (ArcFace/AdaFace/ElasticFace) appear as baselines in the face-morphing work.
> - **Benchmarks:** MNIST and CIFAR-100 appear throughout (Hessian study, NFTS/Meta-Dataset). **SVHN is not present anywhere in this collection**, so its results cannot be established here.
> - **F1/Precision:** used in PBADet (Table 7, hands/feet vs ED-Pose), RLCD (F1 = 2·Recall·Precision over graph structures), and Agreement-on-the-Line (F1 on SQuAD-Shifts).
> - **ResNet-50/SFT fine-tuning and near-linear time:** ResNet-50 is used as the SSL backbone in LDReg (ImageNet linear eval, COCO fine-tuning), the contrastive-learning study (ImageNet-100), and as the SwAV feature extractor (2048-d) in the minimax data-selection paper (which also demonstrates ridge-logistic training). SFT backbones appear in CodeSteer (SFT/DPO) and PCP. The closest match to "near-linear time" is the linear-time HSIC framework (runs in seconds on 100,000 samples) and the output-sensitive parametric-DP results, though neither is a fine-tuning algorithm per se.
> 
> **Bottom line:** the collection covers every requested need except **SVHN**, which is absent; the strongest matched set is PBADet (vision), GeoBFN/ChaosBench (EI-constrained forecasting), JEPA/LDReg (noise-robust SSL), anytime-valid risk-controlling active labeling (deployment), and OctoPack + LoRA/PEFT works (code copilot), with the Hessian-power-law and contrastive-similarity papers supplying the SGD/benchmark/angular-similarity analysis.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:386 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find a small set of recent papers that collectively cover: (1) anchor‑free human part–body association detectors evaluated on standard vision benchmarks (e.g., COCO) with precision/recall; (2) analyses of implicit bias in self‑supervised learning objectives (JEPA vs reconstruction) using losses such as MSE and cosine‑style alignment, and comparisons to cross‑entropy; (3) memory‑efficient training via low‑bit (≈4‑bit) optimizer states for Adam/AdamW/SGD with online implementation; (4) spectral perspectives on deep networks obeying excitatory/inhibitory constraints for time‑series modeling; and (5) Transformer‑based conditional guidance that steers code vs text using supervised fine‑tuning (SFT/DPO) and preference optimization. Prefer works mentioning fine‑tuning (including SFT backbones or LoRA), regularization choices, and results on datasets like COCO/CIFAR‑100/MNIST or with ResNet‑50/Transformers.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：2→3（Δ+1）；rounds：3→4（Δ+1）。**

judge reasoning：

> The generated answer correctly covers all five topics and captures the main quantitative comparisons, but it omits the nuance that BPJDet holds a slight overall AP edge on COCO-HumanParts and contains minor numeric/discrepancy issues (e.g., some BPJDet BodyHands values and the ImageNet scale), so it is good but not perfect.

<summary>展开完整 gold 与两份最终答案</summary>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a cross-paper, result-only comparison that draws directly from the figures/tables in the five provided papers. I group findings by identical datasets first (who is better/worse), then by similar dataset families, and finally by key per-dataset highlights.
> 
> Identical datasets and head‑to‑head comparisons
> 
> 1) Human body/part detection and association (PBADet vs baselines)
> - BodyHands (Table 1):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73.
>   - Best BPJDet baseline (YOLOv5l6): 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39.
>   - Conclusion: On the same dataset, PBADet outperforms all prior methods, including BPJDet, in all three metrics.
> 
> - COCO HumanParts (Table 2 & 3):
>   - Overall detection AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3.
>     • BPJDet is slightly higher on aggregate AP.
>   - Size breakdown (APM/APL): PBADet 66.2/65.0 vs BPJDet 63.8/63.2 – PBADet leads on medium/large objects.
>   - Category APs: PBADet higher on person (62.4 vs 61.3), right foot (30.9 vs 30.2), left foot (31.5 vs 30.9); BPJDet higher on head (56.6 vs 54.6), face (46.3 vs 44.6), right hand (40.4 vs 39.0), left hand (39.6 vs 37.7).
>   - Association mMR−2 (lower is better, Table 3): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves lower average mMR−2 for head (29.2 vs 30.8), face (31.3 vs 31.8), and left hand (41.1 vs 41.6) than BPJDet (YOLOv5l6); PBADet is higher (worse) on feet.
>   - Conclusion: On COCOHumanParts, BPJDet has a slight edge in overall AP, while PBADet is stronger on medium/large objects and feet/person categories and improves several per-part mMR−2 metrics.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Appendix Tables 5 & 6):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): best body MR−2 36.5 (lowest in table) and body AP 91.6; face MR−2 44.7. Pair mMR−2 is ~50.8.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR−2 40.7, body AP 89.5; face MR−2 46.3; pair mMR−2 ~50.1.
>   - Conclusion: PBADet improves body/face detection MR−2 and body AP over BPJDet on CrowdHuman, with similar association mMR−2.
> 
> 2) LLM guidance for symbolic tasks (CodeSteer vs o1/R1 and baselines) on SymBench (Table 1)
> - Average Normalized Score (28 seen + 9 unseen tasks, 100 samples each):
>   - GPT‑4o + CodeSteer: 86.4 total (88.1 seen, 81.3 unseen).
>   - OpenAI o1: 82.7 total; DeepSeek R1: 76.8; o1‑preview: 74.8.
>   - GPT‑4o only (no guidance): 53.3.
>   - Best non‑CodeSteer baseline (Code/Text Choice): 77.9.
>   - Conclusion: On the same benchmark, CodeSteer surpasses o1/R1/o1‑preview and all training‑free and training‑based baselines, and improves GPT‑4o from 53.3 to 86.4.
> 
> - Per‑task head‑to‑head highlights vs o1 (Table 1):
>   - Game 24: CodeSteer 93 vs o1 80; Path Plan 75 vs 74; Standard Sudoku: CodeSteer 100 vs o1 0.
>   - Several logic/string tasks where baselines fail (e.g., Standard Sudoku 0 for text‑only methods), CodeSteer attains high success (often 90–100), indicating robustness when code execution is beneficial.
> 
> - Generalization to other LLMs (Table 2):
>   - Claude‑3‑5‑Sonnet: Ave. Norm. 92.0 with CodeSteer vs 29.1 without.
>   - Mistral‑Large: 59.8 vs 31.0; GPT‑3.5‑Turbo: 42.3 vs 8.6.
>   - Conclusion: Same tasks, same evaluation—CodeSteer transfers well and yields large absolute gains across models.
> 
> 3) Low‑bit optimizers vs 8‑bit and full precision on identical tasks (Table 2)
> - NLU (RoBERTa‑L on GLUE, mean): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9 vs 8‑bit AdamW 89.1 vs 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit Factor 88.9.
> - ImageNet‑1k (Swin‑T top‑1): 32‑bit 81.2 vs 8‑bit 81.0 vs 4‑bit 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9.
> - E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2 Medium BLEU): 32‑bit 67.7 vs 8‑bit 67.5 vs 4‑bit 67.8; 4‑bit Factor 67.6.
> - SQuAD F1 (RoBERTa‑L): 32‑bit 94.6 vs 8‑bit 94.5 vs 4‑bit 94.5; 4‑bit Factor 94.6.
> - WMT14 en‑de SacreBleu (Transformer‑Base): 32‑bit 26.61 vs 8‑bit 26.66 vs 4‑bit 26.28; 4‑bit Factor 26.45.
> - Conclusion: On the same datasets, 4‑bit optimizers match 8‑bit and closely track 32‑bit across vision, NLU, QA, MT, and NLG; small deltas are task‑dependent.
> 
> - Stability & ablations for 4‑bit (Table 1, GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG):
>   - Naïve 4‑bit second‑moment quantization (B2048/DE) is unstable (33–66% runs fail); removing zero point (DE‑0) or using Linear mapping eliminates instability (0%) and restores BLEU ~67.4–67.8.
>   - Rank‑1 normalization + Linear mapping (second moment) achieves highest BLEU 67.8 with 0% instability.
> 
> - Memory and runtime (Table 4):
>   - LLaMA‑7B fine‑tuning: 4‑bit AdamW cuts total memory from 75.4 GB to 31.9 GB (−57.7%); runtime 3.07 h (vs 3.35 h) on 2×A100 80GB; with fused kernels ~3.11 h.
>   - RoBERTa‑L and GPT‑2 Medium: consistent 34–47% total memory reduction; with fused operators, 4‑bit speed matches or surpasses 8‑bit.
>   - Largest trainable model (Table 5): moves OPT capacity from 350M→1.3B (24 GB) and 1.3B→6.7B (80 GB); enables LLaMA‑7B on a single 80 GB GPU.
> 
> 4) Recurrent EI networks: identical tasks across architectures (Figure 2 & text)
> - Tasks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, naturalistic object recognition.
> - Results trend: Column‑EI (ColEI) underperforms DANN and standard RNNs on all four tasks; ColEI is also more variable and benefits disproportionately from gradient clipping. DANN matches standard RNNs.
> - Spectrum–performance link: networks with higher Normalized SVD Entropy (unimodal, clustered singular values) correlate with lower error/greater stability; ColEI degrades with fewer inhibitory units and smaller sizes; DANN robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> 
> 5) JEPA vs MAE on the same synthetic settings (Figures 1–2, Theorems)
> - Distribution 1 (λ and ρ both increasing): both JEPA and MAE learn features in the same (greedy) order by covariance λ.
> - Distribution 2 (λ increasing, ρ decreasing): MAE’s learning order stays tied to λ; JEPA inverts order and learns high‑ρ (high‑influence) features first—effect strengthens with encoder depth L.
> - Temporal linear generative model (Appendix C): empirical λ and ρ trends confirm JEPA prioritizes influential (high‑ρ/low‑noise) features; MAE remains aligned with high covariance.
> - ImageNet‑64 evidence (Appendix D): CCA indicates JEPA’s features from full vs bottom‑variance data align more than MAE’s (JEPA learns perceptual/low‑variance features faster), consistent with the theory.
> 
> Performance on similar dataset families (cross‑paper grouping)
> 
> A) Vision detection with association (crowded people, whole‑body): PBADet consistently improves real‑world body/part detection–association trade‑offs in crowded/whole‑body settings—best BodyHands and CrowdHuman body metrics; on COCOHumanParts, PBADet improves medium/large AP and some parts (feet/person), while anchor‑based BPJDet holds slightly higher global AP and better head/face/hand APs.
> 
> B) Symbolic reasoning and planning (SymBench): CodeSteer steers when to use code vs text. Across 37 tasks, it boosts GPT‑4o from 53.3 to 86.4 Ave. Norm. Score and surpasses o1 (82.7) and R1 (76.8). It also scales to higher task complexity (e.g., Standard Sudoku 100% vs 0% without symbolic tools) and generalizes to Claude/Mistral/GPT‑3.5 with large gains.
> 
> C) Memory‑efficient training at scale (4‑bit optimizers): Across vision (ImageNet), NLU/QA (GLUE, SQuAD), MT (WMT14), and NLG (E2E), 4‑bit matches 8‑bit and tracks 32‑bit accuracy while cutting optimizer memory ~2–4× (overall training memory −34% to −58%), enabling larger models (e.g., LLaMA‑7B on a single 80 GB GPU) with stable training once the zero‑point issue is removed.
> 
> D) Sequence modeling/time‑series like tasks (RNNs): ColEI’s spectral pathologies cause worse learning and stability on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and naturalistic sequence tasks; DANN’s unimodal, clustered spectra make it match standard RNNs and be robust to EI ratios/sizes. Normalized SVD Entropy predicts performance across EI ratios and widths.
> 
> E) Self‑supervised representation learning (JEPA vs MAE): On controlled synthetic distributions and linear temporal models, JEPA’s implicit bias favors high‑influence (high‑ρ) features and resists noisy dimensions, especially with depth, whereas MAE focuses on high‑variance (high‑λ) directions. Small‑scale ImageNet analyses support that JEPA learns bottom‑variance (perceptual) directions earlier.
> 
> Per‑dataset (or task) highlights (selected rows from tables/figures)
> - PBADet – BodyHands (Table 1): Hand AP 89.1 / Cond. Acc 92.62 / Joint AP 85.98 (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39.
> - PBADet – COCOHumanParts (Table 2): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) APM/APL 66.2/65.0 (higher than BPJDet’s 63.8/63.2); feet APs 30.9/31.5 (PBADet) vs 30.2/30.9 (BPJDet); BPJDet higher on head/face/hands.
> - PBADet – CrowdHuman (Table 5): PBADet (YOLOv7) best body MR−2 36.5 and body AP 91.6; face MR−2 44.7.
> - CodeSteer – SymBench (Table 1): Ave. Norm. 86.4 total; major boosts on tasks where code wins (e.g., Standard Sudoku 100 vs 0 for text‑only baselines; Game 24: 93 vs o1’s 80).
> - CodeSteer – Transfer (Table 2): Claude Ave. Norm. 92.0 (vs 29.1), Mistral 59.8 (vs 31.0), GPT‑3.5 42.3 (vs 8.6).
> - 4‑bit Optimizers – GLUE (Table 2 & 7): 4‑bit AdamW equals or slightly exceeds 32‑bit and 8‑bit averages; per‑task medians (Table 7) remain within noise of 32‑bit, confirming lossless fine‑tuning.
> - 4‑bit Optimizers – E2E‑NLG ablation (Table 1): unstable 4‑bit second‑moment quantization fixed by removing zero point (DE‑0) or using Linear mapping; Rank‑1 + Linear reaches BLEU 67.8 with 0% instability.
> - EI RNNs – Four tasks (Fig. 2): ColEI shows worse final performance than DANN/standard RNN; gradient clipping benefits ColEI more, confirming sensitivity to spectral pathologies; NSE tracks error across EI ratio and width.
> - JEPA vs MAE – Synthetic & temporal model (Figs. 1–2, Sec. 4): JEPA flips learning order to high‑ρ features when λ and ρ trends conflict; effect grows with depth; in temporal settings JEPA avoids noisy modes that MAE learns early.
> 
> Summary of “who wins where”
> - Human part–body association: PBADet is best on BodyHands and CrowdHuman detection metrics; on COCOHumanParts, BPJDet keeps a slim edge on total AP while PBADet leads on medium/large sizes and several categories (feet/person) and improves some mMR−2 parts.
> - Symbolic reasoning with code/text steering: CodeSteer gives the highest average score on SymBench (86.4), beating o1/R1 and improving GPT‑4o by +33.1 points; also generalizes to Claude/Mistral/GPT‑3.5 with large gains.
> - Memory‑efficient training: 4‑bit optimizers match 8‑bit and are close to 32‑bit across ImageNet/GLUE/SQuAD/WMT14/E2E, while cutting memory 34–58% and enabling larger models; stability hinges on removing zero in second‑moment quantization and using Rank‑1 normalization.
> - EI RNNs in time‑series/sequence tasks: Standard RNNs ≈ DANN > ColEI in final accuracy and stability; Normalized SVD Entropy predicts performance across EI ratio/width; gradient clipping especially helps ColEI.
> - JEPA vs reconstruction (MAE): In controlled studies, JEPA learns high‑influence (predictive, low‑noise) modes first and avoids noisy directions; MAE focuses on high‑variance modes. Small‑scale ImageNet evidences JEPA aligns better with perceptual (bottom‑variance) subspaces.
> 
> These results strictly reflect the reported tables/figures and emphasize identical-dataset head‑to‑heads (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman, SymBench, GLUE/ImageNet/SQuAD/WMT14/E2E, adding/sequential‑MNIST/PTB/naturalistic object recognition) and consistent trends on similar families of tasks.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here is a small set of five papers that collectively cover all five topics, with an analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Part-body association detection
> **PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)**
> - Anchor-free part-to-body center-offset detector built on YOLOv5/YOLOv7, evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, COCO-WholeBody, BodyHands, CrowdHuman.
> - **COCOHumanParts all-category AP:** 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet's 30.8/31.8 (YOLOv5l6) — a large gain in the original-category metric.
> - **BodyHands (YOLOv7) ablation:** Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each improve Cond. Accuracy (80.78 → 92.62) and Joint AP (78.07 → 85.98).
> - vs pose estimator ED-Pose on COCO (precision/recall/F1 for all parts): PBADet 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs ED-Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51 — substantially more robust.
> 
> ## 2. Implicit bias in SSL objectives
> **How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Analyzes JEPA vs MAE (reconstruction) using MSE-style L2 objectives (JEPA: ‖VW̄x−SG(W̄)y‖²; MAE: ‖VW̄x−y‖²) on deep linear networks.
> - Key finding: JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient ρ), while MAE prioritizes high-variance features (high λ) — JEPA can even reverse feature-learning order. This bias appears only for deep encoders; reconstruction can learn noisy features JEPA avoids.
> - ImageNet experiments: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE, measured by CCA (JEPA mean CCA higher on "bottom" variance data). Cross-entropy/neural-collapse comparisons appear only as related-work references, not core experiments.
> 
> ## 3. Memory-efficient low-bit optimizer states
> **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - Compression-based framework for Adam/AdamW/SGD(M) with online compress/decompress of states each step (small block B128 for first moment, zero-point-excluding linear/rank-1 quantizer for second moment, optional factorization).
> - Results (4-bit vs 32-bit AdamW): GLUE RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9; ImageNet Swin-T 80.8 vs 81.2; NLG GPT-2M 67.8 vs 67.7; SQuAD 94.5 vs 94.6; WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B Alpaca→MMLU 54.9 vs 56.4 — lossless on fine-tuning, comparable on pre-training. Memory: LLaMA-7B 75.4→31.9GB (57.7% saved), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU.
> 
> ## 4. Spectral analysis of EI-constrained networks
> **Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - RNNs obeying excitatory/inhibitory constraints (ColEI vs DANN) for time-series tasks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, naturalistic object recognition).
> - Spectral properties, not sign constraints, dominate: ColEI's column-mean rank-one structure gives multimodal, dispersed singular spectra vs the unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur form of standard/DANN RNNs; sign constraints only account for ~1% of the error gap (0.7–1%) out of 2.3±0.6%.
> - Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; small networks with few inhibitory units or skewed E:I ratio perform worst (sequential MNIST), while DANN stays robust (NSE ≈ 0.95 even with 1 inhibitory unit). Gradient clipping mitigates ColEI's instability.
> 
> ## 5. Transformer conditional guidance (code vs text)
> **CodeSteer: Symbolic-Augmented Language Models via Code/Text Guidance (ICML 2025)**
> - A Llama-3.1-8B "CodeSteerLLM" is fine-tuned with multi-turn SFT (12k trajectories) then DPO (5.5k preference pairs) to steer a TaskLLM between code and text, with symbolic/self-answer checkers.
> - On SymBench (37 tasks), CodeSteer-augmented GPT-4o scores **86.4** vs 53.3 unaided, beating OpenAI o1 (82.7), o1-preview (74.8), and DeepSeek R1 (76.8); it generalizes to other TaskLLMs (avg +41.8 gain on Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Mistral-Large, GPT-3.5). Ablations: generic agent variants score only 69.5–67.0, confirming SFT/DPO guidance is what drives the gain. Full-parameter fine-tuning (4×H100, 4–10 epochs) is used.
> 
> ## Cross-paper comparison
> - **Evaluation domains differ**, so results are not directly comparable across papers: COCO/mAP metrics (PBADet), CCA/feature-order dynamics (JEPA), accuracy/BLEU/F1 plus memory savings (4-bit optimizers), test error (EI RNNs), and normalized task scores (CodeSteer).
> - **Regularization/fine-tuning themes:** PBADet relies on task-alignment learning; the SSL paper shows objective choice is itself an implicit regularizer; 4-bit optimizers preserve accuracy via quantization/factorization without extra tuning; the Dale's-Law paper identifies initialization spectrum as the effective regularizer; CodeSteer uses SFT+DPO and answer-sampling temperature (1.5) with reward-hacking safeguards.
> - **Consistent qualitative findings:** (a) anchor-free + part-to-body design outperforms anchor-based (PBADet 85.98 vs 78.13 JointAP); (b) JEPA's implicit bias beats reconstruction for perception (CCA evidence); (c) 4-bit states are near-lossless while cutting memory ~43–58%; (d) spectrum quality (NSE) predicts EI-RNN learning, with DANN matching standard RNNs; (e) preference-tuned guidance (SFT+DPO) yields the largest gains over base LLMs (+33 points on SymBench).

**community 最终答案**

> Here is a small set of recent papers that jointly cover your five topics, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Selected papers
> 
> **(1) PBADet** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc…`) — one-stage anchor-free part–body association detection. Evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman; ablations on association loss, multi-scale offsets, task-alignment.
> 
> **(2) "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde03…`) — implicit bias of JEPA self-distillation vs MAE reconstruction, both formulated as MSE losses (L_MAE = E‖g(f(x))−y‖², L_JEPA = E‖g(f(x))−f(y)‖²), on deep linear networks. Companion: **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (doc `160e1407…`) — analysis of InfoNCE/cosine-style alignment vs cross-entropy-type losses; **LDReg** (ICLR 2024, doc `51526068…`) — regularization against dimensional collapse.
> 
> **(3) 4-bit Optimizers** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e145…`) — memory-efficient training with ≈4-bit Adam/AdamW/SGDM states via an online compress–decompress framework (Alg. 1).
> 
> **(4) "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`) — spectral analysis of excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) constrained RNNs for time-series modeling (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn TreeBank).
> 
> **(5) CodeSteer** (ICML 2025, doc `78f9e5f2…`) — Transformer-based multi-turn guidance steering code vs text, trained with SFT (12k trajectories) + DPO (5.5k pairs) on Llama-3.1-8B, evaluated on SymBench with GPT-4o.
> 
> ## Experimental comparison and analysis
> 
> - **Detection (1):** PBADet's anchor-free part-to-body offset beats anchor-based BPJDet: on BodyHands, AP 89.1 vs 85.3 (BPJDet), conditional accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80, joint AP 85.98 vs 78.13, with fewer params (36.9M vs 41.2M). On COCO val vs the pose estimator ED-Pose, precision/recall/F1 rise from 24.09/45.51/31.51 to 39.41/63.09/48.52 for all parts. On COCO-HumanParts, YOLOv7-based PBADet reaches AP 42.7/41.5 (original/subordinate) vs 42.5/… for baseline; ablations show task-alignment and the association loss give the largest gains.
> 
> - **SSL objectives (2):** The JEPA paper proves JEPA and MAE have identical minimizers in the linear setting but different *dynamics*: MAE greedily learns high-variance (λ) features, while JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient ρ), reversing learning order when ρ and λ anti-correlate — this bias only appears for deep encoders. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace than MAE (CCA), explaining why reconstruction (MSE in input space) is sub-optimal for perception. The contrastive-embeddings paper adds the cross-entropy connection: InfoNCE/SigLIP optima form a simplex ETF (positive cosine similarity 1, negative −1/(n−1)); mini-batches raise negative-pair similarity variance, and their auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves top-1 accuracy and temperature robustness on CIFAR-10/100 (ResNet-18) and ImageNet-100 (ResNet-50). LDReg shows regularization choice matters: raising local intrinsic dimensionality improves SimCLR/BYOL/MAE linear evaluation and COCO detection on ResNet-50/ViT-B, while global covariance regularizers barely help.
> 
> - **Optimizer memory (3):** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (RoBERTa-L: 89.1 vs 88.9), ImageNet (Swin-T: 80.8 vs 81.2), E2E-NLG (GPT-2M: 67.8 vs 67.7), SQuAD, and WMT14 MT (26.28 vs 26.61), while cutting memory up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9GB) and enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU. The online implementation (per-step compress/decompress, layer-wise) also speeds up FSDP fine-tuning via reduced communication. Key design: excluding the zero point when quantizing the second moment (zero-point problem) plus rank-1 normalization; factorized second moment ("4-bit Factor") adds further savings.
> 
> - **Spectral/EI analysis (4):** ColEI RNNs (columns sign-constrained to obey Dale's Law) learn poorly because their initial recurrent weight spectrum is multimodal/dispersed (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), whereas DANN and standard RNNs have unimodal, quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur spectra. Sign constraints account for only ~1% of the error gap; spectrum matters more. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error across network size and E/I ratio — e.g., small balanced networks beat larger skewed ones. Gradient clipping mitigates instability; DANN RNNs are robust even with one inhibitory unit.
> 
> - **Guidance fine-tuning (5):** CodeSteer's SFT+DPO-trained Llama-3.1-8B steers GPT-4o from 53.3 to 86.4 average score on SymBench (37 tasks), beating o1 (82.7), o1-preview (74.8), DeepSeek-R1 (76.8), and generic agent baselines (67.0–69.5), and transfers to other TaskLLMs (~41.8-point average gain). Design choices quantified: doubling weights of the final two SFT turns (to avoid multi-turn gradient cancellation), score-difference>2 DPO pair filtering with positive-score constraint (anti reward-hacking), and checkers (Symbolic, Self-answer) all contribute; limitations include medium-complexity robustness gaps.
> 
> **Cross-cutting observations:** (2), (3), and (5) all show that *loss/regularization choices* (MSE vs alignment vs cross-entropy; zero-point exclusion; SFT-turn weighting/DPO filtering) drive most gains, while (1) and (4) show that *architectural/spectral structure* (anchor-free offsets; initial singular-value spectrum) matters more than parameter counts or sign constraints.

### paperscope:results_comparison:392 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively tackle scalable and reliable deep learning across vision, sequences, and RL: (a) a single-pass, anchor-free detector that associates human parts with the correct person; (b) analyses of recurrent nets that enforce excitatory/inhibitory sign structure and show how the singular-value spectrum at initialization, more than the sign constraints, drives learning; (c) theory for joint-embedding/self-distillation objectives (JEPA-style) in deep linear models explaining why latent prediction with cosine-like similarity and MSE/CE surrogates biases toward high-influence features; (d) memory‑lean training by quantizing Adam/SGD states to around 4 bits with smarter block/row/column scaling and zero‑free quantizers; and (e) a top‑down, LLM‑guided strategy/option generator for RL that turns natural-language subgoals into shaped rewards for Transformer agents. Please include works that discuss regularization, feature embeddings, and report metrics like F1/Precision/AUROC, and that are relevant to time‑series or vision backbones (e.g., ResNet/Transformers) and standard losses (cross‑entropy vs MSE).Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

Table 7):\n  Precision/Recall/F1 for smaller parts (hands/feet) on COCO val (IoU 0.5): PBADet outperforms ED-Pose notably (all parts F1: 48.52 vs 31.51). On CrowdHuman, PBADet achieves best MR−2 for body/face and best body AP. Result: 4-bit matches 8-bit/32-bit.\n- CLS (Swin-T on ImageNet-1k top-1): 32-bit 81.2; 8-bit 81.0; 4-bit AdamW 80.8; 4-bit Factor 80.9.
