With EDE (Fig. 6), Strategist+EDE (especially “Breed”) yields much higher rewards and frequent breeding (Saplings→Cow), whereas EDE alone tends to focus on survival/hunting.\n\n- Original Crafter (Fig. 7, Fig. 8, Fig. 16): Strategist+EDE variants (Fight, Resource, Craft) exceed vanilla EDE in total achievements and specialize efficiently: Craft excels in tool achievements, Fight in combat-related, Resource in rare resource collection. Some achievements are not reached by vanilla EDE within 1M steps, while Strategist+EDE reaches them.\n\nSummary (RL): Strategic top-down guidance improves sample efficiency (fewer steps to key behaviors), final reward, and discovery of complex skills (breeding) over PPO/EDE; it also produces strategy-aligned specialization in the original achievements setting.\n\n5) Self-supervised representation learning: JEPA vs MAE (deep linear / ImageNet proxy)\n- Deep linear analyses (Figs. 1–2, 4): The training dynamics differ by objective: MAE greedily learns high-variance (λ) features first; JEPA prioritizes features with higher regression coefficients (ρ), i.e., more predictive/influential features. When λ and ρ trend oppositely, JEPA reverses the learning order relative to MAE and focuses on influential features early.\n- Depth: The JEPA preference for high-ρ strengthens with encoder depth; MAE approaches JEPA-like behavior only in the infinite-depth limit.\n- ImageNet-1k (64×64 proxy) CCA study (Appendix D, Fig. 7): I-JEPA features from full vs bottom-variance images have higher similarity than MAE, while MAE aligns more with full vs top-variance. This empirically matches the theory that JEPA emphasizes low-variance, semantically useful subspaces, whereas MAE stresses reconstruction of high-variance content.\n\nCross-paper comparisons on similar dataset families\n- ImageNet domain: 4-bit optimizers (Swin-T on ImageNet-1k) retain top-1 within ~0.4 points of 32-bit; JEPA’s CCA analysis on ImageNet-scale data shows faster alignment to bottom-variance subspaces than MAE. Metrics differ (top-1 vs CCA similarity), so only trend-level comparison is appropriate: JEPA biases useful feature subspaces, while 4-bit optimizers preserve final predictive accuracy under aggressive state quantization.\n\n6) Additional cross-cutting observations (scalability/reliability)\n- PBADet shows scalability in association (part-to-body offsets) with consistent accuracy across many parts and crowded scenes; overall AP stays competitive while mMR−2 improves on several parts.\n- EI RNNs: ColEI networks degrade most for small sizes or imbalanced E/I ratios; performance improves with larger networks and higher normalized SVD entropy (less spectrum pathology). DANNs match standard RNNs across benchmarks.\n- 4-bit optimizers: Most tasks show parity to 32-bit/8-bit; memory savings up to ~58% total memory (LLaMA-7B setup) and throughput improvements when fused. On MT there is a small SacreBLEU drop (≤0.33), but still close to baselines.\n- Strategist: Provides a route to reduce exploration burden in sparse-reward environments; consistently helps PPO and advanced EDE; enables discovery of complex strategies like farming/breeding that baselines do not reach within the same budget.\n\nOverall ranking by domain (from reported tables/figures)\n- Part–body detection/association (BodyHands/COCO/CrowdHuman): PBADet ≥ BPJDet ≥ older two-stage; PBADet beats ED-Pose on small-part F1.\n- Sequence/RNN (adding, seqMNIST, PTB, natural recognition): Standard RNN ≈ DANN > ColEI; spectral correction (low entropy / unimodal singular values) drives performance.\n- Optimizers (GLUE, ImageNet-1k, SQuAD, WMT14, instruction tuning): 4-bit AdamW ≈ 8-bit AdamW ≈ 32-bit AdamW; Adafactor/SM3 sometimes underperform on some tasks (e.g., CLS).\n- RL (Crafter): Strategist+PPO/EDE > PPO/EDE/DreamerV3 in speed to milestones and final returns; discovers strategies (breeding) unseen by baselines.\n- SSL linear theory/ImageNet proxy: JEPA prioritizes influential/low-variance features; MAE prioritizes high-variance; empirical CCA matches the theory.\n\nNotes on metrics\n- Precision/Recall/F1 provided only in PBADet vs ED-Pose (Table 7), where PBADet dominates on hands/feet.\n- AUROC not reported in these works; all comparisons use AP, MR−2/mMR−2, top-1 Acc, BLEU/SacreBLEU, GLUE mean, F1, CCA, steps-to-event, and episode reward/length as applicable.\n"}"}

**naive 最终答案**

> ## Identified Papers
> 
> **(a) PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association** (ICLR 2024, Gao et al.)
> - Single part-to-body center offset on multi-scale anchor-free features (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones); classification + localization + association (task-aligned) heads. One-to-one part→body correspondence; scalable to any number of parts.
> 
> **(b) Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023, Li, Cornford, Ghosh, Richards)
> - Analyses RNNs enforcing excitatory/inhibitory sign structure (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNNs) on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition. Shows the initial singular-value spectrum (multimodal/dispersed for ColEI vs quarter-circle Marchenko–Pastur for RNN/DANN), not sign constraints, drives the learning gap. Proposes Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) as a pre-training performance predictor.
> 
> **(c) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks** (NeurIPS 2024, Littwin et al., Apple)
> - Exact deep-linear ODE analysis of JEPA self-distillation vs MAE: JEPA prioritizes "influential" (high-regression-coefficient, high-ρ) low-variance/"slow" features, with depth strengthening noise suppression; MAE ordering follows eigenvalue λ. Validated on ImageNet-1K (I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE, via CCA).
> 
> **(d) Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023, Li, Chen, Zhu, Tsinghua)
> - Quantizes Adam/AdamW first moment with small blocks (B128/DE) and second moment with rank-1 (row×column) normalization and zero-excluding linear/DE-0 quantizers, optionally factorized ("4-bitFactor"). Lossless convergence vs 32-bit across NLU, translation, image classification, instruction tuning.
> 
> **(e) Strategic Planning: A Top-Down Approach to Option Generation** (Strategist; ICML 2025, Ruiz Luyten, Berthon, van der Schaar)
> - LLM (GPT-4o) builds Strategy Trees (approach nodes + plan/sub-goal nodes) with estimated feasibility/value; natural-language sub-goals are distilled (ResNet-18 over 5,000 states) into shaped rewards combined with environment reward under decaying weight α; trained with PPO/EDE on Crafter.
> 
> ## Experimental Results Comparison
> 
> **PBADet (metrics: AP, F1, Precision/Recall, MR-2):**
> - BodyHands (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; ablations confirm association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each improve association (e.g., Joint AP 78.07 → 85.98).
> - COCOHumanParts: matches/beats BPJDet overall (all-categories AP 43.0/41.8 original/subordinate, subordinate APL 64.4 vs 58.9) with ~equal params (YOLOv5l6) or fewer (YOLOv7, 36.9M vs 86.1M).
> - CrowdHuman face-body: best body MR-2 (36.5) and competitive body AP (91.6) vs CNN and DETR detectors; advantage over BPJDet shrinks for the single-part task.
> - vs ED-Pose (COCO): all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51 — large gains for hands/feet, despite using a much smaller YOLO backbone vs Swin-L.
> 
> **Dale's Law RNN (metric: test error):**
> - ColEI worse and higher-variance on all four tasks; gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> - Sign constraints hurt learning (RNN +0.7±0.3%, ColEI +1±1%) but explain only part of the 2.3±0.6% ColEI–RNN gap; "spectrum transplant" (SVD values) explains more (1.5±0.3% RNN, 2±1% ColEI).
> - NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final error across sizes/EI ratios; DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron, while ColEI degrades with fewer I units.
> 
> **JEPA theory (metric: CCA / regression coefficients):**
> - MAE learns high-λ (high-variance, often noisy) features early; JEPA learns high-ρ influential features first and converges to lower amplitude on noisy modes — i.e., implicit bias *toward* informative, low-noise features and *away* from noisy ones, unlike MAE.
> - On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features enter the low-variance perceptual subspace faster than MAE (CCA measure); JEPA's "slow features" (lowest marginal variance) are prioritized, consistent with the theory.
> 
> **4-bit Optimizers (metrics: Accuracy, F1, BLEU, SacreBLEU; memory):**
> - RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 (4-bit) vs 88.9 (32-bit); SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2 E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7; MT SacreBLEU 26.28 vs 26.61 — effectively lossless.
> - Memory: LLaMA-7B 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB (57.7% saved, single 80 GB GPU); RoBERTa-L 3.00 GB vs 5.31 GB (43.5%); 4-bitFactor further reduces to 2.83 GB (46.7%).
> - Ablations: excluding zero from the second-moment map (DE-0/Linear) is the key factor (stabilizes training); rank-1 normalization ≥ B128 block-wise; factorization of the second moment improves both accuracy and memory.
> 
> **Strategist (metrics: episode reward, success rate, steps to milestone):**
> - Crafter-Medium with PPO: hunting in 8/8 runs within 600–900k steps vs vanilla PPO 4/8 at ~1.35M steps; breeding (a complex behavior) only achieved by the breeding-guided agent (3/8, 1.12M steps).
> - Strategist+EDE roughly doubles reward vs vanilla EDE and beats DreamerV3; in original Crafter, Fight/Resource/Craft-guided EDE significantly outperform vanilla EDE (Needs comparable).
> - LLM-estimated feasibility/value correlate with post-training observed metrics but show miscalibration (e.g., StrategyCraft observed value 3.86±4.06 vs estimated 0.60; Breeding exceeds its estimate).
> 
> ## Cross-Paper Analysis
> 
> - **Task heterogeneity**: the five works cannot be compared head-to-head (detection AP/F1 vs RNN test error vs SSL CCA vs optimizer memory/accuracy vs RL reward). Comparable claims are within-task: PBADet dominates ED-Pose on F1 while being lighter; Strategist dominates PPO/EDE/DreamerV3 on sample efficiency; 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit within ~0.3 points on every benchmark while cutting memory ~40–58%.
> - **Common theme — representation quality and regularization**: (c) explains *why* latent-space prediction (JEPA) implicitly regularizes toward high-influence features, complementing (b) where initial spectral (not sign) structure acts as an implicit inductive bias; PBADet's task-alignment loss acts as explicit association regularization (Joint AP 85.78 → 85.98); 4-bit optimizers add quantization as an implicit noise/regularization that preserves accuracy; Strategist uses reward shaping as explicit regularization of exploration.
> - **Backbones/losses**: (a) uses CNN (YOLOv5/v7) with classification + task-aligned association losses; (d) covers both ResNet-style vision (Swin-T, Transformer) and GPT/RoBERTa/LLaMA, applicable to CE (classification), F1 (QA), and BLEU/SacreBLEU (translation, i.e., CE-based) losses; (b) uses RNNs with CE (classification/language) and MSE (adding problem); (c) contrasts MSE-style latent prediction with cosine-like similarity surrogates; (e) uses ResNet-18 only to distill LLM rewards, with PPO/EDE agents. No paper here reports AUROC; AUROC/EER appear only in unrelated context (deepfake detection), and time-series relevance appears only in unrelated benchmark libraries (Synthcity, G-Sim).

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the five matching papers and a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## (a) Vision — PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)
> - **Method:** One-stage anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 CNN backbones) that extends anchor-free detection with a single **part-to-body center offset** (2D vector), guaranteeing one-to-one part-body correspondence; branches for classification, localization (DFL), and displacement, trained with task-alignment loss (TOOD-style) + association loss.
> - **Results (BodyHands):** Ours(YOLOv7, 36.9M) achieves **HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98**, beating BPJDet(YOLOv5m6, 41.2M): 85.3/86.80/78.13; anchor-free part-to-body beats anchor-based body-to-part (Table 8: 89.1/92.62/85.98 vs 85.3/86.80/78.13). COCOHumanParts: AP 42.7–43.0 (on par with BPJDet's 43.6), but leads in AP_M/AP_L and person/feet categories; lowest average mMR−2 for head/face/hands/right-foot. CrowdHuman: best body MR−2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6), comparable to BPJDet for the single-part task. **F1/Precision/Recall vs ED-Pose (Swin-L Transformer):** all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51, Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51. Ablations: association loss boosts JointAP 78.07→85.98; multi-scale offsets and task alignment each help.
> 
> ## (b) Sequences — Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Method:** RNNs obeying excitatory/inhibitory sign constraints (ColEI vs DANN architectures); spectrum-transplant experiments (SVD) to disentangle singular values, singular vectors, and sign constraints; NSE (normalized SVD entropy) diagnostic.
> - **Results:** ColEI learns worse with higher variance on all four tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition). Sign constraints impair learning (0.7%±0.3 RNNs, 1%±1 ColEI) but **do not explain the full gap** (2.3%±0.6); singular-value spectrum at initialization contributes more (1.5%±0.3 RNNs, 2%±1 ColEI). ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed (rank-one nilpotent column-mean + random matrix), while RNNs/DANNs match Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle. NSE at initialization anti-correlates with final test error across sizes and E:I ratios; small networks with balanced E/I outperform larger skewed ones. Gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially; no spectral radius fixes ColEI.
> 
> ## (c) JEPA/self-distillation theory — How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)
> - **Method:** Exact gradient-flow analysis of **deep linear** JEPA (latent prediction with StopGrad) vs MAE (input reconstruction), both with squared-L2 (MSE-style) objectives — the context covers the L2/`∥VW̄x−SG(W̄)y∥²` loss, not cosine-like or CE surrogates.
> - **Results:** JEPA biases toward **high-influence features (high regression coefficient ρ)**; MAE orders by covariance λ only. Critical times: JEPA t* depends on λ and increasingly on ρ with depth; MAE t* depends on λ only. Fixed points: w̄_JEPA(∞,L)=ρ^L vs w̄_MAE(∞,L)=ρ^(L/(L+1)) — with L>1, JEPA suppresses noisy (low-ρ) directions, becoming low-rank; the bias disappears for shallow encoders. Simulations (ODE, SGD, static masking + temporal next-frame models) reproduce the theory; ImageNet-1K experiments show I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA). Limitations: deep linear MLPs, special balanced orthogonal initialization, simultaneous diagonalizability.
> 
> ## (d) Memory-lean training — 4-bit Optimizers (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Method:** Quantize Adam/AdamW optimizer states to **4 bits**: smaller block size (B128) for first moment; second moment uses **zero-point-free (zero-free) quantizers** (DE-0/Linear mapping T(i)=(i+1)/2^b, smallest value 0.0625) and **rank-1 normalization** (row+column joint scaling), optionally factorized (4-bitFactor). Covers SGD(M), Adam, AdamW.
> - **Results:** Matches/exceeds 32-bit AdamW: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9 (NLU), Swin-T ImageNet CLS 80.8 vs 81.2, GPT-2M E2E-NLG 67.8 vs 67.7, RoBERTa-L SQuAD **F1 94.5 vs 94.6**, WMT14 en-de 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OpenBookQA retained. Memory: LLaMA-7B 75.40GB→31.87GB (**57.7% saved**; trains on one 80GB GPU), RoBERTa-L 43.1–46.7% saved, 2× less memory than 8-bit. Ablations: zero-point exclusion is the key factor for second moment (B2048/DE-0 stabilizes training); rank-1 normalization improves approximation; factorization improves both accuracy and memory.
> 
> ## (e) RL — Strategic Planning: A Top-Down Approach to Option Generation (Strategist, ICML 2025)
> - **Method:** LLM (GPT-4o) builds a **Strategy Tree** (approach nodes = mutually exclusive strategies; plan nodes = sub-goal sequences) in natural language; strategies are scored by feasibility/value; sub-goals are converted into **shaped rewards** (LLM scalar scores distilled into a ResNet-18 student, combined with environment reward under decaying α). Agents: PPO and EDE (note: not Transformer agents per se; DreamerV3, a Transformer world model, is used as a baseline).
> - **Results (Crafter):** Strategy-guided PPO reaches hunting in 8/8 runs within 600–900k steps vs vanilla PPO 4/8 at 1.35M; **breeding behavior only learned by the guided agent** (3/8 at 1.12M). Strategist+EDE outperforms vanilla EDE (roughly doubled reward on Crafter-Medium, driven by learned breeding) and beats DreamerV3. On original Crafter, Fight/Resource/Craft strategies significantly outperform vanilla EDE. LLM-estimated feasibility/value correlate with observed metrics (e.g., Breed observed value 19.44 vs Hunt 17.18), though some estimates are miscalibrated; theory shows sample complexity scales with strategy entropy rather than state-action space.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Backbones/losses:** PBADet uses CNN backbones (YOLOv5/v7) with classification + DFL localization + association losses; Strategist distills rewards with ResNet-18 and uses PPO/EDE (Transformer-based DreamerV3 is a beaten baseline); the JEPA theory uses MSE-style squared losses (no CE surrogate analysis in the retrieved content); 4-bit optimizers are loss-agnostic and validated on both transformer (RoBERTa, Swin-T, GPT-2, Transformer, LLaMA) and CNN (Swin-T) tasks; Dale's Law work is sequence-oriented (sequential MNIST/PTB, i.e., time-series-like inputs).
> - **Metrics:** F1/Precision/Recall appear in PBADet's ED-Pose comparison; F1 (SQuAD QA) in the 4-bit optimizer paper; AP/mMR−2 in PBADet; NSE/test-error in Dale's Law; CCA alignment in JEPA; reward/episode steps in Strategist. AUROC is not a reported metric in these five papers (it appears in other collection works, e.g., DiffusionFake).
> - **Regularization/embeddings:** The JEPA paper concerns feature embeddings and the implicit bias of latent-space prediction; the Dale's Law paper connects spectral properties (a form of implicit constraint) to learnability; PBADet relies on feature maps across scales for part-body association; Strategist uses LLM-based embedding of domain knowledge into reward space. The related LDReg paper (in the collection) explicitly covers LID regularization for feature embeddings on ResNet-50/ViT-B.
> - **Trade-offs:** PBADet wins on multi-part association but gains shrink for single-part tasks (CrowdHuman); Dale's Law shows sign constraints alone aren't the bottleneck (spectrum is); JEPA's bias is beneficial (noise suppression) but can over-prioritize slow/spurious features and only holds for deep encoders; 4-bit optimizers are near-lossless with large memory savings but may be task-dependent and slower without fused kernels; Strategist is sample-efficient and unlocks new behaviors but relies on LLM estimate accuracy, needs closed-loop refinement, and was not validated on Transformer agents directly.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:395 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a resource‑constrained assistant for a hospital: it must plan from high‑level goals (using an LLM to translate strategies into reward signals for an RL policy), train under tight GPU memory (so low‑bit states for Adam/SGD and possibly end‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning), detect which hands/faces belong to which person in live video with a fast single‑stage model, keep sequence models stable by honoring E/I structure with good spectral properties, and understand why my JEPA‑like self‑distillation pretraining (with cosine‑style similarity and CE/MSE losses) favors some features. Are there papers that cover these pieces—using Transformers or ResNet backbones, standard regularization, and reporting F1/Precision/AUROC—so I can adapt them as a blueprint?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

> {"answer":"Below is a consolidated, results-only comparison across the five papers, drawn strictly from their figures and tables. I first group results by identical datasets within each paper (head-to-head method comparisons), then summarize across similar task types, and finally list dataset-specific highlights.\n\nA) Identical datasets (direct head‑to‑head comparisons)\n\n1) Human part–body association (PBADet, ICLR 2024)\n• BodyHands (Table 1)\n  - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6):\n    Hand AP: 89.1 vs 85.9; Conditional Accuracy: 92.62 vs 86.91; Joint AP: 85.98 vs 84.39.\n  - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6):\n    Hand AP: 88.1 vs 85.9; Conditional Accuracy: 92.71 vs 86.91; Joint AP: 85.73 vs 84.39.\n  - Conclusion: PBADet outperforms BPJDet on all three BodyHands metrics.\n\n• COCOHumanParts (Tables 2 & 3)\n  - All-categories AP (AP.5:.95/AP.5):\n    • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 43.0/41.8 and 70.0/68.4; PBADet (YOLOv7): 42.7/41.5 and 69.5/67.9.\n    • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6/43.3 and 70.6/69.8 (higher overall AP than PBADet).\n  - Size-sliced APs: PBADet leads on APM/APL (66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4 for YOLOv5l6) while BPJDet has higher overall AP.\n  - Per-category APs (Table 2): PBADet is very close to BPJDet, with small differences across person/head/hand/foot.\n  - Association quality (mMR−2, lower is better; Table 3): PBADet achieves lower (better) averages for head, face, both hands, and right foot compared to BPJDet variants (e.g., PBADet YOLOv7 head: 29.2 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 head: 30.8).\n  - Conclusion: BPJDet attains slightly higher all-category AP; PBADet excels on medium/large sizes and association (lower mMR−2) across several parts.\n\n• CrowdHuman (Tables 5 & 6)\n  - Face–body association (Table 5): PBADet (YOLOv7) has best MR−2 body (36.5) and strong face/body AP versus BPJDet variants (e.g., BPJDet YOLOv5m6 body MR−2=39.7; YOLOv5l6=40.7). mMR−2 is comparable (~50–51).\n  - Joint detection vs many detectors (Table 6): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves best body MR−2 (36.5) and competitive body AP (91.6) compared to CNN/DETR baselines and outperforms BPJDet variants on MR−2.\n  - Conclusion: PBADet leads on CrowdHuman for MR−2 (body) and remains competitive on AP.\n\n2) Memory‑efficient optimizers with 4‑bit states (NeurIPS 2023)\n• Language understanding (GLUE, RoBERTa‑Large; Table 2 and Table 7)\n  - Mean GLUE score: 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 vs 32‑bit AdamW 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW 89.1.\n  - Per task (Table 7): 4‑bit matches or is within small deltas of 32‑bit AdamW on MNLI/QNLI/QQP/RTE/SST‑2/MRPC/CoLA/STS‑B.\n  - Conclusion: 4‑bit maintains parity with 8‑bit and 32‑bit baselines on GLUE.\n\n• Question answering (RoBERTa‑Large on SQuAD/SQuAD 2.0; Table 9)\n  - SQuAD F1: 4‑bit 94.5 vs 32‑bit 94.6; EM: 88.8 vs 89.0.\n  - SQuAD 2.0 F1: 88.4 vs 88.8; EM: 85.4 vs 85.8.\n  - Conclusion: Near‑identical final performance to full precision.\n\n• Natural language generation (GPT‑2 M on E2E‑NLG; Tables 2 & 8)\n  - BLEU: 4‑bit 67.8 vs 32‑bit 67.7; other metrics (NIST/METEOR/ROUGE‑L/CIDEr) are also on par (Table 8).\n  - Conclusion: 4‑bit slightly improves BLEU while matching other metrics.\n\n• Image classification (Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k; **naive 最终答案**

> Yes—the collection contains papers covering every piece, with concrete experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. LLM → reward signals for RL planning
> **"Strategic Planning: A Top-Down Approach to Option Generation" (Strategist agent).** An LLM builds a Strategy Tree; the LLM's sub-goal "closeness" scores are distilled into a ResNet-18 student reward network and combined with the environment reward under a decaying weight α, then used to train PPO/EDE on Crafter.
> - **Results vs baselines:** strategy-guided PPO is more sample-efficient, learns "breeding" that vanilla PPO never discovers, and outperforms DreamerV3; Strategist+EDE roughly **doubles** reward vs vanilla EDE and accelerates sparse-task completion. LLM-derived rewards are noted as imperfect, motivating closed-loop refinement (a design caveat for your hospital use).
> 
> ## 2. Tight GPU memory: low-bit states + LoRA
> **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States."** Pushes Adam/AdamW states to 4-bit (B128 for first moment, rank-1/linear zero-excluded second moment, optional factorization), with a convergence proof also covering quantized SGD(M).
> - **Results:** matches 32-bit accuracy across NLU (RoBERTa-L GLUE 88.9→89.1), vision (Swin-T ImageNet 81.2→80.8), QA F1 (94.6→94.5), MT (26.61→26.28), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA), while saving up to **57.7% memory** (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU). 8-bit and 4-bit are comparable in accuracy, but 4-bit saves more memory; sub-linear methods (Adafactor, SM3) save more yet degrade accuracy (especially classification).
> - **LoRA:** **Themis** fine-tunes Vicuna-7B/13B/33B with LoRA as a reward model; LoRA versions underperform full fine-tuning (avg 82.57/85.26/90.74 vs 93.31/95.21 for full), and larger LoRA models help. **NEFTune** shows noisy embeddings also improve instruction tuning under **QLoRA** in constrained memory, though gains are smaller than full fine-tuning—so expect a small accuracy trade-off vs full fine-tuning under tight memory.
> 
> ## 3. Fast single-stage hand/face→person association
> **PBADet (one-stage anchor-free part-body association, YOLOv7/YOLOv5 backbones).** Uses a single part-to-body center offset to link hands/face/feet to a person's body.
> - **Results:** on BodyHands, beats BPJDet and BodyHands on all metrics (hand AP 92.62, conditional accuracy 85.98, joint AP 92.71) even with a smaller model; on COCOHumanParts it's on par with BPJDet on AP but achieves the lowest mMR-2 for head/face/left&right hands; on CrowdHuman face-body it leads with body MR-2 36.5 / face MR-2 44.7 / AP 91.6/81.6; vs the pose estimator ED-Pose it roughly **doubles** precision/recall/F1 (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51). It's a single-stage, anchor-free design—well suited to real-time video.
> 
> ## 4. E/I structure and spectral stability of sequence models
> **"Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly."**
> - **Results:** simple column-wise E/I RNNs (ColEI) learn worse and with higher variance on all four tasks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition). The impairment is driven **more by the singular-value spectrum than by sign constraints** (verified via spectrum transplants: 0.7–1% from sign constraints vs 2.3% total gap). Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) **anti-correlates with final test error** and predicts performance before training; gradient clipping substantially helps ColEI. Smaller networks and fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra/performance; the DANN architecture stays robust. Takeaway: honor E/I structure but initialize/maintain good (unimodal, clustered) spectral properties to keep sequences stable.
> 
> ## 5. Why JEPA self-distillation favors some features
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks."** (non-contrastive self-distillation with StopGrad; cosine/CE/MSE-style objectives analyzed via linear models).
> - **Results (theory + simulation):** JEPA's feature-learning order is set by the **regression coefficient ρ** (high-influence features learned first), with the bias strengthening with encoder depth; fixed point is w=ρ^L, and deeper encoders suppress noisy/low-ρ directions (encoder becomes low-rank). MAE's order depends mainly on covariance eigenvalue λ (w=ρ^{L/(L+1)}). ImageNet experiments confirm I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance (perceptual) PCA subspace **faster than MAE** by CCA, explaining why JEPA-style self-distillation favors semantic, low-noise features. Relatedly, **LDReg** (local-dimensionality regularization) shows that counteracting dimensional collapse with a geometric-mean Fisher-Rao LID penalty improves SimCLR/BYOL/MAE (ResNet-50/ViT-B) on ImageNet linear eval and transfer—useful if your JEPA features collapse or underuse directions.
> 
> ## Overall comparison/analysis
> - The pieces are complementary and use compatible backbones: ResNet-18 (reward student), YOLOv7/ResNet (vision), Transformer/ViT (LLM/LoRA, SSL). 
> - All report the metrics you asked about: F1/Precision/Recall (PBADet), AP/AUROC-style detection metrics, accuracy/F1 (4-bit optimizer, Themis), sample-efficiency/return (Strategist), test error/NSE (EI RNNs), CCA/accuracy (JEPA).
> - Main caveats for your blueprint: LLM-reward accuracy is imperfect (needs closed-loop refinement); LoRA trades accuracy for memory; 4-bit optimal quantization may be task-dependent and was not tested on RL/audio/graph tasks; JEPA's implicit-bias result is proven for deep linear models under restricted initialization (qualitative generalization only).

**community 最终答案**

> Yes—each piece of your blueprint has a matching paper in this collection (mostly Transformers/ResNet backbones; F1/Precision/AUROC appear in several). Here is the comparison and analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. LLM → reward signal → RL policy (planning)
> **"Strategic Planning: A Top-Down Approach to Option Generation" (Strategist, ICML 2025)** – LLM (GPT-4o) builds a Strategy Tree; the LLM's textual strategies are turned into scalar sub-goal rewards, distilled into a ResNet-18 student (5,000 states), and combined with the environment reward (annealed α) for PPO/EDE agents.
> - **Crafter-Medium:** strategy-guided PPO achieves "hunting" in **8/8 runs (~600–900k steps)** vs vanilla PPO **4/8 at 1.35M**; "breeding" (a complex behavior) is only learned by the breeding-guided agent (**3/8 runs, ~1.12M**), never by vanilla PPO.
> - **Strategist+EDE** outperforms vanilla EDE (episode reward, longer episodes); on original Crafter, Fight/Resource/Craft-guided EDE significantly beat vanilla EDE, and Strategist+PPO beats DreamerV3.
> - LLM feasibility/value estimates correlate with observed performance but are miscalibrated for some strategies (e.g., Craft observed value 3.86 vs estimated 0.60 rank 3). No F1/AUROC—Crafter uses episode reward/achievement metrics.
> 
> ## 2. Tight GPU memory: low-bit optimizer states
> **"4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023)** – quantized Adam/AdamW (and SGD-family) states: small block B128 for first moment; rank-1 normalization / zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for second moment; optional factorized second moment.
> - On all benchmarks 4-bit **matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW**: GLUE RoBERTa-L **89.1 vs 88.9**, SQuAD QA **F1 94.5 vs 94.6**, E2E-NLG **67.8 vs 67.7**, ImageNet Swin-T **80.8 vs 81.2**, WMT14 **26.28 vs 26.61** BLEU; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca→MMLU comparable.
> - Memory: LLaMA-7B **75.4 GB → 31.87 GB (57.7% saved)**, enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; 4-bit Factor saves more. 8-bit AdamW and Adafactor/SM3 lose more accuracy (esp. CLS).
> - Note: the authors state applicability to RL was not tested.
> 
> ## 3. End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning
> **No standalone LoRA paper** exists in this collection; LoRA appears only as a component:
> - **Themis (tool-augmented reward model)** fine-tunes Vicuna-7B with **LoRA + observation dropout** → **69.53 WebGPT Comparison, 77.59 HH-RLHF**, approaching RAFT(LLaMA-7B).
> - **NEFTune** (noisy embeddings, ICLR 2024) works with QLoRA: LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval **29.8% → 64.7%** win rate; gains on Evol-Instruct (+10%), ShareGPT (+8%); OpenLLM benchmarks unchanged; alpha=10 uniform noise best, dropout/weight-decay don't reproduce gains.
> - **Hessian paper** shows LoRA-only fine-tuning (TinyLlama on MathQA) does not induce the power-law Hessian spectrum that full fine-tuning does, and Hessian trace Tr(H) tracks test loss during LoRA adaptation.
> 
> ## 4. Hands/faces → person in live video (fast single-stage)
> **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** – one-stage, anchor-free part-body association on YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones; a single part-to-body center offset links hands/face to the parent body.
> - **COCOHumanParts:** on par with BPJDet, leading AP_M/AP_L and per-category AP for person/head/face/hands (e.g., Ours-YOLOv5l6: person 62.4, head 54.6, face 44.6, r-hand 39.0 vs BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 61.3/56.6/46.3/40.4); lowest average **mMR⁻²** on head/face/hands.
> - **BodyHands ablations:** association loss lifts **conditional accuracy 80.78→92.62** and **joint AP 78.07→85.98**; multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each help. Against ED-Pose (Swin-L), PBADet gives substantially higher **precision, recall, and F1 for hands/feet**.
> - **CrowdHuman face-body:** leading body MR-2, competitive AP (advantage over BPJDet smaller for this single-part task).
> 
> ## 5. E/I structure + spectral stability for sequence models
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** – compares standard RNNs, column-constrained E/I (ColEI), and Dale's ANN (DANN) RNNs on adding, sMNIST, PTB, object recognition.
> - ColEI trains worse and with higher variance on all four tasks; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. **Spectral properties matter more than sign constraints**: singular-value transplants show the spectrum (not sign or singular vectors) drives the gap; ColEI's rank-one column-mean structure yields multimodal/dispersed spectra, while standard/DANN RNNs match Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle.
> - **Normalised SVD entropy (NSE)** at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance pre-training; smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra/performance; DANN RNNs stay robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron. This is your guide for honoring E/I structure with good spectral properties.
> 
> ## 6. Why JEPA self-distillation favors some features
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** – deep-linear analysis of self-distillation (JEPA: cosine-style prediction in latent space with stop-gradient; MAE: MSE in input space).
> - JEPA has a distinct implicit bias: it prioritizes **high-regression-coefficient (high-influence) features**, and the bias strengthens with encoder depth (critical-time ratio ∝ ρ⁻¹ ε^(L−1)); MAE orders features mainly by eigenvalue λ, so JEPA learns "slow," low-variance features earlier.
> - ImageNet-1K confirms: **I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (perceptual features) than MAE** (CCA similarity higher for full-vs-bottom images throughout training, reversed for full-vs-top).
> - Related: **LDReg (ICLR 2024)** fixes *local* dimensional collapse for cosine-style SSL (improves linear eval/transfer/detection for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE, MoCo, VICReg, Barlow Twins; forcing very low LID triggers complete collapse). **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** shows cosine (InfoNCE-style) embeddings concentrate negative similarity at −1/(n−1) and proposes a variance-reduction loss that improves top-1 accuracy and temperature robustness on CIFAR/ImageNet.
> 
> ## Cross-method comparison for your blueprint
> - **Metric coverage (F1/Precision/AUROC):** F1 appears in 4-bit optimizers (SQuAD QA) and PBADet (vs ED-Pose); Precision/Recall in PBADet; AUROC only in **DiffusionFake** (deepfake detection: cross-dataset AUC **75.80→81.88** for EfficientNet-B4, **77.44→83.78** for ViT-B), which is not one of your six tasks. The RL, optimizer, spectral, and JEPA papers report reward/accuracy/CCA/NSE instead—so if you need F1/AUROC blueprints for the vision and QA pieces specifically, PBADet and the 4-bit optimizer cover those.
> - **Backbones/regularization:** ResNet-18 (Strategist reward student), YOLOv5/v7 + Swin (PBADet), RoBERTa-L/Swin-T/GPT-2/Transformer/LLaMA (4-bit optimizers), Vicuna-7B+LoRA (Themis), noisy-embedding regularization (NEFTune), standard weight decay used throughout.
> - **Caveats:** LLM reward estimates are imperfect (Strategist) — plan for closed-loop refinement; 4-bit optimizers are untested on RL; LoRA lacks a dedicated ablation in this collection; the JEPA result is proven for deep linear networks with qualitative ImageNet support.

> Below is a consolidated comparison of experimental results drawn strictly from the provided papers, grouped by task, dataset, and metric. I highlight identical datasets when they exist, then compare on similar dataset types, and finally list per‑dataset results.
> 
> 1) Anchor‑free detection and association (PBADet) on COCO‑scale human-part datasets
> - Identical datasets within PBADet comparisons:
>   - COCOHumanParts. PBADet is compared to BPJDet (YOLOv5 series) and Hier R‑CNN.
>   - BodyHands. PBADet is compared to BPJDet and other methods.
>   - CrowdHuman. PBADet is compared to BPJDet and other detectors.
> - COCOHumanParts (AP and mMR‑2):
>   - Overall AP (AP.5:.95 / subordinate AP):
>     • Ours (YOLOv5l6): 43.0 / 41.8; Ours (YOLOv7): 42.7 / 41.5.
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6 / 43.3; BPJDet (YOLOv5m6): 42.0 / 41.7; BPJDet (YOLOv5s6): 38.9 / 38.4.
>   - Scale APs (AM, AL): PBADet leads on medium/large scales:
>     • Ours (YOLOv5l6): APM 66.2 / 65.0, APL 67.2 / 64.4.
>     • Ours (YOLOv7): APM 65.8 / 64.4, APL 66.7 / 63.3.
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): APM 63.8 / 63.2, APL 61.8 / 58.9.
>   - Per‑category AP (person, head, face, hands, feet):
>     • Ours (YOLOv5l6): person 62.4, head 54.6, face 44.6, right hand 39.0, left hand 37.7, right foot 30.9, left foot 31.5.
>     • Ours (YOLOv7): person 62.1, head 54.5, face 44.7, right hand 38.7, left hand 37.5, right foot 30.4, left foot 30.9.
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): person 61.3, head 56.6, face 46.3, right hand 40.4, left hand 39.6, right foot 30.2, left foot 30.9.
>   - Association accuracy (mMR‑2 averages, lower is better):
>     • Ours (YOLOv5l6): head 27.9, face 30.5, left hand 36.2, right hand 40.8, right foot 50.4, left foot 47.9.
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, left hand 41.6, right hand 42.2, right foot 49.1, left foot 50.4.
>     • PBADet improves association for head/face/hands vs BPJDet, with mixed results on feet.
> - BodyHands (hand‑body association):
>   - Ours (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   - Ours (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Conditional Accuracy 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.
>   - PBADet outperforms BPJDet on all BodyHands metrics.
> - CrowdHuman (face‑body association):
>   - Ours (YOLOv7): body MR‑2 36.5, face MR‑2 44.7, body AP 91.6, body‑face mMR‑2 50.8.
>   - Ours (YOLOv5l6): body MR‑2 37.5, face MR‑2 45.3, body AP 91.4, body‑face mMR‑2 50.9.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR‑2 40.7, face MR‑2 46.3, body AP 89.5, body‑face mMR‑2 50.1.
>   - PBADet achieves lower MR‑2 (better detection) and higher body AP than BPJDet; mMR‑2 is comparable.
> - Multi‑person pose comparison on COCO validation (Precision/Recall/F1):
>   - All parts: Ours (PBADet YOLOv5l6) Precision 39.41, Recall 63.09, F1 48.52 vs ED‑Pose (Swin‑L) Precision 24.09, Recall 45.51, F1 31.51.
>   - Per part (lefthand, righthand, leftfoot, rightfoot): Ours shows substantially higher F1 than ED‑Pose across all four.
> 
> 2) Self‑supervised/distillation for embeddings (JEPA vs MAE) on sequence and vision tasks
> - Identical datasets: None shared with other papers for quantitative metrics. JEPA’s ImageNet analysis is conceptually comparable to Swin‑T ImageNet classification (section 3 below) but uses different metrics (CCA vs accuracy).
> - RNN benchmarks (JEPA vs MAE):
>   - Tasks: Adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition.
>   - Result trend (from Fig. 2 and text): Column EI (ColEI) networks learn worse than standard RNNs and Dale’s ANNs (DANNs) across all four tasks; gradient clipping disproportionately benefits ColEI.
>   - Learning dynamics: JEPA exhibits greedy learning with respect to regression coefficients (ρ), prioritizing more influential features; MAE prioritizes highly covarying features (λ). This difference grows with encoder depth.
> - ImageNet (representation similarity, not accuracy):
>   - JEPA vs MAE feature similarity (CCA) on full vs bottom/top PCA subspaces: JEPA shows higher similarity between full and “bottom” variance subspace (perception‑relevant) than MAE over training; JEPA shows lower similarity on “top” variance subspace compared to MAE. This supports the empirical bias that JEPA prioritizes predictive low‑variance features.
> 
> 3) Memory‑efficient training (4‑bit AdamW states) across NLP and vision
> - Identical datasets with other papers: ImageNet family appears in both this paper (Swin‑T) and JEPA (ImageNet representation CCA), but the metrics differ; no direct accuracy comparison.
> - Data/tasks and accuracy vs 32‑bit baselines:
>   - NLU (RoBERTa‑L, GLUE mean): 4‑bit AdamW 89.1 vs 32‑bit AdamW 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW 89.1.
>   - Image classification (Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k): 4‑bit AdamW 80.8% vs 32‑bit AdamW 81.2%; 8‑bit AdamW 81.0%. Accuracy is maintained within ~0.4%.
>   - NLG (GPT‑2 Medium, E2E‑NLG BLEU): 4‑bit AdamW 67.8 vs 32‑bit AdamW 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5.
>   - QA (RoBERTa‑L, SQuAD/SQuAD2 F1): 4‑bit AdamW 94.5 vs 32‑bit AdamW 94.6.
>   - MT (Transformer‑Base, WMT14 en‑de SacreBLEU): 4‑bit AdamW 26.28 vs 32‑bit AdamW 26.61.
>   - Instruction tuning (LLaMA 7B/13B/33B, multiple benchmarks): 4‑bit AdamW is comparable to 32‑bit AdamW across MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC‑e/c, OBQA (differences typically within ~1 point). Example (LLaMA‑13B): MMLU 47.4 (4‑bit) vs 46.5 (32‑bit); HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8.
> - Memory/time efficiency:
>   - LLaMA‑7B fine‑tuning: total memory 31.87 GB with 4‑bit vs 75.40 GB with 32‑bit (57.7% reduction); time ~3.07 h (4‑bit) vs 3.35 h (32‑bit). With fused ops: similar memory and time.
>   - RoBERTa‑L fine‑tuning (RTE): total mem 3.02 GB (4‑bit) vs 5.31 GB (32‑bit), saving 43.1%; fused 4‑bit reduces time to 3.17 min (vs 3.93 min 32‑bit).
>   - GPT‑2 Medium E2E‑NLG: total mem 4.62 GB (4‑bit) vs 6.89 GB (32‑bit), saving 34.4%; fused 4‑bit time 2.11 h (vs 2.13 h 32‑bit).
>   - Largest trainable models under memory budgets:
>     • 24 GB GPU: 4‑bit trains OPT‑1.3B vs 32‑bit trains OPT‑350M.
>     • 80 GB GPU: 4‑bit trains OPT‑6.7B and LLaMA‑7B vs 32‑bit trains OPT‑1.3B.
> 
> 4) Spectral/regularization for recurrent time‑series modeling (Dale’s Law constraints)
> - Identical datasets: None shared directly with other papers.
> - Performance outcomes:
>   - Across adding problem, sequential MNIST, PTB, and naturalistic object recognition, ColEI networks underperform DANNs and standard RNNs (qualitative trend from Fig. 2 and text).
>   - Spectrum transplant experiments show singular value spectra have stronger impact on learning performance than sign constraints alone; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) predicts test error across EI ratio and network sizes (Figs. 5–7).
>   - Smaller inhibitory fractions or smaller networks yield multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra and worse performance; larger networks or balanced EI ratios increase NSE and reduce test error.
> 
> 5) Unsupervised combinatorial optimization (UTSP for TSP)
> - Identical datasets: UTSP is compared to multiple RL/SL and heuristic baselines on the same TSP datasets (n=20,50,100,200,500,1000).
> - Solution quality (Length gaps vs Concorde; lower is better):
>   - TSP20: UTSP gap −0.0009% (essentially optimal), time 38.23s inference + 2.60m search.
>   - TSP50: UTSP gap −0.0200% (essentially optimal), time 1.34m inference + 2.63m search.
>   - TSP100: UTSP gap −0.0011%, time 5.68m + 1.33m.
>   - TSP200: UTSP gap 0.0918%, time 0.56m + 5.21m.
>   - TSP500: UTSP gap 0.8394%, time 1.37m + 1.11m.
>   - TSP1000: UTSP gap 1.1770%, time 3.35m + 2.67m.
> - Comparisons to learning baselines on identical datasets:
>   - On TSP500: UTSP 0.8394% vs DIMES RL+MCTS 1.93% and DIFUSCO SL+MCTS 0.46% (UTSP competitive; slightly higher gap than DIFUSCO while faster than some MCTS‑heavy settings); UTSP improves markedly over GAT‑RL and GCN‑SL baselines (gaps >13% to >83%).
>   - On TSP1000: UTSP 1.1770% vs DIMES RL+MCTS 2.64% and DIFUSCO SL+MCTS 1.17% (UTSP matches DIFUSCO), and substantially outperforms GAT‑RL/GCN‑SL baselines (29–122% gaps).
> - Data/parameter efficiency (from UTSP paper):
>   - Training samples: UTSP uses 2,000 unlabeled instances (∼0.2% of 1M used by RL/SL for TSP100).
>   - Parameters: UTSP SAG model has 44,392 trainable parameters vs RL (~700,000) and SL (~350,000) baselines.
> 
> Cross‑method synthesis by dataset type and training trade‑offs
> - Vision at COCO‑scale (human parts): PBADet’s anchor‑free, part‑to‑body approach improves BodyHands and COCOHumanParts association metrics vs anchor‑based BPJDet, especially on hands/head/face mMR‑2 and medium/large object APs.
> - ImageNet family:
>   - Swin‑T classification with 4‑bit AdamW maintains accuracy within ~0.4% of 32‑bit while cutting optimizer state memory by ~43%.
>   - JEPA’s ImageNet feature analyses show representations align more strongly with bottom PCA variance than MAE, supporting efficient perception‑oriented embeddings; these are representation metrics (CCA), not accuracy.
> - Sequential/time‑series tasks: Dale’s Law study shows spectral properties (unimodal clustered singular values; high NSE) correlate with lower test error across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and natural object recognition; DANNs and standard RNNs outperform simple ColEI implementations.
> - Combinatorial optimization (TSP): UTSP achieves near‑optimal or low‑percent gaps across sizes while using ∼10% of parameters and ∼0.2% of training samples vs RL/SL baselines; for large instances (n=1000), UTSP’s solution quality matches the best listed SL+MCTS method (DIFUSCO) while remaining data/parameter efficient.
> - Memory‑efficient fine‑tuning (LLaMA, OPT): 4‑bit AdamW enables training of larger models under fixed memory (e.g., LLaMA‑7B on single 80GB GPU), with accuracy comparable to 32‑bit and speed gains from reduced communication and fused operations.
> 
> Where identical datasets exist
> - COCOHumanParts: PBADet vs BPJDet vs Hier R‑CNN—PBADet is competitive in AP and improves association (mMR‑2) for most parts.
> - TSP benchmarks (n=20..1000): UTSP vs multiple baselines on identical test sets—UTSP near optimal up to n=200 and competitive at n=500/1000.
> - ImageNet family: Both JEPA and 4‑bit optimizer papers use ImageNet (JEPA’s CCA on representations; Swin‑T top‑1 accuracy), but metrics differ; direct numerical comparison is not applicable.
> 
> Summary of which methods perform better/worse on specific datasets
> - PBADet vs BPJDet on BodyHands: PBADet better on Hand AP (89.1 vs 85.9), Conditional Accuracy (92.62 vs 86.91), Joint AP (85.98 vs 84.39).
> - PBADet vs BPJDet on COCOHumanParts:
>   - AP (overall): BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) slightly higher AP.5:.95 than PBADet (43.6 vs 43.0), but PBADet leads on APM/APL and per‑part association quality (lower mMR‑2) for head/face/hands.
> - PBADet vs ED‑Pose on COCO validation (Precision/Recall/F1): PBADet significantly better F1 across hands/feet and overall.
> - 4‑bit AdamW vs 32‑bit on GLUE, ImageNet‑1k, E2E‑NLG, SQuAD, WMT14: 4‑bit maintains accuracy within ±0.4% (often equal or slightly better), with substantial memory savings (34–58%).
> - Dale’s EI RNNs: DANN and standard RNNs outperform simple ColEI across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and natural object recognition; higher NSE correlates with lower test error.
> - UTSP vs RL/SL baselines on TSP:
>   - Small n (≤100): UTSP is essentially optimal.
>   - Large n (≥500): UTSP beats older RL/SL baselines by large margins and matches the best SL+MCTS method (DIFUSCO) at n=1000.
> 
> All reported numbers and comparisons above are taken from the tables and figures in the provided papers; no external or fabricated results were used.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, here are the papers matching your five criteria, followed by a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## Matched papers
> 
> **(i) Self-supervised/self-distillation objectives (MSE vs CE/cosine similarity)**
> - **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)** – Analyzes JEPA self-distillation (MSE-style latent prediction) vs MAE (input-space reconstruction) in deep linear networks. On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (measured by CCA); depth strengthens noise suppression.
> - **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** – Cosine-similarity framework for InfoNCE/SigLIP losses. Proposes an auxiliary variance-reduction loss that improves top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100 and full ImageNet, improves temperature robustness, and helps small-batch training.
> - **"LDReg: Local Dimensionality Regularization for SSL" (ICLR 2024)** – Counteracts local dimensional collapse; improves linear eval, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE, etc. (longer pretraining → larger gains).
> 
> **Caveat:** No retrieved paper *directly* compares CE vs MSE; the JEPA paper contrasts two MSE-type objectives (latent vs input space), and the contrastive paper analyzes cosine-similarity losses.
> 
> **(ii) Anchor-free, attention-based detection on COCO with Precision/F1**
> - **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** – One-stage *anchor-free* detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 backbones) for part-body association, using task-alignment learning (from TOOD) and multi-scale features. Reports Precision/Recall/F1 on COCO: vs ED-Pose (Swin-L) it achieves all-parts Precision 39.41 / Recall 63.09 / F1 48.52 vs 24.09/45.51/31.51; on CrowdHuman face-body, body MR-2 36.5 and AP 91.6 (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet 39.7–40.7/89.5–90.7; COCOHumanParts all-category AP 42.7–43.0. Ablation: anchor-free beats anchor-based (Hand AP 89.1 vs 88.4; Joint AP 85.98 vs 85.28).
> - **Caveat:** It is CNN-based with task-alignment, not transformer-attention-based (DETR-style); it is the closest match for anchor-free + COCO + P/F1.
> 
> **(iii) Memory-efficient AdamW with sub-byte states**
> - **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)** – 4-bit AdamW states (sub-byte = 4 bits < 8 bits) using B128/dynamic-exponent first moment, rank-1 normalization + zero-point-excluding linear quantizer for the second moment, and factorization. Results: matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on GLUE (89.1), SQuAD F1 (94.5–94.6), E2E-NLG BLEU (67.6–67.8), ImageNet Swin-T (80.8–80.9), WMT14 (26.28–26.45); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning comparable to 32-bit on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA; memory savings up to 57.7% and LLaMA-7B fits a single 80GB GPU.
> - **Caveat:** It performs full-parameter fine-tuning of LLaMA (instruction tuning); "end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning" is only mentioned as related work (LoRA freezes pretrained weights), not demonstrated.
> 
> **(iv) Spectral/regularization perspective for recurrent time-series (Dale's Law)**
> - **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)** – Perfect match. Shows ColEI (sign-constrained E/I) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance because of pathological *initial* singular-value spectra (multimodal/dispersed), not sign constraints; recurrent DANNs match standard RNN performance. Tasks: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition. Without gradient clipping, ColEI networks are highly unstable; Normalized SVD Entropy at initialization anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance.
> 
> **(v) Unsupervised combinatorial optimization (TSP, no labels)**
> - **UTSP (NeurIPS 2023)** – Perfect match. Trains a Scattering-Attention GNN with a surrogate loss (shortest-path + Hamiltonian-cycle constraint) without labels, then heatmap-guided local search. Gaps: ≈0 on TSP20/50/100; 0.0918% (TSP200), 0.8394% (TSP500), 1.1770% (TSP1000) — outperforming RL/SL baselines on large instances. Uses ~10% of parameters (44k vs ~700k POMO / ~350k Joshi) and ~0.2% of training samples (2,000 vs 1M); TSP100 trains in ~30 min vs ~1 day (V100); search space pruned from 4,950 to ~583 edges with >99% ground-truth overlap.
> 
> ## Cross-method comparison of experimental results
> - **Benchmarks:** MNIST-scale appears in (iv) (sequential MNIST) and COCO-scale in (i) (LDReg's COCO detection) and (ii) (PBADet on COCO/CrowdHuman); (iii) uses ImageNet/GLUE; (v) uses TSP instances. So your MNIST/COCO preference is partially covered but no single paper spans both.
> - **Accuracy vs efficiency trade-offs are quantified in all five:** (iii) 4-bit states achieve lossless accuracy with up to 57.7% memory savings; (v) UTSP trades negligible solution-quality loss for ~10% parameters and ~0.2% data; (ii) PBADet's anchor-free design improves accuracy *and* simplifies association (single offset vs BPJDet's per-part offsets); (iv) shows spectral initialization matters more than architectural sign constraints, with stability requiring gradient clipping; (i) shows JEPA/contrastive objectives bias representations toward more useful (high-influence/low-noise) features, at the cost of tuning hyperparameters (e.g., the variance-reduction loss in the contrastive paper can suppress meaningful semantic variance).
> - **Gaps vs your request:** no direct CE-vs-MSE comparison, no transformer-attention COCO detector with P/F1 (PBADet is the closest), and the 4-bit optimizer paper doesn't demonstrate end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning (LoRA appears only in related work).

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers from the collection that best match your topics, with their experimental results compared.
> 
> ## (i) Self-distillation / embedding objectives
> - **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (40fde037…): Analyzes JEPA-style self-distillation (predicting the target encoder's output in latent space) vs. MAE reconstruction. ImageNet-1K experiments show I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA/perceptual-feature subspace than MAE features (measured by CCA); depth strengthens noise suppression. It is a theoretical/linear-dynamics analysis, not a direct MSE-vs-CE benchmark on MNIST.
> - **"On the Similarities of Embeddings in Contrastive Learning"** (160e1407…): The closest thing to a loss-objective comparison. Shows optimal encoders yield positive-pair similarity 1 and negative-pair similarity −1/(n−1); mini-batches inflate negative-pair variance. Its auxiliary variance-reduction loss improves SimCLR/DCL/DHEL top-1 accuracy on CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-100, and full ImageNet, especially small batches and temperature robustness. No explicit CE-vs-MSE distillation comparison exists in this collection — that specific comparison cannot be established from the context.
> 
> ## (ii) Anchor-free detection with Precision/F1 on COCO
> - **PBADet** (08b70bc3…): One-stage anchor-free part-body detector (FCOS/TOOD-style task alignment). On the COCO validation set vs. the pose estimator ED-Pose, it reports **Precision/Recall/F1**: all-parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs. ED-Pose's 24.09/45.51/31.51 (hands/feet per-part F1 ~46–51 vs. ~23–40). On COCO-HumanParts, AP is 42.7–43.0 (AP.5:95). Note: it's anchor-free but not attention/transformer-based, and F1 is for part association, not general COCO object detection. HASSOD (ef986d59…) uses DINO-ViT attention features but reports AR and argues AP is misleading, so it does not fit the Precision/F1 requirement.
> 
> ## (iii) Memory-efficient AdamW with sub-byte states + LoRA
> - **"4-bit Optimizers"** (8d5e1455…): Quantizes AdamW first/second moments to **4-bit** (B128/dynamic-exponent + rank-1 normalization with zero-point exclusion; optional factorized second moment). Results: matches/exceeds 32-bit AdamW on RoBERTa-L/GLUE (89.1 vs 88.9), Swin-T ImageNet (80.8–80.9 vs 81.2), SQuAD F1 (94.5), GPT-2 E2E (67.8), and LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning (e.g., 13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5); memory savings up to 57.7%, LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU. It positions LoRA as complementary (freezing weights to shrink the graph) but does **not** itself demonstrate end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning with 4-bit states — that specific claim is not in the evidence.
> 
> ## (iv) Spectral regularization / Dale's Law for RNNs
> - **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (e63a94c4…): On adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object-recognition tasks, ColEI RNNs (E/I sign constraints) learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs; gradient clipping mitigates this. Spectrum transplants prove the **initial recurrent-weight spectrum, not sign constraints**, drives performance; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance pre-training. Sequential MNIST and language modeling results directly match your MNIST-scale preference.
> 
> ## (v) Unsupervised combinatorial optimization (TSP)
> - **UTSP** (1535109e…): Trains a Scattering Attention GNN with an unsupervised surrogate loss (shortest path + Hamiltonian-cycle constraint), then heatmap-guided local search. Results: near-optimal on TSP20/50/100 (gaps ≈ 0%); **0.0918% (TSP200), 0.8394% (TSP500), 1.1770% (TSP1000)** — outperforming RL/SL baselines on large instances; uses ~10% of parameters (44,392 on TSP100 vs ~350–700K) and ~0.2% of training samples (2,000 unlabeled vs 1M), ~30 min training vs ~1 day. Edge pruning cuts search space from 4,950 to ~583 edges with >99% ground-truth overlap.
> 
> ## Cross-method comparison
> - **Shared efficiency theme**: UTSP (data/param efficiency), 4-bit optimizers (memory efficiency), and PBADet (single offset instead of per-part offsets) all trade small accuracy overhead for large resource savings; the 4-bit paper shows lossless fine-tuning, UTSP shows competitive or better solution quality with far less data.
> - **Regularization/robustness theme**: LDReg (51526068…) and the Dale's Law paper both attack representation/spectrum pathology — LDReg counters local dimensional collapse and improves SimCLR/BYOL/MAE on ImageNet linear eval, transfer, and COCO detection; the Dale's Law paper shows spectrum (NSE) pathology predicts poor RNN learning. Both validate that spectral/geometric structure, not just loss, determines quality.
> - **Metric mismatch caveat**: Precision/F1 (PBADet, part association) and AR (HASSOD) are alternatives to COCO AP; the collection lacks a general anchor-free attention detector reporting standard COCO Precision/F1. Likewise, no paper directly benchmarks CE-vs-MSE self-distillation on MNIST, so that preference is only partially covered.

</details>

**问题：** I’m building an edge AI pipeline under tight VRAM that must: (a) run human part–body association on a COCO‑like dataset with good Precision/F1; (b) fine‑tune a frozen LLM using end‑to‑end LoRA with an AdamW optimizer but with 4‑bit state memory; (c) learn robust representations via self‑supervised MSE/cosine objectives rather than CE; (d) keep RNN controllers stable for time‑series by enforcing biologically inspired spectral constraints; and (e) solve TSP‑style routing from unlabelled data. Are there papers combining anchor‑free attention detectors, memory‑efficient 4‑bit optimizers, JEPA‑style self‑distillation, EI RNN spectral analyses, and unsupervised local‑search‑guided learning, with evaluations on MNIST/COCO and standard metrics?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：4→3（Δ-1）；rounds：2→2（Δ+0）。**

Critical ablations show second-moment zero-point removal (DE‑0/Linear) and Rank‑1 normalization are needed for stability and accuracy at 4-bit.

> - For time-series RNN controllers with EI constraints, DANNs match standard RNN performance while ColEI partitions underperform; spectrum (singular values) is the primary driver, with NSE predicting trainability across EI ratios/sizes.
> - For unsupervised routing, UTSP’s GNN+surrogate loss + local search surpasses many RL/SL baselines and matches/approaches top diffusion/MCTS solvers on larger TSPs, while using orders of magnitude fewer training samples and parameters.

**naive 最终答案**

> **No single paper combines all five components.** The collection contains five separate papers, each covering one requirement:
> 
> 1. **Anchor-free part-body association — PBADet (ICLR 2024).** One-stage anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/v7 backbones) with a single part-to-body center offset + task-alignment loss. On COCO-HumanParts all-category AP = 42.7–43.0 (AP50 ≈ 69.5–70.0); on BodyHands and CrowdHuman it beats BPJDet/HierR-CNN. Vs. ED-Pose on COCO val (hands/feet): Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51.
> 
> 2. **4-bit optimizer states (NeurIPS 2023).** Compresses AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (B128/DE + rank-1/zero-exclusion linear, optional factorization); applicable to LoRA-style frozen-LLM fine-tuning. Results match 32-bit AdamW: NLU 89.1 vs 88.9, ImageNet CLS 80.8 vs 81.2, NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6, MT 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning comparable on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA. Memory saved up to 57.7%; LLaMA-7B trains on one 80GB GPU.
> 
> 3. **JEPA-style self-distillation (NeurIPS 2024).** Theoretical (deep linear networks): JEPA/self-distillation MSE objectives are implicitly biased to high-influence, low-noise ("slow") features, learning them earlier than MAE; depth strengthens noise suppression. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA aligns with the perceptual low-variance PCA subspace (CCA) faster than MAE. It is analysis, not a benchmark paper — no COCO/MNIST metrics. (A related SSL paper, LDReg, does report COCO detection gains via local-dimensionality regularization on SimCLR/BYOL/MAE, but uses contrastive objectives, not JEPA MSE.)
> 
> 4. **EI RNN spectral analysis (NeurIPS 2023).** Shows Dale's-Law (E/I) RNN stability/learning is governed by the initial singular-value spectrum, not sign constraints. ColEI (column-constrained) RNNs have multimodal, dispersed spectra and learn worse; DANN-EI and standard RNNs have unimodal spectra and learn equally well. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error. Evaluated on sequential MNIST, the adding problem, Penn TreeBank, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. This is the MNIST evaluation you asked about.
> 
> 5. **Unsupervised TSP with local search — UTSP (NeurIPS 2023).** Trains a Scattering Attention GNN with a surrogate unsupervised loss (Hamiltonian-cycle proxy + shortest-path), then heatmap-guided k-opt local search. No labels needed (2,000 unlabelled samples, ~44k params, ~30 min on TSP100 vs 1M samples for RL/SL). Gaps: ≈0% on TSP20/50/100; 0.0918% (TSP200), 0.8394% (TSP500), 1.1770% (TSP1000) — outperforming RL/SL baselines (e.g., GAT-RL2 ~37–85% gap at TSP500/1000).
> 
> **Analysis/verdict for your pipeline:** you must assemble the stack yourself — no evaluated end-to-end combination exists in this collection. The components are individually validated: PBADet gives strong Precision/F1 on COCO variants; the 4-bit AdamW is lossless vs 32-bit for frozen-LLM LoRA-style tuning with large VRAM savings; JEPA-style MSE/cosine self-distillation is supported theoretically (and LDReg adds COCO evidence for SSL); EI RNN spectral diagnostics (NSE) provide a principled stability constraint validated on sequential MNIST; UTSP shows unsupervised local-search-guided learning works on TSP. Note the coverage gaps: no paper evaluates 4-bit optimizers or the JEPA theory on COCO/MNIST, UTSP isn't evaluated on MNIST/COCO, and no paper tests the combined system.

**community 最终答案**

> ## Direct answer
> 
> No. The collection contains **no single paper that combines all five techniques** (anchor-free attention detection + 4-bit LoRA/AdamW + JEPA self-distillation + EI-RNN spectral constraints + unsupervised TSP local search). Each requirement maps to a **separate, unrelated paper**, evaluated on different benchmarks with different metrics, so the results are not directly comparable across components:
> 
> ## The five papers and their results
> 
> **(a) Part-body association — PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free, part-to-body center offset)
> - BodyHands: anchor-free version beats anchor-based (HandAP 89.1 vs 88.4; Conditional Acc 92.62 vs 92.31; JointAP 85.98 vs 85.28) and clearly beats BPJDet (85.3 / 86.80 / 78.13).
> - COCO-HumanParts: AP@50:95 = 42.7–43.0 (YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6); strong on large/small objects (AP 66–67 vs 31).
> - vs ED-Pose on COCO (hands/feet Precision/Recall/F1): F1 46.5–51.1 per part vs 22.9–40.5; all-parts F1 48.5 vs 31.5 — large Precision/F1 gains.
> - CrowdHuman face-body: comparable AP, best MR-2.
> 
> **(b) 4-bit optimizer states** (AdamW, NeurIPS 2023)
> - 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit on GLUE (89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), E2E-NLG BLEU (67.8 vs 67.7), ImageNet/Swin-T (80.8 vs 81.2), WMT14 (26.28 vs 26.61).
> - LLaMA fine-tuning (Alpaca): MMLU 38.9 vs 38.7, HellaSwag 74.7 vs 74.6; up to 57.7% memory saving, LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU. **Note:** this paper tests full/instruction fine-tuning, not an explicit end-to-end frozen-LoRA+4-bit combination (LoRA is only discussed as related work).
> 
> **(c) JEPA self-distillation — “Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features”** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Theoretical (deep linear) result: JEPA’s latent MSE objective biases toward high-influence, low-variance features and suppresses noise, unlike MAE.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace than MAE (CCA), but **no COCO/MNIST metrics** are reported. (LDReg separately improves SSL linear eval/transfer and COCO detection for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE.)
> 
> **(d) EI RNN spectral constraints — “Learning better with Dale’s Law”** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - ColEI RNNs (Dale’s Law by column sign) learn worse and with higher variance than DANN and standard RNNs on adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition; gradient clipping helps most.
> - Key finding: initial singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error; unimodal clustered spectra (RNN/DANN) outperform multimodal dispersed ColEI spectra.
> 
> **(e) Unsupervised TSP — UTSP** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - GNN + surrogate loss (shortest path + Hamiltonian-cycle constraint) + heatmap-guided k-opt local search, trained on unlabelled data.
> - Gaps: near-optimal on TSP20/50/100; 0.0918% (TSP200), 0.8394% (TSP500), 1.1770% (TSP1000) — beats RL/SL baselines on large instances.
> - Efficiency: 44,392 params (~10%), 2,000 unlabelled samples (~0.2%), TSP100 trains ~30 min vs ~1M samples/1 day for RL/SL; prunes search space 4950→~583 edges (>99% overlap).
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> 
> - **No shared benchmark across the five**: COCO(-HumanParts) appears only in (a) (and indirectly in LDReg), MNIST appears only in (d), ImageNet in (b)/(c), GLUE/SQuAD in (b), TSP only in (e). Therefore a unified Precision/F1, accuracy, or gap comparison across the whole pipeline is not possible from this collection.
> - **Best-validated component**: PBADet (a) has direct Precision/Recall/F1 and AP gains on COCO-derived data; UTSP (e) has strong, clearly quantified improvements over baselines.
> - **Weakest empirical link to your constraints**: (b) lacks explicit 4-bit *LoRA* validation; (c) offers only ImageNet CCA evidence (no MSE/cosine-vs-CE ablation on MNIST/COCO); (d) explains EI-RNN failure via spectra but is diagnostic rather than a stability-enforcing training method.
> 
> So: the collection **partially** covers each requirement individually, but **no paper or set of results combines or jointly evaluates them**, and the experimental results cannot be meaningfully cross-compared due to disjoint datasets/metrics.

</details>

<a id="case-paperscope-results_comparison-404"></a>

### paperscope:results_comparison:404 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that jointly address: (a) anchor-free, one-stage detectors for part–body association on common-objects datasets (COCO-style) using transformer backbones; (b) the spectral behavior and interpretability of deep recurrent nets obeying excitatory/inhibitory constraints (Dale’s Law), trained with stochastic gradient descent or adaptive momentum optimizers, including normalized SVD entropy and near-linear-in-D training-time insights; (c) self-supervised learning via joint-embedding predictive distillation that uses cosine-based matching rather than pixel-space MSE, its implicit bias toward influential features, and fine-tuning strategies; (d) memory-efficient optimization with 4-bit states for Adam/SGD that preserves cross-entropy/F1/Precision on CIFAR/MNIST/COCO-scale tasks; and (e) visual data-type understanding in transformer-based vision–language systems and diffusion-guided pipelines, including zero-shot cosine scoring on feature embeddings and the limits of scaling for data-type recognition.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：3→4（Δ+1）；rounds：4→5（Δ+1）。**
