**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Overview and scope across the five papers: each work evaluates different methods on distinct tasks and datasets, so there is no single evaluation dataset shared by all papers. Where identical datasets exist within a paper, we compare methods head‑to‑head; across papers, we compare on similar task families (e.g., detection on COCO-style data, classification on ImageNet-1k, sequence modeling on MNIST, vision–language data-type identification). Below, we summarize experimental results strictly from the figures and tables provided.
> 
> 1) One-stage, anchor-free part–body association (PBADet) vs. baselines on detection datasets
> - Identical datasets (BodyHands): PBADet outperforms prior body–part joint detectors.
>   • BodyHands (Table 1):
>     - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.62; Joint AP 85.98.
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.71; Joint AP 85.73.
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9; Conditional Accuracy 86.91; Joint AP 84.39.
>     Conclusion: Using identical data, PBADet improves all metrics over BPJDet, with the largest gains in Conditional Accuracy (≈+6 points) and notable gains in Joint AP.
> - Identical datasets (COCOHumanParts): Anchor-free PBADet competes closely with anchor-based BPJDet on detection AP and improves association quality.
>   • All categories AP (Table 2):
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.0 / subordinate 41.8 (close to BPJDet YOLOv5l6 43.6 / 43.3); APM 66.2/65.0 and APL 67.2/64.4 (PBADet higher than BPJDet’s 63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9). Person AP also slightly higher (62.4 vs 61.3).
>   • Association mMR−2 (Table 3): PBADet reduces average miss-match rates in most categories compared to BPJDet:
>     - Head (27.9 vs 30.8), Face (30.5 vs 31.8), Left-hand (36.2 vs 41.6), Right-hand (40.8 vs 42.2), Left-foot (47.9 vs 50.4). Right-foot is the one exception (PBADet 50.4 vs BPJDet 49.1).
>     Conclusion: On COCOHumanParts, PBADet attains comparable overall detection APs, improves medium/large APs and per-category association reliability (lower mMR−2) for head/face/hands and left foot; right foot association is slightly worse.
> - Identical datasets (CrowdHuman): PBADet improves detection robustness vs. joint detectors and remains competitive on association.
>   • CrowdHuman (Tables 5–6):
>     - Body MR−2 (lower is better): PBADet YOLOv7 36.5 (best among joint detectors; BPJDet YOLOv5l6 40.7).
>     - Face MR−2: PBADet YOLOv7 44.7 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 46.3.
>     - Body AP: PBADet YOLOv7 91.6 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 89.5.
>     - Pair mMR−2 (body–face): PBADet YOLOv7 50.8 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6 50.1 (slightly worse; single-part pairing narrows PBADet’s advantage).
> - Ablations (Table 4, Table 8):
>   • Removing association loss (Lassoc) collapses Conditional Accuracy from 92.62 to 80.78 and Joint AP from 85.98 to 78.07; multi-scale anchors and task alignment each contribute additional performance.
>   • Anchor-free and part-to-body association definitions outperform anchor-based and body-to-part setups.
> 
> 2) Spectral behavior of EI recurrent nets (Dale’s Law) on sequence/vision benchmarks
> - Identical datasets per figure (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition): Across all tasks, ColEI (column-sign constrained EI) underperforms Standard RNNs and DANNs, while DANNs match Standard RNN performance.
>   • Figure 2 shows ColEI’s lower accuracy and higher variance across seeds on all tasks; gradient clipping benefits ColEI more than the others (Appendix Figure 10).
> - Spectrum transplant experiments (Figure 4): Quantified contributions to performance gaps.
>   • Sign constraints degrade performance by ≈0.7% ±0.3% (RNNs) and ≈1% ±1% (ColEI), but the singular value spectrum accounts for a larger drop: ≈1.5% ±0.3% (RNNs) and ≈2% ±1% (ColEI).
>   Conclusion: The spectral properties (e.g., multimodal, dispersed singular value distributions with large modes) are more impactful than sign constraints for learning.
> - EI ratio and network size (Figures 5–7):
>   • ColEI performance improves with more inhibitory units and larger networks; Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) strongly anti-correlates with test error across EI ratios and sizes.
>   • DANN spectra remain unimodal and clustered (NSE ≈0.95), and performance is robust even with very few inhibitory neurons.
>   Conclusion: Better singular value clustering (high NSE) predicts better learning; DANN achieves high NSE and stability without sacrificing EI constraints.
> 
> 3) Self-supervised linear analysis: JEPA vs MAE (deep linear, cosine-based joint-embedding vs pixel-space reconstruction)
> - Controlled Gaussian-feature experiments (Figure 1, Figure 2):
>   • Distribution 1 (λ and ρ increasing): both objectives learn features greedily by λ.
>   • Distribution 2 (λ increasing, ρ decreasing): MAE retains λ-based learning order; JEPA reverses order, prioritizing features with larger regression coefficients ρ.
> - Depth effects (Theorem 3.2, Corollary 3.3, Figure 4):
>   • JEPA’s bias toward influential (high-ρ) features strengthens with depth; MAE’s dynamics depend mainly on covariance λ; critical-time analyses (Theorems 3.4–3.5) formalize this.
> - Temporal generative model (Figure 3):
>   • With higher noise σ and differing autocorrelations γ, JEPA favors less noisy, more predictive modes (higher ρ), while MAE does not; simulations match analytical predictions.
> - ImageNet study (Appendix D, Figure 7):
>   • JEPA exhibits higher representation similarity (mean CCA) for full vs bottom-variance subspace than MAE; trend reverses for full vs top subspace—supporting JEPA’s bias toward perceptually informative, lower-variance features.
>   Conclusion: In the tested linear and synthetic settings, JEPA’s latent-space prediction with cosine matching preferentially learns influential, low-variance features (stronger with deeper encoders), whereas MAE emphasizes highly covarying features—even if noisy.
> 
> 4) Memory-efficient optimization with 4-bit states (accuracy vs 8/32-bit baselines; throughput/memory)
> - Identical datasets within paper; comparisons across optimizers (Table 2):
>   • NLU (RoBERTa-L on GLUE): 4-bit AdamW 89.1 matches 8-bit AdamW 89.1 and exceeds 32-bit AdamW 88.9; Adafactor and SM3 trail (89.1 vs 87.5 for SM3).
>   • ImageNet-1k (Swin-T): 4-bit AdamW 80.8 is near 32-bit 81.2 and 8-bit 81.0; Adafactor and SM3 lower (80.0 and 79.0).
>   • NLG (GPT-2 M on E2E-NLG BLEU): 4-bit AdamW 67.8 equals/slightly exceeds 32-bit 67.7 and 8-bit 67.5; other metrics (NIST/METEOR/ROUGE-L/CIDEr) remain comparable (Table 8).
>   • QA (RoBERTa-L on SQuAD/SQuAD2.0): 4-bit AdamW F1 (94.5 on SQuAD; 88.4 on SQuAD 2.0) closely tracks 32-bit (94.6; 88.8) and 8-bit (94.5; 89.0) (Table 9).
>   • MT (Transformer Base WMT14 en-de): 4-bit AdamW 26.28 SacreBleu very close to 32-bit 26.61; 8-bit 26.66.
>   • LLaMA instruction tuning: 4-bit AdamW maintains or matches 32-bit performance across MMLU and commonsense (Table 3).
> - Memory/throughput (Table 4, Table 5):
>   • LLaMA-7B: 4-bit AdamW reduces total memory from 75.40 GB to 31.87 GB (–57.7%) with similar training time; enables training larger models—OPT-6.7B and LLaMA‑7B on a single 80 GB GPU (vs OPT‑1.3B with 32-bit).
> - Ablations (Table 1, Table 6):
>   • Second-moment zero-point removal is critical; rank-1 normalization + linear mapping for v_t yields best stability and accuracy.
>   • Factorizing second moments further reduces memory with accuracy comparable to 4-bit AdamW.
>   Conclusion: Across identical datasets, 4-bit optimizers preserve task metrics (Accuracy, BLEU, F1, SacreBleu) while significantly reducing memory, outperforming SM3 and often matching 8/32-bit AdamW.
> 
> 5) Visual data-type understanding in VLMs (zero-shot cosine/log-likelihood; scaling and fine-tuning)
> - Identical datasets within paper; zero-shot across 27 data-types (Figure 3A, 4):
>   • Contrastively-trained VLMs (e.g., CLIP) outperform large autoregressive LMMs: best C‑VLM mean informedness µI ≈ 0.47 (SyntheticTypeIdent) and ≈ 0.50 (NaturalTypeIdent); best LMM µI ≈ 0.22 and ≈ 0.25.
>   • Per data-type: models perform better on style/semantic types (e.g., PENCIL SKETCH, CARTOON) and struggle on pixel/geometric types (e.g., GAUSSIAN NOISE, rotations).
> - Scaling behavior (Figure 3B): Weak scaling laws for both CLIP and IDEFICS; projections indicate models would need >10^12 parameters to reach strong µI (>0.7), suggesting scaling alone is insufficient for data-type identification.
> - Embedding/pre-training analyses (Figure 5; data abundance correlations in Table 7):
>   • CLIP image embeddings cluster by semantics, not data-type; LAION-2B-en abundance scores correlate with VLM performance across data-types (Spearman r≈0.56 Synthetic; r≈0.49 Natural; stronger for CLIP-only r≈0.61 Synthetic).
> - Fine-tuning with data-type signals (Tables 1–2):
>   • CLIP ViT-B-32 fine-tuned on TeDaTy:
>     - SyntheticTypeIdent: ID µI improves from 0.451 (zero-shot) to up to 0.780 (Freeze-Text) and 0.777 (Freeze-Image); OOD µI ranges 0.370–0.469.
>     - NaturalTypeIdent: ID µI improves to 0.691 (Full), 0.654 (Freeze-Image), 0.646 (Freeze-Text); OOD µI ≈ 0.412–0.474.
>   • Otter-LLaMA-7B: ID µI increases from 0.051 (zero-shot) to 0.120 with TeDaTy+COCO+IN100k; OOD µI (≈0.166–0.276) preserved.
>   • Training-free few-shot methods fail: TIP‑Adapter and in‑context learning do not provide robust gains (Figure 6).
>   Conclusion: Zero-shot VLMs recognize semantics well but not visual data-types; adding data-type information through fine-tuning significantly boosts in-distribution identification, with modest generalization to held-out data-types.
> 
> Cross-paper synthesis by dataset/task type:
> - COCO-style detection (PBADet vs baselines on COCOHumanParts): PBADet achieves similar overall AP to BPJDet and better medium/large AP and lower mMR−2 for most parts; its anchor-free part-to-body center offset improves association accuracy, especially on BodyHands and CrowdHuman.
> - ImageNet-1k classification (4-bit optimizers vs 8/32-bit): Swin‑T shows near-identical accuracy with 4-bit AdamW compared to 8/32-bit, validating memory-efficient training without accuracy loss.
> - Sequential MNIST and language modeling (Dale’s Law): DANNs match Standard RNNs and outperform ColEI consistently; spectrum (singular values) explains more performance gap than sign constraints; NSE predicts learning.
> - Vision–language data-type recognition (VLMs; cosine/log-likelihood scoring): CLIP-like models (cosine similarity) outperform large LMMs; scaling is weak; fine-tuning with data-type-annotated mixtures (TeDaTy) increases informedness substantially.
> 
> Identical datasets across papers: None of the five papers share the same evaluation dataset. Overlaps occur only in source data (e.g., COCO and ImageNet used to build/augment training sets), but the evaluation tasks and datasets differ (COCOHumanParts vs TypeIdent; ImageNet-1k classification vs data-type identification). Where identical datasets exist within a paper, we have reported direct method comparisons and numerical results above.
> 
> Key methodological patterns tied to results (derived strictly from figures/tables):
> - Cosine similarity evaluation benefits contrastive VLMs on zero-shot data-type identification (TypeIdent).
> - Fine-tuning with explicit data-type text captions (TeDaTy) drives large ID gains for both CLIP and Otter.
> - Memory-efficient 4-bit Adam/AdamW with rank‑1 normalization and linear second‑moment quantization preserves task metrics on GLUE/ImageNet/SQuAD/WMT/E2E and enables larger models (OPT-6.7B; LLaMA-7B) under fixed memory budgets.
> - EI RNNs adhering to Dale’s Law learn well when spectral properties are unimodal/clustered (high NSE; DANNs), and poorly when spectra are dispersed/multimodal (ColEI), with spectrum more impactful than sign constraints.
> - JEPA’s cosine-based latent matching prioritizes influential (high-ρ) features—particularly with deeper encoders—over MAE’s covariance (λ) bias, aligning with improved similarity in bottom-variance subspaces on ImageNet.

**naive 最终答案**

> I found five relevant papers, but several of the requested aspects are only partially covered by the collection. Here is the mapping and comparison.
> 
> **1. (a) Anchor-free one-stage part–body association — PBADet (ICLR 2024)**
> - One-stage, anchor-free detector using a single part-to-body center offset; branches for box/class/association with TOOD task-alignment; supports any number of parts without extra offsets.
> - **Caveat:** backbones are CNN-based (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 adapted to anchor-free heads), **not transformer backbones**. DETR-family models (Deformable-DETR, PED-DETR, Iter-E2EDET) appear only as comparison baselines.
> - Results: BodyHands — Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98, beating BPJDet (85.3/86.80/78.13); anchor-free beats anchor-based YOLOv7 (89.1 vs 88.4 Hand AP). COCOHumanParts: AP .5:.95 43.0/41.8 (original/subordinate) with YOLOv5l6; best CrowdHuman body MR-2 (36.5) and comparable body AP to DETR detectors (91.6 vs 92.5 for Iter-E2EDET).
> 
> **2. (b) Spectral behavior of Dale's-Law RNNs — "Learning better with Dale's Law" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - ColEI RNNs (column sign-constrained E/I) learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs across adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, naturalistic object recognition.
> - Spectral cause: ColEI weight matrices have a rank-one nilpotent (column-mean) component, giving multimodal, dispersed singular values (vs. quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur for standard/DANN); sign constraints alone explain only part of the deficit.
> - Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; larger networks and balanced E:I ratios raise NSE and improve learning; gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> - **Not found in the collection:** "near-linear-in-D training-time" insights, and no explicit SGD-vs-Adam/momentum comparison (training uses projected gradient descent). The closest optimizer-spectral content is the Hessian power-law paper (ICML 2025), which shows power-law Hessian spectra under SGD/Adam/AMSGrad/Adai etc. on MNIST/CIFAR, with slope predicting generalization — but that concerns Hessians, not recurrent E/I weights.
> 
> **3. (c) JEPA self-distillation implicit bias — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Analyzes JEPA (non-contrastive self-distillation with StopGrad, e.g., BYOL/I-JEPA/data2vec) vs MAE in deep linear networks. JEPA prioritizes high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ), with the bias strengthening with encoder depth; MAE's ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ, so it can learn noisy, high-variance features.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (which holds perceptual features) than MAE features, measured by CCA.
> - **Cosine-based matching:** the JEPA paper's formulation is latent MSE; the scaled-cosine-similarity objective is documented for BYOL in the LDReg paper (L_BYOL = 2 − 2 p·e′/(‖p‖‖e′‖)). **Fine-tuning strategies** are not detailed in these documents (only that JEPA reaches better downstream classification with fewer optimization steps).
> 
> **4. (d) 4-bit optimizer states — "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - 4-bit AdamW / 4-bit Factor compress first moment (B128/DE) and second moment (rank-1/linear, zero-point excluded; optionally factorized), preserving performance: GLUE 89.1 (vs 88.9 32-bit), Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 (vs 81.2), SQuAD F1 94.5 (vs 94.6), BLEU 26.28 (vs 26.61); up to 57.7% memory savings, LLaMA-7B trainable on one 80GB GPU.
> - **Not covered:** the requested CIFAR/MNIST/COCO-scale cross-entropy/F1/Precision numbers are absent (vision results are ImageNet-1k only); empirical SGD experiments are not reported (a convergence proof for quantized SGD(M) is given, but results are Adam-based). The Hessian paper separately reports SGD/Adam on CIFAR-10/100 and MNIST accuracy, but not with 4-bit states.
> 
> **5. (e) Visual data-type understanding — "Visual Data-Type Identification" (ICLR 2024)**
> - New task + two datasets (SyntheticTypeIdent 27 types, NaturalTypeIdent 25 types); synthetic style/semantic types generated with the Kandinsky 2.1 **diffusion** model; zero-shot evaluation of 39 VLMs (100M–80B).
> - C-VLMs (CLIP/CoCa) scored by **cosine similarity between image and data-type-text embeddings**; LMMs by log-likelihood. Contrastive VLMs outperform much larger auto-regressive LMMs (e.g., OpenFlamingo, IDEFICS); scaling yields marginal gains — power-law fits imply >1 trillion parameters needed for mean informedness >0.7.
> - Style/semantic types (cartoon, sketch) easier than simple geometric/pixel manipulations (rotation, noise); data-type abundance in LAION-2B correlates with performance (r≈0.56–0.61; r≈0.80 with semantic-similarity search). Fine-tuning with data-type-aware captions (TeDaTy) improves ID and often OOD performance; few-shot training-free adaptation (TIP-Adapter, in-context) does not help because CLIP's embedding space lacks data-type discriminability.
> 
> **Cross-method analysis**
> - The only fully-matching papers are (1)-partially (CNN not transformer), (2)-partially, (3)-partially, (4)-partially, (5)-mostly. The transformer-backbone condition in (a), near-linear-in-D training-time in (b), cosine-matching+fine-tuning in (c), and CIFAR/MNIST/COCO 4-bit metrics in (d) are **not supported** by the provided documents.
> - Consistent theme across (c) and (e): embedding-space similarity (cosine) prioritizes semantic/influential features while low-variance perceptual/data-type information is under-represented — JEPA's bias explains why it learns semantically rich features quickly, and the VLM study shows data-type skills do not emerge from scaling alone, mirroring JEPA's focus on influential rather than variance-dominated features.
> - (2) and (4) both emphasize that the whole spectrum (NSE; power-law Hessian) rather than single statistics (max singular value; sharpness) drives learning and generalization, with NSE predicting E/I RNN performance pre-training and power-law slope predicting test error/LLM generalization.
> - Numerically, PBADet's gains are largest for multi-part association (Cond. Acc. +5.8 over BPJDet) but shrink for single-part face-body on CrowdHuman; 4-bit optimizers are effectively lossless (≤0.4 point drops) while halving-to-4× reducing optimizer memory; VLM data-type informedness is far below semantic performance (chance = 0), with no model achieving strong data-type identification.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved documents, here is what can and cannot be matched to each of your five requirements, followed by a comparative analysis of the experimental results.
> 
> ## (a) Anchor-free one-stage part–body association
> **PBADet (doc 08b70bc3…, ICLR 2024)** matches most of (a): a one-stage, anchor-free detector for part–body association using a single part-to-body center offset, evaluated on COCO-style/common-objects datasets (COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman, BodyHands, plus AnimalPose/AP-10K).
> - **BodyHands:** Ours(YOLOv7) → Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98, beating BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) (85.9/86.91/84.39) and Mask R-CNN/BodyHands baselines; anchor-free beats anchor-based in ablations (89.1/92.62/85.98 vs 88.4/92.31/85.28).
> - **COCO-HumanParts:** Ours(YOLOv5l6) AP 43.0/41.8, AP₅₀ 70.0/68.4; on par with BPJDet, leading on person/feet AP and lowest mMR-2 for most parts.
> - **CrowdHuman (face–body):** Ours(YOLOv7) body MR-2 36.5, face 44.7, AP 91.6/81.6.
> - **Caveat:** PBADet uses **YOLOv5/YOLOv7 (CNN) backbones, not transformer backbones**. A Swin-L transformer backbone appears only in the ED-Pose comparator (which PBADet outperforms in hand/foot precision-recall-F1). No retrieved paper provides a transformer-backbone anchor-free part–body detector, so that specific sub-requirement is unmet.
> 
> ## (b) Dale's-law RNNs: spectra, NSE, optimizers, near-linear-in-D training
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (doc e63a94c4…, NeurIPS 2023)** matches the spectral/interpretability part:
> - ColEI (simple E/I column-split) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN RNNs on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition; gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> - The cause is the **initial singular-value spectrum** (multimodal/dispersed, rank-one nilpotent column-mean term), not sign constraints per se; singular-value transplants show spectra matter more than sign constraints.
> - **Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error** across network size and E/I ratio; DANN stays robust (NSE ≈ 0.95) even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> - **Caveats:** the retrieved text does not confirm "trained with SGD or adaptive momentum optimizers" explicitly, and the **"near-linear-in-D training-time insight" is not present** in any retrieved chunk. The related Hessian power-law paper (582d138d…) covers SGD/Adam/AMSGrad/Yogi/RAdam on MNIST/CIFAR but concerns Hessian spectra, not Dale's-law RNNs or D-scaling of training time.
> 
> ## (c) JEPA/self-distillation, cosine matching, implicit bias, fine-tuning
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (doc 40fde037…, NeurIPS 2024)** matches the core: JEPA (online encoder predicting a target encoder's latent, vs MAE's pixel-space MSE) is **implicitly biased toward high-influence features (large regression coefficient ρ)**, increasingly with encoder depth, whereas MAE prioritizes high-covariance (λ) features. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA).
> - **Cosine-based matching** is documented in BYOL (scaled cosine similarity loss) in the LDReg paper (51526068…); LDReg also reports linear-eval gains (BYOL 68.5 vs 67.6 baseline) and improved COCO detection/segmentation transfer.
> - **Fine-tuning strategies** appear mainly in the data-type paper (CLIP: freezing the vision encoder boosts ID and even OOD; freezing the text encoder boosts ID but hurts OOD) and in NFTS (aa60be77…, per-layer freeze/fine-tune + adapters: 80.7 vs 76.6). No single paper ties cosine-JEPA bias, fine-tuning, and downstream metrics together.
> 
> ## (d) 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/SGD
> **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (doc 8d5e1455…, NeurIPS 2023)** matches most of (d) for **Adam/AdamW**:
> - 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on all fine-tuning tasks and is comparable on pretraining: NLU 89.1 vs 88.9, Swin-T ImageNet CLS 80.8 vs 81.2, NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, **QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6**, MT SacreBLEU 26.28 vs 26.61.
> - Memory: LLaMA-7B 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB (57.7% saved); 4-bit Factor saves up to 46.7% (RoBERTa-L); enables LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU. Adafactor/SM3 degrade (especially CLS). A convergence proof for quantized **SGD(M)** is in the appendix.
> - **Caveat:** no explicit **CIFAR/MNIST/COCO-scale** results and no explicit cross-entropy/Precision metrics are reported for the 4-bit optimizers (F1 appears only for QA); the MLMC paper (fe0a4443…) does 2-bit SGD on CIFAR-10 but is about communication compression, not 4-bit optimizer states.
> 
> ## (e) Visual data-type understanding, zero-shot cosine scoring, scaling limits
> **"Visual Data-Type Understanding Does Not Emerge from Scaling VLMs" (doc b0d9a0b2…, ICLR 2024)** matches (e) fully:
> - 39 VLMs (100M–80B), zero-shot evaluation; C-VLMs scored by **cosine similarity between image and text embeddings** of data-type descriptions.
> - **Scaling limits:** scaling yields marginal gains for CLIP; the largest autoregressive LMMs (OpenFlamingo) perform *worse* than smaller contrastive models; power-law fits indicate >1 trillion parameters would be needed for strong data-type ID (informedness >0.7).
> - Style/semantic types (cartoon, sketch) easier; pixel/geometric types (rotation, noise) hard. CLIP's embedding space separates animal classes (KNN informedness 0.96–0.97; linear probe 0.99) far better than data-types (0.29–0.40; 0.84). Data-type info is scarce in LAION-2B (r≈0.80 with semantic search).
> - Fine-tuning with TeDaTy (8 types) improves ID and often OOD; COCO-only fine-tuning degrades ID; Otter transfer improves ID up to 2×.
> - Diffusion involvement is indirect: Kandinsky 2.1 was used to *generate* style/semantic data-type images for the benchmark; no diffusion-guided *recognition* pipeline is evaluated.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - The five requirements map to **five largely independent papers**; no single method jointly addresses all.
> - **Strongest matches:** (a) PBADet (except transformer backbone), (c) JEPA implicit bias (except a dedicated cosine-loss + fine-tuning study), (d) 4-bit Adam (except CIFAR/MNIST/COCO metrics), (e) data-type ID.
> - **Unmet/unsupported:** transformer-backbone part–body detector; near-linear-in-D training time for Dale's-law RNNs (and explicit optimizer detail); CIFAR/MNIST/COCO cross-entropy/Precision results for 4-bit states.
> - **Cross-cutting themes worth noting:** cosine/embedding-space scoring is the common mechanism in (c) and (e) (BYOL cosine vs CLIP zero-shot cosine), both showing that *latent-space objectives (JEPA, contrastive CLIP) favor semantic/influential features over pixel-level ones* — the JEPA theory explains why pixel-space MSE (MAE) is suboptimal, which parallels (e)'s finding that VLMs learn semantics but not appearance-based data-types. Spectral structure is the analytical lens in (b) (singular-value spectrum/NSE) and the Hessian paper, both using it to *predict* trainability/generalization before or during training. (d) is orthogonal and shows that strong accuracy can be preserved under aggressive memory compression, which would be a natural practical enabler for the large models in (a)/(e) — but such a combined study is not present in this collection.

Can you point me to works that cover the detector design, spectral diagnostics, low-bit optimizers, JEPA-style self-supervision, and the limits of scaled VLMs on data-type identification?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of the experimental results reported in the five papers you provided, organized around datasets and task families, and highlighting where methods outperform/worse than baselines. I explicitly flag where the same datasets are used across works (few), then compare results on similar task types and finally on each paper’s specific datasets.
> 
> A) Identical datasets across the five works
> - There are no truly identical evaluation datasets used across all (or most) of the five papers. The closest overlaps are: (i) COCO-family data appear in two works (PBADet evaluates on COCO-HumanParts; the VLM paper uses COCO images in its TeDaTy training mixture, but not for evaluation; the 4-bit optimizer paper does not evaluate on COCO tasks), and (ii) ImageNet appears in two works (4-bit optimizers evaluate Swin-T on ImageNet-1k; the VLM paper uses ImageNet subsets only as part of its TeDaTy training mixture, not for evaluation). As a result, direct cross-paper head-to-head numbers on the same test set are not available.
> 
> B) Comparisons within similar task families
> 1) Human part–body association (anchor-free detection) in COCO-like scenes (PBADet)
> - BodyHands (hand–body association):
>   - PBADet vs prior SOTA (BPJDet, YOLOv5 variants):
>     • PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
>     • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): Hand AP 85.9, Cond. Acc. 86.91, Joint AP 84.39
>   - Summary: PBADet achieves higher Hand AP and substantially higher Conditional Accuracy and Joint AP than BPJDet across matched backbones, with PBADet/YOLOv7 the best.
> - COCO-HumanParts (six parts: head, face, L/R hands, L/R feet):
>   - Overall AP (.5:.95) and subordinate AP:
>     • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 43.0 / 41.8
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6 / 43.3
>     → BPJDet slightly higher on the overall AP summary, but PBADet is competitive.
>   - Per-category AP (higher is better):
>     • PBADet (YOLOv5l6): person 62.4, head 54.6, face 44.6, r-hand 39.0, l-hand 37.7, r-foot 30.9, l-foot 31.5
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): person 61.3, head 56.6, face 46.3, r-hand 40.4, l-hand 39.6, r-foot 30.2, l-foot 30.9
>     → PBADet better on person and feet; BPJDet better on head/face/hands.
>   - Average miss matching rate mMR−2 (lower is better):
>     • PBADet (YOLOv7): head 29.2, face 31.3, l-hand 41.1, r-hand 42.7, r-foot 52.6, l-foot 52.5
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, l-hand 41.6, r-hand 42.2, r-foot 49.1, l-foot 50.4
>     → PBADet has lower (better) mMR−2 on head/face/left hand; BPJDet lower (better) on both feet.
> - CrowdHuman (face–body association):
>   - Body MR−2 and Face MR−2:
>     • PBADet (YOLOv7): body MR−2 36.5 (best among listed), face MR−2 44.7
>     • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR−2 40.7, face MR−2 46.3
>     → PBADet improves body MR−2 and face MR−2 vs BPJDet.
>   - mMR−2 (body–face pairing, lower is better): PBADet ≈ 50.8–50.9 vs BPJDet 50.1–50.6 (very close).
> - Takeaway: In multi-part association (COCO-HumanParts) PBADet trades wins with BPJDet (PBADet better on person/feet AP, BPJDet better on head/face/hands AP), while on BodyHands and CrowdHuman PBADet consistently improves key metrics (Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP, MR−2 for body/face).
> 
> 2) Spectrally stable EI-constrained RNNs (Dale’s Law)
> - Across 4 tasks (adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank language modeling, Naturalistic object recognition), Column EI (ColEI) underperforms Standard RNNs and DANN EI networks; performance is also more variable across seeds for ColEI.
> - Scaling/eigen-spectrum findings:
>   • ColEI exhibits multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra with large singular-value modes, correlated with poor learning and instability (especially without gradient clipping).
>   • DANNs (and standard RNNs) show unimodal spectra consistent with random-matrix theory; they learn well and are robust.
>   • Spectrum “transplant” experiments: substituting ColEI’s spectrum into standard RNNs harms learning more than imposing sign constraints; conversely, giving ColEI a standard RNN spectrum helps more than removing sign constraints. Conclusion: spectral properties matter more than sign constraints for learning quality.
>   • Normalised SVD Entropy (NSE) strongly anti-correlates with error; higher NSE (more clustered singular values) predicts better performance. ColEI’s NSE improves with more inhibitory units and larger widths; DANNs maintain high NSE even with few I units.
> - Takeaway: For EI-constrained recurrent controllers, diagnostics based on the singular-value spectrum (e.g., NSE) better predict and improve stability/accuracy than only enforcing sign constraints.
> 
> 3) Self-distilled JEPA-style representation learning vs MAE (deep linear analysis)
> - Core experimental result (deep linear networks): JEPA demonstrates a distinct implicit bias to learn features with large regression coefficients (influential features); MAE prioritizes high covariance/variance features.
> - Controlled synthetic/temporal linear models:
>   • When feature covariance and regression coefficients disagree across features, JEPA reverses learning order relative to MAE and learns the predictive/low-variance (i.e., less noisy) features first; MAE stays tied to variance.
>   • This depth-dependent effect strengthens as the encoder depth increases.
> - ImageNet-64 evidence (appendix): As training progresses, I-JEPA’s learned features align faster with the “bottom” variance subspace reported as more discriminative for perception; MAE aligns more with top-variance subspace.
> - Takeaway: For self-supervised representation learning under resource constraints, JEPA-style objectives are experimentally shown (in tractable linear models) to avoid noisy pixel features and to prioritize predictive structure; this effect requires depth and does not appear with shallow encoders.
> 
> 4) Memory-efficient 4‑bit optimizers (Adam/SGD-class) without accuracy loss
> - Language understanding (GLUE, RoBERTa-L, mean across tasks):
>   • 32‑bit AdamW: 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW: 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW: 89.1; 4‑bit Factor: 88.9
>   → 4‑bit matches 32‑bit and 8‑bit.
> - QA (SQuAD):
>   • SQuAD v1.1 F1: 32‑bit 94.6; 4‑bit 94.5 (EM 88.8 vs 88.8)
>   • SQuAD v2.0 F1: 32‑bit 88.8; 4‑bit 88.4 (EM 85.8 vs 85.4)
>   → Essentially parity (F1/EM gaps ≤0.4 absolute on SQuAD2.0).
> - NLG (GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG, BLEU):
>   • 32‑bit AdamW 67.7; 8‑bit AdamW 67.5; 4‑bit AdamW 67.8; 4‑bit Factor 67.6
>   → 4‑bit slightly exceeds 32‑bit on BLEU in this setup.
> - Image classification (Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k, top‑1):
>   • 32‑bit AdamW 81.2; 8‑bit AdamW 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9
>   → 4‑bit within 0.4–0.5% top‑1 of full precision.
> - Machine translation (Transformer‑Base, WMT14 en‑de, SacreBLEU):
>   • 32‑bit AdamW 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; 4‑bit 26.28; 4‑bit Factor 26.45
>   → Small drop (≤0.33 BLEU) with 4‑bit.
> - LLaMA instruction-tuning (Alpaca) evaluated on MMLU and commonsense benchmarks:
>   • 4‑bit AdamW matches or is within noise of 32‑bit AdamW across 7B/13B/33B models (e.g., 13B MMLU: 46.5 vs 47.4).
> - Memory/time efficiency:
>   • LLaMA‑7B FSDP: total memory 75.40GB → 31.87GB (−57.7%); training 3.35h → 3.07h (and 3.11h fused).
>   • RoBERTa‑L fine‑tune (RTE): 5.31GB → 3.00GB (−43.5%); time 3.93min → 3.17min (fused).
>   • GPT‑2 Medium E2E: 6.89GB → 4.62GB (−34.4%); time 2.13h → 2.11h (fused).
> - Ablations addressing 4‑bit stability/accuracy:
>   • Second-moment “zero-point” quantization problem is key: introducing DE‑0 (no zero level) or Linear mapping for v_t, and Rank‑1 normalization, removes instabilities and yields BLEU up to 67.8 while keeping 0% training failures.
> - Takeaway: With the proposed quantization (small blocks for m_t; zero-free linear mapping + rank‑1 normalization or factorization for v_t), 4‑bit optimizers retain CE/F1/Precision-level metrics across vision/NLP at near‑parity with 32‑bit while cutting optimizer memory roughly 2× vs 8‑bit and much more vs 32‑bit.
> 
> 5) Visual data-type identification with VLMs (zero-shot cosine vs fine-tuning)
> - Datasets: SyntheticTypeIdent (27 data-types × 50 animals) and NaturalTypeIdent (25 data-types × 50 animals).
> - Zero-shot scores (mean informedness, higher better; chance=0):
>   • Best contrastive VLM (C‑VLM): µI ≈ 0.47–0.50
>   • Best LMM (autoregressive VLM): µI ≈ 0.22–0.25
>   → C‑VLMs (e.g., CLIP with cosine similarity) outperform substantially; the largest LMM (IDEFICS‑80B) underperforms smaller CLIPs.
> - Scaling laws:
>   • Weak scaling for CLIP and IDEFICS families; extrapolation suggests >1T parameters would be needed to approach strong data-type identification (µI > 0.7) via scaling alone.
> - Per data-type trends:
>   • VLMs are reasonably good on stylistic/semantic types (e.g., PENCIL SKETCH, CARTOON), but struggle badly on simple geometric/pixel types (e.g., ROTATION, GAUSSIAN NOISE, HIGH/LOW CONTRAST).
> - Why poor zero-shot? Two findings:
>   • CLIP embedding space clusters strongly by semantic content (animal category) but is largely invariant to data-type; only a few types (TATTOO, PATCH&RESHUFFLE, TYPOGRAPHIC) cluster.
>   • Pretraining distribution analysis (LAION‑2B‑en) shows higher abundance/alignment for stylistic data-types (cartoon/sketch, etc.) and scarcity for simple pixel/geometric transforms; Spearman correlations between a data-type abundancy score and average model informedness are high (e.g., r=0.557 SyntheticTypeIdent; r=0.489 NaturalTypeIdent; stronger for CLIPs).
> - Few-shot training-free adaptation fails:
>   • TIP‑Adapter with CLIP reduces or does not improve µI as shots increase (1–48); in‑context learning with Otter shows a small gain at 2-shot but degrades with more shots.
> - Fine-tuning (TeDaTy mixtures) helps:
>   • CLIP ViT‑B‑32: Zero-shot µI≈0.45; after fine-tuning on TeDaTy with image-encoder frozen: ID µI up to 0.777–0.780, and modest OOD µI up to ≈0.469; COCO-only fine-tuning does not help and can degrade.
>   • Otter-LLaMA‑7B: Zero-shot µI≈0.051 (Synthetic) / 0.102 (Natural); after rand+COCO+IN100k mixture: ID µI≈0.120 (Synthetic) / 0.166 (Natural) while maintaining OOD.
> - Takeaway: VLMs do not acquire robust visual data-type understanding from scaling. Cosine-similarity zero-shot is best among current options but remains low. Fine-tuning with data-type-aware mixtures (TeDaTy) substantially raises in‑distribution identification while offering limited OOD gains.
> 
> C) Performance on specific datasets (paper-by-paper highlights)
> - PBADet:
>   • BodyHands: PBADet/YOLOv7 achieves Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Acc. 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 (best among reported); PBADet/YOLOv5l6 surpasses BPJDet/YOLOv5l6 on all three metrics.
>   • COCO-HumanParts: PBADet/YOLOv5l6 offers better AP on person and feet; BPJDet/YOLOv5l6 better on head/face/hands. mMR−2 shows PBADet lower (better) on head/face/left-hand, BPJDet lower on feet.
>   • CrowdHuman: PBADet achieves best body MR−2=36.5; face MR−2 improves vs BPJDet.
> - Dale’s Law (EI RNNs):
>   • Across adding problem, seqMNIST, PTB, naturalistic recognition: ColEI < Standard ≈ DANNs; spectral properties (NSE, singular value clustering) predict and explain performance; spectrum > sign constraints.
> - JEPA vs MAE (deep linear):
>   • Experiments confirm: JEPA’s training dynamics prioritize high-regression-coefficient (influential) features; MAE prioritizes high-variance features; effect grows with encoder depth; on a temporal model, JEPA prefers slow, predictable modes; ImageNet-64 evidence shows faster alignment with discriminative subspaces for JEPA.
> - 4‑bit optimizers:
>   • GLUE mean: 4‑bit=89.1 equals 32‑bit (88.9) and 8‑bit.
>   • SQuAD1.1 F1: 4‑bit 94.5 vs 94.6 (32‑bit); SQuAD2.0 F1: 4‑bit 88.4 vs 88.8.
>   • E2E‑NLG BLEU: 4‑bit 67.8 vs 67.7.
>   • ImageNet top‑1 (Swin‑T): 4‑bit 80.8 vs 81.2.
>   • WMT14 BLEU: 4‑bit 26.28 vs 26.61.
>   • Large memory savings (e.g., LLaMA‑7B −57.7% total mem) and parity/near-parity runtime.
> - VLM data-type identification:
>   • SyntheticTypeIdent/NaturalTypeIdent zero-shot: best C‑VLM µI≈0.47–0.50; best LMM µI≈0.22–0.25; weak scaling; large gap on simple pixel/geometric types.
>   • Fine-tuning CLIP (TeDaTy, freeze-image) lifts ID µI to ≈0.78; OOD µI modest (≈0.47). Otter improves ID roughly 2× without hurting OOD.
> 
> D) What performs better/worse (by task)
> - COCO-like part–body association: PBADet is superior to two-stage and extended-representation anchor-based baselines on BodyHands and CrowdHuman, and is competitive/trade-off on COCO-HumanParts with per-category strengths (feet/person) versus BPJDet (head/face/hands).
> - EI-constrained RNNs: DANN EI architectures and standard RNNs outperform ColEI across benchmark tasks; spectrum-aware initialization/diagnostics (e.g., high NSE) predict better learning.
> - JEPA-style SSL vs MAE: In deep linear/synthetic settings, JEPA better prioritizes predictive, low-variance features, avoiding “noisy pixels”; MAE favors high-variance features.
> - 4‑bit training: Proposed 4‑bit AdamW/Factor achieves accuracy/EM/F1 nearly equal to 32‑bit/8‑bit while substantially reducing memory; the key is zero-free second-moment quantization with rank‑1 normalization or factorization.
> - VLMs for data-type identification: Contrastive VLMs (CLIP) beat LMMs; scaling is weak; zero-shot cosine similarity remains low overall; training-free few-shot (TIP-Adapter, in-context) is ineffective; fine-tuning with data-type-aware mixtures significantly improves ID performance (especially in-distribution).
> 
> E) How these results align with your requirements
> - Anchor-free detector linking parts to people: PBADet’s one-stage, anchor-free part→body center offset design delivers state-of-the-art on BodyHands, better body/face MR−2 on CrowdHuman, and competitive results on COCO-HumanParts.
> - Spectral diagnostics for EI-constrained RNNs: The Dale’s Law study shows that normalized SVD entropy and singular-value spectra at initialization strongly correlate with performance and stability; DANNs (EI) match standard RNNs, ColEI underperforms; spectrum matters more than sign constraints.
> - 4‑bit optimizer states for Adam/SGD: The 4‑bit paper demonstrates near‑parity CE/EM/F1/Precision across GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG, ImageNet‑1k, and WMT14 with large memory reductions; second-moment quantization without zero-point and rank‑1 normalization/factorization are pivotal.
> - JEPA-style self-supervision to avoid noisy pixels: The JEPA study experimentally shows (in deep linear settings) that JEPA is biased toward influential, predictive features rather than high-variance (noisy) features; the effect strengthens with depth.
> - Frame filtering by visual data-type via transformer VLMs: The data-type identification study shows that zero-shot cosine-similarity (CLIP) is best among current VLMs but still limited; fine-tuning with data-type-aware mixtures (TeDaTy) substantially lifts in‑distribution identification; scaling LMMs alone does not help.
> 
> In sum: the experimental evidence supports (i) adopting PBADet for efficient part–body linkage in COCO-like scenes, (ii) using spectrum/NSE diagnostics (and DANN-style EI) for stable EI‑RNN control loops, (iii) deploying 4‑bit AdamW with the proposed second-moment quantization to fit training in memory without harming CE/F1/Precision, (iv) preferring JEPA-style SSL when you want to avoid learning noisy pixel features, and (v) implementing a CLIP-like zero-shot cosine stage for data-type filtering but planning to fine-tune on a small, data-type-annotated mixture for robust deployment.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the works matching your five requirements, with their key experimental results compared.
> 
> **1. Anchor-free detector (PBADet — "One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association", ICLR 2024)**
> Uses a single part-to-body center offset to link hands/face/feet to the correct person. Results:
> - *BodyHands*: Hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 (YOLOv7) vs. best BPJDet 85.9/86.91/84.39 — outperforms all baselines, even with a smaller model (36.9M vs 41.2M).
> - *COCOHumanParts*: overall AP on par with BPJDet (43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3) but leads per-category AP for person (62.4 vs 61.3), left/right foot, and has the lowest mMR⁻² on head, face, hands, right foot. Advantage over BPJDet is smaller on single-part (face-body) CrowdHuman.
> - *vs. ED-Pose (pose estimation)*: far higher precision/recall/F1 for hands/feet (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51).
> - Ablation: anchor-free part-to-body (89.1 Hand AP, 85.98 Joint AP) beats anchor-based body-to-part BPJDet-style (85.3, 78.13), confirming the anchor-free design helps association.
> 
> **2. Spectral diagnostics for EI-constrained RNNs ("Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective", NeurIPS 2023)**
> - ColEI RNNs (simple E/I column constraints) learn worse than standard and DANN RNNs across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition, with higher seed variance; gradient clipping helps ColEI much more.
> - Spectrum "transplant" experiments show the singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints (which only explain ~1% of the gap vs 2.3% total).
> - Key diagnostic: Normalized SVD Entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error across sizes and E:I ratios — usable to predict trainability before training. ColEI has multimodal/dispersed spectra vs the Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle of standard/DANN RNNs; small networks with fewer I units have worse spectra and learn worst. Implication: for your control RNNs, check the initial singular-value spectrum (NSE), not just spectral radius.
> 
> **3. 4-bit optimizer states ("Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States", NeurIPS 2023)**
> Covers Adam/AdamW/SGD(M) with quantized states:
> - Accuracy is essentially lossless vs 32-bit AdamW: NLU RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9, QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6, NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, MT 26.28 vs 26.61; Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2 (slightly lower); LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning comparable or better on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA.
> - Memory: up to 57.7% total-memory savings, ~2× smaller states than 8-bit AdamW (4-bitFactor ~4×), trains 4× larger OPT models, LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU.
> - Key techniques: small block size (B128) for the first moment; zero-point-excluding linear/DE-0 mapping and rank-1 normalization for the second moment (zero-point problem otherwise destabilizes training: 33% unstable runs, BLEU 66.6); factorized second moment; convergence proof given for quantized SGD(M). Note: evaluated only on language/vision tasks, not RL/audio.
> 
> **4. JEPA-style self-distillation ("How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features", NeurIPS 2024; plus LDReg)**
> - Theory (deep linear analysis): JEPA is implicitly biased toward high-influence (high regression-coefficient ρ) features and learns noisy, high-variance features slowly, converging to lower-amplitude weights; MAE's ordering depends mainly on eigenvalue λ. Depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA embeddings align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA), supporting that JEPA avoids noisy pixel features for representation learning.
> - Complementary: LDReg (ICLR 2024) fixes *local dimensional collapse* in SSL and improves linear eval on ImageNet (SimCLR 64.8 vs 64.3; BYOL 68.5 vs 67.6; MAE 57.6 vs 57.0) and COCO detection/segmentation (SimCLR 37.15 vs 36.48 APbb at 1000 epochs) — useful if your joint embeddings collapse dimensionally.
> 
> **5. Limits of scaled VLMs for data-type identification ("Visual Data-Type Understanding Does Not Emerge From Scaling VLMs", ICLR 2024)**
> Directly matches snow/blur/rotation filtering:
> - Zero-shot evaluation of 39 VLMs (100M–80B) via cosine-similarity text matching on 27 data-types: models are decent on style/semantic types (cartoon, pencil sketch) but fail on simple pixel/geometric types — Gaussian noise, rotations, snow, defocus blur.
> - Scaling gives marginal gains: power-law fits imply >1 trillion parameters needed to reach mean informedness >0.7 — "scaling appears impractical." Contrastive VLMs (CLIP, CoCa) beat much larger autoregressive LMMs (OpenFlamingo, IDEFICS, LLaVA); LLaVA-13B can underperform LLaVA-7B.
> - CLIP's embedding space separates animal classes (linear-probe informedness 0.99; KNN 0.94–0.97) far better than data-types (0.84; KNN 0.29–0.40) — the space is largely invariant to data-types.
> - Data-type scarcity in LAION-2B pretraining strongly correlates with performance (r≈0.80 with semantic-search abundance), explaining the blind spot.
> - Training-free few-shot adaptation (TIP-Adapter, in-context learning) does **not** help and can hurt; fine-tuning with a data-type-rich mixture (TeDaTy) does help: CLIP ID informedness rises from 0.451 to 0.669–0.777 (freezing the image encoder is best and even improves OOD), Otter from 0.051 to ~0.09–0.12 — but COCO-only fine-tuning degrades performance.
> 
> **Cross-cutting takeaways:** PBADet is the drop-in anchor-free detector (best on multi-part association, hands/feet); NSE gives you a pre-training spectral diagnostic for your EI RNNs; 4-bit AdamW/4-bitFactor gives near-lossless training within memory budgets (CE/F1/accuracy preserved); JEPA self-distillation is theoretically and empirically the right choice to avoid noisy pixel features; and for runtime data-type filtering, zero-shot cosine matching with VLMs is unreliable for snow/blur/rotation — plan fine-tuning with data-type-aware captions rather than scaling up model size.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the relevant works and a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Anchor-free detector: PBADet (part-body association)
> **Paper:** "PBADet: A One-Stage Anchor-Free Approach for Part-Body Association" (ICLR 2024). One-stage anchor-free detector linking parts (head, face, left/right hand, left/right foot) to the parent body via a single part-to-body center offset.
> 
> **Results:** On COCOHumanParts, PBADet (YOLOv5l6) reaches AP 43.0/41.8 (all categories), on par with BPJDet but leading on AP_M, AP_L, person and feet; it achieves the lowest mMR-2 for head, face, both hands and right foot. Ablations show the anchor-free part-to-body design beats anchor-based body-to-part (Hand AP 89.1 vs 85.3; Conditional Accuracy 92.62 vs 86.80; Joint AP 85.98 vs 78.13 vs BPJDet's 78.13). Against the pose estimator ED-Pose on COCO val (hands/feet only), PBADet gives far higher Precision/Recall/F1 (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51; e.g., left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87). On CrowdHuman face-body, it achieves leading body MR-2 and competitive AP, though its advantage over BPJDet is smaller for this single-part task.
> 
> ## 2. Spectral diagnostics for EI RNNs
> **Paper:** "Why Dale's Law Constrained Recurrent Neural Networks Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023).
> 
> **Results:** Column-constrained EI (ColEI) RNNs learn worse than standard RNNs and Dale's ANN (DANN) RNNs on all four benchmarks (adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition) with higher seed variance; gradient clipping helps ColEI far more. The key finding: **spectral properties matter more than sign constraints** — sign constraints account for only ~0.7–1% error, while the remaining gap (~2.3%) comes from the singular-value spectrum. ColEI has multimodal, dispersed singular values (from a rank-one nilpotent column-mean term) vs unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur spectra for standard/DANN RNNs; constraining spectral radius does not fix this because it does not constrain the nilpotent contribution. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization **anti-correlates with final test error** across sizes and E/I ratios, so it is a pre-training diagnostic: small high-NSE networks outperform large low-NSE ones.
> 
> ## 3. 4-bit optimizer states
> **Paper:** "Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States" (NeurIPS 2023).
> 
> **Results:** 4-bit AdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW across tasks — GLUE/RoBERTa-L (89.1 vs 88.9), SQuAD F1 (94.5 vs 94.6), E2E-NLG (67.8 vs 67.7), ImageNet/Swin-T (80.8 vs 81.2), WMT14 (26.28 vs 26.61) — and is comparable on LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tuning (MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC, OBQA), with convergence curves closely aligned to 32-bit. Memory savings reach 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4 GB → 31.9 GB). The framework also covers SGD(M) with a convergence proof; sublinear-memory alternatives (Adafactor with β1=0, SM3) degrade accuracy, especially on image classification. So 4-bit states preserve F1/accuracy without hurting metrics; the paper reports loss curves rather than CE directly, but they track the full-precision baseline.
> 
> ## 4. JEPA-style self-supervision
> **Paper:** "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self-Distillation Networks" (NeurIPS 2024).
> 
> **Results:** In deep linear networks with exact gradient-flow ODEs, JEPA self-distillation is biased toward **high-influence (high-regression-coefficient) features**, prioritizing "slow," low-variance features; depth strengthens noise suppression. MAE's learning order depends mainly on eigenvalue λ, so MAE is not biased against noisy features — it can learn them faster and with higher weight amplitude, while JEPA converges to lower amplitudes on noisy features. ImageNet-1K experiments confirm I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace (where perceptual features live) than MAE features, measured by CCA — supporting JEPA-style objectives for representation learning that avoid noisy pixel-level features. (Complementary context: LDReg shows SSL representations can suffer local dimensional collapse, and regularizing local intrinsic dimensionality improves linear evaluation, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR/BYOL/MAE.)
> 
> ## 5. Limits of scaled VLMs on data-type identification
> **Paper:** "Visual Data-Type Understanding Does Not Emerge from Scaling Vision-Language Models" (ICLR 2024).
> 
> **Results:** Zero-shot evaluation of 39 VLMs (100M–80B) on SyntheticTypeIdent (27 types, 1,350 images) and NaturalTypeIdent (25 types, 1,250 images), covering snow, defocus blur, rotation, noise, etc. Contrastive VLMs (CLIP-style, cosine-similarity matching of image to data-type text prompts) **outperform much larger autoregressive LMMs** (log-likelihood scoring, e.g., OpenFlamingo, IDEFICS), which show a pronounced drop at the largest scales. Scaling gives only marginal gains for CLIP (weak power laws: I ≈ 0.26·S^0.08 and 0.01·S^0.25; reaching informedness 0.7+ by scaling appears impractical). Style/semantic types (cartoon, sketch) are easier; basic manipulations (rotation, gaussian noise, patch-and-reshuffle) are hardest. All models identify animals far better than data-types; data-type information is scarce in LAION-2B, and its abundance strongly correlates with performance (r≈0.80 with semantic search; 0.776 for CLIP-only). Fine-tuning with TeDaTy (8 types, captions containing data-type info) significantly improves identification and often OOD generalization; training-free adaptation (CLIP TIP-Adapter, Otter in-context) also helps.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Detector (PBADet) and JEPA (self-supervision) both shift away from pixel-level/hand-crafted representations:** PBADet's single part-to-body offset gives cleaner part-person correspondence than anchor-based multi-offset schemes (and beats them by ~4–8 points in ablation), just as JEPA's latent-space prediction beats MAE's pixel reconstruction at suppressing noisy features — both favor compact, semantic structure over redundant/low-level detail.
> - **Spectral diagnostics (NSE) and low-bit optimizers are both about safe efficiency under constraints:** NSE lets you predict EI-RNN trainability *before* training (anti-correlated with error), while 4-bit optimizer states preserve accuracy while cutting memory up to ~58%. Both are "lossless" diagnostics/tools: NSE costs nothing at runtime, 4-bit states cost no accuracy.
> - **The weakest link in the stack is the VLM data-type filter:** unlike the other four components (detector, RNN, optimizer, JEPA all match or beat their baselines), zero-shot VLMs fail badly on exactly the runtime-relevant types (snow, blur, rotation), scaling does not fix it, and the fix requires either fine-tuning with data-type-labeled captions (TeDaTy) or training-free adaptation — consistent with the resource-constrained design goal, fine-tuning (possibly with 4-bit optimizers) is the practical route.
> - **Cross-cutting caveat:** the JEPA result is proven for deep linear models (qualitative on ImageNet), the spectral result is diagnostic (NSE) rather than a fix, the 4-bit results cover Adam/AdamW (SGD(M) only via framework/proof), and the VLM result shows cosine zero-shot matching is fundamentally limited for this task.

</details>

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and synthesis of the experimental results reported across the five papers, aligned to the themes of training dynamics and efficiency in deep networks/Transformers, memory‑lean optimization, implicit biases in joint‑embedding vs reconstruction, and efficient one‑stage detection.
> 
> 1) Memory‑efficient optimizers (4‑bit) vs full‑precision/8‑bit/factorization
> - Benchmarks and identical datasets:
>   - NLU (RoBERTa‑Large on GLUE aggregate): 32‑bit AdamW 88.9; 8‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit Factor 88.9. Accuracy is maintained at 4‑bit relative to 32‑bit and 8‑bit (Table 2).
>   - QA (SQuAD/SQuAD 2.0): 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit AdamW within noise (e.g., SQuAD F1: 94.5 vs 94.6; SQuAD 2.0 F1: 88.4 vs 88.8; Table 9).
>   - Image classification (Swin‑T on ImageNet‑1k top‑1 acc): 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9 (Table 2). Pretraining‑scale task shows minimal loss (≤0.4 pt) at 4‑bit.
>   - NLG (GPT‑2 Medium on E2E‑NLG, BLEU): 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5; 4‑bit AdamW 67.8; 4‑bit Factor 67.6 (Table 2). Other metrics (METEOR/ROUGE/CIDEr) remain within error bars (Table 8).
>   - MT (Transformer‑Base on WMT14 En‑De, SacreBLEU): 32‑bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; 4‑bit AdamW 26.28; 4‑bit Factor 26.45 (Table 2). Small drop vs 32‑bit.
>   - Instruction‑tuning (LLaMA 7B/13B/33B): 4‑bit AdamW matches or slightly trails 32‑bit AdamW across MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC‑e/c, OBQA (e.g., LLaMA‑13B MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; ARC‑e 64.1 vs 63.6; Table 3).
> - Efficiency results on identical training setups (Table 4):
>   - LLaMA‑7B (FSDP, 2×A100 80GB): 4‑bit AdamW saves 57.7% total training memory (31.9 GB vs 75.4 GB) and slightly reduces wall‑time (3.07 h vs 3.35 h); a fused 4‑bit version keeps the same memory and time.
>   - RoBERTa‑L (RTE task): 4‑bit reduces total memory by 43.5–46.7% vs 32‑bit; fused 4‑bit matches or beats 8‑bit run‑time (3.17 min vs 3.38 min for 8‑bit) with more memory saved.
>   - GPT‑2 Medium: 4‑bit saves 34–36% memory; fused 4‑bit brings time back in line with 32‑bit.
> - Trainable model size within fixed memory (Table 5): 4‑bit expands the largest fine‑tunable OPT model from 350M→1.3B on 24GB and 1.3B→6.7B on 80GB; enables LLaMA‑7B on a single 80GB GPU.
> - Stability/accuracy under 4‑bit (Table 1 ablations): Key to 4‑bit is second‑moment quantization without zero‑point (DE‑0 or Linear) and small‑block/Rank‑1 normalization. With these, 4‑bit achieves the same BLEU on E2E‑NLG as 32‑bit (≈67.7–67.8) with 0% instability; by contrast, naive 4‑bit with zero‑point showed up to 66% unstable runs.
> - Summary: Across identical datasets (GLUE, SQuAD, ImageNet‑1k, E2E‑NLG, WMT14, LLaMA instruction‑tuning), 4‑bit AdamW/Factor matches 8‑bit and essentially matches 32‑bit for fine‑tuning, while cutting total memory by ~35–58% and sometimes improving end‑to‑end time.
> 
> 2) Prompt‑based continued pretraining (PCP) vs conventional TAPT and FT baselines
> - Across 16 GLUE/related tasks (Tables 1, summary panel):
>   - Fully‑supervised: TAPT often harms prompt‑based FT (hard/soft) on sentence‑pair tasks (e.g., MNLI/MNLI‑mm/SNLI/QNLI/QQP/STSb average declines). PCP improves prompt‑based FT on 100% of tasks (both hard and soft), whereas TAPT only helps in a minority.
>   - Semi‑supervised (16 labels/class): PCP yields large absolute gains for prompt‑based FT. Examples:
>     • QNLI (soft): 64.2→84.3 (+20.1 pts); TAPT: 64.2→55.0 (–9.2).
>     • MNLI (hard): 67.3→75.6 (+8.3); TAPT: 67.3→50.7 (–16.6).
>     • CoLA (hard): Matthews 7.2→25.0 (+17.8); TAPT: 7.2→1.4 (–5.8).
>     • QQP F1 (soft): 66.5→72.3 (+5.8); TAPT: 66.5→58.3 (–8.2).
>   - Fully‑supervised single‑sentence tasks: PCP adds consistent small gains (e.g., CoLA soft 61.3→62.0; SST‑2/5/MR/CR small +0.1 to +1.4) where TAPT is mixed or negative (e.g., CoLA 61.3→52.6 with soft TAPT).
> - Against semi‑supervised SOTA (FixMatch, FlexMatch, AdaMatch, Dash) on 5 public text datasets (Table 2): PCP + prompt‑based FT (hard/soft) attains the top or second‑best Macro‑F1 on 4/5 datasets and the best mean across settings, without iterative student–teacher loops or heavy augmentation.
> - Data efficiency and scaling (Fig. 4, Table 3): PCP helpful with only 100–1,000 unlabelled samples; benefits grow with model size (RoBERTa‑Base→Large). Even with larger continued pretraining corpora, PCP continues to outperform TAPT.
> - Lower bound analysis (Fig. 3): PCP with random labels still improves prompt‑based FT in >50% of cases on these tasks; pseudo‑labels from a trained model consistently outperform random labels.
> - Summary on identical datasets: For the same GLUE/related tasks and label budgets, PCP consistently improves prompt‑based FT (hard/soft) where TAPT often degrades it—especially on sentence‑pair tasks—demonstrating better training dynamics when templates are included in continued pretraining.
> 
> 3) One‑stage, anchor‑free part–body association (PBADet) vs BPJDet/Hier‑R‑CNN and others
> - Identical datasets and metrics:
>   - BodyHands (Table 1): PBADet surpasses BPJDet across all reported metrics.
>     • PBADet‑YOLOv7: Hand AP 89.1; Conditional Accuracy 92.62; Joint AP 85.98.
>     • PBADet‑YOLOv5l6: 88.1; 92.71; 85.73.
>     • Best BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9; 86.91; 84.39. Thus, +5.7 pts Cond. Acc. and +1.6 pts Joint AP over strongest BPJDet with smaller/similar backbones.
>   - COCOHumanParts (Table 2): Overall AP.5:.95 and per‑category APs are on par or better than BPJDet and better than Hier‑R‑CNN in many columns. PBADet leads in APM/APL and the “person/feet” categories (e.g., PBADet‑YOLOv5l6 person 62.4 vs BPJDet‑YOLOv5l6 61.3; right foot 30.9 vs 30.2; left foot 31.5 vs 30.9). Subordinate APs also competitive.
>   - Association error (Table 3, mMR−2 averages): PBADet achieves the lowest average miss‑matching rate across head, face, both hands, and right foot, indicating more reliable part‑body linking.
>   - CrowdHuman (Appendix Table 5/6): For face‑body association, PBADet‑YOLOv7 has best MR−2 for body (36.5) and face (44.7), and best AP for body (91.6). Overall mMR−2 remains ≈50.x (comparable to BPJDet). PBADet maintains stronger detection–association balance vs CNN/DETR crowded‑scene baselines.
> - Efficiency: One‑stage, anchor‑free head with a single 2D part‑to‑body offset reduces representation size vs body‑to‑part (e.g., 10 vs 15 fields for 3 parts) and simplifies decoding (nearest‑center assignment), which aligns with the observed accuracy gains and robustness as the number of parts grows.
> 
> 4) Spectral constraints and EI (Dale’s Law): training dynamics and stability
> - Identical tasks across models (ColEI vs DANN RNN vs standard RNN):
>   - On adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task (Fig. 2): ColEI RNNs learn worse (higher error/poorer final accuracy) and show higher variance; DANN RNNs match standard RNNs.
>   - Gradient clipping helps ColEI much more, indicating intrinsic instability.
> - Spectrum transplant experiments (Fig. 4): Replacing spectra shows the singular value distribution at initialization matters more for learning than sign constraints per se. The multimodal, dispersed spectrum with large singular values in ColEI explains exploding/vanishing dynamics; making spectra unimodal/clustered restores much of the performance gap.
> - NSE (normalized SVD entropy) vs performance (Figs. 5–7): NSE tracks learning quality; reducing inhibitory proportion or network size lowers NSE and harms performance. Small ColEI nets with realistic E/I ratios train worst; DANN and standard RNNs keep high NSE and stable learning.
> - Summary: The experimental comparisons across the same tasks show that spectral properties—not just the EI sign constraints—drive the inferior training dynamics of ColEI RNNs; DANNs’ spectra resemble standard RNNs, explaining their strong performance.
> 
> 5) JEPA vs MAE (deep linear analysis): implicit bias and training order
> - Shared synthetic settings (linear encoders/decoders; two data distributions):
>   - Both JEPA and MAE display greedy learning, but the order differs under distribution 2: JEPA prioritizes high‑influence (high regression‑coefficient ρ) features even when covariance λ is lower; MAE prioritizes features with larger λ (Fig. 1 & 2). With depth, JEPA’s bias toward high‑ρ strengthens; MAE’s order remains λ‑driven.
>   - Analytical results (Eqs. 7–14) match simulations; JEPA’s critical time depends more on ρ and depth than MAE’s.
> - Empirical indication on vision features: In a 64×64 ImageNet setting, JEPA features align earlier with the lower‑variance “bottom” PCA subspace, while MAE focuses more on variance‑explaining subspaces (Appendix D/Fig. 7), consistent with the theory that JEPA prefers predictive, less noisy features.
> - Summary: On identical synthetic tasks, JEPA and MAE learn the same modes but in different orders; JEPA’s depth‑dependent bias toward influential features contrasts with MAE’s variance‑driven bias, explaining better early semantic learning under JEPA‑style self‑distillation.
> 
> Cross‑paper takeaways on training dynamics and efficiency
> - Memory/time efficiency: 4‑bit AdamW/Factor preserves accuracy across standard image/text tasks (GLUE, SQuAD, E2E‑NLG, WMT14, ImageNet‑1k) while cutting total training memory by up to ~58% and enabling much larger models under a fixed budget. Stability at 4‑bit hinges on avoiding a zero‑point in second‑moment quantization and using small‑block/Rank‑1 normalization.
> - Pretraining strategy: Including templates in continued pretraining (PCP) produces consistent gains for prompt‑based FT on GLUE‑style benchmarks—especially sentence‑pair tasks—where conventional TAPT often degrades performance. PCP accelerates learning with only 100–1,000 unlabelled samples and scales with model size.
> - Spectral/stability insights: For recurrent deep nets obeying Dale’s Law, initialization spectra predict training viability better than sign constraints alone; measuring NSE offers a practical diagnostic. This mirrors the quantization ablations: careful treatment of distributions (spectra/zero‑points) is critical to stable, efficient training.
> - Efficient one‑stage detection: PBADet’s anchor‑free, single‑vector part‑body association improves both detection (AP) and association (mMR−2) vs anchor‑based/extended representations across BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, and CrowdHuman, while simplifying decoding.
> 
> Overall, on identical datasets and similar task types, the methods consistently show: (i) 4‑bit optimizers deliver near‑parity accuracy with substantial memory/time wins; (ii) PCP reliably improves prompt‑based FT where TAPT is unstable or harmful; (iii) spectral initialization governs EI‑constrained RNN learning more than sign constraints; (iv) JEPA’s implicit bias toward “influential” features contrasts with MAE’s variance bias; and (v) PBADet’s one‑stage anchor‑free design yields superior or comparable detection/association metrics with a simpler pipeline.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the provided collection, the papers matching your criteria are:
> 
> **1. Memory-lean 4-bit optimizers — "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States" (NeurIPS 2023, doc 8d5e1455…)**
> - Compresses Adam/AdamW optimizer states to 4-bit (B128/DE first moment, Rank-1/Linear second moment, optional factorization). Matches the "~4-bit state, reliable cross-entropy/F1" requirement.
> - Results (vs 32-bit AdamW): RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; Swin-T ImageNet CLS 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2M NLG 67.8 vs 67.7; SQuAD QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6; WMT14 MT 26.28 vs 26.61 — match or exceed on fine-tuning, comparable on pretraining; memory saved up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU).
> - Caveat: it does **not** use MNIST/CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50; vision uses Swin-T/ImageNet-1k. The MNIST/CIFAR-100+ResNet/LeNet backbones appear instead in "Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure" (doc 582d138d…, ICML 2025), which analyzes Hessian power-law spectra/generalization (e.g., Pearson 0.72 with LeNet test error on CIFAR-10; d_ks predicts LLM generalization up to 0.98; LoRA-only fine-tuning does *not* induce power-law structure, full FT does) — but that paper is not a 4-bit optimizer.
> 
> **2. Implicit bias of JEPA vs MAE — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024, doc 40fde037…)**
> - Deep-linear analysis: JEPA is biased toward high-influence (high-ρ) features; MAE orders features mainly by eigenvalue λ; depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression. Objectives are MSE-based (MAE) and latent MSE (JEPA); no explicit CE-stability study.
> - ImageNet-1K: I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE. Related SSL work: LDReg (doc 51526068…) counteracts local dimensional collapse, improving SimCLR/BYOL/MAE linear evaluation and transfer with ResNet-50/ViT-B on ImageNet.
> 
> **3. Spectral perspective on Dale's Law — "Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly" (NeurIPS 2023, doc e63a94c4…)**
> - Exact match (normalized SVD entropy/NSE guidance). ColEI RNNs learn worse and with higher variance across adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and object recognition; gradient clipping mitigates. Singular-value transplants show the singular-value *spectrum* (not sign constraints or vectors) matters. NSE anti-correlates with final test error (higher NSE ⇒ better learning); DANN RNNs have standard-like spectra and learn as well as standard RNNs; small networks/fewer I units worsen spectra and performance.
> 
> **4. Prompt-based continued pretraining — PCP (NeurIPS 2023, doc af1b1cf8…) and GOT-D (ICLR 2024, doc bb21f950…)**
> - PCP: continued pretraining with templates + golden/pseudo labels before prompt-based FT; consistently improves prompt-based FT by up to 20.1% absolute across 21 tasks, while conventional TAPT can hurt (e.g., −9.2% case); ablations show templates alone or pseudo-labels alone hurt — both are needed. It does **not** test LoRA (only notes PEFT compatibility as future work).
> - GOT-D: optimal-transport data selection for two-stage "pre-fine-tuning," selecting samples that shift the pretraining distribution toward the target (closest to a "D^c complement/subset" idea, though the exact D^c notation is absent). Results: GPT-2 detoxification −30% toxicity at 10K samples; +1.13% average over 8 domain tasks at 150K; GPT-2 XL AG News +13.9% and GPT-neo BoolQ 57.7 vs 53.3 (DSIR)/51.2 (TAPT) at 40K; scales to millions of samples within a single GPU hour (near-linear-ish efficiency bonus).
> 
> **5. One-stage anchor-free part-body detection — PBADet (ICLR 2024, doc 08b70bc3…)**
> - Exact match, reported with F1/Precision (not only AP). BodyHands: HandAP 89.1 vs BPJDet 85.3, Cond. Acc. 92.62 vs 86.80, JointAP 85.98 vs 78.13 (YOLOv7). COCOHumanParts: AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7), 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6), outperforming BPJDet and HierR-CNN. CrowdHuman face-body: best body MR−2 (36.5) with competitive AP. vs ED-Pose (Swin-L) on COCO val: all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51 — PBADet dominates on F1/Precision. Extends to quadruped AnimalPose/AP-10K.
> 
> **Bonus (near-linear time / diagrams):** GOT-D reports single-GPU-hour scaling (minutes on one GPU for millions of samples) and provides a pipeline diagram; PCP and PBADet both include explicit pipeline/overview figures; the MLMC distributed-training paper (doc fe0a4443…) gives convergence-rate analysis and communication-efficiency plots (CIFAR-10/ResNet18, 2-bit compression) relevant to training efficiency.
> 
> **Comparison analysis:** The 4-bit optimizer and PBADet are the strongest "practical-metric" papers: the former preserves loss/F1 within ~0.1–0.3 points of full precision at ~2–4× smaller optimizer memory, and the latter improves F1 by ~17 points over ED-Pose while being lighter (36.9M params, 1024 input vs 700M+/1536). The JEPA and Dale's-Law papers are more mechanistic/spectral: both show that *spectral/feature-prioritization* structure (NSE; influential-feature bias) predicts learning success better than superficial constraints (sign constraints; reconstruction fidelity). PCP vs GOT-D are complementary continued-pretraining strategies — PCP uses templates+pseudo-labels to fix prompt-FT (its ablations show either component alone fails), while GOT-D uses OT-gradient data selection to fix conventional FT, both giving consistent gains at small budgets (hundreds to 40K samples). The Hessian power-law paper ties these themes together: MNIST/CIFAR-100/ResNet spectra, generalization, and the LoRA-vs-full-FT distinction (only full fine-tuning induces the power-law structure). Note that no single paper covers all requested points: the exact "MNIST/CIFAR-100 + ResNet-50 + 4-bit optimizer," "D^c notation," and "LoRA with D^c-like pseudo-label subsets" combinations are not present in the collection and cannot be confirmed from these documents.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, the five requested topics map to these papers, and here is a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Memory-lean optimizers — "4-bit Optimizers" (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e1455…`)
> - Method: quantize Adam/AdamW first/second moments to 4-bit (smaller block size B128 for first moment; rank-1 normalization, zero-point-excluded linear quantizer, or factorization for second moment).
> - Results vs 32-bit AdamW (Table 2): NLU RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9; CLS Swin-T/ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2; NLG GPT-2M 67.8 vs 67.7; QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6; MT 26.28 vs 26.61 — i.e., matches or slightly exceeds full precision. Memory: LLaMA-7B saves 57.7% (31.87 vs 75.40 GB), RoBERTa-L 43.1% (4-bit AdamW) / 46.7% (4-bit Factor); 4-bit Factor states ~4× smaller than 8-bit.
> - Caveat: benchmarks are GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/WMT/Alpaca, **not** MNIST/CIFAR-100 with ResNet-50, and no explicit Precision metric is reported (QA F1 is preserved at 94.5).
> 
> ## 2. Implicit bias of JEPA vs MAE — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde037…`)
> - Theoretical (deep linear nets, exact gradient-flow ODEs): JEPA biases toward high-influence features (large regression coefficients); MAE orders features mainly by eigenvalue λ (high variance, even if noisy). The JEPA bias requires a **deep** encoder and largely disappears when shallow.
> - Experiment: on ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster (CCA) with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features.
> - No direct MSE-vs-CE stability experiments; collapse risk of the plain JEPA objective is acknowledged but not empirically quantified in this paper.
> 
> ## 3. Spectral perspective on EI (Dale's Law) — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c4…`)
> - Findings: ColEI RNNs (simple column sign-constrained) train worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANN EI nets on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition. Singular-value spectrum transplant shows the **spectrum**, not sign constraints, matters more (sign constraints cost ~0.7–1%, full gap ~2.3%).
> - Guidance metric: normalized SVD entropy (NSE ∈ [0,1]) anti-correlates with final test error; large networks with balanced E/I ratios have higher NSE and train better; gradient clipping substantially helps ColEI.
> 
> ## 4. Prompt-based continued pretraining — PCP (NeurIPS 2023, doc `af1b1cf8…`)
> - Method: MLM continued pretraining on task texts wrapped in prompt templates with golden/pseudo labels; then prompt-based FT (hard or soft) of RoBERTa-base/large.
> - Results: consistent gains for prompt-based FT across 21 tasks, up to +20.1% absolute, while conventional TAPT can drop 9.2%; works with only hundreds of unlabeled examples; outperforms semi-supervised SOTA without iterative/self-training or augmentation. Ablations: templates alone or labels alone each hurt vs combined; prolonged FT (+5× steps) gives only +0.1% (vs PCP's +8.1%).
> - Caveat: experiments are prompt-based FT (soft/hard) on RoBERTa; **no LoRA/SFT experiments** — PEFT compatibility is stated as future work.
> 
> ## 5. Efficient part–body association — PBADet (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc3…`)
> - One-stage anchor-free detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7) with a single part-to-body center offset (one-to-one, always valid even for invisible parts), task-alignment (TOOD-style) supervision, multi-scale offsets; Figure 2 gives the pipeline diagram.
> - BodyHands ablations (YOLOv7): full model Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 vs baseline w/o association loss 89.1/80.78/78.07; w/o multi-scale 88.8/91.64/85.46; w/o task-align 89.0/92.08/85.78. Anchor-free beats anchor-based with same part-to-body definition (Joint AP 85.98 vs 85.28) and beats BPJDet's body-to-part (78.13).
> - CrowdHuman face-body: Ours(YOLOv7) MR-2 36.5/44.7 (body/face), AP 91.6/81.6 vs BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 40.7/46.3/89.5/81.6. COCOHumanParts all-category AP 42.7/41.5 (YOLOv7) and 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6). Against ED-Pose, PBADet reports substantially higher precision, recall and F1 for hands/feet — i.e., practical F1/Precision metrics are present (mainly via the ED-Pose comparison).
> 
> ## Cross-method analysis
> - Reliability under compression: the 4-bit optimizer is the only one claiming "lossless" metrics vs full precision (F1 94.5, accuracy ≈ full), but its task set differs from the requested MNIST/CIFAR-100/ResNet-50 setting, so that specific claim is **not verified in the collection**.
> - Training-dynamics analyses: the JEPA paper is theoretical (deep linear) with one ImageNet CCA confirmation; the Dale's-Law paper is empirical and identifies an initialization-time diagnostic (NSE) predictive of training success — the two complement each other (theory vs spectral diagnostic) but use different models/tasks and no shared benchmark.
> - Fine-tuning efficiency: PCP shows continued pretraining can *hurt* and that template+pseudo-label prompting is what helps; the Hessian paper (doc `582d138d`) additionally shows LoRA-only fine-tuning does **not** induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does — so for LoRA backbones the PCP-style benefits are untested.
> - Detection: PBADet is the only method with a full ablation chain showing which components (association loss, multi-scale offsets, task alignment) drive gains, and it reports F1/Precision (vs ED-Pose) in addition to AP — matching the "practical metrics" request; it also includes pipeline diagrams (Figure 2).
> - Near-linear time complexity: only tangential support exists — the linear-time HSIC test (doc `58063efa`, O(nD²)) and constant-memory BSO spiking optimizer (doc `4741ca1f`) discuss complexity, but neither belongs to the five requested topics.
> 
> **Bottom line:** each requested item is covered by one paper, but several of the user's specific expectations are not fully met in the collection: no 4-bit optimizer results on MNIST/CIFAR-100/ResNet-50 with Precision (only GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet with Accuracy/F1/BLEU), no JEPA MSE/CE stability comparison (only regression-coefficient vs eigenvalue bias, deep-linear theory + ImageNet CCA), and no LoRA/SFT variant of PCP.

End‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning or an SFT backbone is preferred, and I’ll validate on small/standard datasets (e.g., MNIST/CIFAR‑100) before deployment. Can you point me to works that cover these needs together?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
