**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Integrated comparison of experimental results across the five works
> 
> 1) Real‑time part–body association (vision): PBADet vs prior detectors on identical datasets
> - BodyHands (hand–body association; identical test set)
>   - PBADet outperforms BPJDet across all key metrics.
>     - Hand AP: PBADet (YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6) 89.1/88.1 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 85.9.
>     - Conditional accuracy: 92.62/92.71 vs 86.91.
>     - Joint AP: 85.98/85.73 vs 84.39.
>   - Conclusion: PBADet’s one-stage anchor-free, part-to-body offset design yields higher detection and association accuracy than the anchor-based body-to-part offsets.
> - COCOHumanParts (multi‑part association; identical test set)
>   - Overall detection (all categories, AP.5:.95/AP.5/APM/APL):
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 43.0 / 70.0 / 66.2 / 67.2.
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6 / 70.6 / 63.8 / 61.8.
>     - Trade-off: PBADet is slightly lower on headline AP.5:.95/ AP.5, but higher on medium/large objects (APM/APL) and per-category feet AP (r-foot 30.9, l-foot 31.5 vs 30.2/30.9).
>   - Association robustness (average mMR−2, lower is better) per category:
>     - PBADet (YOLOv5l6) achieves best mMR−2 in 6/6 categories (head 27.9; face 30.5; left hand 36.2; right hand 40.8; right foot 50.4; left foot 47.9) vs BPJDet (30.8/31.8/41.6/42.2/49.1/50.4).
>   - Conclusion: PBADet improves association reliability (lower mismatching rates) and medium/large-scale AP; headline mAP parity vs BPJDet.
> - CrowdHuman (face–body association; identical val set)
>   - Body detection MR−2 (lower is better): PBADet (YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6) 36.5/37.5 vs BPJDet 40.7–39.7.
>   - Body AP: 91.6/91.4 vs 89.5–90.7.
>   - Pair mMR−2: PBADet ~50.8/50.9 vs BPJDet ~50.1–51.4 (comparable).
>   - Conclusion: PBADet improves body detection recall/precision; pair mismatching similar to BPJDet on this single‑part benchmark (face‑body).
> - Summary on similar dataset types
>   - Multi‑part settings (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts): PBADet consistently improves association metrics and often detection quality; in single‑part association (CrowdHuman) PBADet’s advantage narrows to detection metrics while association parity holds.
> 
> 2) Memory‑efficient training (NLP & vision): 4‑bit optimizers vs 8‑bit/32‑bit on identical datasets
> - GLUE‑style NLU (RoBERTa‑L; identical tasks aggregated)
>   - Mean accuracy/correlation: 32‑bit AdamW 88.9; 8‑bit 89.1; 4‑bit AdamW 89.1; 4‑bit Factor 88.9.
>   - Conclusion: 4‑bit matches or equals 32‑bit/8‑bit on NLU.
> - SQuAD & SQuAD 2.0 (RoBERTa‑L; QA; identical datasets)
>   - SQuAD F1: 32‑bit 94.6; 8‑bit 94.5; 4‑bit 94.5; 4‑bit Factor 94.6.
>   - SQuAD2 EM/F1 (per‑task table shows near‑parity across optimizers; no degradation reported for 4‑bit variants relative to 32‑bit).
>   - Conclusion: F1/EM maintained under 4‑bit.
> - ImageNet‑1k (Swin‑T; classification)
>   - Top‑1 Acc: 32‑bit 81.2; 8‑bit 81.0; 4‑bit AdamW 80.8; 4‑bit Factor 80.9.
>   - Conclusion: 4‑bit incurs ≤0.4 pt drop vs 8‑bit and ≤0.4 vs 32‑bit; within typical tuning noise; preserves CE‑optimized accuracy.
> - E2E‑NLG (GPT‑2 Medium; BLEU)
>   - BLEU: 32‑bit 67.7; 8‑bit 67.5; 4‑bit 67.8; 4‑bit Factor 67.6.
>   - Conclusion: 4‑bit equals or slightly exceeds 32/8‑bit.
> - WMT14 En–De (Transformer‑Base; SacreBLEU)
>   - SacreBLEU: 32‑bit 26.61; 8‑bit 26.66; 4‑bit AdamW 26.28; 4‑bit Factor 26.45.
>   - Conclusion: small drop (≤0.33 BLEU) under 4‑bit; still close.
> - Instruction tuning (LLaMA 7B/13B/33B; identical evaluation sets)
>   - 7B MMLU 5‑shot: 32‑bit 38.7 vs 4‑bit 38.9; HellaSwag 74.6 vs 74.7; ARC‑e 61.5 vs 61.2 (±0.3); ARC‑c 45.1 vs 44.4; OBQA 43.4 vs 43.0.
>   - 13B: 4‑bit equals or slightly improves over 32‑bit on most tasks.
>   - 33B: near‑parity (minor fluctuations per task).
>   - Conclusion: 4‑bit preserves instruction‑tuning performance across model sizes.
> - Efficiency (identical training configs)
>   - LLaMA‑7B (2×A100‑80GB, FSDP): total mem 75.4 GB→31.9 GB (−57.7%); small speedup from reduced communication.
>   - RoBERTa‑L (single 4090): total mem 5.31→3.00 GB (−43.5%) with fused kernels; throughput similar to or better than 8‑bit.
>   - GPT‑2 Medium (4×4090): 6.89→4.62 GB (−34.4%); fused kernels restore 4‑bit speed to 32‑bit levels.
> - Takeaway on similar dataset types: Across classification, QA, NLG, and MT, 4‑bit optimizers keep CE/F1/Precision-level performance essentially stable vs 32/8‑bit and deliver 35–58% memory savings.
> 
> 3) Prompt‑template & pseudo‑label updates without heavy loops: PCP vs TAPT and semi‑supervised SOTA on identical datasets
> - Fully‑supervised (16 NLP tasks; identical test sets)
>   - Prompt‑based FT (hard/soft) + PCP improved on 100% (16/16) of tasks; TAPT improved on ≤37.5% (hard) and ≤50% (soft) of tasks.
>   - Representative gains: on CoLA (soft), MCC 61.3→62.0 (+0.7); on MNLI/MNLI‑mm/SNLI/QNLI, PCP adds +0.4 to +1.9 points over prompt‑FT baselines, while TAPT often hurts (e.g., MNLI −2.6 for hard; −1.1 for soft).
> - Semi‑supervised (16 per class; identical test sets)
>   - Sentence‑pair tasks (largest deltas): QNLI hard 66.5→85.1 (+18.6); soft 64.2→84.3 (+20.1). CoLA hard 7.2→25.0 (+17.8); soft 4.9→21.5 (+16.6). TAPT frequently degrades (e.g., MNLI hard −16.6; soft −16.1).
>   - Single‑sentence: consistent improvements of +1–7 points across SST‑2, MR, MPQA, Subj, TREC.
>   - PCP improves on 100% (16/16) of tasks for both hard and soft prompting in semi‑supervised settings; TAPT improves 0–75% depending on task type and method, and is consistently poor on sentence‑pair tasks.
> - Against semi‑supervised SOTA (FixMatch, FlexMatch, AdaMatch, Dash) on 5 benchmarks (IMDB, AG News, Yelp, Yahoo, Amazon)
>   - PCP (hard/soft prompts) achieves the best or second‑best Macro‑F1 in 4/5 datasets and most label budgets. Example: Amazon‑200 labels: PCP‑hard 59.64 vs FlexMatch 54.19 (+5.45); Yelp‑200: PCP‑hard 63.15 vs Dash 58.85 (+4.30). One exception: IMDB‑20 where FixMatch edges PCP (95.26 vs 93.53 soft), but gap narrows at larger label counts.
>   - Complexity: PCP avoids iterative teacher–student or heavy augmentation; it pretrains with prompt templates plus (gold or pseudo) labels via MLM then does one prompt‑fine‑tune pass.
> - Data/scale sensitivity (similar dataset types)
>   - PCP is effective with only hundreds to ~1k unlabeled examples (e.g., strong gains observed with 1k examples; runtime <10 minutes on 2×3090).
>   - Scaling backbone (RoBERTa‑Base→Large) improves PCP consistently; PCP remains superior to TAPT at both scales.
> - Ablations (specific datasets): removing labels or templates from PCP degrades performance; random labels help >50% of cases but pseudo‑labels from the prompt‑FT model perform best.
> - Overall conclusion: PCP is a robust alternative to TAPT for prompt‑based FT, especially on sentence‑pair tasks where TAPT often harms; PCP also competes with or surpasses leading semi‑supervised methods while being simpler.
> 
> 4) Avoiding noisy features in representation learning: JEPA vs MAE (similar task families)
> - Controlled deep‑linear analyses plus simulations show:
>   - JEPA prioritizes “influential” features (high regression coefficient ρ), often reversing the learning order seen with MAE (which follows covariance λ). The effect strengthens with encoder depth (L>1).
>   - In temporal generative models, JEPA focuses on less noisy, predictive modes (higher ρ), whereas MAE reconstructs highly covarying content (including noisy parts).
>   - Empirically (ImageNet‑64/CCA diagnostics): features learned by I‑JEPA align more with low‑variance/perceptual subspaces (bottom PCA), matching recent findings that JEPA emphasizes semantic over pixel‑level detail.
> - Takeaway for similar dataset types: To avoid noisy features, JEPA‑style predictive learning in latent space is advantageous, especially with deeper encoders; MAE’s reconstruction objective tends to favor high‑variance (noisy) directions.
> 
> 5) Enforcing Dale’s Law in recurrent controllers: spectral pitfalls and fixes on identical tasks
> - Across identical tasks (adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition):
>   - Simple column‑constrained EI RNNs (ColEI) learn substantially worse than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs; they are also more unstable and sensitive to gradient clipping.
>   - Spectrum transplant experiments show the singular‑value spectrum matters more than sign constraints per se: transplanting ColEI’s dispersed/multimodal singular values into standard RNNs degrades performance nearly as much as a full ColEI, and vice‑versa.
>   - Network size and E/I ratio: small networks and fewer inhibitory units exacerbate ColEI’s spectral pathologies and reduce performance. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) predicts learning outcomes: higher NSE (more unimodal/clustered singular values) correlates with lower error across EI ratios and sizes.
>   - DANN RNNs have spectra like standard RNNs and learn as well; they remain robust over EI ratios and sizes (even with a single inhibitory unit).
> - Conclusion: When enforcing EI constraints (Dale’s Law), prioritize spectral regularity (unimodal, clustered singular values) over raw sign constraints; NSE can serve as a diagnostic before training.
> 
> What performs best where (summary by identical or closely matched settings)
> - Part–body association (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman): PBADet ≥ BPJDet ≥ Hier R‑CNN for one‑stage association accuracy and robustness, especially in multi‑part scenarios.
> - Optimizer compression on GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/E2E/WMT14: 4‑bit optimizers ≈ 8‑bit/32‑bit on CE/F1/Precision metrics, with up to ~58% memory savings; small trade‑offs (e.g., ≤0.33 BLEU drop) are rare and modest.
> - Prompt‑based fine‑tuning (GLUE family & related): PCP consistently beats TAPT for prompt FT; delivers the largest gains on sentence‑pair tasks in semi‑supervised settings; competes with or surpasses FixMatch/FlexMatch/AdaMatch/Dash while avoiding iterative loops.
> - Representation learning (JEPA vs MAE): for noise‑resilient features, JEPA’s latent prediction compresses toward informative, low‑variance structure, while MAE emphasizes reconstruction of high‑variance content.
> - EI recurrent controllers: Standard/DANN RNNs outperform ColEI on all tested tasks; improving ColEI’s spectrum (increasing NSE) narrows the gap; spectrum matters more than sign constraints.
> 
> Practical implications for the requested pipeline
> - End‑to‑end LoRA/SFT fine‑tuning with prompt templates and pseudo‑labels: Use PCP to pretrain with templates + pseudo‑labels via MLM, then prompt‑fine‑tune once; expect consistent gains over TAPT and competitive results vs semi‑supervised loops.
> - Optimizer state compression to ~4‑bit: Adopt the 4‑bit AdamW with small block sizes (B128/DE for m; rank‑1/linear for v) to keep GLUE/SQuAD/F1/Precision stable; memory drops by 35–58% and throughput can match 32‑bit with fused kernels.
> - Multi‑person part–body association: PBADet gives best hand/face/feet association robustness and state‑of‑the‑art body/part AP in single‑stage real‑time settings; strongest gains in multi‑part datasets.
> - Representation learning: Prefer JEPA‑style latent prediction to avoid noisy features in both static and temporal data; deeper encoders reinforce this bias toward informative features.
> - EI‑constrained recurrent controllers: If enforcing Dale’s Law, adopt DANN architectures or explicitly shape singular‑value spectra (target higher NSE) to avoid ColEI’s failure modes.
> 
> Datasets noted as identical or explicitly compared across methods
> - BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman: PBADet vs BPJDet (and with Hier R‑CNN qualitatively) on the same splits.
> - GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/E2E/WMT14: 4‑bit vs 8‑bit vs 32‑bit optimizers on the same tasks/datasets.
> - GLUE‑like single‑sentence and sentence‑pair tasks: PCP vs TAPT vs prompt‑FT/CLS FT on the same splits; semi‑supervised uses the same label budgets.
> - Sequential MNIST, adding problem, PTB, naturalistic recognition: Standard RNN/DANN vs ColEI on the same tasks.
> 
> Overall: The presented results collectively support a resource‑constrained pipeline in which (i) 4‑bit optimizers preserve CE/F1/Precision while cutting memory roughly in half; (ii) PCP provides a simple, non‑iterative way to leverage prompts and pseudo‑labels that consistently beats TAPT and is competitive with self‑training; (iii) PBADet is the best available one‑stage anchor‑free choice for multi‑person part–body association; (iv) JEPA‑style training avoids noisy features; and (v) spectral regularity (NSE) is the key to stable EI‑constrained recurrent controllers.

**naive 最终答案**

> No single work covers all four needs together; the collection addresses each one separately. Here are the relevant works and a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> **1. 4-bit optimizer states — "4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - Uses smaller blocks (B128) for the first moment, zero-point-excluding linear/rank-1 quantization for the second, optional factorization (4-bit Factor).
> - Results (Table 2): vs 32-bit AdamW — NLU RoBERTa-L 88.9→89.1, CLS Swin-T 81.2→80.8, NLG GPT-2 67.7→67.8, QA 94.6→94.5, MT 26.61→26.28. So fine-tuning metrics (incl. QA F1) are essentially lossless; pretraining-style tasks (CLS/MT) are "comparable" but slightly below.
> - Memory: LLaMA-7B −57.7%, RoBERTa-L −43.1%, GPT-2M −34.4%; 4-bit Factor ~4× smaller states than 8-bit; enables LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU and 4× larger OPT models. Ablations: quantizing both moments costs ~0.4% on Swin-T; rank-1/factorization recovers accuracy. Note: on LLaMA-33B commonsense/MMLU, 4-bit AdamW dips slightly (56.4→54.9 avg). Limitation: optimal quantization is task-dependent.
> 
> **2. JEPA vs noisy features — "Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Analytic (deep linear) result: JEPA greedily prioritizes *influential* features (large regression coefficient ρ), while MAE prioritizes high-variance (λ) features even if noisy. Depth strengthens this noise suppression; JEPA converges to *lower* amplitude weights on noisy directions, so noisy features are less likely to be used downstream. 1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE. ImageNet: I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance perceptual PCA subspace faster than MAE.
> - Practical takeaway: prefer JEPA-style latent prediction (with stop-grad) over pixel reconstruction; depth and a high-ρ bias are the mechanism that filters noise.
> 
> **3. Prompt-based continued pretraining — "Prompt-based Continued Pre-training (PCP)" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - Finding: conventional TAPT is *not* reliably beneficial — it can hurt (up to 9.2% decline), especially for sentence-pair tasks and prompt-based FT. PCP instead presents prompt templates + golden/pseudo labels under MLM before prompt-based FT.
> - Results: consistent gains for prompt-based FT (hard/soft) on 21 benchmarks, up to 20.1% absolute; outperforms SOTA semi-supervised methods (FixMatch, DASH, etc.) *without* iterative loops or augmentation; effective with only hundreds of unlabeled examples; works across model/dataset sizes. Ablation: templates alone or pseudo-labels alone both hurt vs the combination; prolonged FT (5× steps) only adds 0.1%, so gains aren't from longer training. Limitation: encoder-only models only.
> 
> **4. Dale's Law (EI) spectral pitfalls — "Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - ColEI (column-sign-constrained) RNNs learn worse than standard RNNs (gap ~2.3%±0.6% on sequential MNIST), with higher variance and instability without gradient clipping. Cause: rank-one nilpotent column-mean term → multimodal, dispersed singular-value spectrum (pathological), not sign constraints per se (spectrum transplants show spectrum matters more).
> - Recurrent DANNs have unimodal spectra like standard RNNs and match their performance, robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron (NSE ≈ 0.95). Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error — usable as a pre-training diagnostic. Small networks/fewer I units → worse spectra and learning.
> 
> **Also relevant to your pipeline:**
> - **PBADet (ICLR 2024)** — one-stage anchor-free part-to-body association (hands/face in multi-person scenes). On BodyHands it beats BPJDet/BodyHands on hand AP, conditional accuracy, and joint AP (smaller YOLOv7 model outperforms BPJDet YOLOv5m6); on COCOHumanParts it leads AP_M/AP_L and lowest mMR−2; vs ED-Pose, F1 for hands/feet is far higher (e.g., all-parts 31.51→48.52). Its compact part-to-body offset representation is efficiency-friendly for real-time use.
> - **NEFTune (ICLR 2024)** — noisy embeddings improve instruction FT (AlpacaEval 29.8→64.7) and work with QLoRA, fitting your resource-constrained fine-tuning; no gain on OpenLLM-style metrics.
> - **Hessian power-law study (ICML 2025)** — LoRA-only fine-tuning does *not* induce the power-law Hessian structure that full fine-tuning does, suggesting LoRA and full-parameter FT may differ in generalization behavior (relevant to your "LoRA vs SFT backbone" choice); it also validates on MNIST/CIFAR-10/100.
> 
> **Bottom line:** for your stack, the 4-bit optimizer paper covers CE/F1-stable compression; the JEPA analysis explains noise suppression; PCP covers prompt-template + pseudo-label continued pretraining without iterative loops; and the Dale's Law paper explains the spectral pathology (use NSE as a diagnostic, prefer DANN-style parameterization over ColEI). PBADet covers the part-body association module. These works are complementary but none jointly spans all four areas.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the works in the collection that map to your pipeline needs, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. 4-bit optimizer states (stable CE/F1/Precision)
> **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Method: compress Adam/AdamW first moment with small block size (B128), second moment with zero-point-excluded linear/rank-1 quantization, optionally factorized ("4-bit Factor").
> - Results (Table 2): vs 32-bit AdamW — NLU (RoBERTa-L): 89.1 vs 88.9; ImageNet CLS (Swin-T): 80.8 vs 81.2; NLG: 67.8 vs 67.7; QA F1 (SQuAD): 94.5 vs 94.6; MT: 26.28 vs 26.61. So CE/F1-style metrics are essentially lossless; memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B, one 80GB GPU). LLaMA fine-tuning on Alpaca also matches 32-bit. Note: works with fine-tuning (LoRA-style frozen-backbone is mentioned as complementary, though LoRA itself doesn't replace optimizer-state compression).
> 
> ## 2. JEPA-style representation learning (avoiding noisy features)
> **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features: The Implicit Bias of Deep Linear Self Distillation Networks"** (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Method/result: exact deep-linear analysis shows JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (large regression coefficient, ρ) and suppresses noisy, high-variance directions; suppression grows with encoder depth (JEPA fixed point = ρ^L, MAE = ρ^(L/(L+1))). MAE instead learns highly covarying features even when noisy.
> - Empirical confirmation on ImageNet: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance (bottom 25% PCA) perceptual subspace than MAE features (CCA similarity higher for JEPA on bottom-subspace, reversed on top-subspace). Implication: use a deep JEPA encoder and expect implicit noise rejection; shallow encoders lose this bias.
> 
> ## 3. Prompt-based fine-tuning via continued pretraining + pseudo labels (no iterative loops)
> **"Don't Stop Pretraining? Make Prompt-based Fine-tuning Powerful Learner" (PCP)** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Method: continued pretraining on task-related text wrapped in prompt templates with golden/pseudo labels (MLM objective), then prompt-based FT. No iterative self-training loop.
> - Results: conventional TAPT **hurts** prompt-based FT (up to 9.2% decline, especially sentence-pair tasks), while PCP consistently improves prompt-based FT by up to **20.1% absolute** across 21 benchmarks (single-sentence + sentence-pair), in semi- and fully-supervised settings, with only hundreds of unlabeled examples. PCP also beats state-of-the-art semi-supervised approaches with greater simplicity. Ablations: using only templates or only pseudo labels both hurt vs PCP; prolonged fine-tuning (5k steps) only +0.1%, vs +8.1% for PCP.
> 
> **Related: GOT-D** (optimal-transport data selection for pre-fine-tuning) — on BoolQ with 40k budget: GOT-D 57.7 vs DSIR 53.3 vs TAPT/c 51.2; GPT-2 XL AG News zero-shot +13.9%. Useful if you want to select task-related text for that continued-pretraining step.
> 
> ## 4. Spectral pitfalls for EI (Dale's Law) recurrent controllers
> **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Method/result: comparing ColEI (column sign-constrained) RNNs vs recurrent DANNs vs standard RNNs on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, object recognition.
> - Key findings: the problem is **not** sign constraints per se — it's the **initial recurrent-weight spectrum**. ColEI's weight matrix = rank-one nilpotent (column means) + zero-mean random matrix, producing a multimodal, dispersed singular-value distribution; standard RNNs/DANNs have unimodal quarter-circle/Marchenko-Pastur spectra. Spectrum transplant experiments show spectrum matters more than sign constraints (sign constraints account for only ~1% error vs ~2.3% total gap). Gradient clipping mitigates ColEI instability. Small networks / fewer I units worsen spectrum and performance; DANN is robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron. Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error — a practical diagnostic.
> 
> ## Part-body association (your real-time multi-person component)
> **PBADet** (one-stage anchor-free part-body association) — on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts it outperforms BPJDet and HierR-CNN; on CrowdHuman face-body association it achieves leading body MR-2 with competitive AP; vs ED-Pose it gives substantially higher precision/recall/F1 for hands and feet.
> 
> ## Coverage note
> No single work in this collection covers all four needs together; you'd combine the above five papers. The closest "pipeline-adjacent" items are the 4-bit optimizer paper (resource-constrained fine-tuning, also evaluated on instruction tuning/LLaMA) and PCP (prompt templates + pseudo labels without iterative loops — matching your requirement 3). The collection does not contain a paper combining 4-bit optimization with JEPA or with Dale's-law RNNs, so cross-method interactions (e.g., 4-bit states + JEPA training, or EI spectral fixes under 4-bit quantization) are not established in this context.

**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a consolidated comparison of experimental results across the five provided papers. For each work, I report results directly from their figures/tables and compare methods on identical datasets, similar dataset types, and specific datasets. I also point out where datasets overlap across papers.
> 
> 1) Anchor-free human part–body association detection (PBADet, ICLR 2024) versus prior detectors and pose estimators
> - Identical datasets: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman (also overlap on COCO with ED-Pose).
> - BodyHands (Table 1):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7, 1024 px): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6, 1024 px): Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 1536 px): Hand AP 85.9, Cond. Acc. 86.91, Joint AP 84.39.
>   - Conclusion: On the identical BodyHands dataset, PBADet exceeds BPJDet across all reported metrics (higher Hand AP, Conditional Accuracy, Joint AP), even when using the same YOLOv5l6 backbone.
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2, per-category AP; Table 3, average mMR−2):
>   - Overall AP (AP.5:.95 original / subordinate): PBADet YOLOv5l6: 43.0 / 41.8 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6: 43.6 / 43.3 (BPJDet slightly higher on overall AP).
>   - Scale AP: PBADet leads on APM and APL (PBADet YOLOv5l6: 66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6: 63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9).
>   - Per-category AP: PBADet YOLOv5l6 vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6: person 62.4 vs 61.3 (PBADet better), feet categories (PBADet 30.9/31.5 vs BPJDet 30.2/30.9; small edge to PBADet), while BPJDet is higher on head/face/hands AP.
>   - Association quality (average mMR−2; lower is better):
>     • PBADet YOLOv5l6 achieves lower mMR−2 than BPJDet YOLOv5l6 on head (27.9 vs 30.8), face (30.5 vs 31.8), left hand (36.2 vs 41.6), right hand (40.8 vs 42.2), and left foot (47.9 vs 50.4); right foot is higher (50.4 vs 49.1). PBADet YOLOv7 also lowers head/face and left hand relative to BPJDet l6, but has higher right hand/right foot.
>   - Conclusion: On COCOHumanParts, PBADet improves association robustness (lower mMR−2) in most categories versus BPJDet, while overall detection AP favors BPJDet slightly; PBADet excels on medium/large object AP.
> - CrowdHuman face-body association (Table 5; Table 6):
>   - PBADet YOLOv7: Best body MR−2 (36.5), best body AP (91.6), face MR−2 44.7, body-face mMR−2 50.8.
>   - BPJDet YOLOv5l6: body MR−2 40.7, body AP 89.5, face MR−2 46.3, mMR−2 50.1.
>   - Conclusion: On CrowdHuman, PBADet improves body and face detection MR−2 and body AP over BPJDet; association mMR−2 is comparable.
> - COCO multi-person pose comparison (Appendix A.2, Table 7; identical COCO validation set):
>   - Parts (Precision/Recall/F1 across selected hands/feet): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) outperforms ED-Pose (Swin-L) across all four parts and overall (e.g., all parts: Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51).
>   - Conclusion: On COCO keypoint-driven parts, PBADet yields higher Precision/Recall/F1 than ED-Pose when evaluated against part bounding boxes.
> 
> 2) Excitatory–inhibitory RNNs under Dale’s Law (NeurIPS 2023): spectral behavior and training stability
> - Identical datasets: adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition.
> - Methods compared: standard RNNs, ColEI (column-sign constrained EI), and DANN RNNs.
> - Performance comparisons (Figure 2):
>   - Across all four tasks, ColEI networks learn worse and more variably than standard RNNs and DANNs (higher error, slower/unstable learning). Gradient clipping benefits ColEI substantially more.
>   - Varying spectral radius (Appendix Figure 9): ColEI’s performance depends differently on radius than standard/DANN; still inferior at best regimes.
> - Stability and spectrum (Figures 3–7):
>   - ColEI exhibits dispersed/multimodal singular value spectra with larger modes; standard/DANN show unimodal clustered spectra, aligning with better performance.
>   - Lower inhibitory proportion and smaller networks degrade ColEI learning and increase spectrum pathology; DANN learning is robust to EI ratio and network size.
>   - Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) correlates with performance: higher NSE predicts better ColEI outcomes across sizes/ratios.
> - Conclusion: On identical tasks, standard RNNs and DANNs consistently outperform ColEI; spectrum clustering (high NSE) predicts better learning. ColEI requires more gradient clipping and favorable configurations to approach performance levels.
> 
> 3) JEPA vs MAE in deep linear settings (NeurIPS 2024): implicit bias and training dynamics
> - Datasets/experiments: synthetic Gaussian features (Distribution 1 & 2) and linear temporal model; Imagenet (64×64) representation analyses.
> - Identical/similar settings:
>   - Synthetic feature learning order (Figure 1): On Distribution 1 (λ and ρ both increasing), both objectives exhibit greedy dynamics prioritizing larger λ; on Distribution 2 (λ increasing, ρ decreasing), JEPA reverses the order and prioritizes high-ρ (influential) features, while MAE retains high-λ prioritization.
>   - ODE simulations (Figure 2 & 4): JEPA shows greedy dynamics w.r.t. ρ (depth-dependent), MAE shows greedy dynamics w.r.t. λ; deeper JEPA accentuates prioritization of high-ρ features.
>   - Temporal linear model (Figure 3): With u(t) autocorrelation γ and noise σa per mode, λ decreases while ρ increases from feature 1 to 2; JEPA learns higher-ρ (less noisy, more predictive) features sooner; MAE is agnostic to ρ and favors highly covarying features.
> - Imagenet (Appendix D, Figure 7):
>   - JEPA full vs bottom-PCA similarity grows faster and higher than MAE; JEPA full vs top-PCA similarity is lower than MAE, consistent with JEPA focusing on lower-variance, more perceptual subspaces.
> - Conclusion: JEPA implicitly prioritizes influential features (high regression coefficients ρ), especially with deeper encoders; MAE prioritizes high covariance λ. On Imagenet, JEPA features align more with the low-variance (perceptual) subspace than MAE.
> 
> 4) Active, anytime-valid RCPS (NeurIPS 2024): label-efficient guarantees with predictors
> - Identical datasets: Imagenet (used for calibration experiments) and controlled numerical simulations.
> - Labeling policies compared: “pretrain,” “learned,” “oblivious” (random budget), “all” (label everything).
> - Numerical simulations (Figure 2): α=0.05, β*≈0.5578.
>   - Safety: All methods keep the safety violation rate below α=0.05.
>   - Utility/efficiency: “pretrain” and “learned” achieve uniformly lower final β̂ (closer to β*) and reach lower β̂ with fewer labels than “oblivious” and “all.”
> - Imagenet (Figure 3):
>   - Safety: All methods maintain violation rates below α=0.05.
>   - Utility/efficiency: “pretrain” and “learned” again achieve lower average β̂ across labels and lower final β̂ than baselines.
> - Conclusion: Across identical setups (simulation, Imagenet), actively using predictors (“pretrain” or learning them) yields more label-efficient risk control (lower β̂ sooner) under anytime-valid guarantees; naïve baselines query more labels for worse utility.
> 
> 5) CleanDiffuser (NeurIPS 2024): diffusion models in decision making, benchmarking and design analyses
> - Identical datasets: D4RL (HalfCheetah, Hopper, Walker2d; Kitchen; Antmaze), plus IL benchmarks (PushT, Relay Kitchen, Robomimic).
> - Offline RL (Table 1):
>   - Locomotion (Medium/Medium-Expert/Medium-Replay): DQL achieves the highest average score across the 9 locomotion tasks (average 89.0), exceeding IDQL (84.1), DD (83.2), AdaptDiffuser (82.4), SynthER (69.4), Diffuser (78.2), EDP (82.4 on average). Specific highlights:
>     • Hopper-medium-replay: DQL 101.6 (best); IDQL 99.4; DD 99.2; AdaptDiffuser 91.2.
>     • HalfCheetah-medium: DQL 52.3 (best); IDQL 51.5; DD 45.3.
>     • Walker2d-medium: DQL 86.8 (best); IDQL 88.1 (slightly higher on Walker2d but DQL leads overall average).
>   - Kitchen (Mixed/Partial) average: IDQL (66.6) > DQL (63.0) > DD (65.8) > AdaptDiffuser (53.7) > Diffuser (54.1). On individual tasks, DD often strong on Mixed Kitchen (75.0 best for DD), while IDQL dominates on Partial Kitchen average.
>   - Antmaze (Play/Diverse): DQL dominates (average 81.3), with IDQL next (59.8), Diffuser/Decision Diffuser much lower (e.g., Antmaze medium: Diffuser 6.7; DD 8.0) and AdaptDiffuser below DQL/IDQL.
>   - Conclusion: On identical D4RL tasks, diffusion policies (especially DQL) generally outperform diffusion planners (Diffuser, DD) and data synthesizer (SynthER); IDQL is competitive especially in Kitchen and some locomotion tasks; DQL is strongest on Antmaze.
> - Offline IL (Table 2):
>   - Low-dimensional observations, average LAST/MAX:
>     • DiffusionPolicy (DiT1d) 0.90/0.96 (best), Chi_UNet1d 0.85/0.93; ACT 0.79/0.89; LSTM-GMM 0.66/0.84; DiffusionBC (Pearce_MLP) 0.65/0.73.
>     • Specific examples: square-mh—DiffusionPolicy DiT1d 0.87/0.96, higher than ACT (0.46/0.72) and DiffusionBC.
>   - Image observations, average LAST/MAX:
>     • DiffusionPolicy (DiT1d) 0.88/0.91 (best), ACT 0.87/0.88; Chi_UNet1d 0.80/0.85; LSTM-GMM 0.65/0.81; DiffusionBC (DiT) 0.51/0.57.
>     • Tasks like pusht-image: DiffusionPolicy variants reach ~0.99–1.00, ACT also 0.99–1.00; DiffusionBC with Pearce_MLP much lower.
>   - Conclusion: On identical IL tasks (PushT, Relay Kitchen, Robomimic), DiffusionPolicy (especially with DiT1d) achieves top average success/coverage; ACT is competitive but generally slightly behind DiffusionPolicy; DiffusionBC trails.
> - Design & sampling analyses:
>   - Sampling steps/backbone (Figures 6, D.2): For IDQL and DD across D4RL tasks, 5 sampling steps often suffice; increasing steps can cause “sampling degradation” (performance decreases), especially in medium-expert MuJoCo/Kitchen. SDE solvers (DDPM, SDE-DPM-Solver++) tend to perform better for diffusion policies but show more degradation risk than ODE solvers; high-order ODE solvers do not consistently outperform first-order.
>   - EMA rate (Figure 7): Higher EMA (e.g., 0.999–0.9999) yields more stable and higher performance and alleviates training degradation; near-convergence often at ~5×10^5 gradient steps.
>   - Model size (Appendix D.1, Table 4): Increasing model size does not universally improve performance; DD benefits in some Kitchen/Antmaze cases, IDQL gains are minor. Algorithm choice dominates over raw size.
>   - IL inference speed/model size (Appendix D.3, Table 5): DiffusionPolicy with Chi_UNet1d best performance but slowest inference (~0.405 s) and largest model; DiT1d is faster (~0.194–0.217 s) with strong performance; ACT fastest (~0.006 s) but slightly lower success.
> 
> Cross-paper dataset overlaps and comparative takeaways
> - COCO: Used by PBADet (COCOHumanParts for detection/association) and ED-Pose (pose); PBADet surpasses ED-Pose on Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet on COCO validation.
> - Imagenet: Used by JEPA (representation similarity) and RCPS (anytime-valid calibration). Both observe improved outcomes using model-aware approaches—JEPA features align with bottom-PCA; RCPS “pretrain/learned” policies achieve lower β̂ under label budgets.
> - Sequential tasks (adding, seq MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition): EI RNN paper shows standard/DANN outperform ColEI across identical tasks; spectrum clustering (NSE) predicts performance and stability.
> - D4RL/IL benchmarks: CleanDiffuser provides extensive identical-task comparisons—diffusion policies (DQL/IDQL) generally beat planners (Diffuser/DD) on RL; DiffusionPolicy beats ACT/LSTM-GMM/DiffusionBC on IL.
> 
> Overall summary of which performs better/worse on identical or similar datasets
> - Human part–body association (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman): PBADet outperforms BPJDet on BodyHands and improves association robustness (mMR−2) across most COCOHumanParts categories; slightly trails BPJDet on overall COCO AP but leads on medium/large AP scales; PBADet improves MR−2 and AP on CrowdHuman.
> - EI RNNs: Standard RNNs and DANNs > ColEI on all identical sequential tasks; ColEI requires favorable spectra/ratios and gradient clipping to reduce instability.
> - JEPA vs MAE: On synthetic and temporal models, JEPA prioritizes influential features (high ρ), MAE prioritizes high covariance (λ). On Imagenet, JEPA aligns more with perceptual (low-variance) subspaces.
> - Active RCPS: Predictor-aware policies (“pretrain/learned”) > baselines (“oblivious/all”) on simulations and Imagenet—lower β̂ with fewer labels; all methods control safety at α=0.05.
> - Diffusion in decision making: On D4RL, DQL is strongest overall (especially Antmaze), IDQL excels in Kitchen and competitive elsewhere; diffusion planners trail. On IL, DiffusionPolicy (DiT1d) best averages; ACT second; DiffusionBC lower.
> 
> All comparisons above are derived from the figures/tables of the provided papers; identical dataset usages are explicitly noted where present.

**naive 最终答案**

> I found five papers matching the requested topics. Here is a brief comparative analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## (a) PBADet — One-stage anchor-free part-body association (ICLR 2024)
> - **Setup match:** Anchor-free detection for part→body association with CNN backbones (YOLOv5l6, YOLOv7), **SGD optimizer** (YOLOv7 scheduler), classification branch with **task-alignment (TOOD) classification loss**, and COCO-family benchmarks (COCOHumanParts, BodyHands, CrowdHuman). Note: it uses SGD (not Adam), and the classification loss is the TOOD/DFL task-aligned loss rather than plain cross-entropy.
> - **Results (comparative):**
>   - BodyHands: HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98 (YOLOv7), beating BPJDet (YOLOv5l6: 85.9/86.91/84.39) with fewer params (36.9 vs 86.1M).
>   - Ablation (Table 8): anchor-free (89.1/92.62/85.98) > anchor-based part-to-body (88.4/92.31/85.28) > BPJDet body-to-part (85.3/86.80/78.13) — both anchor-free design and part-to-body definition improve association.
>   - COCOHumanParts AP.5:.95 = 42.7 (YOLOv7) / 43.0 (YOLOv5l6); leads in AP, APM, APL for person/feet; lowest mMR⁻² for head/face/hands/right-foot.
>   - CrowdHuman face-body: best body MR⁻² 36.5 and body AP 91.6 vs BPJDet (40.7/89.5); advantage smaller because it's single-part.
>   - vs pose estimator ED-Pose on COCO val: much higher Precision/Recall/F1 (all parts 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs 24.09/45.51/31.51).
> 
> ## (b) Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Setup match:** EI recurrent nets obeying biology-inspired constraints (Dale's law: ColEI and DANN), spectral analysis, training stability, stochastic optimization (projected SGD/gradient descent). Trained on adding, sequential MNIST, Penn Treebank, object recognition.
> - **Results:** ColEI learns worse and with **more variance during training and across initializations** than standard RNNs and DANN; **without gradient clipping ColEI is highly unstable**. Spectral behavior is the key: ColEI has multimodal/dispersed singular-value spectra (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), while standard RNNs/DANN match random-matrix unimodal spectra (Marchenko–Pastur/quarter-circle). Spectral-transplant experiments show the spectrum matters more than sign constraints (which cost ~0.7±0.3% for RNNs, 1±1% for ColEI, vs 2.3±0.6% total gap). **Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error** and predicts performance across network size and E:I ratio; DANN stays robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> 
> ## (c) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024, Apple)
> - **Setup match:** implicit bias of JEPA self-distillation toward informative features in **deep linear settings**, trained with **SGD** on deep linear MLPs.
> - **Results:** JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient ρ) in step-wise fashion with depth strengthening the bias, whereas MAE only prioritizes high-variance features (ordering by λ); JEPA is slower to learn noisy features and converges to lower-amplitude weights for them; JEPA prefers "slow," low-variance features. ImageNet I-JEPA experiments confirm it aligns faster with the low-variance PCA (perceptual) subspace than MAE (CCA).
> - **Caveat:** The specific datasets/metrics named in your question — CIFAR-100, MNIST, SVHN with AUROC/F1/Precision — are **not** used in this paper. Its evidence is Gaussian toy-data simulations (batch 1000, 5000 iterations, SGD) plus ImageNet with CCA feature-similarity; the MNIST/CIFAR-100 appearances in the collection belong to other works (e.g., the Hessian power-law paper), not the JEPA study.
> 
> ## (d) Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Active Labeling (NeurIPS 2024)
> - **Setup match:** anytime-valid sequential risk-controlling prediction sets with active labeling under a **label budget**, online updates, via e-processes/testing-by-betting — directly applicable to safety gating of model outputs (e.g., medical lesion segmentation, QA, robotics).
> - **Results:** guarantees risk control at all timesteps simultaneously with probability ≥1−α even on adaptively collected data; optimal labeling policy ∝ conditional-risk std, optimal predictor = conditional risk; regret bounds link policy/predictor error to wealth-process growth. Experiments (simulations and ImageNet, θ=0.1, α=0.05): learned/pretrained policies cut risk faster with fewer labels than "all"/"oblivious" baselines while keeping violation rates below α.
> 
> ## (e) CleanDiffuser — modular diffusion library for decision making (NeurIPS 2024 DB)
> - **Setup match:** easy-to-use modular library for diffusion-model-based decision making with core sub-modules (diffusion models/solvers — DDPM/DDIM/DPM-Solver(++)/EDM/RectifiedFlow; network architectures; guided sampling) and efficient dataloaders/env wrappers; integrates 9 algorithms (Diffuser, Decision Diffuser, AdaptDiffuser, Diffusion Policy, DiffusionBC, DQL, EDP, IDQL, SynthER) across 37 RL/IL environments; ~10 lines of code per algorithm.
> - **Results (empirical insights):** results match/exceed official baselines on D4RL (15 tasks) and IL benchmarks (22 tasks); diffusion policies excel in IL but are slower than ACT; ablations show **5 sampling steps are often enough and more steps can degrade**, SDE vs ODE solvers differ, and **algorithm choice dominates model size**.
> - **Caveat:** CleanDiffuser itself does **not** discuss LoRA/SFT fine-tuning, feature embeddings, self-supervised learning, or vision-language models. Those themes appear only in *other* papers in the collection (NEFTune on noisy embeddings + QLoRA; Themis on LoRA; CodeSteer on SFT/DPO; the Visual Data-Type Identification VLM paper; RTB's Stable-Diffusion LoRA fine-tuning; 4-bit Adam optimizers), not in the diffusion library paper.
> 
> ## Cross-paper comparison
> - **What the experiments actually support:** (a) validates that the anchor-free formulation + part-to-body definition beats anchor-based body-to-part association on COCO-scale human-part data; (b) shows spectral initialization (NSE) — not sign constraints — governs EI-RNN learnability and that such nets need gradient clipping to stabilize; (c) shows JEPA's deep linear dynamics select informative (low-variance/high-ρ) features where MAE does not; (d) shows betting-based anytime-valid sets are label-efficient under budgets; (e) shows modularity/algorithm choice dominate diffusion-policy design in decision making.
> - **Gaps vs the question's framing:** (a) uses SGD, not Adam, and a task-aligned loss rather than plain cross-entropy; (c) does not use CIFAR-100/MNIST/SVHN or AUROC/F1/Precision — those claims are unsupported in the retrieved collection; (e) does not cover LoRA/SFT/VLMs/SSL within the library paper itself, so those aspects cannot be verified from CleanDiffuser alone.

> 
> **(a) PBADet: One-Stage Anchor-Free Part-Body Association (ICLR 2024)**
> - Anchor-free one-stage detector (YOLOv5/YOLOv7 CNN backbones) associating human parts to bodies via a single part-to-body center offset; losses are IoU + DFL + task-aligned classification + association loss; trained with **SGD** (as in YOLOv7) for 100 epochs at 1024×1024.

Ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task alignment each improve association accuracy.
> 
> **(b) Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - Studies excitatory–inhibitory recurrent nets (ColEI sign-constrained vs DANN vs standard RNNs) on adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, naturalistic object recognition, using projected gradient descent and gradient clipping.
> - Results: ColEI learns worse and with higher seed variance; the singular-value spectrum (multimodal/dispersed) matters more than sign constraints (spectrum transplant experiments). Gradient clipping helps ColEI most; smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance; normalized SVD entropy (NSE) at initialization anti-correlates with final error and predicts performance.
> 
> **(c) How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Analyzes implicit bias of joint-embedding self-distillation in deep linear networks trained with SGD on Gaussian data; JEPA prioritizes high-influence (high regression coefficient ρ) features, increasingly with encoder depth, while MAE orders by variance λ.
> - Experiments: ImageNet-1K I-JEPA vs MAE show JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features (measured by CCA). Note: the paper does **not** use CIFAR-100/MNIST/SVHN or AUROC/F1/Precision metrics — those specifics are not in this paper.
> 
> **(d) Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Sequential, anytime-valid RCPS with active labeling under a label budget (e-processes/betting; IPW; optimal policy ∝ conditional-risk std dev; regret bounds).
> - Results (simulations + ImageNet, θ=0.1, α=0.05, label budget B=0.3): learned/pretrained labeling policies reach the target β* with fewer labels than "all" and "oblivious" baselines, while keeping the safety-violation rate below α at all times — suitable for safety gating of model outputs.
> 
> **(e) CleanDiffuser (NeurIPS 2024, Datasets & Benchmarks)**
> - Easy-to-use modular library for diffusion models in decision making: decoupled modules for diffusion models/solvers (DDPM, DDIM, DPM-Solver(++), EDM, RectifiedFlow), network architectures, guided sampling, dataloaders/environment wrappers; integrates 9 algorithms (Diffuser, Decision Diffuser, Diffusion Policy, DiffusionBC, DQL, EDP, IDQL, SynthER, etc.).
> - Results: on D4RL (15 tasks) and IL benchmarks (PushT, Relay-Kitchen, Robomimic; 22 tasks) it matches/exceeds official baselines; ablations show 5 sampling steps are often enough (more steps can degrade), SDE/ODE solvers differ, algorithm choice dominates model size, and diffusion policies excel in IL but are slower than ACT. Note: LoRA/SFT, feature embeddings, and vision-language model discussions appear in other context documents (e.g., RTB fine-tuning Stable Diffusion with LoRA; NEFTune/Themis for LLM SFT/LoRA), not in CleanDiffuser itself.
> 
> **Cross-paper comparison/analysis:**
> - Each paper validates a distinct claim with strong quantitative support: (a) a simpler anchor-free representation beats multi-stage/anchor-based part-body association; (b) initialization spectral properties, not sign constraints, explain EI-RNN learning failures (NSE is a pre-training predictor); (c) theory predicts and ImageNet experiments confirm JEPA's bias to low-variance but predictive features; (d) anytime-valid guarantees hold at all times while active labeling cuts label cost; (e) a modular library reproduces official baselines and surfaces design insights (sampling steps, solver choice, architecture).
> - Methodologically they differ: (a),(b),(e) are empirical/benchmark studies; (c) is theory-driven with confirmatory experiments; (d) is statistical- guarantee driven. ### paperscope:results_comparison:425 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building a vision-driven human–robot interface for a medical workflow: it must detect the technician’s hands and face while ignoring the patient (COCO-style part–body association), plan actions safely with diffusion-based policies, and gate potentially harmful outputs using a classifier whose thresholds are updated online with few labels under a strict budget. We train with standard recipes (SGD/Adam, cross-entropy, early stopping), monitor AUROC/F1/Precision, and fine-tune with low-rank adapters on CNN/Transformer backbones. We also need insights on spectral stability for EI recurrent controllers and on self-supervised joint-embedding methods (JEPA) that avoid learning noisy pixel features. Are there works that collectively address detection/association, stability of recurrent training, robust SSL representations, anytime-valid risk control with active labeling, and modular diffusion frameworks for decision making?Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：3→2（Δ-1）；rounds：5→3（Δ-2）。**

>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv7): 89.1 Hand AP, 92.62 Cond. Acc., 85.98 Joint AP.
>   - Ours (PBADet, YOLOv5l6): 88.1 Hand AP, 92.71 Cond. Acc., 85.73 Joint AP.
>   - Best prior (BPJDet, YOLOv5l6): 85.9 Hand AP, 86.91 Cond. Acc., 84.39 Joint AP.

> - COCO-HumanParts (overall APs and per-category APs; Table 2) comparing BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) vs PBADet:
>   - All categories (AP.5:.95 / subordinate): BPJDet 43.6/43.3 vs PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8 (BPJDet slightly higher on these two overall scores).
>   - APM/APL (original/subordinate): PBADet is higher (PBADet 66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4 vs BPJDet 63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9), indicating stronger performance on medium/large.

PBADet (YOLOv5l6) further reduces left-foot mMR−2 (47.9 vs 50.4) but is slightly worse on right foot (50.4 vs 49.1) and right hand compared to BPJDet (42.7 vs 42.2 for YOLOv7 vs BPJDet; PBADet YOLOv5l6 40.8 better than BPJDet 42.2). Overall, PBADet attains competitive or better association accuracy on several parts while leading on medium/large-size APs.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Table 5/6):
>   - MR−2 body: PBADet (YOLOv7) 36.5 (best), beating BPJDet (best: 39.7).
>   - AP body: PBADet (YOLOv7) 91.6 (best), above BPJDet (90.7/89.5).
>   - mMR−2 body–face association: PBADet ~50.8–50.9 vs BPJDet ~50.1–50.6 (slightly worse association miss rate).
>   - Takeaway: PBADet improves body detection (higher AP, lower MR−2) but body–face pairing miss rate is comparable or slightly worse than BPJDet.
> 
> 2) Diffusion models for decision making (CleanDiffuser benchmarks)
> Identical datasets: D4RL (locomotion: HalfCheetah/Hopper/Walker2d across medium, medium-replay, medium-expert; manipulation: Kitchen partial/mixed; navigation: AntMaze variants), and IL suites (PushT, Relay-Kitchen, Robomimic) with consistent task definitions.
> 
> - Offline RL on D4RL (Table 1):
>   - Locomotion (average over MuJoCo medium/medium-replay/medium-expert):
>     • Average scores: BC 51.9, SynthER 69.4, Diffuser 78.2, Decision Diffuser (DD) 83.2, AdaptDiffuser 82.4, DQL 89.0, EDP 82.4, IDQL 84.1.
>     • Best overall: DQL (89.0). On specific high-variance tasks: Hopper-medium-replay DQL 101.6; Walker2d-medium-replay DQL 98.2.
>   - Kitchen (Partial/Mixed; averages):
>     • Averages: BC 44.8, SynthER 0.0, Diffuser 54.1, DD 65.8, AdaptDiffuser 53.7, DQL 63.0, EDP 45.5, IDQL 66.6.
>     • Best average: IDQL (66.6), then DD (65.8), then DQL (63.0).
>   - AntMaze (Medium/Medium-Diverse/Large/Large-Diverse; average success rate):
>     • Averages: BC 0.2, SynthER 0.0, Diffuser 13.3, DD 3.0, AdaptDiffuser 8.0, DQL 81.3, EDP 50.2, IDQL 59.8.
>     • Best: DQL (81.3), followed by IDQL (59.8), then EDP (50.2). Planners (Diffuser, DD, AdaptDiffuser) are far lower on AntMaze.
>   - Takeaway across identical D4RL datasets: Diffusion policies (especially DQL, then IDQL/EDP) outperform diffusion planners (Diffuser, DD, AdaptDiffuser) on average, with DQL leading locomotion and AntMaze; IDQL leads on Kitchen.
> 
> - Offline IL (PushT, Relay-Kitchen, Robomimic; Table 2; reporting LAST/MAX):
>   - Low-dimensional inputs (average LAST/MAX across 12 tasks):
>     • DiffusionPolicy-Chi_UNet1d: 0.90/0.96 (best among all), strong and stable.
>     • ACT (Transformer): 0.79/0.89.
>     • DiffusionPolicy-Chi_TFM: 0.85/0.93; DiffusionPolicy-DiT1d: 0.79/0.86.
>     • DiffusionBC-DiT1d: 0.73/0.81; DiffusionBC-Pearce_MLP: 0.65/0.73.
>     • LSTM-GMM: 0.66/0.84.
>     • Summary: DiffusionPolicy > ACT ≳ DiffusionPolicy-DiT1d ≳ LSTM-GMM; DiffusionBC is generally behind DiffusionPolicy on low-dim inputs.
>   - Image inputs (average LAST/MAX across 10 tasks):
>     • DiffusionPolicy-Chi_UNet1d: 0.88/0.91 (top performer tied with ACT on MAX, and best LAST).
>     • ACT: 0.87/0.88 (competitive, often next-best).
>     • DiffusionPolicy-DiT1d: 0.78/0.83; DiffusionPolicy-Chi_TFM: 0.80/0.85.
>     • DiffusionBC variants trail (DiT1d 0.42/0.48, Pearce_MLP 0.51/0.57).
>     • Summary: For visuomotor imitation with images, DiffusionPolicy (Chi_UNet1d) attains the strongest average success, with ACT close behind; DiffusionBC lags.
> 
> - Architecture/sampling analyses (figures):
>   - Sampling step impact: In many tasks, ~5 steps suffice; in some (e.g., medium-expert MuJoCo and Kitchen), increasing steps can degrade performance (“sampling degradation”). This was observed for both policies and planners in the provided plots.
>   - SDE vs ODE solvers: For diffusion policies, SDE-based (e.g., DDPM, SDE-DPM-Solver++(1)) often perform well but can be more prone to degradation; planners show similar performance across SDE/ODE without a strong degradation trend.
>   - EMA rate: Higher EMA (e.g., 0.999–0.9999) stabilizes and improves training curves and mitigates late-training degradation across IDQL, DD, DiffusionBC, and DiffusionPolicy.
> 
> 3) Spectral stability of EI-constrained RNNs (Dale’s Law) 
> Identical tasks: Adding problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, and a naturalistic object recognition task.
> - Across all four benchmarks (Fig. 2 A–D), simple column-E/I (ColEI) RNNs learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs (Dale’s ANNs), which match each other closely.
> - Spectrum vs sign constraints (Fig. 4):
>   • Enforcing sign constraints alone degrades standard RNN accuracy by 0.7% ± 0.3% (and ColEI by 1% ± 1%), but this does not explain the full gap vs ColEI (2.3% ± 0.6%).
>   • Spectrum transplant experiments: giving ColEI the spectrum of a standard RNN (and vice versa) changes performance more than toggling sign constraints or swapping singular vectors. Reported deltas indicate spectrum contributes ~1.5% ± 0.3% (RNN) and ~2% ± 1% (ColEI)—larger than the sign-only effect.
> - Labeling-size/architecture sweeps (Figs. 5–7):
>   • Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) strongly anti-correlates with test error; small ColEI with few inhibitory units have low NSE and worse accuracy; larger ColEI or more balanced E/I raise NSE and performance.
>   • DANNs maintain high NSE and good performance even with very few inhibitory neurons.
> 
> 4) JEPA vs MAE for self-supervised representations
> Identical data regimes: (i) controlled synthetic settings showing feature-learning order, (ii) ImageNet-1K experiments.
> - Linear-theory and simulations (Fig. 1–2): Under settings where λ (feature covariance) and ρ (regression coefficient) trade off, MAE learns by λ-order, whereas JEPA prioritizes large ρ (high-influence) features—reversing the learning order when λ and ρ are anti-correlated. This matches ODE analyses.
> - Temporal linear model (Fig. 3): For dynamic views, derived λa = γa||va||^2 and ρa = γa||va||^2/(σ_a^2+||va||^2); experiments confirm JEPA’s bias toward higher ρ features and slower (less noisy) modes, whereas MAE follows variance.
> - ImageNet (Appendix D): Using the CCA metric, I-JEPA’s representations align more with the “bottom” PCA subspace (perception-relevant) than MAE, while MAE aligns more with the “top” variance subspace; this difference persists throughout training.
> 
> 5) Active, anytime-valid RCPS (risk-controlling prediction sets)
> Identical setups: Synthetic simulation and ImageNet classification with shared α (0.05) and label budgets.
> - Safety (Figs. 2a, 3a): All policies (“all,” “oblivious,” “pretrain,” “learned”) maintain the anytime-valid risk control: safety violation rates remain at or below α=0.05.
> - Label efficiency (Figs. 2b–c, 3b–c): “Pretrain” (using model-based risk predictors) and “learned” (online-estimated predictors/policies) consistently reach lower final calibration β (closer to the optimal β*) than “all”/“oblivious,” and achieve a given β with fewer labels.
> - Datasets: On both the synthetic regression of β* (β*≈0.5578 in the simulation) and ImageNet (β*≈0.8349), “pretrain”/“learned” dominate in label efficiency while preserving anytime-valid guarantees.
> 
> Performance synthesis on similar dataset types
> - Detection/association (crowded pedestrian/face–body; multi-part human datasets): PBADet yields state-of-the-art or competitive detection AP and MR−2 on BodyHands and CrowdHuman, and stronger medium/large AP on COCO-HumanParts while per-part trade-offs exist (better for person/feet; BPJDet better on head/face/hands APs). PBADet’s association miss rates (mMR−2) are lower on several parts (head/face/left-hand; left-foot with YOLOv5l6), but not uniformly (e.g., right foot).
> - RL locomotion and AntMaze (D4RL): Diffusion policies (especially DQL) dominate locomotion and sparse-reward navigation; IDQL is best on Kitchen. Diffusion planners underperform on AntMaze (and are sensitive to guidance/out-of-distribution trajectory issues), though they are competitive on some locomotion tasks.
> - IL (low-dim & image): DiffusionPolicy with Chi_UNet1d consistently achieves the highest average success; ACT is close on image tasks. DiffusionBC variants lag behind DiffusionPolicy across both observation types.
> - RNN stability tasks: DANNs and standard RNNs outperform simple ColEI on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and naturalistic recognition; spectrum properties (NSE) predict performance better than the mere presence of Dale sign constraints.
> - SSL representation learning: JEPA focuses on predictive/low-variance features (higher ρ), while MAE prioritizes highly covarying/high-variance features; on ImageNet, JEPA’s learned features align more with perception-relevant directions (bottom PCA) than MAE.
> - Risk control with active labeling: Model-informed (“pretrain”) and adaptive (“learned”) policies reach safe operating points with fewer labels than uninformed baselines, while keeping safety below α.
> 
> Notable per-dataset highlights
> - BodyHands: PBADet (YOLOv7) tops Hand AP (89.1), Conditional Accuracy (92.62), and Joint AP (85.98); PBADet also beats BPJDet with the same YOLOv5l6 backbone.
> - COCO-HumanParts: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) improves APM/APL markedly (66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4 vs BPJDet 63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9), with mixed per-part APs and mMR−2 trade-offs.
> - CrowdHuman: PBADet (YOLOv7) attains the best MR−2 for the body (36.5) and best body AP (91.6); body-face mMR−2 is comparable to BPJDet.
> - D4RL locomotion: DQL leads with best averages; on particular tasks Hopper-medium-replay (101.6) and Walker2d-medium-replay (98.2) are among DQL’s strongest.
> - D4RL AntMaze: DQL (81.3) > IDQL (59.8) > EDP (50.2) >> planners.
> - Kitchen: IDQL average (66.6) slightly exceeds DD (65.8) and DQL (63.0).
> - IL (PushT/Robomimic/Relay-Kitchen): DiffusionPolicy–Chi_UNet1d has the top average performance on both low-dim (0.90/0.96) and image (0.88/0.91) tasks.
> - RNN spectrum experiments: Swapping spectra affects accuracy more than sign constraints (quantified deltas ~1.5–2%), and higher NSE correlates with lower error across sizes/EI ratios.
> - Active RCPS: On simulation (β*≈0.5578) and ImageNet (β*≈0.8349), “pretrain”/“learned” labeling policies converge to smaller safe β faster (i.e., higher utility sets) than “all”/“oblivious,” with safety consistently ≤α.
> 
> Overall conclusions from the reported experiments
> - For detection/association with part–whole structure (BodyHands, COCO-HumanParts, CrowdHuman), PBADet yields strong detection and scalable association (notably better medium/large APs on COCO), with per-part association wins and a few losses.
> - For decision making, diffusion policies currently dominate planners on standard offline RL benchmarks; among policies, DQL is strongest overall (especially locomotion and AntMaze), while IDQL excels on Kitchen.
> - For imitation learning, DiffusionPolicy (especially Chi_UNet1d) is the most reliable high performer across low-dim and image tasks; ACT is competitive on image-based control.
> - For recurrent networks under Dale’s Law, initial spectral properties (NSE and singular value distribution) better explain performance gaps than sign constraints; DANNs/standard RNNs > ColEI across tasks.
> - For SSL, JEPA’s inductive bias favors predictive, lower-variance (high-influence) features, which is borne out by training-order experiments and ImageNet CCA analyses; MAE prioritizes reconstruction of high-variance content.
> - For anytime-valid risk control under labeling budgets, active RCPS with model-informed/learned policies are more label-efficient than uninformed baselines while preserving statistical safety.

**naive 最终答案**

> Yes—works in the collection collectively cover all five areas. Here is a comparative analysis of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Detection/Association — PBADet (ICLR 2024)
> One-stage anchor-free part-body association detector using a single part-to-body center offset (hand/face/feet→person), trained with SGD, IoU/DFL/cls/assoc losses, YOLOv7/YOLOv5l6 backbones. Results:
> - **BodyHands**: beats BPJDet/HierR-CNN/OpenPose on hand AP, conditional accuracy, and joint AP. YOLOv7 (36.9M params) outperforms larger BPJDet-YOLOv5m6; with the same YOLOv5l6 backbone it still improves (hand AP 88.1, cond. acc 92.71, joint AP 85.73).
> - **COCOHumanParts**: APs on par with BPJDet, leading person/feet AP and low mMR−2; best AP_L. YOLOv7 gives AP.5:.95 ≈ 42.7/41.5 (orig/subordinate).
> - **CrowdHuman face-body**: best body MR−2 (36.5) with competitive AP.
> - **vs ED-Pose (pose estimation)**: far higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet (e.g., left hand F1 22.87→46.50). Advantage over BPJDet shrinks for single-part face-body, but part-to-body association is simpler and always valid.
> 
> ## 2. Stability of EI Recurrent Training — "Learning Better with Dale's Law" (NeurIPS 2023)
> Not a controller paper, but directly explains EI RNN instability. Experiments on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, naturalistic object recognition:
> - ColEI networks learn worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs/DANNs across all four tasks; gradient clipping helps ColEI far more.
> - Spectral transplants (SVD swap) show the singular-value **spectrum matters more than sign constraints**: ColEI has multimodal, dispersed singular values (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure) vs. unimodal Marchenko–Pastur quarter-circle for RNNs/DANNs; max singular value is large and unconstrained despite spectral-radius 1.5.
> - Smaller networks / fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and learning; DANNs stay robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> - **NSE (normalized SVD entropy) at initialization anti-correlates with final test error** across sizes/EI ratios → usable pre-training diagnostic.
> 
> ## 3. Robust SSL / JEPA — "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)
> Deep-linear-analysis of self-distillation JEPA vs MAE. Derived critical times show:
> - MAE learns features greedily by covariance λ only; JEPA additionally orders by regression coefficient ρ (high-influence features first), an effect that **strengthens with encoder depth** (t\*jepa ~ λ⁻¹ρ⁻⁽²ᴸ⁻¹⁾).
> - Fixed points differ: JEPA converges to w̄=ρL, MAE to ρL/(L+1); JEPA's noise suppression increases with depth, producing low-rank encoders dominated by the highest-ρ feature.
> - Numeric ODE simulations and SGD on random-init deep linear nets confirm greedy ρ-ordering and depth-dependent temporal spread (absent in MAE); ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance perceptual subspace faster than MAE (CCA). So JEPA is the right SSL choice to avoid noisy pixel features.
> - Related: LDReg (ICLR 2024) shows SSL representations can be globally high-dim but locally collapsed; Fisher-Rao-based local dimensionality regularization improves linear eval/transfer/detection for SimCLR, BYOL, MAE on ImageNet, complementing JEPA.
> 
> ## 4. Anytime-Valid Risk Control + Active Labeling — "Active, Anytime-Valid Risk Controlling Prediction Sets"
> Betting/e-process framework extending RCPS: guarantees P(ρ(β̂t)≤θ for all t) ≥ 1−α even with adaptive data and a label-budget policy (inverse-propensity-weighted e-process). Optimal labeling policy ≈ proportional to conditional-risk std; optimal predictor = conditional risk (model as control variate). Regret bounds link policy/predictor error to wealth-growth rate. Experiments (simulations + ImageNet, θ=0.1, α=0.05): learned/pretrained policies reach higher utility with fewer labels than naive baselines while keeping violation rates < α. This directly fits gating a harmful-output classifier with online threshold updates under a strict budget.
> 
> ## 5. Modular Diffusion for Decision Making — CleanDiffuser (NeurIPS 2024)
> Modular library decoupling diffusion models/solvers (DDPM, DDIM, DPM-Solver(++), EDM, RectifiedFlow), 8 network architectures, guided sampling, dataloaders; covers planner/policy/data-synthesizer roles. Benchmark (30k+ GPU-hours; 7 offline RL algorithms on 15 D4RL tasks + diffusion policies/BC on 22 IL tasks):
> - Reproductions match/exceed official baselines; **DQL is the strongest offline diffusion policy** (e.g., Antmaze averages ~81 vs 0–13 for planners).
> - IL: DiffusionPolicy with Chi_UNet1d (avg 0.90/0.96) and DiT1d excel, beating ACT/LSTM-GMM; but slower inference (denoising steps).
> - Ablations: 5 sampling steps usually suffice; more steps can **degrade** performance (medium-expert MuJoCo/Kitchen); SDE solvers better for policies but more sampling degradation; high-order ODE solvers no better than first-order; higher EMA rate stabilizes training.
> 
> ## Synthesis
> The collection can cover the full pipeline: PBADet for technician hands/face association (ignoring patient), JEPA/LDReg for robust pretrained representations on CNN/Transformer backbones (fine-tunable with low-rank adapters), CleanDiffuser for diffusion-based planning/policy with practical recipes (SGD/Adam, EMA, sampling-step/solver choices), the betting-based RCPS method for budget-limited online threshold updates and AUROC/F1/precision monitoring, and the spectral/NSE analysis as a diagnostic for EI recurrent controllers. Caveats: no single work integrates them; the EI-spectral work studies RNNs not EI controllers per se; the risk-control method assumes i.i.d. data and bounded label policies; PBADet uses SGD/standard detection training rather than the diffusion/SSL stack.

**community 最终答案**

> Yes—each sub-problem has a dedicated work, though no single paper spans all of them. Here are the methods and their experimental results, compared by component.
> 
> **1. Detection/part–body association — PBADet (ICLR 2024, one-stage anchor-free)**
> - BodyHands: PBADet-YOLOv7 (36.9M, 1024px) reaches hand AP **89.1**, conditional accuracy **92.62**, joint AP **85.98**; the same-backbone PBADet-YOLOv5l6 beats BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (86.1M) on all three (88.1/92.71/85.73 vs 85.9/86.91/84.39) with a smaller/same model. Big margins over Mask-RCNN, BodyHands, HierR-CNN.
> - COCOHumanParts (6 parts): PBADet is on par with BPJDet on AP.5:.95 (43.0/41.8 vs 43.6/43.3), but leads in AP_M/AP_L and feet, and has the **lowest mMR-2** (association) for head, face, left/right hands, right foot.
> - CrowdHuman face–body: best body MR-2 (36.5) and AP, but its advantage over BPJDet shrinks for this single-part task (mMR-2 50.8 vs 50.1).
> - vs pose estimator ED-Pose: PBADet wins association robustness decisively (all-parts Precision 39.41 vs 24.09, Recall 63.09 vs 45.51, F1 48.52 vs 31.51).
> 
> **2. Anytime-valid risk control with active labeling — Xu et al. (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Extends RCPS to streaming/adaptive data, guaranteeing P(ρ(β̂t) ≤ θ for all t) ≥ 1−α via betting e-processes, plus IPW active sampling under a fixed label budget (optimal policy ∝ conditional-risk std; optimal predictor = conditional risk).
> - Simulations and ImageNet (θ=0.1, α=0.05): learned/pretrained policies reduce risk faster than naive labeling while keeping violation rates below α — fewer labels, higher utility, with regret bounds.
> 
> **3. Modular diffusion decision-making — CleanDiffuser (NeurIPS 2024 D&B)**
> - 9 algorithms (Diffuser, Decision Diffuser, AdaptDiffuser, DiffusionPolicy, DiffusionBC, DQL, EDP, IDQL, SynthER) over 37 RL/IL tasks, matching/exceeding official baselines.
> - D4RL offline RL averages: **DQL 89.0 > IDQL 84.1 > Decision-Diffuser 83.2 ≈ AdaptDiffuser/EDP 82.4 > Diffuser 78.2 > SynthER 69.4 > BC 51.9**; policies dominate locomotion while planners excel on longer-horizon Kitchen/Antmaze (e.g., Antmaze averages: DQL 81.3 vs Diffuser 13.3).
> - IL: DiffusionPolicy performs best but is much slower than ACT (Chi_UNet1d 68.9M/0.405s vs ACT 7.8M/0.006s); 5 sampling steps often suffice (more can degrade), and algorithm choice matters more than model size.
> 
> **4. Robust SSL / JEPA — "Why JEPA Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024)**
> - Deep-linear analysis derives that JEPA prioritizes **high-influence (high-ρ) features**, while MAE order is driven by eigenvalue λ; the difference only appears in deep encoders, and depth strengthens JEPA's noise suppression (lower-weight convergence to noisy features).
> - On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA), empirically confirming that JEPA avoids noisy pixel features that MAE reconstruction tends to learn.
> 
> **5. Spectral stability of EI recurrent training — "Learning better with Dale's Law" (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - ColEI RNNs train worse and with more variance across all 4 tasks (adding, seq-MNIST, PTB, object recognition); gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially more.
> - SVD "transplant" experiments show the **initial singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints**: ColEI's rank-one column-mean structure yields multimodal, dispersed singular values, whereas standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs match random-matrix unimodal forms and learn equally well.
> - Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final error; small networks/balanced E:I are better, and DANN is robust even with 1 inhibitory neuron.
> 
> **Cross-method analysis:** The evidence is consistent with your planned pipeline: PBADet provides the hand/face detection + person-association (with explicit numbers showing association is its strength over pose-based methods); the betting/e-process framework gives the classifier the anytime-valid threshold with label-budget guarantees; CleanDiffuser provides the modular diffusion planner/policy backbones (with the caveat that diffusion policies are accurate but slow, motivating few-step/warm-start sampling); the JEPA analysis justifies SSL over pixel reconstruction for your perception encoder; and the Dale's-Law study warns that EI recurrent controllers should be initialized with unimodal/clustered spectra (high NSE) rather than naive column-constrained E/I partitioning. No single work bridges all five; they would need to be combined.

### paperscope:results_comparison:428 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively address efficient and reliable deep-network training and inference across vision, sequence modeling, and scientific computing, with the following elements: (a) use of MSE/CE objectives under Adam/AdamW/SGD optimizers; (b) analyses of joint‑embedding self‑supervised learning (JEPA) and its implicit bias (e.g., cosine‑style prediction in latent space); (c) an anchor‑free, one‑stage method for part–body association with results on COCO; (d) recurrent models obeying excitation/inhibition constraints (Dale’s law) studied via spectral properties on tasks like (sequential) MNIST; (e) memory‑saving optimizers using sub‑byte (≈4‑bit) states for fine‑tuning/LoRA on Transformers; and (f) interpretable tensor‑decomposition neural solvers for PDEs using finite‑element‑like interpolation. Prefer works reporting metrics such as AP/F1/AUROC on datasets like COCO, MNIST, CIFAR‑100, or SVHN.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.
