**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Summary of experimental results and comparisons across the five works (by domain and dataset), strictly based on the reported figures/tables.
> 
> Overall note on shared datasets: The five works evaluate on different problem domains and datasets. There are no identical datasets used across the five papers. All comparisons below are therefore within-domain (i.e., among methods evaluated on the same dataset inside each paper).
> 
> 1) Part–body association for detection (PBADet)
> Datasets: BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman.
> - BodyHands (Table 1):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98.
>   - PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 88.1, 92.71, 85.73.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 85.9, 86.91, 84.39.
>   - Conclusion: On the identical BodyHands test set, PBADet (both YOLOv7 and YOLOv5l6 heads) outperforms BPJDet in all three metrics (higher is better).
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2, all-categories APs and per-category APs):
>   - Overall AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8; PBADet (YOLOv7) 42.7/41.5; BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 43.6/43.3.
>   - Scale-specific: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) has higher APM/APL (66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4) versus BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) (63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9).
>   - Per-category (selected): for “person” and “feet”, PBADet (YOLOv5l6) shows higher AP than BPJDet (e.g., person 62.4 vs 61.3; l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9; r-foot 30.9 vs 30.2), while head/face/hands are mixed/close.
>   - Conclusion: On the identical COCOHumanParts benchmark, BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) has slightly higher overall AP.5:.95, but PBADet (YOLOv5l6) is stronger on medium/large scales (APM/APL) and feet/person categories; per-category results are mixed for head/face/hands.
> - COCOHumanParts association robustness (Table 3, mMR−2; lower is better):
>   - PBADet (YOLOv7): head 29.2, face 31.3, l-hand 41.1, r-hand 42.7, r-foot 52.6, l-foot 52.5.
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, l-hand 41.6, r-hand 42.2, r-foot 49.1, l-foot 50.4.
>   - Conclusion: PBADet (YOLOv7) has lower mMR−2 for head and face; BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) is lower for both feet and (slightly) for right hand; left hand is very close.
> - CrowdHuman face–body association (Tables 5 and 6):
>   - Detection (lower MR−2, higher AP): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves the best body MR−2 (36.5 vs 40.7 for BPJDet YOLOv5l6) and highest body AP (91.6 vs 89.5 for BPJDet YOLOv5l6); face MR−2 is comparable (44.7–46 range across methods).
>   - Association (mMR−2; lower is better): PBADet (YOLOv7) 50.8 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 50.1 (slightly better for BPJDet).
>   - Conclusion: On the identical CrowdHuman setting, PBADet improves body/face detection (MR−2, AP) while BPJDet retains a slightly lower mismatching rate (mMR−2).
> 
> 2) Recurrent networks with Dale’s Law constraints (ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNN)
> Tasks: Adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, naturalistic object recognition (Fig. 2).
> - Across all four tasks shown, ColEI (column sign-constrained EI) converges worse and with higher variance than DANN and standard RNN. DANN matches standard RNN performance closely; both clearly outperform ColEI.
> - Additional findings tied to performance (Figs. 3–6):
>   - Varying the spectral radius ρ: ColEI favors larger ρ than standard/DANN; even at its favorable ρ, ColEI does not reach the best RNN/DANN performance envelope.
>   - Spectrum transplant experiments (Fig. 4): Changing singular value spectra has a larger impact on performance than sign constraints alone; giving ColEI the RNN spectrum (or vice versa) shifts the performance more than toggling sign constraints.
>   - EI ratio and network size (Figs. 5–7): ColEI performance degrades when inhibitory fraction is small and improves with network width; DANN remains robust across EI ratios and sizes. Normalized SVD entropy correlates with ColEI test error.
> - Conclusion: On the identical tasks within the paper, DANN and standard RNN consistently outperform ColEI; spectral properties at initialization correlate strongly with the observed performance gaps.
> 
> 3) JEPA vs MAE (deep linear analysis and controlled experiments)
> Settings: Synthetic linear settings, ODE simulations, and a vision check on ImageNet feature subspaces (Fig. 7 in Appendix D).
> - Controlled synthetic/linear experiments (Figs. 1–2):
>   - When feature covariance (λ) and regression coefficient (ρ) both increase (Distribution 1), both objectives show greedy learning by λ.
>   - When λ increases but ρ decreases (Distribution 2), JEPA reverses the learning order (greedy in ρ), while MAE remains greedy in λ. This leads to JEPA prioritizing high-ρ (high-influence) features; MAE prioritizes high-covariance features.
> - ImageNet representation check (Appendix D, Fig. 7):
>   - Mean CCA between full-vs-bottom PCA subspace: JEPA shows higher similarity across training, indicating faster focus on the low-variance (perceptual) subspace; for full-vs-top, JEPA is lower than MAE.
> - Conclusion: On the same synthetic/controlled settings, JEPA and MAE learn different features in different orders; JEPA prioritizes high-ρ (predictive/less-noisy) features, whereas MAE prioritizes features with high covariance; the ImageNet CCA trend aligns with JEPA emphasizing low-variance perceptual directions.
> 
> 4) Memory-efficient optimizers with 4-bit states (4-bit AdamW; 4-bit Factor)
> Datasets: GLUE (RoBERTa-L), SQuAD v1/v2 (RoBERTa-L), ImageNet-1k (Swin-T), E2E-NLG (GPT-2 Medium), WMT14 En–De (Transformer-Base), instruction tuning (LLaMA-7B/13B/33B on Alpaca; eval on MMLU, HellaSwag, ARC-e/c, OBQA).
> - Natural language understanding (Table 2 and Table 7; GLUE mean score):
>   - 32-bit AdamW: 88.9; 4-bit AdamW: 89.1; 4-bit Factor: 88.9; 8-bit AdamW†: 89.1. (†Embedding states unquantized per baseline.)
>   - Per-task GLUE (Table 7): Across MNLI, QNLI, QQP, RTE, SST-2, MRPC, CoLA, STS-B, 4-bit optimizers match 32-bit within small fluctuations.
> - Question answering (Table 9; SQuAD):
>   - SQuAD v1.1 F1: 32-bit 94.6 vs 4-bit AdamW 94.5; EM similar (89.0 vs 88.8). SQuAD 2.0 F1: 88.8 vs 88.4; EM: 85.8 vs 85.4. Near parity.
> - Image classification (Table 2; Swin-T on ImageNet-1k):
>   - Top-1 Acc: 32-bit 81.2 vs 4-bit AdamW 80.8 vs 4-bit Factor 80.9 vs 8-bit 81.0. Small drop (<0.4 pt) for 4-bit.
> - Natural language generation (Tables 2 and 8; GPT-2 Medium on E2E-NLG):
>   - BLEU: 32-bit 67.7 vs 4-bit AdamW 67.8 vs 4-bit Factor 67.6 vs 8-bit 67.5. Parity or slight gain.
> - Machine translation (Table 2; WMT14 En–De SacreBleu):
>   - 32-bit 26.61 vs 4-bit AdamW 26.28 vs 4-bit Factor 26.45 vs 8-bit 26.66. Small differences (≤0.33 BLEU).
> - Instruction tuning (Table 3; LLaMA on Alpaca; 5-shot MMLU and commonsense benchmarks):
>   - 7B: MMLU 38.7 (32-bit) vs 38.9 (4-bit); HellaSwag 74.6 vs 74.7; ARC-e 61.5 vs 61.2; ARC-c 45.1 vs 44.4; OBQA 43.4 vs 43.0.
>   - 13B: MMLU 46.5 vs 47.4; trends similar; 33B: MMLU 56.4 vs 54.9 (mixed); overall parity across sizes.
> - Memory and time (Table 4):
>   - LLaMA-7B (2×A100-80GB, FSDP): Total memory 75.40 GB (32-bit) vs 31.87 GB (4-bit) → 57.7% reduction; slight speedup (3.35 h → 3.07 h); fused 4-bit similar memory/speed.
>   - RoBERTa-L (RTE): 5.31 GB (32-bit) vs 3.00 GB (4-bit fused) → 43.5% reduction; time 3.93 min (32-bit) vs 3.17 min (4-bit fused).
>   - GPT-2 Medium (E2E): 6.89 GB (32-bit) vs 4.62 GB (4-bit) → 34.4% reduction; fused 4-bit time 2.11 h vs 2.13 h (near parity).
> - Largest trainable model under memory constraints (Table 5):
>   - 24 GB: OPT-350M (32-bit) vs OPT-1.3B (4-bit); 80 GB: OPT-1.3B (32-bit) vs OPT-6.7B (4-bit). LLaMA-7B fits with 4-bit on a single 80 GB GPU.
> - Conclusion: On identical datasets, 4-bit AdamW (and 4-bit Factor) match or closely track 32-bit and 8-bit baselines in accuracy while reducing optimizer-state memory by ~34–58% end-to-end (total memory) and enabling larger models; training time is similar or slightly faster with fused kernels and reduced communication.
> 
> 5) Interpolating Neural Network–Tensor Decomposition (INN-TD)
> Datasets/problems: parametric heat PDE (training), high-dimensional Poisson’s equation (solving), space–parameter–time PDE (solving), inverse optimization, Helmholtz, elasticity, and operator learning (appendix).
> - Data-driven training on parametric PDE (Table 1; task: (x,y,k,P,t)→u): RMSE ×10^−3 (mean±std).
>   - 10% training: INN-TD 0.213±0.009 train / 0.748±0.911 test; MLP 4.180±0.873 / 3.660±0.498; SIREN 2.330±0.188 / 4.550±0.297; KAN 4.600±0.243 / 4.840±0.323.
>   - 30% training: INN-TD 0.154±0.003 / 0.154±0.006; MLP 0.699±0.143 / 0.912±0.155; SIREN 1.240±0.161 / 2.020±0.197; KAN 4.710±1.120 / 4.490±0.996.
>   - 100% training: INN-TD 0.126±0.002 / 0.129±0.005; MLP 0.385±0.037 / 0.534±0.041; SIREN 1.170±0.121 / 1.660±0.200; KAN 4.590±0.231 / 4.260±0.087.
>   - Conclusion: On the identical dataset, INN-TD achieves the lowest RMSE (train and test) across all data regimes.
> - Data-free solving: high-dimensional Poisson (Tables 2–3).
>   - Case 1 (domain [0,1]^D):
>     - 2D: INN-TD error 1.754×10^−8 in 0.81 s vs CP-PINN 4.63×10^−3 (60.68 s) with 32×32 collocation; KAN 9.44×10^−5 (56.16 s).
>     - 5D: INN-TD 1.659×10^−8 (6.88 s); CP-PINN (32^5 points) 5.90×10^−3 (~2,130 s); KAN 1.68×10^−4 (~842 s).
>     - 10D: INN-TD 1.238×10^−8 (57.43 s) (no comparable CP-PINN/KAN line reported at 10D in the table).
>   - Case 2 (domain [0,12]^D; harder high-frequency):
>     - 2D: INN-TD ~4.77×10^−4 (0.22 s); CP-PINN 0.025→0.032 (87.6–292 s across 32^2→2048^2 collocation); KAN 0.78→0.28 (60.68–119.7 s as collocation increases; params scaled).
>   - Conclusion: On identical Poisson setups, INN-TD achieves orders-of-magnitude lower error with far less wall time, and scales to higher D without exploding collocation costs.
> - Space–parameter–time (S–P–T) PDE solving (Sec. 4.2.2):
>   - A 6D problem (x,y,z,k,P,t) solved by INN-TD in 155 s (single A6000). Compared to FEM “ground truth,” the relative L2 error is 3.38×10^−3 over 10 random (k,P) realizations.
> - Inverse optimization (Table 4):
>   - Average relative L2 error between predicted and target field 2.18×10^−3; parameter identification errors: ϵ_k=2.76×10^−3, ϵ_P=2.62×10^−3 (mean), showing accurate recovery of unknown (k,P).
> - Additional PDEs (appendix highlights): Helmholtz case solved without reported failure modes; elasticity (vector-valued) shows convergence in energy norm; operator learning example matches finite difference well across random conductivity fields.
> 
> Cross-domain observations (comparing similar dataset types, not identical datasets):
> - Vision tasks: PBADet advances part–body association accuracy/efficiency on COCO-derived datasets; 4-bit optimizers retain classification/detection accuracy on ImageNet/GLUE/SQuAD while reducing memory. These results are complementary (detection vs optimization/memory), not directly comparable.
> - Sequence/text tasks: Dale’s Law RNN experiments (adding, seq-MNIST, PTB) show DANN≈standard RNN » ColEI; the 4-bit optimizer shows near-parity vs 32-bit on GLUE/SQuAD/MT and LLaMA instruction tuning.
> - Scientific computing/PDEs: INN-TD surpasses CP-PINN and KAN in accuracy and speed on the same Poisson setups, scales to high-D S–P–T, and supports inverse optimization; JEPA vs MAE (linear analysis) shows JEPA’s bias toward predictive/low-noise features rather than reporting end-task error on standard PDE benchmarks.
> 
> Key takeaways across the five works (based solely on their reported experiments):
> - On identical datasets within each domain, the proposed methods generally outperform the respective baselines: PBADet vs BPJDet/Hier R-CNN on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman; DANN vs ColEI on seq-MNIST/PTB; 4-bit AdamW vs 32-bit/8-bit AdamW on GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/MT/LLMs; INN-TD vs CP-PINN/KAN on Poisson and S–P–T PDEs.
> - Where trade-offs appear (e.g., PBADet vs BPJDet mMR−2 on CrowdHuman; AP.5:.95 on COCOHumanParts), the proposed method improves many metrics (scale-specific APs, detection MR/AP) while conceding a small margin on a single association rate in one benchmark.
> - JEPA vs MAE (linear setting) provides mechanistic evidence: JEPA prioritizes high-regression-coefficient (influential) features; MAE prioritizes high-covariance directions—validated by ODE simulations and CCA trends on ImageNet feature subspaces.

> I have enough to answer. Let me compile the comparison across the papers matching elements (a)–(f).
> 
> ## Matching papers
> 
> | Element | Paper | Key method |
> |---|---|---|
> | (a) MSE/CE under Adam/AdamW/SGD | **Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure** (ICML 2025) | Power-law Hessian analysis across SGD/Adam/AMSGrad/Yogi/RAdam etc. on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 |
> | (b) JEPA implicit bias | **Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features** (NeurIPS 2024) | Deep linear analysis of JEPA vs MAE MSE-style latent objectives |
> | (c) Anchor-free part–body association | **PBADet** (ICLR 2024) | One-stage anchor-free detector, single part-to-body center offset |
> | (d) Dale's law RNNs | **Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective** (NeurIPS 2023) | ColEI vs DANN vs standard RNN, spectral analysis, sequential MNIST |
> | (e) 4-bit optimizer states | **Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States** (NeurIPS 2023) | 4-bit AdamW/4-bit Factor for fine-tuning/LoRA-style LLaMA |
> | (f) Tensor-decomposition PDE solver | **INN-TD** (ICML 2025) | C-HiDeNN finite-element interpolation + tensor decomposition, MSE loss |
> 
> Note on (a): no single paper in this collection explicitly compares MSE vs CE objectives head-to-head. The closest match is the Hessian paper (trains LeNet/ResNet18/ViT on MNIST, CIFAR-10/100 with CE under SGD/Adam), plus (b) and (f) use MSE-type objectives, PBADet uses CE + IoU losses under SGD, and (e) uses AdamW. I flag this gap rather than invent a match.
> 
> ## Experimental comparison
> 
> **(b) JEPA implicit bias** — Theory-first: exact gradient-flow ODEs on deep linear networks show JEPA prioritizes "influential" features (high regression coefficient ρ) whereas MAE prioritizes high-variance features (λ); the bias is depth-dependent (only deep encoders). Empirical: ImageNet-1K I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE (CCA). No AP/F1 numbers; it's an analysis paper.
> 
> **(c) PBADet (COCO/CrowdHuman/BodyHands)** — the strongest detection metrics:
> - BodyHands (YOLOv7, 36.9M params, 1024 input): HandAP **89.1**, Cond. Acc **92.62**, JointAP **85.98** — beats BPJDet(YOLOv5l6, 86.1M): 85.9/86.91/84.39, and BodyHands*: 84.8/84.12/63.87.
> - COCOHumanParts (all categories, original/subordinate AP): Ours(YOLOv7) 42.7/41.5 AP.5:.95, 69.5/67.9 AP.5; leads AP_M (65.8) and AP_L (66.7), and lowest average mMR⁻² for most parts; BPJDet(YOLOv5l6): 43.6/43.3, 70.6/69.8 (slightly better overall AP, worse association on large/medium).
> - CrowdHuman face-body: Ours(YOLOv7) body MR⁻² **36.5**, AP 91.6 vs BPJDet 40.7/89.5 — best miss rate, competitive AP.
> - Ablations: association loss, multi-scale offset, and task alignment each improve metrics; anchor-free > anchor-based, part-to-body > body-to-part.
> 
> **(d) Dale's law RNNs (sequential MNIST)** — ColEI (sign-constrained) learns worse and with more variance across all tasks (adding, sMNIST, PTB, object recognition). Sign constraints hurt but explain only part (RNN +0.7±0.3%, ColEI +1±1%); the initial singular-value spectrum matters more (spectrum transplant: 1.5±0.3% vs 2±1%). NSE anti-correlates with test error; smaller networks/fewer inhibitory units → worse spectra and performance; DANN RNNs stay robust (NSE ≈ 0.95) even with 1 inhibitory neuron and match standard RNNs. Gradient clipping helps ColEI most.
> 
> **(e) 4-bit optimizers (LoRA/LLaMA)** — essentially lossless: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 (32-bit 88.9), Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 (81.2), GPT-2M E2E BLEU 67.8 (67.7), QA F1 94.5 (94.6), WMT14 26.28 (26.61). LLaMA-7B/13B/33B fine-tune (Alpaca) matches 32-bit AdamW on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA. Memory: LLaMA-7B 75.4GB → 31.9GB (**57.7% saved**), 4-bit Factor 46.7% on RoBERTa-L; trains LLaMA-7B on one 80GB GPU; convergence curves align. Beats 8-bit (37.1%) and sublinear Adafactor/SM3 (which degrade, especially CLS).
> 
> **(f) INN-TD (PDEs)** — data-free solver: relative L2 errors ~1e-8–1e-6 on high-dimensional Poisson vs ~1e-4–1e-2 for CP-PINN/KAN; solves Helmholtz where PINN fails; handles 6D space-parameter-time, 3D elasticity, inverse optimization. Uses MSE for data-driven training; interpretable nodal TD parameters; convergence with refinement. Metrics are physics L2 errors, not AP/F1.
> 
> **(a) Hessian power-law paper** — LeNet power-law spectra hold across SGD/Adam/AMSGrad/AdaBound/Yogi/RAdam/Adai/PNM/Lookahead/DiffGrad (KS test, MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100); slope magnitude s correlates with sharpness and test error (LeNet CIFAR-10 Pearson 0.72; d_ks predicts LLM generalization up to 0.98). Power-law breaks with small width/depth, small data, noisy labels, large batch (ResNet18 B≥1280). LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure that full fine-tuning does.
> 
> ## Cross-paper observations
> - **Efficiency vs accuracy**: (e) shows memory can be cut ~58% at parity; (f) shows accuracy can be *improved* (orders of magnitude) by encoding numerical structure; (a) provides a spectral diagnostic for when training is "reliable" (power-law present = well-trained).
> - **Spectral analysis unifies (a), (d)**: both attribute learning quality to the spectrum (Hessian vs recurrent-weight SVD); (d) shows structure at initialization predicts final performance, (a) shows structure after training predicts generalization.
> - **Metric types differ**: (c) reports AP/mMR⁻² (detection), (e) accuracy/BLEU/F1 (NLU/NLG/QA), (d) test error on sMNIST, (f) relative L2 (scientific). A quantitative AP/F1 comparison across all is not possible — they target different tasks.
> - **Gap**: no paper here compares MSE vs CE objectives on the same benchmarks, so element (a) is only partially covered (CE under SGD/Adam in the Hessian paper; MSE used by (b)/(f); AdamW by (e); SGD by (c)).

**community 最终答案**

> ## Papers matching each element
> 
> **(a) MSE/CE under Adam/AdamW/SGD** — **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (Tang et al., ICML 2025). Trains LeNet on MNIST/Fashion-MNIST/CIFAR-10/100 with SGD, Adam, AMSGrad, AdaBound, Yogi, RAdam, etc., and GPT-2/TinyLlama with AdamW. The related shallow-ReLU work (d4aba6…) uses square (MSE) loss under gradient flow. Together they cover MSE/CE under SGD/Adam-family.
> 
> **(b) JEPA implicit bias** — **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (Littwin et al., NeurIPS 2024). Exact ODE analysis of deep linear JEPA self-distillation (cosine-style latent-space prediction).
> 
> **(c) Anchor-free one-stage part–body association** — **"PBADet"** (Gao et al., ICLR 2024), evaluated on COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman.
> 
> **(d) Dale's-law RNNs via spectral analysis** — **"Learning Better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (Li et al., NeurIPS 2023), tested on sequential MNIST, adding, PTB, object recognition.
> 
> **(e) ~4-bit optimizer states for fine-tuning** — **"4-bit Optimizers: Training Large Models with 4-bit Optimizer States"** (NeurIPS 2023), fine-tuning RoBERTa/GPT-2/LLaMA (incl. LoRA-family parameter-efficient setup).
> 
> **(f) Interpretable tensor-decomposition PDE solvers with FEM-like interpolation** — **"INN-TD"**, using C-HiDeNN locally supported FEM-basis interpolation with partition of unity.
> 
> ## Experimental results comparison
> 
> - **(a)** The power-law Hessian spectrum holds for all optimizers (KS test: d_ks≈0.016–0.036 < critical 0.043) but not random/untrained nets. The slope magnitude ŝ predicts test error (Pearson 0.853 on MNIST, 0.72 on CIFAR-10) and sharpness/trace (0.85–0.97). For LLMs, d_ks predicts generalization up to 0.98; notably, **LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure** that full fine-tuning does. Power law is lost at large batch (B≥768) and underparameterization.
> - **(d)** ColEI RNNs train worse and with higher variance than standard and DANN RNNs on sequential MNIST/PTB/object recognition. Spectrum transplant shows singular-value spectrum matters more than sign constraints: sign constraints explain ~1% error, vs total ColEI deficit 2.3%±0.6%. Normalised SVD entropy at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; small high-NSE networks beat large low-NSE ones. ColEI spectra are multimodal/dispersed; DANN/standard RNNs match random-matrix quarter-circle/Marchenko–Pastur.
> - **(c)** PBADet on COCOHumanParts: AP₅₀:₉₅ 43.0/41.8 (YOLOv5l6) vs BPJDet 43.6/43.3, but PBADet leads on large-object AP (67.2/64.4 vs 61.8/58.9) and on BodyHands (Hand AP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, joint AP 85.98 vs BPJDet 85.3/86.80/78.13). On CrowdHuman it attains the best body MR-2 (36.5) and body AP (91.6). Ablations confirm association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each help.
> - **(e)** 4-bit AdamW matches 32-bit AdamW: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9, Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, GPT-2 E2E BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6, WMT SacreBLEU 26.28 vs 26.61; LLaMA-7B/13B/33B MMLU/commonsense fine-tuning is on par. Memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 75.4→31.9 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU. Sublinear-memory baselines (Adafactor, SM3) degrade, especially on classification.
> - **(f)** INN-TD data-driven: RMSE 0.126/0.129 (×10⁻³) at 100% training vs MLP 0.385/0.534, SIREN 1.17/1.66, KAN 4.59/4.26. Data-free high-D Poisson: relative L2 error 1.75e-8 (2D, 0.81 s) to 1.24e-8 (10D), beating CP-PINN (4.63e-3) and KAN (9.44e-5) by orders of magnitude with far less time, and converging with refinement.
> 
> ## Cross-paper analysis
> 
> - Only (c) and (e) report standard benchmark metrics the prompt prefers (AP on COCO; F1/accuracy); (a) reports MNIST/CIFAR-100 accuracy/KS statistics; (b) is mostly theoretical with ImageNet CCA validation; (d) reports sequential-MNIST test error; (f) reports RMSE/L2 error on PDEs. So the AP/F1/AUROC preference is only partially met.
> - Complementary focus: (a)+(b) explain *why* networks train and what optimizers/losses induce structure (Hessian power law; JEPA vs MAE implicit bias); (d) shows spectral initialization dominates sign constraints for reliability; (e) addresses memory-efficient reliability of AdamW at sub-byte precision without accuracy loss; (c) and (f) apply the recipes to vision detection and scientific computing, respectively.
> - Key tension: (a) finds LoRA fine-tuning lacks the full fine-tuning Hessian structure, while (e) explicitly targets LoRA-type fine-tuning efficiency — together they suggest memory-saving optimizers and spectral-structure analyses operate at different granularities.
> - Caveat: I cannot independently verify these numbers from external sources; they are reported here as stated in the retrieved documents, and cross-method comparison is limited because each paper uses different tasks and metrics.

>     – APM/APL: PBADet-YOLOv5l6 66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4 vs BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9 (Table 2).
>     – Per-category AP: PBADet-YOLOv5l6 has higher AP for person (62.4 vs 61.3) and both feet (r-foot 30.9 vs 30.2; l-foot 31.5 vs 30.9); BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 is higher on head (56.6 vs 54.6), face (46.3 vs 44.6), and hands (r-hand 40.4 vs 39.0; l-hand 39.6 vs 37.7) (Table 2).
>   • Association robustness (lower is better, Table 3 mMR−2): PBADet-YOLOv5l6 achieves the lowest mMR−2 on head (27.9), face (30.5), left hand (36.2), right hand (40.8), and left foot (47.9) compared to BPJDet variants; BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 is best on right foot (49.1 vs PBADet-YOLOv5l6 50.4) (Table 3).
> - Pose-vs-detection on COCO val (PBADet vs ED-Pose, Table 7):
>   • Using the same COCO validation split for small parts (hands/feet), PBADet yields consistently higher Precision/Recall/F1 than ED-Pose (Swin-L). For all parts combined: PBADet P/R/F1 = 39.41/63.09/48.52 vs ED-Pose 24.09/45.51/31.51. Per-part gains mirror this trend (e.g., left hand F1 46.50 vs 22.87; right hand 47.34 vs 24.17; left foot 51.08 vs 40.46; right foot 50.34 vs 40.34) (Table 7).
> 
> 2) ImageNet
> - Active, anytime-valid RCPS (Fig. 3): On ImageNet, the active labeling policies (“pretrain”, “learned”) achieve lower final β̂ (higher utility under the same risk θ) with fewer labels while keeping the safety violation rate below α=0.05, outperforming “all” and “oblivious” baselines.
> - JEPA vs MAE (Appendix D of JEPA paper): On ImageNet-1K (64×64), the JEPA feature space shows higher mean CCA alignment between full and bottom-PCA images, and lower alignment for full vs top-PCA images than MAE over training epochs (Fig. 7), indicating JEPA learns features aligned with lower-variance (perceptual) subspaces, consistent with their theory.
> 
> B) Similar task types (vision detection/association, sequence/RNNs, video-RL, calibration)

> B1) Vision: part/body detection and association
> - BodyHands (identical dataset across methods, PBADet Table 1):
>   • PBADet vs BPJDet and prior baselines: PBADet-YOLOv7 achieves Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; PBADet-YOLOv5l6 achieves 88.1 / 92.71 / 85.73. These exceed BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (85.9 / 86.91 / 84.39) and other legacy baselines (e.g., OpenPose, Mask R-CNN variants) (Table 1). Gains are largest in Conditional Accuracy (≈+5–6 points vs BPJDet-l6) and Joint AP (≈+1.3–1.6 points).
> - COCOHumanParts (identical dataset across methods, discussed above):
>   • Tradeoffs: BPJDet-l6 slightly higher overall AP (AP.5:.95) but PBADet stronger at APM/APL and some categories; PBADet achieves lower mMR−2 on most categories (Table 2–3).
> - CrowdHuman (PBADet Appendix Tables 5–6):
>   • Face-body association (Table 5): PBADet-YOLOv7 attains best detection MR−2 for body (36.5) and face (44.7) and best body AP (91.6). Association mMR−2 is comparable (50.8–50.9), slightly above BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (50.1).
>   • Compared to crowded-pedestrian detectors (Table 6): PBADet-YOLOv7 has the best body MR−2 (36.5) and competitive body AP (91.6) against specialized CNN/DETR-based methods, while providing joint detection ability.
> 
> B2) Sequence modeling / RNNs with Dale’s Law constraints (NeurIPS 2023)
> - Identical tasks across architectures (Figures 2–7): Adding Problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank language modeling, naturalistic object recognition.
>   • Across all four tasks, standard RNNs and DANN RNNs learn faster and to lower test error than ColEI (EI column-sign-constrained) RNNs (Fig. 2A–D). Gradient clipping helps ColEI substantially more (Appendix Fig. 10).
>   • Spectrum transplant (Fig. 4): Replacing spectra shows singular-value spectrum mismatches account for a larger performance gap than sign constraints per se; the average performance drop from constraining signs alone (~0.7%±0.3% for RNNs; ~1%±1% for ColEI) is smaller than the gap induced by adverse spectra (Fig. 4C).
>   • EI ratio and width effects (Figs. 5–7): For ColEI, fewer inhibitory units and smaller networks produce more pathological spectra (lower normalised SVD entropy, larger max singular value) and worse test error; in contrast DANN spectra/performance are robust to EI ratio and size. Normalised SVD entropy predicts ColEI performance across sizes/ratios (Fig. 7D).
> 
> B3) Video-based representation learning for downstream RL (ICLR 2024)
> - Identical domains across methods (GridWorld; ViZDoom Basic; ViZDoom Defend the Center):
>   • No exogenous noise: Forward Modeling and Temporal Contrastive both learn representations that enable successful RL (GridWorld Fig. 2a; ViZDoom Defend the Center Fig. 4a), consistent with the upper bounds proved.
>   • With temporally correlated exogenous noise (observation/reward/both): Forward Modeling degrades, Temporal Contrastive often fails (GridWorld Fig. 2b–d; ViZDoom Defend the Center Fig. 4b–d). Qualitative reconstructions show Temporal Contrastive fixates on moving distractors, while Forward Modeling still captures task-relevant structure (Figs. 3 & 5). ACRO (trajectory-based) stays strong under exogenous noise and outperforms video-only methods, aligning with the lower-bound that video pretraining can be exponentially harder under exogenous noise (Theorem 2).
>   • Robustness trends: Increasing the size/count of exogenous distractors degrades Forward Modeling more; ACRO remains comparatively robust (Fig. 6; Fig. 9). With strictly iid noise, Forward Modeling and ACRO maintain performance (GridWorld Fig. 10); in ViZDoom Basic, Temporal Contrastive handles iid Gaussian noise well (Fig. 11a).
> 
> B4) Calibration / anytime-valid risk control with active labeling (NeurIPS 2024)
> - Simulations and ImageNet (identical settings across methods): For a fixed target risk θ and label budget B=0.3, the active policies (“pretrain”, “learned”) consistently reach lower β̂ (higher utility) with fewer labels than “all”/“oblivious”, while keeping the safety violation rate below α=0.05 (Figs. 2–3). This holds across synthetic and ImageNet experiments.

> C) Dataset-by-dataset summaries (specific results)
> 
> 1) BodyHands (PBADet Table 1; identical dataset for all listed methods)
> - Best overall: PBADet-YOLOv7 (89.1 Hand AP; 92.62 Conditional Accuracy; 85.98 Joint AP) and PBADet-YOLOv5l6 (88.1; 92.71; 85.73). Both exceed BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (85.9; 86.91; 84.39) and prior baselines.

> 2) COCOHumanParts (PBADet Tables 2–3; identical dataset)
> - Overall AP (AP.5:.95): BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 slightly higher (43.6/43.3) vs PBADet-YOLOv5l6 (43.0/41.8) and PBADet-YOLOv7 (42.7/41.5).
> - Mid/Large objects: PBADet leads (APM/APL higher by ≈2–6 points).
> - Per-category AP: PBADet-YOLOv5l6 better on person and feet; BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 better on head/face/hands.
> - Association robustness (mMR−2): PBADet-YOLOv5l6 lowest for head, face, both hands, and left foot; BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 lowest for right foot.
> 
> 3) CrowdHuman face-body association (PBADet Tables 5–6; identical dataset)
> - Detection: PBADet-YOLOv7 best MR−2 (body 36.5; face 44.7), highest body AP 91.6.
> - Association (mMR−2): PBADet ~50.8–50.9, comparable but slightly above BPJDet-l6 (50.1).
> - Against crowded-detector baselines: PBADet achieves the best body MR−2 while maintaining competitive AP.
> 
> 4) COCO validation (PBADet vs ED-Pose Table 7; identical dataset)
> - Parts (hands/feet): PBADet substantially higher Precision/Recall/F1 across left/right hands and feet; all-parts F1 48.52 (PBADet) vs 31.51 (ED-Pose).
> 
> 5) Adding Problem, Sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, Naturalistic Object Recognition (Dale’s Law paper; identical benchmarks across RNN variants)
> - Standard RNNs ≈ DANNs > ColEI in learning curves and final test error; spectral properties (unimodal clustered singular values) are the key explanatory factor. Sign constraints alone account for smaller performance changes than spectrum (Fig. 4).
> 
> 6) GridWorld; ViZDoom Basic; ViZDoom Defend the Center (Video pretraining for RL; identical domains)
> - No exogenous noise: Forward Modeling and Temporal Contrastive both enable successful RL.
> - With exogenous noise: Forward Modeling degrades moderately; Temporal Contrastive often fails; ACRO (trajectory-based) is most robust. Larger or more distractors hurt the video methods more (Figs. 2,4,6,9–11).
> 
> 7) ImageNet (RCPS; identical dataset across labeling strategies)
> - With θ=0.1 and α=0.05, “pretrain”/“learned” active policies achieve lower β̂ with fewer labels than “all”/“oblivious,” while respecting the safety violation rate ≤ α (Fig. 3).
> 
> D) Cross-cutting takeaways tied to training choices and metrics
> - CNN backbones and anchor-free design (PBADet) improve association robustness and efficiency at scale: higher APM/APL on COCO-HumanParts and better body/face detection MR−2 on CrowdHuman; but BPJDet can retain a slight overall AP advantage and better APs on some small parts (hands/head/face).
> - Spectral properties dominate training performance under Dale’s Law constraints: DANNs (and standard RNNs) with unimodal clustered singular spectra train well on Adding/Seq-MNIST/PTB/NOR; ColEI’s multimodal dispersed spectra harm learning—improving spectra (not just relaxing sign constraints) closes the performance gap.
> - JEPA vs MAE (linear theory + ImageNet evidence): JEPA’s learning dynamics prioritize influential (high-regression) features and emphasize lower-variance subspaces; ImageNet feature-CCA confirms JEPA’s stronger alignment with the “bottom” PCA subspace than MAE during training.
> - Anytime-valid, label-efficient calibration: Active policies using model predictions (“pretrain”, “learned”) reduce queried labels to reach smaller β̂ while maintaining risk control (α=0.05) on both simulations and ImageNet; the baselines either use more labels (“all”) or converge more slowly (“oblivious”).
> - Video pretraining for RL under exogenous noise: Without exogenous noise, both Forward Modeling and Temporal Contrastive yield usable representations. Exogenous noise breaks Temporal Contrastive first (learns to track distractors), Forward Modeling next, while trajectory-based ACRO remains strongest—matching the theoretical upper/lower bounds reported.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here are the five papers matching your request, followed by a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. PBADet — One-stage anchor-free part–body association (ICLR 2024)
> - **Setup:** YOLOv7 (36.9M) and YOLOv5l6 (86.1M) CNN backbones, **SGD** optimizer, AMP, 100 epochs, 1024×1024; evaluated on **COCO**-based datasets (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts), CrowdHuman, AnimalPose/AP-10K.
> - **Results:** BodyHands — HandAP 89.1, Cond. Accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98, beating BPJDet (85.9/86.91/84.39) and MaskRCNN/BodyHands baselines by large margins. COCOHumanParts — AP on par with BPJDet but leads AP_M/AP_L/person/feet and lowest mMR-2 for most parts. CrowdHuman face-body — best body MR-2 (36.5). vs. ED-Pose (Swin-L Transformer) on COCO val: **Precision/Recall/F1** all-parts 39.41/63.09/**48.52** vs. 24.09/45.51/31.51.
> - **Ablations:** removing the association loss drops Cond. Accuracy 92.62→80.78 and JointAP 85.98→78.07; multi-scale offsets and task-alignment each contribute.
> 
> ## 2. Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective (NeurIPS 2023)
> - **Setup:** standard RNN, ColEI (sign-constrained columns), and DANN RNNs on adding, **sequential MNIST**, Penn TreeBank, naturalistic object recognition.
> - **Results:** ColEI learns worse and with much higher variance on all four tasks; gradient clipping helps ColEI most. Sign constraints account for only part of the gap (0.7%±0.3% RNN, 1%±1% ColEI vs. full 2.3%±0.6% difference). Spectrum "transplants" show the **singular-value spectrum at initialization**, not sign constraints/vectors, dominates (1.5% vs 2% error contributions). Normalised SVD entropy (NSE) anti-correlates with final test error and predicts performance before training; small balanced-E/I networks can beat larger skewed ones. (Error-rate metrics on MNIST, not Precision/F1.)
> 
> ## 3. Why JEPA avoids noisy features (NeurIPS 2024)
> - **Setup:** exactly solvable deep linear networks (gradient flow and **SGD** simulations on Gaussian data), plus linear generative models (random masking, temporal model) and ImageNet-1K.
> - **Results:** JEPA shows a distinct implicit bias — greedy learning toward **high-regression-coefficient (influential) features**, whereas MAE (reconstruction/MSE) only prioritizes high-variance (λ) features, even if noisy. This bias strengthens with encoder depth (fixed point w̄_JEPA=ρ^L vs w̄_MAE=ρ^{L/(L+1)}; JEPA suppresses noisy directions increasingly with depth). On ImageNet-1K, I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA), explaining why latent-space prediction beats pixel reconstruction for downstream tasks. (No direct CIFAR-100/ResNet-50 result in the retrieved content.)
> 
> ## 4. Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets (NeurIPS 2024)
> - **Setup:** e-process/betting framework; active labeling with label budget B=0.3, θ=0.1, α=0.05. Simulations (P~Uniform[0,1], FPR risk) and **ImageNet** classification with pretrained classifiers.
> - **Results:** learned and pretrained label policies reach lower β̂ (closer to β*=0.5578/0.8349) than "all"/"oblivious" baselines uniformly across number of labels, while all methods keep safety-violation rate below α=0.05 (anytime-valid risk control holds at all times). Optimal predictor = conditional risk; optimal policy ∝ conditional std dev; O(√T) regret via ONS. This is the "safety calibration" component.
> 
> ## 5. Principled representation learning from videos for RL (ICLR 2024)
> - **Setup:** autoencoder, forward modeling, temporal contrastive learning vs. ACRO (trajectory-based), evaluated in GridWorld, ViZDoom basic, and ViZDoom Defend the Center; convolutional encoder/decoder, PPO with frozen representation.
> - **Results:** without exogenous noise, forward modeling and temporal contrastive both enable successful downstream RL (provably polynomial sample complexity). With **exogenous noise**, temporal contrastive **completely fails** (it can minimize its loss by focusing purely on noise), forward modeling degrades (reconstructions still capture state-relevant info), autoencoder is unpredictable, while **ACRO (trajectory data) stays robust** — performance gap widens as noise size/count grows. Under iid Gaussian pixel noise, temporal contrastive filters noise better. Lower bound: video-only pre-training can be exponentially worse than trajectory-based pre-training under exogenous noise.
> 
> ## Cross-paper analysis
> - **Shared principle:** all five argue that *what objective/constraint you optimize* shapes which features are learned — PBADet (part-to-body offset design), Dale's Law (spectrum vs. sign), JEPA (latent vs. pixel prediction), and video-RL (forward vs. contrastive under noise) all show the objective determines robustness; RCPS adds a statistical safety guarantee on top of any black-box model.
> - **Training choices:** only PBADet explicitly reports **SGD** (with YOLO CNN backbones) and **CNNs vs Transformers** (beating the Swin-L-based ED-Pose with a lighter CNN); the JEPA paper uses SGD/ADAM-free gradient-flow analysis with CNNs only implicitly. No paper reports ResNet-50 or CIFAR-100 experiments in the retrieved content — those specifics (plus an explicit SGD-vs-Adam study) cannot be established from this collection.
> - **Metrics:** **Precision/Recall/F1** appear explicitly only in PBADet's ED-Pose comparison; COCO AP/MR-2 in PBADet; error rates in the Dale's Law paper; risk/β̂/label-efficiency in RCPS; RL reward and reconstruction quality in the video paper.
> - **Embeddings/calibration:** JEPA links latent embeddings to PCA/CCA feature alignment; RCPS is the calibration piece (anytime-valid risk control); the video paper links learned embeddings to downstream RL performance under noise.
> - **Caveat:** the five papers are complementary rather than directly comparable — they target different modalities (vision detection, neuroscience RNNs, SSL theory, statistical calibration, RL), so "comparing" their numeric results is only meaningful within each paper's own baselines. A principled unifying theme across them is robustness/feature selection through well-chosen objectives and constraints, with statistical safety guarantees as the calibration layer.

Lowest average mMR−2 on head/face/hands/right-foot.
> - CrowdHuman face–body: Ours(YOLOv7) body MR−2 36.5, face MR−2 44.7, body AP 91.6 — beats BPJDet (MR−2 39.7–41.3) and all two-stage/DETR baselines on MR−2.
> - BodyHands ablation (YOLOv7): Full model Hand AP 89.1, Conditional Accuracy 92.62, Joint AP 85.98; removing the association loss drops Cond. Acc. to 80.78 and Joint AP to 78.07 — association loss, multi-scale offset, and task-alignment all matter.
> - Vs. ED-Pose (Swin-L): substantially higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands and feet.
> 
> **2. Dale's-Law RNN spectral analysis (sequential MNIST, PTB, adding, object recognition)**
> - ColEI (column-constrained E/I) RNNs learn worse on all four tasks and are more seed-variable; gradient clipping helps them most.
> - Spectrum transplants show singular-value spectra matter more than sign constraints or singular vectors (spectrum/vector/sign contributions ≈1.5–2% vs full 2.3% gap).
> - Normalized SVD entropy at initialization anti-correlates with final test error; smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units worsen spectra and performance, while DANN (Dale's ANN) RNNs stay robust and match standard RNNs.
> 
> **3. How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features (joint-embedding self-distillation)**
> - Deep-linear analysis: JEPA learns "influential" features (high regression coefficient ρ) first, with depth amplifying the bias; MAE orders features only by covariance λ. Critical-time formulas and fixed points (w̄_JEPA(∞,L)=ρ^L vs w̄_MAE(∞,L)=ρ^{L/(L+1)}) differ; a 1-layer JEPA equals an infinite-depth MAE.
> - Verified by ODE simulations, SGD-trained random-init linear nets, linear generative models (masking, temporal), and ImageNet-1K where I-JEPA aligns faster with the low-variance PCA/perceptual subspace (CCA) than MAE.
> 
> **4. Active, anytime-valid risk-controlling prediction sets (ImageNet + simulations)**
> - With θ=0.1, α=0.05, label budget B=0.3: "pretrain" and "learned" labeling policies reach lower β̂ (closer to β* = 0.8349 on ImageNet, 0.5578 in simulations) than "all"/"oblivious" at every label count, while all methods keep safety-violation rates below α. Optimal predictor = conditional risk; optimal policy ∝ conditional risk std-dev.
> 
> **5. Video-based representation learning for RL under exogenous noise (GridWorld, ViZDoom)**
> - Without exogenous noise, forward modeling and temporal contrastive learning both enable efficient downstream RL (polynomial sample complexity, theory + practice). With exogenous noise, temporal contrastive completely fails (it can cheat by predicting the noise), forward modeling degrades but retains state-relevant structure, and trajectory-based ACRO stays strongest; a lower bound shows an exponential identifiability barrier for video-only data. Temporal contrastive is better than forward modeling for iid Gaussian pixel noise.
> 
> **Related: LDReg (self-supervised, practical training choices)**
> - On ImageNet with ResNet-50 and ViT-B, LDReg improves linear evaluation and transfer (CIFAR, Food-101, Birdsnap, Cars, DTD) and COCO detection/segmentation for SimCLR/SimCLR-Tuned/BYOL/MAE — the paper that most directly matches your SSL + ResNet-50/COCO/CIFAR, feature-embedding, and backbone criteria.
> 
> **Cross-cutting analysis**
> - *Objective choice shapes representation robustness*: (3) and (5) both show that latent-space prediction (JEPA; forward modeling) resists noise/influential-feature bias better than reconstruction (MAE; autoencoder) or classification-like objectives (contrastive, which can exploit noise). (2) shows the analogous effect at the architecture level: initialization spectra (not sign constraints) determine whether biologically constrained RNNs learn.
> - *Noise robustness is a common stress test*: (5) and (2) quantify degradation under exogenous/structured noise and identify failure modes (contrastive collapses to noise; ColEI spectra become pathological), while (3) explains why JEPA-style objectives avoid noisy features.
> - *Safety/calibration is orthogonal to representation quality*: (4) provides distribution-free anytime-valid guarantees on top of any black-box model, trading label budget for risk control; its "learned/pretrain" policies mirror the transfer-learning theme of (1) and LDReg.
> - *Metric regimes differ sharply*: detection papers report AP/MR−2/Precision/Recall/F1 (COCO-family); SSL papers report linear-eval accuracy, CCA alignment, and downstream transfer (COCO, CIFAR); RNN work reports test error and spectral diagnostics (NSE); RL work reports task success/reconstruction under noise; calibration work reports risk violation rates and label efficiency. There is no single shared metric — the common thread is that all validate on ImageNet/COCO/MNIST/CIFAR-family or RL benchmarks and connect training choices (backbone, objective, initialization, labeling policy) to measured robustness/calibration.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:437 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** I’m building an end-to-end system that: (1) pretrains detectors from unlabeled videos to reliably link hands/face to the correct person; (2) uses those video embeddings to initialize an RL policy; and (3) gates model outputs with anytime-valid risk thresholds while labeling only the most useful points. We need guidance on avoiding spurious features in self-supervised pretraining (JEPA-style vs reconstruction), dealing with exogenous noise in time-series, anchoring detectors without anchors, and applying active, sequential risk control. Our stack mixes CNNs and Transformers trained with SGD/Adam, standard losses (MSE, cross-entropy), and we’ll evaluate with Precision/F1 on COCO-like data as well as MNIST/CIFAR-100. Please point to works that together cover part–body association, self-distillation biases, spectral constraints in deep nets, and active anytime-valid risk-controlled prediction sets—ideally with insights transferable to vision-language models and adapter-based fine-tuning.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

**score：3→4（Δ+1）；rounds：3→3（Δ+0）。**

> Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results strictly extracted from the provided figures, tables, and text. I group results by identical datasets first, then by similar dataset types, and finally by specific datasets where applicable.
> 
> 1) Identical datasets (same benchmark, multiple methods compared)
> 
> A. BodyHands (hand–body association)
> - Methods compared: PBADet (ours), BPJDet (various YOLOv5 variants), prior baselines (OpenPose, MaskRCNN variants, BodyHands).
> - Metrics (Table 1): Hand AP (↑), Conditional Accuracy (↑), Joint AP (↑).
> - Key results:
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7, 1024): Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Acc. 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 — best among all reported methods.
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6, 1024): Hand AP 88.1, Cond. Acc. 92.71, Joint AP 85.73 — also better than BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) Joint AP 84.39.
>   • Conclusion: PBADet outperforms BPJDet and earlier two-stage or pose-based baselines across all BodyHands metrics.
> 
> B. COCOHumanParts (multi-part–body association: head, face, hands, feet)
> - Methods compared: PBADet (YOLOv7, YOLOv5l6), BPJDet (YOLOv5{ s6, m6, l6 }), Hier R-CNN baselines.
> - Metrics (Table 2): Overall AP.5:.95 and AP.5 (all categories, original/subordinate), size-wise APM/APL; per-category APs; (Table 3) average mMR−2 (↓) by category.
> - Overall detection (Table 2):
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): AP.5:.95 43.6/43.3; PBADet (YOLOv5l6): 43.0/41.8; PBADet (YOLOv7): 42.7/41.5. Thus, BPJDet l6 has slightly higher overall AP.5:.95, but see size and category breakdowns below.
> - Size breakdown (Table 2):
>   • APM / APL — PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 66.2/65.0 and 67.2/64.4 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9. PBADet leads for medium and large objects.
> - Per-category APs (Table 2):
>   • Person: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) 62.4 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 61.3 (ours better).
>   • Feet: PBADet (YOLOv5l6) r-foot 30.9, l-foot 31.5 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) r-foot 30.2, l-foot 30.9 (ours better on both feet).
>   • Head/Face/Hands: PBADet slightly lower than BPJDet (e.g., head 54.6 vs 56.6; face 44.6 vs 46.3; r-hand 39.0 vs 40.4; l-hand 37.7 vs 39.6 for YOLOv5l6).
> - Association quality (mMR−2, Table 3; ↓ better):
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): head 29.2, face 31.3, l-hand 41.1, r-hand 42.7, r-foot 52.6, l-foot 52.5.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): head 30.8, face 31.8, l-hand 41.6, r-hand 42.2, r-foot 49.1, l-foot 50.4.
>   • Interpretation: On head/face/left-hand, PBADet (YOLOv7) is slightly better (lower mMR−2) than BPJDet (YOLOv5l6). On right-hand and feet, PBADet (YOLOv7) has higher (worse) mMR−2 than BPJDet (YOLOv5l6). (Averaging across categories depends on the specific model pairing; the table shows category-wise trade-offs.)
> - Conclusion: On COCOHumanParts, PBADet matches or exceeds BPJDet on medium/large objects and person/feet AP, while BPJDet retains small overall AP.5:.95 edge and better AP on head/face/hands; mMR−2 shows mixed category-wise tradeoffs.
> 
> C. CrowdHuman (face–body association and joint detection in crowds)
> - Methods compared: PBADet (YOLOv7, YOLOv5l6), BPJDet (YOLOv5 variants), other crowded detection baselines (DETR/CNN variants, etc.).
> - Metrics (Table 5): body MR−2 (↓), face MR−2 (↓), body AP (↑), mMR−2 body-face (↓).
>   • PBADet (YOLOv7): body MR−2 36.5 (best among listed), face MR−2 44.7, body AP 91.6 (ties/competitive with top DETR baselines), mMR−2 50.8.
>   • BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR−2 40.7, face MR−2 46.3, body AP 89.5, mMR−2 50.1.
> - Joint crowded detection comparison (Table 6): PBADet (YOLOv7) achieves best body MR−2 (36.5) among both EI joint detectors and other crowded person detectors, with competitive AP (91.6).
> - Conclusion: On CrowdHuman, PBADet improves body MR−2 and body AP over BPJDet, while mMR−2 for face–body pairing is comparable.
> 
> D. COCO (pose vs part–body association; qualitative/quantitative cross-task check)
> - Methods compared: PBADet vs ED-Pose (on COCO validation; Appendix Table 7 and Fig. 5).
> - Metrics (Table 7): Precision/Recall/F1 (↑) for left/right hands and feet.
>   • PBADet (YOLOv5l6) F1 substantially higher vs ED-Pose (e.g., left hand 46.50 vs 22.87; right hand 47.34 vs 24.17; left foot 51.08 vs 40.46; right foot 50.34 vs 40.34; all parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51), under the evaluation protocol described in the paper (IoU-based for PBADet, keypoint-in-box for ED-Pose).
> - Conclusion: For bounding-box-based part–body association, PBADet yields higher F1 than a state-of-the-art pose estimator on hand/foot parts in the reported setup.
> 
> E. GridWorld and ViZDoom (video pretraining for RL)
> - Methods compared: Forward Modeling, Temporal Contrastive Learning, Autoencoder (with/without VQ), ACRO (trajectory-based representation) across identical domains under different noise conditions (Fig. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7–13).
> - Findings consistent across both domains:
>   • No exogenous noise: Forward Modeling and Temporal Contrastive both succeed in downstream RL (high returns); reconstructions show they capture task-relevant structure (e.g., walls in GridWorld) (Figs. 2a, 4a, 3 top row).
>   • With exogenous noise (observation and/or reward): Temporal Contrastive performance degrades sharply (often fails); Forward Modeling is somewhat robust at low noise but degrades as exogenous noise increases (Figs. 2b–d, 4b–d; reconstructions in Fig. 3 bottom & Fig. 5 show contrastive focusing on exogenous diamonds).
>   • Increasing exogenous difficulty: As noise size/number increases, video-based methods degrade markedly; ACRO (uses action-labeled trajectories) remains strong and degrades much less (Figs. 6 and 9).
>   • IID noise: Forward Modeling (and ACRO) handle IID noise well (GridWorld Fig. 10). In ViZDoom with IID Gaussian noise, Temporal Contrastive excels relative to the exogenous case (Fig. 11a vs 11b), aligning with theory (contrastive is sensitive to temporally correlated exogenous distractors but robust to IID noise).
> - Conclusion: On identical RL domains, Forward Modeling and Temporal Contrastive succeed without exogenous noise; in the presence of exogenous noise, Forward Modeling is more robust than Temporal Contrastive but still degrades; ACRO (trajectory-based) performs best and remains more stable as noise increases.
> 
> F. ImageNet (two separate tasks; not directly comparable metrics but on the same dataset)
> - JEPA vs MAE (representation quality tracking; Appendix D Fig. 7):
>   • I-JEPA shows higher mean CCA similarity between features learned on full vs bottom-variance subspace (full_bottom) than MAE during training; conversely, JEPA shows lower similarity for full vs top-variance subspace (full_top) than MAE. This supports that JEPA prioritizes semantically useful, lower-variance ("influential") features more quickly.
> - Active anytime-valid RCPS (Fig. 3):
>   • Label policies using pretrained/learned predictors achieve lower final β̂ (closer to β*) with fewer labels than baselines (“all” or “oblivious”), while controlling safety violation rates below α = 0.05. (Same pattern seen in both simulation and ImageNet labeling experiments.)
> - Note: Although both use ImageNet, the tasks and metrics differ (CCA for representational alignment vs β̂ for risk control), so results are not directly comparable.
> 
> 2) Similar types of datasets/tasks (cross-dataset patterns)
> 
> A. Part–body association across human-centric detection datasets
> - BodyHands → PBADet clearly leads (Table 1).
> - COCOHumanParts → PBADet competitive overall: stronger on medium/large scales and person/feet APs; BPJDet slightly higher overall AP.5:.95 and better on head/face/hands AP; mMR−2 shows category-wise splits.
> - CrowdHuman → PBADet improves body MR−2 and AP vs BPJDet; pairing mMR−2 similar.
> - Overall pattern: PBADet’s one-stage anchor-free, part-to-body center-offset design shows consistent gains in crowded/body-centric metrics (MR−2, AP for person), and tradeoffs with BPJDet on certain part categories (head/face/hands).
> 
> B. Pretraining from videos for RL vs trajectory-based pretraining
> - On identical RL domains (GridWorld, ViZDoom), trajectory-based ACRO consistently outperforms video-only pretraining when exogenous (temporally correlated) noise is present; video-only Forward Modeling is more robust than Temporal Contrastive but still sensitive to the amount of exogenous noise (Figs. 2–6, 9–13).
> 
> C. Self-supervised representation learning in vision (JEPA vs MAE)
> - On ImageNet, JEPA training prioritizes low-variance, influential features (higher CCA with bottom variance subspace; lower with top), while MAE more closely tracks reconstruction of higher-variance components. The empirical curves support JEPA’s bias predicted by the deep linear analyses (Fig. 7).
> 
> D. Risk-controlled prediction sets with active labeling (RCPS)
> - On simulation and ImageNet, predictor-informed active policies consistently achieve lower β̂ with fewer labels and maintain target safety (α=0.05) compared with naive strategies (Fig. 2–3 in RCPS paper). This demonstrates label-efficiency improvements that are complementary to pretraining paradigms above but use different objectives/metrics.
> 
> E. EI-constrained recurrent networks (Dale’s Law)
> - Across adding problem, sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, and a naturalistic object recognition task:
>   • Column EI (ColEI) RNNs train worse and show higher variance across seeds than standard RNNs and DANNs; performance improves markedly with gradient clipping but remains below the others (Fig. 2A–D).
>   • Spectrum transplant experiments: giving ColEI the RNN singular value spectrum (and vice versa) shows spectra are more predictive of performance than sign constraints alone; NSE (normalized SVD entropy) correlates with error (Fig. 4–7).
>   • Small networks and skewed E/I ratios → degraded spectrum (multimodal, dispersed) and worse learning; DANNs are robust even with very few inhibitory units.
> - While not the same benchmarks as the detection or ImageNet tasks, the consistent trend is that spectral properties (unimodal, clustered singular values; high NSE) predict better learning across tasks.
> 
> 3) Specific-dataset highlights (selected concrete numbers for clarity)
> - BodyHands (Table 1): PBADet (YOLOv7) Hand AP 89.1, Cond. Acc. 92.62, Joint AP 85.98 (best); PBADet (YOLOv5l6) Joint AP 85.73 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 84.39.
> - COCOHumanParts (Table 2): PBADet (YOLOv5l6) APM 66.2/65.0, APL 67.2/64.4 vs BPJDet (YOLOv5l6) 63.8/63.2 and 61.8/58.9; per-category person AP 62.4 vs 61.3 (ours better); feet APs better for PBADet; hands/head/face APs higher for BPJDet. (Table 3) mMR−2 mixed across categories.
> - CrowdHuman (Table 5/6): PBADet (YOLOv7) body MR−2 36.5 (best listed), body AP 91.6.
> - COCO (Table 7): Part F1 (PBADet vs ED-Pose): left hand 46.50 vs 22.87; right hand 47.34 vs 24.17; left foot 51.08 vs 40.46; right foot 50.34 vs 40.34; all parts 48.52 vs 31.51.
> - ImageNet (JEPA vs MAE): JEPA’s mean CCA higher for full_bottom and lower for full_top than MAE across training epochs (Fig. 7), indicating JEPA focuses earlier on low-variance, influential features.
> - ImageNet (RCPS): Pretrain/Learned labeling policies attain lower final β̂ with fewer queries than All/Oblivious, while safety violations remain under α=0.05 (Fig. 3).
> - RL (GridWorld/ViZDoom): No noise → Forward Modeling & Temporal Contrastive succeed; exogenous noise → Contrastive fails early; Forward degrades as noise grows; ACRO strong and most robust (Figs. 2, 4, 6, 9–11).
> 
> Summary of better/worse by setting
> - Human part–body association (BodyHands, COCOHumanParts, CrowdHuman): PBADet consistently improves BodyHands metrics; leads on medium/large objects and person/feet APs on COCOHumanParts; best body MR−2 on CrowdHuman. BPJDet can be stronger on head/face/hands AP and overall AP.5:.95 on COCOHumanParts.
> - Video pretraining for RL (GridWorld/ViZDoom): Forward Modeling > Temporal Contrastive under exogenous noise; both succeed without exogenous noise; ACRO (trajectory-based) > video-only methods when exogenous distractors increase.
> - Representation learning bias (ImageNet): JEPA > MAE for quickly aligning with low-variance, semantic feature subspaces; MAE emphasizes reconstruction of high-variance components.
> - Active risk control (ImageNet & simulation): Predictor-informed (pretrain/learned) label policies > All/Oblivious in achieving smaller β̂ with fewer labels at the same safety.
> - Dale’s-law RNNs: DANN/standard RNN > ColEI across tasks; spectra (unimodal, clustered) > sign constraints alone for performance; NSE reliably predicts outcomes.
> 
> Notes
> - Where the same dataset appears across different papers (e.g., ImageNet), the tasks and metrics differ (CCA vs β̂), so cross-paper numeric comparison is not applicable; results are reported within each paper’s metric space.
> - All numeric values above are taken from the provided tables/figures; qualitative trends (e.g., robustness to exogenous noise, spectral pathology effects) reflect the empirical plots and authors’ descriptions in the text.

**naive 最终答案**

> Here is a compact mapping of the retrieved works to your pipeline, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## 1. Part–body association without anchors
> **PBADet** (doc `08b70bc3…`) — one-stage, anchor-free detector linking hands/face/feet to a parent body via a single part-to-body center offset (vs BPJDet's body-to-part offsets, whose representation grows with #parts and breaks when parts are occluded).
> - BodyHands: YOLOv7 achieves hand AP 92.62 / joint AP 85.98 vs BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) 86.91 / 84.39; outperforms BodyHands (83.44/63.48) and Mask R-CNN variants.
> - COCOHumanParts (6 parts): AP on par with BPJDet but leads person/feet APs and lowest mMR⁻² for head/face/hands.
> - CrowdHuman (face–body): body MR⁻² 36.5 (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet 39.7–41.3; advantage shrinks for this single-part task.
> - vs pose estimator ED-Pose on COCO: hands/feet Precision/F1 far higher (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51).
> - Ablations: association loss, multi-scale center offsets, and task-alignment learning each add accuracy; also transfers to quadruped (AnimalPose/AP-10K).
> 
> ## 2. JEPA vs reconstruction (spurious-feature avoidance)
> **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features"** (doc `40fde037…`) — deep-linear analysis: JEPA implicitly prioritizes *influential* (high regression-coefficient, low-variance) features, while MAE prioritizes high-variance/noisy features; the bias strengthens with encoder depth. ImageNet experiments: I-JEPA aligns with the low-variance PCA (perceptual) subspace faster than MAE (CCA similarity). Caveat: JEPA can still be vulnerable to *spurious/slow* features.
> **LDReg** (doc `51526068…`) — counters local dimensional collapse (underfilling) via Fisher-Rao local intrinsic dimensionality; improves SimCLR, BYOL, MAE (also MoCo/VICReg/Barlow Twins) on ImageNet linear eval, transfer, and COCO detection/segmentation; longer pretraining → larger gains; global variance/covariance regularizers barely helped, and forcing very low LID causes collapse.
> **HASSOD** (doc `ef986d59…`) — self-supervised object detection with part-to-whole hierarchy (whole/part/subpart masks from DINO features + Mean Teacher); Mask AR improved 20.2→22.5 on LVIS and 17.0→26.0 on SA-1B with ~1/5 images and 1/12 iterations of CutLER; supports detector pretraining without labels.
> **DiffusionFake** (doc `fc4f3d19…`) — reconstruction-guided training forces detectors to capture source/target (disentangled) features; cross-domain deepfake AUC rises 75.80→81.88 (EfficientNet-B4) and 77.44→83.78 (ViT-B), a concrete example of steering away from spurious cues.
> 
> ## 3. Exogenous noise in time-series
> **Misra et al., "Towards Principled Representation Learning from Videos for RL"** (doc `631d23bf…`) — theory + experiments (GridWorld, ViZDoom):
> - No exogenous noise: forward modeling and temporal contrastive learning both provably work and enable efficient RL.
> - Exogenous (temporally correlated, action-independent) noise: temporal contrastive learning *completely fails* (it can minimize the loss by focusing purely on predictable background noise); forward modeling is more robust (larger margin, recovers state structure in reconstructions) but also degrades as noise grows; both fail at high noise levels — an exponential identifiability barrier vs action-labeled trajectories.
> - i.i.d. Gaussian pixel noise: temporal contrastive is actually *better* at filtering it.
> - Trajectory-based ACRO is the strongest and degrades least — relevant if you can obtain action/reward labels.
> 
> ## 4. Video embeddings → RL policy
> **RaMP** (doc `528b3e89…`) — self-supervised RL pretraining on offline trajectories with *random features as pseudo-rewards*, then regress features to a new reward and plan via MPC. On Meta-World, Hopper, D'Claw it adapts faster than MBPO/PETS/SF/CQL; NN random features beat polynomial/Gaussian; matches Dreamer on pixel tasks except Pixel Door Open. This is the closest match for initializing an RL policy from self-supervised embeddings.
> 
> ## 5. Spectral constraints in deep nets
> **"Why Dale's Law Constrained RNNs Learn Poorly"** (doc `e63a94c4…`) — spectral properties at initialization matter *more than sign constraints*: ColEI networks get multimodal, dispersed singular value spectra; normalised SVD entropy (NSE) at init anti-correlates with final test error (sequential MNIST, Penn Tree Bank, object recognition); gradient clipping mitigates. Diagnostic: measure the spectrum before training.
> **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure"** (doc `582d138d…`) — well-trained nets (LeNet, GPT-2, TinyLlama) show power-law Hessian spectra; power-law slope predicts generalization (Pearson 0.72 on CIFAR-10 LeNet; d_ks predicts LLM generalization up to 0.98). Directly relevant to your adapter-based fine-tuning: *LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law structure that full fine-tuning does*, and for LoRA adapters the Hessian trace (not d_ks) is the more reliable generalization indicator.
> 
> ## 6. Active, anytime-valid risk control
> **Xu et al., "Anytime-Valid Risk-Controlling Active Labeling"** (doc `cda0aa75…`) — extends RCPS to streaming/adaptive data: e-process/betting gives risk control that holds simultaneously at all times (P(ρ(β̂t)≤θ for all t) ≥ 1−α); active labeling via inverse propensity weighting under a label budget; the optimal label policy is proportional to conditional-risk standard deviation; the optimal predictor is conditional risk (control variate). Experiments (θ=0.1, α=0.05 on ImageNet): learned/pretrained labeling policies cut risk faster than naive baselines while keeping violation rates below α. Limitation: i.i.d. assumption; potential extension to covariate/label shift and adaptive conformal inference.
> 
> ## 7. Vision-language / adapter-based fine-tuning insights
> - **Visual Data-Type Identification** (doc `b0d9a0b2…`): freezing the vision encoder during CLIP fine-tuning gives large ID gains and even improves OOD; COCO-only fine-tuning degrades ID performance; data-type information scarcity in LAION-2B correlates ~0.80 with performance — a caution about spurious distributional shortcuts in VLM fine-tuning.
> - **NFTS** (doc `aa60be77…`): per-layer freeze/adapter search for few-shot adaptation; adapters preferred at early/late ResNet-18 layers; combining fine-tuning with adapters helps; Meta-Dataset gains +1.9% (ResNet single-domain), +2.3% (multi-domain), +1.6% (ViT-S) over TSA/ETT.
> - **NEFTune** (doc `fad0fb20…`): adding noise to embeddings during instruction tuning improves LLaMA-2-7B AlpacaEval win rate 29.8→64.7 and works with QLoRA; a simple regularizer relevant to adapter training (note: dropout/weight decay did not reproduce gains).
> - **Hessian/LoRA analysis** (doc `582d138d…`, above) — spectral diagnostics for deciding when adapter fine-tuning is well-behaved.
> 
> ## Comparative analysis
> - **Detection**: anchor-free + single part-to-body offset (PBADet) consistently beats anchor-based/body-to-part (BPJDet) and multi-stage methods on BodyHands/COCOHumanParts/CrowdHuman, and beats a pose estimator on Precision/F1 for small parts; self-supervised HASSOD shows part-whole hierarchy can be learned without labels.
> - **SSL objective**: JEPA-style latent prediction beats pixel reconstruction (MAE) for perceptual, low-variance features and is less prone to fitting noise — but is not immune to spurious/slow features; LDReg fixes a complementary failure (local dimensional collapse) and transfers to detection; under *exogenous* temporal noise, forward modeling beats temporal contrastive, and trajectory data (ACRO) beats all video-only methods; under *iid* noise temporal contrastive wins.
> - **Spectral diagnostics**: both papers agree spectral structure (init SVD for RNNs; Hessian power-law for feedforward/LLM training) predicts learning/generalization better than sign constraints or sharpness alone, and spectral fingerprints differ for adapter (LoRA) vs full fine-tuning.
> - **Risk control**: the anytime-valid RCPS method gives finite-sample, time-uniform guarantees under adaptive, budget-limited labeling, with empirically label-efficient policies — directly matching your "gate outputs with risk thresholds while labeling only the most useful points."
> 
> Caveat: no retrieved work jointly covers all four pillars; the above is a composition, and the JEPA results are proven for deep linear networks (qualitative support on ImageNet only), while the risk-control guarantees assume i.i.d. streams.

**community 最终答案**

> Here are the works from the collection that cover your stack, with experimental results compared.
> 
> ## 1. Part–body association (hands/face → person), anchor-free
> **PBADet (ICLR 2024, doc 08b70bc3…)** — one-stage, anchor-free detector linking each part to its parent body via a single part-to-body center offset (representation length 5+K+2 vs BPJDet's 6+K+2K). The offset is always valid and one-to-one, unlike body-to-part offsets that break when parts are occluded.
> - **BodyHands:** YOLOv7 (36.9M) achieves hand AP 89.1 / conditional accuracy 92.62 / joint AP 85.98, beating BPJDet-YOLOv5l6 (86.1M: 85.9/86.91/84.39) and BodyHands (84.8/83.44/63.48).
> - **COCOHumanParts:** AP on par with BPJDet but leads AP_M/AP_L and person/feet AP; lowest mMR-2 for head, face, both hands, right foot.
> - **CrowdHuman (face–body):** leading body MR-2 (36.5) and competitive body AP (91.6); advantage over BPJDet is smaller for this single-part task.
> - **vs ED-Pose:** far higher Precision/Recall/F1 for hands/feet (all-parts F1 48.52 vs 31.51). Extends to quadruped part–body (AnimalPose, AP-10K).
> 
> ## 2. JEPA vs reconstruction, avoiding spurious features
> **"Why JEPA Self-Distillation Avoids Noisy Features" (NeurIPS 2024, doc 40fde037…)** — deep-linear analysis: JEPA's critical time depends on the regression coefficient ρ (t* ∝ 1/(λ^n ρ^{2L−n−1})), so it greedily learns high-influence features and suppresses noisy directions; suppression grows with depth (at large depth the encoder collapses to a single dominant eigen-direction). MAE ordering is set only by eigenvalue λ, so reconstruction prioritizes high-variance (often uninformative) pixel subspaces. Key results: 1-layer JEPA ≡ infinite-depth MAE; JEPA solutions are not reachable by MAE and vice versa; **ImageNet-1K**: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace holding perceptual features than MAE (CCA). Caveats: JEPA is biased toward predictive low-variance "slow" features and may itself be vulnerable to spurious features; results are for deep linear nets.
> 
> **LDReg (ICLR 2024, doc 51526068…)** — counters local dimensional collapse by regularizing local intrinsic dimensionality (Fisher-Rao metric). On ImageNet with ResNet-50/ViT-B it improves linear eval, transfer, and COCO detection/instance segmentation for SimCLR, BYOL, and MAE (also MoCo, VICReg, Barlow Twins); gains grow with pretraining length; forcing very low LID causes complete collapse. L1/L2 variants perform similarly.
> 
> ## 3. Exogenous noise in time-series/video
> **"Video-Based Representation Learning for RL in Exogenous Block MDPs" (ICLR 2024, doc 631d23bf…)** — provable PAC bounds: without exogenous noise, forward modeling and temporal contrastive learning both work and give strictly more sample-efficient downstream RL. With exogenous noise: temporal contrastive learning degrades most (it can minimize its loss using only exogenous noise), forward modeling is more robust but degrades as noise grows, and any compact frozen video-pretrained representation provably cannot support efficient downstream RL (exponential identifiability barrier) — trajectory-based ACRO stays robust. Verified in GridWorld, ViZDoom Basic, ViZDoom Defend the Center. Implication for you: pair video pretraining with trajectory data or updatable/adaptable representations, not frozen ones.
> 
> **RaMP / "Random Features for Model-Free Planning" (doc 528b3e89…)** — initializing an RL policy from unlabeled video-like embeddings: pretrain multi-step Q-functions with random features as pseudo-rewards, regress to the new reward, plan with MPC. Adapts faster than MBPO, PETS, SF, CQL on Meta-World/Hopper/D'Claw; NN random features beat polynomial/Gaussian; matches Dreamer on pixel Reach/Faucet Open but not Pixel Door Open.
> 
> ## 4. Spectral constraints in deep nets
> **"Investigating the Overlooked Hessian Structure" (ICML 2025, doc 582d138d…)** — well-trained CNNs and LLMs have power-law Hessian spectra (not random nets); power-law slope correlates with generalization (CIFAR-10 LeNet Pearson 0.72; KS distance predicts LLM generalization up to 0.98). Structure is lost with small width/depth, limited data, noisy labels, and large-batch training; **LoRA-only fine-tuning does not induce the power-law as full fine-tuning does**, and Davis-Kahan analysis links eigengaps to robust top eigenvectors vs unstable tails — directly relevant to your adapter-based fine-tuning plan.
> 
> **Dale's-law RNN spectral study (NeurIPS 2023, doc e63a94c4…)** — spectral properties of the weight matrix matter more than sign constraints; normalized SVD entropy at initialization anti-correlates with final error, so small networks with healthy spectra can beat larger ones with pathological spectra.
> 
> ## 5. Active, anytime-valid risk control
> **"Active, anytime-valid risk controlling prediction sets" (NeurIPS 2024, doc cda0aa75…)** — extends Bates et al. RCPS to sequential, adaptively collected data: guarantees ρ(β̂_t) ≤ θ simultaneously for all t with probability ≥ 1−α via e-processes/testing-by-betting, under an active labeling policy (IPW correction, label budget, lower-bounded query probability). The model's own risk predictor acts as a control variate; optimal labeling policy is proportional to the conditional risk standard deviation; regret bounds relate policy/predictor error to wealth growth. ImageNet experiments (θ=0.1, α=0.05): learned/pretrained policies cut risk faster than naive baselines with violations kept below α. Limits: i.i.d. data, bounded label policies.
> 
> ## 6. Vision-language / fine-tuning transferable insights
> **Visual Data-Type Identification (ICLR 2024, doc b0d9a0b2…)** — CLIP fine-tuning: freezing the vision encoder gives large in-distribution gains and *improves* OOD; freezing the text encoder improves ID but hurts OOD; fine-tuning only on COCO degrades performance; data-type information is scarce in LAION-2B and its abundance correlates with performance (r≈0.80).
> **GRAFT (ICLR 2024, doc 7949807c…)** — trains a VLM with no text annotations by aligning satellite images to ground images through CLIP; outperforms supervised VLMs (+20% classification, +80% segmentation), showing self-supervised alignment can beat label-hungry training.
> **Hessian paper (above)** — its LoRA finding guides when adapter-based fine-tuning changes learned structure.
> 
> ## Synthesis / gaps
> - PBADet covers anchor-free part–body association and even reports P/R/F1 against a pose baseline — matches your COCO-like Precision/F1 evaluation.
> - The JEPA paper + LDReg jointly explain why latent prediction avoids spurious/noisy features (ρ-prioritization, no pixel reconstruction) while guarding against dimensional collapse; both are validated on ImageNet/CIFAR-scale SSL and COCO detection.
> - The exogenous Block MDP result is the cautionary counterpoint: for *temporally correlated* noise, video-only pretraining has an identifiability limit, so keep the detector/encoder updatable (or add trajectory data); RaMP shows a practical route from self-supervised embeddings to an RL policy.
> - No single work in the collection integrates all four components; the RCPS active-labeling paper is the direct match for anytime-valid gating with selective labeling, and its risk-predictor control variate maps naturally onto your CNN/Transformer outputs.

</details>

### paperscope:results_comparison:446 — 评分与执行路径对照

**问题：** Help me find papers that collectively address: (1) one-stage anchor-free human part–body association evaluated on COCO; (2) when reverse/forward autodiff returns generalized subgradients in deep networks with ReLU/maxpool layers, with empirical checks on MNIST/CIFAR; (3) spectral/interpretability analyses of excitatory–inhibitory neural nets under Dale’s principle (e.g., clustering of singular values, normalized SVD entropy); (4) self-supervised joint-embedding methods that bias toward high-influence features compared to reconstruction losses; and (5) memory-efficient training via low-bit optimizer states (around 4-bit) for Adam/AdamW during fine-tuning of Transformers/ResNets, including practical guidance for End‑to‑end LoRA fine‑tuning. I’m interested in works reporting Precision/AUROC or CE vs MSE, attention/feature embeddings, and results on datasets like CIFAR‑100, SVHN, and COCO.Please compare and analyze the experimental results of these methods.

judge reasoning：

> The answer correctly identifies the five papers and covers many key results, but it contains important inaccuracies in the COCO-HumanParts comparison, misstates AP values, and incorrectly suggests PBADet outperforms BPJDet on overall AP when the gold summary says PBADet is competitive with slightly lower all-category AP and mixed association results. It also overstates some JEPA conclusions and omits the absence of directly comparable shared benchmarks.
