**Gold（保持结果文件中的原始内容；部分条目本身为序列化字典字符串）**

Gold 1：

> Below is a comparison and summary of experimental results drawn only from the provided papers, figures, and tables. I organize by (A) identical datasets across methods (if any), (B) similar dataset/task types, and (C) per‑paper, per‑dataset results comparisons. Where metrics differ across works, I avoid cross‑paper comparisons and note incompatibilities.
> 
> A) Identical datasets across the five papers
> - No shared benchmark appears across the five papers with directly comparable metrics. The closest overlaps are:
>   - MNIST: used differently. The EI‑RNN spectral paper evaluates sequential MNIST classification and the AD‑Clarke paper trains small fully‑connected networks on MNIST only to check AD correctness conditions (no accuracy reported). Metrics are incompatible for comparison.
>   - COCO: PBADet evaluates COCO‑HumanParts (derived from COCO) with detection/association AP and mMR−2; no other paper reports comparable COCO metrics.
>   - ImageNet: the 4‑bit optimizer reports supervised Top‑1 accuracy on ImageNet‑1K with Swin‑T; the JEPA paper reports feature similarity (CCA) on 64×64 ImageNet for representation analyses, not classification accuracy. Metrics are incompatible.
> 
> B) Similar dataset/task types
> - Vision detection/association on COCO: Only PBADet reports these metrics. It compares to BPJDet/Hier‑R‑CNN baselines on identical splits and metrics; see Section C‑1.
> - Vision classification (ImageNet): The 4‑bit optimizer reports Top‑1 accuracy differences across optimizers for Swin‑T; JEPA reports CCA dynamics (not accuracy). No direct cross‑paper accuracy comparisons are possible.
> - Sequence modeling/classification (MNIST/PTB): The EI‑RNN paper contrasts RNN variants on sequential MNIST and Penn Treebank (language modeling) with learning curves; no comparable baselines from other papers use the same metrics on these tasks.
> - Transformer fine‑tuning tasks (GLUE/SQuAD/E2E/WMT; LLaMA instruction tuning): Only the 4‑bit optimizer paper reports these with standard metrics, comparing many optimizers on identical settings; see Section C‑2.
> - Autodiff correctness checks: The AD‑Clarke paper verifies sufficient conditions (not downstream accuracy) on MNIST fully‑connected nets and CIFAR‑10 convolutional nets; see Section C‑3.
> 
> C) Per‑paper, per‑dataset experimental comparisons
> 
> C‑1) One‑stage anchor‑free part‑body association (PBADet)
> - BodyHands (Table 1; Hand AP↑, Cond. Accuracy↑, Joint AP↑):
>   - Ours (YOLOv7, 1024): Hand AP 89.1, Cond.Acc 92.62, Joint AP 85.98
>   - Ours (YOLOv5l6, 1024): Hand AP 88.1, Cond.Acc 92.71, Joint AP 85.73
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6, 1536): Hand AP 85.9, Cond.Acc 86.91, Joint AP 84.39
>   - Conclusion: On identical dataset/metrics, PBADet (both YOLOv7 and YOLOv5l6 heads) outperforms BPJDet on conditional accuracy and joint AP, and improves hand AP.
> 
> - COCO‑HumanParts (Table 2; all‑categories APs and per‑category APs; Table 3; average mMR−2↓):
>   - All‑categories AP.5:.95 (original/subordinate):
>     - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): 43.6 / 43.3
>     - Ours (YOLOv5l6): 43.0 / 41.8
>     - Ours (YOLOv7): 42.7 / 41.5
>   - Scale‑specific AP (ours vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6):
>     - APM (medium): Ours (v5l6) 66.2 / 65.0 vs BPJDet 63.8 / 63.2
>     - APL (large): Ours (v5l6) 67.2 / 64.4 vs BPJDet 61.8 / 58.9
>   - Per‑category AP (ours vs BPJDet YOLOv5l6):
>     - Person: Ours (v5l6) 62.4 vs 61.3
>     - Feet (r‑foot/l‑foot): Ours (v5l6) 30.9 / 31.5 vs 30.2 / 30.9
>     - Heads/Faces/Hands: Ours (v5l6) are similar or slightly lower (e.g., head 54.6 vs 56.6)
>   - Association quality (Table 3, mMR−2↓; lower is better):
>     - Heads/Faces/Hands: Ours (YOLOv7) lower (better) for head (29.2 vs 30.8), face (31.3 vs 31.8), left hand (41.1 vs 41.6), but right hand slightly higher (42.7 vs 42.2) than BPJDet (YOLOv5l6).
>     - Feet: Ours (YOLOv7) worse (higher) for r‑foot (52.6 vs 49.1) and l‑foot (52.5 vs 50.4).
>   - Conclusion: On COCO‑HumanParts, PBADet improves scale‑specific AP (APM/APL) and person/feet APs and achieves competitive all‑categories AP compared to BPJDet; association mMR−2 is better for head/face/left‑hand but worse for feet.
> 
> - CrowdHuman (Appendix Table 5; detection MR−2↓, AP↑, and body–face mMR−2↓):
>   - Ours (YOLOv7): body MR−2 36.5 (best), face MR−2 44.7, body AP 91.6, body‑face mMR−2 50.8
>   - BPJDet (YOLOv5l6): body MR−2 40.7, face MR−2 46.3, body AP 89.5, mMR−2 50.1 (slightly lower)
>   - Conclusion: PBADet improves body/face detection MR−2 and body AP; body–face mMR−2 is comparable but slightly worse than BPJDet.
> 
> - Comparison to multi‑person pose estimation (Appendix Table 7; parts precision/recall/F1↑ on COCO val keypoint‑to‑box matching):
>   - Ours (YOLOv5l6) vs ED‑Pose (Swin‑L):
>     - Left hand F1: 46.50 vs 22.87; Right hand F1: 47.34 vs 24.17; Left/Right foot F1: 51.08/50.34 vs 40.46/40.34; All parts F1: 48.52 vs 31.51
>   - Conclusion: For part detection with association, PBADet substantially improves F1 over pose‑estimation outputs matched to part boxes.
> 
> C‑2) Memory‑efficient training with 4‑bit optimizer states
> - NLU (GLUE; RoBERTa‑Large; Table 2 & Table 7; mean and per‑task scores ↑):
>   - 32‑bit AdamW: Mean 88.9
>   - 8‑bit AdamW: 89.1
>   - 4‑bit AdamW: 89.1; 4‑bit Factor: 88.9
>   - Adafactor (32‑bit): 89.1 (β1>0), 89.3 (β1=0)
>   - SM3 (32‑bit): 87.5 (notably lower)
>   - Per‑task: 4‑bit AdamW tracks 32‑bit AdamW closely across MNLI/QNLI/QQP/RTE/SST‑2/MRPC/CoLA/STS‑B; SM3 underperforms across several tasks.
>   - Conclusion: 4‑bit AdamW matches 32‑bit/8‑bit AdamW on GLUE; SM3 lags.
> 
> - QA (SQuAD/SQuAD2.0; RoBERTa‑Large; Table 2 & Table 9; EM/F1↑):
>   - 32‑bit AdamW: SQuAD F1 94.6; SQuAD2.0 F1 88.8
>   - 8‑bit AdamW: 94.5 / 89.0
>   - 4‑bit AdamW: 94.5 / 88.4; 4‑bit Factor: 94.6 / 88.9
>   - Conclusion: 4‑bit optimizers achieve comparable EM/F1 to 32‑bit and 8‑bit baselines.
> 
> - Image classification (ImageNet‑1K; Swin‑T; Table 2):
>   - 32‑bit AdamW: 81.2 Top‑1
>   - 8‑bit AdamW: 81.0
>   - 4‑bit AdamW: 80.8; 4‑bit Factor: 80.9
>   - Adafactor: 80.0 (β1>0), 79.5 (β1=0); SM3: 79.0
>   - Conclusion: 4‑bit methods are within ~0.3–0.4% Top‑1 of 32‑bit AdamW and outperform SM3; Adafactor lags.
> 
> - NLG (E2E‑NLG; GPT‑2 Medium; Table 2 & Table 8; BLEU/NIST/METEOR/ROUGE‑L/CIDEr ↑):
>   - 32‑bit AdamW: BLEU 67.7
>   - 8‑bit AdamW: 67.5
>   - 4‑bit AdamW: 67.8; 4‑bit Factor: 67.6
>   - Adafactor/SM3: 67.2 / 66.9 BLEU
>   - Conclusion: 4‑bit AdamW slightly exceeds 32‑bit/8‑bit on BLEU and matches other metrics.
> 
> - MT (WMT14 en–de; Transformer‑Base; Table 2; SacreBLEU ↑):
>   - 32‑bit AdamW: 26.61
>   - 8‑bit AdamW: 26.66
>   - 4‑bit AdamW: 26.28; 4‑bit Factor: 26.45
>   - Adafactor: 26.52 (β1>0), 26.45 (β1=0); SM3: 22.72
>   - Conclusion: 4‑bit AdamW/Factor attain comparable BLEU to 32‑bit/8‑bit; SM3 substantially worse.
> 
> - LLaMA instruction tuning (Alpaca; evaluation on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC‑e/ARC‑c/OBQA; Table 3; 5‑shot or standard accuracies ↑):
>   - Across 7B/13B/33B, 4‑bit AdamW matches or is within noise of 32‑bit AdamW (e.g., for 13B, MMLU 47.4 vs 46.5; HellaSwag 79.0 vs 78.8; ARC‑e 64.1 vs 63.6; ARC‑c 48.0 vs 48.3; OBQA 45.2 vs 45.2). Training loss curves overlay closely.
>   - Conclusion: End‑to‑end fine‑tuning with 4‑bit optimizer states preserves instruction‑tuned performance across scales.
> 
> - Memory/time efficiency (Table 4 & Table 5):
>   - LLaMA‑7B FSDP (2×A100‑80G): Total mem ↓ from 75.4 GB (32‑bit) to 31.9 GB (4‑bit), ~57.7% reduction; wall time similar or slightly improved with fused kernels.
>   - RoBERTa‑L (single 4090): 3.31–3.17 min/epoch with fused 4‑bit; total mem 3.00 GB (4‑bit) vs 5.31 GB (32‑bit).
>   - GPT‑2 Medium (4×4090): total mem 4.62–4.44 GB (4‑bit/Factor) vs 6.89 GB (32‑bit); fused 4‑bit similar time to 32‑bit.
>   - Largest trainable model (Table 5): On 80 GB GPU, 4‑bit enables OPT‑6.7B and LLaMA‑7B fine‑tuning, versus OPT‑1.3B with 32‑bit.
> 
> - Key ablations (Table 1; GPT‑2 Medium on E2E; stability and BLEU):
>   - Quantizing 2nd moment with a zero‑point (DE) leads to instability or lower BLEU; removing zero (DE‑0) or using linear mapping stabilizes and restores BLEU (~67.4–67.8) without needing stable embeddings; rank‑1 normalization improves further; factorization of 2nd moment also works.
>   - Swin‑T ablation (Table 6): Quantizing both moments with B128/DE and Rank‑1/Linear preserves ImageNet Top‑1 (80.8–80.9) vs 81.2 (32‑bit). Smaller block size on the 1st moment helps.
> 
> C‑3) Autodiff returns generalized subgradients (Clarke) in practice
> - Fully‑connected nets on MNIST (Section 4, Scenario 1; sufficient condition from Theorem 5):
>   - Three 2‑hidden‑layer MLPs (hidden sizes 256/64) with ReLU6, HardTanh, or HardSigmoid, trained with SGD (B=128) on MNIST. Throughout 20 epochs (469 steps/epoch), the linear independence condition on the layer inputs held whenever non‑differentiable points were touched (e.g., average “touches” 0 for ReLU6, 9.8 for HardTanh, 13.8 for HardSigmoid). Conclusion: AD computed a Clarke subderivative at all training steps checked.
> 
> - Convnets on CIFAR‑10 with non‑trivial maxpools (Section 4, Scenario 2; Theorem 8 via Algorithm 2):
>   - VGG11 / VGG11‑BN / ResNet18 (halved channels for VGG variants). Across 7,820 training steps per run (5 runs), the constructed linear program (defining non‑empty feasible set P_l) was always feasible per layer when required, implying AD returned a Clarke subderivative at all steps.
>   - Tie events (|S_j|≥2) in max operations occurred frequently in early layers (e.g., VGG11 first layer: ~3.2% of max ops had ties; ~1436 steps had non‑trivial ties), yet the conditions for correctness remained satisfiable. Average |S_j \ T_j| when non‑empty was ≈1–2.
> 
> C‑4) Spectral/interpretability analyses of EI RNNs under Dale’s law
> - Benchmarks (Fig. 2A–D text):
>   - Across the adding problem (T=20), sequential MNIST (3×100), Penn Tree Bank (3×500), and a small naturalistic object recognition task, Column‑EI (ColEI) RNNs learned worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and recurrent DANNs; gradient clipping helped ColEI more.
> 
> - Spectrum transplant and sign constraints (Fig. 4):
>   - Freezing signs impairs both RNN and ColEI slightly, but does not explain the full performance gap; transplanting ColEI’s singular‑value spectrum into a standard RNN degrades learning more than sign constraints alone, indicating spectrum drives most of the gap.
> 
> - EI ratio and network size (Figs. 5–7):
>   - Lower fraction of inhibitory units (higher E:I) reduces normalized SVD entropy (NSE) and degrades ColEI learning; DANNs remain robust. Increasing width improves ColEI spectra and performance (despite large max singular values), and NSE anti‑correlates with test error.
>   - NSE at initialization predicts performance across sizes and EI ratios; small nets with high NSE can outperform larger nets with lower NSE.
> 
> - Eigen/singular distributions (Fig. 3):
>   - ColEI: non‑uniform eigenvalue distributions and multimodal, dispersed singular spectra with a mode of large singular values; DANNs/standard RNNs: unimodal quarter‑circle‑like singular spectra with smaller spread. This aligns with ColEI’s poorer optimization dynamics.
> 
> C‑5) Self‑supervised JEPA vs MAE: implicit bias and limited empirical checks
> - Deep linear theory and simulated dynamics: JEPA prioritizes features with larger regression coefficients (high influence), especially for deeper encoders, while MAE prioritizes high‑variance (co‑varying) features. When λ (variance) and ρ (regression coefficient) trade off oppositely across features, JEPA reverses learning order relative to MAE (Fig. 1, Fig. 2).
> - Temporal generative model (Eq. 16; Fig. 3): For two features with similar correlation λ but different noise σ^2, ρ increases as noise decreases; JEPA converges to lower‑amplitude weights and learns the lower‑noise (higher‑ρ) mode earlier.
> - ImageNet (64×64) feature dynamics (Appendix D, Fig. 7): I‑JEPA’s representations have consistently higher full↔bottom PCA‑subspace CCA and lower full↔top CCA versus MAE throughout training, indicating faster alignment with lower‑variance (perceptual) subspaces. No classification accuracies are reported here, only representation similarity.
> 
> Summary of which methods perform better/worse on their own identical datasets
> - PBADet (COCO‑HumanParts / BodyHands / CrowdHuman): PBADet outperforms BPJDet on BodyHands across all reported metrics; on COCO‑HumanParts PBADet improves APM/APL and person/feet AP, with mixed outcomes on association mMR−2 (better head/face/left‑hand; worse feet); on CrowdHuman, PBADet improves body/face detection MR−2 and body AP with comparable mMR−2.
> - 4‑bit optimizers (GLUE/SQuAD/ImageNet/E2E/WMT/LLaMA): 4‑bit AdamW and 4‑bit Factor match or closely track 32‑bit AdamW and 8‑bit AdamW on all tasks, while substantially reducing memory (up to ~58%) and enabling larger models. Adafactor is mixed; SM3 often underperforms.
> - EI RNNs: DANN RNNs and standard RNNs outperform ColEI across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and a naturalistic vision task; spectra (singular‑value distributions) explain more variance in performance than sign constraints alone; NSE at initialization predicts learning.
> - AD correctness in practice: On the examined MNIST MLPs and CIFAR‑10 convnets (VGG/ResNet), the sufficient conditions for Clarke‑subgradient correctness held at all steps checked; AD’s output thus belongs to the Clarke subdifferential across the runs.
> - JEPA vs MAE (self‑supervised): In deep‑linear and controlled generative settings, JEPA prioritizes high‑influence/low‑noise modes versus MAE’s high‑variance bias; on 64×64 ImageNet, I‑JEPA’s learned features align faster with low‑variance subspaces (higher bottom‑CCA, lower top‑CCA) than MAE.
> 
> Notes on datasets with no cross‑paper comparability
> - Although several works touch ‘MNIST’ and ‘COCO’ families, the metrics differ (e.g., sequential MNIST vs MNIST FC‑nets without accuracy; COCO‑HumanParts AP/mMR vs no COCO in other works), precluding cross‑paper performance comparisons.
> 
> All numerical values and qualitative orderings above come directly from the provided tables/figures and their captions in the respective papers; I did not introduce any external results or metrics.

**naive 最终答案**

> Based on the retrieved collection, here are the papers matching your five topics, with experimental results compared.
> 
> **1. One-stage anchor-free part–body association on COCO — PBADet (ICLR 2024)**
> - Proposes a single part-to-body center offset on anchor-free multi-scale heads (YOLOv5/v7 backbones), with classification, localization, and displacement branches plus task-alignment learning.
> - COCOHumanParts all-category AP (original/subordinate): Ours(YOLOv7) 42.7/41.5, Ours(YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8; AP50 69.5/70.0, AP75 65.8/66.2, APL 66.7/67.2 — outperforming HierR-CNN (up to 42.0/38.8) and BPJDet (43.6/43.3 AP50 70.6). On CrowdHuman face-body, it reaches body MR-2 36.5 (YOLOv7) vs BPJDet 40.7, with competitive AP (91.6 vs 89.5).
> - Ablations (BodyHands): full model 89.1 HandAP / 92.62 Cond. Accuracy / 85.98 JointAP; removing association loss drops Cond. Accuracy to 80.78. Anchor-free part-to-body beats anchor-based body-to-part (89.1 vs 85.3 HandAP).
> - Note: reports AP/MR-2 metrics, not Precision/AUROC.
> 
> **2. Reverse/forward autodiff and generalized subgradients (ICLR 2024, "What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute...")**
> - Theorems: AD always returns an element of the Clarke subdifferential when the minibatch size is 1 and non-differentiable neurons have distinct biases (Theorem 1); this can fail with minibatches ≥2 or absent/shared biases (Lemmas 2–3); proper proxy derivatives restore correctness for any batch size (Theorems 4, 6); maxpool networks are safe only with trivial maxpools.
> - Empirical checks: MNIST MLPs (ReLU6/HardTanh/HardSigmoid, SGD, B=128, 20 epochs) — AD satisfied the sufficient condition and returned a Clarke subgradient at every training step; CIFAR-10 VGG11/VGG11-BN/ResNet18 with maxpools — the condition was always satisfied, so AD always computed a Clarke subdifferential element.
> 
> **3. Spectral/interpretability of excitatory–inhibitory nets under Dale's law (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - ColEI RNNs (sign-constrained columns) learn worse and with more variance than standard RNNs and Dale's-ANN RNNs on adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition.
> - Spectral analysis: ColEI singular-value spectra are multimodal and dispersed (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), unlike the unimodal clustered (quarter-circle) spectra of standard/DANN RNNs; maximum eigenvalue constraint does not bound the largest singular value.
> - Normalized SVD entropy (NSE) quantifies spectrum pathology and anti-correlates with final test error: smaller networks or fewer inhibitory units reduce NSE and impair learning; DANN stays robust (NSE ≈ 0.95 even with 1 inhibitory neuron). NSE at initialization predicts performance across EI ratios and sizes.
> - Note: no SVHN or Precision/AUROC results.
> 
> **4. Self-supervised joint embedding biased to high-influence features (NeurIPS 2024, "How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features")**
> - Deep linear analysis of JEPA (self-distillation) vs MAE (reconstruction): the only difference in the ODEs is an exponent; MAE feature-learning order is set by eigenvalue λ, whereas JEPA is also ordered by regression coefficient ρ — a greedy bias toward high-influence features that strengthens with encoder depth (critical-time theorems, Corollary 3.6). On distribution 2 (opposing λ and ρ trends), JEPA completely reverses MAE's learning order.
> - ImageNet-1K experiments: I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features than MAE features (CCA).
> - No CE-vs-MSE comparison or CIFAR-100/SVHN results. (LDReg, ICLR 2024, is related: local-dimensionality regularization improves SimCLR/BYOL/MAE on ImageNet and downstream COCO detection/segmentation; the contrastive-embedding-similarities paper reports CIFAR-10/100 gains, but neither matches the JEPA high-influence bias analysis exactly.)
> 
> **5. Memory-efficient 4-bit optimizer states for Adam/AdamW (NeurIPS 2023)**
> - Technique: B128/dynamic-exponent for the first moment; zero-point-excluding linear (DE-0/Linear) or Rank-1 normalization for the second moment; optional factorization ("4-bit Factor"). Practical guidance: keep the same hyperparameters as full precision ("out-of-box transfer"), use B128 for the first moment, exclude zero from the second-moment map, and factorize the second moment for extra savings.
> - Results vs 32-bit AdamW: RoBERTa-L GLUE 89.1 vs 88.9; Swin-T ImageNet CLS 80.8 vs 81.2; GPT-2M E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7; SQuAD F1 94.5 vs 94.6; Transformer WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61. LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning: MMLU 38.9/47.4/54.9 vs 32-bit 38.7/46.5/56.4 — comparable, no degradation with scale; memory savings up to 57.7% (LLaMA-7B: 31.87 GB vs 75.40 GB), enabling LLaMA-7B on one 80 GB GPU.
> - LoRA is discussed only as a complementary technique (freezing pretrained weights and tuning low-rank adapters); the paper does not provide an End-to-end LoRA fine-tuning guide, and no dedicated end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning paper exists in this collection.
> 
> **Cross-paper analysis / gaps**
> - The five topics are covered by five distinct papers with no shared datasets, so results cannot be compared across topics. Within topics: PBADet's anchor-free part-to-body design dominates anchor-based BPJDet on both COCOHumanParts and BodyHands; the AD paper shows Clarke-subdifferential correctness holds empirically in real training despite failure cases; the Dale's-law paper shows spectrum (NSE), not sign constraints, drives poor EI learning; the JEPA paper shows latent-space prediction reorders feature learning by influence (ρ) in a way reconstruction (MAE) does not; the 4-bit optimizer paper shows 4-bit states are effectively lossless for fine-tuning and modest for pretraining.
> - Items you asked for that are not reported in these papers: Precision/AUROC (the five papers report AP/MR-2, accuracy, BLEU/F1, error rates), CE vs MSE comparisons (the JEPA paper contrasts latent prediction vs reconstruction, not CE vs MSE), and SVHN (no retrieved paper uses SVHN). CIFAR-100 appears only in the contrastive-embedding and Hessian papers, not in the five target works; COCO appears in PBADet and (as downstream detection) in LDReg.

**community 最终答案**

> Based on the collection, here are the five papers that collectively address your topics, with a comparison of their experimental results.
> 
> ## The five papers
> 
> 1. **PBADet** (ICLR 2024, doc `08b70bc…`) — one-stage anchor-free part–body association via a single part-to-body center offset (YOLOv5l6/YOLOv7 backbones), evaluated on COCO-HumanParts, COCO-WholeBody, BodyHands, CrowdHuman.
> 2. **"What Does Automatic Differentiation Compute for Neural Networks?"** (ICLR 2024, doc `c9b4b87…`) — proves forward/reverse AD returns a Clarke subderivative (generalized subgradient) for ReLU/maxpool nets under distinct-bias/rank conditions; verified empirically on MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet.
> 3. **"Learning better with Dale's Law: A Spectral Perspective"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `e63a94c…`) — spectral/interpretability analysis of excitatory–inhibitory RNNs (ColEI vs DANN), singular-value clustering and normalized SVD entropy (NSE).
> 4. **"How JEPA Avoids Noisy Features"** (NeurIPS 2024, doc `40fde03…`) — self-supervised joint-embedding (JEPA/self-distillation) biased toward high-influence (high regression-coefficient) features vs MAE-style reconstruction losses.
> 5. **"Memory Efficient Optimizers with 4-bit States"** (NeurIPS 2023, doc `8d5e145…`) — 4-bit Adam/AdamW optimizer states (B128/DE first moment, Rank-1/Linear or factorized second moment), evaluated on fine-tuning Transformers (RoBERTa, GPT-2, LLaMA) and Swin-T.
> 
> ## Experimental comparison
> 
> **Part–body association (PBADet).** On COCO-HumanParts, Ours(YOLOv7) reaches 42.7/41.5 AP(.5:.95) and Ours(YOLOv5l6) 43.0/41.8, outperforming BPJDet(YOLOv5l6) (43.6/43.3 original, 63.8/63.2 subordinate vs 65.8/64.4 and 66.2/65.0 for ours) and Hier-RCNN. On BodyHands (YOLOv7), the full model gives HandAP 89.1, conditional accuracy 92.62, JointAP 85.98; ablations show the association loss, multi-scale offsets, and task-alignment each matter. On CrowdHuman face–body, ours achieves the best body MR-2 (36.5) with competitive AP.
> 
> **Autodiff subgradients.** The theoretical claim holds under distinct bias parameters (batch size 1) but can fail with minibatches/shared biases; a rank condition covers FC nets, and shared-bias safety holds only for trivial maxpools. The LP-checkable sufficient condition is verified on MNIST MLPs and CIFAR-10 VGG/ResNet in practical training, i.e., AD "almost always" returns a Clarke subderivative in realistic setups. This is theory/verification rather than accuracy benchmarks.
> 
> **Dale's-law spectral analysis.** ColEI (column-partitioned E/I) learns worse and with higher variance than standard RNNs and DANN across adding, sequential MNIST, PTB, and object recognition. The cause is spectral, not sign constraints: ColEI's initial recurrent weights have multimodal, dispersed singular values (rank-one nilpotent column-mean structure), while DANN/standard RNNs match Marchenko–Pastur/quarter-circle form. Normalized SVD entropy (clustering of singular values) anti-correlates with final test error across EI ratio and network size; gradient clipping mitigates the deficit, and DANN stays robust even with one inhibitory unit.
> 
> **JEPA vs reconstruction.** In deep linear networks, JEPA prioritizes high-influence features (large regression coefficients ρᵢ) whereas MAE prioritizes high-variance features regardless of informativeness; the bias weakens for shallow encoders. ImageNet-1K confirms I-JEPA features align faster with the low-variance PCA subspace containing perceptual features (measured by CCA) than MAE features. So joint-embedding methods systematically beat reconstruction losses for perception tasks.
> 
> **4-bit optimizers.** 4-bitAdamW matches or slightly exceeds 32-bit AdamW on all fine-tuning tasks — GLUE/RoBERTa-L 89.1 vs 88.9, GPT-2M E2E-NLG BLEU 67.8 vs 67.7, QA F1 94.5 vs 94.6 — and stays comparable on pretraining (Swin-T ImageNet 80.8 vs 81.2, WMT14 26.28 vs 26.61). LLaMA-7B/13B/33B Alpaca fine-tuning matches 32-bit on MMLU/HellaSwag/ARC/OBQA, with up to 57.7% memory savings and LLaMA-7B fit on one 80GB GPU. LoRA-related guidance: the paper builds on the microsoft/LoRA codebase for E2E-NLG hyperparameters (batch 8, lr 4e-5, 5 epochs, label smoothing 0.1) and, in related work, frames LoRA as freezing pretrained weights and tuning only low-rank parameters, combinable with 4-bit optimizer states — but it does not itself provide a dedicated end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning protocol.
> 
> ## Caveats on datasets/metrics you asked for
> 
> - **CIFAR-100** appears in the Hessian-spectrum paper (LeNet/ResNet18 power-law results), not in the five core papers above; the autodiff paper uses MNIST + CIFAR-10.
> - **SVHN** does not appear in any retrieved document, so no Precision/AUROC or accuracy results for SVHN can be established here.
> - **AUROC/Precision** results exist in DiffusionFake (deepfake detection: AUC/EER on FF++, Celeb-DF, etc.) and LDReg (COCO detection/instance segmentation), but those are not among the five matched topics; the five papers above report AP/mAP (PBADet), accuracy/BLEU/F1 (4-bit), error rates/NSE (Dale), CCA alignment (JEPA), and verification outcomes (AD).
> 
> So the five papers collectively cover all five topics, with the caveat that SVHN results and a dedicated end-to-end LoRA fine-tuning guide are not present in this collection.

## 9. 核验与限制

所有 trace 副本 SHA-256 与服务器采集记录一致，所有模型轮次与 results.jsonl 的 rounds 一致。总体分数、token、耗时和题数已与原汇总交叉核对。没有新增 API 请求、重新评分、修改 gold 或调整实验配置。五组新实验共 532 对 QA；本报告只覆盖标题所示组。完整派生数据与提取脚本见 [summary.json](/Users/yunhaoz/Developer/MyProjects/community_wiki/data/analysis/trace_comparison_20260921/summary.json)、[analyze.py](/Users/yunhaoz/Developer/MyProjects/community_wiki/data/analysis/trace_comparison_20260921/analyze.py)。

本报告没有随机化重复试验或固定检索轨迹的消融，无法识别“社区算法单独造成的准确率变化”。特别是 query 已变、后续读取不同、judge 本身有尺度差异时，只能报告证据支持到的机制层级。
